## Volume Front Matter

### Series Title Page

**Complete Course of Patrology**, or universal, complete, uniform, convenient, economical library of all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprinting of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have survived through the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, carefully collated with one another and with several manuscripts, and corrected with the greatest diligence; continuously enriched with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; augmented with all works discovered after the extensive editions produced during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume and each author of any importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject matter below; enlarged with works both doubtful and apocryphal, and with others possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: namely, one of subjects, by consulting which whatever any one of the Fathers has written on any theme may be seen at a glance; and the other of Sacred Scripture, from which it may readily be discovered which Fathers have commented on the individual texts of each book of Scripture and in which places of their works they have done so. An exceptionally accurate edition, and one easily preferable to all others if the cleanness of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the works reprinted, the very convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the entire work, and the low price are taken into consideration; above all, this collection is single, methodical, and chronological, and brings together for the first time in our library six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, gathered from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.

**First Series**, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church from Tertullian to Gregory the Great. Edited by J.-P. Migne, editor of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or of the complete courses in each branch of ecclesiastical learning.

# The Complete Works of Augustine, Bishop of Hippo

## On the Gift of Perseverance

### [Column 993]

## Notice Concerning the Book on the Gift of Perseverance

Augustine proceeds to refute the remaining errors of the semi-Pelagians of Marseille. Just as he dealt for the most part in the preceding book with the beginning of faith, so in the opening parts of the following book he discusses at length the perfection of perseverance. For from the letters of Prosper and Hilary the holy Doctor understood that the enemies of predestination and grace were drawing nearer to the Pelagians through this twofold error: that they “so place both the beginning of faith and perseverance to the end in our power,” as he says here, section 34, “that they do not think these are gifts of God, nor that, in order that we may have and retain them, God works upon our thoughts and wills.”

Although in this later book he also responds to some of their other questions against predestination, nevertheless, because at the very beginning he proposes to discuss perseverance, the book came commonly to be called either “On the Gift of Perseverance” or—what is the more common title in ancient manuscripts—“On the Good of Perseverance.” Under the latter title it was formerly cited by Remigius, archbishop of Lyons, in his *Book on Maintaining the Truth of Scripture*, chapter 9; by Florus, or by the commonly attributed Bede, in the commentary on Paul; by Hincmar in his *Book on Predestination*, chapter 1; and elsewhere.

Prosper, however, who had seen the first and more reliable copies of the works dedicated to Hilary and himself, reports at the beginning of his *Replies to the Extracts from the Genoese* that the same title had been given to both books: “In the books,” he says, “of blessed memory, Bishop Augustine, whose title is *On the Predestination of the Saints*.” An old codex from Noailles agrees with Prosper, adding at the end of the first book: “Here ends the first book of blessed Augustine, bishop, *On the Predestination of the Saints*. The second begins.” At the end of the second it reads: “Here ends the second book of Saint Augustine, bishop, *On the Predestination of the Saints*.”

Bellarmin speaks of these same books in Book 2 of *On Grace and Free Choice*, chapter 11:

“It is established,” he says, “that a complaint was brought before the Apostolic See, under Pope Celestine, by Prosper and Hilary: namely, that certain priests in Gaul were criticizing Saint Augustine’s doctrine of predestination. What Celestine replied is clear from his Letter to the Gauls, in which, among other things, after praising Saint Augustine in lofty terms, he added the following: ‘Hence let resistance be made to such men, whom we see growing wickedly,’ and so forth.

“And because the Gauls replied that Saint Augustine’s doctrine had indeed been commended by the Pontiff, but that those two books—*On the Predestination of the Saints* and *On the Good of Perseverance*—had not specifically been approved, Saint Prosper, in his *Book Against the Collator*, demonstrates at the end that the Pontiff could not have failed to approve these books, since he approved Augustine’s doctrine and these books do not dissent from the others, and so forth.

“Then, in that letter, chapter 2, Celestine praises Augustine in such a way as to say that he had always been regarded by the Roman Church as an excellent teacher and had never even by rumor been touched by any sinister suspicion. But how could Celestine have said these things if Augustine had written falsely that the faith of predestination had always existed in the Catholic Church and that no one could dispute against it except by error? For if Augustine’s opinion concerning predestination were false, Augustine could not be defended from grave rashness, since he would not merely have contended so fiercely for falsehood but would also have dared to present it as the Catholic faith, and so forth.

“Finally, at the council of seventy bishops Gelasius not only approved all the writings of Saint Augustine and Saint Prosper but also condemned the booklets of John Cassian and Faustus of Riez, although he knew that the chief dispute between Prosper and Cassian, and thereafter between Fulgentius and Faustus, concerned the writings of Saint Augustine *On the Predestination of the Saints* and *On the Good of Perseverance*.”

### [Column 993]

# The Second Book of Saint Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, on the Gift of Perseverance, Addressed to Prosper and Hilary

[Note: Written after the *Retractations*, in the year of Christ 428 or 429.]

[Note: The book addressed to Prosper and Hilary, *On the Gift of Perseverance*, the second book, was reviewed and corrected against the same manuscripts and printed editions as the book *On the Predestination of the Saints*, which we identified above, columns 959–960.]

[Note: We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractations* and the *Confessions*, volume 1. M.]

## (C)

In the first part of the book he proves that the perseverance by which one perseveres in Christ to the end is a gift of God. For one would mockingly ask this of God if one did not believe that it is given by God. Moreover, according to the exposition of the martyr Cyprian, scarcely anything else is requested in the Lord’s Prayer than perseverance; by this very exposition the enemies of grace are shown to have been refuted before they were born.

He teaches that the grace of perseverance is given to some through God’s mercy, and not according to the merits of those who receive it, while to others it is not given according to God’s just judgment. Why one adult rather than another is called, just as why one of two infants is taken up and the other left behind, is inscrutable. More inscrutable still is why, among two godly persons, perseverance is granted to one and not to the other. Yet this is entirely certain: the former is among the predestined, while the latter is not.

He observes that the mystery of predestination is demonstrated by the Lord’s words concerning the people of Tyre and Sidon: had the signs performed among them been performed among the people of Chorazin, they would have repented. He shows that the example of infants is effective for confirming the truth of predestination and grace in adults, and he replies to a passage from the third book of his work *On Free Choice* that his opponents have improperly cited for this purpose.

In the second part of the work he refutes their claim that the definition of predestination is opposed to the usefulness of exhortation and correction. He asserts that predestination is beneficially preached so that a person may glory not in himself but in the Lord. The objections they raise against predestination can likewise be turned, in no dissimilar way, either against God’s foreknowledge or against that grace which they agree is necessary for all other goods, except the beginning of faith and the perfection of perseverance.

For the predestination of the saints is nothing other than God’s foreknowledge and preparation of those benefits by which all who are delivered are most certainly delivered. Nevertheless, he commands that predestination be preached in a suitable manner, and not in such a way that among the uneducated crowd it may appear to be refuted by the very fact of its preaching. Finally, he commends to us the Lord Jesus as the most illustrious example of predestination set before our eyes.

# Chapter One

### 1

We must now discuss perseverance more carefully, for in the preceding book, when we were treating the beginning of faith, we also said something about it. We therefore assert that perseverance is a gift of God—the perseverance by which one perseveres in Christ to the end.

By “the end” I mean the point at which this life comes to an end, during which alone there is danger of falling. Thus, as long as someone is living this life, it is uncertain whether he has received this gift. For if he falls before he dies, he is certainly said not to have persevered, and this is said most truly.

How, then, can someone who did not persevere be said to have received or possessed perseverance? If someone has self-control but falls away from it and becomes incontinent; if likewise he has justice, patience, or faith itself, he is rightly said to have possessed these things and no longer to possess them: for he was self-controlled, or just, or patient, or faithful for as long as he was so. But when he ceased to be so, he is no longer what he was.

How, then, was one who did not persevere persevering? For by persevering a person demonstrates that he is persevering, and this man did not do so.

But lest anyone resist and say, “If, after becoming faithful, a person lived, for example, ten years, and in the middle of that period fell away from the faith, did he not persevere for five years?” I do not dispute about words, if that too is thought to deserve the name perseverance, as belonging to its own period. But the perseverance of which we are now speaking—the perseverance by which one perseveres in Christ to the end—must in no way be said to have been possessed by one who did not persevere to the end.

Indeed, a faithful person who lived faithfully until death possessed this perseverance even for one year, or for however short a time one can imagine, more truly than someone who lived for many years but departed from the stability of faith a short time before death.

# Chapter Two

### 2

With this established, let us see whether this perseverance, of which it is said, “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 10:22), is a gift of God.

If it is not, how is the Apostle’s statement true: “To you it has been granted for Christ’s sake not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him” (Philippians 1:29)? One of these belongs to the beginning and the other to the end; yet both are gifts of God, because both are said to have been granted, as we have already stated above.

For what is a more genuine beginning for a Christian than to believe in Christ? What is a better end than to suffer for Christ? [Note: Thus in Erasmus, the Lyons edition, the Venetian edition, and the Louvain edition. In B: “What end is better than to suffer for Christ?” M.]

As for the fact that one should believe in Christ, some contradiction has been discovered by which it is said that the gift of God is not the beginning but the increase of faith. By the Lord’s gift we have answered that opinion sufficiently and more than sufficiently.

But what can be said concerning why perseverance to the end is not granted in Christ to one to whom it is granted to suffer for Christ—or, to speak more explicitly, to whom it is granted to die for Christ?

The apostle Peter also demonstrates that this is a gift of God when he says: “It is better, if the will of God should so desire, to suffer while doing good than while doing evil” (1 Peter 3:17). When he says, “if the will of God should so desire,” he shows that this is divinely granted, and not to all the saints, that they should suffer for Christ.

For those whom the will of God does not wish to reach the experience and glory of suffering [Note: The printed editions read, “For those whom God does not wish”; the manuscripts, “For those whom the will of God does not wish.”] nevertheless reach the kingdom of God, if they persevere in Christ to the end. But who could say that this perseverance is not granted to those who die in Christ through bodily illness or some other circumstance, when a much more difficult perseverance is granted to those who undertake death itself for Christ?

It is much more difficult to persevere where the persecutor is working to prevent perseverance, and where the person endures even to death in order to persevere. That perseverance is therefore more difficult to have, while this is easier; but for the One to whom nothing is difficult, it is easy to grant both.

For God promised this when he said: “I will put my fear into their hearts, so that they will not depart from me” (Jeremiah 32:40). What else does this mean than: “My fear, which I shall place in their hearts, will be such and so great that they will cling to me perseveringly”?

### 3

But why is this perseverance requested from God if it is not given by God? Is this also a mockery in prayer, when something is requested from him which is known not to be given by him, but which, without his giving it, is in human power? And is that thanksgiving also a mockery if thanks are offered to God for what he himself did not give or accomplish? [Note: The manuscripts read “if thanks are offered to God for this”; the printed editions read “if thanks are offered to God for that.”]

But what I said there—in the preceding book, section 39—I say here as well: “Do not be deceived,” says the Apostle; “God is not mocked” (Galatians 6:7).

O human being, God is witness not only of your words but also of your thoughts. If you sincerely and faithfully ask something from so great a giver, believe that you receive from the one from whom you ask what you ask. Do not honor him with your lips while exalting yourself over him in your heart, believing that what you pretend to pray for from him actually comes from yourself.

Or is this perseverance perhaps not requested from him? Anyone who says this must be refuted not by my arguments but overwhelmed by the prayers of the saints. [Note: All the manuscripts read “overwhelmed.” The printed editions read “recalled.”]

Is there anyone among them who does not ask God to persevere in him, when, in the prayer called the Lord’s Prayer because the Lord taught it, the saints’ prayer is understood to request scarcely anything other than perseverance?

### 4

Read more attentively its exposition in the book of the blessed martyr Cyprian, which he composed on this subject and entitled *On the Lord’s Prayer*. Observe how many years beforehand an antidote was prepared against the poisons of the Pelagians that were to come.

For, as you know, there are three things which the Catholic Church especially defends against them. First, that the grace of God is not given according to our merits, since all the merits of the righteous are gifts of God and are conferred by God’s grace. Second, that no one lives in this corruptible body in any degree of righteousness without some sins. Third, that a human being is born subject to the sin of the first human being and bound by the chain of condemnation, unless the guilt contracted through generation is loosed through regeneration.

Of these three, the last—the one I have placed in the final position—is the only one not treated in the aforementioned book of the glorious martyr. But the other two are discussed there with such clarity that the aforementioned heretics, those new enemies of the grace of Christ, are found to have been convicted long before they were born.

Among these merits of the saints, then, which are nothing other than gifts of God, he speaks as follows of perseverance also being a gift of God:

“We say, ‘Hallowed be your name’: not that we wish God to be hallowed by our prayers, but that we ask from him that his name be hallowed in us. For by whom is God hallowed, when he himself hallows? But because he said, ‘Be holy, because I also am holy’ (Leviticus 19:2) [Note: The manuscripts read “just as I also am holy”; they consistently had this reading above in the book *On Rebuke and Grace*, section 10.], we ask and pray for this: that we who have been hallowed in Baptism may persevere in what we have begun to be.”

A little later, continuing to discuss this very matter and teaching that we ask perseverance from the Lord—which we could in no way do rightly and sincerely unless this too were his gift—he says:

“We pray that this hallowing may remain in us. And because our Lord and Judge warns the one whom he has healed and brought to life not to sin, lest something worse happen to him (John 5:14), we make this prayer continually; we ask this day and night: that the hallowing and giving of life which is received from God’s grace may be preserved by his protection.” [Note: The Vatican manuscripts read “healed and justified.” Shortly afterward they likewise read “that hallowing and justification.”]

This teacher therefore understands us to ask the Lord for perseverance in hallowing—that is, that we may persevere in hallowing—when, having been hallowed, we say, “Hallowed be your name.”

For what else is it to ask for what we have received than to ask that this also be granted to us: that we may not cease to possess it? [Note: The manuscripts read “be granted to us”; the printed editions read “grant.”]

Therefore, just as a holy person, when asking God to make him holy, asks that he may remain holy; so also the chaste person asks to remain chaste, the self-controlled person to remain self-controlled, the just person to remain just, the devout person to remain devout, and so forth. These are among the things which we defend against the Pelagians as gifts of God. Without doubt, such persons ask to persevere in the good things which they know they have received.

And if they receive this, then surely they also receive perseverance itself—the great gift of God by which his other gifts are preserved.

### 5

What of the words, “Your kingdom come”? Do we ask for anything else than that what we do not doubt will come to all the saints may also come to us?

Thus here too, since they are already holy, what do they pray for except that they may persevere in the holiness given to them? For God’s kingdom will certainly come not to others but to those who persevere to the end.

# Chapter Three

### 6

The third petition is, “Your will be done on earth as it is in heaven”; or, as it is read in most manuscripts and more commonly repeated by those who pray, “as in heaven, so on earth.” Most understand this to mean: “As the holy angels do your will, so may we also do your will.” [Note: Erasmus, the Lyons edition, the Venetian edition, and the Louvain edition add here: “may do.”] [Note: Supply: “may do.”]

But that teacher and martyr wishes heaven and earth to be understood as spirit and flesh, and wishes us to pray that we may do God’s will with both in agreement.

He also saw in these words another meaning compatible with sound faith, about which we have already spoken above: namely, that the faithful—who, clothed with the heavenly human being, are rightly called by the name “heaven”—are understood to pray on behalf of unbelievers, who are still earth and bear only an earthly human being through their first birth.

Here he clearly shows that the beginning of faith is also a gift of God, since the holy Church prays not only for the faithful, that faith may be increased or persevere in them, but also for unbelievers, that they may begin to possess the faith which they entirely lacked and against which they bore hostile hearts.

But now we are not discussing the beginning of faith, about which we have already said much in the preceding book. We are discussing that perseverance which must be possessed to the end. Even the saints who do God’s will ask for this perseverance when they say in the Prayer, “Your will be done.”

For since God’s will is already done in them, why do they still ask that it be done, unless so that they may persevere in what they have begun to be?

It could, however, be said here that the saints do not ask that God’s will be done in heaven, but that it be done on earth as it is in heaven: so that earth may imitate heaven—that is, that a human being may imitate an angel, or an unbeliever a believer. Accordingly, the saints ask that what does not yet exist may come to be, rather than that what exists may persevere.

For however greatly human beings may excel in holiness, they are not yet equal to God’s angels. God’s will is therefore not yet done in them as it is in heaven.

If this is so, then in the part where we wish human beings to become believers from unbelievers, what is being desired seems to be not perseverance but a beginning. But in the part where we wish human beings, in doing God’s will, to become equal to God’s angels, when the saints pray this they are shown to be praying for perseverance, since no one reaches that supreme blessedness which is in the kingdom unless he has persevered to the end in the holiness which he received on earth.

# Chapter Four

### 7

The fourth petition is, “Give us this day our daily bread.” Here the blessed Cyprian shows how perseverance is also requested in this petition. Among other things he says:

“We ask that this bread be given to us daily, so that we who are in Christ and daily receive the Eucharist as the food of salvation may not, because some more serious offense intervenes and, being kept from it and not communicating, we are barred from the heavenly bread, be separated from Christ’s body.”

These words of the holy man of God plainly show that the saints ask perseverance from the Lord when they say, with this intention, “Give us this day our daily bread”: namely, that they may not be separated from Christ’s body but may remain in that holiness in which they commit no crime deserving to separate them from it.

# Chapter Five

### 8

At the fifth place in the Prayer we say, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.” In this petition alone perseverance is not found to be requested.

The sins are past, and we pray that they may be forgiven us. Perseverance, however, which saves us forever, is necessary for the time of this life—not for the time already completed, but for that which remains until its end.

Nevertheless, it is worthwhile to observe briefly how even in this petition, by Cyprian’s tongue, the heretics who would arise long afterward were already pierced as by an unconquerable weapon of truth. [Note: Earlier editions read “of the most vehement”; the present reading is “of the unconquerable.”]

For the Pelagians also dare to say that a just person has absolutely no sin in this life, and that the Church exists in such people already in the present time without spot, wrinkle, or anything of the kind (Ephesians 5:27), and that this Church is the one and only bride of Christ.

It is as though she were not Christ’s bride who throughout the whole earth says what she learned from him: “Forgive us our debts.”

But observe how the most glorious Cyprian destroys these men. When explaining the passage from the Lord’s Prayer itself, he says among other things:

“How necessarily, how wisely and salutarily we are reminded that we are sinners, since we are compelled to pray for sins: so that, while pardon is sought from God, the mind may recall its own conscience. No one should please himself as though innocent and, by exalting himself, perish more grievously. He is instructed and taught that he sins daily, since he is commanded to pray daily for sins.

“Thus, finally, John also said in his Letter: ‘If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us’” (1 John 1:8), and so forth, which it would be tedious to insert here in full.

### 9

Now when the saints say, “Do not bring us into temptation, but deliver us from evil” (Matthew 6:9–13), what else do they pray for than that they may persevere in holiness?

For once this gift of God has been granted them—a gift shown clearly enough to be God’s gift precisely because it is requested from him—no saint fails to hold fast to perseverance in holiness to the end.

No one ceases to persevere in the Christian commitment unless he is first brought into temptation. If, then, what he prays for is granted to him—that he not be brought into temptation—he certainly persists, by God’s gift, in the sanctification which he received by God’s gift. [Note: The printed editions read, “there is no saint who does not hold fast.” The manuscripts read, “no saint fails to hold fast.”]

# Chapter Six

### 10

“But they do not wish,” as you write, “this perseverance to be preached in such a way that it cannot either be earnestly obtained or stubbornly lost” (*Above, in Hilary’s Letter*, section 3, columns 949–950).

Here they do not attend carefully enough to what they are saying. For we are speaking of that perseverance by which one perseveres to the end. If it has been given, one has persevered to the end; but if one has not persevered to the end, it has not been given. We have already treated this sufficiently above. (*Above*, section 1.)

Let people therefore not say that perseverance to the end has been given to anyone until the end itself has arrived and the person to whom it was given has been found to have persevered to the end.

We call a person chaste whom we know to be chaste, whether or not he is going to remain in that chastity. If he possesses any other divine gift that can be held and lost, we say that he has it for as long as he has it; and if he loses it, we say that he had it.

But perseverance to the end—since no one possesses it except one who perseveres to the end—many may possess, but no one can lose. For there is no need to fear that, once a human being has persevered to the end, some evil will arise in him by which he will fail to persevere to the end.

This gift of God can therefore be earnestly obtained; but when it has been given, it cannot be stubbornly lost. For when someone has persevered to the end, he can lose neither this gift nor the other things which he could have lost before the end.

How, then, can that be lost by which it comes about that even what could have been lost is not lost?

### 11

But perhaps someone will say that perseverance to the end is indeed not lost once it has been given—that is, once one has persevered to the end—but that it is lost in a certain sense when a person acts stubbornly so that he cannot reach it. We might say that a person who did not persevere to the end has lost eternal life or the kingdom of God—not because he had already received and possessed it, but because he would have received and possessed it if he had persevered.

Let us set aside disputes over words, and let us say that even certain things which are not possessed but are hoped for as things to be possessed can be lost. [Note: The printed editions read “but are hoped to be possessed”; the manuscripts read “but are hoped for as things to be possessed.”]

Let anyone who dares tell me whether God cannot give what he commanded to be requested from him. Anyone who understands this does not merely fail to understand but is insane.

God commanded his saints to say to him in prayer, “Do not bring us into temptation.” Whoever is heard when he asks this is not brought into the temptation of stubbornness, by which he could or might deserve to lose perseverance in holiness.

### 12

“But,” they say, “each person abandons God by his own will, so that he deservedly is abandoned by God.”

Who would deny this? But for that very reason we ask not to be brought into temptation, so that this may not happen. And if we are heard, it certainly does not happen, because God does not permit it to happen.

For nothing happens except what he himself either does or permits to happen. He is therefore powerful both to turn wills inclined toward evil toward good and to redirect and guide wills prone to fall into a path pleasing to him.

Not without reason it is said to him: “You, O God, turning us, will revive us” (Psalm 84:7). Not without reason it is said: “Do not give me up so that my foot may be moved” (Psalm 66:9). Not without reason it is said: “Do not hand me over, Lord, to the sinner according to my desire” (Psalm 140:9). Finally, not to mention many things, since more may occur to you, not without reason it is said: “Do not bring us into temptation.”

For whoever is not brought into temptation is certainly not brought into the temptation of his own evil will; and whoever is not brought into the temptation of his own evil will is not brought into any temptation at all.

“Each person is tempted,” as it is written, “when he is drawn away and enticed by his own desire”; but “God tempts no one” (James 1:14, 13)—that is, with a harmful temptation.

There is, however, also a useful temptation, by which we are not deceived or overwhelmed but tested [Note: The Amiens and Erasmus editions and the manuscripts read “when we are not deceived.”], according to what is said: “Test me, Lord, and try me” (Psalm 26:2).

God therefore tempts no one with that harmful temptation signified by the Apostle when he says, “Lest the tempter have tempted you and our labor be in vain” (1 Thessalonians 3:5). That is, he does not bring or lead anyone into temptation.

To be tempted without being brought into temptation is not evil; indeed, it is good. For this is to be tested.

When we therefore say to God, “Do not bring us into temptation,” what do we say except, “Do not allow us to be brought into it”?

For this reason some pray in this form, and it is read in many manuscripts; the most blessed Cyprian also used it: “Do not permit us to be led into temptation.”

In the Greek Gospel, however, I have nowhere found anything except, “Do not bring us into temptation.”

We therefore live more securely if we entrust everything to God, rather than entrusting ourselves partly to him and partly to ourselves. This the venerable martyr understood. For when explaining the same passage of the Prayer, he says after other things:

“When we ask that we may not come into temptation, we are reminded of our weakness and frailty, as we ask in this way so that no one may presumptuously exalt himself, no one may arrogantly and proudly claim anything for himself, and no one may count the glory of confession or suffering as his own. For the Lord himself, teaching humility, said: ‘Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation; the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak’ (Matthew 26:41). Thus, when humble and submissive confession comes first, and everything is given to God, whatever is asked earnestly with fear of God is granted by his mercy.” [Note: The same manuscripts read “claim”; the printed editions read “say.”]

# Chapter Seven

### 13

If there were no other proofs, this Lord’s Prayer alone would suffice for us in the case of the grace which we defend, because it has left us nothing in which we may glory as in something belonging to us. [Note: Some manuscripts read “has left nothing”; others read “leaves nothing.”]

For even that we may not depart from God, it shows to be given only by God, since it shows that it must be requested from God. Whoever is not brought into temptation does not depart from God.

This is not at all within the power of free choice as human beings now possess it; it had been within human power before the fall. Yet how powerful that freedom of the will was in the excellence of the first condition is evident in the angels: when the devil fell with his own, they stood in the truth and merited attaining the perpetual security of not falling, in which we are now entirely certain that they remain.

After the human fall, however, God willed that it belong solely to his grace that a human being should approach him; and he willed that it belong solely to his grace that a human being should not depart from him.

14. He placed this grace in him in whom we have obtained our lot, having been predestined according to the purpose of him who accomplishes everything. And so, just as he works that we may approach, so he works that we may not depart. Therefore it was said to him through the prophet [Note: [Col. 1001] Several manuscripts read, “through prophecy.”]: “Let your hand be upon the man of your right hand, and upon the son of man whom you strengthened for yourself; and we shall not depart from you” (Psalm 79:18–19). This is certainly not the first Adam, in whom we departed from him, but the last Adam, upon whom his hand rests so that we may not depart from him. For Christ in his entirety, together with his members, exists for the sake of the Church, which is his body, his fullness. Therefore, when God’s hand rests upon him so that we may not depart from God, [Col. 1001] God’s work reaches us—for this is what “God’s hand” means [Note: [Col. 1001] The particle enim (“for”) is absent from the old Corbie codex.]—by which work [Note: [Col. 1001] All our manuscripts and three Belgian manuscripts read “by which” (quo); the printed editions read “because” (quoniam).] it comes about that we remain in Christ with God, not departing from God as we did in Adam. For in Christ we have obtained our lot, having been predestined according to the purpose of him who accomplishes everything. This hand of God, then, is not ours, so that we may not depart from God. I repeat: it is the hand of him who said, “I will put my fear in their heart, so that they may not depart from me” (Jeremiah 32:40).

15. For this reason he also wished us to ask him not to lead us into temptation, because, if we are not led into temptation, we [Col. 1002] depart from him in no way. This could have been given to us even without our praying; but he wished us to be admonished by our prayer as to from whom we receive these benefits. From whom, indeed, do we receive them, if not from him who commanded us to ask for them? In this matter the Church should not await elaborate arguments, but should attend to her daily prayers. She prays that unbelievers may believe; therefore God turns them to faith [Note: [Col. 1002] The printed editions read, “turns them to faith.” The manuscripts omit “them.”]. She prays that believers may persevere; therefore God grants perseverance to the end. God foreknew that he would do these things [Note: [Col. 1002] Am. and Er.: “God foreknew that this would happen.” The Louvain editors corrected the text on the evidence of the Belgian manuscripts, supported by our French and Vatican manuscripts.]. This is the predestination of the saints, whom he chose in Christ before the foundation of the world, so that they might be holy and blameless before him in love; predestining them for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ, for himself, according to the good pleasure of his will, to the praise of the glory of his grace, with which he graced them in his beloved Son. In him they have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of his grace, which he lavished upon them in all wisdom and understanding, making known to them the mystery of his will according to his good pleasure, which he purposed in him, for the dispensation of the fullness of times, to restore all things in Christ, things in heaven and things on earth, in him. In him we have also obtained our lot, having been predestined according to the purpose of him who accomplishes everything (Ephesians 1:4–11). Against so clear a trumpet-blast of truth, what human voices would any person of sober and watchful faith admit?

## CHAPTER VIII

16. “But why,” he says, “is God’s grace not given according to human merits?” I answer: Because God is merciful. “Why, then,” he says, “is it not given to everyone?” Here too I answer: Because God is judge [Note: [Col. 1002] The printed editions read, “a just judge.” “Just” is absent from the manuscripts.]. Thus grace is given freely by him; and by his just judgment toward others it is demonstrated what grace accomplishes in those to whom it is given. Let us not, then, be ungrateful that, according to the good pleasure of his will, to the praise of the glory of his grace, merciful God liberates so many from such a deserved destruction; for if he liberated no one from it, he would not be unjust. For all, from the one man, were judged to go into condemnation—not an unjust condemnation, but a just one. Therefore, let the one who is liberated love grace; let the one who is not liberated acknowledge what is owed. If goodness is recognized in the remission of a debt and equity in its collection, no iniquity is found anywhere with God.

17. “But why,” he says, “in the case not only of infants but also of twins, whose condition is one and the same, is the judgment so different?” Is not the question similar to asking why, in different circumstances, the judgment is the same? Let us recall, then, those laborers in the vineyard who worked all day and those who worked for one hour: the circumstances of the labor expended are different, yet the judgment in the payment of the wage is the same [Note: [Col. 1003] Several manuscripts read “in the giving back” instead of “in the payment.”]. Did both groups hear anything else from the householder when they murmured [Col. 1003] except, “This is what I will”? His generosity toward some was such that there was no injustice toward others. Both groups, indeed, are among the good; nevertheless, insofar as justice and grace are concerned, it may rightly be said to the guilty person who is condemned concerning the guilty person who is liberated: “Take what is yours and go; but to this one I wish to give what is not owed. Is it not lawful for me to do what I will? Or is your eye evil because I am good?” (Matthew 20:1–15). If this person then says, “Why not to me also?” he will rightly hear: “O man, who are you to answer back to God?” (Romans 9:20). In one person you see him as a most benevolent giver, and in yourself as a most just exactor, yet you see him unjust toward no one. For even if he punished both, he would be just; the one who is liberated has reason to give thanks, while the one who is condemned has no grounds for reproach.

18. “But if,” he says, “this was necessary, so that, by not condemning everyone, he might show what was owed to all and thus commend his grace more gratefully to the vessels of mercy [Note: [Col. 1003] Am. and Er. and several manuscripts read, “in the vessels.”], why will he punish me rather than him, or liberate him rather than me, when our condition is the same?” I do not say this. If you ask why, I confess that I do not find what to say. If you ask why this too is so, then I answer: just as his anger in this matter is just and his mercy great, so his judgments are inscrutable.

19. Let him continue and say: “Why did he not grant perseverance to the end to certain people who served him in good faith?” Why do you think, except because the one who says, “They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us” (1 John 2:19), does not lie? Are there, then, two human natures? Certainly not. If there were two natures, there would be no grace; for no one would receive gratuitous liberation if what was owed to nature were being restored.

Human beings, however, think that all who appear to be good believers ought to receive perseverance to the end. But God judged it better to mingle certain people who would not persevere with the definite number of his saints, so that those for whom security is not beneficial amid the temptations of this life might not be secure. For many are restrained from destructive arrogance by the Apostle’s words: “Therefore, let the one who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall” (1 Corinthians 10:12). Whoever falls, falls by his own will; whoever stands, stands by God’s will. For God is able to make him stand (Romans 14:4); therefore he does not establish himself, but God does. Nevertheless, it is good “not to be high-minded, but to fear” (ibid. 11:20). In his own thought, however, each person either falls or stands. As the Apostle says—and I recalled this in the preceding book—“We are not competent to think anything as from ourselves, but our competence is from God” (2 Corinthians 3:5). Following him, blessed Ambrose also dares to say: “Our heart and our thoughts are not in our power.” Everyone who is humbly and truly devout recognizes this as entirely true.

20. Ambrose said this in the book [Col. 1004] he wrote On the Flight from the World, where he taught that this world must be fled not bodily but in the heart; and he argued that this cannot be done without God’s help. For he says:

“Our discourse about fleeing this world is frequent; and would that our disposition were as cautious and watchful as our discourse is easy. But, what is worse, the allure of earthly desires frequently steals in, and a cloud of vanities occupies the mind, so that you think about and turn over in your spirit precisely what you are striving to avoid. It is difficult for a human being to guard against this, but impossible to strip it off entirely. Finally, the prophet testifies that this is rather a matter of prayer than of achievement when he says: ‘Incline my heart to your testimonies, and not to avarice’ (Psalm 118:36). For our heart and our thoughts are not in our power; they unexpectedly cloud and confuse the mind and spirit, and draw them elsewhere than you have determined. They recall us to secular concerns, implant worldly matters, thrust pleasures upon us [Note: [Col. 1004] The Corbie and Manessier manuscripts read, “thrust pleasurable things upon us.”], and weave in seductive things [Note: [Col. 1004] All our manuscripts read, “interweave.”]. At the very moment when we are preparing to raise our mind, caught up in empty thoughts [Note: [Col. 1004] The Noailles manuscript reads, “when inserted.”], we are often cast down to earthly things” (On the Flight from the World, chapter 1).

It is therefore not in human power but in God’s power that human beings have power to become children of God (John 1:12). For they receive this power from him who gives the human heart devout thoughts, through which it has faith that works through love (Galatians 5:6). To take up and hold fast this good, and to advance perseveringly in it to the end, “we are not competent to think anything as from ourselves, but our competence is from God”; in his power are our heart and our thoughts.

## CHAPTER IX

21. Why, then, out of two infants equally bound by original sin is one taken up and the other left behind? And why, out of two ungodly adults, is one called in such a way that he follows the one who calls, while the other is either not called or not called in the same way? The judgments of God are inscrutable. But out of two devout people, why is perseverance to the end granted to one and not granted to the other? The judgments of God are even more inscrutable.

Nevertheless, this must be absolutely certain to the faithful: one is among the predestined, the other is not. For if they had been of us, says one of the predestined, who had drunk this secret from the Lord’s breast, “they would certainly have remained with us.” What does this mean, I ask: “They were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us”? Were not both created by God, both born from Adam, both made from the earth, and had they not received souls of one and the same nature from him who said, “I made every breath” (Isaiah 57:16)? Finally, had not both been called, and followed the one who called them; had not both been justified from among the ungodly, and both been renewed through the laver of regeneration?

But if the one who certainly knew what he was saying heard these things, he could answer: “These things are true; in all these respects they were of us. Nevertheless, according to another distinction, they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us.” What, after all [Note: [Col. 1004] All manuscripts read tamen (“nevertheless”).], is this distinction? The books of God lie open; let us not turn our eyes away. Divine Scripture cries out; [Col. 1005] let us give ear. They were not of them because they were not called according to the purpose; they were not chosen in Christ before the foundation of the world; they had not obtained their lot in him; they had not been predestined according to the purpose of him who accomplishes everything. For if this had been true of them, they would have been of them and would undoubtedly have remained with them.

22. Not to mention how possible it is for God to turn human wills, turned away and hostile, toward faith in him, and to work in their hearts so that they yield to no adversities and depart from him after being overcome by no temptation—since he can also do what the Apostle says, namely, not permit them to be tempted beyond what they can bear (1 Corinthians 10:13)—let us not mention that. Certainly God could have removed from this life, before it happened, those whom he foreknew would fall.

Are we going to return to arguing how absurd it is to say that dead people are judged even for those sins which God foreknew they would have committed if they had lived? This is so abhorrent to Christian—or indeed to human—sentiments that it is shameful even to refute it. Why not also say that the Gospel itself was preached, or is still preached, with all the labor and sufferings of the saints in vain, if people could be judged, even without having heard the Gospel, according to the obstinacy or obedience that God foreknew they would have had if they had heard it?

Nor would Tyre and Sidon be condemned, although they would receive a lighter punishment than those cities in which the Lord Christ performed miraculous signs [Note: [Col. 1005] Am., Er., and several manuscripts read, “and signs.”] before people who did not believe; for if those signs had been performed among Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented in sackcloth and ashes. So speak the utterances of truth, in which the Lord Jesus, through his own words, reveals to us more profoundly the mystery of predestination.

23. If we are asked why such great miracles were performed among those who, though they saw them, would not believe, and were not performed among those who would have believed if they had seen them, what shall we answer? Shall we say what I said in that book in which I answered six questions of pagans—without prejudice, however, to other explanations that wise people may investigate?

When the question was asked why Christ came after such a long time, I said that he foreknew that, in those times and places where his Gospel had not been preached, all such people would have been at its preaching as many were in his bodily presence, who refused to believe in him even after he had raised the dead. Again, shortly afterward, in the same book and in the same question, I said: “What is surprising, I ask, if Christ knew in earlier ages that the whole world would be full of unbelievers, so that he rightly did not wish the Gospel to be preached to those whom he foreknew would not believe either his words or his miracles?” (Letter 102, question 2).

Certainly we cannot say this about Tyre and Sidon. In them we recognize that these divine judgments belong to those causes of predestination without prejudice to which hidden causes I then said that I was answering. It is easy for us to accuse the unbelief of the Jews as arising from free will, [Col. 1006] since they refused to believe in the great works of power performed among them. The Lord also reproved and condemned this, saying: “Woe to you, Chorazin and Bethsaida! For if the works of power that were performed in you had been performed in Tyre and Sidon, they would long ago have repented in sackcloth and ashes.”

But can we say that the people of Tyre and Sidon also would have refused to believe if such works of power had been performed among them, or that they would not have believed if they had been performed? The Lord himself testifies concerning them that they would have undertaken an act of great humility and repentance if those signs of divine power had been performed among them. And yet they will be punished on the day of judgment, although with a lesser punishment than those cities that refused to believe when works of power were performed among them. For the Lord continued: “Nevertheless I say to you, it will be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon on the day of judgment than for you” (Matthew 11:21–22).

These people, therefore, will be punished more severely, and those more lightly; nevertheless, they too will be punished. Furthermore, if the dead are judged according to the deeds they would have performed if they had lived, then, since these people would have become believers if the Gospel had been preached to them with such great miracles, they ought certainly not to be punished. But they will be punished [Note: [Col. 1006] Here chapter 10 begins in Am. and Er.]. Therefore it is false that the dead are judged according to what they would have done if the Gospel had reached them while they were alive.

And if this is false, there is no reason to say that infants who perish by dying without Baptism undergo this on account of a merit consisting in the fact that, if they had lived and the Gospel had been preached to them, God foreknew that they would have heard it unbelievingly. It remains, therefore, that they are held bound by original sin alone and, for this alone, go into condemnation. We see [Note: [Col. 1006] So the manuscripts. The printed editions read, “since we see.” And below: “regeneration is granted through God’s gratuitous grace.”] that to others who have the same condition it is granted only through God’s gratuitous grace to receive regeneration; and that, by his hidden yet just judgment—for there is no injustice with God (Romans 9:14)—some who will perish after Baptism by living most wickedly are nevertheless kept in this life until they perish. They would not perish if bodily death, preceding their fall, came to their aid.

For no dead person is judged on the basis of the good or evil things he would have done if he had not died. Otherwise the people of Tyre and Sidon would not suffer punishment according to what they had done, but would instead, through great repentance and faith in Christ, obtain salvation according to what they would have done if those evangelical works of power had been performed among them.

## CHAPTER X

24. A certain Catholic disputant, a man of no small distinction, explained this Gospel passage in such a way that he said the Lord had foreknown that the people of Tyre and Sidon would later depart from the faith after believing in miracles performed among them, and that in his mercy he had therefore not performed those miracles there; for they would have become liable to a heavier punishment if they had abandoned the faith they had held than if they had never held it.

As for what still deserves to be asked about the view of this learned and exceedingly acute man [Note: [Col. 1006] The manuscripts read, “what merits still deserve to be asked about.”], why should I discuss it now, when that very view supports the matter we are treating? For if, out of pity, the Lord did not perform among these people the works by which they might have become believers [Col. 1007], lest they be punished more severely when they later became unbelievers—something he foreknew they would do—then it is shown clearly enough that no one is judged for sins that he was foreknown to have committed if, in some way, help was given to him so that he would not commit them. Thus Christ is said to have helped the people of Tyre and Sidon, if that view is true: he preferred that they not approach the faith rather than that they depart from the faith through a much greater crime, which he had foreseen they would commit if they had approached it.

Although if it is said, “Why did it not happen that they believed instead, and why was it not granted to them that, before they abandoned the faith, they should depart from this life?” I do not know what could be answered. For the person who says that the benefit of not beginning to possess what they would have abandoned with greater impiety was granted to those who would have abandoned the faith clearly indicates that a person is not judged according to what he is foreknown to have done wickedly if, by some benefit, he is aided so that he does not do it.

Thus help was also given to the one who was taken away, “lest wickedness change his understanding” (Wisdom 4:11). But why were the people of Tyre and Sidon not helped in such a way that they would believe and then be taken away, lest wickedness change their understanding? Perhaps the person who chose this way of resolving the question would answer that. But as far as my present argument is concerned, I see that it is enough for people to be shown—even according to this view—not to be judged for things they did not do, even if they were foreseen as going to do them.

Nevertheless, as I said, I am ashamed even to refute the opinion according to which, in those who are dying or dead, sins are punished [Note: [Col. 1007] Most manuscripts read, “sins that were foreknown are punished,” omitting “sins.”] which they were foreseen as going to commit if they lived, lest we seem to have thought it worthy of serious consideration when we preferred to restrain it by argument rather than pass over it in silence.

## CHAPTER XI

25. Accordingly, as the Apostle says, “It is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Romans 9:16). He also helps infants whom he wishes to help, even though they neither will nor run; he chose them in Christ before the foundation of the world, intending to give them grace freely—that is, with no preceding merits of their faith or works. Even when it comes to adults whom he foresaw would believe in his miracles if those miracles had been performed among them, if he does not wish to help them, he does not help them; concerning them he secretly but justly made another judgment in his predestination.

For there is no injustice with God; rather, his judgments are inscrutable and his ways unsearchable (Romans 11:33). Yet “all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Psalm 24:10). Unsearchable, therefore, is the mercy by which he has mercy on whomever he wills, with none of that person’s preceding merits; and unsearchable is the truth by which he hardens whomever he wills (Romans 9:18), with that person’s preceding merits, indeed, but often merits shared with the one on whom he has mercy.

As with two twins, one of whom is taken up and the other left behind, the outcome is different while their merits are shared: in them one is liberated by God’s great goodness, while the other is not condemned by any injustice of his. Is there injustice with God? Certainly not; but his ways are unsearchable. Therefore let us believe without hesitation in his mercy in those who are liberated and [Col. 1008] in his truth in those who are punished; let us not attempt to investigate what is inscrutable or search out what is unsearchable.

For he perfects his praise from the mouths of infants and nursing children (Psalm 8:3), so that, when we see that in the case of those whose liberation is preceded by no good merits, and in the case of those whose condemnation is preceded in both by nothing but shared original sin, we may by no means hesitate to believe that the same occurs in adults. That is, we should not think that grace is given to anyone according to his merits, or that anyone is punished except for his merits, whether the causes of those who are liberated and punished are equal, or whether they have unequal evil causes. Thus “the one who thinks he stands should take heed lest he fall” (1 Corinthians 10:12), and “the one who boasts should boast not in himself but in the Lord” (ibid. 1:31).

26. But why do people, as you write, “not allow the case of infants to be brought forward as an example for adults” (above, in Hilary’s Letter, no. 8), when, in opposition to the Pelagians, they do not hesitate to affirm original sin, which entered the world through one man, and that all went from one man into condemnation (Romans 5:12, 16)?

The Manichaeans do not accept this either. They not only refuse to grant any authority to all the Scriptures of the Old Instrument; they also interpret those writings that belong to the New Testament in such a way that, by a kind of privilege—or rather sacrilege—they take what they wish and reject what they do not wish. I was arguing against them in the books On Free Choice, from which these people think they should prescribe against us.

For that reason I did not wish to disentangle in detail the very difficult questions that arose, lest the work become excessively long, since in that context the authority of the divine testimonies did not assist me against people so perversely disposed. And I could, as I did, conclude with certainty that, whichever of the alternatives I was not affirming definitively might be true, God was nevertheless to be praised in all things, without any necessity of believing, as they wish, that two substances—good and evil—coeternal and mingled together exist.

Finally, in the first book of the Retractions, which you have not yet read, when I came to revise those books—namely, On Free Choice—I spoke as follows:

“In these books,” I said, “many matters are discussed in such a way that certain questions arising in the course of the argument, which I either could not untangle or which at that point required a lengthy discussion, were deferred. Thus, from either side, or from all sides of those questions in which it was not apparent what agreed more closely with the truth, our reasoning was nevertheless brought to this conclusion: whichever of the alternatives was true, God was to be believed, or even shown, to be worthy of praise.

That discussion was undertaken on behalf of those who deny that the origin of evil derives from free choice of the will and contend that, if this is so, God must be blamed as the creator of all natures. In this way they wish, according to the error of their impiety—for they are Manichaeans—to introduce a certain nature of evil, immutable and coeternal with God” (Retractions, book 1, chapter 9, no. 2).

Again, a little later, in another place, I said:

“Then it was said,” I said, [Col. 1009] “that God’s grace liberates [Note: [Col. 1009] The printed editions read “may liberate”; the manuscripts read “liberates.” The Retractions here read “may liberate.”] from the misery most justly inflicted upon sinners, because a human being could fall voluntarily, that is, by free choice, but could not rise by that same power. To this misery of just condemnation belong the ignorance and difficulty suffered by every human being from the beginning of his birth; and no one is liberated from this evil except by God’s grace.

The Pelagians do not wish this misery to descend from a just condemnation, since they deny original sin. Yet even if ignorance and difficulty were the natural beginnings of human beings, God would still not thereby be blameworthy but praiseworthy, just as we argued in the third book of the same work.

That discussion is directed against the Manichaeans, who do not accept the holy Scriptures of the Old Instrument, in which original sin is narrated; and whatever they read about it in the apostolic writings they contend, with detestable impudence, was inserted by corruptors of the Scriptures, as though it had not been said by the Apostles.

Against the Pelagians, however, we must defend what both Scriptures commend, which they profess to accept” (Retractions, book 1, chapter 9, no. 6).

I said these things in the first book of the Retractions when I was revising the books On Free Choice. I did not say only these things there about those books, but many others as well, which I thought would be lengthy and unnecessary to insert into this work addressed to you. I think you too will judge this once you have read everything.

Although, then, in the third book On Free Choice I discussed infants in such a way that, even if what the Pelagians say were true—namely, that ignorance and difficulty, without which no human being is born, are natural beginnings rather than punishments of nature—the Manichaeans would nevertheless be defeated, since they wish there to be two coeternal natures, that of good and that of evil, must faith for this reason be called into doubt or abandoned—the faith that the Catholic Church defends against the Pelagians themselves, affirming that there is original sin, the guilt contracted through generation and discharged through regeneration?

If these people also confess this with us, so that together we may destroy the Pelagian error in this matter, why do they think it necessary to doubt that God, through the sacrament of Baptism, rescues even infants to whom he gives his grace from the power of darkness and transfers them into the kingdom of the Son of his love (Colossians 1:13)?

In the fact, then, that he gives grace to some and does not give it to others, why do they refuse to sing to the Lord “mercy and judgment” (Psalm 100:1)? But why it is given to these rather than to those—“Who has known the mind of the Lord?” (Romans 11:34). Who can investigate what is inscrutable? Who can search out what is unsearchable?

## CHAPTER XII

28. It is therefore established that God’s grace is given not according to the merits of those who receive it, but according to the good pleasure of his will, to the praise and glory of his grace (Ephesians 1:5), so that the one who boasts may boast in no way in himself but in the Lord (1 Corinthians 1:31). He gives it to those whom he wishes, because he is merciful; and even if he does not give it, he is just. He does not give it to those to whom he does not wish to give it, in order to make known the riches of his glory in the vessels of mercy (Romans 9:23).

By giving some what they do not deserve, he clearly wished to show that his grace is gratuitous [Col. 1010] and therefore genuine; by not giving it to everyone, he shows what everyone deserves [Note: [Col. 1010] So the manuscripts. The printed editions read, “what everyone would deserve.”]. He is good in the benefit granted to some and just in the punishment of the others; good in all, because it is good when what is owed is repaid; and just in all, because it is just when what is not owed is granted without anyone being defrauded [Note: [Col. 1010] Earlier printed editions read “what is owed.” The reading “what is not owed” is more appropriate and is found in the codex of the Church of Reims.].

29. God’s grace is defended as without merits—that is, as true grace—even if baptized infants, as the Pelagians believe, are not rescued from the power of darkness because, as the Pelagians think, they are held guilty of no sin, but are merely transferred into the kingdom of the Lord. Even in that case, the kingdom is given without any good merits to those to whom it is given, and without any evil merits it is not given to those to whom it is not given.

This is what we customarily say against those same Pelagians when they object that we attribute God’s grace to fate, because we say that it is not given according to our merits. It is they, rather, who attribute God’s grace in infants to fate, since they say that fate exists wherever there is no merit [Note: [Col. 1010] See Book 2 Against the Two Letters of the Pelagians, nos. 11–12.]. For, even according to the Pelagians themselves, no merits can be found in infants explaining why some of them are sent into the kingdom while others are alienated from the kingdom.

Just as now, in order to show that God’s grace is not given according to our merits, I preferred to defend this according to both interpretations—according to ours, namely, that infants are held bound by original sin, and according to the Pelagians’, who deny that original sin exists—and yet I must not for that reason doubt that infants possess something for him to forgive, the one who saves his people from their sins (Matthew 1:21); so in the third book On Free Choice I resisted the Manichaeans according to both interpretations, whether ignorance and difficulty, without which no human being is born, are punishments or natural beginnings. Nevertheless, I hold to one of these positions, which I also expressed clearly enough there: that this is not the nature with which human beings were created, but the punishment of the condemned (chapters 20 and 23).

30. It is therefore useless to appeal against me to the antiquity of that book of mine, as though I should not defend the case of infants as I ought, and by that means demonstrate, in the clear light of truth, that God’s grace is not given according to human merits.

For if, when I began On Free Choice as a layman, I completed it as a presbyter [Note: [Col. 1010] Am. and Er.: “I began as a layman in Rome and completed it as a presbyter in Africa.”], I were still uncertain about the condemnation of infants who are not reborn and the liberation of those who are reborn, I think no one would be so unjust and envious as to prevent me from making progress or judge that I must remain in this uncertainty.

But it can more rightly be understood that I should not be thought to have been uncertain about this matter merely because, in opposing those against whom my argument was directed, I seemed to need to refute them in such a way that—whether the punishment of original sin existed in infants, as the truth holds, or did not exist, as certain people in error suppose—the belief in a mingling of two natures, good and evil, which the Manichaean [Col. 1011] error introduces, would nevertheless in no way be accepted.

Far be it from us to abandon the case of infants in such a way that we say we are uncertain whether infants who are regenerated in Christ, if they die, pass into eternal salvation, while those who are not regenerated pass into the second death. For what is written—“Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death; and so death passed into all human beings” (Romans 5:12)—cannot rightly be understood otherwise.

Nor does anyone, little or great, escape the everlasting death most justly assigned as the retribution for sin except the one who died without any original or personal sin of his own, in order to forgive both our original and our personal sins.

But why these rather than those? Again and again we say, and we are not weary of saying: “O man, who are you to answer back to God?” (Romans 9:20). “His judgments are inscrutable, and his ways unsearchable” (ibid. 11:33). Let us add this also: “Do not seek what is too high for you, and do not investigate what is too strong for you” (Sirach 3:22).

31. For you see, dearly beloved, how absurd it is,

[Note: Col. 1011. Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read “you see, dearly beloved,” omitting “for.”] and how foreign to the soundness of faith and the sincerity of truth, to say that infants who have died are judged according to what they were foreseen to be going to do if they had lived. Those who wished to be so far removed from the error of the Pelagians were compelled to adopt this view—although they still considered it necessary to believe, and even to put forward in argument, that the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord, by which alone we are helped after the fall of the first man in whom we all fell, is given according to our merits. Pelagius himself condemned this before the Eastern bishops who were acting as judges, out of fear of his condemnation.

But if this is not said—namely, that the dead are judged according to the good or evil works they would have done if they had lived, and therefore according to works that did not occur and, even in God’s foreknowledge, were not going to occur—[Note: Col. 1011. Lovaniensis reads “presence”; corrected from the manuscripts.]—if, then, this is not said, though you see with what error it is said, what remains except that we should acknowledge, with the darkness of contentious dispute removed, that God’s grace is not given according to our merits, as the Catholic Church defends against the Pelagian heresy, and that we should see this most clearly in the case of infants?

For God is not compelled by fate to help some infants and not to help others, when their condition is the same in both cases. Or shall we suppose that human affairs in the case of infants are governed not by divine providence but by chance events, when rational souls are involved that are either to be condemned or to be delivered? After all, not even a sparrow falls to the ground without the will of our Father who is in heaven (Matt. X, 29). Or must the death of infants without Baptism be attributed so entirely to the negligence of their parents that the heavenly judgments play no part in it—[Note: Col. 1011. All the manuscripts read “must be attributed back” (retribuendum est).]—as though those who die badly in this way had themselves, by their own will, chosen negligent parents from whom they would be born? What shall I say of the fact that an infant sometimes dies before help can reach it through the ministry of the one baptizing?

For often, although the parents are hurrying and the ministers are ready for Baptism to be given to the infant, it is nevertheless not given because God does not will it, since he did not keep the child in this life a little longer so that Baptism might be given. What, moreover, shall we say of the fact that it was sometimes possible for the children of unbelievers to be saved from going to perdition, while it was not possible for the children of believers to be helped by Baptism? Here it is certainly shown that there is no partiality with God (Rom. II, 11); otherwise he would deliver the children of his worshipers rather than those of his enemies.

## CHAPTER XIII

32. Since we are now discussing the gift of perseverance,[Note: Col. 1012. Amiens, Erasmus, and the manuscripts read “concerning the good” (de bono) rather than “concerning the gift” (de dono).] what is the meaning of this: that help is given to one who is going to die unbaptized, so that he does not die without Baptism, while help is not given to one who has been baptized and is going to fall, so that he may die before falling? Unless perhaps we are still willing to listen to that absurdity according to which it is said that it benefits no one to die before falling, because, according to them, he will be judged according to the actions that God foresaw he would perform if he lived. Who could patiently hear such perversity, so violently opposed to the soundness of faith? Who could endure it?

And yet those who do not acknowledge that God’s grace is given not according to our merits are driven to say this. But those who refuse to say that each of the dead is judged according to what God foresaw that person would have done if he had lived—because they see with what manifest falsehood and absurdity this is said—have no remaining reason to say that God’s grace is given according to our merits, a doctrine that the Church condemned among the Pelagians and caused Pelagius himself to condemn, when they observe that some infants who have not been regenerated are taken from this life to eternal death, while others who have been regenerated are taken to eternal life; and that among those who have been regenerated, some depart from this life persevering to the end, while others are kept here until they fall—though they certainly would not have fallen if they had departed before they fell; and again, that some who have fallen do not depart from this life until they return, though they would certainly perish if they departed before returning.

33. From this it is sufficiently and clearly demonstrated that the grace both of beginning and of persevering to the end is not given according to our merits, but according to God’s most secret—and likewise most just, most wise, and most benevolent—will. For those whom he predestined, he also called (Rom. VIII, 30), with that calling of which it is said, “The gifts and calling of God are irrevocable” (ibid. XI, 29).

No human being may be declared with certainty to belong to this calling until he has departed from this world. In this human life, however, which is a time of testing upon the earth (Job VII, 1), “let the one who seems to stand take heed lest he fall” (I Cor. X, 12). For this reason, as we have already said above (chap. 8, §19), those who will not persevere are mingled, by God’s most provident will, with those who will persevere, so that we may learn not to be wise in lofty things but to associate with the lowly (Rom. XII, 16), and to work out our own salvation with fear and trembling. For “it is God who works in us both to will and to work, according to his good pleasure” (Phil. II, 12–13).

We therefore will, but God works in us the willing; we therefore work, but God works in us the working, according to his good pleasure. It is fitting for us both to believe and to say this. It is pious and true, so that the confession may be humble and submissive, and everything may be attributed to God.

With our minds engaged, we believe; with our minds engaged, we speak; with our minds engaged, we do whatever we do. But with regard to the path of piety and the true worship of God, we are not competent to think anything as though from ourselves, “but our sufficiency is from God” (II Cor. III, 5). “For it is not in our power to control our heart and our thoughts.” Therefore the same Ambrose who said this also says (On Flight from the World, chap. 1):

> “Who, then, is so blessed that he may always ascend in his heart? But how can this happen without divine assistance? Certainly, in no way. Finally,” he says, “the same Scripture says above: ‘Blessed is the man whose help is from you, O Lord; ascents are in his heart’” (Ps. LXXXIII, 6).

In saying this, Ambrose was not merely reading it in the sacred Scriptures; as we must undoubtedly believe concerning that man, he also felt it in his own heart.

Therefore, when it is said in the sacraments of the faithful, “Let us lift up our hearts to the Lord,” this is the Lord’s gift. After these words have been spoken, the priest reminds those to whom they are said to give thanks for this gift to the Lord our God, and they respond that it is right and just (In the Preface before the Canon of the Mass).

Since our heart is not in our own power but is lifted up by divine assistance, so that it may ascend and set its mind on the things above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God, and not on the things of earth (Col. III, 1–2), to whom should thanks be given for so great a thing except to the Lord our God, who, by this benefit, delivering us from the depths of this world, chose us and predestined us before the foundation of the world?

## CHAPTER XIV

34. But they say that “the definition of predestination is opposed to the usefulness of preaching” (above, in the Letters of Hilary and Prosper, cols. 947–954). As though it were opposed to the Apostle when he preached! Did that teacher of the nations not commend predestination so many times in faith and truth, and yet never cease preaching the word of God?

Because he said, “It is God who works in you both to will and to work, according to his good pleasure” (Phil. II, 13), did he therefore not himself exhort people both to will what pleases God and to work? Or because he said, “He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion until the day of Christ Jesus” (ibid. I, 6), did he therefore not himself urge people to begin and to persevere to the end?

The Lord himself certainly commanded people to believe, saying, “Believe in God, and believe in me” (John XIV, 1). [Note: Col. 1013. Lovaniensis reads “you believe”; Amiens, Erasmus, and the manuscripts read “believe,” in accordance with the Greek.] Yet this does not make false his statement, nor does it make his definition void, when he says, “No one comes to me”—that is, no one believes in me—“unless it has been given to him by my Father” (ibid. VI, 66). Nor, conversely, because this definition is true is that command therefore void. Why, then, do we consider the definition of predestination useless to preaching, command, exhortation, and correction—all of which divine Scripture frequently employs—when that same divine Scripture commends it?

35. Will anyone dare to say that God did not foreknow to whom he would give the ability to believe, or whom he would give to his Son so that he would not lose any of them (John XVIII, 9)? If he foreknew these things, he certainly foreknew his benefits by which he deigns to deliver us.

This, then, is the predestination of the saints: nothing other than the foreknowledge, namely, and preparation of God’s benefits, by which all who are delivered are most certainly delivered. [Note: Col. 1014. Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “This predestination of the saints is nothing other than foreknowledge, namely,” etc.]

But where are the others left except in the mass of perdition, by a just divine judgment? Where were the Tyrians and Sidonians left, who could also have believed if they had seen those miraculous signs of Christ? But since it had not been given to them to believe, even the means by which they might believe were denied them.

From this it appears that some people possess, in their very nature, a divinely bestowed gift of understanding, by which they may be moved to faith if they either hear words suited to their minds or see signs suited to them.
