Yet if, by God’s deeper judgment, they have not been separated from the mass of perdition by the predestination of grace, then neither the divine words nor the divine deeds by which they could have believed, if they had heard or seen such things, are brought before them.

The Jews, too, were left in that same mass of perdition, although they were unable to believe in deeds of such great and evident power performed before their eyes. Why they were unable to believe, the Gospel did not conceal, saying:

> “Although he had performed so many signs before them, they did not believe in him, so that the word of the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled, which he said: ‘Lord, who has believed our report, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?’ And for this reason they were unable to believe, because Isaiah said again: ‘He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, lest they see with their eyes, understand with their heart, and turn, and I heal them’” (John XII, 37–40).

The eyes of the Tyrians and Sidonians were not blinded in this way, nor was their heart hardened in this way, for they would have believed if they had seen signs such as those witnessed by these others.

Yet it did not benefit the Tyrians and Sidonians that they were able to believe, because they had not been predestined by him whose judgments are inscrutable and whose ways are unsearchable. Nor would it have harmed the Jews that they were unable to believe, if they had been predestined in such a way that God would illuminate their blindness and wished to remove their stony heart from them.

What the Lord said about the Tyrians and Sidonians can perhaps be understood in some other way. Nevertheless, he unquestionably confesses that no one comes to Christ unless it has been given to that person, and that it is given to those who were chosen in him before the foundation of the world. From him the divine utterance is heard by the ears of the flesh, though not by deaf ears of the heart.

And yet this predestination, which is explained clearly enough even in the words of the Gospel, did not prevent the Lord from saying, for the sake of beginning, what I mentioned shortly before: “Believe in God, and believe in me”; and, for the sake of perseverance, “It is necessary always to pray and not to lose heart” (Luke XVIII, 1).

Those who have been given the gift hear these words and act upon them. Those who have not been given it do not act upon them, whether they hear them or do not hear them. “To you,” he says, “it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of heaven, but to them it has not been given” (Matt. XIII, 11).

The one belongs to the mercy, the other to the judgment, of him to whom our soul says, “I will sing of mercy and judgment to you, O Lord” (Ps. C, 1).

36. Therefore the preaching of persevering and advancing faith must not be hindered by the preaching of predestination, so that those to whom it has been given to obey may hear what they ought to hear [Note: Col. 1015. The printed editions read “and to whom it has been given to obey”; “and” has been deleted on the authority of the manuscripts.] (for “how will they hear without a preacher?” [Rom. X, 14]).

Nor, conversely, must the preaching of predestination be hindered by the preaching of faith that advances and remains to the end, lest the one who lives faithfully and obediently exalt himself on account of that obedience as though it were his own good and had not been received. Rather, “let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord” (I Cor. I, 31).

“For there is nothing in which one should boast, since nothing is ours.” Cyprian saw this with the greatest fidelity [Note: Col. 1015. The Corbie manuscript reads “most faithful.”] and defined it with the greatest confidence (To Quirinus, book 3, chap. 4), thereby surely declaring predestination to be most certain.

For if “there is nothing in which one should boast, since nothing is ours,” then certainly one should not boast even of the most persevering obedience, nor should it be called ours as though it had not been given to us from above.

Therefore this too is God’s gift: that God foreknew he would give it to his called ones with that calling of which it is said, “The gifts and calling of God are irrevocable” (Rom. XI, 29), as every Christian confesses.

This, then, is the predestination that we faithfully and humbly preach.

Yet that same teacher and doer—who believed in Christ and lived in holy obedience with the greatest perseverance even to suffering for Christ—did not therefore cease preaching the Gospel, exhorting people to faith and godly conduct, and urging perseverance even to the end, because he had said, “There is nothing in which one should boast, since nothing is ours.”

There he clearly declared the true grace of God, that is, grace that is not given according to our merits. Since God foreknew that he would give this grace, predestination was undoubtedly preached in these words of Cyprian. If it did not prevent Cyprian from preaching obedience, it certainly ought not to prevent us.

37. Although, therefore, we say that obedience is God’s gift, we nevertheless exhort people to obedience. [Note: Col. 1015. The Noailles manuscript reads “all people.”] To those who obediently hear the exhortation of truth, the gift of God itself has been given—that is, the gift of hearing obediently. But to those who do not hear in this way, it has not been given.

For it is not just anyone but Christ who says, “No one comes to me unless it has been given to him by my Father” (John VI, 66); and, “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of heaven, but to them it has not been given” (Matt. XIII, 11).

And concerning continence he says, “Not all receive this word, but those to whom it has been given” (ibid. XIX, 11).

When the Apostle was exhorting married couples to conjugal chastity, he said, “I wish that all people were as I myself am; but each has his own gift from God, one in this way and another in that” (I Cor. VII, 7). Here he sufficiently shows that not only continence is God’s gift, but also the chastity of married people.

Although these things are true, we nevertheless exhort people to them, insofar as each of us has been given the ability to exhort; for this too is his gift, in whose hand are both we and our words (Wis. VII, 16).

Thus the Apostle says, “According to the grace given to me, like a skilled architect I laid a foundation.” And elsewhere: “As the Lord gave to each, I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth. So neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything, but God who gives the growth” (I Cor. III, 10, 5–7).

Accordingly, just as the one who has received this gift exhorts and preaches rightly, so the one who has received this gift certainly hears the one exhorting and preaching rightly with obedience.

This is why the Lord, although he was speaking to people whose bodily ears were open, nevertheless said, “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Luke VIII, 8), for he undoubtedly knew that not all possessed such ears.

The Lord himself shows from whom those who possess them receive them, when he says, “I will give them a heart to know me and ears that hear” (Baruch II, 31).

The ears for hearing, then, are the very gift of obeying, so that those who possess them may come to him, to whom no one comes unless it has been given to him by his Father.

We therefore exhort and preach. Those who have ears for hearing listen to us obediently; those who do not have them experience what is written: “Though hearing, they do not hear” (Matt. XIII, 13)—hearing with the bodily sense, but not hearing with the assent of the heart.

But who has come to know why some have ears for hearing and others do not—that is, why it is given to some by the Father to come to the Son, while it is not given to others? Or who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor (Rom. XI, 34)? Or, “Who are you, O man, to answer back to God?” (ibid. IX, 20).

Is what has been made clear therefore to be denied because what is hidden cannot be comprehended? Shall we therefore, I ask, say that something which we plainly see to be so is not so because we cannot discover why it is so?

## CHAPTER XV

38. But, as you write, they say:

> “No one can be stirred by the goads of correction if it is said in the assembly of the Church, with many people listening: ‘The matter stands thus, according to the settled definition of God’s will concerning predestination: some of you have come from unbelief to faith, having received the will to obey; or, having received perseverance, you remain in the faith. But the rest of you, who linger in the pleasure of sins, have not yet risen because the assistance of merciful grace has not yet raised you. Nevertheless, if there are any among you who have not yet been called, but whom grace has predestined to be chosen, you will receive that same grace, by which you will desire and become elect. And if there are any who are obeying, but who have been predestined to be rejected, the power to obey will be withdrawn, so that you will cease to obey.’”

When these things are said, they ought no more to deter us from confessing the true grace of God—that is, grace that is not given according to our merits—and from confessing the predestination of the saints according to that grace, than we are deterred from confessing God’s foreknowledge if someone speaks to the people about it in this way:

> “Whether you are now living rightly or not, you will later be such as God foresaw that you would be—good, if he foresaw you as good; evil, if he foresaw you as evil.”

If, after hearing this, some people turn toward torpor and laziness, and, inclined away from labor, go after their desires toward lust, must what was said about God’s foreknowledge therefore be thought false? If God foresaw that they would become good, will they not be good, however great the wickedness in which they are now involved? But if he foresaw that they would be evil, will they not be evil, however much goodness they may now display?

There was a certain man in our monastery who, when the brothers corrected him for doing certain things that ought not to be done and failing to do things that ought to be done, would answer: “Whatever I am now, I will be such as God foresaw that I would be.” He was certainly speaking the truth, but this truth did not advance him toward good. Indeed, it advanced him so far toward evil that, abandoning the company of the monastery, he became a dog returning to its vomit. Yet what he will ultimately be is still uncertain.

Must what is truly said about God’s foreknowledge therefore be denied or left unspoken on account of souls of this kind [Note: Col. 1017. The printed editions read “on account of causes of this kind”; nearly all the manuscripts read “souls.”]—especially when, if it is not said, others are led into other errors?

## CHAPTER XVI

39. There are also people who either do not pray or pray coldly because they have learned from the Lord’s statement that God knows what we need before we ask him (Matt. VI, 8).

Will the truth of this statement therefore be abandoned or erased from the Gospel on account of such people? On the contrary, since it is clear that God has prepared some things to be given even to those who do not pray, such as the beginning of faith,[Note: Col. 1017. Lovaniensis reads, “since it is clear that God [gives] some things even to those who do not pray,” omitting “to be given”; the word occurs in the other printed editions and in the manuscripts.] and other things to be given only to those who pray, such as perseverance to the end, the person who thinks that he possesses the latter from himself does not pray to have it.

We must therefore beware lest, while fearing that exhortation may grow cold, prayer be extinguished and pride kindled.

40. Let the truth therefore be spoken, especially when some question urges that it be spoken; and let those who can receive it receive it. Otherwise, perhaps, when it is kept silent for the sake of those who cannot receive it, not only will they be deprived of the truth, but those who can receive the truth—and through it guard against falsehood—will be captured by falsehood.

It is easy, and even useful, to keep some truth silent for the sake of those who cannot receive it. For what else is meant by the Lord’s saying, “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now” (John XVI, 12)? And what else is meant by the Apostle’s saying, “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as people of the flesh; as infants in Christ, I gave you milk to drink, not solid food, for you were not yet able—but even now you are still not able” (I Cor. III, 1–2)?

Nevertheless, through a certain manner of speaking, what is said can be both milk for infants and solid food for the mature.

For example, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John I, 1): what Christian can keep silent about this? Who can comprehend it? Or what could be found in sound doctrine greater than this? Yet it is not kept silent from infants or from the mature, nor is it hidden from infants by the mature. [Note: Col. 1017. Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read, “and it is not kept silent from infants, and it is hidden neither from the mature nor from infants.”]

But the reason for keeping silent about the truth is one thing, and the necessity of speaking the truth is another. It would take too long to seek out or insert all the reasons for keeping silent about the truth. One of them, however, is this: that we should not make those who do not understand worse while wishing to make those who understand more learned. When we keep something of this kind silent, the more learned do not indeed become more learned, but neither do they become worse.

But when the matter is such that if we say the truth, the one who cannot receive it becomes worse, while if we keep silent, the one who can receive it becomes worse, what should we think ought to be done? Should we not rather speak the truth, so that the one who can receive it may receive it, than keep silent, so that not only do both fail to receive it, but the more intelligent person himself becomes worse?

If he heard and received it, many others would learn through him as well. The more capable he is of learning, the more suitable he is for teaching others.

The enemy of grace presses and urges by every means that people believe grace is given according to our merits, and thus that grace is no longer grace (Rom. XI, 6). Are we unwilling to say what, with Scripture as our witness, we can say? We fear, apparently, that by speaking we may offend the one who cannot receive the truth; yet we do not fear that by keeping silent the one who can receive the truth may be captured by falsehood?

41. Either predestination must be preached in the manner in which holy Scripture plainly declares it—that among the predestined the gifts and calling of God are irrevocable—or it must be confessed that God’s grace is given according to our merits, which is what the Pelagians think, although this opinion, as we have often already said, is recorded as condemned by the proceedings of the Eastern bishops and as condemned from the mouth of Pelagius himself (On the Proceedings of Pelagius, §30).

Those on whose behalf we are undertaking this discussion are so far removed from the heretical perversity of the Pelagians that, although they are not yet willing to admit that those who become obedient and remain obedient through God’s grace are predestined, they now nevertheless admit that grace precedes the will of those to whom it is given. They do this precisely so that grace may be believed to be given freely, as the truth declares, rather than according to the preceding merits of the will, as the Pelagian error protests against the truth.

Grace, therefore, precedes faith. Otherwise, if faith preceded grace, the will would undoubtedly precede it as well, since faith cannot exist without the will. But if grace precedes faith because it precedes the will, then it certainly precedes all obedience. It also precedes charity, by which alone God is truly and gladly obeyed. Grace works all these things in the person to whom it is given and whose every one of these qualities it precedes.

## CHAPTER XVII

What remains among these good things is perseverance to the end. It is asked of the Lord in vain every day if the Lord does not work it by his grace in the one whose prayers he hears.

See now how far it is from the truth to deny that perseverance to the end of this life is God’s gift, when he himself gives this life its end whenever he wills. If he gives a person death before an impending fall, he makes that person persevere to the end.

But even more marvelous and evident to the faithful is the abundance of God’s goodness: this grace is given even to infants, who are not of an age at which obedience can be given to them.

Therefore, whatever gifts God gives to anyone, he undoubtedly foreknew that he would give them and prepared them in his foreknowledge. “Those whom he predestined, he also called” (Rom. VIII, 30), with that calling which I am never weary of recalling, and of which it is said, “The gifts and calling of God are irrevocable” (ibid. XI, 29).

For to arrange in his foreknowledge—which cannot be deceived or changed—the works he will accomplish is precisely, and nothing other than, to predestine.

Just as the person whom God foreknew would be chaste, although that person is uncertain of it, nevertheless acts so as to be chaste, so the person whom God predestined to be chaste, although uncertain of it, does not for that reason fail to act so as to be chaste, because he hears that by God’s gift he will become what he will be. Rather, his charity rejoices, and “is not puffed up” (I Cor. XIII, 4), as though he had not received it. The preaching of predestination, therefore, not only does not hinder this work; it also assists it, so that when a person boasts, he may boast in the Lord (ibid. I, 31).

42. What I have said about chastity can be said with complete truth about faith, piety, charity, perseverance, and—to avoid going through each item—about every obedience by which God is obeyed.

But those who assign only the beginning of faith and perseverance to the end to our power, so that they do not think these are God’s gifts and that God works our thoughts and wills in order that we may possess and retain them, while they concede that he gives the other things when they are obtained by the believer’s faith [Note: Col. 1019. Some manuscripts read “when believers obtain them by faith.”]—why are they not afraid that the definition of predestination will hinder exhortation to those things and their preaching? [Note: Col. 1019. Lovaniensis alone reads, “exhortation to them, and the preaching of the other things”; less correctly.]

Or perhaps they do not say that even these things have been predestined? Then either they are not given by God, or he did not know that he would give them. But if they are both given and foreknown by him as things he would give, then he certainly predestined them.

Just as these people themselves exhort others to chastity, charity, piety, and the other things that they confess to be God’s gifts, and cannot deny that they were foreknown by him and therefore predestined, and just as they do not say that their exhortations are hindered by the preaching of God’s predestination—that is, by preaching God’s foreknowledge of these future gifts of his—so let them see that their exhortations to faith and perseverance are not hindered if these too are said, as is true, to be God’s gifts, foreknown by him, that is, predestined to be given.

Rather, this preaching of predestination hinders and overturns only that most pernicious error by which it is said that God’s grace is given according to our merits, so that the one who boasts may boast not in the Lord but in himself.

43. To explain this more clearly for the slower among us, let those whose intelligence has been granted the power to fly ahead bear with my delay in explanation. [Note: Col. 1019. Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read “rememoration” instead of “delay.” The Reims manuscript reads “to prevail” instead of “to fly ahead.”] The Apostle James says, “If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives to all generously and does not reproach anyone, and it will be given to him” (James I, 5).

It is also written in the Proverbs of Solomon, “For the Lord gives wisdom” (Prov. II, 6). And concerning continence we read in the Book of Wisdom, whose authority was used by great and learned men who treated the divine utterances long before us:

> “Since I knew that no one can be continent unless God gives it, and this itself was wisdom: to know whose gift it was” (Wis. VIII, 21).

Wisdom and continence, then—to say nothing of the other things—are God’s gifts.

These people agree with us here. For they are not Pelagians, so as to oppose this evident truth with harsh and heretical perversity. “But,” they say, “faith obtains these gifts from God for us,” and that faith begins from us. They insist that both beginning to have this faith and remaining in it to the end belong to us, as though we did not receive this from the Lord.

Here they are undoubtedly contradicting the Apostle, who says, “What do you have that you did not receive?” (I Cor. IV, 7). They also contradict the martyr Cyprian, who says, “There is nothing in which one should boast, since nothing is ours” (To Quirinus, book 3, chap. 4).

When we have said this and many other things that I am reluctant to repeat, and have shown that both the beginning of faith and perseverance to the end are God’s gifts; that God could not fail to foreknow any of his future gifts—both what gifts would be given and to whom they would be given [Note: Col. 1020. The printed editions read “future gifts would be”; “would be” is absent from the manuscripts.]—and therefore that those whom he delivers and crowns were predestined by him, they think that they must answer:

> “The definition of predestination is opposed to the usefulness of preaching, because, when this is heard, no one can be stirred by the goads of correction.”

In saying this, they do not want God’s gifts to be preached to people as the means by which they come to faith and remain in the faith, lest, when those who hear it consider that it is uncertain to human ignorance to whom God grants these gifts and to whom he does not grant them, more despair than exhortation seem to be produced.

Why, then, do they themselves join us in preaching that wisdom and continence are God’s gifts? If, when these are preached as God’s gifts, the exhortation by which we urge people to be wise and continent is not hindered, what reason can there be for them to think that exhortation is hindered by which we urge people to come to faith and remain in it to the end, if these too are said to be God’s gifts, as the testimony of his Scriptures confirms?

44. Let us leave continence aside and discuss wisdom alone in this passage. Surely the Apostle James mentioned above says:

> “The wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, open to persuasion, full of mercy and good fruits [Note: Col. 1020. The Corbie manuscript reads “full of mercy and good works”; the other manuscripts and the printed editions read “full of mercies”], impartial, and without hypocrisy” (James III, 17).

Do you see, I ask, from how many and how great goods wisdom descends from the Father of lights? [Note: Col. 1020. The margin of the Erasmus edition gives the alternative reading “supported” (fulta).] For, as the same Apostle says, “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (ibid. I, 17).

Why, then—to pass over the other matters—do we correct the impure and contentious, while nevertheless preaching to them that wisdom, pure and peaceable, is God’s gift? Why do we not fear that, disturbed by uncertainty about the divine will, they may find more despair than exhortation in this preaching, and that they may be stirred not by the goads of correction against themselves but rather against us, because we correct them for not having what we say is not brought forth by human will but bestowed by divine generosity?

Finally, why did the preaching of this grace not deter the Apostle James himself from correcting the restless and saying:

> “If you have bitter jealousy and contention in your hearts, do not boast and lie against the truth. This is not the wisdom that descends from above, but earthly, natural, demonic; for where jealousy and contention are, there is instability and every evil work” (James III, 14–16).

Therefore, just as the restless are to be corrected, both by the divine utterances that bear witness and by the very actions that these people share with us, and just as this correction is not hindered by our preaching that the peaceful wisdom by which the contentious are corrected and healed is God’s gift, so unbelievers, or those who do not remain in the faith, are to be corrected. This correction is not hindered by the preaching of God’s grace, which commends faith itself and remaining in it as God’s gifts.

For even though wisdom is obtained through faith, as James himself, after saying, “If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives to all generously and does not reproach anyone, and it will be given to him,” immediately adds, “But let him ask in faith, without doubting” (ibid. I, 5–6), it does not follow that, because faith is given before the person to whom it is given asks for it, faith should be said not to be God’s gift but to come from us, simply because it was given to us without our asking.

The Apostle says most plainly: “Peace to the brothers and charity with faith, from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ” (Eph. VI, 23). From the one, therefore, come peace and charity; from that same one comes faith. For this reason we ask him not only to increase faith in those who possess it, but also to give it to those who do not possess it.

45. Nor do those on whose account we say these things—those who loudly claim that exhortation is hindered by preaching predestination and grace—exhort people only to those gifts which they maintain are not given by God but come from us, such as the beginning of faith [Col. 1021] and perseverance in it to the end. That is what they ought to do if they wished to exhort only unbelievers to believe and believers to remain believing. [Note: Am. and Er.: “as believers.” The Noailles manuscript: “as credulous.”] But with regard to those things which they do not deny, together with us, to be gifts of God, so that together with us they may demolish the Pelagian error—such as chastity, continence, patience, and the other virtues by which one lives rightly, and which are obtained from the Lord through faith—they ought merely to have shown that these should be prayed for and to have prayed for them, whether for themselves or for others; they ought not to have exhorted anyone to undertake and retain them. Yet when they also exhort people to these things, as they are able, and acknowledge that people ought to be exhorted to them, they plainly show that exhortations are not hindered by that preaching, whether exhortations to faith or to perseverance to the end, since we preach that these too are gifts of God, bestowed on no one by oneself but by him.

46. “But,” they say, “each person abandons the faith through his own fault, when he yields to temptation and consents to it, and by that temptation he is led to abandon the faith.” Who denies this? But it does not therefore follow that perseverance in faith is not a gift of God. The one who says, “Do not bring us [Col. 1022] into temptation” (Matthew 6:13), asks for it daily; and if he is heard, he receives it. Thus, by asking daily that he may persevere, he plainly places the hope of his perseverance not in himself but in God.

I do not wish to enlarge upon this in my own words; rather, I leave it to them to consider, so that they may see what sort of thing it is that they have persuaded themselves of: “that the preaching of predestination brings more despair than exhortation to those who hear it.” For this amounts to saying that a person despairs of his salvation precisely when he has learned to place his hope not in himself but in God, although the prophet cries: “Cursed is everyone who places his hope in man” (Jeremiah 17:5).

47. These gifts of God, then, which are given to those called according to God’s purpose—among which are beginning to believe and persevering in faith to the end of this life—as we have established by so many arguments and testimonies: these gifts of God, I say, would not be foreknown by God if there were no predestination of the kind we defend. But they are foreknown. This, therefore, is the predestination we defend.

## CHAPTER XVIII

This same predestination is therefore sometimes signified also by the name “foreknowledge,” as the Apostle says: “God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew.” Here what he says, “foreknew,” is not rightly understood unless it means “predestined”; the context of the passage itself shows this. [Note: The printed editions read “the context of the expression itself”; the manuscripts, more correctly, read “the context of the passage itself.”] For he was speaking of the remnant of the Jews who were saved while the rest perished. Earlier he had said that the prophet declared to Israel: “All day long I have stretched out my hands to a people that does not believe and contradicts.” And as though someone had replied, “Where, then, are God’s promises to Israel fulfilled?” he immediately added: “I ask, then, has God rejected his people? Certainly not; for I too am an Israelite, of the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin.” [Note: The printed editions have “of the tribe of Benjamin”; “of the tribe” is absent from the manuscripts and from the Greek text of the Apostle.] It was as though he were saying, “For I too belong to that very people.”

Then he added the point under discussion: “God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew.” And to show that the remnant had been left by God’s grace, not on account of their merits from works, he continued: “Or do you not know what Scripture says in the passage about Elijah—how he appeals to God against Israel?” and so forth. “But what,” he says, “does the divine reply say to him? ‘I have kept for myself seven thousand men who have not bent the knee to Baal.’” He does not say, “Seven thousand have been left to me,” or, “They have left themselves to me,” but, “I have kept them for myself.”

“So therefore,” he says, “at the present time also a remnant has been made through the election of grace.” [Note: The printed editions add “has been saved.” It is absent from the manuscripts and from the Apostle’s Greek text.] “But if it is by grace, it is no longer from works; otherwise grace is no longer grace.” And connecting this with the words I have already inserted above, he asks, “What then?” and answers that question: “What Israel was seeking, it did not obtain; but the election obtained it, while the rest were hardened” (Romans 10:21–11:7).

In this election, therefore, and in this remnant made through the election of grace, he wished the people to be understood whom God did not reject precisely because he foreknew them. This is that election by which he chose in Christ those whom he wished, before the foundation [Col. 1023] of the world, to be holy and blameless in his sight in love, predestining them for adoption as sons (Ephesians 1:4–5).

Therefore no one who understands these things is permitted to deny or doubt that, when the Apostle says, “God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew,” he wished predestination to be signified. For he foreknew the remnant that he himself was going to make according to the election of grace. This, then, is what “predestined” means. Certainly he foreknew if he predestined; but to have predestined is to have foreknown what he himself was going to do.

## CHAPTER XIX

48. What, then, prevents us, when we read in certain interpreters of the word of God about God’s foreknowledge and the subject is the calling of the elect, from understanding that same predestination? Perhaps they chose to use this word in that context because it is more easily understood and does not conflict with—indeed, it agrees with—the truth preached concerning the predestination of grace. [Note: The printed editions have “however”; the manuscripts have “for.”]

I know that no one has been able to argue against this predestination, which we defend according to the holy Scriptures, except by falling into error. Yet I think that, for those who seek the opinions of interpreters on this matter, the holy men Cyprian and Ambrose, renowned everywhere for their commendable faith and Christian teaching, whose very clear testimonies we have set forth, ought to be sufficient. They ought to be sufficient for both purposes: so that people may believe and preach in every respect the free grace of God, as it must be believed and preached, and may not think that this preaching is opposed to the preaching by which we exhort the sluggish or rebuke the wicked.

For when these men preached God’s grace in such a way that one of them said, “In nothing should we glory, since nothing is ours” (Cyprian, To Quirinus, book 3, chapter 4), while the other said, “Our heart and our thoughts are [Col. 1024] not in our power” (Ambrose, On the Flight from the World, chapter 1), they nevertheless did not cease to exhort and rebuke people so that the divine commands might be fulfilled. Nor did they fear that anyone would say to them, “Why do you exhort and rebuke us, if nothing good that we may possess is ours?” [Note: The printed editions have “if we have no good thing that is ours.” We have preferred the reading of the older manuscripts.] “and if our heart is not in our power?” The holy men could not have feared that such things would be said to them, because they understood that only a very few are granted to receive the teaching of salvation directly from God himself or through the angels of heaven, without any human preaching, whereas many are granted to believe God through human beings.

However the word of God is spoken to a person, there is no doubt that, when he hears it in such a way that he obeys it, this is a gift of God. [Note: The manuscripts read “so that he may hear it”; the printed editions have “who hears it in such a way.”]

49. Therefore the excellent interpreters of the divine utterances mentioned above both preached the true grace of God, as it must be preached—namely, grace preceded by no human merits—and earnestly exhorted people to carry out the divine commands, so that those who had the gift of obedience might hear the commands to which they ought to obey.

For if any merits of ours precede grace, then the merit must consist in some deed, word, or thought, where the good will itself is also understood. But the one who says, “In nothing should we glory, since nothing is ours,” has very briefly embraced every kind of merit. The one who says, “Our heart and our thoughts are not in our power” has not omitted deeds and words either; for there is no human deed or word that does not proceed from the heart and thought.

What more could the most glorious martyr and most lucid teacher Cyprian have done on this subject than to remind us that, in the Lord’s Prayer, we ought even to pray for the enemies of the Christian faith? There he showed what he thought about the beginning of faith—that this too is a gift of God—and he demonstrated that the Church of Christ prays daily for perseverance to the end, since God grants this also only to those who persevere.

The blessed Ambrose, explaining the evangelist Luke’s words, “It seemed good to me also” (Luke 1:3), says:

“It can be that it did not seem good only to him who declares that it seemed good to him. For it did not seem good merely by human will, but as it pleased him who speaks in me, Christ, who works so that what is good may also seem good to us. For he has mercy on whom he wills, and he calls him. Therefore the one who follows Christ, when asked why he wished to be a Christian, can answer, ‘It seemed good to me also.’ When he says this, he does not deny that it seemed good to God; for the will of human beings is prepared by God” (Proverbs 8, according to the Septuagint).

“For God to be honored by the saint is the grace of God” (On Luke, in the exposition of the preface).

Likewise, in the same work—that is, in the Exposition of the Same Gospel—when he came to the passage where the Samaritans refused to receive the Lord as he was going to Jerusalem, he says:

“Learn at the same time that he did not wish to be received by those who turned toward him with an unsimple mind. For if he had wished it, he would have made the devoted out of the undevoted. But why they did not receive him, the evangelist himself recalls when he says: ‘Because his face was set toward Jerusalem’” (Luke 9:53).

“The disciples, however, eagerly desired that he be received within Samaria. But God calls those whom he deigns to call, and makes religious the one whom he wishes” (Book 7 on Luke, no. 27). [Note: Several manuscripts have “whom” rather than “those whom.”]

What could we seek that is clearer or more emphatic from interpreters of the word of God, if we take pleasure in hearing from them what is clear in the Scriptures themselves?

But let us add a third witness to these two, who ought to have been sufficient: Saint Gregory, who also testifies that both believing in God and confessing what we believe are gifts of God. He says:

“Of one Godhead, I ask you, confess the Trinity; or, if you prefer, say that it is of one nature; and he will ask from the Holy Spirit that the word ‘God’ be given to you.” [Note: In the Vatican manuscripts, the word “God” is omitted. But once this word is removed, Gregory’s sentence is incomplete. In Greek it reads: *Mias theotētos, ō houtoi, tēn Triada homologēsate, ei de boulesthe, mias physeōs; kai tēn Theos phōnēn para tou Pneumatos hymin aitēsomen: dōsei gar, eu oida, ho to prōton dous, kai to deuteron, kai malista.* That is: “Men, confess the Trinity of one Godhead, or, if you prefer, of one nature; and we shall ask from the Spirit for you the word ‘God.’ For he who gave the first will certainly give the second, and especially so.” The Louvain scholars note that Augustine, who evidently did not have access to a Greek exemplar, read “he will ask” rather than “we shall ask,” perhaps through the fault of the translator or manuscript; and that the added explanation—“that is, God will be asked,” and so forth—was inserted to clarify the sentence. Likewise, below, the words “he who gave the ability to believe will also give the ability to confess” are printed in italics, because it is uncertain whether they belong to the translator or to Augustine.]

That is, God is asked to permit you to receive the word [Col. 1025] by which you may confess what you believe. “For he will give it—I am certain of this; he who gave what comes first will also give what comes second” (Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 44, On Pentecost): he who gave the ability to believe will also give the ability to confess.

50. These such great teachers say that there is nothing about which we may glory as though it were ours, since God has not given it to us; they say that even our heart and thoughts are not in our power; they attribute everything to God and confess that we receive from him the grace by which we are converted to him so as to remain with him; that what is good may also seem good to us and we may desire it, so that we may honor God; that we may receive Christ; that we may be made devoted and religious out of the undevoted; and that we may believe in the Trinity and confess with our voice what we believe.

They plainly attribute all these things to the grace of God, recognize them as gifts of God, and testify that they come to us from him, not from ourselves. Would anyone say that they confessed God’s grace in this way while daring to deny his foreknowledge, which not only the learned but even the unlearned confess?

Moreover, if they knew that God gives these things in such a way that they did not fail to recognize that he foreknew he would give them, and that he could not be ignorant of those to whom he would give them, then without doubt they knew the predestination which we defend more laboriously and carefully, as preached through the Apostles, against the new heretics.

Yet when they preached obedience and fervently exhorted people to it, each as he was able, no one could rightly say to them: “If you do not want obedience—the obedience to which you inflame us—to grow cold in our hearts, do not preach to us this grace of God, which you admit God gives and to which you exhort us so that we may do these things.”

## CHAPTER XX

51. Therefore, if both the Apostles and the teachers of the Church who succeeded and imitated them did both things—truthfully preaching the grace of God, which is not given according to our merits, and instructing people in devout obedience to salutary commands—what is there that these men, shut in by the invincible force of truth, think they can rightly say?

They say: “Even if what is said about the predestination of God’s benefits is true, it nevertheless ought not to be preached to the peoples” (above, in the letters of Prosper and Hilary).

It must certainly be preached, so that whoever has ears to hear may hear (Luke 8:8). But who has them, if he has not received them from the one who says, “I will give them a heart to know me and ears that hear” (Baruch 2:31)? Certainly, let the one who has not received them reject this preaching. [Note: The Noailles manuscript has “does not grasp it.”] But let the one who grasps it take and drink; let him drink and live.

Just as devotion must be preached, so that the one who has ears to hear may rightly worship God; chastity must be preached, so that the one who has ears to hear may commit nothing illicit with the sexual organs; and love must be preached, so that the one who has ears to hear may love God and neighbor—so this predestination of God’s benefits must also be preached, so that the one who has ears to hear may glory not in himself but in the Lord.

52. As for their claim “that it was unnecessary for so many hearts [Col. 1026] of the less intelligent to be disturbed by a disputation of this kind, since the Catholic faith had been defended no less usefully for so many years without this definition of predestination, both against others and especially against the Pelagians, in so many preceding books by Catholics, both others’ and our own” (above, in Hilary’s letter, no. 8, columns 957–958)—I am greatly astonished that they say this and fail to observe, leaving aside other matters here, that our own books were written and published before the Pelagians began to appear. They should see how, in many passages of those books, without knowing that the Pelagian heresy was to come, we were already striking it down by preaching the grace through which God frees us from our evil errors and ways—not on the basis of our preceding good merits, but according to his free mercy.

I began to understand this more fully in the discussion that I wrote to Simplicianus, of blessed memory, bishop of the Church of Milan, at the beginning of my episcopate, when I also learned and asserted that the beginning of faith is a gift of God.

53. What could have become more widely and more delightfully known among my little works than the books of my *Confessions*? I published those books before the Pelagian heresy existed, and in them I certainly said—and said repeatedly—to our God: “Give what you command, and command what you will” (Book 10, chapters 19, 31, 37).

When these words of mine were mentioned in Rome by a certain brother and my fellow bishop in the presence of Pelagius, he could not bear them. He objected with some agitation and nearly quarreled with the one who had mentioned them.

But what does God command first and above all except that we believe in him? He therefore gives this also, if the words “Give what you command” were rightly said to him.

In those same books, when I related my conversion (Book 3, chapters 11–12, and Book 9, chapter 8), I said that God turned me toward the faith which I had been laying waste with my most wretched and frenzied talk. Do you not remember that I narrated it in such a way as to show that I had been granted not to perish through the faithful and daily tears of my mother?

There I certainly preached that God, by his grace, turns toward the true faith the wills of human beings that are not only turned away from the true faith but even opposed to it.

As for the progress of perseverance, you know how I prayed to God for it, and you can review it whenever you wish. Of all the gifts of God which, in that same work, I either desired or praised, who would dare not only to deny but even to doubt that God foreknew he would give them and could never have been ignorant of those to whom he would give them?

This is the clear and certain predestination of the saints. Necessity later compelled me to defend it more carefully and laboriously, when we were already arguing against the Pelagians. For we have learned that each heresy has introduced its own questions into the Church, against which divine Scripture must be defended more diligently than it would have been if no such necessity had compelled us.

What, then, compelled the passages of Scripture in which predestination is commended to be defended more extensively and explicitly by this labor of ours, except that the Pelagians say that God’s grace is given according to our merits? And what is that other than a complete denial of grace?

## CHAPTER XXI

54. To destroy this opinion, therefore, which is displeasing to God and hostile to the free benefits of God by which we are delivered [Col. 1027], we defend, according to the Scriptures, what we have already said at length: that both the beginning of faith and perseverance in it to the end are gifts of God.

For if we say that the beginning of faith comes from us, so that by it we may merit receiving the other gifts of God, the Pelagians conclude that God’s grace is given according to our merits. The Catholic faith so recoiled from this that Pelagius himself, fearing condemnation, condemned it.

Likewise, if we say that our perseverance comes from ourselves and not from the Lord, they reply that we possess the beginning of faith from ourselves in the same way as its end. They argue as follows: we possess the beginning from ourselves much more if we possess perseverance to the end from ourselves, since completing is greater than beginning. Thus they again conclude that God’s grace is given according to our merits.

But if both are gifts of God, and God foreknew that he would give these gifts—for who can deny this?—then predestination must be preached, so that the true grace of God, that is, grace not given according to our merits, may be defended with an impregnable bulwark.

55. In the book entitled *On Rebuke and Grace*, which could not be sufficient for all our friends, I think I presented perseverance to the end as a gift of God (*On Rebuke and Grace*, no. 10) in a way that, unless my memory deceives me, I had previously written nowhere, or almost nowhere, with such explicitness and clarity. But I have now said this, not as though no one before me had said it.

For, as we have already shown, blessed Cyprian, in his exposition of the Lord’s Prayer, explained our petitions in such a way that he said we ask for perseverance in the very first petition. He asserted that we pray for this when we say, “Hallowed be your name” (Matthew 6:9), even though we have already been sanctified in baptism: namely, that we may persevere in what we have begun to be.

Let those who love me—and to whom, because of their love, I ought not to be ungrateful—consider this. Apart from the matter now under dispute, they profess, as you write, to embrace all my works. Let them consider, I say, whether in the later portions of the first of the two books that I wrote to Simplicianus, bishop of Milan, at the beginning of my episcopate, before the Pelagian heresy appeared, there remains anything that could cast doubt on the claim that God’s grace is not given according to our merits; and whether I did not deal there sufficiently with the fact that the beginning of faith is a gift of God; and whether, from what is said there, it does not consequently become clear—even if it is not expressly stated—that perseverance to the end is given only by him who predestined us for his kingdom and glory.

Furthermore, did I not publish many years ago the letter that I wrote to the holy Paulinus, bishop of Nola, against the Pelagians—the letter which they have only recently begun to oppose? Let them also examine the letter I sent to Sixtus, a presbyter of the Roman Church, when we were engaged in the fiercest struggle against the Pelagians; they will find it to be like the letter to Paulinus.

Let them therefore recall that these things were said and written against the Pelagian heresy several years ago, although it is astonishing that they now displease them.

I do not, however, want anyone to embrace all my writings in such a way as to follow me unless he has first recognized that I have not [Col. 1028] erred in those matters. [Note: The manuscripts read “that I have not erred”; the printed editions have “that I do not err.”]

For this reason I am now producing books in which I have undertaken to revise my shorter works: I do not want to show that I myself followed myself in everything. Rather, I think that, by God’s mercy, I have written while making progress, though I did not begin from perfection. Indeed, I would speak more arrogantly than truthfully if, even now, at this stage of life, I claimed to have reached perfection in writing without any error.

But it matters how much and in what matters one errs, and how readily one corrects the error, or with what obstinacy one tries to defend it. A person is one of good hope if the last day of this life finds him making such progress that what was lacking in his progress is added to him, and he is judged more as one to be perfected than as one to be punished.

56. Therefore, if I do not wish to be ungrateful to people who loved me because some benefit of my labor reached them before they loved me, how much more must I avoid being ungrateful to God, whom we would not love unless he had first loved us and made us lovers of him? For love is from him (1 John 4:7), as those whom he made great said—not only his lovers [Note: The Erfurt edition has “those who pray.”] but also his preachers.

What could be more ungrateful than to deny the very grace of God by saying that it is given according to our merits? The Catholic faith recoiled from this in the case of the Pelagians; it charged Pelagius himself with this capital offense; and Pelagius himself condemned it—not indeed out of love for God’s truth, but from fear of his own condemnation.

Whoever, as a faithful Catholic, recoils from saying that God’s grace is given according to our merits should not withdraw even faith itself from God’s grace, through which he obtained mercy so as to become faithful. [Note: Most manuscripts, here and in the following passage, have “because” instead of “through which.”] Accordingly, he should attribute perseverance to the end also to God’s grace—the perseverance by which he obtains the mercy he daily asks for, so that he may not be brought into temptation.

Between the beginning of faith and the perfection of perseverance lie those things by which we live rightly, which they themselves agree are also given to us by God when faith obtains them through prayer. God foreknew that he would bestow all these things—namely, the beginning of faith and all his other gifts up to the end—on those whom he called.

It is therefore the height of contentiousness to oppose predestination or to doubt predestination.

## CHAPTER XXII

57. Yet predestination must not be preached to the peoples in such a way that, among an uneducated multitude or one of slower understanding, it seems to be refuted by its very preaching. The same appears to happen with God’s foreknowledge—which they certainly cannot deny—if people are told: “Whether you run or sleep, you will be what the one who cannot be deceived foreknew you would be.”

But it is the work of a deceitful or inexperienced physician to apply even a useful medicine in such a way that it either does no good or does harm.

Instead, one must say: “Run in such a way as to obtain the prize” (1 Corinthians 9:24), and recognize through your very running that you were foreknown as people who would run lawfully; and, in whatever other way God’s foreknowledge can be preached, it should be preached so that human sluggishness is driven away.

58. Although the settled decree [Col. 1029] of God’s will concerning predestination is indeed such that some are converted from unbelief to faith after receiving the will to obey, or persevere in faith, while the rest who linger in the delight of damnable sins, if they too are predestined, have not yet risen because the help of merciful grace has not yet raised them—if some have not yet been called, though his grace predestined them to be chosen, they will receive that same grace by which they may will and become elect; whereas if some obey but have not been predestined for his kingdom and glory, they are temporary and will not persevere in that obedience to the end—

although these things are true, they must not be said to the many who are listening in this way, so that the words may be turned directly toward them and they may be told the words that you included in your letter and that I quoted above:

“Such is the settled decree of God’s will concerning predestination that some of you have come from unbelief to faith after receiving the will to obey.”

Why is it necessary to say, “some of you”? If we are speaking to the Church of God, if we are speaking to believers, why should we seem to insult the rest by saying that some of them have come to faith? We can say more appropriately: “Such is the settled decree of God’s will concerning predestination that you have come from unbelief to faith after receiving the will to obey, and, having received perseverance, you remain in the faith.”

59. Nor should the following statement be made at all: “But those among you who linger in the pleasure of sins have not yet risen because the help of merciful grace has not yet raised you.”

It can and should instead be said in this way: “But if any of you still linger in the pleasure of damnable sins, take hold of the most salutary discipline. Yet when you have done so, do not become exalted as though it came from your works, or glory as though you had not received it. For it is God who works in you both to will and to work, according to his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:13), and “your steps are directed by the Lord, so that you may will his way” (Psalm 36:23). From the goodness and rightness of your running, learn that you belong to the predestination of divine grace.

60. Likewise, the following statement is too harshly expressed: “But if there are any among you who have not yet been called, and whom grace has predestined to be chosen, you will receive that same grace by which you may will and become elect,” if we consider that we are speaking not to just anyone but to the Church of Christ.

Why not rather say: “And if there are any who have not yet been called, let us pray for them, that they may be called”? Perhaps they have been predestined in such a way that they are granted in response to our prayers and receive that same grace by which they may will and become elect.

For God, who has fulfilled everything he predestined, wished us to pray even for the enemies of the faith, so that from this we might understand that he also grants unbelievers the gift of believing and turns those who are unwilling into willing believers. [Note: All the manuscripts have “believers,” not “unbelievers.”]

61. As for the words that are connected with this, I wonder whether anyone weak in the Christian people can hear them patiently in any way when they are told: “And if any of you obey, if you are predestined to be rejected, the powers of obedience will be withdrawn, so that you may cease to obey.”

What does this seem to mean other than cursing, or in some way prophesying [Col. 1030] evil? But if it is pleasing or necessary to say something about those who do not persevere, why not at least say it as I said shortly before: first, let it not be said about the very people who are listening in the congregation, but about others in relation to them. That is, let it not be said, “If any of you obey, if you are predestined to be rejected,” but, “If any obey,” and let the rest be expressed in the third person, not the second. [Note: Am., Er., and many manuscripts read: “let it be expressed in the third person of the verb, not in the second.”]

For something undesirable and abhorrent is being described, and it is pressed upon the faces of the hearers in the harshest and most offensive way by direct address when the person speaking to them says: “And if any of you obey, if you are predestined to be rejected, the powers of obedience will be withdrawn, so that you may cease to obey.” [Note: Am., Er., and the manuscripts read *compellando* (“by directly addressing them”); the Louvain edition has *compellendo*, but the Louvain scholars themselves note that this is not a proper substitution, since the reference is to expression in the second person, by which those present were directly addressed.] [Note: The printed editions have “when someone speaks to those to whom he is speaking”; the manuscripts read “when the one who speaks to them says.”]

What does the meaning lose if it is said instead: “But if there are any who obey, yet have not been predestined for his kingdom and glory, they are temporary and will not persevere in that obedience to the end”?

Is not the same matter expressed more truthfully and appropriately in this way, so that we do not seem to wish evil upon the hearers themselves as though it were something desirable, but report concerning others what they hate and do not think applies to them, while hoping and praying for better things?

In the manner they think it should be stated, the same sentence could be pronounced in nearly the same words even concerning God’s foreknowledge, which they certainly cannot deny: “And if any of you obey, if you are foreknown to be rejected, you will cease to obey.”

This is certainly most true. But it is thoroughly reprehensible, inappropriate, and unfitting—not false in expression, but not salutary when applied to the illness of human weakness.

62. I also do not think that the manner which we said should be used in preaching predestination is sufficient for someone speaking to the people unless he adds this or something similar:

“You ought therefore also to hope for and ask in daily prayers for the very perseverance in obedience from the Father of lights, from whom every good gift and every perfect gift descends” (James 1:17). By doing this, trust that you do not stand outside the predestination of his people, because he himself grants you even the ability to do this.

But let it be far from you to despair of yourselves because you are commanded to place your hope in him, not in yourselves. For “cursed is everyone who places his hope [Col. 1031] in man” (Jeremiah 17:5), and “it is good to trust in the Lord rather than to trust in man” (Psalm 117:8), because blessed are all who trust in him.

Holding fast to this hope, serve the Lord in fear and rejoice before him with trembling (Psalm 2:13, 11). For no one can be secure concerning eternal life, which God, who cannot lie, promised to the children of the promise before eternal times, until this life—which is a trial upon the earth—has been completed (Job 7:1). But he will make us persevere in him to the end of that life, to whom we say daily, “Do not bring us into temptation” (Matthew 6:13). [Note: The Vatican manuscripts have “you” rather than “us.”]

When these and similar things are said, whether to a few Christians or to the multitude of the Church, why should we fear preaching the predestination of the saints and the true grace of God—that is, grace not given according to our merits—as holy Scripture preaches it?

Or should we fear that a person will then despair of himself, when he is shown that his hope must be placed in God rather than in himself? Would he not instead despair when, in his pride and misery, he placed his hope in himself? [Note: Three manuscripts have “most faithless” rather than “most miserable.”]

## CHAPTER XXIII
63. And would that those who are slow of heart [Note: [Col. 1031] Several manuscripts read *tardicordes*, “slow-hearted.”] and weak, who cannot—or cannot yet—understand the Scriptures or their interpretations, would hear or fail to hear our disputations on this question in such a way that they would look more attentively to their prayers, which the Church has always had and will have from its beginnings until this age comes to an end. For concerning this matter, which we are now compelled not merely to mention but plainly to uphold and defend against the new heretics, she has never been silent in her prayers, even though at times, when no adversary was pressing the issue, she did not think it necessary to bring it out in sermons. When, indeed, has prayer not been offered in the Church for unbelievers and her enemies, that they might believe? When has any believer had an unbelieving friend, neighbor, or spouse and not asked the Lord to grant that person an obedient mind toward the Christian faith? Who, moreover, has ever failed to pray for himself, that he might remain in the Lord? Or who, when a priest invoked the Lord over the faithful and said, “Grant them, Lord, to persevere in you until the end,” has dared to criticize him—not only aloud, but even in thought—and not rather, with a believing heart and confessing mouth, replied “Amen” to such a blessing, since in the Lord’s Prayer itself the faithful pray for nothing else when they say above all, “Do not lead us into temptation,” except that they may persevere in holy obedience?

Therefore, just as the Church was born, grows, and has grown in these prayers, so also was she born and grows in this faith: the faith by which it is believed that God’s grace is not given according to the merits of those who receive it. For the Church would not pray that faith be given to unbelievers unless she believed that God turns toward himself the wills of human beings, whether turned away from him or set against him. Nor would the Church pray that believers persevere in the faith of Christ, neither deceived nor overcome by the temptations of the world, unless she believed that the Lord so holds our heart in his power that, although we hold the good only by our own will, we nevertheless do not hold it unless he himself works in us even to will.

For if the Church asks these things from him but thinks that they are given to her by herself, she offers not true prayers but perfunctory ones—which God forbid should be true of us. For who would truly groan, desiring to receive from the Lord what he prays for, if he thought that he obtained it from himself rather than from him?

64. Especially since we do not know what we ought to pray for; but, the Apostle says, “the Spirit himself intercedes for us [Note: [Col. 1032] All manuscripts read: ‘intercedes with inexpressible groanings,’ omitting ‘for us.’] with inexpressible groanings.” “And he who searches hearts knows what the Spirit intends, because he intercedes for the saints according to God’s will” (Rom. 8:26–27). What does “the Spirit himself intercedes” mean except “he causes us to intercede,” with inexpressible but genuine groanings, since the Spirit is truth? He is the one of whom he says elsewhere: “God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father’” (Gal. 4:6). And here, what is “crying” except “causing us to cry,” by that figure of speech by which we call a day joyful when it makes people joyful? He makes this clear elsewhere, where he says: “For you did not receive the spirit of slavery again unto fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Rom. 8:15). There he said “crying”; here, “in whom we cry,” thereby explaining how he had said “crying”—namely, as I have already explained, “causing us to cry.” Here we understand that it is itself also God’s gift that we cry out to God with a truthful heart and spiritually.

Let them therefore consider how greatly those are deceived who think that it originates with us, rather than being given to us, that we ask, seek, and knock. They say that this is what it means for grace to be preceded by our merit, so that grace follows when we receive because we ask, find because we seek, and have the door opened because we knock. They do not wish to understand that it is also a divine gift that we pray—that is, that we ask, seek, and knock. “For we have received [Note: [Col. 1032] Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read: ‘we receive.’] the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father.’” Blessed Ambrose also understood this. For he says (in his *Commentary on Isaiah*): “To pray to God is also a work of spiritual grace; as it is written, ‘No one says, “Jesus is Lord,” except in the Holy Spirit’” (1 Cor. 12:3).

65. These things, then, which the Church asks from the Lord, and has asked ever since she began to exist, God foreknew that he would give to his called ones in such a way that he had already given them in predestination itself. The Apostle declares this without ambiguity. For when writing to Timothy he says: “Work together for the Gospel according to the power of God, who saves us and calls us with his holy calling, not according to our works, but according to his purpose and grace, which was given to us in Christ Jesus before eternal times, but has now been manifested through the appearing of our Savior Jesus Christ” (2 Tim. 1:8–10).

Let the person who claims that the Church once did not possess the truth of this predestination and grace, which is now defended with more diligent care against the new heretics—let that person, I say, dare to claim that she once did not pray, or did not pray sincerely, either that unbelievers might believe or that believers might persevere. If she has always prayed for these good things, she certainly has always believed that they are gifts of God; nor was it ever permissible for her to deny that they were foreknown by him. Consequently, the Church of Christ has never been without faith in this predestination, which is now defended against the new heretics with renewed concern.

## CHAPTER XXIV

66. But why say more? I think I have shown sufficiently—or rather, more than sufficiently—that it is a gift of God both to begin believing in the Lord and to remain in the Lord until the end. As for the other good things that pertain to a godly life, by which God is rightly worshiped, even those on whose behalf we are undertaking this work concede that they are gifts of God. Moreover, they cannot deny that God foreknew all his gifts and those to whom he was going to bestow them.

Therefore, just as the other gifts must be preached so that the one who preaches them may be obediently heard, so predestination must be preached so that the one who obediently hears this teaching may glory not in a human being—and therefore not in himself—but in the Lord. For this too is God’s command; and to obey this command—to glory in the Lord—is itself, like the other things, a gift of God: “Let the one who glories, glory in the Lord” (1 Cor. 1:31). I do not hesitate to say that whoever does not possess this gift possesses whatever other gifts he may have in vain.

This is what we hope the Pelagians may possess; and we hope that these people of ours may possess it more fully. Let us therefore not be eager in disputations and sluggish in prayers. Let us pray, beloved; let us pray that God may grant the grace of understanding and confessing to our enemies also, and especially to our brothers and those who love us, that after the immense and ineffable ruin in which we all fell in one man, no one is liberated except by God’s grace; and that this grace is not returned as something owed according to the merits of those who receive it, but, as true grace, is freely given without any preceding merits.

67. There is no more illustrious example of predestination than Jesus himself. I have already discussed this in the first book (*On the Predestination of the Saints*, nn. 30–31), and I have chosen to commend it at the conclusion of this work. I say, then, that there is no more illustrious example of predestination than the Mediator himself.

Whoever among the faithful wishes to understand it correctly should pay attention to him and find himself in him—by “the faithful” I mean one who believes and confesses that he possesses a true human nature, that is, ours, although, through the singular assumption of that nature by God the Word, it was exalted into the one Son of God, so that the one who assumed and what he assumed are one person in the Trinity. For the assumption of a human being did not produce a quaternity; rather, the Trinity remained, that ineffable assumption effecting the truth of one person in God and man.

For we do not say that Christ is God only, as the heretics called Manichaeans do; nor man only, as the heretics called Photinians do; nor do we say that he is man in such a way that he lacks anything certainly belonging to human nature—whether a soul, or a rational mind within the soul, or flesh not taken from a woman but made from the Word after the Word had been converted and changed into flesh. These three false and empty alternatives produced the three various and divergent factions of the heretics called Apollinarians.

Rather, we say that Christ is true God, born of God the Father without any beginning in time, and likewise true man, born of a human mother in the fullness of time. Nor does his humanity, by which he is less than the Father [Note: [Col. 1034] All manuscripts read: “by which the Father is greater.”], diminish anything of his divinity [Note: [Col. 1034] The manuscripts read *divinitati*; the printed editions read *divinitatem*.], by which he is equal to the Father.

These two, however, are one Christ. According to his divinity he most truly said, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30); and according to his humanity he most truly said, “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28).

Therefore, the one who made him, from David’s seed, a just man who would never be unjust, without any merit of a preceding will on his part, himself makes just people out of the unjust, without any merit of a preceding will on their part, so that he may be the head and they his members. The one, therefore, who made him a man without any preceding merits of his own, without sin—whether inherited by origin or committed by will—for him to be forgiven, himself makes believers in him, without any preceding merits of theirs, so that he may forgive all their sin. The one who made him such that he never had and never would have an evil will himself makes a good will in his members out of an evil will.

He therefore predestined both him and us: in him, so that he might be our head; in us, so that we might be his body. He foreknew not our preceding merits but his own future works.

68. Those who read these things, if they understand them, should give thanks to God. Those who do not understand them should pray that he may be their interior teacher, from whose presence come knowledge and understanding (Prov. 2, according to the Septuagint). But those who think that I am mistaken should consider carefully, again and again, what has been said, lest perhaps they themselves be mistaken.

As for me, since through those who read my labors I become not only more learned but also more corrected, I recognize that God is favorable toward me. And I especially expect this from the teachers of the Church, if this work has come into their hands and they deem it worthwhile to learn what I write.

## FULGENTIUS, AT THE END OF THE BOOK ON THE INCARNATION AND GRACE OF OUR LORD JESUS

[Col. 1033]

The God who created the human being himself prepared, through his predestination, the gift of illumination for believing, the gift of perseverance for advancing and remaining steadfast, and the gift of glorification for reigning, for those to whom he wished to give them. For he does not accomplish the work in any other way than he has disposed it in his eternal and unchangeable will.

If anyone refuses to receive with the credulity of his heart or to profess with the confession of his mouth the truth of this predestination—by which the Apostle testifies that we were predestined in Christ before the foundation of the world—and if, before the final day of his present life, he does not cast off the obstinacy of his impiety by which he rebelliously resists the living and true God, it is clear that he does not belong to the number of those whom God freely chose and predestined in Christ before the foundation of the world for the kingdom.

Nevertheless, prayer by the faithful on their behalf must not cease, nor may charity toward them ever grow cold, so that God may grant them the grace of his illumination, through which the seed of the divine word may bear fruit in them. For that word sounds in vain upon outward ears unless God, by a spiritual gift, opens the hearing of the inner human being.

[Col. 1035] From the same Fulgentius. Pope Adrian I, in his letter to Egila and in his letter to the bishops of Spain.

God prepared works of mercy and justice in the eternity of his unchangeableness. And just as he was never ignorant of his future works, so he was never unprepared in preparing those same works. Therefore he prepared merits for human beings who were to be justified, and he prepared rewards for those same people who were to be glorified. But for the wicked he did not prepare evil wills or evil works; rather, he prepared just and eternal punishments for them.

This is the eternal predestination of God’s future works. Just as we recognize that it has always been conveyed to us through apostolic teaching, so also we confidently preach it, and so forth. Let all the faithful therefore hold to the truth of predestination, because whoever does not believe in the divine purpose in this predestination will not attain the glorious effect of that same predestination.

# [THE UNFINISHED WORK AGAINST JULIAN]

[Col. 1035]

## PREFACE TO THE UNFINISHED WORK AGAINST JULIAN’S SECOND REPLY

At last we have reached Augustine’s final work. In it, the blessed defender of Christ’s grace, while restraining the attack of the heretic Julian, who was assailing him anew, is overtaken by death before completing the work itself and is called from the midst of the battle into heaven to receive his crown.

Before presenting our observations on this work, however, it will not be out of place to discuss the origins and character of Julian himself, who was among the most ardent and notorious patrons of the Pelagian heresy and the most insolent of Augustine’s adversaries, and to review his deeds and writings.

## ON JULIAN AND HIS WRITINGS

Julian was born to Memorius and Juliana, both of whom were distinguished in reputation for piety. Marius Mercator, in his *Memorandum of Notes on Julian’s Writings*, calls Memorius “a bishop of holy and blessed memory,” and Juliana, Memorius’s wife, “a first-rate woman,” of whom, he says, “you will find nothing more honorable among the most revered matrons.” Shortly afterward, speaking of Memorius and Juliana together, he says: “Those who knew the holy character, holy life, and way of life of those people” (below, Appendix, part 2).

Jerome Vignierius reports in his preface to Augustine’s *Unfinished Work*, from an unpublished writing of Fulgentius, that Julian’s father Memorius himself was also distinguished by nobility of birth.

Memorius is no less worthy of commendation because he was joined to Augustine by friendship and the exchange of letters. Concerning him the holy Doctor says in the first book against Julian: “I certainly have not forgotten your father Memorius, of blessed memory, who had entered into no small friendship with me through correspondence and had made you yourself very dear to me” (above, *Against Julian*, book 1, no. 12). A letter written to Memorius still exists among Augustine’s letters, numbered 101.

Ughelli adds Memorius to the bishops of Capua, although he relies on no adequate authority, placing him immediately after Vincent, who is famous from the history of Athanasius.

According to Augustine (below, *Unfinished Work*, book 6, chapter 18), Julian was born in Apulia, perhaps at Eculanum or Eclanum—provided that the city, although it had already been included within the boundaries of Campania for three hundred years, was still called by this name in Apulia, since it had once been counted among the cities of Apulia.

His father Memorius, being a pious man, brought his son to the church as soon as possible and wished the grace of Baptism to be given to him while he was still an infant (above, *Against Julian*, book 1, no. 14; below, *Unfinished Work*, book 2, chapter 2), “not knowing how ungrateful he would be toward that same grace” (above, *Against Julian*, book 6, no. 17).

Gennadius attributes to him a keen intellect, a thorough knowledge of the sacred Scriptures, and such wide learning in Greek and Latin literature that Julian, before the impiety of the Pelagian heresy was discovered in him, gained a celebrated name among the teachers of the Church (below, Appendix, part 2).

Nevertheless, Mercator is justified in saying that, when arguing against Augustine, he “wandered about with harsh loquacity, wishing to display himself as eloquent and learned” (ibid.). Some think that Prosper also designated him by the following verse, which seems simultaneously to report and suggest the place of his episcopate, as well as his character and talent for writing:

“Or hearts swell with this Campanian grass.”

Prosper again calls him in his *Chronicle* “the most boastful advocate of the Pelagian error” (ibid.).

Saint Augustine likewise rightly calls him “a young man of the utmost confidence” (above, *Against Julian*, book 2, no. 30). He says that Julian was stronger in tongue than in mind (below, *Unfinished Work*, book 3, chapter 52); and he is also described as “most loquacious in debate, most slanderous in controversy, and most deceitful in profession” (ibid., book 4, chapter 50).

When he had reached adulthood, his father gave him a wife. Augustine testifies in several places that Julian was bound by the marriage tie (above, *Against Julian*, book 3, nos. 28, 46, and elsewhere).

Certainly it must be acknowledged that his family had a very close relationship with Bishop Paulinus of Nola, since Paulinus considered himself by no means unworthy to celebrate Julian’s marriage with a pious epithalamium, which is still read among his works.
