[Col. 1037] In this poem he urges Julian, whom he still calls a boy, and his wife, Jam, to preserve a modesty worthy of an episcopal household both during the solemnity of their marriage and throughout the entire course of their lives. He even prays that they may practice perpetual virginity.

In some printed editions of the poem the title is: “Epithalamium on Julian, son of the bishop Memorius, and on Jam, a most illustrious woman, his wife.”

From this Vignierius argues that Julian’s wife was distinguished by ancient and consular nobility. He also refers to the following testimony from an unpublished work of Fulgentius as applying to the same Jam: “Nor was it enough for him to have added the fasces of the Aemilii to his paternal nobility, which he shamefully stained with degenerate heresy.”

A certain bishop named Aemilius was in fact present at the wedding. But Paulinus does not say that he was Jam’s father, as Vignierius was the first to assert; and the very fact that Paulinus does not say this supplies an argument on the contrary side. Indeed, he repeatedly calls Julian and his wife “the children of Memorius,” or “the household of Memorius.” From this it may reasonably be inferred that, if Aemilius was related to either of them, he was related only at a remote degree.

Paulinus observes that Memorius fulfilled his duty toward Aemilius when he placed the couple in his hands—Aemilius, who joined the heads of both under the peace of marriage, covered them with his own hand, and consecrated them with prayer.

We do not know whether Memorius was supposed to render this service to Aemilius because the wedding was being celebrated in his presence, or because of the man’s outstanding reverence. For Paulinus portrays this Aemilius as the father of Julian, Jam, and Memorius himself, and as a man whose own virtue had earned him exceptional honor and respect.

For this reason some think that he was the same Aemilius who, together with two others, was sent by Honorius and the bishops of the West to Arcadius concerning the case of John Chrysostom and in the year 406 earned the title of confessor (Baronius, under the years 405 and 406). The *Metaphrast* likewise calls him bishop of Beneventum.

But we do not sufficiently understand why Paulinus sang as follows in the epithalamium:

“Rise, Memorius; honor your father, embrace your brother:

In Aemilius, one name belongs to both for you.

Memorius is younger and older; and so forth.

He is son and brother, Memorius; he rejoices to be present,

Their common father to himself and to his children.”

Perhaps Memorius should be understood as older in dignity and as a brother because he was a bishop, but as a son and younger in birth or age because he was begotten by Aemilius, or at least born later than he.

As for what John Garnerius writes—that Aemilius, as bishop of Beneventum, was metropolitan of Memorius (on chapter 4 of Mercator’s notes on Julian)—the testimony of Ughelli and of the *Sacred Geography* shows that at that time the metropolitan dignity did not belong to Beneventum. Nor do we think that the same writer’s claim can be defended: namely, that Aemilius, although already dead, was introduced into the poem by poetic fiction, which Garnerius considers quite ingenious (in Mercator, dissertation 1, chapter 6, *On Julian*).

Paulinus further teaches, in the following verses of the epithalamium, that Julian had already been enrolled among the clergy and appointed to the office of reader before he entered into marriage:

“Let the cleric love his wife Cecoram [reading uncertain], with Christ attending,

And love her beautiful with the light of his heart;

And let the reader learn from heavenly history that she was made, by divine gift, as a help to her husband.”

From this rank of reader he was promoted to a higher one. Whether his wife had already departed this life, or whether both of them maintained continence, it is certain that he held the office of deacon in the year 408 or 409, when Augustine wrote to his father and described him as still a young man.

In that hundred-and-first letter the holy Bishop gives an exceptional indication of his interest in Julian and asks his father to order Julian to come to him for a time.

Finally, Julian was raised to the episcopal order. Although Augustine very often calls him “son,” he nevertheless acknowledges the honor of his episcopate when he breaks out in the exclamation: “O the character of bishops of every sort!” (above, *Against Julian*, book 4, no. 57).

Moreover, Augustine says that the letter to the bishop of Thessalonica was not Julian’s alone but was shared by him with many Pelagian bishops (above, *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, book 2, no. 1). Julian himself also calls Bishop Turbantius, to whom he dedicated his first work against Augustine, “brother” (below, *Unfinished Work*, book 1, chapter 1).

Prosper mentions Julian’s episcopate in his *Chronicle* under the year 439, and there is no doubt that it was long since stripped from him because of his heresy (below, Appendix, part 2).

Innocent I had ordained him, as Mercator writes in his *Memorandum against the Pelagians* (ibid.). But there was once disagreement among scholars over which church he governed. In Gennadius’s book *On Ecclesiastical Writers* he was called “bishop of Capua”; in Prosper’s *Chronicle*, “Julian of Atella”; in the letter of Peter the Deacon to the African bishops exiled in Sardinia, “Julian of Eclanum”; and in Pope Gelasius’s decree on apocryphal writings, “of Celanum.” Bede also gives him this latter title in the preface to the first book of his *Commentary on the Song of Songs*.

Although Bede’s words, “Julian, bishop of Celanum in Campania,” can absolutely be interpreted to mean that Julian was a native of Celanum but held a Campanian episcopal see, the same kind of interpretation could be applied to the titles by which Prosper calls him Atellanus, Peter the Deacon Eclanensis, and Gelasius Celanensis: these designations could refer to his birthplace just as well as to his episcopal see. Nothing, then, would prevent us from believing that he had sat at Capua, unless it were observed that in Gennadius, in the more reliable manuscripts—including the very ancient Corbie copy followed in the Appendix—there is no mention at all of Julian’s episcopate.

In the same way, more recent editions of Prosper, on the basis of manuscripts of better quality, substitute “Eclanensis” for “Atellanensis.” Paying no attention to this correction, Pierre-François Chiffletius wished the original reading of Prosper to be preferred, and held that Julian had truly held the see of Atella, once celebrated among the cities of Campania, from whose ruins Aversa was later built between Naples and Capua (Chiffletius, in *Pauline Illustrated*, part 2, chapter 29).

But Marius Mercator, Julian’s contemporary, rival, and fellow countryman, settles the controversy. In express words he calls him at one time “bishop of Eclanum,” and at another “ex-bishop of the town of Eclanum” (below, Appendix, part 2). It is therefore not difficult to reconcile with Mercator Peter the Deacon, Gelasius, and Bede by changing or transposing a single letter.

This city, once famous but now buried beneath its ruins, was called Eculanum or Eclanum by the ancients. It was situated in the Hirpini, in the farther principate, fifteen miles from Beneventum, toward the southeast. Some think that it was later called Quintodecimum, and that in our own time some of its ruins and deserted walls can be seen near Mirabella.

The episcopal see was transferred from Eclanum to Frequentum, in Italian Frigento or Fricento. Frequentum was joined to the bishopric of Avellino on 7 May in the year 1465 or 1466. It is reported that this region was once included within the boundaries of Apulia but had been added to Campania as early as the time of Hadrian (Noris, *History of Pelagianism*, book 1, chapter 18).

After his parents had died—no one has been able to discover in what year this occurred—Julian took responsibility for his two sisters, but discharged this duty honorably neither toward himself nor toward them.

“We know, we know,” says Mercator, “what one of them said or reproached you with when, because you were too severe, you rose up against the ruin of her modesty; and how at once you remained silent, not daring to inflict any further distress of your censure upon her grief” (below, Appendix, part 2).

That is to say, as usually happens, the corruption of his morals followed immediately upon the corruption of his faith in Julian.

It is entirely uncertain when he began to imbibe the poison of the Pelagian heresy. Bede writes that Pelagius taught him while he was still “a little boy,” and that he was nourished by Pelagius himself “like a little snake in a serpent’s cave,” when Jerome was publishing his dialogues against the Pelagians in the year 415 (ibid.).

But if one interprets these words of Bede strictly and down to the letter, one will find them plainly false. Julian had passed beyond the years of childhood long before the year 415, and it is not likely that he was then in Palestine, where Pelagius was residing that year, unless he was perhaps the very person whom Jerome calls Annianus, a pseudo-deacon of Celedae.

Some mutual acquaintance between them, however, could have arisen at Rome before the year 408 or 410, when Pelagius left the city. This same Julian may perhaps reasonably be judged to have been one of those about whom Augustine wrote to Paulinus in the year 417, immediately after the death of Pope Innocent: men who said that they would sooner defect from Pelagius than acknowledge original sin, although Augustine had been informed that they were from the city of Nola (Letter 186, no. 29).

Elsewhere the holy Doctor says that if Julian had been willing to listen to blessed Innocent, who presided over the Roman Church, he would at that time have freed his dangerous youth from the Pelagian snares (above, *Against Julian*, book 1, no. 13).

Mercator testifies that he retained the Catholic position for as long as the aforementioned pontiff lived. This can appropriately be related to what the same author says in the same place: Julian did not withdraw from communion with Innocent even after Pelagius and Coelestius had been condemned, but continued in communion with the very man who had condemned them until his death (below, Appendix, part 2).

Nevertheless, Augustine clearly declares that Julian embraced the heresy while Innocent was still alive, in these very words: “At that time you would have freed your dangerous youth from the Pelagian snares” (above, *Against Julian*, book 1, no. 13).

A certain paralogism of his is reported. While he was living at Rome with the principal leaders of the faction, he attempted to force less educated people to admit that the guilt of human origin was a mere invention (below, Appendix, part 2). In the judgment of John Garnerius, this may fit the year 417 (Garnerius, in Mercator, dissertation 1, chapter 6, *On Julian*).

If we ought to attribute to him the definitions that Augustine refutes in his book *On the Perfection of Human Righteousness*, as Garnerius thinks, there will be no doubt that he had become a thorough Pelagian as early as 415.

This much is certain: when the Pelagians were condemned by Pope Zosimus in the year 418, Julian refused to subscribe to the pontifical judgment. For that reason he was stripped of his dignity by the pope and expelled from Italy (below, Appendix, part 2). We find that he sent two letters to this same pontiff concerning questions of grace (below, *Unfinished Work*, book 1, chapter 18).

Jerome Vignierius assigns to the earliest period of Julian’s heresy what Gennadius reports: that Julian distributed his possessions to the poor during a time of public famine and poverty, and by this appearance of charity attached very many people to his heresy, especially among those who seemed more devoted to piety (below, Appendix, part 2).

Concerning this, we can observe only that Augustine states in his final work that Julian was “fed in idleness by the wretched people whom he had deceived” (below, *Unfinished Work*, book 2, chapter 51), and that he could not devote himself to writing and dictating books if people did not supply him with food and provide suitable expenses (ibid., book 3, chapters 1 and 44). This sufficiently indicates that he was then living without income of his own or the produce of his possessions. Yet no one should infer from this that Augustine knew for certain that Julian had spent everything in order to relieve the poverty of others.

In what seems to have been the year 419, he wrote, together with other bishops of the same sect, to Rufus, bishop of Thessalonica. He also sent letters to friends at Rome in order to confirm them in their error. Around the same time he attempted to refute Augustine’s earlier book *On Marriage and Concupiscence* in four volumes.

Later, when he was compelled to change his residence, he traversed seas and lands with the companions and colleagues of his error. He visited the East, that is, Asia Minor, and finally gained some measure of peace in Cilicia with Theodore of Mopsuestia, whom they make equally the father of the Pelagian and Nestorian heresies.

There he composed eight more books against Augustine. Nor will we doubt that he was the one who persuaded Theodore himself to publish his five books against the defenders of original sin. Yet Theodore branded him with the mark of anathema in a provincial synod scarcely had he departed from Cilicia (below, Appendix, part 2).

He had already left Italy in the year 421, when Bishop Alypius brought six of Augustine’s books against him there. For when Julian published his eight books against the holy Doctor, he had heard nothing at all of that work of Augustine’s (below, *Unfinished Work*, book 4, chapter 38).

From the time he left Cilicia until the year 428, we find no mention of him anywhere. But Julian is presented as the leader and chief of those bishops who, having been deprived of office because they denied original sin, sought the protection of Nestorius around the year 428.

Hence Mercator writes in his preface to Nestorius’s sermons against the Pelagian heresy:

“Although Nestorius rightly thought and taught against the wicked and impious definition of Pelagius or Coelestius, he nevertheless judged that Julian, the ex-bishop of Eclanum, together with his associates—whose heresy he was the standard-bearer and champion, and who had long before been stripped of office and deposed by apostolic judgment—should meanwhile be received into friendship, promising him hope of absolution. He also consoled Coelestius himself by his letters, copies of which we have appended.

“Whether he did this through malice or through folly cannot easily be known: he thought that those whose distorted opinions, apart from his own impiety which led him even to condemnation, he rightly opposed in thought and teaching should nevertheless be his friends, and that they should be nurtured and indulged with the hope of a vain promise. Yet they were condemned again and again, together with their aforementioned patron, at the Council of Ephesus by 274 bishops.”

For the rest, the same heretics were entirely unable, through Nestorius, to achieve that they should not be expelled from Constantinople at the emperor Theodosius’s command—the same city from which Julian had previously been expelled along with Coelestius.

Julian is not only placed first in each of Nestorius’s two letters to Celestine, ahead of the other Pelagian bishops expelled from the West; he is likewise named first after Pelagius and Coelestius among those notable Pelagians whose condemnation was read and confirmed at the Ephesian synod in the year 431 (below, Appendix, part 2).

Not long afterward, under the pontificate of Sixtus III, and, if Prosper’s *Chronicle* is to be trusted, in the year 439, Julian attempted by various devices to impose upon the Church and to insinuate himself into her communion under a false appearance of correction, in order to recover the episcopal dignity from which he had so long suffered being deprived.

But the Roman pontiff, strengthened by the urging of the deacon Leo—undoubtedly the same man who later succeeded him in the Apostolic See—uncovered Julian’s frauds through his vigilance, firmly opposed them, closed every avenue to his wicked schemes, rejected the deceitful beast, and brought joy to the whole Catholic communion (ibid.).

Jerome Vignierius says that he has arguments persuading him that Julian was once again compelled to flee Italy by Pope Sixtus and came to the island of Lerina. There, after staying for several months, he was received by Faustus, later bishop of Riez, to whom he administered the poison of his heresy.

“This,” says Vignierius, “we shall discuss in its proper place, if God grants us strength and years; and we shall establish it with the remaining proofs, both from Fulgentius and from others, as well as with many things of this kind that are unknown to many” (Vignierius, *Preface to the Unfinished Work*).

To these words of Vignierius John Garnerius adds: “The learned man means by Fulgentius the books that that holy bishop wrote against Faustus, which the same Vignierius possessed in a manuscript when he was alive” (Garnerius, in Mercator, dissertation 1, chapter 6, *On Julian*).

After Sixtus’s death, one may infer that Julian returned to Italy, from which he was again driven out by Pope Leo, because an author of that same period, in the fourth part, sixth chapter, of his book *On the Promises and Predictions of God*, reports that the Pelagians, and especially Julian, were crushed by the blessed pontiff. Vignierius adds that this unfortunate heretic, after long wanderings here and there—for which Fulgentius, as he says, calls him a second Cain, that is, a fugitive and exile from every place—finally took up residence in a certain village in Sicily as his last refuge, where he taught the members of his sect their letters, having become a schoolmaster after being a bishop. Augustine had assigned this occupation to him many years earlier as especially suited both to his devotion to these studies and to the vain glory that he sought from his knowledge of them (*Below, Imperfect Work*, book 2, chapter 51).

Vignierius further adds that, after Julian had ceased to live there, the Pelagians wrote this epitaph on his tomb:

> Here rests in peace Julian, a Catholic bishop.

Since this epitaph was still being read in the ninth century, certain supporters of Semi-Pelagian doctrines attempted to restore his memory. But learned Catholic prelates demonstrated that the Pelagians had always appropriated the name “Catholic”; consequently, there was nothing to prevent such a title from being placed on him, while he was nevertheless regarded as having died in heresy. He died, as Gennadius writes, during the reign of Valentinian III, son of Constantius, and therefore before the year 455 (*Below, Appendix*, part 2). Nevertheless, Vignierius maintains that Julian prolonged his life until the time of Fulgentius—according to Pierre-François Chifflet, Fulgentius was born in 467 and consecrated bishop in 507 [Chiffletius, *Notes on the Life of Fulgentius*, p. 355].

While Gelasius held the Apostolic See, John, patriarch of Alexandria, pronounced an anathema against Coelestius and Julian, as Photius records (*Below, Appendix*, part 2 [Col. 1043]); Peter the deacon did the same in his letter to Fulgentius and the other African bishops in exile.

As for Julian’s writings, although Gennadius says that, before revealing Pelagius’s impiety in himself, Julian was distinguished among the teachers of the Church (*Below, Appendix*, part 2), nothing that he published during that period has so far been found. But once he began openly to profess this heresy, he never ceased trying, through his writings, to draw others into its snares. For this reason he sent two letters to Pope Zosimus in the year 418. Then, after Augustine had written the first book *On Marriage and Concupiscence* to Count Valerius, Julian published four books addressed to Bishop Turbantius in which he refuted that one book. Moreover, when excerpts from this work of Julian’s had been delivered to Valerius, he arranged for them to be conveyed to Augustine; the holy Doctor immediately answered them by publishing a second work with the same title, longer than the preceding one—that is, the second book *On Marriage and Concupiscence*. At the same time he composed his four books addressed to Boniface, in order to blunt two letters of the Pelagians which, apparently, Julian himself had written immediately after issuing his first response to the work *On Marriage and Concupiscence*. Finally, after receiving that first response of Julian’s, which consisted of four books, Augustine defeated it in a great work divided into six books.

Meanwhile, when the second book *On Marriage and Concupiscence* had fallen into Julian’s hands, he brought eight books into the field, so to speak, against that one book; Augustine routed them in his final work, of which we shall speak shortly. Vignierius cites, in this connection, the following words of Fulgentius from an unpublished work:

> Nor was it enough for him to have attached the fasces of the Aemilii to his ancestral nobility, which he disgracefully stained with a degenerate heresy. He attacked the aged Augustine, so that he might become more famous, with youthful ardor; but he was repressed, and thereby won for himself throughout the world as much hatred as he had intended to establish renown for himself among all people. What he had seized upon as an opportunity for a little glory was, with the Lord mocking, turned into disgrace.

(Vignierius, Preface to the *Imperfect Work*.)

Bede also numbers among the books of this heretic a certain Commentary on the *Song of Songs*, preceded by a treatise entitled *On Love*, because Julian had intended in it to disclose the distinction between sacred and profane love. But Bede asserts that, while pretending to discuss that subject, Julian was laboring to strengthen his heresy. Bede both quotes and refutes various passages, taken partly from this treatise and partly from the remainder of the Commentary; at the same time he warns that these writings should be read only with great caution, or rather not read at all. He also mentions a certain *Discussion* in which Julian argued about the good of constancy (*Below, Appendix*, part 2). As for the letter to Demetrias, which Bede attributes to Julian, it is generally acknowledged to belong to Pelagius himself.

Marius Mercator reports that Julian also defended in several books what Pelagius taught: that a human being, if he wished, could be without sin (*In the notes to* chapter 6). Julian, however, speaks less frequently on this subject in the books of his that survive. From this John Garnerius conjectures that Julian may have published other works. The same consideration also leads him to believe that the definitions which Augustine refutes in his book *On the Perfection of Human Righteousness* should be attributed to Julian. Yet this Pelagian position rests solely upon the foundation that the heretic maintained: namely, that nature is still equally strong and sound in all human beings, just as it was in Adam. Julian was unremitting in defending this view.

Garnerius further attributes to Julian (*In Mercator, Dissertation* 5, and in the appendix to Dissertation 6, chapter 4) the Latin translation, extracted by Jacques Sirmond from ancient manuscripts, of the little book of faith written in Greek by Rufinus, a presbyter of the province of Palestine. He likewise assigns to the same author, Julian, on the strength of no slight arguments, another little book of faith (*Below, Appendix*, part 2), composed in Latin and addressed to the Apostolic See in the name of several heterodox bishops who, refusing to subscribe to the condemnation of Pelagius and Coelestius, appealed to a plenary synod.

Finally, certain homilies of John Chrysostom, translated from Greek into Latin by Annianus, also display Julian’s style. Indeed, not only was it easy for copyists to err in the author’s name, so that, through corruption of the first syllable, *Julianus* became *Annianus*; we also observe in the dedicatory letters prefixed to these homilies that Julian’s character, ideas, and personal expressions are present (*Below, Appendix*, part 2, “On Annianus, the Pseudo-Deacon of Celeda”). Moreover, just as Jerome said of Annianus, the pseudo-deacon of Celeda, “He feeds most abundantly in order to supply frivolous words for another’s blasphemy” (ibid.), so Augustine, in the work that follows, repeatedly objects to Julian that he himself is fed by deceived wretches so that he may devote himself to writing books in defense of the Pelagian heresy (*Below, Imperfect Work*, book 2, chapter 51, and book 3, chapters 1 and 44).

## ON THE WORK THAT FOLLOWS

We have already noted that, after Julian had issued four books in response to the first book *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, the holy Doctor refuted certain excerpts from the first of these in his second book *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, and afterward demolished all four books together in a more extensive work of six books against Julian. Alypius brought that second book *On Marriage and Concupiscence* with him to Italy around the year 421 (*ibid.*, book 1, chapter 7). Julian immediately attacked this second book with another response, although he had not yet seen the six books by which Augustine had demolished his first response, nor had he heard anything about them—not even knowing whether that first response had been read by the holy Doctor (*ibid.*, book 4, chapter 38). Nor should it seem surprising that this was so, for Julian was in Cilicia when he composed his second response against Augustine. [Col. 1045] Mercator, however, appears to have convinced himself that Julian acted deceptively in this response, pretending not to know of Augustine’s six books (*Below, Appendix*, part 2).

In this later response, therefore, Julian set eight books against one book of Augustine, which he did not even attack in its entirety (*Below, Imperfect Work*, book 2, chapter 127, and book 3, chapter 143). He was not abundant but tiresome in his wandering verbosity to those who cling to the substance of things and despise superfluous words (*ibid.*, book 3, chapter 20). The first six of these eight books are found in Augustine’s refutation. In them Julian scarcely ever calls Catholics anything other than “Traducians” and “Manichaeans.” Above all, he everywhere assails the holy Bishop with insults, repeatedly calling him there also “the Carthaginian disputant” (*ibid.*, book 1, chapter 7), “the most foolish of all men” (*ibid.*, book 2, chapter 28), and “the most witless” (*ibid.*, book 3, chapter 145); he likewise calls Alypius “the household slave of his sins” (*ibid.*, book 1, chapter 7). But the insults of heretics become a distinction for defenders of the faith.

Julian dedicated this second response to a certain Florus, prominent among the bishops of the Pelagian faction, whose notable imposture is also recounted; because of it, he was expelled from Italy during the pontificate of Leo (Prosper, *On the Promises and Predictions*, part 4, chapter 6).

Although this second response of Julian’s seems to have been composed in the year 421, or not long afterward, as we said earlier, it had not yet come into Augustine’s hands—not when he wrote the book *On Rebuke and Grace* (compare *On Rebuke and Grace*, chapter 11, with *Imperfect Work*, book 4, chapter 84), nor when he completed the second book of the *Retractions*. In that work, chapter 67, he testifies that he did not know whether he would undertake any further composition in the future. Indeed, he was already preparing the third book of the *Retractions* when he had not yet seen it.

At that time, however, Alypius traveled to Rome for the third time and took care, through his diligence, that a transcript of it should be delivered to Augustine (Letter 224). At first he sent him only the first five books, lest he lose the opportunity, promising that the other three would follow as soon as they had been copied, and meanwhile asking that Augustine not delay undertaking the refutation. At that time Augustine was occupied with reviewing his letters and sermons, and he considered this examination a matter of greater necessity than could reasonably be neglected. Moreover, such absurd nonsense occurred in this new response of Julian’s that the holy Doctor was reluctant and ashamed to answer it. Nevertheless, lest it should appear that no answer was available for less experienced readers who might have read Julian’s response without detecting its weakness, Augustine was compelled to undertake this refutation.

He responds to Julian in the following manner: first he presents the heretic’s words, then adds his own response to them, preserving the same numbering or division of the books. Thus the six books of this work each set one of Julian’s six books before the reader—specifically, the first six of the eight written to Florus—together with Augustine’s responses to the individual passages.

Augustine worked on this book until the very end of his life. Prosper says in his *Chronicle*, under the year 430, that Augustine continued it while surrounded by the Vandals within the walls of Hippo:

> Augustine, a bishop outstanding in every respect, died on the fifth day before the Kalends of September, responding to Julian’s books amid the attacks of the besieging Vandals at the very end of his days, and persevering gloriously in defense of Christian grace.

But, overtaken by death, Augustine was compelled to leave the work unfinished, as Possidius states in the fourth chapter of his Index, in these words:

> Against Julian’s second response: an unfinished work.

Vignierius nevertheless calls it complete, asserting that, according to his testimony, the word *unfinished* is absent from various manuscripts of Possidius. We, however, found it in every copy that we examined. To support his opinion, he adds that, after Julian’s words in the sixth book, there appears the closing formula, “Here ends Julian’s book.” Yet we point out in its proper place that the same formula was appended by copyists to the first book and that we saw it there in the Marian manuscript.

There is no need to dwell on Vignierius’s further conjecture that Augustine perhaps summarized Julian’s seventh and eighth books in his own sixth book, since this sixth book is neither longer than the others nor bears anything that could serve as evidence of a completed work. Thus, when Mercator says that Augustine overthrew Julian’s eight later books by placing his individual responses beneath the individual chapters (*Below, Appendix*, part 2), he indicates nothing other than that Augustine overthrew Julian’s final work, consisting of eight books, in such a way that each response was placed beneath the individual chapters of the books being refuted. Mercator is evidently alluding there to the actual words of Augustine’s preface.

In any event, since previously only the first two books were available, published from a Gallican manuscript by Claudius Menard, deputy governor of Anjou, Vignierius was not unjustified in claiming, after he himself supplied the remaining four books from a Clairvaux copy, that this work is now complete, because Augustine did not proceed beyond these six books in the work.

Pope Agatho of Rome cites several passages from the fifth book of this work in a letter to the emperors. These passages were carefully checked and examined at the Sixth Council, session 10, against the Latin copy of the same work then preserved in the library at Constantinople (see Noris, Appendix to the *History of Pelagianism*, p. 174). The same work is cited by Maximus of Aquileia at the Lateran Synod held in the year 649. Prosper had drawn testimonies from these same books in his *Book of Sentences*, and Bede in his work on Paul—not only in the commonly circulated version, which is known to belong to Florus, but also in the genuine and hitherto unpublished version that we possess in parchment. Lupus of Ferrières and Servatus Lupus likewise praise these books in their little works.

The contents of the books are as follows.

In the first, Julian’s first book addressed to Florus is refuted. The accusations that he directed there against Augustine and the Catholic faith, which confesses original sin, are disproved, especially on three grounds. [Col. 1047] The passages he attempted to attack from the first portions of the second book *On Marriage and Concupiscence* and from the first book *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians* are defended. Certain scriptural authorities for grace, which he interpreted according to the Pelagian doctrine, are also vindicated.

In the second, Julian’s second book is examined. It deals with the Apostle’s words to the Romans, chapter 5: “Through one man sin entered into this world,” and so forth. It is shown that Julian, rejecting the Catholic interpretation—according to which Augustine, in book 2 of *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, chapter 27, explained these words as referring to Adam’s sin transmitted through generation to all his descendants—labors in vain to make them understood according to the Pelagian heresy as referring to an example of sin passing not into all descendants, but only into sinners by imitation.

In the third, Augustine shows that Julian perversely abuses scriptural testimonies from Deuteronomy, chapter 24; the Fourth Book of Kings, chapter 14; and Ezekiel, chapter 18, in an attempt to persuade others that God imputes no sins of parents to their children. Augustine then shows that Julian argues in vain in an effort to extricate himself from the passage in the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 11; that passage would overturn the response in which Julian so insistently maintained in his preceding book that the Apostle said in Romans, chapter 5, “one through whom sin passed,” so that “generation” would not be understood.

Afterward Augustine shows Julian returning to statements from the second book *On Marriage and Concupiscence* and treating Augustine unjustly. Julian again complains that Augustine denies both human free will and God as creator of those who are born. Moreover, by comparing Augustine’s statements with a certain heretical letter of Mani, Julian claims that the holy Doctor offers no arguments other than those found in Mani and that, just like Mani, Augustine declares human nature evil.

In the fourth, Augustine continues to refute the adversary, who in his fourth book argues against those passages of the second book *On Marriage and Concupiscence* that extend from chapter 4 through chapter 11. He maintains that the concupiscence of the flesh is evil and was not implanted in human beings by God the Creator, and that this is taught in the very passage he employed for this purpose from the First Letter of John, chapter 2: “Everything that is in the world is the concupiscence of the flesh . . . which is not from the Father,” and so forth. He argues that concupiscence belongs to the nature of animals, but nevertheless to the punishment of the human being himself. The shame of the members, he maintains, arose only after sin, because of the rebellious movements of lust.

Furthermore, to prevent anyone from supposing that there was absolutely any concupiscence of the flesh in Christ, Augustine argues vehemently against Julian. He teaches that infants are born subject to original guilt, not through the exercise of their own will, but through the contagion of the sin voluntarily committed by the first parent. He also maintains that the passage he cited from the Book of Wisdom, chapter 12—“For he was not ignorant that their nation was wicked,” and so forth—serves to demonstrate the defect of our origin.

In the fifth, Augustine confirms and defends against the adversary’s accusations what he wrote in the second book *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, chapter 12 and several following chapters. In particular, he defends the claim that sound nature would not possess the shameful movement of the members that corrupted nature possesses, and consequently that the one born from it needs to be born again.

He next defends what he complained about in chapters 14, 20, and 26: namely, that Julian had misused two apostolic testimonies, 1 Corinthians 15 and Romans 1, as well as the evangelical saying in Matthew 7:17, or 12:33. He also defends his assertion in chapter 28 that evil, or an evil will, could arise from God’s good work because that work, although good, was made from nothing and not from God. Finally, he defends what he taught in chapter 17: that God creates the wicked in the same way that he feeds and nourishes the wicked.

In the sixth, Augustine shows that Julian fights in vain in his sixth book against what was asserted in the second book *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, chapter 34: namely, that through Adam’s sin human nature was changed for the worse, so that it became not only sinful but thereafter generative of sinners. Augustine teaches that by sinning Adam lost the powers of free will, by which, while they remained intact, a human being could both act rightly if he wished and refrain from sin if he did not wish to sin.

He rejects the definition of freedom that the adversary habitually brings forward, namely, “The possibility of sinning and not sinning,” and so forth. He proves that the pains of women in childbirth, thorns, labors, sweat, and the other miseries of mortals are punishments for sin. Above all, he proves that death itself is a punishment for the human being, who had been divinely constituted in such a way that, unless he sinned, he would not die.

In the final portion of the book, Augustine examines and refutes Julian’s exposition of the Apostle’s words in 1 Corinthians 15, “As all die in Adam,” and the following statements in the same chapter. Finally, throughout almost the whole book he demonstrates that the Catholic doctrine of original defect—which Julian everywhere strives to drag into the Manichaean heresy—not only stands far removed from that heresy, but also that the Pelagians can never overcome that heresy except with the aid and profession of the Catholic doctrine itself.

## FROM LETTER 224 TO QUODVULTDEUS

I am responding to Julian’s eight books, which he published after the four to which I had previously responded. When our brother Alypius received these at Rome, he had not yet copied them all; but he did not wish to let pass the opportunity that had presented itself, by which he sent me five of them, promising that he would soon send the other three and pressing me urgently not to delay my response.

Compelled by his urgency, I proceeded more slowly with the work I was doing, so that I might fail neither of the two works: I devoted the days to one and the nights to the other, whenever I could be spared from the other occupations that continually came upon me from one side and another. I was engaged in a task of the greatest necessity, for I was revising my little works; and if anything in them offended me or might offend others, I was working either to criticize it or to defend what ought and could be read.

I had already completed two volumes, having revised all my books, whose number I had not known; I discovered that there were 232. The letters remained, and afterward the popular treatises, which the Greeks call homilies. I had already read a great many of the letters, but had not yet dictated anything from them, when these books of Julian’s also began to occupy me. I have now begun to answer the fourth of them. When I have explained it and answered the fifth, if the other three have not arrived, I plan—if God wills—to begin what you request as well, carrying on both works together: this one and the work of revising my little books, with the night and day hours assigned separately to each.

[Col. 1049]

# ST. AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO: AN UNFINISHED WORK AGAINST JULIAN’S SECOND RESPONSE, COMPRISING SIX BOOKS

[Note: Written by Augustine in the final years of his life. Each of the six books represents one of Julian’s six books—the first six of the eight later books addressed to Florus—together with Augustine’s responses to the individual passages.]

[Note: The *Unfinished Work Against Julian’s Second Response* has been corrected in innumerable places on the authority of four ancient manuscripts of the highest quality. One, designated Colb., was supplied by the Colbert Library, but it is mutilated by two-thirds; it is the very manuscript from which Claudius Menard had copied the first two books and published them in print in 1617. Another, designated Clar., was supplied by the abbey of Clairvaux; Jerome Vignierius later used it to publish all six books. From it, Dom Mathurin Henault, a monk of that same abbey of Clairvaux, collected with immense care and labor readings differing from Vignierius’s edition for the benefit of our edition. The third, Port., came from the Carthusian monastery of Portes, which adorns the province of Bugey in France. The fourth, Mar., of perhaps the same antiquity as the preceding one—that is, written approximately six hundred years ago, though with exceptional and particular diligence—was made available to us by the Premonstratensian abbey of St. Marianus at Auxerre.]

[Note: We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractions* and *Confessions*, volume 1. M.]

(C, S)

## Preface

Against the Pelagian heretics, who say that Adam would have died bodily even if he had not sinned, and that the human race was not corrupted in him—whence it follows that they maintain that deaths, deadly diseases, and all the evils we see, including those suffered by infants, would also have existed in paradise even if no one had sinned [Note: In the printed editions, “infants” has been substituted for “in paradise”: wrongly, and contrary to the evidence of the ancient manuscripts.]—I wrote a book to Count Valerius [Note: The manuscripts connect these sentences in a continuous sequence. Vignierius, however, following Menard, begins the preface here with “I wrote a book to Count Valerius,” and places the preceding words before the preface as a kind of title. Paludanus deletes these same words as though added by another hand.], whose title is *On Marriage and Concupiscence*. I did so because I had learned that the Pelagians had accused us before him of being condemnatory of marriage. In that work, therefore, I distinguished, as best I could in argument, the good of marriage from the evil of carnal concupiscence, which conjugal chastity uses well.

After receiving that book, the illustrious man sent me on a little sheet [Note: Printed editions have “on little sheets.” The manuscripts have “on a little sheet.” See above, *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 2, no. 2.] several sentences excerpted from a work of Julian, the Pelagian heretic. In that work Julian seemed to himself to have answered in four books the one book of mine that I have mentioned as having written *On Marriage and Concupiscence*. These excerpts had been sent to Valerius by someone whom I do not know, who arranged for them to be taken from Julian’s first book as he wished [Note: The Colbert manuscript reads *putavit*, “he thought.” The other manuscripts, Clar., Port., and Mar., read *curavit*, “he arranged.”]. Valerius asked me to answer them as quickly as possible.

It then happened that, under the same title, I also wrote a second book, against which Julian composed another eight books with excessive verbosity. I am now responding to these, presenting his words and adding my response to each passage, as seemed appropriate for their refutation; for, after the first four of his books had come into my hands, I refuted them clearly enough in six books [Note: At this point we restore *six books* from the manuscripts.].

## BOOK ONE

[Col. 1051]

A response is made to Julian’s first book addressed to Florus. In this first book Julian constructs accusations against Augustine and against the Catholic faith by which we confess original sin, relying especially on three arguments. First, he maintains that, if God is just, no sin belonging to another can be imputed by him to infants. Second, since sin is nothing other than an evil will, which is free to abstain from what it wrongly desires, there is therefore no sin in those who are being born, since the exercise of the will cannot be found in them. Third, the freedom of choice granted to the human being consists in the possibility of committing sin and abstaining from sin; therefore free choice is denied by those who say that sins are natural.

With a spiteful tongue he also attacks certain passages from the first portions of the second book *On Marriage and Concupiscence* and from chapter 2 of the first book *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*. He likewise attempts to interpret, according to the Pelagian doctrine, the authorities cited in defense of God’s grace, which liberates us from slavery and condemnation—namely, from the Gospel of John, chapter 8; the Apostle to the Romans, chapters 6, 7, and 9; and the Second Letter to Timothy, chapter 2.

[Col. 1051]

### I. JULIAN

Although I am burdened by great anxieties [Note: Vignierius and three manuscript books read “labors.”], which, when I contemplate the condition of the Churches in these times, arise partly from indignation and partly from pity, I had nevertheless not abandoned faith in my promise: namely, that, having become a debtor [Note: Printed editions have “having become a debtor by promising.” The words “by promising” are absent from three manuscripts.], I would also take care to discharge the debt.

For in the books that I dictated against Augustine’s writings to our brother Bishop Turbantius, a man conspicuous for the great brilliance of his virtues, I promised that, if no unfortunate event occurred to obstruct my efforts, I would immediately confront all the arguments of those who, in accordance with the opinion of the Manichaeans, defended the transmission of sin—that is, natural evil. From this undertaking I have until now been held back by various and unavoidable necessities.

### AUGUSTINE

Would that, after those writings of yours and after these praises by which you call Turbantius a man conspicuous for the great brilliance of his virtues, you imitated him by being freed from your error! A response has been made to those books of yours, and it has been shown to you which Catholic lights, most brilliant in their interpretation of the holy Scriptures, you are attempting to obscure with this reproach—that is, by calling them Manichaeans.

### II. JULIAN

But as soon as I was permitted to draw breath, my plan was to fulfill my promise briefly, to the greatest extent that the nature of the matter itself allowed, unless you, most blessed father Florus, had once again wished me to enter upon a more demanding undertaking. Since you possess such authority through the reverence owed to your holiness that I regard sluggish obedience to your commands as irreligious, you easily obtained from me that I should extend into longer paths the concise brevity I had chosen.

You will therefore favor the work undertaken on your authority. For this reason above all I have inserted your name, so that my style might proceed with greater confidence and cheerfulness under the protection of such a command. My intention, then, had been to adopt a reasonable brevity: for in those four books the truth of the Catholic faith, for which and with which we earn the hatred of a world passing away, had crushed almost everything that had been drawn from the Manichaeans and uttered by Augustine against us. It had been armed both with unconquerable arguments and with testimonies from the sacred law, so that scarcely anything remained, if we had fair judges.

### AUGUSTINE

Against those four books of yours I wrote six books. After the commemoration of the Catholic teachers—whom you make Manichaeans by accusing me under this charge, although they learned and taught these things in the Catholic Church—which I explained in the first two volumes, I answered each of your remaining four books with one book of my own. [Col. 1052] I exposed the darkness of your heresy with the light of Catholic truth, which you abandon and thereby become blind and insane; and, like a new heretic, you seek fair judges in a matter over which there has never been any controversy in the Church of Christ—as though judges could seem fair to you unless they had been deceived by your error.

But what better judge could you find than Ambrose? Concerning him your teacher Pelagius says that not even an enemy dared criticize his faith and his utterly pure understanding of the Scriptures [Note: See above, *On the Grace of Christ*, no. 47]. Would this man, then, with his utterly pure understanding of the Scriptures, retain the most impure doctrine of the Manichaeans when he said, “We are all born under sin; our very birth is in guilt” (Ambrose, book 1 *On Repentance*, chapter 2)? You should therefore now judge how impurely you criticize this Catholic doctrine, and do not delay correcting yourself under Ambrose’s judgment.

### III. JULIAN

Nevertheless, I had passed over certain testimonies of the Scriptures by which they think that something can be brought against us, although I had promised to explain them. My purpose was to show that the obscure expressions of the law, which our enemies habitually appropriate, do not prejudice clear truth, and that they must be understood according to what is confirmed by the most complete authorities of Holy Scripture and by irresistible reason.

For it is evident from this very point how ignorant and profane an interpreter of the divine law anyone is who thinks that the law’s sanction defends what justice cannot vindicate [Note: This is the manuscript reading. Printed editions have “may appear.”].

### AUGUSTINE

What you say, rather, cannot be defended by any consideration of justice. For the misery of the human race, from which we see no human being free from birth to death, does not belong to the just judgment of the Almighty if there is no original sin.

### IV. JULIAN

For if the law of God is the source and teacher of justice, then God’s equity can be assisted by its aids but cannot be attacked. The nature of things therefore allows no support for iniquity to be drawn from the force of that Scripture, whose sole purpose in being promulgated was that, through its testimonies, remedies, threats, and punishments, iniquity might be destroyed.

### AUGUSTINE

Its testimonies declare that the human being was made like vanity and that his days pass away like a shadow (Psalm 143:4). Scripture shows that he is born with this vanity—not only through the truthful text by which his condition is lamented, but also through the laborious and sorrowful care by which he is educated.

In its remedies we read that, even when an infant has been born, a sacrifice is to be offered for sin (Leviticus [Col. 1053] 12:8). In its threats we read that the soul of an infant would perish if he were not circumcised on the eighth day (Genesis 17:14). In its punishments we read that even infants were ordered to be killed when their parents had provoked God to anger, so that they might be destroyed in military slaughter (Joshua 6:21 and 10:32).

### V. JULIAN

Therefore nothing can be done through the law of God against God, the author of the law. By this one concise argument everything usually brought forward by those who err is excluded. But, in order to teach how rich is the truth in which we believe, we also customarily bring the light of interpretation to those passages of Scripture whose meaning has been obscured by the complexity of their wording. Thus, once their dignity has been disclosed, they may possess the nobility of their origin and may not be separated from the sacred lineage [Note: The Marian manuscript reads “from the sacred *stegma*.” The others have “from the sacred *stemma*,” that is, from the line and sequence of the sacred books.] as illegitimate or degenerate.

### AUGUSTINE

On the contrary, you are attempting to obscure the lights of the holy Scriptures, which shine with certain truth, by the confusion of your perverse arguments. For what is clearer than what I have just said: “The human being was made like vanity; his days pass away like a shadow”? This certainly would not happen if he remained in the likeness of God, in which he was created.

What is clearer than the statement, “As all die in Adam, so also all will be made alive in Christ” (1 Corinthians 15:22)? What is clearer than the statement, “For who is clean from filth? Not even an infant, whose life upon the earth is but one day” (Job 14:4, according to the Septuagint)? There are many other passages that you attempt to wrap in your darkness and, through empty verbosity, twist into your perverse meaning.

### VI. JULIAN

This, then, was the only thing I was still intending to pursue according to our custom: namely, to free from the interpretations of the Traducians those passages of the divine law that had been subjected to insult. I intended to show that they were divine by demonstrating that they were just.

AUG. You call the Traducians—Cyprian, Ambrose, Gregory, and their other associates who confess original sin—by an insulting name. But it is not surprising that the new heretics impose a new name upon the Catholics from whom they have departed: others did the same when they likewise went out.

### VII. JUL.

But since you pressed this upon me insistently—or rather, ordered it by the authority of your office—that I should answer the book of the African writer which Alypius recently brought to the comes Valerius, that household servant of his sins, my reply has consequently become longer.

AUG. This African disputant is a great punishment for you; and long before you were born, the African Cyprian was prepared as a great punishment for your heresy.

### VIII. JUL.

For he has again produced monuments of his intellect and faith [Note: [Col. 1053] The printed editions have: “documents, so that they may be understood.” The manuscripts have: “monuments” (or “monumenta”), “which can be understood.”], which can scarcely be understood, are most difficult to explain, and can hardly be heard without horror; yet they can be refuted with the greatest ease and pierced most sharply [Note: [Col. 1053] Thus Menardus and two manuscripts. But Vignierius has: “yet they may be refuted more easily, and that they may be pierced most sharply.” Two manuscripts, Mar. and Clar., have: “somewhat pierced most sharply”; in manuscript Mar. these words are placed before “yet they can be refuted with the greatest ease.” Morel, *Elem. Crit.*, p. 367, thinks that the words “somewhat pierced most sharply” should be removed, as they perhaps invaded the text from the margin. M.], and, out of respect for decency, committed to oblivion and exterminated from memory.

AUG. Those who read do not judge as you wish.

### IX. JUL.

His first book, therefore—the only one published before this one—accuses us of being new heretics (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 1, no. 1), because we oppose the opinion which, whitewashed [Note: [Col. 1054] Menardus has: “whitewashed” in the feminine form.] like a tomb—though, according to the Gospel’s saying, outwardly clothed in a clean color, it is inwardly filled with filth and iniquity (Matt. 23:27)—belches forth, under praise of Baptism, the filth of the Manichaeans [Note: [Col. 1054] Codex Colbertinus has: “belches forth the natural sin of the Manichaeans.”] and natural sin, thereby contaminating the pure Sacraments of the Catholic Church, which until now have remained undefiled.

AUG. The ancient Catholic faith, proclaimed by the most distinguished teachers who lived before us, demonstrates that you are new heretics, since you have only now begun to attack it. Yet one should answer not all your insults so much as your accusations, which with the most shameless forehead and most insolent tongue you hurl not only at me, but also at Ambrose, Hilary, Gregory, Cyprian, and the other most renowned teachers of the Church.

### X. JUL.

He also praises a powerful man [Note: [Col. 1054] Valerius, book 1 of *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, no. 2.], because, when we were loudly demanding nothing other than that judges be appointed for so serious a matter, so that what had evidently been done by underhanded means [Note: [Col. 1054] Two manuscripts have the plural: “had evidently been done.”] might be corrected rather than punished by a judicial inquiry [Note: [Col. 1054] Menardus has: “might be submitted to examination.”], he used the weight of his dignity to obstruct us and did not allow us to obtain either time or a place for a hearing [Note: [Col. 1054] Two manuscripts have: “he obstructed us, and did not allow us to obtain a hearing, a time.” Vignierius has: “he obstructed us, did not allow a hearing, a time,” omitting *nec*. The reading of Menardus, together with manuscript Colbertinus, is more correct: “nor did he allow us time for a hearing.”]. Whether the man to whom this is written acted as wickedly as this praise testifies, let him decide for himself. Yet insofar as we had formed a better judgment of him, the mention of his name, honorably inserted in my little work, made that clear. Nevertheless, that book may perhaps contain falsehoods about its patron. But its author faithfully reveals what he desires: namely, that a battle be fought against reason [Note: [Col. 1054] The printed editions have: “as it is against reason.” We remove *est* on the authority of the manuscripts.], against the faith, and against all holiness of conduct and doctrine, with savage force and blind powerlessness.

AUG. May it be far from Christian authorities of the earthly commonwealth that they should doubt the ancient Catholic faith and, on that account, grant its attackers a place and time for examination, rather than, being certain and firmly grounded in it, impose disciplinary restraint upon enemies such as you. For what was done because of the Donatists was forced by their most violent mobs; they did not know what had previously taken place, which ought to have been shown to them. May God avert such mobs from you, though by God’s favor you do not have them.

### XI. JUL.

After these matters had been set forth in the opening portions of the volume, he proceeded to distinguish marriage and concupiscence, as he had promised in the title [Note: [Col. 1055] Thus manuscripts Mar. and Colb. The printed editions have: “proceeded from a distinction.”], and thereafter provided throughout the work a demonstration of his skill and ability. For, harassed by the final necessity of choosing between denying those who confess and confessing those who deny [Note: [Col. 1055] The printed editions have: “by the denial and the confession.” The conjunction *et* is redundant here; it is absent from the manuscripts.], he publicly exposed the kinds of misery his foul conscience suffered.

AUG. Insult as much as you can. Who cannot be insulting?

### XII. JUL.

I therefore answered his earlier work in four books, with the ability supplied by truth. I had first declared that I would pass over what appeared to have no weight in support of his doctrine and what could expose me to the charge of excessive talk if I pursued every weak and empty point. Indeed, if I had been permitted to observe this rule as I ought—that is, if they had not deserved opposition by reason of their incompetent profession—almost all his inventions would have been consigned to public contemptuous silence [Note: [Col. 1055] The printed editions have: “his inept inventions.” The manuscripts correct this reading.]. But since, as affairs hasten toward the worse—which is an indication that the world is approaching its end—folly and depravity have also gained dominion in the Church of God, we serve as ambassadors for Christ and, according to the share allotted to us, bring whatever aid we can [Note: [Col. 1055] Vignierius has *operis*, “work,” instead of *opis*, “aid.”] to the defense of the Catholic religion. Nor are we reluctant to commit to writing the remedies we prepare against the poisons of errors [Note: [Col. 1055] Manuscripts Mar. and Port. have: “their poisons.”].

AUG. Folly and depravity gave birth to you; but if they had gained dominion in the Church, they would certainly have kept you there.

### XIII. JUL.

As I testified, then, I had declared that in my first work I would not discuss every kind of Traducianism that needed defense, nor repeat everything contained in that book, but would contend with those points in which he had placed the substance and force of his doctrine. Anyone who is even a moderately attentive reader of both works will recognize that I faithfully fulfilled this promise. But, secure in the integrity of my conscience, I both exhort and challenge our opponent: if he thinks that I have omitted some argument brought forward by him which he himself judges to have any importance, let him produce it for public examination and prove me guilty of fear and deceit.

AUG. I do not believe that you thought the things you omitted were of no importance. Yet even if I grant that you thought so, a Catholic and intelligent reader who has both my one book and your four and applies diligence will discover that this is not so.

### XIV. JUL.

I certainly explained some of the testimonies of Scripture at greater length and others more briefly, because I promised to deal with them fully in the work that followed. Thus nothing of all Augustine’s arguments and propositions remained there unrefuted, and nothing was completed by me otherwise [Col. 1056] than I had promised. I exposed many things in his inventions as false, many as foolish, and many as sacrilegious.

AUG. You say this, certainly—but you say it. The one who reads and understands, if he is not a Pelagian, does not say this.

### XV. JUL.

By this declaration we need not fear a reputation for arrogance, because we acknowledge not that truth has been defended by my talent, but that the weakness of our talent has been assisted by the strength of truth.

AUG. You would have said “crushed,” if you had wished to speak the truth.

### XVI. JUL.

Since it is clear that these matters were fulfilled exactly as I have said, I cannot sufficiently marvel at the shamelessness of the man who, in this recent work of his, accuses my books of falsehood, while nevertheless testifying that they had not yet come into his hands (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 2, no. 2). It is hard enough that the habit of sinning produces love of wrongdoing; but nothing is harder than that it extinguishes shame. Although it was clear that this resulted from habitual wickedness, present dangers have nevertheless taught us more than any of us could have supposed. For when would I have believed that a Numidian’s forehead had become so hardened that, in one work and one sentence, he would confess both that I had spoken falsely and that he had not read what I had said?

AUG. If you did not do this, the man did who selected from your books what he thought ought to be sent to the comes Valerius. Since I did not believe that he had done this deceitfully, I attributed to the author what I ought to have attributed to the excerptor. I had not yet read your books, but I had read what he had excerpted from them. If you had thought of yourself as a human being, when you saw that this could have happened, you would never have sought so malicious an accusation against the man on this occasion.

### XVII. JUL.

For, writing to the man whom he admires as devoted to his books, although he is occupied with the exertions of military service, he indicates that some sheets had been brought to him by Alypius, headed as follows:

> “Heads from Augustine’s book, against which I have excerpted a few passages from the books.”

Then he says:

> “Here I see that the man who sent these writings to Your Eminence wished to excerpt them from some books—so I suppose—for the sake of a quicker reply, so that he would not delay your urgency. When I considered what books these might be, I supposed them to be those which Julian mentions in the letter he sent to Rome, a copy of which also reached me [Note: [Col. 1056] Here the manuscripts omit *simul*, “also.” In the second book of *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, no. 2, the same particle is absent from several manuscripts.]. For there he says: ‘They also say that these marriages which are now being contracted were not instituted by God, as is read in Augustine’s book, against which I have now replied in four little books.’”

And after these words he adds again in his own discourse:

> “I believe that these passages were excerpted from those little books. It might therefore perhaps have been better for our purpose to devote our efforts to refuting and disproving the whole work of his, which he explained in four volumes, unless I had also been unwilling to delay my reply, just as you did not delay transmitting the writings to which a response was required” (*ibid.*).

He therefore shows [Col. 1057] most plainly here that he suspects those excerpts were hastily collected from my work, while he admits that he did not know the complete books—yet he dares to say that he was able to answer them.

AUG. Why would I not dare, since I certainly ought not to doubt that you said empty things in them? For you could not speak against the truth except by speaking emptiness. Nor was my judgment mistaken: when I read your books, I found them to be such as I had presumed they would be before reading them.

### XVIII. JUL.

He also mentions a letter which, he says, I sent to Rome. But from the words he quoted, we could not recognize what document he was discussing [Note: [Col. 1057] The printed editions have “but by the words,” omitting *per*. The manuscripts Clar., Mar., and Port. have the particle here.]. For I sent two letters to Zosimus, formerly bishop of that city, concerning these questions; but I did so at a time when I had not yet begun my books.

AUG. This letter was not addressed to Zosimus, but to seduce those in Rome who might be seduced by such persuasion. But if you do not recognize it, let it not be yours. Would that those books also were not yours, but someone else’s, so that through them you might be a stranger to the truth from afar.

### XIX. JUL.

Moreover, let him use the evidence of the letter by which he either learned or fabricated that I had explained my reply against the new Manichaeans—since he disdains to appear an opponent of the old ones—in four volumes. Why did he not take care to learn what we had objected? Why did he not make an effort, since he was about to engage with me [Note: [Col. 1057] Vignierius emended *qui cum*, against the manuscripts, to *quo cum*. Julian likes this construction, familiar from Cicero and Terence; thus Terence, *Eunuchus*, act 4, scene 6, line 21: “with whom you have business.”], to understand it, but, driven by the most disgraceful levity, did he enter the greatest contest with his eyes covered, like the *Andabatae*? He defends this conduct by an argument of such a kind that he says he wished, in his headlong reply, to imitate the haste of his patron, who had hurried in transmitting the sheets—as though he could not most honorably have intimated that he ought to be granted some time to reach the reading of the published work. Among the learned, it is a disgrace to fail in the seriousness of writing, and through impatience in deliberation to attack what one does not know.

To this he adds that, intending to bring an accusation of deceitfulness against us—namely, that our craft had abbreviated the sequence of his statements [Note: [Col. 1057] Vignierius has: “that I had abbreviated the sequence of his statements.” But the manuscripts have: “which craft”—that is, the craft itself—“had abbreviated the sequence of his statements.” Menardus, approaching this reading, published: “which had lain aside the sequence of his statements.”]—he placed confidence in these excerpts, which appear more likely to have been composed through his own falsehood and malice than through the ignorant simplicity of any one of us. But whatever the motive and whatever the author of this may have been, it nevertheless helps us in two ways: for it simultaneously revealed both the extent of his levity and the extent of his weakness. He demonstrated that, although he ought not to speak, he cannot keep silent, and that, from a few half-complete and torn-apart sentences rather than assembled ones, he was nevertheless so broken by my first book alone [Note: [Col. 1057] Thus Menardus. But the manuscripts have: “he advanced, having been made broken.” Vignierius has: “he approached, broken.”] that he stirred the hearts of the common people against us with highly effeminate cries—as will become clear from the progress of our disputation.

[Col. 1058] AUG.

Why are you angry with me because your books could reach me only after a delay, or because, while seeking them, I could not find them quickly? Nevertheless, I was able—and absolutely ought—to examine plainly, with open rather than clouded eyes, whatever the sheet sent to me contained, whoever its author and whatever its character, so that it would not be thought invincible, and to refute it without delay. For even if I could never have found your books, I ought still to have answered, with all the strength I possessed, whatever the man who thought it worth sending to so great a person believed to have any importance, lest anyone reading it should be deceived by it.

You would not have brought this charge against me unless you were speaking—if I may not say with extinguished eyes, then certainly with closed eyes. Yet you would never say that we stirred the hearts of the common people against you unless you knew that the Christian multitude, of both sexes, was not ignorant of the Catholic faith which you are trying to overthrow.

### XX. JUL.

Here too, as in the earlier work we produced, I warn the reader that I shall not set down every one of his words exactly, but only those headings by which, once they have been destroyed, the opinion of natural evil may be crushed.

AUG. The things you omit will perhaps be gathered either by us or by others, so that it may become clear why you omitted them [Note: [Col. 1058] Two manuscripts have *et*, “and,” instead of *ea*, “the things.”].

### XXI. JUL.

Although this was fully accomplished in the first work, nevertheless, since he has now proposed that certain matters from only one of my books be refuted, and since, as I stated beforehand [Note: [Col. 1058] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have *prolocutus*, “having spoken beforehand.”], he accuses me of having truncated to a large extent the headings of his statements which I inserted, I shall first show that I did not do what he criticizes, and that he himself has practiced it most shamelessly in this very work [Note: [Col. 1058] Vignierius has *ut*, “that.” The manuscripts’ *et*, “and,” is better.]. Then I shall prove that, in the very brief and cut-down sentences which he inserts from my writings—writings by which he had been attacked—he opposed them with no solid answers at all, so that those matters remain unassailed and he confesses here things more plainly deserving of detestation than our discourse had labored to explain [Note: [Col. 1058] Manuscripts Port. and Mar. have *operatio*, “work” or “activity,” instead of *oratio*, “discourse.”].

AUG. I have already answered these points above.

### XXII. JUL.

Let us therefore, astonished, hear what he wrote against me.

> “He set down to you these words from my book, which I sent to you and which you know very well, and which he attempted to refute:
>
> “ ‘They most maliciously proclaim that we are condemners of marriage and of the divine work by which God creates human beings from males and females, because we say that those who are born from such a union draw original sin, and we do not deny that, whatever their parents may be, they nevertheless remain under the devil unless they are reborn in Christ.’
>
> “In these words of mine he omitted the Apostle’s testimony which I inserted, because he felt himself heavily burdened by it. For when I had said that human beings draw original sin, I immediately added:
>
> “ ‘Concerning this the Apostle says: Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death, and so it passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned’ (Rom. 5:12).
>
> “After omitting this testimony, as we have said, he joined together the other matters mentioned above. For he knows how Catholic hearts of the faithful customarily receive these apostolic words [Col. 1059], which he omitted—words so upright and shining with such great light that the new heretics endeavor to obscure and distort them through dark and twisted interpretations.
>
> “Next he appended other words of mine, where I said:
>
> “ ‘Nor do they observe that the good of marriage cannot be accused on account of the original evil drawn from it, just as the evil of adultery and fornication cannot be excused on account of the natural good born from it. For just as sin, whether it is drawn from one source or the other by little children, is the work of the devil, so a human being, whether born from one source or the other, is the work of God.’
>
> “Here too he omitted the matters in which he feared Catholic ears. For before we reached these words, we had said:
>
> “ ‘Since we say this because it is contained in the most ancient and most firmly established rule of the Catholic faith, these recent and perverse advocates of a doctrine who say that there is no sin in little children which is washed away by the bath of regeneration make a faithless or ignorant accusation—as though we condemned marriage, and as though we said that the work of God, namely, the human being born from it, is the work of the devil.
>
> “ ‘After omitting these words of ours, those of ours which he quoted follow, exactly as written above’ ” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 2, nos. 3–4).

How long will you continue, by saying such things, to mock the simplicity of devout hearts and inexperienced ears? To what end will unrestrained shamelessness flaunt itself? When you wrote these things, did neither the judgment of learned men, nor reverence for the future judgment, nor the very written records themselves move you? Now expose your deception! Do you not see that you have been caught? What each of us wrote in the first and second works—whom do you suppose is ignorant of it? It was entirely fitting, and proper, to address you in the manner in which the eloquent Consul thundered against a public parricide [Cicero, *First Oration against Catiline*].

AUG. You do well [Note: [Col. 1059] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have: “You did well.”] to inform us, lest we fail to recognize that you have taken and adapted these words from Cicero’s invectives. But we do not fear Julian when we see him become Tullian; rather, we grieve to see him become insane when we see him lose Christian understanding.

For what is more insane than to bar the physician Christ from little children by saying that there is nothing in them which he came to heal? Cicero, inveighing against a parricide of his country, was defending the state which its king Romulus founded by gathering together sinners from every direction. But you both proclaim that so many little children who die without holy Baptism have no sin and prevent them from approaching the city of the King in whose image they were made.

### XXIII. JUL.

You pretend that I omitted the Apostle’s testimony, although it can neither help you nor was omitted by me; rather, it was inserted in the order in which you had placed it. And just as it was faithfully mentioned in the first book, so also in the fourth book of my work it was explained, although cursorily and briefly [Note: [Col. 1059] See above, book 6 against Julian, no. 75.]. Nor did I omit the mention of the Catholic Church which you had inserted for the purpose of deceiving those whom you wished to abandon the Catholic faith and to rejoice in being called “Catholic” in a pitiable way.

Although there was no force of argument in such words, I nevertheless presented the heading of your statements in no other way than you had arranged it. Read my published books; and, seeing the faithful character of my reply, which you accuse of fraud, pronounce meanwhile that I speak the truth. But you, if your habitual conduct permits it, blush.

Now, however, after the inexcusability of your falsehood has been exposed—a falsehood always disgraceful, but still more disgraceful when it invades the place of a censor and reproaches another’s honor for its own deformity—answer this: what do the name of the Church or the words of the Apostle have in common with Manichaean opinions, so that you complain that they were omitted with such great malice?

AUG. I have already answered above this slander of yours, by which you accuse me of falsehood because your words were not set out completely. But you would not so readily attribute to me what that excerptor did if you did not wish to deceive those who read these things.

### XXIV. JUL.

This was always the greatest distinction between the Manichaeans and Catholics, and a very broad boundary by which the doctrines of the pious and the impious are separated from one another; indeed, it is a great mass [Note: [Col. 1060] Three manuscripts have *mole*, “mass,” rather than *moles*, “magnitude.” One of these, Marianensis, has: “all our statements.”] dividing our doctrines from theirs in depth as great as that between heaven and earth: we ascribe every sin to an evil will, whereas they ascribe it to an evil nature. Following different errors, but proceeding as though from the head of this fountain, they consequently arrive at sacrileges and crimes. Catholics, by contrast, beginning from a good starting point and advancing with good progress, reach the summit of religion, which reason fortifies and piety supports [Note: [Col. 1060] Thus manuscripts Mar. and Port. The printed editions have “are carried forward.”].

You therefore attempted to assert natural evil, with a profane desire indeed but an ineffective intention, by appropriating the Apostle’s testimony. Through this same writing I show that he understood nothing of the kind that you are trying to persuade us of: in contradictory ways, you confess him to be a Catholic while judging that his words support a Manichaean [Note: [Col. 1060] Morel thinks the reading should be: “which you are trying to persuade us of, although in contradictory ways you both confess him to be a Catholic and judge that his words support a Manichaean.” See *Elementa Critica*, p. 233. M.].

AUG.
