If you were thinking with a Christian heart, you would blush, tremble, and fall silent when you claim that Catholic teachers support a Manichaean [Note: [Col. 1060] The printed editions have: “you claim that the Catholic teachers support the Manichaeans.” Three manuscripts have: “you claim that the Catholic teachers support a Manichaean.”]—teachers who understood the apostolic words to mean that little children draw original sin, and who did not, in your insane fashion, praise nature as though it were sound, but applied Christian medicine to heal it.

### XXV. JUL.

Did not Adimantus and Faustus—the latter of whom you call your teacher in your *Confessions* [Note: [Col. 1060] Compare *Confessions*, book 5, chapters 6 and 7.]—do the same, following the tradition of their heresiarch, snatching and scraping together the more obscure statements either from the Gospel [Note: [Col. 1060] The printed editions have: “the heresiarchs, by the tradition of whom they made obscure those things which were either from the Gospel.” The manuscripts more correctly have: “the heresiarch of whom”—that is, the founder of the Manichaean sect—“by whose tradition they made the more obscure statements,” and so forth.] or from the Epistles of the Apostles, in order to defend a profane doctrine by the authority of names? Yet why do I speak of the Manichaeans? Absolutely all heresies fortify their inventions—by which they have deviated from piety and faith—with expressions and statements from Scripture.

AUG. They turned obscure statements toward their own doctrine; you attempt to obscure clear statements through your own doctrine. For what is clearer than what the Apostle says: that sin entered this world through one man, and through sin death, and so passed into all human beings (Rom. 5:12)? If the Apostle were compelled to prove this, he would offer as witness the misery of the human race itself, which begins with the cries of little children [Note: [Col. 1061] The manuscripts have: “which begins with the cries,” omitting *a*, “from.”] and reaches even to the groans of the very old. For this great misery would in no way be inflicted upon human nature under the care of the omnipotent and just God unless, in the two human beings, the whole race had been driven from the happiness of paradise into this misery of sin by the desert of sin.

### XXVI. JUL.

Are the authors of the sacred books therefore to be approved as authors of error, or will the dignity of Scripture expiate the crimes of those who perish?

AUG. Say this to yourselves.

### XXVII. JUL.

Let the desire for undisciplined interpretations therefore be extinguished. Let it be believed that words cannot act against the manifest justice of God. If they belong to a person whom it is necessary to venerate, let them be defended by explanations consistent with divine equity; but if they were spoken by an author who need not be feared, let them also be rejected as unqualified.

Thus the judgment of God is now being discussed—of whom it is said [Note: [Col. 1061] The manuscripts have “is written.”]: “God is faithful, in whom there is no iniquity; the Lord God is just and holy” (Deut. 32:4). And again: “The Lord is just, and he loved justice; his countenance saw equity” (Ps. 10:8). And again: “All your judgments are equity” (Ps. 118:172). There are innumerable testimonies in which divine equity is proclaimed in the sacred books. Yet no one, whether Gentile or heretic, except the Manichaeans and Traducians, has doubted it.

AUG. From this equity comes the heavy yoke upon the sons of Adam from the day they leave their mother’s womb (Ecclus. 40:1). Whoever denies original sin absolutely asserts that this is unjust [Note: [Col. 1061] The printed editions have: “asserts that you claim it to be unjust, because you deny original sin.” The manuscripts have: “asserts that it is unjust, whoever denies original sin.”].

### XXVIII. JUL.

Nature teaches [Note: [Col. 1061] The printed editions have: “and nature teaches.” Manuscript Mar. has: “nature teaching,” which is preferable. [*docente natura*]], and has so generally impressed this upon all people, that God is just, that it is evident that there is no God who can be shown not to be just. A human being, therefore, can also be just; but God cannot be anything except just.

AUG. Say this to yourselves.

### XXIX. JUL.

Since he is the one true God whom we believe in and whom we venerate in the Trinity, without doubt he is most just in every respect according to the rational order of judgment [Note: [Col. 1061] Codex Port. has: “the one true God whoever he is.” The same codex has: “he is most just in the administration of every judgment.” Mar. and Clar. have: “he is most just in all judgments and in reason.”].

AUG. Say this to yourselves—and show that it is just that a child should be born amid such manifest misery, or into such manifest misery, when he does not draw original sin.

### XXX. JUL.

By the laws of this one, it cannot be proved and vindicated that what is admittedly unjust exists [Note: [Col. 1062] Thus manuscripts Port., Mar., and Clar.; the printed editions have *id*, “this,” instead of *ita*, “thus.”]; for if this could happen, his entire divinity would become worthless. Accordingly, the doctrine of injustice will be shown to be established by the Scriptures by the one who can approve that the Trinity in whose divinity we believe may be deprived of the glory of divinity.

AUG. You speak truly—but say this to yourselves [Note: [Col. 1062] Two manuscripts, Mar. and Port., have the singular “say this to yourself.”], who are trying to take away from Christ the glory by which he heals little children.

### XXXI. JUL.

Since no reason supports this and no piety does either, either teach that natural sin can exist or that it can justly be imputed to anyone, or withdraw from contaminating the sacred Scriptures, whose statements you think sanction what you are compelled to confess is unjust [Note: [Col. 1062] The printed editions have: “you withdraw, from whose statements you think that what is unjust is sanctioned.” The manuscripts Port., Mar., and Clar. correct the reading.].

AUG. You are mistaken. Rather, you are compelled to confess that the heavy yoke upon little children is unjust if, just as they have no personal sin, they also draw no original sin.

### XXXII. JUL.

But if you do neither of the things we have mentioned, and you claim to believe in this God whose institutions you think reinforce injustice, recognize that you are much worse than the ancient Manichaean, since you have such a God as Manichaeus imagined to be the enemy of his own god.

AUG. You rage against little children more cruelly than the Manichaeans. They at least wish the soul—which they consider a part of God—to be healed in the little child through Christ. But you, although you say that the child has no evil at all, either in soul or in flesh, permit it to be healed through Christ in no respect. And you, distinguished preachers, preach Jesus in such a way that you deny him to be the Jesus of little children [Note: [Col. 1062] Manuscript Colbertinus has “Christ.”]. Read in the Gospel where he received this name (Matt. 1:21), and do not deny the Savior to little children whom he does not save [Note: [Col. 1062] The printed editions have “do not begrudge”; this is not a bad reading. But the manuscripts have “do not deny.” One manuscript, Port., reads approximately: “Read in the Gospel, and do not deny the Savior to little children who are saved.”].

### XXXIII. JUL.

What evasions, then, will you bring against me here—what pillows of lies and absurdities which the prophet Ezekiel attributes to the fornicating Jerusalem (Ezek. 13:18), on which feminine souls may lie while holding the names of mysteries, when they have committed sacrilege against divinity itself by their uncovered profanation? Remove all your tricks and the troops of little crowds whom you have so often summoned as advocates, and teach that what you are trying to affirm through the sacred Scriptures is just [Note: [Col. 1062] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have: “what you are trying to establish firmly through the Scriptures.”].

AUG. The troops of little crowds whom you mock know the Catholic faith, and confess that infants are saved by the Savior [Note: [Col. 1062] We restore the word *salvari*, “to be saved,” from the manuscripts.]. For that reason they detest the error of the Pelagians, who deny this.

### XXXIV. JUL.

So that our discourse may not be extended into endless volumes, let the genus, species, distinction, mode, and quality of the matters under discussion be discerned here—here, I say [Col. 1063] [Note: [Col. 1063] Vignierius has: “our discourse here of the matters under discussion.” Menardus has: “our discourse, thus, of the matters under discussion.” M.]. Indeed, let us inquire more carefully whether they exist, from where they come, where they are [Note: [Col. 1063] We restore *ubi sint*, “where they are,” from the manuscripts.], what they deserve, and from whom. In this way we shall neither wander for long through the winding paths of disputation, nor fail to see clearly what must be held.

AUG. That is why you wrote eight books against my one [Note: [Col. 1063] Against the second book of *On Marriage and Concupiscence*.], because you did not wish to dispute for long through your dialectical abridgments [Note: [Col. 1063] Vignierius has *qui*, “who.” The manuscripts have *quia*, “because.”].

### XXXV. JUL.

Here, then, the account of the Creator and the creature is at issue—that is, of God and the human being. He judges; this one is judged. Therefore, let us examine what is the nature of justice and guilt.

Justice is, both as the learned customarily define it and as we are able to understand it, a virtue—if we may, following the Stoics, prefer one virtue to another—the greatest of all virtues, diligently performing its office of restoring to each person what is his, without fraud and without favor.

AUG. Then say by what justice the heavy yoke of such great and manifest misery was assigned to little children. Say by what justice one little child is adopted [Note: [Col. 1063] The printed editions have: “say also by what justice that little child is adopted.” The manuscripts omit “also” and have “may be adopted.”] in Baptism while another dies without this adoption. Why is this honor not common to both, or why is alienation from this honor not common to both, when the cause—whether good or evil—is common to both? You do not say, because, being more Pelagian than Christian, you do not understand either the grace of God or the justice of God.

### XXXVI. JUL.

But if Zeno did not permit it to be called the greatest virtue—he who so confirms the union and unity of the virtues that, wherever one is present, he says that all the virtues are present, and wherever one is absent, all are absent, and who says that true virtue is that which is perfected by this fourfold union—then even so he will provide us with great assistance when he teaches that neither prudence, nor courage, nor temperance can be contained without justice. In accordance with this truth Ecclesiastes also declares: “Whoever sins in one thing will lose many good things” (Eccles. 9:18).

AUG. Hear the same Ecclesiastes saying: “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity. What abundance does a human being have in all his labor at which he labors under the sun?” (ibid. 1:2–3), and so forth. And tell me why the human being was also made like vanity (Ps. 143:4), when he had been made like truth. Or do you exclude the little children from this—those whom we see, as they grow and even when they are well educated, diminishing by progress the great vanity with which they were born, yet never entirely free from it until all the days of vanity have passed like a shadow?

### XXXVII. JUL.

This august virtue, then, the examiner of each person’s merits, flickers in the works of the image of God—that is, in the human soul—according to the measure and powers of the creature itself. But in God himself, the creator of all things from nothing, it shines forth immense and brilliant through the eternal orbit [Note: [Col. 1063] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have “through an everlasting age.”].

Its origin is divinity; its age is eternity; and eternity knows neither ceasing nor beginning, whether in one direction or the other. Thus, just as God is its genus—by which term I wish nothing other than its origin to be understood—so its species appears in the promulgation of laws and in the effects of judgments.

Augustine: If God is the origin of righteousness, as you admit, why do you not admit that righteousness is given to human beings by him, and instead want the free choice of the human will, rather than God’s gift, to be righteousness—so that you may be among those of whom it is said, “Being ignorant of God’s righteousness, and seeking to establish their own, they are not subject to the righteousness of God” (Rom. 10:3)? Be ashamed at last, I beg you, and ask righteousness from him who is, as you have been compelled to admit, the origin of righteousness.

### XXXVIII. Julian

[Note: [Col. 1064] The editions read “we may not unreasonably understand the difference,” omitting “its”; the latter is present in the manuscripts.]

[Note: [Col. 1064] Vignier reads “and varying.” The particle “and” is deleted on the authority of the manuscripts.]

We may not unreasonably understand its difference as a varying dispensation according to the suitability of the times. For example, sacrifices from livestock had been commanded in the Old Testament. At that time, fulfilling this belonged to reverence for the command; now, however, the cessation of such sacrifices serves the righteousness that gives the command just as the offering then served it. Its measure—or condition—is that it commands no one more than his strength can bear, and that it does not blunt mercy. Its quality is understood as that by which it tastes sweetly to devout minds. It is therefore undoubtedly righteousness, without which deity does not exist; if it did not exist, God would not exist. But God does exist, and therefore without ambiguity righteousness exists. It is nothing other than a virtue embracing all things and restoring to each what is his, without fraud and without favor. It consists above all in the depth of divinity.

Augustine: You defined righteousness as a virtue embracing all things and restoring to each what is his, without fraud and without favor. Accordingly, we see that it restored a denarius without fraud to those who had labored throughout the whole day in the vineyard: this had been agreed upon and settled; they could not deny that they had been hired for this wage (Matt. 20:1–13). But tell me, I ask you, how did it give the same amount without favor to those who had worked there for one hour? Had it perhaps lost its righteousness? Restrain yourself, then. Divine righteousness defrauds no one, but grace gives many things to those who have not deserved them.

[Note: [Col. 1064] The manuscripts read this way. The editions, however, have: “but it gives much grace to those who do not deserve it.”]

But why it gives one person this and another that, consider what you add next. You say most truly that it consists above all in the depth of divinity. In this depth lies the truth that it is “not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Rom. 9:16). In this depth lies the fact that one infant is adopted into honor through the laver of regeneration, while another is left in disgrace, not to be admitted to the kingdom, although neither possesses merit in either direction through the choice of the will.

### XXXIX. Julian

[Note: [Col. 1064] At this point, on the authority of the old codices, we restore “in themselves neither.”]

Its testimony, whether from its author or from the good and the wicked, deserves recognition: it has rightly advanced the former and rightly condemned the latter. But when it permits mercy to be generous toward those who in themselves deserve neither good nor evil, it perceives no injustice; for even this very fact—that God is merciful toward his work when he is not compelled to severity—is a large part of righteousness.

Augustine: At least attend to the word “mercy” and consider from what it is derived. What need, then, is there for mercy where there is no misery? Moreover, if you say that there is no misery in infants, you deny that mercy should be shown them; if you say that there is misery in them, you demonstrate an evil merit.

[Note: [Col. 1065] The editions, omitting the word “misery,” had this reading: “Moreover, if you say that there is no guilt in infants, you deny that mercy should be shown them; if you say that there is no…” The manuscripts correct the text.]

For no one can be miserable under a just God unless he deserves it. Look: two infants lie there. One of them dies baptized; the other dies unbaptized. To which of them do you say that God was merciful? If to one, show the evil merit of the other, since you deny original sin. If to both, show some good merit in the baptized one, since you deny grace where there is no partiality. And say, if you can, why he did not wish to adopt both, since he certainly created both in his own image. Is he just in such a way that he is not omnipotent—if he wished to do so but could not? Certainly neither of them willed anything, lest you refer the impediment of divine power to the merit of the human will. To neither of them, certainly, can God say, “I wanted to, but you did not.”

Or, if the infant does not wish it for the reason that he cries when he is baptized, then let both be left unadopted, for both refuse; and yet one is taken up and the other left, because the grace of God is great and the righteousness of God is true. But why one rather than the other? The judgments of God are inscrutable.

### XL. Julian

Those whom he created because he wished to, he does not condemn unless they are despised; and if, when they are not despised, he makes them better through consecration, he suffers no loss of righteousness and is adorned by the generosity of mercy.

Augustine: You say that he condemns no one except the one who despises him. Say whether he despises his own image unless it has despised him. If you do not dare say this, explain why he rejects those whom he does not adopt as infants, though you will find that he was rejected by them only if you find them in Adam.

[Note: [Col. 1065] The manuscripts read “by whom”; the editions read “in whom.”] There you will find at the same time that, by righteousness, all deserve to be despised, and yet, because of ineffable and inscrutable grace, not all are despised.

### XLI. Julian

Having thus explained the divisions of righteousness that we set out above, let us examine what the definition of sin is. Certainly, the writings of philosophers and of those who were Catholics provide me abundantly with what we seek. But I fear that you will oppose me; and that, if I summon the senate of philosophers, you will immediately arouse against us the workshop laborers and the whole mob.

[Note: [Col. 1065] The editions read “that you will be broken.” Three manuscripts—Claramontanus, Marianus, and Portus—read “that you will oppose me.”]

Augustine: You are insulting the weak things of the world, which God chose in order to confound the strong (1 Cor. 1:27). In the end, they themselves confound those who trust in their own strength. What am I to say? “You are they”? Even while I say nothing, you plainly reveal yourselves, although you do not keep silent.

### XLII. Julian

You shout together with women, all the camp-followers, and the tribunes, to whom your colleague Alypius recently brought eighty or more horses fattened throughout all Africa.

Augustine: Either you are slandering, or you do not know what you are saying; and therefore you speak this either as a liar or as a reckless man. What could be more wicked than you, if you invented these things yourself? What could be more foolish, if you believed those who invented them?

[Note: [Col. 1066] The editions read “What could be more wicked?” omitting “than you”; this is restored from the Claramontanus, Marianus, and Portus manuscripts.]

And what of the fact that you even dared to write this, without fearing that your book might reach those places where my colleague Alypius was welcomed as he crossed or came by land and sea? There, your falsehoods are so clearly exposed that they cannot be read without ridicule—or rather, detestation of you. What is this comparable to—not, I say, to shamelessness, but to madness?

### XLIII. Julian

[Note: [Col. 1066] The word “in accordance with” was absent from the editions and is restored from the same three manuscripts.]

You are by no means willing to submit to the opinions of learned men, adding, in accordance with what suits your understanding, that the Apostle said, “God made foolish the wisdom of the world” (1 Cor. 1:20). Yet you can despise our disputants without fear, since you are not pressed by the authority of such men.

Augustine: You despise those whom, while they teach original sin, you resist so obstinately that you even accuse them of being Manichaeans—naming me and indicating them.

### XLIV. Julian

What then? I will entirely yield to you, and in this place give up all those whose assistance I might have used. I will be content with the definition that, after the secret teaching of the Manichaeans, escaped from your honorable mouth as evidence of good nature.

In the book entitled either *On Two Souls* or *Against Two Souls*, you speak as follows:

“Wait; first let us define sin. Sin is the will to admit or retain what righteousness forbids and from which it is free to abstain. Although, if it is not free, it cannot be called will, I preferred to define it in a cruder rather than a more meticulous manner” (ch. 11).

[Note: [Col. 1066] The editions read “to lose”; the manuscripts read “to admit,” or “to ammit.” Augustine, in the definition cited, later says “the will to retain or obtain,” as below at chapter 47.]

Augustine: Here sin has been defined as what is merely sin, not as what is also the punishment of sin. For this was the subject that had to be discussed when the origin of evil was being sought—namely, the kind of sin committed by the first human being before every human evil.

[Note: [Col. 1066] The Marianus manuscript reads “before every human evil.” The Portus manuscript reads “before all the evil of humanity.” The editions have “before the evil of all human beings.”]

But you either cannot understand this or do not wish to.

### XLV. Julian

O shining gold in filth! What truer or fuller statement could have been made by anyone, even an orthodox person?

[Note: [Col. 1066] The Portus manuscript reads “clearer” rather than “fuller”; later it agrees with the Marianus manuscript in reading “could have been said by anyone, even an orthodox person.”]

“Sin is,” you say, “the will to admit or retain what righteousness forbids and from which it is free to abstain.”

Ecclesiasticus shows this: “God made human beings and left them in the hand of their own counsel. He placed before them life and death, water and fire; whatever pleases them will be given them” (Ecclus. 15:14 and following). And God says through Isaiah: “If you are willing and listen to me, you shall eat the good things of the land. If you are unwilling and do not listen, the sword shall consume you” (Isa. 1:19). And the Apostle says, “Recover your right mind justly” [or “You righteous, recover your right mind”] “and do not sin” (1 Cor. 15:34); and again, “Do not be deceived: God is not mocked. For whatever a person sows, that he will also reap” (Gal. 6:7–8).

[Note: [Col. 1067] Two manuscripts read “righteous.” The Greek, however, has *dikaiōs*, “justly.”]

Augustine: These testimonies were spoken concerning that will in which each person does what he wills: so that, if this will is not possessed, it may be sought from the one who works in us both to will (Phil. 2:13); but if it is possessed, works of righteousness may be performed and thanks given to him who has worked it.

### XLVI. Julian

The will, then, is a movement of the mind that possesses the right to determine whether it runs more toward the left, toward what is wrong, or turns to the right, striving toward what is lofty.

Augustine: What, then, does “Do not turn aside to the right or to the left” mean (Prov. 4:27)?

### XLVII. Julian

It is the movement of the mind of one who, having reached an age at which he can use the judgment of reason, is shown punishment and glory, or conversely advantage and pleasure.

[Note: [Col. 1067] The Portus codex reads “or conversely disadvantage.”] Assistance, and as it were an opportunity, is offered; necessity is not imposed on either side.

This will, which alternates between the two, received the origin of its possibility in free choice. The existence of the action itself it receives from itself. It is not truly will before it wills, nor can it will before it has been able both to will and not to will; and in the matter of sin it does not possess both—that is, willing and not willing—before it attains the use of reason.

When these points are gathered together, it becomes clear that you defined it most truthfully: “Sin is the will to retain or admit what righteousness forbids and from which it is free to abstain.” This sin, which has become clear to be nothing other than will, plainly received its genus—that is, its very origin—from one’s own desire. Its species is found in each individual, who are called atoms. Its difference lies both in the variety of faults and in the circumstances of the times. Its measure is immoderation itself; for if it is the measure to serve the one whom you ought to serve, anyone who neglects this sins by transgressing the true measure.

Yet it may be subtly said that the measure of sin is that no one sins beyond what he can do. For if someone sins beyond his ability, he sins with an ineffective will; and even this could have been done by will alone. Its quality is to be assigned to the vice by which it is shown what bitterness it brings, whether by disgrace or by pain.

Sin therefore exists because, if it did not, you would not follow errors. It is nothing other than a will exceeding the path on which it ought to remain and from which it is free not to deviate. It arises from desire for what is forbidden and exists nowhere except in the person who both had an evil will and could have lacked it.

[Note: [Col. 1067] The manuscripts read “arises”; the editions read “arose.”]

Augustine: This is Adam, whom the definition I gave—which pleased you—had in view when I said, “Sin is the will to retain or obtain what righteousness forbids and from which it is free to abstain.”

For when Adam sinned, he had absolutely no evil in himself by which he might be driven unwillingly to do evil, and because of which he might say, “I do not do the good that I want, but the evil that I do not want—that I do” (Rom. 7:19). Rather, by sinning he did what righteousness forbade and from which it had been free for him to abstain. For one who says, “The evil that I do not want—that I do,” is not free to abstain from it.

[Note: [Col. 1068] Departing from Menard’s edition, Vignier substituted “For,” against the testimony of our manuscripts, which read “Is it that?”]

Accordingly, if you distinguish these three things

[Note: [Col. 1068] The editions read “thus”; the manuscripts correct this to “if.”]

and understand that one thing is sin and understand that one thing is sin, another the punishment of sin, and a third both together—that is, sin in such a way that it is also itself the punishment of sin—you understand which of these three belongs to the definition in which there is a will to do what righteousness forbids and from which it is free to abstain.

Sin, then, defined in this way, is neither the punishment of sin nor both together. These three kinds also have their own species, about which it would now take too long to discuss.

Of these three kinds, if examples are sought, the first kind is found in Adam without any difficulty. Human beings do many evil things from which they are free to abstain, but no one was as free as the one who stood before his God, by whom he had been created upright, entirely uncorrupted by any vice.

The second kind, in which there is only the punishment of sin, is found in the evil that a person does not perform in any way but merely suffers—for example, when someone who has sinned is killed for his crime or is tortured by any other bodily punishment.

The third kind, in which sin itself is also the punishment of sin, may be understood in the case of the person who says, “The evil that I do not want—that I do.” To this also belong all the evils which, when done through ignorance, are not thought to be evil, or are even thought to be good.

[Note: [Col. 1068] The manuscripts read “when evils are done.”]

[Note: [Col. 1068] The manuscripts read “when evils are done.”]

For blindness of heart, if it were not sin, would be unjustly reproved. Yet it is justly reproved when it is said, “Blind Pharisee” (Matt. 23:26), and in many other places in the divine utterances. Again, if the same blindness were not the punishment of sin, it would not be said, “Their malice blinded them” (Wis. 2:21). And if it did not come from God’s judgment, we would not read, “Let their eyes be darkened, so that they may not see, and bend their backs continually” (Ps. 68:24).

Moreover, who willingly chooses to be blind in heart, when no one wants to be blind even in body? Therefore original sin belongs neither to the first of the things we listed, where there is a will to do evil from which one is free to abstain—for otherwise it would not exist in infants, who do not yet exercise the choice of the will—nor to the second, which we mentioned. For we are now discussing sin, not punishment, which is not sin, although it follows deservedly upon sin.

Infants indeed suffer this punishment, because “the body is dead because of sin” (Rom. 8:10).

[Note: [Col. 1068] Vignier and two manuscripts read “for.”] Yet bodily death itself, or any bodily suffering, is not sin. Rather, original sin belongs to the third kind, in which sin is such that it is also itself the punishment of sin. It exists in those who are born, but begins to appear in them as they grow, when wisdom becomes necessary for the foolish and self-control for those who desire evil.

[Note: [Col. 1068] This has been restored with the help of the manuscripts: “but begins to appear in them as they grow.” The editions, omitting these words, had approximately: “while wisdom begins to appear.”]

Yet the origin even of this sin descends from the will of the one who sinned: “Adam existed, and in him we all existed; Adam perished, and in him all perished” (Ambrose, book 7 on Luke 15, no. 234).

### XLVIII. Julian

It deserves execration from honorable people and lawful condemnation from that righteousness whose whole case is at issue here. Therefore, with all the curtains drawn aside, bring forth at last into the light what teaches you that sin is natural.

Certainly, nothing above has been falsely established, whether concerning the praise of divine righteousness or the definition of sin. Show, then, that these two things can be found in infants: if there is no sin without will; if there is no will where freedom has not been unfolded; if there is no freedom where there is no capacity for choice through reason—by what monstrosity is sin found in infants who do not possess the use of reason?

Therefore they possess neither the capacity to choose nor, consequently, the will; and these points being irrefutably granted, they possess no sin at all.

Pressed by these massive difficulties, let us see where you have burst forth. “Infants,” you say, “are weighed down not by their own sin, but by another’s.” It is not yet clear what evil you think. We suspect that you brought this forward to arouse hatred against some person whose wickedness you wished to express, like a Carthaginian orator.

In whose case, then, did an external crime burden unblemished innocence?

[Note: [Col. 1069] The Marianus and Portus manuscripts read “will burden.”] Who was that person who condemned these infants as guilty—so senseless, so savage, so forgetful of God and equity, barbarous and rebellious?

[Note: [Col. 1069] The manuscripts read “and equity”; the editions have “and fairness.”]

We commend your talent entirely. Your learning is evident. You could not otherwise have alleged a figure worthy of the hatred of the human race—a judge, or rather a tyrant, I do not know whom—than by swearing that he not only did not spare those who had committed no sin, but also did not spare those who could not even have sinned.

[Note: [Col. 1069] The editions omit “even,” which is present in the manuscripts.]

A good conscience often struggles before a suspicious mind in defending itself, lest it may perhaps have committed a wrong, because it could have committed one. But someone is absolutely acquitted of a crime when the very impossibility of the act defends him. So reveal who this condemner of the innocent is.

You answer: God. You have indeed struck the mind; but because so great a sacrilege scarcely wins belief, we are uncertain what you have said.

[Note: [Col. 1069] Menard reads “you answer”; Vignier, “you might answer”; the manuscripts read “answering.”]

[Note: [Col. 1069] Vignier alone reads “we are uncertain.”]

We know that this name can be used ambiguously: “There are gods many and lords many; yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things” (1 Cor. 8:5–6). Which God, then, are you calling to account?

[Note: [Col. 1069] The editions read, “What then? Do you call God inexorable?” The reading has been corrected according to the Marianus and Portus manuscripts.]

Here, most devout priest and most learned rhetorician, you exhale something more grievous and more horrifying than either the valley of Amsanctus or the pit of Avernus—or rather, something more criminal than the idolatrous worship itself committed in those places.

[Note: [Col. 1069] Vignier has “the valley of Consentius.” The Marianus and Portus manuscripts read “the valley of Amsanctus.” It is a lake in Italy among the Hirpini, with sulfurous waters emitting a pestilential and deadly odor. Virgil discusses it in *Aeneid* 7.563–570, as does Cicero in *On Divination* 1.]

“You say” that God himself, who “commends his love toward us” (Rom. 5:8), who “loved us and did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us” (Rom. 8:32), himself judges in this way; he himself is the persecutor of those who are born; he himself consigns infants to eternal fires for an evil will, although he knows that they could possess neither a good nor an evil will.

After such a judgment—so monstrous, sacrilegious, and fatal—if we were using sound judges, I ought to report nothing except your execration. With just and appropriately weighty seriousness, I would judge you unworthy of debate, since you had fled so far from religion, learning, and finally common sense that you considered your own Lord, whom scarcely any barbarian would consider criminal.

[Note: [Col. 1070] The manuscripts read “just”; the editions have “righteousness.”]

Augustine: It is no great matter that you see infants do not possess their own will for choosing good or evil. I wish you could see what the one who wrote to the Hebrews saw when he said that Levi, son of Israel, was in the loins of his father Abraham when Abraham paid the tithe, and therefore that Levi also paid the tithe in him (Heb. 7:9–10).

If you had a Christian eye for this, you would perceive by faith—or, if you were unable to do so by understanding—that all who were to arise from Adam through the concupiscence of the flesh were in Adam’s loins. After the sin through which his nakedness was announced to him, Adam felt, looked upon, was ashamed of, and covered that concupiscence.

Hence my teacher Ambrose, whom even you, through the mouth of your own teacher, have praised outstandingly, says:

“What is more serious,” he says, “is that Adam girded himself with this interpretation in the place where he ought rather to have girded himself with the fruit of chastity. For in the loins with which we gird ourselves, certain seeds of generation are said to exist. And therefore Adam was wrongly girded there with useless leaves, where he signified not the future fruit of generation but certain future sins” (*On Paradise*, ch. 13).

He also rightly says what I mentioned shortly before: “Adam existed, and in him we all existed; Adam perished, and in him all perished.”

Not seeing this, you chatter blindly against me; but whatever you say against me, you certainly say also against him. Would that my reward with him were as common as the insult I hear from you that I share with him.

What is this that you shout and say: “If we were using sound judges, I ought to report nothing except your execration”? Can I deal with you more generously, more kindly, or more liberally than by placing among us as judge the very man whose judgment your teacher Pelagius has already given?

Here he is—the one who shone among Latin writers like a beautiful flower, whose faith and most pure understanding of the Scriptures even an enemy did not dare criticize. This is what Pelagius judged about Ambrose (Pelagius, *On Free Choice*, book 3).

What, then, did Ambrose judge concerning the matter at issue between us? Above I stated his opinions about original sin, without obscurity or ambiguity. But if that is insufficient, listen further:

“We are all born under sin,” he says, “our very birth being in fault” (Ambrose, *On Repentance*, book 1, ch. 2 or 3).

What do you answer to this? Pelagius made that splendid statement about Ambrose; Ambrose plainly pronounced this statement on my behalf and against you. Rebuke the man of whom your teacher says that even an enemy did not dare criticize him. Since you seek sound judges, declare this man unsound, so that you may openly confess yourself insane.

But you, a very devout man, are indignant that unregenerate infants, if they die before exercising their own will, are said to be condemned because of another’s sins—by the one who “commends his love toward us,” who “loved us and did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us”—as though fools and ignorant people like you did not complain even more gravely against him when they say:

“Why does he create those whom he foreknew would become wicked and be condemned? Why, finally, does he allow them to live until they reach damnable impiety, when he could remove them from this life before they became such—if he loves souls, if he commends his love toward us, if he did not spare his Son, but delivered him up for us all?”

When they are told, “O man, who are you to answer back to God?” (Rom. 9:20), and “His judgments are inscrutable” (Rom. 11:33), they grow angry rather than calm down. But “the Lord knows those who are his” (2 Tim. 2:19).

If, then, you wish to use sound judges, listen to the sound judge whom your teacher praised in a singular way:

“Adam existed,” he says, “and in him we all existed; Adam perished, and in him all perished.”

“But,” you say, “they certainly ought not to have perished because of another’s sins.”

They are another’s, but they are paternal sins; and therefore, by the law of sowing and generation, they are also ours. Who frees anyone from this destruction except the one who came “to seek what was lost” (Luke 19:10)?

In those whom he frees, then, let us embrace mercy; in those whom he does not free, let us acknowledge a judgment that is indeed most hidden, but without any doubt most just.

### XLIX. Julian

[Note: [Col. 1071] The manuscripts read “fought”; Vignier reads “might have fought.”]

Manichaeus invented and believed that the God of light had fought with the prince of darkness, and he added that the substance of the God of light was held captive in this world. Yet he tries to excuse such great misery under the appearance of piety, asserting that, as a good citizen, God fought for his homeland and therefore exposed his limbs so as not to lose his kingdoms.

[Note: [Col. 1071] The Marianus and Portus manuscripts read “asserts.”]

You, who had learned these doctrines, observe how much you have gained by abandoning them, even temporarily. You say that God did not endure the necessity of war but committed the injustice of judgment; that he is subject not to dark enemies but to obvious accusations; and finally, that he did not expose his substance but violated eternal righteousness.

I leave it to others to judge which of you is worse.

[Note: [Col. 1071] The editions read “Which of you is worse,” omitting “in what respect,” which is found in the manuscripts.]

Nevertheless, this much is clear: you both return to one and the same impious opinion. For Manichaeus also attributes injustice to his god when he alleges that, on the last day, he will condemn the limbs he delivered up. And you assert him miserable precisely by that through which he corrupted the glory in which he shone and, by persecuting the innocence he created, lost the righteousness by which he was most holy.

[Note: [Col. 1072] The Marianus manuscript reads “corrupts.”]

Thus the god whom you introduce is superior to the one your teacher invented by as much as being defeated in battle is more excusable than being defeated by vice.

Augustine: If you are pleased by the innocence of infants, remove from them, if you can, the heavy yoke that is upon the children of Adam from the day they leave their mother’s womb (Ecclus. 40:1).

But I think that the Scripture which said this knew better than you what the innocence of a creature and the righteousness of the Creator are. Who would not see that, if infants possess the innocence you proclaim, God’s righteousness cannot be present in their heavy yoke? Since divine righteousness is present in their heavy yoke, they do not possess the kind of innocence you proclaim.

Unless perhaps, as you struggle with this question, a just but somehow weak God can help you: he could not help his images so that they would not be oppressed by the misery of a heavy yoke, although he wished to do so because he is just, but could not because he is not omnipotent. Thus you may escape these difficulties, but you lose the foundation of the faith by which we first confess in the Creed that we believe in God the Father almighty.

Your god, then, in the face of so many and such great evils that infants suffer, will have to lose either his righteousness, his omnipotence, or his very care for human affairs. Whichever of these you say, consider what you will be.

[Note: [Col. 1072] The editions read “consider what you have done.” The manuscripts correct the reading.]

### L. Julian

Remove yourself, then, with such a god of yours, from the midst of the churches. He is not the one in whom the Patriarchs, the Prophets, and the Apostles believed, in whom the early Church, which is enrolled in heaven, hoped and hopes (Heb. 12:23). He is not the one whom rational creation believes to be judge, whom the Holy Spirit declares will judge justly.

No prudent person would ever have shed his blood for such a Lord; for he did not deserve the affection of love, so that anyone should undertake the burden of suffering for him.

Finally, if the one whom you introduce existed anywhere, he would be proved guilty, not a god, and would have to be judged by my true God, not judge in place of God.

To make you understand the first foundations of the faith: our God, the God of the Catholic Church, is unknown to us in substance and likewise removed from sight;

[Note: [Col. 1072] The editions read “alone”; the manuscripts more correctly read “solely.”]

 “no human being has seen him or can see him” (1 Tim. 6:16). Eternal and without beginning, he is likewise holy and just, without defect; most omnipotent, most equitable, most merciful, made known solely through the splendor of his virtues; creator of all things that did not exist, dispenser of all those that exist, examiner of all who are, who will be, and who have been, on the last day;

[Note: [Col. 1072] The Portus codex reads “of all those.”] he will move earth, heaven, and all the elements together; he will raise the ashes and restore the bodies—but he will do all these things solely on account of righteousness.

Augustine: If you worship the God of the Patriarchs, why do you not believe that circumcision on the eighth day, which was commanded to Abraham, was a prefiguration of regeneration in Christ? If you believed this, you would see that the soul of an infant could not justly be cut off from its people if he was not circumcised on the eighth day (Gen. 17:12–14), unless it had been bound by some sin.

If you worship the God of the Prophets, why do you not believe that God repeatedly said through them, “I will repay the sins of the fathers upon the children” (Exod. 34:7; Jer. 32:18)?

If you worship the God of the Apostles, why do you not believe that “the body is dead because of sin” (Rom. 8:10)?

If you worship the God in whom the early Church, which is enrolled in heaven, hoped and hopes, why do you not believe that infants are to be rescued from the power of darkness (Col. 1:13), since for this reason the Church breathes upon them and exorcizes them, so that the power of darkness may be driven out from them?

But the one whom rational creation, which is in his saints and faithful people, hopes as judge—read to us, besides the kingdom prepared for the good and punishment for the wicked, what third place he has prepared and promised for your unregenerate innocents.

[Note: [Col. 1073] The editions read “where read to us.” The word “where” is absent from the manuscripts.]

How can you say that no prudent person shed blood for the Lord whom we worship, when the most glorious Cyprian worshiped him and shed his blood for him? Cyprian suffocates you in this very question when he says that an infant born carnally from Adam contracts the contagion of ancient death through his first birth (Epistle 64, to Fidus).

Do you see that you are rather the guilty one, who blaspheme the God of these holy martyrs?

[Note: [Col. 1073] The manuscripts read “the guilty one.” The editions have “See to it that you are not rather guilty.”]

You say that you worship the most omnipotent, most equitable, and most merciful God. But he is truly omnipotent who could unquestionably remove from the children of Adam the heavy yoke under which they are oppressed from the day of their birth—or rather, could ensure that they were not oppressed by any such yoke at all.

But he is truly most equitable who would in no way impose that yoke, or permit it to be imposed, unless he found in them the sins with which they were born, whose guilt that same most merciful God would remove from the regenerate.

[Note: [Col. 1073] The passage is restored with the help of the old codices. The editions read, corruptly, “or rather, he would in no way impose it,” omitting the words “that they should not at all be burdened by any such yoke,” and what follows.]

If you took delight in divine righteousness, you would certainly see that from it comes—not unjustly beginning with infants—the human misery known to all, by which this life proceeds from the first cries of those being born to the final breaths of those dying; while happiness is promised to the holy and faithful only in another life.

[Note: [Col. 1073] Vignier reads “re-promised.” Menard and the manuscripts read “promised.”]

### LI. Julian

For this God of mine, whom every creature and Holy Scripture declare to me to be such as I believe him to be, I would more correctly have said that I should not consider you worthy of a literary contest.

[Note: [Col. 1073] Vignier and Menard read “to say”; the manuscript reads “I would say.”] But since this task has been imposed upon me above all by holy men, confessors of our own time—that I should examine what weight and reason your statements possess—it was appropriate first to show that you do not believe in the God who has always been preached in the Catholic Church and will be preached wherever that Church exists until the end.

Augustine: Rather, I have shown that you did not show what you claim to have shown; and, if you are not excessively blind, I have taught that I believe in the God who has always been preached by the Catholic Church.

### LII. JULIAN

Now, accordingly, I shall examine by what testimonies you try to affirm this position, which overthrows the faith of devout people. But since I have undertaken to oppose your second book, which Alypius brought, so that the sequence of the reply would not be confused [Note: [Col. 1074] The printed editions read, “so that the truth of the replies would not be confused.” But the manuscripts of Mar., Port., and Clar. read, “so that the sequence of the reply would not be confused.”], I must still respond briefly, until the argument reaches the testimony of the Apostle, by which you think yourself very strongly fortified. To the words of yours that I quoted above, you add the following:

> “In those matters, therefore, which he omitted, he feared this: for it agrees with the whole heart of the Catholic Church and, as it were, with a clear voice summons forth the faith itself, handed down and established from ancient times; and it vehemently attacks those against whom we have spoken, because they say that there is no sin in infants to be washed away by the bath of regeneration. For everyone hastens to the Church with infants for no other reason than that in them original sin, contracted through the first birth, may be expiated through the regeneration of a second birth.
>
> “Then he returns to our earlier words, which I do not know why he repeats: ‘We say that those who are born from such a union draw original sin, and, whatever sort of parents they are born from, we do not deny that they still remain under the devil unless they are reborn in Christ.’ He had said these words shortly before as well. Then he added what we said about Christ: ‘Who did not wish to be born from the same union of the two sexes.’ But here too he omitted what I had written: ‘So that, rescued by his grace from the power of darkness, they may be transferred into the kingdom of him who did not wish to be born from the same union of the two sexes.’
>
> “Observe, I beg you, which of our words he avoided, like one altogether hostile to the grace of God that comes through Jesus Christ our Lord. For he knows that, according to that statement of the Apostle in which he spoke of God the Father—‘Who rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love’ (Colossians 1:13)—infants are most wickedly and impiously separated from that kingdom [Note: [Col. 1074] The printed editions read, “and most impurely.” But the manuscripts, as in the second book On Marriage and Concupiscence, read, “most impiously.”]. Therefore, without doubt, he preferred to omit these words rather than include them” (On Marriage and Concupiscence, book 2, §§4–5).

Am I hostile to the grace of God, you most shameless of men, when in my first book—from which you have torn these words away from their context so that you might babble something without reason—I condemned, with a pure and full confession, your mouth steeped in Manichaean mysteries?

### AUGUSTINE

Will you manufacture a good case for yourself by hurling insults? Tell me whose mouth among my own you claim to have condemned, just as you boast that you condemned mine [Note: [Col. 1074] Thus the manuscripts of Port. and Mar.; Vignierius, however, reads: “Say whose mouths of mine, and mine, you condemn, just as you boast that you condemned them.”]. You are going to say, “the Manichaeans,” but as a slanderer, not as a speaker of truth. For I detest both the Manichaeans and their assistants, among whom you seek primacy [Note: [Col. 1074] Two manuscripts, Port. and Mar., read *appetitis*, “you seek”; the other books more correctly read *appetis*, “you seek”—spoken to Julian.], and, with our Lord God [Col. 1075] assisting and supporting us, I refute both groups by Catholic truth.

But I shall identify my own authorities, whom you accuse against me all the more wickedly because you do so more craftily. In this controversy, where the question of original sin is at issue, Cyprian is mine. Although he said that an infant had committed no sin, he nevertheless did not remain silent about the fact that the infant contracted the contagion of sin from Adam through the first birth (Epistle 64, to Fidus).

Hilary is mine. In explaining the words found in the Psalm, “My soul shall live and shall praise you,” he says: “He does not reckon that he lives in this life, since he had said, ‘Behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and my mother bore me in sins’” (Psalm 50:7). “He knows that he was born under the origin of sin and under the law of sin” (On Psalm 118, 175).

Ambrose is mine, the man whom your teacher praised so outstandingly. He said: “We are all born under sin, and our very birth is in fault, as you have it in the words of David: ‘Behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and my mother bore me in sins.’ Therefore Paul’s flesh was a body of death” (On Repentance, book 1, chapter 2).

Gregory is mine. Speaking about Baptism, he says: “Venerate the birth through which you have been freed from the bonds of earthly birth” [Note: [Col. 1075] The printed editions read, “for which you have been freed.” The manuscript reading has been restored.](Oration on the Nativity of Christ).

Basil is mine. Speaking about fasting, he says: “Because we did not fast, we fell from paradise; let us fast, so that we may return to it” (Sermon 1 on Fasting).

John of Constantinople is mine. He says: “Adam committed that great sin and condemned the entire human race together” (Homily on the Raising of Lazarus).

All these men, and their other companions who held the same view, whom it would take too long to name, are mine [Note: [Col. 1075] He mentioned these and many others above, in his earlier work Against Julian, book 1, chapters 3–6, and elsewhere.]. If you acknowledge them, they are yours as well; but they are my teachers and your critics.

How, then, have you condemned my mouth and the mouths of those who are mine, when you yourself are condemned all the more by the most harmonious and truthful mouth of those whom you see to be mine? Do you dare, with a mind most darkened, a forehead most shameless, and a tongue most impudent, to charge these lights of the City of God with being Manichaeans? If you do not dare, why do you dare to charge me with this for no other reason than that I say what those men say whom you do not dare to accuse?

### LIII. JULIAN

Here, then, is the order of the words that I set forth, when I had said that God is the author of heaven and earth and of all that is in them, and therefore also of human beings, for whose sake all things were made.

“I am not unaware,” I said [Note: [Col. 1075] Thus the manuscripts. Menardus reads *quod*, “that”; Vignierius reads *in quo*, “in which.” Julian said this in his first work addressed to Turbantius; Augustine refuted it above, in book 3 Against Julian, §8 and following.], “that when we say these things, it will be spread about concerning us that we do not consider Christ’s grace necessary for infants. This greatly and deservedly offends Christian peoples—provided, however, that they do not regard us as the authors of the impious statement itself. For in that way they would neither incur guilt by believing something false about their brothers nor prove themselves zealous for the love of the faith.

“Therefore this part [Col. 1076] must be defended by us against the assault of vanity, and the mouths of our slanderers must be stopped by a brief confession. We therefore confess Baptismal grace to be useful to every age to such an extent that we strike with an eternal anathema all who think it unnecessary even for infants.

“But we believe this grace to be rich in spiritual gifts, adorned with many benefits and revered for its virtues; and, according to the kinds of infirmities and the diversity of human conditions, it heals by one power, both granting remedies [Note: [Col. 1076] Menardus reads, “the sole giver of remedies”; Vignierius, “the unique giver of remedies.” The text is corrected according to the manuscripts.] and bestowing gifts. Once it is applied [Note: [Col. 1076] Menardus reads *amovetur*, “is removed,” corruptly. Here Julian is professing concerning the rite of Baptism what Pelagius had professed before him in his Statement of Faith, §7, below in the Appendix, part 2: “‘We hold one Baptism,’ he says, ‘which we assert is celebrated with the same words of the sacrament for infants as for adults.’ See also the Statement of Faith of the Pelagians in the Appendix, §6, written by Julian.], it must not be changed according to circumstances; for it already distributes its gifts according to the capacity of those who approach it.

“For just as all the arts do not themselves suffer either loss or increase according to the diversity of the materials that they undertake to cultivate, but, remaining always the same and operating in one manner [Note: [Col. 1076] Perhaps, *eaedem*, “the same [arts].”], are adorned with diverse effects [Note: [Col. 1076] The printed editions read *affectu*, “disposition”; the manuscripts differ.], so also, according to the Apostle, there is ‘one faith, one Baptism’ (Ephesians 4:5). They are multiplied and expanded in their gifts, yet the orders of the mysteries are not changed.

“But this grace does not oppose justice, which washes away the stains of iniquity. It does not create sins but cleanses them; it absolves the guilty and does not accuse the innocent. For Christ, who is the redeemer of his own work, continually increases his benefits toward his image by generous giving; and those whom he made good by creation, he makes better by renewal and adoption.”

This grace, then, through which pardon is given to the guilty, spiritual illumination, adoption as children of God, citizenship in heavenly Jerusalem, sanctification, transfer into the members of Christ, and possession of the kingdom of heaven—whoever thinks it should be denied to some people deserves the execration of all good things.

### AUGUSTINE

Among all these gifts of God’s grace that you have listed, you do not wish that the first one you mentioned—pardon being given through it to the guilty—should apply to infants, whom you deny to have contracted any guilt from Adam.

Why, then, does God deny many other things to infants who die at that age without this grace? Why, I ask, are they not given spiritual illumination, adoption as children of God, citizenship in heavenly Jerusalem, sanctification, transfer into the members of Christ, and possession of the kingdom of heaven? Would God deny so many gifts, so necessary, to so many of his images, who according to you possess no sin at all, when the contrary will of infants does not prevent this benefit from coming from him, in whose hands supreme power lies?

Certainly, to remove this reproach from yourselves—that you are said to deny infants the grace of Baptism—you said that whoever thinks this grace should be denied to some people deserves the execration of all good things [Col. 1077]. Therefore the justice of almighty God would not deny it to countless infants who die under his omnipotence without it, if they deserved no evil according to his hidden judgment.

From this judgment, owed to all who come from Adam’s stock, let everyone who is freed according to grace, not according to what is owed, glory not in his own merits but in the Lord.

If you wish, then, to escape the reproach by which you have become hateful to the Catholic Church, allow Christ to be Jesus for infants. This will certainly not happen if he does not confer upon them the reason why he received this name—that is, if he does not save them from their sins (Matthew 1:21).

Concerning this grace, therefore, say what the Catholic and learned teacher Gregory said, so that you may escape the offense of Christians about which you complain: “Venerate the birth through which you have been freed from the bonds of earthly birth.” You plainly confess that infants have no part in this grace so long as you deny that by a heavenly birth they are freed from the bonds of earthly birth.

### LIV. JULIAN

Since I have defended this point as far as the present place allowed, let us return to the place from which we digressed; we shall speak more fully about this same matter wherever it is appropriate.

Behold how clearly I have condemned both those who deny Baptism to infants and you, who dare to stain God’s justice by prejudging it. I have declared that I hold nothing other than that the established mysteries must be administered at every age in the very words in which they were handed down [Note: [Col. 1077] The manuscript of Mar. reads, “in the words in which they were handed down,” which is no less correct.], and that they must not be changed according to the variety of circumstances.

Rather, the sinner is made perfectly good from evil, while the innocent person, who has no evil of his own will, is made better from good—that is, best. Thus both, consecrated, pass into the members of Christ: one discovered in an evil life, the other in a good nature.

The former corrupted by wicked action the innocence he had received at birth. The latter, without praise and without guilt of will, possesses only what he received from God the Creator. Happier in his untainted primeval state [Note: [Col. 1077] The same manuscript of Mar. reads, “darkened,” rather than “unclouded.”], he could not corrupt the goodness of his simplicity; he has no merit arising from his actions, but retains only what he possessed by the favor of so great an Artisan.

### AUGUSTINE

Why, then, is a heavy yoke upon him from the day he leaves his mother’s womb (Ecclesiasticus 40:1)? Why is his body so corruptible that his soul is weighed down by it (Wisdom 9:15)? Why is his mind so dull that even through blows his sluggishness must be instructed?

How long, Julian, will you be heavy of heart? How long will you love vanity and seek falsehood (Psalm 4:3), by which your heresy may be supported? If no one had sinned, and if human nature had remained in the goodness in which it was created, would a human being even in paradise have been born into these miseries—to say nothing of others?

### LV. JULIAN

Therefore, just as that age proclaims Christ’s mercy by being renewed—that is, advanced through the power of the renewing mystery—so it proves either by accusation or by aggravation the judge’s iniquity and the disgrace of justice.

### AUGUSTINE

From what former state is that age said to be renewed, when it is new by birth? These are deceitful lips. If you wish to recognize the oldness from which infants are renewed by Christian grace, listen faithfully to what the man of God Reticius, bishop of Autun, said. He once sat as a judge with Melchiades, bishop of Rome, and condemned the heretic Donatus.

Speaking about Christian Baptism, he says: “No one is unaware, therefore, that this is the principal indulgence in the Church, in which we set forth the whole burden of the ancient crime and erase the old offenses of our ignorance; where we also strip off the old man together with his inborn crimes” [Note: [Col. 1078] See above, book 1 Against Julian, §7.].

Do you hear that he speaks not only of crimes committed afterward but also of the inborn crimes of the old man? Was Reticius a Manichaean? How, then, can you deceitfully say that infants are renewed in Christian regeneration, when you refuse to acknowledge in the old man the evils generated by the burden of the ancient crime?

Furthermore, if, as you say, that age proves the judge’s iniquity by being aggravated, was it not aggravated by the heavy yoke imposed upon the children of Adam? Yet God is not thereby unjust; and therefore it was rightly aggravated. This age has no evil merit if there is no original sin.

### LVI. JULIAN

Infancy, therefore, is not shown to be guilty by the unity of the sacrament; rather, by the truth of judgment it is approved as nothing other than innocent.

### AUGUSTINE

You think you have discovered why infants are baptized. Say why they are exsufflated. Certainly, the great and invincible statement of your author Pelagius is considered decisive, where he says: “If Adam’s sin harmed even those who did not sin, then Christ’s righteousness also benefits even those who do not believe” [Note: [Col. 1078] See above, On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins, book 3, §2, and below, the Commonitorium of Mercator, in the second part of the Appendix.].

What, then, do you say about infants when they are baptized? Do they believe, or do they not believe? [Note: [Col. 1078] The printed editions read *dicis*, “do you say,” and below *dixeris*, “if you say”; the manuscripts consistently have the plural, *dicitis*, “do you say,” and *dixeritis*, “if you say.”]

If you say, “They do not believe,” how does Christ’s righteousness benefit even those who do not believe, so that they may possess the kingdom of heaven? [Note: [Col. 1078] At this point a negative particle was missing; later Vignierius, contrary to the manuscript evidence, supplied it in two places thus: “Or if it does not benefit, as you are compelled to confess: therefore Adam’s sin did not harm them.”] Or, if it does benefit them, as you are compelled to confess, then Adam’s sin harmed those who did not yet possess the will to sin in the same way that Christ’s righteousness benefits those who did not yet possess the will to believe?

But if you say, “They believe through others,” then they also sinned through another. And since it is true that they believe through others—for this reason they are called believers throughout the whole Church—they plainly belong to what the Lord said: “Whoever does not believe will be condemned” (Mark 16:16).

They will therefore be condemned if they do not believe through others, since they are unable to believe by themselves. But they could not in any way be justly condemned if they were not born under sin and therefore also under the prince of sin [Note: [Col. 1078] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read, “are born.”].

For this reason, then, they are also exsufflated. Remove from them your deceptive vanity. Allow the infants to come to Jesus (Mark 10:14), who saves his people—which certainly includes them—from their sins (Matthew 1:21).

### [Col. 1079] LVII. JULIAN

Although reason, which does not allow things joined by their own law to be divided, compels me to linger over explaining the condition of infants, the loss of those being born would otherwise be easier to bear if majesty itself were not endangered along with them [Note: [Col. 1079] Thus the manuscripts read *si non compericlitaretur*; the printed editions, *si non cum eis periclitaretur*.].

Therefore, excuse God and accuse the infant. Let him be shown just in what he does, since God cannot be God without justice; and let any person whatsoever suffer punishment.

But as matters now stand, the things that you think are joined together, apart from sacrilege, strongly contradict one another. You say that because idolaters, parricides [Note: [Col. 1079] The printed editions read, “just as idolaters and parricides.” Some manuscripts omit “just as.”], and infants are initiated by the same mysteries [Note: [Col. 1079] On the authority of the manuscripts, *unis*, “the same,” has been restored.], all the wicked can be convicted. And you add something much more absurd: that the author of this sacrament, of which we are speaking, imputes the sins of others to the innocent [Note: [Col. 1079] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read, “that the author of this sacrament, of which we are speaking, imputes the sins of others to the innocent.”].

This is what I said was contradictory, because the nature of things does not permit God at one and the same time to be so merciful that he forgives each person who confesses his own sins, and so cruel that he thrusts the sins of others upon an innocent person.

Once you grant one of these, you have taken away the other [Note: [Col. 1079] The manuscripts read *tulisti*, “you have taken away”; the printed editions, *sustulisti*, “you have completely taken away.”]: if he grants pardon to the guilty, he does not accuse the innocent; if he accuses the innocent, he never spares the guilty.

### AUGUSTINE

You, rather, make God unjust when it seems unjust to you that he repays the sins of fathers upon their children—a thing that he both frequently declares in words and demonstrates in deeds.

You, I say, make God unjust, under whose omnipotent care you see infants weighed down by the heavy yoke of misery, while you insist that they have no sin, thereby accusing both God and the Church: God, if they are burdened and afflicted undeservedly; the Church, if they are exsufflated as those who are not subject to the right of the devil.

But where did you dream that we equate the original sins of infants with those of idolaters and parricides? Nevertheless, the remission of sins placed in the mysteries is true with regard to sins—whether greater or lesser, many or few, or individual sins. But where there are no sins at all, as you say is the case with infants, it is false.

Original sins are alien in such a way that there is no decision of our will in them; yet because of the contagion of origin they are found to be ours as well.

What, then, is the basis of your outcry when you say that God cannot both forgive the sins proper to adults and impute alien sins to infants? Why do you refuse to consider that he forgives both only in those reborn in Christ, while he forgives neither in those not reborn in Christ [Note: [Col. 1079] The manuscripts read *dimittat*, “he forgives”; the printed editions, *dimittantur*, “are forgiven.”]?

These are the mysteries of Christian grace, hidden from the wise and prudent and revealed to infants (Matthew 11:25). If only you were among them, and did not, as though great, trust in your own strength, you would surely understand that the injustice of the first man is imputed to infants born into the world for the suffering of punishment in the same way that the righteousness of the second man is imputed to infants reborn for the attainment of the kingdom of heaven—even though by their own will and action they are found to have imitated neither the former in evil nor the latter in good.

### [Col. 1080] LVIII. JULIAN

I omitted nothing from your words, therefore, compelled—as you say—by fear. What could I fear in the monuments of so elegant an intellect, except perhaps only this: that I am enduring horror from the attack upon your obscenity?

### AUGUSTINE

If you had bought these insults, I would call you extravagant. They lie beside you free of charge; why not enjoy them, since they feed your slanderous spirit?

### LIX. JULIAN

Listen, then, briefly, in response to what you have said. Those are not the hearts of the Catholic Church with which your speech agrees, if they disagree with piety and reason [Note: [Col. 1080] The printed editions read *quibus*, “with which”; the manuscripts, *quae*, “which.”]. They do both when they neither form a proper judgment about God’s justice nor understand the wisdom and riches of the mysteries that they accuse.

This is not the faith handed down and established from ancient times, except in the council of the wicked, inspired by the devil, brought forth by Manichaeus, celebrated by Marcion, Faustus, Adimantus, and all their satellites, and now—something we deeply lament—vomited by you into Italy [Note: [Col. 1080] Thus the manuscripts and printed editions; some read, “into Italia.”].

### AUGUSTINE

With what mouth, with what forehead, do you call the agreement of so many Catholics, who were teachers of the Churches before us, a council of the wicked?

As though, if the bishops whom I mentioned above, to omit others—Cyprian, Hilary, Ambrose, Gregory, Basil, and John of Constantinople—were sitting in a council of bishops, which you say ought to be convened not for the sake of healing but boastfully because of your questions, you would easily find some bishops who remain today whom you could equal, much less surpass, in the ecclesiastical teaching handed down from ancient times [Note: [Col. 1080] The printed editions read, “and others.” The manuscripts more correctly read, “some of those.”].

Since these men themselves produce clear and unmistakable statements against you concerning original sin—both those I cited shortly before and many others—do you dare to call their agreement in Catholic truth a council of the wicked? Do you consider how you might answer them, rather than how you might flee if you refuse to agree with them?

But since you said that I vomited into Italy what you lament, I turn against your forehead that same bishop of Italy whom your teacher praised: Ambrose.

“ We are all born under sin,” he says, “and our very birth is in fault, as you have it in the words of David: ‘Behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and my mother bore me in sins’ (Psalm 50:7). Therefore Paul’s flesh was a body of death, as he himself says: ‘Who will free me from this body of death?’ (Romans 7:24). ‘But Christ’s flesh condemned sin, which it did not experience by being born, and which it crucified by dying, so that in our flesh there might be justification through grace, where previously there had been defilement through guilt’” (On Repentance, book 1, chapter 2 or 3).

This, then, is the faith that I say was handed down and established from ancient times. You reject it, and do not consider whom you are resisting. Can you say that it was inspired by the devil? Is this man a Manichaean? Is he Marcion, Faustus, or Adimantus? Certainly not; he is far different from and far opposed to them.

Let Pelagius himself say who this man is. He is the one—the very one—whose faith and most pure understanding of the Scriptures not even an enemy dared to criticize.

What is this, Julian? Where do you see yourself? The man whose faith not even an enemy dared to criticize held the faith that you criticize in such a way that you attribute it to councils of the wicked.

Behold, it is not theirs but Ambrose’s, because it is true, because it is sound, because, as I said, it was handed down and established from ancient times. It is also mine.

I did not vomit it into Italy, as you say you lament. Rather, I received the bath of regeneration from this Italian bishop, who proclaimed and taught it [Note: [Col. 1081] Two manuscripts omit “and taught” after “proclaimed it.”].

Since this faith is Catholic and yet is not yours, where, then, are you? Look, I beg you, and return. It is in your interest to see, not to envy; we desire your return, not your destruction.

### LX. JULIAN

There is no sin in a human being if there is no personal will or consent. Every human being who has even a slight degree of understanding agrees with me on this without hesitation.

But you concede that there was no personal will in infants. It is not I but reason that draws the conclusion: therefore there is no sin in them.

They are not brought to the Church, then, for this reason—that they may be disgraced, or rather that they may disgrace God. They are brought so that they may praise God, whom they proclaim to be the author both of natural goods and of spiritual gifts.

### AUGUSTINE

They are not disgraced when they are exsufflated; they are rescued from the power of darkness. Nor do they disgrace God; rather, the one whose creation they are requires them to have him as their Savior. Therefore, by being reborn, they are transferred from Adam to Christ.

When you said, “There is no sin in a human being if there is no personal will or consent,” you would have stated the truth more fully if you had added, “or contagion.”

### LXI. JULIAN

But if original sin is contracted through the first birth, it may indeed condemn marriages instituted by God; nevertheless, it cannot be taken away from infants, since what is born into a person remains with that person until the end, because it has adhered to him from the causes of his beginnings.

### AUGUSTINE

It does not condemn marriage, because marriage itself is not the cause of sin. And it is removed by that Almighty who was also able to be born as a human being without it [Note: [Col. 1081] Vignierius reads *ut*, “so that.” The manuscripts more correctly read *et*, “and.”].

### LXII. JULIAN

We are not, then, bringing any charge against you as though you condemned marriage or as though you said that the human being born from it is the work of the devil. We do not make this objection in bad faith, nor do we draw it incompetently; rather, we carefully and straightforwardly observe the consequence of the statements involved.

Physical marriage is never without sexual union. You say that all who are born from that union belong to the devil. Beyond doubt, you declare that marriage belongs to the jurisdiction of the demon.

### AUGUSTINE

Do we say that marriage in paradise could have existed without bodily union if no one had sinned? But the evil that conjugal chastity now makes good use of would not have been there.

That evil comes from the wound inflicted by the devil’s cunning. From this arises the guilt of mortal offspring; from this comes the fact that the one who is born is under the prince of sins until he is reborn in Christ, who had absolutely no sin. From Christ alone the bond of death is loosed, because he alone was free among the dead.

### LXIII. JULIAN

You say that sin is drawn from the condition of nature, while you wish this evil to have arisen from the will of the first man. I postpone here the response by which you will be convicted of lying without shame.

But concerning the present passage, I gather and accept what reasoning wisdom teaches: namely, that you unambiguously define a diabolical nature. For if there is in it or through it something on account of which a human being is possessed by the devil, then it is irrefutably of the devil, through which he was able to claim God’s image for himself.

Indeed, it is not God’s image if, by its birth, it is in the devil’s kingdom.

### AUGUSTINE

You believe—but you believe the folly of one who merely speculates, not the wisdom of one who reasons. Allow infants to be rescued from the power of darkness so that they may be transferred into Christ’s kingdom.

By saying that they do not possess the contagion of the ancient offense, and thus removing them from the mercy of the Savior who saves his people from their sins, from which he was named Jesus (Matthew 1:21), you achieve nothing except that God’s anger remains upon them. Job spoke of this anger when he said:

> “A human being born of woman is short-lived and full of anger; like a flower of the grass he withers, and he flees like a shadow and does not remain. Have you not also cared for him, and have you brought him into judgment before you? For who will be clean from defilement? Not even one, even if his life upon earth should be only one day” (Job 14:1–4, according to the Septuagint).
