But evidently, merciful man that you are, you pity God’s image lest you say that it is born carnally under sin. How cruel is this empty mercy of yours, which denies infants the mercy of their Savior, who came to seek what was lost (Luke 19:10)!

Through those defilements, therefore, without which the man of God says that no human being exists—even if his life upon earth is only one day—the devil claims God’s image, not through the substance that God created.

Nature has been corrupted; it is not itself corruption.

But you say [Note: [Col. 1082] Vignierius’s edition reads *tum*, “then”; the manuscripts read *tu*, “you.”]: “Nor is it God’s image if, by its birth, it is in the devil’s kingdom.”

What if someone else were to say to you: “It is not God’s image if, though guilty of no sin, it nevertheless does not enter the kingdom of God”? Would you not have nothing to answer if you did not wish to answer falsely?

Certainly, a human being is God’s image because he was made in God’s likeness. Why, then, has he also been made like vanity, on account of which his days pass away like a shadow (Psalm 143:4)? You will not separate infants from this vanity, since their days also pass away like a shadow.

Finally, will you separate them from the living as well? Listen, then, to the one who says in the Psalm: “Behold, you have made my days old, and my substance is as nothing before you; nevertheless every living human being is altogether vanity” (Psalm 38:6).

Since every living human being is God’s image, tell me from where every living human being is also vanity.

But what will you say, since you do not wish to acknowledge that one of these conditions comes from God’s creation, while the other arose from the condition of sin?

Permit us, we ask, to have the living human being, who was made in the likeness of God, rescued from the power of darkness, under which he was made like vanity. Let him now, for the present, be rescued from the obligation of guilt; and after this corruptible life, from every kind of vanity as well.

### [Col. 1083] LXIV. JULIAN

If, then, you read my work, you will cease to wonder why I returned to the words of yours that I had quoted above.

I had promised that from your writings I would prove that, between the impiety you had imbibed and the envy you feared, you had uttered both things at once: what Catholics commonly assert and what the Manichaeans commonly assert.

The order of the words there is therefore directed against your head, although you have now falsely claimed, with the brazen face of a sycophant, that it was interpolated [Note: [Col. 1083] Vignierius’s edition reads *amotus*, “removed.” The text is corrected according to the manuscripts.].

I know that I made a great promise: namely, to prove from the words of my opponent both that those who deny that human beings are the work of God are rightly condemned and that the very man who confesses this does nothing other than establish as the devil’s property whatever proceeds from the fruitfulness of marriage.

By this method, the Manichaean opinion will also be destroyed according to the laws of its own defense. But the entire opening of his book made this public. For he says that human beings who are born from marriage—that is, from males and females—are a divine work. By this statement he overturns everything he was about to argue and agrees with us when we say that those who dare to deny these things are impious.

One part, then, has already been settled. It remains for me to show that he asserts what he had recently attacked.

With these words I reviewed part of your statement, in which you had said:

> “We say that those who are born from such a union draw original sin; and, whatever sort of parents they are born from, we do not deny that they still remain under the devil unless they are reborn in Christ and, rescued by his grace from the power of darkness, are transferred into the kingdom of him who did not wish to be born from the same union of the two sexes.”

Why, then, do you think that this can excuse you from the error of the Manichaeans? You dared to insert a statement with which you had struggled with all the powers of your intellect. This is not a defense of your error but evidence of singular folly: you think that, after the manner of Calliphon, virtue and vices, justice and iniquity, can be brought together in alliance by your speech.

But as for what the Apostle says—“Who rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love”—read the fourth book of my work. Then it will become known to you what the Teacher of the Gentiles understood.

AUGUSTINE: To our sixth book a reply was made in your fourth, and now I chiefly urge those who wish to know how far you deviated from the truth there, and how thoroughly you were refuted by the truth, to read both what you wrote and what I wrote. As for this little document, in which certain passages extracted from your books have been written down, you are free to charge me with what was done by the man who sent it to the person who sent it to me. For he inserted in it from your work whatever he wished and omitted whatever he wished [Note: [Col. 1083] On the authority of the old books we add: “from your work.”]; hence I have already given you a brief but sufficient answer above. Why do you attempt to obscure the Apostle’s plain statements with your obscure ones? He who preached God says, “He delivered us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of his beloved Son” (Colossians 1:13); and you say that this was said by him, except with respect to infants [Note: [Col. 1084] Vignierius reads “concerning him.” Other books, more correctly, read “by him.”].

If, then, infants are not delivered from the power of darkness, they are not dead; if they are not dead, Christ did not die for them. Yet you confess that Christ died even for them; and the Apostle likewise says, “One died for all; therefore all died” (2 Corinthians 5:14). This conclusion of the Apostle is invincible; and therefore, since he died also for infants, infants too certainly died.

Moreover, Christ died “to destroy him who held the power of death, that is, the devil” (Hebrews 2:14). Allow infants, then, to be delivered from the power of darkness so that they may live. What, then, is this charge you bring against me—that I follow the practice of Calliphon, or that I suppose that in my discourse virtue and vices, justice and iniquity, can be brought into alliance? God forbid that I should hold or teach such a thing in either heart or speech. I congratulate you, however, on having understood this philosopher so well. For when he supposed that the human good consisted in virtue of soul and bodily pleasure [Note: [Col. 1084] See Cicero, book 2 of the *Academica*, book 2 of the *De Finibus*, and Lactantius, *On False Wisdom*, book 3, chapter 7], you say that he wished to join virtues and vices together. Accordingly, as was proper, you judged the desire for bodily pleasure to be a vice; therefore lust is a vice—the very lust that you praise. Thus truth slipped in somehow into your understanding, so that, abandoning for a little while the cause you had undertaken, you said what we say.

LXV. JULIAN: Therefore I was rightly, and with justice, accused of a debased [Note: [Col. 1084] The manuscripts of Mar. and Port. read “delighted”; that is, “distinguished.” Cicero used “a chosen evil” in his speech *For His House*.] and feeble inconsistency, by which you had arranged both to declare beforehand that you did not condemn marriage [Note: [Col. 1084] So the manuscripts. The printed editions read “promise.”] and to say that, because of the union of man and woman—which plainly proceeds from the institution and nature of marriage, or rather in which alone, so far as our dispute is concerned, the reality of marriage consists—human beings are transferred into the jurisdiction of the devil.

AUGUSTINE: If the reality of marriage consists solely in the union of man and woman, then the reality of adulteries is the same as that of marriages, because this union of the two sexes exists in both. But since that is utterly absurd, the reality of marriage does not consist, as you rave, solely in the union of male and female, although without it marriage cannot propagate children. Rather, there are other things properly belonging to marriage by which marriages are distinguished from adulteries: for example, fidelity to the marriage bed, the ordered care of begetting children, and—what is the greatest distinction—the good use of an evil thing, that is, the good use of carnal desire, which adulterers use badly.

LXVI. JULIAN: You attempted to persuade us that this union was so execrable that you wanted it understood that Christ chose to be born of a virgin mother not because of the splendor of the sign, but because the union of the sexes was to be condemned. What, then, could ever have been said by anyone more wicked or shameless than this: that you set two persons, as though they were kings contending for possession of humanity, apart by these marks, and separated their two kingdoms, saying that whatever marriage produced belonged to the devil, while God’s was only what the virgin had borne? What else is this than to display the one who made the virgin fruitful as utterly impoverished through the poverty of his portion, and at the same time to deny that he was the creator of those who proceed from human marriages?

Let the diligent reader therefore retain the written record of your words and know that you, a faithful disciple of the Manichaeans and chief of the Traducian sect, have condemned nothing other than the union of lawful marriage.

AUGUSTINE: You do not possess senses trained to separate good from evil. The nature and substance of human beings and angels, whether good or evil, subsist by God the Creator; but the vices of natures and substances—which the Manichaeans call natures and substances, though truth denies that they are so—God, being just and almighty, permits to exist by a judicial ordering. These vices themselves are evil, and they cannot exist except in good things and in good natures.

Everything that is subjected to the devil by God’s judgment is indeed in the devil’s power, but it cannot be alien from God’s power, under which the devil himself has been placed. Since, therefore, all angels and all human beings are under God’s power, your empty verbosity is futile when you say that God and the devil divided among themselves which of those whom they possess each should hold under his own power [Note: [Col. 1085] The printed editions read “certain ones.” The manuscripts are corrected to “those whom.”].

But consider for a little while against whom you spew these insults on which you feed. Here is Ambrose himself. See what he says concerning the matter against which you rage: “How,” he says, “could he alone have been just, when every generation had gone astray, unless, being born of a virgin, he had been entirely exempt from the condition of an implicated generation?” (*On the Ark*).

Listen further—listen, and restrain your insolent tongue by striking your forehead: “For it was not intercourse with a man that opened the secrets of the virgin womb; rather, the Holy Spirit poured an undefiled seed into an inviolate womb. For the Lord Jesus alone among all those born of woman was holy in every respect: he did not experience the contagions of earthly corruption, because of the novelty of his immaculate birth, and he drove them away by his heavenly majesty” (*On Luke*, book 2, 23).

You see plainly who said what I am saying; you see against whom you are speaking in everything you say against me. For if I am on this account a disciple of Manichaeus, then so is he. But the man who said these things before us is not such a disciple. Therefore neither is whoever says these things; rather, whoever contradicts this ancient Catholic teaching is manifestly a heretic.

LXVII. JULIAN: But let us proceed to the rest. Writing about me, after the words of yours that I reproduced above, you add the following:

“After this he inserted a passage of ours, in which we said: ‘For this concupiscence, which is shamelessly praised by the shameless, and which ought to cause shame, would not exist if man had not sinned previously. Marriage, however, would exist even if no one had sinned; for the generation of children would take place without this disease.’ Thus far he inserted my words. For he feared what I added: ‘in the body of that life,’ without which it cannot now take place ‘in this body of death.’ And here, in order not to bring my statement to an end, but somehow to mutilate it, he feared the testimony of the Apostle, where he says: ‘Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the body of this death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord’ (Romans 7:24–25). For there was not this body of death in paradise before sin, which is why we said that in the body of that life, which existed there, the generation of children could have taken place without this disease, without which it cannot now take place in this body of death” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 2, section 6).

You are indeed maintaining your customary practice, and in this work especially you proceed consistently: since you act against the truth, you say nothing true. Yet the multitude of corrections scarcely suffices for the numerous errors of your learning. I shall therefore note briefly here that you deceive; after this work, however, you will understand that I am unaccustomed to falsehood [Note: [Col. 1086] The printed editions read “through”; the manuscripts read “after.”].

Claim the entire possession of this vice for yourself, so that—not without justice—you may hear from the Gospel that you are a liar from the beginning, just as your father is (John 8:44) [Note: [Col. 1086] The Port., Mar., and Clairvaux manuscripts read “not without justice.”]: either the one to whom you say that you belonged as your lord when you were born, or the other, subordinate one, who initiated you into refined rites—though such things cannot be named among decent people.

I have therefore set out in my earlier work the whole passage that you falsely claim was omitted. If you read near the end of the first volume, you yourself will be able to acknowledge how thoroughly and clearly it was refuted by the truth of the argument. It was not your truncated statement, then, but the whole statement that was destroyed by a powerful reply.

Now listen briefly. When the Apostle says, “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the body of this death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord,” he did not refer to the mortality of our body, which the flesh of animals received from the constitution of nature, but to the habit of sinning. From that guilt, after Christ’s incarnation, through the New Testament, whoever turns toward the pursuits of virtue is liberated.

There, therefore, speaking in the person of the Jews who, even after the prohibition of the sacred law, were still wandering through desire for enticements, he showed that at that time there was one aid: that they should believe in Christ. He announced safeguards concerning the future in such a way as to grant pardon for what had been done. He did not press upon the guilty the threat of punishment [Note: [Col. 1086] Vignierius reads “intention,” erroneously.]; rather, he cherished those who ran to him in a most generous embrace—not striking down those crushed by terror, but restoring those corrected by kindness.

Paul himself had already experienced this kindness when he said: “The saying is human: Christ Jesus came into this world to save sinners, of whom I am the first; but for this reason I received mercy, so that in me Christ Jesus might display all patience, as an example to those who will believe in him for eternal life” (1 Timothy 1:15–16).

To make you understand that this referred to an evil life, not to human nature—and lest, because of the reason for Christ’s coming, you should suppose that he declared even infants to be sinners—he says, “In me he displayed all patience.” The patience of God is that of which he speaks to the Romans: “Do you not know that God’s kindness leads you to repentance? But according to your hardness and unrepentant heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath” (Romans 2:4–5).

God’s patience, therefore, is exercised when human conversion is awaited for no short time. But in infants patience cannot appear. For if they had sins belonging to their nature, which the Savior would charge against them, he would certainly be called savage, though falsely called patient. God, however, cannot be anything except compassionate and just—which is what my God Jesus Christ is.

Paul, who for a long time persecuted the Church, and the others in whose person he speaks, experienced Christ’s patience because they were long awaited, although they were liberated late. Thus the Apostle condemns human life, not human nature.

Commending this grace to the Jews—because the law punishes criminals but does not possess any such effectiveness of mercy as Baptism, in which sins of action are cleansed by a brief confession [Note: [Col. 1087] An old Port. codex reads “any.”]—he shows that they ought to hasten to Christ and implore the aid of this forgiveness. They should recognize that the law threatens the wounds of conduct, whereas grace heals effectively and swiftly.

He therefore said that the body of death consists of sins, not flesh. For if he had spoken of the misery of the limbs, which you think was brought about by sin, he would more properly have called it “the death of the body” than “the body of death.”

But so that you may know that, according to the usage of Scripture, sins are called “members,” read the Epistle to the Colossians, where the Apostle himself says: “Put to death your members that are upon the earth: fornication, impurity, and greed, which is idolatry. Because of these things the wrath of God is coming upon the children of disobedience, among whom you also once walked, when you lived in them” (Colossians 3:5–6). See how he calls “members” what he declares to be sins.

And in the same way, concerning the body of sin, he says in the Epistle to the Romans: “Our old man was crucified together with him, so that the body of sin might be destroyed, and that we might no longer serve sin” (Romans 6:6) [Note: [Col. 1087] The printed editions read “this”; the manuscripts read “here.”].

In this same manner, then, he cried out here in the person of the Jews, as we have said: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the body of this death?” That is: Who will deliver me from the guilt of my sins, which I committed when I could have avoided them? The severity of the law does not pardon these sins but avenges them. Who will rescue me from these members—that is, from these vices—which I gathered by imitating the wicked, so as to construct a body full of sin? Who, I ask?

And he answered as though instructed by the voice of the realities themselves: “The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord.” The grace of God, which credits righteousness to the faithful without works, according to what David says: “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered; blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not imputed sin” (Psalm 31:1–2).

Therefore, whoever makes a person blessed is himself blessed also: eternal righteousness, which does not forgive sin unless it could justly have imputed it. It could not justly have imputed it, however, if the one to whom it is imputed could not also have avoided it. No one can avoid what is natural. Therefore, absolutely no one can possess sin by necessity of nature. This brief statement should suffice.

AUGUSTINE: You certainly attempted, by your argument, to turn what the Apostle says—“Who will deliver me from the body of this death?”—into your own sense. But the one who sent the document to the distinguished man saw better that you could not do this; and therefore, when he recalled my words, he omitted that passage, lest your anticipated and published reply should be laughed at.

For who would not laugh at what I do not know whether you have been able to persuade yourselves of, although you thought it should be persuaded to others: that the Apostle introduced the person of the Jews, not yet established under Christ’s grace, saying, “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the body of this death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord”? Is a Jew who is not yet a Christian really the one who says, “The grace of God will deliver me through Jesus Christ our Lord”?

But I shall pass over that. Who could endure the idea that a person is supposed to say, concerning his past sins, “Who will deliver me from the body of this death?” so that they may be forgiven him through the grace of Christ who pardons, when it is perfectly clear from what he came to these words?

Here are his words in our ears. Let us see, then, whether he confesses himself wretched because of what he did willingly or because of what he does unwillingly. The man cries out: “I do not do what I want, but what I hate, that I do.” He cries out: “Now it is no longer I who do it, but sin dwelling in me.” “For I know that good does not dwell in me—that is, in my flesh. For willing is present with me, but accomplishing the good I do not find. For I do not do the good that I want, but the evil that I do not want, that I do.”

He does not say, “I did,” but “I do”; he does not say, “I worked,” but “I work”; he does not say, “I acted,” but “I act”; and this is not what I want [Note: [Col. 1088] The printed editions read “and this I do not want,” omitting “what,” although it was present in the manuscripts.], but what I do not want. Finally, “I delight in the law of God according to the inner person” [Note: [Col. 1088] The printed editions read “why does he delight?”; the manuscripts read “I delight.”]; yet he sees another law in his members, warring against the law of his mind. By that law he is compelled not to do the good he wants, but to do the evil he does not want.

For this reason he exclaims: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the body of this death?” (Romans 7:15–25). And you close your eyes against the clearest truth and explain his groan not as it is evident to everyone, but as it pleases you, saying: “Who will deliver me from the body of this death? That is, Who will deliver me from the guilt of my sins that I committed?” He says, “The evil that I do not want, that I do”; and you say, “that I committed” [Note: [Col. 1088] The printed editions read “which he committed, he saying”; this is erroneous and contrary to the manuscripts.].

Are you so utterly despairing of all the people who read these things that you do not think they will prefer to hear him rather than you, and believe him rather than you? [Note: [Col. 1088] The manuscripts read “all”; the printed editions, “the people.”] Allow the man to ask for God’s grace not only because he has sinned, so that he may be absolved, but also so that he may not sin, so that he may be helped. This is what is happening in this passage.

For one who says, “The evil that I do not want, that I do,” has no occasion here to say, “Forgive us our debts,” but rather, “Do not bring us into temptation” (Matthew 6:12–13). As the Apostle James says, each person is tempted when he is drawn away and enticed by his own desire (James 1:14).

This is the evil of which he says, “I know that good does not dwell in me—that is, in my flesh.” This is the evil in the body of this death. This evil was not in paradise before sin, because this flesh was not yet the body of this death. At the end it will be said to this body, “Where, O death, is your contention?” [Note: [Col. 1089] So the manuscripts. The printed editions read “unto the end.”] But this will be said when “this corruptible body has put on incorruption, and this mortal body has put on immortality” (1 Corinthians 15:53–55). Now, however, it is a body of death, because the Apostle himself said, “The body is dead because of sin” (Romans 8:10).

Hear Catholic interpreters of the Apostle. Receive their words, not mine, though with them I receive your insults. Hear not Pelagius, but Ambrose: “Even Paul’s flesh,” he says, “was a body of death, as he himself says, ‘Who will deliver me from the body of this death?’” (*On Repentance*, book 1, chapter 2 or 3).

“Hear not Caelestius, but Gregory: ‘Within ourselves,’ he says, ‘we are attacked by our own vices and passions, and day and night we are driven by the fiery goads of this body of humiliation and body of death—now secretly, now openly—while the enticements of visible things everywhere provoke and irritate us, and this filth and mire to which we cling exhales through its more capacious veins the stench of its own mud; while the law of sin that is in our members also resists the law of the spirit’” (Gregory of Nazianzus, *Apology 1, On His Flight*).

While barking against these lights of the heavenly city, you say: “He said that the body of death is sins, not flesh,” denying that the Apostle referred this to the mortality of our body, “which,” you say, “flesh received from the constitution of animal nature.”

This is what you hold, the very doctrine that Pelagius hypocritically condemned at the Palestinian hearing: namely, that Adam was made mortal, so that whether he sinned or did not sin, he would have died [Note: [Col. 1089] See the book *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, chapters 11 and 33].

And thus, resisting these men and their other companions in sound faith, resisting so many and such great teachers, you are compelled to fill paradise—even if no one had sinned—with the pain of women giving birth, the labor of those being born, the groans of the sick, the funerals of the dying, and the mourning of those who grieve.

What wonder, then, if you too go out from this paradise, which is the Church—you who make that paradise, from which those who by sinning cast us into these miseries went out, such a place as no Christian, indeed no human being at all, would dare even to imagine, unless he were insane? [Note: [Col. 1089] So the manuscripts. The printed editions read “would dare.”]

LXVIII. JULIAN: For these matters were discussed at greater length in my first work. Yet you do not speak clearly about what death you wish to be understood—the body of which you say was not in paradise before sin—because in the books you published under the name of Marcellinus you professed that Adam was made mortal (*On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, book 1, chapters 3 and 4).

As for what you add, that disease is an affair of marriage, it can be heard gently enough if you say this only about your own parents. For perhaps you may be conscious of some hidden disease of your mother, whom, in the books of your *Confessions*, you indicated—using your own word—was called “a wine-bibber” (*Confessions*, book 9, chapter 8).

But in the marriage of holy people, and in that of all honorable people, there is no disease at all. The Apostle did not grant intercourse as a remedy for disease when, out of reverence for marriage, he was protecting the people of the Church from the disease of fornication. How this interpretation has utterly erased both your forehead and your doctrine is shown near the end of my first volume; it has also been explained throughout the body of that entire reply, wherever the opportunity of the subject required.

AUGUSTINE: Nowhere has your deceit and conscience, condemned by your knowledge, appeared more clearly. For you know—indeed, you know perfectly well; it is so evident that no one who has read those books can fail to know it—that in the books I published for Marcellinus I vigorously opposed the heresy of your party, which was already then beginning to arise, lest it be believed that Adam would have died even if he had not sinned.

But because [Note: [Col. 1090] We restore “because” here from the manuscripts.] I said that he was mortal in the sense that he could die—for he could sin—you wanted to steal upon those who have not read those books, and perhaps will not read them, by an insidious disguise, if they should read what you have written, as though I had said that Adam was made mortal in such a way that whether he sinned or did not sin, he would die.

For this is the matter at issue with you [Note: [Col. 1090] Codex Mar. reads: “For this is where the matter is at issue.”]. The whole question between us and you turns on this: we say that if Adam had not sinned, he would not have suffered bodily death; you say that whether he sinned or did not sin, he would have died bodily.

Why, then, do you pretend not to know what death I wish to be understood—the body of which I say was not in paradise before sin—when you know what I argued in those books, and how openly and clearly I argued it? God would not have said to the sinner, “You are earth, and to earth you shall return” (Genesis 3:19)—which everyone understands to have been said about bodily death—if Adam, even without committing any iniquity, was going to return to earth, that is, to die bodily.

But in thinking that even my mother, who did you no harm and argued nothing against you, ought to be torn apart by insult, you were overcome by the desire to curse, without fearing what is written: “Nor will revilers possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 6:10).

But what wonder is it that you show yourself hostile even to her, since you are hostile to the grace of God, by which I said she was freed from that childish fault? I, for my part, regard your parents as honorable Catholic Christians, and I congratulate them that they died before they saw you become a heretic.

We do not say that intercourse is a disease belonging to marriage [Note: [Col. 1090] Menard’s edition reads: “But now we say that disease belongs to marriage,” a serious and obvious error. Vignierius corrected it on the authority of the Clairvaux manuscript, supported by Port. and Mar.]. What belongs to marriage is to have intercourse for the sake of begetting children, not for satisfying lust. You deny that lust is a disease, although you admit that a marital remedy was provided against it.

For surely, lest fornication be committed, the lust you praise is contradicted, resisted, and opposed. Thus, if the person appointed for the begetting of children transgresses the limit, at least the person who yields to it sins venially with a spouse.

The Apostle was speaking to married people when, after saying, “Do not defraud one another, except by agreement for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer,” he immediately returned to the same subject and said, “Come together again, lest Satan tempt you because of your lack of self-control” [Note: [Col. 1091] Vignierius reads: “And again to them. But if Satan tempt you”; corrected from the manuscripts.]. He immediately added: “But I say this by way of concession, not by command” (1 Corinthians 7:5–6).

This evil, then, is used well only by the chaste intention of propagating offspring. To this evil one yields venially within marriage, not for the sake of offspring but solely for carnal pleasure; against this evil one resists, lest the condemned desire for pleasure be satisfied.

This evil dwells in the body of this death. Because of its movement—which is troublesome even when the mind does not consent—it is said, “I know that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh” (Romans 7:18).

This evil was not in the body of that life, where either, with the genital members also serving the will [Note: [Col. 1091] The printed editions read “where from the will”; the manuscripts read “where, with the genital members serving the will.”], no lust existed, or where it never moved at all against the decision of the will. They were suddenly ashamed when this evil arose (Genesis 3:7) [Note: [Col. 1091] The manuscripts read “were ashamed”; the printed editions, “were repudiated.”]; before they sinned, they were naked and were not ashamed (Genesis 2:25).

You shamelessly scattered praises of this evil [Note: [Col. 1091] Vignierius reads “of this evil, whose praises”; “whose” is absent from the manuscripts.] throughout those four books of yours to which I was compelled to reply in six of mine.

LXIX. JULIAN: For before the Apostle came to this recollection of human misery and divine grace [Note: [Col. 1091] The Clairvaux and Mar. manuscripts read “now.”], he had said: “I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin.” After these words he exclaimed: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the body of this death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Romans 7:23–25).

It is established by those preceding words which you quoted that the Apostle added: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the body of this death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord.” But for the present we are not asking whether the Apostle said this; we are asking with what faith, in what sense, and for what reason he said it.

He called the law in his members—which, through the practice of crimes, was rebellious against holy counsels even at the beginnings of correction—a bad habit [Note: [Col. 1091] In place of “bad,” the printed editions corruptly read “another.”], which educated people of the world commonly call “second nature.”

A little earlier, addressing those to whom he was speaking with reproach, he had said: “I speak in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh. For just as you presented your members to serve impurity and iniquity for iniquity, so now present your members to serve righteousness for sanctification” (Romans 6:19).

And to show that by “flesh” he abusively meant vice, not this body whose causes exist in the seeds, he perhaps adds two chapters later: “When we were in the flesh, the passions of sins, which are revealed through the law, were at work in our members so as to bear fruit for death” (Romans 7:5).

He said, “When we were in the flesh,” as though, when he was arguing, he himself were not in the flesh. But one who knows the Scriptures recognizes this kind of expression [Note: [Col. 1091] The manuscripts read “expression”; the printed editions, “locution.”]. Therefore, wherever the commonness of words introduces a question, the rule of reason must be applied; in accordance with its standard, what seemed to have strayed must be stretched back [Note: [Col. 1092] Codex Mar. reads “flowed away.”].

Furthermore, Faustus, the Manichaean bishop and your teacher, relies especially on this testimony of the Apostle against us. He says that by these words—namely, by the law that wars against the counsel and is said to dwell in the members [Note: [Col. 1092] The manuscripts read “may dwell”; the printed editions, “dwells.”]—the Apostle meant nothing other than an evil nature.

You therefore ought to have done nothing less than interpret this passage in the way they interpret it, lest, when you enter by the same lines that Faustus twisted, you seem not to have argued the matter but to have reproduced what had already been said.

AUGUSTINE: Let not Faustus the Manichaean, but Gregory, a learned Catholic, answer you [Note: [Col. 1092] We restore “let him answer” from the manuscripts; the manuscripts omit “teacher.”]. Gregory did not call the law in our members—which wars against the law of the mind—a bad habit “at the beginnings,” as you say, “of correction,” a habit rebellious against holy counsels through the practice of crimes and commonly called by educated people “second nature.” Rather, he clearly and openly attributed the law of sin in our members to this mortal and earthly body of ours, saying:

“The law of sin that is in our members resists the law of the spirit, while it seeks to lead captive the royal image [Note: [Col. 1092] The manuscripts read “upright,” corruptly.] within us, so that whatever entered into us through the benefit of that divine and original creation may fall as spoil to it. Hence perhaps scarcely anyone,” he says, “governing himself through a long and rigorous philosophy and gradually recalling the nobility of his soul, can draw back and turn toward God the nature of light that is in him, joined to this humble and dark clay [Note: [Col. 1092] The printed editions read “unless by a long”; the manuscripts omit “unless.”].

“Or, if indeed he acts with God’s favor, he will recall both together, provided that through long and constant meditation he grows accustomed always to look upward and to raise by tighter reins the matter bound to him, which drags him downward and weighs him down” [Note: [Col. 1092] The printed editions read “he recalled.”] (Gregory of Nazianzus, *Apology 1, On His Flight*).

Blessed Gregory said these things not at the beginning of his correction, but when he was already a bishop. He wished to explain—or rather to remind us of what is well known—in what sort of immense struggle the saints are placed with their inner vices because of the body that weighs down the soul.

That struggle certainly would not have existed in the place of blessed peace, that is, in the paradise of holy delights, if no one had sinned. The body of this death would not have been there, whose corruption would burden the soul; rather, there would have been the body of that life, where the flesh would not desire against the spirit, so that the spirit would need to desire against the flesh (Galatians 5:17), but human nature would rejoice in the happy concord of both.

If, then, you wished to overcome—not assist—the Manichaeans who introduce another nature and substance of evil, you would certainly not deny, together with your deceivers, these miseries of human life, obvious to all and beginning with infants. Rather, together with Catholic believers and distinguished teachers, you would say from what cause our nature, originally created blessed, fell into them.

LXX. JULIAN: To sum up, therefore, neither have I imposed fraud upon your words, nor have you brought forward anything that you could cover with even the faintest coloring of piety, much less establish by the testimony of Scripture.

The Apostle did not understand what you think he understood. Nor was the condition of sexual union in paradise at all different from what now takes place in marriages. God taught that he himself instituted it both by the constitution of the sexes and the character of their members, and by his repeated blessing.

When these matters have been settled, it becomes clear that all who are deceived by you are more worthy of wrath than of mercy, since, with you as their author, they defame their birth in order to excuse the crimes they commit by an evil will, rather than correct their conduct.

**AUG.** It is a pious action in this life to worship God, to struggle against inward vices by his grace, and not to yield to those vices when they incite or compel us to what is unlawful; and, when one does yield, to seek pardon, while also asking God, with the devotion of religious piety, for help not to yield. But in paradise, if no one had sinned, the pious action of fighting against vices would not have existed, since the continuance of blessedness would have consisted in having no vices.

Yet it is not the mark of men who truly fight against vices to offer the shameless praise of vices that you habitually offer. Was Ambrose, then, when he said, “All human beings are born under sin, and their very birth is in sin” (*On Repentance*, book 1, chapter 2 or 3), either speaking at my instigation or defaming birth so that action might not be corrected? Was Gregory, then, when he said, “Venerate the birth through which you have been freed from the bonds of earthly birth” (*Oration on the Nativity of the Lord*); or when, speaking of Christ or of the Holy Spirit, he said, “Through him the stains of the first birth are cleansed, through which we are conceived in iniquities, and our mothers bore us in sins” (*Oration on Pentecost*); or when Hilary said of King David, “He knows that he was born under the origin of sin and under the law of sin” (*On Psalm 118*, 175)—were these men defaming birth so that action might not be corrected?

Will you dare to persuade your own heart that the conduct of the Pelagians is to be preferred to the conduct of these men? Forgive us: we would never believe that you live better than they did—not even if you did not love the concupiscence of the flesh so much that you would wish to place it in paradise, before sin, in the condition in which it now lusts against the spirit.

For if, as you say, “the condition of intercourse in paradise was no different from that which now takes place in marriages,” then there was also there, before sin, carnal lust, without which the two sexes cannot now unite. If, therefore, you do not wish the genital members, which in that blessedness were not yet objects of shame, to have been able to serve human will without lust in carrying out their function, by which offspring would be begotten, I still ask what sort of lust you believe existed then. Certainly it followed the will whenever it was necessary; but did it also, when it was not necessary for the propagation of children, nevertheless stimulate the mind and drive it to sexual unions, whether those unions were condemnable or, with one’s spouse, venial?

For if it was of the kind it now is, it undoubtedly did this, whether it was resisted through temperance or yielded to through intemperance. Thus a human being would either be compelled to serve lust by sinning or to resist it in an inward battle. If you have any human understanding, you perceive that the one is incompatible with the dignity, the other with the peacefulness of that blessed state.

It remains, therefore, that if lust existed there, it was so subject to the will that it neither dragged a rightly ordered and tranquil mind toward sin nor provoked it to battle, and did not compel a spirit obedient to and enjoying God either to sin or to fight. Since it is not such now, but eagerly rather than obediently desires even what is lawful, while in what is unlawful it either casts down the spirit or lusts against the spirit, recognize the evil contracted through the corruption of nature’s integrity. Married chastity makes good use of this evil in the duty of procreation, and from this evil comes the bond of a generation subject to sin, a bond to be loosed by regeneration.  
[Note: [Col. 1093] Menardus reads, “it would not be a sign”; Vignierius, “it would not be a judgment.” The text is corrected from the manuscripts.]
[Note: [Col. 1093] The printed editions wrongly read, “our ancestors beget us.”]
[Note: [Col. 1093] The printed editions read “you say”; the manuscripts, “you say” (singular).]
[Note: [Col. 1093] Here the particle “now” is restored from the manuscripts.]
[Note: [Col. 1094] The printed editions read “to be saved.”]

**LXXI. JUL.** But enough of this; now I shall take up what follows. “In the body, therefore, of this death—which plainly did not exist in paradise before sin—another law in our members resists the law of our mind; for even when we do not wish it, and when we do not consent, and do not present our members to it so that it may fulfill what it desires, it nevertheless dwells in them and troubles the mind that resists and opposes it; so that the very conflict, even if it is not condemnable because it does not accomplish iniquity, is nevertheless miserable because it does not possess peace” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 2, no. 6).

We teach, on the testimony of universal experience, that the pleasure of all the senses is natural. This pleasure and concupiscence existed in paradise before sin, as the event itself demonstrates: the way to transgression was through concupiscence, which, when the beauty of the fruit had excited the eyes, also aroused the expectation of its pleasant taste.

Therefore this concupiscence, which sins when it does not keep within measure but is a natural and innocent affection when it is kept within the limits of what is permitted, could not have been the fruit of sin. It is shown to have been, not through any fault of its own, but through the will, the occasion of sin. Read also the second book of my work on this subject: you will find that what we say can be made persuasive even to your mind.

But as for what you inserted with a show of cleverness—that there is indeed a law of sin in our members, but that it has sin only when we consent, whereas when we do not consent it merely arouses battle and imposes misery by disturbing peace—who, unless he is foolish, does not see that this is a contradiction?

For if the law of sin—that is, sin—and the necessity of sin are naturally implanted in the members, what benefit is there in not giving consent to it, when, simply because it exists, one must necessarily undergo punishment? Or if it is indeed the law of sin, but when I do not consent to it it does not sin, then the power of the human will is immeasurable, since—if absurdity may be allowed to say so—it compels sin itself not to sin.

But the argument returns to the point that what you say is *asystaton*—inconsistent. For if it does not sin, it is not the law of sin; if it is the law of sin, it sins. But if it sins merely because it exists, how can it be resisted so that one does not sin, when it cannot be driven back so as to cease from the work of sin?  
[Note: [Col. 1094] The printed editions read *repugnans*, “resisting.” See above, *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 2, no. 6.]
[Note: [Col. 1094] The printed editions read *docemur*, “we are taught.” The Claromontanus and Portarum manuscripts read *docemus*, “we teach,” correctly, since Augustine answers: “you say that you teach.”]
[Note: [Col. 1094] Menardus reads “this pleasure and concupiscence”; Vignierius omits “and.” The Marianus manuscript, likewise omitting the particle, reads “concupiscence of pleasures.” Finally, the Portarum manuscript omits “and concupiscence” and reads: “This pleasure existed in paradise before sin.”]
[Note: [Col. 1094] The Marianus and Claromontanus manuscripts read *utile*, “usefully,” in place of *acutule*, “with a show of cleverness.”]
[Note: [Col. 1095] The printed editions read “to them”; the manuscripts, “to it.”]
[Note: [Col. 1095] The Marianus manuscript reads “I do not sin.”]

**AUG.** I already answered your second book in my fourth book, and reproached you for having spoken empty nonsense. But let those who read judge whether one ought to answer a man who advances to such madness that, while admitting sin to be evil, he declares the concupiscence of sins to be good. Nevertheless, we are compelled to answer, unwilling to abandon the slower minds to whom these writings may come.

What, then, are you saying, without knowing what you are saying? Was there, then, even in paradise, before the serpent’s poisonous counsel and before the will had been corrupted by sacrilegious speech, already a desire for the forbidden food? And—what is still more intolerable to say—did it provoke toward evil and yet not itself constitute evil? Did those human beings see the fruit of the forbidden tree and lust after it, but, so that they would not eat, did the concupiscence of the spirit resist the concupiscence of the flesh? And did they live in that place of such great blessedness without possessing peace of mind and body within themselves?

You are not so insane as to believe these things, nor so shameless as to say them. Understand, then—or cease with empty loquacity to obstruct those who understand. An evil will preceded, by which the crafty serpent was believed; and an evil concupiscence followed, by which the forbidden food was desired.

Therefore, it was not that some kind of desire resisted some kind of will there; rather, a depraved desire served a depraved will. Consequently, although both were already evil, the will led the desire, not the desire the will; the desire did not precede the will or resist it. Finally, if the will had been turned away from the unlawful act before the sin was completed, the unlawful desire would have been quieted without any effort.

Speaking of this, blessed Ambrose says: “The flesh, restored to the nature of its vigor, recognizes its nourisher; and, laying aside the boldness of its defiance, it is joined to the judgment of the soul’s moderation—such as it was when it first received the hidden places of paradise as its dwelling, before it had been infected by the poison of the deadly serpent and learned sacrilegious hunger, and before it passed over the memory of the divine commandments, implanted in the soul’s senses, through its zeal for eating. From this, it is revealed, sin proceeded, as though from parents consisting of body and soul: while the body’s nature is tested, the unsound soul suffers with it; and if it had restrained the body’s appetite, the origin of sin would have been extinguished at its very birth” (*Book 7 on Luke 12:52*).

Do you see how the Catholic teacher, endowed with Christian wisdom, already called the very concupiscence of the unlawful food—which you assert to be innocent if it is not permitted to fulfill what it desires—a sacrilegious hunger? Yet if the soul, with its will corrected, had restrained this bodily appetite, then, as he says, the origin of sin would have been extinguished at its very arising. But because the appetite for the unlawful food was not restrained and the sin was brought to completion, the origin of sin was not extinguished; it even flowed down to posterity. So great a dissension between flesh and spirit followed that, as the same teacher says elsewhere, it was turned into nature through the transgression of the first human being (*ibid.*, no. 141).

But against this you say that you “teach, on the testimony of universal experience, that the pleasure of all the senses is natural”—as though in the body, not of this death but of that life, the pleasure of all the senses could not have been naturally sufficient, so that, under the supreme rule of virtue, soul and flesh would be in harmony and nothing unlawful would be desired. [The transmitted reading is corrupt.]

How greatly you err, deriving the holy delights of paradise and that blessedness from this corruption and weakness of nature that now exists! That was one kind of immortality, in which a human being could avoid dying; this is another kind of mortality, in which a human being cannot but die; and there will be a supreme immortality, in which a human being will not be able to die.

Why do you quarrel over contending concupiscence—that is, over the law in the members resisting the law of the mind? It is called the law of sin because it advises sins and, so to speak, commands them; and if the mind serves it, sin is committed without excuse. It is called sin because it was made through sin and desires to sin. Its guilt has been loosed by regeneration; its conflict has been left for the struggle. It is evil—this is clear. We do not resist it by the powers of our will, as you suppose, unless we are divinely aided. This evil must be fought, not denied; it must be conquered, not defended. Finally, if you consent to it, recognize its evil by sinning; if you resist it, recognize its evil by fighting.

[Note: [Col. 1095] The printed editions read “while he confesses”; the manuscripts, “while he admits.”]
[Note: [Col. 1095] The Portarum manuscript reads “good” in place of “the concupiscence of sins.”]
[Note: [Col. 1095] The Marianus and Claromontanus manuscripts read *malesuada*; the Portarum manuscript, *malesuasa*.]
[Note: [Col. 1095] The printed editions read “they lusted”; the manuscripts, “it lusted,” referring to lust.]
[Note: [Col. 1095] “Depraved” had been omitted in the printed editions.]
[Note: [Col. 1095] The printed editions read “thus”; the manuscripts, “hence.”]
[Note: [Col. 1095] Ambrose, and likewise above in Book 2 against Julian, no. 10, reads “the governing soul.”]
[Note: [Col. 1096] The manuscripts read “is revealed”; the printed editions, “is foretold.”]
[Note: [Col. 1096] The Marianus manuscript reads “rebuked” in place of “restrained.”]
[Note: [Col. 1096] The manuscripts read *in iura*; the printed editions, *iniuria*.

**LXXII. JUL.** Or what benefit is there in the moderation of something whose very presence accuses itself? See, then, where your clever arguments lead.

First, nature sins without the will—which is impossible. Second, it is sin and yet does not sin; that is, it is one thing and is not one thing. Further, when it disturbs peace, it is miserable, yet it is not punished for so great a crime as the disruption of tranquility; but when it accomplishes iniquity, it is condemnable.

Yet the law of sin, just as it itself deserves punishment, so excuses the human will. For since the law is compelling, natural, and never departing, it plainly cannot be overcome by the will; and no one is guilty on account of what he could not avoid. Nor does the law itself sin, because it could not do anything else.

But God imputes unavoidable things to guilt, and no one compels him to commit so great an evil. Thus, when all others have been acquitted, this one alone is found guilty: he who, with astonishing audacity, imputes necessity to others, while he himself sins without necessity.

Well done, most noble disputant, in the skill of prudence! By the steps of Punic dialectic, in order to commend gifts, you have overturned judgments; in order to pretend to grace, you have undermined justice; in order to defame nature, you have accused the Creator of human beings; and you have accused him in such a way that your god appears more culpable not merely than some sinner, but even than the law of sin itself.

After this, you most profanely insult Catholic priests by saying that they deny the grace of Christ, whose equity they defend—although we indeed praise the mercy of remedies while the justice of laws remains.

**AUG.** Would that you recognized the Catholic priests who, long before you began to exist, said that the concupiscence of the flesh, which lusts against the spirit, although the spirit also lusts against it, is understood to be the law of sin, resisting the law of the mind after the sin committed in paradise, and that it corrupted human nature. Hence no one is now born without it. In the saints the spirit opposes it so that they may live justly, fighting against it until, when human salvation has been perfected and the flesh is in complete harmony with the spirit, it no longer exists.

Ambrose says that through the transgression of the first human being the dissension between flesh and spirit was turned into nature. Cyprian shows this dissension in the following words—and, I suppose, you do not dare to mock the Punic dialectician in him as you dared to do in my case:

“There is a struggle between flesh and spirit, and a daily conflict between them as they disagree with one another, so that we do not do the very things we wish, while the spirit seeks heavenly and divine things, and the flesh desires earthly and worldly things. Therefore we ask that, between these two, concord be brought about by God’s aid and assistance, so that, while God’s will is done both in spirit and in flesh, the soul, which has been reborn through him, may be preserved. The Apostle plainly and clearly declares this in his own words: ‘The flesh lusts against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh; for these are opposed to one another, so that you do not do the things you wish’” (*On the Lord’s Prayer*).

You do not admit that this concord of flesh and spirit—which Cyprian says we desire and pray for from the Lord—existed in paradise before sin. Or, if it existed, why do you not admit that it perished through the transgression of the first human being, nature having been corrupted, and that miserable discord succeeded the blessed peace of soul and body?

And you are indignant with us because, as though we were Catholic priests—that is, as though we were you—we insult you in our speech by saying that you deny the grace of Christ. Yet you most shamelessly and profanely insult these truly Catholic priests with the words that, in your undigested fury, you spew against me, who follow and defend their faith.

The Apostle says, “Walk by the Spirit, and do not fulfill the desires of the flesh” (Galatians 5:16–17). I ask: why does he call them desires if they do not exist? Why does he forbid them to be fulfilled if they are good? But he continues to show what they are and says: “For the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh; for these are opposed to one another, so that you do not do the things you wish.”

To whom was he saying, “So that you do not do the things you wish”? To Jews, according to your astonishing understanding, who had not yet been established under Christ’s grace—and not to those to whom he had said, “Did you receive the Spirit from works of the law, or from hearing with faith?” (Galatians 3:2)?

He was therefore speaking to faithful Christians, who did not do what they wished because the flesh lusted against the spirit. Why was this so, except because they wished their lower part to consent to their higher part—that is, the flesh to the spirit—but were unable to accomplish what they wished? It remained for them not to consent to that vice, but for the spirit to lust against the flesh.

But even if what you suppose was present in them—that because of a bad habit they lived badly even unwillingly—what becomes of your claim that nature cannot sin without the will, when you admit that these people sinned unwillingly?

Why, then, is the concupiscence of the flesh called sin, or the law of sin, we have already explained above (chapter 71). If it is good not to consent to what is unlawful, then plainly that by which what is unlawful is desired is itself evil, even when the unlawful acts are accomplished neither through consent nor through action.

Moreover, you overturn God’s judgments when you say that the miseries of the human race, beginning with infants, occur without any merit of sin, and when you do not seek God’s gift lest you enter into temptation (Matthew 26:41)—that is, lest you sin. For you trust in your own strength; and either, blind men that you are, you do not see that you have been marked out and condemned in the holy Psalm, or, being foolish, you do not grieve over it (Psalm 48:7).  
[Note: [Col. 1097] The manuscripts read *sicut*, “as.”]
[Note: [Col. 1097] The printed editions read the singular “unavoidable”; the Marianus and Colbertinus manuscripts more correctly read the plural “unavoidable things.” Julian is plainly maintaining that Augustine’s views lead to the conclusion that God imputes unavoidable things to guilt and, all others having been acquitted, is himself alone to be deemed guilty.]
[Note: [Col. 1097] The printed editions read “that corrupted nature perished.” The text is corrected with the aid of the manuscripts: “that nature, having been corrupted, perished.”]
[Note: [Col. 1098] All the manuscripts read “but he still shows what sort they are.”]
[Note: [Col. 1098] The printed editions read “to faithful Christians”; the manuscripts, “faithful Christians.”]
[Note: [Col. 1098] The Marianus, Portarum, and Claromontanus manuscripts omit “even if none.”]
[Note: [Col. 1098] The printed editions read “in the second Psalm”; the manuscripts, “in the holy Psalm.” The reference is to Psalm 48: “Those who trust in their own strength,” etc.]

**LXXIII. JUL.** But let us now proceed to my words, which he extracted from the preface and proposed for refutation:

“I have sufficiently warned that he wished to present my words as though they required refutation, interrupting the sentences in one place by removing their middle portions, and shortening them elsewhere by omitting their conclusions. I have sufficiently shown why he did this. Now let us examine those statements of mine that he presented as he wished, and those that he added. For his words now follow, and, as the man who sent you the little document indicated, he first wrote something from the preface, evidently from those books of which he excerpted a few passages.

“The matter is as follows: ‘The teachers of our time,’ he says, ‘and the authors of the impious sedition that still burns, have resolved to reach the insult and destruction of men whose holy zeal consumes them through the ruin of the whole Church, not understanding how much honor they have brought upon those whose glory they have shown could not be overthrown except together with the Catholic religion. For if anyone says either that human beings possess free choice or that God is the Creator of those who are born, he is called a Coelestianist and a Pelagian. Therefore, lest they be called heretics, they become Manichaeans; and while they fear a false disgrace, they incur a true crime—like wild beasts surrounded by wings so that they may be driven into nets; because they lack reason, they are thrust into genuine destruction by a groundless fear’” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 2, chapters 6–7).

I recognize my words, but not as you have presented them in their entirety. [Note: [Col. 1099] The manuscripts read “in these passages of the contest”; the printed editions, “in these contests.”] And although the substance of the dispute does not consist in these passages, since they are from the preface, nevertheless, so that your frivolity may be made clear, brother most blessed, they were not placed where you put them, but immediately in the first section of the book.

Likewise, when I had said, “the insult and destruction of men whose holy zeal consumes them,” I added, [Note: [Col. 1099] The printed editions read “therefore”; the manuscripts more correctly read “likewise.”] “since no other path lay open, they resolved to reach it through the ruin of the whole Church.” After this I also said, “Because one who confesses free choice and God the Creator is called a Coelestianist and a Pelagian, so that simple people,” I said, “frightened by this unjust accusation, [Note: [Col. 1099] The Marianus and Portarum manuscripts read, “so that simple people might be frightened by an unjust expression.”] might, in order to escape the odium of the name, abandon even the sound faith—plainly believing that neither free choice exists in human beings nor God is the Creator of those who are born, since they had abandoned both doctrines which they had previously affirmed.”

You omitted all of this. After it came the passage you quoted, whose truth and impenetrability will not be difficult to establish. Thus I neither omitted anything from your statements, nor did you report even the first section as I had arranged it. I insist on this so that the seriousness of the Punic writer may stand out.  
[Note: [Col. 1099] Vignierius and the old manuscript of Marignan read, “it will not be difficult to establish by the work.” Perhaps the reading should be, “it will not be difficult for the task to establish.”]

**AUG.** The man who excerpted what he wished from your books and sent it to whomever he wished to read did precisely what you accuse me of doing; nor do I think that you yourself believe otherwise. For in the same book of mine, against which you bark, I certainly stated beforehand to whom I was compelled to respond concerning the document. [Note: [Col. 1099] Vignierius reads “which”; the manuscripts, “against which.”] But you seek, by insulting me, something to say, sensing that in argument you say nothing substantial.

Moreover, even in those words of mine that you immediately propose to yourself as requiring refutation, you could have noticed what I am saying. I would not have said, “It is not as you say, whoever said these things,” if I had been certain that you had said them, rather than the man who sent the writing to me in whatever form he wished and to whomever he wished, and whose document I had undertaken to refute.

But thanks be to God: I responded to your entire work—from which that man excerpted whatever he wished, as it pleased him—with the Lord’s help in such a way that I overturned all the devices you, a new heretic, had erected against the most ancient Catholic faith.

**LXXIV. JUL.** Let us hear, then, what you wrote in reply to these words of mine:

“‘It is not as you say, whoever said these things; it is not so. You are greatly mistaken, or you are preparing to deceive greatly. We do not deny free choice; but “if the Son sets you free,” says the Truth, “then you will truly be free”’ (John 8:36).

“‘You begrudge this liberator to those whom, while captive, you have granted a vain freedom. For by whatever anyone has been defeated, to that he has been assigned as a slave, as Scripture says’ (2 Peter 2:19); and no one is released from this bond of slavery except through the grace of the Liberator, from which no human being is exempt. For through one human being sin entered the world, and through sin, death; and thus death passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 2, no. 8).

The greatness of our cause is indicated not only by the consideration and assessment of the facts themselves, which we defend, but also by your fear. You fight against our blood by pouring out money, distributing inheritances, sending horses, stirring up peoples, and corrupting authorities; yet you are ashamed to profess the faith that is being attacked by us, and you flee to the words of our position, from which you have departed.  
[Note: [Col. 1100] The manuscripts read, “from which you have departed.” The printed editions read, “from which you depart.”]

**AUG.** You either knowingly slander us, if you are the one lying about these things, or, not knowing what you are saying, believe liars. But let what I have already said above in reply to your vanity—or even your malice—be sufficient (above, chapter 42).

**LXXV. JUL.** The crime undertaken by the shameless treachery of Babylon is so wicked that, when it is charged against you by us, you deny it; and what we believe is so holy that you desire to hide beneath its shadow, even with an adversarial mind.

When I set out whatever was held piecemeal in your disputation and compressed the substance of the question into a brief form, so that the cause of the ecclesiastical disagreement—how great and of what kind it was—might be disclosed without smoke or mist, I said that you denied free choice and God the Creator of those who are born. On the other hand, I said that we defend both doctrines, and that for this reason you arouse empty clamor among unlearned ears concerning the names of Catholic men who labor with us for the sake of the apostolic faith that we defend. [Note: [Col. 1100] The Marianus and Portarum manuscripts read “with you.”]

Thus those who had feared being called Coelestianists by you would lose the dignity of the heavenly faith; and those who had dreaded being called Pelagians by you would be plunged into the sea of the Manichaeans. The uninstructed might suppose that they could not be called Christians if the Traducians called them Pelagians, whereas the prudent would determine that it was better to endure the odium and insult of names than to abandon the Catholic faith.

But lest you boast that even this form of insult was invented by your own ingenuity, remember that we customarily receive different names from all heretics. [Note: [Col. 1100] The printed editions omit “we,” reading “to receive different names”; it is restored from the manuscripts.] Yet the Council of Ariminum made especially clear what either ambiguity of wording or the threat of a new name can achieve in minds of leaden weight.

For when, under an Arian emperor, Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria—a man of great steadfastness and sound faith—had opposed the near-total defection of the world from the faith of the Apostles and the impious times, and had consequently been forced into exile, scarcely seven of the six hundred and fifty bishops, as it is said, were found for whom God’s commandments were dearer than the emperor’s: namely, so that they would neither agree to Athanasius’ condemnation nor deny the confession of the Trinity.

But that whole multitude of dejected hearts, beyond fear of personal injury, was chiefly deceived either by the threat of the name, lest they be called Athanasians, or by the trickery of the question.  
[Note: [Col. 1101] Menardus and Vignierius read, “in impiety of the times.” The manuscripts read, “in times of impiety.” The edition of 1635 corrected the text on the basis of the old manuscript read by Menardus and reviewed a second time: “in impious times,” that is, “in wicked times.” The manuscript of Port-Royal agrees. Julian uses the same verb below, chapter 92: “Therefore, cease to make yourself impious,” he says.]

**AUG.** The Arians call Catholics Athanasians or Homoousians, but the other heretics do not. You, however, are called Pelagians not only by Catholics but also by heretics like yourselves and by those who dissent from you, just as the Arians are called Arians not only by Catholics but also by heresies. You alone call us Traducians, just as the Arians call us Homoousians, the Donatists call us Macarians, the Manichaeans call us Pharisees, and the other heretics give us different names.

**LXXVI. JUL.** When the Arians, who at that time held power, proposed the question, “Do you wish to follow the *homoousion*, or Christ?” they immediately answered, as though the issue were a religious name, “We follow Christ,” and rejected the *homoousion*. Thus they went out rejoicing, as though they believed in Christ, whom they had already denied by denying the *homoousion*—that is, that he is of one substance with the Father. [Note: [Col. 1101] The manuscripts read “they rejected”; the printed editions, “to reject.”]

So now you, fabricators of deceit, frighten unlearned ears, so that, if they do not wish to be tainted by the name of men laboring for the faith, they may deny both free choice and God the Creator of human beings. This, then, is what I clearly charged at that point, and the present discussion will make plain how truthfully I did so.

You replied in this way: “We do not deny free choice,” and added nothing of your own. For it followed that, without evasion, you should complete your position: after having first said that you did not deny freedom of choice, you should have added, “But we confess that the freedom of choice given by God remains in human nature.”

**AUG.** How does freedom remain in those who need divine grace in order to be liberated from the slavery by which they have been assigned to conquering sin? It remains because they too are free—but free from righteousness. Hence the Apostle says, “When you were slaves of sin, you were free with respect to righteousness” (Romans 6:20).

**LXXVII. JUL.** By this statement you had indeed supplied something; had you continued to speak against it, you would have appeared excessively shameless, whereas if you had stated everything consistently, you might at least have appeared corrected, even if slowly. [Note: [Col. 1101] The manuscripts read *concinenter*, “harmoniously” or “consistently”; the printed editions, *continenter*, “continuously.”]

But now you say that I am deceiving people, although I prove through you what I charged; and then, in the very matter by which you think you have furnished a consistent argument, you lie. For you say, “We do not deny free choice,” and then add the Gospel testimony: “But ‘if the Son sets you free,’ says the Truth, ‘then you will truly be free’” (John 8:36).

Yet it is established that, in that passage, this was not spoken by our Lord Jesus concerning free choice. Since we shall postpone the exposition of that statement for a little while, let us explain, by definitions and divisions, what each of us means. For, according to the discipline of all teachers, the beginning of an argument ought to be taken from a definition.

**AUG.** Were the Apostles, then, who did not begin their arguments with definitions, unlearned? Yet they were teachers of the nations and despised such teachers, by whom you delight to be puffed up. As for what the Lord said—“If the Son sets you free, then you will truly be free”—you will indeed try to twist it to your position; but when you begin to try, it will become clear that it does not support you.

**LXXVIII. JUL.** For, as that man says, every discussion undertaken rationally concerning any matter ought to proceed from a definition, so that it may be understood what the matter under discussion is (Cicero, *On Duties*, book 1). Thus, just as above we discussed the definition of justice and sin, so now let us consider what definition applies to freedom of choice, so that it may be clear which of us agrees with it and which opposes it. [Note: [Col. 1102] The printed editions omit “with it”; it is restored from the manuscripts.]

Freedom of choice, by which a human being has been emancipated from God, consists in the possibility of committing sin and abstaining from sin.

**AUG.** You say that the human being has been emancipated from God, and you do not consider that emancipation entails that the emancipated person is no longer in the father’s household.

**LXXIX. JUL.** For the human being was made a rational, mortal creature, capable of virtue and vice, who, through the possibility granted to him, could either keep God’s commandments or transgress them; or, through natural instruction, preserve the right order of human society. He would be free to will either side, and in this consists the substance of sin and righteousness.

For when, according to virtue, he gives something to those in need, either from the fountains of mercy or from the abundant breasts of justice, justice itself—which holy will conceived and brought forth within—now performs the action outwardly. [Note: [Col. 1102] The Marianus manuscript reads *indulget*, “bestows,” in place of *immulget*, “milks out.”]

**AUG.** The question at issue between us is whether he conceived justice from his own resources—you who, [Note: [Col. 1102] The printed editions wrongly read “whether justice conceived”; the manuscripts support “whether he conceived justice.”] “not knowing the righteousness of God, wish to establish your own” (Romans 10:3). Holy will certainly conceives justice through holy thought, concerning which it is written, “Holy thought will preserve you” (Proverbs 2:11, according to the Septuagint). But the Apostle says, “Not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think anything as though from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God” (2 Corinthians 3:5).

If you understand this, you will understand that the only free choice deserving praise is that which has been liberated by God’s grace.

**LXXX. JUL.** Likewise, when, by contrast, someone determines to act wickedly to the injury of others and is either unjust or cruel, the action by which he harms others proceeds outward from wickedness, which an evil will has sown and produced within. But when the capacity by which the hidden force of the will may burst forth against one’s neighbors is lacking, nevertheless, in the will alone—which has carried out something good or evil not through a brief impulse but through thought and desire—the principle of either benevolence or malignity has been fulfilled.

**AUG.** Just as you understand that the will, through thought alone, fulfills the principle either of benevolence or of malignity, so may you be corrected and humbly receive grace, if you understand it in the way the Apostle speaks of good and holy thought: that we are not sufficient to think anything as though from ourselves, but that our sufficiency is from God.

You wish to be among those who trust in their own strength (Psalm 48:7), not among those who say, “I will love you, O Lord, my strength” (Psalm 17:2). [Note: [Col. 1103] The printed editions read, “the will alone fulfills the principle either of benevolence or malignity, if you understand it in the way in which”; the Portarum, Marianus, and Claromontanus manuscripts correct the wording as translated.]

**LXXXI. JUL.** Therefore, both the possibility of good and the possibility of evil are good: for being able to do good is the praise of virtue; being able to do evil is the testimony of freedom.  
[Note: [Col. 1103] The printed editions read, “being able to do good of itself is the praise of virtue.” Our reading is found in all the old books.]

**AUG.** Then God is not free, concerning whom it is said, “He cannot deny himself” (2 Timothy 2:13); and concerning whom you yourself also said, “God cannot be anything but just,” and elsewhere, “God,” you say, “cannot be anything but just and pious” (above, chapters 28 and 67).

### LXXXII. JULIAN

By this, therefore, a human being is enabled to possess a good of his own, through which the ability to do evil is subject to him. The whole fullness of divine judgment, therefore, is so closely bound up with this freedom of human beings that whoever acknowledges one of these two knows both. Hence whoever violates one violates both. Thus let the freedom of the human will also be preserved, just as divine equity is preserved. [Note: The printed editions read “which preserves”; the manuscripts have “is preserved,” which is better.]

This is the understanding of free will that has subjected to ecclesiastical truth the opinion of the Fates, the calculations of the Chaldeans, and the fantasies of the Manichaeans. [Note: So the manuscripts; the editions instead read “to ecclesiastical truth.”] This is the understanding that shows you also, together with those whom we have enumerated, to be alienated from Christ. Freedom of the will, therefore, is the possibility either of admitting or avoiding sin, free from a coercive necessity; and, as though in its own right, it possesses the choice of which part of those rising impulses it should follow: [Note: The editions read “which part of suggestion”; *suggestion* is a barbarous word and is not Julian’s, although Augustine calls him “Ciceronian” above, chapter 22. Vignierius and the Porta manuscript instead have “which part of those suggesting.” We follow the Marian manuscript, “which part of those rising,” because Augustine indicates in his reply that he read it this way, when he says that grace is necessary for a person to rise—not for one who is standing, but for one who has fallen. Julian may have written “which part of those rising.” The contrary parts of virtues and pleasures, rising simultaneously to solicit the will, seem to be signified, with an allusion to Tacitus, *Histories* 3.4: “the parties then rising most vigorously.”] that is, either the steep and rugged paths of the virtues, or the sunken and marshy places of the pleasures.

### AUGUSTINE

As long as a human being stood in the good will of free choice, he had no need of that grace by which he might be lifted up, since he was not yet unable to rise. But now, in his ruin, he is free from righteousness and a slave of sin; nor can he be a slave of righteousness and free from sin’s domination unless the Son has set him free.

### LXXXIII. JULIAN

To bring the matter to a brief conclusion: this possibility is on watch for this one purpose—that a human being may neither be driven into sin by anyone nor be dragged away from sin by a captive will. That the will cannot be captured if it itself does not wish to surrender proves the strength whose muscles have continually shone forth, among Gentiles as well as Christians, in contempt of sufferings.

### AUGUSTINE
