This is precisely what your heresy does: for this reason you add “among Gentiles,” lest Christians be thought able either to perform or to have performed the work of pious strength through God’s grace—a strength that is proper to Christians, not something shared by Christians and Gentiles alike. Listen, then, and understand: worldly desire produces the strength of the Gentiles, but the strength of Christians is produced by the love of God, which has been poured into our hearts not through the choice of the will, which comes from us, but through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (Romans 5:5).

### LXXXIV. JULIAN

If, then, as reason has shown, freedom of choice is a repeller of necessities, so that no one can be either good or evil without being free to be the opposite, how did you either confess free will, intending to use such a testimony as applies to captives, [Note: The editions read “which suits captives.”] or insert such a testimony after you had confessed free will? For you say: “We do not deny free choice; but, ‘If the Son sets you free,’ says the Truth, ‘then you will truly be free.’” It is evident that Christ there addressed words to a captive conscience, thereby showing that it was not free but subject to the punishment that condemns sins committed by free will. You have misunderstood this judgment—that is, you have failed to understand it—or perhaps understood it with reference to yourself, [Note: We restore “with reference to yourself” from the manuscripts.] and, dragging it here despite its nature’s resistance, have placed it in a passage where it wholly conflicts with your own statements in its particular meaning. For, if we join the words themselves together: What is set free is captive; what is captive is not free; what is free is not captive.

### AUGUSTINE

One thing is the remission of sins, in the case of things wrongly done; another is love, which makes a person free to do the things that ought to be done. Christ sets free in both ways: by forgiving, he removes iniquity, and by inspiring, he bestows love. [Note: So the manuscripts; the editions read “which made free.”]

### LXXXV. JULIAN

Simply confess one or the other here, and stop quibbling. Either say with us that free will exists, and remove the testimony that was appropriately brought forward in its proper context; or, as in these books that you have now sent through Alypius to Boniface, say that the will is captive, which we call free, and stop denying that you are a Manichaean.

### AUGUSTINE

The madman Manichaeus mixes an immutable substance of evil with the nature of his god, thereby making that very nature of God corruptible, and wants it to be captive under an alien nature. The Catholic faith, however, says that a good but mutable creature was changed for the worse by the will; and therefore, with its nature perverted and corrupted, it is held guilty and servilely detained not under an alien substance but under its own sin. Accordingly, our position differs greatly from his also regarding the liberator himself. Manichaeus says that a liberator is needed in order to separate from us an alien nature; we say that one is needed to heal and give life to our own nature. Show, then, if you can, that you are not Manichaeus’s assistant. For since he undoubtedly believes that the human race is born with the miseries with which he says human beings are born, he undoubtedly agrees with him; and, unwilling to attribute those miseries to the corruption of our nature through sin, you make him attribute them to an alien nature mingled with us. [Note: The words “he undoubtedly agrees” are restored from the ancient books.] [Note: The editions read “he makes”; on the authority of the manuscripts we correct this to “you make,” so that it refers to Julian.]

### LXXXVI. JULIAN

Besides, these two things that you join together—free and not free, that is, free and captive—cannot apply to the matter under discussion; but they testify that you possess singular folly, unprecedented shamelessness, and ancient impiety.

### AUGUSTINE

We call those free for the performance of works of piety to whom the Apostle says: “But now, having been set free from sin and having become servants of God, you have your fruit for sanctification, and the end, eternal life” (Romans 6:22). We can in no way possess this fruit in sanctification—which is undoubtedly love, together with its works—from ourselves; but we possess it through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us. For the God and Teacher was speaking of this very fruit when he said to the branches that remain in him: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5).

But you insult us by saying that singular folly resides in us, because God is our strength and we do not trust in our own strength; and that unprecedented shamelessness resides in us, because we do not praise with your brazen face the desire of the flesh, by which the flesh desires against the spirit; and that ancient impiety resides in us, because, against your recent perversity, we defend—however feebly—the ancient Catholic doctrines taught by those who governed Christ’s Church before us in true piety. Recognize folly in yourself, shamelessness in yourself, impiety in yourself—not, certainly, ancient, [Note: The editions read “not ancient but new,” omitting “certainly,” which is restored from the manuscripts.] but new.

### LXXXVII. JULIAN

But now it is time to discuss the Gospel passage. “Jesus,” says the evangelist John, “was saying to the Jews who had believed in him: ‘If you remain in my word, you will truly be my disciples; and you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free.’” That is, [Note: The editions read *idem* (“the same”), incorrectly.] our Lord Jesus was speaking to those who believed in him, so that, taking pride in no worldly nobility and claiming glory for themselves from Abraham’s seed, they might strive and devote themselves to the virtues, and, after acknowledging Christ, serve no sins, so that with a rejoicing conscience they might retain true freedom and, through the hope of certainties—that is, eternal things—be rescued from desire for all other things, which, because of their fragility, are frequently called vain and false.

Then the Jews answered him, not understanding what freedom Jesus meant: “We are Abraham’s seed, and we have never been slaves to anyone. How can you say, ‘You will be free’?”

Freedom is commonly called by many names: in this passage, holiness; in the Apostle, resurrection, where he says that creation will be freed from slavery to corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God (Romans 8:21); and the freedom that is more familiar, which is mentioned by way of contrast with slavery. By that name freedom of choice is also designated. Let the different matters, then, be distinguished, lest things widely separated be confused through the sharing of a name.

Here, therefore, the Lord does not say that freedom of choice is to be liberated. Since that freedom remains intact, it is appropriate that the Jews, upon receiving pardon, should be freed from guilt and seize that freedom which is greatest before God, so that they may begin to owe nothing to their crimes. Finally, the evangelist continues: “Jesus answered them, ‘Amen, amen, I say to you: everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin. A slave does not remain in the household forever; but the son remains forever. If the Son sets you free, then you will truly be free’” (John 8:31–36).

### AUGUSTINE

Pay attention to what was said: “Everyone who commits sin.” He did not say, “Who committed”; rather, “who commits.” And you do not want him to free human beings from this evil. You do not want him, in this passage, to promise such freedom that we do not commit sin; you want him to free them only because they have committed sin.

### LXXXVIII. JULIAN

He made clear what slavery he was speaking about here: “Everyone,” he says, “who commits sin is a slave of sin.” How forcefully this itself stands against your error, since he says that no one is a slave of sin except one who has himself committed sin; nor can sin cling to anyone unless the person in question has committed it personally, either by action or even by the will alone. [Note: The editions read “or by the will alone”; the manuscripts have “or even by the will alone.”]

He also shows that the whole human race cannot now be possessed by the devil, when he distinguishes between a slave and a son, that is, between the righteous and the unrighteous. For here Christ was separating himself, and likewise each of the saints, from the condition of slaves—just as there were also those before the Old Testament and under the Old Testament whom he declares to remain in the house of his Father and to rejoice at his table (Luke 13:28–29). But this entire exhortation would have been ineptly delivered if it had not been addressed to human beings possessing free choice.

### AUGUSTINE

It is entirely appropriate that those who commit sin are called slaves of sin, so that, once they have received the freedom he promises, they may cease committing sin. For sin reigned in their mortal body, so that they obeyed its desires and presented their members as weapons of iniquity to sin (Romans 6:12–13). Against this evil, therefore, by which they committed sin, they needed the freedom he promised: “Everyone,” he says, “not the one who committed sin, but the one who commits sin, is a slave of sin.”

Why do you try to obscure clear words with murky arguments? They burst forth completely and, even though you resist, overcome your darkness by their brightness. “Everyone,” he says, “who commits sin is a slave of sin.” You hear “who commits,” yet you want not to explain but to substitute: “who committed.” Let those to whom he himself opens the meaning hear, so that they may understand the Scriptures: let them hear, “Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin.” And let them seek to receive freedom, so that they may not commit sin, crying out to him to whom it is said: “Direct my paths according to your word, and let no iniquity rule over me” (Psalm 118:133).

Why do you mock those slow to understand, and present the Lord’s words as though he had said that no one is a slave of sin except the one who has himself committed sin? You act deceitfully; he did not say this. He did not say, “No one is a slave of sin except the one who commits sin”; rather, he said, “Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin.” There are slaves of original sin who have not yet themselves committed sin, [Note: Vignierius reads “who do not commit it themselves.” The manuscripts support the present correction.] and through regeneration they are released from this bond of slavery.

Not everyone who is a slave of sin therefore commits sin; but everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin—just as not every animal is a horse, although every horse is an animal. Where is your dialectic, with which you are accustomed to inflate yourself? Why do these things escape one so learned and acute? Or why do you lay ambushes for the unlearned and the slow, if these things do not escape you?

But which one of us says that the whole human race is possessed by the devil, when there are so many thousands of saints who are not possessed by the devil? We say that those alone are not possessed by the devil whom Christ’s grace sets free—and you are enemies of this grace. For if you did not attack this grace but understood it, you would undoubtedly also see that, both before the Old Testament and during the time of the Old Testament, all the saints were separated from the condition of slaves and set free by that same grace of Christ.

### LXXXIX. JULIAN

Finally, so that you may understand that he reproaches not their nature but their life, what follows is: “I know that you are Abraham’s children.” Behold the freedom they had claimed for themselves on the ground of the dignity of their origin. Now he shows to what slavery they are subject, saying: [Note: Menardus reads: “See that they had called themselves free because of the dignity of their origin; now observe what name of slavery he imputes to them: ‘But you seek to kill me,’ and so forth.”]

“You seek to kill me because my word finds no place in you. I speak what I have heard from my Father, and you do what you have seen with your father.”

### AUGUSTINE

What does “My word finds no place in you” mean if a nature of this kind—one that now needs a liberator—is already capable of his word, even if his grace does not open its understanding, as he opened the understanding of the Apostles so that they might understand the Scriptures (Luke 24:45), and as he opened that of the purple-seller of Thyatira so that she might attend to what Paul was saying (Acts 16:14)?

### XC. JULIAN

See how different are the accounts of nature and of the will. Jesus did not deny that their flesh belonged to Abraham’s seed; but he impressed upon them that, through the iniquity of their will, they had passed over to the devil as the father of their will. He is called their begetter because he is charged with having instructed them in crimes.

“The Jews answered,” he says, “and said to him, ‘Our father is Abraham.’ Jesus says to them, ‘If you were Abraham’s children, you would do the works of Abraham. But now you seek to kill me, a man who has told you the truth that I heard from God; Abraham did not do this. You do the works of your father’” (John 8:37–41).

Do you see what divisions of words Wisdom makes? [Note: The editions read “what divisions of his words Wisdom makes.” “His” is absent from the manuscripts.] He denies that they are Abraham’s children, although above he had said that they were Abraham’s children. But because the discussion concerns different matters—nature and will—he shows that one person is the producer of innocent flesh, while another is the seducer of miserable will.

### AUGUSTINE

You speak truly, but incautiously. In paradise the devil was the seducer of a blessed will, which he made miserable by seducing it; now, however, as you admit, he is the seducer of a miserable will. From this misery, therefore—lest it be seduced by the devil now more easily through it than it was then seduced into it—no one sets it free except the one to whom the whole Church cries out daily: “Lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil” (Matthew 6:13). [Note: The manuscripts read “more easily through it than it was then seduced into it”; the editions have “from that.”]

### XCI. JULIAN

Here, then, when the Lord said, “If the Son sets you free, you will truly be free,” he promised pardon to the guilty, who, by sinning, lost not the freedom of choice but the consciousness of righteousness. Free choice, however, is just as complete after sins as it was before sins; for it is by that very choice that many renounce hidden things of shame (2 Corinthians 4:2), and, casting away the filth of disgraceful deeds, adorn themselves with the insignia of the virtues.

### AUGUSTINE

At least listen to yourself when you say above, chapter 69, that because of the habit of sins it was written: “I do not do what I want, but I do the very thing I hate.” How, then, is free choice free after sins, when, if not through their propagation because you refuse this, still through their habit—which alone, defeated and contorted, you concede to this necessity—it has so lost freedom that its groaning strikes your ears and beats against your forehead when you hear: “I do not do what I want,” and, “I do not do the good that I want, but I do the evil that I do not want” (Romans 7:15, 19)?

### XCII. JULIAN

Stop, then, impiously interpreting Christ’s words—if, indeed, you have any sense of what is permitted or forbidden left to you—in such a way that he appears to have denied free choice, without whose integrity the equity of his own judgment cannot stand.

### AUGUSTINE

On the contrary, the heavy yoke is upon the children of Adam from the day they leave their mother’s womb (Ecclesiasticus 40:1) precisely because the equity of judgment stands. It would be wholly unjust if they did not bear original sin, through which the human being has been made like vanity (Psalm 143:4).

### XCIII. JULIAN

Listen, indeed, to where he displays the power of human freedom: “I have come in my Father’s name, and you did not receive me; if another comes in his own name, him you will receive” (John 5:43). And again: “Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree bad and its fruit bad” (Matthew 12:33). And again: “If you do not wish to believe me, believe the works” (John 10:38).

Most forcefully of all, he says that his purpose was hindered by human will: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, how often I wanted to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were unwilling.” After this he does not continue, “But when you were unwilling, I gathered them”; rather: “Your house will be left to you desolate” (Matthew 23:37–38), showing that they are rightly punished for their evil work but ought not to have been recalled from their own intention by any necessity.

For he had also spoken in this way through the prophet: “If you are willing and listen to me, you will eat the good things of the land; but if you are unwilling and do not listen, the sword will devour you” (Isaiah 1:19–20). How, then, do you not deny free choice when, not indeed in your own words but by the testimony of the Gospel—and, in your understanding, by your own interpretation—you have pronounced it unfree?

### AUGUSTINE

You must be forgiven, since, as a human being, you are mistaken in a matter that is very deeply hidden. Far be it that the intention of the omnipotent and all-knowing God should be hindered by a human being. Those think too little about so great a matter—or are unequal to devising an account of it—who suppose that the omnipotent God can will something but, because a weak human being hinders him, cannot accomplish it.

Just as it is certain that Jerusalem did not wish her children to be gathered by him, so it is certain that, even against her will, he gathered whichever of them he wished. For God, as his human servant Ambrose said, “calls those whom he deigns to call, and makes religious whom he wishes” (*On Luke* 2.58).

Scripture often accommodates itself to human will, so that a person may recognize, when admonished, what he does not possess or cannot do, and ask it from the one from whom all good things come. For if he is heard in the matter about which we were commanded to say, “Lead us not into temptation,” then undoubtedly no one will be deceived by ignorance or overcome by desire.

Therefore it was said through the prophet, “If you are unwilling and do not listen to me, the sword will devour you,” and other statements of this kind: so that, when they found desires within themselves that were victorious, they might know from whom they ought to seek help to repel the evil. But it was said, “Behold, your house will be left to you desolate,” because there were many there whom, by hardening and abandoning them, he had judged worthy of this—by a hidden but nevertheless just judgment.

For if, as you say, “a human being ought not to be recalled from his own intention”—an intention that is certainly evil—“by any necessity,” why is the Apostle Paul, while still Saul, breathing slaughter and thirsting for blood, recalled from his worst intention by a violent bodily blindness and a terrifying voice from above, and why is he raised up from being a fallen persecutor to become a preacher of the Gospel he had attacked, destined to labor more than the others (Acts 9)?

Recognize grace: God calls one person in this way and another in that way, whom he deigns to call; and “the Spirit blows where it wills” (John 3:8).

### XCIV. JULIAN

For in that work which I told you above that you had recently sent to Rome, you disclosed your view more boldly. In the first book, when you had similarly set forth what we charge against you—that you deny free choice—you argue as the most steadfast and subtle of disputants:

“Who among us, then, says that free choice perished from the human race through the sin of the first human being? Freedom did perish through sin, but it was that freedom which existed in paradise: the possession of complete righteousness together with immortality. For this reason human nature needs divine grace, as the Lord says in his Gospel: ‘If the Son sets you free, then you will truly be free’” (John 8:36), “namely, free to live well and justly.

“For free choice did not perish in the sinner to such an extent that they do not sin through it—especially all who sin with pleasure and love of sin, and who are pleased by what they desire. Hence the Apostle says: ‘When you were slaves of sin, you were free from righteousness.’ Behold, they are shown to have been unable to serve sin except through another freedom. They are therefore not free from righteousness except by the freedom of choice; [Note: So Vignierius and Menardus; Menardus, however, gives *voluntas* (“will”) in the margin, a word Augustine himself uses in Book 1 of *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*.] but they do not become free from sin except through the grace of the Savior.

“For this reason the admirable Teacher carefully distinguished the very words: ‘When you were slaves of sin,’ he says, ‘you were free from righteousness. What fruit, then, did you have in those things of which you are now ashamed? For the end of those things is death. But now, having been set free from sin and having become servants of God, you have your fruit for sanctification, and the end, eternal life’” (Romans 6:20, 22). “He said ‘free from righteousness,’ not ‘set free from righteousness’; but he said ‘not free from sin,’ lest they attribute this to themselves. Rather, he most carefully preferred to say ‘set free,’ referring this to the Lord’s statement: ‘If the Son sets you free, then you will truly be free.’

“Since, therefore, the children of human beings do not live well unless they have become children of God, why does this man wish to attribute to free choice the power of living well? For this power is given only by the grace of God, through Jesus Christ our Lord (ibid. 7:25), as the Gospel says: ‘But to all who received him, he gave the power to become children of God’” (John 1:12).

And shortly afterward you say:

“Power is therefore given so that those who believe in him may become children of God. What power can this be, unless it is given by God? No power can arise from free choice, because what the liberator has not liberated cannot be free in the good; but in evil it possesses free choice. In it, either a hidden or manifest deceiver has implanted the pleasure of wickedness, or it has persuaded itself.

“Therefore, as some say that we say—and as this man even dares to write in addition—not everyone is compelled into sin against his will by the necessity of his flesh. Rather, if they are already at an age at which they use the choice of their own mind, they remain in sin by their own will and plunge from sin into sin by their own will.

“But this will, although free in evils because it delights in evils, is not free in good things because it has not been set free. Nor can a human being will anything good unless he is helped by the one who cannot will evil” (*Against Two Letters of the Pelagians* 1.5–7).

In all these words of yours that I have quoted, I see the name of grace intertwined with the denial of free choice in such a way that the evil in your understanding cannot so much be reclaimed by the goodness of the terms as the dignity of those terms is cheapened by their attachment to your doctrines. You have not, therefore, honored yourself by these statements; you have disgraced the very ornaments.

Nevertheless, we separate the things you have joined together, so that the divinity of grace, disentangled from shameful bonds, may neither be shaken by reply nor praised with Manichaean flattery, but commended with the weightiness of Catholics. [Note: The editions read “from obscure” or “unclean” bonds; the ancient manuscripts have the present reading, “from shameful bonds.”]

We therefore confess Christ’s grace to be manifold. Its first gift is that we were made from nothing. Its second is that, just as we are living beings endowed with sensation, so we surpass sentient beings through reason; reason has been impressed upon the soul so that it might be taught to be the image of the Creator. [Note: Perhaps “so that it might be called” should be read.] The freedom granted to the will likewise looks to the dignity of this image.

We also reckon among grace’s benefits the increases of the gifts that it never ceases to bestow upon us. Grace itself sent the law as a help (Isaiah 8:20, according to the Septuagint). Its function was to awaken, through instruction of many kinds, the light of reason that examples of depravity and the habit of vices had dulled, and to foster it by its invitation. [Note: The Clarendon, Marian, and Porta manuscripts read “and to foster its imitators.”]

The fullness of this grace—that is, of the divine benevolence that gave things their cause—therefore looked toward the Word becoming flesh and dwelling among us (John 1:14). For in seeking from his image a return of love, God openly showed how entirely he had acted toward us with immeasurable affection, so that, even if belatedly, we might love in return the one who, commending his love to us (Romans 5:8), did not spare his Son but handed him over for us, promising that, if thereafter we wished to obey his will, he would make us co-heirs of his Only-Begotten Son (Romans 8:32, 17).

### AUGUSTINE

Pelagian, love wills the good, and love is from God—not through the letter of the law but through the spirit of grace. For the predestined, the letter is a help in this respect: by commanding but not helping, it admonishes the weak to flee to the spirit of grace. Thus they use the law lawfully to whom it is good (1 Timothy 1:8), that is, useful. [Note: So the manuscripts. The editions instead read, “If they use the law lawfully.”] Otherwise the letter by itself kills (2 Corinthians 3:6), because, by commanding the good and not bestowing the love that alone wills the good, it makes people guilty of transgression.

### XCV. JULIAN

This grace, then, which in Baptism not only forgives sins but, together with this benefit of pardon, also advances, adopts, [Note: The Clarendon, Marian, and Porta manuscripts read “fits” or “adapts.”] and consecrates—this grace, I say, changes the merit of the guilty; it does not create free choice. We receive free choice at the time when we are created; we use it when [Note: Menardus reads, “We use it when”; Vignierius, “We use it when we acquire”; the manuscripts have “We use it when,” with “at the time” understood.] we acquire the capacity to distinguish between good and evil.

We do not, therefore, deny that innumerable forms of divine assistance are present to the good will, but in such a way that through these forms of assistance the freedom of choice, once destroyed, is neither fabricated anew, nor, after being excluded, is anyone believed to be subject to a necessity of either good or evil. Rather, every assistance cooperates with free choice.

### AUGUSTINE

If grace does not precede in order to operate upon the will, but cooperates with a will that already exists, how is it true that “God is the one who works in you both to will” (Philippians 2:13)? How is it true that “the will is prepared by the Lord” (Proverbs 8:35, according to the Septuagint)? How is it true that “love is from God” (1 John 4:7), when love alone wills the blessed good?

Or, if knowledge of the law and of God’s words produces love in us, so that we love by the choice of our own will—not by God’s gift—what we recognize, because God teaches it, ought to be loved, how is the lesser thing from God and the greater thing from us? For without God’s giving knowledge—that is, without his teaching—we cannot know; yet, if he does not give the love that surpasses knowledge (Ephesians 3:19), we can love. Only new heretics, excessively hostile to God’s grace, can think in this way.

### XCVI. JULIAN

This free choice, then, on account of which alone the Teacher of the Gentiles writes that we shall all be revealed before Christ’s tribunal, “so that each may receive what is due for what he has done in the body, whether good or evil” (2 Corinthians 5:10)—just as Catholics indeed confess, [Note: The Marian and Porta manuscripts read, “just as Catholics who confess to God.”] so you deny it not only together with Manichaeus [Note: So the manuscripts; the editions read “with the Manichaeans.”] but also together with Jovinian, whom you dare to thrust upon us—different, certainly, in kind, but similar in impiety.

To make this clearer, let an examination of the divisions be applied. We say that through human sin not the condition of nature but the quality of merit is changed; that is, even in one who sins there remains the nature of free choice, through which he can cease from sin, just as there was in him the capacity to turn away from righteousness.

### AUGUSTINE

We know why you say that human sin does not change the condition of nature: because you have abandoned the Catholic faith, which says that the first human being was made in such a way that he did not have the necessity of dying; but through sin the condition of nature was so changed that a human being must die. So much so that the Apostle says even to those already regenerated and given life in spirit: “If Christ is in you, the body indeed is dead because of sin, but the spirit is life because of righteousness. If the Spirit of the one who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, then the one who raised Jesus Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in you” (Romans 8:10–11).

He said, “He will also give life to your mortal bodies,” because we hope for this in the resurrection of the flesh, since he had said, “The body is dead because of sin”; yet you do not want the condition of nature to have been changed by sin.

Nevertheless, when Pelagius was charged at the Palestinian judgment with saying that infants newly born were in the condition in which Adam was before sin, he denied that he said this and condemned it. [Note: See *The Proceedings of Pelagius*, §§23, 24, 57.] If he had done so with a truthful heart, perhaps your heresy would by now have perished; at the very least, he himself would have been healed of that plague.

Next I ask whether sinful nature is free from defect. If that is absurd in the extreme, then it has a defect; and if it has a defect, it has undoubtedly been corrupted. How, then, has it not been changed, when, having been healthy, it was corrupted? [Note: We restore this sentence from the Marian, Clarendon, and Porta manuscripts: “How, then, has it not been changed, when, having been healthy, it was not corrupted?”]

Accordingly, even apart from that sin of which John Chrysostom said, “Adam committed that great sin and condemned all in common” (*Homily on the Resurrection of Lazarus*), and even apart from that sin from which human nature originally derives condemnation, how can it reasonably be said that the condition of nature was not changed in the human being who says: “The spiritual law is, but I am carnal, sold under sin; for what I do I do not understand, since I do not do what I want” (Romans 7:14–15), and other statements of this kind—even if he did not derive this change from the condition of his birth but, as you wish, contracted it through the habit of sinning?

Do you see that what you say is empty: that through human sin not the condition of nature but the quality of merit is changed? Unless, perhaps, you say that sin does not change nature but the human being. And what is this except to deny that the human being is nature? When would you say such things if you considered with a sound mind what you are saying?

## XCVII. JULIAN

The Manichaean says that an evil will is inspired by that nature which cannot will the good, but that a good will is infused by that nature which cannot will evil. Thus he imposes necessity upon the natures of individual things, so that their own wills cannot will opposites. [Note: [Col. 1113] The Marianus and Portuensis manuscripts add *et voluntatis* (“and of the will”).] Certainly there is a great gulf between us and him. Let us now see how far you have withdrawn from him.

You say that the will is free, but only so that it may do evil; you deny that it is free in such a way that it may cease doing evil, unless the necessity of willing good has been imposed upon it by that nature which, to use your own words, “cannot will evil” (*Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, Book 1, §7). You therefore define the human race as possessing through free choice nothing other than the ability to sin, and no ability to do anything else. By this you plainly declare that human nature always desires one thing, namely evil, and cannot will the opposite; whereas God’s nature cannot will evil. Therefore, unless God has made human nature evil a participant in its own necessity, there can be no good action in it.

After this, whether or not you love the Manichaean greatly, God sees in the secret of your heart. Yet insofar as the kinship of your doctrines reveals it, you have done absolutely nothing except, by changing the order, to construct the very position that he affirmed.

### AUGUSTINE

Would that you were vigorously destroying the Manichaean, rather than shamefully assisting him. For that man, perverted by excessive madness, does not say that the nature of evil is compelled to do good by another nature—that of the good—which cannot will evil. Rather, he says that the nature of the good is compelled to do evil by the nature of evil, which cannot will good. Thus, in astonishing madness, he wants the nature of evil to be immutable, but the nature of the good mutable.

It is certainly Manichaean to say that an evil will is inspired by the nature that cannot will good. But he does not say that a good will is infused by the nature that cannot will evil, as you more leniently suppose of him. For he does not at all believe the nature of the good to be immutable, such that it could not will evil, while believing that an evil will is inspired in it by that nature which cannot will good. Thus, he holds that through the nature of evil the nature of the good—which he wants to be nothing other than God’s nature—comes to will evil.  
[Note: In the printed editions, *quod* (“which”); we correct it from the manuscripts.]

You therefore assist him by denying that human nature was corrupted by the sin of the first man, so that he may attribute to the nature of evil that he imagines whatever evils he finds in the manifest misery of infants.

Further, since it displeases you that a human being cannot will good unless helped by him who cannot will evil, do you not see that you are contradicting the one who said, “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5), and Scripture, where we read, “The will is prepared by the Lord” (Proverbs 8:35, according to the Septuagint), and where we read, “For it is God who works in us both to will” (Philippians 2:13), and where we read, “The steps of a man shall be directed by the Lord, and he shall will his way” (Psalm 36:23)?

Here I marvel at nothing except how you call yourself a Christian while contradicting so many and such clear divine utterances.

## XCVIII. JULIAN

You are joined with Jovinian in one respect. For in the second book of his work he says that a baptized person cannot sin, but that before Baptism a person can both sin and not sin. Thus he agrees with you that from the time of Baptism a necessity of doing good is imposed upon human beings. This is just as false as your belief that before Baptism human beings possess a necessity of doing evil.

For when you say, “A person cannot will anything good unless he is helped by him who cannot will evil,” you evidently mean that through participation in grace and in a good nature a person acquires the ability to do good; yet you say that this can occur from the time of Baptism.

Thus, poised between impiety and fear, you have fled to the company of Jovinian, but you have not yet left the brothel of the Manichaeans. Nevertheless, Jovinian is more innocent than you by as much as the Manichaean is more profane than Jovinian.

To summarize still more briefly what we have argued: the Manichaean says, “In all human beings, the nature of darkness, which inspires evil will, commits sin, and cannot do anything else.” You say, “In all human beings, nature, infected by the darkness of the first sin and therefore the author of evil will, commits sin, and cannot will good.” Jovinian says, “The human will does indeed commit sin, but only until Baptism; afterward it cannot will anything except good.”

We Catholics—that is, we—say that from beginning to end, without any compulsion arising from nature, the will of each person sins before Baptism; and at the very moment when it sins, it has the power to turn away from evil and do good, so that the reality of freedom may be preserved.

Thus none of you possesses the truth of your doctrines. Yet, since you all set out from the same beginning of error, it would have been less disgraceful if you had admitted the consequences. Since you say with the Manichaean that an evil nature—that is, defective freedom—commits sin, you ought also to have said with him that it can in no way be cleansed. [Note: [Col. 1115] The printed editions read “the evil nature”; the manuscripts support the text given here.] You do indeed affirm this elsewhere, but you should have added what necessarily follows: that therefore it has no need of the sacraments of Baptism.  
[Note: Vignierius reads “of the sacrament.”]

Or, if with Jovinian you assert that good desires are impressed from the time faith is received, you should have said with him that nature was good even before Baptism; although it possessed the possibility of evil, it did not possess its necessity, and thus reached consecration to an inalienable good.  
[Note: Menardus reads *in addissimilabile*; Vignierius, *in inamissibile*. But the Claromontanus, Marianus, and Portuensis manuscripts read *ad indissimulabile*. Julian used this word above, chapter 1.]

In this way, although you would still contradict reason, you would at least not contradict the doctrines of those whom you follow.

### AUGUSTINE

You have forgotten what we say. Please remember. We are the ones who, while you protest, say that even righteous people, so long as they remain in this life, are not without reason to say truthfully of themselves in prayer, “Forgive us our debts” (Matthew 6:12). For if they say that they have no sin, they deceive themselves, and the truth is not in them (1 John 1:8).

What, then, is the point of your empty claim that I am joined with Jovinian in the respect in which he says that a baptized person cannot sin? Heaven forbid that we should be so deaf and mute that we do not hear the voice of baptized people, or fail to say with them, “Forgive us our debts.”

From the moment a person begins to use the power of the will, he can both sin and not sin. But he does not do the one of these without the help of him who said, “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). The other he does by his own will, whether seduced by himself or by another deceiver, or enslaved to sin as a servant.

We know that people were helped by the Spirit of God to will the things of God even before Baptism, as in the case of Cornelius (Acts 10); but some were not helped even after Baptism, as in the case of Simon Magus (ibid., 8). For “the judgments of God are like a great abyss” (Psalm 36:7), and “his grace is not from works; otherwise grace is no longer grace” (Romans 11:6).

Cease, then, to insult us with Manichaeus and Jovinian. If you had eyes, you would see whom you reproach in us—men whom, if we followed them, we could not deny original sin—and if you had any shame, you would be silent. [Note: [Col. 1115] Menardus reads, “to be openly joined to Jovinian’s opinion”; Vignierius, “to be joined in this respect to Jovinian’s opinion”; the manuscripts read, “to be joined with Jovinian in this respect.”]

But you are so slanderous that you say elsewhere that I have asserted that a person cannot be cleansed from sins, although I say that he can be cleansed in such a way that he is brought even to that state where, being perfectly blessed, he cannot sin.

## XCIX. JULIAN

Now, faithless toward everyone, you say that the necessity of sin has been made part of the nature of the flesh.

### AUGUSTINE

Deny that the Apostle said, “When you were slaves of sin, you were free with respect to righteousness.” Or, if you do not deny that he said this, do not accuse him of having spoken incorrectly.

If you do not dare to do that, then deny, if you can, that those to whom he says this possessed free will in evil when they were free with respect to righteousness; or that they possessed free will in good when they were slaves of sin. And dare to say that they were liberated from this slavery by themselves, not by the grace of God—those to whom it is said, “But now, having been freed from sin, you have become slaves of righteousness” (Romans 6:20, 22).  
[Note: Perhaps, “assert that they possessed.”]

But if you say that they were liberated by God’s grace from the guilt of past evils, not from the dominion of sin, by which no one is permitted to be righteous; and that, so that sin would not dominate them, they could have accomplished this themselves if they wished, without needing the grace of the Savior—where do you place the one who says, “I do not do the good that I want, but the evil that I do not want, that I do” (ibid. 7:19)?

If he says this while established under the Law and not under grace, deny that he is groaning beneath the heavy burden of necessity. Assert that he is free for living well and acting rightly through the power of the will, while he cries out to you, “You are lying or deceived; do not do what I want.”

But if, as Ambrose more correctly understood, the Apostle is speaking also about himself, then even righteous people in this life do not possess such freedom of their own will for accomplishing good as they will possess in that life in which it will not be said, “I do not do what I want.”

## C. JULIAN

Therefore, after losing possession of eternity—which, as is established, it never possessed through its own emergence—the will was to remain continually intent upon desiring depravity.

You add, “The will that is free in evil is not free in good.” You call something free that, as you say, cannot will anything except one thing, with no less an avowal of folly than of profanity.

### AUGUSTINE

If nothing is free except what can will two things—that is, both good and evil—then God is not free, since he cannot will evil; yet you yourself said, and said truly, “God cannot be anything except just” (above, chapter 23).

Do you praise God in such a way as to take freedom away from him? Or should you rather understand that there is a certain blessed necessity by which God cannot be unjust?

## CI. JULIAN

Although you are sound in no respect, let the prudent reader carefully consider what you have brought forward. Let us agree that the will can be called free even when it cannot will good; but you assert that this will is liberated in Baptism. [Note: [Col. 1116] The printed editions read *constet* (“is sound”); the manuscripts read *constes* (“you are sound”).]

I ask: in what manner is it liberated? Is it compelled always to will good and unable to will evil? Or is it enabled to desire both? If you answer, “It is compelled always to will good,” you yourself recognize how much of a Jovinianist you are.

But if you say, “How can the will be free if it is compelled always to will good?” I reply: how was it called free beforehand if it was compelled only to will evil?

If, then, you answer that after Baptism the will becomes free in such a way that it can both sin and not sin, by that very answer you will declare that free choice did not exist when it could not do both. You are trapped on every side by the snares of your argument: free choice existed before Baptism; it possessed the ability to do good just as it possessed the ability to do evil; and the entire stage of your doctrine, by which you persuade people that evil is natural, collapses.

### AUGUSTINE

Anyone who has read what I wrote above will find that I have already answered you concerning Manichaeus and Jovinian. But as for your saying that the person whose will we say is prepared by the Lord is made so good in will that he is compelled to will good—which, heaven forbid, should be said by us—your excellent intelligence may judge that.

For if he is compelled, he does not will. And what could be more absurd than to say that someone unwillingly wills what is good?

Consider also what you think about God’s nature, you who say that a person is compelled to will good if he cannot will evil. Is God compelled to will good because he cannot will evil, since he is altogether immutable?

Human nature, however, although mutable, is good insofar as it pertains to what it was created to be. It was made not only without defect, but, even when it is evil through defect, it is capable of that good by which it may become good.  
[Note: The printed editions read *quod* (“which”); all manuscripts read *quo* (“by which” or “whereby”).]

This true judgment overturns the deceptive madness of the Manichaeans.

In Baptism, all sins are therefore forgiven by God’s grace, through which a person is brought to Baptism with a will prepared by him for that purpose, so that thereafter, although his spirit lusts against the flesh in order not to consent to iniquity, the flesh nevertheless lusts against the spirit, so that he does not do what he wills. [Note: [Col. 1117] The manuscripts read “in God’s grace, and to it,” omitting *qua* (“through which”); the Portuensis manuscript reads *nec* (“nor”) for *ne* (“lest”).]

For he also wills not to have this lust of the flesh; but he cannot do so now. Hence he still groans within himself, awaiting “the adoption, the redemption of his body” (Romans 8:23), when he will possess flesh in such a way that he can no longer sin.

Now, therefore, a person not only can sin after Baptism; because even while rightly resisting the desire of the flesh he is sometimes drawn by it into consent, he also commits some sins—venial ones, certainly, but nevertheless some sins.  
[Note: One manuscript reads, “and although some are venial, nevertheless some.”]

He therefore has reason always to say here, “Forgive us our debts” (Matthew 6:12). This Catholic truth also refutes Jovinian’s vanity. What we say both against the Manichaean and against Jovinian overturns your heresy and your slanders.

## CII. JULIAN

But if free choice was not free beforehand for good, and after Baptism became so free that it cannot do evil, then it never possessed freedom of choice at all. It is proved to have sinned without guilt before Baptism and afterward to possess the glory of blessedness without concern for holiness.

### AUGUSTINE

Then God also has no freedom of choice, because he cannot do evil, just as he cannot deny himself (2 Timothy 2:13). He will also bestow upon us that supreme reward: that, although we will not be equal to God himself, we will nevertheless be equal to his angels and will not be able to sin. [Note: [Col. 1117] The particle *ad* (“for”) before “good” in Julian’s preceding statement is restored from the manuscripts.]

We must believe that after the fall of the devil he granted this to the angels as the reward of their good will, by which they stood firm in the truth, so that afterward no new devil would arise through free choice.

## CIII. JULIAN

From this you are plainly convicted of entirely denying your own doctrine, since you claim not to deny free choice while destroying it first by the necessity of evil and afterward by the necessity of good.  
[Note: The manuscripts read as above; the printed editions read, “your doctrines.”]

### AUGUSTINE

As I see it, you are about to say that God is oppressed by necessity, so that he cannot sin; yet he can neither will nor wish to be able to sin.

Rather, if necessity is to be called that by which something must either exist or occur, then that is an altogether blessed necessity by which one must live happily; in that same life one must not die and must not change for the worse.

By this necessity—if it too should be called necessity—the holy angels are not oppressed but enjoy it. For us it is future, not present.

## CIV. JULIAN

Nevertheless, for the complete destruction of your doctrine it is useful to recall your earlier definitions. If sin is nothing other than the will to retain and admit what justice forbids, and from which it is free to abstain, then no sin is found anywhere at all.

### AUGUSTINE

That is a definition of sin considered merely as sin, not also of the punishment of sin, by which the freedom not to sin was lost. From that evil no one liberates us except the one to whom we say not only, “Forgive us our debts,” but also, “Do not lead us into temptation, but deliver us from evil” (Matthew 6:12–13).

## CV. JULIAN

For if justice imputes nothing except that from which it is free to abstain, and if before Baptism there is a necessity of evil, since, as you said, the will is not free to do good and therefore cannot do anything other than evil, then the very necessity that it suffers defends it from the disgrace of evil. For that justice cannot burden it on account of its deeds which does not impute evil unless one is free to abstain from it.

After Baptism, however, if there is a necessity of good, then certainly there can be no sin. See, therefore, how that which reason demonstrates to be sin cannot be found among the offspring, since according to your definitions it is now found not even in conduct.

### AUGUSTINE

You are greatly mistaken, either because you think there is no necessity of sinning or because you do not understand that this necessity is the punishment of a sin committed without any necessity.

For if there is no necessity of sinning—leaving aside the force of that evil which is drawn from original sin, since you wish there to be no such thing—what, I ask, was suffered by the person who, according to your view, was weighed down by such a mass of evil habit that he said, “I do not do the good that I want, but the evil that I do not want, that I do” (Romans 7:19)?

Further, I think you should consider how much labor is required to learn what ought to be desired and what ought to be avoided in the conduct of life. Those who do not know this suffer the necessity of sinning through their very ignorance of what good is to be desired and what evil avoided. [Note: [Col. 1118] The Marianus and Portuensis manuscripts read, “Those who do not know this suffer, through the very ignorance of desiring good and avoiding evil, the necessity of sinning”; the printed editions alter the construction.]

For it is necessary that the person who does not know what he ought to do should do what he ought not to do. Concerning this class of evils, God is petitioned when it is said, “Remember not the sins of my youth and my ignorance” (Psalm 24:7).

If God, who is just, did not impute this class of sins, the faithful person would not ask that they be forgiven. Hence God’s servant Job also says, “You have sealed up my sins in a bag and marked down if I have committed anything unwillingly” (Job 14:17, according to the Septuagint).

You yourself, in the latest book of the four that you published against my one, say that from the emotions and passions of the mind there arises in human beings “an affective quality,” which clings to them so that it is removed either with great exertion or not at all.  
[Note: See above, Book 6 *Against Julian*, §54.]

Therefore, whoever sins through a fear that cannot be separated from him—what else can he do but sin by necessity?

Yet you at least concede that these sins arise from those sins that were committed without necessity, in the case of the person who says, “I do the evil that I do not want.” For the one who is weighed down by the habit of sinning so that he suffers this necessity was undoubtedly not yet weighed down by the necessity of habit before he sinned.  
[Note: The manuscripts read, “earlier, when he was sinning” (*prius cum peccaret*), rather than “before he sinned.”]

Thus, even according to you, the necessity of sinning, from which it is not free to abstain, is the punishment of that sin from which it was free to abstain when no burden of necessity pressed upon it.

Why, then, do you not believe that the ineffably great sin of the first man had at least as much power to corrupt the whole of human nature as the second nature now has in one individual? For you reminded us that learned people call habit “a second nature” (above, chapter 69).

Since, therefore, we acknowledge both the sins committed by human beings not through necessity but through will—sins alone, from which it is free to abstain—and the sins arising from the necessity of ignorance or of the emotions, which are now not only sins but also punishments of sins, and since the whole human race is filled with these, how can you say that according to our definitions sin is found not even in conduct?

But hear what you do not wish to hear. From all sins, whether original or moral, whether already committed or yet to be committed, no one liberates us except the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord. In him we have been regenerated, and from him we have learned to say in prayer not only, “Forgive us our debts”—that is, because we have sinned—but also, “Do not lead us into temptation”—that is, so that we may not sin.

## CVI. JULIAN

Now, having impressed the summary of this argument upon the mind of the prudent reader, let us examine what your Baptism—which you say was provided solely on account of the stirring of the genitals—actually accomplishes in carrying out the office entrusted to it.

It professes to cleanse people from sins. But when the case of the will is brought before justice, the will that could not will anything else is not declared guilty. When the charge of guilt disappears, the entire display of pardon also disappears, because one cannot forgive what one has no right to impute.

Thus Baptism frustrates the effects of its promise, since it finds neither crimes whose remission might be praised nor any debtors to this benefit, by which the bonds of sins might be loosed. For it cannot convict those placed in the refuge of necessity of an evil will. In all these respects, it is shown to be superfluous.  
[Note: [Col. 1119] The Marianus manuscript reads “affections” (*affectibus*); the text and printed editions read “effects” (*effectibus*).]  
[Note: The manuscripts read “nor does it find crimes”; the printed editions read “when it does not find crimes.”]  
[Note: The manuscripts read “by which the bonds of sins are loosed”; the printed editions read “by which the bonds of sins are loosed” in a different grammatical form.]

But since the grace provided by Christ is not superfluous, let its reasonable generosity be maintained: it is by this grace that the sinner’s will is convicted as guilty, since it was certainly able to will good just as it willed evil.

The entire fiction of necessity has therefore vanished. Consequently, there is no sin arising from the condition of nature; free choice persists in human nature. You deny this with the Manichaeans, but we confess it with the Apostles and all Catholics.

### AUGUSTINE

A person to whom justice is unknown must sin. Does it follow that, once he has come to know justice, the sins he committed through the necessity of ignorance should not be forgiven?

Or, because he now knows how he ought to live, should he rely upon himself to live justly, rather than upon the one to whom it is said, “Do not lead us into temptation”?

There is therefore no security of impunity in the necessity of sinning. But so that this necessity may not harm us, he grants deliverance to the one to whom it is said, “Deliver me from my necessities” (Psalm 24:17).

He grants it in two ways: by forgiving past iniquity and by helping us not to enter into temptation. “Each person is tempted when he is drawn away and enticed by his own desire” (James 1:14).

This concupiscence, which you have embraced, is so pleasing to you that when someone is not drawn by it into consent, you think concupiscence itself should be praised—as though a thing that impels someone toward evil were not evil if the person it impels resists rather than yields.

Even if someone consents to it, you make a great display of empty talk insisting that the person who fell, not the desire that impelled him; the person who was drawn, not the desire that drew him; and the person who was enticed, not the desire that enticed him, must be blamed. For, as you define it, he made bad use of a good thing.

You possess such an evil spirit that the desire by which the flesh lusts against the spirit appears good to you.

But you think you have cleverly mocked our position concerning Baptism by falsely claiming that we say Baptism was provided solely on account of sexual activity. We do not say this. We say what you are trying to overthrow by a new and heretical perversity: divine provision was made for the assistance of a second, spiritual birth—which Christ established to take place in himself—because those born carnally according to Adam contract the contagion of ancient death through their first birth (Cyprian, *Letter 64, to Fidus*).

Behold, I have used the words of the African bishop Cyprian, against whom you bark even though he was a martyr, while attacking the firmly established faith of the Church for which his blood was shed.

For just as the Apostle Paul said, “Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death; and so it passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Romans 5:12), so Bishop Cyprian, understanding this Apostle, confessed that those born carnally according to Adam contract the contagion of ancient death through their first birth.  
[Note: The manuscripts read as above; the printed editions read, “and so Cyprian too, as he understood this Apostle.”]

Why, then, do you falsely join yourself to the Apostles and all Catholics, when you openly contradict the Apostle by deceit, and contradict the Catholic bishop and martyr in what he understood together with the Eastern and Western Catholic Church?  
[Note: The word “Church” is restored from the manuscripts.]

## CVII. JULIAN

The explanation you imposed upon the words of the Apostle Paul should properly be passed over with laughter, were it not frightening to those ignorant of the Scriptures.

“When you were slaves of sin,” says the Apostle, “you were free with respect to righteousness.” He certainly could not have said, “You were liberated,” because the language of liberation is appropriately and properly used when a person is freed from harmful things. But people can be called free from virtues when they decide that they owe nothing to virtue.

A person can therefore be called free from both good and evil when, serving one, he strives to owe nothing to the other. But he can be called liberated only from evil, because this word of liberation contains an indication of the distress that is driven away.

What question, then, could be raised against the Apostle here concerning his words, when, according to the custom of the human race, he said that they were free from good but liberated from evil?

“When you were slaves of sin,” he says, “you were free with respect to righteousness. What fruit did you then have in those things of which you are now ashamed?”

But so that you would not think that we become slaves of sin by nature, hear the Apostle himself speaking in the same passage: “Do you not know that to whom you present yourselves as slaves for obedience, you are slaves of the one whom you obey, whether of sin or of obedience to righteousness?” (Romans 6:20, 21, 16).

“You presented yourselves,” he says, as slaves to sin, so that you might understand that he attributes sin to the will, not to birth. For this reason alone, then, he said that they had been free with respect to righteousness: because they had refused to obey its commands.

### AUGUSTINE

If people were said to have been free with respect to righteousness solely because they had refused to obey its commands, then before they received the commands of righteousness, which they refused to obey, they were not free with respect to righteousness and were slaves of sin. Who could say this?

He therefore liberates them from this necessity of slavery who not only gives commands through the Law, but also grants love through the Spirit, by whose delight the delight of sin is overcome. Otherwise that delight remains unconquered and holds its servant. “By whatever a person is overcome, to that he is enslaved” (2 Peter 2:19).

## CVIII. JULIAN

Finally, he immediately adds that they are slaves of righteousness just as they had previously been slaves of sin. From this, if you wish, you can now call them free from sin while they serve righteousness, just as he called them free from righteousness when they served sin.

You have therefore most foolishly attempted to bring an accusation against the apostolic simplicity. For he did not, as you suppose, announce with exceptional vigilance what you imagine; rather, you look at what he said with extraordinary sleepiness.

You argue that he preferred to call them liberated rather than free so that we might understand that through freedom of choice it is indeed possible to do evil, but not possible to become good.

Yet the very order of his words resists you. For if he had thought what you think—namely, that sin occurs only through freedom—he ought to have said, “You were free from sin,” not, “You were free with respect to righteousness,” so that the person for whom freedom itself was working would be called free.  
[Note: The printed editions read, “For if what you think were the case”; the manuscripts read, “For if he had thought what you think.”]

If it is worthwhile even to weigh the significance of grammatical cases, he said that they were free *with respect to* righteousness, not free *from* righteousness. We would therefore be assisted more consistently by this expression if we wished to press such trifles.

But far from it. We understand the Apostle’s meaning and are content with the function of expressions spoken plainly. The Teacher of the Gentiles said nothing other than this: “You were free”—you did not serve—“with respect to righteousness”; “you were liberated”—you received forgiveness of sins—while the freedom of choice remained, through which they were able both to sin before and afterward to obey righteousness.

### AUGUSTINE

From this heretical understanding, according to which you say that grace does not liberate from sin except when forgiveness is granted for the past, and not also so that sin may not dominate when someone is drawn by his own desire into consent, you also contradict the prayers of the saints.

Why is it said to God, “Do not lead us into temptation,” if, so that this may not happen, it lies within the power of our free choice—something naturally implanted in us?

Why does the Apostle say, “We pray to God that you do no evil” (2 Corinthians 13:7), if God does not liberate from sins except by granting forgiveness for past sins?

## CIX. JULIAN

Finally, he shows what his exhortation means by prefacing it: “I speak in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh. For just as you presented your members as slaves to impurity and iniquity for iniquity, so now present your members as slaves to righteousness for sanctification. For when you were slaves of sin, you were free with respect to righteousness” (Romans 6:19–20).

He most orderly calls those free with respect to righteousness who ought to have kept their members in complete sanctification.

But since we have lingered here at some length in order to show that what I said was absolutely certain—namely, that people would deny free choice if they were frightened by your speech and driven into genuine destruction by an empty fear—and that you are the chief denier of free choice, let us return to the book addressed to Valerius.

There we shall first prove that you denied God the Creator, but now, in one place denying it and in another place confessing it much more wickedly than you had denied it.

Indeed, when your earlier book was examined, it became sufficiently clear how plainly you denied that God was the creator of human beings. For you said that “the devil could lawfully pluck the human race as fruit from a shrub planted by him” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, Book 1, §26). Many other statements that you placed there as arguments also contribute to this error.

In this second book, although you do the same thing in the entirety of your doctrine, you nevertheless strive more perniciously to correct the opinion that you previously expressed.

### AUGUSTINE

If the Apostle is not enough for you—he who says, “Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death; and so it passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned”—then Ambrose certainly understood the Apostle not as a Manichaean, although you accuse people of Manichaean faith with that name, but as a Catholic. Understanding him, he said, “We are all nourished under sin, for our very birth is in defect” (*On Repentance*, Book 1, chapter 2).

Behold the source from which the devil lawfully plucked fruit as from his own shrub—not from the nature God created, but from the defect that he himself planted. For those who are born under sin can be under no other author than the author of sin, unless they are reborn in Christ.

## CX. JULIAN

Let us briefly complete the reply owed to the heading that we set out above (chapter 74). I answer consistently and faithfully that we do not begrudge human beings the Lord Jesus Christ as liberator. We warn them so that, by believing you, they may not be broken by despair of amendment and withdraw from Christ’s instruction, as though it commanded what mortal nature, burdened as it is by an inborn evil, cannot receive.

### AUGUSTINE

Death also is inborn. Yet he liberates from it who gives life to those whom he wills (John 5:21). Those who wish to be liberated from inborn evil ought to flee to him. To learn who draws them to do this, read the Gospel (ibid. 6:44).

## CXI. JULIAN

Let them instead run to the one who cries, “My yoke is easy and my burden is light” (Matthew 11:30). In his immeasurable generosity, he both grants forgiveness to the evil will and makes the innocence that he creates good even better by renewing and adopting it.  
[Note: So read in the manuscripts. The printed editions have “to the evil will.” Marius Mercator, in his *Summary of Notes on Julian’s Writings*, read here, “who grants forgiveness to the one acting wrongly.”]

### AUGUSTINE

These are the very people from whom you begrudge the liberator: people whom you deny possess an evil from which they may be liberated.

How, then, do you answer consistently and faithfully that you do not begrudge human beings the Lord Jesus Christ as liberator, when you act rather with stubbornness and faithlessness to prevent people from believing that infants can be saved by him, just as he saves his people from their sins? For this reason, as the Gospel tells us, we have learned that he was called Jesus (ibid. 1:21).

You will therefore not be able to show that you do not begrudge human beings Christ the liberator, since you cannot in any way demonstrate that infants are not human beings.

## CXII. JULIAN

I am therefore astonished that you dared to bring forward the testimony, “By whatever a person is overcome, to that he is enslaved” (2 Peter 2:19). This passage most plainly supports us, since we assert that no one can be subject to the devil unless, after a struggle of the will, he has been overcome by a dishonorable surrender.

You, however, ought not to have appropriated it, since it strongly contradicts you when you persuade people that those who are born are in the kingdom of the devil, although without their own will they could neither have been overcome nor have sinned.

[Additional editorial notes: [Col. 1116] In chapter C, Menardus reads “by which profanity,” and Vignierius “by which profanation”; the manuscripts support “than of profanity.” [Col. 1117] In chapter CII, the manuscripts restore *ad* (“for”) before “good.” [Col. 1118] In chapter CIV, the Claromontanus and Marianus manuscripts read “the whole [destruction]” rather than “the complete [destruction].” In chapter CV, the printed editions read “to justice,” while the manuscripts read “justice”; Menardus reads “what,” and he and Vignierius read “does what they ought not to do,” whereas the manuscripts support “does what he ought not to do.” [Col. 1121] In Augustine’s reply to chapter CVII, the printed editions read “unwilling,” but the Marianus and Portuensis manuscripts read “unconquered,” as translated. [Col. 1123] In chapter CXI, the manuscripts read “and he grants forgiveness to the evil will”; the printed editions read “of evil will.” Marius Mercator, in the *Commonitory of Annotations on Julian’s Writings*, reads: “who grants forgiveness to one acting evilly.”]

Augustine. Those whom you say, being newborn, could neither be conquered nor contend derive their origin from him in whom all sinned—and, what is worse, that man was conquered without a struggle. For Adam existed, and in him we all existed; Adam perished, and in him all perished (Ambrose, Book 7 on Luke, chapter 15, no. 234). Allow the little ones, then, to be found by him who came to seek what was lost (Luke 19:10); otherwise, since they too are human beings, you are plainly envious of Jesus the liberator, however much you think that the cruelty of this error of yours must be concealed by all your verbosity [Col. 1124].

**CXIII. Julian.** Seeing that this indeed counts very strongly against you, as though questioned by that very testimony, “How, then, are little children in the kingdom of the opposing power, if Scripture is believed that everyone, when conquered, is then the servant of the conqueror, and it is agreed that infancy, without the use of reason and will, could neither have fought nor yielded?” you add (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, Book 2, no. 8):

> “Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death; and thus it passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Romans 5:12).

> “Now God is the creator of those who are born in such a way that all proceed from one into condemnation unless they have a liberator through rebirth. He himself is called the potter, making from the same lump one vessel for honor according to mercy, another for dishonor according to judgment” (Romans 9:21), “to whom the Church sings, ‘Mercy and judgment’” (Psalm 101:1).

Although I briefly showed in the fourth book how this statement of yours—that sin entered through one man—ought to be understood, in a passage by which you have stirred the hearts of many uneducated people (*To Turbantius*), nevertheless, with Christ’s help, we shall explain it more fully in this work, so that in the second book, setting aside other matters, the apostolic passage itself may be discussed in full according to its context.

**Augustine.** To what you say you briefly demonstrated in your fourth book, an answer was given in our sixth book (*Against Julian*, Book 6, no. 75 ff.). But when you begin to fulfill the promise you make for this work, it will become clear there how much of a purveyor of empty words you are.

**CXIV. Julian.** Here I should briefly point out that this cannot support the confirmation of that opinion which all learning, all reason, and the law of God prove to be utterly unjust. Let the careful reader therefore attend to what you declared: that God is the maker of evils, and that he creates such beings as, without any merit of their own will, all proceed into condemnation.

**Augustine.** This is what I said: he makes human nature, which is evil through a defect that he himself did not make; and from that nature he himself does something good even when the human beings he makes are evil—for he makes them insofar as they are human beings, not insofar as they are evil. For vessels would not be made for dishonor unless they were evil; yet, through the nature that God makes [Note: [Col. 1124] The printed editions read *fecit*, “made.” The manuscripts read *facit*, “makes.”], they are certainly good. They are evil, however, according to the defect that the enemy has implanted in nature—indeed, contrary to nature, but nevertheless within nature—so that from this there might be an evil nature, that is, an evil human being.

For there can be no evil except in something good, since it can exist only in some nature; and every nature, insofar as it is nature, is good. Pay close attention to how things are said that appear to be contrary to one another but are not—provided, of course, that you have not entirely lost your sight through the smoke of proud contention.

**CXV. Julian.** And lest we fail to know of what period you were speaking [Note: [Col. 1124] The printed editions read *ac ne sciremus*, “and lest we should know.” The manuscripts correct this to *ac ne nesciremus*, “and lest we should fail to know.”], you declare that from Adam, whom you say was one in all, to the end of the age, all who have not been baptized are found liable to condemnation and to the devil [Col. 1125]. In holding this opinion you strive to inflict a much more destructive wound than the one you previously caused. For, in order to remove the odium that was falling upon you because you said that the devil was the creator of human beings, you have been corrected into confessing that God is the creator—but of beings such as Manichaeus assigns to the prince of darkness [Note: [Col. 1125] Thus in all the manuscripts. The printed editions instead read: “but another, such as Manichaeus writes, the prince of darkness.”].

**Augustine.** “All human beings are born under sin, and their very birth is in a state of defect.” This was not said by the filthy heretic Manichaeus, but by the holy Catholic Ambrose (*On Repentance*, Book 1, chapter 2 or 3). Moreover, Manichaeus neither says that every nature, insofar as it is nature, is good, nor says in any way that the nature he calls evil can be healed and made good. The Catholic faith says this concerning human nature, both of the small and of the great, against both Manichaeans and Pelagians—both insane through different diseases, but equally deranged.

**CXVI. Julian.** Indeed, believing that human beings were evil by the condition of their birth, he assigned them an author through whom the guilt of an evil work could be separated from the good God. And because he had gone astray in defining sin, supposing that to be natural which cannot be anything but voluntary, he consequently invented an artificer of the evil of their origin—more religious toward God, more insolent toward nature. You, however, say that they are indeed born evil, but that God is the author of evils: you are more insolent toward God and more respectful toward nature. For nature is defended by the majesty of its author, while the author is accused because of the foulness of his work.

**Augustine.** Accuse God, then, if you please, because of the foulness of his work; for some bodies are born so deformed that, because of their excessive disfigurement, some are even called monsters. It is not another god, as Manichaeus imagines, nor lesser gods, as Plato mistakenly thinks, who are the creators of bodies. Rather, the good and just God certainly produces even such bodies [Note: [Col. 1125] The manuscripts of Marianus and Portus read *corporalia*, “corporeal.”]. If you relate these things to the “heavy yoke upon the sons of Adam” (Ecclesiasticus 40:1), you will find that he is neither evil, such as the one Manichaeus employs in fabricating bodies, nor defeated and entangled and mixed with evils, which Manichaeus is not afraid to believe concerning the good God. Rather, he is plainly just because of original sin, such as the Catholic faith knows him to be—a faith from which your error has departed.

For if no one had sinned, even deformed and monstrous bodies would not have been born in paradise.

**CXVII. Julian.** You did not fear, most wicked man, to attribute to God that which Manichaeus, so that he might not bring it near to him, invented another creator to accomplish. Both of you are indeed enemies of the truth; but before you, he was thought incapable of being surpassed in impiety.

**Augustine.** Before me there was Ambrose, who was not a Manichaean; before him, Hilary and Gregory; before them, Cyprian and the others, whom it would take too long to enumerate—all of whom were not Manichaeans. Yet they taught the Church what they had learned in the Church: that little children bear original sin and must be exorcised in exorcisms, so that they may be rescued from the power of darkness and transferred into the kingdom of their Savior and Lord [Col. 1126] (Colossians 1:13).

Since Christ died even for them—as you too have been compelled to confess—it follows that all were dead; and he died for all, as the Apostle says (2 Corinthians 5:14–15). If, according to your words, the Apostle himself is also a Manichaean, what, then, will you be?

**CXVIII. Julian.** You, however, as the prophet says, have justified your sister Sodom (Ezekiel 16:51); Manichaeus will be thought acquitted if compared with your blasphemies. In the first book of my work I had gloried that I was being torn apart by the mouth through which the Apostles too had suffered abuse. But now I am overwhelmed by the greatness of my good fortune: I am reproached by one who accuses God.

**Augustine.** You are reproached by one who, together with Ambrose and his other companions, proclaims Christ the liberator even of little children. You not only accuse him as a liar when he says that he came to save and seek what was lost (Luke 19:10), but you also contradict him so that he may not seek to save the little ones.

**CXIX. Julian.** From where, then, has such dignity of insult come to me? You could not have conferred anything so remarkable upon me by your praise. You say that my opinions deserve rejection, but that God’s works deserve condemnation; that I argue badly, but that God creates wickedly; that I am in error, but that he rages; that I do not know the law, but that God does not know justice. You shout that I am not a Catholic because I say that Christ provokes those whom he saves; yet you swear that God creates those whom he condemns, and creates them for no other reason than that they should all proceed into condemnation.

**Augustine.** The same thing could be said of God’s foreknowledge, which the faithful cannot deny—and I think neither can you. Or deny that God foreknows that he will condemn many whom he creates, lest he appear to create those whom he condemns.
