And, what is more marvelous and inscrutable, deny that he takes many from this life, lest wickedness change their understanding (Wisdom 4:11), although he cannot be ignorant that they will become evil [Note: [Col. 1126] The negative particle is restored here on the authority of the manuscripts Marianus, Clarus, Portus, and Colbert.].

Give glory to God. Let the ruin of your babbling words yield before the height of his judgments—words seemingly polished and sharp, but really made of glass [Note: [Col. 1126] Thus Vignierius and Menardus. In manuscript B: “as though polished and sharp,” with *et* omitted.].

**CXX. Julian.** Between you and Manichaeus, the composer of your opinions, I see that, through the progress of your learning, a great distance has arisen. Although he introduced two authors, he nevertheless left hope of salvation in that portion of his teaching in which he said that the good God was utterly alien to iniquity and cruelty. You, however, while speaking of one good God, also make him the creator of evils; and thus you have utterly removed both reverence for the deity and hope of salvation [Note: [Col. 1126] Here we add *bonum*, “good,” from the manuscripts.].

**Augustine.** The Manichaeans imagine a God cruelly weak, who handed over his own portion, his own substance, the members of his own nature, to be torn apart and polluted by enemies—enemies whom he saw threatening to devastate him. You, however, who do not deny that God is omnipotent, want him to be believed unjust because of the heavy yoke imposed upon little children, by denying original sin [Col. 1127].

**CXXI. Julian.** There is no one to help the guilty when the one who is himself one, from a desire to create miseries, also punishes those in whom he recognizes nothing other than what he himself made.

**Augustine.** He recognizes there also what he himself did not make: for he did not make sin. Another empty person, just as vain as you, could say [Note: [Col. 1127] Vignierius: “Another, vain like you, could say that another…”], that God, from a desire to create miseries, also creates those whom he could not fail to know he would condemn—far more numerous than those whom he foreknew he would liberate.

**CXXII. Julian.** Now that the abyss of your impiety has been surveyed—although nothing more profane could ever be found—its complete lack of force, and what follows from the matters you had added, will be demonstrated in a brief argument. God, who wished to be called by this name, is believed to be not only omnipotent but also most just. If either of these is absent, neither is present. As the most benevolent creator of human beings, so also is he the most equitable examiner of merits [Note: [Col. 1127] The edition of 1635 reads “examiner of merits.” Vignierius’s edition and the manuscripts Marianus, Clarus, and Portus more correctly read “expunger of merits.” Thus above, in manuscript 37, *expunctrix uniuscujusque meritorum*, “the expunger of each person’s merits,” that is, one who assigns what is due to merits according to the standard of equity. Because names of persons or debts written in registers were customarily marked with a point when they had been settled, this gave rise to the expression “expunger of merits,” meaning one who repays in proportion to merits. Thus Tertullian, *On the Crown of the Soldier*, chapter 1: “Crowned soldiers were marked off in the camps,” which is understood to refer to the donative paid to the soldiers.]. Everything he makes is very good. Therefore no one is naturally evil; but whoever is guilty is accused on account of conduct, not of origin.

**Augustine.** Why, then, is there a heavy yoke upon the origins of little children under the omnipotent and most just God?

**CXXIII. Julian.** Evil, therefore, is not natural; God cannot create the guilty; and he cannot place them in the devil’s kingdom. From these points it will be shown that you too are a Manichaean—or rather, worse than Manichaeus. The fruit of fecundity and natural innocence, entering this human world without sin and under God’s law rather than the devil’s, have shone forth.

**Augustine.** Then Ambrose too, who said, “At the beginnings of their nature, the little ones who have been baptized are reformed from evil” (Book 1 on Luke 1:17, no. 37), is shown to be a Manichaean—or worse than Manichaeus, as you insult him—or else you are mad [Note: [Col. 1127] The printed editions read *in primordio*, “at the beginning.” The manuscript of Portus reads *in primordia*, “at the beginnings,” as in Ambrose and, above, in Book 1 of *Against Julian*, no. 10.].

**CXXIV. Julian.** With this established, attend to what follows from your argument. It is agreed that the prophets, patriarchs, and all the saints of the Old Testament were without baptism, but were created by God and thereafter shone with their own virtues. Are they therefore to be believed to have existed under the devil’s kingdom, destined to be handed over to eternal punishments, contrary to the testimony of the law, because you declare that all were created from Adam for condemnation [Note: [Col. 1127] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read “in condemnation.”]?

**Augustine.** The same grace liberated those ancient righteous people against which you have declared war, although they used different sacraments according to the times. For what we believe concerning Christ, they also believed. There is one God, and one Mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus [Col. 1128] (1 Timothy 2:5). His coming in humility was foretold to them and announced to us; his coming in glory, which will occur at the end, was foretold both to them and to us.

Thus both their faith and ours are one faith in this one Mediator, and the spirit of faith is the same in them and in us. Hence the Apostle says: “But possessing the same spirit of faith, according to what is written, ‘I believed, therefore I spoke’; we too believe, and therefore we speak” (2 Corinthians 4:13).

And so that we may not boast as though this faith came from ourselves, let us hear the same apostle: “By grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not from yourselves; it is the gift of God” (Ephesians 2:8). And elsewhere he says: “Peace to the brothers and love with faith from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ” (Ephesians 6:23).

**CXXV. Julian.** If you should say that you are plainly a Manichaean, even your own patrons will be able to admit it. But if you should understand that the entire army of the true King is fighting against your opinion, and that you cannot prejudice even those patrons, accept that what you had built has been destroyed. Consequently, not all proceed from one into condemnation, but only those who, having rebelled against God’s will, are finally found at the end without repentance and without correction.

**Augustine.** Add also those who have been begotten but not regenerated, because all sinned in one (Romans 5:12).

**CXXVI. Julian.** As for the statement that God is the potter, making from the same lump one vessel for honor and another for dishonor (Romans 9:21), you should not have mentioned it at all. For although it is explained by us consistently, it is entirely opposed to you. When some are said to be made for honor and others for dishonor, the understanding of Catholics is supported: according to the difference of human will, a different outcome for the vessels is proclaimed.

**Augustine.** Listen to Ambrose, who says: “All human beings are born under sin, and their very birth is in a state of defect” (*On Repentance*, Book 1, chapter 2 or 3). Thus, along with his fellow disciples and fellow teachers, who were unquestionably Catholics, he understood what was written concerning sin and death: that it entered through one and passed into all human beings (Romans 5:12).

Understand that this is the lump from which both kinds of vessels are made. For if the solution to this inscrutable question were the one you propose, according to the merits of wills, it would be so obvious that the Apostle would not have been compelled by any difficulty to say, “O human being, who are you to answer back to God?” (Romans 9:20).

The matter concerned those not yet born, one of whom God loved and the other hated—not on the basis of works, but according to his purpose. Hence the discussion reached the point at which it was said that vessels of different kinds are made from the same lump, and that the potter has authority.

**CXXVII. Julian.** But you, who had said above that all proceed into condemnation—what sort of face did you have when you produced the testimony which declares that one proceeds into honor and another [Note: [Col. 1128] The printed editions read “that some proceed into honor and others.” The manuscripts consistently have “one.”] into dishonor?

**Augustine.** Grace liberates those whom it liberates from the condemnation of the whole lump [Col. 1129]—and by denying this you are heretics. As far as origin and its merit are concerned, all proceed from one into condemnation (Romans 5:16). As far as grace is concerned, however, which is not given according to merits, all who are liberated from this condemnation are called vessels of mercy. Those who are not liberated remain under the wrath of God (John 3:36), which comes from God’s just judgment. This judgment is not therefore blameworthy merely because it is inscrutable.

For this reason they are called vessels of wrath: God also makes good use of them, so that he may make known the riches of his glory in the vessels of mercy (Romans 9:23). What is exacted from others when God judges is granted to these when he shows mercy [Note: [Col. 1129] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read “when he has compassion.”]. If you think that these unsearchable ways of the Lord ought to be condemned, listen: “O human being, who are you to answer back to God?” [Note: [Col. 1129] In the Marianus codex appears: “O human being, who are you? Who are you to answer back to God?”]

**CXXVIII. Julian.** Nothing is so contradictory as to say “all” and “not all.” You say that all are made for condemnation by God the potter; the Apostle says that not all are made for condemnation, nor all for honor. In its proper place I shall explain fully what dignity this statement possesses. Yet even in the very formulation of the sentence it is clear that there is great disagreement among you. The potter who fashions everything for condemnation is not the same potter whom Paul says fashions some for honor. Nor do you believe in the potter whom the admirable teacher proclaims, since your potter fashions all for condemnation, whereas the Apostle’s potter fashions many for glory.

**Augustine.** When all are said to proceed from one into condemnation, the lump itself is signified—from which the potter makes some vessels for honor, that is, those who are taken up into grace, and others for dishonor, that is, those who are left to pay what is owed. Thus the children of grace may know that what is given to them would not be unjust if it were exacted from them; and so they may glory not in themselves but in the Lord (1 Corinthians 1:31).

**CXXIX. Julian.** I have said these things so that it might immediately become clear that you possess either singular incompetence or singular shamelessness, since, in place of your own arguments, you use arguments that contradict them. In any case, piety and reason will explain that my God forms no one for dishonor.

**Augustine.** If your god forms no one for dishonor, he is not the God of the Apostle Paul. For Paul was speaking of the true God when he said: “O human being, who are you to answer back to God? Will the thing formed say to the one who formed it, ‘Why did you make me like this?’ Or does the potter not have authority over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?” (Romans 9:20–21).

But you, evidently a great craftsman, bring forth from the Pelagian workshop a better god, one who makes no vessel for dishonor.

**CXXX. Julian.** Rather, he creates all human beings good, as his image, and desires to restore with the generosity of remedies even those who have been destroyed by the perversity of their pursuits. To him the Church sings, “Mercy and judgment” (Psalm 101:1), because he is kind to those who have committed no offense, and justly punishes those who, created good by God, sinned of their own will [Col. 1130] [Note: [Col. 1130] The manuscripts Marianus, Portus, and Clarus read “with a will that persuaded them.”]. Thus the Catholic Church sings this mercy and this judgment. But nothing of this sort can resound in your church, which says that, without justice, without judgment, and without mercy, God the creator of evils forms those whom he will punish, and punishes them for no other reason than that he himself formed them from Adam.

**Augustine.** I have already answered all these points above, but hear briefly what must be said here as well. God does not withhold the goodness of his creative work even from a condemned stock. But if it displeases you that God creates those whom he condemns, contradict him, if you can, so that he will not create those whom he foreknew would become evil, persevere in wickedness to the end, and therefore certainly be condemned.

Or, if you prefer, suggest to him that he should snatch from this life the many thousands of unbaptized little children whom he knows will live ruinously and, condemned by him, will go with the devil into eternal fire—snatch them away while they are innocent and good—so that, if not in his kingdom, they may at least possess eternal life in some place of lesser happiness which your heresy has constructed for such people.

You still have something to suggest, as God’s counselor, concerning his children whom he has regenerated and adopted, yet whom he foresaw would become evil and be condemned: that before they enter into a guilty life, they should be deprived of life itself and belong to his kingdom rather than to eternal punishments.

When you think you have made the envious charge that God creates those whom he condemns, consider how much more enviously another equally vain person could say that God regenerates those whom he condemns, since it lies within his omnipotent power [Note: [Col. 1130] The manuscript of Portus reads “within the power of the omnipotent one.”] to remove them from the trials of this mortal life before they become condemnable.

But if you cannot say these things, cannot contradict God, and cannot offer your counsel to his wisdom—for “who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?” (Romans 11:34)—stop introducing another potter who makes no vessels for dishonor, and refrain from criticizing the one who does make them. Recognize yourself [Note: [Col. 1130] The printed editions omit *te*, “yourself.” It is restored from the manuscripts]. For, so that you may not involve yourself in this sacrilege, the Apostle says to you: “O human being, who are you to answer back to God?”

**CXXXI. Julian.** But now let the dignity of the apostolic statement be defended, lest it be thought that he meant this only of some people, whereas you have judged it of all. The Apostle Paul, therefore, in discussing the questions raised by the Jews [Note: [Col. 1130] Vignierius needlessly corrected *cum quaestionibus*, “with the questions,” to *cum quibusdam*, “with certain people.” Julian is referring to the questions resolved by the Apostle in the Epistle to the Romans.], who, puffed up by the dignity of their ancestry, disdained faithful Gentiles as though they were not their equals, commends both the justice and the grace of God. He argues that their generosity consisted first in the fact that the Jews had been ennobled by the knowledge of the law, and thereafter in the fact that the preaching of Christ had also admitted the Gentiles.

The one creator of both peoples will judge the former through the law and the latter in the law [Col. 1131] (Romans 3:29) because he was not the God of the Jews only, but also of the Gentiles. He renders to each person his due without fraud and without favor, that is, without respect of persons—“favor” being the term that, in the definition of justice, expresses partiality.

Thus he justly condemns those descended from Abraham when they live wickedly and expels them from their inheritance, just as he does Gentiles found engaged in similar conduct. Conversely, he grants the good wills, true faith, and upright actions of both peoples to everlasting joys.

The Teacher of the Gentiles therefore restrains the arrogance of the Jews and shows that the difference lies not in the seeds of the human race but in conduct. Thus they might recognize that, unless they took care to be faithful, they could claim no protection from the privilege of circumcised descent. Jacob and Esau, conceived from one seed and brought forth by one act of childbirth, nevertheless experienced vastly different outcomes according to the diversity of their merits.

**Augustine.** If you understood the Apostle according to the Apostle, you would not mention Jacob’s merits here, where he says that Jacob was loved not on the basis of works, in order to commend grace, which is not given according to our merits. Otherwise, as he himself says, the reward is not reckoned according to grace but according to debt (Romans 4:4). What do these words show except that grace is not owed but freely given?

This is what he was commending when he said: “For when they had not yet been born and had done nothing either good or evil, so that God’s purpose according to election might remain, it was said—not from works but from the one who calls—‘The elder shall serve the younger’” (Romans 9:11–13).

The things you try to obscure are clear. Remove the smoke [Note: [Col. 1131] The printed editions read “remove your smoke.” The manuscripts omit “your.”] and attend to the light of the Scriptures. Grace precedes a person so that he may love God, and through that love perform good works. The Apostle John also shows this most plainly when he says: “Let us love, because he first loved us” (1 John 4:19). Therefore we are not loved because we loved; rather, because we have been loved, let us love [Note: [Col. 1131] Thus the manuscripts Clarus and Marianus. The printed editions read: “Therefore we do not love because we loved; rather, because we have been loved, we love.”].

**CXXXII. Julian.** Esau, being profane and a fornicator, selling his birthright for a single meal (Hebrews 12:16), sought the blessing that he had despised [Note: [Col. 1131] The printed editions read “that he had hoped for.” This is corrected from the manuscripts.], but did not obtain it, although he had sought it with tears. Jacob, however, quiet and gentle, obedient to his parents’ commands and most eager for sanctification, advanced so far [Note: [Col. 1131] Thus in the manuscripts. The printed editions read “proceeded so far.”] that, just as the God of Abraham and Isaac, God was also called the God of Jacob among the holy people.

Since it was evident to all from these examples that God does not, in his just judgment, deny his mercy to good minds in any nation, but allows no evil mind to be defended by the nobility of any stock, the Jews should have understood that the faith of the Gentiles ought not to be despised. For just as the lineage of the Israelites does not protect crimes, so the origin of the Gentiles is no impediment to their virtues [Col. 1132]. The Apostle was dealing with all this in that conflict; yet in certain passages, in order to bend the arrogance of the circumcised, he appeals, under the name of grace, to the mere power of God.

**Augustine.** Then, in order to bend the arrogance of the circumcised, the Apostle lies under the name of grace—God chooses on the basis of works, not grace [Note: [Col. 1132] Thus the manuscripts Marianus and Clarus. The printed editions read “he chose.”]. Who could think such a thing except a heretic who is an enemy of grace and a friend of pride?

The vessel of election, the preacher of the grace by which he was made what he was, cries out that Jacob was not loved on the basis of works. You, however, mention Jacob’s works and insist that he was loved because of them. In doing this, you imagine that you are contradicting me, although you are a new Antichrist and are openly contradicting the one in whom Christ spoke (2 Corinthians 13:3).

**CXXXIII. Julian.** To those who gloried in the observance of ceremonies and sacrifices, and who therefore judged that other nations, consecrated by none of the rites of the law, could neither suddenly be admitted to fellowship with them nor ought to be admitted, he said that even if the highest form of justice had existed in those observances, God would nevertheless have had it in his power to effect a change among the peoples, rejecting whom he wished and accepting whom he wished.

This meaning is expressed under the persona of the Jews [Note: [Col. 1132] The particle *sub*, “under,” is absent from the manuscript of Marianus.]: nothing should now be required from human will, since God has mercy on whomever he wishes and hardens whomever he wishes. To this the Apostle responds, “O human being, who are you to answer back to God?” He then adds the testimony of the prophet Isaiah: “Does the thing formed say to the one who formed it, ‘Why did you make me like this?’” He adds on his own part: “Or [Note: [Col. 1132] Menardus reads also *aut non*; Vignierius reads *annon*, as likewise does the Vulgate. M.] does the potter not have authority over the clay [Note: [Col. 1132] The printed editions read *figulus ex eadem massa*, omitting *luti*, “of clay”; the word is supplied from the manuscripts.], from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?” (Romans 9:18, 20–21).

His meaning is as follows: Since I commended the will of God and set forth the authority of his grace, saying that he showed mercy to whomever he had chosen to show mercy, you, O Jew, brought a charge against me—as though the commendation I had offered of the divine will and power amounted to the destruction of God’s justice.

And because I said, “He does what he wishes,” you argued that nothing should now be required from human will if God did everything according to his own will, since the dignity of persons had excluded the question. For if I had said, “God does what he owes according to the laws of his justice, which judges the merits of individuals” [Note: [Col. 1132] The manuscript of Marianus reads *qui*, “which,” rather than *quae*, “which.”], you would certainly not have raised any objection such as the one you now raise.

But because I said, “God does what he wishes,” you thought that I had stolen something from the dignity of justice. The two statements are therefore the same. For when I say of God, “He does what he wishes,” I say nothing other than, “He does what he ought.” I know that he wishes nothing other than what he ought to wish. Thus, wherever will is inseparably joined to equity, whichever of the two terms I use, I have signified both.

**Augustine.** However you may say that God does what he ought, he owes grace to no one. To many he does not even repay the punishment that their evil works deserve, while he bestows grace that none of their good works deserves [Col. 1133].

What did he owe Paul when he was still Saul and persecuting the Church? Surely, punishment. Therefore, when he struck him down with a voice sent from heaven, blinded him, and drew him with such force to receive the faith that he had been ravaging (Acts 9), he acted unquestionably according to grace, not according to debt, so that Paul might be among that remnant of the people of Israel of whom he says: “So also at the present time there is a remnant according to the election of grace” [Note: [Col. 1133] Vignierius and three manuscripts read “a remnant has been saved, made.” Menardus omits “saved,” in accordance with the Greek text.]: “But if it is by grace, it is no longer from works; otherwise grace is no longer grace” (Romans 11:5–6).

What did he owe those to whom he says, “It is not for your sake that I act, house of Israel, but for the sake of my holy name, which you profaned among the nations”? He says that he will make them do good within themselves, but for the sake of his name, which they profaned—not for the sake of those who profaned it. For if he wished to act for their sake, he would repay them the punishment they deserved, not grant them undeserved grace.

What he says he will do concerns making them do good [Note: [Col. 1133] Thus the manuscripts Marianus, Clarus, and Portus. The printed editions read “so that they may become good.”], not because those who profaned his holy name were good. Finally, he states most plainly that they will do good, but that he himself will cause them to do it. Among other things he says: “I will cause you to walk in my statutes, and to observe and do my judgments” (Ezekiel 36:22, 27).

For these works a reward is reckoned according to debt: a reward is owed if they are performed. But grace, which is not owed, precedes them so that they may be performed. I say that a good reward is owed to good works performed by human beings; but grace is not owed, for grace makes the human beings themselves good out of evil ones.

Finally, you who said that God does what he ought, and who with uplifted neck paraded human merits, tell me, please: by what merits do little children owe the kingdom of heaven? Perhaps you will say that they owe this to his grace, with whose help they have been reborn. Because of this grace, once received, they now deserve to enter his kingdom. But the grace itself, which he offers to those who are to be regenerated, is owed to none of their merits whatsoever.

For this reason your Pelagius, at the episcopal judgment in Palestine, was compelled to condemn—lest he himself be condemned—those who say that God’s grace is given according to our merits [Note: [Col. 1133] *The Proceedings of Pelagius*, nos. 30, 60]. There he unquestionably condemned both you and himself, since you do not cease to say this [Note: [Col. 1133] Vignierius reads: “where he condemned both you and himself, who do not cease to say this.” Menardus reads: “where he condemned both you, who do not cease to say this.” The readings have been corrected from the manuscripts Clarus, Portus, and Marianus.].

The Apostle was commending this grace—truly grace, that is, freely given and owed to no preceding merits—when he said: “For when they had not yet been born and had done nothing either good or evil, so that God’s purpose according to election might remain.” This is the election of which it is also said: “A remnant has been made according to the election of grace; but if it is by grace, it is no longer from works; otherwise grace is no longer grace.”

Therefore here too, after saying “so that God’s purpose according to election might remain,” he immediately added: “Not [Col. 1134] from works, but from the one who calls, it was said, ‘The elder shall serve the younger’” (Romans 9:11–13).

You cry out against this trumpet of truth and say: “In order to bend the arrogance of the circumcised, the Apostle Paul, under the name of grace, appeals to the mere power of God.” What else are you saying than this: “In order to bend the arrogance of the circumcised, the Apostle lies when he says that Jacob was loved not on the basis of works,” although he was loved on the basis of works because he was “quiet and gentle, obedient to his parents’ commands and most eager for sanctification” (above, chapter 132)?

You do not understand that he was not loved because he was such, or was going to be such [Note: [Col. 1134] The manuscript of Marianus omits “because he was such, or.”], but that he was made such because he was loved. Be ashamed. The Apostle does not lie: Jacob was not loved on the basis of works. For if it is by grace, it is no longer from works. He was loved by grace, and the same grace caused him to abound in good works. Spare your soul; do not be an enemy of this grace.

### CXXXIV. JULIAN

Thus that pride which wanted to remain idle, and wished to conceal its sloth under the pretext of necessity, so as to protest against the Gospel when the Gentiles were being received, hears that [Note: Col. 1134. Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read, “would dare to protest against the Gospel, because”]—even if matters were as you imagine—you ought nevertheless to supplicate God, not raise a revolt. By these words he rebuffs the wickedness of the man who, pursuing the ambiguity of the expression, was trying to ascribe to divine necessity the difference of merits arising from the quality of the will, in order to assert that one of two things must be the case: either the Gentiles must not come to share in the promise, or, if God were permitted to do this, the functions of free will must be extinguished. But because this was not sufficient for the argument—for neither was justice, whose authority was commended by such a teacher as God, to be left undefended—he adds, most consistently, that the vessels made for dishonor and those made for honor possess this distinction as the due return of their own will. For if God, wishing to show his wrath and make his power known, endured with much patience vessels of wrath, completed for destruction; and, he says, in order to make known the riches of his glory in vessels of mercy, which he prepared for glory—those whom he also called, not only from the Jews but also from the Gentiles (Rom. IX, 22–24). Certainly here he makes clear what the preceding controversy had obscured: that God’s wrath is not inflicted except upon those vessels that have been completed for destruction, while glory is given to those that have been prepared for this purpose. But from whom such vessels are prepared to receive the things we have mentioned, the Apostle’s own statement makes clear. “In a great house,” he says, “there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and earthenware; some indeed for honor, others for dishonor. If, therefore, anyone cleanses himself from these, he will be a vessel sanctified for honor, useful to the Lord, prepared for every good work” (II Tim. II, 20–21).

**AUGUSTINE.** So then the vessels themselves prepare themselves, making it futile to say of God, “which he prepared for glory”? For this is exactly what you say; and you do not understand that it was said, “If anyone cleanses himself,” in order to show also the work of man through the will. But, ungrateful man, “the will is prepared by the Lord” (Prov. VIII, according to the Septuagint); therefore both things are true: that God prepares vessels for glory, and that the vessels themselves prepare themselves. For when a man acts, God brings it about; because, when a man loves, God first loves.

Read the prophet Ezekiel [Note: Col. 1135. Menard reads, “Read Ezekiel to me.” The error arose because old books write *hezechielem*. Vignierius substitutes “diligently” for “to me”], from whom I recalled above what seemed sufficient (above, ch. 133). You will also find these words there [Note: Col. 1135. The printed editions read, “where you will also find these words.” *Where* is absent from the manuscripts]—that is, that God causes people to do his commandments—people whom he pities, not because of their merits, which he there states to be evil, but for the sake of his own name. Thus, when God, without regard to their merits, causes them to do his commandments, they begin to possess the merits of good deeds. This is the grace that you deny—not grace based on the works that are done, but grace by which they are done.

### CXXXV. JULIAN

Behold the function of free will: “If,” he says, “anyone cleanses himself from association with worthless vessels”—by which name vices are indicated—“he will be a vessel sanctified for honor, useful to the Lord, prepared for every good work.” These vessels, then, are prepared by their own endeavors either for wrath or for glory; while God makes his power known in both cases, either by displaying severity toward the impious [Note: Col. 1135. Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read “in the impious”] or by bestowing blessing upon the faithful. It has thus become clear that the statement of the distinguished teacher neither brought assistance to Manichaean doctrines nor, conversely, armed us in any appropriate manner.

**AUGUSTINE.** Why do you slander? Why do you falsely accuse, without considering which teachers of the Church you are accusing, or what sort of men they are? I answer you in the words not of any Manichaean, but of Saint Ambrose: “God calls those whom he deigns to call, and makes religious whom he wills” (Ambrose, *Book 7 on Luke*, IX, 58). Ambrose understood this truthfully and in accordance with the truth of the divine Scriptures. But the judgment by which he makes some and does not make others is hidden. Therefore it is said to man through man, but not by man [Note: Col. 1135. On the authority of the old books, the words “through man, but” are supplied here]:  “O man, who are you to answer back to God? Does the thing formed say to him who formed it, ‘Why did you make me like this?’ Or does the potter not have authority over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?” (Rom. IX, 20–21).

Remove your clouds from the serenity of these words. They signify that God’s judgment is hidden; yet the words themselves are so clear that they do not permit themselves to be darkened and obscured by your darkness.

### CXXXVI. JULIAN

And therefore this statement also presses you very strongly, since it says that not all are fashioned for condemnation, whereas you declare that all go to condemnation. But you habitually argue most absurdly when you say: “Those are not fashioned for condemnation who are later liberated.” Yet even in this way the surface meaning of the Apostle’s statement cannot agree with you. For when you say, “All are created for condemnation by the law of birth, but some of them—even if very few [Note: Col. 1135. The printed editions read, “but some, namely very few”; the manuscripts read, “but some of them, even if very few”—are liberated from it by the mysteries,” you do not assert what he does, who not only proclaims that some are liberated from among the condemned, but also says that not all are fashioned for condemnation, but some for dishonor and others for honor.

**AUGUSTINE.** When the Apostle said, “From one came condemnation upon all” (Rom. V, 16), he indicated the whole lump, which, wholly corrupted, flowed from Adam. [Note: Col. 1136. Claromontanus and Mar. read “liberated” rather than “to be liberated” in Julian’s preceding sentence.] But when he says that from it vessels are made for honor, he commends grace, by which God both creates and liberates the people whom he makes. When, however, he says that from it vessels are made for dishonor, he displays the judgment by which he creates people but does not liberate them.

This you are also compelled to admit concerning infants, whose one lump you certainly cannot deny, whatever you may think that lump to be. From it, nevertheless, you admit that some are adopted into the kingdom of God; these, without doubt, you concede to have been made vessels for honor. Others, however, are not adopted; these you shamelessly deny to have been made vessels for dishonor, unless you agree with understanding. For even if, as you wish, this is not the punishment of condemnation [Note: Col. 1136. The printed editions omit *ista* (“this”), although it is in the manuscripts], it will at least be the dishonor of the image of God to be separated from the kingdom of God.

But if you persistently [Note: Col. 1136. The printed editions read “persistent,” while the manuscripts read “persistently”] deny that grace, you will show that you belong to this judgment—which would certainly be unjust in the case of infants if original sin did not exist.

### CXXXVII. JULIAN

Once it has become clear that the Apostle spoke of moral conduct, it is equally apparent how great is your poverty of testimonies from the Law, since you seek aid from statements against the thunderbolts of reason [Note: Col. 1136. Menard reads “against the thunderbolts of temptation”; Vignierius, “against such great thunderbolts of reason.” *Such great* is absent from the manuscripts] which, because of their very nature, disdain to help you and cannot help you [Note: Col. 1136. Thus the manuscripts; Vignierius reads, “by their own nature, come to meet [you]”].

**AUGUSTINE.** Against the Apostle, who says that from the same lump God makes one vessel for honor and another for dishonor, and who does not say “another neither for honor nor for dishonor”—which he certainly would have said if he believed what you [Note: Col. 1136. The printed editions add “say”] say about infants—against this divinely thundering voice your reasoning is not thunderous but smoky.

### CXXXVIII. JULIAN

And this has indeed been discussed insofar as it concerns the testimony of the Apostle. But in Isaiah, from whom Paul took the statement itself, God so far from deterring rational creatures from considering his judgment that, just as through the same prophet he had said, “Cease to act perversely, learn to do good, assist the oppressed; and come, let us argue together, says the Lord” (Isa. I, 16–18), so here too he deigns to disclose the rationale of his dispensations, lest he seem to have acted by power alone and not by justice.

To the Jewish people, afflicted in captivity, he announces that the time of redemption is approaching, when they will return to their own land; and he discloses both the cause of their previous sorrows and that of their impending joys:

“Let heaven rejoice from above, and let the clouds pour down righteousness; let mercy spring up from the earth, and let righteousness spring up together. I am the Lord God who created you, making you better; I prepared you like a potter’s clay. Does the one who plows plow the earth all day long? Does the clay say to the potter, ‘What are you doing, because you do not work, because you have no hands?’ Does the thing formed say to him who formed it, ‘Wisely you formed me’? Or does one say to his father, ‘What will you beget?’ and to his mother, ‘What will you give birth to?’ For thus says the Lord God, the Holy One of Israel, who made the things that were to come: ‘Ask me concerning my sons and daughters, and command me concerning the works of my hands. I made the earth and the human being upon it; with my hand I established heaven; I commanded all the stars. I raised up the king with righteousness, and all his ways are straight. He will build my city and bring back the captivity of my people, not with a reward or with gifts,’ says the Lord of hosts” (Isa. XLV, 8–13).

**AUGUSTINE.** If you understood the prophet’s words, you would understand that the king of whom it was said, “I raised up the king with righteousness, and all his ways are straight,” is the mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus. But you would understand him as he ought to be understood.

For you will not dare to say that, because of preceding merits of works, he was made the Son of God from the beginning—that is, from his mother’s womb. By what grace, then, was that human being made good from the beginning? By the same grace human beings who are his members are made good from evil.

For what can you say about Christ according to his humanity—that is, according to the fact that the Word became flesh? He who was God, remained God, and became human; that human being himself was never so human that he was not the only-begotten Son of God, because of the only-begotten Word. He did not acquire this status through merits arising from his own will and conduct. Rather, as Ambrose truly said, “As though born of the Spirit, he abstained from sin” [Note: See above, *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, Book I, no. 40.].

Otherwise, according to you, there would be many such people, if they had wished to be such; and since he alone was such, it was within the power of those who did not wish to be such. If you attend to the impiety of saying or even silently believing these things, then, just as you acknowledge the nature of the Only-Begotten—that “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God”—acknowledge also the grace by which “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John I, 1, 14).

He, therefore, calls those whom he deigns to call, and makes religious whom he wills (Ambrose, *Book 7 on Luke*, IX, 58). He made the human being whom he willed to be the one mediator between God and human beings, without any preceding merits of human will.

### CXXXIX. JULIAN

The meaning of this passage, then, insofar as it concerns the history, is that God speaks to the people:

“I neither handed you over to captivity out of hatred, nor have I now released you from the bonds of Babylonian captivity through forgetfulness of judgment. Rather, insofar as it depends upon me, I am prepared [Note: Col. 1137. The printed editions read, “I am prepared”; *I am* is absent from the manuscripts] to cherish you with continual benevolence; yet justice required of me both that I hand over those who transgressed to their enemies and that I restore and liberate those who had been afflicted.

“For just as one skilled in agriculture does not always devote himself to a single task, breaking up the fields only with the teeth of the plow, but prepares the land for its desired fertility [Note: Col. 1137. The printed editions read “fertility”; Mar. reads “for fertility”] by various methods, so I too vary the turns of my dispensations, so that through both pressures and consolations I may adapt your will to the fruits of justice. [Note: Col. 1138. Mar. reads, “and that I might never have done anything cruelly,” omitting *ever*.]

“Finally, so that you may understand with what equity I deal with you, I could, by my power, disregard your murmuring, so that, just as the formed object cannot say to the potter, ‘What have you done?’ [Note: Col. 1138. Vignierius reads, “Why have you made me thus?” The manuscripts have only, “What have you done?”] I might impose upon you the weight of silence. Yet, against these examples, I summon you to question me concerning my sons and daughters—that is, concerning you and the works of my hands—and to learn that I have acted wholly justly and have never done anything cruelly.”

**AUGUSTINE.** You say what you want to say, not what Isaiah said. He speaks of grace, against which you speak.

### CXL. JULIAN

Thus both the Prophet and the Apostle introduced the potter as an example, assigning him no other function than that of comparison; not, however, in order to indicate that human beings are as worthless before God as clay is in a furnace or on a potter’s wheel.

After completing the exposition we have set forth above, we point out that, according to the more recent interpretation, something else shines forth in the same passage:

“Distill, O heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain down the Just One; let the earth be opened, and let it bring forth the Savior, and let righteousness spring up together. I, the Lord, created him. Woe to him who contradicts his maker, a potsherd among the potsherds of the earth. Does the clay say to its potter, ‘What are you doing?’ and, ‘Your work is without hands’?” (Isa. XLV, 8–9).

By these words, although King Cyrus is expressed according to the historical sense, the incarnation of the Savior is nevertheless expressed according to prophecy. Since he was to be born of a virgin, the obstinacy of the Jews and of all unbelievers is reproved, lest they become hostile to faithful signs. For after he had first said, “Let the earth be opened, and let it bring forth the Savior, and let righteousness spring up together,” he immediately added, “I, the Lord, created him.”

**AUGUSTINE.** Tell me by what works this human being Christ Jesus earned this, and by what righteousness of God he alone earned it; dare [Note: Col. 1138. Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read “you dare”] to chatter about that. Or, if you do not dare, at last confess grace without merits—not only grace that forgives sins in a human being, but also grace that, in human nature, makes righteousness through the Holy Spirit.

For grace did not forgive sins in the human Christ, nor did grace make him such that he was always good from the beginning, just as he was always the Son of God from the beginning. Indeed, just as those who were being lethally tormented by the bites of serpents in the wilderness were instructed to look upon the one who had been lifted up as a sign, lest they perish (Num. XXI, 6–9), so those who are poisoned by your arguments must be instructed to look upon Christ. In the righteousness of that human mediator, let them see grace without merits, and thereby drive away from themselves the venom of your speech.

Finally, in the Prophet’s words—even according to the recent interpretation you mentioned, in which Christ is prophesied more clearly—you found nothing from which to construct your argument except that he was born of a virgin, because it was said, “Let the earth be opened, and let it bring forth the Savior.” But concerning his righteousness, which is likewise foretold there, you wished to say nothing, although you yourself presented the prophetic words in which it says:

“Distill, O heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain down the Just One; let the earth be opened, and let it bring forth the Savior, and let righteousness spring up together.”

Tell me [Note: Col. 1139. The printed editions read, “Tell [me] whom the clouds [rained down as] the Just One,” omitting *me*]: whom did the clouds rain down as the Just One, unless [Note: Col. 1139. Vignierius reads “whom”; Menard and the manuscripts read “because”] it is because the Prophets and the Apostles proclaimed Christ, who was born righteous from the very womb of the virgin? Hence, when it had been said, “Let the earth be opened, and let it bring forth the Savior,” it was immediately added, “and let righteousness spring up together.”

Therefore, it is by that grace [Note: Col. 1139. The printed editions read “by grace”; the manuscripts support “by that grace”] that human beings who are reborn in Christ are made righteous, by which grace Christ was born a righteous human being. Just as he is an example of life, so that by imitating him we may act righteously, so he is also an example of grace, so that by believing in him we may hope to be made righteous by the Spirit [Note: Col. 1139. Menard reads “through him”; Vignierius and the Claromontanus, Mar., and Port. manuscripts read “by the Spirit”], in the manner in which he himself was made righteous—he who was made for us by God wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption—so that, as it is written, “Whoever glories, let him glory in the Lord” (I Cor. I, 30–31).

All whom you have bitten [Note: Col. 1139. Mar. reads the singular, “you have bitten”] with your deadly tooth should therefore look upon this Just One, and they will be healed. That is, they should believe that they receive righteousness from the same source from which righteousness was innate in Christ; and therefore let them glory not in their own will or merit, but in the Lord.

### CXLI. JULIAN

The earth is opened into a sprout before the cultivator’s work receives the seed; this is demonstrated in the childbirth of the virgin, who anticipated and excluded the function of a wife through the gift of motherhood.

What therefore had not previously occurred, almighty God promises that he will do. And, foreseeing the multitude of unbelievers, he adds:

“Woe to those who contradict their maker, a potsherd among the potsherds of the earth.”

That is: woe to those who insist that, despite God’s promise, a virgin could not become fruitful; while they themselves, although formed from seeds established by God, yet through the intervention of God’s power, in their mothers’ wombs, obstinately assert that flesh could not be fashioned from a virgin’s flesh without the ministry of a man.

Thus, obstinate people, what you say is like this: you do not think that I could do this, and you prescribe to me the difficulty of the matter, although it is established that you yourselves were made by my hands. It is as though clay, while being handled by its potter, were to say to him, “You have no hands,” by which it was then being formed into some vessel. [Note: Col. 1139. In the old Codex Mar., before Augustine’s response, the words “The book of Julian is finished” are prefixed; such a notice usually marks the end of the preceding volume.]

So you too, who ask who gave a son to a virgin without male seed, recognize that the same one who made you from seed did this. But since the sacred Scriptures permit varying interpretations, and yet both interpretations agree in pious and religious harmony, let the first book now be brought to an end. Its conclusion nevertheless admonishes us to believe that God is the maker of those who are born, the protector of the innocent, the rewarder of Catholics, and the condemner of Manichaeans [Note: At this point, in the old manuscript Codex Mar., before Augustine’s response, the words “The book of Julian is finished” are prefixed. Such a notice usually indicates the end of the preceding volume.].

**AUGUSTINE.** So that those who read intelligently may know how you tried to obscure the Apostle’s clear words and pervert what is straightforward, I must answer this argument of yours from the same argument of the Apostle.

The blessed Paul wished to show that God is powerful to do what he promised. Here grace is especially commended, and you are its enemies—for it is not in human power that God should fulfill what he promised, but in the power of the one who made the promise [Note: Col. 1140. Mar. and Clar. read “who” rather than “because”]. Wishing, then, to show this, he says:

“The word of God has not failed. For not all who are from Israel are Israel; nor, because they are Abraham’s seed, are all children; but, ‘In Isaac shall your seed be called.’” That is, “Those who are children of the flesh are not thereby children of God; rather, the children of the promise are counted as seed” (Rom. IX, 6–9) [Note: Col. 1140. Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions also read “as seed”].

For this is the word of the promise: “At this time I will come, and Sarah shall have a son.” Keep in mind the children of the promise, because the one who promised is powerful also to accomplish it (Rom. IV, 21).

“Not only this,” he says, “but Rebecca also, having conceived twins from one intercourse with Isaac our father. For before they had been born or had done anything good or evil, so that God’s purpose according to election might remain—not from works but from him who calls—it was said, ‘The elder shall serve the younger.’”

Here too keep in mind election not based on works, which the later prophet in a certain way explained. The Apostle adds:

“As it is written, ‘Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.’”

Here a question arises that could disturb those who do not understand the height of grace. He himself raises it and says:

“What shall we say, then? Is there injustice with God? Certainly not.”

And to teach what he meant by “certainly not,” he says:

“For he says to Moses [Note: Col. 1140. Perhaps the reading should be “to Moses” rather than “Moses”], ‘I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will show compassion to whom I show compassion.’ Therefore it is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy.”

If you had attended to this, you would not have exalted the merits of the will against grace, when you hear: “It is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy.” God did not therefore have mercy because Jacob willed and ran; rather, Jacob willed and ran because God had mercy.

“For the will is prepared by the Lord” (Prov. VIII, according to the Septuagint); “the steps of a man are directed by the Lord, and he wills his way” (Ps. XXXVI, 23).

Then, because this general statement—“It is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy”—was made concerning Jacob, an example is also given from Pharaoh, in connection with the statement, “Esau I hated.” It is added:

“For Scripture says to Pharaoh, ‘For this very purpose I raised you up, that I might show my power in you, and that my name might be proclaimed throughout all the earth.’”

After this he concludes concerning both:

“Therefore he has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills.”

He has mercy, of course, according to grace, which is given freely and not repaid according to merits; but he hardens according to judgment, which is repaid according to merits [Note: We have restored the second clause of the sentence—“but he hardens according to judgment, which is repaid according to merits”—on the authority of the ancient books. It is also found in Bede and Florus.].

To make a vessel for honor from the condemned lump is manifestly grace; to make from it a vessel for dishonor is just judgment. Then, introducing the words of those who dislike this, he says:

“You will say to me, therefore, ‘Why does he still complain? For who resists his will?’”

And restraining them, he says:

“O man, who are you to answer back to God? Does the thing formed say to him who formed it, ‘Why did you make me like this?’ Or does the potter not have authority over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?”

See whether this agrees with what precedes and disagrees with your position. You think this was said according to the merits of wills, contrary to what he himself says:

“For before they had been born, or had done anything good or evil, so that God’s purpose according to election might remain—not from works but from him who calls—it was said, ‘The elder shall serve the younger.’”

And contrary to what he himself says:

“Therefore it is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy.”

It is opposed not only to what precedes, but also to what follows. For he speaks of vessels of wrath that are completed for destruction; and this would be unjust unless the lump, from which all come to condemnation, had already been condemned. He also speaks of vessels of mercy, which he prepared for glory. To mercy freely given, not owed, belongs the preparation of vessels for glory from the condemned lump—not only from the Jews, as he says, but also from the Gentiles.

For this reason he cites testimony from the prophet Hosea: “I will call the one who was not my people, my people”; and from Isaiah: “A remnant will be saved for Israel.” To show that this remnant came to exist through the grace of God, he establishes it by the testimony that follows, saying through the same prophet:

“Unless the Lord of hosts had left us seed.”

Then he shows that the Gentiles apprehended righteousness by faith, whereas Israel did not apprehend it because it sought it not by faith but as though by works. Faith has what he says later:

“For everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved.”

To this salvation belongs the fact that good works and righteousness come to us from God, not from ourselves [Note: The printed editions read, “so that good works may exist, and righteousness may be from God for us.” The reading is corrected from Codex Port.].

Therefore, concerning those who, not by faith but as though by works, stumbled over the stone of stumbling, he continues and says:

“Brothers, the good will of my heart and my supplication to God for them is for salvation. For I bear witness that they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge. For, being ignorant of God’s righteousness and seeking to establish their own righteousness, they were not subject to the righteousness of God” (Rom. IX, 6; X, 3, 13).

This is exactly what you do. You wish to establish your own righteousness, so that God may repay grace according to merits; and you do not wish God’s grace to precede you and make you possess righteousness.

Then, following the connected sequence of his argument, he arrives at the point where he says:

“I ask, then, has God rejected his people? Certainly not. For I too am an Israelite, from the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin. God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew. Or do you not know what Scripture says in Elijah, how he pleads with God against Israel? ‘Lord, they have killed your prophets and demolished your altars, and I alone have been left, and they seek my life.’ But what does the divine response say to him? ‘I have kept for myself seven thousand men who have not bent the knee before Baal.’”

Thus also in the present time a remnant has come into being through the election of grace [Note: Vignierius consistently adds “saved” here and below in Paul’s testimony.].

“But if by grace, then it is no longer from works; otherwise grace is no longer grace.”

Then observe what he adds:

“What then?” he says. “What Israel sought, it did not obtain; but the election obtained it.”

Look back above at what sort of election this is, where he says:

“The remnant has come into being through the election of grace; but if by grace, then it is no longer from works.”

And he relates this to the point from which the present argument began:

“For before they had been born, and had done nothing good or evil, so that God’s purpose according to election might remain—not from works.”

This is the election of grace, not from works, by which [Note: Col. 1142. Bede reads “because”] vessels are made for honor so that they may do good works. Good works follow grace; they do not precede it, because the grace of God causes us to do them. Nor do we establish our own righteousness; rather, God’s righteousness is in us—that is, the righteousness God gives us.

“But the others were blinded” (Rom. XI, 1, 7). This is the judgment by which vessels are made for dishonor; from this judgment it was said, “Esau I hated.” From this judgment it was also said to Pharaoh, “For this very purpose I raised you up.”

Thus it is evident that, by understanding—or rather, failing to understand—the Apostle in this way, you wish to glory in works against grace. By wishing to establish your own righteousness, you are not subject to the righteousness of God.

We, however, proclaim God as the maker of infants; but we do not assign, from the same lump, the middle position of vessels in which they are made neither for honor nor for dishonor—a position the Apostle did not grant. By doing this, you would escape God’s judgment if you could show him to be the condemner of Manichaeans alone and not of all heretics.

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 1141]

The second book of Julian against Florus is refuted. It concerns the Apostle’s words in Romans V: “Through one man sin entered this world, and through sin death; and so into all human beings,” and so forth. Here Julian, rejecting the Catholic interpretation—according to which Augustine, in Book II, chapter 27 of *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, explained these words as referring to Adam’s sin transmitted by generation to all his descendants—labors in vain to have them understood, according to the Pelagian heresy, as referring to an example of sin passing not into all descendants but only into those who sin by imitation.

### I. JULIAN

We would be treated fairly if we were either granted the opportunity to defend the truth before learned judges, or, since this is for the moment denied, were not battered by the tumult of ignorant people.

**AUGUSTINE.** Certainly you seek such learned judges that, unless they have been cultivated and adorned by the liberal disciplines and have not remained ignorant of what even the philosophers of this world thought [Note: Codices Mar. and Port. read “of this age” (*modi*) rather than “of this world” (*mundi*).], they would be unable to judge your statements.

Ambrose was such a man here. If you do not reject him as a judge, you cannot doubt that you have been most justly condemned. For he said:

“We are all born under sin, and our very birth is in fault” (*On Repentance*, Book I, chapter 2 or 3).

By these words he showed that Christ the Savior—that is, Jesus—is necessary for infants. Since you contradict him, you must admit that you wish to have learned judges only in such a way that you do not wish to have Catholic Christian judges.

### II. JULIAN

And because we endure the losses of a trophy being raised for the salvation of the churches [Note: Col. 1143. Thus the manuscripts; Vignierius reads, “And those of a trophy being raised”—a trophy which the prudence of a good cause was about to carry off through the remarkable support of the knowledgeable—or because, at least, the approval of the common people would accomplish nothing else against our humiliation [Note: Col. 1143. Menard reads, “if nothing [else]”; Vignierius, “nothing [else].” The manuscripts read, “or would bring us no other disadvantage except the losses of the trophy which ought to have been raised for our cause by the judgments of the judges”]:  of the two groups of people I mentioned, one would help us and the other would not harm us, if either the former possessed authority or the latter possessed modesty.

But since there is great confusion in affairs and an enormous multitude of fools, the helm of reason is snatched from the churches, so that the popular doctrine may spread its sails with raised horn.

**AUGUSTINE.** If what we assert is a popular doctrine, then this doctrine which you attack among the Christian peoples with a deranged mind is not a doctrine of the Manichaeans. You rightly despise the madness of the Manichaeans in their small number; but you also have your own madness, by which, under the name of Manichaeans, you try to make hostile to us those peoples whom you avoid as judges—as though peoples deceived by your loquacity could call Ambrose a Manichaean, or Cyprian a Manichaean, although they taught that original sin exists for the salvation even of infants.

Ambrose did not create such peoples; he found them. Cyprian himself did not create them; he found them. Your own father found such peoples in the Church when you were baptized, as is said, as an infant [Note: The old Codex Mar. reads “when he was baptized.” But in the earlier work *Against Julian*, Book I, no. 14, Julian himself is addressed: “We have heard that you were baptized as an infant.”]. Finally, you too found such Catholic peoples.

Restrain yourselves. We admit that our doctrine is popular, because we are the people of the one who was called Jesus for this reason: because he saves his people from their sins (Matt. I, 21). When you wish to separate infants from this people, you separate yourselves instead.

### III. JULIAN

Thus it is scarcely permitted to associate with the prudent, while anything at all is permitted with the worthless [Note: This is the reading of the manuscripts. The printed editions read “is fitting” instead of “is permitted.”]. By a decree of sedition, the judgment of virtues has been excluded from the churches. What works against us among the common people is that we refuse to become an addition to error—the common people, I mean, who, weighing the worth of a position by its success, consider it more true when they see that it pleases more people.

**AUGUSTINE.** Does Manichaeism please more people? Are Manichaeans not, like parricides, few and wicked? Do not therefore glory in your small number; and, what is more foolish, do not say that our doctrine pleases more people while charging us with the doctrine of a detestable minority.

### IV. JULIAN

What Cicero said about Epicurus—that it is clear that such things are not stated subtly when people of this kind [Note: Col. 1143. The printed editions read *hujuscemodi*; the manuscripts read *cujuscemodi*] openly profess that they please themselves—these people, in their perverse manner, as in everything else [Note: The printed editions read “as all perverse things.” The manuscript reading is restored here.], think pertains to the testimony of wisdom.

**AUGUSTINE.** But the one who says, “Praise the Lord, all nations; praise him, all peoples” (Ps. CXVI, 1), has defeated and refuted Cicero in this judgment.

You seek not to teach these people truthfully, but subtly to deceive some of them and add them to your small number, by praising the subtlety of a few secular philosophers and criticizing us because our doctrines are not expressed subtly—and therefore people of this kind openly profess that such things please them.

Yet you have said several times that I do nothing more than ensure that I am not understood [Note: See *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, Book I, no. 21.]. How, then, does what I defend please the multitude, unless this multitude is Catholic, and your heresy rightly displeases it?

### V. JULIAN

For it thoroughly delights swelling souls to defame whatever has ever existed, anywhere, among the saints, lest they be corrected by the examples of illustrious works.

**AUGUSTINE.** The swelling souls therefore run after you instead, since you praise lust. Chaste souls, by condemning lust, prove that it is praised when they conquer it.

### VI. JULIAN

It thoroughly delights and profoundly affects them to plead the weakness of nature, to say that the flesh is subject to congenital sins, and not to place the effect of correction in the human will, but to call the crimes of one’s endeavors the functions of the limbs: that this is the Catholic faith, namely, to confess free will, but free will by which a human being is compelled to do evil and cannot will the good.

Augustine. Why are you angry with us, when we seek the result of correction all the more certainly because we ask it more faithfully from the Lord? In vain you stretch out your inflated tongue with boastful speech. We absolutely do not wish to be numbered among those who trust in their own strength (Ps. 48:7). Our soul thirsts for God [Note: [Col. 1144] The printed editions have *Deum sitit*, “thirsts for God.” But the manuscripts have *Deo sitit*, “thirsts for God,” with the dative. He alludes to Psalm 62:2, where one ordinarily reads, “My soul thirsted for you.”], to whom it says, “I shall love you, Lord, my strength” (Ps. 17:2). A human being can will what is good; but the will is prepared by the Lord (Prov. 8, according to the Septuagint). Toward evil, however, the corrupted will turns willingly; and for this reason nature must be healed.

### VII. Julian

But the empty and heretical arguments of those who assert that the just God created the human being free for good work, and that it lies within each person’s power to withdraw from evil and to shine through the pursuit of virtue, serve to pierce with the goad of anxiety and fear those who attribute crimes to the necessity of the flesh.

### Augustine

We do not call empty and heretical those human arguments which assert that the just God created the human being free for a good work. For God created Adam such, and in Adam we were all present; but by sinning he lost himself and everyone in himself. Hence now it is not within the power of the children of humanity to be liberated from evil, unless the grace of God gives them the power to become children of God (John 1:12). Therefore the goad of anxiety and fear is fixed not in those who, as you say, attribute crimes to the necessity of the flesh, but in those who pour out prayers to God so that they may not be led into temptations to crime—lest they consent to your supremely proud and utterly ungrateful arguments against God.

### VIII. Julian

Finally, in Churches that possess great honor [Note: [Col. 1145] Menardus first printed *magnum bonorum*, “a great abundance of goods.” Vignierius corrected this to *magnam bonorum copiam*, “a great abundance of goods.” But the manuscript books Clar., Mar., and Port. have *magnum honorem*, “great honor.” In the 1648 edition, the following was noted in the margin of the codex: “Perhaps, ‘possess a great people of good and evil.’”] and a great people, it is proclaimed that sin has such power that, before the bodily form, before the beginning and arrival of the soul, flying over the seeds once they have been cast, it invades the mother’s secret chamber and makes those about to be born guilty; and that guilt, older than birth itself, awaits the substance of the offspring. This law of sin, thereafter dwelling in the members, compels the captive human being to serve crimes, making him worthy not of punishment for shameful acts but rather of mercy—since what we call the vices of a perverse will is called in the Church by men and women, and by great bishops, “original passion.”

### Augustine

The great bishop Ambrose, whom the mouth of your heresiarch has praised with distinction, answers you and says:

> “Eve gave birth in evil labor, so that childbirth might leave an inheritance to women; and each person, congealed by the pleasure of desire, infused into the genital organs, and coagulated in blood, wrapped in swaddling clothes, might undergo the contagion of sins before he could receive the gift of the life-giving spirit” (Book *On the Sacrament of Regeneration*, or *On Philosophy*).

Therefore, Julian, human nature must be healed by the mercy of God—not, as you foolishly declaim, praised as though it were sound.

### IX. Julian

Thus these harlots of the Manichaeans’ most impure doctrines flatter the ears [Note: [Col. 1145] The printed editions have *scoria dogmatum impurissimorum lenocinatur auribus*, “the dross of the most impure doctrines flatters the ears.” All the manuscripts have *scorta dogmatum impurissimorum lenocinantur auribus*, “these harlots of the most impure doctrines flatter the ears.”].

### Augustine

If you dare, accuse Ambrose of being a Manichaean. Consider against whom you are saying what you wish to appear to be saying against me; and if you have even a little fear of God or human shame, be silent. I ought to hear your abuse of such men not only patiently but even gladly; but you ought, when tearing such men to pieces, to blush before human beings and fear divine judgments.

### X. Julian

This nettle has stirred our enemies, placed in both sexes; formerly, indeed, it was biting because of the vice of bad custom [Note: [Col. 1145] Menardus has *quae dum quidam vitio malae consuetudinis mordet*, “which, while someone bites because of the vice of bad custom.” Vignierius has *quae dum quosdam vitio malae consuetudinis mordet*, “which, while it bites some because of the vice of bad custom.” The reading has been corrected from the manuscripts.], yet it was treated, as it were, with certain ointments of salutary exhortations.

### Augustine

The stinging nettle causes itching—but the person who praises lust does so. If, however, because of bad custom, as you understand [Note: [Col. 1145] So the manuscripts. The printed editions have *sapitis*, “as you understand” in the plural.], a person cries out, “I do not do the good that I want, but the evil that I do not want—that I do” (Rom. 7:19), then surely you admit, at least in this case, that the human will has lost the strength for good works. Unless divine grace comes to its aid, what benefit is there for it in the copious and ornate eloquence of any exhorter?

[Col. 1146] ### XI. Julian

But now, after it began to be offered as a medicine, and authority was added to pleasure, so that, with nearly the whole world in agreement [Note: [Col. 1146] The manuscripts read *consensu*, “with agreement.” The printed editions have *concessu*, “by concession.”], lust—powerful queen of minds, destroyer of honor, and unconquered captor of every soul—might revel: the more honorable the cause of defending truth has become for us, the more difficult it has become. For against headlong peoples who are hostile to their own remedies, the small number of those who administer medicine by their speech has little force. What, then? For their sake, are we to sound the retreat, avenge our insults by silence [Note: [Col. 1146] So the manuscripts. The printed editions have *nostras ulcisci silentio*, “to avenge our wrongs by silence.”], and, from the harbor of our conscience, laugh at the shipwrecks of others? Yet this hatred is opposed, first, by the kindness we owe to the human race; then by the hope and faith that we have in God, who has often lifted up the ruins of desperate ages. Nevertheless, he has granted eternal reward to the steadfastness that he wished to be exercised even to the hour of death, even when no present result followed.

### Augustine

How does God lift up the ruins of evil wills—by which the ages are rightly condemned whenever they are rightly condemned—unless by working good wills in human hearts? Or, if they can, let those wills lift themselves up, just as you have become a great ruin by holding such utter madness. Therefore we pray to God on your behalf; and may he deign to hear us concerning you also, just as he heard us concerning your brother Turbantius [Note: [Col. 1146] Above, book 1, chapter 1.].

### XII. Julian

Rejoicing, then, in this consolation of faith, let us apply ourselves to the work we have begun and fulfill the promises of our disputation, without doubting that this itself is the greatest part of our reward: that we stand upon the citadel of that doctrine which, although the envy of so many—and the error of even more—attacks it, has nevertheless risen above uncertain falls, so that it shines forth as invincible in the possession of victory.

### Augustine

You award yourself the palm against so many bishops of God who, before us, learned and taught in the Church of Christ the things you attack, drinking from and serving the fountains of Israel (Ps. 67:27) [Note: [Col. 1146] The printed editions have *in*, “in the fountains.” The manuscripts have *de*, “from the fountains.”]. What you are doing, then, is not shining in the possession of victory, but flowing shamefully into the sewer of hateful arrogance. For *cluere* means “to prevail” or “to be powerful.” How, then, can you prevail in the possession of victory when you are trying to defile Catholic doctrines—ancient and unconquered?

### XIII. Julian

For if, as both the preceding discussion has made clear and the one that follows will show, whatever belongs to reason, whatever belongs to learning, whatever belongs to justice, whatever belongs to piety, and whatever belongs to the testimony of the sacred writings supports the doctrine we defend, then our enemies achieve nothing by their entire effort except to be proved most foolish among the learned [Note: [Col. 1146] The manuscripts Mar. and Clar. have *impudentissimi*, “most shameless.”], most insolent toward the holy, and most profane toward God.

### Augustine

But you speak falsely. Neither reason, nor sound learning, nor justice, nor piety, nor the sacred testimonies support your doctrine; rather, all these things, as those who understand correctly judge, overturn your doctrine. Reason sees that it can scarcely reach any truth because the sluggishness of nature impedes it. Learning bears the penalty of labor in that same sluggishness of nature. Justice cries out that it does not belong to itself that the sons of Adam should be pressed beneath a heavy yoke from the day they leave their mother’s womb, without any merit of sins. Piety, in opposition to this evil, calls for divine help. The sacred testimonies admonish the human mind that this is so.

### XIV. Julian

And indeed, just as their other writings do, these books against which we are contending testify how little the Traducians possess that they can set against the force of reason by which they are overthrown. They were addressed to a military man [Note: [Col. 1147] The books *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, addressed to Count Valerius.], as he himself can acknowledge—one occupied with other affairs rather than with literature. They ask the aid of power against us, and, on their behalf, commend the decrees of the common people—whether rural or theatrical—which, though they have been promulgated, no history records with what intention.

### Augustine

We do not ask the aid of power against you. Rather, on your behalf, we praise the duty of Christian power, so that you may be restrained from sacrilegious presumption. Consider, then, how you call Cyprian, Ambrose, and so many learned men who write in the kingdom of God “rural” and “theatrical,” and count them among your associates.

### XV. Julian

Nevertheless, we can in no way deny what I have said: that it pleases the crowds very much, though it is base [Note: [Col. 1147] Menardus has *turbis placet, Judaeis tamen*, “it pleases the crowds, yet the Jews.” Vignierius has *turbis placet, videris tamen*, “it pleases the crowds, yet you seem…” A little later they similarly had *et infamationes et hominum morum petulantiam vindicare*, “to justify both slanders and the wantonness of human morals.” The text has been corrected from the manuscripts.], to impute the sins of the will to nature and to justify the wantonness of conduct by the defamation of the seed, so that no one will ever attempt to correct what he expects another to perpetrate in himself [Note: [Col. 1147] Perhaps, “what he knows.”].

### Augustine

Who told you that one person perpetrates another person’s sin [Note: [Col. 1147] So the manuscripts. The printed editions have *quod tibi dixi*, “what I told you.”]? Even the one who says, “It is no longer I who do it, but sin dwelling in me,” immediately adds, “For I know that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh” (Rom. 7:17–18), and thereby shows that whatever it is belongs to him; for the flesh itself belongs to the person who consists of flesh and spirit. And yet you do not wish to agree with Ambrose that this evil—by which the flesh lusts against the spirit—was turned into nature through the transgression of the first human being (Ambrose, Book 7 on Luke 12:52).

But since you too are accustomed to say that these apostolic words express the force of bad custom, what did you mean when you now wished to say, “So that no one will attempt to correct what he knows another to perpetrate in himself”? You certainly wish the person who says, “It is not I who do it,” to correct himself; and you wish this to be accomplished by the strength of his own will, although you see how weak is the will of the person who says, “I do not do what I want.” At least permit this person, I beg you, to ask divine help, since you see that the choice of his own will has failed him.

[Col. 1148] ### XVI. Julian

But the weak defense of a blind opinion multiplies sins rather than diminishing them. Thus this itching of wretched people who make themselves ill [Note: [Col. 1148] The printed editions have *crescentium*, “who increase.” The manuscripts have *aegrescentium*, “who make themselves ill.”] will be able to contribute no weight against reason itself. But because they assert that natural sin is confirmed by certain passages of Scripture, and especially by the words of the apostle Paul—whose interpretation I postponed to the second volume, and the time has come to provide it [Note: [Col. 1148] The printed editions have *distuli, quaerendi tempus est*, “I postponed it; the time has come to seek it.” Corrected from the manuscripts.]—I shall first distinguish briefly, so that the reader may be better instructed, what has been done and what remains to be done.
