It has therefore been shown that nothing can be proved through the holy Scriptures that justice cannot defend. For if the law of God contains the perfect form of justice, then its adversary—that is, injustice—is permitted to acquire nothing through it that belongs to virtue. Consequently, what reason condemns cannot be vindicated by authority.

Next, it was proved that God is known to us through his virtues. His justice, therefore, must be acknowledged in the same way as his omnipotence; for if its destruction is admitted, his whole majesty will begin to totter. For God is so just that, if it were proved that he was not just, it would be proved that he was not God.

And it was concluded that we worship God, supremely just, in the Trinity. It also appeared irrefutably that sin belonging to another cannot be imputed by him to infants.

### Augustine

Why do you not admit that a heavy yoke could not have been imposed by the omnipotent and just God upon the sons of Adam from the day they leave their mother’s womb, without any merit of sin?

### XVII. Julian

But just as we discussed the definition of justice, so also we discussed the nature of sin. Sin appeared to be nothing other than an evil will, which was free to abstain from what it had wrongly desired.

### Augustine

This is entirely the sin of the first human being, from which the origin of evil descended upon humanity. For it was entirely free to abstain from what it had wrongly desired, since there was not yet any vice by which the flesh would lust against the spirit. It did not yet say, “I do not do what I want.” Not yet placed in sinful flesh, it had no necessary need of the help provided by the likeness of sinful flesh.

### XVIII. Julian

And thus, by the clearest testimony, it has been thoroughly demonstrated that there is no sin in those who are born, since the exercise of the will could not be found in them.

### Augustine

And from where does the heavy yoke come, unless because they do not possess the exercise of the will and yet are subject to the bond of origin [Note: [Col. 1148] So the manuscripts. The printed editions have *obnoxium*, “subject,” in the neuter. The manuscript reading is *obnoxiae*, agreeing with the feminine plural subject.].

### XIX. Julian

It has been shown in a lucid discussion that free choice is denied by those who say that sins are natural. The Punic writer, however, denied this—not in his own words, lest it carry less weight, but by the testimony of the Gospel, as though with greater authority; and by explaining it we restored it to the dignity of the Gospel. We also rescued the testimony of the apostle Paul from the snares of the slanderer, and showed, with the prophet as witness, that our God, the fashioner of good vessels, is the creator of all.

### Augustine

You were answered there, and it was shown how far you had strayed from the truth.

### XX. Julian

These matters, then, having been dealt with chiefly in the first book—any one of which is more than sufficient for the victory of truth—it nevertheless remains, by way of abundance, to discuss the judgment of the Teacher of the Gentiles, who said that through one human being sin entered the world (Rom. 5:12). We shall use the definitions we have set forth whenever necessary, both to support our case and to prove that reason did not lie, but that it is a crime against justice to impute the deeds of some to the births of others. Although no one ought to have doubted that this itself is unjust, we shall nevertheless show, by testimonies from the law, either in this book or in the next, that it displeases God and is forbidden by him.

From these arguments it necessarily follows that we are entirely right to defend both that no one is born with sin and that God cannot judge those who are born guilty. Consequently, free choice is as intact as nature in each person is innocent before the exercise of his own will.

### Augustine

Let us see what you are going to say about the apostle’s testimony—just as emptily as you spoke of the preceding matters [Note: [Col. 1149] The printed editions have *quid*, “what.” The manuscripts have *quod*, “that which.”].

### XXI. Julian

The Manichaeans, rebels against both piety and reason, think that sin exists even before the time of the will, although the nature of things does not permit this; they think that God exists whom they argue to be unjust; and they defame the holy pages, whose records they claim prove a crime on the part of the divine nature. Since none of these three things can be demonstrated by reason—that is, neither sin without the will, nor injustice in God, nor perversity in the law—only those people should be shown to be foolish, shameless, and impious [Note: [Col. 1149] So the manuscripts Clar. and Port. The printed editions have *imprudentes et impii demonstrantur*, “are shown to be foolish and impious.”].

### Augustine

Be ashamed. Ambrose was not a Manichaean when he said that a human being undergoes the contagion of sins before receiving the gift of the life-giving spirit (Book *On Philosophy*). Nor did sins arise except from the will, from which they derive their origin. Therefore there is no injustice in God, who for this reason placed a heavy yoke upon those who are born; nor is there perversity in the law, in which this is learned [Note: [Col. 1149] So the manuscripts. The printed editions have *dicitur*, “is said.”] to be most true. You would see this too, if you did not instead have perverse eyes.

### XXII. Julian

Let this, then, above all remain fixed in the mind of the prudent reader: that all the sacred Scriptures contain only what accords with the honor of the Catholic God, as is illuminated by the light of their frequent statements. And if anywhere a harsher expression gives rise to a question, it is certain that the author of that passage did not understand something unjust there; rather, the passage must be understood according to what both clear reason and the radiance of other passages, in which there is no ambiguity, have revealed [Note: [Col. 1149] The manuscripts have *aperuit*, “has revealed.”].

Let us now set forth the words of the man with whom we are dealing. In that chapter of his statements, which he had brought forward as far as his “God the potter of sinners” [Note: [Col. 1150] The printed editions have *peccatorem*, “potter of the sinner,” which is incorrect and conflicts with the manuscripts.], and against which we contended in the preceding book, he said only briefly that through one human being sin entered the world. He did not linger over an exposition of the passage itself.

After discussing at length those excerpts which he confirms were sent to him, he came to one of my statements, which he set before himself as though he were going to attack it. But he reported nothing according to the matter with which he had been challenged. Instead, he hurried to this saying of the apostle, in which Paul says that through one human being sin entered the world. He then attempted to explain the context of the passage according to his own doctrine.

For this reason I hastened, passing over the other matters, to that section. Since I had promised that I would resolve this question in the second volume, I wished both to fulfill the pledge of my promise and to show what his argument amounted to, lest I seem to have acted deceitfully by suppressing his interpretation and introducing instead the interpretation that we confess to be Catholic.

### Augustine

You are going to introduce a Pelagian interpretation, not a Catholic one. The Catholic interpretation is the one that shows God to be just in the case of the many and great punishments and sufferings of infants—punishments and sufferings that none of them would perceive in paradise with any sense of justice if human nature had not been corrupted by sin and deservedly condemned.

### XXIII. Julian

In my first work, then, I reviewed his statement in which he had said:

> “For just as sin, whether it is drawn from this source or that, is the work of the devil, so a human being, whether born from this source or that, is the work of God” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 1, chapter 1).

I now report it here exactly as it appears in my work, from which he had stolen the greater part.

### Augustine

You argue truthfully in the same way that it is true that I stole those things, whereas in fact the person whose little document was sent to me transferred from your work whatever he wished, and in whatever way he wished, according to his own judgment and decision.

### XXIV. Julian

I answered him there:

> “You are indeed evading the issue—let me say this with due respect for your teaching authority [Note: [Col. 1150] The printed editions have: “Answer there, ‘You indeed, let me say this as part of your teaching authority.’” The reading has been corrected from the manuscripts Port., Mar., and Clar. Julian here transfers his reply from the first book of his earlier work addressed to Turbantius; Augustine had already refuted it above, in book 1 of *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, sections 30–31, and in book 3 *Against Julian*, section 51 and following.]. But understand that truth has taken away from you the license to wander wherever you please. For look: we too agree that sin is the work of an evil will, or that it is the work of the devil. But by what means is this sin found in an infant? Through the will? But there was no will in him. Through the form of the body? But God supplied this. Through the entrance of the soul? But the soul, newly created by God, owes nothing to bodily seed. Through marriage? But marriage belongs to the work of the parents, whom you had previously asserted did not sin in this act. If you had not truly granted this—as the course of your argument indicates—then marriage itself must be execrated, since it caused the evil.

> “But marriage has no substance of its own; in its own name it indicates the work of persons. Therefore the parents, who by their union caused the sin, are rightly deserving of condemnation. It can no longer be doubted, then, that the spouses are handed over to eternal punishment, since by their labor the devil came to exercise dominion over human beings. If you grant this, you will lose everything that earlier you seemed to maintain—namely, that you had said the human being was the work of God. For it necessarily follows that, if the origin of offspring comes through the mingling of bodies, and if evil comes into human beings through their origin, and the devil’s right over human beings comes through evil, then the devil is the author of human beings, from whom the origin of those who are born derives.”

After this I repeated his own words again:

> “For just as sin, whether it is drawn from this source or that, is the work of the devil, so a human being, whether born from this source or that, is the work of God.”

And I immediately attacked in this way:

> “When I consider that fearful statement of yours in which you say that marriage is not evil, I cannot contemplate these other statements of yours without laughter. For if you believe that human beings are made by God and that the spouses are innocent, see how it is impossible for original sin to be drawn from them. Certainly the one who is born does not sin; the one who begets does not sin; the one who creates does not sin. Through what cracks, then, do you imagine that sin entered amid so many safeguards of innocence?”

### Augustine

It is enough that I answered these words of yours, even when I had read your own books [See above, *Against Julian*, book 3, sections 54–57]. But here too I remind you that the apostle must be heard rather than you. He pointed out not a hidden crack but an entirely open door through which sin entered the world, and through sin death; and thus death passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned (Rom. 5:12). When you begin to explain these words according to yourselves rather than according to the apostle, then it will become apparent against what rectitude of truth you are struggling with your most tortuous verbosity.

### XXV. Julian

He therefore set forth, in this second book of his, the passage from my earlier work, though with interpolation [Note: [Col. 1151] The printed editions have *scilicet cum interpellatione*, “namely, with interruption.” The manuscripts have *sibi, licet cum interpolatione*, “for himself, though with interpolation.”] (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 2, sections 44–49). For he artfully passed over both the bodily formation that I mentioned and the entrance of the soul—which, as I hope, both reason and the authority of the sacred law and of the Catholic Church confirm to be newly created by God in each individual [Note: [Col. 1151] The printed editions have *ut spero, iste praeteriit*, “as I hope, he passed over.” The manuscripts have *ut spero, arte praeteriit*, “as I hope, he artfully passed over.”].

### Augustine

Whoever reads the six books in which I refuted your four books—the first of which that person, to whom I replied in the book now vainly attacked by your exceedingly verbose folly, excerpted as he wished and in whatever manner he wished—will find that I answered you in my third book in such a way that he can see that I did not artfully pass over what you mention. Rather, the person whose little document I was answering did not wish to transfer this material from your work, either for the sake of brevity or because he did not think it relevant to the issue.

### XXVI. Julian

He then wove together the remaining material, though varied by certain changes of wording. Against these objections of mine he devised nothing with which he could strike back. But, confessing through his lack of argumentative resources that I had gathered the truth, he says that the apostle answers me in all these matters by declaring that through one human being sin entered this world [Note: [Col. 1152] The printed editions have *respondere debere*, “that the apostle ought to answer.” The word *debere* is absent from the manuscripts.].

At this point, what educated person would judge that he had a sound mind, since he did not understand either that he had to pass over the objections against which he could find no answer, or that he had to devise whatever he might set against those objections and connect the apostle’s words in support of it?

### Augustine

But you are more effectively refuted by the apostolic words than by mine. Yet you do not yield even to the apostolic words; you prefer to twist them as well rather than correct yourself.

### XXVII. Julian

I therefore asked, with perfect consistency, that all learning should acknowledge with me [Note: [Col. 1152] So the manuscripts. Menardus has *recognosceret*, “should acknowledge”; Vignierius has *recognoscit*, “acknowledges.”] by what means sin—which is the work of an evil will and is called the work of the devil—could be found in an infant.

If through the will, then there was no will in him; even the man with whom we are dealing confesses this here. If through marriage, then marriage belongs to the work of the parents—no one doubts this—and he had already stated that they did not sin in this union. Or, if the disputant regretted this concession, as the course of his work indicated, he ought to have acknowledged that the parents were guilty, since by their union the devil’s kingdom was prepared against the image of God.

I added, following the necessary steps of the argument, that through original sin the devil must be defined as the author of bodies: for if evil comes into human beings through their origin, and the devil’s right over human beings comes through evil, then the devil is the author of human beings, from whom the origin of those who are born derives.

Since these arguments had detected the Traducians as being shut up in the cave of the Manichaeans [Note: [Col. 1152] Menardus has *Traducianas esse clusuras deprehenderat*, “had detected Traducian enclosures.” Vignierius has *Traducianos essent*—or *esset clusura*—*deprehenderat*. All the manuscripts have *Traducianos esse clusura deprehenderat*. Here *clusura* means the same as *clausula*, that is, the conclusion of an argument.], I turned the key so as to provide an escape for the captives. I also urged him that, if he truly believed that human beings were made by God and sincerely confessed that the spouses were innocent, he should understand that original sin could not be drawn from them.

“Certainly,” I said, “the one who is born does not sin; the one who begets does not sin; the one who creates does not sin. Through what cracks, amid so many safeguards of innocence, do you imagine that sin entered?”

What, I ask, could have been arranged more reverently, more truthfully, more clearly, more briefly, or more firmly than this? After taking three premises that my opponent had conceded, I introduced a fourth, in which the entire conclusion consisted. For just as sometimes, once one or two premises have been taken, a third is necessarily inferred, by what rule was I not permitted, once three things had been conceded to me, to infer a fourth that follows from them? And this was in the second disputation. In the first, moreover, five or more propositions were conceded to me, after which a legitimate and unconquerable conclusion follows.

### Augustine

See how widely you wander, fearing that the apostle’s words, heard without your prejudices, will condemn you, just as they have already condemned you by the judgment of the Catholic Church. But run wherever you wish; linger as long as you wish; multiply your circles in every direction as you wish. Whenever the ship of your deceptions reaches those same words of truth, you will undoubtedly suffer shipwreck.

### XXVIII. Julian

Let us now turn to him. You had granted me that sin is the work of the will. I could immediately have said, consistently, “But there is no will in infants that could sin; therefore there is no sin in infants” [Note: [Col. 1153] The printed editions have *a parvulis*, “from infants.” Corrected from the manuscripts.]. But so that you might be pressed by more witnesses, I asked more cautiously by what means this sin could be found in an infant—perhaps through the will [Note: [Col. 1153] The printed editions have *an per voluntatem?*, “or through the will?” The manuscripts consistently have *ne*, “perhaps through the will?”].

With your consent, I then accepted that there had been no awareness of the will in him. I added the question whether he had perhaps drawn the outlines of his members through the first fault. But you had granted that these were formed by God and were therefore good.

I asked a third question: whether you thought guilt had been brought in through the entrance of the soul. But it was clear that the soul was new and owed nothing to seeds.

Next I proposed whether—since you had nothing left to criticize in these matters—you would call marriage, that is, the mingling of bodies, the work of the devil [Note: [Col. 1153] Vignierius has *an ne*, “or whether perhaps.” M. has the same reading.]. But, with your agreement, I showed that marriage belongs to the work of the parents.

Once all those matters mentioned above had been cleared away, your *tradux* handed over to the devil the spouses who had been the cause of sin. After all this, I struck you with what followed closely upon the argument [Note: [Col. 1153] The printed editions have *induxi*, “I introduced.” All the manuscripts have *impegi*, “I struck.”], saying that you believed the devil to be the author of bodies, since you had assigned to him the work of the sexual union without which the origin of bodies could not exist.

This first disputation showed what disease oppressed you. The second proved both that you were pitiable with such opinions and that Catholics were unconquerable by the support of your fear. Since you granted that human beings are made by God, that the spouses are innocent, and that infants do nothing by themselves, these three premises irrefutably yielded the conclusion that, since the one who is born does not sin, the one who begets does not sin, and the one who creates does not sin, no crack remained through which sin could be shown to have entered.

If, therefore, you dislike the conclusion, deny what you granted. Say either that the one who begot sinned, or that the one who created sinned, or that the one who was born sinned. Of these, one is madness, another is Manichaeism, and the third is worse than Manichaeism: madness, if you say that infants commit sin; Manichaeism, if you accuse the spouses; worse than Manichaeism, if you judge God to be the author of sin.

If all these positions are so alien to the truth that you still fear confessing them openly, with what shamelessness, most deranged of men, do you persist in denying what we have inferred?

### Augustine

When you come to the apostle’s words, you will find there not a crack but an entirely open door through which sin entered the world. You will indeed try to shut it, but you are defeated by the mouths of infants and nursing babies, who seek Christ the Savior rather than you as their praiser, and who testify to their misery far more certainly—not through intricate arguments but through silent tears. If the rectitude and blessedness of the first human being had remained, they could in no way have possessed this misery in paradise [Col. 1154]. Your entire verbosity is overcome by this testimony.

### XXIX. Julian

The case of four persons is at issue here: God the creator; the two parents, from whom the material is supplied to the craftsman; and the infant who is born. You say that sin dwells in this chorus. I ask from whom it comes: from God? You deny it. From the father? You deny it just as much. From the mother? You deny that as well. From the infant? You deny it. And still you do not think the matter concluded, since there cannot be among these four something that none of the four admits.

### Augustine

Say whatever you wish. You will eventually come to the apostle’s words [Note: [Col. 1154] So the manuscripts. The printed editions have *quando*, “when.”], and anyone who recalls them through the separate stages of your arguments—stages we do not wish to repeat continually because of the reader’s weariness—will answer you by that very recollection.

### XXX. Julian

What purpose is served, then, either by rereading the Scriptures or by naming witnesses, when you still cannot define what you think? Why does it help you to teach that Adam sinned, something I do not deny at all? We are asking, now that Adam died so many ages ago, by what means the sin through which the image of God is transferred into the devil’s jurisdiction is found in an infant.

### Augustine

Why do you also refuse to admit the image of God into the kingdom of God when, according to you, it has no merit of sin? Why is blood administered—the blood poured out from the likeness of sinful flesh for the remission of sins—for an infant to drink, so that he may have life, if he comes into death from no origin of sin [Note: [Col. 1154] So the manuscripts. The printed editions have *si de nulla*, “if from no origin.”]?

If this displeases you, openly deny that Christ became an infant [Note: [Col. 1154] These words, *aperte nega parvulum Christum*, “openly deny that Christ became an infant,” are restored from the manuscripts Mar., Clar., and Port.]. Openly deny that he died for infants, he who died for all. From this is inferred what the apostle says: “Therefore all have died, and he died for all” (2 Cor. 5:14–15) [Note: [Col. 1154] So the manuscripts Clar. and Mar. Manuscript Port. has *collegit*, “he gathered,” apparently for *colligit*, “it is inferred.”].

Say openly: “Infants have not died; since they have no sin, they do not need Christ’s death for them, in which they may be baptized.” Now say plainly what you secretly think, since your argument sufficiently betrays what you think. Say, I repeat, that infants become Christians in vain. But consider whether you ought to call yourself a Christian.

### XXXI. Julian

If this is through the union of the parents, condemn marriage by your profession, since you condemn it by your argument, and spare us the trouble by which we convict you of being a Manichaean. But if you do not dare say this, and if, contrary to reason [Note: [Col. 1154] Perhaps, “contrary to your reason.”], you incline toward those who have intercourse [Note: [Col. 1154] The printed editions have *cum cadentibus inclinaris*, “you incline toward those who fall.” The manuscripts have *concumbentibus inclinaris*, “you incline toward those who have intercourse,” that is, those devoted to marriage and lust.], so that through the previously unheard-of monstrosities of your arguments you say that lust is diabolical, that it is situated in the mind of those who have intercourse, and that it belongs to the pleasure of the parents but to the guilt of those who are born, then you certainly reveal your madness and shamefulness.

But I ask you not to claim so much for yourself as to think that we are not free to protect, with honor toward God, the innocence of those who are born, while you are permitted and pleased, while accusing God, to cleanse the members of those who lust from the guilt of the lust you allege.

### Augustine

Praise lust—concupiscence of the flesh—under whatever form of itching you wish. The apostle John says that it is not from the Father but from the world (1 John 2:16); and for this reason the devil is rightly called the ruler of the world (John 12:31). For we know that God made the world.

The conjugal chastity therefore makes good use of this evil of concupiscence of the flesh, and spiritual regeneration releases those who are born from the guilt of this evil that has been drawn from their origin. As long as you do not understand this, you will be not a Catholic but a Pelagian, and you will contradict the holy Scriptures, however much you may seem to defend them.

Whenever you call me a Manichaean on account of this matter that you contradict, you certainly also call Manichaean the man who says that a human being, infused into genital members and congealed by the pleasure of concupiscence, first receives the contagion of sins before drawing in the gift of the life-giving spirit. That man is Ambrose, Julian, in the book *On the Sacrament of Regeneration*, or *On Philosophy*. You call Ambrose a Manichaean, madman.

### XXXII. JULIAN

For when you declare that the lust of the flesh was planted in man by the prince of darkness, and that it is the devil’s shoot, bringing forth from itself the human race as though its own fruits, you plainly reveal that you say not God but the devil is the creator of human beings. By this most impious doctrine, the whole business of marriage—that is, the mingling of the genitals—and all flesh are condemned.

### AUGUSTINE

It is not condemned; but it must not be praised by you as though it were sound [Note: [Col. 1155] Vignierius has *sed non, velut a te, quasi sana laudatur* (“but it is not praised by you as though it were sound”): less well], so that, as you yourself admit, it may be healed by its Creator and Savior. For in those in whom this healing does not occur, it will unquestionably be condemned.

### XXXIII. JULIAN

But when, after this sacrilege, you add and say that you profess the pleasure of procreating spouses to be diabolical, and the movement of the genitals diabolical, but nevertheless that neither the very members that are moved nor the spouses who are affected by pleasure are guilty, while you accuse on behalf of all these things new human beings—that is, the raw work in those who are born—of divinity, you indeed set aside nothing of the impiety of the Manichaeans. Yet you display so monstrous a frenzy of shaken judgment that it would seem more appropriate to indulge it than to cut it off, were it not that your will and zeal in this matter, the overthrow of many, your obstinacy, and the abundance of the Scriptures all spoke otherwise.

### AUGUSTINE

I ought not to hear these insults with indignation, since they are directed against those teachers of the Church who understand that sin entered the world through one man in the manner in which the Apostle speaks rightly, not as the most perverse Julian supposes. Among them, to pass over others, are Cyprian of Africa, Hilary of Gaul, Ambrose of Italy, and Gregory of Greece. By these most learned and prudent judges—such judges as you complain, in your vain presumption, that you cannot find—your heresy was condemned before it was born.

[Col. 1156]

### XXXIV. JULIAN

Read also the fourth book of my work on this subject, and you will understand how much you flatter the devil, whom you call your father, and lust, your mother [Note: [Col. 1156] So the manuscripts Clar., Mar., and Port. The printed editions have *a libidine matris tuae* (“from the lust of your mother”), incorrectly], under the pretext of accusing them.

### AUGUSTINE

I have also read your fourth book, and in my sixth I answered everything you said there. Let the pious reader judge which of us has prevailed.

### XXXV. JULIAN

But now let us examine the Apostle’s words—the Apostle whom you said answered me concerning everything, the passage I cited above:

“To all these objections the Apostle replied. He neither accused the will of the infant, which is not yet his own for sinning; nor marriage, insofar as it is marriage, which has from God not only its institution but also its blessing; nor parents, insofar as they are parents, lawfully and legitimately joined to one another for begetting children. Rather, he says: ‘Through one man sin entered into this world, and through sin death; and so it passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned’ (Romans 5:12).

If these people would apprehend this with Catholic ears and minds, they would not have rebellious spirits against the faith and grace of Christ, nor would they vainly attempt to turn these apostolic words, so clear and manifest, toward their own peculiar heretical meaning by asserting that they were said because Adam sinned first, and that thereafter whoever wished to sin found in him an example of sinning; so that sin passed from that one man into all not by generation, but by imitation of that one man.

Yet surely, if the Apostle had wished imitation to be understood here, he would have said that sin entered this world through the devil rather than through one man, and passed through all human beings. For it is written of the devil: ‘They imitate him who belong to his side’ (Wisdom 2:25). But for this reason he said ‘through one man,’ from whom the generation of human beings certainly began, so that he might teach that original sin had passed into all through generation” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 2, no. 45).

### AUGUSTINE

You have quoted the words of my book. Now say how the words of the Apostle that I set down there are to be understood, so that you may be revealed more and more clearly as a heretic, posing as a praiser in order to take the Savior away from infants.

### XXXVI. JULIAN

Any learned reader of our works will understand that you abuse the ignorance of those who favor you and conceal yourself under the ambiguity of words. But the remaining common crowd—of whom the prophet says to God, “You have regarded human beings as the fish of the sea” (Habakkuk 1:14)—is deceived by reciprocal progression and, ignorant of salutary discernment [Note: [Col. 1156] The printed editions have *progressione decipitur, ac salutifera discretione signatum* (“is deceived by progression and marked by salutary discernment”). The manuscripts give the reading translated here], thinks that everything may be joined to things which it sees joined in words. But what follows from what, and what is contradictory, and what an inviolable and venerable law of speech compels to be inferred from premises once granted—unless one is most learned and attentive, one cannot judge.

### AUGUSTINE

You are still going around seeking dialecticians and avoiding ecclesiastical judges. Say now how “Through one man sin entered into the world” is to be understood—understanding it better, evidently, than the one who said, “All die in Adam,” because “through one man sin entered into this world, and through sin death; and so it passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned.” Thus the death of all is due to his guilt (Ambrose, book 4 on Luke 4:38).

The same man says elsewhere: “There was Adam, and in him we were all; Adam perished, and in him all perished” (book 7 on Luke 15:24).

This is Ambrose, not some ordinary member of the crowd whose ignorant multitude, unable to judge your arguments, you despise with an excessively uplifted neck and insolent face. Ambrose, I say, to whom you are in no way equal in the secular literature of which you are so puffed up; and as for ecclesiastical literature, hear or read who your teacher Pelagius is, and do not embrace a meaning alien to that of so great a teacher.

### XXXVII. JULIAN

This, then, is why, grieving over the ruin of the Churches [Note: [Col. 1157] The manuscripts have *Ecclesiarum* (“of the Churches”); the printed editions have *Ecclesiae* (“of the Church”)], we especially appeal to the judgment of illustrious men, so that it may become clear not merely what is said, but what follows consistently from what is said. For if the matter were debated before such a council, you would certainly not be permitted either to infer what you had denied or to deny what you had affirmed. But in your book, which no standard of shame restrains, you confidently heap together both what Catholics say and what Manichaeans say [Note: [Col. 1157] Two manuscripts, Mar. and Clar., have “both what the Manichaeans confess you heap together”], content with the mere opinion that you will be said to have answered. To consider what weight and consistency your speech possesses, however, you regard as foolish.

### AUGUSTINE

I ask you: say now how “Through one man sin entered into the world” is to be understood. Why do you still slander, insult, and evade? If Cyprian, Hilary, Ambrose, Gregory, Basil, and John of Constantinople, to pass over others, were seated in the council whose judgment you appear to desire, would you dare seek judges more learned, prudent, and truthful? They themselves cry out against your doctrines; they themselves condemn your writings by their own writings. What more do you seek?

I have already taught this sufficiently in the first and second books of my work, six books that I published against your four. But behold, I am still prepared to hear you: say now how what “entered into the world through one man” is to be understood.

### XXXVIII. JULIAN

Finally, when without hesitation you grant what I demanded and consider what follows from it, you confess yourself unequal to the structure we have built, and that the Apostle Paul contradicts all that we have said; yet you introduce him as conceding the very points you had granted. For you say: “The Apostle neither accused the will of the infant, which is not yet his own for sinning” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 2, no. 45). Once this is granted, it is already proved that there can be no sin in the infant, since, according to your own definition, the only condition of sin is the will to admit what justice forbids, and from which it is free to abstain.

[Col. 1158]

### AUGUSTINE

This is a definition of sin as something that is not also the punishment of sin. For when you contend that these are expressions of bad habit [Note: [Col. 1158] Perhaps *conceditis* (“you concede”) rather than *contenditis* (“you contend”)], and thus stifle the expressions of your doctrine [Note: [Col. 1158] Morel, *Elementa Critica*, pp. 311–312, reads: “and thus you stifle the throats of your doctrine”], say, if you dare, how it is free to the human will to abstain from evil when you hear, “I do not do what I want”; or deny that there is evil when you hear, “I do not do the good that I want, but I do the evil that I do not want” (Romans 7:15, 19).

Yet we certainly recognize that this sin is the punishment of sin, and therefore it must be distinguished from that definition of sin in which the will commits what it is free to abstain from [Note: [Col. 1158] The manuscripts have “this it commits.” And below: “Understand what I say”]. Understand what I am saying, and say now, please, how “Through one man sin entered into the world” is to be understood.

### XXXIX. JULIAN

Therefore, if the Apostle did not accuse in the infant a will of its own, which he understands could not even exist there, he plainly declares that no sign of guilt appears in the infant, especially according to that justice which does not impute sin except to one who is free to abstain from it.

But not content merely to grant this, you add: “Nor did the Apostle accuse marriage, insofar as it is marriage, which has from God not only its institution but also its blessing” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 2, no. 45). This alone could equally suffice to overthrow the notion of natural sin. For if the Apostle knows—as he does know—that marriage is not to be accused, and if the sexual union attended by pleasure, instituted and blessed by God, belongs to the union, service, and instrument of marriage [Note: [Col. 1158] Vignierius has “from whose reconciliation, service, and instrument it belongs.” The manuscripts more correctly have: “to whose reconciliation, and service and instrument, it belongs”], then no diabolical possession can spring from these things [Note: [Col. 1158] So the manuscripts. The printed editions have “no diabolical possession can spring from these things”], nor is their fruit guilty before that justice which does not impute sin except where one is free to abstain.

### AUGUSTINE

I beg you, do not imagine that the intercourse of spouses in paradise involved such pleasure as lust now produces—lust that does not arise at the command of the will and that troubles even the minds of the saints with an intrusive insistence, though it must be restrained [Note: [Col. 1158] So all the manuscripts. The printed editions read “to imagine marriage in paradise with such pleasure,” omitting “intercourse”]. Far be it from the faithful and prudent to conceive of paradise as having such pleasure, or such peace and happiness.

### XL. JULIAN

Let us consider the third point as well, so that your benevolence may be seen in your readiness to agree:

“Nor did the Apostle accuse parents, insofar as they are parents, lawfully and legitimately joined to one another for begetting children” (*ibid.*).

Consider what you have said: that parents are not accused by the Apostle insofar as they are parents. Therefore he declares that insofar as they are parents they cannot bear fruit for the devil, and that nothing belonging to them insofar as they are parents pertains to the devil. But children pertain to their parents precisely insofar as they are parents; therefore they are shown to be neither guilty nor under the devil’s rule, nor to be accused by the devil.

To make what we have said clear by repetition:

The union of the sexes contributes to offspring insofar as those who are spouses become parents. But if they should do something more wanton with one another, or wander into illicit adulterous intercourse, this cannot concern the children, who are born from the power of semen, not from the obscenity of vices.

### AUGUSTINE

Do you now admit that even between spouses there can be wantonness in intercourse? Behold what that fine undertaking of yours produces [Note: [Col. 1159] Vignierius has: “Behold what the response you have given to those beautiful things produces for you.” The manuscripts have *tua illa*, omitting *ad*. The word *responsio* is also absent from these manuscripts and from Menardus’s first edition. Julian very frequently says *suscepta tua* (“your undertaking”) to Augustine when speaking of concupiscence, whose defense Julian undertook].

For this does not occur unless one yields to it, when no necessity of begetting offspring drives even spouses united for the purpose of procreation toward that wantonness which you also condemn. You wished to be so great a praiser of it that no one can believe you would dare also to attack it—especially since you were not ashamed to praise it in such a way that it might free you, and to place it even in the blessedness of paradise.

### XLI. JULIAN

Therefore what is conveyed to those born from the begetters is not their crimes but their semen. God instituted the power of semen and, as you are compelled to confess, blessed it.

### AUGUSTINE

God instituted semen. But those who can distinguish its good from its evil in a corrupted nature, so that they neither think nature is evil nor that vice is nature, can themselves discern which of these two belongs to God’s creating and which to his healing [Note: [Col. 1159] The printed editions have “so that neither those who think nature is evil nor those who think vice is nature can discern,” and shortly afterward “they themselves can.” The word “who” is absent from the manuscripts, which have “they themselves can”].

But you cannot do this so long as you are Pelagians, not Catholics. Say now, I ask you, say now how what “entered into the world through one man” is to be understood.

### XLII. JULIAN

Therefore children are not guilty even when their parents sin in begetting them, because the parents pertain to their children insofar as they are parents; and therefore children pertain to their parents only insofar as they are children [Note: [Col. 1159] Perhaps “to that extent”]. For it is clear that the begetters communicate the seeds of nature [Note: [Col. 1159] Menardus has *Naturam* (“nature”), and below *non culpam* (“not guilt”); Vignierius has *Natura* and likewise *non culpa*. The manuscripts have *Naturae . . . . .; non culpae* (“of nature …; not of guilt”)], not of guilt.

If, as reason demonstrates, you also declare that the Apostle confirms this, then rightly, with him as our teacher, we defend that the sins of parents cannot pertain to their children. For the Apostle, illustrious through the Holy Spirit, we instructed by the light of reason, and you, overwhelmed by the weight of the truth you attack, jointly and truly confess that parents are not guilty insofar as they are parents [Note: [Col. 1159] Here the manuscripts add: “insofar as they are parents”]; and that they pertain to their children to that extent; therefore that children, insofar as they are children—that is, before they perform anything through their own will—cannot be guilty.

### AUGUSTINE

Parents are indeed parents by begetting, and children are children by being born [Col. 1160]. Neither begetting nor being born is evil, since each belongs to God’s institution; and both could take place in paradise without shameful lust if no one had sinned.

For if shameful lust had not arisen from sin or been corrupted by sin, it would not be shameful. Either it would not exist at all, and the genital members would serve those who beget just as hands serve those who work; or it would follow the will in such a way that it could never trouble one who did not want it. Chastity teaches that it is not now like this: chastity conquers its movements, both among married people, lest they behave indecently toward one another or slip into adultery, and among those who practice continence, lest by consenting to it they be cast down.

Behold from what original sin is drawn; behold through what the one who came—not to bear his own sin, but to take away ours—did not wish to be born.

### XLIII. JULIAN

Let all the ingenuity of the Manichaean reasoning now exert itself as much as it can [Note: [Col. 1160] Morel thinks one should read: “Let all the ingenuity of the Manichaean nation exert itself as much as it can.” See *Elementa Critica*, p. 156], and let it endure whatever long hardships of thought it wishes. I promise, not arrogantly but religiously, that this structure can never be shaken [Note: [Col. 1160] The printed editions have *structuram* (“structure”), and below, in Augustine’s response, “the structure you call”; the manuscripts have *instructuram* in both places].

### AUGUSTINE

What you call a construction is a ruin for you [Note: [Col. 1160] Menardus and the manuscripts have *ibi* (“there”)], which has so oppressed you that it forced you to praise what you attack—if, indeed, you possess any chastity at all that makes you attack what you praise.

### XLIV. JULIAN

With what face, then, do you add:

“But ‘through one man sin entered into the world, and through sin death; and so it passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned’” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 1, no. 45)?

You interpret this in such a way that the Apostle is said to have declared sin transmitted from that man to his descendants by generation. Earlier you had conceded that the Teacher of the Gentiles accused neither the marriages blessed by God, nor the absence of a will to sin in the one who is born, nor parents who are lawfully and legitimately joined to one another for begetting children. Then immediately you add—as though you had spoken the earlier words while asleep—that guilt is transmitted to descendants by generation.

For if they beget insofar as they are parents, and insofar as they are parents they lawfully and legitimately unite with one another, and if this union is not rejected by the Apostle because it was not only instituted but also blessed by God, with what mouth, under what law, with what face do you affirm that this generation is the cause of guilt, the root of crimes, and the servant of the devil?

### AUGUSTINE

I do not know how many times these things have been said and answered. By your many words you raise a fog that prevents you from distinguishing the evil of vices from the goodness of nature. Repeating the same things again and again to wearisome disgust, you still do not say how “Through one man sin entered into the world” is to be understood.

### XLV. JULIAN

Therefore it does not deserve to be accused by the Apostle, yet it is possessed by the devil; it is instituted by God, yet it is the source of crimes; finally, it is blessed by God, as you admit, yet you accuse it as a diabolical shoot.

### AUGUSTINE

God blessed marriage, not the flesh’s concupiscence that resists the spirit, which did not exist before sin. God did not bless sin, nor that concupiscence which resists the spirit.

The marriage God blessed, if sin had not been committed and nature thereby corrupted, would either have used the genital members as we use the others, obedient to the will without any lust, or shameful lust would not have existed there [Note: [Col. 1161] We have added the word *ibi* (“there”) from the manuscripts], since it would never resist the will, as it certainly does not now. You yourself surely feel this when you dissent from it as it troubles and entices you.

Nevertheless, marriage is still praiseworthy, because it does not institute this evil in human beings but finds it there, and makes good use of that evil for the purpose of begetting, although those who are begotten thereby contract original sin, on account of which they must be reborn.

### XLVI. JULIAN

All learning in literature testifies that you have accomplished nothing against me; and the conflict of your statements demonstrates how you strive against the Apostle and rage against God [Note: [Col. 1161] Menardus and the Portus manuscript have *dejurat*; Clar. has *dejerat*; Mar. has *degerat*].

But now that it has been shown [Note: [Col. 1161] The printed editions have *sed ostendam non posse* (“but I shall show that they cannot be joined”); the manuscripts have *sed ostenso jam* (“but now that it has been shown”) ] that things which the nature of reality separates cannot be joined, let us question the Apostle as well, lest anyone think that the barbarity proved in your opinions lies in his understanding.

### AUGUSTINE

Say now, at least, what you have been postponing through so many winding turns.

### XLVII. JULIAN

I therefore hear Paul declaring:

“Through one man sin entered into the world, and through sin death; and so it passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Romans 5:12).

You affirm that this was said not on account of an example of sin but on account of generation, and you call us heretics because we refer it to examples. You think you are helped by this argument:

“Certainly, if the Apostle had wished imitation to be understood,” you say, “he would have said that sin entered through the devil rather than through one man, and passed through all human beings. For it is written of the devil: ‘They imitate him who belong to his side’ (Wisdom 2:25). But for this reason he said ‘through one man,’ from whom the generation of human beings certainly began, so that he might teach that original sin had passed into all through generation” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 2, no. 45).

But I see that the Apostle said nothing that concerned the defamation of human generation, nothing that concerned the condemnation of natural innocence, nothing that concerned the accusation of God’s work.

### AUGUSTINE

You say “nothing” for a long time, and when you cease repeating that word, you will say nothing. Who would not laugh at you as you try to persuade us that what the Apostle said—“Through one man sin entered into the world”—does not pertain to generation, when that man himself was not begotten by anyone, but from him the rest were to be begotten [Note: [Col. 1161] So the manuscripts. The printed editions have “when he himself was a man not begotten”], while you say it pertains to an example, even though the example of sin that later people were to imitate did not enter the world except through him who sinned without imitating anyone?

For he sinned first. Who among Christians does not know that this was not Adam but the devil? What, then, is it that pleases you, except both not to be silent and to say nothing?

### XLVIII. JULIAN

Finally, you attempted to gather by argument what the words themselves had not indicated: you add that if the Apostle had been speaking of imitation, he ought to have mentioned the devil; but because he wished generation to be understood, he preferred to speak of a man rather than a demon.

I therefore ask what occasion gave rise to this opinion of yours. What? Do you deny that people sin by imitating human beings? And although the matter, established by the testimony of the Scriptures, needs no further proof, hear David:

“Do not emulate those who do evil, nor be jealous of those who do iniquity”; “do not emulate the one who prospers in his way” (Psalm 36:1, 7).

Moreover, all the writings of the Old Testament warn Israel not to imitate the practice of a profane nation.

What necessity, then, forced the Apostle, if he wished imitation to be understood, to name the devil rather than a man, when he knew that people sin by imitating both human beings and the devil? Either prove that people cannot sin by imitating human beings and that this is nowhere contained in the law, and so establish a place for your suspicion [Note: [Col. 1162] The Mar. manuscript has *et asseres* (“and you will establish”)]; or, if it is evident that sins have grown strong in no way more than through the imitation of vices, you have inferred with great ignorance that the Apostle would certainly have spoken of the devil if he had wished imitation to be understood.

### AUGUSTINE

Did I not say earlier that you would say nothing, most talkative man who say nothing by talking? There are indeed sins of imitation in the world, when people follow the examples of sinful people [Note: [Col. 1162] The printed editions have “there are certain sins of imitation in the world, when people follow the sin and examples of human beings.” The manuscripts correct this reading]. Yet the sin which sinners were to imitate did not enter the world through those human beings whom anyone may imitate; it entered through him who first sinned without imitating anyone. This is the devil, whom all who belong to his side imitate.

Likewise, the sin that is not committed by imitation but contracted by birth entered the world through him who first begot a human being. Thus you have said nothing, and you were unwilling to remain silent only in order to deceive some readers and weary others.

### XLIX. JULIAN

Since, then, it is clear that the imitation of evil people may be spoken of not only consistently but necessarily, it is obvious that your argument must for the present be set aside. As for what you add—that it is written of the devil, “They imitate him who belong to his side”—I too agree that this was prudently said by whoever the author of that book may be. But it does not help you to have it written that some sin by imitating the devil unless you prove that people cannot sin by imitating human beings.

### AUGUSTINE

The question here is not whether people sin by imitating human beings. Who does not know that they also sin through such imitation? The question is what kind of sin entered the world through one man: whether it was sin committed by imitation or sin contracted by birth.

The first kind—that is, sin committed by imitation—entered the world only through him who, without imitating anyone, first introduced to those who would imitate him the example of sinning. This is the devil.

The second kind—that is, sin contracted by birth—entered the world only through him who, begotten by no one, first began the succession of origin by which all the others were to be begotten. This is Adam.

Understand, therefore, that your discussion of the imitation of angels and human beings says nothing relevant to the issue; you merely did not wish to remain silent. For we are not discussing every sinner who at some time sinned in the world, but the one through whom sin entered the world. If an example of imitation is sought there, the devil is found; if the contagion of generation is sought, Adam is found.

Accordingly, when the Apostle says, “Through one man sin entered into the world,” he wished the sin of generation to be understood. For the sin of imitation entered the world not through one man but through the devil.

### L. JULIAN

Since both expressions are customarily used—sometimes of one who, imitating the devil, envies; sometimes of one who, emulating a human being, is stained either by envy or by the filth of crimes [Note: [Col. 1163] Perhaps *flagitiorum* (“of crimes”) rather than *flagitiosorum* (“of criminal people”) ]—the word “imitation” can apply to both persons, whether it is spoken of a human being or of the devil. Yet you wished to make yourself absurdly foolish by claiming that Adam could not be indicated through the meaning of imitation.

### AUGUSTINE

Did sin enter the world through just any human being whom another imitates in sinning? Say, if you can, what this means:

“Through one man sin entered into the world, and through sin death; and so it passed into all human beings”—whether it was death, sin, or rather sin together with death.

For the sin by whose imitation people sin entered the world only through the devil, who first did without imitation what others would do by imitation.

### LI. JULIAN

My discourse hastens to the remaining points. But this matter must still be pressed, so that, in divisions as brief as possible, the reader may be supplied with both an understanding of the issue and a memory of it. In nearly all matters the condition of homonyms—what we call equivocal terms—is found.

### AUGUSTINE

You promised to supply the reader with understanding, yet you speak of homonyms and equivocal terms. How, then, will even the Pelagians understand you, unless they are first sent to the schools of dialecticians wherever they may be found, for the sake of hearing these things [Note: [Col. 1163] Morel reads *discenda* (“to be learned”) rather than *dicenda* (“to be said”). See *Elementa Critica*, p. 312]? Or will you perhaps yourself read and explain Aristotle’s *Categories* to them before they read your books?

Why do you not do this as well, most ingenious man, since you feed idly upon those miserable people whom you have deceived?

### LII. JULIAN

But let our discussion now concern the matters at hand. Generation properly belongs to the sexes, whereas imitation always belongs to the mind. This movement of the mind, insofar as the imitator wills it by his capacity, either accuses or advances a person according to the diversity of causes.

Thus, in what is good, one is said to imitate God, angels, and the Apostles:

God: “Be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect” (Matthew 5:48).

Angels: “Your will be done, as in heaven so also on earth” (Matthew 6:10).

The Apostles: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (1 Corinthians 11:1).

In what is evil, one imitates the devil, as it is said: “They imitate him who belong to his side” (Wisdom 2:25); people imitate people: “Do not be like the hypocrites, who disfigure their faces” (Matthew 6:16); animals are imitated when it is commanded: “Do not become like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding” (Psalm 32:9).

These words, whether encouraging or warning, reveal the impulse toward imitation; and if that impulse could not exist, there would be no command to beware of it.

### AUGUSTINE

But the sin of imitation—that is, what is done by imitation—did not enter the world except through him who, in order that others might sin by imitation, sinned without imitation. This certainly is not Adam but the devil.

For when he said “entered into the world,” he indicated the beginning of this sin. If we attend to the sin that sinners were to imitate, it is clear that this beginning was made not through a human being but through the devil.

It remains, therefore, that the sin which entered the world through one man can rightly be attributed not to imitation but to generation.

We rightly give thanks to God because, in speaking against your error, you have confessed—as though truth were flashing before you—that the good will by which we imitate the good is to be attributed not to the powers of our free will but to God’s help. For when you explain what we pray and say, “Your will be done, as in heaven so also on earth,” you have shown that, if we are to imitate the angels, we must not presume upon ourselves but must ask it from the Lord.

### LIII. JULIAN

Just as the word “imitation” is shown to apply commonly to different things, so “generation” truly and properly indicates the substance that generates [Note: [Col. 1164] So the manuscripts. The printed editions have “true and proper”]. It is not properly, but abusively, applied to dispositions or practices.

Yet because this has now become the usage of speech, what it indicates is recognized, and it is not allowed to prejudice proper meanings. Thus the devil is said to generate sinners, according to what the Lord says in the Gospel: “You are from your father the devil” (John 8:44). By this expression he called him the father of criminals because they were convicted of imitating his wickedness. Nevertheless, the meaning is clear, since by the name “father” neither a sex is ascribed to the devil nor an airy substance to those human beings.

Now, then, let it become clear what we intend to establish by this. If a human being were never properly judged to imitate another human being, and the Apostle had said that all sinned through Adam, I would freely prescribe that the Apostle should be defended by the usage of Scripture: just as the Lord called the devil “father,” although he could not beget by substance, so the Apostle would have written that a human being was imitable, lest he be thought to have taught something contrary to evident reason.

### AUGUSTINE

Was Adam first imitable in sin, so that it could rightly be said that this kind of sin entered the world through him? Was not the devil first imitable in sin? The Apostle would therefore have said that sin entered the world through him if he had wished the sin that others would commit by imitation to be understood in that passage.

### LIV. JULIAN

But if I gather the expressions used abusively in the Gospel [Note: [Col. 1165] The printed editions have “if I gather the slanders abusively used in the Gospel.” The manuscripts correct the reading], they will not hold up. Much less did the Apostle Paul provide any occasion for error, since he said nothing improper if he declared that the first human sinner had been an example to those who sinned afterward.

### AUGUSTINE

Then he ought not to have set forth these two persons, one for sin and the other for righteousness—namely, Adam and Christ. For if he had placed Adam as the first sinner because of the sin that the others imitated, he certainly would have placed not Christ but Abel as the first righteous person, because others were to imitate his righteousness. Abel was the first righteous person, imitating no human being but himself to be imitated by others.

But because the Apostle knew what he was saying, he set Adam over against sin and Christ over against righteousness, since he knew the one to be the author of generation and the other the author of regeneration.

### LV. JULIAN

Accordingly, you argued most foolishly that if the Apostle Paul had wished to have sin understood as passing through imitation, he would have named the devil rather than Adam, since it is clear that the evil of both human beings and the devil could have passed on only by imitation.

But now that what you had constructed has been cast down—not so much by my hands as by the hands of reason itself—listen to what we shall bring forward.

### AUGUSTINE

Those who read the words of both of us will judge whether you have cast down what I constructed, or whether you have uselessly laid the hands of your vain opinion—not of sound reason—upon our structure.

### LVI. JULIAN

The Apostle showed that he did not mean that sin passed on through generation [Note: Col. 1165: the manuscripts read “in generation”] when, naming “a man,” he added “one”: for “one” is the beginning of number. And when he explained through whom he meant sin to have entered, he not only named him but also counted him: “Through one man,” he says, “sin entered into this world.” But this one is sufficient for imitation to be offered; he is not sufficient for generation to be accomplished. Sin, then, entered—but through one. It is clear that imitation, not generation, is being condemned here, since generation cannot occur except through two. Therefore, either show that generation arose through Adam alone without a woman—for this too is not beyond the refinement of your intelligence—or, since you see that generation cannot be constituted except through two, agree, even if belatedly, that the work of two was not accused by the number one. “Through one man,” he says, “sin entered into the world.” By saying “through one,” he did not wish two to be understood.

What, I ask, was number doing among these doctrines, that the Apostle, with such care, named not merely “a man” but “one man” [Col. 1166]? Yet the cautious language of a deliberate purpose is apparent. The Holy Spirit revealed it, anticipating and disarming the errors of our times, lest he be thought to have said anything defamatory of the institution of marriage established by God or of blessed fecundity. Since the case required him to retrace the beginnings of sin, he said that sin had passed through that number which could not apply to offspring. Certainly both first human beings had sinned, and both are rightly called a model of sin for those who came after them. Why, then, did the Apostle not say that sin passed through two, which would also have accorded better with the historical account?

But nothing could have been done more prudently by him. He saw that, if he named the two who had provided the beginning and the example of transgression, and affirmed that sin had passed through them, an opportunity for error would arise, so that people might think that by naming two he had condemned sexual union and fecundity. [Note: Col. 1166: The printed editions read, “that by the union of the two names he had condemned fecundity.”] Therefore, with the greatest prudence, he preferred to name one, who, while insufficient as an indication of generation, would be more than sufficient as a sign of example. Thus he would burden imitation with the accusation, without indicting fecundity by the number. To summarize briefly what we have argued: fecundity, instituted in the first human beings, cannot be brought about except through two; but the Apostle declares that sin entered—through one.

### AUGUSTINE

I had already predicted that you would say nothing; and it is clear to anyone, however slow-witted, that this is so. Do sinners not imitate Eve? Or did not the sin of the human race take its beginning especially from her? “From a woman sin had its beginning, and because of her, as it is written, we all die” (Ecclesiasticus 25:33). Why, then, are you unwilling to consider that the Apostle said “one man,” through whom sin entered the world, precisely because he wanted generation, not imitation, to be understood? For just as sin had its beginning from a woman, so generation has its beginning from a man: the man sows first, so that the woman may give birth. Therefore sin entered the world through one man because it entered through the seed of generation, which the woman received from the man and conceived. In this manner the one who alone was born without sin did not wish to be born.

### LVII. JULIAN

It has been irrefutably established that the Apostle showed that this sin was conveyed to posterity through conduct, not through seed. Consider, then, how much falsehood flowed from your mouth: “But the Apostle said ‘through one man,’ from whom the generation of human beings certainly began, so that he might teach that original sin had passed through generation to everyone” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 2, no. 45)—when the Apostle said “through one man” precisely so that it would not be thought that original sin had passed to everyone.

You speak so foolishly that I can scarcely restrain my laughter when you say that generation began from one man, although both the difference of the sexes and the divine text testify that generation could not have occurred unless two human beings first existed—that is, a man and a woman.

### AUGUSTINE

Let those who read this read my earlier reply again; or, if they remember it well, let them laugh at the ravings of this man. I could say, however, that the Apostle said not two men but one man, through whom sin entered the world, because it is written, “The two shall be one flesh” (Genesis 2:24). Hence the Lord says, “Therefore they are no longer two, but one flesh” (Matthew 19:6), especially when a man clings to his wife and intercourse takes place.

From intercourse offspring is generated, drawing along original sin: corruption transmitting corruption, while God creates the nature. Though married couples use this corruption even well, they cannot nevertheless generate nature in such a way that it can be without corruption. But the one who was born without that corruption nullifies it in little children, even against Julian’s will.

### LVIII. JULIAN

Or if, perhaps—for otherwise your doctrine cannot stand—you should answer that Adam conceived and gave birth from himself, no one will doubt that this was not the Apostle’s meaning; but you will show what you would wish to happen to your own sex.

### AUGUSTINE

Do you not fear what is written: “Nor will the revilers possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 6:10)? You would not utter such foul insults, which help you in nothing, except from a desire to revile.

### LIX. JULIAN

But let us set these matters aside [Note: Col. 1167: Vignierius and Menard read, “let us dismiss these matters”] and wear down by the force of reason what appears capable of being brought forward by you at this point. If, then, you say that it is written of this intercourse that “the two shall be one flesh,” and that, according to this, the Apostle said “through one man” in order to designate the limbs of the parents joined to one another, I will answer that this too tells against your impiety.

For it was not said, “The two men shall be in one man,” but “The two shall be one flesh.” By this name of union, that pleasure of those who come together, and that desire which, affecting the senses, throws the limbs into turmoil and, as that prudent man understood, longs to make one flesh, would be shown to have been instituted by God and implanted in bodies before sin.

*[Note: Col. 1167: Menard reads “union” (unionis); the manuscripts read “uniting” (unitionis). The manuscripts read “would be shown”; the printed editions read “is shown.”]*

### AUGUSTINE

If desire alone could make them “two in one flesh”—that desire which you have embraced as precisely the kind that you now both praise and attack, which you confess to be shameful and yet love shamelessly, and which you even dare to endow with possession of paradise—then “the two shall be one flesh” could in no way be understood of Christ and the Church. For you have not strayed so far from the path of truth that you would dare to import this desire even into the union of Christ and the Church. [Note: Col. 1167: The manuscripts read “import”; the printed editions read “impute.”]

Moreover, if Christ and the Church can be “two in one flesh” without this desire, then a man and wife also could have been joined, had no one sinned, not by that shameful desire—which even the person who is not ashamed to praise it is ashamed to acknowledge—but by the charity that rightly deserves praise; and for the purpose of begetting children they could have been “two in one flesh.” [Note: Col. 1167: The Portus manuscript reads “of marriage” (conjugii).]

Accordingly, when the Lord says, “Therefore they are no longer two, but one flesh,” he certainly does not say, “They are no longer two fleshes, but one flesh.” What, then, are “no longer two,” except human beings? [Note: Col. 1167: The printed editions read “except not”; “not” is absent from the manuscripts.] Just as Christ and the Church together are not two Christs but one Christ. Hence it was also said to us [Col. 1168], “Therefore you are Abraham’s offspring,” although it had been said of him, “And to your offspring,” which is Christ (Galatians 3:29, 16).

### LX. JULIAN

Accordingly, the devil can claim nothing for himself, either from its pleasure or from its modesty.

### AUGUSTINE

What do you mean by “from its modesty”? Are you ashamed to name confusion? And yet you say that the shameful desire existed in them even before sin, of whom Scripture says, “They were naked, and they were not ashamed” (Genesis 2:25).

### LXI. JULIAN

Nevertheless, if the Apostle had thought anything of this kind, he would have said that sin entered through one flesh, not through one man. Through generation, the substance of the flesh alone participates in the offspring, because it is not soul from soul but flesh from flesh that is drawn. But in the name “man,” both mind and body are properly indicated. Accordingly, by naming one man, the Apostle neither pointed to the process of fecundity, in which he knew that nothing except the substance of the flesh was imparted, nor did he wish two to be understood. He insisted on one in order to teach that sin passed through imitation, not through generation.

### AUGUSTINE

What, then, does “They are no longer two, but one flesh” mean except “They are no longer two human beings, because of the one flesh”? The flesh itself could also be called “man,” the whole being named from a part, as in “The Word became flesh” (John 1:14), because he became man, of whom this was said.

The Apostle also, when he says, “The outward man is being corrupted” (2 Corinthians 4:16), I think intended the flesh to be understood. For this reason we correctly speak of “a man’s tomb,” although only his flesh has been buried there. Nor was the woman mistaken when she said, “They have taken my Lord from the tomb” (John 20:13), although only his flesh had been placed there.

Since, therefore, the very obscure question concerning the soul remains, it could be said, “Through one man sin entered the world,” even if only the flesh belongs to the process of transmission. Attend to these things, then, and see how little you have said.

### LXII. JULIAN

Here, although truth has already performed its part, I nevertheless offer this reminder so that the attentive reader may remain alert. In this conflict I have surrendered much of my own claim, and, following the provocation of my opponent’s recklessness, I have defended the principles of sound faith so thoroughly that even if the words of the Teacher of the Gentiles were those which the Traducianist thought he had employed, it would nevertheless be clear that he held nothing concerning natural sin. For by naming a man, but one man, he would certainly have condemned not the generation of the offense but its examples.

### AUGUSTINE

You have supplied an example—but of vanity in yourself. For if the Apostle set up the first sinful man, Adam, as an example of sin, then surely he would set up the first righteous man, Abel, as an example of righteousness.

### LXIII. JULIAN

It is established, however [Col. 1169], that the order of the Apostle’s words is not what our enemy supposed. For he argues in this way:

“If the Apostle,” he says, “had wanted imitation to be understood, he would have said that sin entered not through one man but through the devil, and passed through all human beings. For it is written of the devil, ‘They imitate him who belong to his side’” (Wisdom 2:25). “But he said ‘through one man,’ from whom the generation of human beings certainly began, so that he might teach that original sin had passed through generation to everyone” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 2, no. 45).

In this, then, he lies: he asserts that blessed Paul declared that sin entered the world through one man and thus passed through to all human beings. This, I say, is not found in the words of the Teacher of the Gentiles. He did not say that sin passed through, but death.

The order of the words is therefore: “Just as through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death, so it passed through to all human beings, in whom all sinned.” The sublime teacher of the Church weighed what he ought to say: “Through one man,” he says, “sin entered the world, and through sin death; and so it passed through to all human beings.”

He had already named death and sin. Why was it necessary that, in what he said had passed through, he should separate death from the association with sin, unless he wished expressly to show that sin entered this world through one man, and death through sin, but that it was not sin which passed through to all human beings, but death—death imposed by the severity of judgment, avenging transgression and pursuing not the seeds of bodies but the vices of conduct? Unless, of course, he took care to commend and fortify his meaning, lest he be thought to have offered some support to your doctrine.

*[Note: The printed editions read “and.” The manuscripts read “so that.”]*

*[Note: The printed editions read “but death, death certainly, the severity imposed by judgment.” This has been corrected according to the manuscripts.]*

*[Note: Vignierius reads “some supporter.” The manuscripts read “having offered some support.”]*

### AUGUSTINE

In the passage where it is said, “Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death; and so it passed through to all human beings,” it appears ambiguous whether sin, death, or both are said to have passed through all human beings. But what the matter itself demonstrates is entirely clear. [Note: Col. 1169: The printed editions read “is now clearly demonstrated”; the manuscripts read “is so clear,” as do Bede and Florus in their comments on this apostolic passage.]

For if sin had not passed through, every human being would not be born under the law of sin that is in the members. If death had not passed through, all human beings would not die, insofar as this concerns the condition of mortals.

But when the Apostle says, “in whom all sinned,” “in whom” can be understood only as “in Adam,” in whom he says they also die. For it would not be just for punishment to pass through without guilt.

Whichever way you turn, you will in no way overthrow the foundations of the Catholic faith—especially since you yourself contradict yourself. Now you say that not sin but death passed through, although earlier you said that the Apostle insisted on one man rather than two in order to teach that sin passed through imitation, not generation (above, chapters 56 and 61).

Therefore sin passed through together with death. What is the meaning of your present claim that not sin but death passed through?

*[Note: Here we restore, on the authority of the ancient books, “Therefore sin passed through together with death.”]*

### LXIV. JULIAN

Consider, then [Col. 1170], how far you differ from Paul. He says, “through one man”; you say, “through two,” that is, through generation. He declares that in the first man there were both sin and death, but that only death passed on to posterity; you, on the contrary, assert that both sin and destruction ran through to everyone.

*[Note: The manuscripts read “ran through”; the printed editions read “converged.”]*

### AUGUSTINE

The answer has already been given. Let those who wish read what we said above, lest we repeat the same things again and again without purpose.

### LXV. JULIAN

You therefore hide shamelessly under the shadow of his name, although you say things utterly different and contradictory. He condemns the work of human beings; you, the work of God. He condemns the efforts of sinners; you, the innocence and life of those being born. He condemns human will; you, nature.

*[Note: The printed editions read “effort”; the manuscripts read “efforts.”]*

### AUGUSTINE

An answer has already been given above to all these points. The person who remembers it now laughs at you; the person who does not remember it will, after rereading it, certainly laugh at your vanity and pity you.

### LXVI. JULIAN

According to the Apostle, therefore, sin entered this world through one man, and through sin death, because the world saw him as both guilty and destined for condemnation to everlasting death. [Note: Col. 1170: The manuscripts of Marcellinus, Clarus, and Portus read “condemnation”; the printed editions read “dominion.”] Death, however, passed through to all human beings, because one form of judgment also encompassed all transgressors throughout the rest of their life. Yet this death is not permitted to rage against the saints or against any innocent persons; it spreads among those whom it sees imitating the transgression.

### AUGUSTINE

You are saying what was charged against your heresiarch Pelagius at the episcopal judgment in Palestine: that Adam was made such that, whether he sinned or did not sin, he would die.

*[Note: See *The Proceedings of Pelagius*, nos. 23 and 57.]*

You do not wish this death by which we all die—the death of which it was said, “From a woman sin had its beginning, and because of her we all die” (Ecclesiasticus 25:33)—to have passed originally from sin to everyone, lest you be compelled to admit that sin likewise passed originally through everyone.
