You perceive how unjust it is for punishment to pass through without merit.

Nevertheless, what you are trying to overthrow is so Catholic that the man against whom this was charged—as I said—would certainly have left that judgment condemned if he had not condemned it.

Therefore both this death, by which the spirit is separated from the body, and the death called the second death, by which the spirit will be tormented with the body, passed through to all human beings insofar as concerns the merit of the human race. But the grace of God, through the one who came in order by dying to take away the kingdom of death, did not allow death to reign, by that resurrection whose example preceded in him.

This is what the Catholic faith holds; this is what the judges whom Pelagius feared held; this is not what the heretics whom Pelagius sowed hold.

### LXVII. JULIAN

Although that transgression was not made natural, it was nevertheless a form of sin. Therefore, although it does not burden those being born, it accuses those who imitate it.

### AUGUSTINE

Even if you have forgotten the heavy yoke that burdens those being born, we do not cease reminding you of it.

### LXVIII. JULIAN

Judicial death, however, passed through [Col. 1171] in the one in whom all sinned, but by free will. [Note: The printed editions read “in him, in whom.”] By the word “all”—that is, “everyone”—Scriptural usage indicates a multitude, not the totality.

### AUGUSTINE

In vain you try to twist straightforward words and obscure what is clear. “In whom all sinned,” in whom all die: he is Adam. If little children do not die in him, then surely they will not be made alive in Christ. But since “as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive” (1 Corinthians 15:22), those who wish to distort these words are themselves overthrown while the words remain intact.

### LXIX. JULIAN

But let us proceed to the remaining points, so that the sacred discourse may show, through its successive stages, which doctrine the Apostle supports, as has become clear in large measure. [Note: Col. 1171: The manuscripts read “as has become clear in large measure, through its successive stages”; the printed editions read “through largely clear successive stages.”]

“What else,” you say, “do the Apostle’s following words indicate? For when he had said this, he added, ‘Until the law sin was in the world’” (Romans 5:13). “That is, because the law too could not take sin away. But sin was not counted when there was no law. It existed, therefore, but was not counted, because what was to be counted was not displayed; for as he says elsewhere, ‘Through the law comes knowledge of sin’” (Romans 3:20).

“But death reigned,” he says, “from Adam until Moses. This is what he had said above, ‘until the law’—not ‘until Moses’ in the sense that afterward there would be no sin, but because not even the law given through Moses could take away the reign of death, which certainly reigns only through sin.

“Moreover, its reign consists in casting mortal human beings even into the second death, which is everlasting. It reigned, however—in whom? ‘Even in those,’ he says, ‘who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression, who is a type of the one to come’” (Romans 5:14).

“Of whom could this future one be, except Christ? And what kind of type, except one by contrast? Elsewhere he also says, ‘As in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive’” (1 Corinthians 15:22).

“As that in him, so this in the other: this is the type. But this type is not conformable in every respect. Therefore the Apostle, continuing, added, ‘But the gift is not like the trespass. For if many died because of one trespass, much more did the grace of God and the gift in the grace of the one man Jesus Christ abound to many’” (Romans 5:15).

“What does ‘abound much more’ mean? It means that all who are liberated through Christ die temporarily because of Adam, but because of Christ himself they will live without end” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 2, no. 46).

You professed that nothing other than original sin was indicated by the Apostle’s subsequent words. We approved this at the very beginning of our discussion, when you showed that it had not been indicated by him, because he signified that sin passed through one, not two.

### AUGUSTINE

The answer has already been given, and still you speak vanity. Nor is this surprising [Note: Col. 1171: The printed editions read “nor is this surprising,” omitting enim, “for”; the word occurs in all the manuscripts], for you still do not know what I answered. You will be more shameless when you do know, if, abandoning what is vain, you refuse to hold to what is true.

### LXX. JULIAN

Nevertheless, we must examine whether he now indicates what he had passed over. “Until the law,” he says, “sin was in the world.” You say that the Apostle wished this sin to be understood as natural. I ask, then: if it existed “until the law,” why did it cease to exist after the law? I do not agree that “until the law” should be understood as “until the end of the law,” rather than “until its beginning.”

The propriety of the word supports me. In saying that it existed until the law, he shows that it did not exist after the law. Whatever is removed at a particular time was not natural. Therefore, what the authority of the law broke, and by breaking it checked in large measure [Note: Col. 1172: The manuscripts read restinxit, “checked/extinguished”; the printed editions read restrinxit], is shown to have been acquired through imitation, not generation.

### AUGUSTINE

What else can I call this understanding but heretical? If the law took away sin, since you insist that “until the law” must be understood in this way, then righteousness existed through the law. If righteousness existed through the law, then Christ died for nothing (Galatians 2:21).

But if the law did not take away sin so that it ceased to exist—as you had earlier said the law did, and soon afterward regretted saying—but the law nevertheless broke sin, as you later corrected yourself, and extinguished it in large measure, then the one who said, “The law entered in so that the trespass might abound” (Romans 5:20), lied.

But because he spoke the truth, you say nothing; and yet, by saying nothing, you contradict him with heretical obstinacy.

### LXXI. JULIAN

But lest I seem to press you too stubbornly here, let us agree that “until the law” can be understood as “until Christ.” Do you therefore concede that this sin which you call original does not exist after Christ? And how do you say that, in the members of the Apostles, in all the baptized, and even today, after so many centuries since Christ’s coming, the work of the devil, the growth of the hostile power, and the law of sin remain, flourish, and live?

### AUGUSTINE

I do not say this; you say nothing. Sin is one thing, and the desire of sin is another. The person who does not sin by the grace of God does not consent to it. Yet this desire itself is also called sin, because it was made through sin—just as any writing is called the hand of the person by whose hand it was made.

Of him concerning whom it was said, “Behold the Lamb of God; behold, he who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1:29): he dissolves through regeneration the guilt of sin that is drawn through generation. By giving the Spirit, he makes sin not reign in our mortal body, so that we obey its desires (Romans 6:12). Through the daily forgiveness for which we say every day, “Forgive us our debts” (Matthew 6:12), he mercifully erases whatever the desire of sin has persuaded those who are struggling, even while resisting it rightly.

He raises up penitents who have been struck down by a grievous fall. He will bring them to the place where it is wholly impossible to sin and establish them as reigning [Note: Col. 1172: The manuscripts read “he brings and establishes them as reigning”], when it is said, “Where is your contention, O death? Where is your sting, O death? The sting of death is sin” (1 Corinthians 15:55–56).

Behold how that Lamb of God takes away the sin of the world—what the law could not take away.

### LXXII. JULIAN

But let us examine the remaining points. “Sin was not counted,” the Apostle says, “when there was no law” (Romans 5:13). After this you add:

“It existed, therefore, but was not counted, as he says elsewhere, ‘Through the law comes knowledge of sin’” (Romans 3:20).

If, then, knowledge of sin was produced through the law, and you maintain that the sin transmitted before the law was not counted, show that it was counted under the law. For if knowledge of sin came through the law, and ignorance of sin existed before the law, there can be no doubt that this was the principal reason for promulgating the law: so that what had previously lain hidden might be exposed and guarded against.

### AUGUSTINE

You speak truly in saying “so that it might be exposed”; this is also what we say. But “so that it might be guarded against” was accomplished not by the law but by grace, not by the letter but by the Spirit.

For “the law entered in,” not so that sin might be guarded against, but so that sin might abound and grace might abound still more—grace by which sin, once committed, might be erased and its commission prevented.

### LXXIII. JULIAN

Let this, then, be the sum of the dispute: either show that original sin was counted against someone under the law; show that it was exposed; and I will agree that the Apostle spoke of this sin.

### AUGUSTINE

I do show what you challenge me to show. But if you close your eyes to what you do not wish to see, and spread clouds of contention so that others may not see it either—

*[Note: Col. 1173: Codex B reads “if you open your eyes to what you do not wish to see”; Menard and Vignierius follow that reading.]*

Circumcision of the flesh [Note: Col. 1173: the Clarus and Marcellinus manuscripts read “carnal circumcision”] was commanded by the law (Genesis 17:12). Nothing could better signify that original sin is taken away through Christ, the author of regeneration. Every human being is born with the foreskin, just as every human being is born with original sin. The law commanded that the flesh be circumcised on the eighth day because Christ rose on the Lord’s Day, which is the eighth day after the Sabbath’s seventh day.

A circumcised man begets one with a foreskin, transmitting to him what he himself has already lost; likewise, a baptized man transmits to the son whom he generates through the flesh the guilt of the origin from which he himself has been freed.

Finally, the Psalm is written in the law: “Behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother nourished me in the womb” (Psalm 50:7). You would certainly see this and would not dare contradict it if you possessed eyes of faith like those of Cyprian, Ambrose, and the other such teachers of the Church.

### LXXIV. JULIAN

Or, since this cannot be found in the law, agree, most shameless man, that the Apostle spoke of that sin which is acquired through imitation, committed by the will, condemned by reason, shown by the law, and punished by justice.

### AUGUSTINE

It was said of every sin that is taken away through Christ, “Until the law sin was in the world.” It is not taken away by the law, whether it is original sin, added sin, sin that existed before the law, or sin that abounded when the law entered in.

But when you say that the Apostle speaks of the sin “that is punished by justice,” wake up and see that original sin is also there. For otherwise the justice of God would not impose a heavy yoke even upon the very beginnings of little children. Our concern repeatedly calls this yoke to mind, so that, if it does not bend your neck, it may break it.

This sin is also shown by the law and displayed by the commandment of circumcision. If you deny this, tell us by what personal sin the soul of an infant who was not circumcised perished from his people (Genesis 17:14). I know that you do not explain this; but you remain silent in order to weary us.

### LXXV. JULIAN

Moreover, what you invent—original sin—cannot be transmitted through one, because generation is carried out through two.

### AUGUSTINE

The answer has already been given. Read what I have said on this matter, and you will find that you have spoken vanity.

### LXXVI. JULIAN

Nor could it ever exist if it can at some time not exist, because natural things persist from the beginning of the substance to its end.

### AUGUSTINE

You could say this also about death, for we are born with death itself. “The body indeed is dead because of sin” (Romans 8:10). But even if not because of sin, as you foolishly suppose, we are nevertheless born mortal without any doubt. Yet death and mortality will not exist eternally when we live immortally.

Therefore, just as death is original and yet could exist and can cease to exist, while our nature remains in a better condition, so original sin could exist, transmitted through generation, and can cease to exist, removed through regeneration.

*[Note: The printed editions read “removed through generation.” This has been corrected according to the manuscripts of Marcellinus, Clarus, and Portus.]*

### LXXVII. JULIAN

Nor was it shown by the law, nor could it have been shown, because no legislator would ever descend to such madness as to command anyone, “Do not be born in this way or that.” And what ought not to be admonished so that it might be corrected cannot justly be punished.

*[Note: Col. 1174: The manuscripts read, “what cannot be admonished so that it may be guarded against cannot be imputed so that it may be punished”; the printed editions read, “what ought not to be admonished so that it may be corrected cannot justly be punished.”]*

### AUGUSTINE

A command is not given to a human being concerning how he should be born. But a command was given concerning how that parent should live, and he violated the command; from that parent original sin is transmitted.

It is also commanded that an infant be circumcised, and he is condemned unless he is circumcised, although neither anything else nor even circumcision itself is commanded to him personally. Accordingly, although a human being is not commanded how to be born, the world is nevertheless not free from the defilement of sin, nor is the infant whose life is a single day upon the earth (Job 14:4, according to the Septuagint).

Read the words of holy Job, and you will find that you are a liar, while he speaks whom God declared truthful.

### LXXVIII. JULIAN

And what exists “until the law” is shown not to exist after the law; finally, it is shown not to exist after Christ.

### AUGUSTINE

Thus the guilt of this sin is shown not to exist after the abolition of sins, just as death will not exist after the resurrection of the flesh.

### LXXIX. JULIAN

Accordingly, even according to your argument, it has long ceased to exist; according to the testimony of truth, it never existed.

*[Note: Here we restore “according to” from the manuscripts.]*

### AUGUSTINE

Would that you did not exist—those who speak and even write your false testimony against the testimony of truth!

### LXXX. JULIAN

And so that what we have argued may be impressed upon the reader’s memory, you once defined “sin,” and defined it very well, as “nothing other than the will to admit what justice forbids, and from which it is free to abstain.”

### AUGUSTINE

The answer has already been given: this is a definition of sin, not of what is also the punishment of sin (above, book 1, chapter 47).

### LXXXI. JULIAN

That definition also opened the way to understanding the justice of God, so that we concluded that the equity of divine judgment could not stand unless he had imputed as sin something from which he knew that the person afflicted because of it had been free to abstain.

*[Note: In the printed editions the words “imputed as sin, from which he knew” had fallen out here; they are present in the manuscripts of Marcellinus, Portus, and Clarus.]*

### AUGUSTINE

Why, then, are little children afflicted, if they have absolutely no sin? Or was the omnipotent and just God unable to prevent unjust punishments from being inflicted upon so many innocent persons?

### LXXXII. JULIAN

We have established that the Teacher of the Gentiles, armed with the authority of his office, declared that guilt passed into this world through one man. By this designation he separated the work of marriage, which cannot exist without the activity of two. Therefore, we have maintained that one was named by him so that no one would dare understand two.

*[Note: The manuscripts read “therefore we have maintained”; the printed editions read “and therefore we have maintained.”]*

### AUGUSTINE

The answer has already been given. You take constant pleasure in babbling vanity.

### LXXXIII. JULIAN

And indeed, I assert with far greater consistency that the one whom the Apostle calls one is one, in order to teach that the defect was a matter of imitation, not generation, than does the Traducianist, who, by the name of the one said to have been the threshold of sin, applies the matter to the seeds of the will—a thing that the nature of things does not admit.

*[Note: The printed editions read “removes”; the manuscripts more accurately read “applies,” or “brings against.”]*

### AUGUSTINE

Stop repeating what we have already refuted. Why do you compel us to say the same things again and again against such great wisdom of yours, by which you think that generation is not signified where it is said, “Through one man sin entered the world,” because generation occurs through two, not one—as though the sin which you do not wish to have passed through generation but through imitation had been committed by one person?

Since, then, it was itself committed by two, why is it said that sin entered the world through one man, unless because the beginning of generation is not from the woman conceiving and giving birth but from the man sowing? Or because they are no longer two when, through intercourse, they become one flesh?

### LXXXIV. JULIAN

Afterward the discussion also came to the law, up to whose time the Apostle prescribed that sin had not been shown to be in force. You tried to extend that period until the end of the law, without understanding that your argument was useless, since we would compel you to prove that this sin—about which you falsely say Paul spoke, and which you assert reigned until the abolition of the Old Testament—was either counted under the law or could have been counted under it. Or at least you would have to agree that it does not reign after Christ, so that the Apostle’s forcibly distorted statement might conform, however slightly, to your views.

But you can produce none of these things. The purity of our faith, therefore, has been placed on solid ground, and with it agree the principles of reason, the dignity of justice, and the Apostle’s teachings in every respect.

### AUGUSTINE

Both what we have answered and your own words show that you say nothing. When the Apostle says, “Until the law sin was in the world,” he wished every sin, not original sin alone, to be understood. Therefore it was “until the law,” because even the law could not take away sin.

The phrase “until the law” was used so that the statement would include the law itself. Thus it is said in the Gospel, “Therefore from Abraham to David there are fourteen generations” (Matthew 1:17). The number is completed not by excluding David but by including him.

Just as, when we hear “fourteen generations until David,” we do not exclude David but count him as well, so when we hear “Until the law sin was in the world,” we must not exclude the law but count it as well.

For just as David is not outside the number that is said to extend “until him,” so the law is not outside the persistence of sin that is said to have existed “until it.” Accordingly, no one takes away sin—neither even the law, although it is holy, just, and good—except the one of whom it was said, “Behold the Lamb of God; behold, he who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1:29).

He takes them away by forgiving what has been done, which includes original sin; by helping so that sins are not committed; and by bringing us to the life in which they cannot be committed at all.

### LXXXV. JULIAN

But let us examine what follows. After saying, “This pattern is not wholly similar in every respect,” you add: “Hence the Apostle, following this line, added: ‘But the gift is not like the transgression; for if, because of one man’s transgression, the many died, much more did the grace of God and the gift in the grace of the one man Jesus Christ abound for the many’” (Rom. 5:12, 13, 15). You explain this statement as follows: “What does ‘abounded much more’ mean, unless it means that all who are delivered through Christ die temporally because of Adam, but because of Christ himself will live without end?” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 2, no. 46).

The Apostle has certainly declared—on whose meaning our dispute turns—that the Savior’s grace operates more powerfully and more abundantly for the bestowal of salvation than Adam’s sin does for harm, so that he might show that Christ benefited more greatly and benefited more people. His grace, to use his own word, “abounded for the many” more than the transgression of the first man harmed them—the man whom you say bound sin to the seed.

[Note: [Col. 1176] The printed editions read *quam* (“whom/which”); the manuscripts read *quem* (“whom”).]

### AUGUSTINE

He said, “abounded much more,” not “among more people”—that is, not “among a greater number.” For who does not see that there are more people among the human race in whom it did not abound, so that it might be shown what the whole mass deserved by a just judgment, unless the Spirit breathed where he wished, God called those whom he deigned to call, and made religious whom he wished? (*Ambrose*, book 7 on Luke 9).

### LXXXVI. JULIAN

Prove, then, that what the Apostle understood is consistent with your doctrines.

### AUGUSTINE

Let his words be read without the perversity of readers such as yourselves; no other proof will be required.

[Col. 1177]

### LXXXVII. JULIAN

“For if Adam,” you say, “generated all people through natural sin for condemnation, and poured so much poison from his own flesh into his offspring that it disturbed all God’s ordinances in human nature—”

### AUGUSTINE

When an unclean spirit torments a little child, afflicts both its soul and body, and perverts its senses and health, is not the whole of that nature which God established disturbed? Yet, while denying original sin, you find no merit at all for so great an evil. Why do you not here recognize that, through the devil’s poison, all God’s ordinances are disturbed in human nature? Explain the child’s condition; explain the guilt of the one to whom these things happen immediately after birth, since you do not wish to accept the apostolic words as they have been understood since the Catholic Church was established, and as nature itself confesses through evils so plainly visible.

[Note: The printed editions read *dic reatum, et cur recens nato* (“state the guilt, and why these things happen to one newly born”); the manuscripts read *dic reatum ejus cui recens nato* (“state the guilt of the one to whom these things happen immediately after birth”).]

And yet, if we consider the matter rightly, God’s ordinances are in no way disturbed, since, foreknowing the future, he established all things. Nor does he repay to each individual the whole of what the apostate creature deserves; rather, arranging all things “by measure, number, and weight” (Wis. 11:21), he permits no one to suffer an evil that he does not deserve—although no individual suffers as much as is owed to the whole mass.

### LXXXVIII. JULIAN

“So that, without the devil’s gift—which you say sexual desire belongs to—marriage, as God created it, could not exist;

[Note: The printed editions read *quem* (“whom”); the manuscripts read *quod* (“which”).]

indeed, while those marriages which he ordained flew away from the honor of their institution, he would compel and prove that these marriages, whose order remained, together with the movement of the genitals, the modesty of those coupling, the heat and agitation of the limbs, the pleasure of the senses, and the iniquity of those being born, are the work of the devil, not of God.”

### AUGUSTINE

If you distinguish the evil of vices—which cannot exist except in some good—from the goodness of natures, you will neither excuse the devil nor accuse God; neither will you excuse the evil of sexual desire nor accuse the good of marriage.

### LXXXIX. JULIAN

“Finally, the freedom of the will would be overthrown by the impulse of one sin, so that thereafter no one would have the power to reject ancient crimes by choosing virtue; rather, all would be swept into condemnation by the torrent of humanity’s ruin.”

[Note: The printed editions read *subrueres* (“you would overthrow”); the manuscripts read *subrueret* (“it would overthrow”). The reference is to Adam.]

### AUGUSTINE

Why do you not rather marvel at the great misery of the entire human race from the beginning of birth: that no one becomes blessed except from one who is miserable, and that no one is freed from every evil before this life has ended, when God’s grace grants him that freedom? If you marvel at this, you will correct yourself and recognize the just judgment of God—since through one man sin entered the world—in the not-unjust affliction of the human race.

[Note: The manuscripts read *non injusta* (“not unjust”); Menardus and the first Vignier edition read *non justa* (“not just”), incorrectly.]

### XC. JULIAN

“If,” I say, “iniquity brought all these things into the image of the first man, it is altogether clear that Christ’s grace is very weak in its gifts, since it found nothing to heal these many grievous evils; or, if it did find something, declare what it was. Let us now compare each thing individually with its counterpart. If Adam, apart from the acts of the will, overturned the structures of nature itself, Christ ought above all to have restored what Adam had shattered, following the very traces by which Adam had overthrown it.”

[Note: The Codex Portarum reads, “nothing was more fitting for Christ.”]

[Col. 1178]

### AUGUSTINE

He does this, but not in the manner you wish. For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor? (Isa. 40:13; Rom. 11:34).

### XCI. JULIAN

“That is, so that in the marriages of baptized persons sexual desire would in no way be experienced, nor would the genitals be moved in the same way as those of the rest of the nations.”

### AUGUSTINE

Then baptized women ought not to have given birth with groaning, since this—which you cannot deny—is the punishment of the sinful woman.

### XCII. JULIAN

“Finally, after the gift of grace, the modesty of those coupling should depart; the semblance of repose should not pass through the limbs; nor should the senses endure the burdens of pleasure. Finally, free choice should be restored to the baptized, so that, through the correction of nature and the expulsion of the law of sin, you would confess that it is as possible for mortals to shine with the splendor of virtues as to bristle with the filth of vices. Indeed, those who are instructed in the sacraments ought not even to be mortal.”

### AUGUSTINE

And yet, Julian, you are not ashamed to establish marriages of such a kind in paradise, where you admit that those coupling possessed modesty. Was there, then, anything shameful where the Creator—who is to be praised above all—had established nothing except what was worthy of praise? But who can think or say this except one who is not ashamed to praise what he is ashamed of?

### XCIII. JULIAN

“For if medicine contends with a wound, and death is said to have resulted from sin, the removal of sin ought to bring about the removal of death.”

### AUGUSTINE

You still say that Adam was made in such a way that, whether he sinned or did not sin, he would have died. But by saying this your teacher Pelagius himself already condemned you in the Palestinian episcopal judgment—and not without condemning himself, since he did not correct himself.

[Note: *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, nos. 23, 57.]

God, however, does not make his own blessed in this wicked age, although here he forgives their sins and grants them the pledge of the Spirit of grace. Therefore he promised them a future age in which they would suffer no evils—those who either do not use, or use well, the evils of this age, whether pleasurable or savage and harsh. In that age marriages would have been such as they could have been in that paradise if no one had sinned, with nothing shameful in them. Yet they will not be such, because, once the number of the blessed has been completed, there will be no generation for which marriages would be necessary.

### XCIV. JULIAN

“But since none of the things we have mentioned is found to occur in the bodies of the baptized, and since the truth, clearer than the sun, has shown that everything could—and therefore ought—to have been accomplished only through such methods of healing, you must admit either that the things we listed earlier were not caused by sin and therefore were not wounds of nature, so that the rationale of grace may stand, by which it is clear that those things were not moved from their proper order; or else you must deny that there is any healing in Christ’s mysteries [Col. 1179], since, according to you, they could not heal even one of so many diseases.”

[Note: Vignierius and Codex Mar. read “so many diseases of the age.”]

### AUGUSTINE

Rather, if you lived with a sober mind, you ought from this to recognize how great that sin was which entered the world through one man and passed into all people together with death. For even the baptized, although their guilt has already been removed, are not delivered from all the evils of this age—evils with which people die—until after this life, in which we must still be exercised by evils even amid the good things that have been promised.

[Note: The manuscripts of Clar., Mar., and Port. read *cum quibus homines moriuntur* (“with which people die”).]

For if the reward of faith were paid immediately, faith itself would no longer exist. Faith sees the present evils and endures them piously because, not seeing the promised good things, it awaits them faithfully and patiently.

### XCV. JULIAN

“Thus far I have argued as though the Apostle had judged the power of the gifts and the wounds equal, although their effects are contrary.

[Note: The printed editions read *dolorum* (“sorrows”); the older Codex Portarum more aptly reads *donorum* (“gifts”).]

But the greatness of the sound faith that we defend undoubtedly increases when we consider that Paul not only did not place the sickness of sins above the remedies of grace, but even judged the benefits more abundant than the losses.”

### AUGUSTINE

That is true. The losses of the regenerated are temporal, whereas the benefits will undoubtedly be eternal. But tell us by what merit the losses which those being born testify to with their crying are inflicted upon them under the most just and omnipotent Judge, if they draw no sin with them.

### XCVI. JULIAN

“Let the prudent reader consider what this entire discussion has established. The Apostle said that Christ’s gift abounded for salvation among more people than Adam’s fault had harmed.”

### AUGUSTINE

He did not say this, but: “Grace abounded much more for the many” (Rom. 5:15)—that is, it abounded more greatly, not among more people, that is, not among a greater number, as has already been answered.

### XCVII. JULIAN

“By what fault,” you say, “did the disasters we listed above befall nature, when it is clear that not one of them is healed in those who reach Christ’s sacraments? Thus you assert that the iniquity of the first man possessed far greater power to harm than Christ’s grace possesses to heal. From this it has been established that the disagreement between you and the Apostle Paul is as great as that between Catholics and Manichaeans.”

[Note: The manuscripts of Port., Mar., and Clar. read *nec unam in his qui ad Christi perveniunt Sacramenta* (“not even one of them is healed in those who come to Christ’s sacraments”); the printed editions read *nec unam quo ad Christum perveniunt Sacramento* (“not even one, as far as those who come to Christ by the sacrament”).]

### AUGUSTINE

Christ’s grace removes the guilt of original sin, but it removes an invisible thing invisibly. It also forgives all the sins that people have added by living wickedly. “Judgment,” therefore, is “from one offense to condemnation,” because that one offense which is drawn from birth brings eternal condemnation if it is not forgiven. Yet grace does not forgive only this; otherwise it would have merely that much power. Rather, it forgives the other sins along with it; therefore it has greater power. For this reason it is said: “Judgment indeed was from one offense to condemnation, but grace from many offenses to justification” (ibid., 16).

[Col. 1180]

Grace also grants that the spirit desire against the flesh. If a faithful person is sometimes defeated in this struggle in a pardonable way, grace forgives the debt when he prays; and when he is defeated in a damnable way, grace grants a humbler repentance to which it may extend pardon.

Finally, grace grants eternal life to both soul and body. Who could imagine what kind and how great the blessings will be there? How, then, did the iniquity of the first man harm more than the goodness of the second man—that is, Christ—benefited, when the former harmed temporally, whereas Christ both helps temporally and delivers and blesses eternally?

Since this is so, our position is Catholic, not Manichaean; and therefore it is not Pelagian either, because it is Catholic.

### XCVIII. JULIAN

“Quite properly I might despise your frivolous explanation at this point and pass it by without replying, as something clinging too closely to the ground, were I not afraid that this would be attributed more to deceit than to consistency. You speak in this way: ‘What does “abounded much more” mean, unless it means that all who are delivered through Christ die temporally because of Adam, but because of Christ himself will live without end?’ (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 2, no. 46).

“If you had noticed what follows consistently from these words, you would admit that your entire stronghold—that is, the transmission of sin—has fallen. For you say that Christ’s grace abounded much more because through it eternal life is bestowed, whereas through Adam’s sin temporal corruption must be endured. If, therefore, Adam introduced nothing other than bodily death, against which Christ bestowed, by a more abundant benefit, life lasting without end, it is evident that not Adam’s sin but death passed to his descendants.”

### AUGUSTINE

It is evident that you mocked what I said—or rather pretended to mock it—in order to appear to those who do not understand you to be saying something when you were saying nothing.

First, I said that Adam harmed by temporal death those whom Christ’s grace delivers. Those whom it does not deliver by the hidden yet just truth of judgment are punished by eternal death, even if they die as little children. How, then, does it follow from this that not Adam’s sin but death passed to his descendants? It follows only if you want people to believe what your noisy words proclaim, rather than what follows from my words.

We say that both passed over, and we proclaim that Christ removes both: the guilt of sin by the fullest forgiveness of sins, and death by the most blessed resurrection of the saints. Temporal death is not immediately taken away from those who have been regenerated, so that faith may be exercised—the faith by which what is not seen is hoped for.

[Note: The printed editions read *quia* (“because”); the manuscripts of Colb. and Port. read *qua* (“by which”).]

When believers hope for this both for themselves and for their little children, they are certainly believers. This is what we say; this is the Catholic truth that you contradict. Yet whatever you say in your heretical disputations, you speak more against yourselves than against that truth.

### XCIX. JULIAN

“It will follow with complete consistency that everlasting death, that is, eternal punishment, was not transmitted to us, and consequently that there can be no transmitted sin.

[Col. 1181]

“To make clear briefly what must be held: the Apostle places Christ’s gifts above the sin of the first man. Through this sin of yours—that is, transmitted sin—do you say that one death or two deaths passed over? If one, and bodily death, as you have admitted here, it is clear that Christ’s grace surpasses the sin of the first man. And now no one is born a sinner. For if, as you said above, the reign of sin is that a person is hurled into the second death—that is, everlasting punishment—and if you say that through Adam only bodily death was introduced, then neither sin through Adam nor eternal death is transmitted to posterity.”

[Note: The printed editions read *sicut* (“just as”); the manuscripts more aptly read *si, ut* (“if, as”).]

### AUGUSTINE

This has already been answered: you are saying nothing.

The reign of sin also hurls people into eternal death unless it is forgiven through Christ’s grace. Nevertheless, this temporal death too would not exist if Adam had not lost, through the merit of sin, the possibility of not dying. God announced this to the sinner when he said: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. 3:19).

Christ deigned to assume this death without the merit of sin, so that by dying he might indeed go into the earth, but by rising again might lift the earth into heaven. Thus, after destroying eternal death, he did not remove temporal death from the faithful, in order that the faith of the resurrection might struggle against it in the contest of this life.

### C. JULIAN

“But if you say that through Adam’s sin iniquity became natural, and that two deaths occurred—one eternal, the other temporal—and that through Christ’s grace one is meanwhile removed from the person, though not from nature, namely the everlasting one, while temporal death remains, then the Apostle is convicted of falsehood, since he said that grace benefited much more than sin harmed. But the Apostle cannot be accused; therefore you are rightly rejected.”

### AUGUSTINE

I have said that one resurrection of the blessed removes both deaths: the one, so that the soul may not be without its body; the other, so that the soul may not be weighed down or afflicted even by its own body.

Temporal death is left to the faithful for a time so that faith may receive assistance through it, just as afterward it is removed from the condemned, so that the fact that they do not leave their bodies becomes an increase of misery.

Accordingly, it is clear that for those who are regenerated in Christ and depart from this wicked age as the elect, grace benefits more than the sin that entered the world through one man and passed into all people together with death harmed.

The Apostle therefore cannot be refuted, because he spoke the truth. But you either do not understand it, or, in heretical contentiousness, strive to assert what is false against what you understand.

### CI. JULIAN

“The Apostle said that Christ’s grace abounded more than Adam’s guilt. Therefore it is not nature, generation, or fertility that is accused by him, but the will, the choice of evil, and depravity of conduct.”

[Note: The manuscripts read *sed voluntas, electio mali, morum pravitas* (“but the will, the choice of evil, and depravity of conduct”); the printed editions read *sed voluntatis electio, morum pravitas* (“but the choice of the will and depravity of conduct”).]

### AUGUSTINE

If generation does no harm, regeneration does no good. If nature has not been corrupted, little children do not have Christ as their Savior. If the merit of evil and good belongs to the individual’s own will, by what merit does Christ grant the kingdom of God [Col. 1182] to little children, who have used their will in neither direction?

[Note: The printed editions read *sic omne malum* (“thus every evil”); *omne* is absent from the manuscripts.]

Finally, since the Apostle set two persons against each other—one for sin, not the devil but Adam, and one for righteousness, not Abel but Christ—so that the comparison would concern regeneration with generation, not imitation with example: if Adam does not transmit sin to those generated, Christ does not grant righteousness to those regenerated, because little children, whether generated or regenerated, have not exercised their own freedom.

Go now, if you wish, and dare to shout that righteousness is not granted to little children, and that they will not possess righteousness when they inhabit that kingdom where, as it is written, “there will be new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells” (2 Pet. 3:13). Or rave, from the undiluted doctrine with which you are intoxicated, that in that kingdom little children will indeed possess righteousness, but through the merits of their own will and not through the generosity of divine grace.

If you do not dare say this—for you admit that merits are compared here, while rewards are bestowed there—why do you hesitate, or refuse, to admit that they could have sin from Adam without the merits of their own evil will, just as they will receive righteousness from Christ without any prior merits of a good will of their own?

### CII. JULIAN

“Accordingly, if truth still has any place in human affairs, and if the whole world has not become utterly deaf from the clamor of iniquity, then, with reason, argument, the Apostle’s faith, and his very statement as witnesses, everyone will acknowledge that the difference between the Traducians and Catholics is as great as that between Paul and Manichaeus, between wisdom and folly, between reason and madness, and between consistency of speech and the wavering that you endure with such unprecedented disgrace, so that in almost the same verses you deny what you have said and affirm what you have denied.”

[Note: The manuscripts of Clar. and Mar. read *doctorum* (“of learned men”); the printed editions read *dictorum* (“of statements”).]

### AUGUSTINE

It has already been answered. I beg you: if you cannot say anything, be silent if you can. But, what is worse, you cannot even do that.

### CIII. JULIAN

“‘And the gift,’ he says, ‘is not like what came through one who sinned. For judgment came from one offense to condemnation, but grace came from many offenses to justification’” (Rom. 5:16).

You apply the following explanation to these words of the Apostle: “‘From one,’ you ask, ‘what, except an offense? For it follows: “But grace came from many offenses.” Let them say how judgment could come from one offense to condemnation, unless even one original sin is sufficient for condemnation, a sin that passed into all people. Grace, however, is said to come from many offenses to justification because it not only cancels that one sin which is drawn from our origin, but also the other sins added in each person by the movement of his own will.

“‘For if, because of one offense, death reigned through one man, much more will those who receive the abundance of grace and righteousness reign in life through the one Jesus Christ. Therefore, just as through one offense condemnation came to all people, so through one act of righteousness [Col. 1183] justification unto life came to all people’” (Rom. 5:18–19).

After these words of the Apostle, as though you had achieved something, you mock us and say: “‘Let them continue in the vanity of their mind, and say that one man did not transmit a hereditary stock of sin (*propaginem … peccati*), but supplied an example of sin. How, then, did condemnation come to all people through one offense, and not rather through the many offenses of each person, unless the one offense alone is sufficient to bring condemnation even without the addition of the others, just as it brings condemnation to dying little children who are born from Adam if they are not reborn in Christ?

“‘What, then, does this man ask from us that he does not wish to hear from the Apostle—by what means sin is found in a little child: whether through the will, through marriage, or through parents? Let him hear, then, by what means it is found; let him hear and be silent. The Apostle says: “Through one offense condemnation came to all people.”’” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 2, no. 46).

We know that you fear nothing more than an examination that searches out your mind and doctrine. Hence it is that, with all your resources, you obtain from the powers of the world a refusal of investigation. You understand that you must act by force when you are abandoned by the aid of reason.

### AUGUSTINE

Do you wish not to fear authority? “Do what is good” (Rom. 13:3). It is not good to bring forward and assert a heretical interpretation against the apostolic meaning.

Why do you continue to seek an investigation that has already taken place at the Apostolic See, and finally has already taken place in the Palestinian episcopal judgment, where Pelagius, the author of your error, would certainly have been condemned unless he had condemned the doctrines you defend?

The heresy, therefore, has been condemned by the bishops. It is no longer to be examined, but restrained by Christian authorities.

[Note: The word *Damnata* (“condemned”) has here been restored from the manuscripts.]

### CIV. JULIAN

“But your opinion will not carry such weight among the prudent that, since you are the head and cause of these evils, you can withdraw from the central dispute by introducing the Apostle as an objection and suppose that he must be struck on your behalf. Indeed, it is chiefly against you that we arm ourselves with him as teacher and leader.

“To make clear, then, what ought to be said to you: if you and I disagreed on this point because the Apostle confirmed the Manichaean doctrine of natural sin, you would consistently put him forward when I attacked your leader. But since the dignity of the Teacher of the Nations remains inviolable in my eyes, and I will not allow his words to be harmed by your interpretation—which, according to the rule established by reason, I assert to be opposed to a foolish, impure, and impious doctrine—and since I prove that he said nothing in support of natural sin, with what insolence do you intervene, either by making him answer me on your behalf when he is not being questioned, since no one doubts his wisdom, or by loudly accusing me of refusing to hear from the Apostle what, through the sound understanding transmitted to us by the Apostle, I condemn in you?”

[Note: The printed editions read: “who, according to the rule of reason set forth, I assert that you—or I—oppose to a foolish, impure, and impious doctrine.” The manuscript reading is preferable: “which, according to the rule of reason set forth, I assert to be opposed to a foolish, impure, and impious doctrine.”]

[Col. 1184]

### AUGUSTINE

After the Apostle’s words that I introduced, ought you not to have done anything other than remain silent? Yet, saying nothing against them and saying nothing in accordance with them, you do not keep silent toward me. Among other things, you boast that I am the head and cause of these evils—as though I had been the first either to believe in original sin or to discuss its existence.

Do you think that those who will read this are so ignorant that they do not know how many distinguished teachers of the Church before us understood and explained the Apostle’s words in the way the Catholic Church has understood or believed them from its very beginning?

If the words of those teachers are evil, as you do not fear to say, how, I ask you, am I the head and cause of these evils—unless you are the head of those calumnies which, in your madness, you bring against me?

For if you considered with a sound mind the miseries of human life, from the first cries of infants to the final groans of the dying, you would surely see that neither I nor you, but Adam, was the head and cause of these evils. Because you do not wish to see this, you cry out with closed eyes both that God’s judgment is just and that there is no original sin.

You would undoubtedly see how contradictory these two claims are—not, I say, if you were not the head of these evils, for you certainly are not, but if you had a sound head, which you could have if, by following the Catholic teachers, you did not have Pelagius for your head.

### CV. JULIAN

“Let the force of your arguments, then, be brought out. After Paul said that the Savior’s grace had abounded much more for healing than the transgression of the first man had for harming, he continues: ‘And the gift is not like what came through one who sinned; for judgment came from one offense to condemnation, but grace came from many offenses to justification.’

“You insist that this means ‘one offense sufficient for condemnation, namely original sin,’ which ‘passed into all people’; and that grace is said to come from many offenses to justification because it not only cancels that one sin which is drawn from our origin, but also the other sins added in each person by the movement of his own will.

“To confirm this, you argue shortly afterward that, if the Apostle had said that this one offense was sufficient for condemnation because it was received through imitation, he would have had to add that all people go to condemnation not through one offense but through the many offenses committed by each person’s own will.

[Note: The printed editions read *in quibus locis* (“in which passages”); the manuscripts lack *locis*.]

“I warn the attentive reader that the Apostle’s speech must be disentangled here from the snares of the Manichaeans. According to our interpretation, by which the first fault is said to have supplied an example to sinners, you say that the Apostle ought to have stated that death reigned through many sins, just as he said that grace operates from many offenses unto justification.

[Note: The printed editions omit *in* before *justificationem*; it is present in the manuscripts.]

“By this argument, however, you are entirely struggling against yourself. For according to your doctrine, I prove that the Apostle speaks inconsistently when he says, ‘Grace came from many offenses to justification,’ after having said, ‘Judgment came from one sin to condemnation.’

“To leave our territory and enter yours: [Col. 1185] if freedom of choice was first overthrown by sin, and thereafter remained so crippled in the entire human race that it was capable only of doing evil, without having the power to choose the other alternative—that is, to turn away from evil and do good—but, crushed by the necessity of iniquity, was compelled to obey its appetite for crimes; if, with every law of righteousness breached, things that had been voluntary became natural; if the law of sin dwells in the members, having acquired tyranny over the image and work of God through the shame and pleasure of marriage; if the devil’s shrub is planted in the womb before the soul and, growing together with natural increase, sprouts leaves and becomes heavy with poisonous fruit; if, I say, this is what the one fault of the first man produced, then it is more consistent to say that the mortal race goes from one offense to condemnation than that grace frees it from many offenses.

“In this way it may be understood more appropriately that grace is said to free from one offense those whom it frees. For no other offenses are added through the movement of the individual will if the fault of the first parent, having shattered freedom of choice and excluded the desire for goodness, produces every evil by infecting the seed.”

### AUGUSTINE

How can a person who strives to pervert the apostolic words speak except perversely?

When the use of the will is added to that offense which generation transmits—a use of the will that little children do not possess—the tree of many sins grows into many and varied desires. Before this occurred, that one offense alone was already leading the child to condemnation if the child ended this life before reaching the use of the will.

Nor, because a greater condemnation is owed to one who has become mature in a greater and multiplied evil, does it follow that no condemnation was owed to one who was small and whose evil had not yet multiplied. How, then, does regeneration, which removes the evil multiplied through the use of the will, not provide more than generation harmed, when generation transmitted the beginning of this evil—however great and multiplied it might become—before it had yet grown or multiplied, and when it would have remained alone without any growth if no use of the will had intervened to increase and multiply it?

[Note: The editions of Masius and Vignierius read *plura* (“more things”); the manuscripts read *plus* (“more”). Menardus reads *plures* (“more [persons]”), but has *plura* in the margin.]

Before the will is restored to a good freedom for performing true righteousness through the assistance of God’s grace, it is moved—or not moved—to sin by many other causes besides the defect of origin. Consequently, even the ungodly, whom the grace that justifies the ungodly has either not yet helped or will never help, sin some more and others less.

“Judgment,” therefore, is “from one offense to condemnation,” because even those who have drawn that one offense through generation are condemned. “Grace,” however, is “from many offenses to justification,” because it removes not only the sin with which a person is born, but also whatever other sins the use of the will has added to that evil.

This is the Catholic truth of the apostolic words. No amount of heretical loquacity can corrupt it, however much you exercise us with the length of your vanity and talkativeness.

[Note: The manuscripts of Clar. and Mar. read *perplexitate* (“perplexity”) rather than *prolixitate* (“length”).]

[Col. 1186]

### CVI. JULIAN

“Accordingly, if natural sin is the author of such great evils, Christ’s grace does not effect justification by forgiving many offenses; rather, by pardoning one sin, it carries out its work of kindness.

[Note: Codex Port. reads *aucturam* (“will increase”) instead of *acturam* (“will perform”).]

When it promises that it will do this, it will make its promises credible if it cures the things said to have been introduced through the wound of sin. But if, even after the remedies it has brought, the same series of diabolical diseases persists, then gratitude is owed to its desire, and forgiveness to its presumption, because its power, not its will, failed to cure the inborn plagues.”

[Note: The manuscripts read *voto* (“wish”); the printed editions read *voluntati* (“will”).]

### AUGUSTINE

This has already been answered. Understand, and be silent.

Grace makes one person struggle and assists him in one way; it preserves another, victorious without any enemy—external or internal—in eternal peace, in another way. The former is the laborious warfare of the present age; the latter is the blessed rest of the future.

But if you do not wage war within yourself against carnal vices, be ashamed. If you do wage it, be silent.

### CVII. JULIAN

“What, then, has this discussion established? That your interpretation does not agree with the Apostle.

“The Apostle says that many offenses are forgiven through the generosity of grace, whereas your doctrine asserts that one natural sin—which you call the law of sin—forms desires for iniquity in all people. It is therefore clear that you accuse nature, which is God’s work, while he accuses the will.

“He could not have expressed himself otherwise than he did, namely that condemnation can arise from one sin: for that first man supplied an example of sinning through one sin, and just as one transgression was sufficient for him himself unto condemnation, so one fault can be sufficient for others unto guilt.

“For this reason Ecclesiastes says: ‘Whoever sins in one thing loses many good things’ (Eccles. 9:18); and James says: ‘If you observe the whole law but stumble in one point, you have become guilty of all of it’ (Jas. 2:10).”

### AUGUSTINE

Then Adam’s sin harmed Adam alone and not the human race. You will not be so absurd as to say that people are harmed or have been harmed by his sin without knowing or believing whether it existed and what he did.

For even if people imitate something unknowingly, you speak exceedingly foolishly if you say that they are harmed and made sinners by a sin committed thousands of years ago, of which they are unaware—unless you admit that this sin passed into all generations.

But if Pelagius had not condemned those who say that Adam’s sin harmed Adam alone and not the human race, he would have been condemned by the judges, who certainly are not Manichaeans.

### CVIII. JULIAN

“Grace, however, was not given in such a way that it would provide a separate remedy of indulgence for each separate sin, as for separate wounds, or grant forgiveness for various sins through different baptisms. Rather, by the power of the most effective medicine—which is applied to crimes, that is, to acts of an evil will—it provides help universally, so that by the single power of consecration it removes different kinds of guilt.”

AUGUSTINE. However you describe the grace of the Lord [Col. 1187] Jesus Christ as having been given, you separate infants from it, whom you deny can be saved by it. Thus, by dividing the very names according to your own preference, Christ appears to belong to infants because of the kingdom of God, which you concede that only the baptized can enter; but Jesus is wholly alien to them, since he does not work in them the thing from which he receives this name. For it is written, “You shall call his name Jesus,” and immediately, supplying the reason why he is called Jesus: “For he,” it says, “will save his people from their sins” (Matt. 1:21). By denying that this happens in infants, you separate them both from the name Jesus and from his people. And yet you dare to be indignant that you yourselves are rather separated from that same people! As regards voluntary sins, just as judgment, from many sins, leads to condemnation, so grace, from many sins, leads to justification. Why, then, is it said, “Judgment from one sin led to condemnation, but grace from many sins led to justification,” unless because here will is not set against will, nor imitation against imitation, but generation against regeneration? For just as generation has judgment from one sin leading to condemnation, so regeneration has grace from many sins leading to justification. What the Apostle wished to be understood is clear: if you would open submissive ears, you would close your contentious mouths.

**CIX. JULIAN.** Therefore, prudently, when he was speaking about Adam, he named one sin, which he wished to be understood as representing transgression. For this reason, I say, he mentioned one and not many, because he knew that Adam’s one sin alone is contained in the history of the Law. But he praised grace for sending forth those imbued by it from many sins into justification, lest suspicion should arise that the benefit was poor. If he had said, “Grace from one sin for justification,” it would not have appeared that he was abolishing everything so much as individual sins. Thus, by putting one sin first, he preserved the historical account; by adding that grace is from many sins for justification, he commended the generosity and abundance of the mystery.

**AUGUSTINE.** Why, then, did he need to speak about Adam when he was commending the grace of Christ, unless because through the one there is generation, and through the other regeneration?

**CX. JULIAN.** This interpretation, just as it agrees with reason, so it destroys you. By this very admission, you are compelled to confess that in all the preceding words the Apostle was not speaking about the Manichaean “transmission,” since, in recalling grace, he showed that many sins were forgiven.

**AUGUSTINE.** You assist the Manichaeans, since by denying that the original evil is the cause of infants’ misery you give them an opening for introducing another evil nature. Infants would certainly not have this misery in paradise if they were born while the rectitude and blessedness of human nature remained there.

[Note: The Portus, Mar., and Clairvaux manuscripts read, “while the rectitude and blessedness of human nature remained”; the printed editions read, “while the rectitude of nature and human blessedness remained.”]

**CXI. JULIAN.** For he showed that he had also spoken above of that one sin in reference to the kind of sins which he commended as many and all forgiven through grace. But you agree that these many sins are those committed by each individual through the movement [Col. 1188] of his own will; therefore that one sin also belongs to the same category.

**AUGUSTINE.** Along with that one, I say that there are many—not apart from it. It can also rightly be said to belong to the same category if it is referred to its origin, because it too proceeded from the will of the first man, when his sin entered the world and passed through all human beings.

**CXII. JULIAN.** This is so that it may be understood as having been drawn in by each person’s own movement of will, and then not the fruitfulness of seeds but the perversity of pursuits will be accused. Otherwise, if he had wished that one original sin to be understood, he would certainly not have said in what follows that there were many sins, which he testifies were forgiven through grace.

**AUGUSTINE.** Why would he not have said so, unless because the Pelagians want this? But the truth, by which the Pelagian novelty is refuted and its vanity conquered, does not wish it. For the many sins from which grace leads to justification are many together with that one; from that one alone judgment leads to condemnation, even if no others are added.

[Note: Printed editions read, “from which one judgment”; the manuscripts correct this.]

Thus Adam was able to insert one offense into those who were generated, whereas Christ forgives many offenses in those who are regenerated, since it is shown that the latter has benefited more than the former harmed.

**CXIII. JULIAN.** Although the things already said abound in defense of the truth, I nevertheless urge the reader to attend to what we are about to bring forward. For it will become irrefutably clear that in these passages the Apostle Paul discussed not nature but the conduct of mortals. Setting the force of Christ’s grace and of the first sin directly against one another, and comparing the effects of each, he labored to show that the mystery of Christ benefited more than the sin of the first man harmed. But we have shown that this cannot stand in the sense of “transmission.” Thus, just as he intended the many things he enumerated to redound to the praise of grace, so he especially intended this statement to do so: “Judgment from one sin led to condemnation, but grace from many sins led to the justification of life.” The defender of natural evil explained this in the following manner:

> “For this reason,” he says, “it is from one sin to condemnation, because that one sin, which is transmitted originally, is sufficient to lead to condemnation, just as it leads infants born from Adam to condemnation if they are not reborn in Christ, even if there are no other sins. But grace is from many sins for justification because it forgives not only that which is transmitted originally, but also the other sins which each person adds through the movement of his own will” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 2, no. 46).

There you have confessed—although with Manichaean impiety—that sin is indeed natural, but only one sin, on account of which you say that those who are born ought to be condemned.

**AUGUSTINE.** He who said, “We are all born under sin” (Ambrose, book 2 of *On Repentance*, chapter 2 or 3) was not a Manichaean. But you, answer what you are, who separate so many images of God from the kingdom of God without any merit of sin, deny that they are condemned by God’s judgment, and make two eternal felicities: one in the kingdom of God, the other [Col. 1189] outside the kingdom of God. Tell me, I beg you: in that felicity which will be outside the kingdom of God, will anyone reign, or no one? If no one, that felicity will undoubtedly be freer without any king. But if someone will reign in it, who will be king of the images of God without being God? Moreover, if he will be a god, you introduce another god—and you call me a Manichaean?

But if God himself will reign there, whose images are those? Then his images too will be happy in the kingdom of their true God.

[Note: Printed editions read, “his images without the kingdom of their God”; this is corrupt and conflicts with the manuscripts.]

And where will the Gospel statement be: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3:5)?

[Note: Printed editions add, “And where will the Gospel statement be, ‘Unless …,’” but “the Gospel statement” is absent from the manuscripts.]

Or do you finally admit that unregenerated infants will be happy outside the kingdom of God? Tell us, then, what is the merit of this unhappiness, you verbose and contentious men who deny original sin.

**CXIV. JULIAN.** Prove, then, that in them this is fulfilled which the Apostle Paul ascribed to Christ’s grace—namely, that it effects justification from many sins, that is, that by one single forgiveness it grants righteousness to those guilty of several sins. Either, therefore, show that infants are liable to many crimes, so that you may persuade them also that what the Apostle placed in praise of Christ’s generosity applies to them, namely, that they are shown to have been freed from many sins; or confess that in these passages Paul discussed nothing about infants and nothing about human nature, since he testified that those things are forgiven by the liberality of grace which, as you yourself concede, cannot be found in the newborn.

**AUGUSTINE.** What is this that you are saying? What is this that your exceedingly talkative vanity is shouting in your face, lest the most manifest truth enter your ears? Jesus, who saves his people from many sins, does not omit even the individual original sins of infants, because those too are among the many.

[Note: The old Portus codex reads, “What is this, what is this that you are saying?”]

**CXV. JULIAN.** “Grace,” he says, “is from many sins for justification.” You say that infants are liable to no more than one sin. You therefore see the praise of grace limping in their case, because it does not find many sins by whose remission it may be praised.

[Note: The manuscripts read “limping”; the printed editions read “to limp.”]

What the Apostle Paul said, then—“But grace is from many sins for justification”—is shown to be utterly false in the condition of infants. What will you try to leap out of here? Undoubtedly you will say—for your preceding discourse has disclosed this to be your meaning—that the Apostle’s statement, “But grace is from many sins for justification,” is fulfilled in adults, who are convicted of being liable to many sins through the movement of their own will, whereas in infants justification is effected not from many sins but from one.

[Note: The manuscripts read, “What, then, will you try to leap out of here?” The printed editions read, “What, then, will you try to answer from here?”]

**AUGUSTINE.** It would not have been difficult for you to understand that, by this justification which the Savior confers on his own from the forgiveness of many sins, you rather withdraw infants, since you maintain that no sin can be forgiven them. We, however, when we say that all are sent into condemnation through one who sinned, except no age [Col. 1190], because adults too have this sin; and likewise, when we say that grace justifies from many sins, nevertheless except no age. For he who forgives many sins—by “many” all are certainly understood—omits none at all: neither the greater number belonging to the worst sinners, nor the fewer number belonging to some, nor the individual sins of infants.

It would not have been difficult for you to see this, unless you envied infants Christ the physician and absolutely refused to let him be Jesus to them, with dreadful impiety, astonishing blindness, and blasphemous verbosity.

[Note: Printed editions read “blindness of wrath,” a mistake.]

What, moreover, is more insane than to want Christ’s grace to belong only to those who have many sins? By this reasoning—or rather, by this blindness of mind—you withdraw from this grace not only infants, whom you believe to bear no guilt from their origin, but everyone who does not have many sins. For you think the Apostle’s statement, “But grace is from many sins for justification” (Rom. 5:16), must be understood in such a way that no one belongs to this grace unless many sins are forgiven him.

And therefore, since an infant has no sin, as you suppose, when he grows up and begins to sin, if he comes to Christ’s Baptism after committing not merely a few sins but perhaps even one, he will in no way belong to this grace, because he is not sent from many sins to justification but from one. I think the deafness of your hearts is not so dominant that this enormous absurdity will not compel you to blush.

But if someone to whom one sin has been forgiven belongs to this grace, then the Apostle said, “Grace is from many sins for justification,” because he wished the sins of the whole people who are justified through it to be understood: among them some have more, others fewer, and still others only one—which collectively are all many.

**CXVI. JULIAN.** But by this interpretation, which you will be able neither to distort in meaning nor evade, you have lost not only your own tricks but also the fabrication of envy that you were inflaming against us.

[Note: Against the old books, the printed editions read, “which indeed neither to distort,” omitting “the meaning.” Julian is speaking of the interpretation quoted from Augustine, which he himself attempts to distort.] For you loudly accused us of having committed a grave offense against the faith because we say that Christ’s grace is indeed to be handed down in one uniform manner, and that his words and institutions must not be shaken; that he confers equally on all who have been instructed by him the gifts of adoption, sanctification, and advancement; but that he does not find all who approach burdened with the same guilt. Rather, he frees from guilt those who have sinned by their own will—for without its operation there can be no sin—and makes the wicked good; but he finds the innocent happy in their untainted first condition and does not accuse them of any evil work of the will, since he knows that they have had no [Col. 1191] experience of it.

**AUGUSTINE.** O singular insanity! Is this disputation or madness? Infants testify by their weeping that they are born in misery, yet you do not want them to have Christ as Jesus. And you call happy those whom you nevertheless do not admit into his kingdom. If you loved that kingdom with Christian charity, you would judge separation from it to be a great misery.

[Note: The negative particle is omitted in the printed editions here, although it is present in the manuscripts.]

**CXVII. JULIAN.** Rather, he makes the good better, and raises all whom he receives to one and the same hill of sanctification, but does not find all in the same swamp of vices. Instead, he finds some in a state of innocence and others in the pursuits of harmful things.

[Note: The manuscripts read “to raise”; the printed editions read “to transport.”]

Because we say this—something fortified by sound faith, supported by reason, and protected by pious understanding, through which Christ’s grace is rightly praised and no guilt is attributed to God—you say that the authority of the sacrament is tottering. With an acumen blunter than any pestle, you assert that the authority of grace is taken away unless the crime of slander is attributed to it, unless the institutions of justice are perverted, unless the guilt of another’s conscience is thrust upon those who have no knowledge, and, finally, unless grace is said to accomplish nothing if it is not preached as operating uniformly in all.

[Note: The printed editions read “prayer”; the manuscripts read “reason.”]

**AUGUSTINE.** Why did you think that the acumen—not mine, but that of all Catholic disputants, with whom I hold firmly what you are trying in vain to undermine—should be compared to a pestle? Or have you begun to feel that it crushes you in your fragility?

[Note: The manuscripts read “you have begun,” addressed in the singular; the printed editions read it in the plural.]

And yet you who, as though in defense of God’s justice, strive to overturn what the whole Church of Christ believes concerning the condemnation of unregenerated infants will never say from where it is just for a heavy yoke to lie upon infants if they do not bear original sin.

Nor do you notice that you rather pervert the institutions of justice, and those of the omnipotent God, by whom or under whom you say that this punishment is inflicted without any merit upon countless thousands of all human beings—that is, images of God—from the day they come forth from their mother’s womb.

Finally, you will never say from where it is just that infants who die without Baptism, through no fault of their own and often through no fault even of their parents, should be separated from faithful parents and relatives, not admitted to the kingdom of God, and assigned—not among vessels made for honor, like other baptized infants, but among vessels made for dishonor, since there is no third kind of vessel—without any evil merits.

For it displeases your heretical prudence that the Catholic faith believes that, after all went from one person into condemnation, in some the mercy of grace is effected while in others the judgment of truth remains, through the unsearchable ways of the Lord, “which are all mercy and truth” (Ps. 24:10).

**CXVIII. JULIAN.** It is therefore clear that your interpretation has made vanish the whole thing by which you were deceiving minds sullied by folly.

[Col. 1192]

**AUGUSTINE.** You have vanished—but you, who do not wish to see or confess that the forgiveness of sins also belongs to those who have one sin. Infants do not belong to this medicinal grace if they have none; and you impiously kill them because you deny them a Savior.

[Note: The manuscripts read “you impiously kill them”; the printed editions read “you deny them.”]

**CXIX. JULIAN.** For when the Apostle declares, “But grace is from many sins for justification,” and you say that this cannot be true in infants, but is fulfilled only in those who are already of mature age because they have added other sins to that one through the movement of their own will, you undoubtedly confess that the operation of grace differs according to the difference among those who approach it.

Among those who exercise their own will, there is material for grace to boast, because it leads those whom it adopts from many crimes to justification. But in infants, according to you, it promises to remove that one sin in a manner poorer, narrower, and more meager—neither with great power, nor with adequate medicine, nor with honor preserved, nor with secure modesty—which it ought not even to have imputed; and from this one sin it endeavors to send those whom it frees into justification.

**AUGUSTINE.** The answer has already been given: you keep saying the same things because you have nothing to say. When you say that no sin ought to be imputed to infants, you make God unjust, since he has imposed a heavy yoke upon them from the day they come forth from their mother’s womb (Ecclus. 40:1).

Even if Scripture did not say this, who is so blind in mind that he does not see the misery of the human race beginning with infants’ cries? You also make God’s law unjust, which condemns the soul of an infant who is not circumcised on the eighth day (Gen. 17:14). You likewise judge the commandment vain in which an offering for sin is ordered to be made after the birth of an infant (Lev. 12:6–7).

But if this guilt of origin is revealed both by Holy Scripture and by the guilt itself, then this sin too belongs among those many sins from which grace justifies, and through which it makes infants blessed by freeing them from this misery. This does not occur in the present age, which God willed to be punitive for human beings as a whole from the time he expelled the first human beings from the happiness of paradise, but in the future eternity, from which Christ now grants the pledge of the Holy Spirit to his members.

**CXX. JULIAN.** You have therefore confessed that grace operates one way in adults and another way in children. Nor should you think that anything remains to your answer if you say that there is indeed a great difference in the forgiveness of sins, so that, although it finds one sin, it nevertheless finds something to forgive. You accomplish nothing by this argument. For it makes no difference in what respect you confess that one grace has various effects, provided that you confess that its effects can be various.

[Note: The manuscripts read “you should think”; the printed editions read “you think.”]

**AUGUSTINE.** It is one thing to speak of various effects of grace, since Holy Scripture also calls God’s grace manifold (1 Pet. 4:10), and another thing to deny infants the grace of the forgiveness of sins, and to insist that in the Church of truth they are falsely exorcized and breathed upon if they are not rescued from the power of darkness—with great injury to the Creator—if they do not need the help [Col. 1193] of the Savior to be rescued from the power of the deceiver.

**CXXI. JULIAN.** I am satisfied with this much: you have been compelled to grant me that what the Apostle proclaimed in the liberality of grace cannot apply equally to all ages. If you bring forward anything that also confirms the forgiveness being carried out in the first age of the newborn, you have nevertheless not established this: that what the Apostle declared praiseworthy about Christ’s grace is not fulfilled in infants.

For when, in what follows, he preferred the remedy of the mystery to the first man’s sin, which he taught was the pattern, he said, “Judgment from one offense led to condemnation, but grace from many offenses led to justification.” Therefore that by which he preferred grace—namely, that it effects justification from many sins—is not, according to you, established in infants. On this point, although you resisted, you have been forced to admit that grace does not operate equally in different ages.

[Note: Menardus reads, “which was a pattern”; Vignierius, “which into a pattern.” The manuscripts correct these readings.]

[Note: The manuscripts read “you have not established”; the printed editions read “you have removed.”]
