**AUGUSTINE.** The answer has already been given: you speak vanity. The grace of God is glorious even when it forgives the individual sins of each person, because those individual sins too belong to that multitude of sins from which it justifies those whom it saves from their sins (Matt. 1:21). You most properly do not belong to that people, because you do not want infants to belong to it.

**CXXII. JULIAN.** Once this has been accepted by you, it has become clear that there was no need to stir up a charge against human nature merely to prevent it from being said that the grace of Baptism has various effects according to age. With this persuasive pretext removed, if you have any strength, intelligence, or courage, strive to prove natural sin, which you see has been destroyed by reason, authority, and equity.

For what view deceived you into calling the union of bodies, which God instituted, and the pleasure of the sexes that brings about this union—which flourishes both in human beings and in animals, and points to its author as the creator of bodies—the work and offspring of the devil?

[Note: The Portus codex reads, “which God instituted.”]

**AUGUSTINE.** Be ashamed: you are that praiser of lust. Be ashamed, I say. This lust, which pleases you greatly, is something that one who does not wish to commit sin by consenting to its solicitation must necessarily fight. It was not in paradise before sin. Therefore either there was no lust there, or it neither preceded nor exceeded the will of the mind.

It is not like that now. Every human being experiences this in himself—and you are a human being. Restrain your eagerness to resist, and acknowledge the vice from which original sin is derived.

[Note: The manuscripts read “vice”; the printed editions read “beginning.”]

Marriage found this in human beings as they were propagated; it did not create it. Marriage uses this from necessity, and uses chastity well; for this reason it is in no way blamed. In animals this is not evil because in them the flesh does not lust against the spirit. But in human beings this evil [Col. 1194] must be healed by divine goodness, not praised by human vanity.

**CXXIII. JULIAN.** What reason was there, then, for you first to wound innocence with another’s crime, and afterward to attempt to mix the matter of pursuits with seeds?

[Note: The printed editions read, “What evil reason was there, in the first”; wrongly.]

**AUGUSTINE.** You keep saying the same things in the same way; but what you say is certainly vain.

Seeds are good by nature, but seeds too are corrupted, and from corrupted seeds corruptions are propagated. At least the appearance of bodies should teach you this. Although their maker is supremely good and corrupted by no defect, many defective things are nevertheless born. And certainly, if no one had sinned, no such things would be born in paradise.

**CXXIV. JULIAN.** Was this so that you might take away from Baptism the truth of its proper operation? So that you might attribute to God—who is wholly equity, and who cannot be God without justice—the charge of manifest injustice?

**AUGUSTINE.** You rather do this, since, if infants are oppressed by a heavy yoke without any merit of sin, God is unjust. But because he is not unjust, you are calumnious and blind.

**CXXV. JULIAN.** So manifest, I say, that he himself condemned this appearance of injustice, which you falsely claim clings to his judgments, by the authority of his own Law.

**AUGUSTINE.** In his Law it is written that the soul of an infant, if it is not circumcised on the eighth day, will perish from its people (Gen. 17:14). On what merit? Tell me, if you can. But you cannot at all; and yet, by denying original sin, you do not keep silent.

**CXXVI. JULIAN.** What need, then, was there for so many blasphemies if even this position, which you embraced, was not true? Although it had no force, it nevertheless appeared like a sort of plank that you might hold onto amid so great a shipwreck, but which you let go, though late, with your arms exhausted.

To make the matter clear by repetition: you were thought a Manichaean, and tolerated as such by various foolish people, lest Christ’s grace appear not to have one uniform efficacy in all things. For this reason you have now, without our prompting, introduced the following through the stages of your interpretation: you say that the Apostle’s statement, “But grace is from many sins for justification,” can be fulfilled in people of mature age but not in infants; rather, that in infants there is something shorter, narrower, and poorer. Although you invent this, you nevertheless confess that the Apostle never said it.

[Note: The editions of Menardus and Masus read “without our introduction”; the present reading is “without our prompting.”]

**AUGUSTINE.** Let what was answered to you be read again, so that it may be understood that you say nothing and yet cannot keep silent, you talkative man. Grace leads from many sins to justification when Jesus saves his people from their sins. Among those same many sins it also finds the individual sins of infants.

Even if there were no original sins, among those same many sins it would find the individual sins of those older people who are beginning to sin. When such people come to Christ’s Baptism, they could in no way be told, “You cannot be baptized now, because you do not yet have [Col. 1195] many sins; for grace leads from many sins to justification.” They would most truly reply: “Among the multitude of sins from which grace justifies, our individual sins too are included. Some have more, some fewer, and all these together with our individual sins are many.”

[Note: Vignierius reads, “even if there were no sins in them, it would find many.” Menardus and he then read, “the sins of beginners.” The manuscripts correct these readings.]

**CXXVII. JULIAN.** Therefore, according to you too, grace has an equal effect in adoption throughout all ages, but in the forgiveness of sins the measure is not the same in all. But I have acted sparingly and with excessive patience up to this point.

[Note: The manuscripts read “in adoption”; the printed editions read “for adoption.”]

**AUGUSTINE.** If, while speaking sparingly, you say so much that you attack one of my books—not even the whole of it—with your eight books, your frugality is exceedingly lavish and extravagant.

[Note: The book meant is the second book of *On Marriage and Concupiscence*.]

But if you have acted sparingly up to now, why, while shouting against the truth in so many places, have you not spared your own soul?

**CXXVIII. JULIAN.** I am content, then, to prove by the preceding discussion that you too, who were stirring up the greatest sedition against us on this point, say that the forgiveness of sins does not follow one uniform rule in everyone. Thus, even if you could persuade us that this one natural sin exists, it would nevertheless necessarily be clear that those who approach grace do not always have one and the same condition, and that the Apostle’s statement, “from many sins for justification,” is fulfilled only in adults, not also in the first age.

**AUGUSTINE.** According to your empty chatter, it is not fulfilled even in adults, since many adults have only individual sins—even if, according to you, they do not have original sins—when they come to Baptism after beginning to sin. Some have even very few, though not many. They therefore will not belong to this grace of Christ, because it justifies from many sins, which these people do not have. Whoever thinks this way is unspeakably foolish.

Acknowledge Christ as justifying from many sins and saving his people, and understand that among those same many sins the few and individual sins of anyone can be counted. Do not withdraw the infants’ share from this people. Believe that Jesus is necessary even for them. He is called Jesus for no other reason than that he saves his people from their sins—and infants are certainly among that people.

**CXXIX. JULIAN.** Now, consequently, I assert that the Apostle suspected nothing concerning the Manichaean “transmission.” For he showed that it would be a grave insult to the mysteries if they were compared with sins in every respect—that is, if grace did not benefit more effectively than the pattern of sin had harmed. Thus the Teacher of the Gentiles placed the greatest dignity of the Christian faith in this: that he affirmed it to surpass sins. For this reason he took care to place the efficacy of medicine before that of ancient diseases.

**AUGUSTINE.** You deny this medicine to infants, whom you falsely and hostilely insist are saved. But their God, who perfects the praise of his medicine from the mouths of infants and nursing children, certainly also destroys you [Col. 1196], since you offer them a hostile defense when he destroys both the enemy and the defender.

**CXXX. JULIAN.** He therefore showed grace to be praiseworthy if what he said applied to it in every respect: “Judgment from one sin led to condemnation, but grace from many sins led to justification.” By what permission, then, will you deprive Christ’s grace of the praise by which the Apostle wished it to be proclaimed, and cast down the title of dignity by which alone the vessel of election wished its honor to be acknowledged?

**AUGUSTINE.** This does not reach infants if, according to you, they are bound by no sin. But because they are bound, grace, which justifies the multitude of its faithful from many sins, certainly reaches them also in order to heal their one sin, so that from the mouths of infants it may destroy the mouths of lying enemies and defenders.

**CXXXI. JULIAN.** He said, “Grace from many sins for justification.” He preferred the abundance of the medicine to the efficacy of sin. This meaning agrees with Catholic doctrine, which understands that sins are forgiven in those in whom many can be found—that is, sins drawn in through the movement of one’s own will. But in those in whom this movement of their own will is absent—that is, in infants—there are no sins, just as there are not many.

[Note: Menardus reads “of the efficacy of sin”; Vignierius and the manuscripts read “efficacy to sins” (*efficientiae peccatis*).]

**AUGUSTINE.** Then no medicine of the Savior belongs to them, and Christ is not Jesus to them. And you who say this dare to be called a Christian!

Furthermore, if, as you define it, the forgiveness of sins takes place in those in whom many sins can be found, since this is how you understand the Apostle’s statement, “Grace from many sins for justification,” then those who, according to you, do not have original sin but come to the bath of regeneration with one or a few sins do not belong to the forgiveness of sins.

Look at what you are saying. Are you not ashamed? Are you not terrified? Do you not keep silent?

But if people who are beginning to sin, and do not yet have many sins, nevertheless receive grace that justifies from many sins, why are you unwilling to count among those same many sins the individual sins of anyone, except for the purpose of impiously separating infants from it? Thus the worst destruction of iniquity presses upon you, since you also say that older people who are beginning to sin and do not yet have many sins, but only one or a few, are alien to that grace.

**CXXXII. JULIAN.** Therefore, when the Apostle preferred grace to sin, he strengthened our doctrine.

**AUGUSTINE.** Rather, he overturned your doctrine, because this grace which he preferred to sin justifies from many sins. Therefore, since it belongs to the small as well as the great, it passes over no small one: it forgives all the sins of all its people, that is, of the small and the great.

**CXXXIII. JULIAN.** Now show where he equated grace with sin, so that, since your faith cannot accommodate remedies preferred to wounds, it may at least accommodate them when reduced to a narrow comparison, without exceeding it. But if you find this written [Col. 1197] anywhere, it will nevertheless be clear that Paul rejected this opinion. And so that the Apostle’s entire meaning may shine forth concisely, he says, “Grace from many sins for justification.” But even according to you infants do not have many sins, since according to the Apostle they have none.

[Note: Here “none,” restored from the manuscripts, was absent from the printed editions.]

**AUGUSTINE.** Even according to you, those who have only just begun to sin do not have many sins. Yet you cannot deny that they belong to this grace that justifies from many sins when they come to Baptism.

The many sins, therefore, are those of the whole people, in which infants too are included. When grace that justifies from many sins reaches this people of the city of God, it finds there many sins in some, few in others, and individual sins in infants. Taken together, these are certainly all many, and by their multitude they refute your many empty words.

But if, according to the Apostle—as you think—infants have no sin, how then, according to the Apostle, are they dead? For according to you too Christ died even for them: “One died for all; therefore all died; and he died for all” (2 Cor. 5:14, 16).

Julian, this was not said by Augustine but by the Apostle—indeed, by Christ himself through his Apostle. Restrain your empty chatter; yield to God.

**CXXXIV. JULIAN.** It is therefore established that here the Teacher of the Gentiles was not discussing the newborn, but those who already exercise the movement of their own will.

**AUGUSTINE.** Digest the intoxication of your contentiousness, wake up, and understand both the sin and the one sin about which it was said, “For if many died through the one man’s offense” (Rom. 5:15). These many are precisely all those of whom he says elsewhere, “As in Adam all die” (1 Cor. 15:22). There you will also see infants, since, as you yourself concede, Christ died for them too. When the Apostle had said that one died for all, he immediately showed what necessarily followed by saying, “Therefore all died; and he died for all.”

**CXXXV. JULIAN.** But what the Apostle added—“Just as through one offense condemnation came upon all, so through one act of righteousness justification came upon all human beings” (Rom. 5:18)—offers us as much help as it creates uproar in your doctrine.

By placing “all” on opposite sides—terms between which there can be no conjunction—he sends us back to the customary usage of Scripture, so that we may understand that “all” is often said for “many.” For there is great barbarity on the very face of the statement: who are all those who come to justification, if all proceed to condemnation? Or who are all those who proceed to punishment, if all are snatched away to glory? The universality of one side excludes the place of the other.

AUGUSTINE. Therefore, where it is said, “In whom all sinned” (ibid., 12), “all” must likewise be understood as “many,” not “all.” If that is so, you are forced to say that not all sinners sinned by imitation of that one man, but many. If you say that not all but many sinned by his imitation because many, not all, sinned—wishing those who did not sin to be understood as infants—you will be answered that [Note: [Col. 1198] Here too, the word *nec* (“nor”) had been omitted in the printed editions.] the infants likewise did not die in him, and consequently Christ did not die for them, since he died only for the dead, as the Apostle cries out. Thus you will come into conflict with yourself and will utterly separate infants from Christ’s grace, since you will be saying that Christ did not die for them. Consequently, you will also deny that they are to be baptized in Christ. For, as the same Apostle says, “All of us who have been baptized in Christ have been baptized into his death” [Note: [Col. 1198] The manuscript of Port. has *in mortem*, “into death.”] (Rom. 6:3). They, however, are baptized into Christ’s death for whom Christ died. Therefore, you will in no way remove infants from original sin unless you simultaneously make them strangers to the grace of Christ’s Baptism [Note: [Col. 1198] After *feceris alienos*, Vignier added: “Therefore, on both sides they are called ‘all,’ because no one is a stranger to the condemnation of generation.” These words do not occur here in the manuscripts of Mar. and Port., but only below, where Vignier himself repeats them.].

But in what seems to you to be a contradiction between these two statements—that all go into condemnation through Adam and that all again go into justification through Christ—you are altogether mistaken. No human being is drawn into condemnation except through Adam, and from that condemnation human beings are freed through the washing of regeneration; and no human being is freed from this condemnation except through Christ. For that reason “all” are spoken of on both sides: no one comes to the condemnation of generation except through the one, and no one comes to the life of regeneration except through the other. Thus the universality of one side does not exclude the place of the other, because from those very people who universally die in Adam, Christ gives life to whomever he wills. These statements, then, will not seem contradictory to you if you are not yourself contradictory.

CXXXVI. JULIAN. But so that you may also observe here how greatly we are fortified: understand the place of the one who heals by reference to the place of the one who wounds [Note: [Col. 1198] So the manuscripts. The printed editions have *vulnerati*, “of the one wounded.”]. If Christ saved everyone, then Adam too must be imagined to have harmed everyone.

AUGUSTINE. Are all therefore not sent into condemnation through Adam because Christ frees from that condemnation those whom he wills? He himself is likewise said to free all precisely because he alone frees anyone at all, just as he is said to enlighten every human being (John 1:9), because no one enlightens anyone if he does not do so himself.

CXXXVII. JULIAN. If Christ changed the functions of the generative organs, let it be believed that Adam perverted them. If Christ corrected something [Note: [Col. 1198] The manuscripts have *correxerit*, “has corrected.”] in the senses of the flesh, let it be judged that Adam’s fault disgraced them [Note: [Col. 1198] The printed editions have *turbasse*, “disturbed,” a corrupt reading.]. If Christ caused medicine to pass through the line of descent, let Adam be said to have transmitted sin through generation.

AUGUSTINE. I have already answered these points; but hear me briefly now as well. If you were a Catholic Christian, it would be evident to you that Adam transmits sin by generation and Christ removes it by regeneration. Adam generates carnally; Christ regenerates spiritually. Do not, therefore, seek a bodily line of descent in both cases. You understand—if you do not dispute the point—that this line of descent has no bearing on spiritual regeneration. Against the weakness of the flesh, however, Christ’s grace now undertakes the struggle; later it will perfect its healing. As a pledge of that future and perpetual health, he has now given the Holy Spirit (2 Cor. 5:5), through whom charity is poured into our hearts (Rom. 5:5), so that, while the flesh has been left for the present struggle, its weakness may not overcome us.

CXXXVIII. JULIAN. But if, while all these things remain in due order in the one whom they receive from nature, the will is drawn to faith without the compulsion of necessity by exhortations, signs, examples, and the promise either of rewards or of punishments—and if through institutions, mysteries, and gifts the will is cared for not by oppression but by expectation, freedom, and invitation—it is evident that, even if the whole world with one spirit resists, whether roaring or raging [Note: [Col. 1199] So the manuscripts. The printed editions have *rapiens*, “snatching away.”], the will of each person, not his birth, has been stained by imitation of sin.

AUGUSTINE. Whichever way you turn, you will not separate infants from original sin unless you deny that they are dead. If you do that, you will at the same time deny that Christ died for them. But if, so as not to deny this, you confess that infants are dead, you will certainly not deny that they died in Adam [Note: [Col. 1199] The printed editions have: “But if you do not deny this and confess that infants are dead, you will certainly deny that they died in Adam.” The reading has been corrected on the authority of the manuscripts.]. Or, if they did not die there, say where they did.

CXXXIX. JULIAN. Although I have dealt with this rather gently [Note: [Col. 1199] The printed editions have *egerit*, “he has dealt,” erroneously.], even if Christ, from the time when he came, were taught to have both closed the path of death to all human beings and bestowed perpetual life, so that from the day on which the Word became flesh no one at all either fell into sin or feared punishment for sin, nevertheless, the condition of the original injustice would not thereby be shown to be one of the utmost liberality [Note: [Col. 1199] Menardus has *ea conditio*, “that condition.”]. For God can and ordinarily does come to the aid of those who do not deserve it, with praise for his clemency; but he cannot punish those who do not sin without overturning justice.

AUGUSTINE. Since, then, infants are punished from the day they emerge from their mother’s womb by a grievous yoke, acknowledge the just Judge and confess original sin. For, as you yourself also admit, he cannot punish those who possess no merit of any sin without overturning justice.

CXL. JULIAN. Consider, then, what the whole discussion has accomplished. If Christ’s grace and Adam’s fault were judged equal in their different effects, so that they were equal in the number of their operations while differing in the kind of those operations, it had to be shown that grace benefited as many as guilt had harmed, so that the fairness and weight of the balance by which they were being measured might be established. The remedy, therefore, ought also to have come to those very places and parts in which the disease had settled—that is, if the ancient crime had affected anything in the movements of the generative organs, in the sensations of those who engage in intercourse, in the obscenity of the limbs, or in the misery of those being born, it ought to have brought remedies by changing the things just mentioned. Otherwise it would be a great testimony to the weakness of an art that was incapable of benefiting anyone: it would have found no place for the disease and, while natural powers were languishing and overturned, would have applied the inert [Note: [Col. 1199] The manuscripts have *inertiae*, “of inertia.”] remedies of the will.

AUGUSTINE. I have already answered this when we spoke of the difference between the present and the future age [Col. 1200] (above, chs. 93, 94, 106). Here, through the pledge of the Spirit, we receive the strength both to struggle and to conquer; there, without any external or internal enemy, we shall enjoy this ineffable and everlasting peace. Whoever therefore wishes to possess here everything that is to be possessed there shows that he has no faith.

CXLI. JULIAN. In the midst of all this, however, truth has shown that, even if a universal medicine were beneficial to the movements and to mortals [Note: [Col. 1200] The printed editions have *motibus aeque*, “equally to the movements.” All the manuscripts, however, have *motibus atque*. Paludanus corrected the reading to *omnibus aeque*, “equally to all.”] of all, including those who had deserved it through no effort or intention whatsoever, guilt would not thereby immediately harm those being born, since they could have contributed nothing of assent to it. And consequently, even if the assessment of grace and sin were equal, it would nevertheless be clear that even then such a balancing did not stand to the extent of proving anyone guilty at birth.

AUGUSTINE. In that grievous yoke under which even infants are weighed down, how is God just if no one is born guilty?

CXLII. JULIAN. But now, since the Apostle not only did not place grace after guilt but even placed it before guilt, saying that benefits abounded much more widely than losses had entered—and since, according to the doctrine of inherited guilt, it is much more evident that sins have harmed than that grace has benefited—it has been irrefutably established that the Apostle Paul thought nothing about inherited sin, and that the Traducians, together with their Manichaean teachers, have been equally refuted by his judgment.

AUGUSTINE. The Apostle Paul did not say, “Benefits abounded much more widely than losses had entered”; he did not say that. You are altogether mistaken, unless you are deliberately deceiving others. For he said that grace abounded much more in many, not in more people, but that it abounded more greatly. In comparison with those who perish, those who are saved are few; but without comparing them with those who perish, they too are many. The reason why the former are more numerous than the latter is something many wish to know as God’s counsel; but to know it belongs either to very few human beings or to none at all.

The Almighty could have refrained from creating those whom, as one who knows all things, he could not fail to know would become wicked, unless the supremely good God were able to make the best use even of many wicked persons. On this point the Apostle taught us something: namely, that God wished to show his wrath and make known his power by enduring with great patience the vessels of wrath, and to make known the riches of his glory upon the vessels of mercy (Rom. 9:22–23). But the Pelagians do not wish to believe that the whole human stock in one man has been corrupted and condemned, and that grace alone heals and frees it from this corruption and condemnation.

“For the righteous man is scarcely saved” (1 Pet. 4:18). Is it difficult for God to free the righteous? Certainly not. Rather, to show the merit for which human nature was condemned, even the Almighty does not wish to free it easily from so great an evil. Hence sins are easy and righteousness arduous, except for those who love it; but the charity that makes them love it is from God (1 John 4:7).

CXLIII. JULIAN. But since I have been rather lengthy here, let us proceed to the rest.

AUGUSTINE. You say this as though you will be briefer elsewhere, when you inquire at such length how to cast clouds of vanity over the Apostle’s clearest words [Col. 1201].

CXLIV. JULIAN. “He said ‘all’ with respect to condemnation through Adam, and ‘all’ with respect to the justification of life through Jesus Christ, although Christ certainly does not transfer to life all those who die in Adam. Yet he said ‘all’ and ‘all,’ because just as no one comes to death without Adam, so no one comes to life without Christ. It is like what we say about a teacher of letters: if he is the only one in the city, ‘This man teaches everyone here to read and write’—not because everyone learns, but because no one learns except from him. Those whom he had first called ‘all,’ he later called ‘many,’ signifying by both expressions the same people, both all and many. For just as through the disobedience of one man many were made sinners, so through the obedience of one man many will be made righteous” (Rom. 5:19). “Let him still ask how sin is found in an infant. The sacred pages answer him: ‘Through one man sin entered the world’” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 2, §§46–47).

We indeed confess that the Apostle’s pages are sacred, but for no other reason than that, agreeing with reason, piety, and faith, they teach us to believe that God is of inviolable equity, to defend his works as good and honorable, and to vindicate moderation, prudence [Note: [Col. 1201] The printed editions have *prudentiae*, “of prudence.”], and justice in his commandments.

AUGUSTINE. God’s justice itself convicts you in the case of infants, since there would be great injustice if infants too were pressed beneath a grievous yoke without any merit or bond of sin.

CXLV. JULIAN. Consequently, we must deny that anyone can be condemned for another’s sin, deny that any sin passes to descendants by the condition of nature, and believe and assert that a human being born from the fecundity established by God is summoned under the just laws of free choice to avoid everything evil and practice everything good. Nor should he, as you maintain, regard the love and necessity of crimes as belonging to the causes of his substance—that is, as having adhered to the very seeds. Nor should he accept the foolish, insane, and impious claim that, to the dishonor of nature, reason, and God, this is contained in the Apostle’s volume, because he said that through one man sin entered this world and death passed to all human beings (Rom. 5:12), especially since he did not permit anyone to remain long in darkness about this: he added that those whom he had called “all” must be understood as “many,” because they had sinned by imitation, not by generation.

AUGUSTINE. Can you say that not all nations were promised to Abraham’s seed where it is said, “In your seed all nations will be blessed” (Gen. 22:18), because the same nations are also called “many” where we read, “I have appointed you the father of many nations” (ibid. 17:5)? Can you, I ask, say this and, in that passage too, contradict with your empty talk the Scripture that foretells what we see fulfilled in reality? When all nations are promised, what else can “all nations” mean? Through your dialectic you teach that “all” is to be understood not as all, but as “many,” which are not all.

If, however, when “many” are mentioned, “all” may indeed not be understood, while where “all” are mentioned and they truly are all, they may properly also be called “many”—so that those who are all may not be understood as few, as happened with those holy men whom the burning fire was forbidden to consume [Note: [Col. 1202] Perhaps *veritus*, “feared,” rather than *vetitus*, “forbidden.”], who all praised God amid the unharmed flames, yet all of them were few because they were three (Dan. 3:49–51)—what force does your argument have when you refuse to understand “all” as all merely because those same people are called “many”? For those who truly are all are sometimes also called “many,” so that they may be distinguished from those who are all in such a way that they are nevertheless few. All a man’s hairs are indeed also many; all his fingers, however, are few.

CXLVI. JULIAN. Finally, he untangled the whole argument he had made by saying: “For just as through the disobedience of one man many were made sinners, so through the obedience of one man many will be made righteous” (Rom. 5:19). Thus, just as no one deserves the rewards of virtue except one who, after Christ’s incarnation, has striven for them by imitating his holiness, so no one is held as a transgressor in Adam except one who has sinned by imitating the transgression of the first man [Note: [Col. 1202] The printed editions have *quasi primi*, “as though of the first.” *Quasi* is absent from the manuscripts of Clar. and Mar.].

AUGUSTINE. This is the hidden and dreadful poison of your heresy: you want Christ’s grace to consist in his example, not in his gift, saying that people become righteous through imitating him, not through the supply of the Holy Spirit, by whose influence they are led to imitate him, and whom he poured out most abundantly upon his own [Note: [Col. 1202] Menardus reads *quae super spiritum super vos*; Vignierius, *qui suum spiritum super eos*. The reading is corrected on the authority of the manuscripts of Port., Mar., and Clar.]. And as though with particular vigilance you add, “after his incarnation,” evidently because you say that the ancients were righteous without his grace, since they did not have his example.

What if, then, after Christ’s incarnation, before hearing the Gospel, some people set before themselves the examples of the righteous of earlier times and lived righteously? What will you do? Where will you place yourselves? Surely such people do not deserve the rewards of virtue? If righteousness comes from imitating the righteous, then Christ died for nothing (Gal. 2:21), because there were righteous people even before him whom those who wished to be righteous could imitate.

What is the meaning, too, of the fact that the Apostle does not say, “Be imitators of Christ, as I also am,” but says, “Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ” (1 Cor. 11:1)? Did he therefore wish to stand before them in place of Christ? Do you see what evils follow from your position when, with the Apostle setting Adam and Christ before us, you wish to oppose imitation to imitation rather than regeneration to generation? [Note: [Col. 1202] The negating particle has been restored here on the authority of the manuscripts.]

CXLVII. JULIAN. Grace reaches even the innocent, to whom Adam’s guilt did not reach. For this reason he carefully emphasized: “Much more has the grace of God and the gift of the one man Jesus Christ abounded for many” (Rom. 5:15). The earlier equality, then, in the case of an age that uses reason and is engaged in opposing pursuits, indicates imitation; but this preference in the lavishness of grace approves the innocent as consecrated and advanced. Since these things are so, recognize that the Apostle confronts you, not me; understand that he bears arms against you. Even if everything else were lacking, this one point would powerfully overthrow your doctrine and that of your teacher Faustus, from whom you were, as it were, stained at the first touch: he says that through the disobedience of one man many, not all, were made sinners, and that through the obedience of one man the righteous were not all made righteous, but many.

To make the contradiction between you and the Apostle clear to the reader’s understanding, the Apostle declares that not all were made sinners through Adam, whereas you say that absolutely all belong through Adam to the devil’s jurisdiction by natural sin. There can be no doubt that there is a great conflict between you and the Apostle.

AUGUSTINE. He says “all,” and calls those same people “many.” By saying “many” he does not deny “all” [Note: [Col. 1203] Here we have restored *omnes*, “all,” from the manuscripts.], lest he contradict himself, as either your wickedness deceives you or your blindness is deceived. Because the Apostle said both—“all” and “many”—I have shown that these two expressions do not conflict, because those very people are called “many” precisely because they are all, just as “all” are sometimes also called “few.” But when you say “not all” of those whom the Apostle called “all,” you are plainly proved to contradict the Apostle.

CXLVIII. JULIAN. For when you and Manichaeus say, “All are naturally sinners,” while the Apostle says, “There are many sinners, not all,” he removes the accusation from the seeds that arms itself in conduct and destroys original sin. To press the very point we have been discussing: the Apostle stipulates that “many” must be understood as sinners through Adam’s disobedience, and “many” as righteous through Christ’s obedience; he shows that those who are righteous are distinguished from those who are criminal. With what audacity, then, do you attempt to argue that natural sin is proved by these words? When you say that all are born criminal through Adam and therefore belong to the devil, but that some are afterward freed from this by Christ, you do not hold the same view as the Apostle, who says that not all were made sinners through Adam, but many.

AUGUSTINE. Since, as we have already shown, there is no contradiction in the fact that the same people are many and all, the Apostle calls those whom he calls many the same people whom he calls all. “Not all,” however, is not said by the Apostle but by you, and consequently you contradict the Apostle. What the Apostle says is true; what you say is therefore false.

And when you said above that the Apostle had “carefully emphasized that the grace of God and the gift of the one man Jesus Christ abounded for more people” (above, ch. 147), wishing “more people” to be understood because his grace reached infants, to whom the imitation of the first man does not pertain, either a faulty manuscript has deceived you, or you yourself are lying, or you have been misled by someone false or deceitful, or by forgetfulness. The Apostle did not say “more people” (*plures*), but “many” (*multos*). Attend to the Greek text, and you will find πολλούς (*pollous*), not πλείστους (*pleistous*). He therefore said that grace abounded much more in many [Col. 1204], not in more people—that is, not in a larger number—as we have already shown.

For if he had said “more people,” on account of the infants whom grace possesses, while the imitation of the first man does not possess them, he would have spoken falsely and would have been like you. For if all the imitators of Christ after his incarnation, with regenerated infants included, are compared with the sinners whom you wish, on account of free choice, to belong to the imitation of the first man—all those who from Adam himself to the end of the age sin by their own will—it plainly appears which group is much more numerous. Thus your falsehood also defeats you.

CXLIX. JULIAN. If he had thought anything like what you think, he certainly ought to have said: “Through the disobedience of one man all were made sinners, but through Christ’s obedience some of them returned to righteousness.” That is precisely how he would have had to speak if he had wished to convey what you invent.

Nevertheless, with such a statement he could not have maintained the other point as well: that Christ’s grace benefited much more than Adam’s iniquity harmed. Even if we were wholly ignorant of the usage by which many were said to be made sinners through the disobedience of one man, it would still remain firmly established that this does not pertain to original sin, which the Apostle repeatedly applies to many, not to all.

AUGUSTINE. I have already answered concerning “many” and “all.” Is it surprising that the Apostle did not speak in the way you say he ought to have spoken if he had meant what we say? Indeed, even if, according to you, the Apostle had said that many were made sinners through the offense of one man in such a way that those many could not be understood as all, but only as those who sinned by imitating the first man through their own will, he still did not say that some of them were justified through Christ’s obedience, although that is nevertheless true.

What, then, is the meaning of your statement: “If the Apostle had thought anything like what we think, he ought to have said: ‘Through the disobedience of one man all were made sinners, but through Christ’s obedience some of them returned to righteousness’”? Do you mean that you deny that some of those who transgressed the law—the only sinners whom you claim belong to the likeness of Adam’s transgression—were converted to righteousness through Christ’s obedience?

We can therefore say to you in return: If the Apostle had thought anything like what you think, he ought certainly to have said: “Through the disobedience of one man many indeed, but not all, were made sinners, and some of them also returned to righteousness through Christ’s obedience.” Or he would have spoken still more plainly in this way if he had thought anything of the sort: “Many Jews indeed were made sinners through the disobedience of one man; having received the law, they sinned through a similar transgression, but Christ’s obedience also justified some of them.”

If the fact that he did not speak as I have said he ought to have spoken, had he held your view, did not prejudice you, neither should it prejudice me that he did not speak in the way you say he ought to have spoken had he held my view. Since, then, the Apostle spoke as he judged he should speak, we must see which of us agrees with him: whether I, who say that what he says is true—“Through one offense condemnation came upon all human beings,” and “Through the disobedience of one man many were made sinners” (Rom. 5:18–19)—because it is not contradictory that those who are many should be all and that those who are all should be many; or you, who say: “Where he says many, they are many; where he says all, they are not all.”

CL. JULIAN. Your ignorance or shamelessness has therefore been exposed: you either do not care or are unable to explain what is being said. The light of truth itself—which Christ called himself (John 14:6)—has also been displayed, and it has been shown that nothing in the words of the Apostle Paul coheres with the Manichaean, that is, your, madness. Let us now devote ourselves to interpretation, so that, just as it has been shown how Paul cannot be understood, it may become clear how he both ought to be and can be understood.

AUGUSTINE. Thus you are abandoned by truth, and cannot find what to say against the Apostle’s manifest words, so that you call Manichaean what so many holy and distinguished teachers, who learned and taught this in the Catholic Church, understood in them—for, having sound understanding, they could not have understood anything else in words so plain. However violently you rave with the poison of the Pelagian pest, you are compelled to admit that they were not Manichaeans.

CLI. JULIAN. Writing to the Romans, at a time when the mingling of the Gentiles had already begun and the churches were therefore being filled from both Jews and Gentiles, Paul settles the disturbance of both peoples. He insists that the Gentiles cannot dissolve their impiety—by which they had exchanged the glory of God for the likeness of the image of man, birds, four-footed animals, and serpents—through ignorance of the law. For by the force of innate reason they could recognize from the things made by God the God who was made known through his works, even though they did not know the rites of the Jewish ceremonies and he remained hidden in the depth of his substance.

As far as uprightness of life is concerned, each person’s own disposition suggested the rule of the law: namely, that one should do nothing to one’s neighbor that one would not wish to suffer oneself. Thus he proves that the profanation of the Gentiles can rightly be condemned, even if not by the law, nevertheless by the justice that established the law. By that justice, those who sinned without the law will also perish without the law.

He then forcefully breaks the Jews, who were more concerned with the matter because they were especially swollen with contempt for the Gentiles, claiming honor for themselves from the purifications of the law and consequently thinking that Christ’s grace, which forgives sins, had not benefited them as it had the Gentiles, since they had avoided those sins through the institution of the law. He argues that they received all the more through forgiveness because, after the admonition of the law, they had sinned without any ignorance. In this way he proves that they were guilty and could have been severely condemned in the examination of that justice by which those who sinned under the law will be judged through the law: “For it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law will be justified” (Rom. 2:13).

With this purpose he argues throughout the whole book, at once suppressing the pride of the Jews and removing the Gentiles’ excuse for their vanity, so that he may teach that Christ’s medicine benefited both peoples equally.

AUGUSTINE [Col. 1206]. You deny this medicine to infants, whom the law itself commanded to be circumcised on the eighth day, prefiguring the grace of the one whose resurrection was manifested by the Lord’s day—that is, the eighth day after the seventh day, the Sabbath. You neither can nor will attend to the fact that an infant who dies without Christ’s grace will perish in the same way as it was said, “The uncircumcised soul of the infant shall perish from his people” (Gen. 17:12, 14). You cannot find the basis of this destruction so long as you say that infants do not contract the sin of origin.

CLII. JULIAN. He both forgave the crimes of the will, from which it had been possible to abstain, and, through imitation of himself, who was the form and standard of the virtues, granted corrected people the glory of blessed eternity. Although, then, he addresses both nations as the occasion and scope of his book require, in the passages at issue he joins battle especially with the Israelites. They dared to despise those coming from the uncircumcised stock to such an extent that they asserted that these people could not pass into fellowship with them even by the support of faith. Against this arrogance he recalls the origins of the Jewish people and shows, at the very root of circumcision [Note: [Col. 1206] The manuscripts have *et ipsa radice*, “and at the very root,” omitting *in*.], that uncircumcision is not so important that abandoning it makes anyone unjust or removing it makes anyone just.

AUGUSTINE. When the Apostle said these things, he was not dealing with circumcision or uncircumcision, but with the commandments of the law, among which is “You shall not covet” (Exod. 20:17; Deut. 5:21), as he himself also recalled (Rom. 7:7). Why do you evade the issue? You mislead the learned while casting darkness before the unlearned.

CLIII. JULIAN. The promise to Abraham that he would be heir of the world therefore came not through the law but through the righteousness of faith. “For if those who are of the law are heirs, faith has been emptied and the promise has been destroyed. For the law produces wrath; but where there is no law, neither is there transgression. Therefore it is by faith, so that the promise may be secure according to grace for all the seed—not only for the one who is of the law, but also for the one who is of the faith of Abraham, who is the father of us all, as it is written: ‘I have appointed you the father of many nations’—before God in whom he believed, who gives life to the dead and calls things that are not as though they were. Against hope he believed in hope, so that he might become the father of many nations, according to what was said: ‘So shall your seed be.’ And, not being weakened in faith, he considered [Note: [Col. 1206] So the manuscripts. Vignierius has: “And, not being weakened in faith, he did not consider.”] his own body, already dead, since he was almost a hundred years old, and Sarah’s dead womb. Yet he did not waver in unbelief at God’s promise, but was strengthened in faith, giving glory to God, fully knowing that whatever he had promised, he was able also to do. Therefore it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (ibid. 4:13–22).

AUGUSTINE. Are you not ashamed to recall these passages while attacking the grace by which these promises are fulfilled? You speak against God when you say, “We do it”—what he promised that he himself would do. In Isaac, the son promised to Abraham, those people were prefigured—not those who make themselves righteous, but those whom God himself was going to make righteous [Col. 1207]. Hence through the prophet he says to the whole Church: “For I am the Lord, who make you” (Isa. 45:8, according to the Septuagint). Therefore they are called children of the promise, as the Apostle says most plainly: “But it is not possible for the word of God to have failed. For not all who are from Israel are Israel, nor because they are Abraham’s seed are they all children; but ‘In Isaac shall your seed be called.’ That is, it is not the children of the flesh who are the children of God, but the children of the promise are counted as seed” (Rom. 9:6–8).

What God promised, God does. Thus this whole passage builds up those whose hope is in God, just as it overturns those who trust in their own strength (Ps. 48:7). Accordingly, just as it builds up the Catholic faith, so it overturns the Pelagian error.

CLIV. JULIAN. How entirely this passage is hostile to your opinion was discussed in the first work, and, if anything from that discussion needs to be recalled, it will be explained. For now, observe that the promise made to Abraham in reward for his faith—by which he was said to be appointed the father of many nations—shows that he must not be defended as the father of only one people, since he was foretold as the father of many nations. Nor did he receive the reward of his faith in such a way that other believers like him should be thought excluded from sharing in the reward.

“But it was written,” he says, “not for his sake alone that it was reckoned to him, but also for our sake, to whom it will be reckoned if we believe in him who raised Jesus Christ our Lord from the dead, who was delivered up for our offenses and raised for our justification” (Rom. 4:23–25).

AUGUSTINE. Tell us, empty men—not defenders but puffers-up of free choice—who, being ignorant of God’s righteousness and wishing to establish your own righteousness, are not subject to God’s righteousness (ibid. 10:3): tell us, I say, if the Gentiles had been unwilling to believe and live righteously, would the promise made to Abraham have been emptied?

“No,” you will say. Therefore, so that Abraham might obtain the enlargement of his seed as the reward of faith, the will of the Gentiles was prepared by the Lord; and so that they might will what they could also have been unwilling to will, this was accomplished by him who is able also to do whatever he has promised.

CLV. JULIAN. Since Abraham was declared a witness to faith while still in uncircumcision and obtained the enlargement of his seed as the reward for it, by what rule, he asks, do you, Jew, think that the Gentiles do not belong to the fellowship of righteousness when they restore Abraham’s faith by believing equally in God’s powers?

AUGUSTINE. You speak well against yourselves. For if they believe in God’s powers, then, unlike you, they do not trust in their own strength in order to be justified—that is, in order to become righteous—but in the strength of the one who justifies the ungodly.

CLVI. JULIAN. “Why do you think,” he asks, “that nations cannot be brought into Abraham’s family without the consecrations of the law, when it is clear that the promise made to Abraham preceded the law and was not granted through washings [Note: [Col. 1207] So the manuscripts. The printed editions have *ablutioni*, “to washing,” singular.] but through conduct?”

AUGUSTINE [Col. 1208]. If, as you suppose, a human being makes for himself these practices—which you unquestionably wish to be understood as good—God, who foreknew all things, ought to have predicted them, not promised them. In that case it would not be said of him in this matter, “He is able also to do what he promised” (Rom. 4:21), but rather, “He is able also to announce what he foreknew,” or, “He is able also to reveal it.” But when human beings say, “We do what God promised,” they make themselves powerful through boastfulness [Note: [Col. 1208] Menardus and the manuscripts have *instantia*, “persistence” or “zeal.”] and arrogantly accuse him of lying.

CLVII. JULIAN. “For if those who are of the law are heirs, faith has been emptied and the promise destroyed” (ibid. 14). Unless this statement is understood, it raises a very serious question. Beyond doubt, he is speaking of those whom he had previously called “of the circumcision,” whom he knew to claim this for themselves alone, so that they thought no one besides themselves could be admitted to the dignity of Abraham’s seed. He had gathered this through his argument: since not only those who are of the circumcision, but also those who, coming from uncircumcision, wished to follow the footsteps of Abraham’s faith, were rightly reckoned as Abraham’s children—
**AUG.** What if they had not been willing? Would the promise have been nullified? I urge you to understand whose grace you are hostile to when you deny that God works upon human wills in their minds—not so that the unwilling may believe, which is said most absurdly, but so that the unwilling may become willing. It is not like what a human teacher does by teaching and exhorting, threatening and promising in the word of God—which is done in vain unless God works inwardly, by his inscrutable ways, to produce willing. For when the teacher plants and waters with words, we can say, “Perhaps the hearer believes; perhaps he does not believe” [Note: [Col. 1208] From the manuscripts we have added *perhaps he does not believe*.]; but when God gives the growth (I Cor. III, 6), he undoubtedly believes and makes progress. Behold the difference between law and promise, between letter and spirit.

**CLVIII. JUL.** Since, then, above he had acted in such a way that we should understand that the Gentiles could not be excluded from participation in righteousness, but were to be counted among Abraham’s offspring through the same faith as the sons of circumcision, he now asserted that no one from circumcision belongs to the promise given to Abraham. But this is wholly contradictory unless it is understood. What he therefore says—“For if those who are of the law are heirs, faith is emptied and the promise destroyed”—he did not pronounce in the sense that no Jew is believed to become, through faith, an heir of the ancient promise. Rather, a phrase is missing, whose place is supplied by the understanding: that not only those who are of the law are heirs. It would be as though he had said: “For if those who are of the law alone are heirs, faith is emptied.” Indeed, the foreskin would appear to be excluded if the inheritance of blessing reached no one except those who were of circumcision. We must therefore understand the customary usage of Scripture, since what is not expressly said is not thereby immediately denied, and the losses of words are supplied by the work of interpretation.

**AUG.** That is how those who do not understand understand it. Why, I ask, do you not consider that they are not heirs through the law because the law produces wrath? “For where there is no law, neither is there transgression” (Rom. IV, 15). They are heirs through the promise, however, because God himself accomplishes what he promises. For whoever thinks that he fulfills the commands of the law by the choice of his own will, without the Spirit of grace, wishes to establish his own righteousness rather than receive the righteousness of God. For why does the same apostle say, “That I may be found in him, not having my own righteousness, which is from the law, but the righteousness which is through faith, the righteousness from God” (Philipp. III, 9)? Why does he call that righteousness his own which is from the law, and reject that righteousness, but call the righteousness which is through faith not his own, but from God? Is the law not from God? Who but an unbeliever would say this? Rather, he calls it his own righteousness from the law when a person thinks that the law is sufficient for him to carry out the divine commands, trusting in his own strength. But he says that righteousness through faith is from God because God distributes to each person the measure of faith (Rom. XII, 3); and it belongs to faith to believe that God works in us both to will and to accomplish (Philipp. II, 13), just as he worked in that seller of purple, whose understanding he had opened so that she might attend to what Paul was saying (Acts XVI, 14). Accordingly, even those Jews who believed in Christ, among whom Paul also belonged, are altogether to be called heirs through the law [Note: [Col. 1209] The printed editions read, “are not at all to be called.” The negative particle is deleted on the authority of the manuscripts.], but rather through the promise. For this reason it was said, “In Isaac shall your offspring be called,” because “not those who are children of the flesh are children of God, but the children of the promise are counted as offspring” (Rom. IX, 7–8).

**CLIX. JUL.** The apostle therefore gathered the argument in this way: If no one were an heir of blessing except those who are of the law, then, just as the foreskin plainly stood excluded, so it would follow that no one who had been of the law could be deprived of the blessing. That is, if circumcision had such force that without it faith had no force, then, just as it was clear that the Gentiles were rejected, so it would be proved that no Jew could ever go to destruction [Note: [Col. 1209] Menardus: “to prediction.” Vignierius: “to blessing.” The reading is corrected from the manuscripts.].

**AUG.** How did that follow, you coarse dialectician? How did it follow that, if no one were an heir of blessing except those who are of the law, no one who had been of the law would be deprived of the blessing? Does the fact that no one is an heir unless he is baptized mean that all who are baptized are heirs? I say this not because that is the issue being debated between you, but to show how sharp you are, since you call me duller than a pestle (above, ch. 117).

**CLX. JUL.** But now, since you admit that transgressors under the law are not heirs of blessing, because the law produces wrath, it is clear [Note: [Col. 1209] The printed editions read “and it is clear.” The word *and* should be removed in accordance with the manuscripts.] that this promise applies not to circumcision but to faith. The promise would be destroyed if no one were righteous apart from the law, since the law was given four hundred and thirty years after the promise (Galat. III, 17), and it would show Abraham himself, Isaac, Jacob, and all the saints in the middle of their lives [Note: [Col. 1209] Vignierius: “immediately.” The manuscripts have “in the middle of life,” perhaps for “in the middle of their age.”] deprived of the blessing, which could not have been conferred on anyone without the law.

**[Col. 1210] AUG.** Rather, the promise would be destroyed if anyone were righteous through the law. “For if those who are of the law are heirs, faith is made void and the promise is emptied; for the law produces wrath” (Rom. IV, 14–15)—precisely so that God’s grace may be required for escaping wrath.

**CLXI. JUL.** Since this is plainly false—for under the law sinners deserved punishment, and before the law righteousness and faith were not deprived of the fruits of their reward—it is clear that the glory of that promise belongs not to flesh mutilated by the knife, but to minds distinguished by uprightness. There follows, however, a thunderbolt of a sentence against the doctrine of transmission: “For the law,” he says, “produces wrath; but where there is no law, neither is there transgression.” Prove, then, that the law was given to the conceived, and that the law can be given to those being born, so that it can accuse them of transgression. For our part, with the apostle—we defend him as having thought nothing contrary to reason—we believe that there is no transgression at an age in which the law could not exist, because “where there is no law, neither is there transgression.” That law produces wrath, not through any fault of its own, but through the iniquity of those who prefer sins to virtues.

**AUG.** Is this, then, not Christ’s law: “Unless someone is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John III, 5)? You see that this law also applies to infants. Rather, tell me: what transgression was the infant guilty of, whose soul was to perish from his people if he were not circumcised on the eighth day (Gen. XVII, 14), so that he was punished with such a penalty? Unless it is because, although he himself had committed no sin, he was held guilty in the likeness of Adam’s transgression, in whom all sinned (Rom. V, 14, 12). You strive to obscure these apostolic words, so clear, and to twist them, so straightforward, with immense but futile labor.

**CLXII. JUL.** The apostle therefore approved the proposition that it was not written only for Abraham—that it was reckoned to him as righteousness—but also for us, to whom it is undoubtedly reckoned when we believe in God, who raised Jesus Christ from the dead: “He was delivered up,” he says, “for our offenses, and rose for our justification” (ibid. IV, 23–25).

**AUG.** You separate infants from this grace, although you contend that they possess no offense derived from their origin. Consequently, the benefit whereby Christ was delivered up for our offenses does not pertain to them. Yet, while thinking and teaching these things, you dare to call yourselves catholic Christians!

**CLXIII. JUL.** How forcefully he insists that, before the just Judge God, the sins of others do not harm other people. In commending Christ’s death, he carefully declares that Christ suffered death for our offenses—which were both many and ours—and not for one offense belonging to another person, a man long since dead.

**AUG.** The disobedience of one man can certainly and not improperly be called another’s offense, because, before we were born, we had done nothing of our own, whether good or evil. But because we were all in the one who committed it when he committed it, and because that offense was so great and of such a kind that the whole of human nature was corrupted by it—as the manifest misery of the human race itself sufficiently indicates—this offense belonging to another becomes ours through an indebted succession. For this reason a catholic teacher, who correctly understood the apostle, said: “All human beings are born under sin, and their very birth is in fault” (Ambrose, *On Repentance*, book 1, ch. 2 or 3).

If you are willing to follow his understanding, and that of his companions in catholic truth, you will not be compelled to separate infants from the benefit of the death of him who “was delivered up for our offenses”; and “one died for all.” Here the apostle’s next words cry out: “Therefore all died; and he died for all” (II Cor. V, 14–15). You protest, “Infants did not die.” Cry out also what follows: “Therefore he did not die for them.” Then see whether you yourselves are not lying dead [Note: [Col. 1211] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “see whether you too are lying dead.”], since you deny Christ’s death to the dead so that they may not be made alive. You say that the sin of one long-dead man ought not, as you suppose, to be imputed to them [Note: [Col. 1211] Vignierius omits *of one*, which is restored from the manuscripts.].

Nor do you consider that the first man, Adam, had long since died, yet after him came the second man, Christ, although thousands upon thousands of human beings arose between the former and the latter. It is therefore evident that everyone who is born from Adam through the succession of generation belongs to Adam [Note: [Col. 1211] The printed editions read *who is born from her* and, below, *who is reborn in her*; the manuscripts consistently read *him* (*illo*).], just as everyone who is reborn in Christ through the abundance of grace belongs to Christ. Thus the entire human race is, in a certain sense, two men: the first and the second.

**CLXIV. JUL.** Therefore, when he says “many offenses,” he has no suspicion of anything belonging to the Manichaeans—that is, of inherited sin.

**AUG.** But certainly, contentious man, there would be many offenses, possessed by many people—even separate offenses, one belonging to each person—if they came to the bath of regeneration when they first began to sin. According to this—your distortion, not reason—you make all such people strangers to the grace that justifies from many offenses, because you do not want just any human beings, whose offenses are individual, to share in it. How much more numerous, then, are the offenses when those are added which some have in greater number and others in fewer? Yet this grace frees people from all of them, concerning which it was said, “From many offenses unto justification” (Rom. V, 16).

“Adam existed, and in him we all existed; Adam perished, and in him all perished.” Ambrose said this (*Book 7 on Luke* XV, 24)—calumniously, he was not a Manichaean. Cyprian said that infants contract the contagion of ancient death through their first birth (*Letter 64, to Fidus*)—calumniously, he was not a Manichaean. Hilary said that all sinned in the one Adam—calumniously, he was not a Manichaean [Note: [Col. 1211] See the first work against Julian, book 1, nos. 5–11, and book 2, nos. 22–31.]. In what Church did they learn these things? Calumniously, it was not a Manichaean church. And because it was catholic, and remains catholic, it could not endure you, who think and argue against these things; and, so that it might remain catholic, it fortified the weakness of its infants by condemning you.

**CLXV. JUL.** “Therefore, being justified by faith, let us have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we also have access to this grace in which we stand, and we glory in hope of the glory of God” (Rom. V, 1–2). You see, he says, that justification was bestowed on you through the forgiveness of sins. Hold firmly to this harmony, and with equal hearts praise the gifts of the Mediator. By his gift it was bestowed on us that we should have entrance into this grace; and those whom justice held guilty—because nature had not made us guilty, but the will—he restored to freedom and rescued from punishment. He granted that those who had expected eternal punishments might now rejoice in the hope of God’s glory.

**AUG.** This justification is not bestowed through the forgiveness of sins alone, unless you are its authors. For God justifies the ungodly not only by forgiving the evil he commits, but also by granting love, so that he may turn away from evil and do good through the Holy Spirit. The apostle continually asked for this Spirit’s assistance [Note: [Col. 1212] The Mar., Port., and Clar. manuscripts read “ministration,” less correctly. The wording alludes to Phil. I, 19: “through your prayer and the supply of the Spirit of Jesus Christ.”] for those to whom he said, “But we pray to God that you do no evil” (II Cor. XIII, 7). You wage war against this grace, so that you do not defend free will by argument but deceive it through presumption.

**CLXVI. JUL.** But, so that the power and security of this doctrine might be expressed more fully, he pursues what Christian philosophy confers on the faithful: “And not only this, but we also glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation produces perseverance, perseverance approval, approval hope; and hope does not disappoint, because the love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us” (Rom. V, 3–5).

That is: These benefits were not bestowed on us only so that we might one day rejoice in the greatness of the gifts; even now, established amid the burning pressures of anguish, we are cheerful in possessing virtue itself, and we laugh at the fury of our persecutors, judging the cruelty of the ungodly to be more an instruction in perseverance than a disturbance of our joy. Thus we do not refrain from sinning merely for the sake of rewards; rather, we count the very act of not sinning as a reward.

**AUG.** If not sinning is a reward, who gives this reward? I suppose you will not say, “The person gives it to himself,” although the perversity of your heresy forces you to say this. If, then, God gives this reward, so that a person does not sin, I see that it ought rather to be called a gift than a reward, lest it appear that some merits preceded it—especially since Pelagius himself condemned those who say that God’s grace is given according to our merits [Note: [Col. 1212] See the *Book on the Proceedings of Pelagius*, nos. 30 and 60.].

But how this gift is given—that is, the gift of not sinning—you yourself said shortly before when you recalled the apostle’s words: “Because the love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us.” Accordingly, in Christian philosophy, when we glory in tribulations, this does not originate from us, because we have received this also [Note: [Col. 1213] The printed editions read *who*. The manuscripts have *because*.]. Otherwise, as though a person were glorying in something produced by himself for himself, he would be told: “For what do you have that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you glory as though you had not received it?” (I Cor. IV, 7). And yet we glory, not as though we had not received it [Note: [Col. 1213] Here, on the authority of the manuscripts, we restore the words: “And yet we glory, not as though we had not received it.”], but we glory in him who gave this, so that “the one who glories may glory in the Lord” (ibid. I, 31). This is the grace that the catholic faith proclaims. Why, I ask, does your error attack it, when it convicts you even by your own mouth?

**CLXVII. JUL.** Moreover, when we see that the things promised are dealt with in testaments, we count all the good and evil things of the present life as mere playthings, and we assess the faithfulness of God’s promise according to the greatness of his love toward us. For the disappointment of eternal benefits will not refute our hope [Note: [Col. 1213] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read “did not refute.”], since we possess God’s love as the pledge of future blessedness, and it has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us. That is, through the gifts of the Holy Spirit, God has demonstrated his love toward the human race.

**AUG.** You do not want “not sinning” to be among these gifts. Trusting in your own strength, you want to give this to yourself. Do not be angry, I beg you: “Cursed is everyone who places his hope in man” (Jerem. XVII, 5).

**CLXVIII. JUL.** He will therefore faithfully restore everything that he promised to the faithful.

**AUG.** Certainly he will restore even this itself: that they should be faithful. For he promised Abraham the faith of the nations, and a certain great believer says, “I obtained mercy so that I might be faithful” (I Cor. VII, 25).

**CLXIX. JUL.** “For he who did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, through whom he consecrated us by the operation of the Holy Spirit, has undoubtedly given us all things together with him” [Note: [Col. 1213] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read “into the operation.”] [Note: [Col. 1213] The manuscripts read “will give,” in accordance with the Greek *charisetai*.] (Rom. VIII, 32). “For why, when we were still weak, did Christ die for the ungodly at the appointed time?” (ibid. V, 6).

**AUG.** You recall divine testimonies by which your error is overthrown. It was not said, “Christ also died for the ungodly,” but, he says, “he died for the ungodly.” And, as you yourself also confessed elsewhere [Note: [Col. 1213] In the first book addressed to Turbantius. See book 3 against Julian, no. 58, and book 6, no. 8.], he died even for infants. Yet, I do not know with what face, you deny that the ungodliness of the first man passed into them by inheritance [Note: [Col. 1213] Here we add *of the first* from the ancient books.]. How, then, do they belong to him who died for the ungodly?

**CLXX. JUL.** “For scarcely does anyone die for a righteous person; perhaps someone might dare to die for a good person. But God commends his love toward us, because, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us. Much more, then, having now been justified in his blood, shall we be saved through him from wrath. For if, while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, having been reconciled, shall we be saved by his life. And not only this, but we also glory in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received reconciliation” (Rom. V, 7 and following). He has disclosed how wholly Christ acted with compassion: he deigned to die for those who deserved nothing good.

**AUG.** These words of yours are so carefully qualified that they appear to touch infants as well, since you admit that they have deserved nothing good, whom you acknowledge to have done nothing good. But the apostle did not speak in that way; he said that Christ died for the ungodly and for sinners. You have therefore vainly thought that Christ’s great mercy should be diminished. He died for those who deserved evil. You separate infants from so great a benefit of the Savior, because you say that they are saved. But he says, “The healthy do not need a physician” (Matt. IX, 12). Christ is therefore not needed by infants, for whom, according to you, he is not Jesus. But depart, wicked men [Note: [Col. 1214] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read “learn.”]: infants do need him. He also saves them from their sins, since he received that very name for this reason: the angel said, “You shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins” (ibid. I, 21).

**CLXXI. JUL.** They had trampled underfoot reason and the law through love of crimes, following after their desires, which their own conscience, whose power is greatest, chastised. But since it was evident that the prophets too had often striven for justice with contempt of death, and that very many had run toward destruction with an untroubled spirit for great causes and for things shining with the splendor of inherent dignity [Note: [Col. 1214] We restore the negative particle here from the Mar. Clar. manuscripts.], the apostle added this passage lest Christ’s unique virtue should not be made more evident by examples of this kind [Note: [Col. 1214] Masius and the Colbert manuscript read “less clear” (*dilutior*) for “clearer” (*dilucidior*).], thereby showing that his love and courage stand out at a uniquely lofty height.

“I agree that some people, although rarely and scarcely, have nevertheless chosen to die for just and good causes. But the dignity of their undertakings—that is, the renown of the causes for which they had fought—tempered the pain of their dangers. Christ, however, had nothing to love in the pursuits of the ungodly, and he did not disdain to expend himself for those who were deformed by their own will. It is clear that he surpassed all others in virtue, because, even if he can have a few companions in endurance, he can have none in the cause. Let us therefore despair of nothing concerning his generosity, because, if he died for us while we were still sinners, much more, now justified in his blood, shall we be saved through him from wrath.”

**AUG.** Therefore do not remove infants from the number of sinners, since you admit that Christ died even for them.

**CLXXII. JUL.** And after the reconciliation that we deserved to have with God, through the work [Note: [Col. 1214] In the manuscripts: “through the works.”] of the Mediator, we ought to receive eternal joys in our minds, and hope not only for salvation but also for glory.

**AUG.** I ask you to attend to what the apostle says, and why he came to speak of the first man. He was discussing the reconciliation which you too admit was accomplished through Christ the Mediator, from the enmity that we had with God. Behold the apostle’s words: “Therefore, being justified by faith,” he says, “let us have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ.” Shortly afterward: “For if Christ, when we were weak, died at the appointed time for the ungodly.” Again shortly afterward: “But God,” he says, “commends his love toward us, because, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us; much more, now justified in his blood, we shall be saved from wrath through him.”

Attend further: “For if, while we were enemies,” he says, “we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, having been reconciled, we shall be saved by his life.” This reconciliation, which he commended so many times, he also placed at the end, saying, “Through whom we have now received reconciliation”; and then he added, “Therefore, just as through one man sin entered the world” (Rom. V, 1–12).

Just as enmity came through this one man, so reconciliation came through the one Christ. Therefore, whoever says that infants are free from the sin through which enmity arose certainly denies that they belong to this reconciliation, for which Christ became Mediator. Accordingly, he also separates them from the justification that takes place in Christ’s blood. The reason why that blood was shed—when he commended it to be drunk—was stated as nothing other than the remission of sins (Matt. XXVI, 28).

Consequently, if infants have no sins, Christ’s death benefits them not at all. For through it we were reconciled to God when we were enemies, which, according to you, infants were not. And so that we might die to the sin in which there was enmity, “as the same apostle says, all who were baptized into Christ were baptized into his death.” To reach these words, he says: “For if we have died to sin, how shall we live in it?” And immediately, to show that we had died to sin: “Do you not know,” he says, “that all who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death?” (Rom. VI, 2–3).

Where is your freedom and strength of mind? Why are you afraid to say what you are not afraid to believe: that infants ought not to be baptized in Christ, since you say that they have no sin to which they may die?

**CLXXIII. JUL.** “Therefore, just as through one man sin entered this world, and through sin death, and thus death passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned” [Note: [Col. 1215] The manuscripts read, “and thus passed into all human beings,” omitting “death.” But shortly afterward, in the repetition of the same sentence, the manuscripts have “death” and the printed editions omit it.] (ibid. V, 12). To subdue the pride of the Jews, who did not consider the forgiveness of sins as necessary for themselves as for the Gentiles, claiming the holiness of the law as a privilege for their race, he penetrates the disease of human society and traces back the multitude of sinners, so that the authority of antiquity might reveal how much power iniquity had occupied in this world, and so that he might show how many ancient and long-standing crimes, handed down from the obscenity of earlier generations to their descendants through mutual imitation, the grace of Christ had removed.

For this reason he recalls the first man—not the one from whom sin began, since it is clear that the woman sinned first, but the one who, by the privilege of his sex, had assumed the mastery of sin. Through him, therefore, sin entered, and through sin death—undoubtedly that death which is promised to sinners, namely eternal death. “And thus,” he says, “death passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned.” He has plainly shown how this death passed to descendants: through imitation, obviously, not through generation.

**AUG.** You have already been answered as to why he did not name the woman, from whom sin had its beginning, but one man: either so that she too might be understood in him because of the one flesh, or because generation begins from the man, through which he wished to show that sin entered the world.

But you who say that the death which is in sin passed to descendants through imitation, not generation, why do you not openly say that infants ought not to be baptized in Christ Jesus? If they are to be baptized in Christ, since everyone baptized in Christ is baptized into his death, then undoubtedly they too die to sin.
