[Col. 1216] The apostle proved that we had died to sin precisely from this: that we were baptized into Christ’s death. For when he had said, “If we have died to sin, how shall we live in it?”, he immediately showed that we had died to sin by saying, “Do you not know that all who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death?”

Therefore, whoever has no sin has nothing to die to in Baptism [Note: [Col. 1216] The printed editions read “why” (*cur*); the Mar. manuscript more correctly reads “to whom/to which” (*cui*).]. Whoever, when baptized, does not die to sin is not baptized into Christ’s death; and consequently is not baptized into Christ. Why do you evade the issue? Open your hells freely; let those who do not wish their infants, dead in sin, to be made alive in Baptism enter them freely.

**CLXXIV. JUL.** After saying, “It passed into all human beings,” he immediately added, “in whom all sinned.” The phrase “in whom all sinned” indicates nothing other than that all sinned, according to the saying of David: “By what does a young man correct his way?” That is, “How does he correct his way?” “By keeping your words” (Ps. CXVIII, 9). He is therefore said to be corrected in that by which he is corrected. Similarly, the apostle said that death passed into them in that in which all sinned by their own will—not so that the phrase “in which” might point to Adam or sin, but so that it might express that all sinned.

**AUG.** Open your eyes: “In Adam all die.” If infants are not dead in him, they are not made alive in Christ. Why, then, do you rush with them to the Baptism of the life-giver and Savior under a damnable pretense, when, crying out that they are alive and healthy [Note: [Col. 1217] Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read “condemning.”], you do not want them to be made alive and healed?

**CLXXV. JUL.** Numerous examples from Scripture testify that “all” is used for “many,” in accordance with the saying, “All have turned aside; together they have become useless.” A little later he says, “They devour my people as though eating bread” (Ps. XIII, 3–4), showing that this people was distinguished from all those whom he had declared to practice evil.

In the Gospel it is reported, “All the people were shouting, ‘Crucify! Crucify!’” (Matt. XXVII, 23; Luke XXIII, 21). Yet by this general expression neither the apostles, nor Nicodemus, nor the holy women are included. This same apostle, after calling them “all” here, names “many” shortly afterward.

**AUG.** This has already been answered: “all” and “many” are not contradictory, because those “all” are not few but many. And what you recalled from the Psalm—“All have turned aside; together they have become useless”—is entirely true. For it distinguished the sons of human beings, all of whom had turned aside, from the sons of God, who had not turned aside and whom they were devouring. “God looked down upon the sons of human beings”: all these had turned aside. The sons of God were excluded from their number.

Among all these sons of human beings who had turned aside was also that entire people which cried, “Crucify! Crucify!” Those who had already believed in Christ in no way belonged to that people.

If you can, strip away from yourself the claim that one died for all, and dare to say that not all for whom Christ died were dead, when the apostle immediately presses your throat and crushes your most audacious statement by showing what follows: “Therefore all died.” Do not praise the apostle in this way; do not interpret him in such a way that you refuse to hear: “If one died for all, therefore all died” (II Cor. V, 14–15).

Death with sin passed into all these, through him in whom all die. Infants are among them, because Christ died for them also. He died for all for this reason: because all died. Whatever you argue, whatever evasions you make, whatever apostolic words you attempt to overturn or distort, you do not show that infants are free from the death that is in sin, because you do not dare deny that Christ died for them also [Note: [Col. 1217] The printed editions add “who died.” It is absent from the manuscripts.] [Note: [Col. 1217] From the manuscripts we have added “whatever evasions you make.”]

**CLXXVI. JUL.** Let the point we have made, then, be clear. The apostle said “all” and “many,” whom he declares subject to death because they sinned by their own will. He therefore accuses not original but voluntary crime. Indeed, the words indicate nothing else if their meaning and proper force are weighed. For if he believed that sin had passed to descendants by generation—that is, that it had been hurled at those who had not been there—he would have declared falsely that all had sinned.

**AUG.** I could say to you: How did Adam’s descendants follow the example of Adam sinning, when they were not there and neither saw, heard, nor believed the sin itself? But I do not say this. “Adam existed, and in him we all existed; Adam perished, and in him all perished; therefore all die in him” (Ambrose, *Book 7 on Luke* XV, 24) [Note: [Col. 1218] The printed editions read, “Adam sinned, and in him all sinned.” But the manuscripts, as in Ambrose, read, “Adam perished … all perished.”]. Listen to the apostle speaking with complete clarity, rather than to your own tortuous chatter.

**CLXXVII. JUL.** What one person does and directs toward others is not truly said to have been done by all. Either it passed into them, and they did not sin; or they themselves sinned—in which case the language expresses the operation—and it passed into them only through imitation.

**AUG.** If someone brings gout upon himself through intemperance and passes it on to his children, as often happens [Note: [Col. 1218] Thus from Menardus and Vignierius. In B., *happened*. M.], is it not rightly said that this disease passed from the parent into them? Is it not also right to say that they themselves did this in their parent, since, when he did it, they were in him, and thus they and he were still one? They therefore did it—not by the action of human beings, but by the principle already present in the seeds.

What is sometimes found in bodily diseases was known to have occurred in the ancient and great sin of that one first ancestor [Note: [Col. 1218] The printed editions read *illius* (“that one”); the manuscripts read *unius* (“one”).], by which the whole of human nature was corrupted. He said this in language of the greatest clarity, which you strive to obscure: “Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death, and thus it passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Rom. V, 12) [Note: [Col. 1218] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read, “Through the sin of one man, sin entered.”].

He intended to commend Christ’s grace, establishing a pattern by contrast and setting the founder of regeneration against the founder of generation.

**CLXXVIII. JUL.** As for what you thought you could bring against me, either in this book to which I am now replying or in those which you had written to Marcellinus—namely, that sin passed over when, to use your words, “all human beings were that one man” (*On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, book 1, no. 11)—truth easily rubs it away and exposes it to the ridicule of any prudent person [Note: [Col. 1218] The printed editions read *cujusque*; the manuscripts read *cujusce*.].

For such an argument indicates nothing except your impiety—your impiety, I say, in believing that souls are transmitted in the manner once condemned in the profaneness of Tertullian and Mani, just as bodies are transmitted. This is so wicked that, when it was brought against you by us in the letter that we sent to the East, you attempted in the books that you recently sent to Boniface to repel the charge by denying it.

For you say: “But they say that we confess the transmission of souls; I do not know in whose books they have read this” (*Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, book 3, no. 26)—so that, clearly, you may swear that you have said nothing of the kind [Note: [Col. 1218] The manuscripts read *you may swear*.].

But so that your falsehood may be exposed by comparing your own words, how can you say that the transmission of souls—a truly profane opinion—is not held in your thinking, when you profess that all human beings were that one man? If you do not believe that a part of the soul is bound to the seeds, with what mouth do you write that all human beings were the one Adam, since a human being cannot exist except as soul and body together?

AUG. Do you think a human being cannot be called merely the body of a human being, when you know that the only-begotten Son of God himself, our Lord Jesus Christ, crucified and buried under Pontius Pilate—as his whole Church confesses, and many heresies, including yours, also confess—was nevertheless buried only as to his body? Therefore, according to you, Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, our Lord, ought not to have been called buried [Note: [Col. 1219] The printed editions read: “According to his divinity, therefore, Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, our Lord, ought not to have been buried,” etc. The manuscripts provide the corrected reading.], since Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, our Lord, consists not only of a body, but of the Word of God, a rational soul, and a body. Yet when the confession had reached these words, “He was crucified under Pontius Pilate,” it ought to have added, “and his body was buried.” Nor should Scripture have said of the first man himself, who is under discussion, “God formed man from the dust of the earth” (Gen. II, 7), because only the body of a human being is from the earth. Finally, cry out that God himself was mistaken when, threatening death, he said to the man, “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (ibid. III, 19), since according to your teaching he ought rather to have said, “Your body is earth, and it shall go to earth.” Therefore, because “Adam existed, and in him we all existed” (Ambrose, Book 7 on Luke XV, 24)—which Catholic teachers before us learned and taught in the holy Church according to the holy Scriptures—I said, “All of them were that one man.” For those two also, male and female, were no longer two, but one flesh (Matt. XIX, 6). And I said this of all who were to be begotten: when the sin occurred, all of them were that one man. For as yet no one from him had been transferred by generation into a mother; and certainly sons are transferred from males into females. And therefore, in whatever manner and to whatever extent, all who were born from him were that one man, whether according to the body alone or according to both parts of the human being. I confess that I do not know this, nor am I ashamed, as you are, to admit that I do not know what I do not know. Yet for that reason I do not fail to know that it is written of every human being, “Man was made like vanity; his days pass away like a shadow” (Ps. CXLIII, 4), because elsewhere the same holy Scripture says, “Yet every living man is altogether vanity” (Ps. XXXVIII, 6). This would not have come about under a justly creating God if original sin did not exist.

CLXXIX. JUL. Furthermore, even if you refer this solely to the flesh, your folly of understanding still cannot be excused, when you say, “All of them were that one man,” although at the time when Adam sinned there were already two human beings, not one—that is, Adam himself and his wife—from whose substance, not from whose guilt, the human race sprang, in accordance with the way God had established it.

AUG. I have already said it, and here I say it again: I said, “All of them were that one man,” of those whom Adam was going to sow—that is, to beget. Therefore, those who were born drew original sin principally from that one who begot them. But she, who together with him constituted two, conceived and gave birth afterward, although she sinned first. Hence the holy Scripture says that the sons of Levi were in the loins of their father Abraham and that in him they were tithed by the priest Melchizedek (Hebr. VII, 5–10). Read the Epistle to the Hebrews, and correct your language.

CLXXX. JUL. Finally, the holiness of Abel, the son [Note: [Col. 1220] Menardus and Vignierius: “Abel.” M.], celebrated throughout all the Scriptures, testifies that the sin of his parents did him no harm.

AUG. Why, then, did the Apostle not set him forth as one to be imitated, since he was the first righteous man? Instead, when he was speaking of two human beings, one of whom brought condemnation and the other justification, he named Adam and Christ. But if Abel did not have in his members a law opposing the law of his mind (Rom. VII, 23), which, as a righteous man, he overcame in an inward struggle, and if his flesh did not desire against the spirit (Gal. V, 17), then the sin of his parents had done him no harm. But whoever says that Abel was such must say that he did not have sinful flesh. For without doubt the Lord Christ would not have had the likeness of sinful flesh unless the flesh of all other human beings were sinful flesh.

CLXXXI. JUL. On the other hand, Cain—envious and a murderer, begotten from the same nature but not advanced by the same will—is ravaged by trembling that tears his soul to pieces. Therefore the Apostle said that sin entered this world through one man, and death through sin, and thus death passed to all human beings who sinned. This statement, though consistent with Catholic doctrine, provides you no assistance.

AUG. The Apostle shows that death passed along with sin when he says, “And thus it passed into all human beings.” For this reason, when infants are baptized, they are rescued from the power of darkness. Otherwise, as we have already said—and must often say—God’s image would be exorcized and exsufflated with great insult to God, if the ruler of this world, who is cast out (John XII, 31), were not there exorcized and exsufflated, so that the Holy Spirit might dwell there. But the crime Cain committed does not belong to the cause of original sin, because it was committed by the will [Note: [Col. 1220] Vignierius reads, “although it was committed by the will.” Likewise below, chapter 183, “although it is right”; and chapter 186, “although neglecting reason.” The other printed editions and the manuscripts consistently read “because” in these places.].

CLXXXII. JUL. For these matters are arranged by the words in such a way that the preceding example and the subsequent zeal of the imitator are shown.

AUG. It has already been said to you: Abel, therefore, ought to have been set against him from the opposite side, not Christ.

CLXXXIII. JUL. Moreover, if he had wished to show that generation was either infected by sin or made liable to it, he would not have said that sin entered through one man, but through two.

AUG. The answer has already been given. You say nothing, and yet you keep saying it, because you cannot find anything sound to say.

CLXXXIV. JUL. Nor would he have said, “Death passed in him in whom all sinned,” but rather, “In him in whom they flowed from the diabolical desire and flesh of the first man and the first woman.” If he had declared this, the Apostle would not have strengthened your doctrine, but would have overthrown all his own statements. Therefore he accuses the will of those who sin and the example of sin; and consequently both reason and Paul are at war with you.

AUG. Therefore he ought to have placed the example of justification in Abel, the first righteous man, just as you think the example of sin was placed in Adam, the first sinner. Why should we be reluctant to give you the same answer when you are not ashamed to repeat the same thing so often and so fruitlessly?

CLXXXV. JUL. “Until the law sin was in the world; but sin was not reckoned when there was no law. Yet death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression, who is the type of the one to come” (Rom. V, 13–14). He distinguishes the character of sin through a variety of names, showing that one thing is sin and another transgression. In this passage alone he wishes every transgression to be understood as sin, but not every sin as transgression, so that through the term “transgression” the odium of sin might increase, and those who transgressed commandments might appear more guilty than those who sinned by neglecting their inborn reason without the admonition of the law [Note: [Col. 1221] The manuscripts read “administration.”] [Note: [Col. 1221] The printed editions read “of inborn action,” erroneously.] Therefore, before that law which was given through Moses and committed to writing, whose sanction prescribed the pattern of actions, and which those living under it were not permitted to ignore [Note: [Col. 1221] So the manuscripts. The printed editions instead had, for “were not permitted,” “it was not free”; and below, “you bore” in place of “mortals.” “Throughout that intervening period” may perhaps be the correct reading.], during that intervening period between Adam and Moses, the Apostle accuses mortals, polluted by various perversities of conduct, of sin, not of transgression.

AUG. What, then, does this mean: “Death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression”? However you distinguish the words, the Apostle is found to have spoken against you. For if you distinguish the phrase, “Death reigned even over those who did not sin” [Note: [Col. 1221] The printed editions read, “although you distinguish, you will not find.” The manuscripts omit “although” and “you will not find.” Thus, after “you distinguish,” one must supply the words “from the phrase, ‘in the likeness of Adam’s transgression.’” Perhaps the reading should be, “How will it be just?”], how can it be just except on account of original sin? And therefore, as though the question were asked why death reigned even over those who did not sin, the answer is given: “In the likeness of Adam’s transgression”—that is, not on account of their own sins, but because Adam, the transgressor, begot those like himself. Thus those words were expounded even by the Catholic teachers who preceded us. Although that first and single sin, which entered the world through one man, is common to all, for which reason it was said, “In whom all sinned,” nevertheless infants do not have sins of their own. Therefore it could truthfully also be said of them that they did not sin; yet death reigned over them in the likeness, as it was said, of Adam’s transgression.

But if you distinguish the passage as saying, “Death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression”—that is, even over those who did sin, but did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression—you find no one according to your view, because you maintain that all who sinned sinned in his likeness, that is, followed his example. The fox’s den, then, is closed on both sides: there is no way for it to enter and hide, or, if it was already hiding there, no way for it to leave and escape.

CLXXXVI. JUL. Thus those to whom the law was not given are understood not to have transgressed commandments, while they are convicted of guilt because, by neglecting reason—which the inclinations proper to each person proclaim— they violated either the laws of human society or the requirements of modesty. Therefore they are said to have sinned through mutual imitation, but not by transgressing a law that had not yet been promulgated. Until the law, therefore, there was sin, but not transgression; after the law, however, there was not only sin but also transgression. Eternal death also reigned, which God had promised would be assigned to Adam if he sinned. That death, therefore, owed to sin, punitive death, reigned even before the law over those who sinned—as it did among the Sodomites and among those who perished at the time of the flood because of iniquity, though voluntary iniquity, or who were consumed at various ages. After the law it reigned over those whom it found guilty of transgression.

AUG. Since you do not wish any death to be punitive except eternal death, if death is not punitive when it separates the soul from the body, why does nature fear it, when you praise nature so highly that you deny it has been corrupted? Why is it that an infant, once it has advanced even slightly beyond infancy, already fears being killed? Why is the mind not inclined toward death as it is toward sleep? Why are those who do not fear death held in such high regard, and why are they so rare? Why does the very one who said that he desired to be dissolved and to be with Christ (Phil. I, 23) nevertheless not wish to be unclothed, but clothed over, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life (II Cor. V, 4)? Why was Peter told concerning his own glorious end, “Another will gird you and carry you where you do not wish to go” (John XXI, 18)? If, then, death is feared in vain, that very fear is a punishment. But if the soul does not naturally wish to be separated from the body, death itself is a punishment, although divine grace turns it to good use.

CLXXXVII. JUL. Since, according to the justice that judges and does not reckon sin except against one from whom abstaining is free, those who sinned without the law will also be judged without the law, and those who sinned under the law will be judged by the law (Rom. II, 12), when the Apostle says, “But death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression,” he makes clear what he meant: he defines the Jews who sinned under the law as having transgressed in the same way as Adam, because the law of abstaining from the taste of the tree had also been entrusted to that first man—not in writing, but to his ears. In this there was a testing of obedience; by eating against the commandment, he incurred the crime of transgression. Therefore, after the law was given through the ministry of Moses, the people who sinned are likewise shown to have sinned in the likeness of Adam’s transgression [Col. 1223], because, like him, they sinned by transgressing the law. But during the intervening period between the two laws—the first given but unwritten, the second both promulgated and committed to writing—those who sinned are shown not to have been free from sin, but are said to have erred not in the likeness of Adam’s transgression, because they had not received the law.

AUG. When you deny the likeness of Adam’s transgression, you convict yourself: those who sinned without the law are not guilty according to the example of the first man. It is therefore not imitation but generation through which death passed to all human beings through sin. For if this death, which entered the world through the sin of the first man, had passed over the long periods that preceded the law and had begun to spread among the Jews, who became transgressors by violating the law, so as to preserve the likeness of Adam’s transgression, it would not be said of it, “It entered through one man and passed through all human beings.” Whom, I do not say a fool, but even a simpleton, will you persuade that death entered through one man and passed through all human beings, when you say that it bypassed so many nations and so many ages [Note: [Col. 1223] The Clar. and Mar. manuscripts, after “and so many ages,” repeat “and passed through all human beings.”] and reached those who had received the law while leaving the others untouched, although you also say that death reigned over those who sinned not in the likeness of Adam’s transgression, but without transgression because they were without the law? There is absolutely no way for you to correct your error except by returning to the Catholic faith, which sets the first man, the founder of generation, against the second man, the founder of regeneration.

CLXXXVIII. JUL. Adam is called the type of the one to come, that is, of Christ; but a type by contrast, so that just as he is regarded as the type of sin, the other may be regarded as the type of righteousness. Yet Christ’s incarnation was a type of righteousness not the first but the greatest, because even before the Word became flesh, virtues shone forth from the faith that was directed toward God—in the prophets and in many other holy persons. When the fullness of time came, however, the perfect standard of righteousness shone forth in Christ, and he who had been foretold as the father of the future age excelled as the rewarder both of the saints who preceded him and of those who followed [Note: [Col. 1223] So the manuscripts. The printed editions read “shone forth.”]:

AUG. We recognize your heresy. Pelagius defined that the righteous of ancient times did not live by faith in Christ’s incarnation, since Christ had not yet come in the flesh. Yet surely they would not have foretold that future event unless they had first believed. But you fell into this absurdity while defending the possibility of righteousness through nature and the law. Whichever of the two is true, Christ therefore died for nothing.

CLXXXIX. JUL. So also, on the opposite side, Adam is called the type of sin, not the first but the greatest.

AUG. How, then, is it not the first but the greatest? Since, because of the origin of the human race, you do not deny that it was the first, and you cannot explain why you call it greatest unless you admit that Adam sinned so much more grievously because the opportunity not to sin was greater there, where nature had not yet been corrupted and the law of sin did not oppose the law of the mind in the members. With this punishment every human being is born, destined for eternal destruction unless reborn, and lost unless he is sought and found by the one who came to seek what was lost (Luke XIX, 10).

CXC. JUL. I call it greatest not because I deny that the devil was more guilty, but because, when the rationale of the institution was being sought, the Apostle more appropriately mentioned a human being, whom the succession of humankind especially concerns, than an aerial substance. Yet it was established that the first woman had sinned within humanity itself. But because the authority of fathers is more effective and greater in every matter, he said that the man was the type of sin—not the one from whom the offense began, but the one who, through the power of the male sex, is shown to have been more readily imitated. You see, surely, how the consistency of the interpretation testifies that truth lies within it.

AUG. The very form of Christ demonstrates that the Apostle opposed regeneration to generation, not imitation to imitation: the second man, Christ, is opposed to the first man [Note: [Col. 1224] Vignierius reads “because.”]. If, then, those who are reborn do not belong to Christ’s righteousness, those who are born do not belong to Adam’s sin, and Christ is not the type by contrast. But because he is a type, clearly, just as those who are reborn pass into Christ’s righteousness—even infants, although they are unable to practice righteousness—so those born from Adam have passed, or do pass, along with the transmission of sin, although they are not yet able to practice sin. Recognize the type, and do not become distorted by contradiction.

CXCI. JUL. Now consider how greatly the other words of this passage disagree with your interpretation, as do those in which the Apostle declares that death also reigned over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression, who is the type of the one to come. For if he was speaking of natural sin, concerning which, as it seems to you, he had said, “In whom all sinned,” who would those be whom he immediately declares not only not to have sinned in Adam’s transgression [Note: [Col. 1224] So the manuscripts. The printed editions read, “not only of Adam’s transgression” or “not only not in Adam’s transgression.”], but not even to have been liable to the likeness of that fault?

AUG. But you understand it this way because you do not understand it. The Apostle, however, gave the reason why death reigned even over those who did not sin, adding and saying, “In the likeness of Adam’s transgression”—that is, he showed that death reigned even over those who did not sin because they received from Adam’s transgression a certain likeness of the type. For those who are born put on Adam, just as those who are reborn put on Christ.

CXCII. JUL. He says, “Death reigned even over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression.” You see that he clearly made a distinction between those who had gone astray like Adam and those who had gone astray differently.

AUG. If they had gone astray differently, where is the example of imitation? Restore regeneration to generation, not imitation to imitation, and you will find the type commended by the Apostle of truth, not the type fabricated by Pelagius, the author of your error.

CXCIII. JUL. This distinction cannot apply to natural sin. If it did, it would bind everyone together absolutely and equally. There would therefore be no one in whom this evil was not present, and no one would be found of whom it could truly be said that he had not sinned in the likeness of that sin, when all had truly sinned in it.

AUG. What you loudly insist upon retaining is true, and it is against you: original sin bound everyone together absolutely and equally. There would be no one in whom this evil was not present unless divine grace through Christ came to his aid. For the likeness of Adam’s transgression, who is the type of the one to come—that is, of Christ—deserved that death should reign over those who did not sin, that is, who had committed no sins of their own. Just as those who are born are clothed in the first man, so those who are reborn are clothed in the second man.

CXCIV. JUL. The Apostle, then, gathers and declares that there are some who sinned like Adam, and others whom not even the likeness of the ancient transgression touched. It is therefore entirely clear that these are crimes of conduct, not of seed. To review briefly what has been said: the Apostle says that sin entered through one man. Reason shows that this agrees with imitation, not generation, which is the work of two.

AUG. How often you say the same thing, and say nothing! You do not see that if the sin of imitation had begun with the human race, this passage would have said that it entered the world through one woman rather than through one man, since she sinned first, and her husband also imitated her. But because he wanted generation, not imitation, to be understood, he says, “Through one man sin entered the world.” Either he included both in the singular number, on account of what was said, “Therefore they are no longer two” (Matt. XIX, 6), or he chiefly mentioned the one from whom the beginning of generation proceeds, when sowing begins so that conception may follow. We have said these things many times already. But in response to your repetitions, we do not yield by repeating our own answers, though less frequently.

CXCV. JUL. He continued, “And thus death passed into all human beings.”

AUG. What does “thus it passed” mean except “in the manner in which it entered,” that is, with sin or through sin?

CXCVI. JUL. He made a distinction, so that no one would think that sin had passed in such a way that death, which went before, was shown to have followed upon the materials of vengeance that it had found in each sinner through the pursuit of an evil will [Note: [Col. 1225] The printed editions read, “as though even now it had found sinners through the pursuit of an evil will.” The manuscripts provide the corrected reading.]. He therefore shows that nature is not to be accused, but conduct.

AUG. You turn yourself about and turn yourself back for no purpose. Look to Adam and to Christ: he is the type of the one to come. Therefore the one who transfers his righteousness to those who are reborn is not conformed by contrast to Adam if Adam does not transfer sin to those who are born.

CXCVII. JUL. He added that death reigned in him in whom all sinned. By this expression he presented not the ruin of the one being born, but the act of the one acting [Note: [Col. 1225] So the manuscripts. The printed editions read “of the one compelling.”]. Thus he showed that he was accusing depravity, not injuring innocence.

AUG. All sinned in him in whom all die, whose counterpart is the one in whom all are made alive. For just as all die in Adam, so all will be made alive in Christ (I Cor. XV, 22). This was said because, just as no one turns toward death except through Adam, so no one rises to life except through Christ. O man who can say nothing, you could at least keep silent!

CXCVIII. JUL. After this he added that sin reigned until the law, showing that the reign of sin fell when the law was promulgated.

AUG. If the reign of sin fell when the law was promulgated, then righteousness comes through the law. If righteousness comes through the law, then Christ died for nothing (Gal. II, 21). This is the Apostle’s statement, not mine. Come out openly now, enemies of the cross of Christ. Why do you fear Christ’s great people, and not fear Christ’s great judgment? Say openly, “We could be justified by nature; we could be justified by the law. Christ died for nothing.” But because you fear the Christian multitude, you insert a Pelagian statement, and when people ask you why Christ died if nature or the law makes the righteous, you answer, “So that this might happen more easily,” as though it could nevertheless happen, though with greater difficulty, either through nature or through the law. Christ, answer, conquer, and convict them. Cry out, “Without me you can do nothing” (John XV, 5), so that those who cry, “Even if with greater difficulty, we could still do it without you,” may be silent. Or, if they cannot be silent, let them withdraw into some hiding place, so that they do not mislead others. Why, then, does the Apostle say, “Until the law sin was in the world,” unless because the promulgated law also could not take away sin, but he could of whom it was said, “Behold the Lamb of God; behold, he who takes away the sin of the world” (ibid. I, 29)?

CXCIX. JUL. Generation, however, which began from Adam, continues after the law. If it were the source of sins and the devil’s stock, as you argue, this crime would certainly not remain only until the law, but would continue after the law and after Christ. Therefore the sin of which the Apostle declares that it existed until the law and could not remain after the law is proved to belong to conduct, not birth.

AUG. Here you say openly that the Apostle did not say, “Until the law sin was in the world,” because the law also could not take away sin, but because sin could not remain after the law. And you are not terrified by the voice of God, spoken through God’s man as he directs attention to Christ and says, “Behold the Lamb of God; behold, he who takes away the sin of the world”? What are you foolishly saying? What madness possesses you? Not nature, not the law, but “behold him who takes away the sin of the world.” And you dare to say that the reign of sin fell when the law was promulgated and that sin could not remain after the law, although the Apostle says, “If righteousness comes through the law, then Christ died for nothing”; although the Apostle says, “No one is justified by the law” (Gal. III, 11); although the Apostle says, “The law entered so that transgression might abound” (Rom. V, 20); although the Apostle says, “If a law had been given that could give life, righteousness would truly come from the law.” But Scripture imprisoned everything under sin, so that the promise might be given to believers through faith in Jesus Christ (Gal. III, 21–22). If you have ears, now close your mouths. If you wish to open your mouths rightly, first open your ears to the divine voices.

You should also remember that you said generation began from Adam, although you are accustomed to say that generation begins only from two people, and for that reason you did not want the Apostle to be understood as speaking of generation in the sin that he said entered the world through one man. Who would have thought that you could forget what you had said so often and falsely? Yet you forgot it, so that at last you might say something true. Awake [Note: [Col. 1227] Menardus reads, “you would say something true, and you would awaken.” Vignierius reads, “you would say something true, and you would be awakened.” The manuscripts read, “you would say something true. Awake.”]. Listen even to yourself: generation began from Adam, and therefore sin entered through generation—the sin that entered the world through one man [Note: [Col. 1227] The Mar. and Port. manuscripts read, “through generation sin entered the world,” omitting the intervening words.]. For you yourself said, “Generation, which began from Adam, continues after the law.” Therefore the Apostle appropriately named one man from whom sin entered the world, sin that would be transmitted through generation—not the devil, from whom the sin that imitation would follow entered the world.

CC. JUL. “But sin is not reckoned,” he says, “when there is no law” (Rom. V, 13). By this statement, as by all his other statements, he destroyed the opinion of inherited sin.

AUG. Clearly, when there is no law, sin is not reckoned [Note: [Col. 1227] We have restored the negative particle here on the authority of the manuscripts.]—but by human beings, who do not know the inscrutable judgments of God. For if God does not reckon sin when there is no law, by what justice of God will those who sinned without the law perish without the law (ibid. II, 12)?

CCI. JUL. For if inherited sin was not reckoned before the law, and did not exist after the law [Note: [Col. 1227] The printed editions read “through the law.” The manuscripts, more correctly, read “after the law.”], then the poison by which it could harm the human race never had any force [Note: [Col. 1227] The old Port. codex reads “strength.”]. For before the law natural sin was not reckoned; under the law it was not reckoned, because nowhere in the law is it ever taught either to have been pointed out or reckoned. It is therefore evident that the Apostle accuses, before the law, the sin of free will, and after the law, the transgression of free will.

AUG. If original sin is not shown in the law, why, then, is the soul of an infant who has not been circumcised on the eighth day said in the law to perish from its people (Gen. XVII, 14)? Why, when an infant was born, was a sacrifice offered for sin (Lev. XII, 6)? Now, please, be silent. Look at the infant, and imitate one who cannot speak [Note: [Col. 1227] The Mar. and Port. manuscripts read “imitate one who is not an infant.”].

CCII. JUL. It is therefore clear that he said nothing about inherited sin. Although his statements were abundant, in order to prove that the Apostle had thought nothing of natural sin—which cannot exist and is invented by the Manichaeans—he nevertheless, out of an abundance of material, also pressed the distinction that not everyone was polluted by Adam’s transgression, since even among those in whom destruction reigned because of iniquity, many would be found who could be shown to be free from Adam’s transgression.

AUG. Slanderous and wordy man: “We are all born under sin, whose very origin is in fault” (Ambrose, Book 1 on Repentance, chapter 2 or 3)—the man who said this was not a Manichaean, but, as the mouth of your teacher [Note: [Col. 1228] Pelagius.] praises him, a certain beautiful flower shone among ecclesiastical writers. How, then, do you say that not everyone was polluted by Adam’s transgression—and, what is worse, attribute to the Apostle what you foolishly understand—when he says, “Death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who did not sin,” wishing infants to be understood, since they committed no sins of their own? And he adds, “In the likeness of Adam’s transgression” (Rom. V, 14), showing why death reigned over them. We have dealt with this sufficiently above (see chapter 191).

For how did sin enter the world through one man, and death through sin, if death nevertheless reigned over some who did not belong to the sin of that one man? Those over whom death reigned belong to the sin through which it entered. But those who do not belong to the sin through which death entered—who, as you yourself said, did not sin in the likeness of that transgression—do not belong to death. What, then, does “Death reigned even over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression” mean except that death reigned even over those who did not sin, since they committed no sins of their own? Yet it reigned over them in the likeness of Adam’s transgression because, although they committed no sins of their own, they nevertheless belong to the sin through which death entered the world. They bear the likeness of the transgression, not by committing transgression through their own sin, but by being born from the transgressor through whom the whole of human nature was corrupted.

CCIII. JUL. Consider, then, whether you ought still to doubt what we say: namely, that before the exercise of their own will, the innocent—God’s unfinished work—did not sin in Adam, since, according to the Apostle’s testimony, even among the wicked who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression, many are shown to exist.

AUG. The answer has already been given. You must be silent, for you can say nothing except what is perverse, as you strive to distort the Apostle’s words. He said that death reigned even over those who did not sin—that is, over infants who had no sins of their own—in the likeness of Adam’s transgression, who is the type of the one to come. For Christ transfers righteousness to them just as Adam transfers sin; Christ transfers life just as Adam transfers death. Otherwise they will be alien to the type of Christ and will not be Christians. This is indeed what you believe, but you are afraid to say it openly.

CCIV. JUL. But let us examine the rest. “But not as the offense, so also is the gift. For if by the offense of one many died, much more did the grace of God and the gift, in the grace of the one man Jesus Christ, abound unto the many” (Rom. V, 15). He says that the evil of the offense is surpassed by the abundance of grace, and he places the number of those who are saved above those whom he asserts perished through transgression [Col. 1229].

AUG. We have often said this: he does not say “more,” but “many”; nor does he say “more numerous,” but “abounded more,” because those into whom Christ’s life passed will live eternally, whereas death passing into them through Adam harmed them only for a time. See, then, how grace abounded much more greatly in them than sin.

CCV. JUL. If you defend the Apostle’s truth in his words [Note: [Col. 1229] So the manuscripts. Menardus reads, “the words indicate.” Vignierius reads, “the words defend.”], and do not shamelessly think that he lied, explain how this statement, if he was speaking of natural sin, does not bring upon him the shame of a public falsehood. For if original sin existed, making the whole nature of human beings altogether subject to the devil’s jurisdiction, where would there be room for comparing the numbers of the two parties—namely, those who are saved and those who perish? In the Gospel, when the Lord showed the rarity of the blessed, he said: “How narrow and constricted is the way that leads to life, and few are those who find it! How broad and spacious is the way that leads to destruction, and many are those who enter by it!” (Matt. VII, 13–14).

AUG. This is how your interpretation is overturned: there are few who are saved in comparison with those who perish. For without comparison with the latter, the saved are themselves also many; indeed, Revelation says that no one could count their multitude (Rev. 7:9). Therefore, if Paul had said not “many” but “more,” we could not call them fewer; for “more” is a comparative term. It is this word that you insert, not the Apostle.

But even on that reading your argument will not hold. For that imitation of yours which you seem to yourselves to have cleverly devised, against the clearest truth of the apostolic words—namely, that all are thought to belong to the sin of the first man not through generation but through imitation [Note: [Col. 1229] In the printed editions, *imitatione* (“by imitation”), erroneously.]—asserts that many more perish through the offense of one man, or on account of one man’s offense, than are freed by the grace of the one man Jesus Christ. For who does not [Note: [Col. 1229] The negative particle is here restored from the manuscripts.] see that there are more sinners than righteous people? These sinners [Note: [Col. 1229] Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read *peccatoris*.], you say, belong to the one offense—not some of them, but all of them—not indeed through generation, but nevertheless through imitation.

But even if you say that not all sinners, but only transgressors of the law, are bound by the sin of the first man through the bond of imitation, even so, from the time when God’s law was proclaimed among many nations, how broad and spacious is the way that leads to destruction, and how many transgressors enter by it! How narrow and constricted is the way that leads to life, and how few there are who find it! This is plainly in comparison with the many who perish, even if the few who are freed and the baptized infants who die are added to their number.

How, then, could the Apostle have said, “The grace of God abounded much more unto more people”? What you say, he did not say. He said, “It abounded much more unto many,” because, as has already been said, even those who are saved are few in comparison with those who perish; but without comparison with them they are so many that no one could count them. [Col. 1230] Grace abounds much more in them because through Adam they live temporarily, miserably, and mortally, but through Christ they will live most blessedly and without end. Your invention has been thrown into confusion; at last, let your argument be corrected.

**CCVI. JUL.** This matter of “many” and “few,” as you put it, pertains to an infinite quantity, since in mutual comparison either multitude or smallness is found. Thus God, comparing those who are to be saved with the multitude of those who perish, called them few; and here the Apostle, comparing them with those who had sinned as Adam did, declares that those whom Christ’s grace saves are much more numerous.

**AUG.** He does not declare them “more numerous,” but “many.” He spoke in Greek and said πολλούς (*pollous*, “many”), not πλείστους (*pleistous*, “most”). Read, and be silent.

**CCVII. JUL.** Then assert that this belongs to the sin of the Manichaeans—that is, to inherited sin.

**AUG.** Catholic teachers, not the deceived Manichaeans, said that all sinned in Adam. Those who understood the Apostle said this, whereas you deny it in opposition to the Apostle. Therefore you too are deceivers; for you too, like the Manichaeans, though afflicted with a different disease, are insane.

**CCVIII. JUL.** For if natural sin transferred the whole human race produced by human fertility into the kingdom of the devil, and if from that point some are thought to have been liberated through Christ at the end of the world, what truth or what authority does that teacher possess who, against the clear testimony of the whole world, says that righteousness abounded unto more people than guilt? What confidence, then, should be placed in him when he discusses obscure doctrines, if he lies about matters so evident? Since it is sacrilegious to hold this view, but your dogma has compelled you to say it, let the vileness of the Manichaeans be crushed by reverence for the Apostle.

**AUG.** You, rather, strive to cloud what is clear—not only by failing to understand what the Apostle said, but also by changing and inserting what he did not say. He did not say “more”; he said “many.” These many, however, are found to be few when compared with those who perish.

Calumnious, brazen, and verbose man, the Apostle said what Ambrose understood, and Ambrose was not a Manichaean: “All human beings are born under sin, and their very birth is in guilt” (Ambrose, *On Repentance*, book 1, chapter 2 or 3). Listen—as your teacher praised him—to this beautiful flower; and tear from your heart this ugly growth of thorns, that is, the foul cleverness of your wicked contention.

**CCIX. JUL.** The Apostle does not lie. Therefore the grace of Christ abounded unto more people than Adam’s guilt, through whose imitation those who sinned under the law are said to have sinned. Under the law, however, up to Christ, only the Jews transgressed. Compare, then, the Jewish nation alone, and only those of mature age placed under the law and therefore sinning in the likeness of Adam’s transgression, who sinned after receiving the law, with the thousands from the multitude of nations called through the preaching of the Gospel who have been saved by the liberality of grace. Then you will understand that the Apostle Paul truly declared that the grace of God and the gift [Note: [Col. 1230] The printed editions read *et Domini*, corruptly.] of Jesus Christ reached more people [Col. 1231] than the fellowship of the ancient transgression.

**AUG.** Since the Apostle is found to have said not “more,” but “many,” the whole machinery of this argument of yours [Note: [Col. 1231] The printed editions read *tum*; the manuscripts, *tui* (“of yours”).] is overturned—although it is not only Jews, as you wish, who are found to be transgressors, but all who, by transgressing the law proclaimed together with the Gospel, become more culpable. The world is so full of such transgressors, together with the Jews, that in comparison with all of them those who are freed—even with baptized infants added to their number—are few. I have already included this in my previous reply.

The Teacher of the Gentiles clearly cries out against you: “As in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive” (1 Cor. 15:22). Those “all” are not few but many. Accordingly, many die in Adam, and many will be made alive in Christ; but more die in Adam than will be made alive in Christ. Therefore more belong to Adam’s death, while fewer belong to Christ’s life in comparison with them; yet even the latter, considered in themselves, are so numerous that no one could count them (Rev. 7:9).

What, then, does “All shall be made alive in Christ” mean except that no one will be made alive except in him? I offered an illustration of this from a teacher of letters. If there were one teacher in a city from whom everyone there was said to learn letters, this would not mean that everyone learned, but that no one learned except from him (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 2, no. 45). You did not even attempt to refute this expression, because you saw that it was entirely correct and familiar to everyone.

**CCX. JUL.** Having set forth the generosity of grace in the abundance of those saved, he compares the gift and the sin; and most learnedly, in praise of the gift, he adds that one power heals many wounds: “And not as through one,” he says, “so also is the gift.”

**AUG.** He said “through one who sinned,” not “through one sin,” so that when he subsequently says, “Judgment from one offense unto condemnation,” this offense can be understood only as belonging to that one who sinned. You do not want this; but what will you do, since the Apostle said it even against your wishes? Correct yourselves, then. There is nothing else you ought to do here.

**CCXI. JUL.** “For judgment from one offense unto condemnation, but grace from many offenses unto justification” (Rom. 5:16). That is, sins that are grave can each, even singly, be sufficient for the accusation and condemnation [Note: [Col. 1231] The old codices omit “and condemnation.”] of the guilty.

**AUG.** Why did you say “grave,” which the Apostle did not say, unless you saw that if one offense were light, it would not suffice for the condemnation of which he was speaking? This judgment, therefore, does not arise from just any single offense of anyone, but from that one offense committed by the one who sinned—that is, Adam. And still you want to distort the Apostle’s straightforward words, rather than correct your own distorted ones?

**CCXII. JUL.** Grace, however, is not conferred in the same way, so that, being applied equally to individual sins, it is repeatedly brought forth. Rather, once infused by a single force and in a single, concentrated act, it wipes away different and numerous crimes. Therefore he says, “from many offenses unto justification.” That is, having freed human beings from many offenses, it brings them to the glory of the justification granted. He does not, therefore, understand here one sin of Adam, as you suppose; he brought in the numbers “one” and “many” only for this purpose: to direct attention to the praise of grace, because grace was not [Note: [Col. 1232] The negative particle had been omitted in the printed editions but is present in the manuscripts.] repeated as often as sin had been committed by each mortal, as though individual baptisms could remedy only individual sins. [Col. 1232]

**AUG.** You speak as though the Apostle had said, “But grace, once, from many offenses unto justification.” He did not say this. Pay attention to what he said, and correct what you have said. “Grace,” he says, “from many offenses unto justification.”

What relevance here has the fact that all things are forgiven to each person once and at the same time in Baptism? Is not that condemnation to which the final judgment leads undoubtedly inflicted once, for all sins that have not been forgiven? Indeed, condemnation itself occurs once more than the remission of sins through Christ’s grace occurs once. For if someone sins after Baptism, those are not the same sins; rather, through the same grace they are forgiven to those who sin—not once, nor seven times, but even seventy times seven (Matt. 18:22). The same grace daily forgives those who pray even their daily sins, when they say, “Forgive us our debts,” truthfully adding, “as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6:12).

Therefore grace, whether it finds many offenses singly in separate people, or a few in some and very many in others, whether those offenses were committed before Baptism or afterward and are healed by repentance, prayer, and the giving of alms, sends those whom it frees from condemnation unto justification. All these are the many offenses from which grace justifies.

If grace does not come to the aid of a person, then condemnation follows even from one offense—not one that each person commits as his own, for the Apostle was not speaking of that here, but the one that entered the world through the one who sinned. The Apostle expressed this most clearly. He did not say, as you do, “Not as through one sin,” as though he wished a single sin of each person to be understood; rather, he said, “Not as through one who sinned.” Open your eyes and read. Do not, as though speaking to the blind, want to insert one thing in place of another.

**CCXIII. JUL.** But this is what he took care to express: “When individual sins had mortally wounded those who were guilty, this grace, singular and once bestowed, saved human beings pierced by innumerable wounds.”

**AUG.** He said “through one who sinned,” by which Adam is understood—not “through one sin,” where, by changing and inserting a word, you want individual sins of individuals to be understood [Note: [Col. 1232] The manuscripts read *tuo* (“your”)].

**CCXIV. JUL.** “For if, because of one offense, death reigned through one, much more will those who receive the abundance of grace and the gift of righteousness reign in life through the one Jesus Christ” (Rom. 5:17). He consequently affirms what he began to establish, for he set down two statements and intended the concluding phrase to apply to both. Through the one who was the form of sin, and in whose likeness those who sin under the law commit transgression, he declares death to reign; and through the one, those who have obtained the abundance of grace to reign in life. That grace benefits those who imitate virtue.

The question concerning “one,” therefore, has not remained unresolved, because the addition that follows—namely, that those who have received the abundance of grace will reign in life—also settles the first point: no one, evidently, is compelled into death except one who has loved the example of the sinner.

**AUG.** Whose example of the sinner has he loved? Surely that of the first man. For you say that he is the form of sin, because of imitation and not because of generation. Accordingly, as you say [Note: [Col. 1233] Perhaps read *si, ut* (“if, as”).], “No one is compelled into death except one who has loved the example of this sinner.” Therefore those who did not sin in the likeness of his transgression, as you suppose, are not compelled into death.

How, then, do you say that death reigned even over those who sinned by free choice, but not in the likeness of Adam’s transgression, because they sinned without the law? They did not sin by his example, since those who did not sin in the likeness of his transgression did not love the sinner’s example. For to the extent that they are removed from the likeness of this sinner [Note: [Col. 1233] Thus the manuscripts of Mar. and Port.; the printed editions read *peccati* (“of sin”).], they are removed from imitation of his example.

Since death, therefore, also reigned over them, what becomes of your claim that “no one is compelled into death except one who has loved the example of the sinner”—the sinner whom you wish to have been the form of sin because of imitation?

Look: those who did not sin in the likeness of his transgression did not love the sinner’s example; yet death nevertheless reigned over them. Or do you want to return to Catholic truth and acknowledge that death also reigned over those who did not commit sins of their own, but entered under the reign of death, in the likeness of his transgression, through the inherited misery of the stock from which they were born?

This is how the teachers of the Church understood these apostolic words. They saw that they could not rightly be understood unless the origin of sin through an accountable succession were understood in them. For this reason they said that infants born carnally according to Adam contract the contagion of ancient death at their first birth (Cyprian, *Epistle* 64, to Fidus). They were not Manichaeans; rather, by the Spirit of God, who spoke through them, they condemned you Pelagians.

**CCXV. JUL.** The life in which the saints will reign is shown to be eternal; therefore death, which follows voluntary iniquity, must also be believed eternal. Thus, “just as through one offense condemnation came upon all human beings, so also through one act of righteousness justification of life came upon all human beings. For just as through the disobedience of one many were constituted sinners, so also through the obedience of one many will be constituted righteous” (Rom. 5:18–19).

All perplexity has been removed. An impudent accusation is stirred up concerning universality, and a knot is most foolishly sought in a rush. The Apostle declares that not all, but many, learned sins through the disobedience of the first man [Note: [Col. 1233] The manuscripts read “that not all learned sins through the disobedience,” omitting “but many”]; and that many, not all, obtained righteousness through the obedience of the other. Nothing here concerns the origin of humanity; conduct is being revealed in different pursuits. Disobedience and obedience display the activity of moral choices, not of generation.

Certainly, if the Apostle had held your view, where would he have declared more appropriately that all go to condemnation by being born, but few go to life by believing, than in this passage, where the chief point of the discussion had to be completed? He ought to have said: “Just as through the disobedience of one man all were constituted sinners”—or rather, not through disobedience, but “just as through the generation of the first man all were born sinners—so also through the obedience of one many will be constituted righteous.”

**AUG.** Rather, he ought to have said: “Just as through their own disobedience many were constituted sinners, so through their own obedience many will be constituted righteous.” Or, if he had wanted to commend the imitation that you, placed in great difficulties and constrained by persecuting truth, think you have discovered as a way of escape, he ought to have said: “Just as through the imitation of the disobedience of one man many were constituted sinners, so also through the imitation of the obedience of one man many will be constituted righteous.”

Look: I too have said how the Apostle ought to have spoken if he had wanted to say what you say. Do not think it is something great to arrange words according to our own preference rather than to explain the author’s intention in his words.

He therefore said that through the disobedience of one man—whom he knew to be the originator of generation—many were constituted sinners, because that disobedience corrupted human nature; and that through the obedience of one man—who is the originator of regeneration—many are constituted righteous, because the obedience of the one who became obedient unto death, even death on a cross (Phil. 2:8), heals human nature. Thus even those who could not become righteous here through their own conduct are constituted righteous by his grace, such as those who die immediately after the washing of regeneration, whether they are of mature or infant age.

For this reason he preferred to use a future-tense verb and say “will be constituted,” not “were constituted,” because those who will be righteous with that righteousness which will be without any sin will live in the eternity of the future age. But when he speaks of sinners, he does not say “will be constituted,” but “were constituted,” expressing in the past tense this passing age, in which human nature has already been corrupted.

As for “many,” you have already received a sufficient answer: they themselves are all. But those whom the Apostle called “all,” you could explain only [Note: [Col. 1234] “Only” (*nisi*) is restored from the manuscripts.] by contradicting him and saying, “They are not all.” No necessity would compel you to this if you preferred to hold a Catholic rather than a Pelagian understanding. They are called both “all” and “many” in order to distinguish them from those who, although they are all, are nevertheless few.

**CCXVI. JUL.** But if he had introduced the matter in that way, he would have taught no less an impious than a foolish proposition. The comparison itself would then be utterly senseless, since dissimilar things would be brought together for comparison—nature on the one side and will on the other—so that necessity would be assigned to the source of evil, while only freedom would be assigned to the pursuit of good. Indeed, it would no longer be freedom, since the ability to choose the good and avoid the evil would not have been available if there had been natural guilt.

The Apostle, therefore, that wise and learned teacher of the Church, says that through disobedience sin arose and passed on [Note: [Col. 1235] The printed editions had omitted *transisseque peccatum* (“and that sin passed on”).], and that righteousness was multiplied. [Col. 1235]

**AUG.** Where is what you said—that it was not sin but death that passed on (above, chapters 63, 64, 196)? Now you say that through the disobedience [Note: [Col. 1235] The printed editions read “not through disobedience”; *not* is absent from the manuscripts.] of one man, which has been mentioned, sin not only arose but also passed on. Have you perhaps forgotten what you said earlier? Your forgetfulness is to be welcomed, since it compels you to speak the truth.

As for your view that in a comparison of opposing parties it is improper to place the necessity of seed on one side and the effort of the will on the other, you would discover its folly if you saw that, on the evil side, those who belong to the first man drew the contagion of sin through the connection of generation, without any effort of their will, just as those infants who belong to the second man, without any effort of their own will, become participants in righteousness through the peace of regeneration.

If you demand seed on both sides, then just as the carnal seed was corrupted through Adam, so the spiritual seed flourishes through Christ. The Apostle John intimated this seed to us when he said, “And he cannot sin, because his seed remains in him” (1 John 3:9). This will be manifested especially in the future good age, where those who exist will not be able to sin—not in this evil age, where even those who belong to the age that will have no sins still have reason daily to ask the Father for forgiveness of sins.

**CCXVII. JUL.** Accordingly, he destroys the view of natural sin and teaches that the causes of substance and of will are different. And lest this understanding be attributed more to our ingenuity than to apostolic teaching, let us hear what he added to this passage: “The law entered in beside, so that the offense might abound; but where sin abounded, grace superabounded, so that just as sin reigned in death, so also grace might reign through righteousness unto eternal life, through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. 5:20–21).

Then explain how your sin—that is, inherited sin—began to abound after the law, which received its increase after the ministry of Moses [Note: [Col. 1235] The manuscript of Mar. reads: “began to abound through the law, or through the ministry of Moses.”]. [Col. 1235]

**AUG.** Rather, explain how, as you said above (chapter 198), the reign of sin was overthrown by the promulgation of the law, when the Apostle says that sin abounded after the law was promulgated.

I affirm what I said, though even without my affirmation it is clear. Original sin existed before the law, because “through one man sin entered into the world, and death through sin, and so death passed through to all human beings” (Rom. 5:12). It was also voluntary, because “those who sinned without the law will perish without the law” (Rom. 2:12).

But the law entered in beside, so that sin might abound (Rom. 5:20), because to the kinds of sins that existed before the law there was added the one called transgression. “Where there is no law, neither is there transgression” (Rom. 4:15). When sin therefore abounded in all these kinds of sin, grace superabounded (Rom. 5:20), because in those who belong to it grace erases the guilt of all these kinds and, in addition, grants that the delight of sin may be overcome by delight in righteousness, and that one may afterward attain to that life where there will be no sin at all.

How, then, should dissimilar things not be brought together for comparison, as you said shortly before, when this comparison is made from opposites? On one side there is generation, on the other regeneration; on one side the reign of death, on the other the reign of life; on one side abundance, on the other remission of sins; on one side the delight of sin, through the corruption of nature extending to the evil of habit; on the other, the struggle against the desire of the flesh, through the help of the Holy Spirit, extending to the peace of victory, which will suffer no enemy within or without.

Hold fast to this if you wish to be sound, and do not rage against what belongs to sound doctrine.

**CCXVIII. JUL.** Certainly, you maintain that in these passages the Apostle was discussing natural sin. Earlier he had said that it existed up to the law [Note: [Col. 1236] Perhaps read *at* (“but”).], so that it might be understood to have ceased after the law; but now he says of the same sin that it began to grow and abound after the law. We have shown that both statements accord with the Catholic understanding that we follow. But with what impudence is this reconciled with your dogma, so that one and the same sin is said above to have failed after the law was promulgated, but now to have grown? How, then, does natural sin abound after the law?

Did the genital organs begin to move more violently, so that an increase and novelty of movements might seem to add strength to your sin? Or was the law given to those being born, so that those who had been born from the desire that you say is diabolical and the root and fruit of sin [Note: [Col. 1236] The codex of Mar. reads: “that it is a diabolical inheritance and the fruit of sin.”] might be admonished to amend what they had become [Note: [Col. 1236] Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read “what they were going to become.”], and correct the act that their parents had committed when they generated them? Finally, were they compelled to make what had been done undone—something which they, evidently refusing to hear, would incur the crime of disobedience by rejecting? But no fool, much less the law given by God, could have imputed this to anyone [Note: [Col. 1236] The printed editions read: “and this could be commanded by none of fools, much less by the law which God afterwards gave”; corrected from the manuscripts of Mar. and Port.].

**AUG.** Have we ever said anywhere that original sin grew after the law? Or do we want this understood in what the Apostle says, “The law entered in beside, so that the offense might abound”?

It abounded not because the kind of sin that had already existed grew, but because another kind of sin was added—one that did not exist without the law, namely, transgression, as we showed shortly before.

There is the concupiscence of the flesh and the desire of the genital organs, against which the chastity of the saints fights. You are very fond of this concupiscence, even though conjugal modesty itself resists its struggle and uses it rightly only for the procreation of children while opposing its other movements. Because, together with this struggle of its own, you try to admit or introduce it into the peace of paradise, you yourself thereby make sure that you do not enter paradise.

However much you defend and adorn it with praise, it is either a vice or something corrupted. It is rightly hateful to the soldiers of Christ, by whom it is subdued, while you conclude with it by claiming both that you fight against it and that you are not ashamed to praise it.

Through this, the human flesh that is born is flesh of sin. For this reason he who was born in the likeness of the flesh of sin did not wish to be born through it (Rom. 8:3); hence, although he was in true flesh, he was not in sinful flesh.

From this concupiscence, through the generation you accept—indeed, which seems exceedingly beautiful to you but is foul to all the saints—the bond of original sin is drawn, a bond that can be loosed only by regeneration. The former was effected through Adam; the latter is effected through Christ. The former occurred through the one by whom sin entered the world; the latter through the one who takes away the sin of the world. Thus the person who has passed from Adam to Christ recognizes both Adam and Christ.

**CCXIX. JUL.** What, then, was added after the law to natural sin—a sin which is shown not only not to have been prohibited [Note: [Col. 1237] Perhaps read *non prohibitum* (“not prohibited”).] or condemned, but not even lightly censured or faintly revealed in the law?

**AUG.** It is revealed in the law as well, if only the veil is taken away from you (2 Cor. 3:16). What else is shown by the condemnation of the soul of one who is not circumcised on the eighth day (Gen. 17:14)? What else is shown when, after an infant is born, a sacrifice for sin is commanded to be offered (Lev. 12:6)? I have already mentioned this above.

**CCXX. JUL.** Surely you are not so foolish as to say that inherited sin became greater after circumcision had been instituted. How, then, did it abound after the law, when it is neither indicted nor revealed in the law? But observe [Note: [Col. 1237] The printed editions read “attend to this”; the manuscripts, “but observe.” Perhaps read “observe still.”] how well this accords with a sound understanding, which places sin solely in the will of the one who commits it.

The Apostle says that sin existed up to the law (Rom. 5:13), so that after the law there may be understood to have been transgression—namely, the violation of the commandments that had been promulgated. Through this kind of sin, sin abounded when the law [Note: [Col. 1237] “Law” is restored from the manuscripts.] entered in, because the guilt was aggravated by transgression; and the act of an evil will, just as it was sin before the law, began after the law to be transgression. God did not promulgate the law with the intention of making mortals worse by its sanction. For the law is not sin or the cause of sin, but “the commandment is holy and righteous and good” (Rom. 7:7, 12).

Yet because the perversity of those who transgressed wounded itself with the very weapon by which it ought to have been healed, and obstructed God’s purpose so that it was endangered by the very means through which it ought to have been healed, the Apostle says that, judging by the outcome of events, the divine purpose for which the law had been given suffered injury in reputation. And because the result of human correction was not what the giver of the law had intended, but the opposite occurred in very many cases, he says that the efforts of sinners progressed to such an extent that the law appeared to have been given for no other reason than that the wicked might become more wicked and transgression be added to sin.

**AUG.** You say these things because you do not understand God’s purpose in giving the law as the Apostle Paul reveals it. You drive yourself into such blasphemies that you say, “The reputation of the divine purpose for which the law had been given suffered injury,” as though something had happened other than what God had foreseen would happen, and as though what the giver of the law intended had not come to pass when the law was promulgated.

According to your wisdom, then, did God’s intention deceive him, though he foreknew all future things? Do you not attend to what is written: “There are many plans in a man’s heart, but the counsel of the Lord remains forever” (Prov. 19:21, according to the Septuagint)?

If you wish to know, insofar as it is permitted to a human being, the purpose for which the law was given by God almighty, who foreknows all things, consider what the Apostle says: “For if a law had been given that could give life, righteousness would truly be from the law.” And as though we were to say, “Why, then, was it given?” he concludes: “But Scripture confined all things under sin, so that the promise might be given to those who believe through faith in Jesus Christ” (Gal. 3:21–22).

There is the purpose of the law’s being given. Who does not know that, when the law entered in, sin abounded not through any fault of the law but through the fault of human beings? Yet this fault—whereby forbidden things give greater pleasure and the law becomes the strength of sin (1 Cor. 15:56)—is healed not by the letter that kills but by the Spirit who gives life.

Nevertheless, the letter was useful for this purpose: by killing through transgression, as the desire to sin increased through prohibition, it caused the life-giving Spirit to be sought; and it compelled the human being, mortally confident in his own strength, to ask for the help of God’s grace. Under the law—although the law is holy, righteous, and good—he was failing and unable by his own powers to assist himself in doing what is holy, righteous, and good.

**CCXXI. JUL.** Rightly, then, this kind of sin is said to have abounded: it was the will of each person that committed it both before and after the law, but before the law it was sinful, whereas after the law it was also transgressive. Something grows and abounds when it gathers increase within its own kind, just as after Moses the heap of transgression was added to the sin of free will. It belonged to the same kind, although at a different time—that is, to the evil will, which both before and after the law transgressed [Note: [Col. 1238] The manuscripts of Mar. and Port. read “transgresses.”], not under irresistible compulsion but through blameworthy inclination.

Since this is so, nothing from the apostolic words can be made to agree with your view. For when the law entered in, inherited sin is neither taught to have become more abundant nor to have become greater. Nor can that which is shown not to pertain at all to the will of those being born rightly be said to abound through sins of the will. Therefore what the law could neither prohibit nor punish did not abound after the law.

“But where sin abounded, grace superabounded, so that just as sin reigned in death, so also grace might reign through righteousness unto eternal life.”

[Col. 1239] **AUG.** Original sin did not indeed grow after the law. Nevertheless, the law found even that sin, whose abolition it signified through the circumcision of an infant; just as it also found sins of ignorance, which likewise did not grow when the law was given. Indeed, ignorance itself was rather diminished, because knowledge of the law was added.

But sin, without which no one is born, grew through the addition of the will, when original concupiscence drew along the assent of the one who sinned [Note: [Col. 1239] The printed editions read *peccantes a sensu*; corrected from the manuscripts.]. Sin abounded—that is, grew exceedingly—after the knowledge of sin came through the law (Rom. 3:20), and people also began to sin through transgression.

If you will pay attention to this and submit to the truth, you will not be compelled to contradict openly the Apostle, who cries out: “Through one man sin entered into the world, and through sin death, and so death passed through to all human beings” (Rom. 5:12). Since he says that it passed through all, while you say that it did not pass through all, what are you doing except contradicting the Apostle? And if you contradict the Apostle, then certainly you contradict Christ.

Why, then, are you surprised that the Church of Christ abhors you, when by your deadly opinions you try to remove weak infants from the salutary remedies of Christ?

**CCXXII. JUL.** As the Apostle proceeds, he reveals himself more clearly and teaches that, when human salvation had been ruined, God, moved by the abundance of his mercy, brought forth a remedy more effective than usual for desperate circumstances. He wished to bind those whom he had not corrected by commandments through benefits, and thus to demand devotion in the future without imputing what had already been done. Human beings were to strive thereafter to preserve the righteousness that they had obtained through the concise act of faith.

The abundance of preceding sins therefore demanded the aid of such abundant mercy, since, unless there had been so great an abundance of forgiveness [Note: [Col. 1239] Perhaps read *indulgentiae* (“of forgiveness”).], no other discipline could have assisted such serious diseases.
