But in commending this divine benefit, the Apostle saw that an objection might arise from those who could say: “If we properly assess the merits of causes from their effects, and the abundance of sins obtained an overflow of God’s mercy, then we must persist in sins so that grace may not lack abundance.”

Addressing such an opinion, he says: “What then shall we say? Shall we continue in sin so that grace may abound? Certainly not! For how shall we who have died to sin still live in it? Or do you not know that all of us who were baptized in Christ Jesus were baptized in his death?” [Note: [Col. 1239] The old codex of Portus consistently reads here, “into his death,” in the Apostle’s passage.] “Therefore we were buried with him through Baptism into death, so that just as Christ was raised in the glory of the Father, so also we might walk in newness of life.”

AUGUSTINE. Does the fact that you yourselves cite these apostolic words prevent them from choking you, since you recall them so that we may not forget how determinedly you are trying to tear up the foundations of God’s house? Foolish man, when the Apostle had said, “If we have died to sin, how shall we still live in it?” why did he add, “Or do you not know that all of us who have been baptized in Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death?” He did so to prove that those baptized in Christ are dead to sin. [Col. 1240] Are you so deaf that you do not hear these things? Are you so blind that you do not see them? Confess, then, that infants who have been baptized are dead to sin; finally confess original sin. For they had no other sin to which they could die. Or say openly that they ought not to be baptized; or, when they are baptized, that they are not baptized in Christ Jesus; or that they are not baptized into his death. And, if you can, erase the Apostle’s words: “All of us who have been baptized in Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death.” But if you cannot erase these words—as indeed you cannot—then when you hear “all of us,” do not try to exclude infants from it. Allow Christ also to be Jesus for infants, since he saves his people from their sins not by excluding them, but together with them; for this reason the angel said, “You shall call his name Jesus” (Matthew 1:21).

## CCXXIII. JULIAN

He says that we are dead to sin at the time when, in order to receive the gift of pardon, we professed that we renounced the world and all sins; and therefore, mindful of the gift, we ought to live in such a way that we may be shown to have been buried with Christ and may manifest his resurrection through conspicuous holiness. Just as he, after rising from the dead, suffers no bodily weakness and endures no scourges, so we too should strive to be invulnerable to every sin and vice. For “if we have been planted to the likeness of his death, we shall also be to that of his resurrection” [Note: [Col. 1240] The editions read “in the likeness”; the manuscripts read the contrary. The editions read “and his resurrection”; “his” is absent from the manuscripts]; knowing this, that “our old man was crucified with him, so that the body of sin might be destroyed, and that we might no longer serve sin.” For he who has died has been justified from sin” (Romans 6:1–7). He binds the faithful with a clear argument: “If you wish,” he says, “to become participants in his resurrection, imitate also the power of his death, so that, dead to vices, you may live in virtue. For you will then share in that blessedness if you bear the image of his death by dying to sins.” Our old man, then, ought to be taught as affixed to his cross, so that it may destroy the body of sin—namely, through the strength of his passion. By “the body of sin,” Paul, according to his customary usage, means vices, not the substance of the flesh. For he continues: “so that the body of sin may be destroyed, and that we may no longer serve sin. For he who has died has been justified from sin.”

AUGUSTINE. However you interpret “the body of sin,” you will not deny that infants baptized in Christ Jesus are dead to sin, unless you most openly deny that they have been baptized into the death of Christ Jesus; and consequently deny that they have been baptized in Christ Jesus. “All of us who have been baptized in Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death.” Tell us, then, to what sin they die when infants are baptized in Christ Jesus. But you will have nothing at all to say unless, together with the whole Church of Christ, you understand and answer: “Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin, death; and so death passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned.” Behold the sin to which they die when infants are baptized into the death of Christ Jesus. I beg you, do not be like a horse and a mule, which have no understanding (Psalm 31:9). Listen: “If we have died to sin, how shall we still live in it? Or do you not know that all of us who have been baptized in Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death?” Therefore, all of us who have been baptized in Christ Jesus have died to sin, because we have been baptized into his death. Listen to the words, “All of us who have been baptized”; for it does not say infants and not adults, or adults and not infants, but “all of us”—that is, whether infants or adults—who have been baptized in Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death, and consequently have died to sin. If it says “all,” then surely infants also. But to what sin do infants die? At last, I beg you, let generation confess, lest regeneration tell a lie; let sinful flesh be confessed in infants, so that it may not also be denied that the likeness of sinful flesh died for infants.

## CCXXIV. JULIAN

Certainly he was speaking to living people, and he was telling them that righteousness had been conferred through the mysteries. How, then, does he say that the one who died was justified, unless he clearly shows that here “death” means renunciation, and that he assumes the name “death” for this reason: to show that the faithful ought to cease from sins just as the dead cease from their activities?

AUGUSTINE. Contentious man, if in this passage the death spoken of in the Apostle’s words is called renunciation, so that one who renounces sin dies to sin, recall how the mysteries of Baptism are celebrated in the Church of Christ, in which you were baptized. You will find that infants too renounce sin through the mouths of those who carry them, just as they believe through the mouths of those who carry them [Col. 1241]—words restored on the authority of the ancient books: “just as they believe through the mouths of those who carry them”—which perhaps is no longer done among you. For you have advanced in the worse direction, yourselves wandering and leading others into error (2 Timothy 3:17), when those who agree with you say that the infant to be baptized ought not to renounce sin because he did not contract original sin. Or, if he ought to renounce sin, tell us which sin; and correct your error at last.

## CCXXV. JULIAN

“For if we have died with Christ, we believe that we shall also live with Christ, knowing that Christ, having been raised from the dead, dies no more; death shall no longer rule over him. For the death he died, he died to sin once for all; but the life he lives, he lives to God. So you also must consider yourselves dead to sin [Note: [Col. 1241] The editions read “consider yourselves dead with him”; the manuscripts read “consider yourselves dead”], but alive to God in Christ Jesus” (Romans 6:8–11). “Just as Christ,” he says, “who died to sin once—that is, died once because of our sins—no longer dies, but lives in the glory of God, so you too must consider yourselves dead to sin and live for and serve virtue alone.”

AUGUSTINE. O remarkable interpretation! The Apostle says that Christ died to sin, but you say, “That is, because of our sins.” Therefore, when he says, “So you also must consider yourselves dead to sin,” should we suppose that he means, “Consider yourselves dead because of your sins”? Certainly he does not say that here; nor do you understand it in that way. You confess that they are dead to sin so that they might not live to sin. Show, then, that Christ also died to sin, lest the Apostle have spoken inappropriately when he said, “so also you.” He died, indeed, to remove our sins, but he nevertheless died to sin. How could this be, since he had absolutely no sin, neither original nor personal, unless the likeness received the name of the thing of which it was the likeness? For we know that Christ came in the likeness of sinful flesh (Romans 8:3), since he came in true flesh, but not, like other human beings, in sinful flesh. He therefore died to the likeness of sin [Note: [Col. 1242] The editions read “likeness”; more correctly, the manuscripts read “to the likeness”] that he bore in mortal flesh, and thus fulfilled the mystery of our salvation: we were to die to the sin whose likeness he bore. For this reason we are baptized into his death, because just as true death occurred in him, so true remission of sins occurs in us.

But infants are included here also: “All of us who have been baptized in Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death.” People are not baptized in Christ in such a way that some are baptized into his death and others are not. Rather, as he said—the Christ himself speaking through the Apostle—“All who are baptized in Christ Jesus are baptized into his death.” Consequently, all who are baptized in Christ Jesus die to sin. If all are baptized in Christ Jesus, then surely infants also [Note: [Col. 1242] The editions read “they die to sin. All,” omitting “if”; this is restored from the manuscripts]. But to what sin do infants die? At last, I beg you, let generation confess, lest regeneration tell a lie [Note: [Col. 1242] The manuscripts have the verb “let it confess,” used there in a passive sense. The editions read, incorrectly, “let generation confess; let regeneration lie”]; let sinful flesh be confessed in infants, so that the likeness of sinful flesh may not also be denied to have died for infants.

## CCXXVI. JULIAN

Where, then, is nature accused here? Where are the beginnings of the human substance blamed? Where is the motion of generation arraigned? It is clearer than daylight that the Teacher of the Gentiles addresses only the will, so that it may renounce hidden things of shame (2 Corinthians 4:2) and advance toward a better life through the correction of its actions.

But let our exposition now take a shorter route and not continue interpreting the Apostle’s words in these passages. Let us hear him himself discussing his own thoughts. At the end of his argument it will become apparent with whose doctrine and faith he agrees. We say, of course, that the Apostle spoke of the sin of the human will, which exists in each sinner; but you say that he spoke of what you believe was transmitted by generation and received by all without the will. Let our disputes therefore, if you please, cease. To proceed with moderation, let us set aside the Apostle’s dignity, by which the matter could be settled: even if all his words agreed with you in every respect, he nevertheless, given the grandeur of his office, could not have held anything so deformed. The problem is ambiguity of expression, not perversity of meaning. Let us grant him only this in the present matter: that, as a man of untroubled mind, he should be believed to have understood his own writings better than you do.

“Therefore,” he says, “let not sin reign in your mortal body, to obey it” (Romans 6:12). I could say here that the testimony of exhortation proves that he is speaking of sins of the will. For if the evils were natural, they could be defended by justice and finally lamented through mercy; but under no circumstances would people be admonished to avoid them. If any natural evil could exist, no evil would be greater than the madness of anyone who demanded devotion in avoiding natural things. But the Apostle established nothing that could rightly be censured. He therefore shows that sin belongs to the will, since he insists that it must be avoided.

AUGUSTINE. Who does not know that the Apostle is not speaking to infants, but to those who can understand the words of the speaker and, with God’s help, obey the commands? Nevertheless, they too act with regard to their children, so that as the use of reason grows in them, the fruit of obedience may likewise be brought forth, lest they have received the grace of God in vain (2 Corinthians 6:1) when they were regenerated without knowing it.

Yet I speak of that beautiful thing you have embraced, which is disfigured by all its conquerors: I mean the lust of the flesh, through which a human being is born and with which a human being is born. The Apostle commands that this lust of the flesh be restrained and not allowed to reign, and he calls it by the name “sin,” because it derives its origin from the first sin, and because whoever consents to its movements toward unlawful things sins. It will no longer exist in us when we possess an immortal body. Therefore, although he could have said, “Let not sin reign in your body,” why did he add the words “in your mortal body,” unless so that we might then hope that this desire—which he calls sin—will not exist when we no longer possess a mortal body?

Now you tell us why he did not say, “Let sin not exist in your mortal body,” but said, “Let it not reign.” The reason is that this desire, which can exist only in mortal flesh, reigns in those who consent to its desires and perpetrate evil; and once they are enticed by it in whatever direction it leads, they are dragged along in defeat with greater force because they are forbidden by the law, unless they are helped by grace [Note: [Col. 1243] Menard reads “when”; Vignierius, “who”; the manuscripts, “because”]. In those, however, who, by God’s gift, do what is commanded—that is, who do not obey desire when it is stirred and pressing upon them, and do not offer their members as weapons to it—it is present but does not reign.

Its presence is proved by the fact that evil things are desired; its non-reign is proved when they are not done because the delight of righteousness prevails [Note: [Col. 1243] The editions read “its existence is proved,” and below, “if it is not”; the manuscripts read “its presence is proved,” and “it is present”]. For how are we commanded not to obey it unless it commands or persuades? And how could it do this if it were not present? [Col. 1243]

## CCXXVII. JULIAN

“Do not offer your members as weapons of unrighteousness to sin; but offer yourselves to God as living from the dead, and your members as weapons of righteousness to God. For sin shall not rule over you; for you are not under the law but under grace” (Romans 6:13–14). “You ought,” he says, “to serve God more faithfully precisely because you have received greater generosity. Sin ruled over you while punishment for your guilt was impending; but after you received the benefits of God’s grace [Note: [Col. 1243] Thus the manuscripts; the editions read “the benefits of grace,” omitting “of God”] and breathed freely after laying down the burdens of guilt, you ought, admonished by honorable shame, to return thanks to the physician.”

AUGUSTINE. In accordance with your custom—which descends from your error—you recognize grace only in the forgiveness of sins, so that thereafter a person, by free will, may fashion himself righteous. But this is not what the Church says. The whole Church cries out what it learned from the good Teacher: “Do not lead us into temptation” (Matthew 6:13). Nor does the person who says, “We pray to God that you do no evil” (2 Corinthians 13:7), say this. Nor does the person who says, “I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail” (Luke 22:32), say this.

For in this way grace makes us not sin; it does not merely wipe away the sins we have committed. Grace helps in both ways: by forgiving what we have done wrongly and by assisting us so that we may turn away from evil and do good.

## CCXXVIII. JULIAN

But because an occasion arose from the same question that he had explained above—namely, that those who had been freed from the law, which threatened wrath, might be presumed able to sin securely under the kindness of God’s grace—he immediately added: “What then? Shall we sin because we are not under the law but under grace? By no means. Do you not know that to whomever you present yourselves as slaves for obedience, you are slaves of the one whom you obey, whether of sin, or of obedience leading to righteousness?” (Romans 6:15–16).

Do we now believe him concerning the nature of sin, which he has discussed up to this point? “To whomever,” he says, “you present yourselves as slaves for obedience, you are that one’s slaves, whether of sin or of righteousness.” Where, then, is the Apostle indicating that sin which, before the time of the will, before the desire for obedience, before the age of knowledge and conscience, is said to have flown over the very seeds? Certainly this cannot be found anywhere except in the books of the Manichaeans.

AUGUSTINE. They are not Manichaean books in which we read: “For we too were by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Ephesians 2:3). [Col. 1244] You interpret this from the Greek in a new but most shameless manner, as though the Apostle had said not “by nature,” but altogether—namely, “we were altogether children of wrath.” Perhaps you will even dare to correct this in your copies. For you refuse to accept that, unless this faith were both more ancient and more true, all Latin copies would not contain it.

Nevertheless, the Apostle was right to admonish us that we must obey righteousness, not sin, because all human beings are born under sin, and their very birth is in a state of fault (Ambrose, *On Repentance*, book 1, chapter 2 or 3). When the guilt of generation has been absolved by the pardon of regeneration, we must obey the spirit of righteousness, to which we ought to consent, and we must not obey the lust of the flesh, against which we must struggle. We must remember, of course, that this very obedience is also God’s gracious gift, which he promised through the prophet, saying, “I will give them a heart to know me and ears that hear” (Jeremiah 24:7). What else is this than obedience?

## CCXXIX. JULIAN

Moreover, the Apostle shows—if indeed he can obtain any credence from human beings in these times—that he calls no one a slave of sin except those who are clearly shown to have obeyed sin by their own will, and who, through a change of that will—the manuscripts read thus; the printed editions have “through imitation”—began to serve righteousness. He therefore placed obedience at the center and attributed to it the fact that they had previously applied themselves to vices or afterward devoted themselves to virtues.

AUGUSTINE. Those who trust in their own strength (Psalm 48:7) are vain, as you are, and they will be destroyed, as you are [Col. 1245].

## CCXXX. JULIAN

“But thanks be to God that you were,” he says, “slaves of sin, but you obeyed from the heart the form of teaching to which you were handed over; and, having been freed from sin [Note: [Col. 1245] Thus the manuscripts; the editions read “free”], you became slaves of righteousness” (Romans 6:17–18).

AUGUSTINE. Deaf man, hear the Apostle giving thanks to God that they obeyed his teaching from the heart. He did not say, “Thanks be to God because his teaching was preached to you,” but “because you obeyed.” For not all obey the Gospel (Romans 10:16), but only those to whom it has been given to obey. As the Lord says, “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of heaven, but to them it has not been given” (Matthew 13:11).

They would not therefore have obeyed from the heart—that is, from the will—if the will had not been prepared by the Lord. Otherwise the Apostle gives thanks to him falsely for this matter, if he did not himself accomplish it.

## CCXXXI. JULIAN

“From the heart,” he says, “a change of obedience took place; it freed you from sin and made you adhere to holiness.”

AUGUSTINE. But this change is the work of the right hand of the Most High. Hear the man of God confessing this grace in the Psalm, and learn who changes the human will for the better. “And I said,” he says, “‘Now I have begun’; this is the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High” (Psalm 76:11).

## CCXXXII. JULIAN

“I speak as a human being because of the weakness of your flesh. For just as you offered your members to serve impurity and iniquity leading to iniquity, so now offer your members to serve righteousness for sanctification” (Romans 6:19). O teacher filled with the Spirit of God! Truly a golden vessel and a trumpet that rebukes not with broken noises but with clear tones! He wins authority for his speech through the humane character of his exhortation.

AUGUSTINE. O deceiver filled with heretical spirit, attributing everything to human will, contrary to the one who says, “What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Corinthians 4:7). Pelagian man, the Apostle said these things while planting and watering; but because he knew that “neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth” (1 Corinthians 3:7), he not only commanded them but also prayed to God that those to whom he preached his words would do no evil. For elsewhere he plainly says, “We pray to God that you do no evil” (2 Corinthians 13:7).

## CCXXXIII. JULIAN

So that he would not seem to command anything difficult and inaccessible to human beings, he used a word drawn from ordinary usage when he said “human”—that is, easy, manageable, and softened by comparison with the circumstances. “I do not demand from you,” he says, “an effort equal to matters of grandeur; nor do I establish for you, who are undertaking them, commands as new as the resources of the virtues are great. I impose nothing wild, and I point out nothing that can scarcely be borne. For if I commanded something of that sort in proportion to the splendor of righteousness, you would complain of the weakness of the flesh and plead that you could not endure perpetual labor.

“Now, therefore, I address you with this moderation: apply to the virtues [Col. 1246] as much diligence as you previously applied to crimes. Although it is an injustice to honorable things if they are pursued with the same purpose that was devoted to shameful things, this discipline in which you stand is satisfied if you pursue righteousness with the same intention with which you pursued iniquity and impurity.”

AUGUSTINE. Yet they will not do this unless they resist with the strength of love that beautiful thing you have embraced, namely, the lust of the flesh, with which every human being is born: it is the law of the members that is to oppose the law of the mind. A person is guilty through its bond if he is not reborn [Note: [Col. 1246] The Mar. manuscript reads “and through whose bond he will make use”; Port., “has made use”]. Mortals do not overcome it by their own spirit unless they are led by the Spirit of God: “For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are sons of God” (Romans 8:14). Go on, then, and exalt free will against this Christian and apostolic truth; trust in your own strength—not by rising, but by falling.

## CCXXXIV. JULIAN

Let us therefore believe the Teacher of the Gentiles and bear witness to the truth of his teaching. For truly, as he said, what he commanded was human, so that correction of the will might amend the vices of the will.

AUGUSTINE. But this human correction does not occur except through divine assistance. Who corrects the human will except the one to whom it is said, “God of hosts, restore us” (Psalm 79:8), and, “O God, you will restore us and give us life” (Psalm 84:7)? “The steps of a man are directed by the Lord, and he wills his way” (Psalm 36:23). But if they are not directed by him, a person will not will the way of God, even if the law commands him to will it.

## CCXXXV. JULIAN

But if he had thought that this was human, he would have considered the other matter not merely inhuman and not merely wild, but also unjust; not merely unjust, but also insane: namely, that if he knew sin to be born with us, he would reproach the people of his own age for the vices of an ancient birth [Col. 1246]—the printed editions read “of an ancient part,” corrected from the Mar. and Port. manuscripts—and command them to abstain from those things that he believed were innate. He would prescribe with threats that I ought to lay aside things that I had begun to possess before my soul entered my body, and this body entered the world.

AUGUSTINE. Then the lust of the flesh is not innate? Or does the one who says, “Control yourself” (Ecclesiasticus 30:24), and “Flee youthful desires” (2 Timothy 2:22), not command us to abstain from it? Why did he not say, “Flee voluntary desires”? “Youth” is certainly the name of an age; but ages belong to nature, not to the will, and this desire is especially inflamed by youth. Its force is certainly dormant in an infant [the printed editions read “not in an infant”; the same manuscripts lack the negative particle], as are reason and the will itself.

But the Christian eye—not the Pelagian eye—distinguishes what nature receives from the Creator’s institution and what it contracts from the contamination of vice. It praises the Creator for nature’s good and recognizes that nature needs the same Creator as Savior because of the evil by which it has been corrupted. With regard to the guilt with which a human being is born, no command can be given except that the person be reborn.

## CCXXXVI. JULIAN

He would more justly have been admonished by those whom he sought to correct to consider what he commanded and to understand that the first step of consistent counsel is to maintain moderation in commands. A teaching whose equity does not protect it has been stripped of authority; and that teaching is full of authority [Note: [Col. 1247] The editions read “and it is full of authority”; the manuscripts read “of authority,” omitting “is”] which the balance of justice commends. Consequently, it is clear that the Apostle, the revered instructor of the Churches, giving an account of his teaching through counsel, equity, and humanity, thought nothing of natural sin. Rather, he insisted—as the matter stood—that we were slaves of vices only through the will, and that we could likewise serve righteousness through that same will if it were corrected.

But since I have been occupied until now in explaining this passage in order to show that nothing can be defended from the Apostle Paul’s words on behalf of the Manichaeans, and since the truth of his argument has become evident from the context of his speech [Col. 1247]—the manuscripts read thus; the printed editions have “and I think that the truth of his speech is evident from the context”—which he develops throughout the whole body of his statements, let this be the end of the second book. Nevertheless, we must necessarily point out that nothing remains to the Traducianists except shamelessness. For when they confessed that they had no support in reason, they claimed as their entire consolation the Apostle’s statements that have been discussed. Since it has become clear that nothing deformed was prescribed in these statements, and that everything conformed to holiness and reason, it appears that the opinion has fallen which both reason, together with many testimonies of Scripture, and the religion of Catholics—which is directed toward God [Col. 1247]—overthrows; and the opinion concerning this passage no longer protects it [the manuscripts read thus; the printed editions have “the religion of Catholics prevailed, and the opinion no longer protects the passage”].

AUGUSTINE. It is apparent to everyone who reads these things with sound judgment and understanding that, although you said many things against words that were no more mine than they were those of the blessed Apostle, you found nothing to say and produced, through the crooked din of your verbosity [Col. 1248]—the printed editions read “with the whole din”; corrected from the manuscripts—an appearance of having said something to those who do not understand.

Whether you wish it or not: “Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin, death; and so death passed into all human beings” (Romans 5:12). What is the meaning of “so” except “through sin,” not “without sin”? For death would not have passed through unless sin were leading it; death follows sin, it does not precede it. From this come all the miseries of mortals from the day they leave their mother’s womb, as it is written (Ecclesiasticus 40:1) [Note: [Col. 1248] The editions read “Here do not come”; the manuscripts read “From this come,” without the negative]. When you say that these miseries befall infants without any sin, you truly make God unjust and horribly assist the Manichaeans. For, so that they may not make God unjust, the Manichaeans attribute these miseries from the birth of mortals to an immutable nature of evil and to a substance of darkness coming from another origin.

The Catholic faith overcomes both those impious people and you yourselves. It attributes all these things to sin [Note: [Col. 1248] The editions read “sins”; this is corrected from the manuscripts, which read “sin”], which entered the world from the will of the first human being. Death followed it, including this death that drives out the soul and destroys the body—a death that you say would have naturally come to human beings even if they had not sinned.

It follows, therefore, that you must say not only that the domineering lust in which you take such delight, but also the most troublesome fever and the countless other diseases by which we see infants afflicted and dying, would have existed in paradise even if no one had sinned, since you say that infants endure these things without deserving them through any sin [Note: [Col. 1248] Thus the manuscripts; the editions read “as though not”]. Restrain yourselves, I beg you, with your false and harmful praises. Restrain yourselves from infants and nursing children, whom you praise in cruel error as though they possessed no evil. Allow infants to come to Christ the liberator so that they may be liberated. Yield, once conquered and corrected, to the wretched nature that the first human being corrupted, so that the second human being may heal it [Col. 1248].

[Note: Here the copy of Menard, now in the Colbert Library, ends. After the completion of the second book it adds: “I read this at Rome on the ninth day before the Ides of March, against Julian the heretical Pelagian. The second book ends.” These words were perhaps written by the hand of the person who reviewed that very copy.]

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 1247]

Julian’s third book is examined. First, it is shown that he abuses the testimonies of Scripture—namely, Deuteronomy, chapter 24; the Fourth Book of Kings, chapter 14; and Ezekiel, chapter 18—in an attempt to persuade people that God imputes no sins of parents to their children. Next, it is shown that he labors in vain to extricate himself from the passage in the Letter to the Hebrews, chapter 11, through which the reply that he so insistently maintained in the preceding book would be overturned—namely, that the Apostle said “one” through whom sin passed so that generation would not be understood. Later, returning to the statements of the second book concerning Marriage and Concupiscence, Julian acts unjustly toward Augustine by again alleging that Augustine denies both human free will and God as the creator of those who are born. Julian also compares Augustine’s statements with a certain heretical letter of Manichaeus and falsely accuses the holy Teacher of having arguments presented against him no different from those found in Manichaeus, and of declaring human nature evil in the same manner as Manichaeus.

## [Col. 1247] I. JULIAN

Certainly, reverence for every virtue ought to have prevailed among humankind. One ought always to resist crimes with a wise mind [Vignierius reads “with a wise disposition,” omitting “always”], and to earn the Creator’s favor through good pursuits. Finally, since the first and happier stage of continual devotion appears to be both rare and exceedingly difficult, it would have been fitting to reject vices long cherished and return to the aid of correction and repentance.

Certainly, at least in this respect, reverence for God ought to have remained inviolable, so that it would not be necessary for us to vindicate the divine law with such a great struggle [Vignierius, against the manuscripts, reads “with such a great accusation”]. But because the madness of sinners has advanced so far that we must teach, with the greatest efforts, that God is just, let us now fulfill what we promised in the preceding book, presuming upon the aid of that very justice whose cause is at issue.

AUGUSTINE. You seek God’s help so that your vain books may be completed, but you do not seek it so that your perverse thoughts may be corrected. Yet I wish you would say why you ask God’s help in this work, since it lies within your free will either to do this or not to do it. Is it so that those things may be supplied to you that are not within your power and without which this cannot be accomplished—such things as, to omit others, food and leisure themselves?

But God almost always supplies these through the wills of other people. You see, then, that when you ask for help to complete your books, you are asking the omnipotent God to act upon the wills of the people among whom you live, so that what assists you may operate and what hinders you may not. For if people do not wish to supply you with food and suitable expenses, or if they finally refuse to stop disturbing and obstructing you, you will not be able to write or dictate these things.

You therefore hope that, by God’s help, the wills of the people among whom you live may be directed so that you lack nothing necessary. For “the will is prepared by the Lord” (Proverbs 8, according to the Septuagint). Either correct your doctrine now, then, or stop asking for divine assistance in defending it.

## II. JULIAN

Since it had been established in the first volume, through clear definitions, that God is so just that, if it could be proved that he was not just, it would be proved that he was not God; and since no doubt remained concerning this, it also became clear that justice is nothing other than a virtue that never judges anything unjustly, never does anything unjustly, but renders to each person what is his without fraud and without favor—that is, without partiality.

AUGUSTINE. “Without fraud”—you speak truly, so that the undeserving may not be punished. But if God’s justice were “without grace,” Christ would never have died for the ungodly—that is, for those who deserved no good and much evil. Finally, he would never have adopted into his kingdom infants whose good works and will preceded them in no way, nor would he have defrauded other infants in the same condition of participation in that kingdom—he who “never judges anything unjustly, does nothing unjustly, and renders to each person what is his without fraud.”

Recognize, then, that infants who are taken into God’s kingdom are, through grace, vessels for honor; and that other infants who are not taken into that honor are, through judgment, vessels for dishonor. At last, so that you may not make God unjust, confess original sin.

## III. JULIAN

The justice of that virtue would then be established if it punished none of its subjects except for those offenses which were clearly committed by free will.

AUGUSTINE. That too was committed by the free will of the one in whom human nature was condemned, from which human beings are born liable to condemnation unless they are reborn in him who was not born liable [the manuscripts Mar., Clar., and the first edition of Vignier read “of condemnation”]. You wish this Christian doctrine to be overthrown; but while it stands, you yourselves are overthrown.

## IV. JULIAN

Nor would he command human beings to do things that, by their nature, he knew could not be observed; nor would he judge anyone guilty on account of natural conditions.

AUGUSTINE. But Adam existed, and in him we all existed (Ambrose, *Commentary on Luke*, book 7), when he sinned in such a way that he lost all in himself—unless the one who came to seek what was lost (Luke 19:10) wished to free some from that condition.

## V. JULIAN

Nor would he impute the sins of one person to another. Consequently, he would not condemn to eternal punishments, on account of the iniquities of their parents, their innocent children, who had themselves done nothing either good or evil by which they could be shown to have imitated the crimes of their parents. From these points it would be established that God both exists and is just; and it would be clear that, if he were to do anything unjust, he would suffer in his divinity as great a loss as he would have suffered in his equity.

AUGUSTINE. You speak truly. Consequently, he does nothing unjust when he presses the children of Adam with a heavy yoke from the day they leave their mother’s womb. This would certainly be unjust if original sin did not exist.

## VI. JULIAN

Yet, O misery of human error! As I consider the very logic of our dispute, I am shaken by profound grief that this could have become a matter of doubt and that this case could have required defense. I mean that it could have been doubted in Churches professing faith in Christ whether God judged justly—that is, rationally.

AUGUSTINE. Because this is not doubted [the manuscripts read thus; Vignier has “because he did not doubt this”], it is written that “a heavy yoke is upon the children of Adam from the day they leave their mother’s womb” (Ecclesiasticus 40:1). For Pelagian wisdom is not better than the wisdom of the Church.

### VII. JULIAN

But I have become so overwhelmed by reverence for the subject itself that I have forgotten the controversy at issue. For I am astonished that there could have been any doubt about God’s equity, when it is clear that in the synagogues of the Traducianists nothing concerning His iniquity is doubted.

### AUGUSTINE

Because God’s equity is not doubted, the heavy yoke imposed upon the little one is believed to be just; and because this is believed to be just, the little one is therefore not believed to be without original sin. Accordingly, in the Catholic Church—from which the Pelagians went out from among us—it is not as you say that nothing concerning God’s iniquity is doubted, but rather that nothing concerning His equity is doubted. There it is taught and declared that even an infant, whose life upon earth is but one day, is not without the stain of sin (Job XIV, 4, according to the Septuagint); and therefore, in the evils which he suffers, God is recognized as not unjust but just.

### VIII. JULIAN

And this is certainly all the worse in proportion as zeal for evil is graver than neglect of good; as the intention of profanation is more pernicious than doubt concerning truth; and, finally, as it is more criminal to dare accuse God than to refuse to reverence Him.

### AUGUSTINE

Yet you accuse God when, although you see that the little ones are pressed beneath His heavy judgment, you nevertheless deny that they have any sin.

### IX. JULIAN

The fool, as the prophet David testifies, had indeed said in his heart that there was no God (Psalm XIII, 1) [Note: [Col. 1250] Vignierius has *testified* (*testatus est*); the Codex Portarum has *is a witness* (*testis est*)]. Yet he had not said that God did exist but was nevertheless an unjust God. So harmoniously did the voice of all nature resound with the conviction that justice cleaves inseparably to God, that it would be easier to find someone who denied His substance than someone who denied His equity. Someone could arise who thought that what he did not see did not exist; yet no one had been found who called unjust what he believed to be divine.

### AUGUSTINE

[Col. 1251] And you yourself have been found to do so. For to whom but such a person does He say: “You suspected iniquity—that I would be like you” (Psalm XLIX, 21)? But since Catholic Christians know both that God exists and that He is just, they cannot doubt that human beings who die in infancy without being reborn are not unjustly, but deservedly on account of original sin, excluded from the kingdom of God, although they are images of God [Note: [Col. 1251] Here the negative particle has been restored from the manuscripts].

### X. JULIAN

That fool, then, by denying God, seemed to have reached the outermost limit of crime. But the nation of the Manichaeans and the Traducianists has been discovered, and by its profanities that limit has been surpassed [Note: Vignierius reads *is surpassed* (*vincitur*)].

### AUGUSTINE

Knowing what the distinguished and approved teachers of Christ’s Church believed concerning original sin and the justice of God—what I believe they believed, what I teach they taught, and what I defend they defended—I ought to hear your insults in the same way as your praises [Note: Vignierius reads *your* (*tuas*); the manuscripts have *my* (*meas*)].

### XI. JULIAN

But let us return to the point from which we digressed. It had been established that, from the God whom we confess to be the true God, nothing could occur in judgment that opposed justice; and consequently no one could be held guilty for another’s sins. Therefore the innocence of those being born could in no way be condemned on account of their parents’ iniquity, since it would be unjust for guilt to be transmitted through seed.

### AUGUSTINE

Why, then, was it said: “Their seed is accursed from the beginning”? For it was not said in the manner of “the seed of Chanaan and not of Judah” (Daniel XIII, 56), where it was shown whom they had come to resemble and from whom they had degenerated. Rather, He called the seed of those very people accursed, whom He intended to be understood as naturally evil, just as all the children of Adam are, from whom people become children of God by grace.

For where it is said, “Not being ignorant that their nation is wicked, that their malice is natural, and that their thought could never be changed; for their seed was accursed from the beginning” (Wisdom XII, 10–11), I think that nature, not imitation [Note: [Col. 1251] Vignierius reads *change* (*mutatio*). The text is emended from the old books], is being censured. But how could nature be censured except as corrupted by sin—nature which was not created in this condition in the first man? From what beginning, then, was the seed accursed, if not from the time when sin entered the world through one man?

They could not change themselves, but they could have been changed by the omnipotent God; yet He nevertheless did not change them, by an entirely just though utterly hidden judgment. The Apostle knew that he had been changed from this mass not by his own will but by God’s grace, when he said: “We too were by nature children of wrath, even as the rest” (Ephesians II, 3).

### XII. JULIAN

Although this stands in so great a light that nothing either more explicit or truer can be found, I had nevertheless promised to confirm this very point by the testimony of the divine Law: namely, that it is supremely unjust if the crimes of those who beget children are charged against the children they beget, and that God so opposed this that He even prescribed in His own Law that no such deformity of judgment should be committed.

This, then, I had promised to deliver. But since the second book of the Apostle Paul is occupied with the exposition [Col. 1252] of his statements, it is fitting that the fulfillment of the promise should occupy the earlier portions of this volume. We read, therefore, in Deuteronomy, among the catalogue of commandments by which the life and conduct of that people are regulated, that God most explicitly commanded the following as well. For so that it may be understood from the preceding and following provisions among which it is placed:

“You shall not defraud the wages of the poor and needy among your brothers, or of the proselytes who are in your cities; you shall give him his daily wage, and the sun shall not go down upon it—for he is poor, and his hope is in it—and he will cry out against you to the Lord, and it will be sin for you. Fathers shall not be put to death for their children, nor children for their fathers; each person shall die in his own sin” (Deuteronomy XXIV, 14–16) [Note: The printed editions have *their* (*illis*); the manuscripts have *his* (*illius*). The Greek is *autou*].

### AUGUSTINE

He said this concerning children already born, not concerning those condemned in the first parent, in whom all sinned and in whom all die. He did indeed give this command to human judges, so that a father should not die for his son, or a son for his father, when only the father or only the son was found guilty.

But God has not bound His own judgments by this law, whether He judges by Himself or through human beings to whom He gives the prophetic spirit. For when, except for Noah and those with him, He destroyed all the others by the Flood, did He separate the infants who had not yet imitated their parents? Or did that fire consume the Sodomites without their little children (Genesis VII; XIX)? If He had wished to do so, the omnipotent God certainly could have done it.

And that one man Achar, found to have transgressed the commandment, was nevertheless killed together with his sons and daughters [Note: Here and below Vignierius has *Achaz*. The manuscripts consistently have *Achar*, as in the Septuagint]. What shall we say of so many cities conquered under the same commander, Jesus Nave, the man of God? Were not all their inhabitants killed, so that no one who breathed was left alive (Joshua VII; VI; X, and elsewhere)? What evil, then, had the little ones done? Did they not, through the sins of their parents—of which they could as yet be neither conscious nor imitators—undergo a common punishment by divine judgment?

God therefore judges in one way, and commands human beings to judge in another, since God is unquestionably more just than man. You ought to have considered this beforehand, so that you would not linger over examples irrelevant to the case.

### XIII. JULIAN

“You shall not pervert the judgment of the proselyte, the orphan, or the widow; you shall not take a widow’s garment as a pledge, for you were a servant in the land of Egypt, and the Lord your God delivered you from there. Therefore I command you to do this thing” (Deuteronomy XXIV, 17–18).

When God established the form of judgment, He immediately took care to decree that neither parents should be struck for the crime of their children nor children for that of their parents. He showed, therefore, that the beginning and foundation of the justice which He commanded to be preserved in judgment was this: that kinship should not burden the innocent, and that hatred deserved by one person should extend to the whole family.

In the case of actions, then, justice distinguishes those whom relationship joins together. It certainly would not do this if the principle of will and of seed were one and the same, or if the work of free choice passed down to descendants through generative fecundity.

We have therefore demonstrated sufficiently—and more than sufficiently—by this one testimony that the most monstrous perversion of judgment, which the new error embraces, has been crushed by the ancient authority of the enacted Law [Col. 1253]. This judgment was brought forward so unambiguously that it left no room for doubt.

### AUGUSTINE

God resists you, for He said in Leviticus: “Those of you who remain shall perish because of your sins and because of the sins of your fathers” (Leviticus XXVI, 39).

### XIV. JULIAN

In establishing the form that ought to be observed in judicial examinations, God prescribed that the innocent should not be joined to the dangers of their kinship. Just as He separated the father from the punishment of a sinning son, so He separated the son from the condemnation of his father. He plainly showed that the sins of parents cannot pass to their children any more than the sins of children pass to their parents, since the outcome for both persons is alike.

### AUGUSTINE

The little ones suffocate you, for they are so often read to have been killed not even on account of their own sins, but solely on account of the sins of their parents.

### XV. JULIAN

Therefore, whoever says against this judgment that sin is transmitted should also say that sin is transmitted back: if sins descend from parents to children, let them ascend from children to parents. For the authority of the divine Law shows that the crimes of parents do not harm their children in the same way that the crimes of children do not harm their parents.

### AUGUSTINE

The authority of the divine Law did not wish children to suffer penalties for their parents in human judgments, not in divine judgments, where God says: “I will repay the sins of the fathers upon the children” (Deuteronomy V, 9). You should read the words of the Law which you wish to read [Note: The old Codex Portarum has *choose* (*eligere*)] in such a way that you consider yourself likely to hear what you do not wish to hear.

### XVI. JULIAN

Therefore, whoever strives to proceed against this judgment should assert that the very thing was done which had been commanded not to be done. For God’s Law can more easily be denied than corrected; and although denial is profane, correction is still more profane and absurd.

If, then, you revere one of its two decrees but curse the other, you are ungrateful for the part you accept, and you are compelled to obey the part you reject. For by the dignity of the one thing that is dear to you, even that which you reject is defended. And most absurdly, anyone believes that he reveres commandments a part of which he dares to attack.

Consequently, the whole Law may more consistently be denied than corrected. No one but an impious person will attempt to correct it; therefore religious and prudent people accept it whole and praise it whole [Note: Thus Vignierius; in B, *it is regarded* (*suspicitur*). M.].

Nor should anyone be disturbed by seeing that the rite of the ancient sacrifices has ceased with the passing of the Old Testament. The principle of virtues is not the same as that of sacrifices: the perpetuity of commandments is one thing, the temporality of sacrifices another. Yet when Christ came, the one prefigured by the ancient sacrifices, the institutions were fulfilled, not condemned. For they are not said to have been practiced in their own times; rather, when the perfection promised through their observances succeeded them, they came to rest [Note: So the manuscripts. The printed editions have *are proclaimed* (*praedicantur*) rather than *are not proclaimed* (*non praedicuntur*)]. [Note: Perhaps *had come to rest* (*fuerat*) rather than *came to rest* (*fuerant*)].

### AUGUSTINE

What has this to do with the matter? God said that He would repay the sins of fathers upon their children, not sacrifices. And although parents too may imitate wicked children, God never said, “I will repay the sins of children upon their fathers.” But wherever He said this—and He said it often [Col. 1254] (Deuteronomy V, 9; Numbers XIV, 18; Exodus XX, 5; XXIV, 7; and Jeremiah XXXII, 18)—He spoke of the sins of fathers upon their children. In this He clearly showed that He was pursuing the corruption of generation, not imitation [Note: Vignierius has *pursuing* (*prosequentem*); the Codex Marianus has *persecuting* (*persequentem*)].

### XVII. JULIAN

The commandments in which piety, faith, justice, and holiness are contained have not ceased; rather, they have even been increased. And this law concerning the justice to be preserved in judgments, which we brought forward from Deuteronomy, concerns not the age of ceremonies but the perpetuity of commandments. It did not depart with circumcision, but remains with justice.

### AUGUSTINE

It has already been said to you that these judgments were commanded to human beings, not established as prejudgments for God. Finally, if a human judge were to say, “I will repay the sins of fathers upon their children,” he would speak most unjustly and contradict the divine command. Yet God is not therefore either a liar or unjust when He says this.

### XVIII. JULIAN

It is therefore settled, if Moses—through whom God speaks—is believed rather than Augustine—through whom Manichaeus speaks—that children are not held by nature guilty of their parents’ sins [Note: Vignierius reads *affirms that they are not held*. *Affirms* is absent from the Codex Portarum].

### AUGUSTINE

You yourself know that I defend against you the faith which the holy and illustrious Catholic teachers who preceded us learned and taught in the Catholic Church. But because, if you dared to tear them apart, not even your own followers would tolerate you, you have chosen me alone as the target of false accusations and abuse, so that you may persuade people to flee—as though it were something to be avoided—the faith whose defense condemns you.

I also told you earlier that, when I hear insults from heretics in defense of the Catholic faith [Note: Vignierius has *for the Catholic faith*], I regard them as praises. Why do you labor to proclaim to us what we know? Moses spoke truly, but you say nothing. It is not a human being but God who says, “I will repay the sins of fathers upon children.” Nor did God, in this passage, command a human being to do this; rather, He declared what He Himself does.

### XIX. JULIAN

Thus the crimes of those who beget children do not pass to their descendants, although the descendants were born from them, just as the sins of children do not pass to their parents, who could in no way have been begotten from their children. Birth, therefore, cannot harm innocence any more than it can harm what does not exist [Note: In the margin of the old Codex Portarum: *which does not exist*].

### AUGUSTINE

You nevertheless cannot deny that parents can imitate their children, nor that God ever said, “I will repay the sins of children upon their fathers.” Therefore, when He says that He repays the sins of fathers upon children, He censures not imitation but generation. It is not as though, from that one man in whom nature itself was changed for the worse, so that human beings must consequently die, the sins of every father are transferred in the same way; nevertheless, in some manner certain sins of certain fathers are repaid upon their children, punished not by imitation but by generation.

For this reason He does not say “unto the third and fourth imitation,” but “unto the third and fourth generation”—against your will, certainly, but nevertheless something that you too hear, whether you wish it or not.

### XX. JULIAN

[Col. 1255] The matter has already been dealt with. Yet, so that the reader may attend to what I am presenting, I offer this reminder.

Suppose there were someone who openly professed what the Traducianist attempts to establish by argument: namely, that he declared war upon the Law of God, despised without fear the judgment we have brought forward, and asserted by whatever means he could that both things which God wished to be observed were false, thereby undermining on both sides, as far as he could, the judgment of which we are speaking. Suppose, moreover, that he held that parents ought to be condemned for the sins of their children and children for the sins of their parents, and that they were accustomed—and obliged—to be so condemned. Even such a person could not assert that sin is transmitted, according to his own opinions [Note: Vignierius omits *or according to his own opinions* and, from the word *could*, made *would seek*. The text has been corrected from the Codices Portarum, Marianus, and Claromontanus].

Why? Clearly, because even if the judgment of the Law were shown to be false—the judgment which testified that such relationships could not be stained by reciprocal crimes—it would nevertheless remain unshaken that sin is not transmitted [Note: The Codex Marianus has *unconceded* rather than *unshaken*].

For by the very fact that the guilt of parents returned upon children and that of children upon parents, it would be clear that what reached children from the sins of their begetters had not arisen from generation, since it had also returned from children to parents, where generation could not be the cause.

Let it therefore be clear what I have accomplished: that the authority of the divine Law is inviolable and cannot be overthrown by any arguments of impiety; that by its sanction it was most plainly and decisively prescribed that the foul opinion and perversion of judgment must be vigorously avoided—namely, that children should be pronounced guilty for the sin of their parents. By this thunderbolt the structure of the doctrine of transmitted sin has burst apart.

Nevertheless, the faith which we defend is fortified by such powerful supports of truth that it cannot be shaken even by that profanation which is capable of denying God’s Law.

### AUGUSTINE

You ask where you may roam, not rich in substance through your wandering loquacity, but hateful to those who cling to realities and despise superfluous words. You are defeated by the adversaries whom you have, and you set before yourself opponents whom you do not have.

For who tells you that what God wished to be observed in human judgments is false, since fathers and children now have their own separate cases pertaining to each person’s life, which is led separately, so that neither children are punished for fathers nor fathers for children? No one opposes either the Law or you when you say this.

Do not become deaf, however, to God, who says: “I will repay the sins of fathers upon children.” And although He says this repeatedly, nowhere does He say that He repays the sins of children upon fathers. Thus you may understand that attention is being directed not to those whom they imitate, but to those from whom they are begotten.

### XXI. JULIAN

Let the discussion now turn to the one with whom we are dealing. Do you submit to the Law of God—at least in your profession, though we know what you do in your arguments—or do you resist it? If you submit, the controversy is ended; if you resist, agreement is ended [Note: Here the words *if you resist, agreement is ended* are added from the manuscripts; supply “with the Law of God.” In the Codices Marianus and Claromontanus, however, *controversy* is read again in place of *agreement*. The Codex Portarum has *assembly*].

If you submit, the Traducianists are overthrown; if you resist, the perfidy of the Manichaeans is exposed [Col. 1256]—provided that it is clear that your opinion in no way agrees with the Law of God.

### AUGUSTINE

I submit to the Law of God; but you do not submit. I do not deny that neither son for father nor father for son ought to be condemned when they have separate cases of their own. But you do not wish to hear the words in Leviticus: “They shall perish because of the sins of their fathers” (Leviticus XXVI, 39); nor those in the Book of Numbers: “Repaying the sins of fathers upon children unto the third and fourth generation” (Numbers XIV, 18); nor those in Jeremiah: “Repaying the sins of fathers into the bosom of their children after them” (Jeremiah XXXII, 18).

You do not hear these and similar passages. You do not submit to these and such testimonies of the Law; and yet you do not cease speaking and charging the Manichaeans against Catholics.

### XXII. JULIAN

Unless perhaps you say that God indeed commanded this, but does not do what He commanded—in fact, that He does the opposite of what He ordered to be done.

### AUGUSTINE

Why do you not consider how foolishly you think this? For God sometimes does something contrary to what He has commanded to be done [Note: The Codex Portarum has *contrary to the things which* rather than *contrary to what*].

There is no need to recall many examples, lest the discussion become lengthy. Here is something known to everyone. Divine Scripture commanded human beings, saying: “Let not your own mouth praise you” (Proverbs XXVII, 2); yet God must not therefore be called arrogant or proud because He never ceases to praise Himself innumerably.

And concerning the matter at hand, I already demonstrated above how God, without any injustice, killed little ones together with their parents because of the parents’ sins, although He commanded human beings, when judging, not to condemn children for the sins of their fathers.

If you had paid attention to these things, you would not say what you are saying. Or if you do pay attention to them and nevertheless say this, then pay attention also to the fact that what you are saying is empty.

### XXIII. JULIAN

Although it already appears, from the mere indication, how profane this is, let us nevertheless examine, with due regard for the divinity whose equity we defend, what it amounts to, even by a brief inquiry.

When God thus becomes a transgressor of His own Law, is He compelled by the necessity of circumstances that press upon Him, or by His own weakness? Or, since neither of these is the case, does He offend through the mere desire to sin [Note: Vignierius omitted this sentence: “Or, since neither of these is the case, through the mere desire to sin”?]?

But even a Manichaean could not say this, and therefore he invented the claim that your God endured a grave struggle.

### AUGUSTINE

You throw words about while facts press hard upon you. God is not a transgressor of His own Law when, as God, He does one thing and, as a human being, commands another.

### XXIV. JULIAN

If, then, neither misfortune, weakness, nor the desire for transgression burdens Him, how can it happen that He destroys by judging the form of justice which He commended by commanding it? Indeed, how can He rage not against this justice but against reverence for Himself?

The power of equity is so great that it reproves those who deviate and is diminished by no authority of those who flee from it. Finally, if He wishes us to do what is just while He Himself does what is unjust, He wishes us to appear more just than He is—or rather, not more just, but equitable while He is iniquitous.

### AUGUSTINE

What are you saying, man who are so greatly foolish? The higher divine justice is, the more inscrutable it is than human justice, and the farther it is removed from it [Col. 1257].

For what just human being allows a crime to be committed when he has the power to prevent it [Note: So the manuscripts. Vignierius reads: “when he has the power not to allow it”]? Yet God allows such things, although He is incomparably more just than all just people and His power is incomparably greater than all powers.

Consider these things, and do not compare God the Judge with human judges. One must not doubt that He is just even when He does what appears unjust to human beings and what would be unjust if a human being did it [Note: So the old Codex Portarum. The Codex Marianus, together with Vignierius, has *would be unjust* rather than *would be unjust* in the alternate grammatical form preserved in the edition].

### XXV. JULIAN

Is what He Himself does just—namely, charging the sins of some people against others—while He commands us to do what is unjust, pronouncing each person guilty for the offenses of his own will?

### AUGUSTINE

Read what was answered you above, and learn, if you can, how original sins can be understood both as alien and as ours—not alien in the same way as ours. They are alien because no one committed them in his own life; yet they are ours because Adam existed, and we were all in him (Ambrose, Book VII on Luke XV).

### XXVI. JULIAN

What, then, is the source of such envy or such malice in Him? It is envy if He deceived His creature by commanding him not to strive, as far as he could, to imitate His virtues. It is malice—or rather cruelty—if He punishes mortals for unjust actions which they committed while obeying His Law.

### AUGUSTINE

I already demonstrated above that God justly does certain things which a human being would do unjustly. God also justly avenges injuries done to Himself; but human beings are told: “Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but give place to wrath; for it is written, ‘Vengeance is mine; I will repay,’ says the Lord” (Romans XII, 19).

### XXVII. JULIAN

Or perhaps He does not punish—which indeed He does prudently—but even rewards servants who obey His commandments, although those commandments teach injustice? And what benefit did His envy bring Him, if mortals reached by doing unjust things the same destination they would have reached by preserving justice? Although those whom He deceived lose nothing of their happiness, He is nevertheless deprived both of the consciousness and of the honor of goodness and justice.

How much more tolerable would it have been to withdraw their necks from the profession of religion than to lead them through such precipitous and deadly bereavements [Note: So the manuscripts. Vignierius reads *bereavement* (*orbitatis*) in a different grammatical form]?

### AUGUSTINE

You are following yourself and saying nothing. Distinguish divine justice from human justice, and you will see that God justly repays the sins of fathers upon children, although a human being is unjust if he arrogates this to himself in his own judgment.

Do not wander from the just path, so that when you hear that the sins of fathers are avenged upon children, you either refuse to allow God to do this or wish a human being to do it, resisting the divine testimonies or commandments [Note: Vignierius’ edition has *us* (*nobis*). The reading has been corrected from the manuscripts].

### XXVIII. JULIAN

Since God does not permit even His servants to commit anything of the kind which you assert that He Himself perpetrates, it is clear that you have fled no less from His honor than from human reason. Therefore we are not deceived, as you say, by Pelagian error; rather, we are guided by the Law of God when we assert that it is unjust for the crimes of parents [Col. 1258] to be charged against their children.

### AUGUSTINE

God said not once but repeatedly that He repays the sins of fathers upon children. Nowhere, however, did He say that He repays the sins of children upon fathers, or of brothers upon brothers, or of friends upon friends, or of citizens upon citizens, or anything of that kind. Thus we may know that, when this is said, generation, not imitation, is being censured.

You too could understand this in the divine Scriptures if you were not hindered by Pelagian error.

### XXIX. JULIAN

The transmission of sin, daughter of the Manichaeans and your mother, is lamented as having given birth to this monstrosity in our time.

### AUGUSTINE

You are not reasoning but insulting and slandering. Reread the ancient interpreters of the divine word, and see that it was understood long before our time—not in this age—that the Apostle said most explicitly that through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death, and thus passed into all human beings (Romans V, 12). This pertains to generation, which regeneration heals, not to imitation, which you have rather brought forth in this age.

Thus the storm of your novel doctrine has driven you from the face of the Catholic Church, like dust which the wind drives from the face of the earth.

### XXX. JULIAN

It has therefore become clear that what we assert was commanded by God. Although the plain and universally intelligible authenticity of His judgment admitted no blemish of obscurity, let us nevertheless—so that you may not take refuge in the slowness of our understanding and say that we do not understand what was commanded—show by another testimony, now not of a commandment but of an act carried out according to the commandment, how the Law was understood.

We read in the Fourth Book of Kings, concerning Amessias, son of Joas, king of Judah:

“It came to pass,” it says, “after the kingdom was established in his hands, that he killed his servants who had killed his father; but he did not kill their sons, according to the testament of the Law of the Lord, in which it was commanded: ‘Fathers shall not die for sons, nor sons for fathers’” (IV Kings XIV, 5–6).

You see how the reliability of the historical account displayed the justice of the king who judged. Although he had been devoted, it is nevertheless reported that he had stumbled in mind in certain matters; therefore, to confirm his judgment, the authority of God’s Law was added.

So that this act might not lack weight when considered, it is commended as having been carried out according to the Law and covenant of God.

### AUGUSTINE

God wished this judgment to belong to human beings, not to Himself, since He said: “I will repay the sins of fathers upon children” (Deuteronomy V, 9). He also did this through a human being when, through Jesus Nave, He killed not only Achar but also his sons (Joshua VII, 24–25); and through the same leader of His people He condemned the children of the Canaanites, including little ones who had not yet imitated their parents’ sins by their own conduct, to perish together with those parents—not, certainly, with unjust severity [Note: The Codex Portarum has *commanded* rather than *condemned*] (Joshua VI, 21; X, 40).

Do not therefore multiply your writings in a loquacious and empty manner. Attend carefully to the Scripture of God, lest what you think you have opened in one part of it you find closed against you in another [Col. 1259].

### XXXI. JULIAN

People are accustomed to believe two or three witnesses even against a person’s blood; how much more should two sacred witnesses be believed in defense of God’s honor—the Law contained in Deuteronomy and the historical account comprising the deeds of the Kings?

He prescribed how He wished judgment to be conducted; the judgments delivered according to His Law testify how what He commanded was to be received. Is it still doubted that the transmission of sin cannot be proved by the authority of Scripture?

These positions are certainly contrary, the positions for which such lengthy battles are being fought: one defended by you, the other by us. They are so contrary and opposed that you contend by persecution and we by argument, you by fury and we by reason.

Both sides therefore agree that these propositions differ from and oppose one another: that children are punished for their parents’ sins, and that children are not punished for their parents’ sins; that guilt is natural, and that guilt is not natural; that God’s Law prescribes that the sins of parents be charged against children, and that God’s Law prescribes that the sins of parents not be charged against children.

It is manifest that these opinions and judgments, warring against one another, cannot both be true. For the rules of learned disputation also indicate that, when a double opinion arises concerning uncertain matters, both may be false, but both cannot be true.

This can occur with different kinds of things, which are said to possess a middle state; it cannot occur, however, with things that are contraries and lack a middle. These matters are familiar to dialecticians. But, for the sake of the reader unfamiliar with this discipline, we shall disclose the point by an example.

### AUGUSTINE

You seek material with which to fill your exceedingly loquacious books, so that you even attempt to teach their readers dialectic where it is unnecessary. You do not consider how the Church of Christ should reject a dialectician whom it sees to be a heretic.

For who does not understand that you are doing this in order to empty the cross of Christ through the wisdom of speech (I Corinthians I, 17)? Christ shed His blood for all those for whom He died—including, as you admit, the little ones—for the remission of sins.

### XXXII. JULIAN

Let Goliath, for example, be brought into question as to what his complexion was, and let one person assert that he was black while another confirms that he was white. These differing opinions could both be false, but they could not both be true.

For it cannot be true that he was black if he was always white, nor that he was white if he remained black throughout his life. Thus these two opinions, which cannot be true simultaneously, can nevertheless be false simultaneously if his complexion was neither white nor black but yellow—or if it was tempered midway between the contraries, with its whiteness broken but without blackness infused into it.

Different and contrary things, therefore, can more easily both be denied than both be affirmed. But contraries that have no middle—such as good and evil, just and unjust, innocence and guilt—cannot coexist in one and the same thing at one time. Once one of them is posited, the other must necessarily be denied.

Just as a command, counsel, or assistance cannot at one and the same time be both just and unjust in one person, so a human being cannot at the same time be both guilty and innocent, both good and evil [Col. 1260].

### AUGUSTINE

No one is asking what color Goliath was. You are asking this so that you may ensnare people in the colors with which your shape-shifting self is wrapped.

If this dialectic of yours—which does not build you up but inflates you and makes you ridiculous because it makes you a boastful little speaker [Note: Vignierius has *because* (*quam*); the manuscripts have *since* (*quoniam*)]—if this dialectic, I say, which asserts that one person cannot be both good and evil at the same time, is admitted into the laws of Christian disputation, then one human being cannot simultaneously be good by nature and evil by corruption.

Yet the truth cries out that this is possible. You do not deny it, and you yourself are produced as a witness against your own dialectic when, as the matter actually stands, you attribute one of these two things—which you do not doubt are contraries—to the Creator of the human being and the other to the will.

Let your dialectic, then, be ashamed, and let it depart from the disputation of Catholics just as you depart from communion. But if, as we desire, you wish to return, let it remain outside.

### XXXIII. JULIAN

Let the examples therefore be applied to the case. That the sins of parents are charged against children and that the sins of parents are not charged against children cannot both be proved equally just, since they are contraries. But if it is just to hold the offspring of those who beget them guilty [Note: Vignierius reads *not to hold guilty*. The negative particle is absent from the manuscripts], then it must be unjust to say that they are not guilty on account of those same sins.

And just as it is good to command justly, so it is evil to command anything unjustly. Although a clear matter may become less evident through argument, nevertheless, since it is useful to confirm a case already established by the support of the divine Law, let us remain at this point, where no one who stands with a sound mind is permitted to go astray through the precipitous questions now before us.

Do you therefore agree, you who proclaim natural evil, that it was prescribed by God’s Law that children should not be punished for the sins of their parents? Do you also acknowledge that this commandment was understood by that people in precisely the way we now defend that it must be observed?

And therefore do you acknowledge that King Amessias, obedient to God’s commandments, restrained with praiseworthy moderation the indignation he had conceived over the killing of his father? After killing the slayers of his parent, he spared their children—not through cowardice but through justice.

Amessias is indeed praised, and he is said to have done this according to God’s Law. He is commended for having obeyed the Lord’s will. Yet he is also said not to have imitated the devotion of his father David, since he was darkened by remnants of vanity.

Nevertheless, although he had degenerated from the holiness of his family, he maintained in judgment the justice commended by the divine Law. So powerful was his evident reverence for equity.

Consider, then, what evil your faith embraces: you charge God with this iniquity, although we confess Him to be eternal, merciful, and just—an iniquity which neither the pride of a man clothed in purple nor the grief of one bereaved committed.

[Col. 1261] **AUG.** Amessias was a man, and it was not permitted him to judge hidden matters, which he could not know. Therefore, he observed in his human judgment the commandment that had been given, namely, that he should not put sons to death for the sin of their parents. But how could that sin be avenged by human beings—a sin so great that it was turned into nature, a sin which entered the world through one man, without which no human being is born—since it passed into all human beings together with death, so that its punishment accompanies it even to everlasting destruction, except where divine grace has healed generation through regeneration? This, therefore, belongs to God’s judgment, not to that of human beings, just as do many other matters about which human beings cannot judge at all. And therefore He commanded a human being to judge parents and children separately, when they were already living their own lives in different ways; but He Himself judged differently, when, according to His inscrutable justice, He condemned along with the stock the rebellious nature which He knew to be present in the root, although it had not yet sprouted in the shoot—being nevertheless about to free from this condemnation those whom He chose, by an equally inscrutable grace. And although He also repaid the sins of parents living separately to children already living separately—a thing which He did not wish to be permitted to a human judge—He Himself knows why He does these things when He does them, whereas human weakness does not know.

[Note: [Col. 1261] The Portarum codex reads: “why He does this justly.”]

[Note: [Col. 1261] The Mar. codex has *verteretur* (“might be turned”). Other manuscripts have *verteret* (“turned”); here it is used passively, as in that frequently cited passage of Ambrose, *On Luke*, book 7: “Although their dissension, through the transgression of the first man, was turned into nature.”]

[Note: [Col. 1261] Vignierius and Mar. Clar. read *propria vitia habentes* (“having their own vices”). Here we have preferred the reading of the old Portarum codex. Thus Augustine says again below, chapter 38: “They undoubtedly live their own lives separately.”]

**XXXIV. JUL.** But to press the point: it has certainly been established that injustice cannot adhere to God; it has also been established that He Himself prescribed that the sins of those who beget should not harm their children. The very dignity of the One giving the command has indeed asserted that what He prohibits is unjust. Furthermore, to deal with you more generously, I grant you the opportunity to answer concerning the two opinions which I set before you face to face above: namely, whether the sins of parents are to be imputed to their children or are not to be imputed.
