Which do you think ought to be believed to be just? [Note: [Col. 1261] Perhaps, “just.”] If you say that your opinion accords even with the final judgment [Note: [Col. 1261] Morel, *Elem. Crit.*, p. 354, reads: “If you say that your opinion, however, is even suitable to the final judgment.” M.], I ask whether you think the opinion that remains ours is just or unjust. Without doubt you will declare it unjust. Yet it is commanded by the authority of the law to be observed. You see, then, that one of three alternatives necessarily remains: either you must admit that God’s law is unjust—or rather, through the law accuse God Himself of iniquity; or you must take refuge in the statement of your teachers and say that the law given through Moses was not commanded by your God; or, if you do not dare to advance either of these claims, you must admit that the transmission of sin is asserted contrary to the law’s testimony and commandments. For it cannot be believed that you are so foolish as to say that God maintains justice in His commandments but iniquity in His judgments; or, according to your doctrine, that He preserves justice in His judgments but teaches iniquity in His commandments. [Col. 1262] Although we dealt with this above, we have necessarily repeated it now.

**AUG.** You repeat offensively what you speak idly: you have leisure to roll over the same matters with loquacity, matters which you cannot establish by truth; and you say without limit what you cannot establish in any way. For you want it to appear that these two things are contrary to each other: that the sins of fathers are repaid upon their children, and that children are not to be punished for the sins of their fathers—as though I said one of these and God the other. You are deaf: God said both. Therefore both are just, because the Just One said them. But so that you may understand that God did not speak things contrary to each other, distinguish the persons of God as judge and of a human being as judge according to the differing causes. Thus you will neither make God guilty, although He repays the sins of fathers upon their children, nor compel a human being to judge in that manner. But you bring these two things before me as though they were contrary, with such prolixity and perplexity of argument, for no other reason than that you speak much and understand little.

**XXXV. JUL.** But if you say that both are just—both what we say and what you say, that is, both what the law decreed [Note: [Col. 1262] The Portarum codex has: “what the law of God decreed.”] and what the Manichaean and the Traducian have fabricated—then, restraining the power of clear reason, we approach you more kindly and gently. Why, then, if you believe both that what we say is good and that what you say is good, have you stirred up all Italy with such factions? Why did you incite seditions at Rome by hiring crowds? Why did you fatten, from the resources of the poor, throughout almost all Africa, herds of horses which, with Alypius pursuing the matter, you assigned to tribunes and centurions? Why did you corrupt the powers of this world through the inheritances offered by matrons, so that the straw of public fury might blaze against us? Why did you scatter the peace of the Churches? Why did you stain the times of a religious emperor with the impiety of persecutions, if nothing else is being said by us than what you too are compelled to confess is good? [Note: [Col. 1262] Vignierius reads, “if something else is being said by us,” omitting “nothing.” The text is restored from the manuscripts.]

**AUG.** Just as the accusations which you bring against us are false, so the doctrines which you invent for yourselves are false. But say every evil you can against us, lying as you do; we shall defend against you only the Christian and Catholic faith. And why should we return similar curses to you, rather than believe the Gospel and rejoice that, on account of these utterly false curses of yours, our reward in heaven is increased (Matt. V, 11–12)? But how can we believe that, in the matter we are now discussing, both what you say and what we say are good, when we say that God said, “I will repay the sins of fathers upon their children,” whereas you praise what He commanded a human judge—that he should not repay the sins of fathers upon their children—in such a way that you accuse as ours, and condemn as false and unjust, what He Himself said He would repay? And do you not perceive that in this you are resisting and slandering not us but God?

**XXXVI. JUL.** Until now, it is true, I have used milder language. But now the brilliance of fiery reason [Col. 1263] shows that there is no fellowship between evil and good, profane and sacred, pious and impious, just and unjust; and therefore that there is no conflict between God’s commandments and judgments. It is contrary, however, both to impute the sins of some to others and to command that those same sins not be imputed. Since, once one of these two positions is granted, the other must necessarily be removed—that is, if one is taught to be just, the other is taught to be unjust. Yet God’s law prescribed that the sins of parents should not be imputed to their children (Deut. XXIV, 16). Accordingly, by the same authority, the contrary of this—that is, the opinion of the transmission of sin—has utterly collapsed together with the Manichaeans.

**AUG.** I am weary of saying what is true so often, when you are not ashamed to say what is empty so often. God says that the sins of fathers are repaid upon children; God indeed says that the sins of fathers should not be repaid upon children, but He says this to a human being. Both statements must be approved, because God says both.

**XXXVII. JUL.** I have certainly shown that we defend nothing other than what reason first marks as most equitable, what God then confirms by His law, and what, thirdly, was completed in accordance with our assertion when the command was fulfilled with praise for the deed. It has also been impressed upon us that this is true justice, which God showed to be pleasing to Him by commanding it. Accordingly, it has been established that the Manichaean transmission of sin finds no support either in reason or in the testimonies of the law.

**AUG.** The Manichaeans say that nature has always been evil, without beginning; hence they maintain that everything is evil. Catholics, however, affirm what you refused to affirm: that nature was created good but corrupted by sin, and that it needs Christ the physician, from infants to the aged, because He died for all; therefore all died (II Cor. V, 14). Hence the Manichaeans conceive evil as separated from good in such a way that it exists outside it. We, on the other hand, although we separate evil from good by understanding, and [Note: [Col. 1263] The Portarum codex reads *ne* (“not”).] do not believe that what is called evil is any substance, nevertheless do not think that evil is to be separated from those who are being delivered in such a way that it exists outside them. Rather, we know that it must be healed in them so that it may cease to exist. For they call evil an evil substance [Note: [Col. 1263] So the manuscripts. Vignierius has: “For they call evil the substance of evil.”]; we call it a defect of a good substance, and no substance at all. Consider the difference, and cease begrudging Christ the physician to infants who must be healed, lest the wrath of God remain upon them when He says, “I will repay the sins of fathers upon children.” Look at the One who said this: He is God, not Manichaeus. Look at the One who said, “Through a man came death, and through a man the resurrection of the dead; for just as all die in Adam, so also shall all be made alive in Christ” (I Cor. XV, 21–22). He is Christ’s Apostle, not a disciple of Manichaeus. Look at the one who said, “We are all born under sin” (Ambrose, *On Repentance*, book 1, chapter 2 or 3). He is a Catholic bishop, not a Manichaean, nor Pelagius, nor the heretic Pelagian. Therefore, since a human being also punishes the sin of an act, but only God punishes the sin of origin, God, while saying that He repays the sins of fathers upon children, nevertheless commands a human being not to condemn children for the sins of their fathers. Distinguish divine and human judgments, and you will find that these two things are not contrary to each other.

[Col. 1264] **XXXVIII. JUL.** But lest perhaps someone prove so obtuse as to wish it demonstrated to him by clear statements that God judges no otherwise than He commanded human beings to judge—which is certainly a wicked contention—nevertheless, since truth supplies weapons in abundance from all the evidence, I shall not hesitate to point out the most forceful witnesses to this very matter. Thus the prophet Ezekiel, filled with the Holy Spirit, speaks:

> The word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, what is this proverb among you in the land of Israel, in which they say, “The fathers ate sour grapes, and the children’s teeth were set on edge”? As I live, says Adonai the Lord, this proverb shall no longer be spoken in Israel, because all souls are mine; just as the soul of the father is mine, so also the soul of the son is mine: all souls are mine. The soul that sins, it shall die.
>
> But if a man is just, and does judgment and righteousness; if he does not eat upon the mountains, and does not lift up his eyes to the desires of the house of Israel; if he does not defile his neighbor’s wife, and does not approach a menstruating woman; if he does not oppress a man, and returns a pledge to a debtor; if he does not commit robbery, but gives his bread to the hungry and covers the naked with clothing; if he does not lend his money at interest, and does not take more than is due; if he turns his hand away from injustice and renders a just judgment [Note: [Col. 1264] So the manuscripts, following the Septuagint. The printed editions read “a true judgment.”] between a man and his neighbor; if he walks in my commandments and observes my ordinances, doing them: he is just; he shall surely live, says Adonai the Lord.
>
> But if he begets a pestilent son who sheds blood and commits sins, who does not walk in the way of his just father, but eats upon the mountains, defiles his neighbor’s wife, oppresses the beggar and the poor, commits robbery, does not return a pledge, lifts his eyes to idols, commits iniquity, lends at interest and takes more than is due: he shall not live. He has committed all these iniquities; he shall surely die; his blood shall be upon him.
>
> But if he begets a son who sees all the sins of his father which he committed, and is afraid, and does not do according to them—who does not eat upon the mountains, and does not lift up his eyes [Note: [Col. 1264] The Portarum codex has “set his eyes.”] to the desires of the house of Israel; who does not defile his neighbor’s wife, oppress a man, or take a pledge as security; who does not commit robbery, but gives his bread to the hungry and covers the naked with clothing; who turns his hand away from iniquity, does not take interest or more than is due, does justice, and walks in my commandments: he shall not die in his father’s iniquities; he shall surely live.
>
> But his father, because he oppressed with oppression and committed robbery, doing contrary things among my people, has died in his iniquity. And you say, “Why has the son not borne the iniquity of his father?” Because the son has done righteousness, judgment, and mercy; he has kept all my ordinances and done them; he shall surely live.
>
> The soul that sins, it shall die. The son shall not bear the injustice of his father, nor shall the father bear the injustice of his son [Note: [Col. 1264] Here we restore the reading of the old books, Port. and Mar. Clar., in place of the reading which Vignierius had substituted in the remaining passages of Ezekiel [Col. 1265], namely, the wording of the Vulgate version: “and the father shall not bear the iniquity of the son,” and so forth.]. The righteousness of the just shall be upon him, and the iniquity of the wicked shall be upon him.
>
> And if the wicked turn away from all his iniquities which he has committed, and keep all my commandments, and do judgment, righteousness, and mercy, he shall surely live and shall not die. All his offenses, whatever he has committed, shall not be remembered against him; in the righteousness which he has done, he shall live.
>
> Do I desire the death of the wicked, says Adonai the Lord, rather than that he should turn from his evil way and live? [Note: [Col. 1265] The old Portarum codex has “how much more,” or “rather than.”]
>
> But when the just man turns away from his righteousness and commits iniquities according to all the iniquities which the wicked has committed, if he does so, he shall not live. All his righteousness which he has done shall not be remembered; in the offense by which he fell and in the sins which he committed, in them he shall die.
>
> And you say, “The way of the Lord is not right.” Hear now, house of Israel. Is my way not right? Is it not rather your way that is not right? When the just man turns away from his righteousness and commits an offense, he shall die in the offense which he has committed; in it he shall die. And when the wicked turns away from his wickedness which he has committed, and does judgment and righteousness, he has preserved his soul and shall live. For he has turned away from all his iniquities which he committed; he shall surely live and shall not die.
>
> And the house of Israel says, “The way of the Lord is not right.” Is my way not right, house of Israel? Is it not rather your way that is not right? Therefore I shall judge each one of you according to his ways, house of Israel, says Adonai the Lord (Ezek. XVIII, 1–30).

**AUG.** This promise through the prophet Ezekiel belongs to the New Testament, which you do not understand: there God distinguishes the regenerated from the generated, if they are already in the more mature stages of life, according to their own deeds. For those of whom it is said, “The soul of the father is mine, and the soul of the son is mine,” are plainly living their own lives separately. But if the son were still in his father’s loins, as it is written of Levi, that he was in Abraham’s loins when Abraham was tithed by Melchizedek (Hebr. VII, 9–10), it could not then be said, “The soul of the father is mine, and the soul of the son is mine,” since there was plainly one soul.

The prophet, veiling the mystery that was to be revealed in its own time, did not name regeneration, through which each son of man passes from Adam to Christ. But what he did not say at that time, he intended to be understood in this time, when the veil was to be removed for those passing over to Christ. Since you profess to be a Christian, although you show yourself to be an antichrist, endeavoring to make Christ have died in vain, I ask you whether, if a person performs all those works of righteousness which the prophet Ezekiel mentions so repeatedly, he shall live even if he has not been regenerated.

If you say that he shall live, Christ contradicts the antichrist and says, “Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you shall not have life in yourselves” (John VI, 54). Whether you wish it or not, you are compelled to confess that this food and drink belong to the regenerated. But if, crushed under such a weight of authority [Note: [Col. 1265] Vignierius and the Mar. Clar. manuscripts have *obstrictus* (“bound”); Port. has *obtritus* (“crushed”).], you answer that the person who has done all those good things will not live if he has not been regenerated, explain what the reason is. And see that in the matter where the Apostle sets Adam forward on the side of sin and Christ on the side of righteousness, generation is opposed to regeneration, not imitation to imitation.

I shall show you more clearly that what you recall the prophet Ezekiel to have said belongs to the New Testament, in which the inheritance of the regenerated is found—not now, but after you have stated everything that, in your customary loquacity, you are going to say concerning his words.

**XXXIX. JUL.** Does God not appear to be a richly endowed defender of His own judgments [Note: [Col. 1266] “Of His judgments” was absent and has been restored from the manuscripts.], since He has not only judged concerning this question in so many passages but has also argued it? Clearly, foreseeing the errors of our times, He has acted both justly and providently [Note: [Col. 1266] So the manuscripts. The printed editions have *providit* (“He provided”).] through such brightness and abundance of His words: first, so that no one might be shaken by any ambiguity of the questions; second, so that among those who had willingly plunged themselves into shipwreck there might remain no plank of excuse.

He speaks to the Jews, who, having brought captivity upon themselves through their crimes, claimed, to lessen the odium of their own transgression, that it was owed to their parents rather than to their own conduct. And He confronts them with the authority of their fathers. “Why,” He says, “do you have this proverb, saying, ‘The fathers ate sour grapes, and the children’s teeth were set on edge’? As I live, says Adonai the Lord, this proverb shall no longer be spoken in Israel, because all souls are mine; just as the soul of the father is mine, so the soul of the son is mine; all souls are mine. The soul that sins, it shall die.”

**AUG.** When He says, “This proverb shall no longer be spoken in Israel,” He shows that it is customary to say, “The fathers ate sour grapes, and the children’s teeth were set on edge.” He does not condemn it because it was said, but promises a time when it will not be said. Why, then, did they say this, unless they knew that God had said, “I will repay the sins of fathers upon children” (Deut. V, 9)?

**XL. JUL.** To exemplify and confirm the equity of His judgment, God makes use of an oath, and adds force to the authority of His decree by an affirmation. The Apostle understood this kind of speech, and thus argued to the Hebrews: “God,” he says, “desiring to show the heirs of the promise the unchangeableness of His purpose, interposed an oath, so that by two immutable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we may have the strongest consolation” (Hebr. VI, 17–18).

**AUG.** And there too the New Testament was being promised.

**XLI. JUL.** He therefore says that by these two things God shows that He cannot lie: by the fact that He promised, and by the fact that He testifies that He fulfills what He promised. This is not because God is accustomed to have speech that is weak or doubtful without such an affirmation, but so that He might burden His truth with great proofs. He used that form of expression [Note: [Col. 1266] The manuscripts have *elocutionis* (“of expression”) rather than *locutionis*.], which makes even human beings, who are accustomed to deceive, believe.

Thus in the present matter also God warns and prescribes by this solemn affirmation, both so that no one may suspect what the Traducians assert concerning the people, and so that he may recognize that God cannot judge in the manner which He detests: “As I live, says Adonai the Lord, this proverb shall no longer be spoken in Israel.”

[Col. 1267] **AUG.** “It shall not be spoken in Israel”—you would rightly say this if you saw true Israelites who had been regenerated, among whom it will not be said. But among those who are not regenerated it is rightly said, because they are not Israel, according to what the Apostle says to the Romans: “For not all who are from Israel are Israel.” There is no doubt that by this he wished the children of the New Testament, that is, the children of promise, to be understood. Finally, he continues: “But in Isaac shall your seed be called”; that is, “not the children of the flesh are the children of God, but the children of the promise are counted as the seed” (Rom. IX, 6–8).

**XLII. JUL.** What does “It shall no longer be said” mean, when this is asserted to this very day with such efforts by the Manichaeans? But this is what it indicates: no one who belongs to the people of Israel, or who accepts the authority of this Scripture, will dare, after my decision, to believe such a thing [Note: [Col. 1267] So the manuscripts. The first edition of Vignierius has *ac reddere* (“and to render”).]. Moreover, anyone who persists in that opinion and does not obey these Scriptures will neither be numbered among those who are in that true Israel.

**AUG.** If, then, God wishes it understood that after His decision no one will believe this, we must ask why before that decision it was not wrong to believe that the sins of fathers were also repaid upon children. If the question is properly examined, it will be found that “I will repay the sins of fathers upon children” was said on account of liable generation. From this arose that proverb about sour grapes.

But because regeneration is free, the New Testament was promised, where this is no longer said: for the inheritance bringing condemnation, which comes from Adam, is renounced through Christ’s grace when one renounces this world, where the children of Adam must necessarily be burdened beneath a heavy yoke—not unjustly, of course—from the day they leave their mother’s womb until the day of their burial in the mother of all (Eccli. XL, 1). The sacred mysteries, even when infants renounce it, sufficiently show what is being done.

**XLIII. JUL.** After condemning the vanity of that proverb, He established His judgment by its promulgation and by a divine affirmation; and He also deigns to disclose the reason for His justice, namely, why relationships are not burdened with the sins of one another [Note: [Col. 1267] The manuscripts have *alternis* (“of one another”).]. “Because all souls,” He says, “are mine; just as the soul of the father is mine, so also the soul of the son is mine; all souls are mine. The soul that sins, it shall die.” Why, then, this moderation of the sentence is most equitable, He shows also by the ownership of the souls.

**AUG.** This ownership of the souls concerns lives lived separately. For no one can be reborn unless he has been born. Why, then, was Levi tithed while he was in Abraham’s loins, unless because at that time the distinct ownership of his own soul was not yet present in him?

**XLIV. JUL.** “The soul of the father,” He says, “is mine, and the soul of the son is mine.” By this testimony, as by many others, it is taught that the soul owes nothing to seeds, since God claims it for His own right. “It is most unjust and foolish,” He says, “that what is mine, my image, should be burdened by the deeds of others.”

**AUG.** Then you separate the flesh from God’s authority, since you think that He claims only the soul for His own right; and you have forgotten what is written: “Just as woman is from man, so also man is through woman; but all things are from God” (I Cor. XI, 12). This was certainly said either of the flesh or of both together, but not of the soul alone.

But since it pleases you to have God say, “It is most unjust and foolish that what is mine, my image, should be burdened by the deeds of others,” why do you not also [Note: [Col. 1268] The Portarum manuscript reads “here.”] make God say this: “It is most unjust and foolish that what is mine, my image, should, through the faithlessness or negligence of its parents, or of any of those among whom it lives, or through any necessity whatsoever, leave the body without Baptism, and not be admitted to my kingdom, nor live, because it has not eaten holy flesh and drunk blood” (John VI, 54)? Or will you also argue and cry out against this statement of Christ, saying, “Certainly, even if it has not eaten Christ’s flesh or drunk His blood, it will live”? O voice worthy of no one but the antichrist! Go, say these things; teach these things. Let Christian men and women hear you; let people whose minds are corrupted and who are reprobate concerning the faith hear you; let them love you, honor you, feed you, clothe you, adorn you, and, by following one who is lost, lose themselves as well.

But “the Lord knows those who are His” (II Tim. II, 19), and there is no reason to despair even concerning you, so long as His patience is being extended toward you.

**XLV. JUL.** I assigned to this man a condition in which no outsider could harm him against his will, but he would willingly take up either sin or righteousness, either reward or guilt.

**AUG.** This may be said of the first nature of man, not of this nature, which has been corrupted and condemned. For even in paradise, before sin, the corruptible body did not weigh down the soul. Or have you been corrupted in mind to such an extent that you dare even to say this? If you do not dare, explain why the image of God deserved to be weighed down by a corruptible body, when you refuse to acknowledge with the Catholic Church the origin of sin.

**XLVI. JUL.** You are therefore indignant with me because I believe God, who swears, rather than Manichaeus, who dreams—especially since he offers no testimonies or arguments of a sound faith, or of a vigilant intellect. Even if such arguments could never be found strong enough to tear down the foundations of truth, nevertheless, if properly presented, they might at least for the moment offer some consolation against the shame of folly.

God persists in fortifying by an oath what He had made sacred by commanding it. He proceeds to make clear by examples also what He sanctions [Note: [Col. 1268] The printed editions have *sentit* (“perceives”); Clar. and Port. have *sancit* (“sanctions”); Mar. has *sanctit*.], and says that if a man should preserve every form of righteousness with undefiled devotion, and should beget a son who clings to pestilent ways and turns aside from his father’s paths, the son gains nothing from the noble distinction of such a father’s great care for righteousness.

Likewise, in the opposite direction, He sets forth the son of this sinner, who avoids his father’s ways by better judgment, and shows that the parent’s iniquity harms him nothing. He makes the condition of righteousness equal to that of sin, asserting that the vices of those who beget do not pass through seeds, just as virtues cannot pass through them; but that all souls belong to their own right. By this He also shows to be profane what you say, namely, that the souls and bodies of those being born are possessed by the devil’s authority.

**AUG.** You have already been answered: you are speaking emptily and at excessive length. The whole human being—that is, both soul and body—belongs through its substance to the authority of the Creator. But through the defect, which is no substance, he has been enslaved to the devil; nevertheless he remains under the same authority of the Creator, under which the devil himself has also been placed.

**XLVII. JUL.** Having asserted the balance of His examination, He then attacks your opinion in those who held similar views. “And you say,” He says, “Why has the son not received the iniquity of his father? Because the soul that sins, it shall die; but the son shall not receive the injustice of his father, nor shall the father receive the injustice of his son; the righteousness of the just shall be upon him, and the iniquity of the wicked shall be upon him.” Who among us [Note: [Col. 1269] So the manuscripts. Vignierius has *vestrum* (“among you”).] could ever have argued from this with such care as God argued through the mouth of His prophet, by dividing, comparing, and repeating?

**AUG.** And yet, although God has done this, you mix your loquacity into the great clarity of His words, knowing that your case is not a good one.

**XLVIII. JUL.** But He was not content merely to explain this. For the confirmation of this justice He also brings forward an argument from works of mercy, and declares that for those very persons who sinned willingly, if they flee to repentance and amendment, their past errors do not cause harm. “If the wicked,” He says, “turns away from his iniquities which he has committed, and keeps my commandments, all his offenses which he has committed shall not be remembered; in the righteousness which he has done, he shall live.”

That is: since I am so disposed toward clemency that I even forgive their own sins to those who have been corrected, how could I impute the sins of others to those being born? Or do circumstances permit innocence to be guilty before me when it is created, though with me it is efficacious even if restored after interruption?

**AUG.** The case of those who repent is different from that of those who are born. For you cannot show how God is just if, on the one hand, He finds no sins in those being born, and yet, on the other, burdens them with a corruptible body and with so many and such great misfortunes besides.

The evils suffered by infants cannot be counted: fever, cough, scabies, pains in every kind of limb, diarrhea, worms, and countless other things arising from the flesh itself; the torments of their cures, which are more numerous than those of their illnesses; and from outside, the blows of wounds, the injuries of beatings, and attacks of demons. Yet you, wise heretics, so that you may not confess original sin, are prepared to fill paradise with such flowers. If you do not say that these things would have existed there, I ask why they exist in infants who, as you contend, have absolutely no sin. But if you are not ashamed to say that these things too would have existed there, what kind of Christians you are is not something we need to explain.

[Col. 1270] **XLIX. JUL.** This displeased the worshipers of idols; and our faith also displeases you, although you see that it has been formed by this law. The profane therefore said, “The way of the Lord is not right.” “Hear, then,” He says, “house of Israel. Is my way not right? Is it not rather your way that is not right? Therefore I shall judge each of you according to your way, says Adonai the Lord.”

Do you perceive by what testimonies we are fortified? Do we pursue anything ambiguous? Do we hunt for general expressions? Do we defend the faith either by weak arguments or by arguments that are convoluted? We abhor what God abhors; we understand what God explains; we discuss what God discussed; we believe because God swore:

> “The son shall not receive the iniquity of his father, nor shall the father receive the injustice of his son; the righteousness of the just shall be upon him, and the iniquity of the wicked shall be upon him.”

It is clear how God promises that He will judge: namely, that He will neither impute the sins of parents to children nor those of children to parents. Accordingly, it has also been established by the testimonies of Scripture, concerning what reason did not permit to remain in doubt, that God maintains in His judgments the same justice which He maintained in His commandments.

**AUG.** From this at least understand that God spoke these things about fathers and children who were already living separately [Note: [Col. 1270] So the manuscripts; elsewhere, “separate.”], because after He had said, “The son shall not receive the iniquity of his father, nor shall the father receive the injustice of his son,” He immediately added, “The righteousness of the just shall be upon him.” For can it be said of an infant in this world that his righteousness is upon him, when by his own life he is not yet able to live either justly or unjustly? Whatever punishments he suffers in this age, by what merit does he suffer them, if he has drawn no sin from his parents? For the most just God neither inflicts nor permits undeserved punishments to be inflicted upon anyone. Nor can it be said that he suffers these evils to exercise the virtue of an infant, since there is not yet any virtue in him.

But if you consider the future age, which belongs [Note: [Col. 1270] The printed editions add “and” after “belongs”; it is removed on the authority of the Portarum codex.] to the inheritance of the New Testament, then it is also most rightly said of infants who die at that age: “The righteousness of the just shall be upon him, and the iniquity of the wicked shall be upon him.” For the generated will be distinguished from the regenerated in this way: the one will live in that kingdom in which righteousness dwells, while the other will die in that punishment in which iniquity is tormented. But what is the righteousness of the one, except that which passes into him from Christ, in whom all shall be made alive? And what is the iniquity of the other, except that which passed into him from Adam, in whom all die?

**L. JUL.** But lest perhaps you try to deceive the ears of the simpler by such a quibble, saying that God here spoke about those who had reached full maturity—that is, that He said the crimes of parents do not harm those children who have emptied natural evil through the holiness of their own works—it must be shown [Col. 1271] that this trick accomplishes nothing.

Although God prescribed absolutely that the iniquity of parents does not condemn innocent children, but that each person is convicted by his own iniquities, and although no faithful mind could doubt this, let us nevertheless take up again the corpse of your opinion, pierced by so many thunderbolts of the law. How will you understand this discussion of God? Is it that the sins of parents harm neither adult children nor children at birth? Or is it that they are not permitted to harm only those who are already of mature age and are practicing righteousness, while infants, before they exhaust the natural poison through their own righteousness [Note: [Col. 1271] The printed editions have: “before their own righteousness exhausts the natural poison.” The manuscripts correct this reading.], are burdened by the crime of those who beget them, so that what God denied would happen through the prophet does in fact happen?

**AUG.** Rather, what God says elsewhere comes to pass: “I will repay the sins of fathers upon children” (Deut. V, 9). Since He Himself says both—that the sins of fathers do not belong to children and that He repays the sins of fathers upon children—He certainly cannot be contrary to Himself. And therefore, when those who ask how both can be true, one of these is understood to apply to generation and the other to regeneration.

You who corrupt your heart, beware of Him [Note: [Col. 1271] The Portarum codex has: “But you corrupt your heart; beware of Him.”]; and when you hear what is true, do not call it a quibble.

### LI. JULIAN

But to this we return. Therefore also confess that the other matter, which is weighed with equal force, takes place: namely, that the righteousness of parents benefits their children and sanctifies them, and that only those are said not to benefit from it who, having already reached a more advanced age, have worn away their birthright righteousness by their own crimes. Since both things have been denied by God, and one has been explained and emphatically stated by the example of the other, you see that this denial conflicts with your arguments and therefore maintain that it is false with respect to infants; thus, by the condition of those who are born, you invalidate both parts of it. When you do this, you will perpetrate two evils at once: one, that you attack the judgment of God; the other, that you assert that a righteous person is born from a righteous person and a criminal from a criminal.

**AUGUSTINE.** I do not say that the Prophet’s denial is false, but that you have not understood it. For he prophesied regeneration, which alone makes children free from the sins of their parents—sins that pertain to God’s judgment, not to human judgment. But while you deny that generation draws the contagion of ancient death from parents, you attempt to extinguish the very cause of regeneration. Although the washing of regeneration cleanses whatever sins it finds, other sins could also be healed through repentance, as they can in those whom it is not lawful to regenerate a second time. But what is contracted through generation is not loosed except through regeneration.

A righteous person, therefore, is born from God, not from a human being, because he becomes righteous by being born again, not by being born; hence such people are also called children of God. Read the Gospel: “Not from bloods, nor from the will of the flesh, nor from the will of man, but from God they were born” (John 1:13). Why do you seek to join together kinds of things that are so different? Human beings are born from human flesh; they are born again through the Spirit of God. What wonder, then, if, just as a human being derives righteousness from the Spirit of righteousness, so he draws original sin from sinful flesh? For the one human being would not have come to liberate us in the likeness of sinful flesh unless the flesh of all of us were sinful flesh. Since, then, your heresy is hostile to this Christian grace, do you still dare to wonder and complain that Christ’s Church detests you?

### LII. JULIAN

But if, unable to endure the uproar of truth as it cries out against you, you try to escape by another route, you will fall into stronger snares. For if you say, “The Prophet’s statement is indeed true, but only with respect to persons of mature age; it says that relationships are not burdened by mutual guilt. But with respect to infants it is false in one part, where it says that they are not guilty because of the crimes of their parents; while in the other part it is not false, where it asserts that they are not raised up by any virtues of their parents”—then you will plainly reveal the most shameful desire, not to dispute but to fabricate; not to express yourself but merely to talk; and, finally, not the judgment of a sound person but the appetite of a deranged Manichaean. You will do so if you think that, against clear reason, against the honor of God, against examples, against the testimonies of teachers, and against the interpretation of judgments, you may reject whatever you please and adopt whatever delights you.

**AUGUSTINE.** The Prophet’s statement is false in no part. But you, not understanding what is prophesied through it, are—so as not to say that you are lying—certainly, without insulting you, ignorant of what you are saying. For even this claim of yours, that the Prophet asserts “that children are raised up by none of their parents’ virtues,” must be considered carefully: how and to what extent is it to be understood? Do you deny that, through the faith of their parents, children are offered for regeneration to the Church their mother and are baptized by the ministers of God? How, then, are children raised up by none of their parents’ virtues? Will you dare to say that Christian faith is no virtue? Are they not raised up when they are admitted into the kingdom of God by no other means than this same regeneration?

Even in temporal benefits, why is it said to Isaac, “I will do this for you because of Abraham your father” (Genesis 26:24)? Why also is Lot, the son of Abraham’s brother, assisted because of the merits of his uncle (ibid. 14 and 19), if children are raised up by none of their parents’ virtues? Finally, why is his kingdom diminished because of Solomon’s sins, but not taken away entirely because of David’s good merits (1 Kings 11:11–13), if children are burdened by none of their parents’ sins or raised up by none of their virtues?

You who have a tongue but no heart, distinguish these matters. Here, if you can, observe what was prophesied through Ezekiel. It is clear that an unregenerated father does not prevent a regenerated son from attaining eternal life, of which it is said, “he shall live”; nor does a regenerated father benefit an unregenerated son in this same respect. Likewise, a regenerated son neither benefits an unregenerated father nor harms a regenerated father if he is unregenerated, so that the one may live and the other die. But if you cannot see these things, why do you not at least keep silent?

### LIII. JULIAN

Who are you, stirred up by Marcion’s frenzy, to rush into the destruction of justice? Who are you to drag both God’s judgments and his commandments—still slippery with the mysteries of the Manichaeans—under the censorship of your tongue? No one has ever undertaken this except one who first denied them.

Under Manichaean authority, you will dare to rupture God’s testament, which reason, justice, piety, truth, and the faith with which the Prophets wrote have sealed, as though it were an ordered company of sacred witnesses. You lost long ago both the sanctity of understanding and the appearance of religion if you think that, by this statement found in Ezekiel, you can find either support for your cause or escape from its destruction.

**AUGUSTINE.** Verbosity abundantly displays the poverty of its resources where truth is not perceived—or, even if perceived, is despised; where there is not the most empty abundance of words but the most certain abundance of realities. One thing is a straightforward and truthful speaker; another is an eloquent slanderer.[^c0028-1] The Prophet speaks truth about sons and fathers who lead their lives separately; you, under the name of the Manichaeans, slander Catholics who correctly understand the Prophet, in a Pelagian frenzy.

[^c0028-1]: Vignier thinks the reading may perhaps be: “One is an eloquent Truth-speaker, another an eloquent slanderer.”

### LIV. JULIAN

“The iniquity of the wicked,” he says, “shall be upon his own head; I will judge each of you according to his ways. Fathers shall not die for their sons, nor sons for their fathers. The soul that sins, it shall die; for all souls are mine. I will judge each one according to his own iniquities.”

**AUGUSTINE.** The God who says these things is the same God who says, “I will repay the sins of the fathers upon the children.” Unless you understand how both statements are true, do not imagine that you have understood the truthful Prophet, however much I may endure your slanderous verbosity.

### LV. JULIAN

Look at what light, what company of judgments, and what dignity of decisions your traducian doctrine does not fear to insult and attempts to prejudice. Here there is no doubt that you will not be ashamed to say what remains to be said: namely, that you will answer that the Prophet’s statement—or rather, God’s statement through the Prophet—is true, but that the incontrovertible judgment of prudent people teaches that it is utterly unjust for the sins of parents to be charged to their children.

**AUGUSTINE.** Be ashamed, you are the utterly unjust one. For the one who said, “I will repay the sins of the fathers upon the children,” is not unjust.

### LVI. JULIAN

Nor should you think this because the seeds of all human beings are polluted by the guilt of the will, while nevertheless this justice is ineffective in the case of Adam’s crime alone. His is the one sin that is charged to everyone.

What should I do first in response? Should I laugh, since such absurdity demands exceptional laughter? But the destruction of the many whom you deceive calls for compassion and tears. Should I therefore be overcome by serious grief? Yet the monstrosities of your arguments provoke laughter, even though my spirit is sorrowful.

**AUGUSTINE.** Say what you are going to say, distinguished corrector. On whose authority is Ambrose to be considered a deceiver, when your teacher Pelagius said of him that not even an enemy had dared to criticize his faith and his most pure understanding of Scripture?[^c0028-2] Criticize him, then; for you are a stronger and more powerful enemy of the cross of Christ than you would be if you were an enemy of Ambrose. You envy God’s grace more boldly than you would envy that man of God.

Criticize him, I say; ridicule him by attacking him; bewail him in grief. Through the great power of your eloquence, you can lead your vanity into urbanity and transform your senselessness into compassion. Say, then, that this man shamefully erred and unhappily lost his senses when he affirmed that the discord between the desire of the flesh and the spirit had been turned into nature through the transgression of the first human being (Book 7 on Luke 12:52).

For who is born without that discord, since human beings began to be born—being born, of course, in sinful flesh? But you, a very clever man, refusing to believe that that sin was so great and so serious that it could then change nature into this evil and, by the merit of an unspeakable apostasy, make nature condemned together with its offspring, assert as good, while drunk on Pelagian doctrine, what all sober people perceive and judge to be evil.

With wondrous eloquence you can adorn with praise the desire that the saints condemn with groans, and place in the groves of paradise a desire exactly as it now is—forcing itself upon those who do not wish it and challenging the hearts of the chaste to battle—as though it were a beautiful and pleasant tree, even if no one there had sinned. Be ashamed, Pelagian blessedness, and see where you can flee, since the chaste flee from you.

[^c0028-2]: See above, *On the Grace of Christ*, sections 46 and 47.

### LVII. JULIAN

For if any span of time remains to this world, who will be able to believe from the monuments of written literature that there once existed a human being who believed and swore that what was natural was not natural; that what belonged to generation did not belong to generation; and that what pertained to the condition of parents did not pertain to that condition except because they had become parents?

I think that a future generation will judge these inventions—these nausea-inducing statements and these vomitings—to have been fabricated rather than defended by any mortal. For your people and your faith endure these swimmmings, these nauseas, and these vomitings: you say, “The sins of parents cannot pass through nature to their children, because what belongs to the will is not bound to the seeds; but Adam’s sin, which was conceived from the will, passes through nature into all human beings, because what belongs to the will is bound to the seeds. God does not condemn children for the sins of their parents, because that is the height of injustice; yet he condemns Adam’s descendants because of their parents’ sin, which no justice can avenge. Finally, it does not pertain to the condition of generation, because those who are married become parents; but it pertained to Adam for no other reason than that he generated according to the law of marriage.”

Is this guiding a course, or swimming? Is this digesting, or becoming nauseated? Is this taking in something solid, or continually vomiting? In the same words you affirm what you have denied; in the same lines you deny what you have affirmed. And you become angry because we do not yield to a man who, torn apart by a serious illness, cannot retain what he takes in.

**AUGUSTINE.** Far be it from us to say that God does not repay the sins of other fathers upon their children, since divine Scripture so often and so explicitly testifies for which sins of fathers vengeance has come upon their children—to such an extent that, although God spared King Ahab, he delayed avenging one of his grave sins upon his son (1 Kings 21:29).

But who can investigate the manner, rationale, and measure of God’s justice concerning the sins of other fathers, so that they are repaid upon their children? For this reason God reserved these judgments to himself, while he prohibited human beings, when judging, from inflicting such vengeance.

But the apostasy of the first human being, in whom freedom of his own will was at its highest and was hindered by no fault, was so great a sin that human nature collapsed entirely in his ruin. This is indicated by the immense misery of the human race, known to all from the first cries of infants to the final breaths of the dying. Those who deny it therefore claim for themselves a greater share in human misery through such horrible and incredible blindness—as you do when you continue to say, even after the Palestinian judgment, where Pelagius himself condemned you for saying these things, that Adam was made mortal so that, whether he sinned or did not sin, he would have died.[^c0028-3]

But proceed as you please, and even accuse all those many Palestinian bishops of being Manichaeans. Shout that Pelagius yielded for a time to the Manichaeans so as not to be condemned by them. Fill paradise with the fruits of lust; scatter through those happy meadows all the many and great evils that we see infants suffering, as though they were not punitive pains but springtime fragrances.

And ridicule me as though I were swimming, while you perish submerged in these depths. Ridicule me as though I were nauseated and vomiting, while you lie dead and, like rotting corruption breeding worms, stink through your restless verbosity. Accuse me of affirming what I denied and denying what I affirmed, while you have done this instead, as I showed in your previous book; those who read can observe that I did not do so and discover how deceitfully you have said that I did.

Call me torn apart by a serious illness because I cannot retain what I take in, while you, having completely lost the spirit of life, are not even capable of receiving what has been put into you.

[^c0028-3]: *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, sections 24, 57, and 60.

### LVIII. JULIAN

You yourself see that this matter is not worthy of a conflict. Nevertheless, in order to assist unwary minds—which adopt the coarser opinions that flatter their evil habits as a consolation for a wounded conscience—we ask whether you have found such an invention of utter stupidity in some passage of Scripture.[^c0028-4] If you say, “Through one human being sin entered the world” (Romans 5:12), we urge you to reread the earlier book of the present work. If you remember it, you will not be able to use the Apostle’s testimony.

[^c0028-4]: The Portus manuscript has “conceived.”

**AUGUSTINE.** We urge you rather to read the Apostle himself and see that the few words of his which we are discussing are so clearly against you that you have labored in vain—not merely in a little book but in a very long and verbose volume—to twist them, not to your heretical opinion but away from their meaning; not to explain them but to obscure them.

### LIX. JULIAN

But if you say that there is one form of Baptism by which people of different ages are consecrated, you will admit, even without my saying so, that it contains no mention of infected generation, no mention of diabolical flesh, and no mention of Adam. Nevertheless, although this does not concern traducianism, we shall answer it fully in its proper place.

[^c0028-5]: The wording “form of Baptism” is restored here from the manuscripts.

**AUGUSTINE.** When you begin to answer, what will appear in you except, as usual, the heretic?

### LX. JULIAN

At least set forth one statement of the Law against the dignity of so many testimonies brought forward by us, against manifest justice, and against clear reason, by which you may show that you have been deceived. I add this because, even if there were a statement that seemed, through ambiguity of wording, to indicate something of this kind, it would nevertheless be compelled to be interpreted according to the splendor and teaching of other statements, in the manner demanded by justice.

**AUGUSTINE.** The divine testimonies brought against you are certain, not ambiguous, as many have already been brought forward by us. But because they rebuke your darkness, they do not appear luminous to you; and whenever their radiant light troubles you, you close your heart against them, lest the night of error be driven away.

### LXI. JULIAN

Now, since no trace of this opinion is found in the holy Scriptures, while the faith we defend is fortified no less by its own arguments than by examples and testimonies, you are wholly possessed by a deadly obstinacy if you think that the dreams of the Manichaeans must be accepted at the cost of the Law, at the cost of reason, at the cost of prudence, and at the cost of justice.

**AUGUSTINE.** At the cost of the Law, you do not hear, “I will repay the sins of the fathers upon the children” (Deuteronomy 5:9). At the cost of reason, you do not see that the evils suffered by infants who have committed no sins of their own in this life can have just causes before God only in sins of origin. At the cost of prudence, you do not take care to avoid proposing or defending, against the most ancient foundation of the Catholic faith, a novel doctrine that denies original sin. At the cost of justice, you are so unjust that, under my name, you do not fear to charge with the contagion of the Manichaean plague so many holy men—the sons and fathers of Christ’s Church, its disciples and teachers who lived before us—and the Catholic Church itself, the mother of all.[^c0028-6]

[^c0028-6]: The printed editions add “of the Catholic faith.” The manuscripts do not contain “of the faith.”

### LXII. JULIAN

Nevertheless, attend to what we bring forward in this sense. Even if you could prove that Adam’s sin is charged to his children, you would still agree that the crimes of other parents do not harm their offspring.

**AUGUSTINE.** Who would agree with this error except one who does not believe God when he says, “I will repay the sins of the fathers upon the children”?

### LXIII. JULIAN

It was evident that what appeared to make children liable because of the sin of one parent had not been caused by generation but by some other cause.

**AUGUSTINE.** You state most plainly that God is unjust, although he most plainly says that he will repay the sins of fathers upon their children.

### LXIV. JULIAN

And it happened that, just as the judge’s assessment was stained by condemning the innocent, so the condition of generation was vindicated by examples involving other parents. For if the cause lay in the path of descent, if it lay in the act of conception, this condition would pollute every generation.

**AUGUSTINE.** “I will repay the sins of the fathers upon the children,” God cries out. Therefore, because he is truthful, you have strayed from the path of truth.

### LXV. JULIAN

But when the condition appeared different even though the generation was not different, it plainly became clear that, even in that marriage whose guilt its offspring had shared, generation had not been corrupted.

**AUGUSTINE.** Although generation is not different when the mortal are born from the mortal, nevertheless what the Apostle says—“The body indeed is dead because of sin” (Romans 8:10)—does not refer to other fathers but to that one who sinned with such great impiety that we cannot measure or estimate it.

But how great God judged it to be, we have learned from sufficiently reliable witnesses: from divine Scripture, certainly, and from the misery of the human race itself. We see that this misery was repaid to his offspring for his sin, and certainly not by an unjust judgment of God. As Christians, we say that not only eternal death of soul and body, but not even temporal death of the body, nor the many and great evils that we see infants suffering, would have existed in paradise if no one had sinned.

Other fathers, however, even if they commit many sins, sin because the soul is weak and because they sin in a corruptible body that weighs down the soul. Their sins do not make nature mortal, and their sins are repaid upon their children as punishment of a very different and much lesser kind, according to the hidden and just judgment of the one who disposes all things “by measure and number and weight” (Wisdom 11:21) and who truthfully says, “I will repay the sins of the fathers upon the children.”

[^c0028-7]: The Claromontanus and Maranus manuscripts read “than,” rather than “how much.”

### LXVI. JULIAN

What, then, has been accomplished? Evidently, it is so certain that sin is not transmitted that even if you taught that children are punished because of Adam’s sin, it would nevertheless remain established that sins cannot be born with anyone and that guilt does not travel with the seed. For you would admit that this does not occur in every act of generation. Consequently, even if vices were transmitted to persons, they would not be mingled with conceptions.

But now, since you and I agree that the sin of parents could not pass to children except through a defect and guilt of generation; since reason, examples, and the Law agree that the condition of generation could in no way have been corrupted; and since this is also confirmed by your concession—for you say that the sins of no parents except two pass on to their children—it has been conclusively established that neither was the fertility of the first human beings corrupted by the devil nor can any sin be born with anyone.

**AUGUSTINE.** This is not what is said to you; you are saying to yourself what we do not say. The sins of other fathers are repaid upon their children by divine justice, not human justice. God knows when and how he does this most justly; human beings do not know, and must judge according to their knowledge.

A person can know, when judging—although even this is not always possible—what each individual has done. But how does he know by what and what kinds of bonds the nature of a person is connected with the nature from which it arose? We say this one thing: that the alteration of human nature into a condition of mortality, even if there were nothing else, is sufficient for condemnation unless the obligation of generation is loosed by regeneration. We say this although you do not wish to hear it; you do not overcome it by truth, even though you persist in attacking it with verbosity.

[^c0028-8]: The printed editions read “through the deed”; the manuscripts support the shorter reading, “the deed.”

### LXVII. JULIAN

We are therefore asked why we do not agree that sin is natural. We answer: because it has no appearance of probability, much less of truth; no appearance of justice; no appearance of piety; and because it makes the devil appear to be the creator of human beings.

**AUGUSTINE.** It certainly makes him appear to be the creator—but to you, not to those who know how to distinguish defect from nature, even though the defect is in nature. Read the Epistle to the Hebrews and see that solid food belongs to those who have their senses trained to distinguish good from evil; you do not have such senses.

Therefore, when we say, “A human being is born with a defect,” you think that the devil is being called his creator. You are so blind or contentious that you can neither see nor wish to consider even the bodily defects with which some people are born. If you are asked what merits have brought about those defects, you find no refuge except a precipice, so long as you refuse to return to the solid rock of the Catholic Church.[^c0028-9]

[^c0028-9]: The printed editions add “of the faith.” The manuscripts omit it; “of the Church” is understood here.

### LXVIII. JULIAN

Because it attributes the crime of iniquity to God the judge.[^c0028-10]

[^c0028-10]: Vignier reads “to God as judge”; the manuscripts read “to God the judge.”

**AUGUSTINE.** You do this, because, if there is no original sin, the heavy yoke placed upon infants is unjust.[^c0028-11]

[^c0028-11]: The manuscripts read this way. Vignier reads: “because the yoke of grace upon infants is unjust.”

### LXIX. JULIAN

Because it weakens and destroys free will, by which the Church of Christ is especially protected against various errors.

**AUGUSTINE.** You suppress free will by refusing to acknowledge God’s grace, which restores and assists it.

### LXX. JULIAN

By saying that all human beings are so incapable of any virtue that they are filled with ancient crimes in their mothers’ wombs.

**AUGUSTINE.** How could we say that human beings are justified—that is, made righteous—by grace if we denied that they were capable of virtue?

### LXXI. JULIAN

Yet you invent that the force of these crimes not only expels natural innocence but thereafter compels people toward every vice throughout their entire lives.

**AUGUSTINE.** Through God’s grace our necessity is diminished; through God’s grace it comes to an end. Your verbosity has nothing to do here.[^c0028-12]

[^c0028-12]: The Portus manuscript reads “nor” instead of “not.”

### LXXII. JULIAN

You swear that this law of sin remained and continued in the Prophets and Apostles, who were already conspicuous for the great splendor of their conduct and miracles, and even after that grace of Christ’s mysteries which you think can assist all these outrages of your doctrine.[^c0028-13]

[^c0028-13]: The printed editions read “you avoid”; the manuscripts read “you swear.”

**AUGUSTINE.** The Prophets and Apostles faithfully fought against the lust you have embraced—that is, the desire of the flesh opposing the desire of the spirit—because they did not praise it.

### LXXIII. JULIAN

Because it extinguishes every effort toward complete moral goodness; because it consoles and increases the disgrace of moral obscenity by attributing it to the works of God, that is, to human nature; because it subjects all the commandments of the Law to the guilt of impossibility, that is, to iniquity.

**AUGUSTINE.** The one who says, “I do not do what I want, but I do the very thing I hate” (Romans 7:15), places the possibility of his perfection in God’s grace, contrary to you. He does not trust in his own virtue, lest he be vain as you are.

### LXXIV. JULIAN

Because it is no less disgraceful than profane when, as the chief proofs of its assertion, it embraces the shamefulness of the sexual organs.

**AUGUSTINE.** We do not embrace the shamefulness of the sexual organs. Rather, we recognize—what you do not wish to recognize—the origin of that shame. For we hear the clearest testimony of Scripture, against which you make yourselves deaf when you ought to fall silent.

Who, hearing that the first human beings were naked and were not ashamed (Genesis 2:25), would not see how it happened that, after the sin, they were ashamed to be naked and hastened to cover the members of which they were ashamed with whatever coverings they could make (ibid. 3:7)?

Yet a human being has been found who would place even such lust—lust that must be resisted lest one sin, and of which even the shameless are ashamed—in paradise, even if no one there had sinned; nor would he be ashamed to say something so deformed and sacrilegious.

I ask you: if, as we believe, this lust causes you only the trouble of resistance and displays no will of its own, why do you think that such a great reward of praise should be paid to it, even though your judgment about it is false?

### LXXV. JULIAN

And instead of sacred authorities, it swells with accusations against God.[^c0028-14]

[^c0028-14]: Vignier reads “you swell”; the manuscripts, more appropriately, read “it swells.”

**AUGUSTINE.** Is “The body is dead because of sin” not sacred authority? And is “He will give life to your mortal bodies” (Romans 8:10–11) an accusation rather than praise of God? I think that the one who said these things was not an accuser but a preacher of God filled with God himself. Here he shows that Adam was not made as you say, so that, whether he sinned or did not sin, he would die.

### LXXVI. JULIAN

In whose commandments it confirms the tyrannical excess of severity.

**AUGUSTINE.** God’s commandment is not tyrannical; but in order that it may be fulfilled, God himself must be entreated. You do not wish this, because you trust in your own virtue.

### LXXVII. JULIAN

In whose judgments it confirms barbarous iniquity.

**AUGUSTINE.** Because God’s judgment is not unjust, original sin must be recognized in the misery of the human race, which begins with the tears of infants.

### LXXVIII. JULIAN

In whose oaths it confirms the presence of Punic falsehood.[^c0028-15]

[^c0028-15]: That is, Carthaginian or proverbial deceit.

**AUGUSTINE.** When God says, “I will repay the sins of the fathers upon the children,” does he speak in Punic?

### LXXIX. JULIAN

Because, instead of arguments and all syllogisms, it relies upon the dreams and madness of the Manichaeans.

**AUGUSTINE.** Neither was he a Manichaean, nor did he dream, nor was he mad—whether the one who said, “We too were by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Ephesians 2:3), or the one who said, “We are all born under sin, and our very birth is in defect” (Ambrose, Book 1, *On Repentance*, chapter 2 or 3).

### LXXX. JULIAN

These, then, are the reasons that inflame us to attack natural evil, and that make us disdain and despise association with the lost.

**AUGUSTINE.** No one except a lost person would call the pious agreement of so many Catholic teachers an association with the lost.

### LXXXI. JULIAN

These reasons make us no more terrified by the uproar of the whole world than we would be if we saw a gloomy forest of lupines resounding,[^c0028-16] or if we saw it stirred by filthy swine or rushing winds.

[^c0028-16]: Vignier reads “as if”; the manuscripts read “than if.” The printed editions read “thundering”; the manuscripts more probably read “resounding.” Julian alludes to Virgil, *Georgics* 1.75–76:

> Or if you should raise the slender shoots of vetch and bitter lupine,
> their fragile stalks, and a rustling forest.

**AUGUSTINE.** The Catholic Church, spread throughout the whole world, which prudently shuddered at your mouths, is not a forest of lupines; rather, it wished to be safe from lupine bites.

### LXXXII. JULIAN

Therefore we believe that God is just, pious, and truthful. Accordingly, we hold that his Law commanded nothing impossible, that the testimonies confirm nothing false, and that the judgments pronounce nothing unjust. We hold that he is the creator of human beings, whom he creates liable to no crime, but indeed full of natural innocence and capable of voluntary virtues.

**AUGUSTINE.** Why, then, does he not admit his image—unless it has been blown upon and exorcized—to his own life? Is this how the reward of innocence is given? Or is it rather that, because guilt has been contracted through generation and not dismissed through regeneration, life is justly denied and death follows as punishment?

The Apostle would not have detested those alienated from the life of God (Ephesians 4:18) if there were no punishment.

### LXXXIII. JULIAN

Once these points have been gathered together, one of two alternatives must necessarily be accepted: either God is believed to be such as the Manichaean Traducianist invents him, or he is understood, together with all who concede the principles of traducianism, to be such as the honored God is attacked for being.

But God cannot be such as the Manichaean dreams him; rather, he is the pious, just, and true God whom all holy Scripture, the whole Law, and our faith venerate. Accordingly, this is your doctrine, which, just as it is embraced with an insult to God, so is destroyed with honor to him.[^c0028-17]

[^c0028-17]: Vignier reads: “Accordingly, this is your doctrine,” omitting the second “this,” which is present in the manuscripts.

**AUGUSTINE.** If you believe God to be pious, why do you impiously prevent the Savior—that is, Jesus—from receiving infants? If you believe him to be just, why do you believe that a heavy yoke is placed upon infants without any merits of sin? If you believe him to be truthful, why do you not believe him when he says, “I will repay the sins of the fathers upon the children”?

### LXXXIV. JULIAN

It is time for us to proceed to other matters. But the dignity of the case requires us to restore even those things that we think were omitted in the previous book. A prudent reader may perhaps judge this unnecessary; nevertheless, since it is clear that a case entrusted to us amid dangers clings even to minor points, it is our task to remove the consolations by which you have taken away its defenses.

**AUGUSTINE.** Since you have begun to pass on to another matter, we must now demonstrate what we promised earlier: namely, that the prophecy of Ezekiel, in which it is said that the sins of fathers are not repaid upon children, just as the sins of children are not repaid upon fathers, refers to the foretelling of the revelation of the New Testament.

The prophet Jeremiah also says something of this kind, and there he makes clear why it is said. Among other things he says:

“Turn back, virgin Israel; return to your cities, mourning. How long will you turn away, dishonored daughter? For the Lord has created salvation as a new planting, and in this salvation human beings shall go about. Thus says the Lord: Again they shall speak this word in the land of Judah and in its cities, when I restore its captivity:

‘Blessed is the Lord upon his righteous holy mountain.’

And those who dwell in Judea and in all its cities, together with the farmer—and he shall be taken away with the flock;” for I have intoxicated every thirsty soul, and I have satisfied every hungry soul. Because of this I awoke, and I saw, and my sleep became sweet to me.

Therefore, behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and I will sow Israel and Judah with the seed of man and the seed of cattle. And just as I watched over them to uproot and afflict, so I will watch over them to build and plant, says the Lord.

In those days they shall no longer say, ‘The fathers ate a sour grape, and the children’s teeth were set on edge’; but each one shall die in his own sin, and the teeth of the one who ate the sour grape shall be set on edge.’”

It is plainly evident that this refers to the days of the new planting, about which he was speaking when he said this. There, too, the seed of man and the seed of cattle that God promised to sow are to be understood spiritually, so that those who rule and those who are ruled may be recognized.

But because it had become deeply rooted in the hearts of the people that it was written in the Old Testament, “I will repay the sins of the fathers upon the children,” lest anyone should think that God’s Scripture contradicted itself, he immediately added, to show more clearly that one statement belongs to the Old Testament and the other to the New:

“Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and I will complete a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah, not according to the covenant that I established with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt,” and so forth (Jeremiah 31:21–32, according to the Septuagint, chapter 38).

Generation, therefore, belongs to that covenant, while regeneration belongs to this one. Hence, in the former, the sins of fathers are repaid upon children; but in the latter, once the bond of generation has been loosed through regeneration, it is not said, “The fathers ate a sour grape, and the children’s teeth were set on edge.” Rather, “The teeth of the one who ate the sour grape shall be set on edge,” because each person shall die not in his father’s sin but in his own, if he commits it.

But when you have not shown how Scripture is consistent where it says, “The son shall not bear the sin of his father” (Ezekiel 18:20), and where it says, “I will repay the sins of the fathers upon the children” (Deuteronomy 5:9), these statements will remain opposed to each other unless each of the two is referred to its own covenant. The prophet Jeremiah demonstrated this most clearly.

Vignier substituted *nisi* (“unless”) for *sed in* (“but in”). The manuscripts restore the words from *qua* (“where”) through *mentitur* (“is false”). [Col. 1273] The editions and two manuscripts read *vestri Marcionis aestu concitatus* (“stirred by the heat of your Marcion”); the older Portus manuscript omits *aestu* and reads *aestro* in place of *vestri*. The manuscripts read *perrumpere*; Vignier, *prorumpere*. The Portus manuscript reads *inopia copiosa* for *inopiae copiosa*. [Col. 1275] The Portus manuscript reads *conceperis* (“you have conceived”) for *compereris* (“you have discovered”). [Col. 1276] “Form of Baptism” is restored from the manuscripts. Vignier reads *tu* (“you”); the manuscripts, *tot* (“so many”). The printed editions add *fidei* (“of the faith”) to “Catholic Church”; the manuscripts omit it, so it is understood. Vignier reads *judice* (“as judge”); the manuscripts, *judici* (“to the judge”). [Col. 1279] The printed editions read *conspicitis* (“you behold”); the manuscripts, *conspicuis* (“conspicuous”). [Col. 1280] Vignier reads *nullo* (“by no crime”); the manuscripts, *nulli* (“liable to no crime”). The word *reatus* (“guilt”) is restored from the manuscripts. [Col. 1281] Vignier omits the second *hoc* (“this”) in “this is your doctrine”; it is present in the manuscripts. [Col. 1282] The printed editions read *per generationem* (“through generation”); the Maranus manuscript, more correctly, *per regenerationem* (“through regeneration”).

### LXXXV. JUL.

Accordingly, when we had come (Book 2, chapters 56 ff.) to the statement of the Apostle Paul which Traducianus was accustomed to parade before those ignorant of the Scriptures—namely, “Through one man sin entered into the world” (Rom. 5:12)—I first demonstrated, from the testimony of the very wording, that the Traducians had been excluded from the inner meaning of that passage. [Note: [Col. 1282] The Portus codex reads thus; the other manuscripts and the printed editions read “first.”] For when the Teacher of the Gentiles was reviewing the antiquity of sin, he placed, as though a very strong guardian, a definite number beside the preservation of generation, so that, by saying that sin had entered the world through one man, he prescribed that he had intended nothing concerning generation, which could not exist except through two. I also pointed out that a distinction must be made between the union of the parents and the sin of the parents, since he said that sin had indeed entered the world, but through a number that could not apply to offspring.

Throughout the entire little book it was sufficiently established that the nature of sin was not indicated there, but its form: that it consisted in imitation by those who subsequently transgressed, not in something received through generation. But because we read in the Epistle to the Hebrews, concerning the Jews, “From one they came forth, and that one as good as dead”—that is, from Abraham—and because earlier in the same Epistle it is also read of Christ, “He who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all from one” (Heb. 2:11), lest Traducianus seize upon either of these passages, or anything similar if it could be found, and argue that our response had been deprived of all force—our response in which we maintained that “one” was said in the case of him through whom sin passed so that generation might not be understood—since in this Epistle the term “one” had been found to indicate generation, I therefore thought that the matter ought to be reconsidered.

So that the reader may be attentive, I offer this warning: this objection will be destroyed in several ways. In the passage, therefore, where Abraham is mentioned and his wife Sarah is introduced, the order of the words is as follows:

“By faith Abraham, when he was called, obeyed by going out to a place which he was to receive as an inheritance; and he went out, not knowing where he was going. By faith he dwelt in the land of promise as in a foreign land, living in tents with Isaac and Jacob, co-heirs of the same promise. For he was awaiting the city having foundations, whose architect and founder is God. By faith Sarah herself also received power for the conception of offspring, even beyond the proper time of life, because she believed that he who had promised was faithful. Therefore from one they came forth—and that one as good as dead—as numerous as the stars of heaven and as countless as the sand which is beside the seashore” (Heb. 11:8–12).

Since he had therefore mentioned both—Abraham and Sarah—and had said that she was exhausted by the law of old age but had received, through faith, the power of conceiving offspring, he safely added that from one had come forth so many peoples who would be compared with the multitude of the stars.

To explain the union of the parents, the faithful proclamation as well as the truth of what had happened required this wording; [Note: [Col. 1283] Thus the manuscripts; Vignierius reads “of the faithful.”] but to say, in commending the propagation of the multitude, not “from both” but “from one,” was suggested by the art of praise. He wished to show how much that sure faith had deserved, by saying that a multitude exceeding all reckoning had been propagated by God’s power. [Note: [Col. 1283] The printed editions read “power”; the text is corrected from the manuscripts.] He judged that it was more appropriate to the praise of the work to say that they had been begotten from one rather than from two, especially since, in the increase of praise which the final sentence supplied, there was no loss to the historical truth, which he had already supplied above by mentioning both persons. [Note: [Col. 1283] Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read “argument.”]

**AUG.** Anyone who does not understand that you are saying nothing, I do not know what he can understand. You had said that the Apostle stated, “Through one man sin entered into the world,” because that man provided the others with an example of sinning: “For if,” you say, “he had wanted generation to be understood in that passage, he would have said ‘through two,’ not ‘through one’” (Book 2, chapters 56, 183).

Yet if he had wanted an example to be understood, he would rather have said “through one woman,” not “through one man,” since she plainly provided even her own husband with an example of sinning. But because sin entered the world through generation, and is to be healed only through regeneration, he said “through one,” because just as the human example of sin began from a woman, so generation began from a man. [Note: [Col. 1283] The Portus manuscript reads “human.”] For no one doubts that conception, which belongs to the woman, is preceded by insemination, which belongs to the man.

But behold, a most evident testimony has been found—whether by you yourself or by someone who perhaps brought it against you—in which innumerable people are said to have come from one, although they had a man and a woman, plainly two parents, from whom they came forth. Yet this was most correctly said because of the beginning of generation, which comes from the man’s seed.

Finally, when he was setting forth praiseworthy examples of faith, he began with Abel himself, and, after mentioning Abraham, proceeded to Sarah. He had already passed beyond Abraham and was speaking of his wife; yet when he came to mention the generation of the immense people, he returned to Abraham, because he begot what she bore.

If you had reflected as you ought, you would not have blasphemed the faithful preacher of faith who wrote the Epistle by saying that he had been “admonished by the art of praise.” Admonished to do what, I ask? To lie, by asserting that those who came from two had come from one? “Judging,” as you suppose, “that this was more appropriate to the praise of God’s work”? You are greatly mistaken.
