False praise does not please God. You readily offer it, certainly, to lust; but falsity greatly displeases the truth. And why you offer yourself to lust, not as a praiser but as a flatterer, I do not know. Will it love you more for that? You are entirely deceived. It does not love the human being; rather, it goads him to love what he ought not to love.

But if it can be said, in some manner of speech, not falsely but truly, that those who came from two came from one, why do you think that generation could not have been implied where it was said, “Through one man sin entered into the world,” because generation takes place through two, not one? It is known to everyone that either the man who sows generates first, or at least first; while the woman either does not generate but bears, or, if the birth itself can properly be called generation, she first conceives from the man who generates and afterward generates the fetus whom she had conceived.

Accordingly, when the Apostle wished it to be understood that sin entered the world through generation—a sin which Christ would wash away through regeneration—he said “through one man,” who at that time generated either first or rather. Above all, as we have already said—and this must be impressed upon you—if he had said this because of the primacy of the example, he would have said “through one woman,” from whom the first example of sinning in the human race proceeded; and he would more likely have passed over the man, whom the woman’s example had taught to follow her even into sin by imitation.

### LXXXVI. JUL.

Accordingly, in the Epistle to the Hebrews, where the subject is generation, many are said to have come from one; but in the Epistle to the Romans, where the Apostle is speaking about sin, he says that sin entered through one man. By this number he most decisively demonstrated that he had intended nothing concerning generation.

**AUG.** To speak in this way against evident facts is not, as you suppose, praiseworthy eloquence, but unbelievable shamelessness.

### LXXXVII. JUL.

But where it is said of Christ, “He who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all from one” (Heb. 2:11), this can be understood not of Adam but of God, by whose power Christ was made according to the flesh, as was the whole human race. Consequently, the similarity of the wording could contribute nothing toward undermining the Apostle’s understanding, according to which he said that sin entered the world through one man.

Nevertheless, let what follows remain fixed in the mind of the especially prudent reader, so that he may understand that up to this point I have proceeded much more leniently than the matter required. Let us allow generation—which cannot occur except through two—to be shown by many testimonies nevertheless to be customarily said to have been effected through one.

But the opinion of Tradux will gain nothing from this. Why? Clearly because some things we say improperly, and others properly. Therefore, what is proper gives its own names without loss; but what is said by usage is not permitted to impose upon principal realities—that is, proper realities—the prejudices of its definitions. The whole matter is blameless when, by an abuse of language, we assign alien terms to realities about which there is no doubt.

**AUG.** But you are going to introduce doubt even into realities that are clear, when they contradict you.

### LXXXVIII. JUL.

Moreover, when something contrary to everyone’s opinion is introduced in a speech whose very sound provides it with all its defense, it is a grave error if, while its proper name is available, it is labeled with a borrowed and abusive term. Therefore, when the subject is offspring, since no one doubts that everyone who is born has two parents and this requires no supporting argument, it will not harm understanding if I say that he was generated from one. For my statement will not so disturb anyone that he thinks a person could be born either without a father or without a mother.

**AUG.** Someone who is born indeed has two parents; but for him to be born, one generates him by sowing, while the other bears him by giving birth. Thus it is sufficiently clear to whom generation ought chiefly, or first, to be attributed. Cease, then, to cast the clouds of your loquacity over matters placed in the light.

Who speaks in such a way as to say that anyone was generated from one? Whenever anyone hears this, he thinks only of the father, and no one except one father generates a human being by sowing. [Note: [Col. 1285] Thus the manuscripts; Vignierius reads, “nor does anyone sow a human being by generating.”] But people generated from one are rightly said to be two or more when they could otherwise be thought not to have one father.

Yet where father and mother must be understood, who can be said to have been born from one except falsely? If it were clear that two people had walked together or had done something together, would you therefore say without lying that one had walked or that one had done it, merely because it was clear that there had been two? Would your lie not be all the more shameless the clearer the truth was?

The singular number is indeed sometimes used for the plural in figurative speech, as in the plagues with which Egypt was struck, where “frog” or “locust” is mentioned in the singular (Ps. 77:45–46; Ps. 104:34), although there were many. [Note: [Col. 1285] Vignierius reads “or locust, certainly in the singular,” omitting “number,” which is found in the manuscripts.] But if it were said “one frog” or “one locust,” who would doubt that the statement was all the more foolishly false the clearer the truth was?

Stop, then, selling these smokescreens to people who are utterly ignorant of such matters, and understand that sin entered the world through one man, not as you say, but as the Apostle says. Through one man—not through the woman who preceded him by her example, for that would be said of the woman—but through the one who began the generation, because he first sowed what she conceived, and he himself generated what she bore, sin entered the world.

Thus it is written: “Abraham begot Isaac, Isaac begot Jacob,” and this wording continues through the subsequent generations. It is not said, “Abraham and Sarah begot Isaac,” or “Isaac and Rebekah begot Jacob.” And where it was necessary to mention the mothers, the Evangelist does not say, “Judah and Tamar begot Perez and Zerah,” but says, “Judah begot Perez from Tamar” (Matt. 1:2–3). Wherever he adds the mothers, he nevertheless assigns the generation to the fathers, saying not, “He and she begot him,” but, “He begot him from her.”

Hence understand that it was said in this manner that innumerable people were generated from one Abraham, because he alone begot them from Sarah. Therefore it was said, “Through one man sin entered into the world,” so that the beginning of generation might be understood there, which comes from the man—not the example of imitation, which entered the human race through one woman rather than through one man.

### LXXXIX. JUL.

But when the subject is sin, which is falsely represented as innate, contrary to everyone’s opinion and to all reason—

**AUG.** It is not falsely represented as innate contrary to everyone’s opinion and to all reason. Rather, Scripture and the misery of the human race itself testify that original sin is shown against your error.

### XC. JUL.

And this sin is properly said to have passed through one if he provided an example of wrongdoing; but it is most inappropriate to say so if he generated this sin, which could not pass to posterity except through two—

**AUG.** On the contrary, it entered through one, from whom was sown what she bore. The example, however, preceded in her, and he followed it.

### XCI. JUL.

If the Apostle had commended sin as having passed over, but not through one, and if truth had shown that this properly applied to an example, Traducianus acts with intolerable shamelessness when he makes that number reach his own position by an abuse of language.

**AUG.** What is it that you think you accomplish by so often using a new name, almost as an insult, as though the truth of the most ancient Catholic doctrine could be escaped by making the name seem strange? What cannot be mocked in this way? But it is vanity, not wit.

The Apostle says, “Through one man sin entered into the world, and through sin, death; and so it passed through to all human beings.” We both accept these words. Therefore, if we are Traducians because sin was transmitted through generation so that it might pass into all human beings, you are Traducians because you imagine that sin was transmitted through imitation so that it might pass into all human beings. [Note: [Col. 1286] A lacuna in the printed editions, from “you are Traducians” through “it might pass through,” is supplied from the manuscripts.] The Apostle thus appeared first as a Traducian, whether he meant what it is clear that he meant, or what you mistakenly say that he meant. By saying that sin entered the world through one man and passed through to all human beings, he supplied the occasion for this name.

But if the name “Traducian” does not fit these words, where sin is said to have entered through one man and passed through to all human beings, then the name fits neither us, nor you, nor the Apostle. Yet plainly, to say this, to bring it as an accusation, and to repeat it continually and spitefully is entirely suited to your folly.

### XCII. JUL.

For if it is an unheard-of monstrosity for someone, abandoning proper terms, to attempt to construct an otherwise tolerable but novel doctrine through abusive and ambiguous words, then this is infinitely more deformed: Augustine seeks to confirm obscene matters that accuse God’s justice through such double-edged propositions that he admits they sound properly against him but only provisionally in his favor. Would any educated person trust an argument which, when brought into court, is judged by its opponent as native to him, but by its author as a fugitive and kidnapped thing?

**AUG.** You speak about abusive and proper words in such a way that, disregarding the few who understand you and recognize that you are raving, you choose to appear to say something to the many who do not understand you, although you say nothing. I therefore leave you to the few learned people who, even without my demonstrating it, easily understand that you are saying nothing. By refuting you, even when I speak the truth, I would be saying things that many do not understand.

Nevertheless, where it is said, “Through one man sin entered into the world,” because of the author of generation, and therefore as a figure of the future because of the author of regeneration, the words are not abusive but proper.

### XCIII. JUL.

Therefore, what is written in the Epistle to the Hebrews, “All are from one,” requires praise of God, though it comes after the parents have been mentioned. [Note: [Col. 1287] The Portus manuscript reads “praises.”] But what is said of Christ, “He who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all from one,” is referred to God.

**AUG.** Rather, after the parents had been mentioned—especially since he had already passed from the father and was speaking about the mother—the mother herself ought not to have been passed over. He ought to have said, “They came from two,” since they had come from two, not one, so that the praise of God would be true rather than false.

Unless, indeed, this too is true: that they came from one. And it was not said abusively, but properly, because of the father, the author of the seed—not, as you suppose, in order to increase God’s praise by a lie. For to say, “One man did it,” when two or more people did it, can be a figurative expression. But if someone says that one man did what two did, unless one of those two was the author of the deed, he is either lying or mistaken, just as we have already said about the locust and the frog.

### XCIV. JUL.

For the Apostle says likewise to the Corinthians, “As the woman is from the man, so also the man is through the woman; but all things are from God” (1 Cor. 11:12). In the third place, reason demonstrates that even if neither of the two points that supports our position had existed, nevertheless the statement in which Paul argues that sin entered this world through one man had formed no pact with the Manichaeans. [Note: Thus the manuscripts. Vignierius has, “had formed no pact with the Manichaean.”]

**AUG.** Rather, by saying these things you will show that there is a pact. For what pact is there between the Apostle and Manichaeus, when the Apostle says, “The body indeed is dead because of sin,” overturning your heresy, while Manichaeus says that the body is immutably evil because of the coeternal nature of evil alongside the good?

Likewise, in the passage where it is said, “The body is dead because of sin,” the Apostle says, “He who raised Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies” (Rom. 8:10–11); but Manichaeus says that bodies of flesh do not belong to the creation of the good God but to the nature of evil, and that Christ was not raised from the dead because he was not dead. [Note: Here we have added “is evil” from the Portus manuscript.]

You, therefore, who are not Manichaeans but are not sound either, being afflicted by a different plague, tell us how the body is dead because of sin, when you assert that bodily death entered the world not through the sin of that man but by the law of nature.

### XCV. JUL.

Accordingly, our response remains unshaken: it shows that through one man the Apostle alleges not a nature made defective and corrupted through generation, while nature itself remained intact, but only the defective will of sinners.

**AUG.** Are you so blind—or do you so blind people with your murky arguments—that you dare to deny that defective bodies are born? Do bodies not belong to human nature? Or—as the Manichaeans say, whose madness you do not understand but whose position you refuse to notice and consider how greatly you assist—does the good soul remain held in bodies of the race of darkness? [Note: [Col. 1288] Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read “was held.”]

Tell us, then, what merits defective bodies have, since you deny that infants draw any sins from their parents. Behold, the Manichaeans say: “This mortal flesh belongs so entirely not to God’s workmanship but to the race of darkness that even the bodies of human beings, whom you assert to have been made in God’s image, are born not only corruptible and subject to the condition of death, but often defective as well.”

What answer can your heresy give them except that this is a human nature—although under God as creator and maker—such that, even if no one had sinned, human bodies of this kind would have been born even in paradise? O abominable and damnable statement!

But because we do not say that human bodies—not only corruptible and bound to the necessity of death, but also languishing in countless defects, twisted and deformed—would have arisen in paradise without any preceding sin of the parents, and because we judge those who say this worthy of the strongest anathema, we attribute these things not to a nature instituted in the beginning in this way, but to a nature later corrupted through the merit of iniquity. Thus, by the unshaken and ancient stability of the Catholic faith, we overthrow both you and the Manichaeans. [Note: The particle “thus” is restored from the manuscripts.]

### XCVI. JUL.

But let us return to that book which he sent to Valerius, in which he selected for discussion and refutation isolated statements from only one of my books. [Note: [Col. 1288] The Portus codex reads “selected.”] In the first book of the present work I had reached those statements of Augustine in which, having exposed the shamelessness with which he fled the odium of his opinion lest he appear to assert that the devil was the creator of human beings, he declared that God is the author of evil and creates a substance of such character that it receives guilt before it receives the use of reason, and that it is placed in the kingdom of the devil by the hands of its Creator.

**AUG.** Anyone who distinguishes nature from defect does not say what you say; anyone who reads intelligently what I say does not think that I say what I do not say.

### XCVII. JUL.

And that he is the potter who makes vessels of wrath and destruction.

**AUG.** However little you understand how God makes from the same lump one vessel for honor and another for dishonor (Rom. 9:21), he nevertheless does so in such a way that he does not make a third kind of vessel, neither for honor nor for dishonor—the kind you wish infants to be. You consider it no dishonor that the image of God does not enter the kingdom of God.

For you love that kingdom in such a way that you do not believe that not being there is even a slight punishment for a human being, but no punishment at all.

### XCVIII. JUL.

But those who are destined for destruction are compelled to it not through the development of free will, but through the power of their maker.

**AUG.** You can say that God compels not just any human beings, but his already regenerated sons, to destruction, by making them live even though he foresees that they will depart from the faith, when he could snatch them away from here before they were changed by wickedness.

### XCIX. JUL.

And he has undertaken to strengthen this wickedness of a monstrous doctrine by the statements of the Apostle Paul, which I expounded in the context of the entire reading; and I showed that the prophet Isaiah, from whom it was clear that this comparison with the potter had been taken, fully defended the cause of divine justice.

**AUG.** What have you shown to readers and those who understand, except that you attempted, with excessive loquacity, to twist the apostolic words but were unable to do so? [Note: The printed editions have “What did he show to those who were diligent?” The manuscripts correct the reading.]

### C. JUL.

I completed the second book by expounding the Apostle, with Augustine’s arguments set against it, to the extent permitted by the truth that supplied my resources. Let us therefore now return to the order of his book.

**AUG.** You completed the second book not by expounding the Apostle, but under the pretense of exposition, by an empty attack, with vanity rather than truth supplying what you had to say.

### CI. JUL.

After he had brought against me one chapter from the preface of my earlier work, as though it were an objection, and had appended to it his account of God as the potter of sinners, he then accused me—as his own words publicly reveal, with remarkable consistency and purity:

“Therefore, contrary to what you say, deceiving both yourself and others, if someone says either that human beings possess free will or that God is the creator of those who are born, he is called a Coelestian and a Pelagian. For the Catholic faith also says these things. But if someone says that, for rightly worshiping God, human beings possess free will without his assistance, and if anyone says that God is the creator of those who are born in such a way as to deny that he is the redeemer of infants from the power of the devil, that person is called a Coelestian and a Pelagian.

“Therefore, both of us say that human beings possess free will and that God is the creator of those who are born; on this account you are not Coelestians and Pelagians. But that anyone is free to do good without God’s assistance, and that infants are not rescued from the power of darkness and transferred into the kingdom of God (Col. 1:13)—this is what you say. On this account you are Coelestians and Pelagians” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, Book 2, no. 8).

I have often shown that you are swimming in the swamp of your impiety and fear, and it is clear that no prudent reader will doubt this.

**AUG.** Others who recognize you as a heretic know that you are not swimming but drowning; for in that same submersion you have also lost your understanding.

### CII. JUL.

Accordingly, in the first book I showed that I had not lied in writing that all who flee the odium of our association fall into the precipices of the Manichaeans, who deny free will and God as the creator of human beings. I also showed that you had attempted to ward off what you had been, but immediately seized upon it in your unqualified statements, as is revealed by the insertion of passages from the writings you had sent to Boniface (above, Book 1, chapter 14).

Nevertheless, your present response also confesses this. For you said that the Catholic faith is that which believes both in free will and in God as the creator of those who are born. It is certain that all heretics, including the Manichaeans, deny both of these things together with you.

**AUG.** The Manichaeans—as you refuse to see—are rather assisted by you, since you attribute the many and great evils that we see infants suffer not to the merits of sins but to the race of darkness. For you have nowhere to flee when you are asked where these evils come from. But when we refer all these things to the free will of the human being, through which human nature, after being instituted good, was corrupted, Catholic truth conquers you.

### CIII. JUL.

But because you assume only the name of the Catholic faith, as though it were a thin covering, although you have been stripped of its solid substance, you want us to believe that you too hold what Catholics confess: namely, that human beings possess free will and that God is the creator of those who are born.

But if this has been stated by you simply and faithfully, put an end to the contest by remaining silent. Let the report of those who accuse us return to us: let them accuse us of having charged you with something that you have erased by a confident denial. [Note: [Col. 1290] Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read “following.”] Add only this to the statement: if any sect or argument is found that attempts by any reasoning to overthrow this twofold confession, which you have professed to be Catholic, either it is not yours, or you will no longer defend it.

But if you are pleased to defend, by a well-supported argument, what you are going to say you have denied, explain the definitions of free will and surround its boundaries with settled distinctions, as with certain limits.

**AUG.** You are enemies and defenders who, by defending free will, press it down because you do not want the goodness of the omnipotent and true defender to recall it within its proper limits.

### CIV. JUL.

You also assert that God is the creator of people of such a kind as correspond to his hands and to his justice.

**AUG.** O foolish new heretics! If defective works do not correspond to God’s hands, will you dare to remove from God’s hands any human bodies that you see are often born defective? Why do you not, therefore, confess together with Catholic truth that human nature was corrupted by the original free choice of the sinner, a nature from which God produces what corresponds not only to a good craftsman but also to a just judge? Otherwise the Manichaeans will compel you to attribute human bodies to an evil and unjust craftsman.

### CV. JUL.

Certainly, none of this has been done by you. But after you replied that Catholics confess free will, pretending that you are one of their number, you immediately introduced a definition that took away what you had seemed to grant.

For you say: “But if someone says that human beings possess free will for rightly worshiping God without his assistance, that person is called a Pelagian.” And again: “We say that human beings possess free will; but that anyone is free to do good…”

**AUG.** If you had added there, “Heretics say this,” then, although I did not speak those words, you would nevertheless not have departed from my meaning. For it is true that heretics—that is, you yourselves—say that anyone is free to do good without God’s assistance.

But why I did not read there the words “without God’s assistance,” which you yourself just now inserted into this statement as my words, I attribute, as long as I can, to a faulty manuscript rather than to you. Continue, then, with the rest.

### CVI. JUL.

For when you say that we claim that, for rightly worshiping God without his assistance, free will is sufficient for everyone, you are plainly lying. Since the worship of God is understood in many ways—in keeping his commandments, abhorring vices, simplicity of conduct, the ordering of the mysteries, and the depth of the doctrines which Christian faith embraces concerning the Trinity, the resurrection, and many other similar matters—how could we say vaguely that free will is sufficient for worshiping him without God’s assistance, when we read in the Gospel that the Lord says:

“I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to infants. Yes, Father, because such was your good pleasure before you” (Matt. 11:25–26)?

Free will by itself could not discover all these things, whether those contained in doctrines or those contained in mysteries. Nevertheless, reason was able—according to the testimony of the Teacher of the Gentiles—to ensure that idols were not worshiped and that God, who was recognized as the creator of the world itself, was not despised (Rom. 1:20).

Therefore, no prudent person says what you invent, either we or anyone else. Rather, we affirm that human beings are made by God with free will and that they are assisted by innumerable forms of divine grace, so that it is possible for them either to keep God’s commandments or to transgress them.

This is where we defend the existence of free will: when God asserts his goodness in so many ways—by commanding, blessing, sanctifying, restraining, urging, and enlightening—each person who already uses reason possesses the freedom either to keep or to reject God’s will.

**AUG.** You mention so many things by which God assists us—“by commanding, blessing, sanctifying, restraining, urging, and enlightening”—but you do not mention “by giving charity,” although the Apostle John says, “Charity is from God” (1 John 4:7). Hence he also says, “Behold what kind of charity the Father has given us, that we should be called and should be the children of God” (1 John 3:1).

In this charity, which is given to the human heart by the Spirit and not by the letter, that power is also understood of which the same Apostle says in his Gospel, “He gave them power to become the children of God” (John 1:12).

You say that this power comes from human beings to human beings through free will, possessing the spirit of this world and not the Spirit who is from God. Therefore, “you do not know the things that have been given to us by God” (1 Cor. 2:12). For this reason you have neither peace with the Church from which you have gone out, nor charity, which you deny to be God’s gift, nor faith, because you are heretics: “Peace to the brethren and charity with faith,” not from human free will. [Note: Vignierius has “not from human will,” omitting “free”; the latter is found in the manuscripts.]

If you recognize the apostolic doctrine in these words, recognize in your own words that you are a heretic.

### CVII. JUL.

We do not therefore believe that free will is adequate, without God’s assistance, for his worship as it is practiced by those initiated into the mysteries. Rather, we confess free will as a substantial witness to divine equity, so that when the time comes for us to be manifested before Christ’s tribunal and for each person to receive the things proper to the body, according as he has done, whether good or evil, God may be shown to judge nothing unjustly, since he imputes sin to no one except what the person who is punished for it was also able to avoid.

**AUG.** You rightly remind me what I should say against you. Certainly, as the Apostle says, all of us must be manifested before Christ’s tribunal, so that each may receive according to what he has done through the body, whether good or evil (2 Cor. 5:10).

Will you separate infants from this universal judgment? Tell us, then, what good they have done through the body by their own free will, so that they may receive the kingdom of God, so great a good; or what evil they have done by their own will, when as infants they are excluded from this life of God.

If, as you must, you confess that they are made alive in Christ without any works of free will performed by each person through the body, why do you not confess that these others die in Adam, since you know that Adam was, conversely, a figure of the one who was to come, Christ?

Will you open your mouth with your eyes closed and say that for those in whom they were reborn, the spirit of righteousness was beneficial, but for these, in whom they were born, the flesh of sin was not harmful? Who except you would dare to say this?

When people of more advanced age hear or read that each person will receive according to what he has done through the body, they ought not to trust in the power of their own will but rather pray that the Lord prepare such a will for them that they may not enter into temptation.

For “the will is prepared by the Lord” (Prov. 8, according to the Septuagint); and the Lord himself says, “Pray that you may not enter into temptation” (Matt. 26:41); and the Apostle says, “We pray to God that you may do no evil” (2 Cor. 13:7).

### CVIII. JUL.

Therefore your first statement will gain nothing through obscurity. But the second, in which you repeat that although you confess free will, you do not believe that every human being is free to do good, has exposed your entire inward being.

**AUG.** You now compel me to attribute to you what I had shortly before attributed to the manuscript. For behold, you repeat my statement without completing it with my words, which are very necessary and contrary to you.

I said, “No one is free to do good without God’s assistance.” But you say that I confess free will “but not that any human being is believed to be free to do good.” You do not add what I added: “without God’s assistance.”

I do not accuse a thief; I civilly repeat what has been taken away. Return my words, and yours will have no force.

### CIX. JULIAN

“Look, then, we are now pressing the matter, just as we did in the first book, so that you may show how you do not deny free choice [Note: [Col. 1293] Vignierius reads *negatis* (“you deny”) rather than *non negaris* (“you do not deny”). M.]. Let this remain fixed in the mind of our reader: namely, that you have confessed free choice and preach to Catholics that God is the creator of those who are born—two things which no one but a Manichaean has ever denied. But since we have both commonly granted these points, and yet neither for you nor for your doctrine does freedom of choice remain secure, it follows altogether that you and your doctrine hold nothing of the Catholic faith. I therefore ask what free choice is, and what its definition may be.

“Certainly, no alteration of natural things lies within its power. No one has ever changed the functions of his senses within himself—for example, so as to receive voices through his nostrils or odors through his ears. No one has changed the characteristic nature of his sex. No one has been able by free choice to pass into the form of another living creature. No one has been able by free choice to change the hairs of his body into innate fleeces. No one has claimed for himself, according to his own inclination, either a different quality or a different size of body. By such examples one may range over everything that pertains to this condition.

“Let us therefore pass from natural things to an examination of external things. For whom did the fertility of fields, for whom the success of voyages, for whom nobility and wealth, for whom the stability of that very nobility stand within the jurisdiction of the will, so that anyone might confess himself to have been made by God, through free will, either for the acquisition of these things or of things like them? Natural things therefore proceed according to undisturbed orders, whereas external things are always carried along by uncertain accidents.

“In what, then, does free choice consist—that free choice because of which human beings surpass beasts, because of which they were made in the image of God, and upon which alone the justice of divine judgment rests? In what, I ask, is this free choice, which, as it is certain that the Manichaeans deny, so you also admit that Catholics assert? Without doubt, in this: that it should be possible for a human being, without any inevitable compulsion arising from natural conditions, either to turn his will toward crime or to restrain it from crime.”

### AUGUSTINE

“To restrain the will from crime: this very thing, and nothing else, is not entering into temptation. But if we had this within the power of our own will, we would not be admonished to ask it from the Lord in prayer. To whom, then, is it said, ‘Turn away from evil’ (Ps. XXXVI, 27)? This is certainly said so that he may restrain his will from crime.

“And yet, although the Apostle could also rightly have said, ‘We command you not to do anything evil,’ he says, ‘We pray to God that you do no evil.’ [Col. 1294] See why I said—not as you claim that I said—‘No one is free to do good without the help of God.’ This is the help for which the Apostle prayed on behalf of the faithful; he was not taking away the freedom of human choice arising from nature.

“Arrogant and inflated people, do not put your confidence in your own strength. Submit yourselves to God, and pray that you may restrain your will from crime and not enter into temptation. Do not suppose that you are not entering into temptation when by a strong will you restrain the desire of the flesh from some evil deed. You do not know the schemes of the tempter. You enter into a greater temptation when you attribute these things to your own will without the help of God.

“I should certainly like you to explain how you could have said that those things which are called ‘external’ among human goods and evils—such as riches or poverty and the rest—‘are carried along by uncertain accidents.’ For the Catholic faith also so removes these things from human power that it attributes them to divine authority. I say this because I fear that you may perhaps have added this also to your error: that whatever human beings suffer or attain, whether in their bodies or in external circumstances, you deny to belong to divine providence. And thus, whatever evils even infants suffer, you assign to uncertain accidents, attempting in this way to remove them from the judgment of him without whose will, as the Lord himself says, not even a sparrow falls to the ground (Matt. X, 29).

“You see your heresy foundering in the misery of these infants—a misery which, under a just God, would not exist unless human nature, corrupted and condemned by the magnitude of the first sin, had deserved it.”

### CX. JULIAN

“And so that a settled matter may be illuminated by a few examples: it is as free for a human being to wish to commit sacrilege as not to wish it; as free to wish to perpetrate parricide as not to wish it; as free to wish to commit adultery as not to wish it; it is as possible to give true testimony as false testimony; and it is as free to obey God when he commands as to obey the devil when he persuades.”

### AUGUSTINE

“You speak truly. This is free choice; Adam received it in precisely this condition. But what was given by the Creator and corrupted by the deceiver must surely be healed by the Savior. You do not wish to confess this with the Church; this is why you are heretics.

“O man, who do not consider where you are, and who, blind amid evil days as though they were good, exalt yourself: when free choice was such as you describe, the human being had not yet become like vanity, whose days pass like a shadow (Ps. CXLIII, 4). For God, in whose likeness he had been made—and which is renewed from day to day by his grace—is not vanity.

“It had not yet been said, ‘I was conceived in iniquities’ (Ps. L, 7). It had not yet been said, ‘For who is clean from uncleanness? Not even an infant whose life upon earth is but one day’ (Job XIV, 4, according to the Septuagint). Finally, it had not yet been said, ‘I do not do the good that I want, but the evil that I hate, that I do’; and, ‘I know that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh. For to will is present with me, but to accomplish the good I do not find’; and, ‘I see another law in my members warring against the law of my mind’ (Rom. VII, 15, 18, 23).

“This evil was not in Adam when he was created upright, because human nature had not yet been corrupted. He had a ruler, whom he left to free choice; he was not seeking a liberator through whom he might be freed from vice.

“For if those words, ‘I do not do what I want,’ and the other similar statements, belong—as you say—to a human being not yet established under the grace of Christ, then you are also refuted by this: Christ found human beings so weak in will for doing good, and human nature can restore the weakness of free choice for doing good only through the grace of Christ.

“Accordingly, what I said is true: no one is free to do good without the help of God. This is why you removed the words ‘without the help of God,’ so that a field might be opened for you in which you could boast at length—more talkatively than eloquently—about many things by which you would not delight the reader but rather, insofar as you could, hinder one who wished to understand.

“Submit yourselves to God, so that you may be corrected. No one is free to do good without the help of God. Why, then, do you exalt the human will in order to cast yourselves headlong? Pray instead that you may not enter into temptation.”

### CXI. JULIAN

“For this reason, in the preceding sections I assigned greater importance to a perfect will than to the accomplishment of things, since sacrilege, parricide, adultery, and similar acts are easier to avoid than to commit. For the opportunity to carry out what an evil will wishes is not always available to that will [Note: [Col. 1295] We have added this sentence, ‘For the opportunity to carry out what an evil will wishes is not always available to that will,’ from the Portarum manuscript. But something further seems to be missing, such as: ‘Their perpetration is therefore laborious,’ or something similar, to which the contrasting statement would respond: ‘But, on the other hand, abstaining from these things consists in complete ease.’]. On the other hand, abstaining from these things consists in complete ease. Unless perhaps you call this very thing labor: being unwilling to labor.

“I pass over the fact that both the sacred Scriptures—those produced by the Prophets, Evangelists, and Apostles—and disputants shining with Catholic soundness, John, Basil, Theodore, and their like, have commended the view that committing crimes is a much greater labor than avoiding them.”

### AUGUSTINE

“If only you held to the faith of these men and did not deny original sin in infants!”

### CXII. JULIAN

“For the moment, as far as the present matter is concerned, I insist that free choice was given for no other purpose, nor can it be understood in any other way, than that no one should be carried away by a will held captive either toward righteousness or toward iniquity.”

### AUGUSTINE

“He who cries out concerning the law that he sees in his members warring against the law of his mind and taking him captive under the law of sin—‘I do not do the good that I want, but the evil that I hate, this I do’—must surely explain how he is not carried away toward evil by a captive will.

“To speak for the moment according to your position: if this man groans under an evil habit, and, as you say, is not yet established under the grace of Christ, does he have free choice of will or does he not? If he has it, why does he not do the good that he wants, but do the evil that he hates? But if he does not have it because he is not yet under the grace of Christ, then here is what I have already said, and what I see must often be said to you again: no one can have free choice of will for doing the good he wants and not doing the evil he hates except through the grace of Christ—not so that his will may be carried away captive toward good as toward evil, but so that, freed from captivity [Note: [Col. 1296] The printed editions read *libera* (“free”), although all the manuscripts read *liberata* (“freed”).], it may be drawn to its liberator by the generous sweetness of love, not by the slavish bitterness of fear.”

### CXIII. JULIAN

“There are indeed sweet inducements to vices, and the tortures of punishment which persecutors inflict are also frequently bitter; but the former are beaten back by the judgment of moral decency, and the latter are consumed by the greatness of endurance.”

### AUGUSTINE

“You declaim among those who trust in their own strength (Ps. XLVIII, 7). Take heed to yourself, lest you cry out among those who will be tortured because of their pride.”

### CXIV. JULIAN

“Nevertheless, the possession of the virtues is not a burdensome one; outside a certain kingdom of good conscience, it enjoys the promised exaltation of eternal blessedness. Yet the aids of God’s grace are present, and in the sphere of virtue they never abandon the will. Although their forms are innumerable [Note: [Col. 1296] The words ‘of this matter’ are understood.], they are always applied with such moderation that they never displace free choice, but provide supports so long as one wishes to rely upon them; yet they do not oppress a resisting mind. Hence it is that, just as some ascend from vices to virtues, so others fall back from virtues into vices.”

### AUGUSTINE

“How could the aids of God’s grace displace free choice, when they actually free free choice after it has been driven out by vices and subjected to wickedness, so that it may return to its proper place?

“But when you are asked what these aids of God’s grace are, you list what you mentioned above: ‘God helps by commanding, blessing, sanctifying, restraining, urging, and enlightening.’ All these things are also done through human beings, according to the Scriptures. Human beings command, bless, sanctify through the divine Sacraments, restrain by reproving, urge by exhorting, and enlighten by teaching. Yet neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything, but God who gives the growth (I Cor. III, 7).

“This growth consists in each person obeying God’s commands; and this does not happen—when it truly happens—except through love. Thus the Church makes the body grow for its own edification in love (Eph. IV, 16). God alone gives this love, for ‘love is from God’ (I John IV, 7).

“You do not wish to name this love among the aids of grace that you enumerate, lest you concede that the very fact that we obey God belongs to his grace. You think that free choice is removed in this way, although no one can do this except by the will. But what you do not wish to hear is: ‘The will is prepared by the Lord’ (Prov. VIII, according to the Septuagint)—not by words sounding outwardly, but just as God converted the queen when her prayer was heard and changed the king’s indignation into gentleness (Esth. XV, 11).

“For just as he acted in a divine and hidden manner in the human heart, so he works in us both the willing and the doing, according to his good pleasure (Phil. II, 13).”

### CXV. JULIAN

“How, then, do you confess free choice to one to whom you say that only one thing is possible—namely, to do evil—but that it is not possible to turn away from evil and do good (Ps. XXXIII, 15)?”

### AUGUSTINE

“I say that it is possible for the human will to turn away from evil and do good—but for the will which God helps freely, not the will which Julian ungratefully inflates.”

### CXVI. JULIAN

“For the moment I say nothing of the fury with which you rage against the whole law, which you believe commanded mortals to do things for which it saw that they had no capacity.”

### AUGUSTINE

“What you say is false. God commands those things which can be done; but he himself gives the ability to do them to those who can and do them. Those who cannot, he admonishes by commanding them to ask him for the ability.

“And God knows why not all things are done by each of the saints. He provides for the humility of those to whom, as they say every day, ‘Forgive us our debts’ (Matt. VI, 12), he gives such assistance for obedience that there remains something for which he may also grant forgiveness.”

### CXVII. JULIAN

“But I ask with what poets you ran into such a Hippocrene that you fashioned a two-membered beast—not by versifying [Note: [Col. 1297] The printed editions read *criminando* (“by accusing”). The manuscripts more suitably read *carminando* (“by versifying”).], but by blaspheming—whose body you formed from an evil necessity [Note: [Col. 1297] The printed editions read *necessitudine* (“relationship” or “connection”); all the manuscripts read *necessitate* (“necessity”).], and covered only its face with the name of liberty.”

### AUGUSTINE

“You yourself paint whatever pleases you, since you have leisure to roll empty fantasies around in an empty heart. Why do you assign the aids of grace to a good will, when an evil will relies on no aid in order to be evil or to persist in being evil? Or does your scale—whose two sides you try to suspend by equal weights, so that the will may be as free toward evil as toward good—show, by inclining to one side [Note: [Col. 1297] Vignierius reads *vergendo te* (“by inclining you”). The word *te* is absent from the manuscripts.], that you are raving?”

### CXVIII. JULIAN

“For in that work also which you sent to Rome you argue: ‘The will which is free in evils is not free in goods.’”

### AUGUSTINE

“Why do you not add what you read there: ‘if it has not been freed’ (Against Two Letters of the Pelagians, book 1, no. 5)? Or what does the Lord mean when, speaking of the fruits of the vine branches—that is, of good acts—he says, ‘Without me you can do nothing’ (John XV, 5), except that no one is free for doing good whom he himself does not liberate?”

### CXIX. JULIAN

“And here you call him a Coelestian who thinks that anyone is free to do good. You therefore call that free which, you insist, cannot do anything except evil. Find, if you can, another definition of a thing that is not free, and claim this as free.

“If you had fallen so far from your senses that you did not see the definition of the free in its own substance, you ought at least to have understood from its opposite what the essence of freedom was. Suppose, for example, that you could similarly have been uncertain what was meant by the sight of the eyes, and that you defined it in this way: ‘Sight is either having one’s eyes gouged out or being unable to see anything during the time of any obstruction to vision.’ Suppose that you thought this definition applied to sight. You would nevertheless tolerate yourself as you asserted what the explanation of its opposite—that is, blindness—was; and when you could find no other explanation than this, namely, that in an animal whose nature possessed sight, either the destruction of its eyes or the obstruction of thick matter deprived it of the ability to see, you would undoubtedly come to your senses and see that one definition could not apply to contrary things.

“Thus, if blindness could be defined as nothing other than the deprivation of the ability to see in an animal’s eye at the time when it ought to see, then the definition of sight would also be given by negating those conditions by which you had explained blindness—namely, that sight was nothing other than the presence, at the appropriate time, of the proper ability to see when the eyes had neither been gouged out nor obstructed.

“If, after these points had been shown, you obstinately resisted, you would achieve nothing except that your hearers would think either that you were shamefully struggling against your own conscience, or, if you persuaded them that this truly seemed so to you, they would judge that you possessed mental eyes no less gouged out than the man whom you had defined as having sight.”

### AUGUSTINE

“I do not want you to define blindness, but to bring it to an end, and to see that Christ could not rightly have said, ‘Without me you can do nothing,’ if they could have been free to do good without the grace of Christ.”

### CXX. JULIAN

“To apply the example to the present issue, then, you could have understood, even from the definition of the non-free, what you ought now to call free. And even if your understanding had been obscured in defining free choice, so that you thought that something could be called free which was taught to adhere to one of two contraries, you ought to have recognized that a captive—that is, a non-free—thing could not be explained otherwise than as one that was assigned to one of two contraries [Note: [Col. 1298] The printed editions read *videretur* (“might seem”), omitting *uni* (“to one”). The Mar. and Clar. manuscripts read *vindicaretur* (“was assigned”). Perhaps the reading should be *uni diceretur* (“was said to one”). The Portarum manuscript has *uni vindicaretur*.].

“And therefore the name of freedom must be bestowed by negating captivity [Note: [Col. 1298] The Portarum manuscript reads *liberati* (“liberation”).]. Since what was not free was compelled to adhere to one of the contraries, what was opposed to it—that is, what was free—would be allowed to be assigned to neither.”

### AUGUSTINE

“Why do you entangle clear matters with tangled verbosity? A person is free for evil when he does evil willingly, whether by deed, word, or even thought alone. What person of mature age cannot do this? But a person is free for good when he willingly does good, whether by deed, word, or even thought alone. Yet no human being can do this without the grace of God.

“If you say that someone can, you contradict the one who said, ‘Without me you can do nothing.’ You also contradict the one who said, ‘Not that we are competent to think anything as from ourselves, but our competence is from God’ (II Cor. III, 5). I think he said that he was competent to think something good, not evil, not from himself but from God.

“From good thought come good speech and good work. Accordingly, whoever is not competent to think something good from himself is certainly not competent to speak or to do anything good from himself. But if he is under grace, his competence is from God.

“Hence it is said, ‘For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you’ (Matt. X, 20); and, ‘As many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are the sons of God’ (Rom. VIII, 14).

“Considering these things [Note: [Col. 1299] Vignierius reads *Haec ergo intuens* (“Considering these things, therefore”). The Portarum manuscript reads *Haec ego intuens* (“Considering these things, I”). The latter is better, since the contrary statement follows: ‘Considering these things, you feared.’], I said that no one is free to do good without the help of God. Fearing this, you claimed that I had said that no one is free to do good, and you removed the words ‘without the help of God,’ which I had added.

“From this I have no doubt that you already know you have been defeated. But you employ extended empty talk so that you may not appear defeated, defining free will in such a way that it cannot be free unless it can do both things—that is, act well and act badly. Consequently, you must remove freedom from God, since he can have only a good will and cannot have an evil one.”

### CXXI. JULIAN

“Since this is so, and since you most miserably resist this point, it is uncertain what judgment ought rather to be formed concerning you: whether you defend what is false against your conscience, or whether you think what is false to be true. Thus it is uncertain whether you have lost the eyes of reason, although it is certain that you have lost the eyes of faith.”

### AUGUSTINE

“Do you console yourself for having been defeated by hurling insults?”

### CXXII. JULIAN

“To repeat briefly what has been established: free choice, which on the side of evil is aided by the pleasures of vices and the persuasions of the devil, and on the side of good by the teachings of the virtues and the various forms of divine grace, cannot remain free unless both the necessity of righteousness and the necessity of sin are removed from it.”

### AUGUSTINE

“If among the forms of divine grace you included love—which you read most clearly to be not from us but from God, and which God gives to his children—without which no one lives piously, and with which no one lives except piously; without which no one has a good will, and with which no one has anything but a good will, you would truly defend free choice rather than inflate it.

“If by necessity you mean that by which someone is oppressed against his will, then righteousness has no such necessity, because no one is righteous against his will. But the grace of God makes a willing person out of one who is unwilling.

“If no one sinned unwillingly, it would not be written, ‘You have sealed up my sins in a bag and marked whatever I have committed unwillingly’ (Job XIV, 17).”

### CXXIII. JULIAN

“But Catholics confess the truth of this; the Traducians, together with their Manichaean teachers [Note: [Col. 1299] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read *ministris* (“ministers”) instead of *magistris* (“teachers”).], deny it.”

### AUGUSTINE

“These are insults, not judgments. I wish you were able to judge; but what wicked person cannot hurl insults?”

### CXXIV. JULIAN

“We therefore spoke the truth: those who are deceived by you, so that they may not be called heretics, become Manichaeans; and while they fear a false disgrace, they incur a true crime—like wild animals surrounded by wings so that they may be driven into nets and thrust into real destruction by an empty fear.

“We speak of God as the creator of those who are born in such a way that, since it is certain that the God of Catholics, who is the true God, can do nothing evil, human beings made by him cannot in any way be believed to emerge from the hands of that very Creator as wicked and guilty before the use of their will. When you deny one of these two points, you overthrow both. For you say that you indeed believe God to be the Creator, but of evil human beings; and by this you contradict your own doctrine, since you deny that you assert the devil to be the creator of human beings.”

### AUGUSTINE

“Whatever in human beings who are born with a fault belongs to God the Creator is good, because whatever is just is also good. God is the author of natures, not of faults.

“Now let us come to that matter. Let us see what you will say about it: how infants are not delivered from the power of darkness when they are transferred into the kingdom of Christ through the Sacraments of the Church. However many coverings you wrap around yourself with your manifold verbosity, when you come to this point you will appear as a naked heretic.”

### CXXV. JULIAN

“For when you ascribe to God’s work beings of a kind he cannot make, you show that what you had said was made by him does not belong to God.”

### AUGUSTINE

“God alone can make human beings. Say rather how infants are not delivered from the power of darkness when they are regenerated through the divine Sacraments.”

### CXXVI. JULIAN

“Although this matter was treated more fully in the first book, let us nevertheless express here, even briefly, what you think. You fear assigning some substance to the devil’s work; yet you do not fear inflicting upon God not some minor crime but a great one.

“In your view, human bodily nature receives greater reverence than the justice of God. You feared assigning human substance to the devil as though that were something great, while you attached the construction of wickedness to the works of God as though it were something insignificant—that is, to justice and the holiness of God. As though, between two opinions, both of them false, it were not more tolerable to assign flesh to the devil’s works than to assign iniquity to God’s works.”

### AUGUSTINE

“It is you who rather blaspheme the justice of God, under whose omnipotence you say that infants suffer such great evils without any evil deserts. But now say how you separate them from those whom God delivers from the power of darkness in order to transfer them into the kingdom of the Son of his love (Col. I, 13).”

### CXXVII. JULIAN

“For just as here you said that infants are fashioned by God as guilty under the power of the devil, so in the later sections of your book you spewed forth something more dreadful than the sacraments of the Manichaeans when you said of God: ‘Thus he creates evil people, as he feeds and nourishes evil people.’”

### AUGUSTINE

“When you come to those same sections of my book, it will become clear how the statement you now object to was made. For the moment, please say how, when infants are regenerated and transferred into Christ’s kingdom, they are not delivered from the power of darkness.”

### CXXVIII. JULIAN

“Therefore God creates evil.”

### AUGUSTINE

“You do not understand how he says through the Prophet, ‘I create evils’ (Isa. XLV, 7).”

### CXXIX. JULIAN

“And innocent people are punished because of what God does.”

### AUGUSTINE

“They are neither innocent by origin, nor punished because of what God does.”

### CXXX. JULIAN

“And they are possessed by the devil because God does this.”

### AUGUSTINE

“The Apostle also handed a man over to Satan (I Cor. V, 5), but in justice, not in wickedness. And God handed certain people over to a reprobate mind (Rom. I, 28)—if only you yourselves were not among them.”

### CXXXI. JULIAN

“And God imputes to human beings the crime of his own hands.”

### AUGUSTINE

“What infants draw from their corrupted origin is not a crime of God’s hands.”

### CXXXII. JULIAN

“And what the devil subtly, skillfully, and persistently persuaded, God shapes, protects [Note: [Col. 1301] The Portarum manuscript reads, ‘and propagates.’], preserves, and forms.”

### AUGUSTINE

“God does not form what the devil persuaded; rather, from the nature which the devil corrupted, God forms well whatever he forms.”

### CXXXIII. JULIAN

“And he demands from human beings the fruit of goodness when God implanted evil in them.”

### AUGUSTINE

“God did not implant evil. Rather, the evil implanted by corrupted generation God cleanses through regeneration.”

### CXXXIV. JULIAN

“And afterward he lies throughout the entire law, because the Lord is just [Note: [Col. 1301] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read *nititur*, ‘he strives,’ followed by *quam justus sit Deus*, ‘how just God is.’].”

### AUGUSTINE

“You are lying. But you, who deny that the sons of Adam have a sin deserving a heavy yoke (Ecclus. XL, 1), what are you trying to show except that God is unjust?”

### CXXXV. JULIAN

“And he who incurs so many charges is still called God?”

### AUGUSTINE

“Because God incurs no charges, neither does he incur this charge which you attribute to him: that infants, without any desert of original sin, suffer so many and such great evils, whether God himself causes them or permits them [Note: [Col. 1301] Thus the manuscripts. Vignierius reads *illius* (“of that one”) instead of *ullius* (“of any”).].”

### CXXXVI. JULIAN

“The memory of the Manichaeans will perish with a crash, because the Lord remains forever, who has prepared his throne for judgment and will himself judge the world in equity (Ps. IX, 7–9). There is no crime in God. Therefore he does not create evil people, since, if they were evil by nature, God could not create them.

“Accordingly, just as it is characteristic of Catholics to confess God as the Creator of good people, so it is properly characteristic of the Manichaeans to believe God to be the creator of evil people.”

### AUGUSTINE

“If you were not deaf to the divine words where it is said, ‘He will judge the world in equity,’ you would learn the equity of God even in the punishments of infants. By nature they are good, because God creates them; but by fault they are evil, which is why God heals them.

“In this Catholic position, not only does the memory of the Manichaeans perish, but also that of the Pelagians, together with the crash of their verbosity.”

### CXXXVII. JULIAN

“But let us examine the rest.”

### AUGUSTINE

“Look: you are now passing to other words of my book, and you say nothing against what you had proposed from the preceding sections as though it needed to be refuted. For, in order to press you with apostolic authority, I said that you claim that infants are not delivered from the power of darkness and thus transferred into the kingdom of God (Col. I, 13).

“By saying nothing against this, you have indeed appeared, as I predicted above, a naked heretic. But I have not had to labor to strip you, because, against the apostolic faith of the most ancient mother Church, you did not dare to cover yourself with any verbal cloak of empty talk.”

### CXXXVIII. JULIAN

“Listen, then, briefly, to what is at issue in this question. Catholics say that human nature, created by the good Creator God, is good, but corrupted by sin and in need of Christ the physician.

“The Manichaeans say that human nature was not created good and corrupted by sin by God, but was created by the prince of eternal darkness from the commingling of two natures that had always existed, one good and one evil.

“The Coelestians and Pelagians say that human nature was created good by the good God, but that it is so sound in infants at birth that they have no need of Christ’s medicine at that age.

“Recognize, then, your own name in your doctrine, and stop attributing to the Catholics who refute you a doctrine and a name that belong to someone else. For Truth refutes both groups, the Manichaeans and you.

“To the Manichaeans it says: ‘Have you not read that from the beginning he made the human being, male and female he made them? For this reason a man shall leave father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh. Therefore they are no longer two but one flesh. What God has joined together, let no human being separate’ (Matt. XIX, 4–6).

“By this he shows both that God created the human being and that God joined the spouses, against the Manichaeans, who deny both of these things.

“To you, however, he says: ‘The Son of Man came to seek and to save what was lost’ (Luke XIX, 10). But you, excellent Christians, answer Christ: ‘If you came to seek and save what was lost, you did not come to infants. They were not lost, and they were born saved. Go to adults. From your own words we bring a charge against you: “The healthy have no need of a physician, but those who are sick”’ (Matt. IX, 12).

“Thus it comes about that the Manichaean, who says that an evil nature has been mingled with the human being, at least wishes the good soul to be saved from it by Christ. But you maintain that in infants, since they are bodily sound, there is nothing for Christ to save.

“Accordingly, the Manichaean indeed speaks detestably against human nature, but you praise it cruelly. For whoever believes you, its praiser, will not offer his infants to the Savior (On Marriage and Concupiscence, book 2, no. 9).

“I also pointed out in my first work that you do nothing more than arrange to be understood with difficulty.”

### AUGUSTINE

“I am understood perfectly, whether you wish it or not. But since you intend to say nothing against these points, you want it not to be understood that what I said is most true and most firmly established. In the end, the matter itself has shown that you were unable to refute these things.”

### CXXXIX. JULIAN

“And I showed that nearly the greater part of your fabrications is more laborious to understand than to overcome.”

### AUGUSTINE

“And you labor—and, what is worse for you, you are defeated. Yet you do not labor to understand me, which you can do very easily; you labor to refute me, which you cannot do.”

### CXL. JULIAN

“But if I wished to do this point by point, I would seem both tedious by repeating the same things and lengthy by pursuing everything.”

### AUGUSTINE

“See how you act: you want the reader to move far away from what I said and to think that you have answered me, while forgetting the things you had proposed as though they needed to be refuted.”

### CXLI. JULIAN

“Although everything you have published against us is directed toward one end—namely, to persuade people that evils are natural, and that either the devil is the creator of human beings or God the creator of crimes—I nevertheless think that something may be gained for the sake of brevity if I gather together, from different parts, those arguments above all by which, when you are in the dark, you think you defend your entire opinion. I will first assist them with an exposition, so that what they are attempting may become clear; then I will overthrow them, not scattered but collected, not wrapped up but explained.”

### AUGUSTINE

“With a remarkable devotion to brevity, you turn my one book into eight, although you do not shake it even with such prolonged verbosity. Say now, if you can, how you are not compelled to say to Christ—if not in words, then certainly by your perverse opinions themselves:

“‘If you came to seek and save what was lost, you did not come to infants. They were not lost, and they were born saved. Go to adults. From your own words we bring a charge against you: “The healthy have no need of a physician, but those who are sick”’ (On Marriage and Concupiscence, book 2, no. 9).

“Answer this. Why do you try to wrap up and conceal the truth with empty things?”

### CXLII. JULIAN

In the latter parts of your book, after saying, “Thus God creates the wicked, just as he feeds and nourishes the wicked,” you add:

“Because what he grants them by creating them belongs to the goodness of nature; and what he gives them by feeding and nourishing them, thereby increasing them, he certainly grants not to their wickedness but to that same good nature which the good God created. For insofar as they are human beings, their nature is good, and God is its author; but insofar as they are born with sin, destined to perish unless they are reborn [Note: [Col. 1303] Morel, *Elementa Critica*, p. 304, thinks this should be read from Book 2 of *On Marriage and Concupiscence*. M.], they belong to the seed cursed from the beginning (Wis. 12:11), through the fault of that ancient disobedience. Yet the Maker makes good use even of the vessels of wrath, so that he may make known the riches of his glory in the vessels of mercy; so that, if anyone belonging to that same mass is freed by grace, he may not attribute it to his own merits, but ‘let him who boasts, boast in the Lord’ (2 Cor. 10:17).”

Departing from this faith, he does not want those who are born to be under the devil, lest infants be carried to Christ so that they may be rescued from the power of darkness and transferred into his kingdom (Col. 1:13). Thus he accuses the Church, spread throughout the whole world, in which everywhere all infants who are to be baptized are exsufflated for no other reason than that the prince of this world may be driven out from them (On Marriage and Concupiscence, Book 2, §§32–33).

Again, speaking below about concupiscence, without which there can be no intercourse between spouses—a thing which we defend as natural and belonging to God’s work, not as some great good but as a sensation of bodies made by God—you want to attribute it, implanted in human viscera, to the devil, placing your doctrine in his shame [Note: [Col. 1303] Vignier reads *atque in ejus verecundia* (“and in his shame”). *Atque* is absent from the manuscripts.], and strive to assert this in so many writings [Col. 1304]. Concerning concupiscence itself, therefore, you speak here, as often elsewhere:

“Accordingly,” you say, “we do not condemn the honorable intercourse of married couples because of the shameful concupiscence of the bodies. That intercourse could have existed without any preceding commission of sin, and married people would not have blushed because of it; but this concupiscence arose after sin, and the couple, overcome by shame, were compelled to cover it (Gen. 3:7). Hence it has remained for married people of later generations, although they make good and lawful use of this evil, to avoid human observation in such an act and thus to confess what is shameful, even though no one ought to be ashamed of what is good. Accordingly, whoever lawfully has intercourse through shameful concupiscence makes good use of an evil; whoever does so unlawfully makes bad use of an evil” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, Book 2, §36).

### AUGUSTINE

Why is the sentence interrupted, and, with certain things omitted, why is the following added as though it came next: “Accordingly, whoever lawfully has intercourse through shameful concupiscence,” and so on? The words of mine that were omitted are these:

“Thus these two things are set forth together: the good of the union that deserves praise, from which children are generated, and the evil of shameful concupiscence, from which those who are generated must be regenerated, lest they be condemned” (ibid.).

Why do you remove these words of mine from the middle of my sentence, and, after removing them, append other words of mine as though they followed immediately? What are you doing? Why are you doing this? It is not enough that you abandon the things you had proposed to refute from my book in their proper order and proceed to something else, so that the order is disrupted and what you had proposed slips from the reader’s memory. In addition, the things you insert out of order, as you please, you do not present wholly and faithfully, but cut wherever you wish, remove what you wish, and join things together however you wish. Do whatever you want; you will appear convicted and defeated, though against your will.

### CXLIII. JULIAN

The name “evil” is more properly applied to that from which both the wicked and the good feel shame; and we believe the Apostle more readily when he says, “Good does not dwell in my flesh” (Rom. 7:18), than this man, who calls this thing good.

### AUGUSTINE

It would not have been difficult to complete this sentence from my book. I said:

“Than this man, who called that good which, if he is ashamed of it, he confesses to be evil; but if he is not ashamed, he adds an even worse evil to his shamelessness” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, Book 2, §36).

But I do not know why you did not include this, since you could have failed to answer it in the same way as the other things you set down as though they required refutation but did not even touch [Note: [Col. 1304] So the manuscripts. Vignier has *eis non posses respondere* (“you could not answer them”).].

### CXLIV. JULIAN

A little later you add:

“Since human nature, whether born from marriage or from adultery, is God’s work: if it were evil, it would not be generated; if it had no evil in it, it would not be regenerated. To sum up both in a single statement: if human nature were evil, it would not be saved; if no evil were present in it, it would not be saved. Therefore, whoever says that it is not good denies the Creator as the author of what was created good; but whoever denies that evil is present in it begrudges the merciful Savior his mercy toward what has been corrupted. Consequently, in those who are born, neither should adulteries be excused on account of the good that was created from them [Col. 1305] by the good Creator, nor should marriages be accused on account of the evil that is healed there by the merciful Savior” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, Book 2, §36).

Since [Note: [Col. 1305] So the manuscripts. Vignier has *quam* (“which”).] you had endured such a great labor of thought over these many passages from your writings, so that you might appear to say something clever, and since, according to our custom—by which we accomplish nothing craftily—and in view of the security of the truth, because your words can scarcely be understood, they must be clarified by our repetition, we should distinguish them.

You said, then, that the Manichaeans condemn the nature of flesh and assert that humanity was made from the mixture of two natures, one good and the other evil. But we, whom you call heretics, say that human nature was created by the good God, good according to the testimony of its author, and that in infants it is so sound that they have no need of Christ’s medicine. You, however, say that nature was once created good by the good God in Adam, but that it was corrupted by sin and therefore needs Christ’s medicine (*ibid.*).

In the first book of the present work I showed, by joining together the opinions of both sides, how little your faith differs from the profanity of the Manichaeans, since it is plainly descended from it. There it became clear that you are joined to Jovinianus through fear, but to Manichaeus altogether through love.

This, then, must also be discussed by us in the present section. But first I distinguish our statements from yours. You correctly said that we say human nature was created good by the good God; but up to this point the statement is ours. For you either did not see the one part by which our position is completed, or you suppressed it; while you inserted another statement of your own, although it is not ours [Note: [Col. 1305] The negative particle is added here from the Portian manuscript.]. We do not merely say that human nature was created good by God in Adam; we also say that it is created good in every infant by that same God who was the author of the first human being. For this reason we assert that he is the Creator of all human beings.

### AUGUSTINE

What else do we also say concerning the Lord God, the Creator of all human beings? But—far be it from us—you deny that God the Savior is necessary for infants, by asserting that their nature is so good that you say there is nothing evil in it for which it would need Christ as physician.

Answer this point. First refute what you had proposed to refute. Explain why infants who are to be baptized are exsufflated; or, by declaring open war on the whole ancient Church, insist that they ought not to be exsufflated. Do this; stand here; strike this fortress with something that can shake it, if you can. Why do you flee beneath the coverings of your loquacity? Why do you cast up such empty smoke, by which these matters are so covered and obscured that the reader forgets them and supposes that you have said something, although you are wholly unable to answer? [Note: [Col. 1305] The phrase “Why do you cast up such empty smoke, by which” is restored from the manuscripts.]

### CXLV. JULIAN

You have therefore not only removed this part of our statement from our definition; you have also substituted your own in its place. At first sight it might provoke resentment, but once examined it would disappear.

For you stated that we say nature was created good by the good God, but that it is so sound that it has no need of Christ’s medicine. Consider, then, how greatly you suffer from poverty of truth, since even in the very words that are called *antitheses* (ἀντίθετα) you do not hesitate to commit so obvious a theft.

When you had proposed above “good nature,” you added, “so sound.” Is “sound” the antithesis of “good”? Certainly, when we say “good,” we place nothing properly opposite to it except “evil.” But if the occasion requires us to say “sound,” we place “weak” or “sick” on the opposite side: if something is sound, it is not weak; if it is weak, it is said not to be sound. When, however, we say, “This is good,” we set against it not the term “unsound” but the word “evil.”

You ought therefore to have said that we define human nature as created good by God, but that in infants it is so good that it requires no corrector of its formation. Or, if you preferred to indicate what was good by a different term, namely “soundness,” you should have marked the whole statement with consistent wording.

But now you slip like a little lamprey between the stones of your definitions. When truth compelled you to acknowledge that we say human nature was created by the good God and that, in this part of the statement, you saw both much reason and no grounds for resentment, you immediately passed to other words, adding that we defend it as sound in such a way that we believe Christ’s [Col. 1306] medicine is not necessary for it. If you have fallen into this through ignorance, you are exceedingly stupid [Note: [Col. 1306] The printed editions have *barbarissimus* (“most barbarous”), but the manuscripts have *bardissimus* (“most stupid”).]; but if you do it by cunning, you will be found exceedingly crafty.

### AUGUSTINE

When would you say such things, unless you had nothing to say? We were not obliged, as you think, to say “sound” of what we called “good,” lest the opposing terms fail to be true antitheses. If I wished to show how great your ignorance is in saying this, I would be lingering, like you, over matters that are unnecessary.

Remove the superfluous—indeed, even if it were true, it would be of no benefit to you—and say, if you can, how you do not deny that Christ the physician is necessary for infants. Once you begin to say this, it will become clear why you thought it necessary to insert these empty remarks, which do not pertain to the matter at hand [Note: [Col. 1306] So the manuscripts. Vignier has *bona* (“good”) instead of *vana* (“empty”).].

### CXLVI. JULIAN

I shall answer briefly. We do not deny Christ’s medicine to infants, whom we know to be innocent; indeed, we admit that they especially need it in greater abundance. For they are born small and weak. Not only are they unable to nourish themselves by their own labor, they cannot even implore the assistance of their parents. They are exposed to so many dangers that even thicker milk and, very often, the sleep of nursing infants themselves are fatal to them.

### AUGUSTINE

This is why, by inserting superfluous matters, you obstruct the reader’s memory. You do not deny that infants need Christ the physician because of bodily evils, by whose weakness the infirm are corrupted [Note: [Col. 1306] So the manuscripts. Vignier has *validi* (“the healthy”) instead of *invalidi* (“the infirm”).] or killed; yet you deny that they need Christ the physician for the reason that they are under the devil’s power, from which they are to be freed by being baptized and exsufflated.

Thus you make it clear that you proposed this objection as though it required refutation for no other reason than to avoid being detected as afraid of it. You did not attempt to refute it because, coming from a very firm and apparently adamant foundation, the missiles you hurled would rebound against you and destroy you [Col. 1307] instead. For this reason you inserted an unnecessary discussion of antitheses, so that the reader, forgetting that unconquered point, would allow you to draw breath amid whatever utterly empty arguments you introduced, as though you were answering something while saying nothing.
