You brought forward the weakness of an infant’s body, exposed to many dangers, as though infants either suffered from those dangers themselves, or were oppressed by such great weakness, or could experience some evil at that age if human nature had remained as it was established.

Explain, if you can, why the Church of Christ exsufflates infants who are to be baptized; or insist, if you can, that they ought not to be exsufflated; or be silent if you cannot. Indeed, be silent, because you cannot.

### CXLVII. JULIAN

By reason of their mortal body they encounter the hardships of illnesses, the punishments of pain, and the dangers of disease. We therefore acknowledge that Christ’s medicine is necessary not only for infants, who were also made by him, but for the nature of all mortals.

### AUGUSTINE

Do you therefore also believe that all these evils would have existed in paradise if no one had sinned? Do you imagine that human beings would have died there like animals, because you believe that mortality of the body would have been common to all there?

Wretched people! If you considered the blessedness of that place with a Christian mind, you would not believe that the beasts would have died there, any more than that they would have raged; rather, they would have been subjected to human beings with marvelous gentleness and would not have sought food through one another’s deaths, but would have shared food with human beings, as it is written (Gen. 1:29–30).

Or, if extreme old age would have dissolved them, so that only human nature would possess eternal life there, why should we not believe that they would be removed from paradise when they were about to die, or would leave it with an awareness of impending death, so that death would not occur to any living creature in that place of life? For even the human beings who had sinned could not have died if, on account of their iniquity, they had not departed from that habitation of such great happiness.

### CXLVIII. JULIAN

Just as the infirmities of that nature are alleviated in the present life by various kinds of remedies, so they will also be completely removed, though only in the bodies of the righteous, when the resurrection comes.

### AUGUSTINE

Do you include infants among these righteous, although they have done nothing by their own will, whether good or evil? Or do you separate them from the righteous, while nevertheless not separating them from the blessed resurrection of the flesh?

Why, then, did you specify the bodies of the righteous, in which these evils are removed at the coming of the resurrection? But if infants are counted righteous because of the righteousness of the second man, who is the author of regeneration, why are they not counted unrighteous because of the sin of the first man, who is the author of generation?

### CXLIX. JULIAN

You see, then, in how many respects we acknowledge that Christ’s medicine is necessary for human nature. But I know that you will cry out that I am quibbling with you. For you did not mean this medicine, by which bodies are helped, but by the name “medicine” you meant Christ’s grace, which you claimed we deny.

To this one may answer that the fault must be attributed to you, because you did not wish to designate by their proper names the things you wanted to be understood. But since it has perhaps [Col. 1308] only belatedly been understood which medicine you meant, and which medicine you falsely claimed that we confusedly denied, let us also answer the second point you have raised, just as we explicitly stated in our first work:

We confess that Christ’s grace—that is, baptism, from the time when Christ instituted its rite—is so necessary to all ages alike that we strike with eternal anathema anyone who denies that it is useful even for infants.

### AUGUSTINE

We are discussing the medicine by which Christ wished his grace to be named, when he said of himself, “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick” (Matt. 9:12).

You, however, say that Christ’s grace is necessary for infants not for the purpose of healing them, but only for adopting them into the kingdom of God. Do not therefore pretend to answer when you see that you cannot answer.

### CL. JULIAN

Although we repeatedly assert this in clear terms, you have been convicted of public falsehood, since you write that we defend human nature as good in such a way that we deny that Christ’s medicine is necessary for infants while they are sound [Note: [Col. 1308] So the manuscripts. Vignier has *ut sane infantibus* (“so that, in fact, for infants”).].

### AUGUSTINE

I spoke truly. For I meant the medicine of Christian grace, which is conferred only on Christians, not on all human beings, including unbelievers, and certainly not on puppies, piglets, little fish, little worms, or every kind of living creature whatsoever. Without doubt, you deny it to infants, since you maintain that they were generated without any guilt of origin, which is healed by regeneration.

Therefore, having just suffered great embarrassment, you removed the word “medicine” and substituted “grace.” You can say that grace is necessary for infants on account of adoption; but you cannot say that medicine is necessary for them through Christ’s sacraments when you dare to promise them eternal salvation even if they do not become Christians.

You do not want Christ to be Jesus for them. He is called this, as the angel testifies [Note: [Col. 1308] Vignier has “the Apostle”; the manuscripts have “the angel.”], and as the Gospel testifies, because he saves his people—not from diseases and wounds of the flesh, from which he heals all kinds of human beings and every kind of bird and reptile, but from their sins (Matt. 1:21).

### CLI. JULIAN

Yet this grace, since it is also called medicine, while preserving the law of justice, makes some people good out of the wicked; but infants, whom it creates good by formation, it makes better by renewal and adoption.

### AUGUSTINE

Then, insofar as the medicine which Christ provides only to Christians is concerned, what Jesus himself said—“Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick”—is false of infants, whom you say are sound and for whom, in order to avoid resentment, you nevertheless claim that Christian medicine is necessary.

But how does Christ renew those whom he finds new, most recent from birth [Note: [Col. 1308] Vignier has *recentissimosque* (“and most recent”); the manuscripts omit *-que*.], if they carry nothing from the oldness of sin? Will you also say that something not old is renewed, when you read in the Epistle to the Hebrews, “When he says ‘new,’ he has made the first old” (Heb. 8:13)?

Tell us, then, how those who are newly born can be old, when you say they are sound from the oldness of sin. Yet, to avoid provoking true Christians, you pretend that they are renewed by Christ [Col. 1309].

Finally, being healed is one thing, being renewed another. Treatment is necessary for those who are to be healed; restoration is necessary for those who are to be renewed. It is therefore clear that your heresy wholly denies Christian medicine to infants.

### CLII. JULIAN

It is therefore plain that we do not deny that Christ’s grace is useful for infants. What controversy, then, remains, on account of which the Traducianist accuses us of error? Is it that we do not agree that Adam’s nature was good, but that the nature of all human beings was made evil?

I openly confess that we not only refuse to agree with this but also oppose it with all our strength. Let us therefore remove those distorted, childish nets of your inventions and those vulgar phantoms with which you whispered that we deny Christ’s grace to infants in the cradle. Let us contend over the point on which the whole struggle depends.

Accordingly, following the order I promised—since our position has now been defended—let us weigh the views of the Manichaeans, whom you pretended to oppose, and your own.

### AUGUSTINE

You have not defended your position; you have shown that it cannot be defended.

### CLIII. JULIAN

The Manichaean therefore says that the human being was created by the prince of darkness, that is, by the author of evil, from the mixture of two natures, good and evil. What do you say? That human beings are indeed created by the good God, but that all human beings are created evil.

### AUGUSTINE

In a human being who is born there is both nature, which you do not deny is good and for which we praise God the Creator, and vice, which you cannot deny is evil if, under pressure, you confess that Christ the physician is necessary for infants. For you cannot deny that Christ said of himself, “Those who are well have no need of a physician.”

### CLIV. JULIAN

Between you and the Manichaean, then, there is no disagreement concerning the quality of nature, but only concerning its author. You attribute this evil to the God whom you confess to be the Creator of infants, whereas the Manichaean attributes it to the prince of darkness, whom he considered the creator of human nature.

To restore the alliance, therefore, little obstacle remains between you. Yet I shall soon show that, although neither of you appears to bear any trace of truth, the Manichaean’s statements are more mutually consistent than yours.

What do we say? Without doubt, something opposed to both of you: no other nature was either made or mixed by the prince of darkness [Note: [Col. 1309] So the manuscripts. Vignier has *compositam* (“compounded”) instead of *commixtam* (“mixed”).], nor was human nature made evil by the good God [Note: [Col. 1309] So the manuscripts. Vignier has *compositam* (“compounded”) instead of *commixtam* (“mixed”).]. Rather, the one God, the author of all things, not only made human nature good at the beginning, but also makes it good in every individual who is born. Nevertheless, we confess that it needs the assistance of its Creator, useful in many ways and also necessary.

Although the situation is different with respect to created things and gifts, the greater estimation does not here concern the work rather than the craftsman. Both you and the Manichaean therefore affirm natural evil in the same way: both equally say that human nature is evil. But he does so more honestly, you more deceitfully.

For this evil, which you both equally suppose to have been breathed by the devil into human viscera, he does not remove from anyone’s birth. You, however, so that you may appear to differ in some way—though the difference is nonexistent—try to exempt only two human beings from it. Yet you do not say that their persons were free from sin; rather, with the supposed advancement of a more learned intellect [Col. 1310], you say that what became natural through them was not natural in them.

Thus, lest your fraud remain unpunished even here, the addition of folly has chastised the theft you committed from your teacher. To believe something is natural when you admit that it was assumed by the will is an invention not merely of an uneducated mind but of a drunken one.

But we shall deal with this elsewhere. For now let us press the matter at hand. The Manichaean asserts that evil is natural, and you agree. He says that sins are born, and you agree that this is so. He says that human nature is evil, and you confirm this as well. He says that it belongs to absolutely everyone; here you resist and ask that the first union of the two human beings be separated out—although you do not even defend them from guilt, indeed you affirm them to be the authors of natural evil.

Even if we could indulge you in this, your own teacher would not allow it; perhaps he would even chastise your sluggish intellect with the rod, so that you would have to submit to his authority or abandon his school entirely.

Finally, he concludes and says that the author of an evil nature cannot be good; and consequently that the human being whom both of you confess to be naturally evil is the work of the prince of darkness, that is, the devil.

### AUGUSTINE

The Catholic faith says that human nature was created good by the good God but was so corrupted by the great sin of disobedience that posterity also inherited from it the merit and punishment of death. Yet the good God does not withhold his good creative work from that posterity. This faith stands against both you and the Manichaeans.

But you who deny this, please think for a moment about paradise [Note: [Col. 1310] So Vignier. Manuscript B has *cogitare* (“to think”). M.]. Would you like us to place there chaste men and women fighting against concupiscence; pregnant women nauseated, repelled, and pale; some expelling premature births through miscarriage, others groaning and howling in labor; and all the infants born there crying, laughing only late, speaking still later—and then lisping—being led to school to learn letters, crying beneath straps, rods, and whips, with punishments distributed according to the varying abilities of their minds?

Would you also place there innumerable diseases, attacks by demons, and bites from wild animals, by which some would be tortured and others consumed? And those who were healthy would be raised amid the uncertain accidents of life, through the wretched anxiety of their parents. There would also surely be bereavements and mourning, and longing for those most dear who had been lost, together with the pains of the heart.

It would take too long to pursue all the evils with which this life abounds. Yet none of these things is a sin. If such things were destined to occur in paradise, with no preceding sin whose merit could account for them, seek out the people to whom you could preach this—not to believers, certainly, but to mockers.

Indeed, if such a paradise were painted, no one would say that it was paradise, even if the name were written above it. Nor would anyone say that the painter had made a mistake; he would plainly recognize a mocker.

Nevertheless, among those who know you, no one would be surprised if your name were added to the title and it were written: “The paradise of the Pelagians” [Col. 1311].

But if you are ashamed of this—for truly, if you are not ashamed of it, one must suppose that no trace of modesty remains in you—then at last change your perverse opinion, I beg you, and believe that human nature was changed into these miseries by that great sin, and that such things could not in any way have existed in paradise. For this reason those people left paradise, and their descendants also became worthy to endure such things, since the contagion of sin passed to all together with the condition of punishment.

This Catholic doctrine both defends God’s justice, since he would not unjustly have willed the life of mortals to be punitive, and overturns both you and the Manichaeans: you, because you attribute such dreadful misery to paradise; the Manichaeans, because they assert that the nature of their god—and therefore what else but their god himself?—is made miserable by such evils.

Accordingly, I should not be troubled that you set the Manichaean teacher against me, to punish my sluggish intellect with rods. But I beg you to be troubled by this: according to the unspeakable and horrifying monstrosity of your error, you would have been educated with rods even if you had been born among the inhabitants of paradise.

If you shudder with us, as you ought, at this most deformed and absurd notion, I ask you: where does this misery of children also come from—a misery that certainly does not arise from an evil nature, as the Manichaeans foolishly suppose—except from the fact that, through that great sin, human nature was so corrupted and entangled in the most just punishments that from it arose not only the corruptibility of bodies, exposed to so many wretched accidents, but also the slowness of intellects, subject to rods and other beatings?

Thus this wicked age would run its course through evil days until its end, so that even the saints, rescued from eternal punishment by divine mercy [Note: [Col. 1311] Vignier has “rescued from eternal punishment through divine [mercy],” omitting *eruti* (“rescued”); the manuscripts restore it.], after receiving the pledge of incorruptible salvation, would nevertheless be commanded to endure the punishments of this life in the proper use of them, with the reward of patience, rather than deserve to be exempt from them even after the remission of sins.

### CLV. JULIAN

But against this final point you rise up in full force. Once you had boarded the same ship as the Manichaean, and once the same spirit had directed your course, after you had already crossed the strait you nevertheless thought you had to disembark on another shore.

Perhaps, however, through a choice of immediate advantage, your slow hesitation may become more tolerable. Toward what harbor, then, are you steering the vessel?

“I say,” you declare, “that God is indeed good, but that he is also the creator of evils.”

What a flight from danger driven onto the rocks—to have wanted to pour the entire bilge of Manichaeus over the one whom you believe to be God!

### AUGUSTINE

Do you deny that even in wicked human beings the nature of both soul and body is good? God is the creator of this good. The Manichaean calls it evil and assigns an evil author to this good which he calls evil.

He does not even spare the soul. Just as he says that there is a certain soul belonging to the flesh, so he says that an evil nature is coeternal with the good God, so that it cannot be good at all. But he says that another, good soul in the same human being was not made by God; rather, it is God’s substance and nature in that same human being [Col. 1312], forced into the miseries of this mixture, not because of any iniquity of its own but because of God’s evil necessity.

He therefore says that the whole work of creation which is the human being is both evil and the work of an evil author. Do you see how different his doctrines are, and therefore how insanely and impiously foolish he is?

But you, who do not think wicked people can be born because God, being good, creates them, contend, if you can, that bodies also cannot be born defective because God, being perfect, creates them. Finally, contend that just as wicked people cannot be born because God, being good, creates them, so neither can people be born slow-witted or foolish because God, being wise, creates them.

Is foolishness not evil, when Scripture says that a fool should be mourned incomparably more than a dead person (Ecclus. 22:10)? Therefore, just as you do not say with us that God is the author of foolishness, although you admit that foolish people are born while God creates them, so we do not say that God is the author of wickedness; yet, because of the original obligation of sin, we can rightly say that wicked people are born only while he himself creates them, since no one creates human beings except him.

### CLVI. JULIAN

It is therefore absolutely clear that the reasoning of that opinion has greater force: if something evil were created naturally, it would indicate an author like itself.

### AUGUSTINE

Who thinks that way, unless Pelagian heretics? Then, because according to you mortal humanity is created not as a punishment but naturally, it indicates a mortal author like itself. And so that your foolishness may at least blush before fools: because a foolish human being is created naturally, he indicates a foolish author like himself.

### CLVII. JULIAN

Truth prescribes, first, that what exists in such a way that its nature compelled it cannot be called evil—that is, sin. Sin is nothing other than a free will departing from the path of justice [Note: [Col. 1312] So the manuscripts. The printed editions have “the path of injustice.”].

### AUGUSTINE

But this original sin also derives its origin from the will of the one who sinned; thus there is no sin except by the will.

### CLVIII. JULIAN

By what defenses, then, is the innocent nature of all things protected, since, remaining as it was created, it is shown to be liable to no crime?

### AUGUSTINE

But it did not remain as it was created. For that reason it is shown to be liable to sin and made its offspring liable to its own crime as though by inheritance. Yet, insofar as that offspring too is created by God, it is good.

### CLIX. JULIAN

Natural evil therefore cannot exist; consequently, no creature is naturally guilty, and there is no evil author. For evil is found not to be an existing nature. Rather, just as every creature is good insofar as it is created, so God, the author of good natures, is proved wholly good, stained by no crime in his work.

Thus everything the Manichaean had brought forward has been overturned by this single Catholic argument [Note: [Col. 1312] The Portian manuscript has *ratiocinatione* (“reasoning”) instead of *ratione* (“argument”).].

### AUGUSTINE

You speak truly: “Every creature, insofar as it is created, is good.” And therefore, just as we both say this, so we also say what follows: “God, the author of good natures, is proved wholly good, stained by no crime in his work” [Col. 1313].

For the whole point is connected there with the statement that “every creature, insofar as it is created, is good” [Note: [Col. 1313] Perhaps *illi* (“for him”) rather than *illic* (“there”).]. Accordingly, the human being too is good insofar as he is created; but insofar as he is generated from a corrupted origin, he is not good. For that reason he must be regenerated.

### CLX. JULIAN

Yet the one who perished beneath the lightning of such obvious truth seems to breathe somewhat when compared with you. For his entire doctrinal structure collapses when only its foundation is shaken; but in your case three things likewise totter where only one totters in him. Consider, then, whether anything of your building can rise.

Manes [Note: [Col. 1313] The printed editions have *Male*; the manuscripts have *Manes*, the proper name of Manichaeus.], therefore, supposing that sin is natural, although it cannot be anything but voluntary, laid his foundations in emptiness. He then placed the remaining parts beside one another in due sequence, saying: Since sin is natural, nature is evil; but the author of an evil thing cannot be good; and therefore the whole human race must be reckoned as belonging to the prince of darkness.

All of this could certainly have stood if the truth had not first undermined his position: namely, that sin, being the work of free will, cannot be taught to be natural, and that whatever was natural could not be sin.

**AUGUSTINE.** A similar line of reasoning can be woven against you: Since you are not so foolish as to deny that foolish minds—that is, foolish people—are born, then listen to how greatly, through your own foolishness, you have helped Manichaean madness. For he, instructed by you yourself, says that foolishness is natural; hence nature itself is foolish—just as you said, “since sin is natural, nature is evil.” Then he adds that the author of a foolish thing is not wise, just as you said, “the author of an evil thing is not good.” Finally he concludes, “And therefore the race of foolish people must be attributed to the prince of darkness”; and so you too concluded, saying, “And therefore the entire human race must be attributed to the prince of darkness [Note: [Col. 1313] We have restored this from the manuscripts: thus you too concluded, saying, “And therefore the entire human race must be attributed to the prince of darkness.”].”

Behold, Manichaeus has defeated you with your own mouth and slaughtered you with your own sword. What are you going to do? For nothing can help you against him; indeed, what you add and say presses and pierces you still more: “All this could certainly have stood, unless truth had first undermined that first point of his, namely, that sin, the work of free will, cannot be taught to be natural, and that whatever was natural could not be sin.”

How does this help you, and how does it not rather suffocate you more and more? Can you perhaps say that foolishness cannot be natural? Then what Manichaeus first established in a similar argument stands against you: foolishness is natural. You thought that the rest of his claims had been built consequentially upon this as their foundation, up to the summit where he says that such a race of human beings must be attributed to the prince of darkness.

We, however, overturn that first foundation of his. We call foolishness natural because foolish people are born—not because human nature, as originally instituted, is perverse, as Manichaeus foolishly supposes, but because of an accidental defect from which such an origin would justly be derived. Consequently, we concede that what he adds next—that nature itself is foolish—is true because of the defect with which the foolish person was born, not because of the work of the good Creator that exists in him. The person was born foolish through an accidental defect, but the human being was created through God’s action.

Next, he adds that the author of a foolish thing is not wise, understanding the thing itself to mean the human being. We say that this does not follow. We call God the author of the human being who was born foolish, although we do not call him the author of the foolishness itself. For this foolishness is not nature or substance, which is born only through God’s creating; it is a defect of that same nature, occurring with God’s permission. Yet we have no doubt that God permits it by a just judgment.

Thus we overthrow both the Manichaeans, builders of their own ruin, and the Pelagians, the foolish helpers of the Manichaeans.

**CLXI. JULIAN.** Once the first definition had therefore been overturned, the wedge of reason scattered his summit upon the ground. What, then, do you hope for concerning yourself, whose three points are as unstable as his one? First, you say that sin is natural; second, that the good God creates, forms, and extends evil things—that is, sins; third, that a matter involving the will is mixed with the seeds.

Thus the three heads of your definitions each totter on their own: they totter, I say—or rather, like ropes drawn from sand, they fall apart before they can be joined. One of them, namely natural sin, already lies directly demolished in Manichaeus; the other two, which are distinctive to your opinion, have fallen along with the death of Manichaeus, though they have fallen in the customary manner [Note: [Col. 1314] Perhaps, “or sewn together.”].

For if he could not vindicate the birth of human beings as guilty either through an evil nature or through the prince of darkness, how much more foolish are you, who, in order to display the crimes of those being born, have added an accusation against God? Therefore, just as nature cannot be sin—the thunderbolt by which Manichaeus’s doctrine has been shattered—so the conclusion follows that what is sin cannot be natural. A matter of the will does not pass into the condition of substance, as you suppose has happened. It is much more clearly established, however, that the good God never creates evil people. It has therefore become evident that sin cannot be present in the person being born, whom God creates.

**AUGUSTINE.** It is established that the good God does not create evil people in the same way that it is established that the wise God does not create foolish people. If you say, “The wise person creates fools,” the reply will be made to you: “Why, then, does the good person not create evil people?” Accordingly, when you attentively ask where fools come from, although God creates them as human beings, perhaps there you will find the defect of origin, which you refuse to acknowledge as original sin.

Or are you prepared to say that, without any preceding sin of anyone, fools could also have been born in that happiness of paradise—people who could not be educated, I do not say with rods, but not even with clubs? If you do not say this, lest such absurdity encompass all foolishness, then say on what merit the image of God is born with such great deformity of mind that, by no strength of age, no length of time, no labor of study, and no skill of teachers, or punishments of beating, it can reach—not wisdom, but even any useful instruction.

You refuse to believe that the just God therefore dismissed human nature from paradise—that is, from the place of happiness—corrupted and condemned, so that no death would occur there: neither the temporal death of the body, nor the eternal death of the whole human being, nor those many and great evils of minds and bodies that we see in the human race, which had to arise from a corrupted and punished root and a ruined mass. Instead, you assign these evils to this earthly misery of mortals, most justly inflicted, with guilt pursuing those who are born and not withdrawing from those who are reborn through their laborious suffering all the way to bodily death.

**CLXII. JULIAN.** The matter is clear and has already been sufficiently dealt with in the first work. But because you wished to be so crafty as to try to establish some distinction between yourself and Manichaeus, I must now press the case, so that it may be clear that I have met not only your earlier statements but also anything you may attempt to introduce hereafter.

We therefore say that God’s work in the person being born is so good that those things which belong naturally to his substance require no correction. For whoever judges that what he confesses to have been made by God ought to have been made otherwise undoubtedly reproves the one whom he confesses to be the craftsman of a creature needing correction into another form [Note: [Col. 1315] So Port. Other manuscripts, together with the printed editions, read “in place of ‘craftsman’: they carried [or accepted].”].

**AUGUSTINE.** Be quiet, I beg you; you do not know what you are saying. Some people are born with their mouths closed, and physicians have opened them. There was a certain Acatius among us, born in an honorable position among his people. He said that he had been born with his eyes closed; but since they did not open because the eyelids were joined together, a physician wished to open them with a knife. His devout mother would not permit this, but accomplished it by applying a poultice made from the Eucharist [Note: [Col. 1315] We have added “by applying,” on the authority of the ancient manuscripts.] when the boy was already about five years old or perhaps older; he said that he remembered this quite well.

I omit the man in the Gospel born blind, to whom the very Craftsman gave sight, though he had made his eyes deficient in order to commend his miracles. In that case the reason why he was born blind is not concealed: not because of his own sin or that of his parents, but so that the works of God might be revealed in him.

Nevertheless, ask physicians, and let them tell you how many people they help, where they can, so that defects innate in their bodies may not remain, or even kill those who are born with them. For some people, just as others are born with their mouths closed, are born with their lower passages closed; and if these defects remain, they do not allow them to live. When people are assisted by medical skill in such cases, God’s works are not being blamed and corrected.

For what true worshiper of God does not know that such people had to be born as they were born? Yet this too belongs to the afflictions of the human race, in which these evil days are spent—days full of labors, pains, fears, and dangers, by the just judgment of God [Col. 1316]. Far be it from us to suppose that any of these evils existed in the happiness of paradise. Therefore they arose only from the root of sin.

What of the minds themselves? If they are left as they were born and are not cultivated by diligent instruction through the great labor of teachers and learners, is it not evident what they will remain like? But you should fill your paradise with people born defective in both body and soul, so that you may unhappily deny original sin with closed eyes and shamelessly open mouths.

**CLXIII. JULIAN.** Therefore, while preserving in all those being born the degree of probability and the moderate measure of praise owed to natures, we say that increases of divine benefits are useful and necessary for everyone alike at every age. Yet this is so only insofar as neither virtue nor sin is attributed to anyone without that person’s own will.

**AUGUSTINE.** Virtue is not attributed to anyone without that person’s own will; but the will is prepared by the Lord (Prov. VIII, according to the Septuagint), as in the case of that king for whom Esther prayed (Esther XV).

**CLXIV. JULIAN.** Even in this the greater mercy of God is shown, since he sanctifies infants who do not know it. For this pertains to the praise of mercy, when guilt does not stain them while they are unaware; for that belongs to the laws of equity.

**AUGUSTINE.** If no guilt stains them, why are they not all sanctified? And why are all who are sanctified exsufflated?

**CLXV. JULIAN.** But I am speaking of those virtues which we acquire through the practice of perfected reason [Note: [Col. 1316] Codex Mar. reads “will”]. Therefore, since it was necessary to impress this point upon us here too, as often elsewhere, I urge the attentive reader to consider what follows. For he will see that the Traducianists differ in no respect from the Manichaeans, so that they bring against us no arguments other than those found in the Manichaeans’ books. I did this also in the fourth book of my first work.

**AUGUSTINE.** And I answered you in the sixth book of my work.

**CLXVI. JULIAN.** But since, after those works had been published, a letter of Manichaeus was found at Constantinople through your prayer, most blessed Father Flore, and was sent to these regions, it is useful to insert some of it, so that everyone may understand where these arguments for traducianism derive from.

**AUGUSTINE.** How can you say that the letter was found and sent through someone’s prayer, if God does not act upon the wills in human hearts? Certainly the person who found it sought the letter willingly, or was willingly seeking something at the place where he was able to find it; or, when people were willingly speaking about such matters, the person with whom it had been entrusted willingly indicated that he possessed it and could show it and hand it over to anyone who wished to receive it. He too would willingly send it to these regions, or in any other way it was wholly through the will of one person or several people that the letter was found and sent. Yet you say that this happened because a person prayed.

Why, then, do you not confess that, without any external command sounding forth, God, by a hidden impulse, most effectively prepares and arouses human wills to accomplish whatever he wishes—when you do not defend free will as something to be understood, but exalt it in a way that causes it to rush headlong?

**CLXVII. JULIAN.** Although in that first little work I had already discussed concupiscence or the pleasure of the flesh, which is also called lust and which has been implanted in the sexes for the sake of propagation, sufficiently to show that it is nothing other than one of the instruments of the body, equally implanted in rational and irrational beings and pertaining to God’s work, who had endowed our flesh with sensations, nevertheless, because Augustine also presses this matter vigorously and says that it is evil—that is, natural sin and the parent of all sins—and tries especially to establish this through the shame associated with it, while mocking me because I am ashamed to name it directly:

**AUGUSTINE.** I say that the concupiscence of the flesh, by which the flesh desires against the spirit and which is also called lust, is evil. In the present flesh it must be restrained and diminished by good habit; in eternal life it must be healed in every respect. It is not to be separated from us as though some evil substance had been added to or mingled with us, as the Manichaeans foolishly suppose. Yet whatever opinion you hold about it, I would not believe that you could place it in paradise in the condition in which it now exists—so that it urges even the hearts of the chaste, whether married or continent, toward committing unlawful acts, and, unless it is resisted by a stronger will, overthrows them—if I did not find you saying this in your books, filled with vain and insane loquacity.

**CLXVIII. JULIAN.** Therefore I too shall now briefly vindicate the quality of the matter which, in my earlier writings, I defended by distinguishing it from the language of Manichaeus, by exposing those who accuse it while nevertheless professing themselves unwilling servants of it.

**AUGUSTINE.** You can consistently serve the lust you praise; we, however, with the Lord’s help, attack and conquer the lust you accuse.

**CLXIX. JULIAN.** What is therefore retained in your books, old Augustine, is this: “Lust arose after sin, and those who were confounded were compelled to cover it” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 2, section 36).

**AUGUSTINE.** What is therefore retained in your books, young Julian, is that you cannot find anything to say against my books and are seeking accusations to heap upon us with much empty talk.

**CLXX. JULIAN.** And again: “The person who lawfully has intercourse through lust of the genitals uses evil well; the person who does so unlawfully uses evil badly. For it more correctly receives the name of evil than of good, since both the evil and the good are ashamed of it; and we believe the Apostle more readily, who says, ‘Because good does not dwell in my flesh’” (*ibid.*). And elsewhere: “Lust is not the good of marriage, but the obscenity of sinners, the necessity of those who beget, the ardor of wantonness, the shame of marriage” (*ibid.*, book 1, section 13). And this: “What they did afterward through propagation is the good of marriage; but what they earlier covered in confusion is the evil of concupiscence, which everywhere avoids being seen and seeks secrecy in shame” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 1, section 8).

Or perhaps such statements, with which you habitually support this argument, were produced more by your memory than by your intelligence. Manichaeus was afflicted, then, and composed what he thought were sharp arguments; but you, frustrated, thought that what you had read and retained could remain concealed.

**AUGUSTINE.** Who is there who has even a slight knowledge of the Manichaean doctrine and does not know that the Manichaeans say that the concupiscence of the flesh is evil? But this is not peculiar to their doctrine. For what else does the person say who says, “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh; for these are opposed to each other, so that you do not do what you wish” (Gal. V, 17)? What else does the person say who says, “Whoever has loved the world does not possess the love of the Father; because everything that is in the world is the concupiscence of the flesh, the concupiscence of the eyes, and the ambition of the age; it is not from the Father but from the world” (1 John II, 15–16)?

The Manichaeans do not say that the concupiscence of the flesh is evil on the basis of a doctrine proper to themselves; those who are not blind see that the Apostles say this too. But your error helps the Manichaeans in their distinctive and poisonous opinion: you deny that the concupiscence of the flesh—which chastity resists, whether you wish it or not, because it urges people to commit unlawful acts—arose from sin entering the nature that God created good.

Thus you act so that the Manichaeans may conclude that the concupiscence which the struggles of the chaste and the testimony of the Apostles prove to be evil comes from the race of darkness and from an evil substance coeternal with God; and that it is itself not an evil quality to be healed, but an evil substance to be separated [Note: [Col. 1318] Here we have added from the manuscripts, “but an evil substance to be separated.”]—not something that happened to good nature, but something mingled with good nature.

But go on and contrive accusations against us concerning the Manichaean plague. You help them so much that you make them invincible—unless you too, along with them, are conquered by the Catholic truth, which truly is invincible.

**CLXXI. JULIAN.** Listen now and acknowledge what your father wrote to a certain daughter of his, your sister.

**AUGUSTINE.** These are insults—not refined ones, but empty.

**CLXXII. JULIAN.** “Manes, apostle of Jesus Christ, to Menoch, a daughter: May grace and salvation be granted to you from our God, who is truly the true God; and may he himself enlighten your mind and reveal his justice to you, because you are the offspring of a divine race.”

And shortly afterward he says: “Through whom and how you have been made splendid, you may recognize by learning what you formerly were, from what race of souls you emanated—a race that is mingled with all bodies and flavors and adheres to various forms. For just as souls are generated from souls, so bodily formation is fashioned from bodily nature.” Therefore what is born from flesh is flesh, and what is from spirit is spirit. Understand spirit as soul: soul from soul, flesh from flesh” (*Letter of Manichaeus*).

**AUGUSTINE.** If I tell you that I have no knowledge whatsoever of this letter of Manichaeus, although I shall be telling the truth, you will not believe me at all, and, as usual, you will contend with me in empty loquacity. But if Manichaeus said this, what wonder is it that he destroyed himself? For if, just as human flesh is born, the human soul too is born, whether good or evil—and they deliriously claim that two souls exist together in one human being, one evil and the other good, emanating from their different principles—then if the soul is born when the flesh is born, that evil soul is certainly neither coeternal with God nor, contrary to the foolishness of his sect, brought forth from the eternal Father as something good against the princes of darkness.

But however Manichaeus may say that souls are born, what does that concern us? We know and hold that the words of the Lord, “What is born from flesh is flesh, and what is born from spirit is spirit” (John III, 6), do not refer to a human being being born from a human being, but to a human being being reborn from the Spirit of God. For the whole Gospel passage itself does not permit any other understanding.

Go, then, and see to whom you can sell these fables of Manichaeus. Rather, in view of what I said above, show how you are not a helper of the Manichaeans.

**CLXXIII. JULIAN.** You recognize, surely, how explicitly Manichaeus confirms the transmission of souls, and what testimony he uses to disparage the flesh—namely, the one that is constantly on your lips: “What is born from flesh is flesh, and what is born from spirit is spirit” (John III, 6).

**AUGUSTINE.** I have already said how we understand these Gospel words: they teach not generation but regeneration. You tell me, if you can, how you do not assist Manichaeus’s sacrilegious words about the concupiscence of the flesh, which you therefore deny descends into our nature through propagation from the nature of the first man, corrupted by transgression, so that he may rightly be thought to assign it to the race of darkness coeternal with God.

For you most foolishly and shamelessly deny the evil by which the flesh desires against the spirit and against which the inward battles of the chaste are waged.

**CLXXIV. JULIAN.** Therefore he insists, not only by explaining but also by repeating, that it is characteristic of his doctrine to believe in the transmission of souls. He also tries to prove this by comparing it with the generation of bodies: “Just as souls,” he says, “are generated from souls, so the bodily formation is distributed from the nature of a body; and just as flesh is from flesh, so soul is from soul.”

But let us proceed to the rest: “Therefore, just as God is the author of souls, so the author of bodies through concupiscence is the devil, so that, through the concupiscence of the woman, in the devil’s snare, where the devil lies in wait, he hunts not souls but bodies.”

**AUGUSTINE.** Manichaeus could have said that the devil hunts not bodies but souls. For he says that bodies belong to the nature of the race of darkness, from which the devil too comes. Therefore, according to Manichaeus, the devil is said to hunt not the bodies that belong to him, but the good souls that do not belong to him. Our faith, however, knows the good God as the creator of souls and bodies.

**CLXXV. JULIAN.** “Whether through sight, touch, hearing, smell, or taste [Note: [Col. 1319] The printed editions had omitted “or touch.”]. Finally, remove the root of this evil stock, and immediately you will see yourself made spiritual. For Scripture says, ‘Concupiscence is the root of all evils’” (1 Tim. VI, 10).

You see in what spirit and for what doctrine Manichaeus attacks the concupiscence of the flesh, saying that this is the law of sin; if it were removed from bodies, the daughter to whom he writes would see herself made spiritual. Let us hear by what statements of the Apostle he tries to confirm this opinion: “For the flesh is opposed to the spirit, because it is the daughter of concupiscence; and the spirit to the flesh” (Gal. V, 17), “because it is the son of the soul.”

**AUGUSTINE.** Manichaeus supposes that the Apostle’s words refer to two substances, one good and the other evil, rather than to one good substance and a defect of that good substance, contracted through generation from the sin of the first man and healed through the regeneration brought about by the righteousness of the second man. Against both the Manichaeans and you, the Catholic faith powerfully casts this as an utterly invincible weapon and lays both groups low.

**CLXXVI. JULIAN.** You understand that the inner substance of the Manichaean doctrine, by which your faith is compacted, has been exposed. Now he proceeds to accuse us—that is, the Catholics: “Consider, therefore, how foolish they are who say that this bodily formation was created by the good God, although they are certain that it is generated by the spirit of concupiscence.”

**AUGUSTINE.** In this accusation we are both charged by the Manichaeans—you and we—because both of us say that the formation of the flesh was created by the good God. But the Manichaeans say that the spirit of concupiscence is an evil substance, not a defect of a good substance by which the flesh desires against the spirit. We say this in order to refute them, whereas you deny it in order to assist them.

Since they prove that the concupiscence by which the flesh desires against the spirit is evil even though you resist them, if it is not, as you suppose, a defect of a good substance, it will be assigned to an evil substance. That is the doctrine of the Manichaeans, hostile to the Catholic faith with you as its helper.

**CLXXVII. JULIAN.** “When they unite unwillingly in spirit, they act in shameful secrecy, at a time when they hate the light, so that their works may not be revealed. For this reason the Apostle says, ‘It is not of the one who wills’ (Rom. IX, 16), so that this work is to be understood.

For whether we produce something good, it is not of the flesh, because the works of the flesh are manifest: fornication, and so forth; or whether we produce something evil [Note: [Col. 1320] The earlier edition of Vignierius and the Mar. and Clar. manuscripts read: “For whether we generate something good . . . or whether we generate something evil.”], it is not of the soul, because the fruit of the Spirit is peace and joy (Gal. V, 19, 22).

Finally, the Apostle also cries out in Romans: ‘I do not do the good that I wish, but I do the evil that I hate’ (Rom. VII, 19). You see the voice of the rebellious soul defending the soul’s liberty against concupiscence. For he was grieving because sin—that is, the devil—was producing every concupiscence in him.

The authority of the Law indicates its evil character when it condemns all its uses, which the flesh admires and praises. For every bitterness of concupiscence is sweet to the soul; through it the soul is nourished and strengthened. Finally, when the mind restrains itself from every use of concupiscence, it remains vigilant, is enriched, and grows; but through the use of concupiscence it has become accustomed to diminish” [Col. 1321].

Do you understand—or have you at last discovered—from what source you not only derive your understanding but also your speech? You embrace your teacher with such love that you follow not only his journeys but even his footprints. You affirm this throughout all your writings, as do the books you published under the name of Marcellinus and those you sent to Valerius. They all testify that this concupiscence of the flesh, which you also call shameful, was mingled into human bodies by the devil.

**AUGUSTINE.** With what shamelessness do you deny that it is shameful, when you now praise it so freely? I wonder whether you are fighting faithfully. When you had intercourse with your wife, although, fearing nothing, you eagerly pursued the pleasure granted for use, you nevertheless sought secrecy because you were ashamed.

Accordingly, on the position you have adopted, if human happiness had remained in paradise, it would either not have existed there or would not have exerted any of its own motions against the command of the will—motions that would have had to be resisted so that conduct befitting that happiness might be maintained.

But since you have advanced so far in praising it that you claim that lust, such as we now experience it, would have existed in paradise in the same form, troubling the hearts of the chaste who resist it, who does not see that you resist me not with wisdom or eloquence but with shamelessness, because perverse shame prevents you from admitting that you have been defeated?

We therefore say that the concupiscence of the flesh is neither a substance of an evil nature, as the Manichaeans say; nor do we reject every use of it, as the Manichaeans do; nor do we call it good, as the Pelagians do; nor do we praise its movement against the spirit, as the Pelagians do. Rather, we say that it is a defect of a good substance, which entered our nature through the transgression of the first man. This is what Catholic Christians say. We approve the licit and honorable use of this evil for the procreation of children, as Catholic Christians do.

Thus we overcome and avoid both the Manichaeans and the Pelagians. Their errors differ from each other in such a way that the one who appears lesser is shown to be the helper of the one who appears greater. For, when the Pelagians deny that what is plainly evil is a defect of a good substance, they help the Manichaeans, who say that the defect itself is an evil substance coeternal with the substance of the good God.

**CLXXVIII. JULIAN.** This is the daughter of sin and the mother of other sins; and the Apostle Paul complains about it when he says, “I know that good does not dwell in my flesh,” and, “I do not do the good that I wish, but I do the evil that I hate” (Rom. VII, 18, 15). The Catholics have always explained this in such a way that it referred not to the disgrace of nature but to the reproach of habit.

**AUGUSTINE.** And so you are a Catholic, while Ambrose is not a Catholic? People have not been so completely dissipated by the contagion of your vanity—those whom you have been able to deceive—that they dare to implant this in their minds. Therefore pay attention for a little while.

We do not doubt, nor do you or the Manichaeans, that the discord of flesh and spirit of which it is written, “I know that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh; for to will is present with me, but to accomplish the good is not,” and the other statements of this kind—and, much more clearly, “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh; for these are opposed to each other, so that you do not do what you wish” (Gal. V, 17)—exist in human beings.

But there is disagreement about the source of this discord in one human being, and three opinions are put forward in this disagreement: one is ours, another yours, and the third belongs to the Manichaeans.

But lest we seem to be saying arrogantly or deceitfully that ours is the Catholic opinion, let the person whose faith and utterly pure understanding of Scripture even your own Pelagius praises present it—indeed, his enemy did not dare to criticize it [Note: [Col. 1322] See above, *On the Grace of Christ*, sections 46–47].

Ambrose therefore says that this discord of flesh and spirit entered our nature through the transgression of the first man (*Book 7 on Luke*, chapter 12). You say that it arises from the force of habit. The Manichaeans say that it arises from the mingling of two coeternal natures, namely, the good and the evil.

I could now say that anyone wishing to remain Catholic should choose whichever of these three he wishes. For I need not fear that someone fleeing from the Manichaeans might prefer you to Ambrose.

But the person who sees that no one is born without this evil judges your opinion—that this evil grows through the force of habit—to be utterly empty [Note: [Col. 1322] So the manuscripts. Vignierius reads, “he indicates that this evil grows soft through the force of habit, to be utterly empty.”].

For as soon as each person begins to use reason, if he desires chastity, he already feels the concupiscence of the flesh, which had been dormant through age, as though awakening and resisting him; and either, overcome, he is dragged away, or, so that he may not fall into its consent, he fights against it with the Lord’s help, if he is pious.

If you do not wish to accept this, why do you rage against me? Set the Manichaeans and Ambrose against each other, and, as spectators of this contest, choose which side you would favor if you are Catholics. I think that you would judge Ambrose the victor; but because you are not Catholics, we watch securely even so, for Ambrose unquestionably defeats both you and the Manichaeans.

**CLXXIX. JULIAN.** Yet by arguing and employing testimonies of Scripture, you confirm that all the saints were polluted by this concupiscence, which you call the law of sin, and that they all complained about it [Note: [Col. 1322] Vignierius omits the conjunction “and”: “you call the law of sin, confirming all the saints to have been as polluted as they complained.” We have restored it from the Portarum codex.].

**AUGUSTINE.** The saints are not polluted by this evil. They are known to have been, or to be, the strongest conquerors of this evil. Rather, let the most shameless praisers of this evil fear that they may be inexpiably polluted by it.

**CLXXX. JULIAN.** What does Manichaeus say? “Through the concupiscence of bodies, the author is the devil; through it the devil hunts bodies, not souls. Remove,” he says, “the root of the evil stock, and you will become spiritual. Of this the Apostle cries out to the Romans: ‘I do not do the good that I wish, but I do the evil that I hate’” (Rom. VII). He also calls us foolish because we say that this bodily formation belongs to God, although we confess that it was generated through concupiscence [Col. 1323].

You therefore see how great an agreement exists between you and Manichaeus in attacking us. You fight with his words and rely upon his arguments, yet you say that we lie when we call you not only his disciple—as you yourself write that you were—but also still his disciple.

Nevertheless, in this he was more prudent: since he believed that this concupiscence of the flesh had been introduced by the devil, he concluded that whatever appeared to have been produced from the devil’s concupiscence had to be confessed as not belonging to God’s work.

**AUGUSTINE.** Our earlier response, together with the other responses above, is sufficient against all this; let anyone who wishes read them [Note: [Col. 1323] Vignierius reads, “and the other earlier responses.” From Port. we have added “together with,” and from that same codex and other manuscripts, “let anyone who wishes read them.”].

**CLXXXI. JULIAN.** But you are more dull-witted: while saying that the human being is the fruit of the devil’s concupiscence, you nevertheless attribute him to God’s works—not as something good made from evil, but as evil, produced from an evil root, yet having a good author, whose fruit the devil claims for himself as the fruit of his own root.

**AUGUSTINE.** Every human being is in some respect good, even when a person of mature age is an evil human being. For the fact that a person is evil does not take away whatever good exists in him because he is a human being. God is the author of this nature—that is, of this good—whatever evils it derives from origin or adds through the will. For defects are not substance or nature; they are defects of a nature corrupted by those same defects, and they must be healed by the Savior by whom the nature was created.

This overturns both the Manichaeans and you. You are not contending with me but with Ambrose, whom I set against the Manichaeans in this contest; in it he defeats both them [Note: [Col. 1323] So the manuscripts. Vignierius reads, “he will defeat.”] and you.

**CLXXXII. JULIAN.** According to your statements, then, the devil rightly plucks from all those born through concupiscence the fruits of his own tree [Note: [Col. 1323] Book 1 of *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, section 26]. Therefore you blaspheme just as Manichaeus does when we vindicate the concupiscence of the flesh as having been created by God.

**AUGUSTINE.** If you had wished to come to the substance of the matter, the reason why infants being baptized are both exsufflated and cleansed by exorcism would have shown you most openly—not only to the learned but even to uneducated Catholic Christians—that you are a new heretic.

But because you did bring this forward from my book as something to be refuted and then feared to deal with it so greatly that you evaded it through deceptive loquacity, concealing by saying many things what you had left unsaid, I repeat and impress upon you, whether you wish it or not, the Apostle’s statement concerning God the Father: “He has rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love” (Col. I, 13).

If you can, exclude infants from this statement, and dare to say that they are indeed transferred into Christ’s kingdom through regeneration, but are not rescued from the power of darkness. Nevertheless, prepare yourselves to receive most deservedly upon your own faces those same exsufflations that are applied in Christ’s Church both to adults and to infants. For you will have to be exsufflated with such exsufflations as most clearly demonstrate the truth of what you deny.

**CLXXXIII. JULIAN.** And now, that statement of yours which I examined in my earlier work (*the work written to Turbantius*), where you say, “Sometimes lust does not act when the mind wills, although at other times it acts even when the mind does not will it” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 1, section 7), and where you accuse its arrogance because it is stirred against the mind’s will, has been expressed not only in Manichaeus’s ideas but also in his words.

For when he had accused us because we said that human beings are made by God, although we confessed that they are sown through the pleasure of those who unite, he said: “Fools say that what they are certain is generated by concupiscence is created by God, when they unite against the will of the mind.”

AUG. But Manichaeus does not understand that, even from the evil in a human being, God can create what is good, and that the human being himself can make good use of evil through marital chastity, by which he resists that evil that entices him toward damnable shamefulness. But you, who deny that what is evil is evil—why do you resist it, lest you live shamefully? And why, if you consent to it, must you necessarily live shamefully?

**CLXXXIV. JUL.** But when you wrote, “The evil of concupiscence is that it everywhere avoids being seen and seeks secrecy in shame” (*ibid.*, no. 8), Manichaeus likewise says: “They engage in secret shameful acts at the time when they hate the light, so that their works may not be revealed.”

**AUG.** Just as Manichaeus does not know what good is accomplished through the evil of carnal concupiscence, so you also do not know for what evil shame seeks secrecy, even in the good work of marriage.

**CLXXXV. JUL.** But when you say, “The one who lawfully engages in intercourse makes good use of evil” (*ibid.*, book 2, chapter 21), and recall this so as to make the Apostle more readily believed [Note: [Col. 1324] The Portuguese manuscript reads *commoneres* (“you might remind”), rather than *commemores* (“you might recall”).], who said, “Good does not dwell in his flesh,” and wish this “not-good”—that is, the evil dwelling in the Apostle’s flesh—to be understood as carnal concupiscence, Manichaeus made the same claim as you. For after saying, “so that their works may not be revealed,” he says: “For this reason the Apostle cries out to the Romans: I do not do the good that I want, but I do the evil that I hate. For he was grieving because sin—that is, the devil—was working in him every concupiscence. Legal authority indicates the evil of concupiscence, since it condemns all its use, which the flesh admires and praises.”

**AUG.** Does the Apostle condemn every use of carnal concupiscence when he says, “If you marry, you have not sinned; and if a virgin marries, she does not sin” (1 Cor. 7:28)? Manichaeus therefore does not know what he is saying. But neither do you understand what you are saying, since you think that the Apostle meant something other than carnal concupiscence. Concerning this, another apostle says that it is not from the Father but from the world (1 John 2:16); and that the flesh’s concupiscence against the spirit descends from the transgression of the first man—so a Catholic scholar and teacher learned and taught in the Catholic Church [Note: [Col. 1324] The printed editions read “in the Catholic Church.” *Church* is absent from the manuscripts.] (Ambrose, book 7 on Luke 12).

**CLXXXVI. JUL.** But what you thought would greatly help maintain the distinction between you and Manichaeus—namely, when you said that nature was indeed good, but that only the nature created in the first human beings was good, while all nature thereafter had been overturned through concupiscence—Manichaeus argued in the same way:

“It is worthwhile to observe that the first soul, which flowed forth from the God of light, received this bodily structure in order to govern it with its bridle. The commandment came; sin revived, which had seemed captive. The devil found his members [Note: [Col. 1325] The Codex Portarum reads, “the devil found his member,” or possibly “the devil, a member, found…”], led the material of concupiscence astray into it, and through it killed it. The law indeed is holy, but holy for the holy; and the commandment is just and good, but for the just and good.”

Likewise, in that letter to Patricius, he says that something was “as though made from the first flower of substance, and says that it is better than what followed” [Note: [Col. 1325] The same Codex Portarum reads *secutus* (“that which followed”) rather than *secutis*.].

It is therefore no great matter, nor does it advance your defense, that you thought Adam should be separated from the accusation directed against human nature; we shall discuss his condition more fully shortly. For now it is enough to show that nothing in your thinking is so crude that it has not already been worn smooth by Manichaean handling.

**AUG.** Manichaeus says that not only the human being but the whole world, and everything belonging to it, consists of the commingling of two coeternal natures—namely, good and evil. He does indeed attribute to the good God, as craftsman, the very structure of the world, although it is made from the commingling of good and evil; but he says that animals, everything born from the earth, and the human being himself are works of the malignant mind, which he assigns to the nation of darkness.

That is why he says that the “first soul flowed forth from the God of light and received this bodily structure in order to govern it with its bridle.” He is not speaking here about the human being, but about the good soul, which he believes to be a part and nature of God, mixed throughout the whole world and everything in it; in the human being, however, he believes it is deceived through concupiscence. And concerning this concupiscence—which must often be emphasized—he wants it to be not a defect occurring in a good substance, but an evil substance.

He says that Adam was not empty of evil, but possessed less of it, and much more light. Do you see how opposed to this madness is the Catholic faith? That madness says that God’s nature is corruptible and that it is corrupted by commixture with an evil nature. The Catholic faith, however, says that all the evils of the human race—of which we see even infants enduring no small share—and concupiscence itself, by which the flesh desires against the spirit, are derived from a good nature instituted well by the good God, but corrupted by its own will and by the transgression of the first man. By denying this, what are you doing except ensuring that all these evils—which you refuse to have come upon infants from the sin of a good nature—will be attributed to the commixture with an evil nature introduced by the mad error of the Manichaeans?

You see, therefore, even if you do not wish to see it, that the insane and ruined Manichaeans must be conquered together with you, lest, with your help, they prevail; or rather, with the Lord’s help, they have already been conquered together with you.

**CLXXXVII. JUL.** He persists in attacking us and adds:

“But those who have dared to call this concupiscence good, against the Gospel and apostolic books, which they read to no purpose—watch,” he says, “their holy men: at one time sleeping with their daughters, at another engaging in intercourse with several concubines and wives. Nor do they see what the Apostle says: What fellowship is there between light and darkness, between the believer and the unbeliever, between Christ and Belial? (2 Cor. 6:14–15.) They err, heaped together in the cloud of concupiscence [Note: [Col. 1326] Vignierius reads “heaped together in the cloud of the concupiscence of clouds.” The Mar. and Clar. manuscripts read “heaped together in the cloud of concupiscence.”], whose poison they enjoy so greatly that, seized by madness, they think that when they do this it has been permitted by God—as though they did not know that the Apostle said, ‘What they do in secret, it is shameful even to mention’” (Eph. 5:12).

You see, surely, how he harasses the matter of shame and thinks it greatly effective against us that we do not dare to call evil what we nevertheless acknowledge must be covered by shame. You have woven no garment with which to cover the deformity of your doctrine, except the rags in which you grew up under the inheritance of your parent and teacher.

He persists, therefore, in rising up against us and turns directly to the point:

“Come, you defender of concupiscence,” he says, “describe openly its fruits and works. Look: I oppose it and do not fear the light, which it dreads and hates. For everyone who does evil hates the light and does not come to the light, lest his works be revealed” (John 3:20). “Do you see that concupiscence is the origin of evil, through which miserable souls serve lust—not willingly, because this is the one thing we do against the will of the mind?”

That is why you too say:

“For what is the reason that the lips, tongue, hands, and the movements of the back, neck, and sides are placed under our control, so that they may be moved toward their appropriate tasks, whereas, when it comes to the begetting of children, the members created for this work do not serve, but wait for lust, as though it were master of itself, to move them; and sometimes it does not act when the mind wills, while at other times it acts when the mind does not will it?” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 1, no. 7).

You have enumerated all the functions of the limbs and, commending them as servants of the command of the will, call the matter of lust the one thing we do against the will of the mind. What does Manichaeus say?

“Do you see that concupiscence is the origin of evil, through which miserable souls serve lust—not willingly, because this is the one thing we do against the will of the mind?”

But let us see what else he adds:

“Finally, every sin is outside the body, because it is an act; but whoever commits fornication sins against his own body” (1 Cor. 6:18). “For every sin does not exist before it is committed; after it has been committed, only the memory of the deed remains, not the deed’s very form. But the evil of concupiscence, because it is natural, exists before it is enacted; when it is enacted, it increases; after it has been enacted, it is both seen and remains.”

Why, then, do you quarrel with us because we call you a Manichaean, when neither in his writings is anything held other than what you say, nor in yours anything other than what he wants to persuade people of?

Moreover, the saying that runs through your mouths, though infused by you, is contained in that same letter of Manichaeus:

“If sin is not natural, why are infants baptized, when it is evident that they themselves have done nothing evil?”

I said that this saying flies about on many tongues because it is a commoner argument, understood even by the slow-witted. But in your books you place all your hope in it. Your teacher therefore develops this very point as follows:

“Those who must be questioned with these words are: If every evil is an act, why does someone receive purification by water before committing evil, when he has done no evil by himself? Or, if he has not yet acted and must be purified, it is clear [Note: [Col. 1327] Perhaps *liquet* (“it is clear”), rather than *licet* (“although”).] that they display the natural propagation of an evil stock [Note: [Col. 1327] So the manuscripts read. The printed editions have *offendere* (“to offend”) rather than *ostendere* (“to display”).]—those whom madness does not allow to understand either what they say or what they assert” (The Letter of Manichaeus).

Do you hear how he insults us? He calls us mad and says that we understand neither what we say nor what we assert, because we deny the propagation of an evil stock, although we baptize even those who have done no evil—that is, infants—by purifying water.

Many of his opinions have indeed been set down here [Note: [Col. 1327] So the manuscripts read. Vignierius has the singular, “of his opinion.”]; but unless the title identified Menoch’s daughter and Manichaeus, who calls himself Christ’s apostle (above, chapter 172), they would altogether proclaim you their author. Since you say nothing other than what you learned from the teaching of Mani [Note: [Col. 1327] Vignierius conjectures *Mane* (“Manes”).], do you think that Catholics will regard you differently from the one through whom you drank in the sacramental doctrines of this kind?”

**AUG.** At last you have finished what you thought had to be said against us from the letter of Manichaeus—a letter you rejoice to have discovered with the assistance of the speeches of your colleague Florus. In it, certainly, Manichaeus accuses carnal concupiscence, by which the flesh desires against the spirit; and he thinks that this should be held against Catholics, as though they said it was good because they commend the good of marriage with the soundness of the Lord’s and the apostles’ teaching.

For how could Manichaeus distinguish the evil of carnal concupiscence from the good of marriage, when the Epistle to the Hebrews says that solid food belongs only to those whose senses are trained to distinguish good from evil (Heb. 5:14)? But you have plainly fallen unavoidably into this Manichaean bite: you are such a great praiser of carnal concupiscence that you would place it not in the condition in which it could have been—or should have been—there, but exactly in the condition in which it now exists, even in paradise, that is, in a place of such great blessedness. You would therefore have the inhabitants of that place enjoy such blessed peace that they nevertheless would fight against the movements of concupiscence within themselves, in an internal war, lest they slip into agreement with an illicit or dishonorable intercourse.

This evil could not exist in paradise, unless perhaps in that painted paradise of which we spoke above, bearing the superscription, “The Paradise of the Pelagians” (above, chapter 154). Even if concupiscence itself, secretly troubling chaste hearts, could not be represented by any artistic skill of a painter, pregnant women could nevertheless be painted there, rejecting useful foods in disgust, craving harmful ones with foul delight, nauseated, vomiting, growing pale, and sometimes expelling immature fetuses in miscarriage. They could also be shown, even in childbirth, proclaiming their misery through the suffering endured by their mother Eve; and although the picture could not make a sound, it could imitate as best it could the faces of the sad, groaning, and weeping. The infants themselves could all be shown crying, according to the common lot of those who are born, amid various kinds of suffering; and many of them later beneath the blows of their teachers.

If someone ignorant of this painting were to look at it, read the title, and ask its meaning, you would give him this splendid explanation—though it would come from you:

“This would have been the condition of the human race even there, because it is such here, where likewise no origin of sin is drawn from human offspring.”

If he accepted this, he would become a Pelagian. But if he refused to accept such ridiculous folly, you would accuse him of being a Manichaean.

But against this controversy, holy Ambrose, say to them—you who were learned in the Church and a teacher of the Church—that the concupiscence by which the flesh desires against the spirit, and concerning which Manichaeus, not knowing what he is saying, spreads traps for the inexperienced, arose not from a commixture with another nature, as he foolishly claims, but from the transgression of the first man in our good nature, created by the good God (book 7 on Luke 12).

Perhaps you choose, with the most shameless obstinacy, to provide assistance to the utterly impure Manichaeus rather than yield to holy Ambrose. Do as you please; but Manichaeus will not rejoice even with you as his helpers, since, through the Catholic faith, in the name and power of Christ, Ambrose conquers both of you.

For if this concupiscence were such that, by its own carnal movement, it neither preceded nor exceeded the human will, but always followed its decision, Manichaeus would find nothing in it that he could justly condemn; none of us would argue that married people in paradise could not have possessed it; nor would Ambrose say that it had been derived from the transgression of the first man, since he would not see it desiring against the spirit.

But now it is such that it desires against the spirit, even when it does not prevail because the spirit resists it. For that reason it could not have existed in paradise, where the blessed enjoyed that great peace. Nor is it right to believe that God became corrupt through a commixture with an evil nature. It remains, therefore, that the faith of Ambrose should conquer both you and the Manichaeans concerning the contagion of the first sin.

**CLXXXVIII. JUL.** It remains for us to examine that statement of yours which you promised to reduce to a single formulation and which, it must be admitted, you collected briefly and rather cleverly:

“If human nature were evil, it ought not to be generated; if it had no evil, it ought not to be regenerated. And, to conclude both in a single word: if human nature were evil, it ought not to be saved; if no evil were present in it, it ought not to be saved” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 2, no. 36).

Here we must not deprive you of the praise of ingenuity; your reasoning could scarcely have been expressed better in your own interest. Nevertheless, the nature of things does not permit exact cleverness to accomplish anything. It is altogether difficult for you to kick against the goad: whatever you put together dissolves in the fire of the truth brought near to it, no less than ice.

Finally, pay attention to what we now say. You concluded in this way:

“Certainly, if human nature were evil, it ought not to be saved.”

We agree: you spoke entirely truly. If it were evil, it ought not to be saved, because a thing evil and naturally evil would neither deserve nor be capable of salvation. Why would it not be capable of salvation? Because it could not become anything other than what it had been made. Why would it not deserve salvation? Because there would be nothing in it that the mercy of God would deem worthy of liberating.

But when we say, “if it were”—which certainly cannot be [Note: [Col. 1329] The Portuguese manuscript reads *posset* (“could”) rather than *potest* (“can”).]—we are not granting hope of the effect that is denied. Rather, in order to destroy another proposition that arises, we commonly speak of impossible things in this way: “If this or that were so, then without doubt such-and-such would follow.” Since the former cannot be so, the latter also, which had been introduced in order to remove it, is denied all the more.

We have often shown, then, that there cannot be anything evil by nature. Yet, without prejudging this conclusion, we now approve the part of your statement in which you said, “If human nature were evil, it ought not to be saved.”

You placed salvation in baptism and argued consistently: if the Manichaeans were speaking truth when they called nature evil, Christians would be foolish to believe that the remedy for an evil nature should be applied through baptism. Therefore, the person who affirms that human nature is evil is compelled to deny grace. The matter turns back in this way: the person who affirms grace praises human nature, understanding that grace was provided for its salvation.

**AUG.** What you say is not true; you are deceiving or being deceived. For it is not the person who affirms that human nature is evil, but the person who affirms that human nature is itself evil—that is, not the person who says that it is evil, but the person who says that it is an evil thing—who is compelled to deny grace.

For where nature is evil, there it is even more in need of grace. A wicked human being is an evil nature, since a human being is certainly a nature; likewise, an evil woman is an evil nature, since a woman is certainly a nature. How, then, is the person who says this compelled to deny grace, when grace assists evil natures—that is, evil human beings—in ceasing to be evil?
