But we say one thing when we say, “This human being is evil,” and another when we say, “This human being is an evil thing.” The former can be true; the latter cannot. Likewise, if we say, “This human being is vicious,” it can be true; but if we say, “This human being is a vice,” it cannot be true.

Therefore, do not err or lead people into error. Understand me as having said this:

“If human nature were an evil thing, it ought not to be generated; if it had no evil, it ought not to be regenerated.”

It is as though I had said:

“If human nature were a vice, it ought not to be generated; if it had no vice, it ought not to be regenerated.”

Likewise, when I said that I was concluding both points in a single word, I said:

“If human nature were an evil thing, it ought not to be saved; if no evil were present in it, it ought not to be saved.”

It is as though I had said:

“If human nature were a vice, it ought not to be saved; if it contained no vice, it ought not to be saved.”

There: I have made my words clearer—not so that you might find something to say against them, but so that you might understand that you had been unable to find anything to say.

**CLXXXIX. JUL.** Observe, then, what follows from this. The denial of grace is not attached to praise of human nature; rather, these four things are so connected that one cannot be maintained without the other. But disgrace of nature produces denial of grace, and praise of grace produces proclamation of nature. These propositions can be reciprocally exchanged in either direction.

You therefore spoke well when you said, “If human nature were evil, it ought not to be saved.” For the Manichaeans say both things: that the nature of the flesh is evil and that it can neither be saved by grace nor ought to be saved.

**AUG.** But they call the nature of the flesh evil in such a way that they say it is itself an evil thing, not that it possesses evil; for they think that the vice is not something occurring in the substance, but is itself the substance.

**CXC. JUL.** After this you introduce a statement dear to you and say:

“But if no evil were present in human nature, it ought not to be saved. Therefore, whoever says that it is not good denies the good Creator of what was created; but whoever denies that evil is present in it begrudges the merciful Savior of what has been corrupted” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 1, no. 36).

Let the reader pay attention. He will see that you have said nothing other than what you denied should be said. For you declared that evil is naturally present in the thing of which you had said that it was not naturally evil.

**AUG.** I had not said that it was not evil, but that it was not an evil thing. To speak more plainly, I had not said that it was not corrupted, but that it was not a vice. Reread the passage and understand.

**CXCI. JUL.** But “an evil nature” cannot be understood as anything other than possessing innately that which is evil.

**AUG.** Whether the evil is innate, as in mental dullness, or assumed by the will, as in homicide, a human being may be called evil and also an evil nature, because a human being is a nature. Likewise, an evil horse may also be called an evil animal, because a horse is an animal.

**CXCII. JUL.** And to make the conclusion brief and clear: if evil is present in nature in such a way that evil is born from it together with the seeds themselves, it is without doubt proved to be evil.

**AUG.** Even if it is proved to be evil, it is not therefore an evil thing; for although it is proved to be corrupted, it is not therefore a vice.

**CXCIII. JUL.** But if it is defended as good and vindicated from evils, then evil can neither be born from it nor naturally be present in it. Your conclusion has therefore vanished, because the statement you introduced second did not distinguish the first but merely repeated it.

**AUG.** It does not immediately follow that, if it is defended as good, it is vindicated from evils. The same nature is good insofar as it is nature, and evil if it has been corrupted; yet no nature whatsoever is an evil thing.

My conclusion has not therefore vanished, the conclusion in which I said:

“If human nature were an evil thing, it ought not to be saved; if no evil were present in it, it ought not to be saved.”

But if you wish to speak truthfully, say instead that your argument has vanished—the argument by which you wished to refute my conclusion.

**CXCIV. JUL.** You say, “If human nature were an evil thing, it ought not to be saved; if no evil were present in it, it ought not to be saved.” What else have you shown than that one thing ought to be saved for the very reason for which you had denied that it ought to be saved?

**AUG.** It ought to be saved because it is evil, not because it is an evil thing. It is evil not because it is a vice, but because it possesses a vice, just as it is vicious not because it is a vice, but because it possesses a vice.

Because it is vicious, therefore, it ought to be saved. But if nature itself—that is, the substance itself—were a vice, it ought not to be saved.

How, then, did I say that one thing ought to be saved for the reason for which I had denied that it ought to be saved, when possessing a vice is one thing and being a vice is another? It ought therefore to be saved because it possesses a vice, not because it is a vice. But if it were a vice, it ought not to be saved.

You see that answering is not the same as refusing to remain silent: you plainly see that you have answered nothing, and yet you did not wish to remain silent.

**CXCV. JUL.** Thus you have come full circle, restoring by your argument the Manichaean whom you had professedly despised. By saying, “If it were evil, it ought not to be saved,” you had assumed the appearance of an opponent; but by adding, “If no evil were present in it, it ought not to be saved,” you showed yourself to be faithfully serving him.

Once it has become clear that your position is contained in the Manichaean position—namely, that human nature is evil, and that both he and you say that evil is present in it—and once you have declared that an evil nature ought not to be saved, it is completely established that your united ranks attack both nature and grace.

**AUG.** Because you alter my words so as to appear to have answered something, do you therefore make it difficult or impossible for readers either to recall them mentally or to reread them earlier in this very book of yours and see what I said, where you yourself set them down as I had stated them?

I did not say, “If it were evil, it ought not to be saved,” since it ought to be saved precisely so that it may not be evil. I said, “If it were an evil thing, it ought not to be saved.”

It is evil because it possesses a vice; when the vice is consumed, it is undoubtedly made sound. It is not itself the vice; otherwise it would itself be consumed when the vice is consumed.

When the vice is consumed through salvation, what is saved in this way except nature? When it is said that a vice is healed, it is not the vice itself that is saved, but the nature in which the vice was present. If that nature were a vice, it would not be saved but rather brought to an end by healing. Indeed, no healing could occur in that case, because if healing occurred, a healed nature would remain after the vice by which it had not been sound was consumed; but if nature were itself a vice, then, when the vice was consumed, it would not be healed—it would itself be consumed.

Accordingly, human nature ought not to be saved not if it were evil, but if it were an evil thing—that is, if it were a vice. And if no evil were present in it—that is, if it were not evil because of a vice—it ought not to be saved [Note: [Col. 1331] We restore this second member of the sentence from the manuscripts, namely, the words from “if no evil” through “ought not to be saved.”].

There is what I said. Do not, by altering my words, try to make room for your arguments—not for answers, but for quarrels.

**CXCVI. JUL.** It follows that no one can praise the grace of Christ unless he has praised the good work of the Creator in nature.

**AUG.** You have spoken truly. Therefore, even in an evil nature the work of the Creator is praiseworthy, because evil nature, insofar as it is nature, is good; and grace is necessary so that this good may be liberated from evil.

**CXCVII. JUL.** Certainly, the question here does not concern the pursuits of adult human beings, but only the condition of those being born, in whom the state of nature is being examined. You therefore affirm, together with Manichaeus, that this nature is guilty, condemned, and full of evils—that is, crimes—without any admixture of personal will. We, however, maintain that it is innocent, without crime or the evil of sin, and capable of virtue.

**AUG.** We recognize you; indeed, we recognize you as a great protector, since you do not allow the infants whom you protect to be helped by the Savior. But if you do allow it, tell me, please: when they are baptized while bodily sound, from what evil, from what vice, from what part [Note: [Col. 1332] One Portuguese manuscript reads *peste* (“plague”) here.] are they saved?

But what will you say, you who make a paradise for yourself—a paradise that you are not ashamed to fill with the undeserved punishments of infants?

**CXCVIII. JUL.** Do you therefore accuse nature in infants of being criminal, vicious, and condemned by their own will, or by the condition of birth? If by their own will—so that those infants are said to have sinned through their own pursuits—a monstrous opinion arises, but the transmission of sin is denied. For they did not receive from another what they themselves could have committed.

But if they receive so many evils not through their own action but through the condition of birth, they are proved to be naturally unjust.

**AUG.** I accuse neither the nature of infants by their own will—for no one is born because he wishes to be born—nor by the condition of birth, except insofar as they are born miserable, not insofar as they are born.

Human nature would also have been born in paradise, fruitful by God’s blessing, even if no one had sinned, until the number of the saints foreknown by God had been completed. But those infants would not have wept in paradise; they would not have been mute; they would not at some point have been unable to use reason; they would not have lain weak and helpless without the use of their limbs; they would not have been afflicted by diseases; they would not have been harmed by wild beasts; they would not have been killed by poisons; they would not have been wounded by any accident; they would not have been deprived of any sense or any part of the body; they would not have been harassed by demons; nor, when growing into childhood, would they have been subdued by blows or educated through hardships.

Nor would any of them have been born with an intellect so vain and dull that no amount of labor or pain could correct it [Note: [Col. 1332] Vignierius reads *uni* (“to one”); the manuscripts read *ulli* (“any”).]. Except for the size of their bodies, owing to the limited capacity of their mothers’ wombs, they would have been born altogether as Adam was made.

But now they would not be as we see them, nor would they suffer such things, unless human nature had been changed and condemned to these miseries by that great sin. They are therefore in this condition not merely because they are born, but because of the contagion of sin and the condition of punishment.

**CXCIX. JUL.** In what respect, then, do Manichaeus and you differ concerning the judgment on nature? “Because he,” you say, “confesses that it is evil.” If you deny this, declare that it is good, and the dispute is ended. You will immediately be caught in the nets of truth for salvation.

But you object. Let us hear, then, what you produce, O Aristotle of punishments [Note: [Col. 1333] The printed editions read *pendeo* (“I hang”); the manuscripts read *poenarum* (“of punishments”), which is plainly the correct reading.].

“There is so much evil in it,” you say, “that it is possessed by the devil and deserves eternal fire.”

**AUG.** But you, who deny that it is possessed by the devil, undoubtedly deny that it is delivered from the power of darkness when it is transferred through regeneration into Christ’s kingdom. Thus you accuse the entire Catholic Church of a grave crime against majesty.

Under the laws of this world, anyone who spits upon an image of the emperor—even though it is not alive—is held guilty of another crime against majesty. Yet infants are breathed upon in exorcism before they are baptized. Therefore living images are breathed upon—not of some earthly king, but of God.

Rather, it is the devil who is breathed out: he holds the infant guilty through the contagion of sin, so that, once he has been cast out (John 12:31), the infant may be transferred to Christ.

Let Julian’s madness therefore be breathed out, lest the Church be declared guilty of majesty in the cleansing and exorcism of infants. But if the infant is not delivered from the power of darkness and remains there, why are you surprised that he will be in eternal fire with the devil, since he is not permitted to enter God’s kingdom?

Or, because the Pelagians prepare some place outside God’s kingdom—a place of rest and eternal life—for unbaptized infants, is Christ’s statement therefore false?

“He who believes and is baptized will be saved; but he who does not believe will be condemned” (Mark 16:16).

Whoever denies that infants believe through the mouths of those who carry them should also deny that they receive baptism, since they struggle against it in the hands of those who carry them.

**CC. JUL.** But it is so far from being evil that only a Manichaean could accuse it.

**AUG.** Did Manichaeus therefore say, “We are all born under sin, and their very birth is in vice” (Ambrose, book 1 *On Repentance*, chapter 2 or 3)? Since this was said by a learned Catholic teacher, what are you except a deceived and deceiving heretic?

**CCI. JUL.** “Nevertheless,” he says, “I am not a Manichaean, since I absolve it in words and condemn it in judgments.”

**AUG.** You condemn it in judgment—and in an unjust judgment—although you wish it to suffer so many evils without any evil merit.

**CCII. JUL.** What should I first accuse here: the impudence of the liar, the lust of the disputant, or the profanity of one who believes such perversities? Yet I understand that we should use the prophet’s words:

“We are blessed, O Israel, because what pleases God is known to us” (Baruch 4:4).

**AUG.** Is it really known to you what pleases God? Does it please God, you fool, that infants should be oppressed by a heavy yoke without any contagion of sin [Note: [Col. 1333] The printed editions read “it does not please God.” Two manuscripts read “it does not please God.” The Portuguese manuscript, omitting the negative particle, reads “it pleases God?”]?

They therefore draw the contagion from that first and great sin. By refusing to acknowledge this, what are you doing except attributing an unjust judgment to God?

**CCIII. JUL.** The readers’ judgment will supply the task of condemning these attacks; let us proceed to what remains. Certainly, there is no other evil among things that is truly evil except what we call sin.

**AUG.** If the punishments of sinners are not also evils, there is no way for you to defend the truth of God’s statement that he creates evils (Isa. 45:7), since he must not be said to create sins.

**CCIV. JUL.** From what sin, as you say, is natural evil generated in each person? Therefore nothing else is truly evil except evil merit.

**AUG.** Not only evil merit but also the punishment returned for evil merit is evil. For if sin is truly evil, the punishment of sin is also truly evil.

If infants had no evil merit from their origin, whatever evils they suffer would be unjust. These evils therefore could not exist in paradise, because there would be no evil merit there if blessed obedience had continued.

Accordingly, because infants here suffer evils that would not exist there, they also have evil merit, which they would not have except originally.

**CCV. JUL.** If, then, Manichaeus calls nature evil only because he thinks it possesses evil merit, to which he believes punishments must be assigned; and if you affirm that human nature contains evil, recognizing no other evil than what Manichaeus recognizes—namely, carnal concupiscence, which you preach was infused by the devil [Note: [Col. 1334] So the manuscripts read. The printed editions have *inustam* (“branded upon” or “burned into”) rather than *infusam* (“infused”).]—and say that it possesses such evil merit that you persist in assigning it to eternal torments, then without doubt, like Manichaeus, you declare it to be utterly evil and condemned.

**AUG.** Now be ashamed. Carnal concupiscence is not from the Father but from the world—that is, from human beings, whose offspring fills the world. The Manichaeans, however, attribute it to the nation of darkness, with your assistance, since you refuse to allow this evil to have been turned into our nature through the transgression of the first man, in accordance with Ambrosian—that is, Catholic—faith (book 7 on Luke 12).

**CCVI. JUL.** Let us therefore see how the second part of your statement also returns to this point. For you said:

“Whoever says that human nature is not good denies the good Creator who created it; but whoever denies that evil is present in it begrudges the merciful Savior of what has been corrupted” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 2, no. 36).

If, then—as you were compelled to admit—the person who denies that it is good also denies its good Creator, namely God; and if being evil is nothing other than naturally possessing evil merit, then your own confession supports our truth: you deny that God is the good Creator of human beings, whose nature you swear is evil, both by its vices and by its punishments.

**AUG.** Human nature, although it is evil because it has been corrupted, is not an evil thing, because it is nature. No nature, insofar as it is nature, is an evil thing; rather, it is wholly good, and without this good no evil can exist. For a vice cannot exist except in some nature, although nature can exist without a vice, either because it was never corrupted or because it has been healed.

If the Manichaeans understood this, they would certainly not be Manichaeans, introducing two natures from contrary parts of good and evil. If you see what difference there is between us and the Manichaeans, be silent. If you do not see it, be silent.

**CCVII. JUL.** We therefore do not begrudge it a Savior, since we defend it by the dignity of its Creator. But we deny that it is an evil thing, lest we become Manichaeans; and we deny that evil is present in it, lest, under changed names, we be Manichaeans in equal number.

AUGUSTINE. You are altogether opposed to the Manichaeans when you say that nature is not evil; but you are Pelagians when you say that evil is not present in it. Without knowing it, you support the Manichaeans by saying that the evil which is plainly present in it does not arise from the transgression of the first man, so that they may conclude that there is another substance and nature of evil.

CCVIII. JULIAN. We say that being corrupted in each individual, now acting according to his own choice either by doing good or by doing evil, is a merit of the person, not of nature. And therefore we assert that through the grace of Christ that can be healed which can be corrupted, since nothing else is shown to have been wounded than what is taught to have been healed.

AUGUSTINE. Certainly you begrudge infants the Savior; you ought to be exsufflated, like they are, if you believed that this would benefit you, so that you might be rescued from the power of darkness and transferred into the kingdom of Christ.

CCIX. JULIAN. In the baptized, however, it is not the lust of the flesh [Note: [Col. 1335] Perhaps: “of lust.”]—which is natural—that is removed, but the guilt of evil lust.

AUGUSTINE. The apostle John said that the lust of the flesh is not from the Father but from the world (1 John II, 16), thereby making it understood to be evil. But you say that it is not the lust of the flesh, which is natural, but evil lust that bears guilt. For in your view even when fornication is desired, the lust of the flesh is not evil, because, as you say, the person who uses a good thing in that way uses it badly. The thing itself, then, is always good, as you wish, whether someone desires marriage or adultery through it: for if marriage is desired, he uses a good thing well; if adultery, he uses a good thing badly. Fight, therefore, with the apostle John, not with me. For you do not agree with him when he says that the lust which he calls the lust of the flesh is not from the Father but from the world, so long as you say that the lust of the flesh, even when something evil is desired through it, is good, and therefore never evil. But believe me: no Christian exists who would not prefer to agree with the apostle John rather than with you.

CCX. JULIAN. Accordingly, it is also demonstrated by the testimony both of the Creator of the human race and of the Redeemer that there is no sin [Note: [Col. 1335] Thus the manuscripts. Vignier has “of redemption.”].

AUGUSTINE. What do you mean by saying, with excessive thoughtlessness, that no sin is present in nature? As though sin could be present anywhere except in a nature, even if it was not contracted by origin but committed by the will. Whether it is the sin of an angel or of a human being, it is clear that it is present in an angel or in a human being. Who, then, would so depart from the nature of things as to deny that a human being or an angel is a nature? What, moreover, do you mean by speaking with your eyes closed? What, I ask, do you mean by saying that lust is not sin? Do you not see that you are arguing against the Apostle? For he plainly showed that lust is sin when he said: “I would not have known sin except through the law; for I would not have known lust unless the law said, ‘You shall not lust’” (Rom. VII, 7). What could be said more clearly than this testimony, or more vainly than your opinion?

CCXI. JULIAN. And, to review what has been done: by the testimony both of God’s commandments and of his judgments, I demonstrated that the doctrine of transmission is an enemy of God’s justice.

AUGUSTINE. Rather, it has been shown that you are enemies of God’s justice: you make him unjustly impose upon the children of Adam, from the day they leave their mother’s womb, a heavy yoke (Ecclus. XL, 1), while you deny original sin. This has been demonstrated both by the testimony of Scripture and by the very sufferings of infants, which could not exist in paradise except in your own paradise [Note: [Col. 1336] Pelagius, *On Free Choice*, book 3.].

CCXII. JULIAN. I proved by inserting his writings that the lust of the flesh, implanted by God the Creator of bodies for the purpose of arranging the reproductive function between the sexes, is accused by none but a Manichaean.

AUGUSTINE. We have shown, by the clearest proofs both of divine authority and of sober reasoning, that you assist the Manichaeans by attributing the lust of the flesh—which divine Scripture teaches to be evil, for through it “the flesh lusts against the spirit” (Gal. V, 17)—to a race of darkness coeternal with God, since you refuse to let it belong to original sin and even dare to place it in God’s paradise.

CCXIII. JULIAN. I demonstrated that you have no arguments for the transmission of sin other than those that a Manichaean would have used.

AUGUSTINE. You are convicted and compelled to confess that Ambrose was not a Manichaean—he who, as an invincible champion of the Catholic faith [Note: [Col. 1336] Perhaps “defender” should be added.], overthrew both the Manichaeans and you, and who said that the conflict between flesh and spirit, in which flesh lusts against spirit through your assumed condition, was turned into our nature through the transgression of the first man (Ambrose, *On Luke*, book 7, chapter XII). You are forced to this conclusion even by the testimony of your own leader [Note: [Col. 1336] Pelagius, *On Free Choice*, book 3.], who praises that same bishop.

CCXIV. JULIAN. I exposed you as a denier of free choice and of God the Creator of those who are born by examining your position.

AUGUSTINE. Innumerable sacred testimonies proclaim that, by confessing God’s grace, I am not a denier of free choice—the free choice that you exalt only to destroy—but rather its defender, while you deceive it by trusting in its own power [Note: [Col. 1336] Perhaps “cast it down.”]. And what we have both said will show readers that we do not deny God as the Creator of those who are born, but that you deny God as the Savior of those who are born.

CCXV. JULIAN. I reproached you for declaring nature evil by explaining the position that you had promised to sum up in a single word [Col. 1337].

AUGUSTINE. I demonstrated that human nature is not evil, but that evil is present in it: the first by the substance of that nature itself and by God, its Creator; the second by the misery of that nature and by God, its Savior. A diligent and intelligent reader could discover that you were unable to dissolve my reasoning, even if I had not answered you.

CCXVI. JULIAN. Therefore I trust that even the slowest to understand, or those deceived by your favor [Note: [Col. 1337] Thus the manuscripts. Vignier has: “even the slowest to understand, or one deceived by your favor.”], can see that you merely shun the name of Manichaean; otherwise, in every respect, together with all the followers of the transmission doctrine, no less filthy than foolish, you cling to its teachings.

AUGUSTINE. It is altogether otherwise, and contrary to what you think, than what you say is clear even to the slowest. For this is rather clear even to the slowest: if they do not consider it burdensome to devote careful attention to the writings of both of us, they will see that I demonstrated not merely that I am an enemy of the error of the Manichaeans and, with God the Truth assisting, have overthrown their wicked teachings, but also that you assist the madness of the Manichaeans so greatly that they would boast of being altogether unconquered, unless by the Catholic faith—which we defend through God’s mercy—they were defeated, not through you or by you, but rather together with you.

You chose me alone as the person whom you might assail with the Manichaean name and charge, reviling me all the more offensively the more frequently you repeated it, because you thought that in this way you could destroy without provoking envy the most firmly grounded Catholic faith that reproves you, together with the very well-known multitude of its illustrious and holy defenders, who learned and taught what we have learned and teach—not by the truth of the charge brought against me, but by the horror of an impious name.

But “the firm foundation of God stands, having this seal: ‘The Lord knows those who are his’” (2 Tim. II, 19). As for the words of my book that you proposed as though they needed refutation: you tested only a very few of them, as if merely to create the appearance of some sort of battle, and avoided many more, extensive passages interwoven with your cloudy verbosity. Since it would take too long to demonstrate this here, I leave it to the reader, so that he may notice and discover it for himself.

## BOOK FOUR

[Col. 1337]

Augustine continues to refute Julian, who in his fourth book argues against passages from the second book *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, extending from chapter four through chapter eleven. He argues that the lust of the flesh is evil and was not implanted in human beings by God the Creator, and he maintains that this is taught by the very passage he employed for the purpose, from the First Epistle of John, chapter 2, verse 16: “Everything that is in the world is the lust of the flesh,” and “which is not from the Father,” and so forth. He further argues that this lust belongs to the nature of the beast, but nevertheless to the punishment of the human being himself. He maintains that shame concerning the members arose only after sin, because of the rebellious movements of desire. Moreover, he vehemently argues against Julian lest anyone think that there was any lust of the flesh at all in Christ. He teaches that infants are born liable to original guilt, not through the exercise of their own will, but through the contagion of the sin voluntarily committed by the first parent. He also argues that the passage he himself produced from the Book of Wisdom, chapter 12, verses 10 and 11—“not ignorant that their race was evil”—serves to demonstrate the defect of our origin.

[Col. 1337]

### I. JULIAN

I think that a careful reader may wonder why, although I divided my little work into a definite number of books according to the customary practice of writers, I nevertheless resolve in one book questions belonging to another. Thus, in the third volume I argued that the Apostle’s meaning [Note: [Col. 1337] Perhaps: “to the Apostle’s meaning.”], when he said that through one man sin entered the world (Rom. V, 12)—a phrase by which he crushed the opinion of original evil—had, when challenged by the assertion that the Jewish race descended from one Abraham (Heb. XI, 12), contributed nothing, or at least nothing significant [Note: [Col. 1337] Vignier has *nuntio* (“I announce”); the manuscripts have *numero* (“number”).] [Note: [Col. 1337] The Portus codex has *concisus* (“abridged”); the printed reading is uncertain.].

Let that reader, then, to whom I now undertake to give satisfaction, suppose that this should have been placed in the second volume. Let him know, therefore, that the reliability of this response—by which even matters thought to have been omitted are supplied in the following book—neither harms the controversy nor results from any confusion caused by haste, but arises both from the necessity of the issues and from a deliberate plan.

There is, indeed, an abundance of great intellects whose examples could vindicate such continuity of style. But it is foolish boasting to summon the support of resonant ancient names in defense of a straightforward matter, and to make the security of one’s procedure suspect by defending it in this way.

I therefore brought the second book, which I had intended for the defense of the Apostle’s statements, to a necessary conclusion, lest the addition of minor questions extend it to excessive length [Col. 1338]. But when I had fulfilled the task of serious discussion, I also wished to meet foolish questions, and to show consideration for even the slowest people, who can be stirred by even the most feeble objections. Therefore I decided to show in the third book in what way many could be said to have been born from one.

It is also entirely appropriate that the following volume should discharge the debt owed by the preceding one, so that there may appear to be harmony among the books and readers may be invited to learn the work as a whole. Even if they think that some matters were postponed at the beginning, they will understand that nothing was omitted.

Having therefore shown that what we have done accords with the faith [Note: [Col. 1338] The printed editions have *fideli* (“faithful”); the manuscripts have *fidei* (“of faith”).] and with the industry of the work, let us engage the Manichaeans [Note: [Col. 1338] By the name “Manichaeans” he also means Catholics; hence the addition found in the Portus codex—“and the Traducians”—is superfluous.] on behalf of God’s works and laws. From the former we repel the deformity of natural evil; from the latter, the iniquity of deadly judgments. We teach that, in the precepts of the former, justice has lost nothing of its own goodness, and that, in the seeds of the latter, the devil has mingled nothing of his own evil. Finally, we teach that the former are worthy of God as ruler, and the latter most worthy of God as Creator.

### AUGUSTINE

The Manichaeans would regard your engagement with them as a great help, so that they might not be defeated in our engagement, unless the Catholic faith also defeated you together with them. For the discord between the lusts of the flesh and the spirit, and the miseries of the human race, with which the nature of mortals is filled—beginning with the weeping and sufferings of infants—are not permitted to be attributed to the mixture of the two natures that they introduce, because all these things are attributed by divine authority and most truthful reasoning to a nature corrupted by sin, which God created good and, though corrupted, does not abandon by the gift of its fertility and by his good work.

By denying this, you try to break the weapons by which they are defeated. But those weapons are so firm and unconquerable that, whether they reach you after being thrust through and killing them, or reach them after being thrust through and killing you, they strike both sides down.

### II. JULIAN

If you believe these two things—that God’s works are neither evil nor his judgments unjust—the entire doctrine of the transmission of sin is crushed [Note: [Col. 1339] Morel, *Elem. Crit.*, p. 265, thinks that the reading should be: “if you believe thus.”]. Conversely, once the impiety of the transmission doctrine is embraced, these two things—God’s creation and his judgment, through which alone God can be understood—are destroyed.

### AUGUSTINE

God’s works are not evil, since he works good even from whatever evils there are, and since he mercifully assists in healing infants whom he brought forth well from the mass lost through the transgression of the first man. Nor are his judgments unjust, since, by placing a heavy yoke upon the children of Adam from the day they leave their mother’s womb (Ecclus. XL, 1), he avenges nothing except the merits of sins.

When these things are believed and understood, both the error of the Manichaeans and that of the Pelagians is extinguished: that of the Manichaeans, because they wish these evils of the human race to be attributed to some evil beginning coeternal with God; that of the Pelagians, because they refuse to attribute them to sin.

### III. JULIAN

Let us now weigh the points that the defamer of natural things has woven together. But, so that our reader may be supplied with both understanding and discernment concerning matters entangled in mutual response, I shall indicate the kind of contest in which he struggles.

He professes in his writings to oppose what he says was sent to him in a brief document, and he sets down and sneers at certain fragments of my statements that are not found in my work.

### AUGUSTINE

Thanks be to God that, from the very four books of yours from which he extracted what he wished in the manner he wished—and whose brief document was sent to me—I have answered all of it in six books [Col. 1339]. I suppose you will not say that I intended to refute certain things that are not contained in your work. But even if you say this and prove it, I ought also to be grateful that you did not say what you ought not to have said. Would that you had said none of the words of yours that are rightly censured.

### IV. JULIAN

He therefore speaks to Valerius:

“Observe how he thinks he can make himself agree with us under the title prefixed above. ‘God,’ he says, ‘who had fashioned Adam from clay, constructed Eve from a rib and said, “She shall be called Life, because she is the mother of all living things.”’

“It is not written that way, but what does that have to do with us? Memory often fails in words, provided the meaning is retained. Nor did God give Eve the name by which she was called, ‘Life’; her husband did. For this is how he speaks [Note: [Col. 1340] Perhaps: ‘it is read’]: ‘And Adam called the name of his wife Life,’ because she is the mother of all living things (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 2, no. 12).

“What astonishing learning in a teacher, who does not allow anyone to depart even slightly from the language of Scripture! He charges us with ignorance, but graciously deigns to pardon the forgetfulness that had caused me to say that the woman was given the name Life by God. Thus, on this brief occasion, he tried to appear both learned and kind.

“But just as his diligence in discovering the name-giver of the woman is not to be admired, so his shamelessness cannot be tolerated: he wishes to pardon what he cannot prove blameworthy. For the matter is not read in my work as it is held in his notes.

“I had first set down the testimony of the Law, by which the Creator of all things is shown to have said, ‘It is not good for the human being to be alone; let us make him a helper corresponding to him’ (Gen. II, 18). Then I said: ‘What does this mean: “It is not good for the human being to be alone”? Surely God had not made anything that could rightly be called not good, especially since he had made all things not merely good but also very good. How, then, does he say, “It is not good for the human being to be alone”?’

“By this statement the condition of the creature is not reproved; rather, it is shown that a solitary condition could have been harmful to the human race unless succession had been produced through the service of the different sex. For even if Adam is thought to have been able to become immortal had he not sinned, it is nevertheless clear that he could never have become a father unless he had found a wife. She, taken from the side of the sleeping man, heard at her first address what work she had been prepared for: ‘She shall be called Life, because she is the mother of all living things.’

“By these words it was shown that thereafter no human being could exist or live who had not been sustained by the benefit of conception. Therefore, although it is clear that, in a matter of no great importance, I said nothing in such a way that anyone could accuse it except with singular shamelessness, the mark of public falsehood has been branded upon the poorest of all people. When he wishes to give what he does not possess, he commits a double offense at once, through lack of legal right and through the ostentation of generosity.”

### AUGUSTINE

If you did not set down the words of the divine Book as I found them in that brief document, I pardoned not you but the person who wrote them that way. Both of us ought to pardon him. But if you think that I did not find this in the document and nevertheless falsely inserted those words as though I had found them there, so that I might attribute something to your error, then I certainly pardon you now for having formed so bad and false an opinion of me.

### V. JULIAN

After criticizing this with such gravity, he proceeds to the remaining matters and reminds his patron to attend to what follows.

“God, then,” he says, “the creator of the male and female, formed members suited to generation. But, inserting only this much from the head of my statements and passing over altogether many lines in which the novelty of souls, owing nothing either to flesh or to seed, is chiefly emphasized, he adds my words:

“‘Thus he ordained bodies to be generated from bodies; yet the power of his working intervenes in their production, administering all that exists by the power through which he created it. If, then, offspring exists only through sex, sex only through the body, and the body only through God, who could doubt that fertility is rightly attributed to God?’

“After setting this down from my work, he commends it because he too admits that these statements are Catholic. Who, then, would not think that the man had been changed? But he does not forget himself. He considers the condition of a perverse doctrine and of modesty to be alike, so that the former may be restored by a conspicuous fall just as the latter here grows hard through constant friction.

“He therefore approves my statement and voluntarily drives the sword of prejudice into his own faith; yet afterward, as though still possessing his full strength, he claims that something remains for him to fight. For he continues:

“‘After these things, which have been stated truthfully and Catholicly—or rather, which have been written truthfully in the divine Books, though not stated by this man in a Catholic spirit, since they were not uttered with the intention of a Catholic heart—the Pelagian and Coelestian heresy now begins to be introduced because of the reason for which he said them. For observe what follows.’

“Here again he adds our words:

“‘What, then, does the devil recognize as his own in the sexes, by which he may rightly claim their fruit? Their difference? But this is in the bodies that God made. Their intercourse? But it is claimed no less by the privilege of blessing than by that of institution. For it is God’s voice: “A man shall leave father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh”; and it is God’s voice: “Increase and multiply and fill the earth.” Or perhaps fertility itself? But fertility itself is the reason for which marriage was instituted.’

“To this he replied that the devil does not recognize in the sexes either their difference, their intercourse, or their fertility as something by which he may rightly claim their fruit. But, after dismissing all these, he found something to attribute to the devil, and attacked our modesty under the name of fear: among so many gifts of bodies and sexes, he said, we had been afraid to name the lust of the flesh.

“Thus he speaks against me to his patron:

“‘But this man did not wish to name among all these things the lust of the flesh, which is not from the Father but from the world (1 John II, 16), whose prince is said to be the devil. The devil did not find this lust in the Lord, because the Lord, being human, did not come to human beings through it. Hence he himself also says: “Behold, the prince of this world is coming, and he will find nothing in me” (John XIV, 30)—certainly no sin, neither what is drawn from one who is born nor what is added by one who lives.

“‘This man did not wish to name it among all the natural goods that he mentioned, although it is the thing by which marriage too is put to shame, even though marriage boasts of all those goods. For why is the work of married people withdrawn and hidden even from the eyes of their children, unless it is because they cannot praise intercourse without shameful lust? Even those who first covered their shameful parts blushed because of it (Gen. III, 7): parts that had previously not been shameful, but were to be proclaimed and celebrated as the works of God’ (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 2, nos. 12–14).

“I dealt, most blessed father Flore, in the four books of my first work with the cause of marriage, the cause of intercourse, the cause of bodies, the cause of the sexes, the cause of God’s work, and finally the cause of God’s reputation—which, just as it is necessarily praised for the excellence of his works, is wounded by their infamy. Throughout the entire work, wholly unobscured truth made it clear that the devil had added nothing either to the formation of the body or to sense. It is therefore thoroughly demonstrated that the opinion of the transmission of sin has been drawn from the clay of Manichaeus.”

### AUGUSTINE

How you proceeded in those four books of yours, and how you were refuted by our response, so that it became clear that you had accomplished nothing, can readily be understood by those who read both my books and yours. Indeed, even when yours are not read but only mine, your heretical doctrine is seen to have been destroyed in them.

But although you responded to one of my books with those four of yours in such a way that you scarcely touched a third part of it and refuted none of it [Note: [Col. 1342] Thus the manuscripts. Vignier has: “but responding in this way to that one book of mine and to those four of yours.”], you presumed so much upon them that, against another one of my books on the same subject, you wrote these eight of yours—as though you thought I could be frightened not by the strength of arguments but by the number of volumes [Note: [Col. 1342] Thus the manuscripts. Vignier has: “endured.”].

You felt so completely that you had gained nothing from that fourfold response that this eightfold one seemed necessary to you. If your verbosity advances through such increases, who would not be frightened—not by the truth, but by the multitude of your books, whose number I am reluctant to calculate? You are a man of astonishingly abundant eloquence: first you thought four of yours should be returned for one of mine, and eight of yours for another. Who would not fear that you might be planning to return more than a thousand of yours for my six, if you already return sixteen for the first of them and then pursue each of the following books by doubling the number of the preceding one, showing us how much you speak without understanding what you are saying?

### VI. JULIAN

Nevertheless, since this matter was fully established there, it may also be briefly revisited in the present discussion. Let us therefore turn to the man with whose learning we are contending.

You agree, surely, that we rightly gathered that, if offspring existed only through sex, sex only through the body, and the body only through God, it could not be doubted that fertility belonged to God’s works, and that the prince of darkness recognized nothing of his own in the sexes by which he might retain their fruit by asserting his legal right. For the difference belonged to sex, intercourse to the difference of the members, and the fruit of fertility to God, who had also instituted those who beget [Note: [Col. 1342] Vignier has *fuerit*; the manuscripts have *fuerat*, “had been.”]. Consequently, nothing remained for which the fertility of intercourse could be assigned to the devil.

What comfort or defense do you think is afforded you by the modesty of my language, because I did not wish to name the lust of the flesh in this passage? Even if I had passed over it in silence throughout the entire work, that matter would nevertheless have incurred no blame or insult, since it was defended under more honorable names [Note: [Col. 1342] Thus the manuscripts. Vignier has: “which was marked by more honorable names.”], and indeed under the clearest expressions of understanding [Note: [Col. 1342] The manuscripts of Mar. and Clar. have *clausissimis*; perhaps “most obscure.”].

Suppose, then, that I wished more prudently than the nature of the undertaking required to conceal in silence [Col. 1343] the name of the matter that we cover with clothing. Is the whole basis of reasoning and the whole truth therefore to be sacrificed? Is understanding, the judge of matters, therefore to lie prostrate because something cannot always be brought before the ears with the same propriety with which it can be brought before the eyes?

Nevertheless, what deformity is there in naming the lust of the flesh—a term that I too used when the passage required it, and that you, although you affirm that you feel it to be untamable, nevertheless mention frequently?

### AUGUSTINE

I call it tameable—that is, the flesh—but tameable by those who conquer it, not by those who praise it.

### VII. JULIAN

A little later you say:

“By what, then, are infants under the power of the devil, when they are born from bodies that God made, from the intercourse of the sexes that he distinguished in forming but joined in blessing, and when God multiplied fertility by implanting it, and God himself made the infants from the substance of the seed? If you confess that through God there exist the substance of bodies, through God the generative organs of bodies, through God the intercourse of the generative organs, through God also the power of the seeds, and through God likewise the form and life of all who are born, what do you think remains for which you attribute so many works of God to the devil?” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 2, no. 15).

Therefore you call the body of another discussion a heresy, although you confess that all its members are upright and Catholic.

### AUGUSTINE

Do we not call the Novatians, Arians, Eunomians, and certain others heretics even when they have confessed the entire Creed? To say nothing, then, of the other matters belonging to your heresy, how can you not wish us to call you heretics when you deny that infants are rescued from the power of darkness when they are transferred to Christ? In the case of these infants, when they are about to receive the Holy Spirit, the whole ancient Church—which praises the name of the Lord from the rising of the sun to its setting—blows away and exorcises the unclean spirit.

### VIII. JULIAN

After praising our summary, which is so fortified by truth that it was brought in its entirety against you and which you could not profane even by abuse, you nevertheless criticize its effect.

### AUGUSTINE

You do not understand that what you call its effect is your defect. For those true statements that you make as though you were Catholics do not produce the consequence by which you are heretics.

As Catholics, you say that offspring is through sex, sex through the body, and the body through God, from which it follows that fertility is rightly attributed to God. But does it follow from this that such a human being is not born with the stain of sin, even if his life upon the earth is only a single day (Job XIV, 4, according to the Septuagint)?

You are not heretics because you say those true things, but because you deny what is likewise true. For God is certainly not the author of stupidity, and yet he is the author of a fetus even when a stupid person is born. Understand, if you can, how a defect can be born with a human being from his origin, although God is not its author, when no one but God is the creator of that human being.

You should also remember that you have departed from your own doctrine, by which you deny that God works the will in human minds. I praised your words—which I admit are also spoken by Catholics—by my will, yet you say that I praised them because God compelled me. Behold how God works in us both willing and acting (Phil. II, 13), something that you habitually deny even against the Apostle.

### IX. JULIAN

“For if,” I said, “offspring exists only through sex, sex only through the body, and the body only through God, who could doubt that fertility is rightly attributed to God? This is so certain that even your own mouth has been moved to praise it” [Note: [Col. 1344] Two manuscripts have *concluserit*, “has concluded.”].

But after the praise you gave this passage, you warn that heresy is being introduced, although the statements I added merely repeated, with an explanation, what had already been set forth.

### AUGUSTINE

Did you say, among the statements that I had admitted you made truly: “What, then, does the devil recognize as his own in the sexes?” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 2, no. 13)?

Here you began to introduce the meaning of your heresy: as though the devil could not recognize anything of his own in the sexes because the body and the sex exist through God the Creator. Yet the devil himself recognizes both what belongs to God and what belongs to the devil, the former in his nature and the latter in his defect.

Thus in the sexes he recognizes what belongs to God, just as he recognizes the sex itself, the body, and the spirit. But he also recognizes what belongs to him: that by which the flesh lusts against the spirit. The former things come from the Creator, whose vengeance the devil could not escape; the latter comes from the wound he inflicted.

### X. JULIAN

For I say:

“What, then, does the devil recognize as his own in the sexes, so that he may rightly possess their fruit, as you say? Their difference? But this is in the bodies that God made. Their intercourse? But it is claimed no less by the privilege of blessing than by that of institution. Or perhaps fertility itself? But fertility itself is the reason for which marriage was instituted.”

What, then, was new here? What disagreed with the conclusion above that you had approved, so that you thought it should be censured after being praised? Certainly nothing. What, then, is to be inferred from such an ugly inconsistency? Since the discussion was not changed by me [Note: [Col. 1344] Here we restore the negative particle from the manuscripts.], while your assessment of my statements was changed, your intention is shown to be most depraved and your reasoning weak.

### AUGUSTINE

You are surprised that, after praising God’s works, I censured your insidious question. In asking, you said: “What, then, does the devil recognize as his own in the sexes?” And, wishing to persuade people that he recognized nothing of his own in the sexes, you mentioned things that truly do not belong to the devil: the difference by which the female sex differs from the male; intercourse, by which the two sexes unite so that children may be generated; and fertility, by which the children themselves are generated.

We admit that all these things would have existed in paradise even if no one had sinned. But that other thing would not have existed there—the thing they experienced when they covered their shameful parts, although before they sinned they were naked and were not ashamed.

You passed over this lust of the flesh, by which the flesh lusts against the spirit, without which no human being is born; and you passed over this discord between flesh and spirit, which the Catholic teacher—so highly praised by your Pelagius in his own words—learned had been turned into our nature through the transgression of the first man (Ambrose, *On Luke*, book 7, chapter XII).

Why, then, did you remain silent about this? When you asked what the devil recognized as his own in the sexes, you named other things that do not belong to the devil, but refused to give your question the answer concerning what does belong to him. I censured your deceitful question, not the divine works that I rightly praised.

### XI. JULIAN

And that your praise of what is Catholic is a matter of fear [Note: [Col. 1345] Vignier has *est*, “is”; the manuscripts have *esse*, “to be.”], not of faith.

### AUGUSTINE

The one who, through praise of what is Catholic, demonstrates and overthrows your error knows our faith.

### XII. JULIAN

Therefore, when you censure what you praised, this is not judgment but madness.

### AUGUSTINE

I do not censure what I praised. I praised what you said truly; but I censured the fact that you questioned deceitfully, seeing what answer you ought to receive and nevertheless remaining silent about it as though it did not exist. Whether this is a matter of judgment or madness, you will see once you have ceased raging.

### XIII. JULIAN

You will never be without that madness unless you first reject your obscene doctrine. For, caught between the shame of repentance—which Christians have never rejected—and the poverty of your argument, and enduring grievous Symplegades, you must either follow the good statements with which you have been overwhelmed or tear them apart.

### AUGUSTINE

It is not a good statement, Julian, to deny that Christ is Jesus for infants, or to confess that Jesus—that is, the Savior—is Jesus for infants in the same way as for the whole mortal creation, concerning which it is said: “You will save human beings and beasts, O Lord” (Ps. XXXV, 7).

He did not receive such a name because he came in the likeness of sinful flesh. Rather, the angel says: “You shall call his name Jesus; for he will save his people from their sins” (Matt. I, 21).

It is not a good statement to separate infants from this people and therefore to say that Christ is Jesus for them also because he saves them—not from their sins, but from their scabies.

Come to your senses, I beg you. I think you were not born of parents who believed these things; and certainly you were not reborn in a Church that believed them.

### XIV. JULIAN

Let us nevertheless see what part of my statements you have seized upon and attack under the name of error.

“But this man,” you say, “did not wish to name among all these things the lust of the flesh, which is not from the Father but from the world, whose prince is said to be the devil, who did not find it in the Lord, because the Lord, being human, did not come to human beings through it” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 2, no. 14).

Certainly you said that I was introducing heresy, but you add none of my statements to prove this.

AUG. I add those statements of yours in which you asked, “What does the devil recognize as his own in sexual matters?” You were speaking deceitfully, for you saw—and kept silent about—the lust of the flesh, against whose movements even chaste marriages must often struggle [Col. 1346], and you pressed me with a most fraudulent question, as though there were nothing that could be answered. Or, if you did not see it, you were certainly introducing your heresy through that very blindness.

### XV. JUL. 

But you say that I did not wish to name the lust of the flesh. What I did not wish to name, I kept silent about; and if I kept silent [Note: [Col. 1346] The printed editions read, “and if I did not keep silent.” The word “not” is absent from the manuscripts.], I said nothing that you could criticize. Who, then, persuades anyone of error by keeping silent? O new and hitherto unheard-of monstrosities of accusation! He says that a perverse doctrine is constructed by my silence [Note: [Col. 1346] Vignier reads “you say.” M.].

AUG. Not by silence, but by a deceitful question, as I demonstrated above. Yet silence too is rightly censured when what ought to have been said is left unsaid precisely so that it may not be apparent that the question could have been answered.

### XVI. JUL. 

Let all prudence weigh this and laugh at the spitefulness of the speech displayed under the name of silence [Note: [Col. 1346] Thus the manuscripts. The editions, “let it see.”]. You admit, then, that I said nothing that you can charge against me.

AUG. On the contrary, what you said by questioning is most rightly charged against you. For, so that it might be thought that there was nothing that could be answered, you refused to say what could have been answered. Or, in any case, why should I not charge you with the very blindness by which you could not even see it?

### XVII. JUL. 

While attacking our silence, you brought forward what once could not be defended, but now, after the publication of the Manichaean letter whose arguments I set out in the third book, can no longer be concealed.

AUG. Neither does Manichaeus truthfully condemn the lust of the flesh [Note: [Col. 1346] In Marcellus Claromontanus and the editions, before “condemns,” there stood: “and most invincibly against the followers of Manichaeus and Pelagius.” This gloss was transferred here from the margin; we have removed it on the authority of the Codex Portarum.], nor do you truthfully praise it. He does not condemn it because he does not know from where this evil comes; you praise it because you deny that it is evil. He attributes it to a nature alien to us, mingled with our nature; you refuse to admit that it belongs to our corrupted nature. He thinks that through it a part of God is corrupted [Note: [Col. 1346] The two lines beginning “you, because you do not wish it” and ending “a part” were omitted in the editions; we have restored them on the authority of the manuscripts.]; you try through it to dishonor even the happiness of paradise.

### XVIII. JUL. 

“He did not wish,” he says, “to name the lust of the flesh, which is not from the Father but from the world, whose prince is said to be the devil; he did not find it in the Lord, because the Lord, being human, did not come to human beings through it” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 2, no. 14). Thus, in the very words of Manichaeus, you profess that the lust of the flesh was not made by God but by the world—whose prince, nevertheless, you say the devil is.

AUG. Do I say that the devil is the prince of the world, while the Lord himself does not say this? Would I have said it unless I had read that he himself said it? Since you too have read it, why did you think it should be brought against me? Yet it does not follow that the devil is therefore prince of heaven and earth and of every heavenly and earthly creature, in accordance with the statement, “The world was made through him.” Rather, he is called the prince of the world because the inhabited earth is called “the world” insofar as it is occupied by human beings of the sort with which it is filled, according to the statement, “The world did not know him” (John 1:10); and according to the statement that the devil is called “the prince of this world” (ibid. 12:31); and according to the statement, “The world is placed in the power of the evil one” (1 John 5:19); and according to the statement, “Because you are not of the world, therefore the world hates you” (John 15:19); and innumerable passages of the same kind.

Accordingly, as the Holy Scriptures teach us, we understand “world” sometimes in a good sense and sometimes in an evil sense, according to the difference of the contexts. To its good belong heaven and earth and every creature of God in them; to its evil belong “the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the ambition of the age”—or, as you yourself put it, “the pride of life.” As, then, “world” is read sometimes in a good sense and sometimes in an evil one, so, if you can, find the lust of the flesh or the lust of the eyes ever placed in a good sense. But you will not find it so, any more than you will find “the pride of life,” which is added as a third to those two evils [Note: [Col. 1347] Here too the editions had omitted “evils.”].

### XIX. JUL. 

I said that you had used wholly Manichaean expressions because, although some of these words are found in the Letter of the Apostle John, it is nevertheless certain that he, as a teacher of the Church, did not understand anything there about the flesh, the sense of the flesh, or marital concupiscence in the way Manichaeus constructs his argument by appropriating the apostle’s words. I therefore rightly said that they were Manichaeus’s words, since they served his meaning and ought properly to be regarded as expressions of his intention. Just as, in Saint John, they are to be revered with apostolic dignity because they convey the truth, so, in Manichaeus, the shadowed signs of those words should not be regarded as expressing it.

AUG. Why do you add “marital” and say “about marital concupiscence,” clothing your shameful conception in the honorable name of marriage? The Apostle John spoke of the lust of the flesh, not of marital concupiscence. The latter could have existed in paradise even if no one had sinned, as an appetite for fertility rather than a craving for pleasure; or, at any rate, it would always have been subject to the spirit, so that it would move only at the spirit’s will, never lusting against the spirit so that the spirit would be forced to lust against it. Surely there could have been no discord between flesh and spirit in a place of such great happiness, among human beings enjoying such great peace.

### XX. JUL. 

When the Apostle John summoned the faithful to the summit of every virtue and extended their pursuit of holiness to the height of the Lord’s way of life, he gathered together, under the single name of “the whole world,” all the allurements of present goods and pleasures, as a concise summary, and said: “Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him; because everything that is in the world is the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, which is not from the Father but from the world. And the world passes away, and its lust; but whoever does the will of God remains forever” (1 John 2:15–17). As far as the surface of the words is concerned, he declares war on all the elements and announces that the world and everything in the world are not from the Father and ought not to be loved.

AUG. You say this pointlessly. No Catholic, not even an ignorant one, understands “world” in this passage as referring to the elements. For when he says of the Lord Christ, “He is the propitiation for our sins, and not for ours only but also for those of the whole world” (1 John 2:2), no one is so foolish as to think that the sins of the elements are meant here. Everything called “world” in this passage is therefore understood only in relation to human beings, who are spread throughout the world—that is, throughout the whole inhabited earth.

Indeed, the Apostle called the human life lived not according to God but according to human beings “the world” in this passage. Therefore he forbids it to be loved and says that everything in the world is the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the ambition of the age, or the pride of life, which is not from the Father but from the world. If you can, show from some passage of the Holy Scriptures that the lust of the flesh is ever named in a good sense; and do not cast the fog of loquacity over plain facts.

### XXI. JUL. 

He is certainly an apostle and especially beloved by the Lord Jesus. Yet unless his intention were indicated either by the Gospel he wrote or by the authority of his Letters, these words that we have quoted could bring no prejudice against realities, and would have to yield to all the Scriptures that assert that the world was made by God [Note: [Col. 1348] The editions read “believe.” The manuscripts’ “yield” is better.]. But he himself fortified the Gospel he composed with a reverent beginning [Note: [Col. 1348] Thus the manuscripts. The editions read, “he fortified the Gospel he composed with a reverent beginning.”]. “The Word was God; all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made. … He was the true light, which enlightens every human being coming into this world. He was in the world, and the world was made through him. … The Word became flesh, so that he might dwell in us” (John 1:1, 3, 9, 10, 14). By these testimonies he left no obscurity in his meaning. He showed that he knew and affirmed God to be the creator of the whole world and of everything in the world, and he made it thoroughly clear that no avenue to their doctrines lay open to the Manichaeans. For one who affirms God to be the creator of all natures may, without compromising faith, use the names of substances metaphorically to signify immoderate desire.

AUG. But you refuse to understand the lust of the flesh as evil even when it is immoderate [Note: [Col. 1348] The editions read “is moderate,” and shortly afterward, “those who use it moderately.” Both places have been corrected on the authority of the manuscripts.]. You call it good, and say instead that those who use it immoderately use a good thing badly. Accordingly, if the lust of the flesh is good, then moderate lust is moderately good, and immoderate lust is immoderately good; but to use it moderately is, as you say, to use a good thing well, while to use it immoderately is to use a good thing badly.

Wine is certainly good, for every creature of God is good (1 Timothy 4:4); and one who uses a little wine uses a good thing well, while one who uses too much uses a good thing badly. But John would never say that wine is not from the Father, as he said that the lust of the flesh is not from the Father. You therefore cannot find any lust of the flesh that is not from the Father, since even the immoderate is good according to you; rather, the person who uses a good thing immoderately—that is, who uses a good thing badly—is the one who is not good.

Why, then, do you hesitate to say briefly and openly what you say obscurely through long winding arguments: that what John said is false and that you speak the truth? For his statement, “The lust of the flesh is not from the Father,” is false if the lust of the flesh, as you say, is good even when someone uses it immoderately, while the person who uses the good thing badly is the one who is evil [Note: [Col. 1349] Vignier reads “but the lust of the flesh”; and shortly afterward, “if he is evil.” The manuscripts have “if” in the former place and “but” in the latter.].

### XXII. JUL. 

He therefore commands that the world and the things in the world not be loved, and says that the love of God cannot exist in lovers of the age. But he does not intend, by this designation of the world that must not be loved, to make us understand that it has a creator other than the true God. Rather, he wishes the faithful to recognize that no desires of the present life should be preferred to virtues, lest their minds, occupied either with acquiring wealth or seeking pleasures, be drawn away from the vigor of Christian philosophy, which is the true philosophy.

“For everything that is in the world is the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, which is not from the Father but from the world. And the world passes away, and its lust; but whoever does the will of God remains forever.” By the name “world,” therefore, he indicated the customs of human beings who think that nothing exists after this life, as well as the various displays and luxuries of mortals.

AUG. Thus, if “by the name ‘world’ he indicated the customs of human beings who think that nothing exists after this life, as well as the various displays and luxuries of mortals,” then these customs contain the things he said are in the world and are not from the Father. Your own beautiful conception holds the first place among them—namely, the lust of the flesh.

But you appear to have wished the lust of the eyes to be understood in the customs of people who think that nothing exists after this life, because, clinging to the things they see, they refuse to believe what they do not see; in the displays of mortals, the ambition of the age or the pride of life; and in luxuries, the lust of the flesh. Thus you seem to encompass all three things mentioned by John.

Yet how could there be the luxury that you condemn unless one consented to the lust of the flesh, which you do not think should be condemned and which you even praise by calling it good? What could be more insane than to call luxury evil and the lust of luxury good? What could be more insane than to think that the apostle, by the name “lust of the flesh,” accused not the lust of the flesh itself but rather luxury, which does not exist at all unless someone is enticed, drawn, and possessed by the lust of the flesh? As though so great a teacher had not found grounds for accusing lust, but only grounds for accusing the luxurious person in its name—although the luxurious person would not deserve accusation unless he obeyed its desires.

Stop speaking much while understanding little. However great the flood of your loquacity with which you are swept into the depths, you will never achieve this: that luxury should be evil, while desiring the things that belong to luxury should not be evil, even if one does not consent to such desire in order to avoid committing the evil.

### XXIII. JUL. 

For in his Gospel too he had said, “The world was made through him, and the world did not know him” (John 1:10). This was not so that the elements, lacking reason, might appear capable either of seeing or of denying Christ, but so that the crowd of unbelievers might be signified by the name “world.”

In the same way, in the present passage he says that everything in the world—that is, every class of human beings so attached to pleasures that they measure all the goods of rational creatures by the trappings of power or the burdens of wealth—has swollen with detested pride, which is not from God, that is, does not please God, but is from the world, conceived through the perversity of the human will.

“And therefore,” he says, “it ought not to corrupt you through its rivalry; for whoever does the will of God becomes a participant in eternal blessedness and does not pass away with the fragility of present things.”

Thus the Apostle John commanded that the world be hated, just as the Lord in the Gospel showed that not only the body but even our own soul must be hated: “Whoever does not hate father or brother, and even his own soul, is not worthy of me” (Luke 14:26). Certainly the mind of the faithful cannot hate itself, since with highly discerning love it purchases its own happiness even through sufferings and dangers.

What, then, have we established? That the Apostle John, following the custom of the Scriptures, by the word “world” struck not at the nature of things but at the vices of wills; and thus denied that the lust of the flesh is from God, just as he denied that everything in the world is from God.

Manichaeus, seizing upon this according to his own perfidy as though it followed from the apostle’s meaning, confirms that neither the lust of the flesh, nor the flesh itself, nor finally the whole world was made by God. Following him, you believe that the lust of the flesh was created not by God but by the devil.

AUG. I call that lust of the flesh evil which John says is not from the Father, and which Ambrose says was turned into our nature through the transgression of the first human being (*Book 7 on Luke 12*). Therefore John, wishing human beings to be understood, says that it is from the world.

Manichaeus too calls this lust of the flesh evil, but does not know from where it comes. You, however, call it good because you too do not know from where it comes; and by denying that it exists where Ambrose says it exists, you make Manichaeus appear rightly to attribute to himself the nature of evil, which he foolishly thinks coeternal with God.

Thus, so that both you and Manichaeus may be refuted, the bishop Ambrose explains what the Apostle John says. What the transgression of the first human being turned into nature is certainly not an evil coeternal with God [Col. 1351]. Let Manichaeus therefore be silent. Yet it is evil; let Julian also be silent.

### XXIV. JUL. 

It is therefore clear that blessed John gave you no occasion for error, while you absorbed what Manichaeus put forward. And now that the apostle’s reputation has been defended, let us briefly construct an argument on this point: what do you think Saint John intends when he declares that the lust of the flesh and the lust of the eyes are not from God? Does he mean the very kind of lust, which, permitted when moderate but forbidden when excessive, falls into vice? Or only the excess, which is recognized as voluntary rather than natural?

AUG. If it falls into vice, then at least concede that it is evil. But why do you still insist that it is good, and say that the person who exceeds its permitted measure uses a good thing badly? On that account, it is not the lust itself but the person who uses it badly who falls into vice. Do you see how little you know what you are saying, since you do not even remain consistent with your own definition?

### XXV. JUL. 

If you say that by the name “lust” even that enjoyment is meant by which the permitted pleasure of natural things is experienced, so that the lust of the flesh appears to be condemned universally, then you also declare the sense of the eyes, the world itself, and everything in the world to have been created by the devil, because all are equally said not to be from God. If you agree to this, you will not thereby become a Manichaean; you are one even now. But just as your arguments once showed that you were one, so too you will now make it evident by your profession.

If, however, fearing that your error has been exposed, you say that the apostle, by “the lust of the flesh,” “the lust of the eyes,” and “the world,” noted not the things themselves—which are harmless when kept within their permitted limits but become blameworthy when they run into what is forbidden—then it will be clear that what we established in the first work is true: it is not the kind, species, or measure of natural desire that incurs guilt, but only its excess.

Therefore, henceforth beware of this testimony of the apostle, and do not pollute it even by a light reference. If you do, you will be approved as having defended nothing but as having been openly exposed [Note: [Col. 1351] The editions read, “but will appear publicly ruined.” Our reading is more polished and is found in the ancient books.].

AUG. But, contentious man, the measure of desire that you say has been permitted is not preserved when one consents or yields to the desire that urges him and proceeds into its excess. To prevent that excess, one resists the evil.

For who would doubt that something is evil if, when you obey it, you do evil, but, when you oppose it, you do good? Whoever therefore wishes to live temperately should not consent to the evil that you praise; and whoever wishes to live faithfully should not agree with you when you praise evil. Thus, in order to avoid you, let him know that the lust of the flesh is evil; and, in order to avoid both you and the Manichaeans, let him know from where it comes.

### XXVI. JUL. 

I dealt with this passage in the second book of my earlier work and showed that in human beings the lust of the flesh, which provokes the appearance [Note: [Col. 1351] The manuscripts read “hope.” The passage is obscure and corrupt.] of taste and of the eyes, existed before guilt.

AUG. I gave a sufficient answer to this second book of yours in my fourth. For here, as there, you babble empty things. You have in no way shown that the lust of the flesh, by which the flesh lusts against the spirit, began to exist in human beings before guilt.

Whatever it was that those two human beings sensed as something new in their limbs after the sin, on account of which their shame covered their shameful parts (Genesis 3:7), was certainly brought about by guilt.

### XXVII. JUL. 

Here, however, I necessarily demand by what dreams it was revealed to you that you thought the lust of those who have intercourse was signified by the word “lust.” Let us suppose, without prejudice to the resources of truth that a lengthy argument has disclosed, that it has not yet become clear that the sense of the flesh belongs to the same author to whom its form belongs.

AUG. There is one kind of bodily sense by which the flesh in some manner announces bodily things that are present to the spirit; and there are other movements of carnal lust by which the flesh, lusting against the spirit, rushes into all sorts of forbidden and shameful acts unless the spirit itself also lusts against it. This discord of flesh and spirit is attributed not to the creator of the flesh or of the senses but to the evil persuader and the transgressing human being by those whose sound faith condemns the insane error of the Pelagians and Manichaeans.

### XXVIII. JUL. 

But if this is presented as ambiguous, you will immediately be enveloped in a thick cloud of doubt. For this lust of the flesh is in no way confined to an indication of the genitals [Note: [Col. 1352] Thus the manuscripts. The editions read “judgment.”].
