I could say that ears thirsting for various songs are struck by this word; I could say that the palate of gluttons is chastised; I could say that noses lingering over perfumes are censured; in short, everything except what you suppose is included. Where there is no specific pressure from the word, the choice is free.

Either deny, then, that the things we have mentioned are desired, and, as you usually do, contradict everyone’s conscience; or, if shamelessness has not yet become so hardened in you that you can resist these facts, agree that the condemnation of genital pleasure is not found even in the words.

AUG. You speak as though we said that the lust of the flesh burns only for genital pleasure. Whenever the flesh lusts against the spirit through any bodily sense, it is recognized as the same lust; and since, unless the spirit lusts more powerfully against it, it drags a person toward evil, it is proved to be evil.

On its account Scripture says, “What has been created more wicked than the eye?” (Sirach 31:15). Certainly God, the creator of all bodies and senses, created the eye, not wickedness. There you may understand—if you do not resist the truth—that evil is present in our nature even when it is being created, although it is created by the good God as a good thing and created well.

But learn from Ambrose where this evil comes from, lest you lend support to Manichaeus in introducing another nature—that is, the nature of evil—as coeternal with God.

### XXIX. JUL. 

What assistance, then, can it be to you that, amid the union of the sexes and the fertility of those who unite, I refused to rend it under the name of concupiscence, since neither you nor Manichaeus can approve it as diabolical? The consequence of the preceding argument had already made it clear that the sense by which the body of those united is affected belongs to the activity of the same maker to whose institution bodies, marriages, and seed are referred.

AUG. The power of sensation is one thing; the vice of lusting is another. Distinguish these two carefully; do not fall into disgraceful error. The power of sensation is one thing, I say; the vice of lusting is another.

Read the Gospel: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matthew 5:28). He did not say, “Whoever looks,” referring merely to sensing through the bodily sense called sight. Rather, he says, “whoever looks in order to lust,” which means looking toward evil.

Sight, therefore, is a good sense of the flesh; but the lust of the flesh is an evil movement. If a married person uses this evil well, he does not make it good; he compels it to serve a good work. Through it he accomplishes something good only if he does nothing for its sake. But if he does something—even with his wife—for its sake, the apostle would not grant him pardon on account of the grace of marriage (1 Corinthians 7:6) if he did not recognize that sin is present.

### XXX. JUL. 

After the first work that I published for Saint Turbantius, it should certainly be unnecessary to discuss further the natural shamefulness of these matters, since the issue was treated there so fully that no ambiguity could arise here unless minds had been completely abandoned.

AUG. Perhaps Saint Turbantius, after reading the work that you say you wrote for him, was thereby moved to breathe again within the Catholic faith, because he recognized that you had failed in such a cause.

### XXXI. JUL. 

Yet since the defender of propagation [tradux] cannot be turned aside from it even by the slightest fingernail, and wears out my modesty with rhetorical elegance, why does it help to decide the very matter of sexual union, for different persons [perhaps “names”], with the restraint fitting to the actions performed?

In this passage and in those below, where I said, “Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh” (Genesis 2:24)—“so that the prophet might express the faithfulness of the works, he came close to the danger of shame”—he, as though finding plunder, exults, rejoices, and cries out:

“An entirely open confession, extorted by the force of truth!” Let the reason be stated why, in expressing the works of God, the prophet came close to the danger of shame. Is it really the case that human works ought not to be shameful but plainly objects of glory, while divine works are shameful? Is it really the case that, in speaking and describing the works of God, the prophet’s love or labor is not honored but his modesty is endangered? What could God have done that would make his herald ashamed to say it?

And what is more serious, why should a person be ashamed of a work that was done in him not by a human being but by God, when all craftsmen act with as much labor and diligence as they can [Note: [Col. 1353] The manuscripts read “with as much labor as they can.”—*The second book On Marriage and Concupiscence*, no. 22, has “when all craftsmen work with as much labor as they can,” with this note: “The better manuscripts read, ‘when all craftsmen work with as much labor as they can.’” M.] so that they will not be ashamed of their works?

But surely we are ashamed of what those first human beings were ashamed of, when they covered their shameful parts. That is the penalty of sin, the wound and trace of sin, the enticement and fuel of sin, the law in the members resisting the law of the mind. We are ashamed of this, and rightly ashamed.

For if this did not exist, what could be more ungrateful or irreligious than for us to be ashamed in our members not of our own vice or punishment but of the works of God? (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 2, no. 22).

It has certainly become clear how he exults. He cannot restrain his joy. He seizes upon my statement by which he can show that natural concupiscence is evil and attribute it to the works of the devil. He says that this statement was extorted from my mouth by the force of truth, and proclaims that it is utterly criminal and profane to admit that what we say was made by God must be covered by shame.

But, moved by excessive eagerness, he could not weigh what he was saying. For while asserting that nothing in the works of God is shameful, yet asserting that the function of the genitals is shameful and therefore cannot be attributed to the works of the Creator, he suddenly confessed that it had been assigned to our bodies not only as something honorable but also as something just, not only by God as creator but also by God as judge.

I showed in the third book of my earlier work that the same thing cannot be both punishment and guilt.

AUG. You did not show what you vainly boast that you showed. Indeed, at one point you yourself forgot what you had said earlier and admitted that guilt is also the punishment of the sinner.

When I answered you above (*Against Julian*, book 5, no. 10), I demonstrated clearly enough that, through the apostle too, sins are punished by sins. Speaking of certain people who had exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of an image of corruptible human beings, birds, four-footed animals, and serpents, he immediately showed that this sin was punished by other sins: “Therefore God handed them over to the desires of their hearts, to impurity, so that they dishonor their bodies among themselves” (Romans 1:23–24), followed by the other matters he adds there.

Nor would the Psalm say, “Add iniquity upon their iniquity, and let them not enter into your righteousness” (Psalm 68:28) [Note: [Col. 1354] Vignier omits “and.” M.], unless, by the just judgment of God, prior sins were punished by the addition of sins.

### XXXII. JUL. 

There is therefore no need to labor further over this. I do, however, commend the sharpness of the disputant [Note: [Col. 1354] Thus the manuscripts. Vignier reads “acidity.”], who says that what he claims was rendered by God was not created by God, declaring that what he wants to belong to God’s judgments does not belong to God’s works.

AUG. It is clear that you do not understand how it was said, “God did not make death” (Wisdom 1:13), although by his judgment the one who sins dies. It therefore belongs to his judgment that the sinner should die; yet death does not belong to his work, because God did not make death.

His judgment is just: each person perishes through his own sin, although God does not make sin. Thus he did not make death, yet he kills the one whom he judges worthy of death.

Hence it is written, “God did not make death,” and it is written, “Death and life are from the Lord God” (Sirach 11:14). Anyone who distinguishes divine judgments from divine works clearly sees that these two statements are not contradictory [Note: [Col. 1355] Prosper, in *The Book of Sentences*, sentence 303, inserts here the words: “for it is one thing not to have instituted mortality in creating, and another to punish the sinner in judging.” These words are entirely absent from the manuscripts of this work.]. If you had been able to understand this, you would certainly not have uttered such empty nonsense.

### XXXIII. JUL. 

Thus there is no shame in his works, but in his judgments there is the greatest deformity. It is certain that guilt deserves punishment. Does it follow, however, that the confusion appropriate to guilt returns in the punishment, so that what the guilty person did is called without shame, while what God did in judging cannot be spoken without disgrace?

AUG. Why do you entangle what has been explained and roll up what has been unfolded, so that, for slower minds of the sort found in greater numbers among human beings, you may appear to say something when you say nothing?

You are a man who tries to persuade by shamelessness rather than eloquence that there is either no deformity or very little deformity in the fact that, although the flesh ought to be subject to the spirit, it lusts against the spirit; or that God’s judgment is not just when he abandons the delinquent to himself, so that he becomes his own punishment, although God had been his true happiness; or that each person ought to be ashamed of his sin rather than of his punishment.

Many people do not blush for their sins if no punishment follows that they feel and that makes them ashamed; punishment makes them ashamed of what impunity would not have made them ashamed.

But who, against obvious facts, would wish to be eloquent unless he had deserted the truth? We freely say both things: what a person did willingly and what he suffered unwillingly—that is, both the disobedience of the spirit and the lust of the flesh against the spirit. You were ashamed to name one of these, lest you remind us of the basis on which we could convict your error.

And now, when you already name the lust of the flesh and lust, you fear being said to be ashamed of the name of your conception. You therefore fear shame more, and do not fear error.

### XXXIV. JUL. 

It is clear, then, that our accuser is rolling in the same mud that he abhors. For when he invents the claim that the punishment of lust was justly imposed, and insists that this justice belongs to the divine judgment, yet does not deny that the pronouncement of the judgment is a work of God from which he says lust arose, and admits that it is shameful, he has plainly brought back into God’s work the very shame that he had driven away.

AUG. It has already been said to you: “God did not make death.” Yet in the pronouncement of his judgment God said, “You shall surely die” (Genesis 2:17). See: God caused the sinner to receive what God himself did not make.

Nevertheless, because God is the God of vengeance (Psalm 93:1), he also says that he creates evil things (Isaiah 45:7); and certain things are said to have been created for vengeance in the Book of Ecclesiasticus (39:33).

But when sin is also the punishment of sin, God does not make sin by an unrighteous work; rather, by a just work he makes sin become the punishment of the sinner.

Who could deny that it is sin to believe lying prophets? Yet this was the punishment of King Ahab, inflicted by divine judgment, as the history of Kings testifies (1 Kings 22). No one is therefore so foolish as to think that the lies of false prophets ought to be praised, or to call God the author of lying, when by a just judgment he causes someone whom he sees to deserve such punishment to be deceived by a lie.

Read and understand; and do not, by the tumult of your loquacity, drown out the understanding you need.

### XXXV. JUL. 

As though this were not enough, he added, as a sort of special culmination of wickedness, that he called such a punishment inflicted by God an enticement and fuel of sin, a law in the members that invincibly resisted the law of our mind. By this kind of vengeance, God would multiply crimes rather than punish them; and although angry with the evil will by which the error had been committed, he would leave behind a necessity for further sinning.

What sort of judgment this is, let the fury of Manichaeus determine. It remains clear that this judge whom Augustine invents pretended to hate sin, but otherwise clings to sins with such affection that they could not find a more attentive nurturer.

AUG. Read what is written: “Because they did not approve of having God in their knowledge, God handed them over to a reprobate mind, to do what is not fitting” (Romans 1:28). See how certain sins are also the punishments of sinners.

To understand how God does this, reread what I reminded you above concerning King Ahab. His sin was certainly that he believed the false prophets; yet, because God was taking vengeance, that sin was also the punishment of the sinner.

Consider these things, and do not bark against the truth, lest this punishment be recognized in you as well.

### XXXVI. JUL. 

What, then, do you want, most subtle disputant? Is modesty concerning God’s works sacrilegious because everything God has made ought to be performed openly, lest our hesitation appear to accuse the maker?

The Apostle Paul therefore erred when, describing God’s works, he said: “Our less honorable members have greater honor; and God composed the body, giving more abundant honor to the member that lacked it, so that there might be no division in the body” (1 Corinthians 12:23–25).

Augustine. Read carefully, and inspect the Greek codex; you will find that the Apostle called “dishonorable” [Note: [Col. 1356] *Tà aschêmona*.] the things that you call “more shameful.” And when you ask why those things are dishonorable which previously had been so honorable that those two were naked and were not ashamed (Gen. II, 25), you will discover—unless the vehemence of contention blinds you—that sin preceded this condition. Nor did God make anything dishonorable in the first human beings, just as God did not make death, although only God makes the body; and yet the Apostle truly says, “The body indeed is dead because of sin” (Rom. VIII, 10).

### XXXVII. Julian

The caution exercised regarding honorable things is also mistaken when it casts the shadows of shame over natural matters. You yourself, then, should drive away in the sight of the people the remnants of food, which you certainly admit have nothing to do with lust; indeed, in order to lend authority to your doctrine by your example, do everything in church that you say ought to be done at the bidding of the will. Content yourself [Note: [Col. 1356] Vignierius: *commentusque*, “having invented”; the manuscripts: *contentusque*, “contenting yourself.”] with concealing only the act of intercourse—which perhaps you have abandoned both because of your former resolve and now because of old age—and say that it is a grave sacrilege if a thing that has God as its creator avoids public view.

Eat, then, in the forum, or in the synagogues where your disputations resound; and when your clothing has become burdensome under the blazing sun, covering only that part of your body which the devil has moved, walk about naked in the rest, since you declare it ungrateful and profane if anything attributed to God’s works is covered. Yet when you do none of these things—if, that is, you have done so without succeeding [Note: [Col. 1357] So the manuscripts. Vignierius has *perficiendo*, “by accomplishing.”]—you confirm by the works themselves one of two alternatives: either that all these things belong to the devil, since you do not perform them in public view, or that your doctrine has fallen—not in your heart, perhaps, but with your belly as witness.

### Augustine

Of the things that modesty conceals, some are objects of horror and others of desire. The former are hidden so that they may not be loathed, as the discharges of remnants from food; the latter so that they may not be desired, or so that what is usually done through them may not prompt desire. Such are those members that, by modesty itself, are properly called “shameful,” or when the very act of desire is carried out through them.

The other parts of the body, farther removed from these, when one is ashamed to leave them naked or to uncover them, are concealed for the same reason, since the desire of the flesh is fed more broadly through the eyes. Thus those shameless men wished to strip the chaste Susanna as far as they could (Dan. XIII, 32).

It can therefore rightly be understood that God also commended care for this same modesty when he clothed those who, having made themselves loincloths, were ashamed of their nakedness, clothing them also in tunics—indeed, in tunics of skins (Gen. III, 21), so that death, now joined to their corruptible bodies, might be signified.

As for eating in public, custom forbids it wherever custom forbids it, and one is rightly ashamed to act contrary to custom. For the ancient Romans, as you yourself have read, dined and took their midday meal in the open. What, then, is the point of your wandering into emptiness—not by reasoning, but by abuse? Look back at those first parents, who were naked and were not ashamed; observe what they covered, and acknowledge what they felt.

From loincloths they proceeded to tunics. From that point the covering of the human body began and increased, when the name “shameful” was imposed upon human members. There is greater care for modesty where chastity resists desire. For rational nature is ashamed to have in its flesh something against which it must necessarily struggle if it does not wish to be dishonored by immodesty—whether the married, lest they be defiled by illicit intercourse, or the continent, lest they be defiled by any intercourse at all.

This discord between flesh and spirit could not have existed in paradise, if no one had sinned. It did not, however, take possession of us through the mingling of some alien nature. From where, then, did it come to us, except from the transgression of the first human being?

### XXXVIII. Julian

These are foolish matters, and they bring more abuse upon our style than labor; but they necessarily follow from your faith [Note: [Col. 1357] The editions have *etiam*, “also,” in place of *tuam*, “your.” The manuscripts support the correction.]. Nevertheless, to keep the reader attentive, I offer this further reminder.

You attempted to assert that God’s work is proved not to be shameful. But since you were unable to accomplish this, you nevertheless promised most categorically that, if it were shown to be God’s work, you would remove modesty from lust. I approved this in the first work to such an extent that I do not think you will doubt it when you read it. Yet since this fiction of yours indicates that those books have not yet come into your hands, I shall not hesitate to demonstrate the same point here as well.

Who, then, do you think created irrational animals, which at fixed seasons are stirred by the most ardent lust, so that the savagery of each species is also sharpened? Then the boar is fierce; then the worst tigress. “Above all, the fury of mares is remarkable” (Virgil, *Georgics* III, 248, 266). Truly the grasses swell. Truly the abundance of tender moisture overflows. “And herds seek intercourse on appointed days” (ibid. II, 324, 331, 329).

It would take too long to go through each case. All the species that flight lifts aloft, that swimming plunges beneath the surface, that wandering scatters through the air, across the waters, and through the forests—and that neither reason has exalted nor guilt depressed—are inflamed by the well-known pleasure of bodily union.

Did they receive, then, the ardor of the sexes that they suffer through the work of God or of the devil? You will undoubtedly cry out: “God’s.” God, then, kindled the sexes with natural pleasure—a conclusion which, more consistently than you, the Manichaean, deny.

For Manichaeus, from whom you learned to condemn the desire of the flesh, considering what he ought to say, pursues everywhere the thing he had defined as diabolical and removed from God’s works, wherever he could find it. And therefore, just as he assigned human bodies to the devil through desire, so through human beings he assigned all animals to the devil as their creator.

But you, while remaining thus far in the camp of Manichaeus and honoring his great beast, the dragon, from which you breathe deadly poison into unhappy minds through natural evil and the crimes of marriage, nevertheless do not wish to cast at all natures the arrows taught by your master. You are more friendly toward the irrational animals—though you spare them for this reason, that you may accuse the condition of rational beings with greater authority—and you agree that in their bodies God did what you say the devil did in ours, although you admit that the same thing exists in human beings, but more mildly than in beasts.

Thus, so that the prudent reader may understand what has been accomplished, you do not deny that bodily lust in animals was made by God. Therefore that affection, which is found more intensely in substances that have taken nothing from the devil’s evil, not even by a slight inclination of the will, is not unworthy of God’s works.

Since, then, desire has been defended by the example of animals and also by the dignity of its author, it is neither evil nor diabolical: God, the maker of bodies, made it, and it is possessed by a nature free from sin. Once this has become clear, I ask whether you agree that God made this lust which human bodies experience.

If you agree, the dispute is over: you will have been corrected, and Manichaeus will remain crushed. But if you say, “It could not have been made by God in human bodies,” I reply that you consider that pleasure and desire of the flesh unworthy of human, though not of divine, works. For there can be no doubt that, if you say that what you confess to have been made by God anywhere could not have been made in human beings [Note: [Col. 1358] Perhaps *in homine*, “in the human being.”], you are not removing from desire the testimony it deserves; rather, you are seeking what human bodies do not deserve.

See, then, what sort of profanity marks the end of your sect [Note: [Col. 1359] The editions have *fimus*, “we are,” but the manuscripts have *finis*, “end.”]. You say that what was not unworthy of the work of the Creator is unworthy of mortal flesh [Note: [Col. 1359] The editions have *mortali*, “mortal,” though the manuscripts differ.]. Thus, in this sense, you have not censured lust; you have exalted the human being whom you intended to accuse.

Such is the consistency and such the reward of one who declares war on truth: his effort is always struck down by consequences contrary to his intention. I therefore now rise against your words with greater consistency, as every prudent person recognizes:

“Is reason not heard when God’s works are censured and described? Are not the examples of all natures considered? Is human madness carried so far that a person thinks something inconsistent with his own viscera which he sees flourishing by God’s work in the beings that share his nature?” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence* II, 22). For the origin and constitution of our bodies are no different from those of mute animals.

### Augustine

Then say that resurrection and everlasting incorruption are not owed to human bodies, because they too, like those of beasts, are earthly. Say that the end cannot be different where the origin is not different. Say these things, if you wish, and display, against the evangelical Scriptures, how much you have advanced in secular literature by the force of empty verbosity.

But if you will not dare say this, confess, in accordance with the Christian faith, that it is also part of the human being’s punishment that he is compared with senseless cattle and made like them (Ps. XLVIII, 13). This misery, then, belongs to the human being, whereas cattle cannot be miserable. So also the desire of the flesh is a punishment for the human being, not for the beast, in which the flesh never desires against the spirit.

Do you wish to equate mortal natures in such a way that you assert that in beasts also the flesh desires against the spirit? If you do not, then do not be like a horse and mule without understanding (Ps. XXXI, 9). Recognize that the lust of which we speak would not have existed in paradise if no one had sinned—the lust by which the flesh desires against the spirit.

There is no such lust in cattle, from which you have furnished such advocacy for your position, allowing yourself to be verbose on behalf of those mute creatures. For if human lust did not make the flesh desire against the spirit, but if such desire in human beings were of a kind that arose at the bidding of the will whenever action was needed and, when it was not needed, offered no incitements with which our will would have to struggle by restraining and curbing them, we would have no charge against you for wishing to locate it in paradise—that is, in the dwelling place of such great happiness—in so unhappy a form.

### XXXIX. Julian

Just as we have received the image of God through the rational faculty of the mind, so we experience communion with cattle through the affinity of the flesh. Although its form is different, it is nevertheless one substance, derived from the matter of the elements; and, according to the merits of the rational soul, it will see eternity, either miserable through sufferings or glorious through rewards.

### Augustine

If, as you admit, earthly flesh, corruptible like that of cattle, is nevertheless, according to the merits of the rational soul, destined to see eternity with a very different end, why do you not accept that, according to the merits of the image of God—which had not been disfigured by any sin—flesh was originally created in such a way that, although made from earthly matter, it would have remained in eternity and incorruption if no one had sinned?

It would not have been a corruptible body weighing down the soul—that is, the image of God—but would have been so subject to it that, for the begetting of children, the genital members too would have moved at the bidding of the will, just like the other members through which we perform various tasks. Or the desire of the flesh would have been of such a kind that it would not arise unless the soul—that is, the image of God—willed it, nor would the overflow of pleasure cause the mind’s thought to sink down.

For if this were its condition even now, it would not be said of it that it is “not from the Father but from the world” (I John II, 16)—that is, from human beings, who through it and with it are born into the world and who will certainly perish unless they are reborn to God.

Therefore, although bodily matter is common to us and to cattle, it is rightly believed that, by virtue of the image of God, its beginning was originally different, before sin had begun [Note: [Col. 1360] The editions have *meritum*, “merit”; the manuscripts support the correction to *merito*, “by virtue of.”], just as its end is different after sin has been assumed.

### XL. Julian

By what reasoning, then, would it be unworthy—not of the image of God, since the substance of the soul is different from that of the flesh, but of the dissoluble servant of the image of God—which had not been unworthy to be created by God himself?

God therefore made bodies; God distinguished the sexes of bodies; God made genital members; God implanted the affection by which these bodies would be joined to one another; God also gave the power of seeds; God works in the secrets of nature from the matter of seeds. God makes nothing evil, nothing guilty.

### Augustine

“God makes nothing evil, nothing guilty”—but only insofar as God makes it, not insofar as it comes from a corrupted and condemned mass, from which he makes it.

### XLI. Julian

God made lust in human beings just as in cattle. But in cattle God left their impulses without restraint, whereas in human beings God established a measure through reason. Prudence and decency, which God gave him, provide him with clothing. Therefore God censures neither its measure nor its kind, but its excess—an excess arising from the insolence of free will—which accuses not the condition of nature but the merit of the agent.

### Augustine

Why, then, does lust resist the spirit in human beings, which it does not do in cattle, unless it belongs to the nature of cattle but to the punishment of human beings—either because it exists, though it would not have existed, or because it resists, though it would have been subject if it had not been made or corrupted by sin?

For if “God left the impulses unrestrained in cattle,” then surely, since you call these impulses lusts, you admit that they are restrained by human beings. Yet they would be restrained for no reason unless they moved in a defective manner.

You say that God established a measure for lust in human beings. Why, then, does it not remain within the measure divinely established in it, but exceed that measure unless it is restrained? How, then, can that be called good which drives and compels a human being to do evil if it is not resisted?

Do you not see that the extraordinary defense you have undertaken concerning human nature was either born from sin or corrupted by sin? And is this not why the first human beings covered their shameful members after sin, whereas before sin they were naked and were not ashamed?

What do you mean by saying, “Prudence and decency, which God gave him, provide the human being with clothing”? Then before sin human beings were foolish and indecent, imprudent and shameless, since they were not ashamed of their nakedness? Thanks be to sin—for otherwise they would have remained so.

But since it is absurd to say this, clearly natural prudence and decency covered the shameful members, although before sin they had not been shameful. Thus excess belongs to lust in sin, but its impulse too belongs to a defect. Those first human beings were ashamed of this impulse, for they did not wish to leave naked the members that your proposed interpretation claimed were troubling them against their will.

### XLII. Julian

Now attend to what follows from your opinion. Evidently, whatever is believed to be good ought not to be covered by shame. We, however, have taught that the pleasure [Note: [Col. 1361] Perhaps *voluptatem*, “pleasure,” in place of *voluntatem*, “will.”] naturally implanted in the sexes is not so evil as to be unrelated to God’s work.

Accordingly, you must either abandon your impiety or your modesty. But what are these things to us? [Note: [Col. 1361] Thus Vignierius and Morel, *Elem. Crit.*, p. 61. In B: “But what are we? These things, however. Can an Ethiopian change his skin,” etc., with this note: “After ‘But what are we?’ understand ‘we think.’ Or perhaps read: ‘But, as Jeremiah says, If an Ethiopian can change his skin,’ etc.” M.] “If an Ethiopian can change his skin, or a leopard its spots” (Jer. XIII, 23), so may you wash yourself clean of the mysteries of the Manichaeans.

### Augustine

Rather, you will not cease assisting the Manichaeans unless, with Ambrose and all Catholics, you say that this defense you have undertaken—which even the Manichaeans prove to be evil—passed into our nature through the transgression of the first human being. Otherwise, according to those impious heretics whom you unwittingly assist, so manifest a defect of the human being will be believed to have a beginning coeternal with God.

### XLIII. Julian

It follows, then, that you should lay aside modesty and, while remaining on friendly terms with your teacher, join yourself to the Cynics. Yet the arguments of certain Stoics also accompany them, as Cicero reports in *On Duties*:

“They attack common decency, because we call things that are not shameful in fact disgraceful in words; but things that are shameful in fact we call by their proper names. To commit robbery, to perpetrate fraud, to commit adultery is shameful in fact, but is not called obscene; to beget children is honorable in fact, but obscene in name. And many other arguments to this effect,” he says, “are advanced by them against modesty. But let us follow nature and flee everything that shrinks from the approval of the eyes and ears” (*On Duties* I).

You, then, who reject this natural principle, the genuine source of decency, must either say that robbery, sacrilege, and parricide—all of which have the greatest shamefulness in fact but no obscenity in their names—are more foul and profane than begetting children, as the duty of modesty requires; or, if you are ashamed to accuse marriage to such an extent that you would make it outweigh even crimes, exhort married couples to call that union as confidently and freely as we customarily name parricide and robbery.

Furthermore, if you add that the joining of bodies intended for the production of offspring is not stained by any wickedness, but can be considered good in its proper measure, in order—as usual—to mock Christian ears, then embrace the deed of Crates [Note: [Col. 1362] We add the name *Crates* from the manuscripts.] of Thebes, a wealthy and noble man who was so devoted to the Cynic sect that, abandoning his ancestral wealth, he moved to Athens with his wife Hipparchia, who was equally devoted to that philosophy.

When he wished to have intercourse with her in public, as Cornelius Nepos relates, and she drew a cloak over them to conceal the act, he beat her and said: “Clearly you are still insufficiently instructed in your senses, since you do not dare to do openly, in the presence of others, what you know you are doing rightly.”

Such a practice is entirely appropriate to your flocks, so that natural acts—because through them the things created by God are approved as good for the multiplication of bodies—may be performed without any objection on grounds of shame.

Restore gratitude, then, to the four-footed animals. Since, through their examples, they protect the sense of your bodies from the possession of the devil and from the mouth of Manichaeus, follow their freedom in intercourse as a testimony to the goodness of the act. It is fitting that those who have offered patronage to your members should provide instruction in your morals as well.

And, to make clear by repetition what we have dealt with [Note: [Col. 1362] Marked in an ancient hand in the margin of the Portus manuscript.]: you said that, if God had made lust, it should not be concealed by any shame. Although we fully treated this matter in the four books of the earlier work, here too we have demonstrated, by the testimony of all animals—which for the moment you admit were created by God—that the lust of the sexes was created by God, while we nevertheless acknowledge that in human beings it should be covered by shame.

Your doctrine therefore entails that, after a long return, you present to us the beauty of the Cynics and practice before the eyes of the city those things that are natural because they were made by God.

Do you perceive with what entangled lights you have rushed into my position, in which I said: “To express the prophet’s faith in God’s works, he came close to the danger of shame”? For just as your teacher, in accordance with his fables, attacks this statement—as I set out his arguments in the preceding book—because he denies that all bodies were made by God, so you have shamelessly dared to handle what you confess to have been created by God, although you fearfully acknowledge him as the creator of bodies whose sensation you attribute to the prince of darkness.

This, surely, has been worn down by the power of truth as much as by the faith with which the Evangelist said: “All things were made through God, and without him nothing was made” (John I, 3).

### Augustine

Could you compare beasts with human beings in the concupiscence or lust of the flesh unless you also believed that those first parents of the human race, although they bore corruptible bodies, would have died even if they had not sinned?

The Catholic Church condemns this recent error of your heresy [Note: [Col. 1362] The word *errore* (“error”) is omitted in the editions, though it occurs in the manuscripts.] so decisively that Pelagius, your leader, when this was brought against him among other charges before the fourteen Eastern bishops who heard his case, condemned it himself through fear of his condemnation [Note: [Col. 1363] See above, *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, nos. 24, 57, 60.].

In that judgment you yourself have certainly also been condemned, since you say that Adam was made in such a way that, whether he sinned or did not sin, he would have died—contradicting the Apostle, who says, “The body is dead because of sin” (Rom. VIII, 10).

Moreover, if those bodies would not have died without sin preceding them, then they were certainly not corruptible, lest they weigh down those blessed souls. For “the corruptible body weighs down the soul,” as it is written (Wis. IX, 15).

Accordingly, just as death and corruption could fail to be common to the bodies of beasts and human beings, although earthly matter was common to them, so lust need not have been common to them in the begetting of children. In human beings it would either not have existed at all, so that, just as the other members are moved by the will to perform their appropriate tasks, the genital members too would have been moved by the will for the work of generation; or it would not have been such as it is in beasts, but would have served the will, never lowering the mind from vigilant thought, and not even finally doing so through pleasure.

But now, because sin preceded us and human nature was changed for the worse, things have become punitive for it that are appropriate to the nature of cattle. Yet in this evil—in which the flesh desires against the spirit—there is greater cause for shame, because between two things, both of which belong to our nature, one of which ought to rule and the other to serve, there has arisen not merely a discord to be mourned but one that must also be deeply blushed for.

What, then, did the irrelevant aid of the Cynics summoned by you accomplish? On this path of your error, when you were failing away from the road, even the animals you compared with human beings could not help you.

### XLIV. Julian

The time warns us to pass on to other matters. But since it is certain that you have nothing to sell to inexperienced ears except the shamefulness of natural acts, I shall touch as briefly as I can on what is thought to remain.

Who, then, would deny that this decency by which we cover our genital members varies according to persons, places, occupations, and customs? Thus, in public gatherings, greater nakedness is more obscene, whereas in baths it has no shamefulness. Thus one is the attire of the bedchamber, half-naked and unconcerned; another is the attire of the forum, more careful and more elaborate.

What of the fact that, as a testimony to frequent familiarity, negligence attends upon caution, and the more unknown or distinguished the person present, the more carefully one’s dress is arranged? What of the fact that no one has charged sailors and many craftsmen with the fault of nakedness?

And lest this simplicity be attributed more to persons than to their occupations, even the Apostle Peter, in accordance with the custom of everyone, was fishing naked in a boat after the Lord’s resurrection (John XXI, 7) [Note: [Col. 1363] Vignierius has *nudus piscabatur*, “was fishing naked,” omitting *in navigio*, “in a boat,” which is found in the manuscripts.].

Direct your eyes from here to the services of physicians: they bring their art, in the interest of health, into the regions of shame. Nakedness is even honorable for athletes. Indeed, not only among young men and their wanton companions, but among entire peoples, both sexes are exposed, and intercourse takes place without the choice of privacy.

What wonder, however, if the Scots and the barbarism of neighboring peoples do this, when the philosophy we mentioned above held the same opinion, and when the doctrine of the Traducianists has reached this point?

What measure of modesty, then, will be maintained, or what boundary will there be amid so many differences of modesty, and amid acts of intercourse that are partly necessary and partly defended by social custom—by which it could be shown that the devil mingled natural sexual ardor with the sexes?

Accordingly, just as the defense of your opinion has been dissolved by occupations, places, customs, arts, and entire peoples together, so what we defend by reason itself and by the teaching of the Apostle Paul remains invincible: God, the author of all things, created all bodies, all members of bodies, and all bodily senses; but he ordered them in such a way that modesty would cover some of our members according to the requirements of time, while natural decency would present others, for which it would be as indecorous to provide covering as it would be inappropriate to expose the genital secret.

### Augustine

Rather, you cast the guilt of impropriety upon those of whom divine Scripture says, “They were naked, and they were not ashamed” (Gen. II, 25). Certainly at that time they were upright, just as they had been made upright: for, as we read, “God made the human being upright” (Eccl. VII, 30).

At that time, then, when their uprightness was so great, were they so perverse as to expose the secrets of their genital members imprudently, shamelessly, indecently, and improperly? Recognize, therefore, that there was not yet a cause for shame, when those members that are now properly called shameful were not yet shameful.

The law resisting the law of the mind did not yet dwell in their members, without which no one is now born. By the just judgment of God—who deservedly abandoned the one who had abandoned him—the disobedience of the flesh had not yet been repaid to disobedient humanity.

For it is not the case that the disobedience of the flesh does not consist in desiring against the spirit merely because, when the spirit also desires against the flesh, it is not permitted to accomplish what it attempts. This, then, did not yet exist when they were naked and were not ashamed.

They therefore did not improperly expose the secrets of their genital members in true nakedness [Note: [Col. 1364] Morel, *Elem. Crit.*, pp. 281–282, reads this passage: “They therefore did not expose the secrets of their genital members in free nakedness.”]. Rather, they had not yet experienced anything improper in their genital members.

Why do you gather empty words like light leaves, so that you too may cover your carnal contention against spiritual authority—as though the flesh desired against the spirit? Why do you ask what measure or boundary of modesty should be maintained amid all the differences produced by various necessities, occupations, opinions, and customs, whether right or perverse?

Here you have human beings—not members of some people such as the Scots, but the parents of all peoples; not corrupted by some perverse opinion, like the Cynics and others disfigured by a similar irreverence, but created upright by God; not constrained by the work of some necessity, as Peter’s nakedness was, with which you thought yourself covered, but free in the paradise of delights.

Look at them: before sin, they displayed freedom; after sin, they taught modesty. Before sin they were naked and were not ashamed; after sin they were ashamed of their nakedness. Before sin they left their genital members uncovered, since they were not yet shameful; after sin they covered their genital members, since they had become shameful.

These witnesses, therefore, are fully adequate to refute both the obstinacy of the Pelagians and the shamelessness of certain peoples and of the Cynics: by their nakedness they show that the members were not shameful before, but became shameful afterward.

### XLV. Julian

Having now completed this matter, insofar as the subject permitted, I come to what you said: that this natural concupiscence did not exist in Christ. For you attack me as follows:

“But in all these matters he did not wish to name the concupiscence of the flesh, which is not from the Father but from the world; and the devil is called the prince of this world. He did not find it in the Lord, because the Lord did not come to human beings through it” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence* II, 5).

You have therefore declared that Christ, whom the Catholic faith confesses to have been truly human in every respect, did not possess in his own flesh this concupiscence that the Apostle John says is not from the Father but from the world.

John, however, as his words have taught, declares that the concupiscence of the flesh and the concupiscence of the eyes, together with the whole world, are not from the Father (I John II, 16). We have shown how this ought to be understood.

### Augustine

You did indeed show it—but you showed how you understood it, or rather how you failed to understand it, not how it ought to be understood. On this matter I answered you in that very disputation of yours, which was not truthful but loquacious, contending for the truth [Note: [Col. 1365] We have added *certans*, “contending,” from the older books.].

### XLVI. Julian

Yet you embrace the very name “concupiscence” and wish the sense of the eyes to have been absent from Christ’s body just as the sense of his viscera was.

### Augustine

You would not say this if you possessed sound sense—not of the body, but of the mind.

### XLVII. Julian

Let the reader now attend with his whole mind, for he will see the heresy of the Apollinarists restored, with the addition of Manichaeism through you.

Apollinaris is said initially to have introduced such an incarnation of Christ that he claimed only a body had apparently been assumed from human substance, while the deity itself had taken the place of the soul. Thus Christ seemed to have assumed not a human being but a human corpse.

When this began to be overturned by both reason and the testimony of the Gospel—since by that very fact the whole falsehood had to be exposed, namely, that Christ had said he was a human being, whom the Jews pursued as one speaking the truth, if he had assumed flesh alone, since a human being could not exist without soul and body together; and since he had said in the Gospel, “I have power to lay down my soul, and I have power to take it up again” (John X, 18)—for what soul would be laid down if he had not assumed one?—then, after he had been overthrown by the authority of such testimonies and by manifest reason, he devised another position from which his heresy, which persists to this day, would arise.

He said that Christ did indeed have a human soul, but that the senses of the body were absent in him, and he declared him incapable of suffering [Note: [Col. 1365] The editions have *esse pronuntiavit*, “declared him to be.” On the authority of the Portus manuscript, we have removed *esse*.] with respect to all sins.

### [Col. 1366] Augustine

Epiphanius, the bishop of Cyprus of holy memory, said in the little work he published concerning heresies that some Apollinarists said that, in the Lord Jesus Christ, the body was consubstantial with the deity; others denied that he had assumed a soul; and others, because it was said, “The Word became flesh” (John I, 14), argued that he had not assumed flesh from created flesh—that is, from Mary—but that the Word had become flesh. Later, however, devising I know not what, they said that he had not assumed a mind.

As for your claim that the Apollinarists asserted that the senses of the body were absent in Christ [Note: [Col. 1366] This phrase, “that the senses of the body were absent in Christ,” is omitted in the editions and restored here from the manuscripts.], and that they declared him incapable of suffering, I have found it nowhere except in this book of yours, nor have I ever heard it from anyone.

But since I see that you are looking for a place to spread your empty talk, so that, though verbose, you may appear abundant, I shall answer briefly: Let anyone who believes either those things that I mentioned above as being said by the Apollinarists, or that Christ did not possess the senses of the body and was incapable of suffering, be anathema.

And so that you too may recognize yourself: Let anyone who believes that the flesh of Christ desired against the spirit be anathema.

### XLVIII. Julian

Not one who avoided sins by the power of judgment, but one who, because of the fortunate condition of flesh separated from our sensations, could not experience the desire of vices.

### Augustine

We do not say that “Christ, because of the fortunate condition of flesh separated from our sensations, could not experience the desire of vices.” Rather, we say that, with perfect virtue and with flesh generated not through the concupiscence of the flesh, he did not possess the desire of vices.

For it is one thing not to have an evil desire, and another not to be able to experience it. He would have experienced it if he had possessed it. The sense by which he could experience it was not lacking in him; rather, the will by which he would not possess it was present.

Nor should you be surprised that Christ, although truly human, was nevertheless wholly good and did not wish to possess an evil desire. For who except you denies that the desire by which evil things are desired is evil? Who, I ask, except you, attempts to persuade us that the desire which he admits to be the desire of vices is not itself a vice, and that what becomes an evil deed if one consents to its persuasion is not evil?

Christ could have experienced this desire if he had possessed it, and he could have possessed it if he had willed to do so [Note: [Col. 1366] So the manuscripts. The editions have *haberet*, “if he possessed it.”]. But far be it from him to will this.

Nevertheless, if he had possessed an evil desire—or, to use your expression, “the desire of vices”—it would have begun in him from his own will, because he was not born with it as we were.

Accordingly, his virtue consisted in not possessing it; our virtue consists in not consenting to it. In this we imitate him: just as he did not sin by not possessing it, so we do not sin by refusing to consent to it; and just as he willed and was able not to possess it, so let us will to be free from it, since we shall be able to be free from it.

For his grace will free us from this body of death—that is, from the flesh of sin. He came to us in the likeness of sinful flesh, not in sinful flesh.

### XLIX. JULIAN

[Note: [Col. 1366] Printed editions: “So gravely, as the matter itself shows, toward the end of the Catholics’ flattery” ([Col. 1367]). But all manuscripts read “grave”; and among them the manuscript of Mar. reads “faith.”]

Such grave flattery toward the Catholic faith—as the matter itself shows—was not merely unnecessary but even profane. For when he wishes to show that something more was present in Christ’s body, lest he should be made contemptible by sharing our flesh, he deprived him of the integrity of his natural senses, failing to see how great a destruction of the truth was being brought about by corrupted flattery. The Catholic objection, stirred up against this, rightly protested: for in such a faith the mysteries of Christ would suffer greater damage than his members.

For if Christ was made, as they say, from David’s seed (Rom. 1:3), made from a woman, and made under the law (Gal. 4:4), so that he might give us an example and that we might follow his footsteps—he who committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth (1 Pet. 2:22)—yet he did not assume in every respect the properties of our substance, if he bore either flesh without a soul or a human being without the senses with which nature has endowed us, then he is not shown to have fulfilled the pattern of the example or the law.

For what praise was there in despising the allurements of the senses when, by nature’s favor, he was incapable of them? What was remarkable about restraining the eyes of his flesh when, with their aid, they did not wander? What was great about turning his nostrils away from alluring odors to which they could not be exposed? What was astonishing about maintaining daily strict moderation at meals when he could not feel their stimulants? Finally, what difficulty could there have been in extending fasts to forty days if hunger could not trouble him? What honor would the discipline of the ears deserve—ears that received nothing but honorable sounds—if he suffered from an inborn deafness toward improper ones? And what glory would there be in chastity if virility was absent rather than desire, and what was thought to arise from strength of spirit actually came from weakness of the members?

### AUGUSTINE

[Note: [Col. 1367] Vignierius reads “greatest of all,” omitting “of human beings,” which we add from the manuscripts.]

These things are rightly said—not against Apollinaris or any Apollinarian, whom I do not think ever said that Christ’s flesh lacked the senses of the human body—but against anyone who says this.

We say that Christ perceived beautiful and ugly things through his eyes; fragrant and foul odors through his nostrils; musical and discordant sounds through his ears; distinguished sweet from bitter by taste; and judged rough and smooth, hard and soft, cold and hot by touch. Whatever else can be sensed and perceived through the body’s senses, he could sense and perceive. Nor did he lack the capacity to beget, had he willed it. Yet his flesh never lusted against the spirit.

If, as you think, abstaining from sins is a great good because there are lusts to be conquered, but would not be a great good if those lusts were absent, then each person will be more praiseworthy in virtue in proportion to how lustful he was in the flesh. Accordingly, Christ, according to this dreadful and detestable perversity of yours, ought to have been the greatest of all human beings in virtue and also the most lustful in the flesh.

[Note: [Col. 1368] Here “senses” is added on the authority of the manuscripts.]

If you perceive how impious this is, do not delay changing your judgment. Distinguish lusts from the senses: lusts are felt within the various senses rather than themselves doing the sensing. Otherwise, the more ardent someone’s lust, the more vigorous his senses will appear; and Christ will be thought to have burned with the more violent lusts in proportion as his senses were purer.

### L. JULIAN

Finally, what crown of endurance would there have been if the pain of wounds and blows, the route to the soul being intercepted by the senses, could not reach the soul?

What, then, did Apollinaris’s flattery accomplish? Clearly, it caused all the beauty of the virtues that Christ had expressed in himself to wither, emptied of praise wrongly attributed to his nature, and it stripped the sacred teaching of the Mediator of all the splendor of its truth and exposed it to ridicule.

Moreover, he not only destroyed the distinction of Christ’s deeds, making him happier by birth than by virtue; he also subjected him to accusations of deceit if he were to say to mortals: “Stretch yourselves toward endurance under a man who feels nothing, and come through real crosses to the virtues of a false body”; or: “Imitate chastity, overcoming the sure inducements of your nature, in one whom weakness made appear chaste.”

Certainly nothing more profane or more wicked could be devised than such arguments.

Apollinaris, however, had not said all these things. By that one assertion of his—that the man Christ lacked those senses which nature has implanted and which fall into vices not through use but through excess—he silently accepted all these consequences reported by the Catholics, because of the prejudice created by his opinion. For Catholic faith is constructed by affirming all these things, while the Apollinarian heresy is formed and condemned by denying them or drawing such consequences.

You, therefore, must consider what judgment ought to be formed about yourself. You condemn sexual intercourse like Manichaeus; you separate Christ’s flesh from communion with human beings according to the Manichaeans; you accuse the lust of the flesh in accordance with the statements of your teacher Manichaeus; and you say that the lust of the senses [Note: [Col. 1368] Codex Port., “of the sexes.”] was not present in Christ’s body, either according to the Manichaeans or according to the Apollinarians. Yet you want us neither to call you an Apollinarian nor a Manichaean.

Although I yield and grant you this favor—and I do not regret my generosity—you may, through my indulgence, avoid appearing to be a follower of Apollinaris, for he was the inventor of the lesser impiety. But it is not in your power to be called anything other than a Manichaean.

### AUGUSTINE

Ambrose was neither an Apollinarian nor a Manichaean, but a conqueror of heretics. Through your position he said that whatever human being might be born [Note: [Col. 1368] We have added the verb “might be born” from the trustworthy manuscript of Portus. Augustine is referring to the passage from Ambrose cited below, chs. 55–56, and also above, *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 1, no. 40, and book 2, no. 15.] could not be without sin, understanding and expounding the apostle Paul as he ought.

But you help the Manichaeans all the more—the more often I have shown this—the more you think yourself alien from them. You are a new heretic, a Pelagian: exceedingly loquacious in disputation, most calumnious in controversy, and most deceitful in profession. Finding nothing to say, you say many empty things; you charge Catholics with a false crime and falsely claim to be Catholic.

### LI. JULIAN

In the third book of my first work I showed that, if natural sin were believed, it would necessarily have to be said that Christ too derived guilt from Mary’s flesh; and that you placed him under the power of the devil when you asserted that the whole substance of human beings belonged to the devil’s jurisdiction.

### AUGUSTINE

What you recall having shown in the third book of your work, I have reproached you for not having shown in my fifth.

### LII. JULIAN

Leaving this aside for the present, I demand to know where you have read that Christ was naturally a eunuch.

### AUGUSTINE

Where did you read that I said this, unless you are making a calumny, as you usually do?

The capacity to beget children is one thing; we do not say that this was lacking in Christ’s flesh, as we know that it is lacking in the flesh of eunuchs. The lust of vices is another thing, which you try to persuade us Christ possessed while boasting that you are a Christian.

For, as you said shortly before, “Christ would also be subjected to accusations of deceit if he said to mortals, ‘Stretch yourselves toward endurance under a man who feels nothing.’” As though it followed that someone who wishes and is able not to have evil desires would not feel inflicted pains.

Or, to compose your own words, if he were to say: “Imitate chastity, overcoming the inducements of your nature, in one whom weakness made appear chaste.”

You are such an excellent lover of chastity that, in your view, the more chaste person is the one who desires illicit intercourse but resists his desire so as not to commit it, rather than the one who does not even desire such evils—not through the impossibility of the flesh, but through the highest perfection of virtue. Indeed, the former is chaste, while the latter is not chaste at all but only appears to be, since, according to you, if he were chaste he would naturally desire these evils but would restrain that natural desire by strength of spirit.

Thus the absurdity I have already exposed follows you: each person is considered more chaste in will the greater the lust of his nature he has overcome and the less he has allowed it to issue into any excess of lust, however great it may be. Whoever restrains a lesser lust for wrongdoing is therefore less chaste, because, according to your wisdom—or rather madness—one who does not desire what is unlawful is not chaste at all.

See what you insanely try to impose upon Christ: that he was by nature the most lustful of all, because by the power of his will he could thus be the most chaste of all. For, as you argue, the spirit of continence would be greater in him in proportion to the greater lust of the flesh that he restrained. [Note: [Col. 1369] The manuscripts read as above. The printed editions have “the appearance is greater.”]

Your exceedingly beloved position has brought you to this destruction.

### LIII. JULIAN

Although he was born of a virgin as a sign, he was not so averse to the male sex that he did not assume its reality. Whole in every respect in his mother’s womb, whole in body, a true human being and a perfect man, if the apostle Peter is to be believed when he speaks in Acts (Acts 2:22, 33), he was conspicuous in untouched chastity, always guarding both his mind and his eyes with the heart’s vigilance never relaxed.

But that he accomplished all this through strength of mind, not through weakness of flesh, is testified by the lust of the flesh, mingled with the senses of his entire body; by the reality, soundness, and condition of his members; and by his sleep, food, beard, sweat, labor, cross, and spear. [Note: [Col. 1370] Printed editions read “flesh,” contrary to the manuscripts.]

He therefore did not lack bodily senses, but governed them. This is why the faith of Catholics insults the Gentiles and the Manichaeans: because the word of the cross, just as the word of his flesh, is foolishness to those who are perishing, but the power of God to those who are being saved.

This is how he commended his love to us: everything that the impiety of Manichaeus tears apart, the piety of the Mediator assumed.

Therefore I am not ashamed of anything in my Lord. I hold to the reality of his members, in which he came for my salvation, so that I may receive the solidity and stronghold of his example.

### AUGUSTINE

The reality of Christ’s members is one thing, which every Christian acknowledges in Christ [Note: [Col. 1370] Vignierius has “every Christian acknowledges: something else,” omitting “in Christ,” which we restore on the authority of the manuscripts.]; the lust of sins is another, which you wish to impose upon Christ.

You say that the lust of the flesh—that is, lust, which you more willingly call “natural desire”—is a good. Yet you condemn its excess in such a way that anyone who allows it to cross the limits conceded to it incurs guilt as one who misuses a good, while anyone who lets it proceed as far as what is lawful and permitted, but no farther, is worthy of praise as one who uses a good well. [Note: [Col. 1370] Thus the manuscripts; Vignierius reads “will be.”]

Since we see that some people are born with greater lust pressing upon them and others with less, if both are chaste by resisting it, you are compelled to say that the former use a greater good well and the latter a lesser good well.

Under your instruction, then, each person will possess more abundantly this good of yours in proportion to how lustful he is; and he will labor more intensely in the struggle for chastity against his lust in proportion to the abundance of this natural good. He will therefore also be more praiseworthy in this virtue in proportion to the strength with which he resists the greater good, than if he resisted a lesser one.

Since Christ unquestionably lived most chastely in mortal flesh, you will consequently assign him a greater natural lust in proportion to the greater strength you cannot find in restraining lust.

Thus, without the charge of deceit, he would say to his followers: “Imitate my chastity, overcoming the inducements of your nature.” For these inducements are good, yet they must be restrained and conquered, just as I had them, but restrained and conquered greater ones, lest you say to me: “You conquered because you lived most chastely in your mortal flesh because, by nature’s good fortune, you had only the smallest lusts, which you could conquer most easily.”

“Be chaste, then, because, in order to remove from you every excuse for imitating me, I wished to be born more lustful than you, and yet I never allowed my greatest lust to cross the permitted limits.”

Your heresy has produced these dreadful monstrosities.

### LIV. JULIAN

I declare that all holiness in him rested upon the gift of the mind, not upon any weakness of the flesh. In this way both his nature is defended by its condition and assumption, and human life is directed by imitation of his virtues.

Of these two, one cannot be praised without the truth of the other: the sacred work will possess as much dignity as the truth of the human body possesses; and the defense of the flesh will be as strong as the holiness of his conduct requires.

Conversely, condemnation of one affects both, since as much will be taken away from his virtues as from his limbs. [Note: [Col. 1371] Thus the manuscripts; printed editions read “deeds.”] If anything is scraped away from the solidity of his substance, the entire adornment of his conduct perishes, and the losses of his birth rebound upon the injury done to his endurance.

Finally, if the substance of his flesh is diminished by the removal of any natural feature [Note: [Col. 1371] The manuscripts read “exception”; the printed editions have “removal.”], the entire display of his virtues vanishes.

Therefore I will deny nothing in the members of the Mediator made from a woman that is known to be natural. And see how different are the limits of reason and of modesty: the Christian faith is not ashamed to say that Christ had genitals, although in us we conceal them as honorably as we can.

### AUGUSTINE

The Christian faith is indeed not ashamed to say that Christ had genitals. But you ought to have been ashamed—or rather, you ought to have trembled lest you say—that Christ’s genitals were at some time, even against his will, aroused by lust. [Note: [Col. 1371] Printed editions read “nor to say,” and shortly afterward, “ought to have wished.” Both places are corrected from the manuscripts.] For he did not at any time ought to have desired this, since he lived a celibate life; and that part of his holy body ought not to have risen toward any illicit use against his holy purpose.

Every class of saints suffers the sort of lust that you try to impose upon the Holy of holies.

If you do not dare say that Christ’s genitals customarily became aroused and erected against his will by lust [Note: [Col. 1371] Vignierius reads “customarily became aroused,” omitting “and erected,” which we add from the manuscripts.], why, wretched man, do you dare believe it? Why do you dare attribute such lust to Christ’s nature that you compel people to imagine what you do not dare say?

### LV. JULIAN

Nature has therefore prescribed that there are certain things which reason, faith, and religion alike pronounce, yet modesty and propriety of conduct do not allow to be exposed to the eyes.

In this way the Teacher of the Gentiles also assigns truth to Christ’s flesh and holiness to his spirit:

“Great is the mystery of piety: he was manifested in the flesh, justified in the spirit, appeared to angels, was preached among the nations, was believed in the world, and was taken up in glory.”

Just as the apostle commended this as something to be believed with truth, so at the end of the age he announced that its opponents would arise. For he immediately continues:

“In the last times some will depart from the faith, attending to deceitful spirits and doctrines of demons, speaking lies in hypocrisy, having their conscience branded, forbidding marriage, and commanding abstinence from foods that God created to be received with thanksgiving by the faithful and by those who know the truth; for every creature of God is good” (1 Tim. 3:16; 4:4).

The contamination of the churches that you have spewed forth from your pursuit of Manichaeus, and the transgression of those who depart from the faith—which consists in proclaiming natural evil and condemning marital intercourse—the Apostle both foresaw and punished, showing not only what would be said but also what would follow from it.

### AUGUSTINE

And yet you, who can do nothing but belch calumnies and vomit insults, did not dare contradict the words of the Catholic man of God, whom you cannot call a Manichaean, when he silenced you by saying that no one can be born without sin from the intercourse of male and female (Ambrose, *On Isaiah*).

I recalled these words of his in my first book addressed to Valerius. You attempted to refute it in four books, but were afraid to touch this point. [Note: Augustine refers to *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 1, no. 40, and book 2, nos. 14–15.] In the work to which you are now replying, I did not keep silent about the same words (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 1, no. 40, and book 2, nos. 14–15). Yet you remain silent before them, although you do not hesitate to accuse me while carefully avoiding the name of the one whom you do not openly dare to oppose.

### LVI. JULIAN

When the Apostle says that abstinence from foods would have to be taught, he does not, among prudent people, condemn Christian moderation or declare that there could be people who would indicate the danger of starvation. Rather, he shows what would follow when people arose who said that all animals, because they were born through lust and sexual intercourse, had been created by God as food for mortals but were polluted by a diabolical evil. He expressed the consequence: namely, that foods would have to be renounced if their propagation were believed to be diabolical.

Accordingly, you remove this charge of bodily intercourse from animals so that the pretense of your argument may remain. Yet you say that human beings, made in the image of God, belong to the devil’s jurisdiction because of the very lust by which they beget children.

Thus you and Manichaeus have one and the same reason for condemning substances and transferring them to the devil. But Manichaeus condemns all living creatures because of the affection felt in the natural act; you condemn not all creatures, but—what is more shameful—the better ones. [Note: [Col. 1372] Thus the manuscripts; Vignierius reads “all.”]

You absolve pigs, dogs, and asses so that you may appear to avoid the Manichaeans; but because of the same thing as Manichaeus, you condemn all human beings made in the image of God. Establishing natural evil nowhere except in the image of God, you preach against us as accuser of the saints and patron of asses.

### AUGUSTINE

What is this that you say, calumniator of Catholics and ally of the Manichaeans? What is this that you say—something of which you ought to be ashamed even if you had an asinine forehead?

Could not someone of the same mind as you call the accuser of the saints and patron of asses a person who said that human beings can become miserable through ignorance of the truth, but that asses cannot be miserable through not knowing the truth? Yet he would speak most truly.

Why, then, do you not understand that it is likewise true that human beings cannot be born without sin from the intercourse of male and female, while asses can?

Do you think you escape the blows of authority and reason pursuing you because, in the fellowship of lust, you yoke human beings and asses to the chariot of your error?

Ambrose was speaking not about beasts but about human beings when he said: “It has therefore been established that, from man and woman—that is, through that bodily intercourse—no one appears to be free from sin” (*On Isaiah*).

Was this man—the doctor of the Church—therefore an accuser of the saints and patron of asses? [Note: [Col. 1373] Vignierius reads: “Was this doctor of the Church therefore …?”]

Certainly the body of both an ass and a human being is corruptible. Yet it does not burden the ass; it burdens the human soul. For Scripture says of the human being: “The corruptible body weighs down the soul” (Wis. 9:15).

So recognize in lust both the nature of the beast and the punishment of the human being, if you do not possess an asinine soul.

### LVII. JULIAN

Christ, therefore, was no less truly human than truly God, and lacked nothing natural. But it was right that, since he gave an example of perfection, he should excel in every pursuit of virtue.

His chastity, exalted by continual integrity and moved by no desire of lust, having remained a virgin in holy mind [Note: [Col. 1373] Codex Port. reads “because.”]; the greatness of his spirit, mastering all the senses; and his triumph over pains—these made him both imitable in his humanity and astonishing in his sublimity to all the faithful.

### AUGUSTINE

You say that Christ’s chastity was exalted by continual integrity. But you are a man to whom chastity does not appear complete when, through the greatness and perfection of a good will, unlawful things are not only avoided but not even desired.

Whoever desires evil things, even if, while resisting his desire, he does not commit them [Note: [Col. 1373] Printed editions read “and not resisting”; corrected from the manuscripts.], fulfills what is written: “Do not go after your lusts” (Sir. 18:30). But he does not fulfill what the law says: “You shall not covet” (Exod. 20:17).

Christ, therefore, who fulfilled the law most perfectly, desired nothing unlawful. He did not possess the conflict between flesh and spirit that, through the transgression of the first man, entered human nature. He was born from the Spirit and the Virgin, not through the lust of the flesh.

In us, however, the flesh desires unlawful things against the spirit, so that it would completely fulfill them unless the spirit also desired against the flesh in such a way as to conquer it.

You say that Christ’s mind mastered all the senses. But what must be subdued is what resists. Christ’s flesh had nothing untamed and did not resist the spirit in anything, so that it would need to be subdued by him.

With this example of perfect purpose before him, every imitator ought to strive toward this: to desire and endeavor not to possess at all the desires of the flesh that the Apostle forbids to be fulfilled (Gal. 5:16). In this way he can lessen them through daily progress, until he has none through perfected salvation.

### LVIII. JULIAN

You have therefore spoken with the utmost profanity, saying that Christ’s flesh did not possess what belongs to human nature. Certainly you drew this not from any reasonable stream of Scripture but from the filth of the Manichaeans, by which you were deceived.

But, to make the abundance of arguments for defending the truth more evident, let us grant that you dreamed that Christ did not possess the lust of the flesh as you describe it—something that had certainly already been condemned, first in the madness of Manichaeus and later in that of Apollinaris. [Note: [Col. 1374] Vignierius reads “wished”; the manuscripts more correctly read “had not wished.”]

What could this support for your doctrine, since it would not immediately follow that something was evil merely because Christ did not wish to assume it? For, as the merits of good things gradually increased, one could say that he advanced through what was best without condemning, by choosing what was higher, the good things placed beneath it.

Just as he did not dishonor marriage by pursuing integrity, so he would not have condemned the sensation of genital flesh if he had not wished to possess its possibility even in his own substance.

### AUGUSTINE

I have already said that Christ not only did not commit unlawful acts but did not even desire them, in order to fulfill the law that says: “You shall not covet.”

This indeed flows from the stream of Holy Scripture into the hearts of the faithful, not from the filth of the Manichaeans, and it extinguishes your heretical doctrine.

You say that I dreamed that Christ did not possess a lust of the flesh resisting the spirit—yet you did not spare even Christ from these dreams of yours.

We know that Christ slept. If this position of yours was in him, then, without doubt, while his senses were asleep such dreams sometimes deceived him, so that he seemed even to have intercourse with himself; and thus, with his flesh aroused by this good of yours, his genitals would be extended in vain and he would discharge useless semen. [Note: [Col. 1374] Vignierius has “if”; the manuscripts have “to himself.”]

If you tremble to believe this about Christ’s flesh [Note: [Col. 1374] Thus the manuscripts; printed editions read “to say.”]—and you are not so stone-like that you do not tremble at it, although I spoke it without a trembling heart in order to refute you—then you must certainly admit that such a lust of the flesh was absent from Christ’s nature not only without any loss but with the praise of perfect virtues, even though we know that such lust is not absent from the flesh of other human beings, including the saints themselves.

You say that it does not follow that this is evil even if you grant that Christ did not wish to assume it, just as he did not condemn marriage merely because he did not wish to marry. This can be said about the lust of animals, which is not evil for them because they do not possess the good of reason, and therefore their flesh does not lust against the spirit.

But whatever resists the spirit of a human being wishing to do good is not good, however volubly you defend it.

Christ therefore abstained from sin in such a way that he also abstained from every desire for sin: not by resisting it once it existed, but by ensuring that it never existed at all—not because he could not have possessed it if he had wished, but because he could not rightly have wished for it, and because the flesh of sin, which he did not bear, could not compel him to possess it even against his will.

Accordingly, that perfect man was not born through lust, which indiscriminately desires both unlawful and lawful things, but from the Holy Spirit and the virgin Mary. Whatever he desired was lawful; whatever was not lawful, he did not desire.

Born from flesh that had conceived through the Holy Spirit, far be it from him to possess within himself any conflict between flesh and spirit.

### LIX. JULIAN

To make the matter clear by some example: it is better to possess reason than not to possess it. Human beings were made rational, whereas animals are irrational.
