Yet it does not follow, merely because human nature surpasses quadrupeds, that quadrupeds should be called either evil or the work of the devil.

Suppose, then, that when Christ formed his members he did not wish to mingle with them the sensation of the genitals, since he would not use it. Did he therefore do something evil when he formed the members of Isaac, Jacob, and all the others, giving them both sex and sensation? Or, when he came to these things [Note: [Col. 1375] Codex Port. reads “or came to these things,” omitting “to.”], did he summon the devil to his aid so that he might mingle necessary pleasures with the members he himself had assembled?

Thus you have not been able to gain anything at all—either in this work or in the earlier one, as we have shown with God’s help—against the divine works through the person of Christ. For it has become clear that the Savior’s body possessed nothing less of human nature.

### AUGUSTINE

On the contrary, it has become clear that human nature now possesses less of all these things—integrity, rectitude, and salvation—than it possessed when it was first created.

Christ came to restore, correct, and heal this nature: whole without any corruption, upright without any perversity, and saved without any desire for sin.

### LX. JULIAN

Accordingly, sin cannot exist in that nature, since in him, in whom it is whole, no iniquity was found.

### AUGUSTINE

You blaspheme monstrously, Julian, by equating Christ’s flesh with the flesh of other human beings and failing to see that he came not in sinful flesh but in the likeness of sinful flesh (Rom. 8:3). This would in no way be true unless the flesh of other human beings were sinful flesh.

### LXI. JULIAN

The lust of the sexes, therefore, whether it was present in Christ’s flesh or was not present, is not shown to be evil or diabolical.

### AUGUSTINE

The lust of the flesh is evil even when it is not consented to for the purpose of evil. For it is the lust by which the flesh desires against the spirit, even when, because the spirit desires against it, it does not accomplish what it attempts—that is, an evil act.

### LXII. JULIAN

I hasten to other matters, but I am held here in profound amazement at what you have said. What such madness possesses you against another, if you do not understand the Scriptures or weigh your own statements? You argue continually in such a way that whatever you cast forth returns upon you with greater force.

You certainly said that there is no cause of shame except the lust of the flesh appearing in the movements of the genitals. [Note: [Col. 1375] The printed editions have “To whom evil?” This has been corrected with the aid of the Portus manuscript.]

### AUGUSTINE

I did not say this. There are other causes of shame as well: either lest something be done that is improper, or because it has been done.

But when the cause of the particular shame we are now discussing is sought, the truest explanation is found in what caused these members specifically to be called shameful. Previously they had not been shameful, when those human beings were upright and perfect, naked and unashamed.

If you had wished to think about this intelligently, you would not have impudently resisted the most obvious truth.

### LXIII. JULIAN

To judge that anything which God is believed to have made is shameful, apart from this lust of the flesh, is sacrilege. [Note: [Col. 1375] Thus the manuscripts; printed editions read “sacrilegious.” They also read “to indicate” for “to judge,” and “shamelessness” for “modesty.”] Yet Christ did not possess this lust of the flesh, which causes shame for mortals.

What answer, then, could you have given to this? You did not see it: namely, that Christ, naked—that is, Christ himself—ought to have joined public gatherings, and ought to have shown no regard for modesty, lest he incur the sacrilege you devise by being ashamed of his own works and those of the Father in his flesh, which did not possess lust.

But if he lacked lust and nevertheless performed the office of modesty, then, even according to you, it is irrefutably proved that modesty is owed to the human body, not to heat.

### AUGUSTINE

By that sharp and refined reasoning of yours, one would have to deny that John’s baptism was given for repentance from sins, because Christ was baptized with it even though he had absolutely no sin.

But if he could be baptized for another reason, not the reason applicable to others—that is, not because of sinful flesh, which he did not possess, but because of the likeness of sinful flesh, which he assumed in order to free flesh from sin—then he could also cover his members for a reason different from that applicable to others: namely, so that he might conform to those who cover their shameful parts, although he himself had nothing shameful.

Just as he was baptized in conformity with penitents, although he had nothing requiring penitence to be washed away, so the things required by sinful flesh were appropriate to the likeness of sinful flesh.

Moreover, the naked appearance of the human body, wherever it is unusual, offends human sight. Therefore the angels who appeared to human beings in human likeness wished to appear clothed, as human custom required.

But if we recall where this custom originated, the cause of the first sin presents itself: those human beings who, before they sinned, were decently and honorably naked in a place of such great blessedness, had not yet been confounded by their flesh, which, having been made disobedient to the disobedient, lusts against the spirit. [Note: [Col. 1376] The printed editions have “of lust”; the reading is corrected according to the manuscripts of Mar. and Port.]

Christ’s clothing therefore does nothing to help you, so that you may not be an impudent defender of the lust of the flesh.

### LXIV. JULIAN

You therefore see that you called it sin without reason, if [Note: [Col. 1376] “If” is added from the Portus manuscript.] we admit that a covering ought to be applied to those works that God made—a covering that our Lord and the fashioner of humanity instituted, and that the man Christ practiced.

Let reverence for the Redeemer grant pardon, since, in asserting the truth of the mystery and destroying the crimes of the Manichaeans, we speak boldly about his flesh. If faith did not demand it, modest reverence would not touch upon it.

### AUGUSTINE

You do not speak boldly about true things concerning Christ’s flesh, but unhappily about false things—not, as you flatter yourself, to destroy the crimes of the Manichaeans, but rather to assist them.

If you intend to defeat the Manichaean, do not say that what is evil is good; instead, explain where the evil comes from, since you cannot show that it is good.

Because you refuse to say with Ambrose that this comes from the transgression of the first man (Ambrose, book 7 on Luke 12), you undoubtedly make the Manichaean boast that he speaks truth about another’s nature.

### LXV. JULIAN

“But this man,” you say, “did not wish to name the lust of the flesh. He is silent because he is ashamed; and, with a remarkable—if it may be said so—shamelessness of shame, he is ashamed to name what he is not ashamed to praise” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 2, no. 17).

You therefore disapprove because, according to the Apostle, we know that our more shameful parts must be covered with the necessary propriety (1 Cor. 12:23), since in this we follow the Creator’s counsel: what he placed in a secret part of the body, we cover with an equally modest covering. [Note: [Col. 1377] Perhaps “we follow.”]

### AUGUSTINE

You make the astonishing claim that Adam and Eve followed the Creator’s counsel when they abandoned his command by following the counsel of the deceiver.

Before they committed this evil, while they were still upright and perfect, did they not follow the Creator’s counsel by leaving naked what he had placed in a secret part of the body and not taking care to cover it with a modest covering?

Most shameless man, it is worse to praise what they felt when they were ashamed than to uncover it.

### LXVI. JULIAN

These different modes of expression—which you not only fail to imitate but even condemn, and whose services assist us—were devised not by the cultivation of all languages but by the refinement of Greek and Latin.

Other languages, which are called natural because the pursuit of wealth or elegance has contributed nothing to them, employ entirely plain names for the members. Thus among the Hebrews, whose language preserves the purity of the Scriptures, everything is designated by its proper terms.

### AUGUSTINE

You are greatly mistaken, as though figurative speech did not exist in Hebrew expression, in which the words are certainly not proper but transferred.

But whatever the case may be, how does this help you? [Note: [Col. 1377] This sentence is omitted in the printed editions: “But whatever the case may be, how does this help you?” It is restored from the manuscripts.]

In the sacred Hebrew Scriptures it is certainly written both when those first human beings were naked and were not ashamed, and when they were confounded by their nakedness and what members they covered (Gen. 2:25–3:7), so that we might know what they felt and from what they were confounded.

If you wish to cover in this matter the source of your own shame, then at last be silent.

### LXVII. JULIAN

With the same confidence with which the feet and knees are named, the genital organs of both sexes are also named. For my part, even when authority supports this usage, I have not neglected the aids of more decorous expression, since neglect of propriety is rightly open to criticism, and decorum must be preserved in words no less than in actions, insofar as the nature of the case permits. Therefore, because natural concupiscence could not be convicted by the reproach of shame, and was defended by the dignity of its Creator, it was vindicated from the jurisdiction of demons and placed among the works of him who made the world and the bodies—not as though it were some great good, since it is common to human beings and animals alike, but as a necessary instrument for the sexes. No one accuses the bodies except Manichaeus and his heir, the Traducian; thus it becomes clear that the whole fiction of natural sin, whose entire support rested upon accusations against nature, has completely vanished.

[Note: [Col. 1377] Vignierius reads *absit* (“may it be absent”); Marcellinus Clarus reads *adsit* (“may it be present”); Codex Port. reads *sit* (“is”).]

[Note: [Col. 1377] Vignierius reads *apparet autem* (“but it appears”). The particle *autem* is redundant and is absent from the manuscripts.]

### AUGUSTINE

Here you are still calling it “natural concupiscence”; here, as far as you can, you are still concealing what your adopted cause is, so that it cannot be understood, beneath an ambiguous garment of words. Why do you not say “concupiscence of the flesh,” but instead say “natural concupiscence”? Is not the concupiscence of blessedness natural concupiscence? Why do you speak ambiguously? Give the thing you have undertaken to defend its proper name. What are you afraid of? Or, perhaps disturbed by its bad cause, have you forgotten what it is called? Rather, with your memory fully alert, you do not wish to call it “concupiscence of the flesh.” For you know that those who have read this expression in the holy Scriptures only in reference to an evil reality are offended by its praise.

But by using this name and calling it natural concupiscence, you try to place it among the works of him who—as you say, and as is true—made the world and the bodies, although John says that it is not from the Father (1 John 2:16). God certainly made the whole world and all bodies. But for the corruptible body to weigh down the soul, and for the flesh to desire against the spirit, is not part of the prior nature of the human being as created; it is the subsequent punishment of one condemned.

“You say,” you continue, “that no one accuses it except Manichaeus and his heir, the Traducian.” I am glad to receive your insults together with those whom you dare to blame in me, though you do not dare to name them. Does the one who says that the concupiscence of the flesh, against the spirit, was changed into our nature through the transgression of the first man not accuse your adopted cause? (Ambrose, Book 7 on Luke 12.) And who is this? Clearly the man whose faith and utterly pure understanding of the Scriptures even your enemy has not dared to criticize, just as your author Pelagius praises him (Pelagius, *On Free Will*, Book 3; cited in Augustine, *On the Grace of Christ*, §§46–47). Defend your adopted cause against this accuser. Revile this teacher of mine, and that teacher of yours who praises him, for it, as much as you can, so that you may demonstrate that your patronage is sufficiently free and faithful; lest desire, having you as its defender, abandon you as timid—although it will find no other who blushes less on its behalf.

### LXVIII. JULIAN

For this reason I necessarily asked what the devil could claim as his own in the sexes, by which he might rightfully harvest their fruit, since he had neither joined together the flesh, nor formed the limbs, nor given the genital organs, nor distinguished the sex, nor ordered marriage, nor endowed with honor or sprinkled with pleasure the intercourse without which marriage cannot exist.

### AUGUSTINE

The devil had indeed done none of these things. But he had persuaded the human mind to disobedience, which was followed by the punitive and shameful disobedience of the flesh; from this original sin would be derived, through which whoever was born would be subjected to the devil, and would perish with that same devil unless reborn.

### LXIX. JULIAN

In these arguments, then, attempting to confront you with the fear of a stag and the cunning of a fox, you imposed this upon the patron to whom you were writing: that, because of the natural sense of the body—that is, the concupiscence of the flesh—the prince of darkness ruled over the works and image of God; whereas it was necessary that the same author be assigned the sense of the flesh to whom the nature of the flesh also belonged.

[Note: [Col. 1378] Codex Port. reads *discessionibus* (“departures”); the printed editions read *dissertionibus* (“arguments” or “discussions”).]

### AUGUSTINE

You do not know what you are saying. The sense of the flesh is one thing; the concupiscence of the flesh is another. The latter is perceived through the sense both of the mind and of the flesh, just as the pain of the flesh is not itself the sense, but cannot be perceived unless sensation is present.

Through the sense of the flesh, which is called touch, rough and smooth things, like other things, are perceived differently. But through the concupiscence of the flesh, lawful and unlawful things are desired without distinction; they are judged not by desiring but by understanding, and one abstains from unlawful things only by resisting concupiscence.

Evil works therefore are not avoided unless evil concupiscence is restrained. Yet you, with horrifying shamelessness—or rather madness—call this concupiscence good. You neither blush nor shudder that you have reached such disgrace, that no one is delivered from his evil unless he does not consent to your good.

The concupiscence of the flesh, by which forbidden things are desired, is therefore not from the Father. You think—or rather wish others to think—in vain that when the apostle John said this, he meant concupiscence of the flesh as a term for sexual excess. Quite plainly, if sexual excess is not from the Father, neither is that from the Father which, when consent is given to it, conceives and gives birth to sexual excess. For by those movements to which we are commanded to resist, what, I ask, is it attempting except to reach sexual excess?

How, then, is that good which attempts to reach evil? How is that our good which attempts to reach evil? How is that our good which compels us toward evil?

[Note: [Col. 1379] The word *jubemur* (“we are commanded”) has been restored from the manuscripts.]

[Note: [Col. 1379] Vignierius reads: “How, then, is that good which attempts to reach evil? How is that our good which drives us toward evil? It must be healed,” and so forth.]

This evil, then, must be healed, Julian, by divine goodness—not praised by human vanity, wickedness, and impiety.

[Note: [Col. 1379] Vignierius reads “by wickedness and impiety praised.”]

### LXX. JULIAN

It is therefore evident that you did not strive to refute the objections, but to mock pitiably the patron to whom you were writing; and he might have thought that you had brought forward some crude matter which you could rightly attack, although by your concession concerning the preceding points and the creation of bodies you had already praised it.

### AUGUSTINE

I praised the creation of bodies, which is good even in an evil person—not the evil without which no one is born. Since you refuse to say with Ambrose from where this evil comes, you assist Manichaeus, who says that it comes from another nature.

### LXXI. JULIAN

I nevertheless admit that you thought far too carefully about what you should say; your talent and your diligence are evident. You weighed with great skill what ought to be asserted in support of the transmission of sin. No one else could have written more cunningly in favor of natural evil. You yourself could not have presented it so artfully unless the inventions of your old teacher had aided your talent.

### AUGUSTINE

I proudly declare that my teacher, both against you and against Manichaeus, is Jesus. I confess—although you deny it—that Jesus also belongs to little children, because Adam perished, and in him all perished (Ambrose, Book 7 on Luke 15:24). They are saved from perdition only by him who came to seek what had perished (Luke 19:10).

### LXXII. JULIAN

You understood, indeed, that since little children merit nothing of their own, guilt could not be attached to them without the condemnation of their bodies. For that reason, the assistance of Manichaeus was necessary, so that he might exclude the concupiscence of the flesh from the works of God and assign both marriage and the bodies themselves to the devil as their creator.

### AUGUSTINE

I have no need of Manichaeus’s assistance. Rather, by fighting against him, I repel the assistance you provide him with the help of God. God grants me this help also through his most illustrious companions—not only through the Prophets and Apostles, whose words you perversely attempt to distort [Note: [Col. 1380] This is the manuscript reading; the printed editions read *prorsus* (“altogether”)], but also through the later teachers of his Church: Irenaeus, Cyprian, Hilary, Ambrose, Gregory, Basil, John, and many others, soundest in faith, keenest in intellect, richest in doctrine, and most renowned in reputation.

All of them, while preserving the praise of bodies and marriage, confessed original sin, knowing that Christ—something you impiously deny—is also the Jesus of little children. For he saves his people, among whom those little children also belong, not from fevers and other such diseases and accidents—for in his abundant goodness, surpassing all flesh, he grants this even to non-Christians—but, as Christians, from their sins (Matthew 1:21).

You do not shrink from calling these so many and such great sons and fathers of the Catholic Church Manichaeans, though they taught this from her summit after learning it at her breast. When you attack me alone as though openly, you accuse them all the more obliquely, and therefore all the more treacherously—and the more treacherously, the more wickedly. Your own words entirely convict you in this great crime. You slander me with that most abominable name for no other reason than that I say of original sin what they say.

### LXXIII. JULIAN

Your retreat from the truth, then, and your flight from it, were caused by the deformity of the cause you defend.

[Note: [Col. 1380] The marginal reading of Codex Port. is *diffunderis* (“you are spread abroad”) for *defunderis* (“you are poured away” or “you depart”).] But if you wished to pass over to the Catholics, you would carry out and complete what we assert with far greater elegance.

[Note: [Col. 1380] Vignierius reads *tu* (“you”); the manuscripts read *tute* (“you yourself”).]

### AUGUSTINE

O tongue-filled face and blinded mind! Are those not Catholics to whom I cling in the fellowship of this faith, which I defend against your empty words and curses? Are Irenaeus, Cyprian, Hilary, Ambrose, Gregory, Basil, and John of Constantinople—not to mention others and repeat the same names—not Catholics? And are Pelagius, Coelestius, and Julian Catholics? Dare to say this, if you can. If you do not dare, why do you not rather return to those from whom I do not depart? Why do you admonish me to pass over to the Catholics? Behold the Catholic lights; open your eyes. You pass over to those whom you slander through me, and at once you will restrain yourself and fall silent concerning me.

### LXXIV. JULIAN

Although I would not dare to pronounce you lacking in sharp and vigilant intelligence, I do see in your choice to undertake this task a judgment that is so slow and deformed.

### AUGUSTINE

Tell us, then, from where slow intelligences arise. For Adam was not made such. You refuse to admit that through his sin human nature was changed for the worse, and that this harms those who are born with respect to all the vices they suffer.

[Note: [Col. 1381] The editions omit this entire response of Augustine, although it is present in all the manuscripts. Augustine presses Julian with the same argument below, Book 5, chapter 11.]

### LXXV. JULIAN

If, with completely sound faith, and in the manner of a student merely displaying the power of your learning, you attempted to shake things that cannot be overthrown, intending nevertheless, when the playful contest was over, to award the palm to those whom you had opposed, we would approve your literary study but censure its irreligious example.

But since you pursue with the most shameful obstinacy a doctrine not even coated with the corrupted color of plausibility, which you cannot defend with any testimony of the law—for such testimonies never prejudice reason—and which nevertheless, horrifying in its impiety, prostrate in its stupidity, is pierced by decency, argument, and sacred law nowhere except among the private parts of desires, one of three conclusions follows: either you must be judged to possess a leaden sharpness of understanding, or to be held in the chains of that sorcery which, as we have heard, belongs to the mysteries of the Manichaeans, or to suffer both at once.

[Note: [Col. 1381] Codex Port. reads *voluptatum* (“pleasures”) instead of *voluntatum* (“desires”).]

### AUGUSTINE

However much you may appear to fight against the divine testimonies we bring before you in the name of reason, you do not overthrow them. They torment you when you kick against the goad.

[Note: [Col. 1381] *Cum* (“when”) is added here from Codex Port.]

Say, as much as you can, “among the private parts of desires,” to the man who tells you that one conceived through the intercourse of the two sexes is not free from sin (Ambrose, *On Isaiah*). This is Ambrose, Julian. He defeats you, and you would not dare deny that he is a Catholic; you certainly will never call him a Manichaean. Defend your adopted cause against this accuser.

Moreover, you affirm that I am either leaden in understanding, or held by Manichaean sorcery, or suffering both at once. We have already answered you often enough concerning Manichaean sorcery and your insult, and perhaps we shall answer again at a more appropriate time, when necessity requires it.

Now answer concerning the leaden sharpness of understanding, verbose heretic. Surely no one would refuse, if it lay within human power, to be born intellectually vigorous and extremely sharp in understanding. And who does not know how rare such people are? Yet even all those very few, when compared with the intellect of the first human being who was made, are judged dull as lead.

For at that time, unlike now, the corruptible body did not weigh down the soul (Wisdom 9:15). Either it was not corruptible, because Adam would not have died unless he had sinned; or, if—as you recent heretics say—he would have died even had he not sinned, he was nevertheless not created in such a way that his soul would be weighed down by his body, since God had made him first and he had not yet done anything evil.

Who would deny that this is punishment, except one who is weighed down more heavily than others? If, then, Manichaeus asks from where comes this evil of slowness—not in bodies but in the very human intellects in which the image of God exists, a slowness that gradually proceeds as far as laughable—or rather, as Scripture warns, lamentable—foolishness (Sirach 22:10), we answer that this and all the other evils with which we cannot deny or doubt that human beings are born must be attributed to the sins of the first two parents and of those who followed, since they cannot be attributed to the will of those being born.

As for other animals, if some are born with the defects of their kind, why should it be surprising if harmful spirits take them into their power, just as they took possession of pigs, as we know (Matthew 8:32)? These evil spirits can corrupt the very seeds of animals, just as human beings corrupt the limbs of irrational animals.

The question concerns human beings, in whom the image of God would never suffer the punishments of the various defects with which we see them born—punishments that could not be unjust—unless the preceding sins of those who beget them had caused them. By denying this, you abandon the Catholic faith and assist the wicked doctrine of Manichaeus, as far as he himself would not have dared hope, so that he may appear certain and secure in refusing to confess the true God as the maker of human beings and in introducing a race of darkness.

[Note: [Col. 1381] The words “and he had not yet done anything evil” have been restored from the evidence of ancient books.]

[Note: [Col. 1381] Perhaps *homines* (“human beings”) should be supplied after “with which we are born.”]

[Note: [Col. 1382] The printed editions, together with Marcellinus Clarus, read *mentem* (“mind”); Codex Port. more suitably reads *gentem* (“race” or “nation”).]

### LXXVI. JULIAN

We, however, have nothing in our intellect of which we should believe ourselves worthy of admiration, because we understand that neither sin can exist without the will, nor bodies without God, nor the senses of bodies without bodies, nor marriage without intercourse, nor those who are born without God as the agent. We firmly hold it as indubitable that nothing taught to be unjust is divine, and that nothing divine can be taught as unjust.

It is no less clearly unjust than the things we have mentioned if the sins of some are imputed to others who were not there, much less consented. Therefore, enlightened by these suns, we rightly despise the caverns of the Manichaeans [Note: [Col. 1382] The manuscripts read *Manichaeorum* (“of the Manichaeans”); Vignierius reads *Manichaei* (“of Manichaeus”)], who think either that sin can exist without the will; or that human beings are not made by God; or that the sense of bodies belongs to one author and bodies to another; or that there is a God who is overwhelmed by accusations of iniquity; or that the one regarded as the eternal creator of all is pressed down by the crime of injustice; or that justice retains any shadow of legitimacy if the wills of some are attached to those who have come into being from others.

Accordingly, we attribute the merits of the parties to their deeds, not to their intellects.

### AUGUSTINE

I have already answered everything you have said. Your arguments are not strengthened against me merely because you repeat them so often and so offensively. Say instead, if you can, from where human intellects are generally born with such great corruption, when we agree that God, who made the whole human being, is just, while you deny any original sin.

You would not say that we impute the sins of some to others who were not present when they were committed if you recalled what is written: Levi was in Abraham’s loins when Abraham was tithed by Melchizedek, priest of the Most High God (Hebrews 7:9–10). There you would see, if obstinacy did not blind you, that the human race was in Adam’s loins when he committed that great sin.

### LXXVII. JULIAN

But let us return to the case. After you said that I had not wished to name concupiscence because it was not from the Father but from the world, whose prince the devil is called; that he found it not in the Lord, because the Lord came to human beings as man not through it (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, Book 2, §41).

Here it must be noted that, although you were speaking of a natural reality and had said that it was from the world, you added that the devil ought to be regarded as prince of the whole world, thereby confessing him to be the author not of voluntary acts but of natural things—that is, of natures.

### AUGUSTINE

Where I wrote “concupiscence of the flesh,” you removed “of the flesh,” which I had said. And where I wrote “the devil is called the prince of the world,” you added “whole” and said “the prince of the whole world,” which I did not say.

Do as you please; say what pleases you, or even what pleases those whom you please. I said “concupiscence of the flesh,” which John says is not from the Father but from the world (1 John 2:16)—that is, from human beings who are born in the world and will perish unless they are reborn in Christ.

This concupiscence of the flesh is not sexual excess when it is resisted; it is sexual excess when it is fulfilled, that is, when it reaches the point toward which it drives. Hence the apostle Paul says: “Walk by the Spirit, and you will not fulfill the desires of the flesh” (Galatians 5:16). He did not say, “You shall not have them,” for he knew that this gift would indeed be ours, but would not belong to the present life.

I said that the devil is the prince of the world, just as divine Scripture calls him that (John 12:31; 14:30; 16:11), not as your vanity suspects or slanderously alleges. I did not therefore say that the devil is the author of natures, but that he is the prince of the world—that is, of human beings, with whom the world is filled, who are born in the world and are not reborn in Christ.

For those who are reborn in Christ cast out the prince of the world. This is signified by the mysteries when even little children who are to be baptized are exorcized and exsufflated. Answer these points, if you can.

Do not try, with your extremely verbose vanity, to make the reader vain, to turn him away from and lead him astray from the matter at hand. Say, if you dare, that desiring evil is good. Say that evil works are not from the Father, but that the concupiscence of evil works is from the Father. Say that the devil was not called the prince of the world. Say that the world does not mean the human beings established in the world. Say that the world cannot be understood in the evil sense as unbelieving human beings, with whom the world is filled throughout the earth, and again in the good sense as believing human beings, with whom, though fewer, the world is likewise filled throughout the earth, being similarly called “the world”—just as it is not absurd for a tree full of fruit to be said to be full of leaves as well.

Say that, when little children are baptized, they are not rescued from the power of darkness, and that throughout the entire Catholic Church the images of God are exorcized and exsufflated with great insult to God. Or say that they are possessed by the devil without any bondage of sin.

If you dare to say these things, you will soon be exposed. If you do not dare, you will not thereby remain hidden.

### LXXVIII. JULIAN

After saying this, then, you added: “Hence the Lord himself also says, ‘Behold, the prince of this world is coming, and he found nothing in me’” (ibid., 14:30). And you added from yourself: “Certainly nothing of sin, neither what is drawn from one at birth nor what is added by one who lives.”

Show, then, that the Lord said in the Gospel that he did not have the sin that would be drawn from one at birth.

[Col. 1384]

### AUGUSTINE

You show that the Lord said that he had no stain, without which Job says that not even an infant exists, whose life upon the earth is only one day (Job 14:4, according to the Septuagint). Nevertheless, when he says, “Behold, the prince of this world is coming, and he will find nothing in me,” we do not understand even that stain to be present, if we understand correctly.

For if, from what he said, we are to understand what he did not say, then he did not name the devil, but called him the prince of the world. And he says, “He will find nothing in me”; he does not say, “He will find no sin in me.” Yet we state things he did not say, understanding them from what he did say.

### LXXIX. JULIAN

Why do you deceive unhappy souls, lying that what has not been shown has been shown?

[Note: [Col. 1384] The manuscripts read *indicatum* (“shown”); Vignierius reads *judicatum* (“judged”).] The Lord says in the Gospel: “Behold, the prince of this world is coming, and he found nothing in me.” It is certain that the devil found no sin in him, since he was overcome in every temptation—whether the temptation by which he tested the one who was hungry or the one whom he later proclaimed—as though he had brought persecutors against him.

The Savior therefore declares that the devil found no sin in him. He would certainly have found some if anything had been drawn from the condition of the flesh, since he too had been made from a woman, born from the seed of David and from a stock descended from Adam.

### AUGUSTINE

But the virgin had not conceived him through the concupiscence of the flesh. Therefore the propagation of the flesh passed into him without the propagation of sin, so that in him there was not sinful flesh but the likeness of sinful flesh, which would save sinful flesh.

Accordingly, before Adam sinned, he had neither sinful flesh nor the likeness of sinful flesh, because he would not have died unless he had sinned. But after he sinned, sinful flesh already begot sinful flesh, because he begot it through that concupiscence of the flesh which before sin was either entirely absent in him or did not resist the spirit; for that reason, he was not ashamed to be naked.

Christ, however, was not born through that concupiscence of the flesh. He was therefore born without sin, which all sinful flesh draws along with it, plainly on account of which all die, although he himself did not possess sinful flesh. Nevertheless, he too died because of the likeness of sinful flesh.

For if he had not died, he would not only have lacked sinful flesh—as he did—but would also not have displayed its likeness, which he had assumed for our salvation.

You, therefore, who cannot deny that Christ came not in sinful flesh but in true flesh nevertheless in the likeness of sinful flesh, must demonstrate what sinful flesh is. For if there is none, there is certainly no likeness of it.

Since Christ alone had the likeness of sinful flesh without being sinful flesh, because he was not born through sexual intercourse, what remains except that the flesh of all who are born from such intercourse is sinful flesh? They belong to the world whose prince is the devil, and they are not delivered from that evil unless they are reborn in Christ.

[Note: [Col. 1384] The manuscripts read *cum* (“with”); the printed editions read *eam* (“it”).]

### LXXX. JULIAN

The devil would therefore have found natural guilt in him, if any existed. He would have held the body subject to it if he had poisoned it either in the first parent or in the mother herself. It would not matter whether the intention of the will, delayed and rendered ineffective by the conditions of its material, resisted nature: struggling against nature, it would not purge the one born but would exasperate the tyrant. Apart from the fact that the will could not have been free if nature had been captive.

If sin existed in the very sense and condition of the flesh, if human nature itself belonged to the dominion of demons, Christ would either have become guilty or would not have become human. Therefore, if a curse is attributed to the nature of humanity, then either guilt will also be attributed to him who became flesh in order to dwell among us, or his humanity will be taken away.

[Col. 1385]

### AUGUSTINE

Neither will guilt be attributed to him, in whom the prince of the world could find no sin, nor will his humanity be taken away, since he possessed both a human soul and human flesh—although he did not possess sinful flesh, but the likeness of sinful flesh.

### LXXXI. JULIAN

The Manichaean did both: having imagined that evil exists naturally in the flesh, he said that Christ did not possess flesh, lest he confess that in him there was iniquity.

### AUGUSTINE

The heretic Manichaeus denies that Christ had flesh. The Pelagian heretic wishes to equate sinful flesh with Christ’s flesh. The Catholic Christian distinguishes the likeness of sinful flesh from sinful flesh, so as not to blaspheme Christ’s flesh.

[Note: [Col. 1385] The word *carni* (“with flesh” or “to flesh”) has been added here from the manuscripts.]

### LXXXII. JULIAN

But the Catholic faith has crushed this man in both respects, declaring that evil is not naturally present in the flesh and therefore that Christ lacked nothing of humanity and possessed no iniquity.

The one conscious of his dispensation therefore cries out: “Behold, the prince of this world is coming, and he found nothing in me”—certainly nothing that could accuse him, because he could not defame a nature whose will he had not bent toward sins.

### AUGUSTINE

Rather, there was nothing of sin in him—neither what is drawn from one at birth, because he was conceived in no iniquity, nor what is added by one who lives, because he was deceived by no temptation. The first is why we read, “In iniquities I was conceived” (Psalm 50:7); the second is why we say, “Lead us not into temptation” (Matthew 6:13).

### LXXXIII. JULIAN

The very reason for tempting Christ was that the devil wished, according to his customary art, to capture him by persuasion, since he could corrupt no one by creating.

### AUGUSTINE

He does not corrupt by creating, since he creates no one. He corrupted by evil persuasion what he found created good. For he is not the author of the nature that is created in human beings by the goodness of God, but of the fault with which a human being is born from parents descended from the corrupted first human beings.

What wonder, then, if he tempted the one in whom there was no sinful flesh? Sinful flesh was not present even in those whom he first cast down by tempting them. Through their concupiscence of the flesh, concerning which they were ashamed, sinful flesh was propagated; the likeness of sinful flesh, which possessed no evil, would heal it from this evil.

[Col. 1386]

### LXXXIV. JULIAN

Therefore Christ’s incarnation vindicates the work of his divinity. Bringing my nature to me and his will—of which he offered me a mirror and a rule—and declaring that the devil found no sin in him, he shows that guilt does not arise from the creation of the flesh but solely from the will that assumes it.

Finally, just as nowhere in the Scriptures is Christ said to have fled from the sin that he knew was drawn from those being born, so it is also clearly demonstrated by testimony that the justice of the human being he assumed rested not upon a difference of nature but upon voluntary action.

### AUGUSTINE

You say that it is “nowhere written that Christ fled from the sin which he knew was drawn from those being born.” What would he flee from that he himself had not drawn, but had come to save those who had drawn it? What, I ask, would he himself flee from, since no one flees from it except by fleeing to him?

You also say that “clear testimony demonstrates that the justice of the human being assumed by the Son of God rested not upon a difference of nature but upon voluntary action.” Is it really the case that Christ did not even have this difference in nature: that he was born from a virgin in such a way that he was already not only the Son of man but also the Son of God?

Did this assumption, which made God and man one person, contribute nothing to the excellence of justice in that man, which you say arose in him from voluntary action? Has your defense of free will driven you headlong against the grace of God to such an extent that you say even the Mediator, in order to be the only Son of God, earned this by his own will? And do you say that what the whole Church confesses is false: that it believes in Jesus Christ, the only Son of God the Father almighty, our one Lord, born of the Holy Spirit and the virgin Mary?

According to you, the Word of God did not assume a man so that he might be born from a virgin. Rather, after being born from a virgin, he advanced through the power of his own will and caused himself to be assumed by the Word of God. He did not possess such a great will through that assumption; he reached that assumption through such a great will. The Word did not become flesh in the virgin’s womb; rather, this happened later through the merit of that man and through his human, voluntary virtue.

From this it also follows that, just as you believe he was assumed by the Word of God because he willed it, so you must believe that many others could have been assumed in the same way if they had similarly willed—or could be, if they should will it. Thus human sluggishness of will would make him the only one, although there could have been many if human beings had willed it.

If you say these things, where is your shame? If you do not say them, where is your heresy?

### LXXXV. JULIAN

The apostle Peter says: “Christ died for us” [Note: [Col. 1386] The manuscripts read “for you”], “leaving you an example so that you might follow his footsteps, who committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth” (1 Peter 2:21).

Certainly the Apostle’s statement agrees with the Lord’s voice. The Lord says in the Gospel: “The prince of this world came, and he found nothing in me” (John 14:30). The teacher of the Church confirms the same thing and says that there was no sin in Christ. But he explains by what means he did not have sin, with a truthful testimony: “Because,” he says, “he committed no sin.” He did not say, “Because he did not assume sin,” but, “Because he committed no sin.”

### AUGUSTINE

Certainly, the one who did not draw original sin had no sin, because he committed none—just as Adam himself, because he did not have original sin, would have had no sin if he had not committed any.

### LXXXVI. JULIAN

But if guilt existed in nature, Peter’s statement was uninstructed.

[Note: [Col. 1387] Codex Port. reads *imperfecta* (“imperfect”) for *imperita* (“uninstructed” or “unskilled”).] He would have judged that the testimony of spotless holiness could be satisfied if Christ’s acts were free from crimes, while it was believed that sin dwelt in him through a natural poison.

Therefore, if he had perceived anything concerning natural evil, he would have mentioned this matter more carefully and emphatically, writing: “Christ left us an example, who neither committed sin nor acquired the sin that we draw by being born;” and then it would rightly follow that no deceit was found in his mouth.

Moreover, if he had thought this, he would never have mentioned him as an example. Whom would he have shown to human beings as worthy of imitation if an external nature of the flesh had distinguished him, and if the difference of substance had condemned the standard of his teaching?

[Note: [Col. 1387] The manuscripts read *externae* (“external”); Vignierius reads *externa* (“external,” agreeing with a different construction).]

[Note: [Col. 1387] Codex Port. reads *discresset*, apparently an orthographic form of *discrevisset* (“had distinguished”).]

[Note: [Col. 1387] The manuscripts read *censuram* (“the standard”); Vignierius reads *censura* (“judgment” or “censure”).]

### AUGUSTINE

Others certainly understand how empty your statement is, even if you do not. When the apostle Peter proposed Christ to human beings as an example to imitate, what need was there for him to say anything about original sin, as though anyone could, by imitating Christ, bring it about that he was born without original sin, as Christ could? In the same way, no one could imitate Christ so as to be born, as he was, of the Holy Spirit and the virgin Mary.

Therefore, in order that we may imitate Christ, our will is formed; but in order that we may be freed from original evil, our nature is regenerated.

### LXXXVII. JULIAN

Moreover, the opinion of natural sin would not only diminish the force of emulation; it would also undermine the credibility of the praise bestowed upon him. With what gravity, with what confidence, could one say that there was no deceit in his mouth, if he had come in a different condition of flesh from ours? He would then be convicted of having acted deceitfully in evil not only by teaching, which is the lesser matter, but also by being born, which is the greater.

What sort of thing would it be for him to compel human beings established in natural evil and under the kingdom of the devil, sinning under the pestilential necessity of inborn corruption and naturally serving the law of sin that ruled in their members, to imitate him even under threat of punishment, and to impose his justice upon human beings of that flesh? He had been so terrified by its evil that, although he wished to express an image of holiness under its appearance, he nevertheless avoided the truth of its nature.

How much more rightly would the sickness of sinners and the security of those under compulsion say to him: “When we are well, we all give sound advice to the sick” (an allusion to Terence, *Andria*, Act 2, Scene 1, line 9); “if you were as we are, you would think very differently indeed”?

What, then, has your impiety accomplished? Necessarily, if sin is believed to exist naturally in our flesh, Christ must either have assumed this flesh and become subject to this evil, or he did not assume it and was defeated—not by the falsehood of his birth, but nevertheless by the irresolvable iniquity of voluntary fraud.

Since the whole of this is so foul with such great blasphemous filth that it can scarcely be set forth without horror, even when it is being torn apart, let the dignity of the Mediator attend his example and work, and our faith, which vindicates the truth both of him and of the words of his Apostle. It never ceases to proclaim that Christ, true man, assumed from the womb of Mary flesh of the same nature as ours; that he was true in every respect as a human being; and that he had no sin.

To indicate this, it is enough for the apostle Peter to say that he committed no sin, teaching that one who had not committed sin could not possess it. “No deceit was found in his mouth.” He offered a holy example to those who shared his nature, the nature that he himself had made in all respects. Therefore it is clear that sin is not innate, since Christ did not possess it—Christ who, while preserving the honor of his divinity, became flesh for this very purpose: that he might be imitable for us.

[Note: [Col. 1387] Perhaps *argueret* (“would undermine” or “would accuse”) should be read instead.]

[Note: [Col. 1387] Codex Port. reads *putaret* (“would think”); *imperaret* (“would command” or “impose”) appears to be the preferable reading.]

AUG. What then, you very talkative and very foolish man, if people were to say to Christ, “Why are we commanded to imitate you? Were we born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary? Finally, can we possibly have as much virtue as you, who are so human that you are also God, and in this respect coeternal with the Father and equal to the almighty Father in omnipotence?” Was he therefore not to be born in this manner, or taken up in this manner by the Word of God into the unity of his person, lest men unwilling to imitate him be given such an excuse?

Yet Christ himself set before us the Father for imitation, although the Father was certainly never a man; and whoever both wishes and is able, through his grace, to imitate him without any diminution or weakening of his divinity—by loving their enemies and doing good to those who hate them—does not say to him, “You can do this because you are God, and because your enemies can do you no harm; but we are weak human beings, and we are commanded to love those who inflict so many and such great evils upon us through their persecutions.” In the same way, Christ’s imitators do not say to him, “We cannot do the things which you exhort us to do by your example, because your excellence is far greater than our weakness.” Therefore he did not need, because he was born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary, to have a desire by which he might desire evil things—even if, by resisting it, he did not do them—lest people say to him, “First acquire evil desires, and conquer them if you can, so that by conquering ours we may be able to imitate you.” [Note: The printed editions have *et sic* (“and thus”). The manuscripts correct this to *etsi* (“even if”).]

Moreover, Julian, what do you say about the one who says, “I do not do what I want, but I do what I hate” (Romans 7:15)—the one whom you assert is oppressed even to this necessity not by the desire with which he was born, but by an evil habit? Did Christ not provide such people with an example for them to imitate? Did he despise them and wish them to remain strangers to the practice of his virtues? If they were to say to him, “You do not know what we suffer under the burden of the habit that oppresses us. You are not oppressed by it, and therefore you speak as you do. When we are well, we all readily give sound advice to the sick,” would you be pleased if Christ too were oppressed by such a habit and overcame it, so that, once their excuse had been removed, he might be imitated by such people? Or will you now laugh at your own empty talk and be silent before us?

**LXXXVIII. JUL.** Once these matters have been dealt with as the situation required, I am glad to confront you, even if only moderately, concerning the confidence with which, while praising Jerome’s writings, you say that there was no sin in Christ, although in that *Dialogue* which he composed under the names of Atticus and Critobulus, with remarkable elegance and in a manner befitting such a faith, he attempts, by the testimony of a “fifth Gospel” which he says he translated, to show that Christ possessed not only natural but also voluntary sin, because he recognized that he needed to be cleansed by John’s baptism.

He also fastens upon him an accusation of falsehood from another testimony of the evangelist John. [Note: The printed editions have *affuit*; this is corrupt for *assuit* (“fastens upon”).] Concerning this work, in the letter which you sent to Alexandria, you boast in such a way as to say that Pelagius, overwhelmed by the mass of Scripture which Jerome had brought against him, could not defend free choice. But that work was answered by a Catholic man who had been attacked. I have now recalled it only so that you might recognize that you agree neither with the holy Scriptures nor even with the supporters of your own doctrine.

[Note: Julian seizes upon Jerome’s words in the third book, chapter 1, of the *Dialogue against the Pelagians*: “In the Gospel according to the Hebrews—which is indeed written in the Chaldean or Syriac language, but in Hebrew letters, and which the Nazarenes use to this day—according to the Apostles, or, as most people think, according to Matthew, and which is also kept in the library at Caesarea, the narrative relates: ‘Behold, the mother of the Lord and his brothers were saying to him: John the Baptist baptizes for the remission of sins; let us go and be baptized by him.’ But he said to them: ‘What sin have I committed, that I should go and be baptized by him? Unless perhaps this very statement is itself ignorance.’” Jerome does not say in this passage that he translated this Gospel into Greek and Latin, but says so in the *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*, in the chapter on James, the brother of the Lord.]

**AUG.** If you had quoted Jerome’s words, perhaps I could have shown how they ought to be understood without the blasphemy which you are trying to impose upon him. Even if I could not do so, I would not therefore think that his faith—which he held together with the other eminent teachers of the Catholic Church—should be rejected merely because something might be found in his writings, if indeed it were found, in which he did not agree with them.

But against you, speaking of this man himself, it is enough for me that, although he holds the same view of original sin which you reject so vehemently that you call me a Manichaean for holding it, [Note: Perhaps read *inde me*: “call me a Manichaean on that basis.”] you nevertheless do not dare to call him a Manichaean. Here it is clear that you are deceived by imprudence, but that you accuse me contrary to your own prudence.

For my part, I opposed you not with a sentence recalled from Jerome, but with one recalled from Ambrose; and not a sentence expressed in my own words, but in his (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 1, no. 40, and book 2, nos. 14–15). In that sentence he says that Christ could not have been free from sin in any other way than by being free from that conception which is produced by the union of man and woman. Here you see that it follows that if I am a Manichaean because of this opinion, Ambrose too must be one. But since he is not, this opinion neither makes nor demonstrates anyone to be a Manichaean. Although you see this—for it is not such a thing that you cannot see it, or can fail to see it—you are nevertheless so abandoned by the goodness of your case that you slander me with the name of Manichaean, not through unwitting ignorance but through shamefaced deceit. [Note: So read all the manuscripts. The printed editions have: “not through shameless ignorance but through shameless deceit.”]

**LXXXIX. JUL.** You abandon the Manichaeans when they condemn swine and goats, although you accompany them in their condemnation of human nature; and together with them you overthrow in Christ not the appearance of flesh, but the force of his example. For the moment, you remove natural sin from Christ in your words, lest you also appear to place him under the power of the devil—something even the Manichaean himself did not do.

But you praise Jerome [Note: Vignierius reads *quia* (“because”); the old Portus codex reads *qui* (“who”).], who did not fear to blaspheme Christ in such a way as to say that he had also entered into familiarity with voluntary crimes. Thus, rolling about without deviation amid the various filth and fictions of your friends, you vent your fury solely upon Catholics because they say that God is not the author of evil; that human beings created by him are not naturally evil; that God’s laws are just; that his image can turn away from evil and do good; and that Christ committed no sin either in his members, in his commands, or in his judgments. Therefore, although you may be distressed by an assertion of the truth, we nevertheless believe that the prudent are being instructed and that some even of those whom your lies have wounded can be healed.

**AUG.** I answered you above concerning Christ’s example: we must neither deny his excellence—by which, although he was a completely upright man, he was nevertheless born of the Spirit and conceived without fleshly concupiscence [Note: The printed editions read *concupiscentiae*; all the manuscripts read *concupiscente*.], and lived the most righteous life of all human beings—nor use that excellence as an excuse for failing to strive to imitate him according to our measure.

Faithful married people do not imitate his celibacy; nevertheless, so that they may not commit adultery or any illicit intercourse, they do imitate him. Nor, if those who lead a holy celibate life imitate him more fully, can they for that reason imitate him in this also: that he not only did not commit illicit acts, but did not even desire them. For one leading a holy celibate life, every intercourse is illicit, since not even marital intercourse is licit to such a person.

What, then, is surprising if one born of the Spirit [Note: Vignierius has “of the Holy Spirit.” The word *sancto* is absent from the manuscripts.] and the Virgin had no evil in himself? Who, unless weighed down by more serious evils, would deny that there is an evil against which even the saints daily ask the Father at the Lord’s instruction? For when we say, “Do not bring us into temptation” (Matthew 6:13), we ask God to protect us against our concupiscence. “Each person is tempted,” as it is written, “when he is drawn away and enticed by his own concupiscence” (James 1:13).

Therefore, may this Father whom we ask turn concupiscence away from us, rather than permit us to dare say that what the concupiscence of the flesh draws us toward is not from the Father, while the concupiscence itself which draws us is from the Father; or that what it draws us toward is evil, but that the thing which draws us is not evil. But if the truth proclaims that concupiscence is evil, then surely the one who was born without any evil did not possess it; and consequently, just as he did not commit sin, so he did not desire sin.

We imitate him, then, when we do not commit sin—not by lacking the concupiscence of sin, but by not consenting to it. Nevertheless, when we live well, we imitate that Holy One of holy ones in such a way that there remains a reason for us to say in our prayer, “Forgive us our debts” (Matthew 6:12).

I did not praise Jerome in the way Pelagius praised Ambrose, saying that even an enemy did not dare criticize his faith and his most pure understanding of Scripture (*On the Grace of Christ*, nos. 46–47). Accordingly, if something displeases me, I criticize it in the writings of a friend just as I do in my own. [Note: The printed editions have “in the writings of an enemy.” The manuscripts more appropriately read “in the writings of a friend.”] But it is one thing for a Catholic to err in some place, and another to establish or maintain a heresy of great error.

**XC. JUL.** Let this suffice for now; let us come to the matter in which a large part of the dispute is concentrated, and by whose force the Manichaean ambassador, examined and exhausted, produced evidence of his fidelity in answering as impressive as his intelligence was elegant.

After he had praised and approved my statements quoted above, without anything new intervening, he proceeded to the part in which the argument promised by us was completed. For when I asked by what means those whom God had made were under the devil, I replied in his own name, “By sin, not by nature.” Then I added on my own behalf, “But just as, as you yourself acknowledge [Note: The Portus codex reads *non abnuis* (“you do not deny”).], a fetus cannot exist without the sexes, so neither can sin exist without the will.” Do infants, then, have a will at the time of their conception, although they do not yet have a soul? Or do they have one at the time of their emergence, although they do not yet have the use of reason?

When he reached this point, he proposed only this from our objections: “But just as a fetus cannot exist without the sexes, so neither can sin exist without the will.” And he replied, “Yes indeed, so it is; for ‘through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death, and so it passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned’” (Romans 5:12). “Through the evil will of that one man all sinned in him, when all were that one man; and for this reason each individual drew original sin from him” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 2, no. 15).

I therefore urge the reader to examine our conflict attentively. What did it profit you, most learned of bipeds, not to complete my statement, when, even if the explanation of the earlier statement were contained in the part you suppressed, the entire force of the argument would nevertheless reside equally in what you yourself brought forward?

I faithfully stated what you yourself usually report, as your agreement also made clear [Note: Vignierius reads *manifestatur* (“makes clear”); the manuscripts read *manifestavit* (“made clear”).]; and when I asked by what means infants whom God had made were under the devil, I answered on your behalf: “By sin, not by nature.” Surely you see that I committed no deception here. I stated what is in the mouth of the Traducianist, although it is not part of the doctrine. To this I added: “But just as a fetus cannot exist without the sexes, so neither can sin exist without the will.”

By shameless deceit you made this divisible: for when recalling what we had said—“Just as a fetus cannot exist without the sexes, so neither can sin exist without the will”—you kept silent about what followed concerning the will of infants, and replied, “Yes indeed, so it is: for ‘through one man sin entered the world’; through the evil will of that one man all sinned in him.”

Is this an answer? Is this argument? Is this, finally, even a regard for sobriety? Learned people certainly laugh at the cleverness of sophisms when, through the sharing of terms, the simplicity of the respondent is mocked. Those very sophisms, although not solid in truth, are at least colored by an urbane surface; but this monstrosity of an argument is neither solid in truth nor smoothed over by sophistry.

I certainly said that sin cannot exist without free will. Once this is conceded, your doctrine is destroyed, since you think that there is guilt in human nature without any will whatever.

**AUG.** I had read only that part of your work which was contained in the little document sent to me. Later, when I found your books from which someone had excerpted that passage, I answered all of it.

We too say that sin cannot exist without free will. Nevertheless, our doctrine is not destroyed, as you claim, when we assert the existence of original sin. For even this kind of sin was reached through free will—not the free will of the one who is born, but of the one in whom all originally existed when he corrupted the common nature by an evil will. [Note: So read the manuscripts. The printed editions have: “because this too.”]

Infants therefore do not have, at the time of their conception or birth, a will to sin. [Note: The printed editions add *liberam* (“free”).] But that first man, at the time of his transgression, committed that great sin by free will, and from that free will human nature contracted the contagion of original sin, so that the holy man most truthfully said, “I was conceived in iniquities” (Psalm 50:7); and another holy man likewise said, “Who indeed is clean from defilement? Not even an infant whose life upon the earth is one day” (Job 14:4, according to the Septuagint). These utterances of truth mock the vanity of your loquacity.

**XCI. JUL.** With what impudence, then, do you both approve my statement and refuse to abandon your doctrine, when the statements of the two parties cannot be joined by any agreement, since their opposed propositions cannot both share in the truth?

Just as, if I agreed that sin is natural, I would necessarily have to abandon the authority of the statement which maintains that sin cannot exist except in free will, so you, by agreeing with me that I spoke correctly when I declared that no sin exists without the will, ought immediately to have rejected the opinion by which you believed sin to be natural.

**AUG.** It is one thing to say that sin cannot exist without free will—which we too say, since original sin could not have existed without the free will of the first man—and another thing to say, as you yourself did, that sin cannot exist except in free will, which we do not concede.

For original sin is not in the will of the one being born; yet it is not in the will of the first man either, although it could not have existed without that will. It is one thing, therefore, to say, “Sin cannot exist without the will,” and another to say, “Sin cannot exist except in the will.”

For if we correctly say, “Without conception there cannot be a birth,” it does not follow that we can correctly say, “A birth cannot exist except in conception.” These are so different that conception cannot exist either in conception or in birth. Sin, however, can exist in the will, as it did in the case of the first man; and it can also exist not in the will, as is the original sin of every person being born, which is entirely in no one’s will—but not without the will of that first man.

That holy man too who said to God, “You have sealed up my sins in a bag and marked down whatever I have committed unwillingly” (Job 14:17), certainly did not have in his will the sin which he committed unwillingly. What of the one who says, “I do not do the good that I want,” and immediately adds, “but the evil that I do not want, that I do” (Romans 7:15)? Is he to be said to have sin in his will, according to your own position, since you want him understood to be compelled by the force of habit to sin against his will?

Stop, then, slipping in through proximity and gradually crossing the boundary, so that because we say “without free will,” you assert that we are saying “sin cannot exist except in free will”—as if we were to say, “Coal cannot exist without fire,” and you were to claim that we were saying, “Coal cannot exist except in fire.”

If you did not know this, admit that you were not an intelligent disputant. But if you did know it, then you were an unintelligent man to hope that you would have an intelligent reader.

**XCII. JUL.** For it is obvious that whatever is natural is not voluntary.

**AUG.** If whatever is natural is obviously not voluntary, then our wish to be saved and blessed is not natural. Who would dare say that except you? Or perhaps, once warned, not even you.

**XCIII. JUL.** If, then, sin is natural, it is not voluntary; if it is voluntary, it is not innate. These two definitions are as contrary to each other as necessity and will are contrary, and the confirmation of each arises from the mutual negation of the other. For just as the voluntary is nothing other than what is not compelled, so the compelled is nothing other than what is not voluntary. These two therefore cannot exist simultaneously or, as it were, live together, because their nature is such that one lives only when the other is extinguished.

**AUG.** Why do you not notice that sin can also be involuntary, certainly in the case of the one who says—whatever the reason for his saying it—“If I do what I do not want, it is no longer I who do it, but sin dwelling in me” (Romans 7:19)? Why do you not notice that there is also a necessity by which we must wish to live happily, and, with your eyes closed, oppose one to the other as though the will could not belong to necessity or necessity to the will? [Note: Vignierius, together with the manuscripts, has “so he opposes one to the other”; the word *alteri* is omitted. The manuscripts preserve it.]

**XCIV. JUL.** Since, then, this is so unshakable that it cannot be overturned by any argument, choose whichever you prefer and consistently affirm either our statement or your own, so that you may attribute guilt either to necessity or to the will.

When I say “whichever you prefer,” I am not warning you as though your opinion were still hidden—you who have learned through the Manichaean to introduce accusations against nature—but I say this so that the truth of your argument may be exposed.

**AUG.** Whether you like it or not, since you say this so often, you must also hear this so often [Note: Vignierius, together with the manuscripts, reads *cur* (“why”).]: the man who said that the dissension between flesh and spirit was turned into nature through the transgression of the first man was not a Manichaean (Ambrose, book 7 on Luke 12).

By denying this as the cause of this evil with which every human being is born [Note: The printed editions read *malum* (“evil,” accusative); the manuscripts more aptly read *malo* (“evil,” ablative).], although you are not allowed to deny that everyone is born with this evil, you make the Manichaean say that another nature has been mixed into us, and he will prevail unless he perishes, overcome together with you.

**XCV. JUL.** Let the prudent and attentive reader weigh what you have answered me. We are certainly speaking of infants, who have no will of their own minds, and concerning whom the question is by what means they are under the devil, although God made them and you agree that they themselves have done nothing evil.

You proclaimed that they belong by right to the devil because of sin, not because of nature. Our reply rose up against this: “But just as a fetus cannot exist without the sexes, so neither can sin exist without the will.” To this you replied, “Yes indeed, so it is”—that is, sin cannot exist without the will. Yet after affirming this, with what impudence [Note: The old Portus codex reads *qua pudentia* (“with what modesty”).] did you add, “But through one man sin entered the world, through the will of that one man”?

**AUG.** Because the discussion concerned infants, was I therefore not to show that what you had said was also consistent with my position—that sin cannot exist without the will—since even original sin has no cause except the will of the one from whom the origin itself is derived?

Although you had said this with an opposing intention, I nevertheless replied that it was not opposed to me and conceded that it was true; and I showed what you had not seen—how it was not opposed to me.

For according to your intention you could have said that sin cannot exist without the personal will of the one whose sin it is. If you had said this, I certainly would not have conceded it; for original sin is transmitted without the personal will of the one being born. [Note: So reads the manuscript of Portus. The other manuscripts, together with the printed editions, have *eadem* (“that same”) instead of *enim* (“for”).]

Nevertheless, you did speak truly in saying that sin cannot exist without the will, because original sin itself was brought about by the will of the one who first sinned by that will through which human nature was corrupted. Thus whatever human beings were born through the concupiscence of the flesh—which is veiled by the confusion of the guilty—would not be freed from guilt unless reborn through the grace of the Spirit.

**XCVI. JUL.** Were you being questioned about Adam’s actions, or had it been asked whether he had sinned by his will? That question will indeed soon be brought against you. Let it be that you enjoy mocking others; how deformed it is for you to impose upon yourself! I cannot persuade myself that you suffer such great deformity through opinion rather than fraud.

In one and the same sentence you agree that sin cannot exist without the will, and immediately add that the sin which you had not said could remain without the movement of a free mind reigns in all human beings without the will.

**AUG.** Why do you insert your own words as though they were mine, so that anyone hearing or reading this, without noticing it, is deprived of my meaning? I did not say that sin cannot remain without the will, but that it cannot exist without it.

How great the difference is, I shall make clear from your own words. When you said, “A fetus cannot exist without the sexes,” who would not agree that you spoke the truth? A fetus does not exist in any other way than through the sexes of male and female. But if you had said, “A fetus cannot remain without the sexes,” who would grant that this was true? A fetus remains without the sexes of its parents, although it could not exist without them; nor do the parents who caused it to exist themselves cause it to remain.

So too, sin—which cannot exist without the will—can remain without the will. Thus Adam’s sin also, since it is the very thing which remains originally in his descendants except in those to whom it is forgiven in Christ, is plainly said not to exist in them without the will only insofar as it is referred to that will by which it came to be that what remained in his descendants should exist—not to the will by which it came to be that what already exists should remain and could now remain without the will.

But if you say that “to exist” is the same as “to remain,” I will not quarrel over words; I simply state that, insofar as remaining is concerned [Note: Vignierius reads *quantum altius ad manendum*; the manuscripts read *quantum attinet ad manendum*.], every sin can exist without the will. For who is there who would even wish the sin which he did not commit willingly to remain? And yet sin remains against the sinner’s will when it was committed by the will. It therefore remains until it is forgiven; and if it is never forgiven, it will remain forever. For it was not falsely said in the Gospel, “He will be guilty of an eternal sin” (Mark 3:29).

**XCVII. JUL.** Furthermore, since a difference of prepositions is found in many statements, you said, “Sin cannot exist without the will,” and you replied, “But sin exists through the will of one man.” Does the response that follows, introduced by the preposition governing the accusative case, agree with the earlier definition, which is fortified by the preposition governing the ablative case?

The question was whether guilt could exist without the will, and it had been established that it could not. You added that sin entered through one man, although the question was not through what it had begun, but without what it could not exist. [Note: The manuscript of Portus reads: “Then why is there now much dissonance and diversity in the prepositions?”]

**AUG.** I said that sin cannot exist without the will in the same way that we say that apples or grain cannot exist without roots. In this matter, even without offending grammarians, we can say that apples or grain cannot exist except through the root.

Since, then, both expressions are correctly used—although one is stated with a preposition governing the ablative and the other with a preposition governing the accusative—why do you spread snares for us from the cases of nouns, like spiders’ webs, becoming weaker the more subtly you weave them? Go catch dying flies in those little nets. The men whom we follow in order to scatter your little traps were not like that.

The Apostle was not like that when he said, “The body is dead because of sin” (Romans 8:10). Hilary was not like that when he said: “All flesh is from sin, that is, derived from the sin of Adam our parent.” [Note: So read the manuscripts here. The printed editions have *parente* (“parent”) rather than *parentis* (“of the parent”), as in book 1 of *Against Julian*, no. 9.]

Ambrose was not like that when he said: “We are all born under sin, and our very birth is in corruption” (*On Repentance*, chapter 2 or 3).

Would that you might instead be caught firmly and beneficially in the nets of these fishermen of Christ! Then, corrected, you would decline the accusative case—by which you yourself have been accused by yourself—and the ablative case—by which you have been removed from the Catholic Church—more properly. But if you follow the prepositions correctly and without corruption, why do you not, laying aside your arrogance, place these teachers of the Church before yourself?

**XCVIII. JUL.** Surely the detestable theft is apparent, and it was immediately punished by the retribution that clings to sins: namely, before it could advance into the destruction of its hearers, it ensnared its own author.

For, behold, it is not denied that the first man incurred some sin; rather, the question is how this sin could be found in those being born. Define what you think was the condition of the first sin. You say, “It was voluntary; for sin cannot exist without the will.” We approve this.

But you then add, “This sin, which cannot exist without the will, clings to those being born without the will.”

**AUG.** It clings through contagion, not through choice.

**XCIX. JUL.** What you had conceded is therefore false: that sin does not exist without the will. For although it was committed through the will, it could nevertheless pass to others without the will.

**AUG.** What I conceded is not false, because original sin was not made without the will of the one from whom the origin of those being born derives. But what could not be committed by him without the will could pass to others without the will through contagion.

Consequently, it could not exist without the will in order that there might be something which could pass into others without the will—just as grain could not exist without roots in order that there might be grain which could pass into other places without roots. [Note: Here we add from the manuscripts: “without the will.”]

**C. JUL.** Sin therefore now exists without the will, since it is found in those from whom you remove the evil will. [Note: So reads the manuscript of Portus. Mar. has “from whom you remove the evil of the will”; the printed editions have “from whom you remove evil wills.”]

**AUG.** Sin certainly exists without the will—that is, it remains. For it would not remain unless it were something that could remain; but for there to be something that remained without the will, it was brought about only by the will—provided that sin is merely sin and not also punishment, for through punishment each person sins unwillingly.

Thus both statements are true: sin cannot exist without the will, and sin can exist without the will—just as both are true of a fetus: it cannot exist without the sexes of its parents, and it can exist without the sexes of its parents. The first statement is made because without them it cannot come into existence; the second because without them it can remain.

You yourself spoke well in one place of both sin and a fetus when you said: “Just as a fetus cannot exist without the sexes, so neither can sin exist without the will.” Therefore, just as we understand that a fetus cannot exist without the sexes of its parents because without them it cannot come into existence, and that it can exist without the sexes of its parents because it can remain without them once it already exists, why should we not understand sin in the same way: that it cannot exist without the will because without it it cannot come into existence, and that it can exist without the will because it can remain without it once it already exists?

**CI. JUL.** See, then, where your acumen leads you: you are trying to persuade us that something does not exist by means of that through which it can exist.
