**AUG.** What then, you great defender of free choice—even against the grace of God—will you deny that something can fail to exist through free choice although it can exist through free choice? [Note: The printed editions read *per quod liberum arbitrium*; the manuscripts read *per liberum arbitrium*.] Sin comes to exist through free choice when a person sins if he wishes; and sin fails to exist through free choice when a person does not sin if he does not wish to.

Behold, we have found something—and the very thing under discussion—which does not exist through that by which it can exist: that is, through free choice. What is the matter, contentious man? Is this where my acumen will lead? Or have your eyes here lost their sharpness? Do not be hasty. It is better to attend to what you are saying than to contend merely in order to contradict.

**CII. JUL.** That is, sin exists without the will through that by which it cannot exist without the will.

**AUG.** Sin is certainly not without the will through that by which it cannot exist without the will; rather, the two occur through different causes, and yet both are possible. It cannot exist without the will because without the will it cannot come into existence; but it can exist without the will because what has come into existence can remain without the will.

**CIII. JUL.** Thus its condition loses itself through its own condition, and it exists without that without which it was defined as unable to exist. This is to deny reality. What did Anaxagoras ever say like this, who maintained that snow is black?

You are inventing a denial of the nature of something through its own consequences. Although necessity and will are contrary, so that, as we showed above, they destroy each other by mutual opposition, you subject one to the effect of the other through a new and impossible alliance and a monstrous relationship. You say that necessity arose from the consequences of the will, so that the will destroyed itself by its own multiplication and, having produced its own state, changed it; and, to express the matter in its own terms, after the will began to exist, it ceased to be will. [Note: Vignierius has “on account of which the will began to exist.” The manuscripts have “after the will began to exist,” as also below in Augustine’s response.]

What could be imagined more obtuse—or, I will not say obtuse, but more insane—than this? Since these two things cannot exist together, namely necessity and will, and since you have affirmed what we said, that sin cannot exist without the will, and have also agreed that there is no will in infants, you are forced, with your throat twisted, to acknowledge that there is no sin in them—although you professed that sin cannot exist without the will.

AUG. You would not say that necessity and will cannot exist simultaneously if you knew what you were saying. For since there is a necessity of dying, who can deny that there can also be a will? Hence the Apostle says that he desires to depart and be with Christ (Phil. 1:23). Therefore, when one who must die wishes to die, necessity and will exist together—something which you had denied could occur through a vain will, with no necessity.

But that necessity also frequently arises from will, and is contrary to will, is utterly foolish to deny. For one who voluntarily inflicts a mortal wound upon himself dies even if he does not wish to die. Likewise, one who voluntarily commits a sin [Note: [Col. 1398] So the manuscripts. Vignierius reads: “has committed.”] has sin unwillingly: unchaste willingly, guilty unwillingly. The sin remains against his will, although it would not have occurred without his will. Thus sin both cannot exist without will, because it is committed only by will, and can exist without will, because what was done voluntarily remains even against the will. And necessity too can exist without will, when will has produced it without necessity.

For even the man who says, “I do not do what I wish,” is plainly oppressed, according to you, by the necessity of habit [Note: [Col. 1398] The word “of habit” is restored here from the manuscripts.]. Yet, lest you take freedom of choice away from him, you insist that he made this necessity for himself by his own will. And you do not believe that something of this kind occurred in human nature: that, from the will of the first man, from whom the human race derives its origin, the necessity of original sin arose in his descendants.

Behold: what you proposed as impossible has become possible through the force of habit—habit which was not without reason called by some “a second nature.” You said that we speak something more absurd than the man who said that snow was black, “so that sin should lose its own condition through its own condition, and exist without that without which it has been defined as unable to exist.” Does it not lose its own condition through its own condition, so that through the force of habit it comes to exist without will, when habit itself was produced only by will? Is not the nature of this thing denied in its effects, since habit is the effect of will, being generated from will, although what it does claims that it does not do by will?

You say that “necessity and will are contrary, so that they destroy one another by mutual opposition,” and on this basis you accuse us of “subjecting one to the effect of the other, saying that necessity arose from the effects of will,” although you see that the necessity of habit is the most evident effect of will. Has not what seemed impossible to you—“the will destroyed itself through its own multiplication and changed its proper condition by what it produced”—happened when repeated will produced the necessity of habit [Note: [Col. 1398] Vignierius: “produced the necessity of its own habit.” “Its own” is absent from the manuscripts.]? If, on your authority, necessity destroys will, has this not happened? But if it does not destroy it, surely in a man weighed down by the mass of habit the will of righteousness and the necessity of sin can exist together.

[Col. 1399] “For to will lies close beside me”—this is a declaration of will; “but to accomplish the good I do not find” (Rom. 7:15, 18)—this is a confession of necessity. Yet [Note: [Col. 1399] Vignierius reads “thus”; the manuscripts read “you.”] you said that will and necessity cannot exist together, although you see that they exist together when they agree and exist together when they fight.

That other point is laughable, which you put forward as impossible—“nothing,” you said, “more obtuse, or rather more insane, can be imagined than that, after will began to exist, it ceased to be will”—as though this did not happen when a person begins to will something evil, then immediately repents and ceases to will it.

Nevertheless, while speaking in this way, you say that with “a twisted throat” you “force me to concede that there is no sin in infants,” although you do not, even with a twisted throat, break the bond of Catholic truth—by which, unless you agree with it, you are most wretchedly strangled.

**CIV. JUL.** But as for what you added—“Through one man sin entered the world”—although, as has been shown, you placed it most incongruously here, how it is to be understood was explained in the second book. But now that the present discussion has been completed, I wish to reconsider your most acute [Note: [Col. 1399] Portarus reads: “most carefully considered.”] statement. For you say: “Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death; and so it passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Rom. 5:12). “Through the evil will of that one man, all sinned in him, when all were that one man; and for that reason each individual drew original sin from him” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 2, no. 15).

“You say,” I repeat, “that they sinned when all were that one man.” But I had already marked that you wrote this to Marcellinus (*On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, book 1, no. 11, and book 3, no. 14). By this testimony you are convicted of believing and embracing the transmission of souls, taken especially from the very entrails of Manichaeus [Note: [Col. 1399] Perhaps “taken” should be feminine, referring to *tradux* understood as feminine.], whose views I inserted in the third book. This is so deformed that, although you indicate it, you dare in no way to profess it openly. But let us defer this for the moment; it is strangled both by the obscenity of its first advocate and by the fear of its successor—that is, by your fear.

For the present, however, it is useful to observe how greatly you are thrown into confusion in argument. You say: “Through the evil will of that one man, all sinned in him, when all were that one man.” If all were that one man, how did all sin through his evil will, when all those whom you say were in him could have sinned by their own will? Indeed, to turn the argument back upon you, how much more wretched was he than all the rest, since he alone bears the blame, although, according to your doctrine, all sinned in him!

Therefore infants possessed a will—not merely before they were born, but before their great-grandparents were generated. They exercised freedom of choice before the seeds of their substances were laid down. Why, then, are you afraid to say that at the time of their conceptions they possess a free will by which they do not naturally draw sin but voluntarily commit it, if you believe that those conceived today [Col. 1400] possessed, so many ages ago, awareness, judgment, and the effectiveness of will? You did not hesitate to state this in the books you published under Marcellinus’s name, plainly to show the madness by which the enemies of God are possessed. For there you say: “Those infants sinned in Adam, so that they might be created like him” (*On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, book 1, no. 11).

What could sound more deceitful, more insane, and more foul than “they sinned beforehand so that they might be created”? That is, by acting they earned the right to exist as beings capable of action; and their action was older than their substance. It is enough to point out that such inventions are more appropriate to orgiastic rites and thyrsi (Dionysian wands) than to literature.

From this, then, arose the reply in which you say that all sinned in him when that one man was all, and that each individual drew original sin from him. There is no need here to labor to demonstrate that, since will is the act of a person, will cannot exist before the person whose will it is. Rather, I want it chiefly understood that, even according to this opinion, there is no original sin. For if all who sinned were there, they drew nothing from an original evil, because all of them perpetrated it by their own efforts.

The transmission of sin, therefore, is destroyed not only by Catholic truth but also by all the arguments of its own advocate. Such is the nature of falsehood: it does not preserve consistency in its pretense, but, prodigal of shame and covetous of what belongs to another, exposes itself in everything it has appropriated.

**AUG.** The Apostle said that sin entered the world through one man in whom all sinned, and Ambrose understood him in that way. But Julian attempts to twist the same apostolic words into his own perverse meaning. Why does Ambrose himself not answer him? Listen, then, Julian. “All,” he says, “die in Adam, because through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death; and so it passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned. Therefore the guilt of that one man is the death of all” (*Commentary on Luke*, book 4, on 4:38).

Listen to something else: “Adam existed, and in him we all existed; Adam perished, and in him we all perished” (*Commentary on Luke*, book 7, on 15:24). Tell him, if you dare, that when one soul sinned by its own will, so many souls could not perish because they did not yet possess their own wills.

Argue [Note: [Col. 1400] Vignierius reads “And accuse”; the manuscripts read “Accuse.”] against my hesitation concerning the origin of souls, since I do not dare to teach or affirm what I do not know. You may produce whatever pleases you concerning the profound obscurity of this matter. Nevertheless, let this sentence remain fixed and unshaken: “The guilt of that one man is the death of all,” and “in him all perished.” Hence the last Adam came to seek and save what had perished (Luke 19:10).

Tell him: “Then these people also sinned by their own will, those whom you say perished in him who sinned by his own will.” But Ambrose could understand what you cannot: that this is not said on account of the free choice of individuals, but on account of the origin of the seed from which all were destined to come. According to that origin, all were in that one man, and all were that one man, though none of them yet [Col. 1401] existed as individuals in themselves.

According to this seminal origin, Levi too is said to have been in the loins of his father Abraham when Abraham was tithed by Melchizedek. Thus Levi himself is shown to have been tithed—not in himself, but in him in whose loins he was. He neither willed nor refused to be tithed, because he had no will when, according to his substance [Note: [Col. 1401] The Mar. manuscript omits “substance”; perhaps “will” is to be understood there.], he did not yet exist himself. Yet, according to the principle of the seed, it was neither falsely nor vainly said that he was there and was tithed.

For this reason, from the tithing of Abraham’s sons who were in his loins when he gave a tithe to the priest Melchizedek, the one priest was alone excepted to whom it was said: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109:4). Although even he, according to the flesh, is Abraham’s seed, because the Virgin Mary, from whom he took flesh, was descended from that seed, he is nevertheless not subject to the same seed, since he was not conceived from male seed and is free from the bond of generative concupiscence.

So do not, as I was saying, address Ambrose any longer, but address the one who wrote to the Hebrews and said [Note: [Col. 1401] Vignierius reads “hence”; the manuscripts read “him.”]: “And, as one might say, through Abraham even Levi, who receives tithes, was tithed; for he was still in the loins of his father when Melchizedek met him” (Heb. 7:9–10).

Attack him with blind loquacity and say, if you dare: “When Abraham was tithed by his own will, how could Levi be tithed—that is, give tithes [Note: [Col. 1401] The printed editions read “a tenth be given”; corrected from the Portarus manuscript.]—through Abraham’s will, when Levi had no will, because he did not yet exist at all?” By the same reasoning, or rather by this error, you say to us: “When the first man sinned by his own will, how could those who did not yet have their own wills sin simultaneously in him through his will, since according to their substance they did not yet exist as individuals?”

Rather, cease your empty chatter. If you can, understand that all those who had not yet been born and could do nothing good or evil by their own wills could sin in the one in whom they existed according to the principle of the seed, when he sinned that great sin by his own will and corrupted, changed, and subjected human nature in himself—except for the one man who, although begotten from that seed, was not produced according to the principle of the seed. If you cannot understand, believe.

**CV. JUL.** After this reply, he attempts to wipe away another point on which I had challenged him. For after I had inquired about the will of infants, I continued: “But you deny that this exists in those being born—that is, a sinful will—and yet you say that infants are under the devil, nor do you conceal the basis on which you think they live under his power. For you say: ‘Because they are born from the union of the two sexes, they are under the power of the adversary.’”

Thus, from his own testimony, it was clear that he delivers infants over to the devil for this reason: that they were born from the union of the two sexes. By this I showed that he had enslaved to the devil marriages instituted by God, which cannot exist without sexual union.

[Col. 1402] **AUG.** You could not establish this by any reasoning, although you tried with great persistence. Those who read both your accusations and my refutations can see that.

**CVI. JUL.** This, then, he now set before himself and prefaced with my question. “You say, then,” he says, “that they are under the devil because they are born from the union of the two sexes?” Let us hear what sort of answer he offers. “I plainly say,” he says, “that they are under the devil because of sin. But they are not free from sin for this reason: they were born from that union which, without shameful lust, cannot accomplish even what is honorable.” The most blessed Ambrose of revered memory also said this (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 2, no. 15). O the disastrous perversity of the man! O the wicked intention! O the falsity deserving of shame!

**AUG.** Exclaim, exclaim as loudly as you can; add to your exclamations, “O violence!” [Note: [Col. 1402] “O bia” or “O vis!”—“O violence!”] For an innocent man is subjected to violence, so that you are compelled to call Ambrose a Manichaean. “God forbid,” you say, “that I should say so.” Why, I ask? Are you showing here how great is the strength of free choice, when you endure such violence that you say it, and yet do not say it?

Why, then, do you call me what you do not call him, when he said long before what I am now saying, and when, in this position for which you call me a Manichaean, he and I share the same ground? Or, since you cannot find a way out, are you merely pretending to be angry and, though not angry, crying out in confusion?

Yet in your very exclamations I hear: “O the disastrous perversity of the man!” That is, I am a wretched and perverse man because I choose to agree with Ambrose; but I would be blessed and upright if I chose to agree with Julian.

I hear: “O the wicked intention!” Our intention is wicked because we set Ambrose against Julian; but it would be good if we placed Julian before Ambrose.

But what is this third exclamation of yours that I hear: “O the falsity deserving of shame!” Do you say that Ambrose’s opinion is false—that is, that he himself thought falsely? Or that we falsely attribute it to him, since he did not think this and did not say at all what we say he said? Or that, because we do not understand it, we falsely form an opinion about it, although it is itself true [Note: [Col. 1402] Vignierius: “to form a false opinion, since it is false.” The manuscripts read: “to form a false opinion about it, although it is itself true.”]?

But you do not speak so insultingly of Ambrose as to attribute to that man a falsity deserving of shame [Note: [Col. 1402] In Vignierius: “But you do not speak so insultingly of Ambrose as to attribute to that man a falsity deserving of shame.” M.]. You did not dare to say that we composed this statement and falsely pretended that it had been uttered by him. For so many of that teacher’s writings are known that you feared to hurl yourself into such a precipice.

Yet the statement is so clear that anyone who understands it seems not acute but merely unnecessary if he thinks it needs explanation. Finally, so that what I am saying may be considered, I shall place here the very words of that most blessed Catholic bishop.

He says—he whose faith and utterly pure understanding of Scripture your Pelagius says that not even an enemy dared to criticize (*Pelagius, On Free Will*, book 3)—when he was speaking about the Lord’s birth:

“Therefore, although he was tested in all things as a human being and endured everything in the likeness of human beings, yet, since he was born from the Spirit, he abstained from sin. For every human being is a liar, and no one is without sin except God alone. It was therefore maintained,” he says, “that no one who comes from man and woman—that is, through that union of bodies—should appear to be free from sin; but whoever is free from sin is also free from such a conception” (Ambrose, *On Isaiah*).

Since you do not deny that Ambrose said this, and since you see that it is plain and clear, why do you cry out, “O the falsity deserving of shame”? To whom is it deserving of shame, I ask—to him or to me? If to him, consider whom you are insulting; if to me, consider how you are slandering me.

“But you also say this,” you reply. I certainly do, because it is true. If you do not think it true, why, in one and the same statement—which he says and I say—is he not a Manichaean, while I am one? How much more justly do we exclaim here: “O the shameful acceptance of persons!” It would undoubtedly force you to blush, if your brow resembled your mouth.

**CVII. JUL.** Does this man dare to say that he is not a condemner of marriage, and with so great a deception delude inexperienced ears by saying that he has withdrawn from fellowship with Manichaeus—he who, by repeated declaration, places sexual union, the work of marriage, and the affection and feeling of parents in the kingdom of the devil? Adding his own cleverness to these Manichaean inventions, he declares sexual union diabolical and present both in the marital act and in the flesh of spouses [Note: [Col. 1403] So the manuscripts. Vignierius has “of the married person.”], and on its account assigns it to the kingdom of the devil, while nevertheless absolving the agents as innocent. Thus, always hostile to God, he protects those who, as he says, serve the devil through lust.

**AUG.** You are in error, and you lead those who agree with you into error. Those who use the bodies of married partners for the purpose of begetting children, so that those children may be born to be reborn, do not serve the devil through lust. Yet this does not mean that the evil of lust is defended; rather, those who make good use of an evil are defended. For there is also a good use of evil.

Indeed, even in the holy Scriptures the activities of Satan himself are found to have their uses, while his blame remains and praise belongs to the one who makes good use of evil.

**CVIII. JUL.** But the infants whom he says are made by God he subjects to the dominion of the enemy. Thus he does not condemn the work of the demon, whose ministers he absolves from guilt; rather, he condemns the work of God, which pleasure conscious of a devilish service [Note: [Col. 1403] So the manuscripts. Vignierius reads: “of the devil.”] could not attain. Therefore, as an accuser of the marital act but an expiator of lust, an assailant of innocence, and a defamer of divine justice, he did not fear to write: “I plainly say that they are under the devil because they were born from that union.”

When he saw the criminal character of this statement exposed, he attempted to defend it by some authority which he could not produce from Scripture [Note: [Col. 1403] So the manuscripts. Vignierius reads: “prefer.”], and he added that Bishop Ambrose had held the same opinion. It is certainly no wonder that he accuses the dead, when he accuses the innocent.

[Col. 1404] **AUG.** Whoever hears this, what does he think you are bringing against us except that the statement of the most blessed Ambrose which we quoted is not his, but that we fabricated it as though it were his? For I too, when I read these words, thought that you were doing nothing else [Note: [Col. 1404] The Portarus manuscript reads: “that you were doing nothing else.”]. But after I came to what you add, and you did not deny that Ambrose said this, I found you instead to be a dreadful accuser of so great a teacher.

For whatever you say against me, since I say that no one conceived through the union of man and woman is free from sin, you certainly say also against him who said and wrote this before me. But when, refuting and resisting you, I assert that infants are under the devil on account of original sin unless they are reborn in Christ, I defend not only myself but also Ambrose, his other associates, the participants in and teachers of this faith, and the whole Church of Christ. The Church testifies that it has received this, holds this, and faithfully believes this through the exorcism and exsufflation of infants being baptized.

Thus I defend them all against your wicked accusation.

**CIX. JUL.** How much more correctly you would say: “Manichaeus said the same thing in his letter to Patricius; he said it in the letter he wrote to Menoch’s daughter; and he said it in many other writings, which you have thoroughly absorbed.” But you try to draw the bishop of Milan into your fellowship, and because you cannot obtain protection, you wish to find consolation.

**AUG.** What Ambrose said is entirely opposed to Manichaeus. Manichaeus says that the nature of evil belonging to another has been mingled with us; Ambrose says that our own nature was corrupted by the transgression of the first man. In the statement now under discussion, Ambrose defends the birth of Christ’s flesh as distinct from the flesh of other sinners, whereas Manichaeus entirely denies it.

Therefore, what Ambrose believes, I also believe; what Manichaeus believes, neither he nor I believe. Why do you strive to separate me from Ambrose and join me to Manichaeus?

For if it is a Manichaean doctrine to say that original sin is inherited by those who are born, not from the mingling of something alien but from the corruption of our own nature, Ambrose says this with me. Why do you not try to join both of us to the Manichaeans? But if this is not a Manichaean doctrine—as it is not—I say it with Ambrose. Why do you not deign to detach both of us from the Manichaeans?

Why, then, as you say, “do I try to draw the bishop of Milan into my fellowship,” when you vainly try to draw me away from his fellowship? What do you mean when you say, “because I cannot have protection, I wish to find consolation”? With Ambrose, whether you wish it or not, Christ is our common protection in the Catholic faith.

Ambrose is plainly my consolation because, with him, I receive your abuse. Nor does he alone greatly console me in this matter; so do Cyprian and Hilary and others like them, whose Catholic faith you tear apart in me.

Do not, then, begrudge me the consolation that Ambrose, Cyprian, and Hilary provide for my injury. For against your will you are compelled to see how great a difference there is between Pelagius and Coelestius—and any other such person—and the fact that they are consolations of your condemnation.

Moreover, I show Ambrose fighting the Manichaeans on behalf of the Catholic faith, while in this struggle you offer the Manichaeans against Ambrose either consolation when they are defeated, or, worse, assistance while they resist.

For the Manichaeans say that evil possesses its own substance and nature, coeternal with the substance and nature of the good God. “It is impossible,” they say, “for evils to arise from good things.” Ambrose contradicts them and says: “Evils arose from good things; for evils are nothing other than things deprived of good. Yet through evils it came about that good things stood out more clearly. Therefore, the deprivation of good is the root of wickedness” (*On Isaac and the Soul*, chapter 7).

What do you say amid all this? “The nature of things does not allow,” you say, “that anything evil should proceed from good, or anything unjust from just.” We placed these words of yours on the side of the Manichaeans against Ambrose, from that distinguished work in which you attempted to answer my one book in four books (*Against Julian*, book 1, nos. 42–46).

If you were judge in this controversy, Ambrose would plainly be declared defeated by the Manichaeans on the basis of your judgment. And you are not ashamed—though you are an accuser of those whom you openly condemn, a flatterer of those whom you indirectly condemn together with yourself, and an assistant to those about whom you accuse others.

**CX. JUL.** Do the writings of disputants prejudice the law of God or the work of God?

**AUG.** Here you are beginning to confess that this statement was not fabricated by us as though it were Ambrose’s, but truly is his opinion [Note: [Col. 1405] The Codex Portarum reads: “but truly is Ambrose’s opinion.”], since you try to free yourself from him by saying: “Do the writings of disputants prejudice the law of God or the work of God?” But continue. Say the rest, by which you will be judged an even more shameless enemy of the Catholic faith.

**CXI. JUL.** For the moment it is more than enough for me to prove even by this very point that you have nowhere read in the sacred Scriptures what you believe, since in such a matter you have produced nothing except the bishop’s—what you call—little sayings. If you could have brought forward anything more authoritative, you would undoubtedly have refrained from these.

**AUG.** Let those who read judge whether I have not produced divine testimonies, or whether you have not vainly tried to distort those I produced.

**CXII. JUL.** But it is well that you first relieved us of the burden of such persons. For in the book you composed against free choice for Timasius, when the holy Pelagius had recalled the venerable men Ambrose and Cyprian, who had commended free choice in their books, you replied that you were not burdened by the authority of such men, saying that, if they had thought anything wrongly, they had expiated it through the progress of a better life (*On Nature and Grace*, no. 71 and following).

Let your own words serve you for this purpose, so that you may blush to stir up hatred merely by invoking names. As for the sayings of Ambrose or of the others whose reputation you strive to stain by associating them with your own company, they can be defended by a clear and kindly reason.

**AUG.** Who would believe that such blindness of heart could have befallen you, unless he had read these words? You say that if I could have found something more authoritative—that is, if I could have found something of greater authority—I would have refrained from the sayings of disputants, or, as you call them, their “little sayings.” [Col. 1406] Immediately afterward, you yourself say that Pelagius, whom you call holy, brought the venerable men Cyprian and Ambrose forward as witnesses in defense of free choice.

You do not notice how, by saying this, you refute your teacher and your entire heresy. For according to your position, if Pelagius had found something more authoritative in the canonical writings in support of what he defended, he would have refrained from the testimonies of disputants [Note: [Col. 1406] So the manuscripts. Vignierius has “in the Scriptures.”]. Why would you say such a thing unless Ambrose disturbed you so greatly that Pelagius suddenly became his adversary?

“But I relieved you first,” you say, “of the burden of such persons”—namely, Ambrose and his associates. Indeed, you are so weighed down by this burden that you are not merely crushed but ground to powder, becoming the dust that the wind drives from the face of the earth (Ps. 1:4).

For so many, such great, and such holy and illustrious bishops of God, sons of the Catholic Church in learning and fathers in teaching, did not speak about the sin of the first man and the succession of mortals subject to it in such a way that they differed from one another, or that any of them differed from himself. They spoke entirely in such agreement and consistency that anyone who reads them without a heretical frame of mind cannot doubt that Holy Scripture must be understood in this matter in no other way, nor any other faith be regarded as Catholic.

The weight of these men has already broken you so badly that you have undertaken to defend the statements you oppose by “a clear and kindly reason.” Let us hear, then, this clear and kindly reason. If those statements are defended by your reasoning, why are your curses hurled at me on their account? For the very things that you detest and condemn in me are the things you defend in their discussions.

But if they are not defended and are instead more subtly attacked under the name of defense, then far be it from us to call this a clear and kindly reason. It is rather a mocking flattery, called a defense so that the offense against Catholic peoples, who venerate these men, may not be tolerated.

**CXIII. JUL.** For evidently they sometimes spoke more simply, and, while considering something else, did not have to deal with questions arising from the side. Since they frequently praised marriage, did not think that any affection in bodies had been implanted by the devil, and did not subject God’s works—that is, the members of nature—to the devil’s kingdom, but explained, as occasion required, that marriages were instituted by God and endowed with his blessing, as well as defending free choice, it is only human that they should not be judged to stand in fellowship with your crime if you discover something ambiguously or carelessly expressed in their writings.

For just as it does not prejudice the holy Scriptures that all heresies conceal themselves behind, and attempt to defend themselves by, certain testimonies from them, so we will not allow the reputation of Catholic men to be handed over on account of something expressed with insufficient caution. They did not intend either to condemn marriage, to deny free choice, or to wound innocence. If they had intended these things, they would not have strengthened your doctrine but would have forfeited the honor of their office.

**AUG.** O clear and kindly reasoning of defense! Ambrose evidently spoke more simply when he said that no one is free from sin through the union of male [Col. 1407] and female (*On Isaiah*). And, while considering something else and not having to deal with questions arising from the side, he carelessly and incautiously infused the poison that you call Manichaean into his writings and discussions.

Most loquacious man, fearing a human being, you spare the man but do not defend those statements. For if these statements are defended by true reasoning, they are certainly defended truthfully and are true. And if this is so, original sin is rightly asserted and your doctrine is destroyed. But if these statements are defended by false reasoning, then your supposed clear and kindly reasoning is not reasoning but deception.

“But Ambrose frequently praised marriage.” So do we. “He did not think,” you say, “that any affection in bodies had been implanted by the devil.” If you mean a good affection, neither do we; if an evil one, then we do so just as he does.

“Nor did he subject,” you say, “God’s works—that is, the members of nature—to the kingdom of the devil.” As though the members of adulterers were not God’s works and members of nature, although it is nevertheless clear that through vice they are subject to the devil.

“They,” you say, “explained marriages instituted by God and endowed with his blessing, and free choice, as opportunity required.” So do we.

“It is human,” you say, “that they should not be judged to stand in fellowship with your crime.” Rather, it is insane that we should be judged by your crime not to stand in fellowship with them.

You say that “it does not prejudice the holy Scriptures that all heresies conceal themselves behind, and attempt to defend themselves by, certain testimonies from them.” In the same way, you wish “the Catholic disputants not to be prejudiced by certain statements which, as you think, we bring against you as having been expressed with insufficient caution.”

What is this except to say that in the holy Scriptures too the things which heretics appropriate for themselves were expressed with insufficient caution, and therefore are not true? What could be said more wickedly?

Or, if those statements are true but are not understood by heretics as they really are, then the comparison is entirely inapplicable. For if you concede that the statements of Ambrose, Cyprian, and the other Catholics which we bring against you are true, you will establish original sin.

Accordingly, just as we praise marriage with them, confess free choice with them, and defend innocence with them, so say with them that infants are not free from sin. Otherwise, we are with them and you are against them. For you do not defend their statements, as you promised, but criticize them.

According to your doctrine, since you are compelled to condemn those statements and insist that they are false, you are in no way permitted to offer the defense you promised on the authority of those men [Note: [Col. 1407] So the manuscripts. Vignierius has: “and to show that they are false; in no way are you permitted to offer it through their authority.”]. For in your accusation [Note: [Col. 1407] Perhaps “in your excuse” or “defense.”] you try to be a flatterer, and in your flattery you are caught as an accuser.

**CXIV. JUL.** I therefore freely conjecture and declare that if any one of them had survived to these days and had seen the glory of Christian discipline extinguished, free will idle in every matter and attempting to attribute to necessity whatever it commits voluntarily, and the reproach of God’s works and the overthrow of his law being announced to the ears of the people under the name of ineffective grace [Col. 1408], he would have been moved against you with all the bitterness of his anger.

Recognizing also that natural sin cannot be distinguished from Manichaean impiety, he would have defended the Catholic faith more plainly and more cautiously, whether by correcting you or by condemning you.

AUG. Why, then, do you correct us and not also correct yourselves? Where is what you promised, that you would freely conjecture and pronounce? Behold, neither is your vanity free, nor is your freedom genuine: for you were afraid to say that, if Ambrose had survived to these days and heard you, he would first correct himself and then us; yet, like a free man afraid to mutter this aloud, you nevertheless wanted it to be understood. Behold to what these days have come: if Ambrose were alive, he would learn from them that he had been a Manichaean and, after hearing Julian, or Coelestius, or Pelagius himself, ought no longer to remain so, but should be healed from that abominable disease under your instruction and care.

What spectacle would present itself to the mind that imagined it? What would it be like to see Ambrose standing—or, if he allowed it, sitting—before Pelagius and learning about a new paradise filled with the calamities of this age, which we see infants suffer: a place where, even if no one had sinned, the flesh would necessarily lust against the spirit, and, lest it drag the spirit toward unlawful and disgraceful acts, the spirit would also lust against the flesh? Ambrose used to say that this conflict had been changed into human nature through the transgression of the first man (*On Luke*, book 7); but under you as teachers he would no longer dare to say so.

In such a paradise, pregnant women would necessarily grow pale, endure prolonged nausea, and groan and cry out in childbirth; human beings would be born with various defects of character and body; only a few, possessing sound judgment, would learn letters—though with less difficulty, yet not without labor—while the rest would be somewhat slow or altogether dull, and the slower each was, the more likely he would be either to be cut down by the schoolmaster’s rods or to remain uneducated and ignorant. Fools, moreover, would not even be entrusted to teachers, but would be raised merely to be pitied or mocked.

Infants, before they could wish or do anything evil, would be harassed by diseases, tortured by pains, treated with tormenting medicines [Note: [Col. 1408] So the manuscripts. The printed editions, however, read *cruciatibus* (“torments”).], tormented by demons, and forced to die beneath overwhelming disasters.

But if Ambrose, horrified by these things, refused to believe them and replied that none of them would in any way have occurred if no one had sinned, in that place of such great blessedness; and that they could not have existed there even after sin, once those whose transgression had brought these evils about had been expelled; and that consequently they arose from the misery of mortals—a misery that would not exist unless human nature, corrupted and changed by the gravest sin of the first man, had deserved to propagate an age filled with so many and such great calamities; and that even the redeemed, though they have already received the pledge of eternal salvation, are not free from evils of this kind, but will be free from them only when they have departed from this age—if Ambrose gave such a reply, your brilliant syllogisms would prevent him from saying it, lest, by condemning the lust of the flesh and affirming original sin, he should condemn marriage, take away free will, blame the works of God, and bring about the overthrow of the law under the name of grace.

No, plainly no. Be ashamed—or rather, be terrified—to think such things. Indeed, if that man were still alive, he would resist you on behalf of the catholic faith, the grace or justice of God far more vigorously and authoritatively than we do, showing that the things you regard as consequences are not consequences. For one can live rightly without either abolishing or praising evil desire, but by restraining it; the Creator of nature is not blamed when what could be corrupted by an enemy, though not created by him, is shown to require healing from him; marriage is not condemned when it makes good use of shameful desire; free will is not taken away, but it is shown whose gift makes it free for the good; and the law is not nullified by grace, but fulfilled.

That outstanding teacher would argue these points with distinction and would hurl into your shameless faces what we said above about your paradise—things that truly follow from your error and are regarded by all people either with laughter or with horror as insane and deranged.

**CXV. JUL.** For no one is entitled to accept established premises and exclude what follows from them. Therefore, whoever says that infants belong to the devil’s jurisdiction because they are generated from sexual intercourse unquestionably condemns the intercourse itself—in which the work of nature consists—together with the institution of nature itself.

**AUG.** That is how it appears to you. But Ambrose saw what you do not see: that those born from man and woman—that is, through that intercourse of bodies—are not free from sin (*On Isaiah*). Yet he does not thereby condemn the intercourse itself together with the institution of nature.

For the intercourse of husband and wife for the purpose of procreation is a good of marriage. Yet some good works are performed without being free from the evil of vices, just as evil works are performed without being free from the good of the bodily members. However many vices may disgrace any nature, its institution is always good. For just as the institution of the body is good even when someone is born diseased, and the institution of the mind is good even when someone is born foolish, so the institution of the human being itself is good when someone is born subject to the contagion of original sin.

**CXVI. JUL.** Either both are denied together, or both are accepted together; and although the rejection of both lies within one’s power, the choice of one is nevertheless not left to the discretion of the other—unless it is easier to burden illicit intercourse with the fault of the will while defending the fruitfulness of the seed than, by accusing its fruits, to vindicate the union of the sexes. Your hesitation, therefore, which you endure between fear and impiety, will not be able to establish new rules of argument, so that you accept one of two connected things and exclude what adheres to it.

The light-footed deer will feed in the air before the consequence is denied after the premise has been accepted (*Virgil, Eclogue* 1.59). The apostle Paul employs this kind of reasoning when he says: “If the dead are not raised, neither has Christ been raised. If Christ has not been raised, your faith is vain” (1 Cor. 15:16). But now Christ has been raised; therefore it is established that there will be a day of resurrection for the dead [Note: [Col. 1409] The printed editions read *sanctorum* (“of the saints”), contrary to the manuscripts, which read *functorum* (“of the dead”).].

And, to impress this very point upon the reader with a shorter example: let it be questioned whether everything just is good. I ask whether you will admit that everything just is honorable. Once this is granted, I add another question: whether you declare everything honorable to be good as well. Once this too is granted, whether you wish it or not, I conclude: If everything just is honorable, and everything honorable is good, then everything just is good. Whoever wishes to resist this conclusion after accepting the first premises does not shake the structure of the reasoning [Note: [Col. 1410] The printed editions read *quaerit* (“seeks”). The manuscripts’ *quatit* (“shakes”) is more appropriate.], but exposes himself to ridicule.

Let us therefore return to the comparison with our case. The question is whether sin exists in nature. I asked whether you would concede that there is no sin without the will; you agreed, as your own statements testify. I added whether you thought there was a will in an infant; this too you denied. What follows as a third proposition, if there is no sin without the will? This is so certain [Note: [Col. 1410] Perhaps the words “namely, that there is no sin in nature—or in an infant” are missing.] that it could not be thrown into doubt even by the Academics, whose wealth consists in holding nothing certain. Yet when, after accepting the first two propositions, you deny the third, which is the consequence of those two, you do not overthrow the foundations of reasoning but expose your own madness.

**AUG.** Are you so foolish as to think that sin does not exist in nature, when sin cannot exist anywhere except in nature? For it exists either in an angel or in a human being, and both are unquestionably natures. If, therefore, sin existed in neither of these natures, it would exist nowhere at all.

Accordingly, when you proposed the question whether sin exists in nature, you intended to teach that sin does not exist in nature. If you are not excessively vain, you understand that your intention was therefore empty and that you proposed this question in vain.

Behold, I overthrow the foundations of your reasoning—since it is not true reasoning—and yet I do not, as you insultingly claim, expose my own madness, but your error. For after conceding the two propositions you assume, I deny the third because the consequence of those two is not contained in it in the way you suppose.

I concede that there is no sin without the will because sin cannot be committed without the will. But, for another reason, it is also correctly said that sin exists without the will, because it remains as long as it is not forgiven, even after the will by which it was committed has ceased.

Again, I concede that there is no sin without the will because original sin was not committed without the will of the one from whom its origin took its beginning. Therefore, even when I concede that the will to sin is not present in an infant, the third proposition—that sin is not present in an infant—does not follow from these two.

It would follow if, just as I concede that there is no sin without the will, I also conceded that no one’s sin exists without that person’s own will. Thus the infant does not possess the will to sin, but would not possess sin if the one from whom he drew it had not sinned by his will.

Something similar can be said even about human birth. If you were to say, “No one is born except by someone’s will,” I would concede this reasonably enough. But if you were to say, “No one is born except by his own will,” I would not concede it. In this same way, since we are speaking of the infant’s sin, his original sin, like his birth itself, could not exist without a will—but not his own.

[Col. 1411] **CXVII. JUL.** If those priests whose statements we have now vindicated heard this, and I asked them whether conjugal intercourse was good, they would admit that bodies are fashioned by God [Note: [Col. 1411] Perhaps *formata* (“fashioned”) should be read instead of *informata* (“informed”).]. Once this was conceded, I would add whether marriages had been ordained with God’s approval. When this too had been similarly confirmed, I would ask again whether there could be offspring without intercourse. Once this had been denied, what would follow? Clearly, if the body comes only through God, intercourse only through the body, and offspring only through intercourse, then both offspring and intercourse belong to the same author to whom the bodies belong.

**AUG.** Is this really the question at issue between us—whether conjugal intercourse is good? We both say that it is good. Why, then, do you think so badly of those priests, whose statements you do not, as you falsely claim, vindicate but pollute, as though you wished to persuade them of something about which you prove that neither they nor we are in doubt?

Conjugal intercourse undertaken for the purpose of procreation is good. But Ambrose, who said that no one conceived from the intercourse of the two sexes is free from sin, did not condemn conjugal intercourse. He saw the evil whose good use produces what no catholic doubts is a good work.

You speak emptily and waste time on superfluities. You abandon the matter at hand and attempt to teach as though it were doubted—or even denied—what no one doubts. What wonder, then, that you produce so many books, and such empty ones?

**CXVIII. JUL.** To this conclusion, without doubt, prudent catholic men who were priests would assent. Seeing that no one other than the true God had made anything in the sensations of the flesh or in the offspring of the sexes, and that God had made nothing that was evil, while evil was nothing other than an evil will transgressing without any compulsion from natural things, they would certainly declare that the Manichaeans and the Traducians had been shattered by the flashing thunderbolts of catholic reasoning.

**AUG.** Why, then, do you shamelessly lie that you defend and vindicate the statements of those whom you call prudent men and catholic priests, if those very statements are shattered by your thunderbolts? But if they are defended and vindicated, and therefore remain intact, then you are the one struck by their thunderbolts.

What Ambrose said—that no one conceived from the intercourse of the two sexes is free from sin—is either false or true. If you say it is false, then you attack the statements of prudent and, as you admit, catholic priests; you do not defend or expose them to ridicule. But if you concede that it is true, so that they may rightly be defended and vindicated, then you yourself thunder against the statements of catholic bishops.

Why, then, do you boast and say that those most blessed and learned men, if they had heard your syllogisms, would have declared that we, whom you call “Manichaeans and Traducians,” had been shattered by the flashing thunderbolts of catholic reasoning? They would therefore have pronounced against themselves and, under your thunderbolt, shown that they themselves had been shattered together with us.

Why do you not dare to say directly what you are convicted of saying indirectly? We confess original sin together with Ambrose, and you hurl thunderbolts with such force that, because of these statements common to us and him, we are shattered while he is vindicated? You are foolish: you do not distinguish him from us, and you accuse both us and him. Yet you do not strike either us or him with your thunderbolt, if you do not wish to violate the testimony of your teacher Pelagius, who said that no enemy had dared to criticize Ambrose’s faith and his most pure understanding of Scripture (*On the Grace of Christ*, §§46–47).

Thus, although you are clearly an enemy of his faith and of his most pure understanding of Scripture, you do not dare to criticize him. Instead, by criticizing me, you imagine that you demonstrate the evil of what he says. O man struck through, yet not confessing, you are compelled by great force to breathe forth murky fallacies. You pretend, in vain, the assaults of one hurling thunderbolts, when you are rather exhaling the smoke of one who has been struck.

These, certainly, are the arguments by which you attempt to teach that Ambrose and other teachers associated with him did not affirm original sin: “that God fashioned bodies and ordained marriages, and that offspring would not exist without intercourse.” These points are conceded. The further points you add are also conceded—namely, “that offspring and intercourse belong to the author to whom bodies belong,” provided that by intercourse you intended conjugal intercourse when you said this.

Although this is in itself recognized as true, it does not follow from your reasoning. Otherwise, when you say, “If the body exists only through God, and intercourse only through the body,” and from this wish to conclude, “Intercourse belongs to the author to whom bodies belong,” someone else could say: “If the body exists only through God, and adultery only through the body, adultery belongs to the author to whom the body belongs.” You see how great an insult to God this would be, and how much evil your syllogisms teach.

Therefore, just as it does not follow that adultery is to be attributed to God because it takes place only through the body, whose author is God, so it does not follow that intercourse is to be attributed to God because it takes place only through the body, whose author is God [Note: [Col. 1412] We have restored this second member of the sentence—from “so it does not follow” through “whose author is God”—on the authority of the manuscripts.].

Nevertheless, we concede that conjugal intercourse alone, when undertaken for the purpose of procreation, is to be attributed to God as its author—not because this follows from your premises, but because, considered for another reason, it is plainly true.

What you seek to establish from this, however, neither follows from the preceding points nor is true. For because God made the body, because God instituted marriages from whose intercourse offspring arise, and because God creates the offspring of animals themselves, it does not follow that “no one other than the true God made anything in the sensations of the flesh or in the offspring of the sexes.”

Where did the devil make what he did evilly with the first human beings, if not also in their sensations of the flesh? Their sensation was corrupted by evil persuasion when consent to sin was produced. And where did he make whatever evil he afterward did to the human race, if not in the offspring of the sexes—that is, in the children of human beings?

How, moreover, can you say that “God made nothing that is evil”? Is Gehenna not evil for the condemned? Indeed, whoever believes you when you say that “evil is nothing other than an evil will transgressing without any compulsion from natural things”—to say nothing of the innumerable evils that evil angels and human beings suffer unwillingly—will not fear eternal punishment itself, which is both the greatest evil and not an evil will, but the punishment of an evil will.

These are your arguments, by which you think your word is a thunderbolt, though your heart is ash.

**CXIX. JUL.** Cease, then, to accuse men of sound judgment and the bishops of the churches. More negligent speculations should not be subjected to judgment; for it is not brief hesitation but persistent intention that deserves anger. Let us indeed imitate their zeal, by which they built up the peoples through exhortation, entreaty, and correction. Would they have done any of this if, after your manner, they had believed sins to be not voluntary but natural?

**AUG.** We too, according to our limited ability, build up the peoples by exhorting, entreating, and reproving, as Ambrose did. Yet concerning original sin we think and say what Ambrose thought and said—not alone, but together with his other great associates.

When you call these men “bishops of the churches” and “men of sound judgment,” with what kind of judgment do you savagely criticize what they learned and taught with the fullest agreement, and deceptively defend it? You accuse me of being their accuser, although you see that I am their defender against the accusations that you indirectly bring against them.

You say that their “more negligent speculations should not be subjected to judgment.” Is this how you defend and vindicate their statements? Or do you instead condemn and accuse them under the name of negligence, plainly rejecting statements that, because they were negligently uttered, you pronounce false?

We ask you: if you assert that the statements you defend are false, assert that the statements you criticize are true. “It is not brief hesitation,” you say, “but persistent intention that deserves anger,” as though you were producing something by which you could show that they changed their opinion about original sin—not, I do not say, after a brief hesitation, but even after a long-standing conviction, or at the end of their lives [Note: [Col. 1413] The Portus manuscript adds here *cunctationem* (“hesitation”).].

You speak emptily, insanely, perversely, and in a way contrary to your own salvation. Be quiet, I beg you. Why do you talk so much?

**CXX. JUL.** But let us proceed to the remaining points. It is wholly worthless for you to claim that you attribute to the devil not bodies but sins. You deny this altogether, as we have frequently shown, for no other reason than to avoid the disrepute of the Manichaeans, whose poison you breathe into others.

You plainly attribute bodies—bodies themselves—to the prince of darkness. You profess their intercourse to be diabolical; you accuse their genital organs, their movements, and their fruits. From the first lesson you openly reproach the members, not the vices. For you call diabolical what even the Manichaean, as I have shown from his writings, deplores as flourishing in the sexes.

And, so that our reader may receive in a brief repetition something he can retain: either show that infants possess a will, or remove the crime from them. Since you do not do this, but assert that they are possessed by the devil because they were generated from the intercourse of bodies, you show that you assign to the hostile power not sins—which do not exist without the will—but the bodies themselves [Col. 1414].

Therefore, just as that desire which is found both in human beings and in animals is natural and instituted by God, so this desire that you endure amid the variety of your argument, by which you move among differing and opposing doctrines, has been conceived no less from folly than from profanity [Note: [Col. 1414] Vignierius reads *a profanitate est* (“is from profanity”), omitting *concepta* (“conceived”), which has been restored from the manuscripts.].

We are therefore not unjustified in distinguishing Ambrose from your company, nor do we call him, as you ask, a Manichaean.

**AUG.** You have labored altogether in vain to reach that false and ridiculous conclusion through long, twisted, deceptive, and evasive windings, where you say, “It is not unjust that you distinguish Ambrose from our company and do not call him a Manichaean.”

Absolutely: if you do not call him one, you ought not to call me one either. But if you think I ought to be called one, you are compelled to call him one as well, together with all those great and illustrious teachers of the Church who, concerning original sin—the very reason you call me a Manichaean—say, without any obscurity or ambiguity, what I say, as I have shown sufficiently clearly in the first and second books of my six books published against your four.

But your dialectic would supposedly terrify Ambrose, if he had survived to these days, so that, discovering from false consequences that what he had believed was false, he would no longer dare to say that infants born from the intercourse of the sexes are not free from sin, lest he thereby place them under the power of the devil. Then, under your instruction, he would cease to be a Manichaean.

Oh, what a loss for the man who could not hear you!

Therefore, since you say that I am a Manichaean because of this belief, Ambrose, persisting in the same belief, departed this life as a Manichaean—with you as his authority. You ought not, then, to defend him, which you cannot do in any way, but to grieve that you can no longer teach him. If you had been able to do so, corrected and instructed by your teaching, he would surely have forbidden the Church he governed to exorcize and exsufflate those infants who were about to be baptized, lest such a grave and conspicuous insult be offered to God in so many images of God who, as you assert, had been placed under the devil’s power without any reason.

Yet if Ambrose had forbidden this, he would have been expelled from the catholic Church together with you. For it would be absurd to call this “correction” rather than “deception.” It is therefore absurd to suppose that this man would have stood with you against the catholic mother; rather, unconquered, he would have resisted you on her behalf [Note: [Col. 1414] The manuscripts read *sisteret* (“would stand”); the printed editions have *resisteret* (“would resist”).].

What, then, is the reason you think I must be separated from him in this matter? Through the intercourse of the bodies of male and female, I say that no one is born free from sin, just as he did. Yet I do not attribute bodies to the devil as their creator, because neither did he. We both blame the defect of nature, and we both venerate the author of nature.

If, because I say that the lust of the flesh—by which the flesh lusts against the spirit—was changed into nature through the transgression of the first man, had passed into human nature, you claim that I “reproach the members, not the vices,” he did the same. But if the origin of vices comes from one source and the origin of members from another, then neither I [Note: [Col. 1415] Supply: “reproach the members, not the vices”] nor he does so.

Neither Ambrose nor I say that those being born possess a will of their own. Yet both Ambrose and I say that the vice of lust was produced through the transgressive will of the first man, and that those born through sexual intercourse draw original sin from it.

Both of us, therefore, assign human beings, before they are reborn, to the hostile power—not on account of their substance, whose creator is God, but on account of the sin that entered through one person and passed through all human beings, and whose author is the devil.

What is this that you lie about with the most shameless face, claiming to defend and vindicate the statements of Ambrose and others like him? Who is so blind that he does not see that you criticize those statements while I defend them, that you pollute them while I cleanse them?

Ambrose’s statements concern Christ. He says:

“Therefore he, as a human being, was tempted in every respect and endured all things in the likeness of human beings; but, because he was born from the Spirit, he refrained from sin. For every human being is a liar, and no one is without sin except the one God. It was therefore preserved,” he says, “that no one born from man and woman—that is, through that intercourse of bodies—should appear to be free from sin; but whoever is free from sin is also free from conception of this kind” (*On Isaiah*).

You say that these statements are entirely false and that they contain the abominable doctrine of the Manichaeans; and thus you criticize and pollute Ambrose’s statements.

But I declare them entirely true and demonstrate that they are not merely unconnected with the Manichaeans but opposed to them, as I have already done. I, therefore, defend them and cleanse them from your abominable accusations.

Whether he is ours or yours, you must decide. But because you fear the people who love him, you attempt to excuse through sophistry the man whom you are plainly convicted of accusing so savagely.

**CXXI. JUL.** You say that Jovinianus insulted him (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 2, §15); in this, however, I think you are lying. But let us grant that you may truly accuse Jovinianus and that Ambrose was called a Manichaean by him: it is agreed that this was madness. For one who proclaimed good nature, voluntary sins, marriage instituted by God, and infants made by God could not rightly be called a Manichaean. If, then, he thought that the preference of virginity to marriage was an accusation of marriage, he did not know at all what he was saying. For contrariety is one thing, rank or order another. Praise of a good thing is a step toward better things; defamation of nature is a road to Manichaeus. Therefore, since Ambrose did not condemn marriage, nor call the intercourse of spouses either the devil’s work or a necessity of sin, Jovinian acted wrongly in comparing him to Manichaeus and in thinking that there was no difference between an accuser of marriage and a praiser of virginity [Note: [Col. 1415] Perhaps “of virginity” should be added.].

For if Ambrose said that those generated by a lawful bodily union instituted by God, after they had begun to exercise reason, had voluntarily lied through imitation of the upright [Note: [Col. 1415] Perhaps *pravorum* (“wicked persons”), or *proavorum* (“forefathers”), should be read.], he nevertheless did not intend this union to be seen as a necessity of lying, but as an indication of universality [Note: [Col. 1416] The manuscripts read *indicium* (“indication”); Vignierius has *judicium* (“judgment”).]. For his statement, “Those born from parents lie,” is like saying, “Every human being—at least one who is master of his own choice—has at some time lied.” For he knew that no one except Christ had existed without the intercourse of parents. Thus the prudent man meant the conjugal act to indicate not iniquity but universality. But he declared that Christ had avoided every lie, and showed this by the miracle of the woman giving birth; this indeed fiercely provokes Jerome, whose follower you are, and who made a most explicit attempt to fasten a lie upon Christ [Note: [Col. 1416] See above, chapter 88.]. Therefore he was not rightly called a Manichaean (if indeed he was called one), since against your error he repeatedly praised creatures.

**AUG.** We too repeatedly praise creatures. Why, then, do you say that Ambrose does this against our error, when he does it in accordance with our faith? Ambrose himself shows elsewhere in his writings how he understood the words which you were afraid to recall when I put them to you, lest your darkness be refuted by their most brilliant light. He does so in such a way that this judgment cannot seem to have slipped from him once only, as from a careless and incautious speaker, as you call him; rather, he declares with sufficiently clear manifestation that his doctrine of original sin is catholic doctrine.

Why, then, and on what ground, did he say, “It was therefore preserved that no one born from man and woman—that is, through that intercourse of bodies—should appear free from sin; but whoever is free from sin is also free from conception of this kind”? That he intended here not the sins which people commit after beginning to use reason, as you hallucinate [Note: [Col. 1416] In the margin of the Claromontanus manuscript: *hallucinaris*. Perhaps *hariolaris* (“you babble divinations”) should be read.], but original sin, attend to what he says elsewhere: “The Jordan’s turning back signified the future mysteries of the saving laver, through which baptized infants are re-formed from evil into the beginnings of their nature” (*On Luke*, book 1, 1.36 [Note: [Col. 1416] Printed editions and the Marian and Claromontanus manuscripts read *in primordio* (“in the beginning”) for *in primordia* (“into the beginnings”).]). Tell us, Julian: from what evil, if they do not draw original sin?

Hear him again elsewhere: “It was not male intercourse that opened the secret recesses of the virgin womb; rather, the Holy Spirit poured immaculate seed into an inviolate womb. For the Lord Jesus alone, among all those born of a woman, was holy in every respect: by the immaculate newness of his birth he did not experience the contagions of earthly corruption, but drove them away by heavenly majesty” (*On Luke*, 2.23). Answer, Julian: what are the contagions of earthly corruption which the Lord Jesus alone, among those born of a woman, did not experience by the immaculate newness of his birth?

Hear further: “Before we are born, we are stained by contagion.” And shortly afterward: “And if an infant even of one day is not without sin, much less are the days of maternal conception without sin” (*Apology of David*, chapter 11). I can recall many such statements by this man whom you have admitted to be of sound judgment; but what will suffice for one whom these do not suffice? Understand from these, then, how you are not permitted, as you have attempted, to twist and pervert into another sense those things Ambrose said about persons born through the intercourse of bodies: he was not accusing God’s creature, but original sin.

Why do you bring forward Jerome, whose follower you insultingly call me, when no question now concerns his words? Yet if you had produced those words, I would either show that they contain nothing that should displease, or leave them for more intelligent persons to explain; or, if they were unquestionably contrary to truth, I would reject them with the freedom they deserve. Look to Ambrose, whom you do not dare to call a Manichaean, although you call me one because I say concerning original sin what he says. For if you did not call Ambrose a Manichaean because he proclaimed good nature, voluntary sins, marriage instituted by God, and infants made by God, neither would you call me one, since I faithfully proclaim the same things. But if you think I ought to be called a Manichaean because I confess original sin, he confesses this too: why do you not think both of us so? You call me so arrogantly; of him you secretly hold the opinion—not because truth distinguishes us, but because your freedom has rather been extinguished. For what you do not dare say of him, you dare believe. Or if you do not believe these things of him, certainly you do not believe them of me either; for even if you think us mistaken, you can easily see that those are not Manichaeans who do not assert that the proper substance of the sinner, which God did not create, exists, but maintain that original sin has been propagated from the voluntary defect of the nature God created good. You can easily see this, and at the same time see that we are opposed to the Manichaeans; but you keep their name away from Ambrose by flattery and cast it at me by calumny.

**CXXII. JUL.** But just as Ambrose is assailed by that hostile Jovinianus, so, in comparison with you, he is acquitted. When will the judgment of so many prudent men grant you enough that it can deservedly compare you with Jovinianus?

Jovinianus said that there is a necessity of the good; you, of evil. He said that through the mysteries human beings are restrained from error; you say that they are not freed even through grace. He dissolved Mary’s virginity through the circumstances of childbirth; you transfer Mary herself to the devil through the circumstances of birth. He equates what is better with what is good—that is, virginity with marriage; you call marital intercourse diseased and cheapen chastity by comparing it with something utterly foul. Nor do you place a degree between these things; you alter the whole category, preferring virginity not to something good but to something evil.

It is the height of baseness to be unable to please except in comparison with something most repulsive.

What did he ever say about insults to God such as you make? He wished to confuse the rigor of God’s judgment with the side of benevolence; you, with that of malignity. He says that the good and the best will enjoy equal honor with him; you say that the good and the impious—that is, the innocent and the devil—will be tormented with one punishment.

Jovinianus therefore wishes God to appear most merciful; you, most unjust. He says that human beings instructed in God’s mysteries cannot sin; you contend that God himself sins—in his weakness regarding the mysteries, his immoderation in the commandments, and his savagery in judgments [Note: [Col. 1417] The printed editions add here *apud eum* (“with him”), but it is absent from the Marian manuscript and appears to have been taken over by scribal error from the preceding statement, “he says that the good with him…”].

Since, then, the difference between you and Jovinianus is as great as the connection between you and the Manichaean, Jovinianus is proved to be all the more tolerable in proportion as the Manichaean is more terrible than Jovinianus.

AUG. How handsome you seem to yourself when, by comparing me with Jovinian, you try to show that I am worse. Yet I am glad to receive this most lying insult from you together with Ambrose; but I grieve that you are so insane. For you say that I am worse than Jovinian for the very reason that you also say I am a Manichaean. And what is this? Clearly, that original sin which you, together with Pelagius, deny, but which we, together with Ambrose, confess.

Accordingly, in his company, according to you, we are both Manichaeans and worse than Jovinian; and whatever else you may say against us with insolent—not truthful, but abusive—speech, the Lord has taught us to rejoice and exult when we hear such curses, not because they are true, but because we are contending for the truth (Matt. 5:12).

Behold, I do not say that there is a necessity of evil, any more than Ambrose does; and yet I say that infants are restored from evil, as Ambrose also does. Therefore there is no necessity of evil, because what birth transmits is curable by God—how much more, then, what the will adds? [Note: Col. 1418: Thus the manuscripts; Vignierius reads “you say” (dicis).] I do not say that human beings are liberated even by grace—far be it from Ambrose to say that—but I say what you do not wish to say: that they are liberated only by grace, not merely so that their debts may be forgiven, but also so that they may not be led into temptation.

We do not hand Mary over to the devil by the condition of her birth; rather, we say this because that condition is dissolved by the grace of rebirth. We do not place virginity above marriage as though the former were good and the latter evil, but as a better good over a lesser good. We do not, as you slanderously claim, say that the good and the impious are punished with one punishment; rather, we say that the good are punished with none, while the impious are tormented not with one punishment, but with different punishments according to the diversity of their impiety.

We do not say that God sins in his mysteries through weakness, in his commandments through immoderation, or in his judgments through savagery. His mysteries are beneficial to those regenerated by grace, his commandments salutary to those liberated by grace, and his judgments are distributed appropriately to the good and the wicked.

Behold, we remove from ourselves those matters in which you say that we are worse than Jovinian. Remove from yourselves, if you can, those matters in which I shall show that you are worse than that same Jovinian. He said that there is a necessity of the good; you say that the desire of evil is good. He maintained that through the mysteries human beings are restrained from error; you say that the desire to walk on the right path is not inspired by God, but acquired by free choice. He dissolved Mary’s virginity through the condition of childbirth; you equate the very holy flesh born from the Virgin with the rest of human flesh, failing to distinguish “the likeness of sinful flesh” from sinful flesh. He equates what is better with what is good—that is, virginity with marriage; you equate evil with good, for you say that the discord between flesh and spirit is as much a good as the harmony of marriage.

He says that the good and the best will receive equal honor with God; you, however, say that certain good people will not merely obtain no honor in the kingdom of God, but will not even see the kingdom itself. He says that human beings instructed in the mysteries of God cannot sin; you say that human beings can indeed more easily refrain from sin through the grace of God, but can also do so without it through free choice—displaying giant-like audacity in resisting God when he said, concerning good fruits, “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5).

Since, then, you differ so greatly for the worse from Jovinian’s error, you nevertheless subject us to him and rather equate us with the Manichaean—fortified, evidently, by this great defense, as though you had founded a new heresy for the very purpose that, whenever we refute you, we might be unable to compare you with any heretics. [Note: Col. 1419: The printed editions read “he had founded” (condiderit); the manuscripts more correctly read “you had founded” (condideritis).]

Yet in this matter, in which I seem to you so detestable on account of original sin and rather to be equated with the Manichaean, I am with Ambrose, whether you wish it or not. Jovinian called Ambrose a Manichaean, just as you do—but he did so openly, whereas you do so deceitfully. In the end, Jovinian is defeated once, when Ambrose is shown not to be a Manichaean; but because you chose to have a double heart, you are defeated twice. You accuse Ambrose of being a Manichaean; I show that he is not. You deny that you are making the accusation; I show that you are. Both points will be clear to anyone who reads what he said above. [Note: Col. 1419: The Portarum codex reads “what we said” (diximus).]

CXXIII. JUL. But let us examine the rest as well. I think I have instructed the reader sufficiently and more than sufficiently concerning the skill with which he either attacks something I have said or defends his own opinion. It will therefore not be necessary to demonstrate this by repeating all my writings.

Since he scarcely ever brings forward individual, scattered little verses from my book, frequently praising them and sometimes even lightly pricking them with a very brief sneer—although what he thinks should be attacked was not stated by me in the way he supposes—I direct the reader to that work of mine. He will see that the argument agrees with the truth.

But this man, who complained that he had been accused of attacking nature and its seeds, could not maintain his continuous pose of dissimulation. After he had calmed his patron’s hearing by conjuring tricks [Note: Col. 1419: The word praestigiis, “conjuring tricks,” has been added from the manuscripts], he opens his head like a tortoise.
