For after saying that, if Adam had not sinned, human beings could have procreated in the way that we move our joints or trim our fingernails, he added:

“But if the seed itself bears no curse, what is the meaning of what is written in the Book of Wisdom: ‘Not unaware that their nation was wicked, and their natural malice, and that their thought could not be changed forever; for their seed was accursed from the beginning’?” (Wis. 12:10–11).

And he follows the very testimony he has produced with this argument:

“Clearly, whoever he may be speaking about here, he is speaking about human beings,” he says (On Marriage and Concupiscence, book 2, §§17–21).

Behold the man who professed to have abandoned the pursuits of the Manichaeans. Under cover of a statement he does not understand, he declares the seed accursed, malice natural, and the thought of the wicked unchangeable.

There is a report that, at the cataracts (cataclita) of the Nile [Note: Col. 1419: Thus the manuscripts; Vignierius reads catadyta], the inhabitants have been deprived of the use of their ears by the roar of the rushing waters. That may be an invention of popular report, which scatters things larger than they are; nevertheless, the example is useful for chastising the deafness of fools, who, amid the roar of mutual terror, resist the voices of facts like deaf asps.

Augustine cries out: “The nation of human beings is wicked; their malice is natural; their thought is unchangeable forever; their seed is accursed from the beginning.” And there are still people who do not think that he bears the mark of the Manichaean everywhere? Let all the public adherents of that filth be questioned today: if they say anything else, let us be thought to have lied.

Therefore, if malice is natural, how do you pretend that you do not declare nature evil? If the seed is accursed from the beginning, how do you say that you accuse the vices of wills, not of seeds? If the thought of the wicked is unchangeable, how do you swear that you confess free choice? Unless, finally, you are going to say that those Hebrews, Sirach—or Philo, who are believed on uncertain grounds to have been the authors of the book called Wisdom—were Manichaeans.

AUG. Whoever may have been the author of this book, it is good that you do not reject its authority. It is therefore a suitable source from which we may produce against you whatever testimonies we can find. For your teacher Pelagius [Note: Col. 1420: “teacher” is added from the manuscripts] also, in the book he published under the title Testimonies or Chapters, included passages from this book that he believed agreed with his purpose (On the Proceedings of Pelagius, §6).

The fact that the author of this book was not a Manichaean demonstrates sufficiently and quite plainly that even those who are not Manichaeans, and who have deserved to be read and accepted in the Church of Christ, could speak of natural malice without any reproach against the institution and creation of God, the wisest and best creator of all natures.

Thus the Apostle is understood to have spoken in the same sense when he says: “For we too were once by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Eph. 2:3). Some have interpreted this not word for word but according to the sense, saying: “For we too were once naturally children of wrath.” The words “like the rest” show that all are by nature children of wrath, unless divine grace separates some of them from the mass of perdition.

Speaking, then, of those alienated from this grace, the Apostle Peter says: “But these, like irrational animals, creatures of nature, are born for capture and destruction” (2 Pet. 2:12). [Note: Col. 1420: Thus the manuscripts, “mute animals” (muta animalia); Vignierius reads “bloody animals” (cruenta).]

They were not, of course, stripping off the old human being. But unless every human being were born old, no infant would be renewed by being reborn.

Far be it from us, therefore, to suppose that saying that human beings are naturally children of wrath insults the Creator. In the same way, without any insult to him, someone may be called naturally deaf, naturally blind, or naturally diseased; likewise, one person may be naturally foolish, another naturally forgetful, another naturally irascible, and so on through countless other defects, whether of bodies or—what is more serious—of souls, which were created by God’s workmanship and impaired by the hidden but just judgment of that same God.

He himself is the creator of the whole human being. Yet although human nature is to be praised together with its Creator, human nature is in no way vicious together with his blame. We know, therefore, that it is not vices but natures that must be attributed to God the Creator. But whoever wishes to resist the Manichaean must explain where vices come from.

Regarding the defects of other things, which we confess were created by God but subjected by his most wise ordering to good or even evil angels, the answer is easy: the seeds of those things may also be corrupted by those to whom they are subject, so that they not only become defective but are conceived and born defective.

But the subject is the human being, a rational creature; the subject is the image of God. Its nature would in no way have become the devil’s plaything—although we rightly believe him to be the author of vices—unless this had occurred through God’s just judgment on account of original sin.

Finally, you yourselves, as I suppose, do not dare to say—although your doctrine is followed by this dreadful absurdity—that so many and such great natural vices would have arisen in paradise if, with no one sinning, the happiness in which human nature was created had remained. [Note: Col. 1421: humanae, “human,” is omitted in the printed editions, though present in all the manuscripts.]

But by denying original sin, you plainly make a nature that God did not create enter into the world, a nature from whose mixture the vices with which human beings are born arise.

O perverse heretics, helpers of the Manichaeans, slanderers of the Manichaeans, contentious accusers of other Catholics who unanimously speak the same truth against you [Note: Col. 1421: vera, “true,” is here restored from the manuscripts], and deceitful flatterers of still others!

CXXIV. JUL. The reader may now expect to learn how this testimony should be understood. The very man who had appropriated it shows that it certainly has nothing to do with the transmission of sin or with the Manichaean opinion. For he says: “Whoever he may be speaking about here, he is speaking about human beings.” Yet if he were speaking of natural sin, he would certainly be speaking not of some people but of all.

The opinion of the Manichaeans brands the nature of all mortals indiscriminately; but the view under discussion receives from its own plunderer the testimony that it was spoken not about everyone, but about some. From this it is clear that it had no concern with transmission, which by no means strikes everyone but affects the majority.

Since it has therefore been shown that the passage has nothing to do with that profane opinion, let the soundness of the writer be established by the testimony of the book itself. He speaks to God:

“You have mercy on all, because you can do all things, and you overlook the sins of human beings so that they may repent. For you love all things that exist, and you hate none of the things that you have made. How could anything endure unless you had willed it? But you spare all things, because they are yours, O Lord, lover of souls. For your good spirit is in all things. Therefore you correct little by little those who err, and admonish them and speak to them about the things in which they sin, so that, abandoning wickedness, they may believe in you, Lord” (Wis. 11:24–12:2).

AUG. How does God have mercy on all, when another Scripture says, “Do not have mercy on all who work iniquity” (Ps. 58:6), unless it is because even among those on whom he does not have mercy, all human beings are present in such a way that all classes of human beings are understood—as when it is said, “You tithe every herb” (Luke 11:42), meaning every kind of herb?

What help is it to you that the Scripture of the Book of Wisdom was not speaking of all human beings when it said that their malice was natural? The fact that it was speaking of some, not all, does not mean that it also implied that no others were like them, since the Apostle says: “We too were once by nature children of wrath, like the rest.”

At that time, nature did not distinguish the Israelites—even though not all of them, but the godly—from those of whom it was said, “Their malice is natural”; grace distinguished them. For this reason they were also called children of God.

We must also consider how it is said, “You love all things that exist,” since the wicked also exist, while elsewhere it is written, “You hate all who work iniquity” (Ps. 5:5). God therefore loves them insofar as they are human beings, and hates them insofar as they are wicked; he condemns them because they are wicked, and makes them exist because they are human beings. “For you hate none,” it says, “of the things that you have made.”

God therefore loves human beings to such an extent that, even when they are wicked, he loves them as human beings, although he hates them for being wicked. Thus the wicked whom God hates are human beings, because God loves his own workmanship; and they are miserable, because God loves his judgment.

CXXV. JUL. Do you see how hostile to your opinion is the praise offered to God by the man who praises him? He says that God creates souls and loves them. Yet you deny this, swearing that the souls of the innocent are under the devil and hated by God, even though they possess nothing except what they received from their creator.

AUG. Then, according to you, those who are born foolish also receive their foolishness from God the Creator—those whom Holy Scripture says should be mourned more than the dead (Ecclus. 22:13).

Yet God also loves the souls of these people in a certain sense: namely, so that they exist, live, and perceive; and although their mental discernment is dull, so that they nevertheless surpass the animals.

But there is another kind of love, of which it is written: “God loves no one except the one who dwells with wisdom” (Wis. 7:28).

You should say [Note: Col. 1422: Thus the manuscripts; Vignierius reads “you say” (dicitis)], then, how God loves more the souls of infants for whom he provides the bath of regeneration, so that he may send them into the kingdom; and why he does not grant this benefit to others, when no merits of their wills distinguish them and when there is no partiality with God—the very charge you foolishly and habitually bring against us.

Moreover, where it is said, “You love souls,” and not, “You love all souls,” there is no difficulty. Perhaps it is stated in this way to mean that God creates all souls, but does not love all of them; rather, by the generosity of his grace, he distinguishes those whom he causes to dwell with wisdom from the rest, since “God loves no one except the one who dwells with wisdom,” and “the Lord gives wisdom” (Prov. 2:6).

CXXVI. JUL. Your doctrine also does not admit the repentance which he says God grants, since it contains the claim that natural evil and wickedness do not know how to change.

AUG. On the contrary, against you we say that God grants repentance itself. For although each person repents by his will, the will is also prepared by the Lord (ibid., VIII, §LXX), and this is “the change of the right hand of the Most High,” which the sacred Psalm proclaims (Ps. 76:10). For when Peter wept, the Lord looked upon him (Luke 22:61–62). Hence his fellow apostle says of certain people: “Perhaps God may grant them repentance” (2 Tim. 2:25).

When malice is called unchangeable, this is true of the human being, who cannot change it—not of God, who can do all things.

CXXVII. JUL. The fact that he commended God for admonishing sinners to abandon wickedness and believe in him completely overturns the opinion of natural evil, since it is certain that what is congenital cannot be abandoned.

AUG. Congenital things can also be abandoned, but only when the Almighty brings this about in a human being. Corruption, too, is congenital to the body, yet the body will become incorruptible.

CXXVIII. JUL. Having explained God’s patience and his most gentle dispensation—by which he does not desire the death of the dying, except that he may return and live—he continues to confirm what he had said with examples. He mentions those who, living in the land of Canaan, had behaved most wickedly and kindled the anger of the Almighty, so that they might be destroyed by the most just vengeance for the triumphs of the Israelites [Note: Col. 1423: Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read the singular, “triumph” (triumphus)], who were already living under God’s law.

“For you hated those ancient inhabitants of your holy land, because they performed hateful works for you through magical rites and unjust sacrifices, and because they were merciless murderers of children; you willed to destroy them by the hands of our ancestors, so that they might receive a fitting settlement from the children of God—the land which is dearer to you than all others” (Wis. 12:3–7).

This passage bears witness to why God wished the seven nations to perish, after most of them had been destroyed and the Promised Land had been given to the Israelites.

So that it might not appear that there was discrimination among one human nature through some partiality toward persons on God’s part [Note: Col. 1423: Vignierius reads “nor” (nec); the Portarum codex reads “lest” (ne)], the passage explains why the Canaanites deserved to be killed. “You hated,” it says, “those ancient inhabitants of your holy land.”

Why? Certainly, according to you, it ought to have added that they had been generated from a diabolical mixture, that they were possessed by the prince of darkness, and that Adam had corrupted all who were to come from his stock. But none of this is said. What cause does it give for their being hated? Only the works committed through free will.

“You hated them,” it says, “because they performed works hateful to you.” But so that we would not be unaware what those works were—and so that you could not call these deeds of the nations sexual desire—it goes through the specific forms of their conduct.

“They performed magical rites and unjust sacrifices,” it says, “and were merciless murderers of children.” That is, they served magic and sacrifices that were unjust because they were offered to idols after the worship of the Creator had been abandoned. Through these sacrileges [Note: Col. 1423: Thus the manuscripts; Vignierius reads sacrificiis, “sacrifices”] they assigned even their closest relationships to demons, appeasing them by the monstrous slaughter of children.

See, then, how the passage is not speaking of the crime fabricated by the Manichaean—that is, of something naturally attached to all mortals. It says that these people had especially offended in this respect: they did not even refrain from destroying their own infants.

Their children’s death certainly would not have redounded to the murderer’s discredit [Note: Col. 1424: Vignierius reads “of the murderers” (interfectorum); the manuscripts read “of the murderer” (interfectoris)] if, because of one sin, both the parricide and the son were displeasing to God.

AUG. You speak as though all human beings were punished for one particular kind of sin, or as though we said that those who have reached mature age are children of wrath solely because of original sin.

“Whoever does not believe in the Son,” the Son himself says, “shall not have life, but the wrath of God remains upon him” (John 3:36). Yet some are worse than others, and upon them the wrath of God certainly remains more heavily. Nevertheless, not all are overturned and destroyed as were those under discussion, who possessed the land given to the Israelites.

What, then, do you mean when you say, “See how he is not speaking of the crime fabricated by the Manichaean”? You wish original sin to be understood by this. But the Manichaean did not fabricate it. Ambrose, like the other Catholics, confesses it both against you and against the Manichaean. It is not a mixture with an alien nature, which the Manichaean introduces, but a corruption of our own nature through the sin that entered the world through one human being and passed through all human beings—a sin that you deny against the Catholic faith.

Are you so blind that you do not see that if original sin does not exist because it is not mentioned here, then other sins that are not mentioned here will not be sins either, whether lesser or greater? Were the Sodomites not destroyed because it was not said of them that they practiced magic and parricidal sacrifices? Or were these Canaanites not destroyed because it was not said of them that males practiced disgrace with males?

Nevertheless, it has not been left unmentioned that their malice was natural. This is indeed true of all human beings, though it is less in some and greater in others, just as all bodies are corruptible, although they weigh less heavily upon some souls and more heavily upon others, according to God’s judgments—hidden, certainly, but without any doubt just.

What, then, is surprising if, when the reason for such vengeance against them was being explained, not only their voluntary malice but also their natural malice was mentioned? In addition to the common contagion of the human race, something further had been added to them by prophetic cursing. For holy Noah cursed his grandson Canaan, the ancestor of those people (Gen. 9:25). This was not unjust, since only his offspring was subject to the curse through the bond of succession. [Note: Col. 1424: Thus the manuscripts, tantum, “only”; the printed editions read tamen, “nevertheless.”]

This is also apparent in their infants, who were destroyed together with their parents, at God’s command, without exception for any age (Deut. 2:34). The adults had especially displeased God because they were accustomed to pour out the blood of their infants to demons.

Nor did God command that those infants be spared; rather, he expressly commanded that they not be spared at all. Here understand the seed accursed from the beginning. You will certainly not dare to call unjust the one who gave this command.

Had this occurred to you, you would not have separated the innocence of the children from their impious parents by saying that “the parents especially offended God because they did not refrain from destroying their infants. Their death,” you say, “would certainly not redound to the murderer’s discredit if, because of one sin, both the parricide and the son were displeasing to God.”

Do you not see that the murderers of their children displeased God so greatly that he nevertheless ordered those same children to be killed along with them? It does not follow that, because they impiously sacrificed their children to demons, those children should therefore not also perish—not through human crime, but by divine judgment, certainly just although hidden—as seed accursed from the beginning, as in fact occurred.

You do not attend to these things because you are swept along by eloquence without wisdom and wish to be eloquent in a flood of vanity, abandoned by the light of truth.

CXXIX. JUL. “Yet even these,” he says, “you spared as human beings and sent wasps ahead of the army—not because you were powerless in battle to subject the impious to the just, but because, judging them gradually, you gave them a place for repentance. You pricked those very sacrilegious people with the stings of flies, so that they might recognize the power of the avenger through the comic character of their affliction.

“But after, by the counsel of God and through this form of vengeance, their voluntary sins had been revealed—sins whose rejection was awaited and sought [Note: Col. 1425: The Portarum codex reads “whose disclosure was awaited,” or “was awaited and desired” (quorum retectio exspectabatur, vel expetebatur); Morel admits neither “and sought” nor “or desired,” and simply reads “whose rejection was awaited.” See Elementa Critica, pp. 364–365, M.]—then the writer’s invective finally rises against the obstinate profanity of those being punished, and he says that they had entered into such familiarity with crimes that these seemed, in a certain way, innate.

“‘Not unaware that their nation was exceedingly wicked, and their natural malice, and that their thought could not be changed forever; for their seed was accursed from the beginning. And although you feared no one, you gave them the opportunity to repent of their sins’” (Wis. 12:8–11).

“Although,” he says, “you had dealt so kindly and patiently with them, granting them both time for repentance and a watchtower of admonition [Note: Col. 1425: Perhaps spiculum, “dart,” rather than speculam, “watchtower”], so that you might vindicate justice and mercy from every disgrace and every suspicion of cruelty, they nevertheless despised your warnings, having scorned the benefits previously offered—as though they wished to prove themselves descended from that seed of Ham whom blessed Noah, after his nakedness had been mocked, had cursed with a paternal sentence.

“What wonder, then, if the writer, remembering their greater insolence and the severity of the sentence that had struck them, spoke of the stain upon their descendants who did not cease to imitate them [Note: Col. 1425: Perhaps qui, “who,” is missing here], since the Law frequently censures imitation by using terms of kinship for descendants?

“Thus in the Gospel the Lord says to the Jews: ‘You are from your father the devil’ (John 8:44). And Daniel is likewise said to have inveighed against the corrupt elders who nevertheless came from the stock of Israel: ‘Seed of Canaan, and not of Judah’ (Dan. 13:56). The prophet Ezekiel too reproaches the people of Jerusalem: ‘Your mother was a Hittite, and your father an Amorite’ (Ezek. 16:3, 45).

“There is therefore a customary usage in which an insult to a person’s will is accompanied by the defamation of his lineage, and the seeds themselves seem excessively attached to the crime, since they suffer the reproach on account of that person’s merit.”

But the same custom is also preserved on the side of the good, so that when a person appears entirely upright, he is said to flourish with congenital virtues. Thus blessed Job confirms that the compassionate feeling with which he aided the needy was drawn from his breasts—or rather, that it had gone out with him from his mother’s womb (Job 31:18).

Therefore neither resemblance, nor exaggeration, nor ambiguity can prejudice matters that are clear. Since it is certain that mortals are never required to correct natural things, while God commands human beings to desist from evil, it is all the more truly established that natural sin cannot exist.

AUG. You thought you had explained the words of the Book of Wisdom, but you will not be permitted to evade them with words of folly. It is sufficiently clear how that nation was called exceedingly wicked, how its malice was called natural, and how it was called seed accursed from the beginning.

For if, as you suppose, this had been said on account of imitation—that is, because they imitated their ancestor Ham, whom his father Noah cursed on account of his sin—then, when God brought such a just vengeance upon that nation, he would certainly have ordered its infants to be spared. You cannot say that they deserved punishment through imitation of their ancestors.

Since, then, God not only did not command mercy to be shown to them, but himself commanded that they should suffer the same vengeance as their parents, and since he could not command anything unjust, it shines forth clearly that their malice was called natural, and that they themselves were called seed accursed from the beginning, not because of exaggeration or imitation, but because of generation.

Against your error, prophetic authority was vigilant in this very seed under discussion: righteous Noah cursed his sinful son Ham in his son, that is, Canaan, so that we might understand from this that children are bound by the merits of their fathers unless the bond transmitted through generation is dissolved through regeneration.

The Canaanites descended from this Canaan, and they were called seed accursed from the beginning. Their infants too, because they likewise belonged to that seed, were divinely ordered to be killed with their parents—not because of imitation, but because of lineage.

The prophet Daniel wished it to be understood that the impious elders were like these Canaanites when he said to them, “Seed of Canaan, and not of Judah,” as though he were saying, “Like the sons of Canaan, and not like the sons of Judah.” Similarly, it is said, “Brood of vipers” (Matt. 3:7), because of a certain resemblance to viper-like malice. [Note: Col. 1426: malitiae, “malice,” is added from the manuscripts.]

But when the Lord says, “You are from your father the devil,” he truly intends imitation, not seed. Yet he did not say, “You are the devil’s seed.” And where it is written, “Your father was an Amorite, and your mother a Hittite,” it is evident that this was said because those addressed had imitated the people named. Indeed, it does not say there, “Seed of the Amorites” or “of the Hittites.”

Therefore, it is not as you said—that, because of the merit of a will excessively attached to crimes, the seeds themselves suffer reproach. Far be it from us to suppose that Holy Scripture reproaches seeds, which are innocent, as you reproach human beings.

But when holy Job confirms that his compassionate feeling had gone out with him from his mother’s womb, and you think that he said this merely to commend that feeling greatly, not because it was actually so, why, I ask you, do we not agree that some people are naturally compassionate, if we do not deny that some are naturally heartless?

There are indeed certain congenital traits that begin to appear at the age when the use of reason begins, just as reason itself does. Accordingly, commandments for living are given to human beings who are by nature children of wrath because grace is also given, so that the one who commands may also help. In this way not only evils added through the will, but also those generated along with us, are overcome.

What is impossible for human beings is easy for God (Matt. 19:26). But those to whom the grace of God is not given—the grace concerning which it is said, “Who makes you different? What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Cor. 4:7)—become transgressors when the Law comes, not righteous.

Yet even these people live for the benefit of the children of mercy [Note: Col. 1427: The printed editions read “but if for some benefit” (sed si quam ad utilitatem); the manuscripts read “for the benefit” (ad utilitatem)], so that when they see them and understand that what is granted to them is given not as a merited reward but freely, they may not become proud; rather, “the one who boasts, let him boast in the Lord” (2 Cor. 10:17).

CXXX. JUL. Wisdom then continues:

“Who will charge you if nations perish which you made, since there is no other God besides you, who cares for all? But because you are just, you dispose all things justly. You consider it foreign to your power to condemn even one who does not deserve punishment, for your power is the beginning of justice” (Wis. 12:12–16).

This certainly agrees with the common judgment of prudent people, since the greatest sign of justice in God is precisely what the Manichaean and the Traducianist deny with every effort of their fables.

AUG. In reviling others, whom shall I say you resemble, if not yourself? If you understood that God is just, you would never attribute congenital defects, whether of the human body or of the soul—which you cannot deny—to his workmanship, but to his judgment. From this you would understand, rather than deny, original sin, or natural sins. [Note: Col. 1427: Supply naturalia, “natural.”]

CXXXI. JUL. Finally, a little later it continues:

“For by chastising them you made your children of good hope, because, in judging, you give a place for repentance in sins. For if you delivered, with so great a torment of admonition, the enemies of your servants and those deserving of death, giving time and opportunity by which malice might be changed, with how great care do you judge your children, to whose parents you gave both oaths and covenants of good promises? Therefore, while you give us discipline, you scourge our enemies in many ways, so that we may consider your goodness in judging” (Wis. 12:12–21).

AUG. Since God foreknows all future things, the fact that he gave even those people time and opportunity in which their malice might be changed—although it had been said that their thought could not be changed forever—sufficiently demonstrates the meaning of his words: “You gave your sons good hope, because, judging them, you gave them a place for repentance in their sins.”

A time and place for repentance is therefore given even to the children of wrath, handed over to death and destined not to repent, because among them there are, or will arise from them, children of mercy for whom the benefit will come from what benefited those others not.

Thus even over the children of perdition God’s patience is not empty or fruitless. It must benefit those whom divine grace, not human merits, distinguishes from the mass of perdition—whether they give thanks that God’s mercy has distinguished them from the others, or whether, by God’s arrangement, those who will not perish are born from among those who are perishing.

CXXXII. JUL. You therefore observe how the surface of the words has made a distinction between the natures of two peoples: it calls the Israelites children of God and the Canaanites accursed seed. If what the language expresses referred to generations and births, it ought to have said that the generation of the religious was one thing and that of the profane another.

AUG. Is it because, when we hear “children of God,” we understand grace, that, when we hear “children of human beings,” we must not acknowledge and confess nature? What is this, contentious man, except that you do not know what to say?

Recognize what is true; attend to what is clear. The Canaanites were called accursed seed because of such an evil lineage that, when the most just God took vengeance and commanded it, even their infants were not spared [Note: Col. 1428: The Portarum codex reads “even their infants” (nec eorum parvulis), rather than “even its infants” (nec ejus parvulis)], although they had followed their parents without any imitation of their will.

The Israelites, however, were called children of God not because of natural descent, but because of the adoption of grace. Therefore, whether they are called children and children, or seed and seed, how does this agreement of names help you when there is such a great difference in realities?

CXXXIII. JUL. Nevertheless, even according to this absurdity it remained clear that there is no transmission of the first sin, as the interrupted stocks of many nations together demonstrated most fully.

AUGUSTINE. The seed of that one man, which is all human beings, is one thing; the different seeds of the various peoples are another [Note: [Col. 1428] The Codex Port. reads “the seed of the various peoples,” omitting “different.”], and these do not interrupt the former, because everything descends from it. Nor do they, by their variety, cause the sin of the first man—by which human nature deserved to be changed—to be harmful to whatever descendants of his were born much later; rather, they cause it to be more or less harmless. For just as some parents aggravate original sin, so some lessen it; but no one removes it except the one of whom it was said, “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1:29). For him no good in a human being is impossible, and no evil is incurable.

## CXXXIV. JULIAN

Moreover, just as what is said in praise of the Jews does not serve to make anyone believed to shine with an innate holiness, so also what is called natural wickedness does not serve to commend vicious seeds. Yet, without prejudice to nature—whose unshakable order derives whatever it possesses from its own author, God—this variety of expressions either indicates the force of denunciation or performs the office of praise.

AUGUSTINE. If no one possesses innate holiness, how was it said to Jeremiah, “Before you came forth from the womb, I sanctified you” (Jeremiah 1:5)? How also was it said of John the Baptist, “He will be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother’s womb”—as his exultation also showed when the virgin Mary, pregnant, greeted Elizabeth, who was pregnant and married (Luke 1:15, 41, 44)? Or are these statements not declarations of a distinctive quality but merely exercises in praise? Go on, then; rave on. It remains for your madness to say this.

Why do we put Jeremiah and John before the arrogance of your brow, when you do not distinguish Christ himself from sinful flesh, and, saying that no flesh is originally sinful, so equate him with the rest that you are compelled even to deny that he possessed innate holiness—he who was born of the Holy Spirit and the virgin Mary, wholly free from sin because free from that conception which occurs through the intercourse of the sexes?

For Jeremiah and John, although sanctified in their mothers’ wombs, nevertheless drew original sin. For by what other merit would their souls have perished from their people if they had not been circumcised on the eighth day—that is [Note: [Col. 1429] The printed editions lacked “that is.” It is restored from the manuscripts.], if they had not come to Christ’s grace [Note: [Col. 1429] All the manuscripts read “belonged,” rather than “had come to.”]—which bodily circumcision on the eighth day, that is, after the seventh day, symbolized as destined to rise for our justification?

Thus they were both by nature children of wrath from their mothers’ wombs and by grace children of mercy from their mothers’ wombs: for they did not yet possess that holiness which would break the bond of an inherited condition subject to condemnation, a bond that had to be broken in its own time; yet they did possess the holiness that marked out Christ’s herald from his mother’s womb [Note: [Col. 1429] The Codex Clar. reads “heralds.”].

But you wish to be thought a new heretic and a religious natural philosopher [Note: [Col. 1429] The Codex Port. reads “of religion.”] when you say that “natural wickedness” and “accursed seed” are spoken without prejudice to nature, whose, as you say, “unshakable order derives whatever it possesses from its own author, God.” Do not even those who are born foolish admonish you to have a heart, at least? Yet not even fools themselves dare call God the author of foolishness. Nor, as the Manichaean foolishly or insanely supposes, did the commingling of a foreign nature introduce this vice; rather, the corruption of our own nature introduced it.

Those who are sound in the faith therefore find the deserving cause of this vice, and of all the other natural vices, nowhere except in original sin.

## CXXXV. JULIAN

But just as here it is called accursed seed, so elsewhere—indeed, where the authority of the reading is greater—it is called blessed seed. For the prophet Isaiah, speaking about the Israelites, says:

“They shall build houses and inhabit them themselves; they shall plant vineyards and eat their fruit themselves. They shall not build and others inhabit; they shall not plant and others eat. For according to the days of the tree of life shall the days of my people be; the works of their lips shall endure [Note: [Col. 1429] The same manuscript reads “shall endure.”]; my chosen ones shall not labor in vain, nor shall they beget children under a curse, because the seed is blessed by God” (Isaiah 65:21–23).

AUGUSTINE. If you understood this prophecy of Isaiah, you would not bring it against us in order to evade the issue, but rather against yourself in order to be corrected.

You would see here another seed—not mortal but immortal, not carnal but spiritual. John the Evangelist saw this seed when he said, “Everyone who is born of God does not sin, because his seed remains in him” (1 John 3:9). According to this seed, no one sins: for even if he sins as a human being, he nevertheless has another seed, according to which the seed cannot sin, because he has been born of God.

According to this seed, children are not begotten under a curse. In these words of the Prophet you ought to have awakened and observed that this would not have been promised to God’s people as a great gift unless children were begotten under a curse according to the other seed, which is from Adam; but they are not begotten under a curse according to Christ, who is the seed blessed from the beginning.

For he is also the Wisdom of God, of which it was said, “She is a tree of life to all who embrace her” (Proverbs 3:18). Hence this same Prophet—or rather, God through the Prophet—says, “According to the days of the tree of life shall the days of my people be.”

Eternal and immortal life was being promised in these words to spiritual, not carnal, Israelites. There the spiritual vineyards and houses will not be possessed by others after their planters and builders have died, but by those same planters and builders, who will live without end.

Therefore acknowledge two kinds of seed: one of generation and the other of regeneration. Do not be unbelieving, but faithful.

## CXXXVI. JULIAN

Let little children, then, suffer the controversy arising from these verbal contradictions, so that, capable of nothing greater than sounds, they may battle over the cups [Note: [Col. 1430] The printed editions read “peoples.” The old Codex Port. more aptly reads “cups.”—Morel, *Elementa Critica*, p. 173, suggests “little words.” M.] playfully offered them. The Catholic faith, however, neither believes that God’s law quarrels with itself nor admits any authority to the destruction of reason; nor does it listen to any opinion or flattery that would stain divine justice. Rather, since it not only believes but also knows God to be the creator of all natures, it attributes sin to no one other than the free will. Through all this it has no doubt that the transmission of sin is false.

AUGUSTINE. The Catholic faith, rather, has no doubt that original sin exists—a faith defended not by little children but by serious and steadfast men, learned in the Church and teaching the Church, even to the day of their death.

You, however, do not believe that God’s law quarrels with itself, as you say; yet you yourselves quarrel against it with blind impiety or impious blindness. For this is why you boast that you admit no authority to the destruction of reason: so that, by your arguments—which are not arguments but deceptions—you may set aside divine authority rather than explain it.

Yet no one ought to be so dull of heart as to be deceived by the argument of Pelagius, which he produced as though explaining the Apostle. He said: “The body is dead because of sin”—meaning, he claimed, that the body dies to sins when it turns away from sins.

Against this folly one must not argue [Note: [Col. 1430] Here we have added “one must not argue” on the authority of the manuscripts]; rather, the Apostle himself must be read:

“But if Christ is in you, the body indeed is dead because of sin, but the spirit is life because of righteousness. And if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in you” [Note: [Col. 1430] The printed editions read “Christ” instead of “spirit”; corrected from Codex Port.] [Note: [Col. 1431] The Codex Port. repeats here, “who raised Christ from the dead.”] [Note: [Col. 1431] The printed editions read “because of,” rather than “through.”] (Romans 8:10–11).

What could be clearer? What could be more lucid? Who, I ask, except heretical madness would deny original sin in the face of this disclosure?

Because of that sin, the body is still dead, although the spirit is already life because of righteousness. “But,” he says, “God will give life to your mortal bodies.” Who would bark against this truth [Col. 1432] except the rage of vanity, which boasts that it listens to no opinion or flattery that would stain divine justice, while in fact whoever is deceived by you is compelled to deny divine justice?

For if the many defects—whether of body or of mind—with which human beings are born are said to carry no deserving cause of any sin, then without doubt God’s judgment is declared unjust. Thus, while you attribute sins to the will in such a way that you refuse to attribute original sin to the will of the first man, you compel those who believe you to attribute all the evils that infants inherit or suffer to an unjust judgment of God.

# BOOK FIVE

[Col. 1431]

Augustine confirms and vindicates from Julian’s calumnies what he wrote in Book Two of *Marriage and Concupiscence*, chapter twelve and several chapters following it—especially that healthy nature would not possess that shameful commingling or stirring of the members which corrupted nature possesses, and consequently that one who is born from it needs to be born again.

Next, he confirms what he argued in chapters fourteen, twenty, and twenty-six: that Julian improperly abused two apostolic testimonies, 1 Corinthians 15:36, 38 and Romans 1:27, as well as the Gospel saying in Matthew 7:17 or 12:33.

He also confirms what he asserted in chapter twenty-eight: that evil, or an evil will, could arise from the good work of God because that work, although good, was made from nothing and not from God.

Finally, he confirms what he taught in chapter seventeen: that God creates the wicked in the same way that he feeds and nourishes the wicked.

## I. JULIAN

It is established by the dangers of every age that among only a few does incorruptible judgment retain its authority—among those who are devoted to the pursuit of knowledge and desirous of virtue, who can either investigate the truth or dare to defend it once discovered; or, as the Apostle says, who have their senses trained for the discernment of good and evil (Hebrews 5:14). They are not broken by any storms of adversity, since they hear from the same teacher that one must resist sins even unto blood (Hebrews 12:4).

These wise men, whom the masses of fools make appear few, pursue knowledge and courage with equal zeal. Neither achieves its fruit or honor without the other: courage, unless applied through knowledge to the best things, bursts into contemptible madness; and, conversely, laws of examined justice [Note: [Col. 1431] Here “justice” has been added from the manuscripts], unless enclosed by the wall of magnanimity, will immediately lie open to plunder and be led away into servitude to crimes.

These two-horse chariots, without which the errors of the world cannot be conquered, have appeared in different ages only among the very rare individuals who cultivated, joined, and guided them. For the pursuit of knowledge is hindered both by avoidance of labor and by the variety of worldly cares, while fear strikes down steadfastness amid the hardships stirred up by the wicked.

Faithful and wise minds do overcome these kinds of assaults; yet they are so rare that, among crowds of madmen, they seem mad because they do not rave.

AUGUSTINE. Does not this rarity of human beings—which you yourself mention, among whom there are both knowledge and courage [Note: [Col. 1431] So the manuscripts read. The printed editions, however, read “fear.”—]—warn you what you ought to think about the human race and about this entire mass of rational mortal creatures?

Why does not the whole mortal race, or at least the greater part of it, rise by natural inclination to the pursuit of knowledge and the strength of courage, so that we would rather marvel at the very rare individuals who deviate and depart from what nature’s formation desires? Why does it slide into the depths of ignorance and the softness of sloth as though down an incline, pressed by some kind of burden?

You certainly say that avoidance of labor is the cause by which human beings fail to know what they ought to know. But I wish you would say what causes it to be so laborious for a human being, naturally so well constituted, to learn what is useful and beneficial to nature, and thus, fleeing labor, to rest more familiarly and willingly in the darkness of ignorance.

Surely, the great rarity of the talented and studious—through which two qualities one reaches knowledge of human and divine things—and the great multitude of the slow and indolent sufficiently indicate toward what side nature itself is borne, as though by its own weight, even though you deny that nature has been corrupted.

Nor do you think according to the Christian faith about what kind of being Adam was when he gave names to all living creatures (Genesis 2:19)—a sign of the most outstanding wisdom, as we read even in secular literature. For Pythagoras himself, from whom the name of philosophy arose, is said to have declared that the wisest person of all was the one who first assigned names to things.

But even if we had learned nothing of this kind about Adam, it was surely our task, by true reasoning, to infer what kind of nature was created in that man in whom there was no vice at all.

Who could be so dull of mind as to deny that dull or keen intellects belong to nature, or to suppose that slowness of mind or memory or understanding is not a defect of the soul? And what Christian could doubt that those who appear most talented in this world, so full of errors and hardships—whose corruptible bodies nevertheless weigh down their souls—would, if compared with Adam’s intellect, be farther apart from him than tortoises are from birds in speed?

Paradise would therefore have been filled with intellects of such excellence if no one had sinned. For God would have created such people from parents as he had created that man without parents—certainly in his own image. Human beings had not yet become like vanity, so that their days would pass like a shadow in this troubled world (Psalm 143:4).

If that had been the case, would your complaint have had any place? Would the attainment of knowledge have been laborious, so that people would prefer to be ignorant in order to avoid labor? Would we have needed the very courage that, as you rightly say, is found scarcely among the few, where there would have been no hardship that we would have had to endure courageously for the sake of truth?

Since everything has been turned into its opposite, you deny that our nature has been corrupted so that, with your help, the Manichaean may introduce into us a foreign nature mixed with our own. Thus, while you rush forth as its ignorant opponent, you become its unwitting ally.

## II. JULIAN

The book called *Wisdom* also demonstrates this when it expresses the words of the wicked, who, after the shadow of present things has been removed, behold the merits of the blessed:

“We considered their life madness; and how have they been counted among the sons of God?” (Wisdom 5:4–5).

This is why the perseverance of the faithful, defiant against the injustices of the times and choosing rather to be afflicted with the people of God than to have the enjoyment of temporary sin (Hebrews 11:25), is accused by those who say, “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die” (1 Corinthians 15:32), under the name of stubbornness and contentiousness. Nothing is thought more fitting for prudent counsels than to purchase the servitude of a degenerate spirit, or the faithless tranquility of passing moments.

It was chiefly because of this baseness of cowardly hearts [Note: [Col. 1433] The printed editions read “usefulness.” Corrected from the manuscripts.] that the filthy doctrine of the Manichaeans was able to sail through the shipwrecks of the churches. For if a free and manly authority had stood firm in those who held the office of priesthood, the inventions of the Traducianists, which invincible reasoning demolishes, would likewise have been crushed by public assent.

But when nothing is judged more contemptible by people who love the present than religion, the accusation was directed against God, so that we were compelled, through such lengthy discussions, to prove that our God, who is the true God, is faithful in his words, just in his judgments, and holy in his works (Psalm 145:13, 17).

AUGUSTINE. If God is faithful in his words, why do you contradict him when he says, “I will repay the sins of the fathers upon the children” (Deuteronomy 5:9), and insist that this is not true?

If he is just in his judgments, why do you refuse to accept as just this very fact—that the sins of the fathers are repaid upon the children? And why are you not afraid to say that the fact that Adam’s children are weighed down by a heavy yoke from the day they emerge from their mother’s womb occurs without any deserving cause of original sin?

If he is holy in his works, why do you refuse to distinguish from his holy work of forming nature the uncleanness of those who are born—an uncleanness that compelled a man of God to say that no human being is clean from sin, not even an infant whose life upon the earth is but one day (Job 14, according to the Septuagint)? Why do you attribute to his holy work all the many and sometimes very great defects of both minds and bodies?

By refusing to attribute these things to original merits arising from sin entering the corrupted nature [Col. 1434], you certainly open a very broad entrance for the Manichaeans to introduce a foreign nature of evil. You shudder as though accusing their impious doctrine, while in fact you assist those who are in error.

## III. JULIAN

While I have devoted the work of my books to these matters, the defender of natural evil attacks it—although in the preceding discussion of my earlier volumes I have fully and abundantly demonstrated with what strength and in what consistent reply this has been done.

From reading them, I have no doubt that every prudent person—and I testified in this preface that such people are rare—will understand that the enemy of truth is pursuing nothing else than to amuse the ears of the simpler-minded, and to appear to have escaped so long as he seems in some fashion to have replied.

AUGUSTINE. You testify in your preface that prudent people are rare [Note: [Col. 1434] So the manuscripts read. Vignierius has “you testified.”]. Yet you neither say nor learn what the cause of this rarity is, or why even those who have reached prudence through a rare capacity of intellect could not attain useful knowledge without great labor. You refuse to admit that human nature was corrupted through the transgression of the first man.

And yet, for the reading of your books, you send only those same prudent people whom you testify to be exceedingly rare. You think so highly of their intellect that you attempt to refute one of my books with eight of your own, multiplying for them the labor of Adam’s children. Through that labor they may learn that, even if no one had sinned, they would have had to labor in paradise itself in order to learn the books of the educated [Note: [Col. 1434] So the manuscripts read. The printed editions have “of letters”; and in the following line they have “opinion” instead of “knowledge.”], and first the letters themselves.

This is your splendid knowledge, comprehensible to no human beings except the rare prudent ones—and not even to them without miserable labor.

## IV. JULIAN

Although it is therefore abundantly evident that we have accomplished this, nevertheless, since our work is becoming lengthy, the wise reader should understand that brevity would indeed have been desirable to us, but that the necessity of the case required the error of the world—which has been spread more widely by favor—to be overcome by a broader edge of truth.

Our speech is therefore not being extended for no reason. With Christ’s help, I presume that no part of the impiety against which we are contending will be judged to have been sought carelessly, discovered inadequately, or worn down only superficially.

Nor can or should we despair that, as time advances, the storm that has arisen will subside and that, through the authority of the wise, the sluggish crowd that now makes such an uproar will be corrected. Yet our hope is a weaker cause than our conviction; whatever outcome the condition of affairs may receive [Note: [Col. 1434] So the manuscripts read. Vignierius has “although the condition of affairs may receive destruction.”], our reasoning concerning both kindness and faith will remain established for us.

For we do not depend upon the outcome of popular success. The story of the three boys in Babylon is well known. When the most arrogant king compelled them to worship a statue, they resisted with complete faith and were not terrified by the blazing furnace that had been kindled to consume the devout. They replied, as faith and steadfastness required:

“Our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from this furnace, O king; but even if he does not deliver us, know that we will not serve your gods or worship the statue that you have set up” (Daniel 3:17–18).

How holy a hope they joined to judgment, and yet they did not weaken the seriousness of their decision by desire! They neither precipitate the strength of faith through despair nor hold it back through desire. They do mingle hopes, but they do not abandon order. They console endurance [Note: [Col. 1435] The printed editions read “endurance” in the nominative; the manuscripts differ.], but subordinate milder things to what is just:

“It is certain,” they say, “that our God can deliver us; but whether he wishes to do so is uncertain. Therefore, whatever the ambiguous outcome of events, the resolution of the devout remains certain: to reject idols and endure punishments.

“Whatever good our deliverance may confer on others is beside the point. Meanwhile, may unconquered faith preserve true happiness for us. There is therefore no excessive need to gratify softer desires in one whose glory is engaged in adversity.”

From this discipline, left to us by illustrious teachers, we understand that moderation should be maintained in the hopes of prosperity, but permanence in the principles of faith. We desire, with the swelling of persecutions restrained, to assist the peoples as well. But if that does not happen, we remain ready to endure whatever is bitter in insults and dangers rather than fail to abhor the filth and pollution of the Manichaeans.

AUGUSTINE. We have often reminded you how greatly you assist the Manichaeans when you do not attribute the heavy yoke placed upon Adam’s children from the day they emerge from their mother’s womb (Ecclesiasticus 40:1) to the just judgment of God on account of original sin, and thereby make room for the foreign nature of evil taught by their insane error. Whenever it seems appropriate, we will not cease reminding you.

Now, since you boast that you are so courageous, while nevertheless commending your own “moderate hopes” on behalf of many—as you say, “you hope to assist the peoples once the swelling of persecutions has been restrained”—I ask you whether you hope for this from the Lord.

If you do not, these are not Christian hopes. But if you do, how do you expect the Lord to grant this in response to your hopes? Surely, you expect him to turn the hearts of those who are hostile to you toward your favor and love.

If you believe this, you have made progress: he has already begun to convert you yourselves and to change you yourselves for the better. Consider this, I ask you, and hold fast to it. At last confess that the almighty God works the wills of human beings in their hearts and turns those who are hostile to him. In this way you will appreciate his mercy and grace—and, where he does not do this, his hidden but just judgments.

Thus perhaps he will answer our hopes by converting you to the Catholic faith, just as shortly before he converted your Turbantius, who is now ours, through a similar act of his power and mercy [Note: [Col. 1435] The Codex Port. reads, “If you believe this, then he has certainly begun to convert you yourselves.”].

## V. JULIAN

But now let us approach the issue. It has become clear both from my earlier work and from the present one that natural concupiscence, without which there can be no intercourse between the sexes, was established by God, who is the creator both of human beings and of animals (*Marriage and Concupiscence*, Book 2, no. 25).

My opponent’s confession is sufficient to establish this, since natural sin cannot be asserted at all without censuring concupiscence—that is, carnal concupiscence [Col. 1436]—and without defaming intercourse.

AUGUSTINE. Whether you prefer to call it natural or carnal, we censure that concupiscence by which the flesh desires against the spirit and drags one toward unlawful things, unless the spirit desires against it with greater strength.

We say that this conflict did not exist in paradise, when those who were there were naked and were not ashamed. That it began after sin is proclaimed by the fact itself: after sin they covered their nakedness, which had not previously been shameful.

They were naked before not through shamelessness but through innocence; for shamelessness is itself a vice, whereas, when they were not ashamed to be naked, they certainly had no vice.

This evil, by which the flesh desires against the spirit, the heretic Julian calls good. This evil the other heretic, Manichaeus, says was mixed into us from a foreign nature of evil. Ambrose, the Catholic, defeats both of them by saying that this evil was turned into our nature through the transgression of the first man.

## VI. JULIAN

Since this has been demonstrated by us with the ability supplied by truth, no prudent reader ought to doubt it any further. Wherever this appears in the writings of the Traducianist—without which he cannot open his mouth—it should move his listeners not at all, but should testify to the author’s shame. As for us, if circumstances require it, we shall henceforth touch upon it with necessary brevity.

He therefore attacks what I said: “This commingling of bodies, with heat, pleasure, and semen, is made by God and approved as praiseworthy in its own measure” (*Marriage and Concupiscence*, Book 2, no. 25).

But he passed over what I added: “As for the matter which, being naturally established, sometimes becomes even a great gift of the devout, the devil does not dare claim anything from it for himself—not even with your brow” [Note: [Col. 1436] Vignierius reads “may be.” The manuscripts read “be.”].

AUGUSTINE. The person who sent the little book to which I was replying was the one who passed this over—perhaps understanding what you do not understand. You spoke so carelessly that you said: “From a matter naturally established, which sometimes becomes even a great gift of the devout, the devil does not dare claim anything for himself.”

Yet we see that the devil claims human beings themselves, and they have certainly been established naturally. Or are human beings not among those who are rescued from the power of darkness, over which the devil holds dominion? Or are you so foolish as to affirm that the devil does not claim for himself those whom he possesses and keeps subject to his power?

But, to say nothing of those whom you can claim to be possessed by the devil through their own evil will, what will you say about the one whose father replied, when questioned by the Lord, that from childhood he had been tormented by an unclean spirit (Mark 9:20)?

Did not the devil claim his members and senses in order to afflict him—members and senses all naturally established by God as their author, and common gifts of both the wicked and the devout? Although the devil could not do this unless he received power from the good and just God, the creator of human beings, he nevertheless does it, and he shows your exceedingly foolish words [Col. 1437] to be false when you say, “From a matter naturally established, which sometimes becomes even a great gift of the devout, the devil dares claim nothing for himself.”

You ought to have said that, among the good things naturally established, the devil claims nothing for himself—not that he creates nothing. The person who selected from your books certain passages to send to his friend perhaps saw this and spared you by omitting your words.

But I am grateful, because you remind me what I ought to say against your error. Inquire, then, into the merits of the little children whom the devil claims for himself in order to torment them. Since you will not find those merits to be their own, confess that they are original.

For if you persist in denying even this, you will plainly be convicted of accusing God’s judgment: God allows his image to suffer these things at the devil’s hands without deserving them.

## VII. JULIAN

Setting these matters aside, then, he attacks me for not having said, “with lust.” He adds, as the acuteness of his doctrine required:

“The gift of the devout is the fruitful propagation of children, not the shameful commingling of the members; healthy nature would not have had this in the generation of children, but now the same nature, corrupted, does have it. And consequently, the one who is born from it needs to be born again” (*Marriage and Concupiscence*, Book 2, no. 25).

How consistently everything follows! He calls the existence of children the gift of the devout; yet he places under the devil what he confirms God gives—that is, children. He calls lust, which exists in the shameful commingling of the members, diabolical; he does not deny that it exists in the parents, whom nevertheless he absolves from guilt.

“Would you call him born of a human being?” “What the parents do,” he says, “is diabolical, but they are not guilty; that children are born is a work of God, but they are guilty.” And he still thinks that he has been struggling not against God but against the demon?

Most deservedly do those who think there is such a thing as natural sin suffer this madness.

AUGUSTINE. You are the one who rages against God. You plainly accuse him of injustice if, as you insist, Adam’s children draw no evil merits from him, yet God nevertheless weighs them down with a heavy yoke from the day they emerge from their mother’s womb—a condition that you are not allowed to deny.

And, thinking that dull people will read both my words and yours, you claim that I said what I did not say. When would I say, “What the parents do is diabolical,” when I expressly proclaim that what chaste marriages do in their intention to procreate is a good work?

But this commingling would not have been shameful if the sin of the human being, by which nature was corrupted, had not preceded it. From that sin the concupiscence of the flesh became such that no one makes good use of this evil unless he resists its movements—which strive to drag him toward unlawful things—by desiring against it in the opposite direction, through the spirit.

We do not therefore say, “What the parents do is diabolical.” For it is not so diabolical to make good use of an evil that God himself makes good use of the devil.

We do not deny, however, that we say this: “That children are born is a work of God, but they are guilty.” They are not guilty because of God’s work by which they are created so that they may be born, but because of the origin of sin by which they are bound unless they are born again.

[Col. 1438]

## VIII. JULIAN

The history itself also testifies that Adam could not have joined with his wife in any other way than by the manner that became customary, both in the form of the members and in the fact that God’s blessing was pronounced no differently upon animals than upon human beings. Just as the history shows the nature of bodies to have been formed, so it does not assert that it was changed.

Nothing is found against this testimony of the whole universe in God’s law—except in the books of Manichaeus, who fabricates the story that this concupiscence was infused by the prince of darkness.

AUGUSTINE. It is not the form of the members—for it was not changed by the sin of the first man—that establishes that the concupiscence of the flesh was before sin such as it appeared when they covered their shameful parts, of which they were ashamed though you are not. They thus showed that, although the form remained, something in them had nevertheless been changed.

Indeed, when members are born deformed and monstrous, shame itself compels you to confess that, if no one had sinned, such things would in no way have been born in paradise.

As for the blessing of God by which it was said, “Increase and multiply” (Genesis 1:21, 28), why should it be surprising if nature, although corrupted by sin, did not lose it? It did not follow that because nature had lost immortality and happiness, it should also lose fecundity, which was granted even to irrational animals.

In those creatures the flesh, although it desires, does not desire against the spirit. You are trying to introduce into the place of that most blessed peace and freedom the most miserable war or the most shameful rule that you have embraced, since you insist that, even if no one had sinned, the human race in paradise would have been such that we would fight against lust or serve lust if we did not wish to fight.

## IX. JULIAN

We testify both by our work and by our speech that all people ought to be born again through Baptism. But this is not so that, through the bestowal of this benefit, they may appear to have been seized from the devil’s jurisdiction; rather, it is so that those who are works of God may become God’s pledges; that those who are born in a base condition, though not harmfully, may be reborn in a precious condition, though not calumniously; that those who proceed from God’s institutions may be advanced through God’s mysteries; that those who bring the works of nature may receive the gifts of grace; and that their Lord, who made them good by creating them, may make them better by renewing and adopting them.

Therefore, you must admit that it is rightly said: the natural sin that Manichaeus invented—but which you, changing the name, call original—has perished.

Nor does that ancient Catholic faith believe this [Note: [Col. 1438] The manuscripts read “believed this.”] which does not doubt both that little children are made by God and that God makes no evil. Consequently, before the exercise of free will, it places God’s works neither under guilt, through prejudice against nature, nor under the devil’s jurisdiction.

AUGUSTINE. We call it “original sin” rather than “natural sin” for the more significant reason that it may be understood to derive not from a divine work but from human origin [Note: [Col. 1438] Here and a little below, shortly before the end of this response, we have restored two lines, and perhaps as many or more, from the manuscripts]; above all, in order to signify that through one human being it entered the world. It is not abolished by Pelagian argument but by Christian regeneration.

But why you say that all infants ought to be reborn through Baptism, we know well enough: that is precisely why you are heretics. You argue, with this novel pestilence, against the antiquity of the Catholic Church, saying that infants are not rescued by the grace of the Redeemer from the power of darkness, although the Catholic Church exsufflates and exorcizes in their case—the power, plainly, of the devil, not the image of God.

What, then, is the meaning of your statement: “Those who are born cheaply, though not harmfully, may be reborn at great price, though not through slander”; and why do you not consider the very price by which they are reborn nobly? What is it, unless it is the blood of the immaculate Lamb? And the Lamb himself cries out why it was shed [Note: [Col. 1439] Vignierius reads *cum* (“when”); the manuscripts read *cur* (“why”).]. Did he not himself say, “This is my blood, which will be poured out for many” [Note: [Col. 1439] So the manuscripts. In Vignierius, “for you”] “for the forgiveness of sins” (Matt. 26:28)?

Yet you are more wondrous still [Note: [Col. 1439] The printed editions have *mirabilius* (“more wonderfully”). The manuscripts, which are better, have *mirabiliarius* (“wonder-worker”); Augustine uses this word in *Tractate on John* 13.17.]: you say that this blood is poured out even for infants, and you deny that any sins are forgiven them through it; you say that they must be washed, and deny that they are cleansed; you say that they must be renewed, and deny that they must be purified from the old condition; you say that they are to be adopted through the Savior, and deny that they are to be saved.

But we, you say, slander them, because we say that they are dead in their transgressions and in the uncircumcision of their flesh; and therefore that they are baptized into Christ’s death, so that those who had been dead in sin may die to sin. You, however, defend them; by denying that they are dead, you act so that the one who holds the power of death is not driven out from them. Thus they receive no benefit from Christ’s death, although he died, one for all.

When the Apostle had said this, he immediately concluded and said, “Therefore all have died, and he died for all” (2 Cor. 5:14–15). Accordingly, the one who defends infants in such a way as to deny that they are dead does not defend them from death, but presses them into the second death, excluding them from the benefit of him who, as is proclaimed, died only for the dead.

## X. JULIAN

After this, he passed over the whole episode concerning Abraham and Sarah, who received a son as a gift when their bodies were already dead—an example whose support for the truth is understood not only by a wise reader but even by an ordinary one—in such a way as to say that it was not very forceful against him.

That impudence ought at least to have been recalled by the sentence constructed as follows: “And, to close the substance of this discussion briefly, I say: if the one whom God promised was produced through concupiscence, then concupiscence is undoubtedly good, since it fulfills God’s promise; but if he was produced without concupiscence, concupiscence cannot be harmful to the one begotten, since concupiscence was present neither when he was conceived nor when he was born.”

## AUGUSTINE

Who would say that Abraham’s son was generated without carnal concupiscence? For this work could not otherwise have been performed in this body of death, of which the Apostle says, “The body indeed is dead because of sin” (Rom. 8:10).

Abraham made good use of this evil in marital intercourse; but this evil was not present in that body of life which existed in paradise before sin. If, however, carnal concupiscence seems good to you because through it the offspring whom God had promised was produced, then let the devil also seem good to you, because through him the blood of Christ, by which we were to be redeemed, was shed—the blood which God had promised. Or admit that some good can be produced through some evil.

## XI. JULIAN

Passing over these matters, then, this new natural philosopher declares false what we said: “Just as at that time the clay which was taken up was the material, not the author, of the human being, so now that force of pleasure, which produces and mingles the seeds, does not perform the role of divine operation; rather, it offers to God from the treasuries of nature the material from which he deigns to fashion the human being.”

He testifies that these words were correctly spoken by me, except for the statement that the seeds are produced by the force of pleasure; and he philosophizes in this manner: “That pleasure,” he says, “of carnal concupiscence does not produce the seeds, but those things which have already been created in the bodies by the true God are not made by pleasure, but are aroused and emitted with pleasure” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence* 2.26) [Note: [Col. 1440] Here Julian passes over the one by whom the bodies themselves are created.].

This plainly shows that he made the statement not through fraud but through a failure of understanding. For I called the force of pleasure the very constitution of the male body, and I found it necessary to give it the name of virility. This virility, then—which consists in the structure and soundness of the genitals and the internal organs, and supplies the powers both of desire and of production—I called the force of pleasure and concupiscence.

For that reason I preferred to call it not simply “pleasure” but “the force of pleasure,” so that I might indicate the whole ardor which is felt both before the act and during it. For men whose genital members are weakened—that is, eunuchs—do not have semen, although, certainly, some of them are stirred by sparks of extinguished fire [Note: [Col. 1440] So the manuscripts. Vignierius has “fires.”]. Yet because they lack the particular strength of the parts through whose service semen is formed from internal fluids, they are unable to produce offspring.

Thus God established it, so that there would be a force in the body which, unfolding at the proper times, would reach the power of fertility if health were present. Accordingly, semen is produced in bodies with the assistance of mature puberty. Hence premature pleasure does stimulate the sexually immature, but without the laws of age its kindled excitation flashes fruitlessly.

That semen is mingled with pleasure is true; but that one pleasure is the pleasure which rises above the senses, while another is the inner pleasure of the internal organs, nearer to the act’s effect, is discussed at length in the writings of medical authorities. Hence even that Mantuan poet, more knowledgeable about nature than the Carthaginian philosophical quibbler, marks the herds as weakened by emaciation, so that when familiar pleasure arouses them to their first intercourse, they may be kept from both foliage and springs. He says:

> Often, too, they are shaken by running and wearied by the sun,  
> while the threshing-floor groans beneath the heavily beaten grain,  
> and the light chaff is carried away by the winds.  
> This is done so that excessive indulgence may not blunt  
> the generative field and clog its inactive furrows;  
> but so that they may endure a certain dryness in secret,  
> and so that the thirsty creature may seize Venus  
> and store her deep within.  
> (Virgil, *Georgics* 3.130–137)

But in these matters also, since they are not particularly necessary to the argument, it is enough to note the man’s acuity.

## AUGUSTINE

I have already demonstrated above how empty your words are, which you say I passed over. Perhaps even the man who sent the little document saw this and, wishing to spare you, passed over the same things.

As for your verbose discussion of the force of pleasure, which you said produces semen, now that you have found an opportunity to talk, I do not need to resist you; for you yourself mention that these points are not particularly necessary to the argument [Note: [Col. 1441] Vignierius reads “but concerning pleasure.” The manuscripts read “but concerning the force of pleasure.”].

I had understood you to mean by “the force of pleasure” the force by which pleasure could produce something, not the force by which pleasure itself was produced. For we ordinarily speak of the force of a thing as that by which it is able to do something, not that by which another thing, which produces it, is able to produce it.

But, as you have now explained your words, you assert that you called “the force of pleasure” the force through which pleasure can be produced, not the force through which pleasure itself produces what it can produce—as if you were to say that the force of fire is that by which fire itself is kindled so that it may exist, when everyone speaks of the force of fire as that by which it burns or heats whatever it is able to burn or heat.

You have therefore spoken in an unusual manner. But what does that matter to us? However we learned it, once the matter is clear we do not quarrel over words. We agree that not only human beings from the seeds, but the seeds themselves, are works of God, however they may be produced. Thus we need not summon natural philosophers, physicians, or even poets as witnesses where there is no need; nor contend over how one ought to speak when we both hold the thing for which we speak to be true—namely, that the seeds of every nature are works of God.

But what you try to establish from this is false: that the seeds have no defects because God, who is supremely good, is their creator. You would not say this if you knew the principle of seed in the way that the one who said, “Man has become like vanity” knew it. And to show that this applied to the very nature which had fallen into mortality, he added, “His days pass away like a shadow” (Ps. 143:4). He knew that the human being had been made in the likeness of God, yet he distinguished the defect of corrupted human origin from divine creation.

You should have noticed the same point in your own words with which you attacked me. You said, “But in these matters also, since they are not particularly necessary to the argument, it is enough to have noted the man’s acuity,” thereby implying that I am dull because I could not understand your expression in matters which, as you admit, are not particularly necessary to the argument.

I, however, ask you where human beings become dull. For you yourself are not so dull [Note: [Col. 1441] Here, on the authority of the manuscripts, we restore: “for you yourself are not so dull.”] as to deny that dull or sharp intellects belong to human nature. Indeed, as we have already said above, even sharp intellects, when compared with the intellect of the first human being, are dull because of this corruptible body which weighs down the soul (Wis. 9:15). He certainly had not received such a body that his soul would be weighed down by it.

Thus I too would distinguish, in human nature as it now is, between the defect of the intellect and the work of so great an artificer. Defects of human intellects, whatever their extent, cannot rightly be attributed to him [Col. 1442]. By this rule you may learn to distinguish from his creation original sin, although it is congenital in human beings; and you should not deny that it exists merely because God makes human beings, while he does not make sin. In the same way, congenital defects in human intellects are not to be denied because God makes human beings, although all defectiveness is foreign to the divine art of the one who makes them [Note: [Col. 1442] So the manuscripts. Vignierius has “from the divine citadel.”].

God knows how to bring good out of human beings whose substance has been corrupted by sin, just as he knows how to bring good out of human sins, whose defects are voluntary.
