For we see how many good things he brought out of the sin of the brothers who sold their brother through envy (Gen. 37–50), as well as from many other things with which the sacred writings are filled.

## XII. JULIAN

Yet I am astonished at the disputant’s consistency everywhere. He declares that the seeds were created by the true God, by whom the bodies also are created, although they are emitted with pleasure. Thus he confesses that the seeds are made by God, while saying that they contain a diabolical evil; and he is not ashamed to believe that an evil is made by God and then charged against the innocent.

## AUGUSTINE

Evil does not come from God when good is made from evil. The defect of origin which comes from sin is evil, and the human being is born with it; the work of God is good, though not without evil. The guilt of that evil is not charged, as you say, against the innocent, but against the guilty, so that because it was contracted through birth it may be removed through rebirth.

Thus all were in Adam, by the principle of the seed, in his loins when he was condemned; and therefore he was not condemned without them. In the same way, the Israelites were in Abraham’s loins when he was tithed, and therefore he was not tithed without them (Heb. 7:5–10). Those who said these things and took care to commit them to writing for reading in Christ’s Church understood the principle of the seed better than you did. In that Church, those born from Adam are reborn, so that they may not remain condemned in that stock [Note: [Col. 1442] So the manuscripts. The printed editions have “in which.”].

## XIII. JULIAN

“Concupiscence,” he says, “has nothing to do with the seeds, because it was made by the devil. Married couples serve this concupiscence; but God makes the seeds and makes infants from the seeds. Yet,” he says, “the parents who perform the devil’s work are neither guilty nor punished; while infants, whom God created, are assigned to crime and punishments. What the devil made—that is, concupiscence—goes unpunished, and is thereby shown to be good, since it does not deserve punishment; but what God makes is accused and condemned, and is thereby shown to be criminal, since it cannot be defended from punishment or even from the shame of its author. It is believed that the deity does what cannot endure even the extremity of captivity.”

Such is the outcome for those who wage war against the truth: they say nothing that is not impious or insane, while it remains clear that the condition of the innocent is defended by no argument so much as by the profaneness of their accusers.

## AUGUSTINE

Do you make what I say false merely because you say that I say what I do not say? I do not say that concupiscence has nothing to do with the seeds, since those who are born certainly do not arise without concupiscence, and are born from the seed. Rather, I say that God works without any defect of his own even from a corrupted seed.

Nor do I say that the parents who perform the devil’s work are not guilty and are not punished. I say that they do not perform the devil’s work when they use concupiscence not for the sake of concupiscence but for the sake of propagation. For it is a good work to make good use of the evil of concupiscence, as married people do; conversely, it is an evil work to make bad use of the good of the body, as the sexually immoral do.

Nor do I say that concupiscence goes unpunished. It will be destroyed with death when this mortal nature puts on immortality (1 Cor. 15:53). It exists only in this body of death, from which the Apostle longed to be delivered (Rom. 7:24). It did not exist, or was not of the same kind, in that body of life which human beings lost by sinning, although they had been created upright (Eccl. 7:30). Nor will concupiscence, like some substance, be separated and removed from us, to migrate elsewhere [Note: [Col. 1443] So the manuscripts. The printed editions have “to an evil place.”]; rather, like an infirmity, it will perish in the perfection of our salvation.

Indeed, it ceases to exist even now after the death of the body. For it cannot still exist in a dead body, since it can exist only in a body of death; and what will perish in the death of the body will not rise again when the body rises without death. How, then, will it be punished or go unpunished when it will not exist as it perishes?

Those, however, will go unpunished who, because they lacked regeneration, remained without release from its congenital guilt, yet did not yield to its rising and pressing impulses when they urged them to perform unlawful acts; and if they do anything with their spouses from concupiscence not for the sake of offspring but for its own sake, they are healed by subsequent pardon.

That God creates infants from an origin rightly and justly condemned is good, because what he creates is itself good: he creates human beings, and even evil human beings are something good insofar as they are human beings. He is not restrained from the goodness of creating by those whom he foreknew would be condemned; indeed, he knows that they are already condemned by origin. We should therefore give thanks that so many of them are freed from their deserved punishment by undeserved grace.

But if you think it cruel that infants should be condemned when you do not believe that they contract original sin, then it should seem cruel to you that infants are not snatched from this life—infants who, according to you, have absolutely no sin, yet whom God knows will die amid many great sins without any change for the better. For according to human reasoning, it seems more cruel not to deliver, though able, one stained by no small or great sins than to condemn the offspring of a sinner.

When, then, you proclaim with whatever voice you can that the former is just, with what face do you contend that the latter is unjust?

## XIV. JULIAN

After this, he attempts to attack the point which we established by the testimony of the Apostle Paul: that God works the human being from the seeds. He argues that I committed fraud by wishing to apply to this passage statements which were plainly made about grains, as though I had either divided the Apostle’s meaning there, as he now judges, or recalled the testimony for any other reason than to show at its conclusion that God ought to be believed the creator of all seeds [Note: [Col. 1443] Perhaps “to demonstrate in good faith.” Morel, *Elementa Critica*, p. 269, suggests “to show at the end.”].

For blessed Paul, after using examples to establish faith in the resurrection and in daily multiplication [Note: [Col. 1444] The Codex Portarum has “lasting multiplication.”] [Note: [Col. 1444] The printed editions have “confirmed.”], added something that can apply to the whole of nature, saying: “But God gives it a body as he wills, and to each of the seeds its own body” (1 Cor. 15:38)—that is, he gives every seed the body which its particular nature requires.

I did not therefore intend that what was said about grains should be understood of the human being. Rather, I seized upon this statement—that each seed receives its own body from God the author—for the destruction of your position, since your dogma denies it. Thus, contrary to your opinion, I did not mention that statement uselessly, nor did I fraudulently misuse it, as you falsely claim. Nor do you believe, despite your perjury, that the human being is made by God from human seeds. I affirm this not by conjecture but by understanding your own faith.

## AUGUSTINE

Anyone who reads your writings intelligently can see how you introduced the apostolic testimony concerning the seeds sown in the earth, which are not made alive unless they die—for the discussion required this in treating the resurrection of bodies, which was the subject under consideration—and can also see what we replied to you about these matters in the same book which you are now attempting to refute (*On Marriage and Concupiscence* 2.28). He will find that, in what concerns the matter, you said nothing there and say nothing here.

With great effort you try to establish that God makes human beings from seeds, as though we denied this. You bring forward the Apostle as a witness where no necessity of the case requires you to prove it. And, what is more absurd, you wish to interpret as referring to human seeds what he said of grain seeds, because the matter required that interpretation. You quote his words, “What you sow is not made alive,” and suppress what he connects with them: “unless it dies.”

You also suppress what he adds: “And what you sow is not the body that is to be, but a bare grain, perhaps of wheat or of some other kind.” There he makes sufficiently clear what he is talking about. Having suppressed these words, you introduce what follows: “But God gives it a body as he wills, and to each of the seeds its own body” (1 Cor. 15:36–38). You refuse to understand here whose seeds are meant—that is, seeds of wheat or of some other kind, specifically those which, when sown, are not made alive unless they die.

You seek to transfer this statement also to human seeds. Although it may truthfully be said of them that God gives them a body as he wills and to each of them its own body, it cannot be said that human seed, when poured into a woman’s womb, is not made alive unless it dies.

But it can plainly be said of the human body. It will not rise unless it dies, and this is why the Apostle said the whole passage about the seeds of grain.

It therefore seemed to me, not without reason, that you suppressed in this testimony the words by which it would be evident what kind of seeds he was discussing. You introduced him as a witness so that an attentive reader might not be warned—if indeed you were able to anticipate this—that in paradise human beings could have been sown in the generative fields of women through the genitals of men just as grain is sown in the fields by the hands of farmers; so that no stimulus of concupiscence would incite the sowing of a human being, just as no pain would force the birth of a human being.

To those who dislike this tranquility I ask: what in the flesh pleases them except what shames them? Indeed, carnal concupiscence would not be shameful if the flesh were liberated only by what the mind commanded, whenever it commanded it [Note: [Col. 1445] Perhaps “commanded.”] and to whatever extent it commanded it.

But now, since it is not such, why do you support it against us rather than admit with us that it was either born from sin or corrupted by sin?

## XV. JULIAN

Who among prudent people could restrain laughter when he reaches the examples you have supplied? You say:

“His own words would refute this man: a man modestly named but not of religious will, rather of lustful pleasure, and an immodest preacher. He can be convicted from the very seeds which farmers sow in their fields. For why should we not believe that God could have granted the blessed human being in paradise from his own seed what we see granted to farmers from the seed of wheat, so that it might be sown in the same way as this is sown, without any shameful concupiscence?” (*On Marriage* 2.29).

How charmingly the “modest named” and “immodest preacher” produces thoroughly disordered movements and recites the songs of street performers!

But the other passage cannot be read except with the greatest amusement: if Adam had not sinned, then a woman could have been prepared for fertility just as a field is, perhaps so that ears of sons might burst forth through every joint and through the tiny tubes of the body which physicians call *poroi* (πόροι, “pores”); and thus, fruitful in every part, she might sweat out offspring instead of lice [Note: [Col. 1445] The ancient codices consistently have *lita* here and below in Augustine’s response. The printed editions more appropriately have *laeta*, “fruitful.” It seems to allude to Virgil, *Georgics* 1.1: “What makes the fields fruitful.”] [Note: [Col. 1445] The ancient codices have *peduculis*, “lice”; shortly afterward, *peducularia*, instead of *pedicularia*.].

But if some sons also burst forth through her eyes, the lights would be taken from the mother who gave birth; and if helmeted swarms emerged through the globes of her pupils, she would undoubtedly curse blindness and bereavement. Nor would it be difficult for offspring, not born but sweated out, to be killed; and there would be a people, among the doctrines of Manichaeus, either lice-like or public [Note: The Latin pun is between *pedicularia* (“lice-like”) and *publicaria* (“public,” perhaps “common” or “promiscuous”).], just as there was among the fables of the Myrmidons.

Such would be the woman’s means of bearing children. But what could the man accomplish? Surely he would bring up not limbs but tools, and, empty of genitals, would press plows and mattocks into the woman.

Thanks, then, and the greatest thanks, are owed to the error of the first human beings, by which the tortures of such a blessed nature were avoided [Note: [Col. 1445] So the manuscripts. Vignierius has “ferments.”]. Childbirth treats women more gently, and a husband treats his wife more gently, than if women felt plows or if they grew wild throughout their bodies with an intrusive fertility.

“Let the faces of the Manichaeans be filled with disgrace” [Note: [Col. 1445] The Codex Portarum repeats the word: “Let the faces, let the faces of the Manichaeans be filled with disgrace.”], “and let them seek your name, O Lord.” What monstrous arguments and testimonies these are, brought forward against the innocent and against God!

“Why,” he says, “should we not believe that nature could have been made otherwise than we see it made?” As though the question were what God could have done, rather than what he established.

If one wishes, through the lust of speculation, to criticize what has been made by saying that because things could have been made otherwise, what has been established does not bear witness to a good nature, let us declare that God could have made mortals with two heads; therefore those with one head were badly made, and those who stood on their feet were badly made, since they could have been made with heads at both ends. This form sometimes appears in certain little worms, whose belly encloses a vertex formed in two directions, so that they may be understood to begin at both shoulders and end in the middle.

Admit such absurdities, and what end will there be to delirium? God could therefore have made human beings sprout from the earth with flowers. As far as power is concerned, I do not deny that he could have done so; but he chose that they should be born from the two sexes. The question now is what he did, not what he could have done.

At this point the response is insane: “What exists is evil because God could have made it otherwise.” This is to praise God by blaming him, and to proclaim his omnipotence as a stain upon his plan. It is not praise at all, but a grave insult, to attribute strength to God while taking wisdom away from him, and to say that God possessed power but lacked judgment.

Criticism of his wisdom reaches, in effect, a denial of his power: he cannot do everything if he cannot arrange things well. Indeed, if he is deficient in the sublimity of wisdom, nothing remains of the reverence due to divinity. Since it is utterly profane to suspect this, the point returns which strangles your error.

God, who made all things very good, established nothing in such a way that, within the kind of thing that was made, another arrangement could be shown to have been either more fitting or more rational. Endowed equally with wisdom and omnipotence, he would not establish something that a human being could rightly criticize.

Whatever is taught to be natural in all creatures whatsoever has therefore been made in such a supreme manner that attempted correction of it is rightly judged foolish and profane. Thus the form of a horse and the form of an ox differ when compared with one another, yet within their own kinds they possess an apt harmony in every respect. Neither the horse nor the ox ought, or could, have been established otherwise than they are seen to have been formed. By the same rule one may pass through all creatures that swim, creep, walk, or fly, and finally those of the air and the heavens: no form can be shown to have been instituted better than the form suited to the kind for which it was prepared.

So too the human being, whom the generality of walking creatures has already indicated above, was formed throughout in such a way that no one could devise him better. He received, wisely, in his body both places of beauty and places of modesty, so that within himself he might learn both shame and confidence. He would have appeared disfigured if he had been covered everywhere; and he would have become sluggish and negligent if he had always been exposed everywhere.

Accordingly, human fecundity ought to have received the members of both sexes in no other way than it has, with no other arrangement of the internal organs, no other senses, and no other pleasure.

Let us therefore admonish the Manichaeans to stop criticizing the works of divine wisdom and to correct the perversity of their opinions. For it is irrelevant to the question whether human beings are said to have been destined to reproduce in a way different from that attested by the whole universe; nor could they have been made better than they were. Both reason and Scripture testify to this: Scripture cries out that God made all things not merely good but also very good (Gen. 1:31; Sir. 39:21).

Thus, throughout the entire work, the Manichaean doctrine has also collapsed at this point.

We do admit that in the future the bodies of the blessed will be more glorious and will require no assistance. But this too was most wisely established by the most just and wise God: the condition of the reward would not be anticipated or distorted by nature [Note: [Col. 1447] Perhaps “preceded.”]. Rather, there would be a first stage in which natural freedom would stand, and from which, by the right of free choice, it would either descend to the depths of punishment or strive upward to the summit of glory along the paths established by God.

## AUGUSTINE

Julian, you plainly did not think that people would read both my writings and yours. You wrote only for those who, ignorant of or neglecting my writings, and without carefully examining both, would take care to read and know yours alone; and who would believe that I had said nothing except what they found quoted by you in your letter as though it were mine.

I see that this happened because I had said: “Why should we not believe that God could have granted the blessed human being in paradise from his own seed what we see granted to farmers from the seed of wheat, so that it might be sown in the same way as this is sown, without any shameful concupiscence?”

You, as though responding to these words of mine, expanded your empty talk, proceeding and spreading it so far that you claimed I had held that, “if Adam had not sinned, a woman could have been prepared for fertility in such a way that, perhaps, ears of sons might burst forth through every joint and through the tiny tubes of the body which physicians call pores, and that, fruitful in every part, she might sweat out offspring instead of lice,” along with the rest, which I am weary of recounting but which you were not ashamed to heap up.

In these passages you also said of the man that he “would bring up not limbs but tools, and, empty of genitals, would press plows and mattocks into the woman.”

Would these and similar statements—which, when they are read on your behalf by readers who are not merely readers but admirers, they blush for you, if they possess any human feeling—really have allowed you to chatter about my words? You passed over and suppressed them for no other reason than to prepare broader spaces in which you could rave.

For I said that a human being could have been sown, with the genitals obeying the nod of the will. You, however, suppressed the genitals, so that you could go on about children sweating out through the woman’s joints and tiny tubes, like lice, and being born through the pupils of her eyes, followed by blindness.

I repeat: you suppressed the genital members, as though we were saying that, if Adam had not sinned, human beings would lack them. This enabled you to say, with ridiculous—not witty but foolish—banter, that “the man, empty of genitals, would press plows and mattocks into his wife so that she might conceive” [Col. 1448].

Is the question really about the number and shape of the members—members created for generation—which could have remained sound and intact in their proper places, without requiring the stimulus of concupiscence and serving the command of the will?

You did not wish to mention these things when you quoted my words, lest you impose silence upon yourself and be unable to open your mouth on those matters which seemed to you to sound so delightfully witty: children bursting out throughout the body like lice, and farmers’ tools being used to impregnate women. In fact, you presented them with the most absurd vanity.

For the same reason you did not think it appropriate to touch on what I said in the same passage, which you had undertaken to refute, concerning the pains of women in labor. If women gave birth without the torments of childbirth, I think they would have lacked not genital members but punitive torments [Note: [Col. 1448] So the manuscripts. Vignierius has “members” in the dative plural.].

Moreover, divine Scripture—as everyone who reads it knows—testifies that this kind of torment entered the female sex through Eve’s sin (Gen. 3:16).

You preferred to pass over this in my words rather than discuss it, lest it be said to you that, with the genitals of both sexes sound and intact, spouses could have had intercourse in the happiness of paradise without shameful concupiscence [Note: [Col. 1448] Vignierius has “spouses, without shameful concupiscence,” omitting *concumbere* (“to have intercourse”), which is restored from the manuscripts.], just as women could have given birth, with their female genitals sound and intact, without groaning in pain [Note: [Col. 1448] Perhaps “without groaning.”].

But you prefer to place not only the torments and groans of women in labor, but also the other labors and hardships of mortals, in the place of that great blessedness—not from the time of their free choice, but from the day they emerge from their mother’s womb—rather than place there even the shamefulness which you have accepted, at least with the shame proper to it.

And yet, although you deny that nature was changed into this mortality after sin, you admit that after the merit of a good will it will be changed into the glory of blessed immortality.

Infants ascend to the summit of that glory—as you cannot deny—not by the merits of their own will but by those of another’s will [Note: [Col. 1448] So the manuscripts. Vignierius has “would ascend.”]. Yet you refuse to believe that they were cast down into the depths of the miseries we know by the merits of another’s evil will, even though they were in the loins, by the principle of the seed, of the one in whom that will existed.

## XVI. JULIAN

But let us now proceed to the remaining matters. After avoiding the example of Abraham which I had introduced, he attempted to assert that, in the case of Abimelech also—who, it is reported, was healed with his women after Abraham prayed [Note: [Col. 1448] Vignierius omits the name “Abraham,” which we have added from the manuscripts.] so that he could return to the work of generation, from which he had been restrained by the affliction—it may be understood that the women’s womb had been closed not by the removal of concupiscence but by some pain (*On Marriage* 2.30).

This was as though we had asserted with great emphasis that their natural desire had been restored to them. Yet I was content, by those testimonies, to prove only that intercourse, which could not exist without concupiscence, had been obstructed by God’s anger and restored by God’s indulgence, whether the obstacles had been removed or the customary stimulants restored. Nevertheless, the point was not that this was diabolical, but rather that even through this it was shown to belong to God’s work: among the ordinary but harmless instruments of the body, it would sin neither in kind nor in manner, but through excess alone.

AUG. Who would not understand that, if, through God’s indignation, something happened to women’s bodies that prevented intercourse, and consequently offspring—which certainly could not be conceived except by those having intercourse—then, once that impediment had been removed, such intercourse was restored as belongs to this body of death, that is, intercourse with lust? For bodies are restored to the condition they acquired after sin, the condition of mortal nature that compels them toward death. But in that body of life, in which man would not have died had he not sinned, the condition was plainly different. Accordingly, there was there either no lust, or not such lust as exists now, by which the flesh would desire against the spirit, so that it would have been necessary either to submit to it or resist it—of which the one would not accord with dignity, and the other with the peace of that blessed state.

Do not therefore confuse these two lives through heretical perversity. One kind of life is lived in the corruptible body, which weighs down the soul (Wis. 9:15); another kind would have been lived in paradise, had the uprightness in which man was created remained.

[Note: [Col. 1449] After “which weighs down the soul,” we restore *vivitur* (“is lived”) from the manuscripts.] There too, then, there would have been intercourse between husband and wife for the sake of generation; but either with the genital members serving the mind without any lust, or with the movements of lust itself, if there were any, never resisting the will. If it had been of this kind, it would not have been shameful; nor would it have caused the bodily members—which it might either arouse or move by its impulse—to be properly called shameful or compelled them to be covered. That this happened after sin, and could have happened only as the punishment of sin, is testified by God’s words: “Who told you that you were naked, unless you have eaten from the tree concerning which I commanded you not to eat from it?” (Gen. 3:11). That is: “Your nakedness would not have been announced to you unless you had transgressed my law.”

But what does it mean for nakedness to be announced to one who was certainly not unaware of it, unless some movement stimulated him so that, at the unfamiliar sight, he felt himself compelled to notice it and was struck with shame? For sin caused the lower part of man to desire against the higher, that is, the flesh against the spirit. Yet you close your eyes against all this and, although God reveals that man would not have been ashamed of his nakedness unless he had sinned, you assert that he was so constituted that he would have been ashamed of his nakedness even had he not sinned. God says: “Who told you of your nakedness, unless because you sinned?” And you say—to quote your own words, which you spoke shortly before:

“Thus man was formed throughout in such a way that no one could fashion him better. In his body he wisely received both places of beauty and places of shame, so that in himself he might learn both modesty and confidence: lest he appear deformed if he were covered throughout, and lest he become indolent and negligent if he were always exposed throughout.”

According to you, therefore, man became far better by sinning. For unless he had sinned, the man whom God had made upright (Eccl. 7:30) would have lived imprudently, failing to distinguish in his body places of beauty and places of shame; immodestly, by covering none of them; and negligently, by exposing everything. He would not have avoided these vices unless, because he had sinned, his nakedness had been announced to him.

[Note: [Col. 1450] Thus the manuscripts. In Vignierius, *faceret* (“would make”).]

### XVII. JUL.

Since enough has been said about this, let us hasten to those matters which the Manichaean of old brought forward concerning natural evil—cleverly, but, as I shall prove, deceived by the perplexity of his questions. First, however, let us briefly examine what Augustine has brought forward against the testimony of the Apostle.

When I had stated most plainly, even on the testimony of blessed Paul, that this familiar function of the sexes, established by God as the author of bodies, was instituted by him—for, attacking the depravity of those whom madness had driven even to intercourse with the male sex, he says, “Abandoning the natural use of the female, they burned with desire for one another” (Rom. 1:27)—I concluded, on the testimony of the Apostle, that the natural use of woman had been instituted with approval.

In reply, he wrote:

“He did not say ‘conjugal use,’ but ‘natural use,’ intending it to be understood as that which takes place through the members created for this purpose, so that through them the two sexes may unite for procreation. Accordingly, when someone joins himself through the same members even to a prostitute, the use is natural, though not praiseworthy but blameworthy. Therefore, by this designation, namely ‘natural use,’ conjugal intercourse was not praised; rather, it marked out acts of impurity and crime more shameful than if they had used women illicitly but nevertheless naturally” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 2, no. 35).

That is, this use of woman which the Apostle pronounced natural is not to be understood as conjugal, so as to show it good and lawful. Rather, he says, it was called natural because it indicates that the difference of the sexes was established for this purpose: both for intercourse and for childbirth.

Since these contrivances accomplished nothing, why did he linger over them so long? Obviously for the sole reason that those who follow him might think that what they had seen touched upon had been dissolved. But how little he has actually said will be made clear by a brief discussion. The Apostle says that the use of woman was instituted naturally; he did not commend the other kind of intercourse originally ordained. Rather, when discussing that use in which he knew lust to have flourished in every age, he called it natural.

AUG. The natural use of woman occurs when her male partner uses that member by which nature propagates the same kind of living beings. For this reason that member itself is also properly called “nature”; hence Cicero says that a woman dreamed that she had been marked with “nature” (*On Divination*, book 2).

Thus natural use may be lawful, as in marriage, or unlawful, as in adultery. But use contrary to nature is always unlawful and plainly more disgraceful and shameful. The holy Apostle was condemning it both in women and in men, intending them to be understood as more damnable than if they sinned through natural use, whether by adultery or fornication.

The natural and therefore blameless intercourse of those who unite could have existed in paradise even if no one had sinned; for otherwise children could not have been begotten for the multiplication of the human race according to God’s blessing. But who told you that the Apostle called natural that use in which he knew lust to have flourished in every age, except your heresy? Far be it from us to believe that the Apostle thought that shameful lust flourished even at that time when they were naked and were not ashamed.

Nevertheless, even if the Apostle had said what you said—“that lust flourished in the natural use of woman in every age”—I would still find in these words something I could rightly understand, so as not, as you do, to place your shameful lust in the bodies of that blessed life, which were not yet the bodies of this death, with the most foolish mind, the most talkative tongue, and the most shameless forehead.

For from the time when intercourse between the two sexes began, the natural use of woman could certainly not exist without this shameful lust. By then they possessed not the body of that life but the body of this death, since after sin they had left paradise and the male and female first united in natural intercourse. If they had done so before, lust would either have been absent or not shameful. It would not have disturbed one who was unwilling, compelling the chaste person to resist it; rather, either the genital members would have performed their function at the command of the mind without it, or, if it existed, it would have risen when needed, following the will’s calmest command, neither overpowering thought with a turbulent assault of pleasure.

That it is not now of such a kind, it confesses through its many intrusive movements, which must be restrained. Therefore it testifies either that it is a vice or that it has been corrupted. This is the source of the Apostle’s statement: “I know that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh” (Rom. 7:18). This is the source from which original sin is drawn by those who are born. Conjugal chastity makes good use of this evil; religious widowhood and sacred virginity make even better use of it by not using it.

### XVIII. JUL.

This is what we understood, and when we were speaking about the institution of nature, we brought forward what it was evident that the Apostle meant. What, then, have you accomplished by reporting that he called it not conjugal use but natural use? Or with what face do you add that “when someone joins himself through the same members even to a prostitute, the use is natural, though not praiseworthy but blameworthy”? For, to show here as well what we have often made clear—that you never produce even one proposition that does not carry great force against you—if the use of fornication is called natural, though not praiseworthy but blameworthy, because it is the use of a prostitute, you will doubtless admit that conjugal use, because it is honorable and lawful, is not blameworthy but praiseworthy.

AUG. Conjugal intercourse is rightly called blameless, not because it is without evil, but because it makes good use of evil. For making good use of evil is good, just as making bad use of good is evil. Thus married people make good use of the evil of lust, just as adulterers make bad use of the good of the body. I have said this not once already, and I shall not tire of saying it repeatedly so long as you are not ashamed to contradict the truth.

[Note: [Col. 1452] Thus the manuscripts. In Vignierius, *pigebit* (“I shall be ashamed”).]

### XIX. JUL.

And where is your “diabolical crime,” which you were trying to attach to it by that argument concerning shame? For lust is no longer being condemned, since it is felt by the very condition of nature both in forbidden and in permitted use, if only its deviation toward what was not permitted is blamed.

AUG. It is not only “the deviation of lust toward what was not permitted” that is blamed; your great deviation lies in failing to blame it when it impels one toward what was not permitted. For whenever it impels toward what is unlawful, it surely rushes onward unless its perversity is resisted. This is the lust of the flesh, by which the flesh desires against the spirit; and for this reason the spirit also desires against it, lest it rush toward whatever the flesh impels it to do.

Therefore, what impels toward evil is itself evil. But if it does not rush onward because the spirit resists it, man is not conquered by evil. He will be free from every evil only when there is nothing for him to resist.

When this happens, nature will not, as the Manichaean madly claims, be separated from us as something alien; our nature will be healed. If it were already healed from every weakness in the same way that it is healed from guilt through regeneration and the forgiveness of sins, the spirit would not desire against the flesh, so that we would do only what is lawful. Rather, the flesh would consent to the spirit, and nothing unlawful would be desired against it.

### XX. JUL.

To ask the question precisely and briefly: when the Apostle Paul called the use of woman natural, do you think he indicated the possibility and the moral propriety of the act, or possibility alone? That is, by the term “natural,” did he wish us to understand a use which could and ought to take place, or one which could take place but ought not?

If you say, “One which could take place, although it ought not,” as in adultery, then that other disgraceful act also will not be contrary to nature, because it is performed with natural members. But if, shrinking back, you answer—as truth also requires—that the Apostle called natural a use which is intended for offspring and can honorably, indeed naturally, be performed because it both can and ought to be performed—that is, with the bodies of either one or several women, provided that they are permitted by the circumstances of the time—you will undoubtedly admit that your argument was foolish. You will admit that blessed Paul, by the term “natural use,” indicated not fornication, as you had supposed, but the honorable and lawful union of bodies prepared for fertility.

We therefore rightly defend in general what the Manichaean attacked in general. You say that this intercourse of the sexes with pleasure was instituted by the devil, that it is the cause of original sin and the necessity of all crimes, and thus you accuse nature itself. What could we more consistently do than defend, on the testimony of the Teacher of the Gentiles, the universality of nature, and attribute to God’s work what you called naturally evil?

Thus what you call diabolical we proved, in refutation of you, to have been naturally instituted.

[Note: [Col. 1453] Vignierius reads *probaremus institutum*, “we might prove it instituted,” omitting *naturaliter*, “naturally,” which is restored here from the manuscripts.]

This is the legitimate and learned response: what is accused in particular must be defended in particular, and what is attacked in general must be vindicated in general. The Manichaean understood this as well—he whom you equal in guilt but do not equal in intelligence. For that reason he transfers the whole substance of bodies to the devil, whereas you transfer not the whole but, as we said in the preceding book, the better part.

Truth has therefore triumphed, surrounded by sacred defenses. Through the Apostle, by proving that the natural business of married people belongs to God, who is the author of nature, it has shattered your fabrications, by which you swear that this is transgressive rather than natural.

AUG. We have already said sufficiently above which use of woman the Apostle called natural and why he called it natural: namely, because it takes place through the members of both sexes that were instituted for propagating nature. This may be a use such as could have existed in paradise, making use of no evil—either because no lust existed or because, if it existed, it followed only the will’s command—or it may be such as it has been since it first began: lawful, as in marriage, making good use both of the body’s good and of the evil of lust; or unlawful, as in adultery, making bad use of both that good and that evil. Yet even the latter does not depart from those members which are properly called “nature” as well.

There is therefore no reason for you to ask, as you claim, precisely and briefly, whether the Apostle intended by “natural use” one which could and ought to take place, or one which could take place but ought not. For in saying this the Apostle was considering none of these distinctions, but only the genital members natural to both sexes—that is, created for propagating nature.

[Note: [Col. 1453] Vignierius reads *creatura* (“creature”); the old Codex Portarum reads *creata* (“created”).]

For who does not know that lawful use of woman both can and ought to occur, whereas unlawful use can occur but ought not? Yet both are natural, because both take place through the genital members created for the propagation of nature.

Remove your evasive ambiguities; put away the verbose and deceptive smoke of your vanity. The lust of animals is not a vice because their flesh does not desire against the spirit. If the Manichaean had been able to distinguish this, he would neither have alienated the natures of animals from the workmanship of the true God nor have thought that human vices were substances.

But unless you think and maintain, with Ambrose and the other Catholics, that through the transgression of the first man the disagreement between flesh and spirit was turned into our nature (Ambrose, *On Luke*, book 7, 12:53), you will undoubtedly remain, however much you seem to detest the Manichaeans, a detestable accomplice of theirs. You assert to be good what truth proclaims to be evil, and by denying that this evil comes from the corruption of our nature by sin, you enable the Manichaean, with your assistance, to introduce into us the intermixture of an alien nature.

[Note: [Col. 1453] Thus the manuscripts; Vignierius reads *indicat* (“indicates”).]

[Note: [Col. 1453] Vignierius reads *voluisset*, “had wished.” The manuscripts have *valuisset*, “had been able.”]

### XXI. JUL.

With similar acumen you also attempt to undermine what I said: that according to the Gospel testimony a tree must be known by its fruits, so that I might demonstrate what is obvious—namely, that marriages cannot be taught to be good, nor even nature itself, which is replenished through the activity of marriage, be vindicated as belonging to God’s work, if crimes were said to spring from it.

[Note: [Col. 1454] The manuscripts read *operi* (“work”); later printed editions likewise have this reading in Augustine’s response below, chapter 24.]

You replied:

“Was the Lord speaking about that, or rather about the two wills of human beings, the good and the evil, calling the one a good tree and the other an evil tree because good works arise from a good will and evil works from an evil will? If we understand marriage as the good tree, we shall necessarily place fornication, by contrast, as the evil tree. But if he should say that not adultery, but human nature, from which man is born, must be placed there in the position of the tree, then here too the tree will not be marriage but human nature, from which man is born” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 2, no. 43).

[Note: [Col. 1454] Vignierius reads *illius* (“of that”); the manuscripts read *illic* (“there”).]

You are mistaken. There the Lord is not speaking about two wills but about his own person. For although he was doing countless good deeds for the Jews, they never ceased making accusations against him.

[Note: [Col. 1454] Thus the manuscripts; Vignierius reads *innumeris* (“countless [persons]”).] Since they could not attack his works, which they even glorified, they nevertheless accused him of mocking them as a Samaritan and as one possessed by a demon and by the spirit of Beelzebul.

Then the Lord said: “Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree bad and its fruit bad; for the tree is known by its fruit” (Matt. 12:33). That is: Either criticize my works, which the expelled illnesses and restored health proclaim to be good, so that the testimony of my works may prove me wicked; or, if you do not dare to criticize such great benefits, bear witness to the good tree—namely, to me—through the testimony of my fruits, and love the benefactor whom you praise for his benefits.

There, therefore, Christ commanded that his person be recognized from his works. This rightly supported our position, so that we might teach that nature and marriages too must be judged by the quality of their fruitfulness: if the poison of crimes flowed from them, their root also would have to be judged criminal.

See, then, how blind you are in understanding, since you thought you could lighten the burden of my objection by placing fornication opposite marriage, so that, just as marriage appeared to be a good tree, fornication would appear to be an evil tree—and so no fertility ought to come from fornication, lest it be proved evil if good marriages were shown by good offspring to be good. Yet whether a man is born from marriage or from adultery, he proceeds not from the crime but from the nature of the seed.

The crime committed by the will of adulterers does not disturb the substances established by God. Rather, nature exercises itself through its own materials; the sin remains with the author of the unlawful will, while an innocent offspring emerges from the work of the Creator. You too saw that this had to be acknowledged, but let the prudent reader observe how you attempted to evade it.

You say:

“If adultery is not to be placed there in the position of the tree, but human nature, from which man is born, then here too the good tree will not be marriage but human nature, from which man is born.”

This, then, is what you attempted to express: just as a man is not attributed to fornication but to nature, so the sin drawn from legitimate parents is not to be attributed to marriage but to human nature, which the devil infected with the ancient crime.

Thus, in adulterers you blamed the will of those indulging in lust, but praised human nature, from which a man would be born even through illicit intercourse. In legitimate parents, however, you praised marriage, from which you do not say that sin comes, but blamed nature, from which you say that the dreadful crime is infused.

Let my reader be alert here. If you judged human nature praiseworthy in fornication because it made the cause of the person being born undefiled by the crimes of those who came together, how do you criticize this same nature in marriage, when you say that it supplied the cause of the natural crime?

[Note: [Col. 1455] Printed editions read *impolluta* (“undefiled,” nominative); Codex Mar. reads *impollutam* (“undefiled,” accusative).]

You have therefore professed that not marriage but human nature is both a great good and a great evil. For what is worse than it, if it gives birth to crime? What is more detestable, if it is possessed by the devil? Let nature itself see what art it possesses in the seed. For the present, however, it is proved to be of the worst quality in that which contains every good or evil, if it is itself guilty, gives birth to guilt, and is shown to be an accomplice of the devil’s tyranny.

The tree must therefore rightly be known by its fruits, so that what is the cause of evil may most properly be called evil.

AUG. The matter itself sufficiently shows that neither marriage nor adultery is the cause of original evil. For what is good in human nature is born from man by God’s creative work, whereas what is evil, on account of which he must be born again, is drawn from man.

The cause of this evil, moreover, is that “through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death, and so it passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Rom. 5:12). Those who read your words and ours intelligently see how verbosely and fruitlessly you have labored to twist the Apostle’s words into another meaning.

What, then, does the Gospel testimony help you? Why, I ask, did you mention the statement that a good tree produces good fruits when you were speaking of the good of marriage and wanted its fruits to be human beings—as though you were thereby demonstrating that they are born without evil because marriage is good and a good tree cannot produce evil fruits?

Human beings are born from human beings, whether with original guilt, concerning which the Apostle says, “The body is dead because of sin” (Rom. 8:10), or without any guilt, as you contend against the Apostle.

[Note: [Col. 1455] Perhaps *nascantur* (“are born”).] They are not, however, born only through marriage: sometimes marriages are sterile and adulteries fertile.

Whether the Lord wished to suggest, through the two trees, the two wills of which we speak—one good, by which a person is good and which cannot produce evil works, that is, evil fruits; the other evil, by which a person is evil and which cannot produce good works, that is, good fruits—or whether, as you say, he spoke these words about himself to the Jews, those who wish to know read the Gospel and disregard you.

[Note: [Col. 1456] Printed editions read “and disregard you”; this is corrected from the manuscripts.]

When the Lord showed that those should be avoided who would come in sheep’s clothing but inwardly were ravenous wolves, he said: “You will know them by their fruits. Do they gather grapes from thorns, or figs from thistles? Thus every good tree produces good fruits, but the bad tree produces bad fruits. A good tree cannot produce bad fruits, nor can a bad tree produce good fruits” (Matt. 7:16–18).

According to Luke, when hypocrites were being rebuked, these two trees were also mentioned and immediately explained, as the Lord continued:

“The good man brings forth good from the good treasure of his heart, and the evil man brings forth evil from the evil; for from the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks” (Luke 6:45).

But when he said, “Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree bad and its fruit bad”—which you think he said about himself—he immediately explained from what he had spoken:

“For from the fruit,” he says, “the tree is known. You brood of vipers, how can you speak good things when you are evil? For from the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks. The good man brings forth good things from his good treasure, and the evil man brings forth evil things from his evil treasure” (Matt. 12:33–35).

Do you see that you are mistaken, not I? Return, then, to the cause of the evil deed, and you will find an evil will. Return to the cause of original evil, and you will find the evil will of the first man, and a good nature corrupted by it.

### XXII. JUL.

But we say these things to show what the end of your faith is. For the point established in the preceding discussions remains unshaken: nothing is evil except the act of the will of the one who perpetrates what justice forbids; and what is natural cannot be proved evil. This unshaken tower therefore remains, from whose height the raids of various errors are driven back.

AUG. What are you saying? And what are your preceding discussions except the most verbose vanities? What do you mean by saying, “Nothing is evil except the act of the will of the one who perpetrates what justice forbids”? Is the evil will itself, then, not evil, if nothing is evil except its act? For it does not follow that an evil will also has the power to carry out the act. Thus, on your authority, it will not be evil for a man to will evil when he cannot do it.

Who could tolerate such folly—or rather, such madness? We may also point out that if nothing is evil except the act of the will of one who perpetrates what justice forbids, then whatever human beings unwillingly do or suffer will not be evil. The evil of which the Apostle cries out will not be evil: “For I do not do the good that I want, but the evil that I do not want, this I do” (Rom. 7:19). The punishment of eternal fire, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth (Matt. 8:12), will not be evil, because no one will suffer it willingly, and it is not the act of a will that perpetrates what justice forbids, but the punishment of one who is unwilling.

When will you acquire sound judgment, if you do not disastrously lose it—or rather, if you do not go mad?

[Note: [Col. 1457] Codex Port. reads *si non miserabiliter desiperes*, “if you did not miserably lose your reason.”]

What also do you mean by saying, “What is natural cannot be proved evil”? Is natural deafness not evil—to say nothing of countless natural bodily defects—when it impedes even the faith by which the just person lives (Gal. 3:11), since “faith comes from hearing” (Rom. 10:17)?

But if you were not inwardly deaf, you would hear with the ears of your heart when the Apostle says, “For we too were by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Eph. 2:3). Continue, then, and cry out with blind and deaf hearts: “It is not evil to be naturally forgetful, naturally dull, naturally irascible, naturally lustful.” Why do you not confidently utter these foolish words, by which even natural stupidity is said not to be evil?

You are compelled to praise every natural defect because you deny to all original evil the character of guilt. Thus you are driven to say that not only misshapen, weak, and monstrous offspring of the body, but even foolish offspring, would have arisen in paradise had no one sinned—provided that you place your shameful lust, by which the flesh desires against the spirit, among the delights of that most blessed place.

### XXIII. JUL.

But now let us pursue what the passage requires. It is evident that you, a most subtle disputant, have exalted one and the same thing—human nature—with great praises, but stained it with even greater crimes. Yet just as these things cannot occur simultaneously, at one time, through one work, and according to one plan, so natural reason cannot in any way admit these opposites, even successively; rather, it is always wholly of one character—namely, an appraisal as good, never as evil—because the institutions of its maker do not admit an assessment unworthy of his dignity, unless they are bitten by the most polluted tooth of the Manichaeans.

[Note: [Col. 1457] The manuscripts read *uni operi* (“to one work”).]

[Note: [Col. 1457] Thus the manuscripts; printed editions read *subalternatio* (“subalternation”).]

[Note: [Col. 1457] Perhaps: “which, through the dignity of their author, do not admit [of evil].”]

But having completed this point, I ask which empty pretences of marriage you think should be followed. For if you admit that marriage is not the cause of man but nature, and that marriage is not the cause of sin either, but nature, then the marriage to which you were giving praise has completely vanished.

To what, then, is it to be attributed, if it is the cause neither of your evil nor of my good? If you remove man from the honor of marriage, lest you also be compelled to attribute him to fornication; if you remove sin from the necessity of marriage, lest you seem to condemn marriage; what remains worthy of praise in the possession of marriage?

Why are you afraid to violate in speech what you have utterly overthrown by your argument? Of what, then, will it be said to be the cause, if it participates in neither natural evil nor natural good? Is the name and honor of marriage now entirely inactive in human affairs?

But you are distressed—and indeed severely distressed. The gasping old man must therefore be helped. Something remains that you can grant him, without which nothing else can be found: namely, that you may say that this marriage stands at the door so that it does not allow any reputation for obscenity to intrude upon the pleasure of those who unite, but by its own title claims honor and modesty for that activity.

Without cause, then, you wished to corrupt the faith of marriage by deceptive praise. Nothing is more hostile to it than to you.

[Note: [Col. 1458] Vignierius and Codex Clar. read: *nulli es infestus, quam tibi*, “you are hostile to no one as much as to yourself.” Codex Mar. has the reading adopted here: *nulli est infestius, quam tibi*, “nothing is more hostile to it than to you.”]

It utterly drives you away and does not permit the tongues of the Manichaeans to creep in and tear apart the intercourse entrusted to its protection.

[Note: [Col. 1458] Printed editions read *perturbat* (“disturbs”); Codex Clar. more aptly reads *proturbat* (“drives away”).]

“They have,” it says, “meritorious acts worthy of their doctrine, in which they may fulfill themselves during the night hours. The modest pleasure of marriage is protected by guards; crimes are kept away, and the honor of modesty is admitted.

[Note: [Col. 1458] Printed editions read *voluntatem* (“will”); one manuscript, Codex Port., reads *voluptatem* (“pleasure”).]

Honorable marriages and undefiled beds defend the privileges granted them by the Apostle: ‘Marriage is honorable among all, and the marriage bed undefiled; but God will judge fornicators and adulterers’” (Heb. 13:4).

[Note: [Col. 1458] Codex Port. reads *privilegio sibi ab Apostolo concesso defendit* (“it defends the privilege granted it by the Apostle”).]

Where, then, is the criminal intercourse, if the authority of marriage—which you praised—attends upon its activity and secrecy?

AUG. You wished the Gospel testimony that a tree is known by its fruits to benefit not nature but marriage. For these are your words:

“If original evil is drawn even from marriage,” you say, “then the union of marriage is the cause of evil, and that through which and from which an evil fruit has appeared must necessarily be evil, since the Lord says in the Gospel, ‘The tree is known by its fruits.’ How,” you ask, “should you be thought worthy of being heard when you say that marriage is good, from which you declare that nothing other than evil proceeds? It is therefore established,” you say, “that marriages are guilty if original sin is derived from them, and they cannot be defended unless their offspring is proved innocent. But they are defended and pronounced good; therefore their offspring is proved innocent.”

Your words make it sufficiently clear that you intended marriage to be understood as the tree, and the fruits of the tree as the offspring born from the intercourse of married people. But because you were excluded from this position by the clearest reasoning—for such offspring also arise from adulterers—you thought it necessary to flee to nature, in whose height you might lie hidden. Yet you were not discussing nature when, on account of the good of marriage and its good fruits, you blindly employed the analogy of the Gospel tree.

Defend nature, then, against original sin. Leave marriage aside and call nature itself the good tree, because it produces human beings whether from marriages or from adulteries. You call them the good fruits of the good tree so that they may not be believed to have drawn any guilt from a corrupted origin, a guilt that must be removed through regeneration; so that they may not need a savior, nor be redeemed by the blood poured out for the forgiveness of sins.

[Note: [Col. 1455] Perhaps *in remissionem* (“for the remission”).]

Do this as a detestable heretic. Fill God’s paradise—even if no one had sinned—with the lusts of those desiring, the struggles of those fighting against lust, the pains of women giving birth, the cries of infants, the illnesses of the weak, the funerals of the dying, and the grief of mourners. Do this; it suits you. For, according to you, such punishments follow the good fruits of the good tree and reveal a paradise of delights—but one belonging to the Pelagians.

You also mock my dialectical argument with sharp wit, saying that I have exalted one and the same thing, namely human nature, with great praises but stained it with even greater crimes. But I do not take pleasure in having Aristotle or Chrysippus, much less vain Julian with his loquacity, as my teacher. I take pleasure in having Christ as my teacher. Surely, unless human nature were a great good, the man who was God would not have become man for its sake. Unless it had been dead through the great evil of sin, he would not have died for it, though he came and remained without sin.

Again, as though human nature were not sufficient for you—human nature which is born from adulterers in the same condition as from married people—you think we must be pressed on the goodness of marriage. You ask what place marriage has in human affairs if neither the evil is to be attributed to marriage, since it is drawn not from marriage but from an origin corrupted by sin, nor the good, since a man is also born from adulterers.

And because we find that the honor of marriage is distinguished from the shame of illicit intercourse, you think it follows that no original evil is drawn from conjugal intercourse. You fail to see that if the good of marriage were the cause of preventing those born from married people from drawing evil, then the evil of adultery would certainly be the cause of those born from adulterers drawing evil.

Marriage therefore has its honorable place in human affairs—not so that human beings may be born, for they would certainly be born even if, without any law of marriage, both sexes freely united in natural intercourse, but so that they may be born through ordered propagation. Just as mothers are established by childbirth, so fathers may be known with certainty through marital fidelity; and so that your shameful lust may not wander among any women, all the more shamefully because it would do so more freely.

But a man is not, because he is born from marriage with a known father, thereby without need of the Savior through whom he may be born again and freed from the evil with which he is born.

[Note: [Col. 1459] Vignierius reads, “freed from the evil in which he is born”; *cum*, “with which,” has been added from the evidence of the manuscripts.]

There is therefore no criminal intercourse in marriage, as you falsely accuse us of saying. But the chastity of married people is to be praised because it alone can make good use of the evil which you praise disgracefully.

### XXIV. JULIAN

Having disposed of these matters, I shall briefly show how deeply you lie in the abyss of ignorance—you who until now were regarded as exceedingly subtle and acute. You say that you attribute to nature the guilt that passes into offspring, but not to marriage [Note: [Col. 1459] The Codex Port., “but not into marriages.” Perhaps it should be read, “but not in marriages.”]: just as, conversely, you apply the matter to human nature, not to the crime. And therefore you pretend that you praise marriage, lest you be openly discovered to be a Manichaean; but you condemn nature, which you confess both to contain evil and to propagate evil.

Could you never have heard the rules of disputation and the soundest principles of reasoning? For in all the categories, genera embrace more than species; from these, moreover, subordinate genera are formed. Species, in turn, comprise more than individuals; and there are genera within which species are contained, while special species include individuals. Consequently, the disturbance of what is lower does not disturb what is higher; but what is higher, through its own changes, encompasses everything that it contains.

For example, “animal” is a genus [Col. 1460]; but by the breadth of its meaning it contains various species, namely human being, horse, ox, and so forth. If, then, one species perishes, that genus does not experience destruction. Suppose, for instance, that the nature of oxen were to disappear from the world: the genus would certainly not be destroyed, since the nature of the other animals remains. Conversely, if that which is “animal” were removed from the world, all the species undoubtedly included under that genus would perish; for no species of living thing would remain once “animal” had been completely destroyed.

Thus what is higher communicates its own qualities, outcomes, and merits to the species it embraces; yet it does not change into the varieties of its species as though into certain subordinate relations. To apply the example to the present issue: the universality of human nature is a kind of genus of the institutions situated beneath it [Note: [Col. 1460] The printed editions have “irritations”; the old Codex Mar. has “irrationalities.” But below, in chapter 40, where Augustine cites this same passage in his reply, all the books have “institutions.”]. These have, as it were, the status of species: position, bodily members, ranks, movements, and other things of that kind. It therefore communicates its quality to all the subordinate species, but it would not be made liable to its own [Note: [Col. 1460] The Codex Port. has “liable to the guilt of itself.” Morel, *Elem. Crit.*, pp. 354–355, reads “liable to recurrence.” That reading seems difficult to admit. M.] guilt, so as to be entangled in the dangers of the things beneath it.

If, then, nature is condemned and believed to be liable to the devil and guilty, marriage also, which lies beneath it, together with fertility and the whole substance, will be condemned. Marriage, which takes place according to nature, cannot therefore be praised if nature itself is reproached. The beauty of the severed shoots must necessarily die together with its root; and, to state the matter more plainly, the business of marriage cannot be called good if natural intercourse is indicted, since what is depreciated in the genus to which it indivisibly adheres cannot be honored in the species.

Moreover, when an evil will uses natural instruments for shameful acts, that force of pleasure and semen—which never varies according to the will of those who have intercourse—does not suffer any partnership in the crime. Rather, it provides the material for God’s activity, while it is solely the merit of the adulterer that is condemned, not nature.

When, therefore, we were discussing natural things, you condemned nature while praising marriage with extreme dullness; yet it is incontrovertibly established that a genus participates in whatever its species receive. Consequently, either the use that the Apostle calls natural will be judged good and legitimate, and marriages will be honorable, with no natural sin existing; or, if nature is believed to be diabolical, so that there is original sin, the use of marriage also will be pronounced condemnable. Thus, the doctrine of the Manichaeans is being accepted—not soberly, indeed, but openly nevertheless. Since that doctrine is deadly, and since among them there is nothing either of truth, honor, or faith, while among no others can the opinion of natural sin be found, it is clear that, just as we are Catholics, so you are Manichaeans.

### AUGUSTINE

You certainly spoke of a tree and of the fruits by which the tree is recognized, when you thought that in this comparison marriage and offspring were to be understood. But when you were excluded from that comparison because such a fruit can also arise from adulterous intercourse, you fled to nature. Nor could the route taken by your flight escape us: it became quite evident in the words I shall now recall.

For you said, addressing me personally:

> “With similar acumen you also try to undermine what I said—that, according to the gospel testimony, a tree must be recognized by its fruits—so that I might show,” you say, “what is clear: that good marriages cannot be taught; indeed, that nature itself, which is replenished by the operation of marriage, cannot be claimed as God’s work if crimes were said to spring from it.”

By these words of yours you disclosed the course of your flight, naming marriages and adding, “indeed, nature itself, which is completed by the operation of marriage.” You therefore distinguished these two things and clearly showed that nature is one thing and marriage another, by whose operation nature is replenished.

What, then, is the meaning of your later wish to make marriage the species and nature its genus? Is any genus completed by the operation of one of its species? Certainly not. The genus “animal,” for example, is not completed by the operation of a human being, horse, ox, or any other animal that is a species of that genus. Even if one species is absent and removed from the world, the genus nevertheless remains, embracing the remaining species, just as you yourself argued. The genus would not remain complete if it were completed by the operation of the species that had been removed. A genus is not more a genus if it has more species, nor less a genus if it has fewer species; although, if all the species are removed, there will be no genus, just as, when the genus is removed, there will be no species.

Marriage, then, is not a species and nature a genus if nature is replenished by the operation of marriage—just as a crop is not a species of agriculture, since the crop is completed by the work of agriculture.

Furthermore, if you say that nature is the genus and marriage its species, you are unquestionably forced to say that every marriage is nature. A horse is therefore “animal” in every case, although not every animal is a horse, because horse is the species and animal the genus.

Nor, consequently, is any nature made by a human being. For although, as it is written, “a wife is joined to a husband by the Lord” (Prov. 19:14, according to the Septuagint), since it does not happen rightly unless he assists, who does not know that marriages are the work of human beings? But if a human being does not make nature, marriage is not nature, because a human being makes marriage. And therefore, since marriage is not nature, it cannot in any way be a species of nature, as though nature were its genus.

Marriages therefore belong to human customs, whereas human beings themselves belong to nature. It is consequently permissible for us to condemn the evils of corrupted nature and to praise customs that make good use of the good and evil things of nature.

I therefore praise marriages. But far be it from me to praise the evil by which the flesh lusts against the spirit—without which evil no human being can be born, and the guilt of which cannot be removed except by rebirth, although its good use in marital intercourse is praised.

Accordingly, it is not the Manichaeans but the Catholics who say that original sin is not drawn from another person’s intercourse, but from the corruption of our nature; and by denying this, you are heretics.

### XXV. JULIAN

To avoid the odium attached to that name, you make entirely pointless mention of various heresies. For you say:

> “Just as the Arians call Catholics Sabellians, although they make a definite distinction between the persons while preserving the community of nature, so we too impose upon you the name of Manichaeans, although you do not say that marriage is evil, as the Manichaeans say, but say that evil passes into all human beings by the condition of nature” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 2, no. 38).

I do not doubt that these arguments of yours will be laughed at by prudent people. For just as the Arians falsely call Catholics Sabellians, although among us the persons of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are distinguished without any confusion and without any change of substance, while they most stupidly slander us by claiming that there is no difference between one and three, so Catholics rightly and deservedly pronounce you to be Manichaeans, because your own faith compels us to say this.

The Manichaeans assert natural sin; you call it natural. The Manichaeans say that the lust of bodies was planted by the devil; you confirm this through repeated argument. They contend that evil cannot be avoided by free will, since it is natural; you likewise invent free will in the same terms, but one by which evil can be done [Note: [Col. 1462] We have restored from the manuscripts the two lines extending from “you likewise” to “by which evil can be done.”], while one cannot desist from evil.

The Manichaean says that semen is accursed; you attempt to prove this by the authority of Scripture. The Manichaean says that wickedness is unchangeable; you cry out that it is so. But you say that Adam alone belonged to a better nature; the Manichaean also says to Patricius that Adam must be believed to have been better, as though he had been formed from the flower of the first substance.

You say that intercourse is diabolical because of natural impulses, and that human beings are rightly plucked by the devil as fruits from a shrub planted by him; the Manichaean says this too, since you learned to believe and affirm it from him.

The Manichaean says that both nature and marriage are evil; you say that marriage is good, but nature guilty. In this matter you are not more religious, but he is wiser.

Therefore, just as it is false that the Arians say that Catholics are Sabellians, so it is entirely true that Catholics say that the Traducians are nothing other than Manichaeans; and that the distinction between you arose as a deception, not from your faith but from your ignorance.

You and the Manichaean therefore share one faith; but he is less shameless than your dignity proves to be. For it is not easy for a Manichaean—or another Melitidian—to be offended by someone who says that he condemns human nature but does not defame marriage.

### AUGUSTINE

Anyone who reads that book of mine intelligently immediately discovers why I mentioned the Arians and Sabellians, and sees that you are acting deceitfully because you did not wish to recall the whole matter. For I said to you:

> “Just as the Arians, while fleeing the Sabellians, fell into something worse because they dared not distinguish the persons but the natures of the Trinity, so the Pelagians, while perversely attempting to avoid the plague of the Manichaeans, are convicted of thinking more perniciously than the Manichaeans themselves about the fruit of marriage, by believing that infants do not need Christ the physician” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 2, no. 38).

You should have set these words of mine before yourself, or at least this statement of mine, if you wished to answer me in any way. Omitting them, you say to yourself whatever you wish, so that you may appear to have answered me—not by refuting what I said, but by failing to remain silent.

And now, when you say that I hold the same views as the Manichaeans, you are greatly mistaken—or rather, you deceive as many as you can. For the Manichaeans say that evil is coeternal with God, that evil is a substance, and that it is another nature, which cannot be changed into good either by itself or by the good God. They maintain that, through the mixture of this immutable evil [Note: [Col. 1463] The printed editions have “the mixture”; and shortly afterward, “the shadows of piety.” Below, instead of “and a guilty nature,” they had “and that nature.” These and other passages in this response have been corrected according to the old manuscripts.], the good soul—which they dare to believe is the nature of the good God—is defiled and corrupted; and for this reason they hold that a savior is necessary at every age of human life, by whom it may be cleansed, restored, and rescued from such captivity.

But you, while perversely fleeing the Manichaeans, have fallen into such shadows of impiety that, while asserting infants to be free from every evil, you do not think that they need a Savior. And, in helping the very Manichaeans from whom you flee, you somehow encounter them indirectly through the circuitous route of your error: by denying the evil of our corrupted nature, you make whatever evils are rightly believed or plainly found in infants be attributed to a foreign nature’s mixture—as they themselves wish.

The Catholic Church, however, in avoiding both Manichaeans and Pelagians, says that evil is not any nature or substance. But it does not deny that our nature and substance, mutable because it is not God’s nature, has been corrupted by the voluntary evil that passed through one human being into all human beings [Note: [Col. 1463] Vignierius has “that it is mutable.” The word “is” is absent from the manuscripts.]. It confesses that a Savior is necessary for people of every age, so that this evil—which is not incurable by God—may be removed.

Accordingly, we cannot say the same things as the Manichaeans concerning natural sin, the lust of bodies, free will, accursed semen, unchangeable wickedness, the nature of the first human being, sexual intercourse, or the devil’s power over human beings. We do not say that there are two natures and substances, one good and the other evil, eternal without beginning in time and mixed together from some beginning in time; for otherwise, among many absurd and insane ideas, we would also be saying that God’s nature can be defiled and corrupted.

But when you claim that I alone say that marriages are good while nature is guilty, I give you Paul the Apostle—leaving others aside—whom you too proclaim as a praiser of marriage, yet who says concerning the guilt of original nature [Note: [Col. 1464] Perhaps “of original sin.”], “the body is dead because of sin” (Rom. 8:10).

I give you another interpreter of this matter and my teacher, the Catholic Ambrose, who, while praising conjugal chastity, nevertheless says:

> “We are all born under sin; our very origin is in fault” (*On Repentance*, book 1, chapter 2 or 3).

Slanderous, contentious [Note: [Col. 1464] In place of “contentious,” Vignierius substituted “insulting.”], wordy man, what more do you seek?

### XXVI. JULIAN

Enough has now been done against these mockeries. Let us come to that extremely perplexing question which I said above had deceived your teacher himself by its subtlety.

You attempted to meet our objection not by explaining it, but by presenting another, more difficult one. For when I had shown that, in human beings of mature age, while they act through their own will, the innocent beginnings of nature are praised and the deviations of their actions are rightly condemned, and that there are two things to which contrary judgments can be applied; whereas in infants there is only one, namely nature, since there is no will; and that this one thing must be attributed either to God or to the devil; I concluded that, if nature exists through God, original evil cannot exist in it, but if it is transferred to the devil through innate evil, there would be nothing by which human beings could be claimed for God’s work.

When you reached these points, you replied, with your customary faith, that I had drawn a true conclusion, but that in infants there were also two things, namely nature and sin. Yet, if you remember the definitions stated earlier, sin is nothing other than the will to retain or admit what justice forbids and from which it is free to abstain.

Having therefore established that sin is nothing other than the choice of an evil will, you replied, Epicurus of our age, that in infants there is sin but no will. The fourth book has already shown what disgrace this entails.

In these passages, then, when I said, “If sin comes from the will, it is an evil will that makes sin; if it comes from nature, it is an evil nature that makes sin,” you attempted to meet me with a question that clearly was not devised by you. For when we were in Carthage some years ago, a certain man named Honoratus [Note: [Col. 1464] The printed editions have “an honored man.” A little later they have “as our letters indicate.” These readings have been corrected from the manuscripts. Honoratus, Augustine’s friend who at one time adhered to the Manichaeans, is well known from the book *On the Usefulness of Believing*, written to him. Julian sufficiently indicates that he was the same man who, after sending questions to Augustine from Carthage, received from him the famous letter 140 against the Pelagians, entitled *On the Grace of the New Testament*.], your necessary associate and, as your letters indicate, likewise a Manichaean, proposed this very question to me.
