I mention the matter only to make clear that this was the question that had deceived both Mani and Marcion many centuries earlier.

Thus you speak against what I had said—“If sin is in nature, it is an evil nature that makes sin”:

> “I ask him, if he can, to answer. Just as it is clear that all evil works are made from an evil will, as from an evil tree, I ask where he says that the evil will itself—that is, the tree of evil fruits itself—arose from. If from an angel, what was that angel himself except a good work of God? If from a human being, what was that human being himself except a good work of God? Indeed, because the evil will arose from the angel’s will and from the human being’s will, what were these two before these evils arose in them, except a good work of God and a good and praiseworthy nature?

> “Behold, then: evil arises from good, and there was absolutely nowhere from which it could arise except from good. I mean the evil will itself, which was preceded by no evil—not evil works, which arise only from an evil will, as from an evil tree.

> “Yet the evil will could not arise from good because good was made by the good God, but because it was made from nothing, not from God. What, then, does he mean when he says, ‘If nature is the work of God, the devil’s work is not allowed to pass through God’s work’? Was not the devil’s work, when it first arose in the angel who became the devil, born in God’s work? Therefore, if evil, which nowhere existed at all, could arise in God’s work, why could evil that already existed somewhere not pass through God’s work? Are human beings not God’s work? Sin therefore passed through human beings—that is, the devil’s work through God’s work—or, to say the same thing another way, God’s work through the work of God’s work” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 2, no. 48).

All these many words that I have set out from your discourses have completely exposed the head and source of the ancient error. You have brought forward nothing sharper in your statements, nothing more perplexing in your reasoning. Driven about across the entire field of disputation and expelled by the weapons of hostile truth from every position at which you had attempted to stand, you finally reached that cavern which the Manichaean had dug amid the darkness of his questions.

You acknowledged the difficulty of your proposition by saying, “I ask him, if he can, to answer.” Since we both agree that the point is difficult, I warn the reader to attend with his whole mind.

He should first follow the subtle distinctions appropriate to the matter—which, with Christ’s help, I trust will grow richer—and afterward proceed with confidence. You asked, then, where evil comes from. I ask what evil you mean; for this is a common name for guilt and punishment. Punishment, however, is called evil only improperly, since the gravity of the judgment by which it is inflicted vindicates it. You answer that you are speaking of sin, not punishment.

### AUGUSTINE

You have exposed your stupidity as fully as you could by confessing that committing sin is evil, while saying that punishment is not evil but is improperly called evil—the punishment of burning in everlasting fire.

Yet you give an excellent account of such an absurdity:

> “Punishment,” you say, “is improperly called evil, since the gravity of the judgment by which it is inflicted vindicates it.”

If, then, in saying this you measure the punishment of the condemned not by the misery of the one who suffers but by the justice of the one who condemns, say more plainly that punishment is good, although you improperly call it evil.

Punishment is the penalty of sin, and the penalty of sin is certainly just. Punishment is therefore just; and everything that is just is good. Punishment is therefore good.

Do you not see that unless you distinguish the condemned from the condemning in such a way that you assert the condemnation itself—which is punishment and the penalty of sin—to be a good work of the condemning party but the destruction of the condemned to be evil, you are driven to say that human beings reach not the greater evils they suffer—which is true—through their evil works, but rather good things? This is so false, and expressed with such vanity, that to think such things is itself as great an evil as the punishment of a blind heart.

It is therefore not improperly called evil; it is wholly evil for the one who suffers it. But it is good for the one who inflicts it, because it is just to impose punishment on one who sins. If you do not wish to rave, distinguish these matters.

### XXVII. JULIAN

You ask, then, where this evil comes from—the evil that is rightly called evil, namely sin. I answer that it is exceedingly unskillful to ask the origin of a thing whose definition has not yet been established.

Let us therefore first see whether it exists, then what it is, and finally where it comes from. I did this in the first book of the present work, but there I was secure only to some extent. Let us therefore inquire whether evil exists.

### AUGUSTINE

If you said that evil existed while I denied it, then the question between us would concern whether evil existed; and in that question you would undertake to show that evil existed because I had denied it.

But since neither of us denies it and neither of us is uncertain about it, why do you ask that we be uncertain about what is not uncertain, except from a desire to talk—so that you may boast not of the conviction of my words but of the multitude of your books?

### XXVIII. JULIAN

But frequent vices and severe judgments testify that it exists. It is therefore established that sin exists.

We ask what it is: whether it is some body that appears to be composed of many things [Note: [Col. 1466] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have “composed of all things.”], or some singular entity, like one element, or something purified by thought from association with the rest.

It is none of these. What, then, is it? It is the appetite of free will, which justice forbids; or, to use the earlier definition, “the will to do what justice forbids and from which it is free to abstain.”

Consider, then, whether sin can be found outside the limits of this definition, lest what we think we have comprehended wander elsewhere.

Let us consult the justice of the judge, so that its testimony may also make clear whether the whole genus of sin is properly enclosed within these boundaries. Does God impute what he knows cannot be avoided? That would be no justice and the greatest deformity. Indeed, if this were done, sins would not be punished but increased. Guilt is ordinarily punished by a just judge; but if it penetrated the judge himself through a corruption of justice, vengeance would have been taken upon the judge, not punishment inflicted.

Justice therefore does not impute sin except where it is free to abstain. But nothing can be called free unless it stands within the right of an emancipated will, without any unavoidable compulsion of nature.

The definition is therefore excellent and complete:

> “Sin is the will to do what justice forbids and from which it is free to abstain.”

These matters having been settled, let us ask where sin comes from—a question that had been investigated in great confusion before these definitions.

Where, then, does sin come from? I answer: from the free will of the one who acts.

### AUGUSTINE

Is it really from the free will of the one who acts when it is said, “If I do what I do not want, it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells in me” (Rom. 7:20)?

Do you not see that, when you ask where sin comes from and answer, “From the free will of the one who acts,” you are thinking of a sin that is not also the punishment of sin? But when a human being does what he does not want, and the Apostle nevertheless declares that this is sin, that sin does not at all belong to your answer or to the definition you recalled when you said that sin is the will to do what justice forbids and from which it is free to abstain.

For how is it free to abstain when one cries out, “What I do not want, that I do”?

Human nature therefore sinned in one way when it was free to abstain from sin; it sins now in another way, with freedom lost, when it needs the help of a liberator. The former was merely sin; the latter is also the punishment of sin.

### XXIX. JULIAN

But let us see whether what the preceding definition has established is confirmed by everyone’s agreement. Certainly no prudent or Catholic person can doubt either that nothing is sin except what can be avoided, or that justice is nothing except that which imputes to the one it punishes what he himself committed by free will, when he could have avoided it.

### AUGUSTINE

What was imputed to the first human being was something he could have avoided if he had wished. But through his sin the whole nature even of his descendants was corrupted and needs a Savior, so that it may be able to avoid sins when the age arrives at which it can use the faculty of reason.

Before that age, however, there is present, from its origin, a guilt contracted through generation, which must be removed through regeneration. By denying this, you most plainly say that Jesus Christ is not Jesus to infants—although, according to the testimony of the angel, he is called Jesus for this reason: “He will save his people” (among whom you do not wish infants to be included) “from their sins” (Matt. 1:21).

### XXX. JULIAN

Just as these matters no longer deceive us, so they are rejected by the Manichaean and the Traducian with equal zeal. Let us therefore see what they themselves say.

The Manichaean writes that sin is natural; Augustine agrees that sin is natural. Both therefore disagree with the definition we gave above, and they have a partnership in naming natural sin.

Let us also see what they say about the kind of sin—that is, what they think sin is, which they both affirm to be natural—lest perhaps they disagree at the next stage.

What does the Manichaean write to his daughter? He says that the concupiscence of the flesh, and that pleasure destined for the work of fecundity, is proved to be diabolical by the fact that its public operation avoids being seen.

What does Augustine say? The same in every respect:

> “That concupiscence of the flesh is a shrub of the devil; it is the cause, the law of sin, which,” he says, “everywhere avoids being seen and seeks concealment in shame” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 1, no. 26 and no. 8).

Thus they disagree neither about the earlier account of evil nor about the later one.

What is the third point? When the question is now where evil comes from, the Manichaean says, “From the eternal nature of darkness.”

What does Augustine say? “My teacher goes too far in this matter, since he thinks evil never began. It began through the will of the first human being, indeed already through that of the higher nature, namely the angelic nature; but from that time it became natural.” His teacher evidently scourges him and drags him most authoritatively into court [Note: [Col. 1468] In the manuscripts, “most authoritatively.”].

What judgment will the Catholic render between them? Without doubt, he will judge the Manichaean to be exceedingly foolish for thinking that sin is natural, but he will make the idea appear extremely subtle when it is joined with Augustine’s ingenuity.

For how can they agree that sin is natural and confess that this sin is of one species, by which they think the entire human race is possessed? Yet after this, when the disciple dares to say that what he confesses to be innate in all is not natural in one person alone, they will undoubtedly brand him with childish blows and place him under his teacher, who blasphemes more consistently.

Both disciple and teacher will therefore be expelled from the assembly of the pious.

Consider, then, what we concede. You do not approve what the Manichaean says—that evil is natural [Note: [Col. 1468] Thus the manuscripts. Vignierius has “the Manichaean says that sin is natural.”]. Then say that no one is born guilty, and you have escaped, plainly denying original sin. But you do not say this; therefore you confess that you neither wish to abandon your teacher nor to join the Catholics.

### AUGUSTINE

Should we therefore not say that the good God made the world because the Manichaean says this too? Yet when the question is from what he made it, we are distinguished from him.

We say, “From things that did not exist,” because he spoke and they were made (Ps. 148:5). But he says, “From two natures, namely good and evil,” which not only already existed but always existed.

Therefore, the things we do not say together prevent us from being their associates on the basis of the things we do say together.

Likewise, if we are asked whether God exists, both we and the Manichaeans answer, “God exists.” In this both of us are separated from that fool who said in his heart, “There is no God” (Ps. 13:1). But when the question is what kind of God he is, we are distinguished from the wicked fable of the Manichaeans by a great difference.

We say and defend that God is incorruptible; they invent a corruptible God.

When asked about the Trinity itself, both of us say that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are of one and the same nature. Yet neither are we therefore Manichaeans nor are they Catholics, for they say other things about the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit in which we are utterly different from and opposed to them.

Accordingly, we confidently assert the things we say together against the errors of those who deny them. Nor do we fear that they will call us Manichaeans and thereby claim superiority over us because we say with the Manichaeans what they themselves refuse to say, and because of this are refuted by us.

Therefore, just as the Arian is a heretic because he does not say with us that the Trinity has one essence—a statement that the Manichaean also makes—so you are heretics because you do not say with us that sin is natural, although the Manichaean also says this with us.

But we are not therefore Manichaeans, because we do not say what he says in the same way that he says it.

We say that our good nature has been corrupted by the voluntary sin of the one from whom we were born; hence we are all born under sin, and our very birth is in fault, as Ambrose says (*On Repentance*, book 1, chapter 2 or 3). But he conveys to us a foreign evil nature [Note: [Col. 1469] Perhaps “imports”], through whose mixture he asserts that we sin.

Finally, we offer even infants to the Savior for the healing of our nature. He, however, does not think Christ necessary in order to heal our nature in us, but in order to separate from us a foreign nature.

You see, then, how greatly we differ even in the matter that we say together—that sin is natural.

Likewise, in the matter that we say together, that the concupiscence of the flesh is evil, by which the flesh lusts against the spirit, we are found to be most distinct when the question is where this evil comes from.

We say with Ambrose that this foul disagreement between flesh and spirit entered our nature through the transgression of the first human being (*Book 7 on Luke 12:53*). But he and his followers say that, so that flesh and spirit may oppose one another, a foreign nature—which was always evil—has adhered to us.

We therefore seek a Savior so that this defect of ours may be healed. He seeks one so that the foreign nature, which cannot be healed at all, may be taken away from us.

Why do you not attend here also to the great difference separating us in the matter that we say together—that the concupiscence of the flesh resisting the spirit is evil?

Why do you not attend to the fact that we are not Manichaeans because we say certain things with them, whereas you are heretics because you do not say those things with them [Note: [Col. 1469] Vignierius has “because.” The manuscripts have “because.”]?

For if you said with them that evils are natural, and said with us against them where these things come from—because they do not derive from a foreign nature coeternal with God—you would not be Pelagian heretics.

But now, by denying that the concupiscence by which the flesh lusts against the spirit is evil and comes from our corrupted nature, you cause them to conclude that it comes from a foreign nature. Thus you are both new heretics and, by perversely fleeing the ancient heretics, assistants to those whom you flee [Note: [Col. 1469] The printed editions have “whom you flee, you perversely assist.” The manuscripts have “whom you perversely flee,” that is, by proceeding toward perversity. In this sense, *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 2, no. 38, above, chapter 25, says “they attempt perversely to avoid,” and shortly afterward, “you flee perversely.”].

So stop setting the Manichaean teacher against me. Instead, follow Ambrose with me, and look to the Arians and imitate them at least in this respect, in which they have better understanding than you: they do not call us Manichaeans, although we say with the Manichaeans that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have one nature, a point on which they oppose us with the greatest contentiousness.

### XXXI. JULIAN

You thought this a forceful objection: how, in the very first man [Note: [Col. 1470] Vignierius reads “in the man himself.” We have added “first” from the manuscripts.] or in the devil, who had been made an angel, could an evil will have arisen. Yet you say that it arose in God’s work—that is, either in the angel or in man—not because it was God’s work, but because it had been made from nothing. See, then, whether by another route you too are saying that the necessity of evil was eternal. For if this was the cause of evil’s arising in God’s work, namely, that it was known to have been made from nothing; and if, before that which was to exist was made, this nothing always existed—that is, before that which was to exist was made, it had never been anything, and what had never been anything is said to have been nothing—then from eternity that which was not before it was made by God never existed, since God alone has substance without beginning. This emptiness, therefore—that is, nothing—always existed before it was terminated by the existence of things. This nothing, then, was not made; rather, creatures were made, and that nothing ceased to be.

In the creature, therefore, which was made from nothing, you imagine that evil arose for this reason: that it had been made from nothing. You have consequently attributed the arising of evil in man to his origin; and you say that the origin—that is, nothing—was the cause of sin. For, you say, evil arose in man not because he had been made by God, but because he had been made from nothing. If, then, evil arose because the condition of the preceding nothing demanded it—and this nothing was eternal—you have wandered onto a different path [Note: [Col. 1470] We have added “you have wandered” from the manuscripts.], and you remain entirely caught in your teacher’s snare, so that both of you acknowledge evil to be eternal.

Yet in this respect he was more prudent: introducing natural sin, he said that the substance of darkness was eternal and, without the sinner’s will, compelled this evil to be present. He therefore assigned an author to the thing whose necessity he was creating, so that the evil pervading substances would appear to have a coercive power. You, however, with an intellect too leaden to bear, affirm the necessity of evil while denying the author of that necessity. And, just as in the case of infants, so also in the case of the original perpetrator of sin, you leave the work unfinished; and you say that something—I know not what—great can be understood, so that that nothing had great power, although it was nothing.

### AUGUSTINE

Nothing has any power; but it is you who assert that nothing, although it is nothing, has some power. Nor do you understand that, when it is said that God made the things he made from nothing, this means only that he did not make them from himself. For before he made anything, there was nothing coeternal with him that he might make. That, therefore, is “from nothing” which is not from something. For even if God made certain things from other things, those very things from which he made them he had made from no things.

No thing, however, could sin if it had been made from God’s nature; nor would it then have been made [Note: [Col. 1470] Here too, on the authority of the manuscripts, we have restored “nor would it then have been made”; shortly afterward, “and that which he was.”], but whatever it was would have been from him, and would have been that which he was—just as the Son and the Holy Spirit are, since they are from him and are what he is: one by being born, the other by proceeding. They are from him in such a way that he was never prior to them. Therefore this nature cannot sin at all, because it cannot abandon itself, nor does it have anyone better to whom it ought to cling and by whose abandonment it could sin.

Nor, however, was rational creation made in such a way that it had a necessity to sin. Yet it would not have had even the possibility of sinning if it had been God’s nature, since God’s nature neither wishes to be able to sin nor can wish to do so.

### XXXII. JULIAN

You assert that this nothing, from which all things were made, was the cause of sin. Thus the power of this nothing counts for as much with you as the power of the prince of darkness does with the Manichaean. Both of you therefore say that even the first evil had a necessity: he gives it solidity—though evil solidity—and you give it emptiness—equally evil. He therefore speaks of a violent substance; you speak of something equally violent, but of nothing.

Consider, then, the conclusion of your syllogism. Nothing, when not yet anything had been created, was an indication of eternal emptiness; but this very nothing—that is, emptiness—was brought to an end when creatures arose, for it ceased to be nothing when something began to exist. Therefore the nothing itself, even when it existed, did not exist, since it is understood to have existed when as yet there was nothing. But after things were made, this indication of emptiness [Note: [Col. 1471] Thus the manuscripts. Vignierius reads “designation.”], namely nothing, just as it had never possessed substance, so also lost its name; and it came about that what had never existed in reality also lost its very name. By the violence of this nothing, then, you imagine that evil arose both in the angel and in man. What could be said more insane?

### AUGUSTINE

Rather, you seem to rave from a desire to insult. I did not say that nothing was violent, for it is not something that could be violent. [Note: [Col. 1471] Thus the manuscripts. Vignierius reads: “to sin by some force.”] Neither angel nor man was compelled to sin by any force; and they would not have sinned if they had not wished to sin—indeed, they could also have been unwilling. Yet the possibility of sinning would not have been in them if they had been God’s nature.

### XXXIII. JULIAN

You say that a thing which did not exist possessed great power for the sole reason that it had never existed; yet it began to have very great power after it had itself lost its name. This nothing acquired great dominion after even its designation had perished.

### AUGUSTINE

If that which is nothing were something, you could say that it had acquired great dominion. For vanity—or falsehood—dominates you so completely that it compels you to chatter such empty things for so long.

### XXXIV. JULIAN

Well done for the virtue of your wisdom: by the rules of a first argument newly devised by you [Note: [Col. 1471] Vignierius reads “newly devised in your age”; the manuscripts read “newly devised by you.”], you embrace a second denial of beginnings, and join bodies whose heads have been severed. We do not begrudge you your subtleties; indeed, with Christian humanity we pity you, because you found a worthy conclusion for your dogma: beginning with the crimes of the innocent, you arrived at nothing.

### AUGUSTINE

Rather, you have arrived at nothing, and you are so delighted by it that you still do not wish to leave or return from it. You say that I called that which is nothing something, so that you might call so much nothing.

### XXXV. JULIAN

Oh, the soundness, oh, the elegance of the disputant! “Evil,” he says, “did not arise in man because he was made by God, but because he was made from nothing” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, Book 2, no. 48). We have already shown the acumen by which the greatest power has been substituted for this nothing. Now I point out what the preceding conflict also made clear: the first evil was not undertaken by the sinner’s will, if the condition of the stock coming from nothing required it to arise [Note: [Col. 1472] The manuscripts read “lest”; the Portarum codex joins it to the preceding verb: “do you understand?”].

### AUGUSTINE

No condition of a stock coming from nothing required sin to arise. For what is required is compelled to be given or done. But neither the angel nor the man by whom and in whom the first sins arose was compelled to sin by anything; they sinned by free will. They could also have been unwilling, since they were not compelled to will; yet they could not have willed to sin if they had possessed their nature from God and had been made not from nothing.

### XXXVI. JULIAN

You have therefore assigned a nature even to the first evil, but one emptier than the Manichaean’s, though equally eternal. There is no need to fight over this: it is entirely clear that an agreement remains between you, joined by the chain of natural and eternal evil.

### AUGUSTINE

Most foolishly said: that which is nothing cannot be eternal; that which is no thing cannot be eternal; finally, that which is not cannot be eternal.

### XXXVII. JULIAN

I have proceeded as the integrity of the argument demanded, and reason has demolished what you had established by argument: namely, that an evil will arose in God’s work because man had been created from nothing. It has shown that, while changing the terms, you have said the same thing that Manichaeus invented and believed: that the first sin too was generated by the violence of eternal darkness.

### AUGUSTINE

We have already warned you above that what is not cannot be eternal. What, then, is the meaning of your saying that I must be compared with Manichaeus because Manichaeus said that the first sin was generated by the violence of eternal darkness? He assigned substance to those darknesses; I could not assign substance to nothing, so that on this account I too might seem to establish eternal darkness—that is, eternal nothing.

Just as I could not give substance to nothing, so neither could I give it violence or eternity. For, as we have already said, in no way can that which is nothing be violent or eternal. In vain, therefore, have you wished to argue against me concerning what is nothing.

### XXXVIII. JULIAN

But lest, seeing yourself exposed, you attempt to escape by saying that you did not say, “Evil arose in God’s work because it was made from nothing,” but rather, “It could arise because it was made from nothing,” it must be shown by what more violent snares you are entangled.

If you say that you attributed the possibility of evil, not its necessity, to the power of that eternal nothing, we reply that the possibility of an evil will arising in man is certainly nothing other than free choice. For that is why an evil will could arise: so that a good one could also arise. This is the liberty in which reason exercises itself; because of it man is asserted to have been made in the image of God, and by it he surpasses the other creatures.

If, then, the fact that an evil will could arise in man is nothing other than freedom of choice—and this is so great that by its distinguishing marks man surpasses the other living creatures—you, who profess that this possibility was in man not because he was made by God but because he was made from nothing, pronounce that nothing—that is, the ancient emptiness—to be the cause of so great a good, namely free choice. Thus, to make the matter clear by a brief question: when you said, “Nevertheless, a bad will could not have arisen because man was made by God, but because man was made from nothing,” do you believe that this very fact—that a will could arise—is good or evil? That is, do you consider the very capacity for a will to arise, which you attributed to nothing, to be upright or utterly bad?

If you say it is good, then God is not the cause of the good, but nothing is. But if, seeing that this is utterly insane, you declare it evil—since you say that it must be attributed not to God but to nothing—you will testify that we have not craftily assembled anything against you, but that in good faith of argument we have overthrown the bad faith of your dogma. What we have established therefore remains unshaken: you and Manichaeus have both attributed even the evil will of the first man to the necessity of an eternal origin.

### AUGUSTINE

However you looked at it, you could have known what answer might be made to you. But you have tried in vain to resist the truth, as though replying to my words while not replying to my words. You argued as though I had said, “Nevertheless, an evil will did not arise from the good.” I did not say that. I said: “Nevertheless, an evil will could arise from a good being, not because that good being was made by the good God, but because it was made from nothing, not from God” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, Book 2, no. 48). You yourself have also quoted these same words of mine (above, chapter 26).

Why, then, did you think you should answer as though I had said, “Nevertheless, it did not arise,” when I said, “Nevertheless, it could not arise”? For so long you spoke against one who said that the necessity of evil’s arising from the good had burst in because the good itself was made by God from nothing, not from God, although I did not attribute necessity to such a cause, but the possibility of evil. I did not say that evil arose for this reason, but that for this reason evil could arise from the good.

And for so long you accused nothing and made nothing violent, as though nothing had compelled the angel and man to sin by an unavoidable necessity. Now, then, finally return to my words, as you have begun to return. You propose the question to yourself as though it had suddenly occurred to you to ask what I could answer, although I had stated this long before in the book against which you are struggling.

You say that I could reply that I had not said, “Evil arose in God’s work because it was made from nothing,” but, “It could arise because it was made from nothing.” This is precisely what I said. I said, “It could arise”; I did not say, “It arose.” I assigned the possibility of evil to this cause [Note: [Col. 1474] The published editions omit “of evil”; it is present in the manuscripts.], not its necessity.

When rational creation was first made, it was made in such a way that, if it did not wish to sin, it was compelled by no necessity to will it, or even to sin unwillingly—that is, against its will—and do not the good it wished, but the evil it did not wish. In that case it would no longer be merely the sin simply called sin, but also the punishment of sin.

Nevertheless, it could not possibly will anything evil, or even do anything evil unwillingly, unless it had been made from nothing—that is, unless it were God’s nature. For God’s nature alone was not made from nothing, because it was not made at all; and therefore it cannot be changed in any way whatsoever.

When we say this, we are not attributing powers to nothing, as though it could have done or did anything while being nothing. Rather, we are saying that the nature which could sin is not God’s nature. It follows that the nature which is not God’s nature was made; for it is not coeternal with God. And if it was made, it was made from nothing, since even those natures that are made from other natures derive their stock from nothing: the natures from which they were made, before they were made, were nothing—that is, they were absolutely nonexistent.

But you say, “An evil will could arise so that a good one could also arise.” As though either the angel or the man had not been made with a good will. He [Note: [Col. 1474] The Portarum codex reads: “when he was made.”] was made upright, as Scripture says (Eccles. 7:30). The question, therefore, is not from where a good will could arise in him, since he was made with it, but from where an evil will could arise, since he was not made with it.

And you say, without considering what you are saying, “An evil will could arise so that a good one could also arise.” You think this belongs to the nature of free choice, that it can do either—namely, sin or not sin—and you consider man to have been made in the image of God for this reason, although God himself cannot do both. Surely no madman would say that God can sin; or do you dare to say that God does not have free choice?

Free choice, then, is God’s gift, not a gift of nothing. Yet free [Note: [Col. 1474] Here we have added “free” from the manuscripts.] choice is supreme in God himself, who cannot sin in any way. For if he could be unjust, he could also, of course, not be God. If he is God, he is most certainly just. Thus, although he has free choice in the highest and fullest degree, God nevertheless [Note: [Col. 1474] Thus the manuscripts. Vignierius reads “however.”] cannot sin.

The angel or man could therefore sin—and could therefore misuse that gift of God which is free choice—for this reason: he is not God; that is, he was made by God from nothing, not from God himself. Understand, and be silent; or speak about what you have understood, not about what you have not understood.

### XXXIX. JULIAN

Not content to have conquered in one way, I shall expose the falsity of your argument, whose impiety I have disclosed. When you wrote, “An evil will could arise in God’s work not because it was made by God, but because it was made from nothing” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, Book 2, no. 48), you should have noticed how forcefully the examples of other creatures contradicted this: they too were produced from nothing, yet are incapable of an evil will.

Finally, the elements themselves, which truly were made from nothing, cannot possess consciousness of any will by which they might protest through evil movements against the necessity of their origin. Living creatures, however, and the rest with which the world is filled, did not emerge from nothing, but from something already existing. Where, then, is the force of the ancient emptiness that compelled an evil will to exist, when it is evident that no one except a rational animal can sin?

### AUGUSTINE

You could think me convicted of falsity if, when I had said that our bodies can be wounded because they are earthly, you showed me many earthly bodies that cannot be wounded. For a wound can exist only in the body of a living creature, which is called flesh.

Here I should remind you that you failed to see that this proposition does not work both ways. For just as it is true that every body which can be wounded is an earthly body, so it is not also true that every earthly body can be wounded.

Why, then, did your vaunted skill in dialectic fall asleep, so that you did not notice that when I said a rational creature could sin because it was made from nothing, I meant that everything capable of sinning was made from nothing, not that everything made from nothing could sin? You objected to me as though I had said this by citing other things, including the elements of the world, which, although made from nothing, cannot sin—since only a rational animal can sin.

Wake up, then, and see that everything capable of sinning was made from nothing; but it does not follow that everything made from nothing can sin. Therefore do not bring forward other things that were made from nothing and cannot sin. I do not say, “Everything made from nothing can sin”; I say, “Everything capable of sinning was made from nothing.” It is as though I had said, “Every ox is an animal.” It would not have been appropriate to cite against me many animals that are not oxen, since I did not say, “Every animal is an ox,” but, “Every ox is an animal.”

Again, then, I say: everything capable of sinning was made from nothing. I do not say that everything made from nothing can sin, although you act as though I had said this when you mention many things that, though made from nothing, cannot sin. Remove your cleverness, by which you mock dull minds; or your blindness, by which you do not see what is plain.

When I say that a nature created as rational could sin because it was made from nothing, not from God, attend to what I am saying, lest you again throw nothing about with empty loquacity and claim that I said that what is nothing has the power to do something.

What I say is that a nature created as rational could sin because it was made from nothing. What else is this than saying that it could sin because it is not God’s nature? If it had not been made from nothing, whatever it was would naturally have been from God. If it had naturally been from God, it would have been God’s nature. If it had been God’s nature, it could not sin. Therefore it could sin, although it was made by God, because it was made from nothing, not from God.

If you understand this and do not wish to resist the truth, you will cease this dispute on the present question.

### XL. JULIAN

Since this was so clear and obvious, what persuaded you to believe that the violence of the ancient nothing was the cause of the evil will? Clearly it was so that we might understand you to believe all things made from nothing guilty, and to hand the entire world over to the devil.

Since it has therefore become clear to me that the ancient agreement between your doctrines remains, I now answer both you and Manichaeus together. You certainly ask how I, who deny that evil has a nature, can explain where the evil will itself could have arisen in the first man. But I reply that you do not understand what you are saying. For the will is nothing other than a movement of the mind, compelled by no one.

### AUGUSTINE

What is a movement of the mind except a movement of nature? [Note: [Col. 1476] Pope Agatho cites this statement, and several others from this fifth book, in the synodical letter to the Emperors, read at the fourth session of the Sixth Synod, commending Augustine in these words: “Blessed Augustine, the most prudent preacher of truth, in the fifth book of his disputation against Julian the Pelagian, defines what the will is in these words: ‘What is a movement of the mind except a movement of nature?’” etc.] For the mind is unquestionably a nature. Therefore the will is a movement of nature, since it is a movement of the mind.

But earlier, when you placed nature as a genus and subordinated its species to that genus, you certainly spoke as follows: “The generality of human nature,” you say, “is a kind of genus for the institutions situated beneath it. It has, as it were, these species: position, members, orders, movements, and other things of that kind [Note: [Col. 1476] Perhaps “when.”]” (above, chapter 24).

By this argument, then, you asserted that a movement of nature is a species of nature. It follows from your own reasoning—something you do not want to follow—that every movement of nature is nature, if nature is the genus and a movement of nature is its species, just as every horse is an animal because animal is the genus and horse is a species of that genus.

Accordingly, since the will is a movement of the mind, and is thereby shown to be a movement of nature, it is nature according to your argument, because you subordinated such things as species to nature as their genus. Why, then, do you criticize the statement that sin is natural, when [Note: [Col. 1476] Perhaps “when.”] you are demonstrably saying that the will itself is nature?

But let the will not be nature. Certainly, however, it cannot exist except in nature. Insofar as man is concerned, it is a movement of the mind, and the mind is a nature.

Allow, then, please, that sin may be called natural because when man sins, nature sins—for man is a nature. In the same way, spiritual sin may rightly be spoken of when the spirit sins. The Apostle did not err when he said, “the spiritual forces of wickedness” (Eph. 6:12). Those “spiritual” things are certainly natural [Note: [Col. 1476] The printed editions read “are nature.” The manuscripts more suitably read “are natural.”], because spirit is indisputably a nature, whether it is the Creator or created.

Yet when something is committed by an angel or a man who wills it [Note: [Col. 1477] The printed editions read “unwilling.” The manuscripts correct this to “willing.”]—for both angel and man are natures—we do not thereby say that it is natural sin in such a way that what was done was done by necessity. For one who sinned because he willed to sin could also have been unwilling to sin. Man was created in such a way that he could both be unwilling and willing, and had either of these within his power [Note: [Col. 1477] All the manuscripts read this way. Vignierius’ edition reads: “so that he can both be unwilling and willing, and either of these is held in his power.” Augustine is speaking of the first sin of man, which he teaches was committed with that liberty by which he could have been unwilling to sin as well as willing to sin, and not by any necessity such as constrained the one who said, “For I do not do the good that I want,” etc.].

Original sin, however, is one thing. Although those who are born draw it along without their own will, nevertheless its origin was corrupted through the will of the first man. Likewise, there is another matter in the grown man, on account of which he says, “For I do not do the good that I want, but the evil that I do not want, that I do” (Rom. 7:15). Yet even this necessity is not incurable for the one who is told, “Deliver me from my necessities” (Ps. 24:17).

### XLI. JULIAN

You are therefore seeking a necessity for something that cannot exist if it suffers necessity. If an earlier cause is assigned to this free movement of the mind, restless and without coercion, by the movement itself [Note: [Col. 1477] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read “is said.”], it is not generated at all but abolished. For the very name “will” has no force other than that what is moved should not owe its motion to matter.

When, therefore, you seek by the will itself what preceded the origin of the will, you are seeking not its beginning but its destruction. It is not understood to exist at all if it is assigned either to darkness or to nothing; nor can that still be called a will which cannot subsist except in a movement of the mind compelled by no one.

If someone compels it, there is indeed movement, but there is no will; the force of that definition is completed by its second part, namely, “with no one compelling.” If the will is nothing other than a movement of the mind, compelled by no one, then the origin of a thing whose condition is destroyed if it is preceded by something is sought altogether wrongly.

Consider, then, what it is that you ask: “From where,” you say, “could the evil will have arisen in the first man, like an evil tree?” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, Book 2, no. 48). Yet you confess that the will is related to an origin. For the will is a movement of the mind, compelled by no one. All natural things compel what follows to exist; but if the will is compelled by preceding causes, it immediately ceases to be will and loses its defining condition if it receives an origin.

### AUGUSTINE

If the will has no origin because it is not compelled, then man himself has no origin as man, because he was not compelled to exist. How could one who did not exist be compelled? And certainly man is a nature; moreover, you said, “All natural things compel what follows to exist.”

I beg you, attend to what you are saying. Do not move your tongue with your eyes closed [Note: [Col. 1477] The printed editions omit “with your eyes closed,” but the manuscripts contain it.], as one who speaks in sleep.

Nothing that does not exist can be compelled. See also how insane it is to deny that things which have arisen have an origin, since “origin” itself is named from arising. For that which exists and has no origin always existed. But if it did not exist and exists, it arose; if it arose, it has an origin.

The will of sin, therefore, which did not exist and now exists, certainly arose. For if it exists and did not arise, it always existed; but it did not always exist. Therefore it arose.

Now shout against this most evident truth; such conduct suits your empty loquacity. Say, “It arose, but it has no origin,” or, what is even more insane, “It did not exist, and it exists, yet it did not arise.” But if you do not say this, lest you be judged utterly foolish and senseless, seek where the evil will of man arose. You cannot deny that it arose, since you cannot deny that it did not exist and began to exist.

Seek, I say, where it arose, and you will find the man himself. For the evil will arose from him, though it had not previously been in him. Ask also what kind of man he was before the evil will arose from him, and you will find that he was good. For he was made evil by that will which, before it arose from him, was such as he had been made by the good—namely, good.

This, then, is what my teacher and your destroyer Ambrose says: “Therefore evils arose from good things” (*On Isaac and the Soul*, chapter 7). By denying this and saying, “The order of things does not allow anything evil to be produced from the good, or anything unjust from the just,” you do nothing but assist the Manichaeans in introducing a nature of evil from which they say evils arise, so that they may rejoice in you as the patron of their error—unless you too are conquered along with them.

For you are the one who, with marvelous eloquence—or rather madness—defends infants in such a way as to separate them from the Savior; and you attack the Manichaeans in such a way as to raise them up against the Savior.

### XLII. JULIAN

Since the will has been correctly defined as “a movement of the mind, compelled by no one,” why do you seek causes above, which the definition of the will has excluded? Consider, then, what the will is, and you will cease asking where the will comes from.

For the will is a movement of the mind, compelled by no one. If you try to go even half a finger beyond this, you immediately tear apart what has been established.

What, then, does Manichaeus say? “This movement arose for the reason that man was made from the nature of darkness.” What do you say? “Because,” you say, “man was made from nothing.” One therefore says, “The will is evil because man was made from nothing”; the other, “The will in man is evil because man was made from darkness.”

Both of you therefore deny to the will that supplementary condition—namely, “compelled by no one.” For if there was as much power in nothing as in something, and that power compelled this will to exist, it excluded from the will its own defining condition, by which it had been said to be “compelled by no one.”

Yet he did not remove the disgrace of evil any less. For there is no sin that does not come from a free movement of the mind. Thus, at the cost of truth, the accusation of all evil perished; the nature of evil vanished when the guilt of the will vanished; and the guilt of the will vanished when the definition of the will was cut away.

It has therefore become clear that both sin and will have this condition: if they are attributed to preceding causes, they lose both their right and their guilt [Note: [Col. 1478] The printed editions read “and their force.” The manuscripts read “and their right.”]. Where, then, will the nature of evil be, when it has been established that evil does not exist?

### AUGUSTINE

I cannot say how much I marvel at your audacity: how can you speak of the nature of evil when you do not call evil natural? Or how can you refuse to call evil natural when you speak of the nature of evil?

And what could be more foolish than your definitions, when you think that one should not ask where the will comes from because it is a movement of the mind, compelled by no one? For if it is said, as you think, whence it is, then “compelled by no one” will not be true, because that from which it comes compels it to exist. Therefore it does not come from anywhere, lest it be compelled to exist.

What singular folly! Man himself, then, does not come from anywhere, because he was not compelled to exist—for before he existed, there was no one to be compelled.

Yet the will does come from somewhere, and is not compelled to exist. If its origin need not be sought, this is not because the will does not come from somewhere, but because it is clear where it comes from. It comes from the one whose will it is: the angel’s will comes from the angel, man’s will from man, and God’s will from God.

And if God works a good will in man, he does this precisely so that a good will may arise from the one whose will it is, just as he causes man to arise from man. For it does not follow, because God creates man, that man is not born from man.

Each person is the author of his own evil will, because he wills evil. But when the question is why man can have an evil will although he need not have one, the question is not about the origin of the will but about the origin of the possibility itself. Its cause is found to be this: although rational creation is a great good, it is nevertheless not what God is, whose nature alone is unturnable and unchangeable.

When the cause of this is sought, it is found to be that God did not beget it from himself—that is, from his own nature and substance—but made it from nothing, that is, from no thing. Not because nothing has any power—for if it had, it would not be nothing but something—but because for any nature to have been made from nothing means that it is not God’s nature, which alone is immutable.

Nor are those things that were made from other things excluded from this origin, since the things made in such a way that other things were made from them were themselves made from no existing things—that is, altogether from nothing.

All other things can be changed through their different and proper qualities; but among things that use reason, only rational creation is changeable through the will. Whoever observes these matters carefully and intelligently will recognize that you have said much about nothing that is nothing relevant to the issue.

### XLIII. JULIAN

What, then, is evil—that is, sin? The will to pursue what justice forbids and from which it is free to abstain. What is the will itself? A movement of the mind, compelled by no one.

If sin arose from the will, and the will from a movement of the mind compelled by no one, then neither the condition of nothing nor that of darkness caused this movement to exist—a movement that is compelled by no one precisely so that it can be “compelled by no one.”

Accordingly, there is neither natural nor original sin, because these two names indicate one thing: that sin is involuntary. Yet truth has established that nothing can be sin unless it is voluntary. Therefore, whoever says that evil is something demonstrably unoriginated does not prove that sin exists in nature, but shows himself guilty through perversity of judgment [Note: [Col. 1480] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read “through perversity of intellect.”].

Here is the answer to which you thought no answer could be made. The question you regard as unconquerable was altogether an oxymoron [Note: [Col. 1480] From the Greek *oxymōros*: a statement called foolishly pointed, or quickly dissipated.].

### AUGUSTINE

You exult in vain and say, “Here is the answer,” when anyone acute who reads these words of yours—or anyone not very slow who reads mine—immediately discovers that you were unable to answer.

However intricate the confusion with which you try not to disentangle what is tangled but to tangle what is clear, sound minds cannot deny that each person’s will arises from that person, and that a man’s will arises only from man.

Accordingly, since human evils began through an evil will, and we know that before the evil will human nature was good, evils arose from good things. Ambrose says this. By this Manichaeus is destroyed.

Julian denies this on behalf of Manichaeus against Ambrose, saying: “If nature is God’s work, God’s work does not permit the devil’s work to pass through God’s work.” Thus, according to Julian, Manichaeus says that men are not God’s work, since the Apostle says that sin and death—the devil’s work—passed through men (Rom. 5:12). For according to Julian, “God’s work does not permit the devil’s work to pass through God’s work,” while the Apostle says that the devil’s work passed through men. Therefore men are not God’s work.

This is the Manichaean conclusion that comes to him, Julian, through your assistance. But the Apostle, contending for the truth, says that men are God’s work in order to overthrow Manichaeus; and he says that the devil’s work passed through God’s work—that is, through men—in order to overthrow you yourself along with him.

### XLIV

**JULIAN:** Yet I point out that in your writings you are also accustomed not to call darkness a creature, but to say that obscurity remains as the absence of light, so that darkening is nothing other than the exclusion of brightness. What is excluded you call a creature; what remains, darkness. This is indeed a view commonly reported among philosophers; I am not now asking whether it is thought true or false. But I insist on this: you do not say that darkness is anything other than nothing. Yet you argue that evil came to exist in man—that is, in God’s work—because he had been made from nothing. You therefore affirm that nothing was the cause of evil, and you also declare that darkness is nothing. Thus you say that the necessity of evil descends from the condition of darkness. In this, then, you do not differ from your teacher, since you alike assign the evil will to eternal darkness.

**AUGUSTINE:** A little earlier I answered you, as plainly and briefly as I could, when you were saying that nothing comes from nothing; and now you have tried in vain to flee to darkness. You will not escape notice: the light of truth pursues you, saying that creatures were made from nothing—creatures that are not what their maker himself is—so that “nothing” is not thought or understood to be something, nor to possess any power for making; for if it possessed such power, it would not be nothing.

Accordingly, nothing is neither any body nor spirit, nor anything accidental to these substances, nor any formless matter, nor an empty place, nor darkness itself, but absolutely nothing. **[Col. 1481]** For wherever there is darkness, there is some body deprived of light—whether air, water, or something else; for only a body can either be illuminated by bodily light so as to shine, or be deprived of it so as to become dark. Accordingly, the creator of these bodily darknesses is none other than the one who created bodies; and for this reason, in the hymn of the three young men, light and darkness bless him (Dan. 3:72).

God therefore made all things from nothing—that is, if we consider their first origin, he made everything that he made in order that it might exist from things that did not exist. The Greeks express this as **ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων**, “from things that are not.” To prevent this from being believed of the Only-Begotten, who is God from God, light from light, and therefore not from nothing, the Catholic Church vigorously resists the Arians.

When, therefore, we say that an evil will could arise from the good, not because it was made good by the good God, but because it was made from nothing, not from God, we do not assign any nature to nothing. Rather, we distinguish the nature of the maker from the nature of the things that were made. These things can therefore be changed—either by their will, as rational creation can be changed, or by their own qualities, as other things can—because they were made from nothing, not from God, although they were made by none other than God. That is, they are not what that nature is which was not made, and which alone is therefore immutable.

If, then, you wish either to avoid or to defeat the Manichaeans, learn this, understand this if you can, and believe it if you cannot: evil has arisen from good, and evil is nothing other than a lack of good.

### XLV

**JULIAN:** But since truth has exposed and overthrown you both, the consideration of our duty now requires us to explain what it is that had cast obscurity over this question, which has already been disarmed.

Everything that comes to be is said to arise either from the necessary or from the possible. By “necessary” here I do not mean what we ordinarily call useful, but what has been compelled by greater causes. We call necessary, therefore, not what lies within the power of the will, but what undergoes the force of existing. We call possible what experiences no necessity in either direction—neither of existing nor of not existing—but which, in certain circumstances, can both exist and not exist.

Let our reader therefore retain what we are here calling necessary and possible. To begin with great examples: when God made the world, he proceeded from the possible, not from the necessary. That is, it was possible for his omnipotence to create what he created, but it was not necessary; plainly, he was not compelled by anyone to make it, but made it because he willed to do so, and certainly would not have made it had he been unwilling. Yet what was possible for the creator became necessary in the work: it was not possible for the world both to exist and not to exist, once the Omnipotent commanded it to exist; rather, it was compelled to come into existence when the Omnipotent assigned it being.

**AUGUSTINE:** How was the world compelled to exist, when it did not exist before it existed? How can anything be compelled if it does not exist? Would it not have been better for you to say, “The world was made by God’s will, not by its own”?

But continue; let us see what you are trying to establish by this distinction between the possible and the necessary. We could understand it better if you had wished merely to mention it, rather than also explain it. For who does not see that everything that must come to be can also come to be, whereas not everything that can come to be must also come to be?

If, then, you have chosen to call “possible” what can come to be without being necessary, and “necessary” what not only can come to be but must come to be, speak as you wish. Once the things themselves are clear, there should be no dispute about words. It is enough to know that everything necessary is possible, but not everything possible is necessary.

### XLVI

**JULIAN:** What had proceeded from the possibility belonging to the creator therefore passed over into the necessity belonging to the created thing. He also made different natures and different kinds within natures, preserving the order that flowed from the beginning of things, so that some things would be necessary and others possible. Whatever creatures possess naturally, therefore, they have received from the side of the necessary.

**AUGUSTINE:** If whatever creatures possess naturally they have received from the side of the necessary, then human beings do not naturally have sexual intercourse, but naturally have the ability to have sexual intercourse. Nor is what the Apostle called “the natural use of the female” (Rom. 1:27) natural, but only its possibility. For if a man does not wish it, the act itself does not occur, although it can occur if he wishes. Its possibility, therefore, is natural; the act itself is not. For it is not necessary, since it does not occur at all if we do not wish it, and the Apostle was mistaken in saying that the use of the female is natural.

What, then, becomes of your earlier statement that marriage is the genus and species of human nature, since marriages are joined not by necessity but by will? Or had the distinction between these two—necessary and possible—not yet occurred to you when you said this?

And for a human being to be born after the intercourse of the sexes—is that not natural because it is not necessary? For conception and childbirth do not necessarily follow when male and female have intercourse. Yet you defined the possible as what can happen but need not happen. Do we not naturally eat either? This too does not happen if we do not wish it, and so, on your account, it is possible rather than necessary.

But to deny that these things are natural is simply to wish to remove a large part of nature. Your statement is therefore false: “Whatever creatures possess naturally, they have received from the side of the necessary.” For both the things I have mentioned and many others too numerous to mention are possessed naturally, yet they have not been received from the side of the necessary.

### XLVII

**JULIAN:** Those which have perception in their development [perhaps: “things which”] do not always derive from the necessary, but derive many things from the possible. This can be seen in all bodies, though a longer discussion would arise. Let us nevertheless offer a few examples.

It is the nature of bodies that they grow together through composition and are dissolved through division. They are therefore capable of injury, since they can suffer destruction. That they can be wounded, they possess from the necessary; that they are actually wounded, they possess from the possible. Thus the nature of possibility comes from the necessary, although the actualization of possibility is not necessary.

For example, a horse, an ox, and similar animals possess a nature vulnerable to injury, and therefore they are necessarily capable of harm. But it is not always necessary that they be wounded. If they are protected from blows by the care of their keepers, they can remain unwounded; if they are not guarded, they can also be wounded.

There is therefore a great difference between what comes from the possible and what comes from the necessary. Unless this distinction is preserved, one falls into innumerable errors.

To make the matter clear by comparison: certain opponents of medicine fell into error, arguing that this art possesses no usefulness. They reasoned as follows: “Does medicine help those who are going to die, or those who are going to live? If those who are going to die, it accomplishes nothing; if those who are going to live, it is eager to no purpose. Those who were going to die will die even when medicine struggles on their behalf; those who were going to live could have been saved without its assistance.”

What a neat and elegant conclusion! But the defenders of medicine dissolve it in this way: “This art benefits neither those who will live nor those who will die solely from the necessary; rather, it benefits those who will undergo either outcome as a possibility. Medicine does not help someone who is certainly going to die, since it cannot make him immortal; but neither does it help someone who is certainly going to remain unharmed. Rather, it helps the person who, if untreated, may be endangered, but if treated, may be rescued. Thus just as the learned art cannot help either one who will live or one who will die according to the condition of the necessary, so it can benefit both one who will die and one who will live according to the possible.”

Those earlier critics of medical practice therefore began with a proposition concerning the possible and concluded with the necessary. This kind of argument extends to innumerable cases.

For example, the law forbids homicide; it also forbids providing an opportunity for negligence through which one rushes into danger, as in the case of a goring bull (Exod. 21:28–32) or the parapets of houses (Deut. 22:8). But someone might say: “Does this diligence help one who will live, or one who will die? If one who will die, it accomplishes nothing; if one who will live, it offers needless assistance. If both outcomes follow necessarily, both with and without obstacles, then this diligence is contrary to reason.”

But that is false. The law rightly provides the best possible protection for mortals, so that by the resources of diligence they may escape what they could have suffered without diligence. One thing, therefore, comes from the possible and another from the necessary.

Let us now show how these preliminary statements assist us. God made man with free choice and with a good nature, but one capable of the virtues that he might acquire for himself through a devoted will. Free choice could not remain free in any other way than by also possessing the possibility of sinning. He has freedom from the necessary, and will from the possible. He cannot fail to be free, but he cannot be compelled toward either kind of will; and thus he was made the possible effect of a necessary thing.

Sin can occur in the possible, but not in the necessary, because in the necessary the agent is not the one judged, but the author himself. What man can do in his entirety belongs to God; but in what is possible, man himself is considered the agent.

**AUGUSTINE:** What will you say about the devil, of whom it is written, “The devil sins from the beginning” (1 John 3:8)? Does he possess the possibility of sinning or the necessity of sinning? If necessity, you must see how, according to your arguments, he can be excused from guilt **[Col. 1484]**. If possibility, then he can also not sin; he can have a good will; he can repent and obtain God’s mercy, since God will not despise a contrite and humbled heart (Ps. 50:19).

This view was held by certain people, reportedly under the authority of Origen. But, as I suppose you know, the sound Catholic faith has not accepted it **[Note: Manuscripts, “receives it.”]**. Hence some either prove or wish to prove that Origen himself was not implicated in this error.

It remains, therefore, either that, before the punishment of eternal fire, this necessity of sinning is itself a great punishment for the great sin of the devil **[Col. 1484]**, or that he is not thereby excused from guilt, since this very punishment is vengeance for his greatest crime **[Note: So the manuscripts of Marcellinus and Clarus. The printed editions read, “is near the crime.”]**—namely, that he is delighted by evil alone and cannot be delighted by righteousness.

He would not have reached this already punitive necessity of sinning unless he had first sinned by free will, without any necessity. The definition of sin, therefore—doing what justice forbids and from which it is free to abstain—belongs to that sin which is merely sin, not to that which is also the punishment of sin.

### XLVIII

**JULIAN:** Thus he produces both evil and good by his own will; but he owes his good also to God, who supplies assistance to this part—not, indeed, prejudice, but aid.

**AUGUSTINE:** Certainly, as you say, man produces good as well as evil by his own will, and the possibility of both is equally balanced in him; and God supplies assistance for doing good. Why, then, is the nature of mortals more inclined to sin if original sin has done nothing?

Nor is it hidden what kind of assistance you are compelled to admit that God supplies. You say it is the law, not the Spirit, although the Apostle Paul teaches that we are helped through the supplying of the Holy Spirit (Phil. 1:19). I thought this should be recalled, lest those who hear or read your statement about the supplying of divine assistance forget your heresy.

### XLIX

**JULIAN:** This distinction has such force that, if we ignorantly conclude with the necessary what begins from the possible, all crimes return to God. Seeing this, the Manichaean devised darkness as the author of sin; for he was unable to distinguish between the possible and the necessary.

Everything, therefore, that man possesses naturally he has received from the side of the necessary, because he could not have been otherwise than he was made.

**AUGUSTINE:** A little earlier I showed how empty this opinion is. For it is utterly foolish **[Note: The old Codex Port. adds here, “to say”]** to say that human beings naturally possess the possibility of eating, but do not naturally eat foods suited to nature; or that human beings naturally possess the possibility of sexual intercourse, but that the two sexes do not naturally have intercourse through their genital organs.

Who would say this, if he gave even a little consideration to what he is saying? Both things are natural: that these acts can occur and that they do occur. But the former exists even when we do not wish it; the latter exists only if we wish it.

### L

**JULIAN:** But the evil that he commits, he commits from the possible.

**AUGUSTINE:** Consider the one who says, “The evil that I do not want, that I do.” Answer whether someone who does not do the good he wants, but does the evil he does not want, is not under the necessity of doing evil.

If you do not dare oppose the Apostle, behold: the man who acts from necessity destroys and scatters your definitions. For he acts evilly by necessity who does what he does not want to do.

But if what he does unwillingly is merely to desire with the flesh, without any consent of the mind or activity of the limbs, then the desire of the flesh is evil even when he does not consent to it as evil—although you delight in praising it. If, however, this man who cries, “The evil that I do not want, that I do,” is so compelled that he also offers his limbs as instruments to sin, then not only are evils desired from the necessary; they are also committed.

Where are your definitions, which you distinguish with such verbosity? They have vanished and perished like smoke. You commend distinguishing the necessary and the possible with great care, defining the necessary as what must happen and the possible as what can happen but need not happen. You therefore assign necessity to the necessary, while you bind the possible by no necessity.

You do not assign evil acts to the necessary, but to the possible; and, speaking of man, you say, “The evil that he commits, he commits from the possible,” so that no one may be said to do evil by necessity rather than by will.

But there appears one who contradicts you with the greatest force and says: “What is this you are saying? Behold, I do not do the good that I want, but the evil that I do not want, that I do” (Rom. 7:19).

It is well known that the first man did evil by will, not by necessity. But this man who says, “The evil that I do not want, that I do,” shows that he does evil by necessity, not by will; and, while lamenting his misery, he laughs your definitions to scorn.

### LI

**JULIAN:** Unless the possibility had been necessary, the effect of the possible would not have occurred. Thus, that he may be able to do evil and good is necessary; but that he does evil he owes not to the necessary, but to his own possible. Where there is the possibility of either part, there is the necessity of neither.

Thus sin is nothing other than the will to do what justice forbids and from which it is free to abstain. But if will is nothing other than a movement of the mind compelled by no one, then just as God had the possible as the source of his making the world, while the world itself endured the necessary in order to exist, so too something similar is understood in the image of God.

He is not compelled to possess whichever will he chooses; that comes to him from the possible. But the evil that he has done possesses the necessity of guilt. Thus the crime incurs horror from the necessary, although it arose not from the necessity but from the possibility of the agent. The work, therefore, is testimony to the possibility of a living creature possessing free choice.

**AUGUSTINE:** He who reads what we answered you above now entirely disregards you. For the man who says, “I do not do the good that I want, but the evil that I do not want, that I do,” clearly indicates and demonstrates that he is driven by necessity to do evil. Thus what you say is false: “That he does evil he owes not to the necessary, but to his own possible,” along with the other things of this kind that you babble pointlessly.

Thus the definition by which sin is said to be the will to do what justice forbids and from which it is free to abstain includes, as I warned above, the sin that is merely sin, not the sin that is also the punishment of sin. For this man was acting under such a punishment when he did the evil he did not want. If it had been free for him to abstain, he would certainly not have said, “I do not do the good that I want, but the evil that I do not want, that I do.”

Just as we recognize man in the body of that blessed life in which he had the freedom to do whatever he wished, whether good or evil **[Note: Vignierius reads, “where he had free choice.” “Choice” is absent from the manuscripts]**, so recognize man in the miserable body of this death, where he has lost his freedom and you hear him say, “I do not do what I want, but I do what I hate”; and, “I do not do the good that I want, but the evil that I do not want, that I do”; and, “Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7:15, 19, 24).

### LII

**JULIAN:** The blame for this does not return to the necessary, because whatever reaches the necessary strikes the author himself.

**AUGUSTINE:** Does this evil of man, when he says, “The evil that I do not want, that I do,” strike man’s author himself? And yet it is plainly evident that the one who acts in this way has reached the necessary; for he does by necessity what he does not do by will.

### LIII

**JULIAN:** Just as what comes from the necessary cannot be ascribed to my possible, so what comes from the possible cannot be ascribed to the necessary. That is, just as the nature of my body and mind cannot be applied to my will, so that I may appear to be as I am because I wished it—since I could not wish before I existed—so the evil of the will cannot be applied to nature, so that the operations of possibility are mixed with necessity **[Note: The manuscripts of Marcellinus and Clarus read *misceatur*, “be mixed”; Codex Port. reads *misceat*, “mix.”]**.

**AUGUSTINE:** What can be done without being necessary is sufficiently and plainly distinguished from necessity; you call this possible, as though what not only can happen but must happen were impossible.

But since you have chosen to impose these names upon the two things, let us understand them as best we can and endure them. What, then, do you mean when you say, “The evil of the will cannot be applied to nature”? When an angel or a man wills something, does nature not will something? And are neither angel nor man natures **[Col. 1487]**? Who could say this?

If, then, angel and man are natures, nature certainly wills whatever the angel wills, and nature wills whatever the man wills. How, then, can the evil of the will not be applied to nature, when nothing can will except by nature?

Or should the sin of a man’s will not be imputed to him because man is a nature, and, as you say, the evil of the will cannot be applied to nature? Or has your folly advanced so far that you say nature must be charged with what cannot be applied to nature? For who would say that what is imputed to man is not imputed to nature, unless he were so foolish as to deny that man is a nature?

Do you see how much you say without knowing what you say? If you say, “The will cannot be applied to necessity,” even this is not universally true. Sometimes we will what is necessary, as it is necessary that those who live well with perseverance become blessed. Sometimes it is even necessary that we will something, as it is necessary that we will blessedness. Hence there is also a certain blessed necessity, because it is necessary that God live always, immutably, and most blessedly.

But since there are also certain necessities so separate from wills that there is necessity where there is no will, and will where there is no necessity, the statement “The will cannot be applied to necessity” is at least partly true.

But whoever says, “An evil will cannot be applied to nature,” should show us, if he can, either a will—evil or good—where nature is absent, or how any will could exist if there were no nature that willed something.

Consider, then, how far you are cut off from the truth. You say, “An evil will cannot be applied to nature.” But the truth says, “As long as any will exists, it cannot be separated from nature.”

### LIV

**JULIAN:** Not penetrating this subtlety of distinctions, the Manichaean produced against us the ranks of the Traducianists. He argues in this way: “From where is evil?” Plainly, from the will. “From where is the evil will?” He answers, “From man.” “From where is man?” “Through God.” And he concludes: “If evil is from man, and man is through God, then evil is through God.”

After this, as though acting religiously, lest he make God criminal, he assigns a nature of darkness to which we ought to ascribe evil. Hence Augustine too: “From where is evil?” “From the will.” “From where,” he says, “is the will itself?” “From man, who is God’s work.” And he concludes: “If evil is from the will, the will from man, and man God’s work, then evil is through God.”

As though trying to absolve God from this, lest he appear to call God criminal—which his doctrine of transmission asserts—he likewise offered us, in God’s place, something no less violent—namely, darkness—to which we should ascribe this evil. “For,” he says, “evil was not born in man because he was God’s work, but because he was from nothing” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 2, section 48).

As if truth could not answer: With what impudence does your god first falsely declare that there is a will in man, and then condemn it, when he knows that this evil—namely, sin—came by the necessity of darkness, that is, of the ancient nothing?

We have inflected *nothing* through its cases so that the power of the Traducianist, who places his hope in nothing, might become apparent.

Consider, nevertheless, the weakness of the God whom the Traducianist introduces. He was unable to overcome nothing; and when he had made man from nothing, he could not strip him of the condition of evil that came from nothing. Made more bitter by the difficulty of things, he accuses man for his own faults and condemns the crimes of nothing through the destruction of his image.

The old man Manes deals more kindly with him, saying that he was not entirely devastated by the race of darkness; whereas the Traducianist depicts such great weakness in him that he imagines him to have been overcome by nothing.

**AUGUSTINE:** No one is overcome by nothing; but you are overcome by saying nothing. Nor have I placed my hope in nothing; rather, you have brought your loquacity to nothing.
