Certainly, if you correctly understand what you perversely say, in this way God is overcome by nothing, since nothing can overcome God. For what is “nothing” except no thing? In this sense God also cannot overcome nothing, because he does not overcome no thing who overcomes all things; he is above all things.

But, as you say, the Manichaean “did not penetrate the subtleties of your distinctions,” and therefore says: “If evil is from man, and man is through God, then evil is through God.” You suppose that, terrified by this conclusion, we must deny either that man is through God, or that evil is from man, or both—as he does—and thus declare it all false, so that he may introduce to us some substance of darkness that made man and that is itself primarily evil, from which all evil is believed to come **[Note: Codex Port. reads, “from which evil is believed to exist.”]**.

What answer will you, most subtle divider, make to this artifice, which you think must be resisted by wisdom? “I shall say,” you reply, “that evil arose from man through the possible, not through the necessary.” As though he could not answer you: “If evil is from the possible, the possibility is from nature, nature is through God, and therefore evil is through God.”

If you do not fear this conclusion, neither do I fear it. For we both confess that the first man sinned not from the necessary but from the possible.

When we say that man could sin because his nature was not made from God, although he could not exist at all except through God’s creating him, we do not say that this means a necessity of sinning was imposed upon him, as you slanderously claim. He could plainly sin and not sin **[Note: In the printed editions *peccare* has been wrongly replaced by *poterat*, against the manuscripts.]**. But if he had not been made from nothing—that is, if his nature had been from God—he could not have sinned at all.

For who is so insane as to dare say that the immutable and unchangeable nature that is God can in any way sin? Of him the Apostle says, “He cannot deny himself” (2 Tim. 2:13).

We therefore resist both forms of Manichaeism, saying that man was made by the good and just God not in such a way that he had to sin, and that he sinned because he willed to do so, although he could also have willed not to sin.

But when we see such great and manifest evils in his descendants, and you deny that they come through a corrupted origin together with those with whom they are born, rather than through the voluntary acts of human beings, your heresy plainly establishes the Manichaean doctrine in a fortress: it introduces a nature of evil whose mixture has corrupted God’s nature. From this fortress the truth casts down both him and you.

### LV

**JULIAN:** All who declare war against truth suffer this disgrace. Let us therefore collect what we have done.

The question is where that first evil will arose in man. We answer: from a movement of the mind compelled by no one.

It is objected: “Did it appear in God’s work?” We agree that this is true.

We are asked how we can deny natural sin while admitting this. We answer: because this sin exists in God’s work from the possible, not from the necessary.

Natural things, therefore, are necessary, while possible things are voluntary.

**AUGUSTINE:** There are also voluntary things that are necessary, as when we wish to be blessed, and it is necessary that we wish it. There are also natural things that are possible. Thus it is possible for a woman who has intercourse with a man through the genital organs of both to conceive, provided that she is not sterile and he is not sterile; but it is not necessary. It can happen, but it need not happen, and yet it is natural.

Be silent, I beg you. Your definitions are empty, and your divisions are not subtle but childish.

### LVI

**JULIAN:** Accordingly, just as we ascribe sin to a free movement, so we ascribe nature to God the creator. Human nature is therefore God’s good work; free choice—that is, the possibility of doing wrong or doing right—is likewise God’s good work.

Both of these come to man from the necessary; neither of these two things is the cause of evil. They came from the necessary only this far: now the will arises in them, but not from them. For they are capable of will, not full of it; they do not produce differences of merit, but receive them.

**AUGUSTINE:** You rightly confess that nature and free choice are good works of God. But what could be more insane than your assertion that the will arises in them, yet not from them?

Can it really be, Julian, that the will of man does not arise from man, when man is a good work of God? Could it finally have entered your mind that man’s will arises, but not from his free choice?

Tell us, then, from where it arises if not from nature—that is, if not from man himself; if not from his free choice, tell us, I beg you, from where man’s will arises.

You have said where it arises; say also from where. You say: nature and free choice are good works of God. “In these,” you say, “the will arises, but not from these.” From where, then? Tell us; let us hear and learn.

Or show that something arose somewhere when there was no source from which it could arise. The world indeed arose from nothing, but through God’s making it; for if it had no God as its craftsman, it could not arise from any things at all.

If, then, the will also arose from nothing in man or in his free choice, who made it? Or if it was not made but arose, who begot it **[Note: The same codex reads, “but arose.”]**? Is it the only thing among things that began to exist that was made by no one, born from nothing **[Note: The printed editions read “from no one,” and shortly afterward, “from which unwillingly it arose.” The manuscripts have been restored.]**?

Why, then, is man condemned on account of it, when the evil will arose in him against his will, and he was merely capable of it but not effective in producing it?

But if it arose in him with his will, so that he may rightly be condemned, why do you deny that his own will arose from him, when you do not deny that it arose with his will and could not have arisen except with his will?

Since it arose from him, it arose from nature, because man is a nature. And since he could also have willed not to do what he willed to do, it arose from his free choice, which likewise, as you admit, belongs to nature.

Why, then, do you deny with closed eyes what is plainly evident—that the will of man arises from the nature of man—because you fear that the Manichaean may accuse the author of this nature?

To refute that pestilence, it is enough that Catholic truth proclaims that man was so created by the best God that he had no necessity of sinning and would not have sinned if he had not wished to sin, since he could always have willed not to sin.

For who is so blind in mind that he does not see that, just as man was first created, it was a great good of nature to be able not to sin, although it is a greater good to be unable to sin? It was most orderly that the former should first exist as the basis of human merit, and the latter should afterward exist as the reward of one who had merited well.

### LVII

**JULIAN:** The good possibility of evil and good, therefore, does not compel the will but permits it to arise. No one is good, then, merely because he possesses free inclination; for many people are equally free and yet utterly wicked. Nor is anyone evil merely because he possesses free choice; for many share equally in this freedom and are nevertheless excellent.

Man is therefore neither good nor evil simply because he is free; yet he could be neither good nor evil unless he were free.

This possibility, which is displayed under the name of freedom, was established by the supremely wise God in such a way that there is nothing without it which is not compelled to exist through it.

For one capacity for opposites is freed from the prejudice of either side: that is, it cannot be called either the cause or the necessity of an evil or a good will, since it receives both in such a way that it compels neither to exist.

The course of necessary things is therefore singular, and in a certain sense is a single thread **[Note: So the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “The necessary is therefore a singular course, and to be a good thread in a certain manner.”]**, like that geometrical length without breadth; nor can this unity be divided here.

As long as it extends in a single line, it retains the force of its nature. But when it encounters something that branches off in another direction, that necessary course immediately comes to an end **[Note: The manuscripts read *occurrerit*; the printed editions have *occurrit*.]**.

That is: the good God made man good **[Note: Codex Port. reads, “makes man good.”]**.

Additional editorial notes from the source:

- XLVI **[Col. 1482]**: The printed editions read “from which things” (*qua rerum*); the text is corrected from the manuscripts. At “since it does not occur,” Vignierius reads “because,” while the manuscripts read “which.” At “This too,” the manuscripts read thus; Vignierius has “Because of this.”
- XLVII **[Col. 1483]**: At the opening, perhaps read *quae* (“things which”) rather than *qui*. At “certainly going to remain unharmed,” Vignierius reads “is certainly unharmed”; the manuscripts require the addition “going to be.” At “resources of diligence,” the manuscripts read *opibus* (“resources”), the printed editions *operibus* (“works”). At “because in the necessary,” perhaps read “because from the necessary.”
- XLVII, Augustine **[Col. 1484]**: The printed editions omit the words, “you must see how, according to your arguments, he is excused from blame.” At “a great punishment,” the printed editions wrongly read *magna*.
- XLVIII **[Col. 1484]**: The old Codex Port. reads “but for doing good.” Vignierius reads “the human nature of mortals”; *human* is absent from the manuscripts.
- XLIX **[Col. 1485]**: The Codex Port. adds “to say.” At “both things,” the manuscripts read *utrumque* (“both”); Vignierius reads *utrumque* in a differing form.
- L **[Col. 1485]**: All the manuscripts read “who does not”; the printed editions read “when.” Codex Port. reads, “the concupiscence alone of the flesh is evil.”
- LI **[Col. 1486]**: Codex B reads, “Thus any definition comes about”; the text is corrected to “Thus that definition.”
- LIII **[Col. 1487]**: Maximus of Aquileia, in the Lateran Synod of 649, act 5, cites this passage as: “Julian, when an angel or a man wills something, does not their nature will something?” At “because it is necessary,” perhaps read “by which it is necessary.”
- LIV **[Cols. 1488–1489]**: The column references occur at the discussion of the necessity of darkness and at Augustine’s concluding objection.
- LV **[Col. 1489]**: Codex Portarum reads “But” in place of “If.”
- LVI **[Col. 1490]**: Codex Port. reads “that the will of man arises” in place of “that man’s will arises.”
- LVII **[Col. 1490]**: The column reference occurs at the opening of Julian’s discussion of freedom.

AUGUSTINE. Why, then, did you say that a human being is neither good nor evil except by his own will, and that whatever he has from God he has necessarily, not possibly? What you want understood is “from nature,” not “from the will”: so that a human being is good through himself, not through God—or at any rate better through himself than through God. For these are your own words: “No one,” you say, “is good because he is endowed with free choice of will.” And shortly afterward: “Nor is anyone evil,” you say, “because he has free choice of will.” What do these words mean except that God did not make the human being either good or evil, but that the human being makes himself one or the other when he uses his free choice well or badly? What, then, is the meaning of what you now say, “The good God made a good human being,” if he is neither good nor evil by possessing the free choice that God made in him, but becomes good by using it well—that is, when he already wills well himself, not when he possesses the possibility of willing well? And how will it be true that “God made the human being upright” (Ecclesiastes 7:30)? Was he upright because he did not possess a good will, but only its possibility? Then he was also perverse because he did not possess an evil will, but only its possibility; and the good will comes to him from himself, while it was falsely written [Note: Col. 1491: perhaps, “and falsely”], “The will is prepared by the Lord” (Proverbs 8:35, according to the Septuagint), and “God works in you both the willing” (Philippians 2:13). Although you do not even say that the good or evil will comes from himself, but that it arises in him, not from him. Thus, according to your astonishing wisdom, God did not make the human being upright; rather, he made one who could be upright if he wished. Nor does he make himself upright, but somehow becomes upright by some accident, since the will by which he becomes upright arises not from him, but somehow from somewhere else or somehow in him. This is not the wisdom that descends from above, but an earthly, natural, demonic wisdom (James 3:15).

### LVIII. JULIAN

Both the beginning and the good beginning of substance are directed by union with the necessary. It also receives freedom of choice; it is still equally contained within the line of the necessary, but now the necessary has reached its end; from this point wills are split into opposites. Therefore the nature of division does not pertain to the union of the necessary. We are compelled to possess possibility; but we are not compelled to use that possibility either well or badly. Thus even the possibility of sinning, capable of good and evil, is voluntary, since it could not have been capable of its own good unless it had also been capable of what is perverse.

[Note: At this point we have inserted the particle *ergo* (“therefore”) on the authority of the manuscripts.]

### AUGUSTINE

Say rather—if you wish to speak the truth—that human nature was first made capable of good and of evil: not because it could not have been made capable of good alone, but because it had to rise in the most orderly way from that first stage, so that, if it had not sinned when it could sin, it might attain the blessedness in which it could not sin. For, as I have already said, both are great goods, although one is lesser and the other greater. It is lesser to be able not to sin; it is greater not to be able to sin. One had to proceed from the merit of the lesser good to the reward of the greater.

For if, as you say, human nature “could not have been capable of its own good unless it had also been capable of evil,” why, after a life faithfully lived, will it be capable only of good and not of evil—alien, that is, not only from every will or necessity of sinning, but even from the possibility of sinning? Or must we fear that we may perhaps sin even then, when we shall be equal to the holy angels? Of those angels we must believe without hesitation that, as a reward for their perseverance, they received the inability to sin, because they stood when, while others were falling, they too could have sinned.

Otherwise, we should still have to fear that this world might contain many new devils and their new evil angels. The life also of the saints who have departed from their bodies would be suspect to us, lest they too should perhaps have sinned—or perhaps should sin—in the place to which they have gone, if the possibility of sinning remains in rational nature and it cannot be capable of good unless it is also capable of evil. Since this is exceedingly absurd, that opinion must be rejected. Rather, we must believe that this nature was originally made capable of both good and evil so that, by loving one of these, it might acquire merit by which it would afterward become capable of good alone or of evil alone. Yet if it were punished with everlasting condemnation, it would be compelled only to suffer evil, not permitted also to commit it.

### LIX. JULIAN

But as great as the difference between fullness and emptiness is, so great is the difference between possibility and necessity. The possibility of that thing of which something is said to be capable is shown to be empty: for if it were not empty, it would not be possibility. For what would something receive that it already possessed? Necessity, however, indicates not emptiness but fullness: it cannot receive, as though empty, what it is already compelled to be, as though full. Thus there is as much difference between the necessary and the possible as between things filled and things empty.

Therefore, by the very reception of opposing qualities, it is defended against the prejudgments of either quality, of both of which it is equally capable. It has as much necessary good in its nature as pertains to the honor of its author: namely, innocence, naturally unmixed with any evil, receiving the result of its own deed either as the possession of good or as the indictment of evil. What comes to it from itself can be wounded by anyone who sins; but what it has received from God’s work cannot be discolored.

Thus even in evil people the natural assessment of good remains. Nor will it ever be evil that it was able to perform good and evil; yet this will profit nothing the person who has forced the institutions of his necessity not indeed to be condemned, but nevertheless to be of no benefit to him. Therefore, just as in a human being in whom freedom has now been unfolded, when he sins we attribute the evil to the will, but nature to God, the author of creation, so, if an infant who does not possess the use of will and displays nothing except the institutions of nature is said to be full of crime and to have evil from the necessary, while another receives it from the possible, then without doubt the author of the crime is accused who is the author of nature.

### AUGUSTINE

We openly break your rules in the case of adults, so that you cannot transfer them to infants. It was not an infant who said, “I do not do the good that I wish, but the evil that I do not wish, that I do” (Romans 7:19). According to your way of speaking about these matters, there was in him not the emptiness of possibility but the fullness of necessity: it was not empty space for him to receive, but something filled with the evil he had received.

For he does not say, “I am able to do both good and evil”—a possibility that was neither the evil of human nature nor of the will—but, “I do not do the good that I wish.” Nor is that all: he adds, “but the evil that I do not wish, that I do.” Behold, both the good he does not do and the evil he does, according to the constitution you yourself have established, he owes not to possibility but, as that man suffers and confesses, to his necessity. He is weak in removing his miseries, but plainly a very sturdy hammer for smashing your rules.

He wills what is good and does not do it; he does not will what is evil and does it. From where does this necessity come? Catholic teachers recognize it: they understand the apostle Paul to be speaking in these words even of himself, and do not hesitate to say that it comes from the law resisting the law of the mind in the members—a law without which no human being is born. Hence they see that even saints are said to say, “I do not do the good that I wish, but the evil that I do not wish, that I do,” because they see how great a good it is not to desire in the flesh what they reject in mind, and see them will this yet fail to accomplish it; and how evil it is, although the mind does not consent, nevertheless to desire such things in the flesh, and see them refuse this yet do it.

They do this without any condemnation, certainly, because the guilt of this sin has been erased through regeneration and they resist with the mind, lest they complete what they desire in the flesh; but not without some evil of their own, since what is mixed with them is not something foreign but their own nature, both in mind and in flesh.

You refuse to admit this pious and true understanding against the position you have undertaken to defend, as though you did so in order that, in the judgment where you defend it, nothing might be recited against it—not only from the written words but also from the very conduct and groanings of human beings—because you do not wish it to be recited; and recited with such manifest force of truth that not eloquence but only your impudence would remain, by which you could not defend it, but would merely wish to defend it.

For what are you doing when you try to cloud clear matters with a storm of confused loquacity? The Apostle cries out, “I do not do the good that I wish, but the evil that I do not wish, that I do.” He also cries out above, “Now it is no longer I who do it, but sin dwelling in me; for I know that good does not dwell in me—that is, in my flesh” (Romans 7:17–19).

What is this “I do what I do not wish”? And what is “It is no longer I who do it”? What else can it mean but what he explains immediately afterward? By saying, “I do what I do not wish,” he shows that he does it; and again, by saying, “It is no longer I who do it,” he shows that it is not his consenting mind but his desiring flesh that does it. For the flesh acts by desiring, even if it does not draw the mind into consent.

For this reason he adds, “I know that it does not dwell in me.” And explaining what he means by “in me,” he says, “that is, in my flesh, good.” But let these be the words not of the Apostle, as you wish, but of any human being weighed down by an evil habit that he cannot overcome by his will. Is this not strong enough to break and shatter your arguments about the possible and the necessary as childish and frivolous playthings?

For there is sin that is not merely voluntary and possible, from which one is free to abstain, but also necessary sin, from which one is not free to abstain. This is now not only sin but also the punishment of sin. And you do not wish to notice that what is accomplished in each person through the violence of habit—which some learned men have called “a second nature”—was brought about through the penal violence of that first, supreme and greatest sin of the first human being, in all who were in his loins and were to arise through his desire when the human race was propagated; a desire which the shame of sinners covered in the region of the loins.

### LX. JULIAN

But why bring us to infants, when the Manichaean question says that a human being of mature age does not sin by the will? For if evil arose in a human being because he had been made from nothing, and if a human being necessarily had from God that he should be made from nothing, then without doubt he received evil not from possibility but from necessity.

Since this has been destroyed by a lengthy discussion, let us continue to discuss this same matter briefly, so that it may become clearer and clearer through repetition. You ask, then, from where the evil will itself first arose in the first human being. I answer: “From a movement of the mind, compelled by no one.”

You also ask from where the movement itself arose. I answer: “What are you asking? From where it could have existed, or from where it was compelled to exist?” If you say—as you have also written—“From where was it compelled to exist?” I shall say that you are speaking contradictions that cannot stand together (*asystata*). For you ask who compelled what could not exist unless no one compelled it. Since this is dissolved by its own contradiction, a question that has no order has no force.

Therefore you ask most foolishly from where the evil will itself arose. For by this “from where” you seek not its occasion but its origin—that is, its nature. But, as was discussed above, if it receives a nature, it loses the definition by which it was said to be “compelled by no one”; whereas if it retains the definition, it excludes the presumption of birth.

A human being therefore did not sin because he was made from nothing; nor because he was made by God; nor because he was made from darkness; nor because he was made with free choice. He sinned because he willed—that is, he had an evil will because he willed.

### AUGUSTINE

We—or rather, Truth itself—say that among people of mature age some do evil by will, some by necessity, and that the very same people act in some matters by will and in others by necessity. If you think this false, look at the one crying out, “I do not do the good that I wish, but the evil that I do not wish, that I do.” This must be thrown back in your face as often as you say these things, whenever you either pretend not to see this man or perhaps truly do not see him.

Why do you entangle yourself in winding evasions? No one says to you, “A human being had the necessity of sinning because he was made from nothing”; you say this to yourself. He was certainly made in such a way that he had the possibility of sinning from the necessary, but sin itself from the possible.

Nevertheless, he would not even have had the possibility of sinning if he had been God’s nature; for he would certainly have been immutable and unable to sin. He therefore did not sin because he was made from nothing, but he was able to sin because he was made from nothing. There is an enormous difference between “he sinned” and “he was able to sin”: the former is guilt, the latter is nature.

Nor did everything made from nothing have the ability to sin; wood and stones cannot sin. Yet the nature that could sin was made from nothing. Nor is it a great thing to be unable to sin; what is great is to be unable to sin in blessedness. Just as it is not a great thing to be unable to be miserable, since all things that cannot attain blessedness cannot be miserable; but it is great for a nature to be so blessed that it cannot be miserable.

Although this is greater, it is not a small thing that human nature was created in such blessedness that, if it wished, it could be not miserable.

Thus all things are said to have been made from nothing—that is, from things that did not exist—so that we may understand that whatever was made from something that already existed must be referred to the first origin. Flesh, for example, is from earth, but earth is from nothing. In the same way we say that all human beings are children of Adam, although each person is the child of his own father.

Nevertheless, all things that have been made are mutable because they were made from nothing—that is, they did not exist and came into being through God’s making—and they are good, because they were made by the good. Nor would any goods be mutable at all, insofar as they exist, unless there were an immutable good from which they were created.

All evils, therefore, which are nothing other than privations of goods, arose from goods—but from mutable goods. The angel and the human being, from whom evils arose—although those evils need not have arisen if they had been unwilling to sin, since they were also able not to will—may rightly be called good natures, but not immutable ones.

God, however, is so good that he makes good use even of evils. The Almighty would not permit them to exist if he could not make good use of them by his supreme goodness. Otherwise he would rather appear powerless and less good, because he could not make good use even of evil.

Accordingly, you cannot deny that the one who says, “I do the evil that I do not wish,” has already received evil from the necessary, not from the possible. Therefore it is not true, as you say, that “every action of evil comes not from the necessary but from the possible”; rather, some evil is found to come from the necessary as well.

Now see how your elaborate contrivance has collapsed. But when asked from where the evil will first arose in the human being, you think it more cautious to answer, “From a movement of the mind, compelled by no one,” as though you could not answer more quickly and directly, “From the human being himself.”

For the addition “compelled by no one” could have been added by you here as well: “with no one resisting you.” Who would resist you if you said what is true—if you said, “The evil will arose in the first human being from the human being himself, compelled by no one”?

But now, fearing to blame nature, as though some injury would thereby rebound upon its author, you have said what you had long wished to say, and have not departed from nature. For the mind is a nature, and indeed, in the constitution of the human being it is better than the body. You have said that from its movement, compelled by no one, the evil will arose.

Do you not see that what you are not permitted to deny had to arise from somewhere, since before it arose it did not exist? What need is there to ask from where the movement of the mind came, when it is sufficiently clear that the movement of the mind could arise only from the mind?

If you deny this with the utmost impudence and foolishness, you are still asked from where the evil will arose in the first human being. You are no longer permitted to say, “From a movement of the mind, compelled by no one,” because the movement of the mind itself is the will.

Therefore to say, “The will arose from a movement of the mind,” is to say, “The movement of the mind arose from a movement of the mind,” or, “The will arose from the will.”

Or do you say that this movement arose from itself, not from the mind, lest the good nature—that is, the mind itself—thereby be blamed? Let it not, then, be condemned on that account. Who could rightly condemn the mind on the basis of that for which it cannot rightly be blamed?

But you say, “The human being sinned because he willed; he had an evil will because he willed.” You speak most truly. But just as the most brilliant light is not darkness, the evil will arose from him because he willed.

For we do not say—as you slander us, and falsely claim that we have written—that this movement was compelled from somewhere. We say that it arose from somewhere without anyone compelling it, because, although no one compelled it, it nevertheless arose, and because what did not exist before it arose could arise only from somewhere.

If, then, the human being willed, the will arose from the human being. And what was the human being before the will arose from him, except a good nature and a good work of God? The evil human being is also this, insofar as he is a human being and a work of God.

Let Julian, then, be confounded by his own vanity, since Ambrose truly said that evils arose from good things (*On Isaac and the Soul*, chapter 7). Yet because they arose with no one compelling them, God is free from blame; and because he permitted them to exist, he is praised more magnificently for the just and good use he makes of them.

### LXI. JULIAN

The will, therefore, which is nothing other than a movement of the mind compelled by no one, owes its possibility to nature, but its effect to itself. It arose in nature, but from the possible, not from the necessary.

If someone should say here, “But the nature that could have an evil will was evil,” I answer, “But the nature that could have a good will was good.” Thus it will be called at one and the same time both the best and the worst. But the reason of things does not permit one and the same thing, at one and the same time, to be filled with contrary qualities of merit.

If, therefore, it is thought evil because it could do evil, it should be considered good because it could perform good. But, he says, why could it also do evil if it was performing good? I answer: because this good, which is called virtue, could not be its own unless it were voluntary. But it would not be voluntary if it possessed the necessity of good; and it would have endured the necessity of good if it had not possessed the possibility of evil. Therefore, so that the right of good might be preserved, the possibility of evil was admitted.

[Note: The manuscripts read *jus boni* (“the right of good”); the printed editions have *vis boni* (“the power of good”).]

### AUGUSTINE

As I see it, you do not even wish to attribute a good will to nature when the human being was first created—as though God could not make a human being with a good will, while nevertheless not compelling him to remain in it; rather, it could remain in his choice whether he wished always to remain in it or not, and whether, without anyone compelling him, he wished to change from it into an evil will, as in fact happened.

For the human being did not previously lack the will not to sin and then begin his life from a will to sin, in which life God created him upright—certainly as one who could already use reason. Who could tolerate it if someone said that he had been made like infants are born?

That perfection of nature, which was not supplied by years but by God’s hand alone, could not have possessed anything other than a will, and that will could not have been evil. Otherwise it would not have been written, “God made the human being upright” (Ecclesiastes 7:30).

The human being was therefore made with a good will, ready to obey God, receiving obediently a command that he could keep without any difficulty for as long as he wished, and abandon without any necessity when he wished—doing the former not without fruit and the latter not without punishment.

From this, by pious and sober reflection, it is gathered that the first good will was God’s work: with it he made the human being upright, for no one is ever upright unless he wills uprightly. Therefore the good will is not restored after being lost except by the one by whom it was created; nor should the necessity of sin be thought capable of being healed from anywhere except by the mercy of the one whose profound and just judgment brought it upon the descendants of the man who sinned without any necessity.

Hence, after he had lamented the necessity and punishment of the sin dwelling in his flesh, by which he was compelled to do the evil he did not wish, he immediately showed where one ought to take refuge: “Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God, through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Romans 7:24–25).

You surely see how that possibility you think you have discovered as something great does not come to his aid. It has already been lost when evil is done by necessity, and under necessary evil the human being cries, “Wretched man that I am.” But let the one come to his aid whose grace overcomes even those things that you therefore call necessary because they cannot be otherwise.

For what is impossible for human beings is easy for God. It was not necessary for the camel to be unable to enter through the eye of a needle; rather, it was possible for it to enter (Matthew 19:26, 24), just as flesh and bones were brought through closed doors (John 20:26).

You therefore strive in vain to defend a nature that has been corrupted. If you seek to do something useful on its behalf, work for its healing, not its exculpation. Allow it to have done for itself the thing for which it would deservedly be condemned.

For whatever else you say about where the evil will arose, if you deny that it arose from the will itself, you affirm its unjust condemnation. For what else are you saying except, “It did not itself do the thing for which it is condemned”? What, then, is more unjust than to condemn it for something it did not itself do?

But if it did it itself, why do you try to excuse it on the basis of the possible, from which you are shown to accuse it more inexcusably? For you say that “the evil will arose in nature, but from the possible, not from the necessary.”

If this possibility is outside nature, then let the possibility itself, from which the evil will arose, be condemned rather than nature. But if possibility also belongs to nature, nature made the evil will more truly its own, because it was also able not to make it. This is shown by the definition of possibility that you have yourself commended.

No one says to you, “Nature is evil because it could have an evil will.” We, certainly, against whom you are now speaking, do not say this. Why do you linger pointlessly over it?

But in what you said—“This good, which is called virtue, would not be voluntary if it possessed the necessity of good; and it would have endured the necessity of good if it had not possessed the possibility of evil”—you have completely forgotten God. His virtue is all the more necessary the more he wills it in such a way that he cannot not will it.

You yourself said in the first book of this work, “God cannot be anything except just” (chapter 28). If this is to be called necessity, let it be called necessity without reservation, provided that it remains clear that nothing is happier than this necessity, by which it is just as necessary that God not live evilly as it is necessary that he live forever and most blessedly.

For such a necessity is not afraid of your words. You did not wish to say, “He would have had the necessity of good,” but preferred to say, “He would have endured it if he had not possessed the possibility of evil.” Thus you make it appear that God spared the human being lest, like someone afflicted, he should endure the necessity of good by not possessing the possibility of evil. Yet this is so great a good that it was reserved as a reward for the saints—whom you have forgotten just as you have forgotten God.

For we shall not live without virtue at the time when it is granted to us that we can never depart from the Lord, since we shall not even be able to will to do so. Our good will therefore be certain, when, as promised, we shall always be with the Lord (1 Thessalonians 4:16), so that we shall neither wish nor be able to wish to depart from him.

Virtue, then, would not otherwise exist in us unless we lacked an evil will in such a way that we could have one. But, in return for the merit of this lesser virtue, a greater virtue ought to be granted to us as a reward, so that we would lack an evil will in such a way that we could not have one.

O desirable necessity! Truth will bestow it, so that there may be certain security, without which our complete happiness cannot exist—happiness to which nothing remains to be added.

### LXII. JULIAN

But this can be turned against us, so that it may be said: “Nature was adapted to evil. For because evil could not have been voluntary if there had been a necessity of evil, the possibility of good was given so that ownership of evil might be established.”

This is indeed clever, but insane. For everything is assessed from the better side of things. To this is added the dignity of the author, namely God, who did not make the free creature for the sake of those things he was going to punish, but for the sake of those for which he was going to reward it, and therefore gave it the possibility of opposites.

Nevertheless, I do not wish to fight over this; I allow some room for accusation, so that I may prescribe nothing concerning the authority of the maker. Yet the following necessarily follows: this possibility of doing good and evil must be removed from the effect of either will. Consequently, it is proved to be the cause neither of virtue nor of vice.

Let us grant this injustice to honorable things: because they seem to have this in common with the wicked, let the merit of neither a good nor an evil will be attributed to them on that basis. It therefore has testimony to its freedom, that it is innocent, because it is full neither of good nor of evil, but only of the voluntary.

[Note: The manuscripts read *ingenuitatis* (“freedom” or “nobility”); the printed editions have *integritatis* (“integrity”).]

Attribute the possibility of willing to nature; attribute neither a good nor an evil will to nature. It is therefore irrefutably established that the evil will arose in God’s work, but from the possible, not from the necessary. This cannot be charged to the giver of possibility, but to the governor of possibility itself.

### AUGUSTINE

You allow that neither a good nor an evil will should be attributed to nature, but only the possibility of a good or evil will, although both angel and human being are natures. If, as you say, a good or evil will is not to be attributed to nature, then nature must neither be honored for a good will nor condemned for an evil one.

For what is more unjust than to judge it worthy of condemnation for an evil that is not to be attributed to it? Are angel and human being not natures? Who says this except one who does not know what he is saying?

What is attributed to the angel is therefore attributed to nature; what is attributed to the human being is attributed to nature—but to a nature made good by the good God, and made evil by its own will.

Accordingly, the evil rightly attributed to these natures is not attributed to the one by whom they were created, because when he first created them he did not establish them in such a way that they would have any necessity of an evil will, but only a possibility. In that possibility they could acquire merit, and a good will, if not abandoned, could find reward, while if abandoned it could find punishment.

Why, then, do you seek to excuse nature from the malice of the will, when willing or refusing belongs to nature? For there is no evil will except the will of a willing angel or human being, and we cannot in any way say that these are not natures.

Why, I ask, do you attribute an evil will to the human being, so that he may justly suffer punishment for the merit of an evil will, while you do not wish to attribute what you attribute to the human being to nature, as though the human being could in any way not be a nature?

It would be far better for you to speak soundly and say that the evil will of the human being belongs to some nature, because every human being is a nature; but that this nature, when it first did evil, had an evil will not from the necessary but from the possible. For you have chosen these terms to distinguish two things: in the one, something is understood to happen because it must; in the other, something that can happen but need not happen, since it can also not happen.

This is said most truly of the sin of the first human being, or of the first human beings. There remains the one who cries out, “I do not do the good that I wish, but the evil that I do not wish, that I do” (Romans 7:19). He does evil from the necessary: he does not wish it, yet does it. And he breaks your rule, which you fashioned with reckless loquacity, saying that “the cause is proved to belong neither to the necessary in the case of virtue nor to the necessary in the case of vice,” although in this instance its cause is proved to belong to the necessary.

For either the action of evil is not vice, or not doing the good one wishes, refusing the evil yet doing it, is not necessity—or else the necessity of virtue will also be a blessed one for us, when our nature shall be filled with such great grace and “God will be all in all” (1 Corinthians 15:28), so that it cannot will anything evil.

Virtue is justice, and a new heaven and a new earth are promised to us, in which justice dwells (2 Peter 3:13).

Or if, perhaps confused, you say that you fashioned this rule for the present life, not the future one, I do not contend with a defeated opponent. Certainly, you do not deny that it pertains to this life, where you see a human being willing but not doing good, and unwilling yet doing evil. You are therefore forced, against your rule, to attribute this vice to necessity, not to the will.

From this necessity, with which infants too are born, although it begins to appear as age advances, who liberates the miserable human being except the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord (Romans 7:25)? You, enemies of this grace, trust in your own virtue and, against the divine writings that condemn those who trust in their own virtue (Jeremiah 17:5), argue with impious pride.

### LXIII. JULIAN

Let the distinction, then, between those things that come from the possible and those that come from the necessary remain fixed in the mind of the prudent reader; let him apply all natural things to the necessary and voluntary things to the possible, and bring all questions to completion from the side from which they began.

For if he wanders blindly through both, he is plunged through almost every word into countless errors. Since this has become sufficiently clear, it is evident that you were altogether too much in the dark when you concluded: “Just as the evil that did not exist anywhere was able to arise in God’s work, so also what already existed passed naturally through God’s work.”

See into what error you have become entangled. You say that sin conceived by the first will, which comes from the possible, was changed into the necessary, so that just as the free movement of the mind could arise, it might pass over without a free movement into the necessity of natural things.

[Note: The manuscripts read *in naturalium necessitatem* (“into the necessity of natural things”); Vignier has *in naturalem necessitatem* (“into natural necessity”).]

But understand that God is the author of necessary things. If, then, God does in natures what the mind did in sins, he must be guilty in the same way as the one whose will he accuses. Indeed, even more so: for the more necessary something is than something possible, the more criminal it is to implant sin than to usurp it.

Although the nature of things cannot contain this conclusion, I will nevertheless show here that your opinion of God is much worse than the Manichaeans’ opinion. Their god was mutilated by sudden wars; yours has been corrupted by ancient and multiplied crimes.

Accordingly, you disagree with Catholics not only about the question but about God altogether. You do not worship the same God whom we venerate as most just, almighty, and inviolable in the Trinity.

Therefore a thing belonging to the will could not pass through nature. We rightly said, then, that the work of the devil is not permitted to pass through the work of God.

The work of the devil is the sin of the devil and of the evil human being, and it cannot exist in anyone without a free movement of the will. This work comes from the possible to both devil and human being, and it does come from the possible. But the work of God is nature, in which the human being subsists not from the possible but from the necessary. This nature exists for many years without a will, since its power is perceived only at a determinate age.

As long, therefore, as nature exists without a will, it is solely the work of God. But because it has not done this thing, it cannot have sin. It was therefore said irrefutably that the work of the devil is not permitted to pass through the work of God.

No less false than profane is what you said: “The work of the work of God passes through the work of God.” For this is to say, “God sins because the human being whom God made sinned.”

For just as sin exists nowhere except in the work of the human being—and when the human being has sinned, no substance is added to him so that sin may appear prominent there, but only an evil work committed from an evil will, which also assigns an evil merit to the one by whom it was done, so that the one who did evil may be called evil—so likewise, if your god did evil in his work, no substance would indeed be added to him, just as none is added to the human being; nevertheless, the most shameful merit would be assigned to him, so that he would be called evil because he did evil.

An infant, certainly, is shown even then not to be guilty because he has malice from the necessary; for unless the devil had malice from the possible, the infant could not be guilty.

But the God who is the true God of Christians does not do evil. An infant, before the exercise of his own will, has nothing except what God has made in him. Therefore no natural sin can exist.

Since we have broken through the caves of the ancient error with the utmost care, and nothing remains hidden concerning this question, let the diligent reader hold fast the distinction between the necessary and the possible. He will laugh at the fictions of the Manichaeans no less than at those of the Traducianists.

[Additional editorial notes: Col. 1491: The manuscripts read *non quo* rather than *non quod*. Col. 1492: We restore *malos* (“evil”) from the manuscripts. Col. 1493: An old Porto manuscript reads *menti adversantur* (“oppose the mind”). Col. 1494: The manuscripts read *peccati* (“of sin”) rather than *peccandi* (“of sinning”); the same reading occurs below in chapter 61 in the printed editions. Col. 1495: The manuscripts read *quae nulla erant* (“things that did not exist”); the printed editions read *quae de nullo erant* (“things that were from nothing”). An old Porto manuscript reads *nolebas* (“you did not wish”) for *volebas* (“you wished”). The manuscripts read *ea quidem*; Vignier reads *quippe*. Col. 1496: The passage from “Therefore” through “from the will” is added from the Porto manuscript. Agatho, in his Synodal Letter to the Emperors, adds only “that the will arose from the will,” omitting the remaining words. Vignier reads “said that evils arose,” omitting *verum* (“truly”), which is supplied here from the manuscripts. Col. 1497: An old Marian manuscript has *difficultate* (“difficulty”) here again in place of *necessitate* (“necessity”). Col. 1498: An old Porto manuscript reads *Non ergo aliter non esset*; perhaps *Nunc ergo aliter non esset* (“Now, therefore, virtue would not otherwise exist”). The Marian manuscript reads *ex ea quo*. Col. 1499: The Porto manuscript adds *vel bonae, vel malae* (“whether good or evil”) after “possibility of willing.” It reads *compararent* (“they might acquire”), which is acceptable if referred to the natures. The particle *cum* is restored from the Porto manuscript. Col. 1501: An old Porto manuscript reads *perrupimus* (“we have broken through”) rather than *prorupimus* (“we have burst forth”).]

AUGUSTINE. Among people who understand what they read in such a way that they also understand these things you are saying, you have accomplished nothing other than repeating the same points through the same points with such great perplexity, so that it might become apparent that you wished to obscure, rather than refute, my response in the one book of mine which you undertook to answer in eight of yours, since you were unable to dissolve it. Among those, however, who do not understand these things, you have at least accomplished this: that they think you have said something precisely because they do not understand. Accordingly, they must meanwhile be briefly reminded of the matter now under discussion, so that, with the mists of your loquacity removed, they may look upon that very passage of mine and see how unconquerable it is.

You had said: “If nature is God’s work, the devil’s work is not permitted to pass through God’s work.” To this I replied: “What does this mean: ‘If nature is God’s work, the devil’s work is not permitted to pass through God’s work’? Was not the devil’s work, when it first arose in the angel who became the devil, born in God’s work? Therefore, if evil, which nowhere existed at all, could arise in God’s work, why could evil, which already existed somewhere, not pass through God’s work—especially since the Apostle uses this very verb when he says, ‘And so it passed through to all human beings’ (Romans 5:12)? Are human beings not God’s work? Sin, then, passed through human beings—that is, the devil’s work passed through God’s work. To put the same thing another way: the work of God’s work passed through God’s work. And therefore God alone is immutable and of supremely powerful goodness: he who, before any evil existed, made all things good, and who works well in every respect through the evils that arose in the good things made by him” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 2, section 48).

[Note: [Col. 1501] Thus the manuscripts. In Vignier: “evil which did not exist anywhere.”]

Disturbed by the evident force of these considerations, you thought that people’s eyes should be darkened by a long and empty disputation about the possible and the necessary, so that, after this darkness had been cast over them, you might not withdraw your vain position lest it be destroyed, but conceal it lest, once destroyed, it be seen lying exposed. For what difference does it make to the matter we are investigating whether something proceeds from the necessary or from the possible? An angel and a human being certainly sinned. Either dare to say that an angel and a human being are not natures; or, since you are not so insane as to dare say this, you are convicted of saying that nature sinned when an angel sinned, and you are convicted of saying that nature sinned when a human being sinned.

“But,” you say, “he sinned from the possible, not from the necessary.” This is true. Yet an angel sinned; a human being sinned; nature sinned. Thus God’s work—which is an angel, which is a human being—sinned, not because God compelled it, but by its own evil will, which it could also have lacked. Shame, therefore, belongs to that nature which, although it had been made good and was not compelled to do evil, nevertheless did evil. Glory, however, belongs to God, who both made nature good and makes good use of evil, although he did not make the evil.

Since, then, by these and similar true and catholic arguments, nature can both be defended and proclaimed as creative, and be accused and reproved as sinful; and since that very sinful nature can both be praised insofar as God made it and blamed insofar as, with no one compelling it, it defected from him and received its own desert in its descendants—for the very same nature is born in each individual without will which sinned in the one individual by will—what drove you to say, what overwhelmed you so that you wrote: “If nature is God’s work, the devil’s work is not permitted to pass through God’s work”?

O deaf man to the sacred words! O blind man in your inventions! Is sin not the devil’s work? Did it not pass through to all human beings, who are God’s work? Is death, especially the kind of death which you say alone occurred through sin—that is, not bodily death but the death of the soul—not the devil’s work? Did it not pass through to all human beings, who are God’s work?

“But it passed through by imitation,” you say. Nevertheless, it passed through human beings, who are God’s work. “But it passed through from the possible, not from the necessary.” Say whatever pleases you. Nevertheless, it passed through human beings, who are God’s work. Yet you stated without qualification: “The devil’s work is not permitted to pass through God’s work.” You attempted, with such great loquacity, to defend the manifest vanity of this statement—not so that it might be cleared, but so that it might not be seen—in order to become still more vain.

[Note: [Col. 1502] The printed editions read “manifest nature,” against the manuscripts.]

If the apostolic words had not come to mind, words which ought to have prevented you from saying this, why, I ask, did you not consider that it is a greater thing for the devil’s work to exist in God’s work than for it to pass through God’s work? Since you admit the former, why do you deny the latter? Can what you want to happen happen, while what you do not want cannot happen? May God have mercy on you, so that you may cease to be vain.

The Manichaean gladly embraces this position of yours as his friend and argues as follows: “If the devil’s work is not permitted to pass through God’s work, much less is it permitted to exist in God’s work. From where, then, is evil, unless from the source we identify?”

But we answer them: “Say these things to Julian, not to us. The author of this position has been cast out. May he not prejudice us, to be defeated together with you—or rather, already defeated by us together with you.”

## LXIV. JULIAN

You therefore brought forward another point arising from the same obtuseness. For you say: “God creates the wicked in the same way as he feeds and nourishes the wicked” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 2, section 32), because it is written in the Gospel that he makes his sun rise upon the good and the wicked, and sends rain upon the just and the unjust (Matthew 5:45).

What you have joined together is far and wide contrary in character. For the fact that God feeds sinners also, and is kind toward the ungrateful and the wicked, is a testimony to his compassion, not to his malignity. For he does not wish the death of the dying, but that he should turn back and live (Ezekiel 18:32); nor does he quickly punish those who go astray. He does this for no other reason than that his goodness may grant time for repentance. Thus the Apostle says: “Do you not know that the goodness of God leads you to repentance? But according to your hardness and impenitent heart, you are storing up wrath for yourself” (Romans 2:4–5).

He also argues among the Lycaonians and the Areopagites that God did not, even in the times of past ignorance, withdraw the evidences of his providence. For he did not leave himself without witness, “giving,” he says, “rains from heaven and fruitful seasons, filling their hearts with food and gladness” (Acts 14:15–16). Therefore, the fact that he sends rain upon the good and the wicked is evidence of his kindness, by which he endures and awaits those who go astray, so that at last they may withdraw from evil and do good.

So far does he not wish evil to occur that, out of love even for human correction, he feeds the ungrateful also. This is a sign of perfect compassion. But what you say—“He creates the wicked”—is evidence of perfect iniquity. See, then, how ignorant you are of what you are saying: from an example of mercy you wished to establish cruelty.

For it is good to feed even the wicked, so that, if they wish, they may be corrected. But it is criminal to make infants wicked, so that those who cannot will nevertheless be compelled to be unjust. Generosity exercised toward sinners draws them away from evil; it does not compel them into evil. But the creation of the wicked does not draw them away from the worst things; rather, it compels both deed and doer into every impious act.

You are therefore insane when you say, “God creates evil.” But you are even more insane when you attempt to affirm this by the testimony of the Gospel, and by that testimony in which there is a great argument for divine goodness. Consider, then, how much more forcefully the matter now turns against you: it is manifest that God, who feeds even the wicked so that by his patience he may make them good, does not create the wicked.

But if he creates the wicked, then he neither loves nor rewards the good, nor can he himself finally possess anything good, since creative power, more effectively and violently than any evil will, would inflict harm—not only possible evils but necessary ones as well. Since this is incompatible with the God of Christians—that is, with him who is called the Father of mercies and the God of consolation (2 Corinthians 1:3), whose judgments are all proclaimed to be just (Psalm 118:75), and who is said to have made all things in wisdom (Psalm 103:24)—you have no communion with us in estimating our God, any more than the Manichaeans do.

[Col. 1504]

Stupid inventions and inherited sins have drawn you to worship an entirely different author, one nevertheless fabricated by the madness of Mani.

[Note: [Col. 1504] We have added the particle “to” (*ad*) from the manuscripts.]

[Note: [Col. 1504] The printed editions have *tamen* (“yet”); Vignierius: “Perhaps, *tam*.” The manuscripts read better: *tamen Manis furore simulatum*, “nevertheless fabricated by the fury of Mani” (that is, of Manichaeus).]

## AUGUSTINE

I shall do what you did not do. What need is there for me even to say what that is? Let those who read judge. For, because you had said “that, according to our understanding, God makes human beings for the devil,” my response came to these words, from which you yourself extracted what you wanted. But even against your will I shall recall what you thought should be passed over.

Among the other matters—which would take too long to state in full—I said: “Does he feed the goats, the sons of perdition, on the left hand, and feed them, nourish them, and clothe them for the devil, because he makes his sun rise upon the good and the wicked and sends rain upon the just and the unjust?” (Matthew 25:33; 5:45). “Thus he creates the wicked in the same way as he feeds and nourishes the wicked: because what he grants them by creating them belongs to the goodness of nature, and what he gives them by feeding and nourishing them provides an increase—not to their wickedness, certainly, but to that same nature which the good God created. Insofar as they are human beings, it is good, belonging to the nature whose author is God. But insofar as they are born with sin and are destined to perish if they are not reborn, it belongs to the seed cursed from the beginning” (Wisdom 12:11), “through the vice of that ancient disobedience. Yet the Maker makes good use even of the vessels of wrath, in order to make known the riches of his glory in the vessels of mercy, so that no one may attribute it to his own merits if, belonging to that same mass, he is liberated by grace; rather, ‘let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord’” (2 Corinthians 10:17).

After saying these things, I added: “From this apostolic and catholic faith, most truthful and firmly founded, this man departs with the Pelagians. He does not wish those who are born to be under the devil, lest infants be carried to Christ so that they may be rescued from the power of darkness and transferred into his kingdom” (Colossians 1:13). “And thus he accuses the Church spread throughout the whole world, in which everywhere all infants who are to be baptized are exsufflated for no other reason than that the prince of this world may be cast out from them” (John 12:31): “it is necessary that the vessels of wrath be possessed by him when they are born from Adam, unless they are reborn in Christ and, having been made vessels of mercy by grace, are transferred into his kingdom” (*On Marriage*, book 2, sections 32–33). Let the person who wishes and is able read the rest there, or listen to someone reading it.

Now, because you left aside these passages, by which what you quoted is established and fortified, and thought that your quotations should be presented as though you were making a bandit’s attack in a deserted place where no defender was present, let those who wish to know what you did read these things—or rather, let them return to the consideration of the same book from which I took these passages—and let them see that those things remain most firmly established which you attempted to shake as though they were weak.

What, then, does it help you that you brought against me those whom God’s patience awaits for correction through repentance, and for whose sake he makes his sun rise and sends rain upon them, when I brought against you the goats of the left hand, whom the one who knows all future things cannot fail to know will live in impiety and crimes without repentance until the end, and therefore will be punished with eternal torment?

Nor does he withhold the good of his creation from those for whom it would not have been advantageous to be born, nor the good of his nourishment and life-giving power—lasting as long as he wills—from those for whom it would have been advantageous to die as soon as possible. Among these there are certainly many who, if they were snatched from this life as infants, would, according to your false heresy, be taken away entirely from everything; according to the catholic faith, however, they would be taken away from the most severe condemnation.

What, then, is the meaning of this further point? Among these goats of the left hand, destined in God’s unfailing foreknowledge for everlasting fire, there are many who, washed in the bath of regeneration, later perish either through apostasy or by living so criminally and disgracefully that they are undoubtedly assigned to the left hand. Yet they are not snatched away, as certain people are, “lest wickedness change their understanding” (Wisdom 4:11).

Nor is God prevented by fatal necessity from granting them this great benefit; nor is he changed by respect of persons when he grants it to others. What place here is there for those “possible” and “necessary” things of yours, which you carefully commend as requiring distinction, when, without your knowing what you are saying, he knows what he is doing—he whose judgments may be hidden but cannot be unjust?

It is not unjust, then, that good things are bestowed upon the wicked. But it is unjust that evils are inflicted upon the good. Say, then, by what justice infants suffer such great evils—evils which we are often reluctant to mention, while you are not ashamed to bring those same evils into paradise, even if no one had sinned.

“They are not created wicked,” you say—that is, they do not draw original sin along with them. By what justice, then, are they pressed down beneath a heavy yoke from the day they emerge from their mother’s womb (Ecclesiasticus 40:1)?

[Note: [Col. 1505] The printed editions read, “What then?” The reading “By what justice?” is corrected from the manuscripts.]

There is such misery in that yoke that we can more easily lament it than explain it. You say that sin cannot be changed from the possible into the necessary—that is, from the voluntary into the involuntary. We have shown that this could happen in the case of the one who says, “What I do not want, that I do” (Romans 7:19). You attribute this to the violence of habit, not to the bonds of a corrupted origin. Yet you see that sin could be transformed from the possible into the necessary, and you are not ashamed of your twisted and deceitful rules.

You do not wish to admit that something of this kind could happen to the entire human race through one human being in whom all were present. Yet you do not deny that, under the care of the almighty and most just God, infants pay so many and such great penalties.

[Note: [Col. 1505] Vignierius reads “most unjust”; this is corrected on the authority of the manuscripts.] You are forced to admit this because it closes your mouths and strikes your eyes if you deny it.

Do you not, then, consider whom you make unjust, when you behold punishments so plainly evident and deny that infants have any evil merits? You thought it false and profane when I said, “The work of God’s work passed through God’s work.” For certainly an angel is God’s work. Therefore sin, which is the work of an angel, is the work of God’s work, but not the work of God himself.

You accuse me concerning these words as though I had said, “God sins, because the human being whom God made sinned.” I did not say this. God’s work sinned—an angel or a human being—but they sinned by their own work, not by God’s work. They themselves are God’s good work; their sin, however, is their own evil work, not God’s.

But which is worse to say: “God also sins, because the human being whom God made sinned”—which I did not say—or to deny original sin in such a way that the unjust punishment of an infant is nothing other than God’s sin? If this cannot be attributed to God, then the infant’s punishment is just. But if it is just, it is punishment for sin. Therefore no one can proclaim God just amid such numerous and such great punishments of infants while denying original sin.

“Therefore,” he says, “it would be evidence of iniquity to create wicked people if he himself had created the evil by which they are wicked.

[Note: [Col. 1506] Perhaps: “you say.”] But now, since human beings are wicked, while he himself creates that by which they are human beings, and since what makes them wicked follows them from a corrupted nature through sin, surely, even when he creates wicked people, he himself is good in what he creates. For they are wicked through a vice which is not a nature; but he creates the nature, which is not a vice, even though it has been corrupted.”

Bestowing the good of creation upon a corrupted and justly condemned stock is like bestowing upon a wicked human being the good of life and health, on account of what makes him human, not on account of what makes him wicked.

[Note: [Col. 1506] The printed editions read “of the Creator” instead of “of creation.”]

As for what you say—“It is criminal to make infants wicked, so that those who cannot will nevertheless be compelled to be unjust”—those who do not exist cannot in any way be compelled to anything. But if they already exist, not yet in the distinct character of their individual person and condition, but in the most hidden manner of the seed, as Levi existed in the loins of Abraham (Hebrews 7:9–10), then through the vice of nature proceeding from the sin of the first human being they are already wicked—not by God’s creation, who does not compel those who cannot yet will to be wicked.

Consider, moreover, the wonders of the grace of Christ, whose wretched enemies you are. Behold, infants who cannot will or refuse good or evil are nevertheless compelled to become holy and just when, resisting and crying out with tears, they are reborn through holy Baptism. For without doubt, if they die before the use of reason, they will be holy and just in the kingdom of God, leading their lives forever in holiness and justice through that grace to which they came not by their own possibility but by necessity, trampling upon and breaking your rules concerning the possible and the necessary.

Without doubt, it is more to refuse to do evil than neither to refuse nor to will it. Yet he both refused and did evil who said, “What I do not want, that I do.” I am not therefore insane, nor do I say, “God creates evil.” For he creates good.

[Note: [Col. 1506] We have added from the manuscripts: “For he creates good.”]

He who, even from corrupted nature itself, creates not the vice but the nature, creates good. That nature, however, bears the vice—not through God’s workmanship, but through his judgment.

But consider whether you are not insane—or, if you are not thoroughly insane, whether you are nevertheless not behaving insanely—when you say that God creates not the punitive evil which is just, but the evil called iniquity. For what else does he do if he either inflicts, or permits to be inflicted, such great evils upon infants who are guilty of no evil?

But you ought not to be addressed and refuted by us; rather, if you could be, you ought to be exsufflated and exorcised by the whole Church—the Church from which you absurdly claim that infants are exsufflated and exorcised.

# BOOK SIX

[Col. 1507]

Augustine shows that Julian argues in vain throughout his sixth book against what was asserted in chapter thirty-four of book two of *On Marriage and Concupiscence*: that by the sin of the first human being human nature was changed for the worse, so that it not only became sinful but subsequently generated sinners. He teaches that the powers of free will, by which human beings, while they possessed them intact, could act rightly when they wished and not sin if they did not wish to, were lost through sin. He entirely rejects that definition of freedom which his opponent habitually brings forward, namely, “the possibility of sinning and not sinning,” and so forth.

He proves that the pains of women in childbirth, thorns, labors, sweats, and the other miseries of mortals are punishments for sin; but above all, that death itself is a punishment for the human being who had been divinely constituted in such a way that, unless he sinned, he would not die. In the final part of the book he examines and refutes Julian’s exposition of the Apostle’s words, “As in Adam all die” (1 Corinthians 15:22), and the statements that follow in the same chapter.

Finally, throughout almost the entire book he demonstrates that the catholic doctrine concerning original corruption—which Julian everywhere strives to drag toward the Manichaean heresy—not only lies far from that heresy but also shows that the heresy can never be overcome by the Pelagians except with the aid and confession of that very catholic doctrine.

## I. JULIAN

I do not doubt that this sort of opinion has thus far prevailed in our dispute to such an extent that it might be thought to concern an involved question rather than the substance of the faith. Those who move about far from spiritual pursuits are stirred only by the little breezes of reputation;

[Note: [Col. 1507] Thus the manuscripts. Vignierius reads “alone.”] and, fearing the disapproval of the times and holding fast neither to the protection of established truth—for, as commonly happens in troubled circumstances, no one is trusted less than oneself—they consider the safer path to be the more frequently traveled.

## AUGUSTINE

Our path is more frequently traveled because it is more ancient; for it is catholic. Yours, however, is less frequently traveled because it is more recent.

[Note: [Col. 1507] The Codex Portensis reads “new.”]

For it is heretical.

## II. JULIAN

This occurs at present for two reasons: both because the Manichaeans’ opinion concerning criminal designs has been approved, and because the storms of persecution that have been stirred up deter impoverished spirits from favoring the truth.

[Note: [Col. 1507] Morel, *Elem. Crit.*, p. 141, reads: “because the Manichaeans’ opinion concerning criminal designs has been brought forward.”]

## AUGUSTINE

How can our path be more frequently traveled on account of the Manichaean position, when they are extremely few? Or how can you suffer persecution for the truth, when you hold infants back from the Savior?

## III. JULIAN

Therefore, the party that consults both pleasure and fear—or luxury accompanied by the crowds of the arena, the circus, or the stage, seeking in every form of depravity to put forward necessity as an excuse, by which the odium of the act is always lightened, and to avoid the crashes of the world through transgression—these are the things that make the defense of vices more popular.

Nevertheless, as I said above, the greater part of the common people has believed that the arguments of the Traducianists and the Catholics agree concerning God.

## AUGUSTINE

The innumerable multitude of the faithful, which was promised to Abraham (Genesis 22:17), is despised by you as a common mob. For evidently, only a few—those whom you make insane by the poisons of a novel pestilence, the Pelagians—can approve what you say: that the evident misery of the human race, which appears in the heavy yoke of the sons of Adam from the day they emerge from their mother’s womb (Ecclesiasticus 40:1), does not arise from the desert of sin by which human nature was corrupted in the first human being.

From this it follows that, if no one had sinned, you are compelled to say that paradise would have contained not only the many and great burdens of suffering which we see infants bear, but also the many and great defects of mind and body with which most people are born.

In that place of happiness and tranquility you also place the concupiscence you have received, by which the flesh desires against the spirit. Yet you accuse us, with closed eyes, as though we were friends of pleasure and luxury, because we fight it as an adversarial vice with the spirit desiring against it. No one falls shamefully and disgracefully into luxury except the person who consents to that received concupiscence of yours, which we condemn and which you defend, when it solicits and persuades him.

## IV. JULIAN

But since both in the first dispute and in the present one Augustine’s argument has made it clear that the God of the Traducianists is not the God whom Christians worship, with harmonious confession, as just and the creator of all, I now foresee that many even of those who have fallen through blind error will be corrected once these matters are recognized.

[Note: [Col. 1508] Vignierius reads “I perceive.”]

## AUGUSTINE

Rather, once they have recognized what we answer your deceitful babbling with the language of truth, no one will remain in the error of your heresy except through excessive dullness or obstinacy.

## V. JULIAN

The Manichaean believes that, against us, human beings are naturally compelled into crimes and wicked acts. He thinks that the origin of darkness supplied both matter for bodies and the basis for crimes; he asserts that sexual pleasure is the corruption of the human race, the champion of the devil’s law, and the force compelling human beings into every disgrace.

The Traducianist, following him in every respect—for he is his heir and offspring—bears witness in many words that natural crimes, an eternal necessity of evil arising from a dark nothingness, and an affection assigned to the senses that pollutes all the saints and places the image of God in the devil’s kingdom, are real.

[Note: [Col. 1508] Thus the manuscripts. In Vignierius: “such.”]

[Note: [Col. 1508] Thus the Codex Portarum. Other manuscripts, together with the printed editions, read: “natural crimes, an eternal necessity of evil.”]

## AUGUSTINE

The Manichaean, in a singular madness contrary to catholic truth, invents a substance of evil coeternal with the good God. But catholic truth confesses that God alone is eternal, without any beginning—not merely good, which he too says, but also immutable, which he does not say.

We therefore proclaim, against the insanity of the Manichaeans, this supremely good and therefore altogether immutable God, to whom no nature is coeternal that is not what he is and that would not exist unless it had been made—not from him, but nevertheless by him; that is, not from his nature, but nevertheless by his power.

We know and say that created nature, which could not have existed at all unless omnipotent nature had made it—although it did not make it from itself—is good, but not equal to the one who made it. For God made all things “very good” (Genesis 1:31), but not supremely good as he himself is. Yet these things, however good they are, would not be good at all unless the supremely good one had made them; nor would any mutable good exist unless the immutable good one had made it.

Accordingly, when the Manichaeans ask us where evil comes from, wishing to introduce evil as coeternal with God, and not knowing what evil is, because they think that it is a nature and substance, we answer them that evil is not from God and is not coeternal with God. Rather, evil arose from the free will of a rational nature, which was created good by the good God. Its goodness, however, is not equal to the goodness of its Creator, since it is not nature but his work. Therefore it had the possibility of sinning, though not the necessity.

It would not have had even the possibility of sinning if it were God’s nature, which neither wishes to be able to sin nor is able to wish to sin. Nevertheless, if this rational nature, possessing the possibility of sinning, had not sinned when it could have sinned, it would have acquired great merit. The reward of that merit would also have been this: that, in greater blessedness, it could not sin.
