But when the Manichaean hears this, he continues and says: “If evil comes from the free will of a rational nature, where do all these evils come from, with which we see those who do not yet use the freedom of the will being born? Where does concupiscence come from, by which the flesh desires against the spirit and draws it toward the commission of sin, unless the spirit desires more strongly against it? Where does such great discord arise in one human being between the two things of which he consists? Where does the law in the members, warring against the law of the mind, come from, without which law no one is born? Where do so many and such great defects of mind and body come from, with which most people are born? Where do the labors and calamities of infants who have not yet sinned by their will come from? When the use of reason arrives, where does such great punishment for mortals come from in learning letters or any arts, so that the torment of blows is added to their sorrowful efforts?”

Here we answer that these evils too derive their origin from the will of human nature, which, by sinning greatly, was corrupted and condemned together with its stock.

From this nature come so many natural goods through God’s workmanship; the evils come through his judgment. The Manichaeans fail to see that these evils are in no way natures or substances. They are called natural, however, because human beings are born with them, as with a root of corrupted origin.

But you, novel heretics, contradict us. Answer the Manichaeans, then. If you deny that human beings are born with so many and such great evils, where is your boldness? If you admit it, where is your heresy?

But you insist that these evils are not evils, and you fill paradise—not the true paradise, but your paradise—with labors, pains, errors, groans, tears, and mourning, even if no one had sinned. If you do not dare to do this, lest you be laughed at even by infants themselves and be judged by the rod to require correction, the Manichaean concludes against you that these evils—which you do not wish to be derived from a corrupted good nature—come from a mixture with evil, which he says is a nature coeternal with and contrary to God.

Thus, when you try to become more distant from the Manichaean, you make yourself his accomplice.

[Col. 1510]

## VI. JULIAN

Now, with the same conclusion but a different beginning, they hurl their weapons of accusation against God himself. For the Manichaean says that the good God does not make evil, but adds that he assigns souls to everlasting fire on account of natural crimes. This is a clear sign of savagery; and thus, by the conclusion of his position, he pollutes with manifest injustice the one whom he had called good.

Augustine, moreover, as though trusting in the patron to whom he is writing, with even greater boldness despises the teacher’s hesitation. He does not hesitate to begin from the point at which the Manichaean arrives, and he declares that God makes and creates evil—that is, sin—although it is clear that this is incompatible with the God whom the faith of Catholics worships.

Let this above all be fixed in the reader’s mind: no greater reason for conflict has ever fallen upon any of the faithful than has fallen upon us; and whoever considers nature itself to be the necessity of crime has no fellowship in the worship of the God of Christians. Since this has frequently been impressed upon us—the usefulness of the principal argument having required repetition—let us now come to an examination of the first human beings, in whose condemnation the Numidian, as though armed with a small shield, confronts our battle line.

## AUGUSTINE

I would think that you do not know what the Manichaean says about the mixture of good and evil substance, unless I knew that you had read what we wrote against that very error. For, thinking that certain testimonies which I brought forward were directed against me, you cited them from the book in which I refuted their opinion concerning two souls established in the human being, one of which was good and the other evil (*On Two Souls*, section 15).

The Manichaean therefore maintains that two souls—or spirits or minds—exist in one human being: one proper to the flesh, evil by nature not through an accidental vice but coeternal with God; the other good by nature, as though a part of God, but polluted by mixture with that evil nature.

[Note: [Col. 1510] An old Codex Portarum reads: “an evil nature, the other a good nature.”]

From this he wishes it to follow that the flesh desires against the spirit, which is evidently good, through its own evil soul, so that it may hold the spirit entangled; while the spirit desires against the flesh so that it may be freed from that mixture. If it cannot achieve this even in the final conflagration of the world, he says that it will then be fastened to the mass of darkness and held in such punishment forever.

Therefore, contrary to what you say, the Manichaean’s God does not “assign souls to everlasting fire on account of natural crimes.” Rather, the souls, good by nature, are assigned to the mass of darkness because of their mixture with another evil nature—a mixture which that god himself brought about—and those whom he cannot free from it are not confined in everlasting fire, since Manichaeus believes in no everlasting fire, but, as I have said, are fastened to the everlasting mass of darkness in which the mind of darkness will be enclosed.

The catholic faith, however, which you abandoned in order to establish a novel sect—not, as you suppose or pretend, as an opponent of the Manichaeans, but rather as their helper—when it hears or reads the Apostle saying, “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh; for these oppose one another, so that you do not do the things you wish” (Galatians 5:17), does not understand two natures, one good and one evil, eternally opposed to each other and later mixed together, as the heretic Manichaeus supposes.

Rather, as the catholic teacher Ambrose recognizes (*Book 7 on Luke*, 12:53), this discord between flesh and spirit has passed into nature from the transgression of the first human being. Thus it is not understood to be the nature of the human being originally instituted, but a punishment changed into nature.

This faith is not the Numidian small shield with which, as though joking, you mock us. It is the truthful shield with which, as the Apostle exhorts, we extinguish all the flaming arrows of the evil one (Ephesians 6:16).

This shield was being used when Cyprian the Carthaginian, already armed and advancing against you who were to come, confronted you—not indeed a Numidian, but nevertheless that Carthaginian whose name your empty loquacity again uses to attack us.

Armed with this shield, that Carthaginian said in his book *On the Lord’s Prayer* that, when we say, “Your will be done on earth as it is in heaven” (Matthew 6:10), we are praying that, with God’s help, harmony may be established between these two things, namely, flesh and spirit.

There the excellent soldier of Christ extinguishes the flaming arrows of the evil one cast both by the Manichaeans and by you.

[Note: [Col. 1511] Vignierius reads: “he extinguishes the flaming arrows of the evil one,” omitting “arrows,” which has been restored from the manuscripts.]

All heretics serve that evil one, and you think that his camp should be enlarged by your enlistment.

By seeking harmony between spirit and flesh, Cyprian teaches against the Manichaeans that both natures of which we consist are good, if the evil of discord is healed by divine mercy. But he resists you, because you call good the concupiscence of the flesh, whose hostility produces the discord that he asks to be healed.

[Note: [Col. 1511] The manuscripts read “good” (*bonum*).] This discord arises when we act well, so that, by the spirit desiring against it, we resist the hostile concupiscence of the flesh.

For if we consent, the harmony of spirit with flesh is not desirable but blameworthy, or even condemnable. He also resists you because you attribute to free will what he understands must be requested from God in order that it may occur in a human being.

[Note: [Col. 1511] The printed editions read: “he also resists you, because by free will”; they omit “he is” and “you attribute,” which have been restored from the manuscripts.]

But you, who ignorantly object to me that I say God creates sin, resist the Manichaean who says that, in the discord between flesh and spirit, two mutually opposed natures, one evil and one good, appear.

There is one answer by which this plague can be defeated: namely, that this discord passed into our nature through the transgression of the first human being. By denying this, you strive to make the Manichaeans prevail, and you make it sufficiently clear that you are a false opponent of the Manichaeans and a genuine helper.

### VII. JUL.

For throughout all his writings he insists that Adam and Eve were created by God only good—that is, not subjected to any natural crime—and that they sinned by free will, but so gravely that all God’s institutions in their nature were overthrown. “For,” he says, “the devil implanted that sin, much greater and more profound than the sins known to human beings. Hence, through that great sin of the first man, our nature there being changed for the worse, it not only became sinful, but also generates sinners; and yet the very sickness by which the power of living well perished is not nature but vice. Therefore that sin, which changed the human being himself for the worse in paradise, because it is far greater than we can judge, is drawn from everyone who is born” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 2, §§57–58). Behold how plainly he has explained what he thought: Those first human beings had a good nature, but they committed a sin so monstrous and immeasurable that they destroyed the virtue of living well, extinguished the light of free choice, and made a necessity of sinning thereafter—so that no one born from their stock could strive for the adornments of virtue, avoid vices, and attain possession of holiness.

### AUG.

You may think that you are saying something to yourself, or even to your Pelagian associates, when, having abandoned divine authority, you boast in human vanity and oppose and obstruct the truth of the holy Scriptures with the arguments of your heart. For if you attended, with a Christian and Catholic mind, to what the Apostle says, “The body indeed is dead because of sin,” you would surely understand that the first man sinned so greatly that, through that sin, not merely the nature of one man but that of the entire human race was changed and fell from the possibility of immortality into the necessity of death. Thus even those who turn to God through the one mediator of God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus, do not immediately receive bodily immortality; rather, they are promised that they will receive it afterward through the Spirit of God by whom they are now indwelt. [Col. 1512]

[Textual note: Vignierius reads “so that it”; following the Portarum manuscript, the text reads “so that even.”]

The same apostle explains this in the same passage as follows: “If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him. But if Christ is in you, the body indeed is dead because of sin, but the spirit is life because of righteousness. If the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in you” (Romans 8:9–11).

The body, then, is dead because of sin, since it bears the necessity of death even in the living. But what sin, if not that of the first man? For through the righteousness of the second man, that is, Christ, blessed life will come to that same body which is now called dead. Hence Christ is also called the second man and the second Adam. Although we see so many generations of human beings to have passed between Adam, the man who was made, and Christ, the man who was born, and although in their sequence no one could be called the second man except Cain, nevertheless, because the first death of the body occurred on account of Adam’s sin, in which this age runs its course, while the second life of the body will occur on account of Christ’s righteousness—and has already occurred in Christ’s flesh, in which the age to come will endure—therefore the one is called the first Adam or man, and the other the second.

And you refuse to understand that his sin was so great that it propagated an age of mortals, while Christ’s righteousness was so great that it propagated an age of immortals? Yet you object to me the greatness of the first man’s sin, which became the cause of so great an evil for all human beings, as though I alone or the first had said this.

Listen to John of Constantinople, a priest of eminent glory [Col. 1513]: “Adam,” he says, “committed that great sin and condemned the whole human race in common” (*Letter to Olympias*). Listen also to what he says in the raising of Lazarus, so that you may understand that bodily death too came from that great sin: “Christ wept because the devil had made mortal those who could have been immortal” (*Homily on the Raising of Lazarus*).

Where, I ask you, did the devil make all human beings mortal, except in the one to whom he inflicted so great a sin of transgression that the human race was cast from the blessedness of paradise into the misery that we see and feel? This is attested not only by bodily death, but also by the many and great evils of the soul itself, which the corruptible body weighs down, and by the heavy yoke upon the children of Adam from the day they leave their mother’s womb. Under this yoke is also what is read in the Psalm: “Every living human being is altogether vanity” (Psalm 38:6).

Since you are unwilling to attribute these evils to that great sin of the first man, what are you doing except bringing them—according to your view—into the paradise of his great happiness, as though they too would have existed there if no one had sinned, while the Manichaeans attribute them to the race of darkness? They are not confounded because you accuse them, but emboldened because you help them—unless, together with you, they are struck down as though pierced by the invincible sword of Catholic truth.

Yet we do not say, as you insinuate, “It is impossible for anyone born from the stock of the first human beings to strive for the adornments of virtue.” Many do strive, in those in whom God works both the willing and the doing (Philippians 2:13); and, with his help, they strive without failing to attain the fruit. But if the corruptible body did not weigh down the soul, they would not have to strive. Accordingly, in paradise—if no one had sinned and there were no heavy yoke upon the children of Adam—they would have obeyed their God easily and happily, without striving.

### VIII. JUL.

He therefore thinks that he can claim the support of those first human beings—that is, of only two—in order to maintain the distinction between the Manichaeans and the Traducianists. There is hardly anything that could be encountered as more extravagant—or, perhaps, more insane—or more shameless than this opinion. [Textual note: Perhaps “more insane” (*amentius*) instead of “more extravagant” (*eminentius*).] “The freedom of choice,” he says, “after it began to make use of itself, lost its powers.”

And so, as we turn to him and examine everything step by step, let us see: You admit, do you not, that the first man was made with free choice and created good by God, polluted by no stain of sin from the beginning; but that he afterward voluntarily transgressed his harmless condition and imposed upon all who would arise from him an unavoidable compulsion to sin. This is certainly your doctrine, which we prove to have been drawn from the mire of Manichaeus, who thinks that Adam’s nature itself, although formed from the flower of the first substance and much better than those who followed, was nevertheless naturally evil.

### AUG.

What has been said above sufficiently indicates both our Catholic doctrine and your heretical doctrine concerning the first human beings and their descendants: the former were created upright by God, while the latter, although produced by the same Creator, nevertheless arose from a nature corrupted by sin and with the bond of sin, and by the condition of their origin were cast down from the salvation in which the human being [Col. 1514] was first made into the sickness of corruption and the necessity of death.

For this reason they need the help of a Savior, who first saves them by the remission of all sins and afterward by the healing of all sicknesses (Psalm 102:3). [Textual note: The manuscripts read “saves” (*salvos facit*); printed editions read “saved” (*fecit*).] To those already baptized and to those who had already received the Holy Spirit the Apostle said: “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh; for these are opposed to one another, so that you do not do the things you wish” (Galatians 5:17).

You deny that free choice lost its powers by sinning—that is, by using itself badly. What will you answer when you hear that, while the flesh desires [Textual note: Vignierius reads “in desiring”; the manuscripts read “while desiring.”] against the spirit, the faithful do not do the things they wish; that even those whose sins have been forgiven in Baptism do not do the things they wish; that those whom the Apostle says received the Holy Spirit through hearing with faith do not do the things they wish (Galatians 3:2); and, finally, that those whom the same teacher of the Gentiles says were called to freedom do not do the things they wish through free choice (Galatians 5:13)?

Next, as so eloquent a defender of desire—as though an outstanding advocate—you dare, in support of your position, to assert that the desire of the flesh, by which it desires against the spirit, existed even in paradise before sin. Do you not see that you are thereby compelled to say that even then free choice was not effective in those first human beings? For if the flesh was even then desiring against the spirit, they certainly were not doing the things they wished.

But since, by free choice—which then possessed entirely sound powers—they undoubtedly did what they wished, that is, they served the divine law not only without any impossibility but also without any difficulty, your position about the flesh desiring against the spirit did not exist there. Through that condition, human beings who have already turned to God through faith, have already been baptized and sanctified, and have been called to freedom, fail to do what they wish in extinguishing vicious pleasure.

That most truthful statement, therefore, which the Catholic faith uttered through Bishop Ambrose, remains true: this vice, by which the flesh desires against the spirit, was turned into our nature through the transgression of the first man (*Book 7 on Luke* 12:53). By this unavoidable and unconquerable weapon of truth both the Manichaean and you are cut down.

For in this matter both of you are utterly mistaken—see [Textual note: An old Claromontanus codex reads “see” (*videre*) for “consider” (*videto*).] which of you is worse: you, because you contend that this pestilence is not an evil; he, because he acknowledges that it is an evil but does not know where it comes from, and, deprived of the Catholic faith, constructs a fable full of lies and indecencies about the mingling of two natures, namely, the good and the evil.

Our righteousness, then, at present is that, having been justified by faith, we have peace with God (Romans 5:1). Against the desire of the flesh that attacks us, however, we must fight, with the spirit resisting through the help of God. [Textual note: The manuscripts read “with the spirit resisting” (*repugnante spiritu*); printed editions read “we resisting” (*repugnantes*).]

The righteousness of this life, therefore, is not to have no vice, but to diminish vices by refusing to consent to them and, by resisting them, to live temperately, justly, and piously. To have no vice against which we must resist belongs to the life to come, which is the reward of the present life rightly conducted: our healing, not—as the Manichaean, whose helper you are, foolishly claims—through the separation of another nature. [Col. 1515]

Behold, our doctrine was not “drawn from the mire of Manichaeus,” as you accuse us. By this doctrine, unless you have lost all understanding, you see the Manichaean himself overthrown together with you.

### IX. JUL.

Our first task, then, in the present matter is to expose the dullness of your understanding; afterward we must show—as we have often already done—that you do not withdraw even one foot from the Manichaeans’ dens and merit-schemes.

To begin with, it is utterly insane to suppose that the matter of choice was mingled with the seeds and that the functions of wills grew into the conceptions, so that, once the clearest and broadest distinction between natures and dispositions had been removed, the will of the first human beings could be said to have been engendered in their descendants.

Everything in the world resists this error. For never have the sons of eloquent men brought the beauty of their father’s art with them in their cries, nor have the offspring of actors stretched out their hands to words with trained movements; nor have the sons of warriors asked the people for a trumpet. It would be possible to pursue all examples of this kind—examples that speak more clearly than thunder.

The whole universe will answer that the boundaries of nature are one thing and those of the will another, and that the conditions of seeds cannot be accessible to the desires of dispositions. [Textual note: Printed editions read “first”; the manuscripts correct this to “accessible” (*pervias*).]

It therefore appeared extremely foolish, indeed the product of desperate stupidity, to believe [Textual note: Printed editions read “and the product of stupidity appeared”; the Portarum codex reads “and it appeared the product of desperate [literally, ‘cast-off’] stupidity.”] that something you admit was voluntary had been turned into nature.

But this other claim is far, far more deformed: you say that the possibility of acting was consumed at the beginning of the act—that is, that free choice, which is nothing other than the possibility of sinning and not sinning [Textual note: The words “and not sinning” were omitted in printed editions and restored from the manuscripts.], subject to the violence of neither side but possessing the power to stand of its own choice on whichever side it wishes, lost the ability to do both as soon as it began to will one of them.

### AUG.

Do you truly not see that, unknowingly but nevertheless persistently, you are assisting Manichaeus through this inflated and frothy din of your loquacity?

Suppose that, when he asks us where evil comes from—a question by which uneducated minds are accustomed to be troubled—we answered that it arose from the free will of a rational creature. He would then say: “From where, then, are all these many evils that occur not to those who are already born and have begun to use their will with advancing age, but with which all or most people are born?”

For the desire of the flesh is congenitally present in everyone—the desire by which the flesh desires against the spirit, even in one instructed in upright faith and the teaching of piety. A certain slowness of mind is also congenitally present in everyone, so that even those called talented learn whatever arts they learn, including those called liberal arts, or attain fuller knowledge of religion, not without some laborious hardship. Some are born with bodies that are deformed and sometimes monstrous; many are forgetful; many are slow and dull in understanding; many are angry; many lustful; and some are born altogether witless and foolish. [Col. 1516]

What else could the Catholic faith answer except that all these evils arose, after the human being sinned and was expelled from paradise—that is, from the place of happiness—from a nature corrupted by the contagion of sin? For if no one had sinned, neither such vices nor any others would have arisen in paradise.

When he heard this, the Manichaean would recite to us your words, if he had them, in which you say that it is “utterly insane to suppose that the matter of choice was mingled with the seeds and that the functions of wills grew into conceptions.” He would also recite whatever else you added in this vein, attempting to prove it from the fact that the sons of eloquent men are not born eloquent, nor actors’ sons actors, nor warriors’ sons warriors.

The Manichaean uses [Textual note: Perhaps “may use” (*utatur*) rather than “uses” (*utitur*).] this assistance from you to attack what we say: that the human nature of the first man was corrupted by sin, even in his descendants [Textual note: The manuscripts read “even in his descendants”; Vignierius reads “even into his descendants.”], who were in him by seminal descent when he sinned in that great transgression. Once he has attacked this, he introduces a mingling of his two natures [Textual note: The Portarum codex reads “of two natures, and,” omitting “his.”] and asserts that, from the mingling, those evils with which human beings are born arise from the evil nature.

But in order to resist me, you are compelled to say something utterly absurd and detestable: namely, that these evils of those being born would have arisen even in paradise if no one had sinned.

Here the Manichaean will press you to say where they would have arisen from. When, forced into great straits, you say that these evils would have arisen from the very natures of those being born, without any merit of the will, you will certainly be accusing the Creator. To avoid doing this, you will flee to the merits of evil wills.

But he will ask: “Whose wills? For there is no will belonging to seeds or to newborn infants.”

What, then, will remain except that, if you wish to escape or overcome the Manichaean, you understand with us that, in the hidden recesses of origins, the seeds of those being born are also secretly entangled, and [Textual note: The conjunction “and” is supplied on the authority of the Portarum manuscript.] with the merits arising from the evil will of their begetters? Yet the sin of the first man was so great that it condemned the whole human race in common, to use the words of Saint John (Chrysostom, *Letter to Olympias*).

From this it follows that these evils would not have arisen if no one had sinned, nor could they have existed in paradise, since those who had sinned left it before they begot children.

By this Catholic doctrine, your attempt to introduce the analogy of the arts is nullified. You reminded us that no one is born with his father’s art. But it is one thing to sin in morals, by which one lives rightly—something that is customarily punished either by laws or by divine judgment—and another to sin in the arts, whether honorable or disgraceful, where something done contrary to an art is called a fault.

Such faults are not condemned by divine law or punished with severity; rather, they are condemned by the human beings whose judgments govern these matters, especially by teachers of those arts when they instruct children, under fear or pain of punishment.

Nevertheless, in this matter we must consider that, if something were taught in paradise that would have been useful for that life to know, the blessed nature would attain it without any labor [Col. 1517] or pain, either with God teaching it or by its own power.

Who, then, does not understand that in this life even the torments of learners belong to the miseries of this age, which was propagated from one person for condemnation (Romans 5:16)? Here too there is this misery: wretched minds do not desire what is good; or, even when the will has already been prepared by the Lord (Proverbs 8, according to the Septuagint), the person living in this age still cries out: “To will lies near me, but to accomplish the good I do not find” (Romans 7:18).

If you hold fast to this, you will conquer the Manichaeans. But because you do not hold fast to it, this faith conquers both of you.

### X. JUL.

Let what we have said now be established: your doctrine differs in no respect from that of the Manichaeans.

There is no doubt that Adam’s nature itself was made most evil if it was formed under this condition: that it possessed a necessity of evil but not of good. That is, even if the crime had been conceived by the will, it would nevertheless become natural in that nature, while goodness would not become natural. It is therefore falsely said that the person sinned by will when he was burdened by the prejudice of a most wicked condition.

It is evident how bound [Textual note: The manuscripts read “bound” (*vinctus*); another reading is “joined” (*junctus*).] to evil he was, who was destined to be filled with inseparable crime. For what substance could you find worse than one that was made so that it could fall into iniquity but could not withdraw from iniquity?

If it had endured such violence on the side of good, and had lost free choice, it would nevertheless have had no one to accuse as its author, since no one would raise a question against him concerning the resources of benevolence. But when such domination is placed on the side of evil, it accuses no one more than the very creator of the human being. And such a God is caressed by the empty flattery of his accusers—that is, of you—although he is proved to be a friend of wickedness by the deformity of his creation.

For who could be persuaded that the first man did not intend crimes, if God deprived him of the possibility of correction; if he affected him with so depraved a mind that his error could not displease him; if he gave him no return to honesty; if he did not make him better after experience; and, lest he should ever feel a desire to recover goodness, removed from him the very possibility of correction?

Plainly, if his condition was such that, so long as he remained in this life, he lost the power of correcting virtue through a single fall, he was instituted for no other reason than that he might fall. Indeed, it is more truly said that he did not fall but always lay fallen, since, as far as morals are concerned, he is not permitted to rise.

What sort of freedom, then, is that which is believed to have been bestowed upon him earlier, if, from two contrary qualities, he necessarily acquired the worse and received the better only from the mutable—and if, once seized by the tyranny of crime, he was stripped of the possibility of repentance?

The condition of the first man was therefore most dreadful from the beginning, if he was so unhappily established by God that, destined to rush into crime, he was bound by a perpetual necessity of sinning. [Textual note: The Portarum codex reads “what he did not will” (*noluit*) for “what he willed” (*voluit*) in the preceding sentence.]

### AUG.

You are saying things which, if you do not neglect to consider them—even when we at least admonish you—you might blush at yourself, shameless though you are.

Why do you not attend to this? If that nature is made most evil which falls into evil through an unjust will but cannot return to good through an unjust punishment, then not merely the human nature that you cast before us [Col. 1518] but the angelic nature also was made most evil.

Unless perhaps you say that even the devil, having fallen from the good by his will, will return to the good he abandoned whenever and if he wishes—and thus restore to us the error of Origen.

If you do not say this, correct what you imprudently said when admonished, and confess that the nature was created good which fell into the evil it made, compelled by no necessity but collapsing through its own will.

It can be recalled to the good it abandoned only by the grace of God, not by the will of freedom [Textual note: Printed editions read “not in the will of freedom”; “in” is absent from the manuscripts.], which it deservedly lost through iniquity.

Another person, erring just as you do, could say: “What substance could I find worse than one made so that it could go into eternal punishment but could not return from it?” Certainly almighty God can rescue whomever he wishes from punishment; but he cannot lie, having threatened that he would not do this when he called that punishment eternal.

But so that you may think sensibly rather than foolishly about this matter, your own definition deceives you—the definition by which, in your earlier exposition [Textual note: The manuscripts read “exposition” (*prosecutione*); Vignierius reads “persecution.”], to which we have already responded, you defined free choice, as you often do elsewhere.

For you said: “Free choice is nothing other than the possibility of sinning and not sinning.”

By this definition you first deprived God himself of free choice, although you do not deny—and often say, truly—that he cannot sin. Then the saints themselves in his kingdom will lose free choice, where they will be unable to sin.

Here, however, you must be reminded what you ought to think about the matter now under discussion: namely, that punishment and reward are contrary to one another, and that two other contraries adhere to these contraries. Thus [Textual note: Vignierius reads “if”; the manuscripts read “thus” (*sic*).], in punishment there is the inability to act rightly, just as in reward there will be the inability to sin.

Attend to the Scriptures, from which you pitiably wander away and are tossed about like a storm-driven traveler by your wandering, windy loquacity. See how it is said: “What Israel sought, it did not obtain; but the election obtained it. The rest were blinded, as it is written: ‘God gave them a spirit of compunction, eyes so that they would not see, and ears so that they would not hear, to this very day.’” And David says: “Let their table become a snare, and a trap, and a stumbling block, and a recompense for them; let their eyes [Textual note: Printed editions read “hearts”; the Portarum codex reads “eyes,” as does the Apostle.] be darkened so that they may not see, and keep their back always bent” (Romans 11:7–10).

Consider also what is said in the Gospel: “For this reason they could not believe, because Isaiah said again: ‘He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, so that they may not see with their eyes, understand with their heart, turn, and I heal them’” (John 12:39–40).

I have recalled these passages so that, if you can, you may understand that it certainly happens through a just punishment that people do not believe with a blinded heart, while through mercy they believe with free will.

For who does not know that no one believes except by the free choice of the will? Yet the will is prepared by the Lord, and no one is completely rescued from the evil slavery deserved by his own merits unless the Lord prepares him through gratuitous grace.

If God did not make willing people out of unwilling people [Col. 1519], we certainly would not pray for those who do not wish to believe, asking that they may wish to do so. The Apostle showed that he did this for the Jews when he said: “Brothers, the good will of my heart and my prayer to God for them is for salvation” (Romans 10:1).

They could not attain this salvation unless they believed willingly. Therefore blessed Paul prayed that they might will it.

Bishop Cyprian also understands the words in the Lord’s Prayer, “Your will be done, as in heaven so on earth” (Matthew 6:10), in this way: we have been instructed to pray for our unbelieving enemies, so that, just as we believe—we who are already heaven, bearing the image of the heavenly man—so they too may believe, who are earth because they bear only the image of the earthly man (*On the Lord’s Prayer*).

### XI. JUL.

The alliance between you and the Manichaeans plainly endures: they by explicit profession, you by argument, both assert that the nature of the first man was evil.

Although this entire position is full of absurdities and lies—as I set aside the legions of the saints and take Abel as the first example of righteousness after Adam’s sin [Textual note: The manuscripts read “take up” (*arripiamus*); Vignierius reads “receive” (*accipiamus*).]—it is refuted by Abel’s remarkable holiness. Born from sinners, he showed by the outcome of his virtue itself that he had not been deprived of the power to live well.

Nevertheless, let us set these matters aside and press the opinions of the Traducianist faction.

What, then, do you suppose free choice was like when it was bestowed upon the first human beings? Certainly it enabled their minds to alternate between movements, either to do evil or to withdraw from evil, either to abandon or to preserve righteousness.

There would therefore have been no will to sin unless the possibility of willing had preceded it.

After they began to use this by their own will—that is, by a movement of the mind compelled by nothing—you say that they lost free choice. [Textual note: Morel, *Elementa critica*, p. 94, reads: “After these [namely the first parents mentioned above] began to use it by their own will, that is, with no movement of mind compelling them, you say that they lost free choice.”] What could be imagined more insane than this?

To keep the force of your argument clearly expressed, you say that the thing perished because of the will which was given for no other reason than the will. For sin is nothing other than an evil will, while freedom was given for this sole purpose: not to compel the will, but to permit it to arise.

Yet you say that this freedom [Textual note: The Portarum codex reads “this freedom”; other manuscripts and printed editions read “your freedom.”] lost its own condition through the operation of the will, so that it is believed to have perished through the very thing by which it alone is shown to be active.

An evil will, then, is not a fruit but a testimony of freedom. Freedom is nothing other than the possibility of good and evil, but voluntarily.

How, then, could it perish through the very thing by which it reveals that it was established, when an evil will and a good will are not destructions but proclamations of freedom?

Accordingly, just as duties and distinctions differ, so does your opinion differ from the account of free choice, whose destruction you think is derived from its own praises.

What new or unexpected thing happened from the human being’s sinning [Textual note: The manuscripts read “what unexpected thing from one sinning”; the printed text reads “what unexpected thing when one sinned.”], through which God’s institutions were overthrown? The human being was made capable of sinning and not sinning. [Col. 1520] When he sinned, he did what he ought not to have done, but nevertheless could do. Through what, then, would he lose that capacity which had been established for this purpose: that he might be able to will and able not to will what he willed?

### AUG.

You repeat the same things again and again. Anyone who reads what I have already said above will see that I have responded to them.

But since you persist and insist that the freedom to act well or badly cannot perish through its own bad use, let blessed Pope Innocent, bishop of the Roman Church, answer you. In his reply concerning your case to the African episcopal councils, he says:

“Once having possessed free choice, while using his goods too carelessly, he fell and was plunged into the depths of transgression; thereafter he found no way by which he could rise. Deceived forever in his freedom, he would have remained beneath the oppression of this ruin [Textual note: The manuscripts read *oppressu*; Vignierius reads *oppressus*.], unless the coming of Christ had, by his grace, raised him up” (*Letter 181 among Augustine’s letters*, §7).

Do you see what [Textual note: Printed editions read “does”; corrected from the Portarum manuscript to “teaches” (*sapiat*).] the Catholic faith teaches through its minister? Do you see that the human being possessed the possibility of standing and falling in such a way that, if he fell, he would not rise by the same possibility by which he had fallen—the punishment, namely, following the guilt?

For this reason Christ’s grace, for which you are miserably ungrateful, came to raise up the one who was lying fallen. [Textual note: The manuscripts read “in your case”; Vignierius reads “in our case.”]

In another letter, which he wrote concerning you to the Numidians, he says: “Therefore they attempt to take away the grace of God, which we must seek even after the freedom of our original state has been restored to us” (*Letter 182 among Augustine’s letters*, §4).

You hear that freedom is restored, yet you insist that it did not perish. Content with human will, you do not seek the divine grace that our freedom understands to be necessary even after it has been restored to its original condition.

I ask you, then, whether the freedom of the person who says, “I do not do what I want, but I do what I hate,” and, “To will lies near me, but to accomplish the good I do not find” (Romans 7:15, 18), has already been restored to its original state—and whether the freedom of those to whom it is said, “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh, so that you do not do the things you wish” (Galatians 5:17), has been restored.

I suppose you are not so foolish as to say that these people possess the freedom of the original state. Yet if they had none of it, they could not even will what is holy, just, and good.

There are people whom it delights to sin so much that they do not wish for, and hate, righteousness. No one can even will righteousness unless the will is prepared by the Lord, so that the desire of the will precedes the accomplishment of righteousness and the realization of power gradually follows—more quickly in some, more slowly in others, each according to what the Lord has given.

He alone can restore a human being’s salvation, increase what has already been lost, and also grant this: that the person can no longer perish.

Among those who have been set free is the holy Abel, whom you say was not deprived of the power to live well. He certainly was not deprived of it—but only after he began to possess it. Before that, who is clean from defilement? Not even an infant, whose life upon earth is but one day (Job 14:4, according to the Septuagint).

All who are redeemed, therefore, are redeemed by him who came to seek what was lost; even before he came in the flesh, he redeemed them through the very faith by which it was believed that he would come. [Col. 1521]

They are redeemed into the freedom of everlasting blessedness, where they can no longer serve sin.

For if, as you say [Textual note: Vignierius reads “if you say”; the manuscripts read “if, as you say.”], only the voluntary possibility of good and evil is freedom, then God does not have freedom, since there is no possibility of sinning in him.

But if we seek the free choice that is innate in the human being and wholly incapable of being lost, it is that by which all human beings wish to be happy—even those who do not wish for the things that lead to happiness.

## XII. JULIAN

Then, to follow the steep consequences of your opinion [Note: [Col. 1521] So the Port. manuscript; Vignierius has *prorupta* (“bursting forth”).], you argue that free choice was so ordered that, as a deserved consequence of the will, it would lose its power and thereafter endure the necessity of the condition it had chosen. So listen to what we reply. Do you think that man was created in such a way that he would suffer the necessity of the chosen condition in either direction—that is, so that, if he had willed the good, he could no longer sin, and if he had chosen evil, he could no longer amend his ways? Or do you think that only the evil direction was to be followed by necessity, while nothing of the sort would occur in the good direction, which would always remain exposed to the dangers of change?

Choose either of these two alternatives. If you say that a nature was made which would suffer necessity only in the case of evil, no doubt will remain that it must be defined as utterly wretched, since it is subjected only to the violence of the worse direction. It would also be proved that Adam was of an evil nature, and no shadow of voluntary action would remain under which you could conceal the deed. But if you acknowledge that the same thing would also have followed in the case of good—that is, that if he had willed the good, he could no longer sin—I ask: Why, then, did he sin? Why did he not suffer any necessity of the good, so that he might appear impenetrable to the devil’s snares, since he is found to have been obedient to God for some time before he sinned?

For he did not immediately, as soon as clay was warmed by the entrance of the soul, blaze up into a desire for an evil will. On the contrary, we read that, after he had been transferred to cultivate and guard paradise, he received a command from God to eat of all the fruits, but obediently to abstain from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. Before, therefore, a body was formed from his side for his wife, he remained obedient to the command, an innocent cultivator [Note: [Col. 1521] So the manuscripts. The printed editions instead have “guardian.”] of the pleasant land; afterward, he obtained a helper like himself as a companion.

The faith of Scripture has indeed impressed these distinctions of time upon us. Once he saw that a woman had been prepared for him, he served God’s command with such diligent devotion that he even disclosed to the woman the law he had received. Thus he was not merely the guardian of the divine command but also its preacher: he taught Eve both the reverence due to the one who commanded, the nature of the service required, and the reason for fear.

That is why the woman too, when she confronted the attacking devil, carefully resisted him. Although God had commanded her nothing, she rejected the serpent’s first lies and said that it was not abstinence from all the trees, as he had falsely claimed, but that, with permission to enjoy the abundance of everything else, caution regarding only one little tree had been commanded, and that the threat of death had been set before them—a threat that would rightly follow transgressors. [Col. 1522] [Note: [Col. 1522] Perhaps *quae* (“which”), rather than *qui*.]

It is therefore not evident that Adam guarded the command for only a short time; Eve too is shown to have had a devoted concern, though she fell through her love of knowledge and divinity. Why, then, did that righteousness and devotion—which flourished in Adam for a long time and in Eve for some time—not remove the possibility of sinning, so that the necessity of the good might make them impenetrable to criminal suggestions?

They were obedient for as long as they wished, yet by the merit of their devotion they did not lose the capacity to transgress. In the end they fell (Genesis II–III). Therefore, after they had sinned, it is equally clear that they could not have lost the power of correction. And so, here too, as everywhere else, you have completely lost everything you had fabricated: that sin of the first human beings neither imposed the necessity of any crimes nor passed into nature, just as the righteousness that preceded it neither imposed the necessity of virtues nor claimed for itself the pathways of reproduction.

## AUGUSTINE

Everything you have said at such length and with such a tangle of words can be stated briefly as follows. You ask: Why did Adam, by acting badly, lose the ability to act well, while, by previously acting well, he did not lose the ability to sin? You want it to be understood that, if this is so, man was made not of a good but of an evil nature, in which an evil action had more power to prevent him from acting well than a good action had to prevent him from acting badly.

In the same way, you could say that man was created with evil eyes, because when he extinguishes them, he becomes unable to see, whereas by seeing he does not become unable to extinguish them. Or you could say that the whole human body was badly constituted, because it lies within a person’s power to kill himself but not within his power to raise himself from the dead; through death it comes about that he cannot bring himself back to life, while through life it does not come about that he cannot kill himself.

If you do not say this, because you see how absurd it is, why do you say that God created human nature badly, if an evil will made man unable to return to the good, although a good will did not make him unable to go over to evil? For he was created with free choice in such a way that, if he wished, he could refrain from sinning—not in such a way that, if he wished, he could sin with impunity.

What, then, is surprising if, when he transgressed—that is, when by corruption he changed the uprightness in which he had been made—the inability to act rightly followed as a punishment? As long as he remained in that same uprightness, in which he could refrain from sinning, he did not therefore receive something greater—namely, the inability to sin—because he did not choose to remain in what he had received all the way to the end of his reward.

What the saints will receive, who in the future age will possess spiritual bodies, Adam would have received without the intervention of death: ascending from the condition in which he could avoid death to that in which he could not die, and ascending from the condition in which he could avoid sin to that in which he could not sin. For he had been made not in a spiritual body but in an animal body, although, had he not sinned, he would by no means have died. As the Apostle says: “Not first what is spiritual, but what is animal; afterward, what is spiritual” [Col. 1523] (1 Corinthians XV, 46).

Hence blessed Ambrose says in *On Paradise* that Adam was made in the shadow of life, from which he could fall—not by necessity but by will. Had he remained in it, he would have received that life of which the shadow was a figure, the life that the saints will receive and from which they will be entirely unable to fall.

He understands this mortality, in which the present age runs its course, conversely as the shadow of death. But the death of which this is the shadow he identifies as the death called the second death (Revelation XX, 6), from which no one, once he has entered it, will return. Those who are freed from this shadow of death are prepared not to return to the shadow of life but to proceed to that life from which no one can ever depart.

Adam himself will also be there, because it is rightly believed that, at the Lord’s coming and descent into the underworld, he was already released from the bonds of hell, so that the first creation of God, who had no human parent but only God as creator, and the first father of Christ according to the flesh, would not remain any longer in those bonds and would not perish in eternal punishment.

But where judgment exalts mercy [Note: [Col. 1523] The manuscripts Clar. and Mar. have *superexaltatur* (“is exalted above”); Port. has *superexsulat* (“is banished above”).] (James II, 13), merits are not to be considered, but grace. Its height is so great, so inscrutable and unsearchable, that, after the sentence was pronounced, “Unless someone is born again of water and the Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of God” (John III, 5), we sometimes see that faithful parents who have deserved well are not granted that their children should be in the kingdom of God with them. Unregenerate infants depart this life, although at times their own parents ardently desire it and the ministers of the sacraments eagerly hasten to it; yet the all-powerful and most merciful God does not delay their death even briefly, so that, born of Christian parents, they may depart hence reborn [Note: [Col. 1523] The printed editions have “may not depart.” The negating particle is removed on the authority of the manuscripts.] and not be lost to Christ’s kingdom and to their own parents; instead, before they are baptized, they expire.

At other times, to the infant children of unbelievers—even of those who blaspheme Christ’s grace itself—when, by God’s marvelous governance, they are brought into the hands of Christians, this grace is granted: they come into God’s kingdom, separated from their impious parents. If you are asked what kind of justice this is, you certainly do not find it in that dialectical and philosophical discourse in which you think you have argued most diligently about God’s justice. For “the Lord knows the thoughts of the wise, that they are futile” (Psalm XCIII, 11); and, hiding these things from the wise and prudent, he revealed them to little ones (Matthew XI, 25)—that is, to the humble, who place their confidence not in their own power but in the Lord. You either do not deign to be such a person at all, or not yet.

If, then, you ask where or when man is granted the inability to sin, seek the rewards of the saints, which they ought to receive after this life. But if you do not believe that the free choice of man, by which he could and ought to have acted rightly, failed through the evil of sin, at least attend to the one who says: “I do not do what I want, but I do what I hate.” You do not want him to be suffering from a corrupted origin, but from a prevailing evil habit; and thus you too admit that free choice can fail by using itself badly. Yet you do not want free choice in human nature to have been corrupted by so great a sin—one greater and worse than every evil habit—although you say that evil habit has such power in corrupting it that a man cries out that he wants to perfect the good but cannot.

The immutable freedom with which man is created and was created is the freedom of the will by which we all want to be blessed and cannot not want it. But this is not sufficient for anyone to be blessed, nor for him to live rightly in the way by which he may be blessed. For the immutable freedom of the will by which a person wants and is able to act well is not innate in man in the same way as that by which he wants to be blessed; everyone wants this, including those who do not want to act rightly.

## XIII. JULIAN

What, then, has been established? One of two things must be necessary: either you must confess that Adam was made of a good substance, that his nature was not destroyed by a voluntary condition, and abandon natural sin; or, if you maintain that he is, as you have hitherto believed, the cause of natural evils, you must declare him to be of the worst substance and to belong to your god—that is, to yours and Manichaeus’ god.

## AUGUSTINE

Our earlier reply shows that what you think has been established has not been established. For when the question between us was whether this freedom, together with which man was created, could be corrupted by the evil use of free choice, so that one who had lived badly would not be fit to live well unless healed by the power of grace, then—to omit the many other things said in that same reply—we find a man saying, with the highest authority of the divine Scriptures: “I do not do the good that I want, but the evil that I do not want, this I do.”

In these words it clearly appears that free choice has been corrupted by its own evil use. Before the sin by which man misused free choice, when he had been established in the happiness of paradise and with great facility for doing good [Note: [Col. 1524] The printed editions have *felicitate* (“happiness”). The Port. manuscript’s *facilitate* (“facility”) is preferable.], he could not have said this.

But you attribute this not to human nature corrupted in the first man but to the evil habit of each person. You say that, willingly but unable to overcome it because it prevails over him, and unable to find his freedom intact for perfecting the good, he is compelled to say these things—as though he suffered the force of evil habit as something insuperable, so that he asks to be freed from it by God’s grace unless nature has been weakened.

For the one who said these things, when he reached the point at which he says, “I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin which is in my members,” cried out: “Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Romans VII, 15, 23–25).

Interpret the “body of death” as you wish. Nevertheless, while free choice and nature had been weakened, he said this and desired to be freed by God’s grace from the body of death, [Col. 1525] where he did not do the good he wanted but did the evil he hated.

But you are defeated by a still clearer proof: that sin of the first man was so great that it was greater and worse than every violence of habit, since the evils of children are brought forward to you. Such evils certainly would not have existed in paradise if human nature had remained in that upright happiness in which it was made, so that it would not have been expelled from there.

To say nothing of such matters, which we have already discussed in several places, and to pass over not only uninstructed but also unteachable infancy: suppose that a boy received from his teacher something to commit to memory, wished to retain it but was unable to do so. If he could speak, would he not speak most truly by saying: “I see another law in my soul, warring against the law of my will and taking me captive under the law of the rod, which hangs over my members? Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death?”

“For the corruptible body weighs down the soul,” so that it cannot retain what memory wishes to hold. And who frees us from this corruptible body except the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord? This occurs either when, having been stripped of it and redeemed by Christ’s blood, the soul rests, or when this corruptible body puts on incorruption (1 Corinthians XV, 53), and, after the sufferings of the body, our mortal bodies—which died because of sin—are made alive through the Spirit of Christ dwelling in us.

Against this grace you defend free choice [Note: [Col. 1525] The Port. manuscript has *arbitrio* (“by free choice”), rather than *arbitrium* (“free choice”).] as an enslaved will to sin. But we are far from Manichaeus: in human nature, whether in adults or in infants, we confess both the defect and the physician.

## XIV. JULIAN

Thus far I have argued as the custom of our faith required. But, not content with this alone, I will deal with you courteously and deliberately assume a role that may appear to favor the opinion of your teacher. I will do this so that you may be compelled to attack Manichaeus, if you disagree with him.

For it will be regretted by this very fact that there is no cunning in our assertion, since the Traducianist [*Traducianus*] has found nothing with which he can resist Manichaeus. Thus it will become clear how great a conspiracy exists between you, and how you arrange everything through mutual concessions, when no quarrel could be stirred up between you.

Let the reader keep in mind, then, the purpose for which I have undertaken this course. I shall now speak in the language of the role we have assumed.

They are altogether mistaken who think that this bodily composition is suited to righteousness [Note: [Col. 1525] We restore *habilem* from the manuscripts.]. The base nature of flesh and blood resists every good pursuit. Whatever impulses arise through the allurements of the senses slide toward the disturbance, indeed the overthrow, of the mind. Cast down into this mud by I know not what misfortune, the mind loses its noble flashes in the mixture of filth.

The mind itself, insofar as it can, strives toward its proper place, that is, toward higher things; but it is afflicted by an earthly prison. Finally, when it wishes to soar toward chastity, it experiences the glue and birdlime of obscene pleasure arising from its scorched entrails.

Again, if it desires generosity and liberality, it is bound by the tightest shackles of greed, which is concealed under the appearance of frugality. [Col. 1526] But if it wishes to stand in some serene stability and unshaken constancy, it is immediately overwhelmed by the hail of fear and storms of grief; growing pale before every uncertainty, it is not allowed to remain master of its own judgment. Add to this the darkness of unknown things, by which it is surrounded amid filth.

What quality worthy of praise shall we suspect in that living creature which has neither vigilant eyes for choosing what is useful nor enough capacity, amid the storms of desires and dangers, to count its own shipwrecks?

Yet let no one claim that these things happened spontaneously to a substance that had been corrupted. The original constitution of the first human beings is found to have been subject to these sufferings. To establish this also by the testimony of Moses, whom Catholics venerate: the first human beings experienced the slaughterhouse of fear. The threat of danger terrified them if they did not obey; and, judging from the comparison of circumstances, we suppose that they were more fearful than their descendants, since they were tormented by a punishment not yet known to anyone.

Why would they be shaken by the threat of death if they did not know what harm death would bring? They were surely troubled only by suspicions of evils. In what tranquility, then, could that mind remain which so harsh a winter of fear disturbed?

Moreover, how profound was their ignorance, and how harsh the condition of enduring it, since they could not be freed from it except by transgression? For they would not acquire the knowledge of good and evil without undertaking a condemnable act.

“You will say,” he continues, “that innate desire also rendered this blind and suffering creature thus, being provoked both by the beauty and by the sweetness of the forbidden thing.” As though all this were insufficient to express the misery of that condition, it is exposed to assault by the higher nature.

Who, then, would be so foolish as to think that anything good existed there where he admits that so many instruments of misery had been established?

This flesh, therefore, of the worst condition and the worst nature, in these first human beings displayed what it had possessed from the beginning. But the good God could not have fashioned so evil a substance. What remains, then, except that we confess one being to be the giver of the soul and another the creator of beings made of clay?

The battle line of Manichaeus, whose role I had assumed, now stands arranged. You understand what we should await: namely, that the one who opposes him should demonstrate this by a corresponding attack. Let your doctrine therefore clash with his; it will become clear whether it can move even slightly without bringing ruin upon itself.

He certainly declared not only that all people born from the mingling of bodies are guilty, but also that Adam himself brought with him the necessity of guilt from the composition of his entrails and from the filth of the clay from which he was made.

“The nature of flesh,” he says, “was harmful in the first human beings. It enclosed, dampened, and extinguished the very spark of the soul that shone faintly through its devotion to honesty.”

Catholics are utterly foolish, he says, when they oppose the testimony of sinners and refuse to accept their own evidence: they see that they do not do the good they want but perform the evil they abhor, and yet they think that there is no necessity of evil in the flesh.

Let the Traducianist confront these words, spoken with such hostility, if he can. Meanwhile I stand by as a spectator and await the outcome of your conflict. [Col. 1527]

What, then, will you answer to one who swears that an evil nature existed even in the first human beings? Without doubt you will reply that God, the maker of human beings, could not have created the evil thing he created, and that, because God, who does not make evil, made human beings, they are by no means proved to be naturally evil.

You have said something, and truthfully; but consider whether you ought to have said this in my hearing. I do not much care by what power you have shaken Manichaeus; meanwhile, you have passed entirely over to my side. Since I have caught you, I take pleasure in mocking you. I receive your profession with loud applause and remind you to remember it.

By the dignity of the author—that is, God, who does not make evil—you declared that his works must be pronounced good. Do you therefore think that all human beings born from the sexual union established by God are made by God or by the devil?

If by God, how dare you pronounce them guilty and evil, when you have said that the sole proof that Adam could not have been made of an evil nature is that he was created by God, who is supremely good?

If, then, it is a valid argument by which we believe that the guilty substance of the first human beings was not instituted—namely, that God created it, whom we acknowledge to be good—then this same testimony remains as your destruction: it proves that all who are born from marriage cannot be created wicked, because God created them, whom we acknowledge to be good.

But if, even after this, your raging shamelessness persists in swearing both that infants are made by God and that they are nevertheless naturally evil, then, for a Catholic—and likewise for our God—these falsehoods cause no prejudice. It nevertheless remains established that you have not attacked Manichaeus, since he gladly embraces what you accuse God of. You have merely lost the point by which you had tried to prove that Adam was of a good condition.

## AUGUSTINE

When you propose to me, with eloquent blindness, that I undertake a contest against the Manichaean for you to watch, you imprudently undermine your own position; and you have even made it possible for people who are slow-witted to understand how, by the pestilential breath of your doctrine, you assist that most dreadful plague which the fatal error of Manichaeus introduced. For when anyone hears or reads all that you have said so copiously and eloquently about the miseries of this mortal and corruptible life, he will recognize that you have pursued truths—not only in your speech, but also in the very realities of human affairs. Indeed, Manichaeus, to whom you supplied words as though he were speaking against us, had nothing great or difficult to observe in this mortal life, which was deservedly expelled and cast down from the happiness of paradise because of sin [Note: [Col. 1527] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have *detecta est* (“was exposed”).]—whether he merely chattered about these things as you have done, or more fully and abundantly, since they are so obvious that they are repeatedly read in many places of the divine Scriptures: the burden of the corruptible body, and the burdening of the soul that comes from it [Note: [Col. 1527] The old Marcellian codex reads *ex illa* (“from it,” feminine), rather than *ex illo* (“from it,” masculine).].

Hence, even in the saints struggling in the contest of this life, “the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. 5:17): the spirit, as the most glorious Cyprian says, seeks heavenly and divine things, while the flesh desires earthly and worldly things (*On the Lord’s Prayer* [Col. 1528]). This is the conflict which the aforementioned martyr carefully and eloquently explains in the book he wrote *On Mortality*, saying, among other things, that we have a continual and troublesome struggle with bodily vices and worldly enticements.

Now blessed Gregory sets this contest, which we have in “this body of death,” before our eyes in such a way that there is no athlete in this combat who would not recognize himself in his words as in a mirror. He says:

> Within ourselves we are attacked by our own vices and passions, and day and night we are pressed by the fiery goads of this body of humiliation and this body of death. Sometimes secretly, sometimes openly, the enticements of visible things provoke and irritate us everywhere; this filth, this mire to which we cling, exhales through its capacious veins the stench of its own mud. Moreover, the law of sin that is in our members resists the law of the spirit, striving to lead captive the royal image that is within us, so that whatever entered into us through the gift of God and of that first creation may become its spoil.  
> (Gregory of Nazianzus, *Apologia I, On His Flight*)

I have set these words of the man of God both in the second book of the six which I published against your four [Note: [Col. 1528] Chapter 3.] and in this work [Book 1, chapter 67], when I was replying to your first volume, where you thought that the “body of death,” from which the Apostle says that he is liberated by the grace of God (Rom. 8:24–25), should be understood differently.

And when Saint Ambrose had said, “We are all born under sin; their very birth is in fault, as you have it written when David says, ‘For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother bore me,’” he immediately added: “Therefore Paul’s flesh was a body of death, as he himself says, ‘Who will deliver me from the body of this death?’” (*On Repentance*, book 1, chapter 2 or 3).

What wonder, then, if Manichaeus, looking upon the evils of this life, and upon this body of death that weighs down the soul, and upon the disagreement of flesh and spirit, and upon “the heavy yoke” laid upon the children of Adam “from the day of their leaving their mother’s womb until the day of their burial in the mother of all” (Ecclus. 40:1), says through your mouth, as though against us, things such as we see Gregory saying against you?

It is therefore clear that both Manichaeans and Catholics confess the evils of this life—which is “a temptation upon the earth” (Job 7:1, according to the Septuagint)—the evils with which the world is filled because of the heavy yoke of the children of Adam from the day of their leaving their mother’s womb until the day of their burial in the mother of all. But it is also clear that they do not both say the same concerning the origin of these evils, and that there is a great difference between them [Note: [Col. 1528] Vignierius reads *vos* (“you”); the manuscripts, *eos* (“them”).]: the Manichaeans attribute them to an alien evil nature, whereas Catholics attribute them to our own good nature, corrupted by sin and deservedly punished.

You, who do not wish to say what we say, what do you yourself say? How do you answer Manichaeus concerning the origin of these evils with which human beings are born—evils that would not have arisen in paradise if no one had sinned, and there our nature, not corrupted but upright, had remained as it was created [Note: [Col. 1528–1529] The printed editions read *permanente?*; more correctly, *permaneret?*, as in the ancient codices, whose support also restores the two immediately following lines.]? If the congenital defect by which “the flesh desires against the spirit” is not from nature corrupted at its origin, tell us where it comes from.

If there is a congenital defect in which a human being cries, “I know that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh: for to will is present with me, but to accomplish the good I do not find” (Rom. 7:18), and if it is not from the nature corrupted by the transgression of the first human being [Note: [Col. 1529] On manuscript authority, *corrupted* is added.], tell us where it comes from. But if these defects are not congenital [Note: [Col. 1529] The printed editions also lacked *are not* at this point; it is supplied from the manuscripts.], tell us where they come from.

“From the habit of sinning,” you will say, “which each person has acquired by free choice.” Here, meanwhile, you confess what you do not wish to confess: namely, that freedom of will could be destroyed by its own bad use, since it was made less capable of accomplishing the good by accomplishing evil. But was anyone made dull of heart by the will? Was anyone made forgetful by the will? Was anyone made foolish by the will? These and other defects of the mind and spirit themselves—defects with which no one doubts that human beings are born—if you say that they are not from a corrupted origin, tell us where they come from. Surely you will not say that paradise could have possessed these things if no one had sinned.

Finally, tell us whence it comes that the corruptible body weighs down the soul, beneath whose miserable burden all human beings who are not completely senseless groan. Surely you will not say that the first human beings were created in such a way that the soul of one of them was weighed down by a corruptible body; nor that anyone is born after their great sin without such a body.

Why, then, do you introduce Manichaeus speaking against us with such verbosity, when, by denying what we say, you cannot answer him? Cyprian answers him by demonstrating that flesh and spirit are so discordant that the concord of both must nevertheless be sought from God the Father (*On the Lord’s Prayer*). Gregory answers him: although he had said of the flesh things such as you have composed for Manichaeus to say against us, he nevertheless testifies that both must be recalled to God, with God himself propitious—that is, both spirit and flesh. Ambrose answers him: after saying that the flesh must be joined to the governance of the more moderate soul, he adds:

> What sort was it, he says, when it received the secrets of paradise to inhabit, before it had learned, infected by the poison of the pestilential serpent, the sacrilegious hunger?  
> (*Book 7 on Luke*, 12)

By these statements the Catholic bishops taught sufficiently and quite openly that the nature of the flesh is not evil, but that it has a defect; and when this defect has been healed, it returns to the condition in which, as it was first established, it burdens the soul with none of its corruptions and has no discord with the spirit through contrary desire. For Manichaeus was deceived by this discord into imagining that an alien evil substance had been mingled with us.

If you wished to follow with us the faith of these Catholic bishops, you would overthrow the Manichaeans rather than assist them. But now you are trying not to destroy them, but rather to build them up. By denying the evils that human beings draw from a corrupted origin when they are born, you do not make us believe that there are no natural evils, since they are far too evident. Rather, you cause these things to be thought to come from an alien evil nature which, according to the madness of the Manichaeans, has been mingled with us—not to flow from our own good nature, corrupted by the transgression of the first human being, as the sound teaching of Catholics declares [Note: [Col. 1529] The printed editions have: “these natural evils are thought to be those which are mingled with us.” The manuscript reading has been restored here.].

“But,” you say, “Manichaeus so detests the flesh of the first human being itself, such as it was before he sinned, that he strives to show it to have been evil.”

Thus you introduce him speaking in such a way that he creates some task of answering not only for me, but also for you. For when he says that it was made by an evil creator [Note: [Col. 1530] The manuscripts read *cum conditore factum esse* (“to have been made with the creator”).], we answer him together that so good a creature—one that could have refrained from sinning if it had wished—notwithstanding that it is not equal to its Creator, could have had no creator except a good one.

But when he calls the fear of death, which God threatened it with if it sinned, miserable—even before it had sinned—we answer together that, for a human being who could never have sinned if he had never wished to sin, the avoidance of that punishment which was to follow sin was a tranquil precaution, not a troubled fear.

We can indeed answer the common adversary in common, as has been said. But against Manichaeus I increase my praise of that rational creature, which was not only tormented by no fear but also enjoyed great happiness, because it had the power not to suffer the evil of death, from which the hearts of all, or nearly all, the faithful shrink.

Since your error is opposed to this faith of ours—for you think that Adam would have died whether he sinned or did not sin—what answer do you give Manichaeus when he says that the nature was created miserable which, whether sinning or not sinning, was tormented by fear of impending death?

If you say that Adam was created in such a way that he did not fear death, which would certainly come at some time, you will undoubtedly admit that the nature found in his descendants is born miserable, since we see that the fear of death is so congenital even in them that those who desire, through faithful hope, the joys of the future life nevertheless struggle with the fear of death in this life. They do not wish to be unclothed, but to be clothed over, so that, as far as their will is concerned, this life may not end in death, but what is mortal may be swallowed up by life (2 Cor. 5:4).

Thus, if you place the fear of death in paradise before sin, you are defeated by the Manichaeans, who think—and wish it to be thought—that human nature was created miserable even in the first human being. But if you answer that the fear of death, by which the mind of mortals is goaded not without misery, did not exist before sin, you are defeated by us, since nature would not have been changed for the worse unless it had been corrupted.

Again, in what you make Manichaeus say against us—that “the blind and wretched animal was also made restless by an innate desire, which the beauty and sweetness of the forbidden object provoked”—recognize, Julian, the shipwreck of your doctrine upon an unavoidable reef.

We say that in that blessed condition there was no desire that resisted the will. But if those human beings desired something, from what did they rather wish to abstain? Beyond doubt, desire resisted their will. Thus you have made Manichaeus say through your own words something not against me, but against yourself.

For if they were such that desire resisted their will, then the flesh was already desiring against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh. Here the defect of the flesh is most clearly understood—the defect on account of which the Apostle said to the faithful, “For these are opposed to one another, so that you do not do the things that you wish” (Gal. 5:17).

There is no saint who does not wish to prevent the flesh from desiring against the spirit, although he resists it so that he does not fulfill the desire of the flesh by consenting to it, hearing the same Apostle where he says: “But I say, walk by the Spirit, and you will not fulfill the desires of the flesh” (Gal. 5:16–17).
