He does not say, “Do not have the desires of the flesh as adversaries,” because he saw that perfect peace between flesh and spirit could not be accomplished in this body of death. Rather, he says, “You will not fulfill the desires of the flesh,” thereby setting before us the struggle that we must wage against the resisting flesh, so that we do not fulfill its desires by consenting to them, but overcome them by resisting.

Peace, however, in which we did not endure those desires as adversarial and resisting, existed in the body of that life which we lost when the nature of the first human being was corrupted by transgression.

For if there was not peace between flesh and spirit even there before sin, and if what Ambrose said is false—that their discord was turned, through the transgression of the first human being, into our nature (*Book 7 on Luke*, 12:53)—then, God forbid, the statement that you made Manichaeus speak against us will be true: namely, that the first human being was created a miserable creature, whom innate desire made restless, and whom the beauty and sweetness of the forbidden object provoked.

We, however, say that the human being was so blessed before sin, and possessed such free will, that, while observing God’s command with the great strength of his mind, he did not suffer the flesh to resist him in any struggle and felt nothing at all arising from any desire that he did not wish to feel. His will was first corrupted by the serpent’s poisonous persuasion, so that desire arose which followed the will rather than resisting it; and once sin had been committed, the desire of the flesh also resisted the weakened mind as a punishment.

Accordingly, unless the human being first did by sinning what he wished, he would not suffer by desiring what he did not wish.

This is how we defeat Manichaeus when he tries to introduce an evil creator of human nature. But you, who chose for yourself, according to your own pleasure, the position of spectator while we were fighting, and who judged that these very words of yours should be handed to Manichaeus against us—by what method, I ask, and with what strength will you dare resist him, since you say that the desire of the flesh, such as it now is and as we see it fighting against the spirit, was also such in paradise before sin?

Whether you wish it or not, therefore, we remove you from the seats of the theater into the arena, and turn you from a spectator into a combatant. Enter the contest, and, if you can, defeat our common adversary, since you too profess that you worship God as the creator even of the flesh.

Defeat, then, the enemy who tries to persuade us that the God who created the flesh is evil—the flesh whose desire was already resisting the spirit, which had not yet been corrupted by transgression, and was making the human being miserable by its conflict.

Or will you say, “Certainly he possessed such a desire, and yet he was not miserable”? Is this to overcome the adversary, or rather to assist Manichaeus and rebel against the Apostle?

Have you so forgotten who said, “I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind,” and who, after such words, added, “Wretched man that I am”?

If Adam, while willing to obey the divine command, was provoked by desire to eat the forbidden food, and if the desire of the flesh, which you say he possessed even then, resisted the spirit that desired obedience, would he not most truly have said, had he wished to say it: “I delight in the law of God according to the inner human being; but I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind”?

How, then, was the human being not miserable, when after such words the Apostle says, “Wretched man that I am” (Rom. 7:22–24)? Finally, how was he not miserable, and how did he have free will, if, while the flesh desired against the spirit, he was—as the Apostle himself testifies—unable to do what he wished?

Therefore, if you say that the desire of the flesh before sin was such as it now is, Manichaeus will unquestionably defeat you. Come over to my position, and let us both approve Ambrose, who says that, through the transgression of the first human being, the discord of flesh and spirit was turned into our nature; thus we may both defeat Manichaeus.

Through the words you composed for him, as though he were going to recite them, and through what is usually debated in the schools of rhetoricians—speaking words belonging to another—he said that Adam was created not only wretched but also blind. Blind in what sense, unless because he did not know sin, concerning which it is said in the praises of Christ, “Him who knew no sin he made sin for us” (2 Cor. 5:21)? Whatever evils are learned not through wisdom but through experience are fortunately unknown to the one who does not know them.

But perhaps you too will say with me, against Manichaeus’ accusation concerning the ignorance of the first human being: what answer you should give him concerning bodily death and the desire of the flesh, in accordance with the answers we have now given you, consider for yourself.

For these two most obvious facts show that the condition of the first human beings, who were not born from any parental stock, was one thing, while the condition of those who are created by God and also begotten by human beings is another. From the first human beings they receive the pattern of their formation; from their parents they derive the liability of their origin. They owe their formation to the Creator’s workmanship, their obligation to judgment, and their liberation to the Creator’s beneficence.

When the Manichaeans look upon the evils with which these descendants are born, they try to introduce an evil maker of the human being. But the very structure of the flesh testifies that God is its maker—as I say nothing here about the soul, which is the life of the flesh—from whom come all good things, whether heavenly or earthly. The flesh is so good that the blessed Apostle took its structure as an image for the highest praise of love, by which faithful people, as members of Christ, are joined to one another in a peaceful bond of unity (1 Cor. 12:12).

Thus, both those first human beings, who were made without defect, and their descendants, who were born with original defect, could have been created only by a good Creator, on account of the exceedingly evident goodness of nature.

## XV. JULIAN

But let us not press the first part of the contest too far. Let us allow you, as your argument proceeds, to prove the goodness of Adam’s nature. You certainly say:

“A just God would not impose upon a human being a law of devotion if he knew that the human being was subject to the necessity of sinning. For if he demanded righteousness of will from one whom he knew to be of an evil nature, when that person transgressed he would not be declaring him guilty, but would be proclaiming himself an enemy of righteousness. Yet the just God imposed a law upon the human being and promised that he would punish him if he transgressed. It is therefore established that, being good by nature, he could have sinned in no other way than by the will alone.”

You see, surely, how legitimate is the conclusion that I have brought forward in your name. This is altogether the sword which, flashing in the hands of Catholics, ravages both Manichaeans and Traducianists. But I have mixed you into it too much because of your name, since for the moment I had wished the answer to appear to have been made in your place.

The solid answer has shaken Manichaeus. I pursue the august argument with fitting praise; but observe that with the oil of this praise I am sharpening the sword against you. Repeat, then, please, what you had said.

“A just God,” you say, “would not impose a law upon a human being if he were evil by nature. But the one who imposed the law is just. It is therefore now evident that the human being was able to keep what the most equitable God commanded, since, unless he had possessed the power of obedience, there would never have been any rational basis for the command addressed to him.”

What a delightful little chapter! With me as spectator, he attempts to establish from the justice of the one who promulgates the law the goodness of the nature upon which the law is imposed; and he does not see that, before Manichaeus feels even a slight wound, he has already carried ruin to the Traducianists [Note: [Col. 1533] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have *protulisse* (“brought forward”).].

So that you may understand that I am snatching the bloodstained weapons from your half-dead grasp, and that dying eyes may bear witness to the victorious truth (Virgil, *Aeneid* 10.462–463), I shall drive you back upon your own weapons [Note: [Col. 1533] The manuscripts read *librare* (“to brandish”), rather than *vibrare* (“to hurl”).].

If the just God could give Adam a law only if he knew that Adam was free, without any compulsion toward evil, to observe what was just, then unquestionably, in later times also, a law of the same justice—handed down in writing, more widely disseminated, more clearly marked by its distinctions, and made more reverent by increased punishment—would not have been given to human beings if they were either too weak to do good, without the possibility of righteousness, or guilty—that is, evil—from the womb.

For just as the excuse of necessity would acquit such people of every transgression, so the excess of commands, the impotence of penalties, and the injustice of judgments would rebound as a stain upon the author.

This second part, therefore, is closed in the same manner as the first [Note: [Col. 1533] The printed editions have *eluditur* (“is evaded”). The manuscripts of Marcellus and Claromontanus have *cluditur* (“is closed”).]: either you must confess that God’s justice could not command anything unless he had considered that his subjects were able to do it; and that, by the testimony of the first commandment, Manichaeus is destroyed, while by the testimony of the laws that followed, both Manichaeus and the Traducianist are destroyed; or, if impiety abandons this position, then Manichaeus, scarcely struck at all by you, will demonstrate before the whole world that he is your father and your leader, and that, together with you, he has only one contest against us [Note: [Col. 1533] The printed editions read: “and it will be shown before the world that he is with you …” The wording has been corrected from the manuscripts.].

## AUGUSTINE

This, surely, is what you pursued not by eloquence but by verbosity: namely, that the earlier law, which was given in paradise, is a testimony to the goodness of the nature created with free will; otherwise the law would have been most unjustly given to a human being who did not possess free will.

Hence, you say, the later law, which was most fully promulgated in writing, is likewise a testimony to the goodness of the nature created from parents, also without defect and with free will.

While arguing this way, you seem to yourself to be saying something, because you follow either your own clever arguments or human ones. But you do not care to read the divine utterances from which you think you can prescribe to us; or, if you do care to read them, you do not wish—or are unable—to understand them.

But if by chance you understand them while we are arguing, do not be like the one whom Scripture reproves when it says, “A stubborn servant will not be corrected by words; for even if he understands, he will not obey” (Prov. 29:19). Yet he who wishes can also remove from you the heart of stone, by which one does not obey divine words even when they are understood—the heart which, through the holy prophet Ezekiel, he promised to take away from that stubborn people (Ezek. 11:19; 36:26).

In paradise the human being received a law who had been made upright, so that obedience might be shown to be either the sole or the chief virtue of a rational creature. But through transgression of that same law he made himself crooked.

And because he could corrupt himself but could not heal himself, afterward—at the time and in the place when and where the Wisdom of God judged that it should be done—the crooked human being also received the law. It was not given so that he could be corrected by it, but so that through it he might recognize that he was crooked and could not be corrected by himself even after receiving the law. Thus, as sins did not cease through the law but increased through transgression, his pride was cast down and crushed, so that with a deeply humbled heart he might desire the help of grace and, having been slain by the letter, might be made alive by the Spirit.

For if a law had been given that could give life, righteousness would certainly have been through the law. But Scripture confined all things under sin, so that the promise might be given to believers through faith in Jesus Christ (Gal. 3:21–22).

If you recognize the Apostle’s words, you plainly see either what you do not understand or what, although you understand it, you neglect.

The law, therefore, which was given in writing through Moses, is not a testimony to free will. For if it were, the one who says, “I do not do the good that I wish, but the evil that I hate, that I do” (Rom. 7:15), would not belong to it—and you certainly maintain that this person is not yet under grace but still under the law.

Nor is the new law itself, which was proclaimed as destined to go forth from Zion [Note: [Col. 1534] The old Portian codex reads *praedicta* (“foretold”).], and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem (Isa. 2:3)—which is understood to be the holy Gospel—a testimony to free will. Rather, it is a testimony to a will that is to be liberated.

For there it is written: “If the Son sets you free, then you will truly be free” (John 8:36). This was said not only on account of past sins, from which we are liberated by forgiveness, but also on account of the assistance of grace which we receive so that we may not sin—that is, so that we may be made free while God directs our ways, so that no iniquity may rule over us (Ps. 118:133).

The Lord’s Prayer bears witness to this. In it we say not only, “Forgive us our debts,” on account of the evils we have done, but also, “Do not lead us into temptation” (Matt. 6:12–13), precisely so that we may not do evil. Hence the Apostle also says, “We pray to God that you do no evil” (2 Cor. 13:7).

But if this were in our power, as it was before sin, before human nature was corrupted, it would not be asked for in prayer; rather, it would be held by doing it.

Yet after that earlier fall, so great that we fell into the misery of this mortality, God first wished us to struggle, granting that we be governed by his Spirit [Note: [Col. 1535] The printed editions read *agamus* (“that we may act”); all the manuscripts read *agamur* (“that we may be led”).] and put to death the works of the flesh, and that, with him granting the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ, we might afterward reign with him in eternal peace.

Accordingly, unless God is present, no one is fit to struggle against vices: either he will be dragged along by them without a struggle, or, having begun to struggle, he will be overcome in the very conflict.

For this reason, in this combat God wished us to struggle more through prayers than through our own strength, because he himself supplies to those who fight whatever strength we ought to have here, and it is he whom we ask.

If, then, those whose spirit already desires against the flesh need God’s grace for each individual act, lest they be overcome, what freedom of will can those possess who have not yet been rescued from the power of darkness, with iniquity ruling over them, and have not even begun to fight? Or if they have wished to fight, how can they avoid being defeated in the servitude of a will that has not yet been liberated?

## XVI. JULIAN

I do not know whether, now compelled by want, you are attempting something so foolish and so feeble as to say that you cannot prove by any arguments that Adam was created good by God, but that for belief in this you are content with the authority of the text alone—namely, the passage which, after the human being had been formed on the sixth day, reports collectively concerning all creatures: “And God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good” (Gen. 1:31).

You apparently think that Adam too was established as not unjust—not on the basis of the dignity of the craftsman, nor on the basis of an assessment of his justice, but on the basis of the testimony by which created things in general are said to have been made well.

Although this only lightly strikes Manichaeus, so that he laughs [Note: [Col. 1535] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have *redeat* (“returns”).], it nevertheless presents the Traducianist to us as bound and defeated.

Therefore, so that we need not gather the people by means of all the divine testimonies relevant to this matter, we appeal to the authority of the Apostle alone. Foreseeing the disgraceful error, he thundered against you with exalted voice, saying: “For every creature of God is good” (1 Tim. 4:4).

If, then, to prove that the first human being was formed as a good nature it is sufficient that Moses says that God made all things well, and if on this basis you contend that Adam could not be created by God with sin, because he is read to have been established good among the rest, then by the same line of reasoning we shall assert that no one can be born with sin, since the Apostle defends the goodness of every creature of God.

What, then, has been accomplished by these arguments? Clearly this: that what reason had investigated, the outcome of the contest declared between you and Manichaeus. For when, in the proposed contest, you were unable to hurl even one [Note: [Col. 1535] Vignierius reads *ullum* (“any”); the manuscripts read *unum* (“one”).] weapon against your teacher without injuring yourself, it became much more clearly evident that you and the Manichaeans have coalesced into one obscene body of impiety.

For what could be so closely joined together as that which is not separated even by the impact of distinction? The doctrine of the Traducianists perishes in the complete destruction of Manichaeus; there is nothing that strikes him and leaves you untouched. You have the same institutions, the same mysteries, and the same dangers. And do you take offense when I call you the offspring of the old Manes?

**AUG.** You say, then, that I can prove by no arguments that Adam was created good by God—as though I were contending with you about this. Do not both you and I say that Adam was created good—not I alone, nor you alone, but both of us? For we both say that the nature was good which could refrain from sinning if it wished. But since I assert that it was better than you do—for I say also that it could not have died if it had not wished to sin—what do you mean by saying that I can prove by no arguments that Adam was created good by God, when my arguments show him to have been more good than yours do? For my arguments show not only that he could have refrained from sinning if he had wished, but also that he could not have died if he had not wished to sin. Yours, however, make him mortal in such a way that, whether he sinned or did not sin, he was destined to die.

When this was brought forward against Pelagius in the episcopal judgment at Palestine, he himself condemned it so that he might not be condemned (*On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, §§24, 57, 60); and by this he was condemned by his own statement, in accordance with what the Apostle says about a heretical man (Tit. 3:10–11). I also say that Adam did not fear death, since it lay within his power not to die; but you say that he was under the necessity of dying even without any necessity of sinning. If you say that Adam feared death even before sin, what are you saying except that he was created miserable? But if, so as not to be miserable, he did not fear death, although it was to come, then surely he begot his offspring—into whom he implanted the fear of death—as miserable. For who can deny that human beings naturally fear death, so that only rare greatness of spirit enables some not to fear it?

I add this also to the goodness of Adam’s creation: before sin, the flesh did not lust against the spirit in him. But you, who say that the lust of the flesh, such as it now is, would have existed in paradise if no one had sinned, and that it existed in Adam even before he sinned, add this misery also to his condition, through the discord between spirit and flesh. Since, therefore, I show by so many and such great arguments that Adam was created better and happier than you say he was, what possessed you to rave with such folly as to say that I can prove by no arguments that Adam was created good by God, but that, for believing this, I am content with the sole authority of the text because it is written that God made all things “very good”?

I am not so much duller than a pestle, as you abusively say (*above*, book 2, chapter 117), that I would cite against Manichaeus, in refuting him, the authority of this divine book, by which he is not bound. I bring this authority against you when the matter requires it, since it is shared by you and me. But I convict Manichaeus not from the work of God—for he denies that—but rather from the goodness of these created things, compelling him to confess that they have a good creator.

As for what the Apostle says—an Apostle whom the Manichaeans profess to accept—“Every creature of God is good” (1 Tim. 4:4): since it is clear which creation he was speaking about, this testimony would be powerful against them, unless they also maintained that the canonical books, which they accept, contain certain false statements mixed in with them. Accordingly, they must always be pressed concerning the goodness of created things, so that they may confess that God—whose authorship they deny—is their good creator.

Moreover, all creatures are so good that reason demonstrates even those created with defects to be good, and demonstrates this by the very testimony of their defects. For a defect is contrary to nature; and unless nature itself were rightly pleasing, its defect could in no way rightly be displeasing. This is argued at greater length against the Manichaeans in some of our little works, where it is shown that a defect is not a nature, and that, because it is contrary to nature, it is therefore evil; and consequently that nature, insofar as it is nature, is good. From this it follows that the creator of natures can be none other than the creator of good things, and therefore is good—but is better than his creatures by a great distinction and supreme goodness, and cannot be corrupted at all, not by the reception of grace [Note: [Col. 1537] An old Clarendon manuscript reads *praeceptione*, “by the imparting,” instead of *perceptione*, “by the reception.”], but by the property of his nature.

Created natures, therefore—whether they are without defect, or are born subject to defect, or are born already defective—can have no creator except him who creates good things [Note: [Col. 1537] Morel, *Elem. Crit.*, p. 319, reads *ullum creatorem nisi eum*, “any creator except him”; M has the shorter reading.], because insofar as they are natures they are good, even when they are defective. For he is not the author of defects, but the creator of natures. Indeed, the very author of defects is good by nature, since God made him; but he is evil through the defect by which, through an evil will, he departed from the good Creator.

Thus this true reasoning refutes the error of the Manichaeans, who refuse to accept the authority either of the statement, “God made all things, and behold, they were very good,” when no evil yet existed, or of the statement, “Every creature of God is good,” when this evil age already existed, although God is certainly the maker of all ages.

But you, who accept the authority of the divine utterances so that it may rightly be brought to bear against you, why do you not observe that in the book where it is read that God made all things very good, paradise was planted as the best of all places [Note: [Col. 1537] The Portus manuscript reads *optimo*, “best.”], where God so willed that nothing evil should exist that he did not even permit his image to remain there after it had sinned by its own will (Gen. 2:8; 3:23–24)? Yet you do not hesitate to introduce into a place of such great happiness and beauty—where it is to be believed that there could not and cannot have been any defect in wood, hay, fruit, or any crop or animal—all the defects of human bodies and minds, defects with which we allow you to grieve—but not to deny—that human beings are born.

For you must suffer anguish when you find nothing to answer, yet refuse to change so perverse an opinion—an opinion that compels you, by an inevitable necessity, to place in a region of such blessedness and beauty the blind, the one-eyed, the bleary-eyed, the deaf, the mute, the lame [Note: [Col. 1537] The following six words have been restored here from the manuscripts.], the deformed, the twisted, the moth-eaten, the leprous, the paralytic, the epileptic, and those afflicted with various other kinds of defects, and sometimes even monsters of excessive ugliness and horrifying bodily abnormality.

What shall I say about the defects of the mind? Some are naturally lustful, some irascible, some fearful, some forgetful, some slow-witted, some senseless, and some so foolish that a man would rather live with certain animals than with such human beings. Add the groans of women in childbirth, the cries of newborn infants, the agonies of those in pain, the hardships of the sick, the many torments of the dying, and the far greater dangers of the living.

Who can even briefly recall in suitable words all these things, and others like them or worse? According to your error—but plainly against your own sense of shame—you are compelled, either with an utterly shameless brow or with your hand placed over your brow, to locate them in God’s paradise and to say that they would have existed there even if no one had sinned.

Say it, say it! Why should you hesitate to dishonor with so many and such great defects and calamities a place that, by your impious doctrine, you make alien to yourselves? For if you intended ever to enter there, you would never place such things in it.

Or, if shame prevails in your hearts, and you blush, shudder, and fall silent at placing such things in such a place, yet stubbornly cling to your error—that human nature was not corrupted by the transgression of the first man—then answer the Manichaeans when they ask where these things come from, lest they conclude that they arise from the mixture of an alien and evil nature.

When this is asked of us, we answer that these things do not come from a mixture with an alien nature, but from the transgression of our own nature, through him who was cast down in paradise and cast out of paradise, so that condemned nature would not remain in a place of blessedness, and so that the defects and punishments which were deservedly to follow his descendants would not be present in a place where no evils are permitted to exist.

But you, by denying that these deformities and miseries arise from the merits of our corrupted nature, permit the mixture with an alien nature; and thus, miserable as you are, you are compelled both to assist the Manichaeans and, through your error, to bring those evils back into paradise from which your sense of shame had removed them.

### XVII. JUL.

But see how, against you and against Manichaeus—whose ruin continually sweeps you along—our conflict is genuine, and how swift our victory over him will be. We circumscribe all those things that he vomited forth in condemnation of God’s work with the plough of the first definition, and compel him to explain what he thinks sin is. It is plainly nothing other than a will desiring what justice forbids, and from which it is free to refrain.

Once this has been established, all those thorns of objection that had pierced the compact structure of bodies are shown to have been pulled up by the roots—indeed, as he puts it, “rooted out” (*Cicero, On Ends*, book 2).

Now the emotions of fear and the sensation of pain, through which he thought that the storm of human shipwrecks was stirred up, are shown not merely to compel no evil, but—when they have found the barrier of a good will [Note: [Col. 1538] The manuscripts read *contra*, “against,” in Vignier.]—to be helpers and furtherers [Note: [Col. 1538] Perhaps *provectores*, “promoters,” rather than *pervectores*, “conveyers.”] of justice. For who would fear judgment unless warned by fear? Who would be aided by the groans of repentance unless cleansed through pain and inward distress? Finally, what force would the severity of a judge have unless the suffering of inflicted anguish punished voluntary sins?

The testimony of all these things makes clear that sin is nothing other than a free will that disregards the commands of justice. Justice cannot stand in any other way than by imputing as sin what it knows to have been guarded against freely. Consequently, no law can count natural things as guilt, nor can anyone incur a crime that he himself has not committed, when he is able to avoid it.

By this power the Manichaean and the Traducianist are destroyed: having gouged out the eyes of their entire understanding, they try to attach a matter of the will to the seeds of generation.

**AUG.** We have already answered these errors of yours many times. Those who read these answers and commit them to memory do not everywhere need my response wherever you repeat your verbosity. But lest anyone complain that, while the more quick-witted are forgiving toward me, I fail to provide an answer even for the rather slow, I must not neglect them either.

Here, then, I answer you concerning the definition of sin by which [Note: [Col. 1539] The manuscripts read *qua te*, “by which you”; Vignier has *quale*, “what kind of.”] you think you are greatly assisted. That definition determines what sin is when it is not also the punishment of sin: “Sin is a will desiring what justice forbids, and from which it is free to refrain.” This applies especially to the one whose great sin gave rise to misery for his descendants—through the heavy yoke imposed upon them from the day they leave their mother’s womb, and through the corruptible body that weighs down the soul.

For he knew, from the very brief commandment he had received, what justice forbade; and from it [Note: [Col. 1539] The printed editions read *unde*, “from which”; the Marignan manuscript more aptly reads *inde*, “from it.”] it had certainly been free for him to refrain, since the flesh had not yet lusted against his spirit, on account of which evil it was said even to the faithful, “So that you may not do the things that you wish” (Gal. 5:17).

Blindness of heart, by which one does not know what justice forbids, and the violence of desire, by which even one who knows from what he ought to refrain is overcome, are not only sins but also punishments of sins. For that reason they are not included in the definition of sin, which defines sin alone, not what is also the punishment of sin.

When someone does not know what he ought to do, and therefore does what he ought not to do [Note: [Col. 1539] The Portus manuscript reads “what he ought not to have done.”], it was not free for him to refrain from what he did not know he ought to avoid. Likewise, the person who, as you say, is oppressed not by origin but by habit, so that he cries out, “I do not do the good that I will, but the evil that I do not will, this I do” (Rom. 7:15)—how is it free for him to refrain from the evil that he does not will yet does, that he hates yet practices?

If it were within human power to be free from these punishments, God would not be asked to remove them: against blindness, one would not say, “Enlighten my eyes” (Ps. 12:4); and against wicked desire, one would not say, “Let no iniquity have dominion over me” (Ps. 118:133).

Moreover, if these were not sins for the reason that it is not free to refrain from them, it would not be said, “Remember not the sins of my youth and my ignorance” (Ps. 24:7); nor would it be said, “You have sealed up my sins in a bag and noted if I committed anything unwillingly” (Job 14:17, according to the Septuagint).

By that definition of sin, therefore, the Manichaeans are defeated—the sin committed by Adam, who knew what justice forbade and did not refrain from it, although it had been free for him to refrain. But they are defeated by us, because we say that this is the origin of the human evils under which we see even infants weighed down, and on account of which it was also written, when sins were being discussed: “For no one is clean from defilement, not even an infant whose life upon earth is but one day” (Job 14:4, according to the Septuagint).

But by denying this, you try, through a destructive defense, to press our nature down still further, lest in its misery it seek a liberator. When the question is where evil comes from, you permit the Manichaean to introduce a nature alien to God [Note: [Col. 1540] Vignier reads *et Deo*, “and to God”; *et* is absent from the manuscripts.] and coeternal with him.

For when he seeks the source from which to condemn human nature, he does not bring forward the emotion of fear and the sensation of pain—two things that you thought ought to be praised against him, since, as you said, “fear and pain are thoroughly shown to be helpers and furtherers of justice,” when a person does not sin out of fear of judgment or is pained by the stings of repentance for having sinned [Note: [Col. 1540] The old Marignan manuscript reads *pervectores*, as above in Julian’s speech.].

This is not what is being asked of you. The question is: what is the punishment of fear in infants, who do not flee sins, and why are those who commit no sins afflicted by such great pains?

You yourself said: “What would the severity of a judge be worth unless the suffering of inflicted anguish punished voluntary sins?” By what justice, then, are infants punished by the suffering of inflicted anguish when they have no personal voluntary sins?

In them it is plainly evident that your praises are empty and foolish, since you praised fear and pain. These punishments are grievous; newborn and newly formed images of God would not suffer them from the moment of their birth under the most just judgment and omnipotence of God if they did not bear the desert of original and ancient sin.

Finally, if no one had sinned in paradise, and the fertility of married couples had proceeded from that true blessing of God, far be it from us to suppose that anyone there, great or small, would have suffered such torments. For not only pain, which is very evident, but also fear has torment, as divine Scripture testifies (1 John 4:18). Far be it, then, that there should have been any torments in that place of happiness.

At any age, therefore, if no one frightened them, what would they fear? If no one harmed them, what would they suffer? But in this present evil age, into which we were cast from the paradise of delights so that it might run its course amid our miseries, the misery of fears and pains remains even in those whose sins have been forgiven. Thus our faith concerning the future age, where none of these things will exist, is tested not only by our own sufferings but also by those of our infants.

For we do not wish them to be regenerated so that they may not suffer these evils, but so that they may be brought into the kingdom where such things will not exist.

When the Manichaean raises the question where the evils of infants come from, all your verbosity will fall silent as you reject this true and catholic faith and attempt to refute it with the empty clamor of your lips. For when you deny original sin, he will immediately batter your brow and introduce an alien nature as the source of evil.

The catholic faith does not fear what seems to you impossible—“that a matter of the will can be attached to seeds”—when it hears God saying that the sins of fathers are repaid to the third and fourth generation of their children (Exod. 20:5; 34:7). The matter of the will by which fathers sin is indeed attached to seeds when punishment is exacted upon their children.

The father Abraham, by his will, gave tithes to the priest Melchizedek so that he might be tithed by him; yet Holy Scripture testifies that his children also—because they were in his loins—were then tithed (Heb. 7:9–10). This certainly would not have happened if a matter of the will could not be attached to seeds.

### XVIII. JUL.

But, in the name of the faithfulness of our God and of human beings [Note: [Col. 1541] Vignier reads, “But for the faith of our God and of human beings!” The manuscripts correct the text.], could such monstrosities of invention really have been found—so that, deliberately and with sustained effort, they attempt to assert everything in reverse?

For what is more monstrous than what the Carthaginian declares? “Those things,” he says, “which were natural were not perpetual; but those which were undertaken by deliberate choice clung to the first structures of the limbs.

“Adam was made good; he possessed natural innocence. He surpassed the other creatures in a distinctive nobility and shone with the likeness of his Creator. He received free choice in his creation, so that he might move by his own judgment toward whichever side he wished; and by the very condition of his creation, through which he stood above the others, he received the capacity to approach either good or evil, or to withdraw from both.

“But because, with his judgment emancipated, he appropriated the perverse will of a free mind, he overturned all those things that were evidently innate; and only sin and the necessity of sinning clung inseparably to him.”

This is the monstrous invention I mentioned. For it is an unheard-of deformity to say: “An animal was well constituted in which even natural goods were liable to be lost, while voluntary evils adhered to it inseparably.”

**AUG.** When it is said, “An animal was well constituted in which even natural goods were liable to be lost, while voluntary evils adhered to it inseparably,” you think this a “monstrous invention.” And when you suppose that we say these things, you are so violently and fiercely agitated that you cry out in the name of the faithfulness of God and of human beings, as though you were suffering violence because such statements are made.

But I ask you: lay aside these terrifying outbursts, and listen more calmly to what I say. If someone blinds himself by his own will, does he not lose a natural good—namely, sight—and does not a voluntary evil—namely, blindness—adhere to him inseparably? Is an animal therefore badly constituted merely because it possessed a natural good that could be lost and an inseparable voluntary evil?

Why should I not rather cry out, “In the name of the faithfulness of our God and of human beings!”—that a man who wishes to appear very acute, learned, philosophical, and dialectical should fail to see things so obvious and set before his eyes?

For if anyone voluntarily cuts off any bodily member, does he not lose the natural good of bodily soundness and take on the inseparable evil of mutilation? But perhaps you will say that this can happen in the goods of the body, not in those of the mind.

Why, then, when you said “natural goods or voluntary evils,” did you not add “of the mind,” lest your rash and thoughtless [Col. 1542] opinion be overturned by the goods and evils of the body? Or perhaps you forgot? Let us excuse you; it is human to forget.

But the man comes forward who cries out, “I do not do the good that I will, but the evil that I do not will, this I do” (Rom. 7:15), and he shows you that certain goods of the mind can perish through an evil will in such a way that they cannot return through a good will, unless God does what a human being cannot do—God who can restore sight to one blinded by the will and limbs to one mutilated by the will [Note: [Col. 1542] Vignier reads, “and he shows that certain goods …”; “to you” has been added from the Portus manuscript.].

Furthermore, what will you say in answer concerning the devil himself, who irreparably lost his good will? Will you say that it can be restored? Dare to say so, if you can. Or will you rather admit that this too never entered your mind, and that your forgetfulness of these matters caused you to rush into a rash opinion?

At least correct yourself when I remind you. Or does stubbornness prevent you from correcting what thoughtless rashness has said, while shame at making an amendment confirms the error into which you have fallen?

God, as I see, must be entreated on your behalf—the God whom the Apostle entreated for the Israelites, that he might heal them, since they were ignorant of God’s justice and wished to establish their own, and therefore were not subject to God’s justice (Rom. 10:1, 3).

For you too are such people. You want to establish your own justice, which you fashion for yourselves from your own free choice; you do not ask for and receive from God the true justice called the justice of God. This is not the justice by which God is just, but the justice that is given by God—just as salvation is the Lord’s (Ps. 3:8), not salvation by which the Lord is made safe, but by which he makes others safe [Note: [Col. 1542] Vignier reads *sit*, “may be”; the manuscripts read *fit*, “is made.”].

Hence the same Apostle says: “That I may be found in him, not having my own justice, which is from the law, but that which is through faith—the justice that is from God” (Phil. 3:9).

This is the justice of God that the Israelites did not know, and that they wished to establish as their own, the justice that is from the law. When Paul destroyed it, he was certainly not destroying the law, but their pride: they thought that the law was sufficient for them, as though they fulfilled the justice of the law through free choice, and they did not know the justice of God, which is given by God so that, with his help, what the law commands may be done. His wisdom carries both law and mercy upon its tongue (Prov. 3:16, according to the Septuagint): law, because it commands; mercy, because it helps, so that what it commands may be done.

Desire this justice of God, my son Julian; do not trust in your own strength. I say, desire this justice of God. May the Lord grant you to desire it; may the Lord grant you also to possess it.

Do not, swollen with your earthly ancestry, despise this Carthaginian who warns or admonishes you. For do not suppose that because Apulia gave birth to you, the Carthaginians must therefore be defeated by your people, whom you cannot defeat in mind. Flee punishments rather than Carthaginians: you cannot flee Carthaginian disputants so long as you delight in trusting in your own strength.

For blessed Cyprian too was a Carthaginian, and he said: “In nothing should one glory, since nothing is ours” (*To Quirinus*, book 3, chapter 4).

### XIX. JUL.

Let someone say: “What, then? Do you deny that the innocence in which he had been created was corrupted by the admission of voluntary sin? For although the possibility of returning to the good does not perish when iniquity has been committed, it is nevertheless certain that the merit of innocence, with which the human race begins, is destroyed by the fault of the will.”

I do not deny that this is so. But what I want illuminated by these examples is this: since the condition of the qualities by which we are called good or evil is such that they are governed under the authority of the will, and since this has been established with such seriousness that even innocence—which, according to the dignity of the author, precedes the activity of the will and is natural—nevertheless cannot preserve itself by any power when the mind resists, it follows that this right is much more powerful on the side of evil, so that guilt assumed by the will cannot seize a tyranny destructive of reason.

And if the good quality with which human beings were made was not immutable—for a human being would falsely be called free if he could not alter his own movements—then much less could the evil quality become immutable and rational [Note: [Col. 1543] An old Portus manuscript reads “and natural.” Perhaps the text should read, “so that it would be immutable and rational.”], lest reason suffer a prejudice against freedom on the side of evil, which, because of its condition, it had not suffered even from the portion of good.

**AUG.** Look: you too have discovered—although rather late, yet at last it has entered your mind—the point by which your rash opinion is overturned. For you said that the natural good which is innocence can be destroyed by a fault of the will. Thus you have shown that so great a good, belonging not to the body but to the mind itself, pertains so much to nature that God made the human being with that good, and yet that it can be lost.

If this had occurred to you earlier, you would not have thought it monstrous and excessively deformed to say, “An animal was well constituted in which even natural goods were liable to be lost.” You thought that goods or evils—whether voluntary—could be lost, but you are accustomed to proclaim natural things incapable of loss.

For elsewhere you say that “natural things endure from the beginning of a substance to the end of it” (*above*, book 2, chapter 76), in order to maintain that free choice, which God gave to the human being when he created him, cannot be lost. You especially assert that natural goods cannot perish through voluntary evils.

Accordingly, you say that we attempt to assert everything in reverse, as though we said that voluntary evils cannot be lost, but natural goods can. We do not say this. We say that both can be lost: evils introduced through free choice can be lost through divine forgiveness, or through human will when liberated by God and prepared by the Lord.

But you, who say that what can be lost through an evil will is voluntary good, not natural good, have now discovered the contrary and said it yourself: innocence, which is a natural good, can be lost through a voluntary evil.

And if you pay close attention, innocence is a greater good than free choice. Innocence belongs to the category of good things, whereas free choice belongs both to good things and to evil things.

Whether innocence, when it perishes through an evil will, can be restored through a good will is not an insignificant question. For just as bodily limbs, if cut off by the will, are not restored by the will, so we must consider whether, although the matter is unlike—namely, in the mind—something similar occurs in the loss of innocence: whether it can perish through a voluntary movement but cannot return.

Sacred virginity, too, if it perishes through an immodest will, can return to chastity but cannot return to virginity. Yet one may still answer that the integrity of virginity belongs to the body, not to the mind [Note: [Col. 1544] The manuscripts read “the integrity of the virgin,” rather than “of virginity.”]. But when innocence is discussed [Note: [Col. 1544] Perhaps one should add: “when a matter of the mind is under discussion”]—and nevertheless it must be considered whether one who has sinned returns by the will to justice, not to innocence—then the comparison is as follows: just as injustice stands opposed to justice, so what stands opposed to innocence, as its contrary, is not injustice but guilt.

Guilt is not removed by human will, even though it is produced by human will. For one who thinks that a penitent removes his own guilt does not see the truth. Even repentance itself is given by God, as the Apostle confirms when he says, “Lest perhaps God grant them repentance” (2 Tim. 2:25). But God most clearly removes guilt by granting forgiveness to the human being; the human being does not remove it from himself by doing penance.

We must remember the one who found no place for repentance, although he sought it with tears (Heb. 12:17). Thus he did penance and remained guilty because he did not receive forgiveness. Likewise, those who will say among themselves, repenting and groaning in anguish of spirit, “What did our pride profit us?” (Wis. 5:3, 8), will remain guilty forever, because they did not receive pardon. So too the one of whom the Lord says, “It will not be forgiven him, but he will be guilty of an eternal sin” (Mark 3:29).

There, then, innocence has been found to be a great good of the human being, and so natural that the first man was created with it and, as you say, every human being is born with it. Yet it can be lost by human will and cannot be restored by human will.

Guilt, meanwhile, is a great evil and the opposite of innocence. Although it is voluntary and therefore within human power to inflict, it is not within human power to remove.

Do you see how your general rule is broken—the rule by which you thought that we cannot lose a natural good by our will—when something has been found that not only perishes but does not return through human will? God, however, can restore a human being to innocence after removing guilt.

Why, then, do you not believe that the freedom to act well could have perished through human will and cannot return except through divine will, when you hear a human being saying, “I do not do the good that I will, but the evil that I do not will, this I do”; and after these words crying out, “Who will deliver me?”; and then adding, “The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. 7:15, 24–25)?

“But it would falsely be said,” you reply, “that a human being is free if he cannot vary his own movements.” Do you not see that you are taking freedom away from God himself, and from us, when we begin to live immortal with him in his kingdom, where it will no longer be possible for us to vary our movements now toward good and now toward evil?

Yet then we shall be more happily free, when we cannot serve sin—just as God himself cannot. The difference is that we shall be free by his grace, while he is free by his nature.

### XX. JUL.

Next, what flatterer has praised the strength of a glorious soldier with such adulation as the Traducianist has praised the devil? This can be recognized from the weight of his affections [Note: [Col. 1545] An old Marignan manuscript reads *effectuum*, “effects,” rather than *affectuum*, “affections.”].

God made the human being, handling the very material of clay with venerable condescension, so that it might follow the hand of its author when that hand molded it into human form. The image already stood complete, pale and cold [Note: [Col. 1545] The manuscripts in Vignier read *fringensque*], awaiting the spirit by which it might shine and live.

Then the mind, created and inspired by the most august breath of the Creator, moved the filled entrails; then all the senses were roused for the performance of their proper functions. The indwelling spirit gave color to the entrails, heat to the blood [Note: [Col. 1545] Perhaps the readings should be reversed: “heat to the entrails, color to the blood.”], vigor to the limbs, and radiance to the skin.

See what work divine piety undertook in forming and animating the human being. Yet the familiarity of the Creator did not leave him incomplete. He was transferred to a more pleasant place, and the one whom God had mercifully made, he generously enriched.

Nor was he content to grant only this. He illuminated him by sharing conversation with him. He gave him a command, so that, understanding his freedom, he might see that he possessed the means by which he could become more intimate with the Creator. The command was not extended into many requirements, lest he feel the burden of an increased law; rather, by the prohibition of a single little fruit [Note: [Col. 1545] The manuscripts in Vignier read *interdicta*, “prohibitions.”], a testimony of devotion was sought.

Afterward, so that he might have a companion through whom he could become a father, the hand by which he had been created was again ennobled by its touch; and he was continually nurtured and honored by divine conversation.

All these things, therefore—so long, so many, so great: the establishments, gifts, commands, and conversations provided by God—created no necessity of good in the human being. But, on the other side, the devil, no less timid than crafty, mixed a few words with a woman; and he is said to have possessed such power that they immediately became part of natural conditions, indeed overturned everything innate, made the necessity of evil perpetual, and imposed the devil as lord and possessor upon the image of God.

What, then, could be stronger, more excellent, or more magnificent than the opposing power, if by a light conversation it accomplished as much as God could accomplish neither by his works nor by his gifts?

It is therefore clear that you stand on the side of the one whose power you praise so immoderately, and that you have no fellowship in the worship of our God, whom we confess to be both supremely just and omnipotent. He is powerful, and truth surrounds him; he humbles the proud as one who has been wounded—that is, the devil and Manichaeus, and you, his followers, who slander nature so that you may not admit that you sin voluntarily.

Our God himself, therefore, destroys his enemies by the strength of his arm (Ps. 88:9, 11). By that arm, nothing could be brought forward either by you or by the Manichaeans that would not be shattered by the lightning of his truth.

AUG. We are not flatterers of the devil; nor do we, as you abusively charge us, exalt his power—which is subject to God’s power—with the adulatory proclamation of praise. But would that you were not his soldiers, as are all heretics, whose doctrines he hurls, through your tongues, like deadly weapons against anyone he can strike. The Apostle says: “Giving thanks to the Father, who has made us fit to share in the inheritance of the saints in light, who has rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love” (Col. 1:12–13). Yet you forbid us to give these thanks on behalf of little children, asserting that they are not under the power of the devil. Why, unless it is so that they may not be rescued from it, lest the devil’s profits be diminished?

Jesus says—he who, in accordance with his name, saves his people from their sins: “No one enters the house of a strong man to seize his goods unless he first binds the strong man” (Matt. 1:21; 12:29). Yet you insist that little children do not belong to this people of Christ, whom he saves from their sins, since you want them bound neither by their own sins nor by original sins. And when by your deceptive speech you diminish the strength of him whom Truth called strong, you make him, through your error, stronger in overcoming little children.

Jesus says: “For the Son of Man came to seek and to save what was lost” (Luke 19:10). You answer him: “There is no need for you to seek little children, because they were not lost.” Thus, when you repel the Savior’s search from them, you increase the power of the one who wounded them against them.

Jesus says: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners” (Matt. 9:12–13). You say to him: “Then you are not necessary for little children, because they are sinners neither by their own will nor by human origin.” Since, therefore, you prevent those who are not saved from coming to the physician to be saved, the devil’s plague exercises a more powerful dominion over them.

How much more tolerable, then, would it be for you to soothe the devil with false praises like parasites and flatterers than to assist him, as soldiers or bodyguards, with the falsehoods of your doctrines?

You describe in abundant and ornate language how God formed the human being from clay, animated him by breathing, enriched him with paradise, supported him with a commandment, and took such care not to burden him in any respect that he did not spread the commandment across many matters, lest the human being—whom he had created with such benevolence—feel the burden of an expanded law.

Why, then, does the corruptible body now weigh down the soul (Wis. 9:15)? Why, then, is a heavy yoke upon the children of Adam from the day they leave their mother’s womb (Ecclus. 40:1), since he was unwilling even to burden Adam himself with an enlarged law? Surely you see that, if no one had sinned in paradise, the fecundity of married couples would have filled that place of such great happiness with the human race, so that neither a corruptible body would weigh down the soul, nor a heavy yoke oppress those born as human beings, nor labor and pain educate pitiable little children.

Where, then, do these things come from? They are certainly not derived from some evil nature, alien to us and mixed with us, which Manichaeus invents or believes in. They come from the nature corrupted by the transgression of the first human being.

But you, an acute and prudent man, are surprised and do not think it credible that the devil’s few words, mingled with the woman’s, are said to have possessed such power that they overturned all natural goods—as though it were the words of the speaker, rather than the assent of the hearer, that accomplished this. For, as you say, the serpent’s few words were not transformed into the condition of natural things; rather, the human will lost a good that could not be restored by human will, but only by God, who, as the most just, most powerful, and most merciful judge, would determine when and to whom it should be restored [Note: [Col. 1547] The old Port. manuscript reads *judicabat* (“he judged”).].

Just as, in the body—as we have already said—human will can remove a person’s sight; but once this happens, blindness follows, and necessity can endure it though will cannot remove it; so in the mind the human will can destroy a person’s innocence but cannot restore it.

Rather, consider this: the evils with which human beings are born, which could not have been born along with human beings in the happiness of paradise, would certainly not now be born along with them unless the corrupted nature had gone out from paradise. Look at these evident facts. We do not merely conjecture in the dark about the evils of mortals from the day the children of Adam leave their mother’s womb; we see them in the clearest light. Since these evils do not arise from the commingling of another evil nature, they undoubtedly arise from the corruption of our own.

Nor should it seem improper to you that the image of God has been subjected to the devil. This would not happen except by God’s judgment, and this condemnation is not removed except by God’s grace. The one who, by the excellence of his nature, was made in the likeness of God so as to be God’s image has become, through the corruption of his nature, like vanity; and therefore his days pass away like a shadow (Ps. 143:4). Tell me why innumerable images of God, who commit no sins in their infancy, are not admitted to the kingdom of God unless they are reborn. They possess something by which they deserve to lie beneath the devil, and for which they do not deserve to reign beneath God. If you adhered to his light, you would not compare your words, with such arrogance, to lightning.

### XXI. JUL.

It is therefore perfectly clear that Augustine differs in no respect from his teacher, but that in his disputations the nature of Adam no less than that of the rest is declared utterly evil. Finally, let us discuss once more with him something of what we have treated. It is evident that you also do not consider the first sin to be of the same kind as other faults. For when you say that the crimes of later ages cannot pass into nature—for example, that children born of a thief, a parricide, or an incestuous person are not born liable to the sins of their parents—and that no crime is mingled with the seeds except that one, you show most clearly that you do not consider that disobedience to be of the same kind as the other sins.

Consider, then, how brief and clear our question is. If the sin committed by Adam was assumed by the will and could become natural, why are the sins committed daily—sins which a criminal will perpetrates—not accumulated into the deformity and prejudicial condition of the seeds? But if these sins, though no less atrocious and more numerous, cannot be generated in this way, by what law, condition, or privilege is that one alone claimed as innate? If the sins we know, which the law condemns and justice punishes, are of one kind, and if the sin of the first human being was committed by the will and punished by justice, why do we not understand either these sins from that one, or that one from these? Or, if they cannot serve as mutual testimony for one another, with what impudence is that transgression denied to have been of another condition—namely, produced not by the will but by natural corruption?

Finally, dare to define with confidence any sin—not, for the moment, that first one, but even one of those now committed, such as sacrilege, depravity, or some other evil deed—and explain what definition these sins have. Without doubt you will say: “It is a will desiring what justice forbids, and from which it is free to abstain.” For if an evil will did not exist, sin could not exist [Note: [Col. 1548] Vignier reads: “sin would not exist.” The manuscripts read: “sin could not exist.”].

Pay attention to how reasonably we may rise to meet this. O stupidity! O unbearable impudence! You define sin as nothing other than a free will forbidden by justice, although the opinion of natural evil prescribes that there is a sin with which a human being is born, and which is not voluntary. It is therefore not true that there is no guilt except what is voluntarily committed, because there is a crime—and a very great one—that is received not voluntarily but by being born.

Withdraw, then, that definition of sin, which is friendly to Catholics but turns aside to you without even the right of hospitality; and once it has been withdrawn, prove that you are not a fellow soldier of those who attack substance itself out of hatred of corruption.

And to gather together what we have discussed: either no sin will be shown to be voluntary, if there is some natural sin; or no sin will be natural, if every sin is defined as voluntary. The result is that you must either deny that sin can be born and pass over to the faith of the Catholics, or, if you persist in maintaining that some crime—and indeed the greatest crime—can be received by nature without the will, you must also give your name to Manichaeus, to whom you offer complete obedience.

### AUG.

You think you bring great odium upon me when you say that I differ in nothing from my teacher. But I take your abuse as praise of me; and, recalling to my faith not what you intend but what your words convey, I understand them as I ought. You speak the truth and do not know it, just as Caiaphas, the high priest and persecutor of Christ, was thinking criminal thoughts yet uttered salutary words without knowing it (John 11:49–52).

I rejoice entirely that, in this dispute between us, I differ in nothing from my teacher. First, because the Lord himself taught me that little children are dead unless he gives them life—the one who died for all. Explaining this, the Apostle says: “Therefore all have died, and he died for all” (2 Cor. 5:14–15). Yet you contradict this, denying that little children are dead so that they may be given life in Christ, even though you confess that Christ died also for little children.

John, the apostle of the Teacher of all, teaches me the same thing. He says that the Son of God came for this purpose: “to destroy the works of the devil” (1 John 3:8). You deny that these works are destroyed in little children, as though he did not come for them, who came precisely to destroy the works of the devil.

Nor should I deny my teachers, who have helped me to understand this through their literary labor. My teacher is Cyprian, who says that an infant, born carnally according to Adam, drew the contagion of ancient death in his first birth, and for that very reason approaches more easily to receive the remission of sins, since what is remitted to him is not his own sins but the sins of another [Col. 1549] (Epistle 64, to Fidus).

Ambrose is my teacher. I have not only read his books but also heard him speak, and through him I received the bath of regeneration. I am indeed far inferior to him in merit, but I confess and openly declare that in this matter I differ in nothing from my teacher.

Far be it from you to dare to prefer Pelagius, your teacher, to him. Yet against you I take Pelagius himself as my witness concerning Ambrose. Pelagius said that no enemy had dared to criticize Ambrose’s faith and most pure understanding of Scripture (Pelagius, *On Free Will*, book 3). You dare to criticize him in such a way that, when he says that the discord of the flesh was turned into our nature through the transgression of the first human being (Book 7 on Luke 12:53), and whatever else he perceived and said concerning human nature corrupted through Adam, you assert that it is a Manichaean invention.

You do preserve part of your teacher’s testimony concerning this great man, since you do not dare to criticize him openly. But when you abuse me by name with a malicious tongue and brazen face, you certainly also accuse him—and the other great and distinguished teachers of the Catholic Church who thought and spoke the same things—all the more wickedly because your accusation is oblique.

I therefore defend against you both my own faith and the faith of those whom you openly fear to have as enemies and, unwillingly, endure as judges [Note: [Col. 1549] The printed editions read *invictus* (“unconquered”); the manuscripts correct this to *invitus* (“unwillingly”).].

But your arguments will have no force before such judges. In them you compare that great sin—the transgression of the first human being—with the sins of later ages, and you think that, if the nature of the human race was changed by the crime of the first human being, the crimes of parents even now ought to have changed the nature of their children [Note: [Col. 1549] The old Mar. manuscript reads *vitiata est* (“was corrupted”).].

In saying this, you do not consider that, after committing that great sin, those sinners were expelled from paradise and were excluded from the tree of life with such severity. Are the criminals of the present age thrown from this earthly world into some lower lands when they commit crimes here, however great those crimes may be? Are they forbidden the tree of life, which does not exist in this misery?

Yet the place and life of the human race continue, and even the most impious people live within them, whereas we see that the place and life of those impious people could not remain after sin as they had been before sin.

According to your opinion, little children, bound by no guilt, ought as soon as they were born to be carried by angels into God’s paradise as innocent images of God and to be nourished there without any labor or pain, so that, if any one of them sinned, he would deservedly be expelled from there, lest sins increase by imitation.

But now, when only the man who sinned in paradise heard: “The earth shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you; cursed in all your works; and in the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread,” we see no human being exempt from the punishment of labor. That labor certainly would not have burdened the blessed inhabitants of paradise.

And when only his wife heard: “In sorrow you shall bear children” (Gen. 3:16–19), we know no woman who gives birth to be exempt from this punishment.

Are you so absurd, then, as either to think that human beings would have suffered these hardships in paradise if no one had sinned, although it is perfectly clear that God then imposed them only on those transgressing human beings; or to deny that their descendants now endure them, exiles from paradise and suffering so many and such great miseries throughout the earth; or to claim that the more sinful and impious someone is, the more his fields produce thorns and thistles and the more he sweats in labor, and that the more wicked a woman is, the more severe are the pains she suffers in childbirth?

Thus, just as the punishments of human misery, which the children of Adam commonly endure from the day they leave their mother’s womb, belong to all because their parents are common to all, and these punishments came from their transgression, so the transgression of those two must be understood as so great a sin that it could change for the worse the nature of all who are born from man and woman and bind them by a common guilt, as by the document of an inherited debt.

Whoever, therefore, says that the condition of whatever offenses are now committed ought to have been the same as the condition of that offense which was committed amid such great happiness of life and such great ease of not sinning, must also equate the two lives themselves: the life now being lived and the life lived in those holy and blessed delights.

If you see that this is utterly foolish, cease trying to prescribe from the sins of the present age, lest that great sin lose its own force and its distinctive gravity.

Moreover, even in this life that omnipotent and just one who says, “I will visit the sins of the fathers upon the children” (Exod. 20:5), clearly shows that descendants are entangled by the guilt of their parents and, although by a milder bond, become inherited debtors—unless, as we have argued in the earlier parts of this work, the New Testament, not your argument, and the grace of rebirth, not natural generation, release them from the bond of that proverb commonly spoken: “The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children’s teeth are set on edge” (Jer. 31:29).

But that definition of sin—which understands sin as a will desiring what justice forbids and from which it is free to abstain—is the definition of that sin which is merely sin, not of that which is also the punishment of sin. I do not know how many times this has already been said to you in answer to these points. For when someone says, “I do not do the good that I want, but the evil that I do not want, that I do” (Rom. 7:15), it is not free for him to abstain from this evil; and therefore he calls upon a liberator, because he has lost his freedom.

### XXII. JUL.

Time warns us to pass on to other matters, but indignation compels me to remain a little longer in the same place. Do you dare to say that Adam sinned by his will? Where did this dream come to you from? “Because,” you say, “it was unjust for God to impute something as sin unless it was something from which he knew us to be free to abstain.”

What, then? Had that prince of darkness whom you worship trusted this justice for a moment, and, soon demanding it back, deprived this God of all equity, so that the one who had understood from the beginning that nothing could be imputed as sin except what it was free to abstain from would, throughout all remaining time, know that it had not been free for anyone born to abstain?

Finally, how do you know that it was just only that Adam could be punished for a voluntary crime, if you do not know that it is unjust for anyone to be charged with a crime which you admit was assumed without the will?

You must therefore either consider the opinion of the *tradux*—the transmission of sin—to be just, so that it can agree with God’s sentence when he imputes to a little child a sin committed without any will of that child; and you will also be forced to profess it just and consistent with God’s judgments that he imputed to Adam as sin what he knew had been produced in him not by his will but by the deformity of his substance. On this account there will be no transmission at all, nor will nature be blamed as corrupted by the agent’s choice; rather, nature, badly constituted from the beginning, will be blamed, and you will confess yourself to be a Manichaean.

Or, if you recover your senses and say that it is unjust for Adam to be held guilty for the faults of his nature, it follows irrefutably that it is utterly wicked for Abel, Enoch, Noah, and the entire human race to be considered liable to original guilt.

If you bring this crime of judgment against your God, he alone will remain guilty on behalf of all, and it will become clear—as always—that he is not the one whom Catholics worship as the supremely just one in the Trinity.

If you desist from accusing God, you will condemn the Manichaean *tradux*—the transmission of sin—which has until now pierced you through, even if it has returned from the dead.

### AUG.

This is why you are gravely mistaken; this is why you are heretics; this is why, against the Catholic faith—which avoids heretics, follows the divine utterances, and is fortified by them—you dare to construct novel machines from human and empty arguments. You do not know, and because you cannot understand you refuse to believe, how powerful are the bonds of seeds in the succession of generation, and, among creatures whom God willed to be born one from another according to their kind, how great and ineffable are the natural laws of propagation—laws penetrated by no sense and comprehended by no thought.

From these laws arises that implanted affection in the human race by which all people, so far as they themselves are concerned, wish to have children whom they know to be their own. In chaste women, the fidelity of the marriage covenant serves this purpose. For this reason the philosopher Plato rightly displeased us: in the city which he constructs in debate as though it were the best, he judged that women should be used promiscuously. What else did he intend by this than that the older citizens should show all the younger the love which he saw nature itself owes to children, since each person would think that someone could be his child if he saw that person to be of an age at which he might reasonably be believed to have been born from his seed through any unknown woman with whom he had had intercourse indiscriminately?

What of that utterance which Cicero brought forth from the inmost hearts of all fathers and addressed to his son? Writing to him, he says: “You alone are the one by whom I would wish to be surpassed in everything.”

Did not the natural laws of propagation—which, as we have said, are most hidden, yet which we know to have more power than can be believed—bring it about that two twins, not merely not yet begetting but not yet even born, still in their mother’s womb, were called two peoples (Gen. 25:23) [Note: [Col. 1551] Vignier reads *jura fuerunt* (“were laws”). From the manuscripts we correct this here and below to *jura fecerunt* (“made laws”).]?

The same natural laws of propagation brought it about that Israel is said to have served in Egypt (Deut. 14:22), that Israel departed from Egypt (Exod. 14:30), that Israel entered the promised land, and that Israel received good things or experienced evils which God either granted or inflicted upon that people.

It is also written concerning this people: “He will come from Zion, the one who delivers and turns away impiety from Jacob; and this is my covenant with them” [Note: [Col. 1552] The manuscripts read this way. The printed editions instead read: “and he will remove iniquity from Jacob, and this is my testimony to them.”], “when I take away their sins” (Isa. 59:20–21). Yet the man who first and alone received these two proper names had died long before and did not see these good or evil things.

These natural laws of propagation also brought it about that the same people were tithed in Abraham, for no other reason than that they were in his loins when he himself was tithed by his own will (Heb. 7:9–10). That people, however, was tithed not by its own will but by the natural law of propagation.

But how that same people was in Abraham’s loins—not only from him until the time written about in the Epistle to the Hebrews, but also from that time until the present, and from the present until the end of the age, for as long as other Israelites are generated from other Israelites—how, then, could such an innumerable multitude of human beings have been in the loins of one man? Who could explain it in words, or even discover it by thought?

For even the seeds themselves, whose quantity is bodily, though each is small, from which each individual is born—if they were gathered together, those from which all the human beings who have been born, are born, and will be born to the end were produced—they could not have been contained in the loins of one man.

There is therefore some invisible and intangible power implanted in the hidden structures of nature, in which the natural laws of propagation lie concealed. Because of this power, however, it is certainly not falsely said that all who could be propagated from that one through successive generations and proliferations were in the loins of that father.

They were not only there; they were also tithed when he, knowing and willing it, was tithed, while they themselves were tithed without knowing or willing it, because they did not yet exist as beings capable of knowing and willing.

The author of that sacred Epistle said this in order to place the priesthood of Christ—which was prefigured by the priest Melchizedek, who tithed Abraham—above the Levitical priesthood. He also teaches that Levi himself, who tithed his brothers—that is, received tithes from them—was tithed by Melchizedek in Abraham, because he too was in Abraham’s loins when Melchizedek tithed him, that is, received tithes from him.

Accordingly, he does not want Christ, to whom it was said, “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 110:4), to be understood as having been tithed, so that he may rightly be preferred to the Levitical priesthood (Heb. 7). Melchizedek tithed Abraham [Note: [Col. 1552] The two lines beginning “he does not want” and ending “Abraham” have been restored here on the authority of the manuscripts.]; he was not himself tithed, as Levi was in Abraham.

But if it is asked how Christ was not tithed, since it is clear that, according to the origin of the flesh, he too was in Abraham’s loins when that father was tithed by Melchizedek, nothing presents itself except this [Note: [Col. 1553] The word *nisi* (“except”) has also been added here from the authority of the manuscripts; in the immediately following line, *parentum* (“of the parents”) has likewise been restored from the manuscripts.]: Mary, his mother, from whom he assumed flesh, was indeed born from the carnal desire of her parents; but she did not conceive Christ in that manner. She bore him not from male seed but from the Holy Spirit.

He therefore did not belong to the reckoning of male seed through which those who are attested by sacred Scripture to have been tithed in Abraham’s loins were there.
