Now, the desire of the flesh through which the emission of carnal seed is aroused either did not exist at all in Adam before sin, or it was corrupted in him through sin. For either the genital organs could then move appropriately and semen could be infused into the wife’s womb without it, if it did not then exist; or it too could have served the will at its command, if it did exist.

But if it were such now, the flesh would never desire against the spirit. Therefore, either it is itself a defect, if it did not exist before sin, or it was certainly corrupted by sin; and for this reason original sin is drawn from it.

There was therefore in Mary’s body the carnal material from which Christ assumed flesh, but carnal desire did not sow Christ in her. Thus he was born from flesh and with flesh, yet in the likeness of sinful flesh, not as other human beings in sinful flesh. For this reason he dissolved original sin in others through regeneration, but did not contract it himself through generation.

Thus Adam was the first, and Christ the second: Adam was made without the desire of the flesh, while Christ was born without it. But Adam was merely human, whereas Christ was both God and human. Therefore Adam could refrain from sin, unlike Christ, who could not sin.

You strive in vain, then, either to equate with the sin of that man the sins of his children, however great and horrible, or even to prefer them to it. The more exaltedly that nature stood, the more grievously it fell.

That nature was such that it could not die if it had not wished to sin. That nature was such that it had no discord between flesh and spirit. That nature was such that it did not struggle against its vices—not because it yielded to them, but because there were none in it.

You ought therefore to equate the sins of his descendants with his sin only if you can find a nature like his; and you ought to call them greater only if you can find a better nature. For the higher a rational nature is, the worse its fall; and the more incredible its sin, the more damnable it is.

Thus the angel fell irreparably, because “from the one to whom more is given, more is required” (Luke 12:48). He therefore owed more voluntary obedience in proportion to the greater goodness of his nature. Hence he was punished for failing to do what he ought to have done in such a way that he can no longer even will it, having also been destined for eternal torments.

But Adam, together with the innumerable descendants whom no one can count, is liberated from eternal punishment by the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord. Adam was also liberated in himself, although thousands of years after his death, when Christ died for us and descended to the regions of the dead—not by necessity but by power—and released the pains of hell (Acts 2:24).

For Wisdom is to be understood as having led him out of his sin (Wis. 10:2) in this way: through the holy flesh of the only Son of God [Note: [Col. 1553] The old Mar. manuscript reads: “of his Son, God.”], which he generated, the father of the human race—and therefore also the father of Christ, who became human for the salvation of human beings—was then released from those bonds. The Church does not believe in vain that this happened not by his merit but by the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord [Col. 1554].

This, then, is what God imputed as sin to the first Adam: something from which it was free for him to abstain. But that first Adam was of such an excellent nature—because it had not been corrupted—that his sin was as much greater than the sins of others as he himself was better than others.

Accordingly, the punishment that immediately followed his sin appeared so great that he was immediately held by the necessity of dying, although it had been within his power not to die; he was immediately expelled from the place of such great happiness; and he was immediately forbidden the tree of life.

When this happened, the human race was in his loins. Therefore, according to what we said earlier, because of the exceedingly hidden and highly powerful natural laws of propagation, it followed that those who were in his loins and were to come into this world through the desire of the flesh were condemned together with him, just as it followed that those who, by that law of propagation and reckoning of seed, were in Abraham’s loins were tithed together with him.

All the children of Adam were therefore sprinkled with the contagion of sin in him and bound by the condition of death. Accordingly, although they are little children and do no good or evil by their will, because they have been clothed with the one who sinned by his will, they draw from him the guilt of sin and the punishment of death.

Likewise, little children who are clothed with Christ, although they have done no good by their own will, receive from him a share in righteousness and the reward of eternal life. Thus Christ is shown as the pattern of what was to come by contrast, which is why the same Apostle says: “Just as we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of the one who is from heaven” (1 Cor. 15:49).

Since this is so, let anyone who dares say that those who are born are not clothed with the sin and death of the first Adam also say that those who are reborn are not clothed with the righteousness and life of the second Adam—although the former have not committed the sin from which it is free to abstain, nor the latter performed the righteousness which it is free to perform.

### XXIII. JUL.

“That sin, then, which changed the human being himself for the worse in paradise, because it is much greater than we can judge, is drawn from everyone who is born” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 2, no. 58).

Who told you that Adam’s sin was much greater than Cain’s, and even much greater than the sin of the Sodomites? Finally, who told you that it was much more monstrous than yours and Manichaeus’s? Certainly the historical account provides no occasion for this vanity.

He had been commanded to abstain from eating the fruit of one tree. Inexperienced, unskilled, incautious, without the experience of fear and without an example of justice, at the woman’s prompting he took the food, whose sweetness and beauty had enticed him. See [Note: [Col. 1554] The Port. manuscript reads *video* (“I see”).] that this was a transgression of a commandment.

One transgression was committed among the others which the zeal of sinners perpetrated at different times. It was no greater than when the people of Israel used animals that had been forbidden. The cause of the sin lay not in the quality of the fruit but in the transgression of the commandment.

What, then, did Adam do that you accuse his sin of having been beyond human estimation? Unless perhaps, following the mysteries of Manichaeus—who restrains his hands from picking fruit and from every growing thing, lest he tear apart a portion of his god, which he supposes enclosed in bark and grasses—you too think that Adam committed a grave offense because, by eating the fruit, he tore apart the substance of your god.

O madness! “Because that sin is much greater than we can judge,” he says, “it is drawn from everyone who is born.”

So it was a greater crime to eat the fruit when it was forbidden than to stab holy Abel out of murderous envy; than to violate the rights of guests and of the sexes in Sodom; than to sacrifice one’s own children to demons after the law had already been given; than, finally, to subject innocent little children, conscious of no will of their own and newly made by God, to the kingdom of the devil and join them to his merits; than to accuse God of injustice; than to assign honorable marriage to the prince of darkness; and, finally, than to consider little children—because they are born through the pleasure of those who generate them—worse than all the impious, worse than all pirates?

I am not inventing this; I am drawing it together from what you say. You declared that sin to be so much greater and more enormous than every other crime that no guilt could be compared with it. Yet you assert that little children arrive full of this great evil, which outweighs every vice.

We have therefore understood correctly: the more they share in the greater sin, the more they are placed ahead of all criminals in condemnation.

AUG. Because of the words from my book that you have quoted, as though they could be refuted if you were able, where I said, “That sin, therefore, which in paradise itself changed the human being for the worse, because it is far greater than we can judge, is drawn by everyone who is born,” you ask me who told me that Adam’s sin was far greater than Cain’s, and far greater even than that of the Sodomites. I did not, in fact, express this in my own words, but you understood them in this way. For I said that that sin was greater than we can judge; I did not say that it was greater than Cain’s or the Sodomites’ sin.

The taking of the forbidden fruit, since it was punished in such a way that nature, which had possessed the power not to die, acquired the necessity of dying, undoubtedly surpasses every human judgment. To eat the fruit forbidden by God’s law might seem a slight sin; but how highly the One who cannot be deceived judged it is sufficiently shown by the magnitude of its punishment. Cain’s crime, as a fratricide, appears monstrous to everyone, and is plainly a horrible offense. If it is compared, as you do, with the illicit plucking of the fruit by human assessment, the comparison will be judged ridiculous. Yet although the fratricide was destined to die someday, he was not punished by death, by which human courts customarily avenge such crimes.

For God said to him: “You shall work the ground, and it shall no longer give you its strength; groaning and trembling you shall be upon the earth.” When Cain heard that the earth would not give him fruit according to his labor, and that he would be wretched upon it, groaning and trembling, he was even more shaken by fear of death, lest someone do to him what he himself had done to his brother. God therefore placed a sign upon him, so that no one who found him would kill him (Gen. 4:12–15). Here again there was a great fault and a light punishment—but this is how it appears to human judgments, which neither understand these mysteries nor can weigh human faults with the clear and uncorrupted judgment with which God weighs them.

The Sodomites, indeed, were consumed when fire came upon that land from heaven, with a punishment corresponding to their deeds (Gen. 19:1–25). But there were also little children there—pure, through your advocacy, and free from every taint of sin. Yet the just and merciful God did not, by the ministry of angels—which would have been entirely easy for him—snatch so many innocent images of himself from the conflagration of Sodom, nor did the Almighty provide them, as he did the three men in the furnace (Dan. 3:49–50), with harmless flames while their parents were being burned.

Consider these things; think about them carefully and devoutly. When you see little ones and adults alike subjected in this world to miseries of a kind that could in no way exist in God’s paradise if no one had sinned, acknowledge original sin and the just, heavy yoke placed upon the children of Adam from the day they leave their mother’s womb (Ecclus. 40:1). Do not make their burden heavier by your defense, denying Christ the Savior and Life-giver to the sick or the dead.

For if you ask who told me how great a sin Adam committed, it is he himself who told you as well. But if you have ears to hear, you will hear him. You will have them if you do not attribute them to your own judgment, but receive them from him who said, “I will give them a heart to know me, and ears that hear” (Baruch 2:31). Who, except one who lacks such ears, does not hear Scripture saying without any obscurity or ambiguity to the first sinful man, “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. 3:19)? This clearly shows that he would not have been destined to die even in the flesh—that is, to go into the earth from which his flesh had been taken—by the death of the flesh, unless he had deserved to hear and suffer this on account of sin. Hence the Apostle later said, “The body indeed is dead because of sin” (Rom. 8:10).

Who does not hear, except one who lacks such ears, God saying concerning Adam himself, “Lest he should at some time stretch out his hand and take from the tree of life, and eat, and live forever”; and “the Lord sent him forth from the paradise of pleasure” (Gen. 3:22–23)? There, certainly, he would have lived forever without any labor or pain. For that pleasure of paradise—which you must acknowledge, if you have not yet forgotten the Christian name—is to be understood not as disgrace but as blessedness.

[Note: Col. 1556. Vignier reads “unless”; Codex Portianus more correctly reads “if.”]

This punishment, then, which Adam deserved—that he should not live forever, and therefore was sent away from the place of such great blessedness, where, if he had been there and had not sinned, he would undoubtedly have lived forever—how great a punishment it is should teach us how great the sin must have been that deserved to be punished by it.

What are you doing, then, I ask you, when you strive so insistently to diminish Adam’s sin, except accusing God of monstrous and dreadful cruelty—God who punished it with such a punishment, not merely with such severity but with cruelty? If it is wicked to think this of God, why do you not measure the magnitude of the sin—about which human beings cannot judge—by the greatness of the punishment, imposed by a judge incomparably just, and restrain your tongue from sacrilegious talk?

I, however, do not accuse God of injustice. I say that he placed a just yoke upon the children of Adam from the day they leave their mother’s womb. You, rather, make God unjust, because you think that they suffer this without any merit of any kind of sin. I say that those born from the first human being remain under the same enemy—not because of the work God created, but because of the vice the enemy implanted—unless they are reborn in the second human being.

[Note: Col. 1557. On the authority of the manuscripts, we have added: “unless they are reborn in the second [human being].”]

In this you accuse the Catholic Church of the crime of treason against divine majesty, if, as you say, infants are not rescued from the power of darkness when they are baptized, while the Church exorcizes and exsufflates, before their baptism, so many images of God.

Nor do I assign honorable marriages to the prince of darkness; rather, I cleanse them from every fault of lust, provided that they make proper use of them with the intention of procreation. You, however, do not shrink from placing in paradise the evil by which the flesh lusts against the spirit—that is, in a place of such peace, such rest, such honor, and such happiness.

Nor do I, as you slanderously claim, judge little children who have no sin except original sin worse than all the wicked and criminal. For it is one thing to be burdened by a sin committed by oneself, and another to be touched by the contagion of another’s sin, however great it may be. For this reason, as the African Cyprian says, little children approach the remission of sins all the more easily because sins are remitted to them that are not their own but another’s (Epistle 64, to Fidus).

But when you say that little children not only have committed nothing by their own will—as we too say—but also have drawn no sin from their origin, you undoubtedly make God unjust. This has already been said to you often and must be said still more often: he placed a heavy yoke upon them from the day they leave their mother’s womb.

To understand how children born from Adam are bound by participation in that man’s sin and yet are not made equal to his guilt, consider Christ, whom you have read to be “the form of the one to come” (Rom. 5:14). See how little children, reborn in him and made participants in his righteousness, become so; and do not dare to compare them with his merits.

You yourself, in the second book of this work (above, chapters 189–190), said that in Adam the pattern of sin—because Eve sinned first—was not the first but the greatest, just as in Christ the pattern of righteousness is not the first but the greatest, because there were righteous people before him. If you had not forgotten what you said, you would not here diminish Adam’s sin, in whom you confessed that the greatest pattern of sin had appeared.

[Note: [Col. 1557] Codex Port.: “the pattern of sin you confessed,” omitting “had appeared.”]

## XXIV. JUL. Why should you be disturbed by envy of the enemies of innocence, when the wantonness and frenzy of an obscene mouth are not restrained even by reverence for divinity? You accuse little children, but together with God; you attack innocence, but with injury to justice; you deny the truth, but while accusing the one whom you confess to be your God. And so, even if we were to fail for want of rational support, the transmission of sin would nevertheless collapse completely through the deformity of its advocates.

[Col. 1558] AUG. Your abusive loquacity has charged me with the frenzy of an obscene mouth. Am I a defender and praiser of lust? Have I dared to enrich with possession of paradise the desire of the flesh, by which the flesh lusts against the spirit? Into that place of such beauty and peace you have introduced either warfare, against which one laudably struggles when it urges one to sin, or disgrace, to which one shamefully yields.

Why, then, do you rise against me so insultingly and fail to look at yourself? I do not accuse God; but you do, when you say that little children draw no sin from their origin, although he placed a heavy yoke upon them. Nor do I attack innocence with injury to justice; rather, you injure justice when you say that little children possess such innocence—children whom justice would not punish with a heavy yoke if what you yourself think were known to be true.

[Note: Col. 1558. Vignier reads “and”; the manuscripts read “whom.”]

Nor do I deny the truth or accuse God; you do so instead. For the Apostle spoke the truth: “The body is dead because of sin” (Rom. 8:10)—which you deny. How do you not accuse God when you attribute to little children, who possess no original sin worthy of misery, the miseries that you cannot deny?

[Note: [Col. 1558] Here we restore from the manuscripts the words “who possess no original sin worthy of misery.”]

And so your conclusion, which imposes deformity upon us, does not follow the truth of any reasoning.

## XXV. JUL. But why do we so obstinately think that only the reasoning of truth must be followed, when the phalanx of our enemies rests upon the very dangers of reality and rises against us fortified by the support of hardships?

[Note: [Col. 1558] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read “hostile.”]

They wish to establish by the shame of intercourse, the pain of childbirth, and the sweat of labor that faults and punishments are transmitted into seeds, so that by these signs—the difficult labors, the sweating farmers, and the newly cleared fields full of thorns—it may be believed that there is a natural crime, on account of which the human race is exercised by so many troubles. Some think that this was made mortal through Adam’s sin. I said “some” because their leader Augustine was ashamed to say this. For he writes to Marcellinus that Adam appears to have been made mortal, but then, with his customary elegance, adds that death was the wage of iniquity; and although he admits that Adam was constituted mortal according to nature, he declares that he could not have died.

The statements customarily brought against us from Genesis are therefore those by which Adam and Eve are harassed. It is now time to discuss them. “The Lord God said to the serpent,” he says: “Because you have done this, you are cursed above all cattle and above all the beasts that are upon the earth. Upon your breast and belly you shall walk, and you shall eat earth all the days of your life. And I will place enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed. She shall seize your head, and you shall seize her heel.”

[Note: [Col. 1558] The printed editions read “shall trample”; the manuscripts disagree and read “shall seize.”]

“But to the woman he said: Multiplying, I will multiply your sorrows and your groaning; in sorrow you shall bear children, and your turning shall be toward your husband, and he shall rule over you.

“And to Adam he said: Because you have listened to the voice of your wife and have eaten from the tree concerning which I commanded you, forbidding you to eat from it alone, cursed is the earth in your works. In sorrow you shall eat of it all the days of your life. Thorns and thistles it shall produce for you, and you shall eat the grass of the field. In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread, until you return to the earth from which you were taken; for you are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. 3:14–19).

You therefore take these statements as testimony to innate iniquity and proclaim that women would not have suffered pain in childbirth unless, together with Eve’s sin, the misery of her fertility had passed over to them.

[Note: Col. 1559. The manuscripts read “in giving birth”; the printed editions read “in paradise.”] You want the punishment itself to be an indication of sin, so that what the first woman deserved through her offense may be thought to be suffered by every woman without that same iniquity.

“For,” you say, “there would be no pain in the woman giving birth unless there were sin in the one being born.” How astonished I am as I confront these claims is not easy for me to measure. Your opinion has applied so many goads at this point that I can scarcely be moved to engage in the contest. There are more sins against understanding in these objections than there are syllables.

AUG. However much you mock—or pretend to mock—the hardships of the human race with your witty and facetious speech, those very hardships have driven you into these straits, so that you are forced to affirm that God’s paradise would have been a place of hardship even if no one had sinned. If, out of shame, you refuse to make this claim, your own doctrine will compel you to do so. Unless you abandon that doctrine after correction, you will not escape these straits, which press upon you and thrust you into a dreadful precipice.

For you are asked where you think these hardships come from, hardships that we see in both adults and little children. You reply, according to your doctrine, that from its beginning the human race was divinely constituted in this way. Your reply is met with this response: “Then they too would have existed in paradise if no sin had arisen there.”

At this point you will either plunge headlong, change your doctrine, or be corrected in mind—or, shameless in face, remain unchanged. Either you will fill the place of famed happiness with a life of hardship

[Note: Col. 1559. The printed editions read “smokiest”; this is corrected from the manuscripts.]

 and find no eyes with which you dare to look at Christians, however they may be; or, cast down into more horrible depths, you will attribute these human hardships to an alien, evil nature mingled with ours

[Note: Col. 1559. Vignier reads “mingled with an alien evil nature,” omitting “and with ours,” which is present in the manuscripts.]

and be swallowed up in the Tartarean abyss of Manichaeism; or you will confess that this punishment of hardships arises from a corrupted nature, through the judgment of God who punishes, and you will breathe again the Catholic air.

You even say that some think the human race was made mortal through Adam’s sin. You add that you said “some” because I, their leader, was ashamed to say this, although I wrote to Marcellinus that Adam appeared to have been made mortal. Those who have read, or are reading, both your words and mine

[Note: Col. 1559. Vignier reads “read my words”; on manuscript authority, “have read, or” has been added.]

, if they are not Pelagians, certainly see how your tongue has embraced deceitfulness.

I never thought, and never said at all, as you say, that Adam was made mortal in the sense that he would have died whether he sinned or did not sin. These exact words were brought as an accusation against Coelestius in the episcopal judgment at Carthage. They were also brought as an accusation against Pelagius in the episcopal judgment in Palestine (On the Proceedings of Pelagius, §§23, 60; and On Original Sin, §§3–4).

For this is precisely the question at issue between us and you: whether Adam would have died whether he sinned or did not sin. Who does not know that according to the definition by which one is called immortal who cannot die and mortal who can die, Adam could die because he could sin, and therefore could die by the merit of guilt, not by the necessity of nature?

According to the other definition, by which one is also called immortal if it is within his power not to die, who can deny that Adam was created with this power? For whoever had the power never to sin certainly had the power never to die.

This, then, is what is said against you: your doctrine, by which you think Adam would have died whether he sinned or did not sin, is entirely false.

Since this is so, how could I say what you falsely claim I said—that Adam was constituted mortal according to nature, as though he were driven by the necessity of dying—when he could not be driven into death except on account of sin?

[Note: Col. 1560. The negative particle is supplied on the authority of the manuscripts.] Or how do I declare that he could not have died, when I know that he did die?

[Note: Col. 1560. The manuscripts read “that he died”; Vignier reads “that he would die.”] If he could not have died, he would not have died.

But I plainly declare that he could not have died. “Not being able to die” is one thing; “being able not to die” is another. The former is the greater immortality; the latter the lesser. If you distinguish these two, you see both what you say about Adam and what we say against you.

You say: “Whether he sinned or did not sin, he would have died.” We say: “As long as he did not sin, he would not have died; and if he had never sinned, he would not have died.”

Next you recall what is customarily said against you from Genesis. Concerning the pain of the woman giving birth, by which the earlier Eve was punished, you attribute to us something that you want us to be thought to say, or think we say.

We do not say that women would not have suffered pain in childbirth unless the misery of Eve’s fertility had passed over to them together with her sin. Rather, the misery that passed over to them was not the misery of fertility but of iniquity.

[Note: [Col. 1560] These words had fallen out of the printed editions: “the misery that passed over to them was not the misery of fertility but of iniquity.” They appear in all the manuscripts.]

For although fertility was made miserable, iniquity, not fertility, caused this. The misery of childbirth descended from human iniquity, whereas fertility descended from God’s blessing. Or, if you did not mean the misery of fertility in the sense that fertility itself caused it, but that fertility received it, this is our position.

We do not, however, say that women in paradise would also have suffered pain in childbirth. Rather, we infer from this that the pain is a punishment for sin, because it would not have existed in that place, where those who sinned would not have been allowed to remain. You attempt to refute this only by being forced, with your hand placed over your forehead and your eyes closed, to fill God’s paradise not only with human lusts but also with torments.

But what wonder is this, when you wish to fill that place of memorable happiness even with human deaths—deaths of which none, or almost none, occur without some bodily torment?

[Note: Col. 1561. Vignier reads “since indeed you wish to fill it”; the manuscripts read “when you wish to fill it.”]

[Col. 1561] And when your doctrine compels you to utter such monstrosities, you dare to mock those who, heaven forbid, refuse to say such things because they hold what was handed down anciently in the Church of God

[Note: Col. 1561. The manuscripts read “anciently”; Vignier reads “more anciently.”]

, whence it was said, “From a woman sin had its beginning, and because of her we all die” (Ecclus. 25:33). You even insultingly call me their leader, against your own knowledge and conscience.

For you certainly cannot be unaware how many learned men and teachers of the Church, and how eminent they were, said before us that human nature was divinely constituted in such a way that, if it had not sinned, it would not have died. How, then, am I called the leader of these men, whom I do not lead but follow?

I do not say that you are the leader of those who assert that Adam was made mortal in such a way that he would have died whether he sinned or did not sin, and who thus strive to fill the paradise of holy pleasure—where there was such great rest of soul and body—with the torments of the dying, the funerals of the dead, and the mourning of the bereaved.

You are not their leader. Pelagius and Coelestius, who first made these assertions, hold the primacy of this wicked doctrine. Would that, just as you do not lead them, you also did not follow them!

## XXVI. JUL. How insane is this very claim of yours—that you say the pain of childbirth is an attendant of sin, when it so plainly concerns the condition of the sexes more than the punishment of crimes that all animals, stained by no sin, suffer these anguishs and groans in giving birth? This shows that what can be found even without sin is not an indication of sin.

Then, as you advance your argument, you bring forward another claim, much more foolish. “A woman,” you say, “would not feel pain unless she were a participant in crimes.” But immediately you add: “Yet the sin because of which the woman suffers is not found in the one giving birth but in the one being born. For this reason, you say, even baptized women, though free, are agitated by sin”—

[Note: [Col. 1561] Thus the old Codex Portianus. Other manuscripts, together with the printed editions, read: “you say, freely, while sin agitates.”]

“—but they suffer the difficulties of their fertility on account of the iniquity of the children they bear. According to this view, the transmission of sin no longer flows from the mother into the offspring; rather, it flows back from the one being born into the parents. For if a baptized woman feels pain because iniquities are found in the little child, then the transmission of sin begins to be upward rather than downward.”

“But,” you will say, “she is not tormented because her child has iniquity, but because she herself had brought that iniquity with her when she was born.”

Yet you had said that this evil was removed from her by grace. If, therefore, pain adhered to sin, the removal of sin ought to have cured the anguish of childbirth. Or if this anguish cannot exist without iniquity, although it is found in women after baptism, then iniquity too was not removed from them by grace, and the splendor of baptism has faded.

But if, in these mysteries, there was the power and truth that we believe, not that which you imagine, and if all sin was removed, while pain nevertheless remains—the pain generated by the difficulty of childbirth—it is evident that this groaning is an indication of nature, not of guilt. Even you acknowledge that it is suffered by women whom you admit have been freed from the sin of the Manichaeans.

This has appeared from the examples of things alone. But if we also examine the very words of the statement, that wording will dissolve your clouds with a brilliance brighter than the sun’s rays.

For it was not said to the woman, “Pains shall arise in you,” or “I shall generate groans for you,” as though their sensation were instituted after the guilt. Rather, he said, “Multiplying, I will multiply your sorrows.” He showed that something already existed in the natural order which he promised not to create in the sinful person but to multiply.

Things are never multiplied unless they already exist. Before they exist, they may properly be said to be made; to call them increased would be premature.

Finally, so that this may not seem to be our interpretation rather than that of the truth itself, the same order of words is preserved throughout all living creatures. Concerning the human being, before he was made, God said, “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:26). And again, concerning the woman, after the man had been made, he said, “It is not good for man to be alone; let us make him a helper like himself” (Gen. 2:18).

After they had been made, he blessed them, saying, “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth” (Gen. 1:28). Before he was created, it was not said, “Let man be multiplied,” but “Let man be made.” After there existed one who could receive increase, he appropriately added, “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth.”

In this order, therefore, the groans of childbirth—which had been established according to nature in human bodies just as in cattle—were not created in Eve but increased, so that the anguish aroused by that extraordinary circumstance might afflict her. Yet they would not reach women of later generations except through the ordinary measure of nature and the variety of bodies.

Thus the fact that a woman should suffer pain in childbirth came not from sin, but the fact that she should suffer excessive pain did. Likewise, we read that at various times bodily weaknesses came upon certain people because of sins; but this increase of misery did not overturn the sparing measure of the natural order.

Nor does the force of attentive observation encompass everything contained in that same sentence. Some part of it indicates merit; some part designates duty.

“Multiplying, I will multiply your sorrows and your groaning; in sorrow you shall bear children.” Up to this point there is punishment, which the person, not nature, deserved.

From here onward the function of the later sex is simply indicated: “Your turning shall be toward your husband, and he shall rule over you.” This plainly does not pertain to punishment; if it did not exist, it would pertain to guilt. For a woman to be subjected to a man with a modest affection is order, not punishment.

According to the Apostle, “the head of the woman is the man” (Eph. 5:23), because “man was not created for the woman, but woman for the man” (1 Cor. 11:9). If, therefore, she reveres her head with fitting modesty, she preserves the institutions of nature; she is not suffering the torments of sin. But if she rebels against that order, she is guilty.

A function whose neglect is blameworthy is therefore not itself a misery.

AUG. We say that the pain of childbirth is the punishment of sin. For we know that God said this without any ambiguity, and that he said it only to the woman who had transgressed his commandment, and that he said it for no other reason than that he was angry that his commandment had been transgressed. But in order to empty and nullify this anger of God, you said that this punishment is so far from being the punishment of sin that animals, which have no sins at all, suffer groans and pains of this kind in giving birth. The animals did not, of course, tell you whether that groan is one of singing or of pain [Note: [Col. 1563] The old codex Mar. reads, “one of singing, not of pain.” Codex Port. reads, “whether it is one of striving or of pain.”]. We certainly observe that hens about to lay are more like singers than sufferers; after laying, however, they utter sounds of the sort they customarily make when frightened. Moreover, when they are laying they are in complete silence, as are doves and other birds, which become known to those who pay attention.

Who, then, knows whether dumb animals, which cannot indicate what is happening within them, do not experience in the act of giving birth not only no pain but even some pleasure? But why should I investigate the hidden things of nature in this matter, when our case does not depend on them? In any event, if dumb animals suffer no pain in giving birth, your argument is worthless; but if they do suffer, then that very punishment is the punishment of the image of God: to be made comparable to animals. The punishment of the image of God, however, could not be just unless guilt had preceded it.

Far be it from me to say what you thought you had to refute as though I had said it: that the mother suffers in giving birth not on account of her own merit but on account of the merit of the one being born, and that therefore faithful women suffer even after their sins have been forgiven, when the necessity of giving birth presses upon them. Far be it from me, I say, to say this. For, because we say that death is the punishment of sin, must we therefore say that death ought not to have occurred after the remission of sins?

These punishments, which we say are punishments of sin in a nature corrupted by transgression, remain even after the remission of sins so that the faith which we hold concerning the world to come may be tested—a world in which these things will not exist. For it would not be faith if we believed for this reason: that the reward of feeling no pain and not dying would immediately be given to us. With this reason given—that is, that the evils contracted through sin are left to us for the contest of faith, although the guilt of sins has already been removed through Baptism—what force is there in what you said: “If all sin has been removed in the mysteries, and yet the pain produced by the difficulty of childbirth remains, it is evident that this groan is an indication of nature, not of guilt”?

You certainly would not say this, if you either possessed or attended to the power of faith. That power is all the stronger the more earnestly we hope for what we do not see and await the fullness of blessedness through enduring miseries.

“But,” you say, “the very words of God show that this already existed in the natural order, which he promises not to create in the sinful person but to multiply. He does not say, ‘Pains will arise in you,’ or, ‘I will produce groans for you,’ so that their sensation might appear to have been instituted after the guilt; rather he says, ‘Multiplying, I will multiply your sorrows.’” And you add, as though stating a general and definitive rule: “Things are never multiplied unless they already exist; but before they exist, they are properly said to be made, whereas to call them increased is premature.”

First, then, I ask how you can say that Eve’s pains already existed when she had not suffered them: how, I ask, could she already have pains when she felt no pain? If her pains did not already exist in her because she did not possess them, since she felt no pain, then even things that did not exist could be multiplied. And the statement, “I will multiply your sorrows,” is rightly understood as meaning, “I will make them many”; this can happen whether something has already begun to exist or has not yet begun.

You therefore said in vain, “They are never multiplied unless they already exist.” For behold, after sin Eve’s pains were multiplied, although before she sinned there were none. Accordingly, God did not say, “I will multiply your sorrows,” because some sorrows had already begun to exist in her, but because they were going to be many once they began to exist.

“But,” you say, “they existed in the natural order.” If, then, things that have not yet arisen already exist in the natural order, how does what you said help you—that God did not say, “Pains will arise in you,” but “I will multiply your pains,” because they already existed in the natural order? The answer to you is this: he could have said, “They will arise in you,” because he was going to multiply pains that already existed in the natural order, not pains that had already arisen.

Or perhaps you will say that they had already fully arisen in the natural order itself? How much more plainly, then, and more acceptably, can one say to you that the children of Adam already existed in Adam in the natural order when, as blessed John the bishop says, Adam committed that great sin and condemned the whole human race in common [Chrysostom, *Homily on Lazarus Raised*]; or, as his colleague Ambrose says, “Adam existed, and in him we all existed; Adam perished, and in him all perished” [Book 7 on Luke 15]. If you dare to say not merely, “They already existed,” but even that Eve’s pains had already arisen when God threatened that he would multiply them, although we do not dare to say of ourselves, as Adam’s children, that we already existed when that sin was committed.

Yet Eve’s pains, which women giving birth necessarily suffer, did not already exist in the natural order, because it was not necessary for her to suffer them when she began to give birth. They came through the condemnation of guilt, not through the condition of nature.

What do you accomplish by denying this, except that you place human sufferings—even when no one has sinned—in that place of blessedness where human beings were not permitted to remain, although they would already have had to be tormented? I do not know with what face you do this, unless it is because, as opponents of paradise, you take pleasure in dwelling, as it were, against paradise; for Adam too, having been expelled from paradise, was placed opposite paradise (Gen. 3:24, according to the Septuagint).

Since you are thus opposed to paradise, observe with what vanity you argue against paradise. You think that only things which already exist in some respect can be multiplied; before they exist, you think they should be said not to be multiplied but to be made. On this principle, then, no multiple things come into being unless they are multiplied by additions—that is, unless they are made multiple. Accordingly, the “manifold spirit” said to exist in Wisdom (Wis. 7:22), which did not begin to exist but is thus from eternity, was not rightly called manifold, since no additions made it manifold.

What will you say, moreover, about God’s answer to Abraham, where he says, “Multiplying, I will multiply your offspring like the stars of heaven” (Gen. 22:17)? Here we see that God also multiplied the stars of heaven, just as he promised to multiply Abraham’s offspring. Did the stars of heaven first begin to be fewer, so that they could be multiplied, rather than being established as multiple in their own number from the moment they were established [Note: [Col. 1565] We add from the manuscripts, “from the moment they were established.”]?

Why, then, do you not understand the statement, “I will multiply your sorrows,” as though he had said, “I will make your sorrows multiple”? The reason is that you act as though, if possible, you might introduce pains into paradise, contrary to the place in which you were placed, and proclaim that miseries were instituted in a place of such great blessedness before sin.

For when you assert that Eve naturally received childbirth with its pains before she sinned, you call this “natural frugality” [parcimonia naturalis]; yet you do not want it to appear that this frugality was overturned by the increase in the punishment added to the woman when God avenged her sin. For you speak as follows: “But that increase of miseries did not overturn the frugality of the natural measure.”

Thus, according to your teaching, it is natural frugality for women to suffer moderate pain in childbirth; but what was added to Eve on account of sin is an increase of miseries. You do not see, when you say this, that if miseries were increased through sin, they had already been instituted through nature, and that the woman whose miseries were increased on account of sin was already naturally miserable before sin.

You may say that she was moderately miserable through natural frugality; nevertheless, whether you wish it or not, when you say that an increase of miseries was added to her, you plainly confess that she was miserable even before this addition.

Behold what human nature, originally instituted by God, deserves from you; behold what God’s paradise deserves from you. Having been expelled and placed opposite it, you have returned such things in opposition to it that in a place of blessedness you say that miseries were divinely instituted—not begun through sins, but increased through sins.

What is more contrary than misery to blessedness, and blessedness to misery? Or what does it signify that the sinner, expelled from paradise, was placed opposite paradise, except that he was placed in misery, which is without anyone’s contradiction [Note: [Col. 1565] Vign. reads, “without anyone’s doubt.” From the manuscripts we have added, “or contradiction.”] or doubt contrary to blessedness?

And what does nature flee so much as misery? What does it desire so much as blessedness? Indeed, the free choice that we possess concerning this matter is naturally implanted in us so firmly that no misery can take away from us the desire not to be miserable and to be blessed. So much so that even those who are miserable because they live wickedly nevertheless wish to live wickedly, but do not wish to be miserable; rather, they wish to be blessed.

This is the free choice fixed immovably in our minds—not the free choice by which we wish to act well, for we were able to lose that through human iniquity and can recover it through divine grace, but the free choice by which we wish to be blessed and do not wish to be miserable. Neither the miserable nor the blessed can lose it.

For we all wish to be blessed. Even the philosophers of this age, and the Academics who doubt about everything, were compelled to confess this, as their patron Cicero testifies; and they said that this alone was something requiring no debate, since there is no one who does not desire it.

This free choice is aided by God’s grace, so that we may obtain through living well what we naturally desire—that is, to live in blessedness.

And you say that miseries, even if moderate, are nevertheless miseries—contrary to blessedness, as no one denies or doubts—and that they were naturally instituted among God’s first works, without any preceding sin on anyone’s part. Thus, the punishment of the sinful woman, on account of which it was said, “Multiplying, I will multiply your sorrows,” is not the institution of miseries, which, as you say, had already existed in nature, but merely an increase added as punishment.

What am I now to do with you concerning the following words of God? After saying what pertained to punishment [Note: [Col. 1566] Vign. reads, “what pertained to,” omitting “punishment,” which we restore here from the manuscripts], “In sorrow you shall bear children,” he immediately added, “And your turning shall be toward your husband, and he shall rule over you” (Gen. 3:16).

Why should I dispute with you over whether this rule of the husband is a punishment for the woman or an order of nature? God did not mention this order when he created her, but when he punished her.

Yet, as I said, why linger over a matter which, whichever way it is understood, does not hinder our case? Suppose that God suddenly turned from the punishment he was inflicting on the woman to giving a command, and that in commanding rather than condemning he said, “Your turning shall be toward your husband, and he shall rule over you.” What does this have to do with the question of punishment for the sinful woman that we are examining in this discussion?

I am dealing with the miseries which you, having been expelled from paradise and placed opposite it, attempt to locate in paradise; and you attribute them not to the merits of sinners but to God, the creator and establisher of natures, as though he had naturally instituted these things as well—at the cost of your shame and with your mouth blaspheming.

Now say what you also try to persuade us concerning the man’s punishment, since it is already sufficiently clear what this woman—who before sin was naked and was not ashamed—has stripped and confounded you with.

XXVII. JUL. But enough of this concerning the woman; let us proceed to the man’s duties. He says that God spoke to Adam: “Cursed is the earth because of your works; in sorrow you shall eat it all the days of your life. It shall produce thorns and thistles for you, and you shall eat the grass of the field. In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread, until you return to the earth from which you were taken; for you are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. 3:17–19).

Here it is not said, “I will multiply your thorns,” or “your sweats”; rather, they are said to have been created at that time for the first time. But even the objection arising from this is dissolved by an effort no greater than that required in the case of his wife. At the beginning, the curse is directed not against the seed of man but against the soil. “In your works,” he says, “the earth shall be cursed.”

What had the fields deserved—which certainly could have received nothing from Adam’s transmission—to receive the reproach of a curse for another’s voluntary sin? Or was it so that, by the example even of the clods themselves, it might be shown that something can be accursed where there is no guilt?

For if there is sin in the man and a curse in the crop, it is clear that crimes do not always adhere to losses. If, then, the earth is cursed so that the one who sinned may be afflicted, while nevertheless there is no iniquity in the place where the curse is contained, why should it not follow under the same condition that, even if it were shown that some hardships had been imposed upon our nature after the sin of the first man, those who are born would not therefore be miserable in order to be proved guilty, but so that, through a reminder of the first sin, a succeeding affliction might warn those whom it had not made guilty against the evil of imitation?

The earth too, after all, is shown to have endured the reproach of a curse for this reason: to expose the evil of another’s will, not to generate participation in his crime. Unless, perhaps, we believe that God values the earth more dearly than innocence, so that although he does not allow it to be polluted by another’s crime together with the clod, he nevertheless permits infancy to be condemned.

The curse, then, is directed against the earth, yet this very point is not left unexplained. The purpose toward which such a sentence tended, and the manner in which the soil was called accursed, are discussed. “In sorrow,” he says, “you shall eat it all the days of your life.”

Observe, then, in what sense this is to be understood. The earth is called accursed, not because punishment could be inflicted upon it, but by this expression the state of the sorrowing mind is revealed. Since the sorrowing man knew that the earth would be sterile in proportion to the merits of its cultivator, the distress of the hungry laborer attributed to the earth what he himself had deserved; and in his affliction he called accursed the earth whose abundance was closed off for this reason: so that the transgressor might confess that not nature or the earth, but his own will and person, were subject to the curse.

“It shall produce thorns and thistles for you.” He was not content to say, “It shall produce thorns and thistles” [Note: [Col. 1567] On the authority of the manuscripts we have added, “He was not content to say, ‘It shall produce thorns and thistles.’”]; he added, “for you.”

Among other shrubs and thorny bushes, it had long before been commanded to produce them. But now, so that man might be pricked, it is promised that it will become more bristling than usual. Adam could have been severely chastised by this, since after the springs and meadows of paradise even a single thorn could offend him.

But when it says, “In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread,” I do not see that this sufficiently pertains to hardship. For it is also a natural aid that the limbs of workers are refreshed by sweat. The reading itself testifies that labor had been imposed upon cultivation even before sin. For it says: “And the Lord God took the man whom he had made and placed him in paradise, to work it and guard it” (Gen. 2:15).

If, then, even in paradise God did not wish him to receive food wholly unworked, but by imposing the work that he had assigned him aroused his diligence, what new thing do we believe happened to him if he felt sweat while experiencing labor?

The passage continues: “Until you return to the earth from which you were taken; for you are earth, and to earth you shall go.” This final part of the sentence, like that concerning the woman, looks to an indication [Note: [Col. 1567] The printed editions read, “to judgment.” This has been corrected from the manuscripts], not to punishment; indeed, as the matter itself shows, it consoles the man by promising an end [Col. 1568].

Since he had mentioned above pains, labors, and sweats, whose experience nature had assumed but whose excess the person had assumed, lest this seem to extend forever, the indicated limit softens the distress [Note: [Col. 1568] The manuscripts read thus. Vign. reads, “gives life to.”], as though he were saying: “You will not suffer these things forever, but only until you return to the earth from which you were taken; for,” he says, “you are earth, and to earth you shall go.”

Why, after saying, “until you return to the earth from which you were taken,” did he not add, “because you sinned and transgressed my commands”? This would have had to be said if the dissolution of bodies pertained to crimes.

But what did he say? “Because,” he says, “you are earth, and to earth you shall go.” He showed the reason why he would return to the earth: “Because,” he says, “you are earth.” How he would be earth had been made clear by the preceding statement: “Because,” he says, “you were taken from the earth.”

If, then, God said that the reason for returning to the earth was that he had been taken from the earth, and if being taken from the earth could not pertain to iniquity, then plainly it belonged not to iniquity but to mortal nature that one who was not eternal should be dissolved in the bodily part.

That barrenness of the trees, then, that abundance of thorns, and that increased distress of painful childbirth were imposed upon individual persons, not upon the race.

Indeed, Cain and Abel were already born, both of one nature but of different wills. Neither did it benefit Cain, who sinned voluntarily, that the sins of his father had not weighed upon him; nor did it harm Abel that his parents had sinned. Each of them, by his own judgment, publicly showed through a different purpose and a different outcome that no natural predisposition to virtue or vice had inhered in him.

Having undertaken the office of priests, they offered sacrifices to their creator, God. Their unequal care, however, distinguished them in the manner of their service. The divine judgment made this clear: it showed that Abel’s offering was pleasing to God, while to Cain, who had offended him, it disclosed the reason for God’s indignation, saying that he had offered well but divided badly.

Without delay, the profane mind burst into envy; burdened by his brother’s holiness, he gratified envy with fratricide. Thus, on the first occasion, it became clear that death is not itself an evil, since the righteous man was the first of all to consecrate it.

Yet Cain did not escape the anger of God through the audacity of his guilty mind. He is questioned about his brother, convicted of the crime, handed over to punishment, and, beyond the terror that weighed upon him as a mark of his cruelty [Note: [Col. 1568] Codex Port. reads, “and beyond the trembling that weighed upon him on account of his notable cruelty”], he is also punished by a curse upon the earth:

“Cursed are you by the earth, which has opened its mouth to receive your brother’s blood from your hand. When you work the earth, it shall no longer give you its strength” (Gen. 4:3–12).

Behold, once again the earth’s barrenness is imposed as punishment upon the cultivator. Countless torments of the human race [Note: [Col. 1568] Perhaps, “of this sort.”] are promised in Deuteronomy.

What, then? Did the thickets of our lands, whose removal the cultivator watches over armed with a pruning hook, spring up through Cain’s fratricide? And because you think that every owner of thorny ground is made liable by the sin punished through the abundance of thorns, will all infants now be said not only to have eaten apples—although they are born without teeth—but also to have shed Abel’s blood?

It is certainly apparent to what madness the Manichaean doctrine of transmission proceeds [Note: [Col. 1569] So the manuscripts. The printed editions read, “to what it pertains,” omitting “madness.”]. Since it has nothing but insanity, the gravity of the Catholics laughs at your arguments [Note: [Col. 1569] The printed editions read, “truth.” The manuscripts, however, read, “gravity.”], but their compassion weeps over your ruins.

AUG. Indeed, your very prolonged and painstaking discussion of the punishment of the first man accomplishes nothing except that, by diminishing this punishment, you also diminish the guilt itself, which was condemned to bear this punishment. And you do this because of the words in my book to which you are replying, which you set before yourself as though they needed refutation. There I said: “That sin, then, which itself changed man for the worse in paradise, because it is much greater than we can judge, is drawn from everyone who is born.”

Thus, in order that the sin may not seem great enough to have changed nature for the worse, you contend that the punishment it deserved was slight and almost nothing. Hence it is that you twist the accursed earth, imposed in punishment for the transgressor’s works, toward the perversity of your doctrine. Hence it is that you assert that thorns and thistles were instituted even before man sinned, although God does not name them among the things first instituted by him, but threatens them as part of the sinner’s punishment. Hence it is that you have said that the sweat of the laborer, as though it did not seem sufficiently connected with hardship, was also a natural aid, so that the limbs of those who work might be refreshed by sweat—as though, when God said these things, he were not imposing punishment for sin, but additionally granting a reward.

We might indeed say this appropriately if you praised the sweat of labor in such a way as to say that it was instituted at that time. But you now affirm that, even before sin, man was placed in paradise in such a condition that he could not cultivate the earth without labor—as though that strength, and the complete absence of bodily weakness, could not have enabled him to perform what might give delight not only without labor but even with pleasure of mind.

Yet you could not conceal why you said this. For you speak most openly when you add: “What new thing, we ask, happened if he felt sweat, since he experienced labor?” Did you take such delight in bringing not only the sorrows of childbirth among women but also the sweat of labor among men into that most tranquil place of the blessed, that, when God pronounced condemnation, you could say that nothing new happened to the condemned man? Do you mock and despise the severity of God so greatly [Note: [Col. 1569] The manuscripts read thus. The editions have *veritatem* (“truth”) instead of *severitatem* (“severity”).] that what he imposed as punishment you assert was given naturally?

If you say that nothing new happened to the man to whom God said, “In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread,” then deny that God said this in condemnation. Or will you say: “Indeed, by these words he condemned the man, but nothing new happened to the man because of it”? Then he condemned him, but the condemned man was not affected? Was the force of vengeance frustrated, as though God had hurled a weapon but had been unable to strike the one he wished to strike?

“On the contrary,” you say, “he was both condemned, and nothing new happened to him.” Here it is difficult to restrain laughter. For if he was condemned and nothing new happened to him, then he used to be condemned, and consequently he used to sin—for he would not have been condemned unjustly. Or, since no one doubts that he then sinned for the first time, was he accustomed to be condemned unjustly beforehand?

For, unlike what you said about the woman, you did not even admit that this at least was something new that happened to the man: that just as pain in childbirth was added to the woman, so sweat in labor was added to the man. By such an addition—something that had not existed previously—you would have conceded that something new happened to him. But when you say, “What new thing happened to him?” while nevertheless confessing that he was condemned, what else are you asserting than that he was accustomed to being condemned?

Or, if we do not say that something usually happens unless we know that it happens repeatedly, you must surely concede that he was condemned at least once beforehand, when you assert that nothing new happened to him because he was condemned in this way. You see into what precipices your argument has driven you.

Return, then, from the precipice of your laborious discussion, and do not bring labors and pains into the dwelling places of happy joys and into the place of ineffable repose.

Moreover, you also try to bring bodily death into paradise in such a way as to say that it was promised—or rather announced—to the transgressor as a benefit, when God said, “You are earth, and to earth you shall go.” It is as though man did not know that he had been created in such a way that, whether he sinned or did not sin, he would die; and as though God had granted him this knowledge only then, when he condemned him for the iniquity he had committed.

For, discussing these words of God, where he says, “In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread, until you return to the earth from which you were taken; for you are earth, and to earth you shall go,” you say:

“This final part of the sentence, like that concerning the woman, refers to an indication, not to a punishment; indeed, as the matter itself shows, it consoles the man. For because he had previously mentioned pains, labors, and sweats, the experience of which nature had assumed, while the person had borne their excess, lest this seem to continue forever, the indicated limit softens the affliction—as if he were saying: ‘You will not suffer these things forever, but only until you return to the earth from which you were taken; for you are earth, and to earth you shall go.’”

By saying this, you try to persuade us that man was indeed created in such a way that, even if he had remained in the uprightness of life in which he was created, he would nevertheless eventually die through the necessity of nature; but that this had not been announced to him except at the time of his condemnation, so that his misery might receive consolation from the promise of an end and not be thought eternal.

Adam, then, would have thought that he would not die if God had not announced this to him. But God would not have announced it to him unless the sinner had to be condemned. He would therefore have remained in the error by which he believed himself to be eternal, or never destined to die, unless he attained—through the merit of sin—the wisdom by which man comes to know himself.

Do you realize what you are saying? Consider another point. Undoubtedly Adam, not knowing that he would die—for if he had not sinned, he certainly would not have known it—would nevertheless have been blessed if he had been unwilling to sin, even while ignorant of this; and, believing something contrary to the truth, he would not have been miserable.

Do you hear what you are saying? Consider a third point. If, while Adam was living in his righteousness, he believed that he would not die bodily if he did not violate God’s commandment, but learned that he would die only when he violated it, then what we believe is what he believed while he was righteous; whereas you believe that he was not worthy to know this unless he became unrighteous. Thus our error lies on the side of righteousness, while your wisdom lies on the side of iniquity.

Do you understand what you are saying? Consider a fourth point. If God did not announce the future death of his body to that blessed and righteous man, but did announce it to the wretched sinner, then it is more fitting to believe that he wished to torture him also with fear of death, judging him worthy of this torment as well.

For, as nature itself cries out, death is feared more than labor. All people labor so that they may not die, if the choice were offered to them that they should die immediately if they did not labor. But who is found who would rather die than labor? Finally, Adam himself preferred to labor for so many years rather than, by not laboring and dying of hunger, bring both life and labor to an end together.

For in what other sense did Cain, too, naturally fear death more than labor? In what other sense do judges, through judgments that are neither unjust nor inhuman, condemn lesser crimes to labor in the mines, but greater crimes to death? And why are martyrs proclaimed with such glory because they died for justice, unless it is because it is a greater virtue to despise death than labor?

For this reason the Lord did not say, “No one has greater love than to labor,” but rather, “than to lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13). If, then, greater love consists in dying for one’s friends than in laboring for them, who is so blind as not to see that the punishment of labor is less than that of death?

Or, if a man ought to fear labor more than death, how can that nature itself not be wretched which fears death more than labor? And you, without considering these things, say that man was consoled by having his death announced to him, lest he think his labor eternal.

Yet if your doctrine were true—that Adam would have died even if he had not sinned—this would not have needed to be announced to him before the punishment of condemnation began, lest God torture him with fear of death before he sinned. But then, after he had sinned and God judged him fully deserving of punishment, God would also announce that he was going to die, thereby increasing the same punishment, as a just God and avenger of the wrong committed, by the fear of death.

Whoever, therefore, understands these words of God by which Adam was punished, when it was said, “You are earth, and to earth you shall go,” according to the Catholic faith, and does not wish especially to introduce bodily death into paradise, must also introduce diseases there—diseases whose pitiable variety we see afflicting the dying—and will be forced to fill the paradise of holy delight and spiritual and bodily happiness, to which you are not ashamed to be opposed, with pains, labors, and sorrows. You are driven to this, and find no way out, so long as you refuse to change so impious a doctrine.

Whoever, then, as I said, receives and understands these words of God according to the Catholic faith sees the punishment of labor in what was said, “In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread,” and likewise sees the punishment of death in what follows: “Until you return to the earth from which you were taken; for you are earth, and to earth you shall go.”

He therefore understands the words as though God were saying:

“I indeed took you from the earth and made you man. Certainly I could have made it so that the same earth which I made living would never be compelled to be deprived of the life I gave it. But because, being earth—that is, according to the flesh taken from the earth, and not according to me, who took you from the earth—you chose to live, you shall labor in the earth until you return to it. And therefore you shall return to the earth because you are earth; and in just punishment you shall go to the earth from which you were made, because you did not obey the spirit from whom you were made.”

This sound and Catholic understanding is recognized especially because it does not force us to fill the earth of the living with deaths, nor the earth of the blessed with all the grievous and burdensome evils through which human beings suffer in this corruptible body and, unable to endure them, are driven to die.

For you cannot say that people would have died gently in paradise if no one had sinned. That too is against you. If they would then have died gently, whereas now they die so harshly, then human nature was changed through man’s sin. Since you deny this, you are consequently forced to introduce deaths exactly like those we now experience in place of that great happiness and delight; and therefore also innumerable kinds of diseases, so severe and intolerable that human beings are compelled by them to die.

If the appearance of such a paradise makes your faces blush and confounds you even somewhat, you who refuse to confess that our nature could have been changed through sin, change your opinion instead. With the Apostle, confess that “the body is dead because of sin” (Romans 8:10). Say with the Church of God, “Sin began from a woman, and because of her we all die” (Ecclesiasticus 25:33).

Acknowledge with the Church of God that “the corruptible body weighs down the soul” (Wisdom 9:15). For before sin, the body in paradise was not such that the soul was weighed down by it.

Sing with the Church of God: “Man has become like vanity; his days pass like a shadow” (Psalm 143:4). For the one who was made in the likeness of God would not have become like vanity except through sin, so that through the course of the ages and the onset of death his days might pass like a shadow.

Do not cast the clouds of your error over the clearest light of truth. Do not make bitter for the hearts of the faithful the paradise of God, which they ought to love.

What, I ask you, offends you? What offends you in that celebrated place of the blessed and tranquil, that you wish to fill it—with closed eyes, a shameless brow, a stubborn mind, and a most loquacious tongue—with human deaths and, through them, all the evils by which we see the hardships and necessities of the dying abounding? You do this so that you may not be compelled to confess that, through the greatest sin of the first man, human nature fell into these miseries with which you see the human race filled, from the cries of infants to the gasps of the aged.

And because you see that it is unjust for the punishment of parents to pass to their descendants without guilt, you should also concede that the guilt passed to them. I prove that the guilt of the first man was very great—the guilt you tried to diminish as much as you could so that people would not believe that human nature could have been changed because of it—not only through the very miseries of the human race, which begin at the cradles of infants, but also through your own testimony.

For in the second book of this work of yours you placed the greatest pattern of sin in the first man, so that, by contrast, the greatest pattern of righteousness might be commended in Christ (above, book 2, chapters 189–190). You seem to have forgotten that you said this to me. For if you had remembered it, you would certainly never have tried to diminish Adam’s sin with such loquacity.

I, however, demonstrate that that sin was very great by the magnitude of its punishment. For there is no greater punishment than that he should be expelled from paradise and separated from the tree of life, lest he live forever. To these were added the distresses of this life, so that his days would groan amid labors and pass like a shadow.

Indeed, the hereditary calamity of the human race, from infants to the aged, is itself a witness. These miseries would not have the character of punishment unless they were transmitted through the contagion of sin. You obstinately contend with us about this contagion; and, to prevent it from being believed, you diminish both the sin of the first man itself and its punishment, while with the most shameless and impious contention you try to introduce pains, labors, and deaths into paradise.

You also say:

“If the earth is cursed so that the one who sinned may be afflicted, although there is no iniquity where the curse is contained, why should it not likewise follow that, if anything were shown to have been brought upon our nature as a hardship after the sin of the first man, those who are born would nevertheless not be miserable for the purpose of being proved guilty, but so that, through the remembrance of the first sin, a subsequent affliction might impose the warning of avoiding evil imitation upon those whom it had not made guilty?”

I see the straits by which you are pressed. You are compelled to confess the miseries of those who are born, because the force of the evidence presses upon you, and you are not permitted to deny what is set before the eyes of everyone. You do wish to assert that these miseries of those who are born would also have existed in paradise if no one had sinned; but you see that you cannot persuade people with any sort of heart of this.

It remains, therefore, that you confess that the human race was made miserable because of the sin of the first man. But, fearing to say this plainly, you say: “If anything were shown to have been brought upon our nature as a hardship after the sin of the first man.”

What does “if anything were shown” mean? Is the most manifest reality, which you too are now compelled to perceive, not shown? Or must you return to the point from which, through these words, you are gradually attempting to flee, understanding how intolerably absurd it is to believe that the miseries of those who are born would also have existed in paradise if no one had sinned?

And if you shudder to say this—for it is truly something at which one ought greatly to shudder [Note: [Col. 1573] The manuscripts read thus. Vignier’s edition has: “since it is truly something at which one ought to shudder to say it.”—]—why do you say, “even if it were shown,” when it is shown beyond any doubt that not merely some hardships, but all the hardships of those who are born, were brought upon our nature after the sin of the first man, indeed because of the sin of the first man?

“But,” you say, “those who are born are not miserable so that they may be proved guilty.”

Nor do I say, “Those who are born are miserable so that they may be proved guilty.” Rather, I say: “They are proved guilty because they are miserable.” For God is just—as you constantly say against yourself without knowing it. God is just, I say; and therefore he would not permit those who are born either to make themselves miserable or to be made miserable unless he knew them to be guilty.

Thus the Catholic faith understands the Apostle’s statement: “Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin, death; and so it passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Romans 5:12). You are unwilling to refer this to the bond of origin [Note: [Col. 1574] The editions read *sexum* (“sex”); the manuscripts read *nexum* (“bond”), perhaps for *noxam* (“guilt”).], and instead try to twist it toward an example of imitation.

This leads to the following question being put to you: Why, then, do infants, who have sinned through no imitation, testify to the miseries of the human race beginning at the very dawn of life through their innumerable and varied evils? As though overwhelmed by the most severe and unavoidable pressure of indigestion, you burst into these vomitations and say: “Those who are born are not miserable because they are guilty, but so that, warned by this misery, they may take care not to imitate the sin of the first man.”

For I thought this was what you meant to say more plainly and explicitly, though you had expressed it more obscurely and confusedly. But however you state it, who does not see that, in your eagerness to defend your opinion, you entirely refuse to consider what you are saying?

Were innocent people, I ask you, to be punished with misery—not because they had any sin, but so that they would not have any? Then Eve ought first to have been made miserable before she became guilty, so that she might be warned by her misery not to consent to the serpent. Adam too ought first to have been punished with the evil of misery, so that he might not consent to his seduced wife and thereby consent to the evil of sin.

You approve of punishments preceding crimes in order that crimes may be avoided, rather than of punishments following crimes in order that they may be avenged; and thus, perversely, not guilt but innocence is punished—not because sin has been committed, but so that it may not be committed.

Correct, I beg you, this perverse and upside-down opinion. You would certainly correct your tunic if you happened to put your right arm into the left sleeve. I say this because you want sins to be prevented by punishments that precede them, whereas sins that precede are ordinarily and rightly avenged by punishments that follow.

Next, tell us how we are to warn afflicted infants to look upon their misery so that they may not imitate the sin of the first man—infants who are not yet able either to imitate anyone or to be warned.

The earth was cursed. This is where you take your example for your delirium, because you suppose that those who are born could be made miserable so that they might avoid the sins of those who beget them, even though they do not derive original sin from them, just as the earth was cursed because of man’s punishment, although it itself had no guilt.

Why do you not attend to the fact that, just as the earth has no guilt, so it does not have punishment from that curse? Rather, when the earth is cursed, it itself becomes the punishment of the sinning man.

But when those who are born are miserable, they themselves experience their miseries. On your view, they themselves draw no sin from anyone; and, if this is so, they undoubtedly endure undeserved punishments. As I have said, they are not yet able to be admonished about anything, nor are they able to imitate the sin of the first man, on account of which they would need to be admonished [Note: [Col. 1574] The manuscript reading *imitari* (“imitate”) has been restored here.].

Are we to wait until they grow and reach free choice, when they can perceive someone admonishing them, and, by looking upon their misery, refrain from imitating another’s guilt? But where do we place the many who do not know until the day of their death who Adam was, whether he existed, or what he committed? Where do we place the many who die before reaching the age at which they can perceive an admonition? Where do we place those who are born with an intellect so dull and foolish that, even when grown, they cannot be instructed in such matters with any benefit?
