Surely all these are punished with so great a misery without any merit and without any benefit [Note: [Col. 1575] Here the old Codex Port. adds *si* (“if”): “if without any merit and without any benefit”; this is not inappropriate.]. Where is the justice of God? If you considered it, you would never believe that those who are born could be so miserable without the merit of original sin.

But since you spoke conditionally—for you did not say, “Because it is shown,” but said, “If anything were shown to have been brought upon our nature as a hardship after the sin of the first man”—you are prepared, I imagine, to say: “It is not shown.”

And so it remains for you to say that the evils we see infants suffering would also have existed in paradise if no one had sinned, lest you confess that they arose because of the sin of the first man.

Thus, while you seek to escape these knots and try to slip from our hands, you will stand immovable against paradise. You are so opposed to it that, in order to disturb its happiness and tranquility, you introduce into it, with the boldest mouth and most shameless brow, the pains of women in childbirth, the labors of those who work, the tossings of the sick, and the diseases of the dying.

But in praising death you think you have discovered something important to say—namely, that “at the first opportunity it became clear that death is not an evil, because the first righteous man of all dedicated it.”

Then explain how the righteous man could have had nothing to dedicate unless the unrighteous man had built it. For Cain was the author and maker of that death, not Abel. The one who fashioned it, then, dedicated it. The death of a good man was the evil work of an evil man.

But the man who endured evil for the sake of good dedicated not death but martyrdom, bearing the figure of the one whom the Jewish people, like an evil carnal brother, killed.

Therefore Abel is glorious—not because he received anything good from his brother, but because, patiently dying for righteousness, he made good use of his brother’s evil. Just as transgressors are punished by using the good of the law badly, so, conversely, martyrs are crowned by using the evil of death well.

Accordingly, if you do not disdain to say what I see you do not know: death is evil in all who are dying; but among the dead it is evil for some and good for others. Those who have committed laudable discussions of the good of death to writing followed this distinction.

The death of the righteous Abel, dwelling in rest, is therefore not only not evil, but even good. You, however, have introduced into paradise not the rest of the good who are dead, but the torments of those who are dying, so that there might be no rest of the good there.

Or, if you say, “If no one had sinned, people would have died in paradise without torment,” then, at least because scarcely anyone dies without torment outside paradise, you are finally convicted and compelled to confess that human nature was changed for the worse by the sin of the first man.

XXVIII. JUL. What, finally, is to be said about the serpent itself? Do you think that the devil was punished by that curse, or do you suppose it was this ordinary reptile? That is, do you think that the sentence which says to the serpent, “Cursed are you above all sinners and above all the beasts that are upon the earth; upon your breast and belly you shall go, and you shall eat earth all the days of your life” (Genesis 3:14), was fulfilled in the punishment of the devil, or in that of this beast which is brought out of its caves by the warmth of spring?

If you say that this curse applies to this serpent, whose form extends into a limbless body [Latin: *enode*; the precise zoological sense is uncertain], and that it was made earth-eating on account of the merit of that guilt, then the stock of iniquity also rests upon all beasts, which you suppose could be transmitted only through the lust of those who mate. It follows that you would assert that even the lust of serpents—and from that point the lust of irrational animals—was planted by the devil, and that, once the Manichaean doctrine had been exposed, you would chant a song at us [Note: [Col. 1576] The editions read *carnem* (“flesh”); the old Codex Mar. reads *crimen* (“crime”); Codex Clar. more suitably reads *carmen* (“song”).].

But if you profess that whatever is said concerning the serpent was fulfilled intelligibly in the devil, you will undoubtedly agree that what is presented there as vengeance is not now an indication concerning guilty serpents, and that the devil does not eat earth bodily. Even if he then took up the service of the dragon, and paternal severity later broke this as though it were the weapon by which he had used to wound man, nevertheless sin remained solely in the will of the agent.

That foods, thorns, and the sweat of labor were first instituted naturally, then increased judicially in certain cases, and have come down to our own age without any wonder caused by that sin [Note: [Col. 1576] Perhaps *adjunctione* (“addition”). Morel, *Elementa Critica*, p. 316, reads *admigratione*. M.]—these matters are so obvious that they require no lengthier defense.

AUG. Why do you twist your viperous cunning even concerning the serpent? For who, understanding appropriately these words of the divine book that you have recalled, would not see that the sentence was pronounced rather against the devil, who used the serpent for what he wished, in the way he was able [Note: [Col. 1576] Vignier has “used it for what he wished.” We have added, from the manuscripts, “in the way he was able.”], than against the animal itself, whatever earthly creature it may have been?

But because the devil did not act by himself, but through the serpent worked his seductive words, God therefore addressed the serpent in a way that suited the signification of the devil’s wickedness, and the nature of the serpent served as a figure of the devil.

Accordingly, what God said to the serpent—“Cursed are you above all cattle and above all the beasts that are upon the earth; upon your breast and belly you shall go, and you shall eat earth all the days of your life,” and so forth—is understood and explained all the better the more appropriately it is taken as referring to the devil.

But since, even according to the correct faith, these matters are often discussed in many ways, and it does not now pertain to the issue which interpretation among them I choose to present, it is sufficient for me to answer you that the nature of the devil has no connection whatsoever with the bond and succession of descent, which is the matter at issue when the question of original sin is being considered.

As for thorns and the sweat of the laborer, I believe that our earlier response will persuade readers how shamelessly you assert that they were instituted before sin.

For you wish to make paradise such that it cannot reasonably be called God’s, but rather yours. Nevertheless, although you said that thorns were instituted before sin, you did not dare to introduce them into paradise; indeed, you expressly indicated that they were not there. Yet you wished to place labor there, whose burden, even if it does not prick, presses down.

Nevertheless, if you too agree that thorns are not suited to paradise, is it really the case that no change from blessedness into misery occurred, or could have occurred without any merit of sin, in human nature—so that it was previously in a place where thorns were not, and now is in a place where they are?

Let this therefore compel you to acknowledge original sin, at least such a sin as you could not deny the punishment to be, if you do not believe that God is unjust.

XXIX. JUL. Yet, lest we seem to have passed over anything carelessly, consider another point. It is established that this pain of childbirth varies according to the bodies and strength of those giving birth. Certainly barbarian women and the wives of shepherds, who are hardened by exercise, give birth with such ease in the middle of their journeys that, without interrupting the labor of travel, they care for their offspring and immediately carry them along. They do not languish from any difficulty of childbirth, but transfer the burdens of their bellies directly to their shoulders. And generally the poverty of humble women does not require the assistance of midwives.

On the other hand, wealthy women are softened by luxury; and the more attendants each one has to trouble themselves over her, the more she both learns and desires to fall ill, thinking herself in need of as much care as she has an abundance of service.

The hands of rich husbands, certainly, never experience the hardship of the first man among thorn bushes. On the contrary, confident in their resources, they consider it beneath them to devote even a moment to the hopes of fertility; and, placing themselves beyond fear even of famine by expanding their possessions, they give orders repeatedly, as the poet says: “Unyoke the oxen” [Note: [Col. 1577] Vignier reads as the manuscripts: *de junge boves*. Juvenal has *disjunge boves*, “unhitch the oxen.” M.], “until you send truffles” (Juvenal, *Satire* 5, line 119).

If, then, the pain of those giving birth also belongs to the institutions of nature—as is thoroughly demonstrated both by the example of brute animals and by the exact sense of the divine sentence; if the withholding of fruits and the emergence of thorns were created among other things, but were made denser and more troublesome for certain persons; if, finally, just as the difficulty of childbirth itself varies according to bodies, so too does the thorniness of clods vary according to bodies and regions; and finally, if that distress continues after conception within women’s wombs, while the luxury of the wealthy is entirely unaware of it [Note: [Col. 1577] The editions read *luculentorum* (“splendid,” “illustrious”); the manuscripts more suitably read *opulentorum* (“wealthy”).];

if it was expressly stated why the dissolution of the body was going to follow, and it was attributed more to skills than to errors—then here too it is evident that everything agrees with the truth of the Catholics, and that neither women nor thorns are of any benefit to you.

AUG. When you were discussing the punishment that God inflicted upon the first sinners, you had already passed from the woman in such a way that you said, “Let this suffice concerning the woman.” Why, then, did you not keep faith with your promise? Behold, after so much, you return to her; behold, your loquacity is not satisfied with what you had said should suffice concerning the woman. But if you were not so verbose, how would you fill eight books, which you are returning to my single book? Yet say whatever pleases you: behold, after promising sufficiency, we have patiently listened also to your abundance. Why should you waste such fine observations, which later came to your mind? Although this too ought to have occurred to you: that, from your book, which was still in your hands and needed completion, you should remove what you had said, “Let this suffice concerning the woman,” lest you be read as so indecently contradicting your own promise.

But proceed; bring forward, contrary to your promise, what you later thought of. Say that the labor of childbirth varies according to the bodies and strength of those giving birth; and describe barbarian and rustic women as so capable of giving birth that they do not even seem to be in labor—and therefore do not feel merely a small pain in childbirth, but none at all. But if this is so, how does it help you? Are you not speaking against yourself, since you declared these pains to be so natural that Eve could not have given birth without them, even if she had remained in paradise without committing any sin? Are you going to say that your barbarian and rustic women are more fortunate in this respect than that first woman, so that in these lands of misery they give birth without pain to what she could not have done in paradise, had she given birth? It would be as though feminine nature had been changed for the better in them from the way it had been created, and human practice had proved more effective in changing it than divine action had been in creating it. [Note: [Col. 1578] Vignier reads “the practice of changing,” omitting “human”; the manuscripts restore the latter.]

But if you do not want your words to be understood as meaning that fierce and uncivilized women give birth without pain, and you grant them childbirth so bearable and easy that nevertheless you admit that they suffer when they give birth, does it follow that there is no punishment merely because it is less? Whether, then, these women suffer less when they give birth, or whether they endure pains equal to those of other women—or even pains greater than those of some others—with remarkable endurance acquired through practice, without being exhausted and weakened by that torment, they nevertheless suffer; and certainly all who suffer, whether they suffer more or less, greater or lesser punishments, nevertheless without any doubt undergo punishments. [Note: [Col. 1578] On the authority of the manuscripts we add, “nevertheless punishments.”]

If you were to consider yourself not, I do not say, a Christian, but merely a human being, you would more readily maintain that God’s paradise does not exist than make it punitive by your sacrilegious argument.

You elegantly defend wealthy men from the hereditary labor of the first man, while ignoring—or pretending not to know—that the rich labor more bitterly in their thoughts than the poor do in their physical work. Under the name “sweat,” Holy Scripture signified labor in general, from which no human being is exempt: some labor at harsh tasks, others are troubled by anxious cares. The studies of all who learn also belong to these labors. And what produces these studies, except this earth, which its Maker had not made burdensome when he created the first man?

But now, as it is written, “The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks of many things; and we scarcely judge the things that are on earth, and we discover the things that are before us with labor” (Wis. 9:15–16). Whether, then, a person studies useful or useless doctrines of any kind, since the corruptible body weighs down the soul, he must labor. Thus this earth also produces thorns for him.

Nor should the rich be called strangers to these thorns—especially since, in the Gospel, God the Teacher explains that the thorns among which the seeds are sown and by which they are choked so that they do not reach fruition are the cares of this life and the anxieties of riches (Matt. 13:22). He certainly calls not only the poor but also the rich when he says, “Come to me, all you who labor.” Why does he call them, unless because he says shortly afterward, “And you will find rest for your souls” (Matt. 11:28–29)? When will this be, unless when the corruption of the bodies that now weighs down souls no longer exists?

Now the poor labor, the rich labor, the righteous labor, the wicked labor, the great labor, the small labor—from the day they leave their mother’s womb until the day of burial in the mother of all. [Note: [Col. 1579] Thus the manuscripts. Vignier reads: “the righteous, the wicked, and the small labor, from the day of departure.”] So malicious is this age that, unless there is an exit from it, the promised rest cannot come to us. Although, through the transgression of the first man, labor came upon his descendants, nevertheless, even after the guilt of that transgression which we inherited has been dissolved, labor remains as a test of faith and as a contest. For we must struggle against vices and labor in that very struggle until it is granted us to have no adversary.

Therefore, so that good warriors may be brought to their rewards, punishments are turned into battles. The labors of little children also remain after original guilt has been dissolved, although they are taught to have arisen from that very guilt, because it also pleased God in this way to test the faith of their elders, by whom they are offered for regeneration.

What and how great would be faith in invisible things if invisible reward followed immediately, rather than the promised rest being postponed, so that faith would conduct its business with the heart and not with the eyes; and thus the future age, where there will be no labors—a thing we do not yet see—would be believed more sincerely and sought more desirably? Accordingly, God, in marvelous kindness, turns our labors—that is, our punishments—to our advantage.

Desiring to refute these things, you labor uselessly. You labor by producing thorns, not by uprooting them; whereas we labor to uproot your thorns, insofar as the Lord grants it. Unless perhaps you boast that you do not labor because you compose so many books with great ease of intellect, and, just as those barbarian and rustic women give birth to their offspring, so you give birth to thorns without difficulty. But I think that you boast vainly of the ease of your intellect. You certainly labor: for how do you manage not to labor, when you even try to introduce labors into paradise? Indeed, the more impossible this is shown to be, the greater—and the more futile—your labor is found to be.

### XXX. JUL.

I certainly shall not oppose those who maintain that Adam, if he had proved obedient, could have been transferred to immortality as a reward. For we read that Enoch and Elijah were transferred so that they might not see death. But the institutions of nature are one thing, and the rewards of obedience another. The merit of one individual is not so great that it should disturb everything that has been established naturally.

Innate mortality, then, would have exercised itself in the remaining cases even if that first man had passed from a long life into eternity. This is held not by an irrefutable conjecture but by a certain example: for the sons of Enoch could not, through their father’s immortality, be secured against the condition of dying.

Nor should this perhaps be thought to arise: that, if not sinners, nevertheless all the righteous would pass to immortality without the intervention of bodily dissolution. [Note: [Col. 1580] The printed editions read “disputation”; corrected from the Portarum manuscript.] Abel, the first of the righteous, Noah, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and all the hosts of the saints, in both the New and the Old Testament, have demonstrated both their merit by their virtues and mortality by their death.

Christ’s authority also confirmed the matter, which had been settled. When the Sadducees put a question to him by the example of a woman who had had seven husbands, asking, if the raising of bodies were believed, to which husband she would most properly belong, he replied: “You are mistaken, not knowing the Scriptures or the power of God. In the resurrection they will neither marry nor be given in marriage; for neither will they die” (Matt. 22:29–30; Luke 20:35–36).

Aware of his own work, he made clear why he had instituted marriages: namely, so that offspring might make up for the losses caused by death; but that the generous fruitfulness would immediately cease when greedy death had ceased. [Note: [Col. 1580] Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read “sterility,” corruptly.]

If, therefore, according to the testimony of Christ who created it, fruitfulness was created for this purpose—that it might contend with frailty—and if this condition of marriage was ordained before sin, it also appears that mortality does not pertain to transgression but to nature, to which marriage too is said to pertain.

That law, therefore, which was proclaimed—namely, “On whatever day you eat from what has been forbidden, you shall die by death”—is understood as punitive death, not bodily death; it threatens sins, not offspring. No one incurs it except through transgression, and no one escapes it except through correction.

The saying that death is to be inflicted on the day of sin reflects a scriptural custom, by which Scripture often calls someone condemned who is going to be condemned. Hence in the Gospel the Lord says, “Everyone who does not believe in me has already been judged, because he has not believed in the name of the only-begotten Son of God” (John 3:18). This does not mean that unbelief, by which Christ is denied, had already been joined to eternal punishment before the time of judgment, since all who come to faith were previously unbelievers. Rather, so that the severity of the one giving the command might appear, sins are said already to be punishments.

Finally, Adam himself, the book called Wisdom, and the opinion of many assert that he was cleansed by subsequent correction. [Note: [Col. 1580] Supply: “and yet he died,” so that we may know that bodily death does not belong to the punishment of that sin, but to the institutions of nature, as Augustine explains below.]

### AUG.

If, as you say, you do not oppose those who believe that Adam, had he proved obedient, could have been transferred to immortality as a reward, distinguish between immortalities—namely, the greater and the lesser.

For that condition too is not absurdly called immortality in which a person can avoid dying if he does not do what would cause him to die, although he is also capable of doing it. Adam possessed this immortality; he lost it by the merit of his transgression. It was supplied to him by the tree of life. He was not prohibited from that tree when he received the good commandment not to sin, but when he sinned through an evil will. For then he was expelled from paradise, lest he extend his hand to the tree of life, eat, and live forever.

Accordingly, we should understand that he used to receive sacramental nourishment from this tree of life and ordinary nourishment from the others. He was commanded not to eat from the one tree called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. Why, then, should it be thought that he did not eat from the tree of life, since it was far more excellent than the others, and since, except for the one by which he sinned, he had received permission to eat from every tree?

These are the words of God giving the command: “You shall eat from every tree that is in paradise; but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, you shall not eat from it” (Gen. 2:16–17). Likewise, these are the words of the one condemning: “Because you listened to the voice of your wife and ate from the tree concerning which I had commanded you—not to eat from that one alone” (ibid. 3:17).

What, then, was the reason that he did not take particular care to eat from the tree of life, when he had been forbidden only the tree whose use he usurped in sinning? Indeed, if we understand attentively, just as he sinned by eating from the forbidden tree, so he would have sinned by not eating from the tree of life, since he would have begrudged himself the life that came from that tree.

The immortality in which the holy angels live, and in which we too shall live, is undoubtedly greater. It is not an immortality in which a person has the power not to die, just as he has the power not to sin, yet can also die because he can sin. Rather, it is an immortality in which everyone who is there, or will be there, cannot die, because he can no longer sin.

For there the will to live well will be as great as the will even now to live happily, which we see that not even misery has been able to take away from us.

If you say that Adam could have passed into this immortality, unquestionably the greater one, from the lesser one as a reward for obedience without any intervening death, you will say something that right faith ought not to reject. But if you praise the lesser immortality in such a way as to deny the greater, you will be forced to fill paradise with deaths and with the calamities of the dying, who are driven toward death by sufferings they cannot endure; and thus you will disfigure your own teaching so badly that you would wish to flee from it if you could see it in a mirror.

For why would the descendants of the first man, born in paradise—not only the good but also the blessed—be forced to die, if no fault compelled them to leave paradise, where the tree of life existed, where the highest power of living came from it, and where there was no necessity of dying?

Enoch and Elijah were transferred from that necessity. They were on these lands, where the tree of life was not, and therefore the common necessity of death pressed them toward the end of this life. To where should we believe they were transferred, except to the place where the tree of life itself is, so that they might have the power of living and no necessity of dying—just as it would have been in paradise for human beings in whom no desire to sin arose, a desire that would not allow them to remain where no justice would compel them to die?

Therefore the examples of Enoch and Elijah help us rather than you. In these two God showed what he would also have granted to those whom he expelled from paradise, had they not wished to sin: these were expelled from the place to which those two were transported.

We also believe that God’s grace conferred this upon them there, so that they would have no occasion to say, “Forgive us our debts” (Matt. 6:12). For in these lands, where their corruptible bodies weighed down their souls (Wis. 9:15), they struggled against vices in a great contest, so that, if they said they had no sin, they would deceive themselves and the truth would not be in them (1 John 1:8).

They are believed, indeed, to return for a short time to these lands, so that they too may struggle with death and pay what is owed to the offspring of the first man.

Hence it is to be understood that those who had no sin—and their children, if they had remained inhabitants of paradise in the same uprightness—would have persisted more fully in that immortality until they passed into the greater one without any intervening death, if we acknowledge that so long a life was granted to Enoch and Elijah, who, though righteous, were outside paradise on these lands and could not say that they had no sin.

“But,” you say, “when the Lord was questioned about that woman who had had seven husbands, he confirmed by his answer that marriages were instituted so that offspring might make up for the losses of death, and that generous fruitfulness would cease when greedy death ceased.”

You are entirely mistaken to think that marriages were instituted so that the succession of those being born might replace those who died. They were instituted so that the chastity of women might make fathers certain of their sons and sons certain of their fathers. Human beings could also have been born through promiscuous and indiscriminate intercourse with various women, but a definite relationship between fathers and sons could not have existed.

If no one sinned, and therefore no one died, this age would end once the number of the saints had been completed—the number sufficient for the future age—an age in which there would be the possibility both of not sinning and of sinning; and that other age would follow, in which no one could sin.

For if souls separated from bodies can be either miserable or blessed and yet cannot sin, what believer would deny that, in the kingdom of God, where there will be an incorruptible body that will not weigh down the soul but adorn it, and will no longer need food, this disposition will exist: that no sin could occur there—not because no will acts, but because the will is good?

Therefore, when the Lord, speaking about the resurrection, said, “They will neither marry nor be given in marriage; for neither will they die,” he did not say this to show that marriages had been instituted because of those who would die. Rather, once the number of the saints had been completed, no one would need to be born where no one would need to die.

“But,” you say, “Adam is asserted to have been cleansed from his offense by subsequent correction, both by the book of Wisdom and by the opinion of many; and yet,” you say, “he died, so that we might know that bodily death does not belong to the punishment of that sin, but to the institutions of nature.”

As though David did not expiate those two grave crimes—adultery and murder—by repenting in such a way that the very prophet who had terrified him testified that forgiveness had been granted to him. Yet we read that the things God had threatened followed, so that we may understand that the forgiveness served to prevent the man who had committed such great evils from being punished for them with eternal punishment.

Thus there was also something for which repentance benefited the first man: namely, that he might be punished with a long but not eternal punishment. Hence it happened—as is most rightly believed—that his son, that is, the Lord Jesus according to his humanity, when he descended to the underworld, released him from the bonds of hell. [Note: [Col. 1583] The Mar. and Clar. manuscripts read “from eternal bonds.”] [Col. 1583]

At that time he should be understood, according to the book of Wisdom, to have been brought out from his offense, so that this book may be shown to have spoken not of something already done but of something future, although it expressed it through a past-tense verb. For it says, “He brought him out from his offense” (Wis. 10:2), just as it says, “They pierced my hands” (Ps. 21:17), and the other passages there that speak of future things through past-tense verbs. [Note: [Col. 1583] The printed editions read “through future-tense verbs.” Corrected on the basis of the manuscripts.]

Accordingly, through bodily death he paid a temporal penalty for sin, and through repentance something was accomplished so that he might escape eternal punishment. Here the grace of the one who liberates was more powerful than the merit of the one who repents.

You have no means of fortifying yourself against the force of truth. With your devices you will be struck down in the clearest light, and you will not be permitted, by any means whatsoever, to introduce into God’s paradise deaths and countless diseases filled with deadly torments.

Believe God when he says, “On whatever day you eat from it, you shall die by death” (Gen. 2:17). They began to die on the very day when, having been separated from the tree of life—which, being placed in a physical location, supplied life to the body—they received the necessity and condition of death. [Note: [Col. 1583] Vignier reads “behold”; the manuscripts read “certainly.”]

Certainly “the losses caused by death” and “greedy death” are your own words. At least these harsh and dreadful words should have warned you to spare God’s paradise. Does that most renowned dwelling of the blessed offend you so greatly that you send into it death—destructive and greedy?

O enemies of God’s grace, enemies of God’s paradise, how much farther can you go than to fill the sweetness of holy delights with the bitterest punishments, and to wish paradise to be nothing but a lesser hell?

### XXXI. JUL.

There has now been enough concerning Genesis. Let us pass to the Apostle Paul, whom the Manichaean and the Traducianist suppose to support their opinion. When, then, he was discussing the resurrection of the dead, he said: “Just as all die in Adam, so also all will be made alive in Christ” (1 Cor. 15:22).

You used this testimony in the case we have against you; but what you thought it established, because you kept silent about it, I suspect but cannot confidently affirm. For what relevance does “tradux” have, if all are said to die in Adam, since Adam is the name of a human being, whereas “tradux” is an indication of sin and of the Manichaean stain? Unless perhaps you admit that Adam both is and signifies nothing other than sin, so that by this designation the Apostle might seem to have declared that all die in sin. But this is plainly insane.

What, then, is new if, because Adam in Hebrew indicates nothing other than “human being” (which is what its interpretation expresses), the Apostle said, “All die in Adam, and all will be made alive in Christ”—that is, according to the nature of human beings who die, they are raised from the dead by the power of Christ?

Anyone who denies this meaning is insane. For by the power of the same author who established fruitfulness and mortality in this life, all will be raised from their graves, so that each may receive what belongs to his own body, according to what he has done, whether good or evil (2 Cor. 5:10).

Do you therefore think that, in the Apostle’s saying, “Just as all die in Adam, so also all will be made alive in Christ,” bodily death—which is common to the righteous and the unrighteous—or that punitive death assigned to the devil and the impious is being indicated?

If he indicated this ordinary natural death, which is precious even in the saints (Ps. 115:5), which comes equally not only to the good and the bad but also to human beings and animals—if, I say, the Apostle indicated this death here, it is clear that by the name Adam he showed the nature of humanity, and by the name Christ the power of the Creator and the one who raises the dead.

But if you want “All die in Adam” to mean crime here rather than nature, an explanation is available that is as clear as it is certain: namely, that he said, “Just as all”—that is, many—die by imitation of Adam, so “all”—that is, many—are saved by imitation of Christ.

Either, then, he spoke of common death and indicated nature, or of sin and condemned imitation. [Note: [Col. 1584] The Portarum codex reads “accumulated.”] For shortly afterward he added: “Just as we have borne the image of the earthly one, let us also bear the image of the heavenly one” (1 Cor. 15:49). Certainly the bearing of an image could not have been commanded if it were believed to be natural in one of the two conditions.

### AUG.

Who is so negligent of the Apostle’s words as not to see that the Apostle was discussing the resurrection of the body when he said, “Just as all die in Adam, so also all will be made alive in Christ”?

But, in order to expand not your eloquence but your empty talk, you introduce a question where there is none and ask me of what death it was said, “All die in Adam.”

It was plainly said of bodily death, namely, that death by which good and evil must die, not that death by which those who are evil are called dead—dead by that same death. The Lord embraces these two deaths in one brief saying: “Let the dead bury their own dead” (Matt. 8:22).

There is also the death called the second death in the Apocalypse (Rev. 2:11; 20:6, 14; 21:8), by which both body and soul will be tormented in eternal fire. The Lord threatens this when he says, “Fear him who has power to destroy both body and soul in Gehenna” (Matt. 10:28).

Although many deaths are found in Scripture, there are nevertheless two principal ones, the first and the second. The first is the death introduced by the first man through sinning; the second is the death that the second man will bring through judgment.

Just as many covenants of God are mentioned in the holy books—as those who read attentively can observe—there are nevertheless two principal ones, the old and the new.

The first death, then, began when Adam was expelled from paradise and separated from the tree of life. The second death will begin when it is said, “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire” (ibid. 25:41).

When, therefore, the Apostle was speaking of the resurrection of the body, he said: “Through a man came death, and through a man the resurrection of the dead. For just as all die in Adam, so also all will be made alive in Christ” (1 Cor. 15:21–22).

We should not, then, inquire which death is meant in this passage. It is clear that bodily death is meant. Rather, we should attend to the one through whom the death in question came: whether through God, who created the human being, or through the human being, who by sinning became the cause of this death.

But, as I said, we should attend to this matter as something placed openly before us, not search for it as though it were hidden. The Apostle himself removed this question by saying most plainly, “Through a man came death.” And who is this except the first Adam? He is the one of whom it was said, “Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin, death” [Note: [Col. 1585] The printed editions read, “and through man, death”; this is erroneous and conflicts with the manuscripts.]—and in contrast to him the second Adam is set, “who is the form of the one to come” (Rom. 5:12, 14). Hence here too it is said, “Through a man came death, and through a man the resurrection of the dead.”

Thus we must understand his saying, “All die in Adam,” without forgetting his saying, “Through a man came death.” They die in Adam precisely because death came through a man, just as they are made alive in Christ because the resurrection of the dead came through a man.

A man, then, and a man: just as one is this man, so one is that man. And because this one is the second man, that one is the first man. We know, as you mention, that Adam means “human being” in Hebrew. But it does not follow that, as you shamelessly try to persuade us, when the Apostle said, “All die in Adam,” he meant every mortal human being, so that we should think all die not in that first man but in the fact that they are mortal.

Do not obscure what is clear, pervert what is right, or entangle what is simple. All die in the one through whom death came, just as all are made alive in the one through whom came the resurrection of the dead.

And who is this except the second man? Who, then, is that one except the first man? Who, therefore, is this except the one Christ? Who is that one except the one Adam?

“Just as we have borne the image of the earthly man, so let us also bear the image of the heavenly one.” The former is indicated; the latter is commanded. The former is already present; the latter is future.

We have borne the former image by the condition of being born and through the contagion of sin. We bear the latter by the grace of being born again; for now we bear it in hope, but in reality we shall bear it as the reward of rising again and reigning happily and justly. [Note: [Col. 1585] So the old Codex Portarum. Other manuscripts, together with the printed editions, read “in reality.”]

Since these things are so, the death of a human being created and established in such a condition that he would not die unless he sinned is unquestionably punitive. Yet because God, through his grace, turns our punitive evils to our good, the death of his saints is precious in the sight of the Lord.

Through it they struggle, just as through discipline: “Discipline,” as it is written, “does not seem for the present to be a matter of joy but of sorrow; afterward, however, it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have struggled through it” (Heb. 12:11).

But you, who insist that bodily death would have occurred even in paradise, even if no one had sinned, are an enemy of God’s grace and an enemy of the saints, whose death is precious, through which they struggle to enter and dwell in paradise.

For, as far as you are concerned, you introduce into a place of such happiness and rest not only death—that is, the dissolution of the soul from the body, even though the soul does not wish to be stripped but rather to be clothed upon, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life (2 Cor. 5:4)—but also all diseases and every kind of evil by which human beings die because they cannot endure them. I see how great your error is in doing this, but I do not know with what audacity you do it.

### XXXII. JUL.

Let us now examine the entire context of the passage itself. He says:

“If Christ is preached as having risen from the dead, how do some among you say that there is no resurrection of the dead? But if there is no resurrection of the dead, neither has Christ risen. But if Christ has not risen, our preaching is empty and your faith is also empty. [Note: [Col. 1586] Thus the manuscripts; Vignier reads “our.”] We are even found to be false witnesses of God, because we have testified against God that he raised Christ, whom he did not raise. For if the dead do not rise, neither has Christ risen. But if Christ has not risen, your faith is vain, because you are still in your sins; and therefore those who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished. If in this life only we hope in Christ, we are more pitiable than all human beings.

“But now Christ has risen from the dead, the firstfruits of those who sleep, since through a man came death and through a man the resurrection of the dead. For just as all die in Adam, so also all will be made alive in Christ. But each in his own order: Christ the firstfruits, then those who are Christ’s at his coming, then the end” (1 Cor. 15:12–24).

### AUG.

It will become clear in your own lengthy and superfluous discussion that you undertook to examine this entire passage in the Apostle’s Letters concerning the resurrection of the body only to obtain an opportunity to spread your loquacity in abundant—if it may be called so—poverty, and to provide yourself with room for wandering in order to fill so many books.

### XXXIII. JUL.

The excellent teacher constructed his argument with great force and instilled in us hope of sharing in the Mediator, asserting that, insofar as concerns the substance by which he is joined to us, that man had nothing excepted from our condition; and that the opinion which unbelief had adopted could prejudice Christ no less than it could prejudice us.

Thus he mingles Christ’s case with that of human beings in such a way that what is judged in one must necessarily be believed in the other. Human beings had thought at that time that there would be no future resurrection of the dead; nevertheless, they did not deny that Christ had risen. The Teacher of the Gentiles seizes upon this and declares that both sides must be equally exposed to one judgment: either all human beings will rise, or Christ must not be believed to have risen.

Certainly the Apostle would not have had this force in his argument if, according to the Manichaeans and their Traducianist disciples, he distinguished Christ’s flesh from participation in our nature. [Note: [Col. 1586] Thus the Portarum manuscript; the printed editions read “from the nature of communion.”]

### AUG.

Those who distinguish Christ’s flesh from participation in our nature are not Manichaeans; rather, Manichaeans are those who insist that Christ had no flesh at all.

By associating the Manichaeans with us—though they are to be anathematized and condemned together with you—you even assist their cause [Note: [Col. 1586] Thus the manuscripts; Vignier reads “with us.”] when you say that they distinguish Christ’s flesh from participation in our nature—as though they admitted that Christ had flesh which they distinguish in any way from our flesh.

Leave them aside, since they are far removed from us, and also far removed from you, in this question concerning Christ’s flesh. Deal with us in the matter at hand, because you confess with us that Christ had flesh, although you do so differently.

For we do not distinguish it from the nature and substance of our flesh, but from participation in its vice. Our flesh is flesh of sin. For this reason Christ’s flesh was called not “the likeness of flesh,” since it is true flesh, but “the likeness of sinful flesh,” since it is not flesh of sin.

If the flesh of sin were not our flesh, how, I ask you, would the likeness of sinful flesh be Christ’s flesh? Or are you so foolish as to say that something is similar without there being anything to which it is similar?

Listen to Hilary, a Catholic bishop, whom, whatever you may think of him, you certainly cannot call a Manichaean. Speaking of Christ’s flesh, he says:

“Therefore, when he was sent in the likeness of sinful flesh, he did not have sin in the same way that he had flesh. But because all flesh is from sin—that is, descended from the sin of Adam the parent—he was sent in the likeness of sinful flesh, with not sin in him, but the likeness of sinful flesh.”

What will you say to this, most wicked, most loquacious, most insulting, most slanderous man? Is Hilary also a Manichaean?

But far be it from me to consider your insults unworthy of acceptance—not only together with Hilary and the other ministers of Christ, but also together with Christ’s own flesh, to which you are not afraid to inflict so great an insult that you dare to equate it with the flesh of other human beings, which is admittedly flesh of sin—if it was not falsely said that Christ came in the likeness of sinful flesh (Rom. 8:3).

### XXXIV. JUL.

He would never have said, “If the dead do not rise, neither has Christ risen.” For it could have been answered to him: “But Christ, because he was born of a virgin, rose in a special way; human beings, however, because they were born from a diabolical mingling, do not rise.”

But he would immediately reply: “What purpose did his rising serve if it was prepared neither for our hope nor for our instruction? What reason for teaching, what weight of example, would there be if his nature were unlike ours and lacked both the hope of reigning with him and the power to imitate him?”

The Apostle’s faith, then, is far, very far, from this opinion. Filled with the same Spirit as Peter, he knows that Christ died for us for this reason: to give us an example, so that we might follow his footsteps (1 Pet. 2:21).

And because he knew that the cause of so great a mystery was both sacrifice and example, he does not hesitate to declare—indeed, he carefully insists—that Christ the man did not attain anything from which any one of us might be excluded by the disabilities of our nature.

“If there is no resurrection,” he says, “neither has Christ risen. But if Christ has risen from the dead, how do some among you say that there is no resurrection of the dead?”

That is: if you confess that, according to his humanity, he possessed the same nature as we do, how can you think that resurrection occurred in him but will not occur in the rest?

After setting forth these conditions, he completes the argument in every respect: “But now,” he says, “Christ has risen from the dead; therefore there will be a resurrection of the dead.”

AUGUSTINE. To those who think that there is no resurrection of the dead, yet believe that Christ rose, it is therefore said, “If there is no resurrection of the dead, neither has Christ risen”: because Christ rose for this reason, namely, to establish faith in the resurrection of the dead, showing that human beings would rise in the flesh, just as he, having become human, rose in the flesh. Accordingly, it followed that those who did not believe in the resurrection of the dead should deny that Christ had risen. Since, therefore, those with whom he was arguing could not deny the latter, they ought also, once their darkness had been removed, to confess the former.

For if, because of some difference belonging to Christ, people think they are right to deny the resurrection of the dead while nevertheless not denying the Lord’s resurrection, they can also produce other arguments—of which they discover many—by which they may seem to themselves to defend their error. For what if, when they hear, “If the dead do not rise, neither has Christ risen,” they should answer: “But he is not merely human; he is also God, which no other human being is. He was born, as man himself, of the Holy Spirit and of the virgin Mary, which no other human being was. He had the power to lay down his life and to take it up again (John 10:18), which no other human being had. What wonder, then, if he was able to rise from the dead, something no other human being could do?”

If they say this because they grant that Christ alone rose but refuse this to the rest, are we therefore going to deny those great differences between Christ and others, so that we may persuade them of the resurrection of the other dead on the basis of Christ’s equality with them? Thus, without denying that difference—that we confess Christ’s flesh alone not to have been flesh of sin as the flesh of others was, but to have been the likeness of the flesh of sin—we nevertheless maintain that he did not rise alone, but that others too will rise. And we defend it in such a way that we say what the Apostle said: “If the dead do not rise, neither has Christ risen”; but Christ has risen; therefore the dead rise.

For because the merits of origin are not the same in the two kinds of flesh, it does not follow that their earthly and mortal substance is not the same. The likeness of the flesh of sin does indeed have its own distinction, by which it is distinguished from the flesh of sin; but far be it from us to say that Christ, by rising, makes himself unlike those with whom he chose to make himself equal by dying. Therefore we should not equate the likeness of the flesh of sin with the flesh of sin in so far as concerns the distinction between belonging to sin and not belonging to sin, because he did not wish there to be between the two kinds of flesh a difference between rising and not rising, just as he did not wish there to be a difference between not dying and dying.

But what does imitation—which you support when it is unnecessary—have to do with this case? Imitation lies in the will; but when the will is good, it is prepared by the Lord, as it is written: “The will is prepared by the Lord” (Proverbs 8, according to the Septuagint). No one imitates unless he wills to do so; but a human being dies and rises, whether he wills it or not.

Moreover, imitation itself does not always occur only when the nature of the one to be imitated is the same as that of the imitator. Otherwise we could not imitate the justice and piety of the angels, whose nature is different; yet you yourself acknowledged that we ask this of the Lord in prayer when we say, “Your will be done, as in heaven, so on earth” (Matthew 6:10; above, Book 2, chapter 52). Nor would we imitate God the Father, whose nature is very different from ours; nevertheless the Lord says, “Be like your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5:48), and through the prophet it is said, “Be holy, because I am holy” (Leviticus 11:44). Therefore it is not because Christ was in this world in the likeness of the flesh of sin while we are in the flesh of sin that we cannot imitate Christ.

[Col. 1593] The passage from “He says, ‘die’” through “will be made alive” has likewise been restored on manuscript authority. [Col. 1593] Vignierius reads “pertain to that death”; “future” has been added from the manuscripts. [Col. 1593] Perhaps “wished,” rather than “wished.” [Col. 1594] The printed editions here and shortly below read “uttered punishment without guilt”; both places are corrected on manuscript authority to “endured punishment without guilt.” [Col. 1594] The printed editions read “bright”; corruptly and against the manuscripts, which read “to be paid.” [Col. 1595] The manuscripts read “through that human being”; the printed editions, “through human beings.” [Col. 1595] The word “penal,” omitted here in the printed editions, is restored from the manuscripts. [Col. 1595] The printed editions read “penal”; the manuscripts more correctly read “rewarding.” [Col. 1595] The Codex Portarum reads “when he has abolished”; the other manuscripts and printed editions read “when he has made equal,” perhaps for “when he has made obsolete,” that is, “abolished.” Greek: *katargēsē*. [Col. 1596] The printed editions read “resurrection”; corrected from the manuscripts to “by the resurrection.” [Col. 1596] Vignierius reads “under the just and omnipotent God as judge”; “God” is absent from the manuscripts. [Col. 1596] Vignierius reads “created by God”; “good” has been added from the manuscripts. ### XXXV. JULIAN

Let us bring these arguments to their conclusion and say: “If Christ, who became human, did not have natural sin, how do some among you say that innate depravity dominates the image of God? But if there is evil in nature, and Christ, who is found in that same nature, has been placed under the rule of the devil, then, if he is believed to be guilty, our preaching is vain and your faith is empty. The Apostles are found to be false witnesses, because they testified against God by saying that he formed his Son, according to the flesh from the seed of David, innocent and holy, if the guilt of a cursed seed infected him. Surely, if we place our hope in such a Christ, we are more pitiable than all human beings.

“But now Christ, no less truly human than truly divine, born from Adam’s stock, made of a woman and made under the law, committed no sin and therefore had no sin. It is evident, then, that guilt belongs to the will, not to the seed.”

### AUGUSTINE

Your entire structure of reasoning surely rises from this foundation, which you first laid when you said: “If Christ, who became human, did not have natural sin, how do some among you say that innate depravity dominates the image of God?” Once this proposition has been shaken and demolished, everything you subsequently added as though it followed collapses with the greatest ease.

For it does not follow that, if Christ, who became human, did not have natural—that is, original—sin, no innate depravity dominates the image of God. It does not follow that, if the likeness of the flesh of sin had no depravity, that which it resembles—that is, the flesh of sin itself—has no depravity. Rather, it follows that, if there is a likeness of the flesh of sin, there is also flesh of sin. For everything must be like something; and if Christ alone had true flesh, like other human beings, but not the reality of the flesh of sin, only its likeness, then it is necessary not merely that there be another flesh to which this flesh is similar, but that the flesh of all other human beings be nothing other than flesh of sin.

Therefore, even if there is evil in the flesh of sin, it is not in Christ, who came in true flesh—not in flesh of sin, but in the likeness of flesh of sin—in order to heal the flesh of sin. He is not therefore believed to be guilty; rather, our guilt, both original and added, is removed by him. Hence the Apostle’s preaching is not vain: he would not preach in Christ the likeness of the flesh of sin unless he knew that the flesh of others was flesh of sin. Nor is our faith empty, by which your heresy is emptied.

The Apostles are not found to be false witnesses when they distinguish the likeness of the flesh of sin from the flesh of sin—a distinction your heresy does not make. They proclaim Christ as being from the seed of David while nevertheless asserting that he was born of the Holy Spirit and the virgin Mary, not from the desire of the flesh, so that he might have the likeness of the flesh of sin but could not have the flesh of sin.

We are not more pitiable than all human beings because we believe this; rather, we believe in great misery that Christ’s flesh was not distinguished from the flesh of sin. Accordingly, you bring your argument to a vain conclusion when you say: “It is evident, then, that guilt belongs to the will, not to the seed.” You have brought this forward altogether without basis, because I have shown that the preceding propositions, from which you think it has been constructed, do not entail it. And undoubtedly, since there could have been no vices of those being born in paradise unless the seeds too had been corrupted by the evil will of the first parents, those vices could exist after paradise.

Why, then, should it not rather be said to you—as we employ, truthfully, the same form of reasoning that you employed deceitfully: “If Christ the man was sent to human beings in the likeness of the flesh of sin, how can you all say—not merely some among you—that there is no flesh of which this is the likeness, if there is no other flesh of sin? If Christ did not have the likeness of the flesh of sin, then the preaching of the one who said this is vain, and the faith of the Catholic Church, which believed it, is also vain. The Apostle too is found to be a false witness, since he testified against Christ that Christ had the likeness of the flesh of sin, although he did not have it.”

But if we believe this, we do not join ourselves to the faithful. Now Christ was sent in the likeness of the flesh of sin, because he alone had true flesh in such a way that it was not flesh of sin but its likeness. Therefore we must confess that the flesh of other human beings is flesh of sin, to which Christ’s true flesh was made similar, though it was not itself flesh of sin.

[Note: Vignierius reads, “Christ is in the likeness.” We have added “was sent,” because it is found in the manuscripts.]

### XXXVI. JULIAN

The Manichaeans are indeed pierced through—both those who believe in natural sin and those who deny the resurrection of the flesh. “But now,” he says, “Christ has risen from the dead, the first fruits of those who sleep; for since death came through a human being, the resurrection of the dead also came through a human being.”

Here the Apostle is not speaking of the general resurrection, which even the wicked and profane will experience, but only of the resurrection of those who will be transferred into glory. He therefore indicates the blessed resurrection simply by the name “resurrection”; in comparison with it, the resurrection of the wicked is passed over as though it were no resurrection at all.

Here, then, the Apostle, as I said, emphasizes not merely resurrection, which is shared by the good and the wicked, but the blessed resurrection. And although resurrection and the blessedness of resurrection are not one and the same, just as resurrection and the misery of resurrection are not one and the same, nevertheless, because eternal blessedness does not exist without resurrection, that happiness which makes the awakening one not to regret is also signified by its name.

For example, if someone, praising industry, strength, and various pursuits, wished to display them briefly through the life associated with them, he might call one person’s life learned, another’s elegant, and another’s energetic. He would not thereby introduce a distinction such that life appeared to be the same as industry, elegance, or strength. Living is one thing, and pursuing something is another; nevertheless, unless you live, you will pursue nothing.

So too resurrection is not the same as blessedness. There is indeed a wretched awakening of ashes; nevertheless, no one will reign unless he has first risen. The death of the body and the resurrection of the body therefore stand opposite one another. If death were universally penal, resurrection would also be universally a reward. But now resurrection is penal for all who are assigned to eternal fires; therefore death too is not punishment but natural.

For just as the death of the body does not in every case make death regrettable, so resurrection does not in every case make being restored to life pleasing. The goodness of the former lies in the reward of those who rise, and the bitterness of the latter in the burning of those who are punished; both follow according to merits.

It is therefore evident that the Apostle is discussing not natural death but the death of criminals, which perpetual punishment makes unhappy; and not the common resurrection but the resurrection made blessed by eternal glory. Nor, when he discusses persons, does he impose a prejudice upon created beings; rather, while always preserving distinctions and broad boundaries between natures and wills, he sometimes mingles terms so that the particularity of things does not perish through confusion.

“Through a human being, then, death, and through a human being, the resurrection of the dead.” Here he does not say that death was established by a human being, but that it appeared in a human being. Likewise, he does not say that the resurrection of the dead was accomplished by a human being—that is, by Christ—but in a human being, as the same teacher says to the Philippians: “Being obedient unto death, even the death of the cross; therefore God also exalted him and gave him a name above every name” (Philippians 2:8–9).

The assertion of the Apostle Peter also agrees with this: “Men of Israel, listen: Jesus, a man of Nazareth approved by God among you—you killed by the hands of wicked men; God raised him, having loosed the pains of hell.” And again: “This Jesus God raised up, of which we all are witnesses” (Acts 2:22–24, 32).

Thus, just as it was proper to the human being to undergo death without injury to his divinity, so it was proper to divinity to raise that human being from the dead. And what God is declared to perform in the person of the Word, Christ himself also performs. For he had said: “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up” (John 10:18).

Although the Son is one person, therefore, by a legitimate distinction one thing is attributed to the flesh and another to the divinity. “Through a human being, then, death, and through a human being, the resurrection of the dead”—manifested, not created. In every case, both were instituted by God; but in Adam the condition of death became evident, while in the person of Christ the first fruits of resurrection shone forth.

Where, then, the Apostle says, “Through a human being, death,” if you say that this occurred through his will, it has nothing to do with nature; if through nature, it has nothing to do with guilt. The human beings are set opposite one another, one as the author of death and the other as the author of resurrection; and he is unwilling to subject the second to the first.

It follows: “As in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive.” Does he say this—“all shall be made alive in Christ”—also of the wicked, or only of the faithful? If of the wicked, so that all are made alive in Christ, then no one is in punishment. If of the faithful, then not everyone is made alive in the faith of Christ, but only the faithful, although all absolutely are raised by his power, through which they were created.

If, therefore, he is speaking of the death of the body—“In Adam all die”—no guilt is indicated by this expression, since Christ too is found to have died in the same Adam. The truth of the resurrection would not have followed unless the truth of death had preceded it. The Apostle therefore declares that all die in Adam.

If this death indicates nothing other than the dissolution of the body, it certainly has nothing to do with natural sin, nor does it prejudice the innocent if they are said to die in Adam, in whom Christ also died.

But if by “In Adam all die” you wish to understand the inclination of the mind toward sin, and not merely death but guilty and miserable death—that is, death followed by punishment assigned for crimes—Christ could not have been in that Gehenna, nor could the saints. Therefore neither does this prejudice the innocent, who possess no voluntary good and no voluntary evil, but retain only the fact that they were made by God. We consecrate them by the right of Baptism, so that the one who made them good by creating them may make them better by renewing and adopting them.

Therefore, when the Apostle says, “As in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive,” this is as far removed from the suspicion of Manichaean transmission as Christ is from sin. He had no iniquity and possessed nothing less of human nature.

### AUGUSTINE

What is this that you say in arguing against us: “The Manichaeans are indeed pierced through, both those who believe in natural sin and those who deny the resurrection of the flesh”? Are we, like them, either attributing sin to a nature that is alien to us or denying the resurrection of the flesh?

Let the Manichaeans be pierced through by you—those who are pierced through by us along with you, and who are also helped by you. For you deny that the discord between flesh and spirit is to be attributed to Adam’s sin. For, seeking or offering an explanation of the cause of this evil, they conclude that an alien nature of evil, coeternal with the good God, has been mingled with us.

You then explain the following passage, where the Apostle discusses the resurrection of the flesh, and you say that “he is not speaking of the common resurrection, namely, of the good and the wicked, but only of those who will be transferred into glory.” That is indeed so; nevertheless, he is speaking of the resurrection of the body.

The death of the body is therefore set against it in opposition, and two human beings are assigned as the respective authors of these two things—that is, of the death of the body and the resurrection: “Since through a human being came death, and through a human being the resurrection of the dead.” These two human beings are also expressed by their proper names, so that it may be evident of whom this was said; and it is added: “For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive.”

He says “die,” not “will die”; but on the other side he does not say “are made alive,” but “will be made alive.”

Now they die through punishment; then they will be made alive through reward. He is not therefore speaking of that death which will be suffered by those who will be tormented with soul and body in eternal fire. Otherwise he would put the future tense on both sides, and just as he said “will be made alive,” he would also say “will die.”

But when he said “die,” which is something that is happening now, and “will be made alive,” which will happen then, he sufficiently shows that he is speaking of the death in which he says, “Through a human being came death”: the death that dissolves the soul from the body. Yet this also pertains to that future death called the second death, which awaits those who do not have the guilt they drew from Adam through generation removed through Christ by regeneration.

Since, therefore, he is now speaking of the resurrection of the body, which will be future, and sets against it, in opposition, the death of the body, which occurs now—and since these two opposites have individual authors, Adam for death and Christ for the resurrection of the dead—the death is to be understood as penal just as the resurrection is understood as a reward. For the opposite of a reward is not nature but punishment.

And therefore, in this passage, where the resurrection of the body is set against the death of the body, the Apostle is not discussing the common resurrection, which concerns the just and the unjust, but rather that resurrection in which those who will be made alive in Christ will be present, not those who will be condemned by Christ. Yet he himself will raise both groups, for all who are in the tombs will hear his voice, and those who have done good will come forth to the resurrection of life, while those who have done evil will come forth to the resurrection of judgment (John 5:28–29).

Therefore, as I said, I wished to commend the resurrection that belongs to Christ’s benefit, not also the one that belongs only to judgment; so that, since this resurrection is a reward, the death of the body, which is set against it as its opposite, might also be shown to be penal. For just as death is contrary to life, so punishment is contrary to reward.

Since the holy martyrs struggled and conquered through this punishment—that is, through the death of the body—their death, in which they now sleep in the sight of the Lord, is precious not by its own nature but by his gift, as it is written: “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Psalm 115:15).

The punishments of the saints are also, without doubt, precious. But it is not because they are precious that they are not punishments, just as it is not because they are punishments that they are precious. They are precious because they were endured for the truth or borne with piety.

If you held this sound and Catholic understanding, you would not send into God’s paradise—that is, into the place of holy delights—not only the punishments of death but also the deadly illnesses of human beings.

What, then, is every punishment of a human being except punishment of the image of God? If it is inflicted unjustly, the one by whom it is inflicted is certainly unjust. Who, moreover, would doubt that punishment is unjustly inflicted upon the image of God unless guilt had deserved it?

The only mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, endured punishment without guilt, so that he might empty both our guilt and our punishment—not the punishment that had to be paid in this evil age, but the eternal punishment that was owed to us.

And yet, taking upon himself even our own human feeling as death approached, he said: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matthew 26:39). He certainly had the power to lay down his life and take it up again; but by these words the divine Teacher showed that the death which, without any preceding guilt, he accepted for us by will and not by necessity was nevertheless a punishment. He alone endured it for us, without any iniquity of his own.

If, then, this glory of Christ’s mercy—that he endured punishment without guilt for us—is unique, so that although he was not in the flesh of sin, he nevertheless died in Adam, because of the likeness of the flesh of sin and because the flesh of sin descended from Adam, then undoubtedly other human beings, in this evil age outside paradise, deserveably and justly suffer whatever punishments they endure from birth to death. In these punishments they also suffer death, on account of their sins—whether drawn in being born or added by evil living—under the judgment of the just and omnipotent judge.

He would neither inflict nor permit punishments to be inflicted upon his images without cause, since no sparrow falls to the ground without his will (Matthew 10:29), unless he knew that the punishment was justly inflicted.

And what is “justly,” except according to the deserts of sins or the testing of virtues? Thus, even when sins have been forgiven, the pledge of eternal salvation that the reborn receive can be brought to the age to come, while here they pay whatever must be paid in the punitive and evil vanity of this age.

What, then, is the meaning of your statement: “For this reason infants are baptized, so that those whom God made good by creating them he may make better by renewing and adopting them”?

He did indeed make them good, because every nature, insofar as it is nature, is good. But those whom he made good, he would not unjustly make—or permit to be—miserable.

Although you too, when you say that they are renewed, carelessly and unknowingly confess that they are led from the oldness of the old human being, although they are certainly new by birth.

You are therefore compelled to choose one of three alternatives: either fill paradise with the punishments of human beings; or call God unjust in the punishments of his images, which the innocence of infants suffers; or, since both alternatives are detestable and condemnable, acknowledge original sin.

Then understand that all who die the death of the body die in Adam, because through that human being came death—that is, through his guilt and punishment—and that all who are not condemned but made alive through the resurrection of the body are made alive in Christ, because through that human being came the resurrection of the dead—that is, through his righteousness and grace.

Because the death of the body is penal, therefore we see opposed to it, by contrast, the resurrection of the body as a reward only, although there is also a penal resurrection.

### XXXVII. JULIAN

“But each in his own order: Christ the first fruits, then those who belong to Christ at his coming, then the end.” The same Apostle says elsewhere: “Who is the firstborn from the dead” (Colossians 1:18).

“Then those who belong to Christ”—that is, the saints are caught up in the clouds (1 Thessalonians 4:17). “After this, the end,” because they will go into the eternal kingdom, while the wicked will go into eternal fire (Matthew 25:46).

“When he delivers the kingdom to God and the Father, when he has abolished every principality and every authority and power—for he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet. For he has subjected all things under his feet; but the last enemy, death, will be destroyed. When he says that all things have been subjected, clearly it is excepted that one who subjected all things to him. When all things have been subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subjected to him who subjected all things to him, so that God may be all in all” (1 Corinthians 15:23–28).

The kingdom of God and the Father consists in this: once the number of the saints contained in his foreknowledge has been completed, every principality and every power of the adversary will perish. This efficacy of so great a mystery must be such that all the enemies of righteousness are placed beneath the divine feet.

This will occur when eternal death sees itself destroyed and conquered by all the saints. When all those kinds of powers have been subjected both to Christ and to his body through the manifestation of the kingdom, the whole glorified assembly of the saints will certainly not cease to be subject to God. Rather, the entire body worthy of the kingdom of heaven, built under Christ its head, will cleave to the divine will with perfect devotion, so that, once every desire for sins has been extinguished, God may both contain all things and fill them.

### AUGUSTINE

In this part of your argument you pursued almost nothing that pertains to the case being debated between us. Why did you think this entire passage, in which the Apostle discusses the resurrection of the body, had to be inserted, except because of what he says: “As in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive”?

You do not wish to attribute the death of the body to the sin of the first human being, but to nature; and you say that nature was instituted in that first human being in such a way that, whether he sinned or did not sin, he would have died. I think that enough has been answered on that point.

Therefore, setting aside the matters on which you wished to spend excessive time in explanation, it may perhaps be necessary to examine what the Apostle says: “The last enemy, death, will be destroyed”—to determine of which death this was said. Is it the death that exists now, by which the soul is compelled to depart from the body? Or is it the death by which the soul is not permitted to depart from the body, so that both are tormented together in eternal fire? That death certainly does not yet exist; it is future. Nor will it then be destroyed; rather, it will then begin to exist. Who doubts that it does not yet exist now?

But the death that is then common to all who die in the body, and to which the resurrection of the body is opposed—the subject about which the Apostle was arguing when he said all these things—this familiar death of the body, which now occurs and is known to all of us, will then finally be destroyed, when “this corruptible body has put on incorruption, and this mortal body has put on immortality” (1 Corinthians 15:53–54).

We clearly understand that this was said about the resurrection of the body that will then occur, in opposition to the death of the body that exists now.

Therefore, if eternal death, which has never yet existed, cannot then be destroyed, since it will rather begin to exist at that time, and will never be destroyed because it will always exist, it remains that this death which exists now is itself destroyed at the end, when, through the resurrection of the flesh, it ceases to exist.

Moreover, how could it be an enemy if it were natural in such a way that it was not penal? Under the just and omnipotent judge it could in no way be penal unless it had come about through the deserts of sin.

At last, we ask you to correct your understanding and cleanse the paradise of the blessed, which you had contaminated with human punishments.

I cannot express how much I am pleased by your statement that in the kingdom of heaven it will happen that, “once every desire for sins has been extinguished, God will both contain all things and fill them.” Would that you might correct yourself through the reminder contained in this statement of yours, and recognize that the desire for sins—which now, even when restrained, does not cease to resist us in our flesh, but then, as you rightly confess, will be extinguished—is not something you should continue to praise as a good, but rather accuse as an evil!

This is that desire you have accepted, by which “the flesh desires against the spirit,” so that the spirit too must desire against the flesh (Galatians 5:17), lest something be committed for which the human being is condemned.

It is this evil of discord, which you proclaim to have been changed into nature through the transgression of the first human being—although both parties, flesh and spirit, are good and were created by the good God—that Ambrose exposed, neither as a Manichaean nor as an assistant to the Manichaeans, but as their destroyer (Book 7 on Luke 12:53).

### XXXVIII. JULIAN

“Otherwise,” he says, “what will those do who are baptized for the dead, if the dead do not rise at all? Why are they baptized for them? And why are we also in danger every hour? Every day I die, by your glory, which I have in the Lord. If, as a human being, I fought with beasts at Ephesus, what advantage is it to me if the dead do not rise? Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die.”

“If,” he says, “this hope of future glory, through which God will be all in all, is shaken by impious unbelief and the resurrection of the dead is denied, what will those do who are baptized for the dead?”

From this arose the error of certain people, who thought that at the beginnings of the Gospel there was a custom by which those standing by would make professions on behalf of corpses and would even sprinkle the limbs of the dead with baptismal water. This appears to have arisen from ignorance.

For what the Apostle says—“They are baptized for the dead”—indicates nothing other than what he said to the Romans: “We have been buried with him through baptism into death” (Romans 6:4). That is: “With what disposition do we approach the reception of Baptism, except with the intention of mortifying our members in the future and living entirely as dead, if there is no hope that we shall live after death?”

“And why,” he says, “am I also subjected to daily dangers,” continually falling into death inflicted by persecutors, so that I may be able to glory before God in your progress, if the dead do not rise?

“And why did I, as a human being, fight with beasts at Ephesus?” That is, why did I endure the bestial fury of seditious people, if it remains uncertain that the dead rise?

“Do not be deceived: evil conversations corrupt good manners. Some have no knowledge of God. I say this to your shame” (1 Corinthians 15:29–34).

The love of sins, he says, persuades you to doubt the future; judgment is thought not to exist, so that people may sin with greater boldness. Those who deny the resurrection, he says, entirely fail to appreciate God.
