Thus you deny not only recompense but also the power of divinity, for which you ought to be exceedingly ashamed. “I say this to your shame”: such people can be found among you.

### AUGUSTINE

Here too you wished to say absolutely nothing relevant to the matter under dispute between us. Therefore, since the words of the Apostle that you attempted to explain according to your capacity—although in some respects you did not grasp the meaning of their author—are nevertheless not contrary to the faith, I have no need to answer your lengthy exposition.

### XXXIX. JULIAN

“But someone will say: How are the dead raised? And in what body do they come? Fool, what you sow is not made alive unless it first dies. Not every flesh is the same flesh: one kind is human, another the flesh of cattle; another is the flesh of birds, and another of fish. There are also heavenly bodies and earthly bodies; but one is the splendor of heavenly bodies and another that of earthly bodies. One is the splendor of the sun, another the splendor of the moon, and another the splendor of the stars; for star differs from star in glory. So also is the resurrection of the dead.

“It is sown in corruption; it will rise in incorruption. It is sown in dishonor; it will rise in glory. It is sown in weakness; it will rise in power. It is sown an animal body; it will rise a spiritual body.

“So also it is written: ‘The first man Adam was made a living soul; the last Adam a life-giving spirit.’ The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man from heaven, heavenly. As was the earthly, such also are the earthly; and as is the heavenly, such also are the heavenly. And just as we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of the heavenly” (1 Corinthians 15:35–49).

He makes the difficulty of the matter manageable through examples and says that nothing is impossible when omnipotence promises an outcome. But just as he commends the resurrection of bodies by comparing them with seeds, so he also reveals the diversity of those who rise through the variety of created things. Nevertheless, he is speaking throughout of the resurrection of the blessed.

“It is sown,” he says, “in dishonor; it will rise in glory. It is sown in weakness; it will rise in power. It is sown an animal body; it will rise a spiritual body.” This certainly cannot be fulfilled except in the saints. The wicked too are raised, but not into glory; rather, into everlasting shame, as the prophet asserts (Jeremiah 23:40).

Here he appropriately establishes the difference between nature and grace, and recalls the testimony of the Old Testament in which it is said: “The first man Adam was made a living soul.” He adds from his own teaching: “The last Adam a life-giving spirit.”

He shows that the gifts of immortality belong to the life-giving spirit, while the merely living soul belongs to nature, which at some time dies. “This,” he says, “is not therefore the same as what gives life. The life-giving one is he who confers immortality, and this he applies to Christ. The living one is the one who enjoys life, but does not exclude mortality.”

Thus he distinguished both statements by their conclusion, showing that Adam was made living but not immortal, whereas Christ was made a spirit—not merely living, but also conferring resurrection, glorious for his own and eternal for all.

AUG. Was Adam therefore going to die even if he had not sinned, because he had been made with an animal body and not a spiritual one? You are completely mistaken if you think that, for this reason, it was necessary for us to fill God’s paradise with the deaths and punishments of dying creatures, and finally with the disgrace, weakness, and corruption in which human animal bodies are now sown. For the tree of life, which God planted in his paradise, also protected the animal body from death, until, through the merit of persevering obedience, it passed without death intervening into the spiritual glory that the righteous will possess when they rise.

For it was just that the image of God, not darkened or worn away by any sin, should be implanted in such a body—although that body had been created and formed from earthly matter—so that the stability of life supplied by the tree of life might remain with it; and that it might meanwhile live through the living soul, from which no necessity would separate it; and that from there, on account of obedience preserved, it might attain to the life-giving spirit. Thus this lesser life, in which it could both die and not die, would not be taken away from it, but that greater life would be added in which it would live without the aid of any tree and could not die.

For I ask you: what sort of body do you now suppose Elijah and Enoch to have—an animal body or a spiritual one? If you say, “An animal body,” why are you unwilling to believe that Adam, Eve, and their descendants, if they had violated God’s command by no transgression, would have lived, though in an animal body, as these men now live? [Note: [Col. 1598] Vignier has “not”; the manuscripts have “now.”] For those men were in the place to which these men were translated, and these men live in the place from which those men were expelled so that they might die.

The bodily tree of life therefore supplied life to animal bodies just as the spiritual tree of life, which is the wisdom of God, supplies the life of saving doctrine to holy minds. Hence some Catholic interpreters of the divine utterances have preferred to commend a spiritual paradise; nevertheless, they do not resist the historical account, which shows more clearly that it was bodily.

But if you answer that Enoch and Elijah already possess spiritual bodies, why do you not acknowledge that the bodies of the first human beings, and of those who would have been born from them in successive generations, if no sin had existed that would deservedly separate them from the tree of life, could have passed from an animal body into a spiritual one without an intervening death [Note: [Col. 1599] So the manuscripts. The printed editions read “by the death of the Mediator,” omitting “you acknowledge.”]—so that you would not be forced to fill God’s paradise, the place of blessed joys, with the punishments of deaths and dying creatures [Note: [Col. 1599] The printed editions omit “of deaths and”; the manuscripts have it.] and with the tortures of innumerable deadly diseases?

### XL. JULIAN

“But not first what is spiritual,” he says, “but what is animal; afterward, what is spiritual. The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man from heaven, heavenly. Just as we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of the heavenly one.”

Clearly he now turns to matters of conduct, and he wants there to be as much difference between our former and present way of life as there is between mortality and immortality. “The first man,” he says, “was from the earth, earthly; the second man from heaven, heavenly.” By naming substances, he indicates the difference involved in his proposition. For Christ, whom he calls the heavenly man, did not bring his flesh down from heaven; he received it from the seed of David, from the seed of Adam, and within a woman from the flesh of a woman.

He therefore relates “earthly” and “heavenly” to virtues and vices. Finally, he continues: “Just as we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of the heavenly one.” So too in the Epistle to the Romans: “I speak in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh: just as you presented your members to serve impurity and iniquity for iniquity, so now present your members to serve righteousness for sanctification” (Rom. 6:19).

Following the tenor of the exhortation he had begun, he adds something which, unless it is understood, seems to overthrow everything he has said: “This, then, I say, brothers: flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God, nor will corruption possess incorruption.” Indeed, in these passages, in which he had labored over nothing other than affirming the resurrection of the flesh, which he had said would be placed in the glory of the kingdom, he now declares that flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God. If flesh does not possess it, if blood does not possess it, where is the resurrection of the dead whose glory he has just celebrated?

Yet, in accordance with the manner of Scripture, he has named “flesh and blood” as vices, not as substance. Finally, he made this same point clear: “Behold, I tell you a mystery: we shall all indeed rise, but we shall not all be changed.” The excellent teacher understood that above he had claimed the term “resurrection” only for future blessedness [Note: [Col. 1599] So the manuscripts. Vignier reads: “had indicated the term ‘resurrection’ only above the future blessedness.”]; and therefore, lest the matter remain ambiguous, he explained it: “We shall all indeed rise”—behold the common raising up—“but we shall not all be changed”—behold where the resurrection of the blessed lies. The transformation into glory is therefore owed only to those who deserve not God’s anger but his love.

“In a moment,” he says, “in the twinkling of an eye [Note: [Col. 1600] So the manuscripts. Vignier reads “of an eye.”], at the last trumpet; and the dead will rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed.” Here again he turns to those saints whom that day will find in the flesh. He says that in a moment as brief as the final limit of sound can be, those who had died will be raised incorruptible—that is, whole and sound—and those who are found alive will be transformed into glory.

“For this corruptible body must put on incorruption, and this mortal body must put on immortality. But when this mortal body has put on immortality, then will come to pass the saying that is written: ‘Death is swallowed up in your victory.’ [Note: [Col. 1600] The printed editions read “its victory”; the manuscripts read “your victory.”] Where is your sting, O death? Where is your victory? The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law.”

As he often does, he shows that he was speaking only of the resurrection of the saints. He therefore passes over the raising of the impious and declares that it is fitting for corruption to be devoured by the eternity of glory in the bodies of the saints.

“But when this,” he says, “has been accomplished, then it will be possible to mock the devil and everlasting death, which had made this natural corruption appear evil. Then the joys of the saints, seeing the sting of death crushed by them, will rebuke it, saying: ‘Where is your sting, O death? Where is your victory?’ The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law.”

That is: “O everlasting death, you had sin as your sting, by which you wounded those who deserted righteousness. For if you had not been armed with this sting—that is, voluntary sin—you would have harmed no one. You see that this sin and this sting have been broken by the strength of faith, as our reward bears witness, from which you were trying to lead us away. Your sting was sin, and the power of your sin was the law, because where there is no law, there is no transgression” (Rom. 4:15).

Or certainly, although your sting [Note: [Col. 1600] Here “your” is added from the manuscripts.] was sin, it nevertheless became stronger in the minds of transgressors alone after the law of Moses was brought against it. [Note: [Col. 1600] The old manuscript of Mar has: “The custom of the law was brought against it.” We think that it should be read: “The law of Moses was brought against it.” For what Julian adds—“For the law is holy,” etc.—also concerns the Mosaic law; and below, in book 3, chapter 141, he himself fears that Augustine may understand “the power of sin is the law” specifically of the commandment given to Adam.]

Yet the law was not given for the purpose of sharpening it. [Note: [Col. 1600] The Port manuscript has: “so that it might sharpen you.”] For “the law is holy, and the commandment holy and just and good. But sin, in order that it might appear to be sin, was working death in me through what is good, so that through the commandment sin might become sinful beyond measure” (Rom. 7:12–13).

This power, then, which your sting of spontaneous iniquity brought about in us, is shown to have been defeated and broken by the virtues of the faithful, by the crowns already awarded to the faithful. We therefore mock you, giving thanks to our God, who has given us this victory through our Lord Jesus Christ (1 Cor. 15:46–57).

[Col. 1601]

AUG. Enough has already been said above about the image of the earthly man and the image of the heavenly man; and we have answered you that the image of the heavenly man can now be borne by faith and hope, but will be borne in reality, when it has been presented and bestowed, when the spiritual body rises—the body that is now sown as an animal body.

For he assigns these two images—the one of the earthly man and the other of the heavenly man—to two respective realities: the former to the animal body, the latter to the spiritual body. Above he said: “Not first what is spiritual, but what is animal; afterward, what is spiritual”; and immediately added: “The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man from heaven, heavenly. Just as we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of the heavenly one.”

Who is that first man, if not Adam, through whom came death? And who is this second, if not Christ, through whom comes the resurrection of the dead? “For since death came through a man, the resurrection of the dead also comes through a man. For just as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive”—that is, whoever will be made alive will be made alive only in Christ. We have already spoken of this above.

There is certainly no ambiguity [Note: [Col. 1601] The Port manuscript reads “therefore.”] about which two realities these two images refer to: the former refers to death, the latter to resurrection. The former therefore refers to the death of the body, because the latter refers to the resurrection of the body; the former to the animal body, which is sown in disgrace, the latter to the spiritual body, which will rise in glory. We put on the former by being born, the latter by being reborn.

But since we are born under sin and are reborn in the remission of sins, he says: “Just as we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of the heavenly one.” He recalls that the former has already been brought about, while he exhorts us that the latter should come about. [Note: [Col. 1601] So the manuscripts. Vignier has: “that he should bring it about.”]

No one can bring it about that he was not born under the punishment by which his body is sown in disgrace. But unless he is reborn and perseveres in that grace in which he was reborn, he will not attain the condition of the spiritual body, which will rise in glory.

What then do you mean when you say: “Clearly he has turned to matters of conduct, and wants there to be as much difference between our former and present way of life as there is between mortality and immortality”? The Apostle is not turning to something else [Note: [Col. 1601] Vignier reads “that thing”; the manuscripts read “something else.”]; rather, he is completing what he had begun to say about the resurrection of the flesh [Note: [Col. 1601] Vignier reads “what he had begun about the resurrection.” “Of the flesh” has been added from the manuscripts.], to which he contrasts the death of the flesh.

He does not therefore want two ways of life—the bad and the good—to be understood here. Rather, he is asserting that the resurrection of the flesh will come through Christ just as the death of the flesh came through Adam.

Let the man of God do what he is doing; follow him, and do not try to make him follow you. However much you try, he does not follow you.

He plainly contrasts the death of the flesh with the resurrection of the flesh. He plainly assigns separate authors to these separate realities: Adam to the death of the body, Christ to the resurrection of the body. Clearly comparing two images, one of the earthly man and the other of the heavenly man, in opposition to each other, he assigns the former to the animal body, which through Adam deserved to be sown in disgrace, and the latter to the spiritual body, which through Christ will deserve to rise in glory.

Christ is also called a heavenly man according to the flesh, not because he took flesh from heaven, but because he also raised that flesh into heaven.

If good intention and good conduct bring people to the glorious resurrection [Note: [Col. 1602] Perhaps the text should read “that our bodies may attain”; the Port manuscript adds “our bodies.”], was it through an evil intention and the bad conduct of this life—which we led after being born and growing with the advance of age [Note: [Col. 1602] Vignier reads “and we led it with the advance of age,” omitting “growing,” which is found in the manuscripts.]—that we came to be born in an animal body with the inheritance of death? For who acquired the beginning of a sorrowful birth through an evil intention, or through any intention at all? Who by bad conduct brought it about that, however he might have lived, he would have to die?

Certainly, if we wish to relate these two things—the image of the earthly man, which belongs to the animal body, and the image of the heavenly man, which belongs to the spiritual body—to ways of life as well, then, just as we place the resurrection of the spiritual body on the side of righteousness, so we must place the death of the animal body on the side of sin. For just as that resurrection will occur through the righteousness of Christ, so that death occurred through the iniquity of Adam.

If you understand this and agree with this most evident truth, I grant what you say: “earthly” and “heavenly” refer to vices and virtues. For just as Christ’s virtue will cause the spiritual body to rise, so Adam’s vice caused the animal body to die.

The statement of this same Apostle to the Romans therefore does not fit here: “Just as you presented your members to serve impurity and iniquity for iniquity, so now present your members to serve righteousness for sanctification” (Rom. 6:19). There he was speaking about bad and good conduct [Note: [Col. 1602] So the manuscripts; Vignier reads “works.”]; here, however, he is speaking about the resurrection of the body and the death of the body.

But since those who already use reason cannot come to the glorious resurrection that will occur when the spiritual body rises unless they both believe and hope for it, he recalls that we have borne the image of the earthly man, in which death comes through a man, and exhorts us to bear the image of the heavenly man, in which the resurrection of the dead comes through a man. Thus, just as through Adam’s sin we came to the death of the animal body, so through Christ’s righteousness we may come to the resurrection of the spiritual body.

Then he adds: “This, however, I say, brothers: flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God.”

Here we do not criticize you for having believed that “flesh and blood” signifies carnal understanding, not the substance itself of the animal body, which is indeed sown in disgrace but will nevertheless rise in glory and will undoubtedly possess the kingdom of God.

This may also be understood in another way: in this passage the term “flesh and blood” may signify the corruption that we now see in flesh and blood. That corruption certainly will not possess the kingdom of God, because this corruptible body will be clothed with incorruption.

Accordingly, after saying, “Flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God,” as though explaining what he had signified by these terms, so that the very substance of the flesh would not be thought to be meant, he added: “Nor will corruption possess incorruption.” According to this interpretation, what follows also seems more closely connected.

But whichever meaning the author of these words intended by them, neither is contrary to the faith, which holds that the family of God, gathered from all the nations, will possess the kingdom of God in incorruptible flesh.

We therefore do not criticize you [Note: [Col. 1603] Vignier reads “certainly do not”; the Port manuscript reads “therefore do not.”] for something that, even before us, many Catholic interpreters of the divine Scriptures have said: that “flesh and blood” may be understood as referring to people who think according to flesh and blood, and therefore will not possess the kingdom of God. For the same teacher of the nations says: “To think according to the flesh is death.”

But we do criticize you because you do not wish to acknowledge that the death of the animal body occurred through the sin of the first man, although you hear the same Apostle saying: “The body is dead because of sin” (Rom. 8:6, 10). Nor do you dare deny that the resurrection of the spiritual body—which is set in opposition to the death of the animal body—will come through the righteousness of the second man.

You refuse to accept this because you want to fill paradise, that memorable place of blessed delights, with the bodies of the dead and with the tortures of the dying. This we criticize; this we detest; this we judge worthy of anathema.

At the end, against what death will the taunt be directed when it is said, “Where is your victory, O death? Where is your sting, O death?”—unless against the devil, who is also the author of bodily death, or against death itself, the death of the body, which the resurrection of the body will swallow up?

This saying will come to pass when this corruptible body has put on incorruption and this mortal body has put on immortality. For the Apostle says without ambiguity: “When this corruptible body has put on incorruption, then will come to pass the saying that is written: ‘Death is swallowed up in victory. Where is your victory, O death? Where is your sting, O death?’”

To what death will this be said, if not to the death that will be swallowed up in victory? And what death is that except the one that will then be swallowed up, when this corruptible and mortal body is clothed with incorruption and immortality?

The sting of this bodily death is therefore sin, because it is to this death that it will be said: “Where is your sting, O death?” He said that the sting is sin—the sting, namely, through which death came to be, not one which death itself produced, just as a cup of death is that by which death is brought about, not something brought about by death.

How then, as you think, will the taunt be directed not against this death but against eternal death? Will eternal death itself be swallowed up in victory when this mortal body has put on immortality? Has eternal death contended against the saints, so that its fear might be overcome by their struggle—the fear that previously held them captive when, through fearing it, they sinned?

Was it not precisely in order to conquer this death that the Lord died, “and destroyed him who had the power of death, that is, the devil, and freed those who through fear of death were subject to slavery throughout their lives” (Heb. 2:14–15)?

Were they subject through fear of eternal death [Note: [Col. 1603] The word “eternal” is added from the Port manuscript.], when rather those who do not fear it become subject to it? For this reason the Lord, so that this bodily death might not be feared—the fear of which makes people guilty—but rather that eternal death, by not fearing which they become guilty, says most plainly: “Do not fear those who kill the body and afterward have nothing more that they can do. But fear him who has power to destroy both body and soul in Gehenna” (Luke 12:4–5).

This is certainly the second and everlasting death. Against fear of it the saints do not struggle; rather, they struggle against this temporal bodily death. To conquer this one, they fear the other. For when they have conquered this one through devotion and righteousness, they will not experience the other.

Against this death, therefore, not against that one, they will hurl the taunt, saying: “Where is your victory, O death?” Elsewhere it is written: “Where is your contention, O death?” (Hos. 13:14, according to the Septuagint).

Since, then, the sting of this death is sin, how dare you say that it did not happen through the sin of the first man that we were separated from the tree of life in him and punished with bodily death?

What, I ask you, is the reason that, against the evident testimony of the divine utterances, you bark with the foam of your incredible, raging verbosity, as though your soul could not obtain life in God’s paradise unless you brought bodily death into it—with so many and such great bodily diseases, executioners, and heralds of death?

Pay attention to yourself instead, lest, by sending bodily punishments into the place of holy delights, you yourself should suffer in the place of everlasting pains of both soul and body.

### XLI. JULIAN

In this passage Augustine, to be sure, thinks that the sting of death is that ancient sin, not understanding what follows: “The power of sin is the law.” He tries to assert that this law was the commandment given to Adam.

But that law was not the power of sin; rather, it was the kind of sin. For it is one thing to give power to something already existing, and another to bring into existence something that did not exist.

If the eating of that tree had not been forbidden, it would not have been evil. But after it was forbidden and seized through transgression, sin was born there from the one who forbade and the one who despised the prohibition. The law, however, was not given for the purpose of transgression; nevertheless, if a human being had done the same thing—that is, eaten from the tree—he would not have sinned, because the tree was good, unless its taste had been forbidden by the law.

What is intrinsically wrong—for example, parricide, sacrilege, or adultery—is rightly said to have acquired power through the law among transgressors, who are made more desirous by prohibition, since it is recognized as evil even without a promulgated law. But what is not unjustly seized unless it is forbidden is properly called a kind or category there; its strength is not understood to have been conferred upon it by the occasion of the law.

But since I have been more lengthy here, at the end of this book I also remind my reader to examine carefully that no occasion for Manichaean impiety has been encountered in the law of God. If anything seems ambiguous, he should not doubt that it can be explained according to the rules of truth and reason and shown to accord with justice.

We therefore condemn, with the same force that accords with the law of God, both those who say, “There will be no resurrection of the dead through Christ,” and those who likewise assert, contrary to the Apostle, that Christ did not have a body of our nature, through which they honor the doctrines of the Manichaeans.

[Col. 1605]

AUG. I never said that the law given in paradise was what the Apostle meant when he said, “The power of sin is the law.” You have therefore said many things against me to no purpose, as though I had said this.

I have always understood “the power of sin” to mean the law by which sin—already existing, but working less effectively [Note: [Col. 1605] We add here from the manuscripts: “but working less effectively.”]—was strengthened. The same Apostle says of this law: “What then shall we say? Is the law sin? Certainly not. But I did not know sin except through the law. For I would not have known covetousness unless the law had said, ‘You shall not covet.’ But, taking occasion through the commandment, sin worked in me every kind of covetousness” (Rom. 7:7–8).

Behold how the law is the power of sin. Sin was working less effectively when it had not yet produced transgression, because the law had not yet been given: “For where there is no law, there is no transgression” (Rom. 4:15).

There was not yet every kind of covetousness before it grew through prohibition and became so strong that it broke the bond of the very prohibition through which it had grown.

You yourself have shown that you know this by arguing at length in support of this position, although, to demonstrate it, you brought forward other apostolic testimonies rather than the one I have now used—perhaps so that you would not have to admit that covetousness is sin.

For the one who said what I have recalled showed most clearly that it is sin: “I did not know sin except through the law.” And as though we were asking what sin he meant, he says: “I would not have known covetousness unless the law had said, ‘You shall not covet.’”

This covetousness, then, which is certainly evil, by which the flesh covets against the spirit, did not yet exist before that great sin of the first man. It then began to exist and corrupted human nature, as though in transmission, [Note: [Col. 1605] The printed editions have: “as though it were transmission.” The manuscripts Clar. and Mar. have: “as though in transmission.” Port. has: “as though into transmission.”] from which original sin is derived.

Every human being is born with it. The guilt of this covetousness is not removed except in those who are reborn, so that after this absolution no one is defiled by it except one who consents to it in order to carry out an evil deed, when the spirit either does not covet against it or does not covet more strongly than it does.

The sins that are added by the personal will of sinners, and the habit of sinning—which is not without reason commonly called a second nature—add strength to that same covetousness. Yet even then it is not every kind of covetousness. It still has room to grow, because it is weaker so long as sin is committed not knowingly but ignorantly.

That is why he did not say, “I did not have covetousness,” but “I did not know covetousness unless the law said, ‘You shall not covet.’ But, taking occasion through the commandment, sin worked in me every kind of covetousness.”

It is every kind of covetousness when forbidden things are desired more ardently, and when sins already known—once the excuse of ignorance has been removed and transgression of the law has been added—are committed more wickedly.

Hence the law of God, among those whom the grace of God does not help through the Lamb of God who takes away the sin [Note: [Col. 1606] So the manuscripts. Vignier has: “sins.”] of the world, is called not the correction of the sinner but rather the power of sin.

And therefore, after saying, “The power of sin is the law,” as though someone were to answer, “What then shall we do, if sin is not removed by the law but increased by it?” he immediately adds where hope should lie for those who struggle: “Thanks be to God, who has given us the victory”; or, as other manuscripts have—and as the Greek copies also have—“who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.”

Entirely and most truly so. For “if a law had been given that could make alive, righteousness would indeed be from the law. But Scripture confined all things under sin, so that the promise might be given to those who believe through faith in Jesus Christ” (Gal. 3:21–22).

These are the children of the promise and the vessels of mercy. The promise was given to them through faith in Jesus Christ because they received mercy so that they might be faithful. The Apostle says the same about himself (1 Cor. 7:25), so that even faith itself—from which whatever we do temperately, justly, and devoutly begins and to which it is referred—might not be attributed to the judgment of our will as though it were not given to us by God in his mercy. From him even the will itself, as it is written, is prepared (Prov. 8, according to the Septuagint).

For this reason the holy Church, through the mouths of its priests who offer prayers, prays not only for the faithful, that they may not fail in the piety by which they persevere in what they believe, but also for unbelievers, that they may believe.

From the time Adam, through the free choice of the human will, committed that great sin and condemned the whole human race together (Chrysostom, Letter to Olympias), all who are freed from this common condemnation are freed only by divine grace and mercy. Whatever the law of God commands is fulfilled only with the help, inspiration, and gift of the one who commands. He is entreated that the faithful may remain, advance, and be perfected; he is also entreated that unbelievers may begin to believe.

Those who raise up the judgment of the human will against this grace of God, so that they may fall more disastrously from their height, seek to suppress and extinguish these prayers of the holy Church, which are increasing and burning throughout the whole world. Among them you hold a contentious position, either alone or especially, [Note: [Col. 1606] So the manuscripts. Vignier has: “you who hold.”] because you do not want Jesus Christ to be Jesus for little children, whom you insist have not been touched by any original sin.

Yet he was called Jesus for this reason: because he saved his people—not from bodily diseases, which he was accustomed to heal even among those who were not his people, but from their sins (Matt. 1:21).

Although, therefore, in saying “the sting of death is sin” the Apostle unquestionably expressed the death that is opposed to the resurrection of the body about which he was speaking—that is, bodily death, which will itself be swallowed up in victory when the spiritual body rises and no longer exists, since the body too will possess immortality, which no sin can take away—nevertheless, in what he next added, “the power of sin is the law,” he did not mean the law that was given in paradise.

That law could not be the power of sin, since sin did not yet exist. Rather, he called that law the power of sin which entered so that sin might abound and produce every kind of covetousness—that is, not merely the covetousness that arose in paradise and brought death to the body, with which every human being is born; nor merely the covetousness that grew through sins added by each person’s evil conduct; but also that covetousness which, aroused more ardently by a prohibiting commandment, proceeded as far as transgression.

Thus victory—the victory not only over the desire of sin but also over the fear of bodily death, and finally over the weakness of mortality itself—was to be supplied not by the law given through Moses but by grace accomplished through Christ.

Accordingly, the Apostle said: “The sting of death is sin; but the power of sin is the law. Thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.” It was as though he were saying:

“The sting of death is indeed sin, because bodily death itself also came through sin. At the end, the one who caused it—or death itself—will be addressed by those in whom it will be swallowed up as they rise in glory: ‘Where is your victory, O death? Where is your sting, O death?’

“But this sting—that is, sin—which entered through one man and passed into all human beings with death, and which was multiplied by the addition of other sins, the holy, just, and good law could not remove. [Note: [Col. 1607] All the printed editions have this reading, but the sense requires the passage to be read as follows: ‘multiplied by the addition of other sins, it could not be removed by the holy, just, and good law.’ M.] Rather, the law became its power, when forbidden covetousness burned more intensely and reached the accumulation of transgression.

“What then remained except for grace to come to our aid? Thanks therefore be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ. By forgiving our debts and not leading us into temptation, he brings us to the final victory in which bodily death itself is swallowed up, so that whoever boasts may not trust in his own power but boast in the Lord” (2 Cor. 10:17).

This is the right and Catholic faith. In it we have also learned and hold that bodily death was made through the sting that is sin. It differs so greatly from the error of the Manichaeans, and is so opposed to it, that they should rather say with you than with us that Adam was made mortal in such a way that, whether he sinned or did not sin, he would have died.

Yet [Note: [Col. 1608] “Yet” is restored from the manuscripts.] we do not therefore call you Manichaeans because you say this. Nevertheless, you do not see that for the same reason we should not be called Manichaeans by you because both they and we say that covetousness is evil, by which the flesh covets against the spirit.

But you differ from them, in what you say together with them, by a different though still another error: they attribute the death of the flesh to a nature alien to us and mingled with ours, whereas you impose it upon our nature, which has not been corrupted by any sin. Thus you unhappily and indecently fill the paradise of the most honorable and happiest delight with the funerals of the dead and the tortures of the dying. [Note: [Col. 1608] See above, book 3, chapter 154.]

But in saying with the Manichaeans that the covetousness of the flesh, by which it covets against the spirit, is evil and is not from the Father (1 John 2:16), we differ from them not by another, though dissimilar, heretical error, but by Catholic truth.

For we argue, together with the Catholic Ambrose and his associates, that this conflict between the two covetousnesses of flesh and spirit did not come upon us through the mingling of an evil nature coeternal with God, as the Manichaeans say, but entered into our nature through the transgression of the first man (Ambrose, book 7 on Luke 12:53). Against both of you we confidently assert that Christ’s flesh was not, as the Manichaeans say, nonexistent, nor, as you slanderously claim, alien from the nature of our flesh. Rather, we proclaim that it was free from this defect of ours, by which the flesh covets against the spirit, and was entirely undefiled.

But by denying that the things which are evil are evil, and by not referring their origin to the sin of the first man, you do not make them not evil. Rather, with detestable blindness, you assist the Manichaeans in making them believed to be coeternal with the good eternal nature; and you accuse them pointlessly because you are pitiably helping them. [Note: [Col. 1608] In the manuscripts Mar. and Clar., and in Vignier, the following is added: “Here ends the sixth book of Aurelius Augustine, Catholic bishop, against Julian, the heretical Pelagian, successfully.” In Port.: “Here ends the sixth book of blessed Augustine against Julian.”]

## APPENDIX TO VOLUME TEN OF THE WORKS OF SAINT AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, DIVIDED INTO THREE PARTS

The first part contains spurious minor works, namely: the *Hypomnesticon*, or books commonly called the *Hypognosticon*; the book *On Predestination and Grace*; and the short work *On the Predestination of God*.

The second part contains various writings and documents relating to Pelagian history.

The third part contains apologetic minor works of Prosper of Aquitaine on behalf of Augustine against the unjust critics of his doctrine of grace and predestination, as well as Prosper’s *Book of Sentences* drawn from Augustine.

## FIRST PART OF THE APPENDIX, CONTAINING CERTAIN SPURIOUS MINOR WORKS

[Note: [Col. 1611] We compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of *Retractations* and *Confessions*, volume 1. M.]

### [THE HYPOMNESTICON]

[Col. 1609]

## NOTICE ON THE HYPOMNESTICON
This work is divided in printed editions into six books, commonly entitled *Hypognosticon*, that is, “Books of Subnotations.” The first five of these present, respectively, a response to each of the five doctrines of the Pelagians, set down in subnotated form. Yet in the preface by the author himself, and also by the ancients who cite it, it is called *Hypomnesticon*, as if one should say “Memorandum” or, as those ancient writers themselves interpret it, “Memorial.” For it appears to have been the author’s intention to hand down, in summary form and for the assistance of memory, the doctrine of the Catholic Church against the Pelagians: “For, trusting,” he says, “that these matters ought to be answered, as a *hypomnesticon*, I have taken care to make this little book abbreviated.” In the Sorbonne manuscript, however, and in several more recent manuscripts, it is called *The Book of Augustine’s Hypognosticon*; and these same more recent manuscripts do not append the sixth book, which concerns predestination, to the preceding five books.

In the older manuscripts, moreover—namely, the Remigian manuscript, approximately nine hundred years old, the Germanensis, and others—the title prefixed to the work is: *Responses of Saint Augustine against the Pelagians and Coelestians*. After the first book these codices read: “The first response ends. The second response begins.” After the second: “The second response ends. The third response begins.” And similarly after each book up to the fifth, at the end of which appears: “The fifth response ends. A discussion concerning Predestination against the same persons begins.” This is the book commonly called the sixth book of the *Hypognosticon*. Certain Victorine manuscripts present this sixth book alone and separately from the other five, under the following inscription: “Augustine’s Discussion of Predestination against the Pelagians.” The much older Germanensis manuscript also contains it, prefaced as follows: “Here begins blessed Augustine’s work On Predestinations against Coelestius.” In that manuscript, with its first verse omitted, the book begins with the words, “It is especially necessary also to add to this work.” In that codex this sixth book is appended to certain excerpts from Tychonius the Donatist; but Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, in the first chapter of his book *On Predestination*, indicates that he had seen a manuscript in which it was appended after the work *On the Eight Questions of Dulcitius*.

As for the name of Augustine, it was entirely absent from the most ancient Corbie exemplar of this work. Nevertheless, the work is found attributed to Augustine by writers of the ninth century. Among them, Hincmar, in his letter concerning Gottschalk to Amolo and the Church of Lyons, says that Augustine,

“after he had written *On Free Will*, *On Rebuke and Grace*, *On the Perfection of Human Righteousness*, and *On the Predestination of the Saints* to Prosper and Hilary—in which he said nothing concerning the predestination of the reprobate, but concerning the predestination of the saints—at the request of many wrote the book *Hypomnesticon* against Coelestius and Pelagius, treating five questions, and added a sixth in the place of a retraction, concerning predestination, in which he excuses himself by saying that he had not spoken in that sense, nor wished it to be understood that the reprobate had been predestined to destruction, but that punishment had been predestined for those who persevered in iniquity or impiety.”

Remigius, archbishop of Reims, and the Church of Lyons refute Hincmar in the thirty-fifth chapter of their book *On Three Letters*, in these words:

“He also adds something new, which until now has been known to us neither from reading nor from any truthful tradition: namely, that blessed Augustine, after all his books, wrote a certain little work which he calls by the Greek name *Hypomnesticon*, interpreted in Latin as ‘Memorial’; and that in it he disputed against Pelagius and Coelestius concerning five questions; and that whatever he had said in his preceding books concerning divine predestination with respect to the condemnation of the reprobate, he had not said in the sense in which everyone knows and understands that he said it, but in another most absurd and inappropriate sense: so that, when he said that the impious had been predestined to destruction, he did not wish the impious themselves to be understood as predestined to destruction, but—something which no one could believe or even suspect—wished it to be understood that punishment had been predestined for them, and so forth. Who could endure such absurdity, indeed such madness? For we know very clearly that when he wrote the books of the *Retractions*, already old and near death, in which he carefully and faithfully revised all his preceding books, he had by no means yet written this little work. If he had written it, he would certainly have mentioned it among the others.

“It also appears clear that, after his death, when a certain holy bishop and his disciple [Note: [Col. 1611] Possidius.] most carefully reviewed and recorded his life and catalogue—not only of his books, but also of his treatises addressed to the people and his letters to various persons—blessed Augustine had not yet written this little work. For if he had written it, it could certainly have been numbered and commended to memory among the others as especially necessary. But if one of the rulers of the Church who lived after his death simply believed, from the title inscribed with the name of Saint Augustine, without more careful consideration or any necessity compelling him to do so, that the work belonged to the person whose name he found on its front, what prejudice does that cause to the truth? Once carefully sought and found, truth allows no one to err on this matter.

“For the little work mentioned above itself also shows by the clearest indications that it is not Saint Augustine’s: it contains no preface at its beginning in which one could find that he had indicated that he had been asked by someone, or had himself judged it necessary, to write a new work on such a matter—that is, to correct or explain differently in his books the doctrine of predestination.” [Note: [Col. 1611] He is speaking of the sixth book; or he does not deny that the work as a whole lacks every kind of preface, but only one that would indicate that Augustine intended to retract what he had said concerning the predestination of the reprobate.]

“Nor is any such necessity known to have existed that he should again discuss, in a new work, those five questions concerning which he had argued at such length and in such varied ways in his preceding books. The style itself also differs greatly from Saint Augustine’s eloquence. Its meaning is held to be considerably inferior to his meaning. His moderation and humility of character and speech are not preserved in it. It uses testimonies from the Hebrew translation edited by blessed Jerome against those heretics, contrary to Augustine’s custom; for he was accustomed to do this rather from the ancient edition. And it is wholly unworthy to think that so great a man could be found in this little work emptying and destroying the doctrine of predestination—the doctrine which throughout all his writings and preaching he maintained and commended, and which, since he did not criticize it in the books of the *Retractions*, he plainly approved—so that, by reason of this, confidence could no longer be placed even in his *Retractions*.

“It is therefore more credible that the work was written, not long after his death, by someone else, and that it was collected and arranged in abbreviated form, largely according to the manner and pattern of his thought, against the heretics Pelagians and Coelestians, concerning their five more dangerous questions. And because its author appears to have gathered and explained, as though into one whole, the thought of blessed Augustine in this brief work, he therefore wished the name of Saint Augustine to appear in the title of the work itself—as though, if he had wished to call the same little work in Latin ‘Saint Augustine’s Memorial,’ nothing else would have been understood except that what Augustine had discussed in scattered and varied form had been briefly set down and, as it were, placed before the eyes in a single view for the sake of memory.”

And in the ninth chapter of his book *On Maintaining the Truth of Scripture*, replying to the authority of the *Hypomnesticon*, he says:

“It is most manifestly contrary to the thought of the aforesaid Doctor, indeed to Catholic integrity, nor does its style in any way agree with his eloquence.”

Prudentius, bishop of Troyes, uses the same arguments against John Scotus in the fourteenth chapter of his book *On Predestination*, where he proves that the *Hypomnesticon* is not Augustine’s.

John Garnerius, in the sixth dissertation appended to Mercator’s works, *On Writings against the Pelagian Heresy*, conjecturally declares that the true author of the books of the *Hypognosticon* was Sixtus, the Roman presbyter who succeeded Coelestine in the Apostolic See. Anyone who observes, with Garnerius, not only that Mercator gave the same title to his more notable little works against the Pelagians—calling one a book of “Subnotations” and the other a “Memorial”—but also that, in Letter 193, which Garnerius had not yet seen when he was investigating the author of the *Hypognosticon*, Augustine replies to Mercator in its first chapter that he had received with Mercator’s letter another book of his against the new Pelagian heretics, filled with testimonies from Holy Scripture, will more readily attribute it to Mercator.

Nevertheless, although Augustine praises this book of Mercator, its identification with the *Hypomnesticon* cannot be asserted immediately and confidently, because of the style and manner of expression, which in the *Hypomnesticon* we do not find to be entirely the same as in Mercator’s other undisputed little works.

[Col. 1611]

# THE HYPOMNESTICON AGAINST THE PELAGIANS AND COELESTIANS, COMMONLY CALLED THE BOOKS OF THE HYPOGNOSTICON. (C, G, S)

## Preface

[Col. 1611] 1. The adversaries of the Catholic faith, while striving to fight against the rule of truth with diabolical weapons, make us more cautious through the anxiety of resisting them; but they deceive themselves before they are able to wound any one of our number. For when the blind contend to empty the treasures of faith, emptied of the hope of faith, they cause the Church, assisted by God’s grace, to glory in the fullness of faith [Note: [Col. 1612] Thus most manuscripts. The printed editions, however, have: “the fullness of the faith of the Church,” etc.]. [Col. 1613] And while they keep watch in hypocrisy in order to do harm—of whom I think it was therefore said through the prophet, “Sleep has been taken away from their eyes, for they do not sleep unless they have done evil” [Prov. 4:16]—they in a certain way awaken us who are sleeping, so that, having taken up the shield of truth and with our hearts resisting their falsehoods, we may keep watch, while the evangelical trumpet sounds in our ears: “Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation” [Mark 14:38].

Therefore the heretics who attack the Catholic [Note: [Col. 1613] Here the printed editions add “faith.” Several manuscripts have “Church.” The more ancient books have neither.] Church trust in their own strength—that is, in the boldness of their heart—being abandoned by grace; and they glory in the abundance of their riches, namely, in the works of their own will [Note: [Col. 1613] The manuscripts have “they glory.”]. But God has scattered the bones of those who please themselves; they have been confounded because the Lord has despised them [Ps. 52:6].

Let us also trust, as we resist them, in the grace of the Lord, which is our glory, redeeming us from those who surround us, giving us understanding, and instructing us in this way in which we walk [Note: [Col. 1613] Several ancient books have “in which we proceed.”], while he establishes his eyes over us. For our salvation and our glory are in God; God is our help, and our hope is in God.

2. But now it is necessary to explain in the following discourse who or against whom I have spoken these things, and to respond to their perverse doctrines insofar as the Lord in his grace has deigned to instruct us. Accordingly, we must respond concerning the heretics Pelagians and Coelestians, whom the Lord, before the foundation of the world, foresaw would become such through their own fault, and whom, once they had arisen in the world, he condemned by a just judgment [Note: [Col. 1613] In certain manuscripts: “who were excluded.”].

The apostle Peter pointed to these future persons in his Second Letter, saying:

“There were indeed false prophets among the people, just as there will also be false teachers among you, who will introduce destructive sects and deny the Lord who bought them, bringing upon themselves swift destruction. And many will follow their debaucheries, through whom the way of truth will be blasphemed; and in greed they will exploit you with fabricated words. Their judgment has not been idle for a long time, and [Col. 1614] their destruction does not sleep” [2 Pet. 2:1–3].

Therefore, trusting in the teaching of God’s grace that these matters must be answered, I have taken care to make this little book abbreviated, as a *hypomnesticon* [Note: [Col. 1614] The printed editions have *hypognosticon*. Most manuscripts, especially the older ones, have *hypomnesticon*.]. Whoever wishes to read it should not scrutinize the mediocrity of its wording, but the reasoning of its faith; and, if it pleases him, let him give thanks to God [Note: [Col. 1614] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have “to God” in the dative form.], who teaches human beings knowledge.

If there are matters in which we have erred unwillingly—if, indeed, there are any matters requiring correction—let him correct them, with charity in view and God as judge; but let the one who corrects be Catholic in understanding. If, however, someone is ignorant or envious, let him not presume to corrupt what is sound; for he will stand with me before the tribunal of Christ to give an account, whoever he may be.

3. The following, then, is the impious blasphemy of their doctrine:

I. “Adam,” they say, “whether he had sinned or had not sinned, would have died.

II. Yet his sin harmed no one except himself.

III. A human being, through free will—as though sufficient for himself by himself—can fulfill whatever he wishes; or else, through the merits of works, God gives grace to each person.

IV. Sexual desire is naturally good, and there is nothing in it that ought to cause shame.

V. Infants do not carry original sin, nor will they perish from eternal life if they depart from this life without the sacrament of Baptism” [Note: [Col. 1614] In the printed editions “the children of the baptized” is added here; it is absent from the manuscripts.].

O evil doctrine, discovered by the enemy of peace! O doctrine by which the unity of the mother Church of the reborn is torn apart! O doctrine that, under Christ’s name, attempts to overthrow and alter Christ’s foundations! O doctrine with a thousand impious names and a thousand arts of doing harm [Note: [Col. 1614] An allusion to *Aeneid* 7.337–338.]! It takes weapons against the Law from the Law; it attacks the Gospel by fighting from the Gospel; and, to its own destruction, by fabricating falsehoods from truths, it challenges truth to falsehood. But these things are their punishment, which the person who utters them disorderly believes to be victory, so that what is written may be fulfilled in them: “By the things through which anyone sins, by these he is also tormented” [Wis. 11:17].

# BOOK ONE

## In which the first doctrine of the Pelagians is overthrown

[Col. 1613]

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 1613]

1. “Adam,” they say, “whether he had sinned or had not sinned, would have died.”

We answer: You are mistaken, heretic; you are mistaken. It is not so. Or, if it is so and you are not mistaken, establish it by divine proofs. But far be it from us to find in the Holy Scriptures God as the author of death. For it is written:

“Do not court death through the error of your life, for God did not make death, nor does he rejoice in the destruction of the living. For he created all things that they might exist, and he made the generations of the world healthy” [Wis. 1:12–14].

Again, in the same book:

“God created human beings imperishable, and made them in his own image; but through the devil’s envy death entered the world” [Wis. 2:23–24].

If you can see, then see that death came to human beings placed in the paradise of delights not from God as its author, but through the error of life—that is, when, through the reasoning faculty of the soul by which they had been established as good and life-giving, they departed from the divine command, through the envy and deception of the serpent.

You hear the Prophet testifying that God did not make death, but you dare to say that God is its author, although in the book of Genesis he foretold to the first-formed human being what would happen if he touched the forbidden tree. For it is written:

“And the Lord said to Adam: You may eat from every tree that is in paradise; but you shall not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. For on the day on which you eat from it, you shall die” [Gen. 2:16–17].

You hear this, and you dare to call God the author of death? Death, then, coming through the envy of the devil, entered the world, and by the just judgment of God was permitted to rule over the sinner as punishment.

[Col. 1614] For rightly did the one who refused to guard against the death foretold, lest he lose life, lose life himself. Yet the truthful and merciful Lord does not rejoice in the destruction of the living. For what is the destruction of the living except death? It is the death, however, of those who live wickedly, who will perish in the second death—not of the righteous living, that is, of those who seek God, to whom, because of Adam’s sin, which they have carried with them from birth, only the first death, not the second, is due.

If, then, according to you, God is the author of death, he ought to rejoice at the death of the living as at his own good work, because it is written, “The Lord will rejoice in his works” [Ps. 103:31], and because he made nothing that he hated, but everything he made was very good [Gen. 1:31], as it is written:

“For you love all things that exist, and you hate none of the things that you have made; nor did you establish anything while hating it” [Wis. 11:25].

## CHAPTER TWO

2. Or why, in opposition to it, did he assume flesh from the body subject to its sin, without sin, if he himself made it the weapon of the body? For we know that, while making the world, God made nothing contrary to himself. Therefore, if you have not lost your sight through the darkness of death, understand that God the Son assumed humanity in order to conquer death, his enemy, or sin, its mother [Note: [Col. 1614] The ancient codices omit “its mother.”].

For, concerning what was impossible for the Law [Note: [Col. 1614] The printed editions have “impossible for the Law” in the dative; the manuscripts have the genitive form, in accordance with the Greek.], [Col. 1615] Paul, the vessel of election, says: “What was impossible for the Law, in which it was weakened through the flesh, God did, sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and on account of sin condemned sin in the flesh” [Rom. 8:3].

But what is “impossible for the Law” except what it was unable to make either obedient or perfect in the one subject to it? It could neither remove sin nor conquer death. Yet, explaining why it could not accomplish this, he adds: “in which it was weakened through the flesh.”

For by commanding one who is weak without helping him, it is weakened, because through the flesh—that is, through the desires of the flesh arising from sin, which a human being cannot overcome by free choice alone—he cannot become a doer of the Law unless God’s preceding grace is present. Thus the same apostle says: “The Law brought nothing to perfection” [Heb. 7:19].

What, then, does it mean that the Son of God came in the likeness of sinful flesh, except that his flesh had no sin, unlike ours? The apostle Peter says of him: “He committed no sin”—that is, he did not possess sin—“nor was deceit found in his mouth” [1 Pet. 2:22].

By saying “in the likeness of sinful flesh,” he showed that Christ’s flesh was without sin, whereas ours is sinful. He was in the likeness because he was born in true flesh from a virgin’s womb, not through the use of sexual desire as we are, but through a mystical inspiration.

“And on account of sin,” he says, “he condemned sin in the flesh”—namely, in human sinful nature. I call it sinful, not because God was its author, but because a human being transgressed. Assuming flesh, as I have said, without guilt, and crucifying this innocent flesh, he condemned the sin that had condemned us through disobedience in the earthly Adam, in the obedient heavenly Adam.

We die because we have been conquered by sin; but Christ, though innocent, wished to die so that by dying he might take death captive and conquer it. In a certain way he allowed it to rule over him when he patiently offered himself to be killed according to its will. But when death saw in hell, among the wicked, the righteous one, and had no basis for mocking him as it did the others, it could not hold him when he rose again. Rather, defeated, prostrated, and condemned, it fell.

Therefore the Apostle, exalting Christ’s victory over death and rejoicing on behalf of his servants, announces:

“Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more; death shall no longer rule over him. For in that he died, he died to sin once; but in that he lives, he lives to God” [Rom. 6:9–10].

By saying this, what else did he wish us to understand except that God did not make death, nor rejoice in the destruction of the living, since he wished, without sin, to share in the condition of the dead in order to conquer death through the weakness of the flesh?

If you do not believe that through the devil’s envy death entered the world through sin, you assert nothing else except that God made death so that, after human beings to whom he had given his own image had been killed, he would be forced to fight with death, or even to die and rise again.

But far, far be this from the Catholic faith, which believes—under the teaching of the faithful master Paul—that through one human being sin entered the world, and through sin death, and thus passed into all human beings [Rom. 5:12]; and that Christ died for our sins and rose for our justification [Rom. 4:25], reconciling us to God the Father in his own body through the cross [Eph. 2:16].

3. Be ashamed, I beg you, and be silent. For in your own perpetual death [Note: [Col. 1615] The printed editions have “for your perpetual death”; the manuscripts differ.] you accuse God, while excusing the devil in the matter of death—and this because you fear offending not God but the devil.

Tell me, then: if God made death, why did Christ God, according to the flesh, weep for the dead Lazarus [John 11:35]? He ought not to have grieved over what he himself had made. But by grieving and weeping for him, he showed that those whom God had made living, the devil had made mortal through guilt.

He raised Lazarus so that the devil might recognize that he had gained nothing by killing him, and so that no human being belonging to God might despair because of death, since [Col. 1616] those whom the devil thought had perished sleep in God.

“I do not desire,” the Lord says through the prophet Ezekiel, “the death of the sinner, but that he should turn back and live” [Ezek. 18:23, 32].

If, as you proclaim, God is its author, why does he repel death from the sinner by saying, “I do not desire it,” and not allow what belongs to him to remain? “I do not desire,” he says, “the death of the sinner, which I did not make for him; rather, while he was a transgressor against me, he found it for himself. But let him turn back and live”—that is, let him receive again, through my mercy, the life he lost by sinning.

## CHAPTER THREE

4. No believer, therefore, can doubt that the first human beings were made so living that, if in the freedom of the soul in which they had been created immaculate they had despised the serpent’s deadly deception, they would have enjoyed eternal life; but if they had followed it, they would have lost that life.

For this reason God warned them beforehand not to touch what was forbidden, so that whatever adversity later befell them after they had been defeated would be attributed not to the one who had given the warning, but to themselves for their disobedience.

When he had foretold that death would come to those who transgressed, is it to be believed that he himself had made what was to happen? Why did he warn them to avoid it if he himself was its author at their destruction? Yet the death that came through the devil could not have prevailed over them as they sinned unless the Lord, by a just judgment, had permitted it as vengeance for their disobedience.

Thus, that human beings die is the punishment of sin; that they return to life is the work of the merciful Lord. But the one who returns to true life is the one who, through a good way of life proceeding from God’s grace, sanctified by Christ’s blood, enters the kingdom of heaven and, as though returning to his own homeland to please the Lord—a land from which he had been exiled by sin—rejoicing and triumphing over death, says to his soul:

“Return, my soul, to your rest, for the Lord has dealt generously with you; for he has rescued my soul from death, my eyes from tears, and my feet from falling. I shall please the Lord in the land of the living” [Ps. 114:7–9].

Why shall I please him? Because the Lord has dealt generously with me.

The sinner, too, receives life, but he does not return to life. The return to life is in the kingdom of heaven, which no one dying in his sins or without Baptism can possess. He receives life, however, in a body in which he will no longer die physically, but will live in the body in such a way as to be dead in life; or, while living bodily, he will remain forever in punishment, condemned with both life and body together with the devil, the author of death [Note: [Col. 1616] The Corbie manuscript, in a second hand, has “condemned.”].

Therefore the Lord also says in the Gospel to those who will be on the left on the day of judgment—that is, to the impious and sinners:

“Go into the eternal fire, which my Father has prepared for the devil and his angels.”

But to the righteous who will be on the right:

“Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.”

“And then,” he says, “they will go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” [Matt. 25:41, 34, 46].

In that life they will be glorified—that is, changed from corruption into incorruption and from mortality into immortality. They will shine, and, reigning forever with Christ, will exult over condemned death, saying:

“Death has been swallowed up in victory. Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting?” [1 Cor. 15:54–55].

## CHAPTER FOUR

5. Death, then, is the deprivation of life, possessing only a name and not an essence; and therefore God cannot be said to be its author. For whatever we say God has made possesses essence—that is, it is a form or species. “Essence” is derived from *that which is*, and should properly be said only of God, according to what is written in Exodus to Moses: “You shall say to them”—that is, to the people—“He Who Is has sent me to you” [Exod. 3:14].

Nevertheless, one may also say of other creatures that they possess essence, but not in the same way as of God, who has no beginning of his being. Rather, having received their beginning from God, they began to exist as what they are.

Death, therefore, is nothing except a name left behind when life has departed. So hunger is the lack of food; thirst, the want of drink; darkness, the absence of light; barrenness, the lack [Col. 1617] of fruit [Note: [Col. 1617] The manuscripts have “offspring.”]; silence, the absence of voice; want, the deprivation of resources; and so with whatever other things are discovered to be nothing except names through the deprivation of realities.

For I think that death received this name because Adam was killed in paradise by the bite, as it were, of the poisonous serpent—that is, the devil. The serpent deceived Adam by its bite when it persuaded him, through desire, to bite—that is, to eat—what was forbidden. And, as I have said, death therefore received its name as though from a bite.

Hence also the Lord, threatening death through the prophet Hosea, says:

“I shall be your death, O death; I shall be your bite, O hell” [Hos. 13:14].

“Death” and “hell” are understood as spoken in the person of the devil, because through him death—that is, the deprivation of life—befell the transgressing human being; and through him sinners are turned into hell, as into his prison, where he himself has been condemned.

6. But it must be asked how Christ, God the Son of God, became the death of death and the bite of hell.

There is no doubt that he did so in the flesh he assumed, in which death had no claim against him. As he himself says, “The prince of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me” [John 14:30]. After his Baptism he was tempted in the desert, but did not obey the devil’s desires when the devil said, “Tell these stones to become bread” [Matt. 4:3], and so forth.

Or he became death’s death because he allowed himself, righteous and innocent, to be fastened to the cross by the bite of nails and to be pierced by the mouth of a lance [John 19:18, 34]. I have said “the mouth of a lance” in accordance with what is said concerning sinners: “They shall fall by the mouth of the sword” [Sir. 28:22]. A lance is certainly a sword.

And because, descending into hell as into the mouth of death—whence he says in the Psalm, “Let not the deep swallow me, nor let the pit close its mouth over me” [Ps. 68:16], that is, hell—it was impossible for him to be held by the devil, he raised on the third day the human being whom he had assumed for humanity, namely, his flesh, which did not see corruption, and brought him forth from the mouth of hell as Jonah was brought forth from the mouth of the whale.

For hell was to Christ what the whale was to Jonah, as the Lord himself says:

“For just as Jonah was in the whale’s belly three days and three nights, so will the Son of Man be in the heart of the earth three days and three nights” [Matt. 12:40].

He therefore became the bite of hell when he allowed himself to be received by it as food—that is, his flesh—with which hell would not be sated, as it is with sinners, but would itself be swallowed up. For this reason it is said: “Death has been swallowed up in victory.”

I also think that the testimony found in the prophet Amos was spoken for this reason, when the Lord, promising future evils to the sinful people, says:

“Even if they hide from my eyes in the depths of the sea, there I shall command the serpent, and it shall bite them” [Amos 9:3].

What does “Even if they hide from my eyes in the depths of the sea” mean? It means: even if they persist in evil works, turning themselves away from my eyes—that is, from my spiritual commands, because the eyes of God are the Spirit of God, who gave the Law, that is, the commandments—in the depths of the sea, namely, in the depth of despair.

“There I shall command the serpent, and it shall bite them”: there, in that same despair of contempt, I shall command, I shall give power to, the serpent—that is, the devil, who from the beginning [Col. 1618] was called a serpent—and it shall bite them. By the bite of various desires with which he kills those who sin, he will put them to death.

But the bite produces death. It is not itself death, as with wild beasts or every kind of savage animal, which sometimes kill human beings with their bite and yet are not themselves death. Rather, by an incurable bite they cause death—that is, deprivation of life—just as a sword’s blow, a stone’s strike, or anything else can deprive a human being of life by killing him.

## CHAPTER FIVE

7. I must not omit the following, lest perhaps some enemy of the truth who is not a seeker of certain arguments, but an inventor and proposer of tangled questions for the subversion of his hearers, should say:

“If death is nothing except a name, as you argued above, because death saw Christ, the righteous one, in hell among the wicked, and because there was no sin in him was unable to hold him when he rose again, so as to mock him as it did the other sinners, and therefore was defeated, prostrated, and condemned—if, then, death is nothing, how can something that is nothing see, hold, mock, be conquered, be prostrated, or be condemned?”

We answer: What is “nothing” itself? For sometimes, when we name “nothing,” we add “is,” as in the Gospel passage: “Without him nothing was made” [John 1:3]. Is it a substance, or a name lacking substance?

As I have already said, many people commonly say, when something is despised, regarded as insignificant, or entirely nonexistent: “It is nothing.” When, therefore, we say “nothing,” we name an insubstantial name; but when we add “is,” we signify a reality. Why, then, do we say “nothing,” an insubstantial name, as though it truly were something, by adding “is”? Everything we say “is,” we judge to be something. Nevertheless, when we repeatedly say “it is nothing,” in accordance with customary speech we add “is” to “nothing,” although “nothing” is merely a name and not a thing.

So also, in the case of death, according to customary expression or by comparison with an agent, we say, “Death sees,” “it does something,” “it mocks,” or “it has been condemned,” “it has been conquered,” and whatever else can be said as though death itself does or suffers something.

When these things are said of death, they are all referred to the author of death, through whom the deprivation of life was brought about: the devil. For he either does what pertains to death, when he takes captive and kills, or suffers it, when he is conquered and condemned.

The devil is by nature an angel; and what he is by nature is the work of God. But that he is the devil results from his own fault, because he misuses the good of his nature. His evil works, which are called vices, are actions, not things. They are said to act as though by themselves when the devil acts wholly through them and by means of them; or they are said to be condemned when he himself is condemned on account of them. Human beings too are condemned for the sins by which they are condemned when, enticed through free will, they give their assent to them.

Therefore these things will no longer exist in the future age, because they will be condemned in their author, the devil, when he is condemned in Gehenna and will no longer have the power to perform them in order that human beings may sin.

# BOOK TWO

## The second doctrine of the Pelagians is refuted

[Col. 1617]

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 1617]

1. They say: “Adam’s sin harmed no one except himself.” We reply: If the sin of the first human beings harmed only them and none of us, how has the sentence imposed upon them for their sin passed over to us, while the guilt did not pass over to us as well? Unless, perhaps, according to you God is unjust, since, though we were free from their offense, he allowed us to be bound by the chain of their punishment.

For this is the divine sentence pronounced upon them after the sin, after the serpent—the persuader to transgression—had been cursed:

[Col. 1618] “And God said to the woman: ‘Multiplying, I will multiply your sorrows and your groaning. In sorrows [Note: [Col. 1618] The printed editions read: “in sorrow.” The manuscripts: “in sorrows,” in accordance with the Greek Septuagint.] you shall bear children, and your turning shall be toward your husband, and he shall rule over you.’ And he said to Adam: ‘Because you listened to the voice of your wife and ate from the tree concerning which I had commanded you—not to eat from this one alone—cursed is the earth in your works; in sorrows you shall eat from it all the days of your life. Thorns and thistles it shall produce for you, and you shall eat the grass of the field. In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread, until you return to the earth from which you were taken; for you are earth, and into earth you shall go’” (Gen. III, 16–19).

That the whole of human nature, spread throughout the entire world, is bound by this sentence of punishment bears witness in itself, since, according to the testimony of the holy Law, it plainly sees that it labors under ancestral sufferings. By what justice, then, if we are not heirs of our parents’ sin, do we suffer? If natural equity is supplied to you alone, so that your judgments are more just than God’s, sit in judgment between us and God from your throne of pride. For the devil could find no human being so enamored of, or so eager to defend, his error as to criticize or even refute God’s judgments, except Pelagius and Coelestius, who hand down the laws of a new doctrine.

Adam, then, was created naturally without sin. But when the human being sinned, nature sinned, and nature became sinful—that is, possessing the defect of sin, not itself transformed into a defect or into sin. After the sin, therefore, the human being was called a sinner, not “sin.” For “sinner” is derived from sinning; “human being” is not derived from sinning [Note: [Col. 1619] Am. and the manuscripts: “is not said from not sinning.”]. And therefore a sinful human being begot a human being—certainly a sinner—because from a nature corrupted by sin, as I have said, nothing but a corrupted nature is born, that is, a sinful one, in accordance with what the apostle Paul says: “As was the earthly one, so also are the earthly ones” (I Cor. XV, 48). And how could this happen except through the scattering of seed?

## CHAPTER II

2. But you come at me from the opposite direction and say: “Then is the seed sin?” I have already said above that when the human being sinned, nature sinned, and the seeds belong to that nature. The seed, therefore, too, was corrupted, not itself a corruption, as it is written: “For their seed was accursed from the beginning” (Wis. XII, 11). It was accursed, clearly, after the sin, because he says: “Cursed is the earth in your works.” But the defect is not transmitted from the first-created human being except through the emission of seed; nor can a human being come to be except through it [Note: [Col. 1619] Thus certain older manuscripts. The printed editions instead read: “nor can a human being exist without the emission of seed.”].

The Apostle confirms this when he says: “Through one human being sin entered the world, and through sin death; and thus death passed to all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Rom. V, 12). The Lord Jesus Christ alone became human from a virgin without human seed, and was born, God and human being, free from sin.

You hear, then, that through one human being sin entered the world, and through sin death; and that death thus passed to all human beings, in whom all sinned. Yet you dare to say, heretic, “Adam’s sin harmed no one except himself”? Indeed, it harmed only him when he alone existed, together with Eve, his wife.
