But in those two alone we were all present, because they were the nature of the human race, just as now those two are present in all of us, because we are their nature.

## CHAPTER III

3. But you reply, as you are accustomed to reply: “If the Apostle intended it to be understood that he was speaking of sin passing to all human beings through the conception of seed, he would not have said ‘through one human being,’ but ‘through two human beings,’ because a human being cannot be born without a woman, from the male alone.”

If you have not lost the eyes of your heart, pay attention to the statement: “They are no longer two, but one flesh” (Matt. XIX, 6); and again: “The two shall be one flesh” (Gen. II, 24). For this reason the Apostle said “through one human being”: since, when the woman is one flesh with her husband, the offspring is reckoned in the seed.

Listen further to another very wise man speaking to your shame: “From a woman sin had its beginning, and through her we all die” (Eccli. XXV, 33). There you have it, heretic: it has been sufficiently demonstrated to you that sin or death passed into the human race through two human beings.

## CHAPTER IV

4. But I know what you will say next, as you usually say: “When the Apostle said that sin entered the world through one human being, he meant this through imitation of behavior, not through the propagation of seed.”

I reply: If sin consists in imitation of behavior, whom did the devil imitate in order to transgress? Tell us who is found to have been the first sinner. For if I ask about Adam, you may perhaps reply that he imitated the devil. Granted, Adam imitated the devil in order to sin; tell me whom the devil imitated, since you maintain that sin consists in the imitation of behavior passing from one person to another.

But why do I delay, knowing that you will answer nothing? Whom will you say he imitated, when he himself was the author of his own fall? We read nothing else in the book of Genesis about Adam’s sin except that he was disobedient and failed to preserve the divine command.

Let me ask, then, whom Cain, his firstborn son, imitated when he killed his brother (Gen. IV, 8), so that you may show that he learned to commit murder. We read that there were then four human beings: Adam and Eve, Cain himself, and his brother Abel. Among these we find no one who first committed murder except Cain, as I have said. Tell me, therefore, heretic, where he learned this and whom he imitated, if sin is held to pass from one person to another through imitation of behavior rather than being contracted through conception.

Everything that is to be imitated is either seen with the eyes or grasped through a definite report. Or will you excuse murder by saying that it is not sin? And what could be more wicked? Tell me now—tell me, as I ask you again and again—whom Cain saw, or from whom he heard a report that murder had been committed.

But, constrained by the bond of truth and finding no open door by which to escape from your proposition, you will return to the door of the apostle Paul’s statement, so that, if you wish, you may walk along the straight path and tell the truth in answer to my question. Truly, it was not through imitation of behavior but through the scattering of seed that sin entered the world through one human being, and through sin death; and thus death passed to all human beings, in whom all sinned.

From Adam, therefore, his sinful father, Cain first contracted sin in his mother’s womb, and he was the third human being born a sinner from her womb. His inner mind was already captive to the devil through his ancestral sin [Note: [Col. 1620] The printed editions read: “captivated by the devil.” But the manuscripts read: “captive to the devil.” The same manner of expression occurs in Book 3, no. 2, “captive to the devil,” and no. 4, “captive to sin.”]. From there he acquired jealousy; from there he possessed envy and rancor. Thus, not through imitation of behavior but through his own will, he rushed headlong into and committed murder.

For the devil, who inflicted that one sin upon the first human beings when they transgressed, also incites other sins to be committed through the fact that all human beings (except Christ alone, as stated above) have drawn that sin by being born, whenever they consent to him by free choice.

We all therefore draw the sin of the first-created human being into ourselves, not through imitation of behavior but through the conception of seed [Note: [Col. 1620] The manuscripts read: “of seeds.”], as it is written: “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother bore me” (Ps. L, 7).

Sins also arise through imitation of behavior, namely, through imitating the wicked. But the fact that someone imitates the wicked is a defect of a corrupted nature, by which he became wicked and malicious—not a nature created wicked by God. For this reason we are also said by the Apostle, even after baptism, to have been “by nature children of wrath.” Everyone who is born carnally is rightly called by nature a child of wrath (Eph. II, 3), because this is the nature of the first-created human being, which first, in him, justly received the wrath of God the judge on account of the transgression [Note: [Col. 1620] The manuscripts read: “of the just God.”].

For if we did not draw in his transgression, through which, as I have said, he provoked the Lord to wrath, we would never be called by nature children of wrath. And therefore his sin harmed not only him but the entire human race, since together with his condemnation we received his guilt as well [Note: [Col. 1620] The Remigianus manuscript reads: “his condemnation.”].

That we have been wounded by his transgression is proved by the chosen Vessel when he says: “There is no distinction; for all have sinned and lack the glory of God” (Rom. III, 22). By saying “all,” he excluded no one; indeed, he declared the entire human race. For all sinned, since we are all born sinners from one sinner.

For this reason the same apostle says again: “Judgment from one resulted in condemnation” (Rom. V, 16). From whom, if not from Adam, or from his one sin? In what condemnation, if not in the guilt by which he was condemned? And what is “and they lack the glory of God” except the grace of God the Father [Note: [Col. 1621] In this place the word “Father” is absent from some manuscripts.], through Jesus Christ, who is in the glory of God the Father?

And what does “they lack” mean? It means that no one is capable, by himself, of receiving back the life that he loses through carnal birth or through the works of his merits, unless he is spiritually reborn through our Lord [Col. 1622] Jesus Christ. He came, through the undeserved mercy of the Father, of himself, and of the Holy Spirit, to save and seek what had perished (Luke XIX, 10).

For what had perished? Surely not irrational animals? Or does God care about oxen (I Cor. IX, 9)? Certainly the human race had perished through sin; and for this reason, freely handing himself over to death and rising again, the immaculate one redeemed it from sin and death through the generosity of free grace.

# BOOK THREE. Against the third doctrine of the Pelagians

[Col. 1621]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 1621]

1. Again they say: “A human being can, through free choice—as though sufficient for himself—fulfill whatever he wishes; or even God gives grace to each person on the basis of the merits of his works.”

We reply: We rightly say that no one can be sufficient for himself—that is, through free choice—to fulfill whatever he wishes. Only the first-created human being could do so, since the will of free choice in him was sound before the guilt.

For the Law would not have been imposed upon him to keep while he was established in paradise unless he had been free both to will to keep it and to refuse to keep it, as it is written: “And the Lord spoke to Adam, saying: ‘You shall eat from every tree that is in paradise; but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat’” (Gen. II, 16–17), and so forth.

By saying, “You shall eat from every tree that is in paradise,” the Lord permitted him to will in this manner. And by forbidding him—“But from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat”—he warned him against such willing. But by warning him both to will and not to will, he showed [Note: [Col. 1621] Am. and the manuscripts read: “but by teaching beforehand both to will and not to will, to whom, etc.”] to whom he had given free choice for both possibilities.

Using this badly, in his carelessness, he freely yielded consent to the persuasive serpent and passed over the Lord’s command [Note: [Col. 1621] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions instead read: “he passed over.”]. Having lost the good of possibility, he retained only a wounded choice [Note: [Col. 1621] Some manuscripts omit “choice.”] for willing.

Because of this wound, we all limp in our free choice, and our natural power is not sufficient for us to fulfill the good. For, as I argued above, from a nature corrupted by sin—that is, from the first-created human beings, whose nature we ourselves possess, and in whom freedom was corrupted—a human being of sound will cannot arise, one possessing the perfect freedom of choice by which he might be sufficient for himself.

## CHAPTER II

2. To make you understand more clearly that Adam was created with free choice together with the good of possibility, by which he was able to fulfill what he wished, hear what Holy Scripture says in the book of Ecclesiasticus:

“God created the human being from the beginning and left him in the hand of his counsel. He added commandments and precepts: ‘If you wish to keep the commandments, they will preserve you, and to act faithfully will be pleasing forever.’ He placed fire and water before you; stretch out your hand toward whichever you wish. Before the human being are life and death, good and evil; whatever he wishes shall be given to him” (Eccli. XV, 14–18).

What is meant by “He left him in the hand of his counsel” except “He left him in the possibility of his free choice”? For in “hand” possibility is understood. This is the first grace, through which the first human being could have stood firm if he had wished to keep the Lord’s commandments.

Deprived of this through disobedience, the human being was, by a just judgment, made captive to the serpent—that is, to the devil—to whom he preferred to obey rather than God. Therefore it is written: “By whatever anyone is overcome, to this he is enslaved” (II Pet. II, 19); and again: “Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin” (John VIII, 34).

The apostle Paul confirms this when he says to those already baptized: “When you were slaves of sin, you were free from righteousness” (Rom. VI, 20)—that is, you were strangers to righteousness.

The human being could therefore fall by himself, because he willed to do so. But just as he fell by himself, he could not immediately rise from his fall by himself—that is, by his own will—unless he had been raised by the most merciful hand of the Lord, whenever it pleased his kindness.

For this reason it is written: “The Lord lifts up all who fall and raises up all who are crushed” (Ps. CXLIV, 14). But if a human being, by the power of his own will and not through the Lord, is sufficient to rise after being crushed, so that he may return to paradise, from which he was expelled for disobedience, reconciled to God, then “Christ died for nothing” (Gal. II, 21).

And why did the physician wish to come to the healthy, or why did he say that he had come to save and seek what had perished, when, according to your doctrine, he found nothing lost that required saving?

## CHAPTER III

3. Therefore I ask you, holy apostle Paul, chosen Vessel, teacher of the nations: tell us why Christ came into the world, so that we may know what we ought to answer the heretics who proclaim that his coming benefited the human race nothing, since they claim that human beings are sufficient for themselves.

“Faithful is the saying,” he says, “and worthy of all acceptance: Christ Jesus came into this world to save sinners, of whom I am the first” (I Tim. I, 15).

Do you hear, Pelagian heretic, sunk in the sea of perdition, or Coelestian, destined to perish under heavenly judgment, the chosen Vessel sounding the trumpet of truth [Note: [Col. 1622] Some manuscripts read: “the trumpet.”]? “Christ Jesus came into this world to save sinners,” and he says that he himself is the first of them. Yet you try to establish that, when you preach that a human being can naturally do whatever he wishes, Christ found in him no wound to heal and no infirmity to cure with the medicine of his free grace.

You are so deeply submerged in folly that you do not understand that the Lord Christ wished to assume the form of a servant for our restoration, reformation, redemption, and reconciliation. For what need would God have had, if the human nature had remained in its sound condition, to assume our flesh, endure insults, and suffer death at the hands of the Jews through the cross?

All these things the good and merciful Lord deigned to endure for our salvation: he was Lord for wicked and ungodly servants, free for captives, righteous for the unrighteous, life for the dead, hope for the hopeless, reconciliation for those who had offended. As the apostle John says of him: “He is the propitiation for our sins; and not for ours only, but also for the sins of the whole world” (I John II, 2).

The apostle Peter likewise says: “He himself bore our sins in his body upon the tree, so that, having died to sins, we might live for righteousness; by his bruise you were healed. For you were like wandering sheep” (I Pet. II, 24–25).

Again, in the same Epistle, he says: “Christ also died once for our sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, so that he might bring us to God, put to death in the flesh but made alive in the spirit” (ibid. III, 18).

You hear chosen and competent witnesses speaking by the Spirit of God: Christ came as the propitiation for the sins of the world; he therefore bore our sins in his body upon the tree so that we might live for righteousness; by his bruise we were healed, we who were like wandering sheep. You hear that the righteous one died once for our sins, for the unrighteous, so that he might bring us to God—that is, call us back to God, exiles from sin.

Yet, working in the darkness of your conscience, you belch forth clouds with which you try to darken the true light [Note: [Col. 1623] The printed editions read: “to remove.” The manuscripts read: “to darken.”], and you say that a human being can fulfill whatever he wishes through free choice, as though he were sufficient for himself.

The same thing is expressed in that boast which you utter with proud voice: “If I wish, I am holy; if I wish, I sin; if I wish [Note: [Col. 1623] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “if I do not wish.”], I do not sin.”

By saying this you assert nothing other than what has already been stated above: that Christ, when he came, accomplished nothing for us; that he brought us no salvation and no assistance; that his death benefited us nothing; and that our salvation is natural to us.

The catholic faith pronounces an anathema upon those who preach such things. For it believes that Christ is the salvation of the human being from God [Note: [Col. 1623] In the printed editions alone: “in Christ.”], whose wound heals and restores our wounded free choice; who, by his free grace, turns those who have turned away from him back to himself; and who works in them both the will and the ability to please God the Father, himself, and the Holy Spirit through good works. He himself completes their course in this life, through his mercy both going before and following after, for the sake of the true life to come.

Therefore we firmly believe and unequivocally proclaim that human beings possess free choice.

## CHAPTER IV

4. But why it is called free choice must be discussed briefly. I think that “choice” (*arbitrium*) received its name from judging (*arbitrando*) through rational consideration, or from discerning what one chooses and what one rejects. It is therefore called “free” because it is placed within its own power and possesses the possibility of doing what it wishes—which is the movement of a living and rational soul.

But, as I have already said, this condition existed in the first-created human being when he remained unharmed before the sin. For he incurred the offense in no other way than through that by which he was able to resist the persuader and avoid sinning [Note: [Col. 1623] Am. and the manuscripts: “through that by which.” The Ebrulphensis manuscript: “through which.”].

By willing evil, therefore, he rightly lost the ability to will good, since through the ability to will good he could have overcome the will to evil. God justly abandoned him, now held captive by sin, to his corrupted will: the one who, if he had always obeyed God, could have been sufficient for every good thing he wished to do, now suffered this as punishment—the inability to do what he wished.

He did not acquire the will to evil from the condition of his good nature, as though from an inborn evil, as Manichaeus believes. Rather, he conceived it from an accidental, depraved desire, when, as I have already said above, he consented to the serpent—that is, to the devil—in eating the forbidden tree, which he ought to have refused.

As from a corrupted root, all human offspring arising from him contracted this, except Christ alone, who, through the coming of the Holy Spirit and not through human seed, became flesh from the flesh of a virgin.

Through sin, therefore, the human being lost the good of possibility belonging to free choice, but not its name and rational character.

5. We confess that all human beings possess free choice, having indeed the judgment of reason—but not such that, without God, it is capable of beginning or certainly completing what belongs to God. It is capable only in the works of the present life, both good and evil.

By good works I mean those that arise from the good of nature: wishing to work in the field, wishing to eat and drink, wishing to have a friend, wishing to possess clothing, wishing to build a house, wishing to marry, wishing to tend livestock, wishing to learn an art involving various good things, wishing for anything good that belongs to the present life. All these things do not exist without divine governance; rather, they arise from God and through God, or have begun to exist through him.

By evil works I mean such things as wishing to worship an idol, wishing to commit murder, wishing to commit adultery, wishing to seize the property of others, blaspheming the living God forever, wishing to live shamefully, wishing to learn magical practices, wishing to become drunk and live luxuriously, wishing to do anything that is forbidden or unprofitable.

But these things do not belong to the substance of the present life, because they are not from God. Rather, wrongly desired, they stain the life that is from God.

These are the weeds of soul and flesh which the enemy, the human being—that is, the devil—sowed in free choice while Adam was sleeping, that is, while he was not preserving God’s commandment (Matt. XIII, 25). In these matters the wounded and corrupted will is more inclined and ready than it is toward good things.

These are the works of the devil. Christ, the Word of God the Father, who is a two-edged sword, came into this world, was born from a virgin, and cuts them away from the free choice of believers through his free grace, preparing within them a will capable of believing [Note: [Col. 1624] Most manuscripts read: “of progressing.”]—a will through which they may carry out the just [Note: [Col. 1624] The manuscripts read: “united.”] will of God the Father, of himself, and of the Holy Spirit.

6. That these are the works of the devil and are removed through Christ is proved by John, the beloved apostle of Christ, in his Epistle, where he says: “Whoever commits sin is from the devil, because the devil sins from the beginning. For this purpose the Son of God appeared, that he might destroy the works of the devil” (I John III, 8).

The apostle Peter likewise says of Christ in the Acts of the Apostles, among other things: “He went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, because God was in him” (Acts X, 38).

The apostle Paul says to the Hebrews: “He, being the radiance of his glory and the exact representation of his substance, and sustaining all things by the word of his power, having made purification for sins, sits at the right hand of the Father” (Heb. I, 3).

Again, in the same Epistle: “For if the blood of goats and bulls, and the sprinkling of the ashes of a heifer, sanctifies those who are defiled for the purification of the flesh, how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the Holy Spirit offered himself immaculate to God, cleanse our conscience from dead works to serve the living God?” (ibid. IX, 13–14).

Go on, heretic, and, resisting such great teachers of truth, say that free choice has been received from Adam in such a condition that, needing no medicine from Christ, it is sufficient by itself to fulfill whatever it wishes.

You hear that the Son of God appeared in order to destroy the works of the devil. You hear that he went about doing good in order to heal all those oppressed by the devil. You hear that by the word of his power he made purification from sins. You hear that, offering himself immaculate to God, he cleansed our conscience with his blood from dead works so that we might serve the living God.

Yet, ungrateful for his grace, you think that you possess free choice naturally sound?

If the human being is sound, as Adam was first established by God, and, as you say, acquired no defect afterward when he sinned, I ask: From whom did the Son of God, when he appeared, destroy the works of the devil? Whom did he heal, oppressed by the devil, as he went about doing good? In whom did he make purification from sins? Whose conscience did he cleanse from dead works so that it might serve the living God?

Unless perhaps you claim that the Apostles, who are the brightest lights in the catholic Church, preached these things falsely, seeking, as it were, to test the one who spoke in them, Christ (II Cor. XIII, 3).

For what would you not presume to say, deprived as you are of the light of truth, when you refuse to believe either the Law of God, or the Prophets, or the Gospel of Christ and his Apostles singing by the Spirit of God—that the human race was made mortal through the sin of the first human being, that it is subject to other sins because free choice was corrupted, and that the Son of God came to save, restore, and give life to it by taking the likeness of sinful flesh, enduring death, and rising from the dead?

## CHAPTER V

7. Therefore, when we discuss free choice, we are not discussing a part of the human being but the whole. For when the first human being sinned, it was not in some particular part but in the whole nature in which he had been created that he transgressed.

When we mention only the soul, do we sometimes separate the body or the spirit from the soul? Or when we say “spirit,” do we separate the soul and body from the spirit? Or when we call something “body,” do we separate the spirit and soul from the body?

Since free choice was corrupted, therefore, the whole human being was corrupted. Without the assistance of grace, he is neither able to begin nor sufficient to complete what pleases God.

Medicine—that is, the grace of Christ—goes before him so that the corrupted will may be healed, restored, and prepared in him; always needing the assistance of the Savior’s illuminating grace, it may both know God and live according to his will.

When the Lord says through the prophet, “I will give you a new heart and a new spirit” (Ezek. XXXVI, 26), what else does he signify except that the wills of human beings, which fell through the transgression of the old human being, are restored through Christ, the new human being, and prepared for the will of God, as it is written: “The will is prepared by the Lord” (Prov. VIII, according to the Septuagint)?

Again the apostle Paul says: “It is God who works in you both to will and to accomplish, according to his good will” (Phil. II, 13)—that will which, as I have said, has been both restored [Note: [Col. 1625] Some manuscripts read: “created.”] and prepared by the Lord so that it might be good.

The faithful human being, recognizing that he has been enlightened in this will so as to be ever more ready for God’s will, follows by crying out to him: “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me” (Ps. L, 12); and, “Open my eyes, and I shall consider the wonders of your law” (Ps. CXVIII, 18); and, “Make known to me, O Lord, the way in which I should walk”; and, “O Lord, I have fled to you; teach me to do your will, for you are my God” (Ps. CXLII, 8–10).

But if this is not already the voice of one who believes, “how will they call upon him in whom they have not believed?” (Rom. X, 14).

Therefore, while the human being’s will still limps under the defect of free choice, he does not precede God by his own will so as to know and seek him [Note: [Col. 1625] Some manuscripts read: “so as to desire him.” Older manuscripts: “so as to seek grace, as though he would receive it on the basis of merits.”], as though he were going to receive grace in return for merits. Rather, as I have already said, by his most merciful grace God goes before the will of the human being who is ignorant and does not yet seek him, so that he may make that human being know and seek him.

As the apostle John says in his Epistle: “We know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, so that we may know the true God and may be in his true Son. This is the true God and eternal life” (I John V, 20).

And David says in the Psalms: “My God, his mercy shall go before me” (Ps. LVIII, 11); and, “O God, you will turn and give us life” (Ps. LXXXIV, 7).

And the Lord says to his disciples in the Gospel: “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John XV, 16).

The apostle John likewise says: “In this the love of God was revealed among us, that God sent his only-begotten Son into the world so that we might live through him. In this is love: not that we loved God, but that he first loved us and sent his Son as the propitiation for our sins” (I John IV, 9–10).

## CHAPTER VI

8. The apostle Paul teaches that no human merit exists in receiving grace for salvation [Note: [Col. 1625] The manuscripts read: “in receiving grace”; and some omit “for.”]. Writing to the Ephesians, he says:

“But God, who is rich in mercy, because of the great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead in sins, made us alive together with Christ—by whose grace you have been saved. Because of the great love,” he says, “with which he loved us,” not because of our love, as though we had loved him first, when we were dead in sins.

A little later in the same Epistle he says: “For by grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not from yourselves; it is God’s [Note: [Col. 1625] The printed editions read: “for it is God’s.” “For” is absent from the manuscripts and from a.] gift; not from works, so that no one may boast” (Eph. II, 4–5, 8–9).

He says likewise to Timothy: “Therefore do not be ashamed of the testimony of our Lord, nor of me, his prisoner, but labor together with the Gospel according to the power of God, who saved us and called us with a holy calling, not according to our works but according to his purpose and grace, which was given to us in Christ Jesus before eternal times” (II Tim. I, 8).

[Col. 1626] You hear “before eternal times,” when the human being existed in God’s foreknowledge—not “in the age,” because the age did not yet exist. Yet, blind in your resistance to the truth, you place voluntary works before his gift?

For, “seeking to establish your own righteousness, you cannot be subject to the righteousness of God” (Rom. X, 3).

He says likewise to Titus: “But when the kindness and humanity of our Savior God appeared, he saved us—not from works of righteousness that we had done, but according to his mercy—through the bath of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out upon us abundantly through Jesus Christ” (Titus III, 4–6).

What will you answer to these things now, heretic? What will you, enemy of grace, devise to oppose grace, despite the testimony of so great a teacher of the nations, who declares that it is given without any human merits?

Tell me, what are you trying to resist when such an outstanding teacher proclaims the truth? He does not speak from himself and in himself, but from God before God in Christ, preaching the Gospel—that is, in the simplicity and sincerity of God, and not in carnal wisdom.

Hear him testify that he proclaims the truth, and do not be unbelieving but faithful. “The God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ,” he says, “who is blessed forever, knows that I do not lie” (II Cor. XI, 31). Again: “I speak the truth in Christ, I do not lie, my conscience bearing witness with me in the Holy Spirit” (Rom. IX, 1). And again: “I speak the truth in Christ, I do not lie, a teacher of the nations in faith and truth” (I Tim. II, 7).

You hear him say, “I do not lie,” yet you refute him as though he were lying when, on the basis of your perverse doctrine, you announce that grace is given according to human merits, contrary to what he proclaims.

Indeed, see that you are refuting not only Paul but also Christ speaking in him.

## CHAPTER VII
### 9

“But,” you say to me, “if each person does not receive grace according to his own will—the will by which, as we say, he sought God—but God’s grace anticipates his will, so that he may be able to believe in him, why then does he not work this in everyone? Is God a respecter of persons?”

If your understanding, heretic, had been stripped of the darkness of ignorance by the illumination of grace [Note: Am. Er. and some manuscripts read “detected” instead of “stripped”], you would believe only the divine testimonies I have already cited—or those I have not cited—which are found in the Holy Scriptures in countless numbers: namely, that God grants his grace apart from any human merits, through which he reveals himself to them so that they may believe in and serve him. You would not ask—indeed, you would not investigate—why God does not work this in everyone [Note: In the manuscripts: “you would not investigate God, why…”], since he always works well and justly whatever he wills, and no one resists his will; therefore, “whatever he willed, he did” (Ps. 113:3).

So do not ask me, while I fear and tremble at his judgments, why he works this in one person and not in another—his judgments are unsearchable and incomprehensible [Note: Some manuscripts read “and irreproachable”; shortly afterward they read “I believe and revere,” rather than “I believe and fear”]. For what I read, I believe and revere; I do not investigate it. “Who is the human being who answers God? Does the thing formed say to the one who formed it, ‘Why did you make me this way?’ Does the potter not have authority over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?” (Rom. 9:20–21).

But ask him who said, “No one comes to me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (John 6:44); and, “Not all receive this word, but only those to whom it has been given” (Matt. 19:11); and, “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of heaven, but to the others it has not been given” (Matt. 13:11); and, “No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son and the one to whom the Son wishes to reveal him” (Matt. 11:27); and, “Just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he wills” (John 5:21); and, “The Spirit breathes where he wills”; and, “A human being cannot do anything by himself unless it has been given to him from above” (John 3:8, 27).

Ask also him who said, “To you it has been granted on behalf of Christ not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him” (Phil. 1:29); and, “It depends not on the one who wills or on the one who runs, but on God who has mercy”; and, “He has mercy on whomever he wills, and he hardens whomever he wills” (Rom. 9:16, 18). For the Holy Spirit distributes the gifts of his charisms to each person as he wills (1 Cor. 12:11), not as they will. And God has made known “the riches of the glory of his mystery” to those whom he willed, not to those who willed it (Col. 1:27).

“These are all the ways of the Lord: unsearchable mercy and truth” (Ps. 24:10). If you wish to know them, ask Paul, and he will answer you: “Do not be high-minded, but fear. For who has known the mind of the Lord, so as to instruct him?” [Note: In Lov., “who instructed him?”] “Or who has been his counselor? Or who first gave to him, so that he might be repaid? For from him and through him and in him are all things; to him be glory forever” (Rom. 11:20, 34–36).

Ask David also, and he will say to you: “Who is wise and will understand these things?” (Ps. 106:43); or, “Who will speak of the powers of the Lord and make all his praises heard?” (Ps. 105:2).

### 10

Therefore, when the incomprehensible, unsearchable, and ineffable God does these things, he does not do them by partiality or unjust judgment, but by a judgment that is wholly just, profound, and hidden. This is the catholic faith [Note: So read the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “profound and hidden; for this is the faith…”]. If you wish to follow it, you will not be curious and contentious about God’s incomprehensible judgments; rather, with Catholics you will be humble and gentle.

You will not say to God by questioning, “What is your will?” but by trembling, “Your will be done” (Matt. 6:10), because power belongs to God, and to you, Lord, belongs mercy (Ps. 61:12–13).

Because human beings cannot recount God’s judgments in his works, is God therefore unjust? On the contrary, he is just, incomprehensible in the judgment of his justice, and irreproachable in the execution of his will. Let the blameworthy, lying, and unjust human being be silent, so that God, who is irreproachable and truthful and just, may do whatever he wills.

If you consider only the sin of the first human beings, by which the mass of the human race deserved to be condemned—since, according to the testimony of the apostle Paul, “from the one [man] all came into condemnation” (Rom. 5:16) [Note: Am. Er. and the manuscripts read “from that one”]—you will be able to recognize that God’s judgments are entirely just.

For this reason there is an evil merit preceding God’s judgments in human beings, both in infants and in adults, so that they may be punished by his just judgment. But why, as I have said, are not all punished for this prior evil merit, or why are not all saved from it? I, who serve the Lord in fear and rejoice with trembling, sing mercy and judgment to him. For he executes judgment when a cause precedes it, but grants salvation by mercy, anticipating the evil cause [Note: The printed editions read “grants and mercy,” rather than “grants salvation by mercy”].

We are therefore his property. Why, heretic, is your eye evil? The just and merciful master of the household has authority over his own property to do whatever he wishes; that is, over one guilty of death, he is judge and may impose whatever sentence he wishes.

### Chapter VIII

#### 11

Listen still more closely [Note: In Lov., “the human being wounded”], so that we may return to the subject of the preceding discussion: the human being, wounded in free will through Adam’s sin, cannot heal himself without the grace of God—that is, by himself alone—nor can he voluntarily return to paradise to be joined to the company of the saints. Nor does he receive grace through any merits; rather, God accomplishes everything by his mercy.

“A certain man,” says the Lord in the Gospel, “was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and he fell among robbers. They also stripped him and, after inflicting wounds, went away, leaving him half-dead. Now it happened that a certain priest was going down the same road; and when he saw him, he passed by. Likewise a Levite, when he was near the place and saw him, passed by. But a certain Samaritan, while traveling, came near him; and when he saw him, he was moved with compassion. He approached and bound up his wounds, pouring in oil and wine; and placing him on his own animal, he brought him to an inn and took care of him. The next day he brought out two denarii and gave them to the innkeeper, saying, ‘Take care of him, and whatever more you spend, I will repay you when I return’” (Luke 10:30–35).

This certain man is the human race, descending from Jerusalem to Jericho—that is, from paradise to this world. Jerusalem is called thus in Hebrew, but in Latin it is interpreted as “Vision of Peace.” Accordingly, we rightly call paradise the vision of peace. Before the human being sinned, he was in the vision of peace—that is, in paradise—wherever he looked, there was peace and joy.

Descending from there—that is, being humbled and made wretched through sin—he came to Jericho, namely, into the world. Jericho, in which the world is represented, is interpreted as “Moon,” because, just as the moon rises and sets, so also the world: when those who arise in it set, they rise again.

He fell among robbers, namely, the devil and his angels. Through the disobedience of the first human being, as has often been said, the devil stripped and wounded the human race, depriving it of the ornaments of good character and of the good possibility of free will. In that one’s sin he inflicted a wound; in us he inflicted wounds, because through that one sin—which we carry with us at birth—we add many sins.

What does “leaving him half-dead” mean? He is rightly called half-dead: he retained a vital movement, namely, wounded free will, but this alone was not sufficient for him to return to eternal life, which he had lost. Therefore he is called half-dead.

The human race therefore lay wounded in the world. But why did it lie there? Tell me, if it could rise or heal itself by its own power, needing no assistance. It lay wounded because its own strength was insufficient to rise, so that, in order to be healed, it might seek a physician, namely God.

A priest came down the same road; when he saw him, he passed by. Likewise the Levite, when he saw him, passed by. In these two figures—the priest and the Levite—two periods are understood: the Law and the Prophets. The priest represents the Law, through which the priesthood and sacrifices were instituted. The Levite represents the prophecy of the Prophets.

During their times the entire human race could not be healed, because “death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who had not sinned in the likeness of Adam’s transgression, who is a type of the one to come” (Rom. 5:14)—that is, even over all the saints and over infants, who did not transgress as Adam did. Yet, because of the sin of transgression that they drew from him at birth, as though bound by a paternal legal document, they paid the wages of sin by dying. For “the wages of sin is death” (Rom. 6:23).

And because through the Law comes knowledge of sin (Rom. 3:20), not its abolition—for the Law commands a person to recognize that he is a sinner, which he did not know, but it does not remove sin—the Apostle therefore says: “I would not have known covetousness unless the Law had said, ‘You shall not covet’” (Rom. 7:7).

The Law therefore brought nothing to perfection (Heb. 7:19). For “if righteousness comes through the Law, then Christ died for nothing” (Gal. 2:21). If a law had been given that could give life, then righteousness would truly come through the Law. But Scripture confined all things under sin, so that the promise might be given to believers through faith in Jesus Christ, who removes all sins (Gal. 3:21–22).

For Christ is the fullness of the Law and the Prophets. He came not to abolish the Law and the Prophets but to fulfill them (Matt. 5:17).

#### 12

As the priest and the Levite were passing by, the Samaritan, traveling, came near him. The Samaritan is Christ the Savior himself, because “Samaritan” is interpreted as “Guardian.” To him we rightly say: “Guard me, Lord, as the apple of the eye; protect me under the shadow of your wings” (Ps. 16:8).

What does “he came near him” mean? He came in the likeness of sinful flesh—not as the one who lay [Note: So read the manuscripts. The printed editions read “hid”] in sinful flesh. Therefore it says “near him,” because he came in its likeness.

“And when he saw him, he was moved with compassion.” What did he see? The man lying there. Not rising and running? And therefore he was moved with compassion, because he found no merit in him by which he might be considered worthy of healing.

“And he approached and bound up his wounds.” What does “he bound up his wounds” mean? As it is written: “He who knew no sin, for our sake he made sin” (2 Cor. 5:21). That is, “he condemned sin in the flesh” (Rom. 8:3).

“Pouring in oil and wine”—that is, the holy chrism and his blood.

“And he placed him on his own animal”—namely, as an aid of the grace of his incarnation. For, as it is written, “He himself bore our sins and suffered for us” (Isa. 53:4).

“And he brought him to an inn”—that is, granting him faith so that he might believe in him, he brought him into his Church. The Church lies open like an inn to all who walk on the road of faith, so that they may enter it.

“And the next day”—as though at another time, namely after his resurrection and ascension—“he brought out two denarii,” namely, the Old and the New Testament, in which there is one coinage of God the King.

“And he gave them to the innkeeper”: to the apostle Paul, who is a chosen vessel and whose concern is for all the churches (2 Cor. 11:28).

“And he said, ‘Take care of him’”—that is, teach him what pertains to my faith and how he ought to reach complete health.

“And whatever more you spend, when I return I will repay you.” If, therefore, beyond the Gospel, as one who has obtained mercy in order to be faithful, you have understood anything for his benefit, when I return to judge the world and repay each person according to his works, I will repay you.

What did Paul provide beyond the Law and the Gospel? I think it was what he himself says to the Corinthians: “Concerning virgins I have no command of the Lord, but I give an opinion as one who has obtained mercy from the Lord to be faithful”; or also that other statement concerning married people: “To the rest I say—I, not the Lord” (1 Cor. 7:25, 12), and so forth.

#### 13

These matters have meanwhile already been discussed or explained by the great interpreters of the catholic Church. But we defend the boundary of sound faith when we do not move the limits established by the holy fathers; rather, we observe and defend them.

Behold how the wounded free will of the human being is healed. From the day of his coming—the day on which the Lord came to heal the wounded man lying there—until the day of his return, when he will judge the world, he commands the innkeeper to care for the wounded man entrusted to him.

This signifies that from the day on which God, through the movement of his mercy and not through any merit found in the wounded person, grants a human being the grace by which he may be healed, until the day of his assumption, he cannot reach perfection unless he remains under the care of grace.

As Paul, his innkeeper, teaches when he writes to the Philippians: “Being confident of this very thing, that he who began the good work in you will perfect it until the day of Jesus Christ” (Phil. 1:6) [Note: The manuscripts read “who will have begun”].

The apostle Peter likewise says in his First Epistle: “But the God of all grace, who called us into his eternal glory in Christ Jesus, after we have suffered a little, will himself perfect, confirm, strengthen, and establish us. To him be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen” (1 Pet. 5:10–11).

### Chapter IX

#### 14

What else is shown by that lost sheep from the hundred sheep, except free will, which, having lost the good of its possibility through the fault of the first human being, has strayed from the company of the righteous and cannot by itself return to the fold [Note: So read the manuscripts. Am. Er. read “to the enclosure,” Lov. “to the courtyard,” and “to the flock”; these are erroneous]—that is, to paradise, from which it departed—to be restored to the number of the faithful, unless the good shepherd Christ, who laid down his life for the sheep, by his own will and through unmerited grace, calls it back?

He brings back the sheep wandering in the wilderness—that is, from this world, in which the human being has been exiled as a deserter of the divine commandment and wanders by free will in the works of the devil—after placing it upon his shoulders, namely, as an aid of his faith and love (Luke 15:4).

As I have said, the Lord himself proves this when, in the parable, intending the human being to be understood, he says that the sheep wandered away and did not return of its own accord; rather, when sought by the shepherd, it was carried back to its own fold upon the shepherd’s shoulders. Likewise, he says that the man wounded by robbers was carried to the inn not by his own steps but after being placed upon an animal.

Seeing this, the teacher of the Gentiles, with the illumination of the grace of faith, says to those who presume upon themselves: “Therefore it depends not on the one who wills or on the one who runs, but on God who has mercy” (Rom. 9:16).

#### 15

“But,” you say to me, “if finding God depends not on the one who wills or on the one who runs, how is it written in the Psalms, ‘I will confess to him by my own will’ (Ps. 27:7), and again in the Apostle, when, using the image of vessels, he speaks of sinners: ‘If anyone cleanses himself from these things, he will be a vessel for honor, sanctified and useful to the Lord, prepared for every good work’ (2 Tim. 2:21)?”

Receive the account of faith. The condition of one who still does not believe is different from that of one who already believes. Concerning the unbeliever—that is, one who still does not know God—in order that he may know and believe, when there are no good works in him, it is said: “It depends not on the one who wills or on the one who runs, but on God who has mercy.”

For, having his understanding darkened in the vanity of his mind [Note: The printed editions read “and darkened in” as well. The manuscripts do not have “and in”], he cannot see the true light of free will, which enlightens every human being coming into this world, unless God, who in his mercy said that light should shine out of darkness, shines in his heart “for the illumination of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Christ Jesus.”

Then, when the veil—that is, the cloud of sin—has been removed from his heart, he can turn to the Lord, who is Spirit. When he has received the Spirit of the Lord, there will be freedom in him to undertake the Lord’s commandments, because “where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (2 Cor. 3:17).

But he possesses this treasure in an earthen vessel, namely, in his earthly body, so that the excellence of the power may belong to God and not come from him. Therefore, “it depends not on the one who wills or on the one who runs, but on God who has mercy.”

This also occurs in many ways and by many means among those who already serve God, when, through the mercy of his grace, they suddenly attain good things that they neither willed nor pursued.

#### 16

But the voice of one who already believes—that is, one illuminated and restored in free will through the gratuitous grace of the Savior—is: “I will confess to him by my own will.”

Yet, in order that he may confess to him, he does not glory in himself but in the Lord, when he says: “The Lord is my helper and my protector; in him my heart hoped, and I was helped, and my flesh blossomed again.” Therefore he continues: “I will confess to him by my own will” (Ps. 27:7).

Every faithful person’s good will is indeed his own, since in him it has been restored from its fall through Christ so that it might be good. Therefore, whatever good he wills and whatever he is able to do comes from the Lord. For the Lord says in the Gospel to his disciples: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5).

Likewise in the same Gospel, according to John: “A human being cannot do anything by himself unless it has been given to him from above” (John 3:27).

The apostle Paul likewise says to the Corinthians: “We have such confidence through Christ toward God—not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think anything as though from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God, who also made us competent ministers of a New Testament, not of the letter but of the Spirit. For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3:4–6).

#### 17

Thus, then, this too is what the Apostle says: “If anyone cleanses himself from these things, he will be a vessel for honor, sanctified and useful to the Lord, prepared for every good work” (2 Tim. 2:21).

When someone who has already been redeemed through the grace of Baptism sins by his own will and, remaining in his sins, departs from this world, he becomes a wooden vessel, which can easily be consumed by the fire of Gehenna; or certainly an earthen vessel, which can be shattered by the straight rod—the rod of Christ’s kingdom, that is, by the judgment of his equity.

God’s kindness, as the Apostle says, may lead such a person to repentance so that he may be saved (Rom. 2:4). Accordingly, he says again to Timothy: “Perhaps God may grant them repentance for the knowledge of the truth, and they may come to their senses from the snare of the devil, by whom they are held captive for his will” (2 Tim. 2:25–26). God may also feed him “with the bread of tears and give him drink in tears and measure” (Ps. 79:6).

He cleanses himself from such vessels because, while God’s mercy precedes him, he himself acts sufficiently through free will so that he may be cleansed. But if he presumes upon his own will alone, he cannot be cleansed; indeed, he is not even compelled to repent from the heart [Note: The manuscripts read “to be repented of”]. For unless the Lord had looked upon Peter, he would never have been moved to repent and weep bitterly (Luke 22:61–62).

Repentance is therefore an excellent and perfect thing, which restores those who have fallen to perfection. But, as the apostle James says, “every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no change or shadow caused by turning” (James 1:17).

The repentant person must therefore pray for the things that contribute to his cleansing. Hear from where he is to obtain them in order that he may do this. “Likewise,” says the apostle Paul, “the Spirit also helps our weakness. For we do not know what we ought to pray for as we should; but the Spirit himself pleads for us”—that is, makes us plead—“with unutterable groanings” (Rom. 8:26).

### Chapter X

#### 18

There is therefore free will. Whoever denies that it exists is not a Catholic; whoever says that it exists in such a way that, without God, it can neither begin nor complete a good work—that is, a work belonging to God’s holy purpose—is a Catholic.

To whom are these words spoken in the Psalms except to those who possess free will? “Come, children, listen to me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord” (Ps. 33:12). Likewise, the Lord says to his disciples in the Gospel: “Everyone who hears these words of mine and does them” (Matt. 7:24); and again: “You are my friends if you do what I command you” (John 15:14).

The Apostle says to the Corinthians: “This is useful for you, who began not only to do but also to will from the previous year; now complete it also in deed, so that just as the readiness of your will is present, so also may there be completion” (2 Cor. 8:10–11).

There are many other such passages contained both in the Old and in the New Testament; it would be too long to recount them all, because of the weariness of reading.

How could each person be repaid according to his works on the day of judgment unless free will existed? Therefore there is no partiality with God. “All who have sinned without the Law will also perish without the Law, and all who have sinned under the Law will be judged through the Law” (Rom. 2:11–12).

In every holy work, therefore, God’s will comes first and free will afterward: God works, and the human being cooperates. But if you say, as you are accustomed to say, “Because I willed first, God willed,” you are already making merit, so that grace is no longer grace on the basis of works but a reward.

Here the Apostle refutes you, saying: “But if it is by grace, it is no longer from works; otherwise grace is no longer grace” (Rom. 11:6). Grace, therefore, is given, not repaid. For if it were repaid as a debt, the Apostle would not say “not from works,” but “from works.”

### Chapter XI

#### 19

Every Christian, then, to whom it has already been granted by grace to be able to do God’s will, ought to abound in good works, because his labor will not be in vain in the Lord. Yet he must not glory in himself, but always in the Lord, whose grace, as I have said, instructs him to renounce impiety and worldly desires so that he may live soberly, justly, and piously in this world.

As the Apostle writes to Titus: “The grace of our God and Savior has appeared to all people, instructing us to renounce impiety and worldly desires and to live soberly, justly, and piously in this world, awaiting the blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ” (Titus 2:11–13).

Let no one be sluggish or negligent in serving God, nor trust in grace in such a way as to suppose that God does not require works from the free will of the person whom he restored and prepared for himself through the death of his Son. Rather, let him turn away from evil and do good.

Let him watch, seek, ask, knock, and strive to conquer the world and please God. Thus, while he travels across the sea of the world, as has often been said, let him not loosen the anchor of grace, which is fastened around his neck, through confidence in free will [Note: Am. Er. and some manuscripts read “carried back with confidence.” Other manuscripts read “fastened,” and omit “with confidence”].

Whether in favorable sailing, lest he be lifted up, or amid the storms of temptation, lest he be submerged, he will be able to remain secure under God’s direction until he reaches the harbor of paradise. Then, when he has completed his course, he may say confidently with the apostle Paul: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith” (2 Tim. 4:7).

When Paul said this, he did not glory in himself but in the Lord. For he himself said: “Let the one who glories, glory in the Lord” (1 Cor. 1:31). How could he have fought the good fight, finished the course, and kept the faith? He had already said: “Not I, however, but the grace of God with me” (1 Cor. 15:10).

He cut off all human glory and gave glory to God alone when he again said: “So that we might not be confident in ourselves but in God, who raises the dead” (2 Cor. 1:9); and again: “By the grace of God I am what I am” (1 Cor. 15:10).

#### 20

I rightly think that free will may be compared to an animal, which is why it is said: “I became like an animal before you” (Ps. 72:23); grace may be compared to its rider.

Just as a very lively animal is captured from the herd, wandering about, so that it may be broken in for work necessary to human beings, and begins, through the care of the one who tames it, to advance toward his will, so free will, which lives wounded in the human being, is seized by the grace of God from the herd and worldly dissipation [Note: So read the manuscripts. The printed editions read “from the herd of worldly revelry”], in which it had wandered under the devil as shepherd through unsuitable pleasures [Note: The printed editions read “wills”; the manuscripts disagree].

I called the devil a shepherd according to the prophet Zechariah, who says of him: “O shepherd and idol!” (Zech. 11:17).

Grace therefore takes hold of free will, as I have said, in order to tame it, so that, having laid aside the wildness of its evil conduct, it may be humbled and corrected for obedience in the work necessary to the Lord. Thus, through the rider’s constant care, it begins to advance toward God’s will.

For just as an animal, while being directed on the road, is guided by the rider’s hand so that it may proceed along the right path—whether gently or at a run, according to the will of the one seated upon it—until it reaches its appointed destination [Note: The manuscripts read “whether lightly or at a run, that is, according to…”], so free will, once it has begun to be on the road, that is, in Christ—for he says, “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6)—is governed by the direction of grace.

Thus it can walk along the paths of the Lord with an upright heart, whether through the patience of love or with a fervent spirit [Note: The manuscripts read “or fervent in spirit”], that is, according to the distributions of the graces of the Spirit, who divides them to each person as he wills through grace (1 Cor. 12:11), until it reaches the promised kingdom of heaven.

Therefore the Psalmist says: “Your good Spirit will lead me into a level land” (Ps. 142:10).

And just as an animal sometimes, while under its rider and feeding on abundant food, presses against the bridle and is lifted up in its running, but is struck with the rider’s whip so that it may walk according to his will, so free will, when a person forgets God’s grace in prosperity and is lifted up as though glorying in his own ability, is corrected by God’s whip when it is somewhat subdued through various tribulations and afflictions, so that the humbled person may return in his weakness [Note: Am. Er. and the manuscripts read “humility”] to the help of grace.

Thus, when a person riding an animal has completed the journey he undertook, he says, “Today I traveled, for example, thirty miles,” even though the animal, while he was seated upon it, traveled thirty miles. It would not, however, have traveled them unless the rider had both directed it along the road and governed it.

Therefore the rider, whom I have used to represent grace [Note: So read the manuscripts. The printed editions read “whom grace represents”], rightly says, “I traveled thirty miles.” He did it, because he caused the animal to do it; and yet the labor of the journey is attributed to both.

So also grace and free will undoubtedly complete the journey of faith. Free will does so while the Christian performs God’s commandments, but not, as I said above, without grace directing and governing it. Therefore the Psalmist says: “Direct my way in your sight” (Ps. 5:9); and, “The steps of a human being are directed by the Lord” (Ps. 36:23).

Thus neither grace without free will makes a person possess blessed life, nor free will without grace. Yet grace gives infants blessed life without the use of free will. But those who are already capable of reason it anticipates and teaches, so that they may will and be able to do good.

For it is written in the Acts of the Apostles: “God opened the heart of Lydia, a seller of purple, so that she might listen to what was being said by Paul” (Acts 16:14).

Likewise, in the Gospel, concerning the two who were traveling on the road after the resurrection: “Then,” he says, “he opened their understanding so that they might understand the Scriptures” (Luke 24:45).

And in the Psalms: “Blessed is the person whom you instruct, Lord, and teach from your law” (Ps. 93:12).

And in the prophet Ezekiel the Lord says: “I will cause you to do my will and to walk in my commandments” (Ezek. 36:27).

### Chapter XII

#### 21

Receive, from many testimonies, a few examples showing that, by the gift of the grace of God the Father, of his Christ, and of the Holy Spirit, the righteous who lived before the Law or under the Law were both chosen and governed.

In the book of Genesis: “Noah,” it says, “found grace before the Lord God.” It immediately continues: “Noah was a just and perfect man in his generation, and he pleased God” (Gen. 6:8–9).

Notice, therefore, that after he had found grace—God having granted it—he is called just and perfect and said to have pleased God, not before grace.

God took him up for salvation through the election of grace from the company of the wicked, against whom he was justly angered and upon whom he was about to bring the flood. This was not on account of deeds deserving merit, since he was born guilty through Adam’s transgression.

The water of the flood was his baptism, and the ark was the Church—not only for him but also for his wife, his sons, and his daughters-in-law [Note: So read the manuscripts. The printed editions read “and the women”], who were preserved with him for the restoration of the human race.

It is clear, therefore, that this was the faith of salvation for him who had uncircumcision, as it now is through Christ among the uncircumcised nations. For both he and we have been saved by grace, as the Apostle says: “not from works, so that no one may boast” (Eph. 2:8–9).

#### 22

Likewise, there in Genesis the Lord says to Abraham: “Do not fear, Abraham; I will protect you, and your reward will be exceedingly great” (Gen. 15:1).

“I will protect you”—certainly by my grace, by which, before you called upon me, I called you to go out from your land and your kindred and to call upon me (Gen. 12:1).

Therefore Abraham himself also said to the Lord when he appeared to him by the oak of Mamre: “Lord,” he said, “if I have found grace before you, do not pass by your servant” (Gen. 18:1, 3), and so forth.

By grace, therefore, which is not from works, it was said to him: “Your reward will be exceedingly great,” because “no one has first given to God, so that he might be repaid” (Rom. 11:35).

The Apostle confirms this when he says: “What then shall we say that Abraham our father according to the flesh discovered? For if Abraham was justified by works, he has glory, but not before God” (Rom. 4:1–2).

#### 23

Likewise, in Genesis, concerning Joseph, when he had been sold to Potiphar, a eunuch [Note: Older codices read “to Putiphar the eunuch”]:

“His master,” it says, “saw that the Lord was with him, and that whatever he did, the Lord prospered in his hands; and Joseph found grace before his master.”

He did not possess this from himself, but found it, God granting it—the God who was with him, prospered his works, and had given him the interpretation of dreams.

Likewise, when he had been sent to prison: “The Lord,” it says, “was with Joseph, and poured out mercy upon him, and gave him grace before the chief of the prison” (Gen. 39:3–4, 21).

He did not glory in himself because of this grace but in the Lord, whose gift he knew it to be, when he said to Pharaoh concerning the interpretation of his dream: “Without God, no answer of salvation will be given to Pharaoh” (Gen. 41:16).

Likewise, in Exodus: “The Lord,” it says, “gave grace to the people before the Egyptians, and they lent to them, and they plundered the Egyptians” (Exod. 12:36).

For how would those who hated them have given them their vessels of gold and silver, or their clothing, unless it had been the gift of grace?

#### 24

Likewise, in the same book Moses says to the Lord: “Behold, you say to me, ‘Lead this people away,’ but you have not shown me whom you will send with me. And you said to me, ‘I know you above all others, and you have grace before me.’ Now therefore, if I have found grace in your sight, show yourself to me clearly, so that I may see you, and so that I may be one who finds grace before you, so that I may know that this people and this nation have grace before God.”

But this comes from God, not from himself. Indeed, when he says, “If I have found grace in your sight,” he boasts that he has found it, not that he possessed it.

And when he says, “Show yourself to me clearly, so that I may see you, and so that I may be one who finds grace before you,” what else does he indicate but this: “When I see you clearly, may I recognize that it was not a merit of mine but the gift of your grace”? Therefore he says, “so that I may be one who finds grace before you.”

A little later he says to the Lord: “Unless you yourself go out with us, do not lead me away from here. And how will it truly be known that I have found grace with you, I and your people, unless you are with us also? Then I and your people will glory above all the nations that are upon the earth.”

How will we glory? Not in ourselves [Note: The printed editions read “upon the earth. For we are not in ourselves,” omitting “we will glory.” The manuscripts provide the corrected reading], but in you, from whom we have received the grace of glorying.

Likewise, the Lord says to Moses: “I will also do this word that you have spoken, because you have found grace in my sight, and I know you above all others” (Exod. 33:12–17).

But I will do this because, through my mercy, you have found my grace—not because you, born from Adam the sinner, possessed your own grace.

And when the Lord says to Joshua son of Nun, “As I was with Moses, so I will be with you; and I will not abandon you or despise you” (Josh. 1:5), what else does he say than what he said to Moses: “You have found grace in my sight, and I know you above all others”? For Joshua would not have received Moses’ place unless he too had found grace before God.

25. Likewise in the Book of Judges:

“And the angel of the Lord said to Gideon: ‘Because the Lord will be with you, and you will strike Midian as one man.’ And Gideon said to him: ‘If I have found favor in your sight, and you will do according to what you say to me,’ etc.” (Judg. VI, 16–17).

That is: Since I do not recognize myself as capable of fulfilling what you promise, and since my having seen you was not due to my merits, it must have been a gift of God. Therefore he also says, “If I have found favor in your sight.” That he saw the angel by God’s gift is confirmed by the divine voice, when it consoles him in his fear and trembling, saying, “Peace be with you; do not fear; you will not die” (Judg. VI, 23). That is: It was by my grace that you saw the angel; therefore you will live in peace and will do what he announced to you.

Likewise, in the Second Book of Kings:

“And King David said to Zadok the priest: ‘Carry the ark of the Lord back into the city. If I find favor before the Lord, he will bring me back, and I shall see it and its beauty’” (II Sam. XV, 25).

That is: I do not trust in my own strength to be delivered, but in the grace of God, whose power it is to bestow it. Therefore he also says, “If I find favor before the Lord”—which he himself confirms in the Psalms when he says, “The Lord will give glory and grace” (Ps. LXXXIII, 12).

26. For what could have been said or proved more clearly concerning grace and works [Note: [Col. 1634] Am., Er., and the manuscripts read: “concerning the works of grace.”] than what was said to the prophet Jeremiah? Or, even if his name is not mentioned in that passage, did God not accomplish this through his gratuitous grace, when he says to him:

“Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you; and before you came forth from the womb, I sanctified you, and appointed you a prophet among the nations” (Jer. I, 5)?

He plainly displays [Note: [Col. 1634] Manuscript codices read *manifeste*, or *manifestae*; Am. and Er. read *manifestum*.] the gift of grace, and not something arising from works. For what works of his existed when he had not yet been formed in the womb or born from the womb? Therefore it was not on account of works, but from the One who called him, that it was said to him: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you; and before you came forth from the womb, I sanctified you and appointed you a prophet among the nations.” [Col. 1635]

Behold: truly it depends not on the one who wills or the one who runs, but on God who has mercy.

Likewise in Jeremiah:

“And may the Lord,” he says, “give us strength, and enlighten our eyes, and may we live under the shadow of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and under the shadow of Balthasar his son, and serve them for many days, and find favor in their sight” (Baruch I, 12).

Since, evidently, because of our sins—for we were handed over into their power—we do not deserve to find rest, may he grant grace through which we may be able [Note: [Col. 1635] Thus some manuscripts. Certain others read: “until we receive grace through which we may be able.” But the printed editions read: “until we find grace through which we may be able to receive pardon.”].

Therefore he says likewise in what follows:

“Hear, O Lord, our prayer and our supplication, and deliver us for your own sake, and grant us favor before the face of those who led us away” (ibid. II, 14).

“Deliver us,” he says, “for your own sake, and grant us favor”—that is, because power and mercy belong to you, and because you have justly humbled us, for this reason we ask you to grant us grace: for your own sake, not for ours, whom you handed over into captivity on account of the preceding merits of our evils.

27. Likewise, in Solomon:

“The lips of the righteous distill grace” (Prov. X, according to the Septuagint).

That is, by the gift of grace they speak graciously and justly. For they would not distill grace unless they were watered from the fountain of grace.

Likewise there:

“He who loves discipline loves understanding; but he who hates reproof is foolish. Better is the one who finds favor before the Lord” (ibid. XII, 1–2).

For evidently one cannot love discipline and obey the one who reproves him for the Lord’s sake by his own power alone, unless he has been instructed by the gift of grace.

Therefore he says again:

“The heart of a man considers right things, so that his steps may be directed by God” (ibid. XVI, 9).

For the one who has found favor before the Lord already considers the right way; and the Lord directs his steps when, trusting in him and not in himself, he says:

“Perfect my steps in your paths, so that my footsteps may not be moved” (Ps. XVI, 5).

Likewise, in the Book of Wisdom:

“For the grace of God,” he says, “is among his holy ones” (Wis. IV, 15).

Here it is stated universally that none of the holy ones was or is without the grace of God. But in order that grace might be present in them to strengthen them, they received freely through faith what comes from God; they did not possess it before faith. For, as David says, “You will save them for nothing” (Ps. LV, 8).

28. Likewise, in the Book of Tobit:

“But I,” he says, “guarded my soul so that I would not eat of their foods. And because I remembered God with all my heart, the Most High God gave me favor with King Shalmaneser, and I bought everything for him, traveling into the region of Media, until he died” (Tob. I, 12–14).

But when he prefaced this by saying, “Because I remembered God with all my heart,” lest it appear that this was something proper to him rather than a gift, he immediately adds, “The Most High God gave me favor.” Thus he confirms that it was by God’s gift, not by his merits, that he remembered God and found a place of affection before King Shalmaneser.

“For the will is prepared by the Lord” (Prov. VIII, 3, according to the Septuagint), from whom “every good gift and every perfect gift” comes (Jas. I, 17), “so that every mouth may be stopped and the whole world may become subject to God,” because “no flesh will be justified before him by works”; for the righteousness of God, through the anticipation of mercy, has appeared by faith in Jesus Christ upon all who have believed.

Therefore the same apostle adds:

“Having been justified freely by his grace, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus, whom God set forth as an expiation through faith in his blood” (Rom. III, 19–25), and so forth.

Behold: you have heard, “Having been justified freely by the grace of God.” Do not put your own works before it, nor glory in them, because, as was already said above, “no flesh will be justified before him by works.”

## CHAPTER XIII

29. “Then,” you will say, “you condemn the good works of free choice, because you say that righteousness is not owed on account of works. If this is so, why are we commanded by the Apostle to abound in good works, because our labor will not be in vain in the Lord?” (I Cor. XV, 58).

Listen, foolish heretic and enemy of the faith of truth. We do not condemn the good works of free choice which, in order that they may be performed, are prepared through the prevenient grace—not through any merits of free choice, but by grace itself, which causes, governs, and perfects them so that they abound in free choice. For by these works, or by works of this kind, people have been justified, are justified, and will be justified in Christ.

But we condemn, by divine authority, those works of free choice which are placed before grace, and on account of which people are exalted as though they were justified in Christ by their merits [Note: [Col. 1636] Lov. alone reads: “the justified are exalted.”]. “For who has first given to him, and it will be repaid to him?” (Rom. XI, 35).

Paul says this—not from himself, but with Christ speaking in him. Pelagius does not believe it. Tell me, heretic: to whom must an anathema be pronounced?

Rather, let Paul speak with his own mouth, with Christ delivering the sentence:

“But even if we, or an angel from heaven, should preach to you a gospel contrary to what we preached to you, let him be anathema. As we have said before, so now I say again: If anyone preaches to you a gospel contrary to what you received, let him be anathema” (Gal. I, 8–9).

He, in the Spirit of God, says to those who exalt themselves on account of themselves: “Who has first given to him, and it will be repaid to him?” You, in the wisdom of the flesh, which is hostile to God (Rom. VIII, 7), reply: “I first gave to God, and he repaid me.” What remains for you to hear, then, except “Anathema”?

30. But you cry out again and say:

“If there is no merit in the one who acts, how is it written, ‘And you will repay each one according to his works’?” (Matt. XVI, 27; Rom. II, 6).

Listen and understand—if, that is, you have ears for hearing and your heart has not been hardened against understanding. Because of free choice, by which people perform good and evil deeds, it was said that each one would be repaid according to his works.

For a person has evil merit when, having been baptized, he turns away from the good through his own fault and does evil—that is, when he abandons God and loves the world, as the Apostle testifies that Demas and Hermogenes did (II Tim. IV, 9; I, 15). Or when someone, placing his entire hope [Note: [Col. 1636] Lov. reads: “having his whole hope.”] in empty idols, does not wish to know the true God—whom the Most High God has power to [Note: [Col. 1636] The printed editions read: “whom he has power to know in this world.” “To know” is absent from the manuscripts, so that the pronoun “whom” may be understood of the human being; of God, however, “has power” means that he has power either to save that person through undeserved grace or, by a just judgment, to reserve him for Gehenna.] save in this world, if he wills, through undeserved grace, by which he justifies the ungodly, and also, when that person turns away, to reserve him—handed over by a just judgment to a depraved mind—for the future punishment of Gehenna, so that he may repay him according to his works.

He likewise has good merit when he does not resist the good things of God’s grace working in him in all things, but becomes its fellow worker and places all his hope in it; when he offers his ear and heart to God speaking within, that is, in the inner person, and not outwardly to the evil world resounding around him [Note: [Col. 1636] The printed editions read: “in the evils of the world resounding around him.”]—a merit not on account of the present life, as though he were to receive it in the present world, but on account of the true future life, which will be forever and ever.

For “if in this life only we have hoped in Christ, we are of all people most pitiable” (I Cor. XV, 19). “For hope that is seen is not hope; for what a person sees, why does he hope for it? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience” (Rom. VIII, 24–25).

Therefore a Christian ought not to be exalted on account of merits in this world, because no one living in this life will boast that he has a pure heart, nor does anyone say that he is without sin. For in the present life labor has been imposed, so that merits may come into being through the help of grace, not so that the repayment of merits already earned may take place.

Therefore the Apostle also says:

“Not that I have already received it, or am already perfect; but I pursue it, if I may apprehend that for which I have also been apprehended by Christ Jesus” (Phil. III, 12), and so forth.

Whatever a person has attained in the present life, then, is a gift, not a merit. But when “this corruptible has put on incorruption, and this mortal has put on immortality” (I Cor. XV, 53), when there will no longer be any desire for evil but perfect righteousness, so that God may be all in all, then the just will be repaid according to their works. Throughout the whole life of this world, their every merit was grace, so that, rejoicing then, they may rightly say to their soul:

“Bless the Lord, O my soul, and all that is within me, bless his holy name. Bless the Lord, O my soul, and do not forget all his rewards: who is gracious to all your iniquities, who heals all your diseases, who redeems your life from destruction, who crowns you with mercy and compassion” (Ps. CII, 1–4).

Do you hear, Pelagian, “with mercy and compassion,” while in your blindness you exalt yourself as though you were to be crowned for the merits of your own powers alone [Note: [Col. 1637] Some manuscripts read: “your own virtues.”]? Understand that the soul is crowned by the mercy and compassion of God, not by an inflation of merits [Note: [Col. 1637] The printed editions read: “not by the fabrication of merits.” The manuscripts correct this.].

## CHAPTER XIV

31. Therefore all the holy people of God whom I mentioned above, or did not mention, who lived before the coming of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, were saved by no other faith than the one that exists now.

For when the Apostle said in the Epistle to the Hebrews:

“By faith we understand that the ages were fashioned by the word of God, so that visible things might come into being from invisible things. By faith Abel offered to God a greater sacrifice than Cain, through which he obtained testimony that he was righteous, God bearing witness to his gifts; and through it, though dead, he still speaks.
