By faith Enoch was translated so that he would not see death, and he was not found, because God translated him; for before his translation he had testimony that he pleased God. But without faith,” he says, “it is impossible to please God” (Heb. XI, 3–6).

The same applies to the others whom the order of the reading mentions [Note: [Col. 1637] The printed editions read “election”; this is incorrect and disagrees with the manuscripts.].

But it was not by faith alone; rather, it was also by grace, which has now been given through Christ. For neither is faith without grace nor grace without faith, as the Apostle says to Timothy:

“But the grace of our Lord abounded with faith and love that is in Christ Jesus” (I Tim. I, 14).

That the faith which brought salvation through knowledge of God is the same for them and for us, the Apostle demonstrates most clearly when he writes to the Galatians:

“Before faith came, we were being guarded, shut up under the law, for the faith that was to be revealed” (Gal. III, 23).

That is, for the faith which, throughout the silent ages, was always present in God’s servants through the Word of God, and which was to be revealed among the nations through that same Word incarnate. For, as the Apostle again says to the Hebrews, “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever” (Heb. XIII, 8).

The times, therefore, have changed, not the faith.

32. Justification, then, through faith in Jesus Christ has been given, is given, and will be given to believers. This faith is a gift, as grace also is, not a payment. For, as I recalled the Apostle saying above, “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ abounded with faith.”

For which of us possessed faith before it came—the faith which, as the Apostle said, was to be revealed? Let no one boast at all that he produced faith in himself from his own understanding, by which he could believe God. Rather, let him acknowledge that, both before the law, under the law, and after the law, the faith that is in Jesus Christ was revealed to each person for salvation through the illumination of grace that comes from God the Father.

Our Lord and Savior demonstrates this most clearly in the Gospel, where he says to his disciples:

“Who do people say that the Son of Man is?” and so forth.

“But you,” he says, “who do you say that I am?”

Peter answered:

“You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.”

And the Lord said:

“Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jona, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. XVI, 13–17).

Behold the clear gift of faith. Is it not a gift when it is said, “Flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven”?

Likewise the Apostle Paul says to the Galatians:

“But when it pleased him who separated me from my mother’s womb and called me through his grace, to reveal his Son in me, so that I might preach him among the nations” (Gal. I, 15–16). [Col. 1638]

He had learned from the Gospel what the Lord had answered Peter when he confessed him. Therefore he also said:

“But when it pleased him who separated me from my mother’s womb and called me through his grace, to reveal his Son in me.”

It was as though he were saying:

“It was not flesh and blood that revealed the Son of God to me, but the Father who is in heaven.”

Therefore he did not say, “when I wished,” but “when it pleased him who separated me from my mother’s womb”; and he called me not through my merit, but through his grace.

Hence he says again in another Epistle:

“I obtained mercy, so that I might be faithful” (I Cor. VII, 25).

Likewise to the Ephesians, where he says:

“For this reason I, Paul, am a prisoner of Christ Jesus for you Gentiles,” and among what follows:

“Through the Gospel,” he says, “of which I was made a minister according to the gift of God’s grace, which was given to me” (Eph. III, 1, 7).

Hear and believe, Pelagian: according to the gift of grace, each person is faithful, not according to the merit of his own will.

## CHAPTER XV

33. But you say to me—because, with your eyes clouded by heretical grief, you cannot direct your gaze toward the light of truth:

“Then there is absolutely no merit belonging to one’s own will, if you distinguish between will and grace?”

Listen, then, briefly. The merit of one’s own will is good when the gift of grace precedes each person’s will and works so that a person, through his own will, may produce merit.

In order that you may recognize more clearly that grace and faith are gifts which recall a lost human being to salvation, hear the Apostle preaching to the Ephesians:

“By grace you have been saved through faith; and this is not from yourselves: it is the gift of God; not from works, so that no one may boast” (Eph. II, 8–9).

Therefore all who have existed, or exist, or will exist, have believed, believe, and will believe in God through the one faith [Note: [Col. 1638] Ancient manuscripts read: “through united faith.” Certain others, with Ambrose and Erasmus, read: “through the unity of faith.”] and grace that is in Christ Jesus; they have received, receive, and will receive salvation.

For without Christ no human being can believe in God or attain salvation. Thus the Apostle Peter says in the Acts of the Apostles concerning Christ, rebuking the madness of the unbelieving Jews:

“This is the stone that was rejected by you builders, which has become the cornerstone; and there is salvation in no one else. For there is no other name under heaven given among human beings by which we must be saved” (Acts IV, 11–12).

For this reason the Apostle Paul, writing to the Corinthians—that is, showing that all our fathers were redeemed by the same faith [Note: [Col. 1638] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “the same faith.”], by the same sacraments as we are—says:

“For I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses [Note: [Col. 1638] The Ebrulphian codex, following the Greek, reads “into Moses,” rather than “in Moses.”], that is, through Moses, in the cloud and in the sea; and all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them; and the rock was Christ” (I Cor. X, 1–4).

Likewise, in the Second Epistle to the Corinthians:

“But having the same spirit of faith, as it is written, ‘I believed, and therefore I spoke’; we also believe, and therefore we speak” (II Cor. IV, 13).

He entirely removed every doubtful suspicion from the ignorant and fortified our definition with a wall that no battering ram of the heretics could shake, when he writes to the Ephesians:

“One body and one Spirit, just as you were called in one hope of your calling; one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is above all, and through all, and in us all.”

And shortly afterward in the same place:

“Until we all meet in the unity of faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, as a perfect man, according to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ” (Eph. IV, 4–6, 13).

Notice what he says, heretic: “all,” and “in the unity of faith.” But this is the faith that is in Christ Jesus, which, together with grace, as we proved above, was freely granted by God the Father for the salvation of all who believe—not on account of merits.

Let these things, taught by the school of grace that is in Christ Jesus our Lord, suffice concerning grace and free choice. Rather, thanks be to God, who, by giving as much as he wished, permitted us to speak what he wished; and where he wished us to be silent, he set a limit to the tongue.

# BOOK FOUR

Against the Fourth Dogma of the Pelagians

[Col. 1639]

## CHAPTER ONE

1. They also say that lust is a natural good in human beings, and that there is nothing in it of which one should be ashamed.

We answer: Lust is not a natural good in human beings, but an accidental evil brought about through the sin of the first human beings, and something shameful. God is not its author, but the devil. You say that it is a natural good because, in your error and while leading others into error, you believe God to be the author of this plague rather than the devil.

For everything that is naturally good, the supremely good God made from nothing; the devil did not make it. But we say and believe that lust is not a natural good, but a natural evil.

We call it a natural evil not because it was congenitally implanted in nature by God, its creator, but because it passed from a nature that sinned into a sinful nature—that is, because it is the defect of a nature that sins, not nature itself.

For no evil is nature; rather, it is an accidental act arising from the lack of good. Therefore, whatever is not nature, God did not make, because everything he made is nature.

Through this evil in Adam—who, as I have said, wickedly desired an unlawful good—human nature was corrupted, and every person born from the seed bears this corruption.

But perhaps you ask me:

“How could the evil of the serpent, that is, of the devil, pass into the good of human nature?”

Listen. We know that a serpent sometimes kills a human being immediately with its poisonous breath, and sometimes severely afflicts him so that he can die. Therefore I ask you: answer how the breath-borne poison of another nature can so prevail over human nature that it fills all its limbs with its deadly breath and forces the breath of life to depart from it [Note: [Col. 1639] Some manuscripts read “infects.”].

But I know that you will have nothing to say. For you do not believe that human nature was made wretched and mortal by the sin of the first parent, so that it can easily be brought low or killed by any accidental weakness.

Listen, then. Just as now a poisonous substance is inflicted upon a sinner by the pestilential breath of a serpent, and through it he is compelled to die, and a person inspected by a Marsian—that is, an enchanter—is said to have been breathed upon, because, as the saying goes, “the serpent breathed upon him,” and immediately an antidote is prepared for his recovery, by which the poison may be overcome—so then, in Adam when he sinned, after he had imprudently yielded himself to the serpent, that is, to the devil, who persuaded him rather than to God, who warned him not to do it [Note: [Col. 1639] In the manuscripts: “had offered himself as an imprudent and obedient servant.”], when God turned away from him in anger, lust—poisonous and deadly through its deceitful breath—was inflicted upon him [Note: [Col. 1639] Ancient manuscripts read “was inflicted.” The same manuscripts again below, §6, read “was inflicted through sin.”]. Thereafter it oppressed him with such domination that even against his will to sin, just as poison drags a person toward death, it drove him unwillingly to sin—that is, to will evil.

From this he became and was called a sinner, corrupted and vicious; from this he deserved the deprivation of life.

Against this poisonous evil, lest it prevail, the remedy—that is, the antidote—of grace was given through Jesus Christ by the mercy of God [Note: [Col. 1639] More manuscripts read “by God.”], so that the whole human race might not perish utterly.

If you do not wish to believe this, I ask you to say how a serpent can offer poison to a human being with a gentle hiss so that it may kill him—something no human being is unaware of.

But however much you evade the issue, with sin intervening, human nature could be taken captive under the evil of the devil-serpent, just as a human being can be deprived of life by the breath-borne poison of an earthly serpent [Note: [Col. 1639] All the manuscripts read: “with sin and the evil of the devil-serpent intervening, human nature could be taken captive, and an earthly serpent can be deprived of life, and so forth.”]. For we believe that the former could pass into human nature in the same way that we know and see the latter can happen. Neither would that have been possible there nor this here, if our nature had remained blameless. [Col. 1640]

## CHAPTER II

2. We must therefore ask why this evil under discussion is called lust.

Without doubt, the word *libido*—lust—was derived from *libendo*, that is, from *libitus*, “what is pleasing.” But you say to me:

“Then everything that pleases is lust?”

I answer: Not everything that pleases is lust, but everything that pleases wrongly is lust.

For in a good inclination, it cannot be called lust, but will—arising, of course, from the reasoning of the natural mind. But in an evil inclination it is not will but pleasure, which the will of the first parent produced when he transgressed: namely, when he wrongly desired what was unlawful at the serpent’s urging. Through its poisonous hiss, as I have already said above, sinful nature conceived this disease, which it had not possessed before the fault, and transmitted it through the intercourse of the seeds to later generations [Note: [Col. 1640] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “and the seed passed through intercourse.”].

That the first human beings were made without the evil of lust is testified by Holy Scripture when it says:

“And both were naked, Adam and his wife, and they were not ashamed” (Gen. II, 25).

What does “they were not ashamed” mean? It means that they were not, as happened after the sin, harassed by any impulses of lust toward sinning.

The lawful use of the sexual organs for begetting children had been created in their will, not the pleasure of lust. But after the sin had occurred in them, Scripture itself again demonstrates this, saying:

“And their eyes were opened, and they knew that they were naked, and they sewed fig leaves together and made coverings for themselves.”

But were they created with their eyes closed, since it is said, “Their eyes were opened”? And if their eyes had been closed, how would what is written be true:

“And the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was excellent to the eyes and beautiful to behold” (ibid. III, 6–7)?

Their eyes, therefore, were open to behold the works of the Lord, which he created very good; but they were closed through ignorance of evil, which the Creator of all good things did not create.

“And their eyes were opened” when the awareness of guilt struck them, or when they saw—that is, felt—in themselves that, having already been stripped of the peace of soul and body, some exceedingly shameful and precipitous movement had newly arisen. Therefore, ashamed, they ran to the fig leaves and covered with them the limbs troubled by the shame of lust.

But if, according to you, this lust is a natural good and there is nothing in it of which one should be ashamed, I ask for what reason they covered their natural limbs after the transgression instead of remaining as they had been before the sin, when they were naked and were not ashamed.

For when God fashioned the human being according to his image, he created nothing in his form that would cause the human being to be ashamed.

But if they were not ashamed, according to our faith, because of the accidental evil of lust after the sin, then according to your dogma God made something in them that would cause them to be ashamed. For you say nothing else when you proclaim God to be the author of the most shameful lust.

## CHAPTER III

3. But perhaps you reply:

“Far be it from us to say that God made shame in the first parents” [Note: [Col. 1640] The printed editions add here “anyone.”].

Therefore I ask again and again: If God made nothing that could cause shame, and it is said with full confidence that he made absolutely nothing of that kind; and if the evil of lust is not from the devil—for it is not said with right faith that it is not from him, since it is from him—tell us why, after their guilt, they covered their sexual organs, which from the day of their creation they had seen in one another and had not covered.

If you say, “Because of the sin,” then confess and accuse the evil lust whose shamelessness those who possessed shame covered with fig leaves. But if you cannot say this, you openly charge God with being the author of this shame, because, when you deny that their confusion arose from the evil of lust, the human race’s maker is openly accused.

Would that you were ashamed to praise this lust in the same way that they were then ashamed when, being convicted by its movement that they had sinned, they blushed.

What else do the fig leaves indicate, with which, as I have said, they covered their shameful limbs—made shameful through sin, not by God as their author—except a certain shameful itching of lust?

Indeed, why did they cover those parts of the body rather than their hands, with which they touched what was forbidden, or their mouths, with which they ate what they had wrongly desired?

They covered those limbs in which the desire for sin, blazing up, accused the concupiscence of an incontinent throat.

This is your laudable and beloved lust [Note: [Col. 1641] The printed editions read “beloved desire”], through which, as the Apostle says, “the flesh desires against the spirit” (Gal. V, 17). Against this, unless the spirit, hoping in God, desires with strength, neither flesh nor spirit will possess eternal life.

You are so foolish that, while excusing the devil and accusing God, you believe that he made this discord between flesh and spirit.

But far be it—far be it—from Catholic minds to dare to think or say that God is the author of lust.

## CHAPTER IV

4. Trusting in the antidote of grace against this poison, all the saints, disciplining their bodies and bringing them into servitude lest they should perhaps become reprobate in relation to the faith of Christ, have fought and continue to fight bravely.

The Apostle Paul was speaking of this struggle when he said:

“I therefore run, not as uncertainly; I fight, not as one beating the air”; and as though he were answered in opposition, “Who is your adversary, or where is he, against whom you fight?” he replies:

“I discipline my body and bring it into servitude” (I Cor. IX, 26–27).

That is: He is in my body, not in the air, against whom I fight. It is lust, namely, the enemy of my life, which, while I run to please God under the guidance of his grace, attacks and provokes me moment by moment with the goads of various evil inclinations [Note: [Col. 1641] Thus the ancient books. The printed editions read: “while I run and, under the guidance of his grace, wish to please God” (Ambrose and Erasmus read “not wishing”), “with the evil inclinations of various kinds,” etc.]. By hindering the course of my contest, it seeks to make the devil, its author, the victor.

Therefore I discipline my body, where I carry my enemy. Strengthened by the power of grace, which fights in me against my enemy, I fight back for myself.

But I destroy the enemy’s power when, by disciplining my body, I am made weak in myself. For “when I am weak, then I am strong” (II Cor. XII, 10).

“Thanks be to God, who has given us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ” (I Cor. XV, 57).

But if he did not discipline his body for this reason—that he might overcome the desires or impulses of evil concupiscences and lust—then, you who claim to be wiser and teachers than he, explain better why he said he did this.

For you would not proclaim lust to be a natural good if, looking toward chastity, you disciplined your bodies as Paul did. Rather, with shameless faces you live wantonly and praise its movement in public with such immodest speech that it is plain to everyone what you do in secret—if, that is, those whom it does not shame to praise publicly choose even secrecy.

I beg you, be ashamed of what the first parents, as has already been said, were ashamed after the sin—those whose sinful children we also are—and believe that lust is an evil from the devil, not a good from God.

The Apostle calls it a law—that is, an evil habit—and says that it exists in the members in opposition to the law of the mind, so that one may not obey the law of God.

## CHAPTER V

5. Hear, then, how great is the iniquity of this evil and what the weakened human being suffers from it, as the Apostle says and discusses among other things:

“For I did not know concupiscence,” he says, “unless the law said, ‘You shall not covet.’”

He did not say, “I no longer had concupiscence,” but “I did not know”—what? Whether it was evil.

Therefore I had it, but believed it to be a natural good. When, however, the law said, “You shall not covet,” I recognized that concupiscence was not a natural good, but an accidental evil brought about through sin.

“Taking opportunity through the commandment, sin worked in me every kind of concupiscence.”

When, therefore, I hoped that by my own powers I could conquer concupiscence at the law’s command, I was pressed by its stronger goads, and as I was weakened, desire increased.

“For without the law sin was dead.”

What sin? Lust, certainly, which is also called evil concupiscence.

He did not say, “It did not exist,” but “it was dead”—that is, while the commandment of the law, which is opposed to it, did not yet exist, it lay hidden in the sinner, because it was exposed by the authority of the law.

“I was once alive without the law.”

Before I knew the commandment of the law, I thought that I was living in the works of desire [Note: [Col. 1642] The printed editions add here “of the whole.”].

“But when the commandment came, sin revived, and I died.”

It lived first with a death-dealing force under the first law—that is, when it took Adam captive in paradise. It revived through the same deception under the second law and killed me as its captive, the son of the transgressor, because through the law came knowledge of sin, not victory over sin.

“And the commandment that was for life was found by me to be for death.”

He said very well, “was found by me”: God did not give the commandment for death, but it appeared to me to be deadly because I cannot fulfill it by my own strength, although I die not through any fault of the commandment but struck by the goad of concupiscence.

For sin is the goad of death.

“For sin, taking opportunity through the commandment, deceived me, and through it killed me.”

Seeing that I had no power against it through the authority of the law, sin—which, as has often been said, is desire, from which lust arose—deceived me as it had Adam, when the commandment was introduced for transgression and from it I contracted the vice of sin, as though saying again:

“You will not die by death if you eat from the forbidden tree; rather, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like gods, knowing good and evil” (Gen. III, 4–5).

Therefore through it also it killed me.

6. Therefore the law is indeed holy, and the commandment holy and just and good. I do not therefore charge God’s law with the fact that, having been weakened by my fault, I cannot fulfill its precept. Although by commanding it does not help me, nevertheless by its holiness and justice it shows that concupiscence is evil—a fact of which I was unaware—because, he says, “I did not know sin except through the law.” And it taught me that, when I fail in myself, I ought to implore divine assistance in order to overcome its unlawful desires [Note: [Col. 1642] Older books read, “enticing appetites” (*inlices appetitus*).].

What is good, then—has it become death to me? By no means. Has the good commandment, given against the works of death, been changed into death for me? By no means. I die, to be sure, not through any fault in the good commandment, but because, through my fault, I have transgressed the good commandment. Yet, so that sin might appear to be sin, it worked death for me through what is good, so that through the commandment sin might become sinful beyond measure.

Thus, so that the evil of concupiscence—which is the root of all evils—might be recognized as evil, it prevailed in me all the more through the good commandment; it did not fail. For “the law entered in so that the trespass might increase.” The trespass therefore worked death for me, since from the trespass—that is, from evil concupiscence—which weakened my own power to obey the law, trespasses multiplied. And sin became sinful beyond measure through the commandment, since through the law, as I have said, it did not diminish but rather increased into immoderate desires: “for the power of sin is the law,” by prohibiting and not removing it [Note: [Col. 1642] Thus the manuscripts. Am. reads, “and not drawing it out”; Lov. reads, “and not assisting.”].

For we know that “the law is spiritual, but I am carnal, sold under sin.” Therefore, by the Spirit of God—who both teaches and assists, and through whom the law was given—the commandments cannot be fulfilled by carnal will alone [Note: [Col. 1642] The printed editions read, “not by the will of the carnal law alone.” The manuscripts have been followed here.], because through the law I merely recognize my vices; I do not remove them. [Col. 1643] In vain do I rely on the weakness of the flesh. I cannot overcome by myself my enemy, to whom by God’s just judgment I have been handed over because of sin, and to whom the will of the first-formed man sold me [Note: [Col. 1643] The manuscripts read, “with God as the just judge.”].

God commands—indeed, may he bring it about that what he commands comes to pass. “I have been sold under sin”: may he deign, in his mercy, to change his just sentence by which he condemned me as a sinner [Note: [Col. 1643] Thus the Codex Uticensis of Saint Ebrulfus. Other copies, together with the printed editions, read: “may he deign in his mercy to change me, in accordance with his sentence by which he condemned me as a sinner.”]. “The law is spiritual, but I am carnal”: may he himself make me capable of fulfilling his law, so that, girded with the power of the Spirit, and with grace preceding through the trumpet of the perfect law [Note: [Col. 1643] Ancient codices read, “through the trumpet of the holy law.” Perhaps the reading should be, “with grace preceding through the trumpet of the perfect law.”], I may be able to overcome the enemy in my body.

7. For “what I do, I do not understand.” What I desire—that is, the evil things I desire—I do not seek or wish for them to come about, because I was not constituted by nature in such a way. But, when I lend an ear to the law, I am suddenly thrown into confusion by dark and perverse desires, enticed by this evil through which nature has been corrupted by transgression [Note: [Col. 1643] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “But this evil, by which nature was corrupted through transgression, I present its author to the law.”].

For “I do not do what I want, but I do the very thing I hate.” I want to obey the commandment of the law by the effort of my own will, but I cannot; yet while resisting sin, I take pleasure in consenting to it. “If I do what I do not want, I agree with the law that it is good.”

While, then, I want to form no desire for any evil of concupiscence, I do this all the more. Concupiscence is truly a great evil in my members [Note: [Col. 1643] The printed editions add, “I recognize,” but this is absent from the manuscripts.]. It urges me to sin with a certain delight; nevertheless, I agree with the law—that is, I believe and recognize this through the law—because, when the law in its goodness says to me, “You shall not covet,” it indicates that the poison of death is in concupiscence.

“But now it is no longer I who do it, but sin dwelling in me.” Therefore, this evil—which causes body and spirit to disagree—is present in me, not because I desire or produce it. Since the law shows me that it is evil, I strive to agree with the law so that it may not be in me [Note: [Col. 1643] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read, “from which I recognized that it was evil.”]. But since I cannot uproot it by my own willing and ability [Note: [Col. 1643] The printed editions read, “I cannot overcome it.” The manuscripts have been followed here.], that same sin, which was inflicted upon me through sin [Note: [Col. 1643] Elsewhere, “was fastened upon me.”], remaining in me, works against me the things I do not want.

For I know that good does not dwell in me—that is, in my flesh. I am therefore certain that this concupiscence, which opposes my effort, is not good. For when resistance is offered to it and it is thought to have failed, it is renewed all the more forcefully in various desires through its own wickedness.

“For to will is present with me, but to accomplish the good I do not find.” I indeed want both to conquer this sin and to obey the precept of the law. But in order to accomplish both goods, my ability does not suffice for me together with my willing, because “our sufficiency is not from ourselves but from God.” For “I do not do the good that I want, but I do the evil that I do not want.”

Therefore, for carrying out the good, my will, relying upon itself rather than upon God, accomplishes nothing; but toward evil—even what it does not want—it is sometimes inclined so as to want it. “If I do what I do not want, it is no longer I who do it, but sin dwelling in me.”

Thus, when my unwillingness to desire is provoked so that it wills, it is not the resisting will that does this, but the desire of sin, which cannot be overcome by my will alone, because the Lord says, “Without me you can do nothing” (John XV, 5).

8. I therefore find this law for me who want to do good: evil is present with me. For “I delight in the law of God according to the inner man.” Since, then, the evil of concupiscence is present with me—that is, it comes of its own accord and confronts me when it is not desired, and it is possible for the corrupted will to carry it out, because, as has already been said, it cannot be weakened without God—it nevertheless seems to me, when I rely upon myself, that I am able to accomplish the good, namely, the commandment of the law, if, according to the inner man [Col. 1644]—that is, according to the reasoning of the soul—I do not cease to resist with the whole intention of my will and with all the powers of my nature the mortal movements of my body.

But I see another law in my members, opposing the law of my mind and taking me captive in the law of sin, which is in my members. And behold, I see in myself—that is, I feel—a contrary law, namely evil concupiscence, sullied by the disease of lust, confronting, resisting, and prevailing against the law of my mind—that is, against the natural intention of my soul—and leading me captive into the law of sin, which is in my members: that is, into the transgression of the first-formed man, which is in my members. For “through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death; and so it passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Romans V, 12).

## CHAPTER VI

9. Behold what deadly wars, what dangers and shipwrecks have arisen from the evil of your praiseworthy and beloved concupiscence, sown by the devil. Behold whose pestilence you proclaim to be a light burden and an easy yoke. But Paul—whose most open enemies you are, since you do not recognize lust with him as evil—had read that this evil yoke was written of as follows: “A heavy yoke is upon the sons of Adam, from the day they come forth from their mother’s womb until the day of their burial in the mother of all” (Ecclesiasticus XL, 1).

And therefore, against you, he preached to the faithful concerning this yoke, saying, “Do not bear the yoke with unbelievers” (II Corinthians VI, 14): that is, do not become equal to unbelievers by praising with them what is detestable and calling evil good. For “woe to those who call sweet what is bitter, and bitter what is sweet” (Isaiah V, 20).

That teacher of the Gentiles therefore discovered these wars, in faith and truth, according to the wisdom given to him against you, as existing in the whole human race within himself, and he fought vigorously against them. For when, in his own person, he says:

“I did not know sin except through the law”; and, “I did not know concupiscence”; and, “Sin worked in me every concupiscence through the commandment”; and, “I was once alive without the law”; and, “I died”; and, “The commandment that was for life was found by me to be for death”; and, “Sin deceived me through the commandment, and through it killed me”; and, “What is good, then—has it become death to me? By no means”; and, “Sin worked death for me through what is good”; and, “The law is spiritual, but I am carnal, sold under sin”; and, “What I do, I do not understand”; and, “I do not do what I want, but what I hate, that I do”; and, “If I do what I do not want, I agree with the law that it is good”; and, “But now it is no longer I who do it, but sin dwelling in me”; and, “I know that good does not dwell in me—that is, in my flesh”; and, “To will is present with me, but to accomplish the good I do not find”; and, “I do not do the good that I want, but the evil that I do not want, that I do”; and, “If I do what I do not want, it is no longer I who do it, but sin dwelling in me”; and, “I find this law for me who want to do good: evil is present with me”; and, “I delight in the law of God”; and, “I see another law in my members, opposing the law of my mind and taking me captive in the law of sin, which is in my members”—

he plainly testifies that he himself waged these wars against concupiscence.

Yet he does not boast that he achieved the triumph of victory by his own strength. And so, when he had been weakened by such an evil in himself, against himself, and for himself, and had found no assistance toward victory, he was displeasing to himself and lifted his eyes to the fortifications of Christ, by which he might be defended, saying: “Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Romans VII).

It is grace, heretic, by which we are freed from the body of death—that is, from the movements of concupiscence by which our body is struck so that the soul may be destroyed—not the mere power of one’s own will.

## CHAPTER VII

10. Continue, then, through the fields of your loquacity, by which you do not blush to praise the squalor of such great shame, and cry out according to your custom, saying: “Lust is a good genital heat, and there is no reason to be ashamed of it; for if it is said to be evil, marriage will already be condemned, since without it offspring cannot exist.”

Let the most chaste conquerors of your beloved concupiscence consider from this, as much as they please, what it delights you so greatly to praise—or, if it does not please them, when it urges them to be pleased and is conquered by them [Note: [Col. 1645] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “or, if it does not please them, why do you persuade them to be pleased, while chastity is conquered by you?”]—why do you proclaim as good what you feel to be opposed to you? I beg you, be ashamed. No one ever takes pleasure in calling what is his enemy good or adorning it with praises.

You are wholly deceived and deceiving; indeed, you have been deceived and you deceive others. This is not a good heat, nor is it genital in the good genital members that God formed. Rather, as has often been said, it is evil, with the devil as its author and sin preceding it. If by this heat the vigor of your mind were not dissolved toward unlawful things, you would not praise it so freely; rather, as Catholics do, you would condemn it.

11. But again you answer, as I said above, setting up a shield before your dogma so that the simple whom you deceive may be unable to resist you, and you say: “Marriage will be condemned if lust is condemned, because offspring are not begotten without it.”

Why do you strive through your most deceptive assertions to turn day into night? Why do you envelop clear things in clouds? Why do you, burning in the shameful heat that you proclaim to be the best, belch forth the bitterness of smoke upon those who behold the light, so as to disturb the eyes of their hearts?

Marriage, established by God, is very good, and it is in no way condemned when lustful desire is condemned. Marriage was instituted for the procreation of children, as it is written: “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth” (Genesis I, 28). Its lawful use was not instituted in the luxury of lust, but without it, by the command of the most honorable will, solely, as I have said, for the sake of children [Note: [Col. 1645] Lov. reads, “but in the command,” omitting “without it.”].

For before Adam’s sin—when this disease was not yet in them—God said to Adam and Eve, “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth.” But after the sin, as has already been discussed above, their bodies conceived this restless and deadly pestilence through the hiss of the poisonous serpent, by whose cunning flatteries they were deceived [Note: [Col. 1645] In the manuscripts: “by whose cunning.”]. Through lawful use, after they had been expelled from paradise, they transmitted it to their descendants, leaving it in us by hereditary right as a testimony of their sin.

Thus, recognizing from this that we are children of transgressors, let us not boast of ourselves—that is, of our sinful nature—in the sight of God, the just judge; rather, let us always bend our necks to his mercy, which does not rest upon merits, so that he may deign to call us back to paradise, from which he rightly made us exiles [Note: [Col. 1645] The printed editions read, “may he deign to call us back,” and below, “from which he rightly made them.” The manuscripts contain neither “us” nor “them.”].

12. In married people, then, and in every human being, lust is evil. For it sometimes draws people toward unlawful acts, because it is opposed to the sinful will through which it came to exist in the members, to such an extent that by its own burning it drives even married people’s minds, panting for lawful use, so that they act under the impulse of that same permission rather than acting as agents [Note: [Col. 1645] All manuscripts read, “that same permission.”].

The will becomes incontinent when it is enticed [Note: [Col. 1645] Am. Er. and some manuscripts read *illicita* (“unlawful things”).] and overcome by pleasure; yet among married people who make good use of an evil, it is venial. The Apostle shows this when, for the sake of giving themselves to continence and prayer, he enjoins married people to abstain for a time and commands them to return again to one another because of the temptation of incontinence, saying:

“Do not defraud one another, except by mutual consent for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer; and return again to the same relation, lest Satan tempt you because of your incontinence. But I say this by way of concession, not by way of command” (I Corinthians VII, 5–6).

But among adulterers and fornicators, who make evil use of evil, it is damnable. Now, then, understand whether the Apostle promised married people forgiveness for an evil or for a good: whether he commanded them to abstain for a time in order to devote themselves to prayer on account of an evil or on account of a good.

You are wholly mistaken, because God, who commanded that the good be done, nowhere prohibited the good, but prohibited the evil, saying through David: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Psalm XXXVI, 27).

13. It is stated without hesitation that married people make good use of this venial evil for the purpose of begetting children—children who are born through God the creator, not from the evil of accidental lust, but from the good of marital permission.

When a vineyard, abandoned on every side by the farmer, has been overgrown with thorns and, in its season, lying amid the bushes, produces clusters [Note: [Col. 1646] Older codices read *botruos*.], does it produce grapes from the hostile thorns by which it is oppressed? By no means. Rather, from the good of its own nature, though corrupted by the prickles of the thorns, it bears good fruit.

Likewise, if wheat, once it has sprung up, is surrounded and covered on every side by weeds, insofar as it produces an ear, it brings forth a good shoot from the good of its own nature, not from the evil of the weeds by which it is hindered. So children are good fruits from the good of nature, not from the evil of lust, which corrupts and vitiates nature and with which every human being is born.

Everything, then, while remaining in the good of its own nature, withers and grows numb under adversities that are foreign to it [Note: [Col. 1646] Am. Er. and the manuscripts read *miserescit*; the reading is uncertain.], always needing the hand or care of the cultivator so that it may be able to correspond to its nature, into which nothing contrary was implanted by its author, God.

The same thing occurs in our sinful nature: it continually needs God, its author, cultivator, and preserver, so that, by the hand of his grace through Jesus Christ our Lord, it may be purified from the thorns, thistles, and weeds of lust and of all evil concupiscences—which, as we have often said, it acquired not through God as their author but through sin—until it returns to the earth from which it was taken, to be raised again by the same Jesus Christ our Lord and to return from the earth, purified, into the new age.

I repeat again and again, then: evil lust does not hinder the good of marriage [Note: [Col. 1646] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read, “does not contribute to marriage.”], because marriages were not ordered from the beginning amid its filth, as we have already said above. For God, who created bees to produce offspring without intercourse and decreed that all the seeds of the fields should be sown or germinate without lust, would also have permitted human beings, had they not sinned, to arise from human beings in paradise through voluntary intercourse, not through the harlotry of lust.

How this would have occurred I think I have already shown in a chapter of this discussion, insofar as the Lord has revealed it. Therefore, we confess that the permission of marriage is very good, and with Catholic speech we proclaim that evil and pleasurable concupiscence in married people is damnable; and by the authority of the holy Scriptures we condemn your dogma as horrifying in its shamefulness.

## CHAPTER VIII

14. It is Paul, the apostle of Christ—not Pelagius, the disciple of Antichrist, heretic—who says that what is not good dwells in his flesh. Indeed, he most openly calls it evil and testifies that it is sin; he calls it the “goad” of his flesh and declares that it buffets him, lest he be exalted by the greatness of his revelations (II Corinthians XII, 7). Considering its evils [Note: [Col. 1646] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read, “considering its evil.”] in the body of his death, in which he waged an internal war with an invisible enemy, he testifies that he found no remedy for his salvation at all except the grace of God in Christ Jesus, which delivers him.

Writing to the Colossians, he himself says: “Put to death your members that are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, lust, evil concupiscence” (Colossians III, 5), and so forth. Answer this great teacher: why does he command these things to be put to death, if they are natural goods?

But while Pelagius and Coelestius speak in you, you preach the opposite with laudable applause, rather than Christ speaking through Paul, saying: “Make alive your members that are upon the earth: pure fornication, good lust, excellent concupiscence.”

Madman, heretic abandoned to a reprobate mind according to your own will: concerning the evil of these filths, the same apostle again says, writing to the Romans: “Let not sin reign in your mortal body, so that you obey its concupiscences” (Romans VI, 12).

He, teaching the truth, forbids obedience to these impurities; you, in Pelagian error, encourage it. He calls concupiscence opposed to the mind sin; you, by praising it and taking pleasure in it, assert that it is a natural good.

15. Fools, at last become wise, and do not boast of so great an evil or be liars against the truth, which, through the mouths of its saints, calls your praiseworthy and beloved concupiscence evil and punishes lust as impure.

For various temptations arise from these things, and they hinder us at every moment as we strive to please God, as the Apostle James says:

“Let no one who is tempted say, ‘I am tempted by God.’ For God is not a tempter of evils, and he himself tempts no one. But each person is tempted, drawn away and enticed by his own concupiscence. Then, when concupiscence has conceived, it gives birth to sin; and when sin has been brought to completion, it generates death” (James I, 13–15).

See your beloved concupiscence conceiving pain from the seed of your praises [Note: [Col. 1647] The printed editions read, “See your beloved and also praised one conceiving pain.” The manuscript reading has been followed here.], giving birth to sin, and generating death.

When you proclaim God to be its author, you undoubtedly accuse so great an apostle and say that God is the tempter of evils. For according to you he created that by which human beings are tempted, drawn away, and enticed; and consequently he himself made that by which they perish. If you did not think this, you would certainly not say that God made death.

But hear the same Apostle James still striking your empty mouths with the rod of heavenly wisdom: “From where are wars and disputes among you? Is it not from this—from your concupiscences, which wage war in your members?” (James IV, 1).

Do you hear what office your excessively beloved concupiscence performs—that is, wars and disputes, by which it causes our body and spirit to disagree? And does it delight you, heretic, to serve in its hostile camp and under its deadly law?

If you followed the peace of the Catholic faith, you could easily be freed by the rudder of grace from this storm of wars and disputes in which you are tossed about on every side in the sea of your heart, so that you cannot reach the harbor of truth [Note: [Col. 1647] The manuscripts read, “by the rudder of grace you could be freed.” The printed editions read, “you will be able to be freed with grace as your guide.”], and you could recognize the evil that, being placed in evil, you think most beautiful.

16. Hear another apostle reclining upon the breast of Jesus and testifying that concupiscence is not from God the Father but from the world, and that it will pass away with the world. I mean the Apostle John.

“Do not love the world,” he says, “or the things that are in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him. For everything that is in the world is the concupiscence of the flesh, the concupiscence of the eyes, and the pride of life, which is not from the Father but is from the world. And the world passes away, and its concupiscence; but whoever does the will of God remains forever” (I John II, 15–17).

If it pleases you, close the eyes of your hearts still further so as not to see, and block your ears so as not to hear the truth of so great an apostle; then cry out, lest you do any injury to your beloved concupiscence: “The concupiscence of the flesh is from God, not from the world, and therefore genital heat is good.”

## CHAPTER IX

17. But why should I strive to proclaim any further discourse in producing testimonies by which your defense is proved damnable? For if everything were brought forth from the treasures of the divine law, I would run out of time in recounting it. Hear, then, briefly—not brief things, but works of your most beloved heat, immense in crime—which drive the dulled hearts of mortals into unlawful intercourse; and at last be ashamed and fall silent.

Inflamed by this heat and shamefully enticed, a father sometimes turns toward his daughter and commits incest. A son also stains his father’s bed when he sometimes unites with his mother or stepmother. A brother, led by desire, attacks his sister; he does not blush to violate a kinswoman. A virgin does not endure the lawful permission of marriage, but desires intercourse at an unlawful time. A husband, by no means content with the lawful embrace of his wife, contaminates others’ wombs [Note: [Col. 1648] All manuscripts read, “he contaminates forbidden alien wombs.”]. Likewise, a wife, forgetful of her own marriage bed, usurps another’s wife through adulterous love [Note: [Col. 1648] The printed editions read, “forgetful of her own husband’s marriage bed, through adulterous love she occupies the bed of another’s wife.” The manuscripts add neither “husband” nor “bed.”].

For males also, abandoning the natural use of the female, burn with desire for one another, males committing shameful acts with males (Romans I, 27). It is even more horrifying to say what follows than what we have mentioned: that a human being, forgetful of his rational nature, is compelled to mate with an irrational nature, alien to his own [Note: [Col. 1648] Understand: “alien to his nature”], namely, an animal.

What shall I say about the downfall of certain servants of God and sacred virgins, who in this age suffer shipwreck? Or what about the various impurities, in which I think the devil himself, their author, is displeased for your sake? Behold into what filth of disgrace that heat, which you love so dearly, entices and hurls human minds! Behold, you did not tremble to say that such defilement had existed even in the holy members of Christ. Behold of what obscenity and shame you are the fiercest praisers and most shameless defenders; and, if I am not mistaken, so long as it still displeases you not, perhaps even its perpetrators.

For who could think well of you, when he knows that you think well of so great an evil? If, then, there is any shame in you, if there is any decency, if there is any concern for chastity, stop calling and praising as good so great a necessity of evil—that is, concupiscence of the flesh mixed with the filth of lust. Believe that its author is not God but the devil, with the sin of the first-formed man preceding it; and believe that human will alone cannot restrain it in its most shameful movements unless saving grace through Christ our Lord comes to its aid [Note: [Col. 1648] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read, “unless the singular grace of Christ our Lord, the Savior, comes to its aid.”].

# BOOK FIVE  
## Against the Fifth Dogma of the Pelagians

[Col. 1647]

## CHAPTER I

1. Again they say, “Little children do not carry original sin, nor will they perish from eternal life if they depart from this life without the sacrament of Baptism.”

We answer: We have already discussed at length above the original sin by which little children too are held bound, and we have shown by the light of truth that the whole human race limps under this fault. We have also shown that the Son of God came in the likeness of sinful flesh for this reason: that by his death on the cross he might conquer death, and by his gratuitous grace heal our wounds.

Nevertheless, heretic, with the help not only of our Savior Christ but also of the authority of the Scriptures, I will prove that what you proclaim about little children is false. What [Col. 1648] could be said more clearly to show that little children are born subject to Adam’s sin than what was said through David: “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother bore me”?

For when he was lamenting his adultery and the murder he had committed because of Bathsheba, he poured forth this truth in the groaning of his confession, as though he were saying: “It is not only because of this single crime that I am a sinner, as though, before I committed it, I had been without sin” [Note: [Col. 1648] The manuscripts read, “I was without sin,” omitting “not.”]; rather, I was already a sinner from my mother’s womb: “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother bore me.”

Therefore, [Col. 1649] conceived and formed from parents in the defect of sin, I took on the condition through which I committed adultery and murder as personal sins [Note: [Col. 1649] Thus Lov. At Er., Lugd., and Ven., “I took on … I committed.” In B., “I took on … … I committed.” M.]. For when he adds, “For behold, you loved truth” (Psalm L, 7–8), he confesses sins committed by his own will.

For the penitent says truth to God when he hides nothing from him of the crimes he has committed—not because, even if he concealed them by his will, God would be unaware of them; but God wishes truth to be confessed to him so that the penitent may obtain pardon. If some things have slipped from his mind, God wishes him to confess God’s truth, so that, when he says generally, “God, you who know the hidden things of the heart, you know my works, and my offenses are not hidden from you” (Psalm LXVIII, 6), God may grant him pardon. And this, certainly, is the truth of the one confessing, which God loves.

2. Eve therefore borrowed sin from the devil; Adam, by consenting, made the bond; and usury increased for posterity. Hence it is that an infant, bound in his mother’s womb by hereditary right, promises the debt before he recognizes his father’s bond, or even his parent as a debtor.

The usury of this written obligation consists in those most malign passions by which the souls of adults as well as of little children are oppressed. David himself, who said that he was conceived in iniquities and born in sins, shows that no one can be freed from them except through Christ when, in the seventy-first Psalm, he speaks concerning the person of Christ, saying: “He will free the poor from the powerful, and the needy who had no helper”—that is, the human race from the dominion of the devil.

“He will spare the poor and needy, and will save the souls of the poor. He freed their souls from usuries and iniquities” (Psalm LXXI, 12–14). Christ, certainly, paid Adam’s debt, with which he had bound us by usuries, when he permitted his own body, subject to no sins, to be hung upon the cross. For his is the voice in the Psalm: “What I did not seize, then I repaid” (Psalm LXVIII, 5).

Therefore he himself frees the souls of little children as well from usuries and iniquity, because, as the Apostle says, “One died for all”; and again, “Therefore all died” (II Corinthians V, 14). And if all died, they died having been struck by the goad of death; for “the goad of death is sin” (I Corinthians XV, 56).

Tell me, then, when I ask: If a little child, born according to the flesh, has contracted no sin, why is he bound by death’s brief allotment of days? For where there is no sin, there ought certainly to be no death. This is not something I invent, but what the Apostle proclaims: “Through sin, death.” Accordingly, in accordance with your error, God is unjust if he allows a little child who has no sin by which he could be deprived of life to die.

## CHAPTER II

3. But looking back to that deception of your dogma, to which an answer has already been given above, you say to me: “God made death because he made man mortal; but he did not make sin, because in the beginning he forbade man to sin.”

Rather, what else do you say when you believe that God made death, except that God also made sin, so that through sin death could enter the world? For, as must be repeated again and again, when the teacher of the Gentiles says, “Through sin, death,” you answer: “By no means; God did not make sin.”

Then he gave man the occasion to sin, so that, as you say, his work—death—could befall man. For without sin death could not exist; because, whether you wish it or not, “through sin, death.”

“Nor did God,” you say, “give man an occasion to sin by which he could die; rather, he made him mortal.” It has already been answered that it is written: “God did not make death, nor does he rejoice in the destruction of the living” (Wisdom I, 13); and again, “God created man imperishable” [Note: [Col. 1649] All manuscripts read, “incorruptible.”] (Wisdom II, 23).

If, then, he did not make sin, nor give man an occasion to sin—which is rightly said—[Col. 1650] how, according to you, could the good of death, which is not rightly said, come to man through the evil of sin? For “what fellowship has light with darkness? Or what part has justice with iniquity?” (II Corinthians VI, 14).

See, wretched people, if indeed you can see, what friendship you create between God and the devil—something far from the Lord. You say that God made death, and the devil sin—if indeed you assign even this to the devil. Their works therefore became mingled, as they came to one another’s aid by agreement, so that they might deprive man of life; and therefore it was said, “Through sin, death.”

4. Here, then, understand—or rather, let those who are sound in judgment understand—since you are accustomed to call us Manichaeans: which of us is the advocate of the Manichaean plague? Is it we, who say that light has nothing in common with darkness; or you, who confuse the work of light, as you suppose—that is, death—with the work of darkness, the devil—that is, sin?

Unless you believe that both death and sin are evil, and that God is the author of neither, but that the devil inflicted both upon the transgressing first-formed parents [Note: [Col. 1650] Lov. adds here, “inflicted.”], you plainly assist the Manichaeans; indeed, you are like the Manichaeans [Note: [Col. 1650] Several manuscripts read, “indeed, you are perfect Manichaeans.”].

The Manichaean does not believe, but the Catholic does believe Paul when he says that “through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death, and so it passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Romans V, 12).

This is our faith: we unhesitatingly confess that sin is in little children, and that through sin death has passed into all human beings. Little children too are human beings by nature. Therefore, however many there are, they are all human beings; and when it happens to them to die, they die because of sin, which has passed into them not by an act but through a further transmission of conception. For they would not die unless they were killed by the mire of sin.

For, as must often be repeated, “through sin, death,” not without sin. From death, so that they may not perish eternally, they are redeemed by the Lord’s death [Note: [Col. 1650] The printed editions read, “from this death.”]. From this mire of sin, in which they are born filthy, so that they may enter the kingdom of heaven undefiled, they are cleansed through the undefiled blood of Christ in Baptism.

## CHAPTER III
### 5.

Hear also another who inquires into the wisdom of God and through it proclaims the truth to mortals. Hear him speaking in a manner different from David, yet prophesying no differently; indeed, speaking with one and the same Spirit [Note: [Col. 1650] Thus all the manuscripts. The printed editions have, “with a single Spirit.”], he declares that both Adam’s sin and birth itself weigh upon infants.

For David says, as has already been stated above: “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother bore me.” This writer says in the Book of Ecclesiasticus: “A heavy yoke is upon the sons of Adam, from the day they leave their mother’s womb until the day of their burial in the mother of all” (Eccli. 40:1). What is this heavy yoke except sin? And why is it called a yoke unless because it comes from two—Adam and Eve—or presses and crushes the necks of two, namely, male and female, both the older and the younger? For it is a yoke upon both sexes. Therefore he also speaks generally: “A heavy yoke is upon the sons of Adam.” By saying “upon the sons,” he makes no distinction of ages or sexes; and by comparing the yoke with sin, he makes everyone, except Christ, equal as sinners, since Christ was not born, like the others, through ordinary marital intercourse [Note: [Col. 1650] Only the printed editions read, “because of.”].

Bound to this yoke [Note: [Col. 1650] The printed editions read, “this yoke”; the manuscripts, “to this yoke.”]—that is, original sin—the older and the younger alike drag, as though it were a plough, the vice arising from birth itself [Note: [Col. 1650] The manuscripts have, “vices arising from it.” The Ambrosian manuscript has, “by the vice arising from it [....].”], as long as we are in the body of death. By the ploughshare of its desires [Note: [Col. 1650] The printed editions read, “of its desire.”] our earth is furrowed—that is, corrupted. For this reason, I think, it is said in the Book of Wisdom: “But the corruptible body weighs down the soul” (Wis. 9:15).

From the labor and burden of this yoke, or from the corruption caused by the plough, no one is released by his own will and power, [Col. 1651] except by the one who judges justly and shows mercy without owing it, who says:

> “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matt. 11:28–30).

But how those called to him are to go, he himself shows when he says: “No one comes to me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (John 6:44).

In place of the harsh and heavy yoke of sin, under which those born according to the flesh are weighed down, he commands those who are called to take upon themselves the easy yoke and the light burden. Above we have already explained why sin is compared to a yoke; now we must understand the spiritual yoke and burden of Christ. I say that it is charity, by which we are commanded to love God and neighbor, because upon these two commandments, as upon a yoke, the whole Law and the Prophets depend (Matt. 22:37–40).

For what is sweeter or lighter [Note: [Col. 1651] The printed editions have, “and gentler.”] than charity, by which God, loving us, joined the two peoples—Jews and Gentiles—in the unity of faith by the bond of grace, and made the two one? Christ’s yoke, therefore, hangs upon the necks that the yoke of sin had pressed; it does not weigh them down but lifts them toward heaven. For charity, without which no one can please God, never fails (1 Cor. 13:8), and it covers a multitude of sins (1 Pet. 4:8).

It is also the light burden: whoever possesses it carries God, because “God is charity” (1 John 4:8). Therefore the Apostle also says: “Glorify and carry God in your body” (1 Cor. 6:20).

### 6.

Infants too belong to this calling. They are taken up through the faith of those who believe, not through the obedience of their own will, but through the abundant love of charity. For this reason it is said of them in the Psalms: “For even those who do not believe dwell with the Lord God” [Note: [Col. 1651] The manuscripts omit “the Lord God.”] (Ps. 67:19).

Unless the easy yoke and light burden of Christ’s charity are bestowed upon them by the gift of grace, they cannot rest from the labor and burden of the original yoke. For they are weighed down by the labor and burden of various sufferings, which we see and marvel that they endure while still at the breast. They are sometimes tormented by demons; they are also tortured by various pains and wounds; and, as I have said, they are afflicted by many kinds of misery. In all these sufferings, although they cannot say what they are undergoing [Note: [Col. 1651] The manuscripts read, “although.”], they nevertheless somehow declare that they are tortured by diverse punishments when, pierced by the goad of pain, they utter confused cries of lamentation.

If these infants, who are flesh of sin because they are from the sinful flesh of the first parents, do not suffer because they have been struck by the sting of the protoplasts’ sin, then, according to your error, God either made nature such that the soul is tormented by penal sufferings, or else he is unjust, permitting holy innocence, wholly free from every fault, to be oppressed by such great dangers and sometimes even deprived of life amid them [Note: [Col. 1651] Lovaniensis adds here “who,” and below, after “is afflicted,” reads, “he is cruel or certainly unjust.” But all the manuscripts disagree.].

Unless you believe that they suffer these things because of original sin, you unquestionably accuse God, who made all things “very good.” But far be it from us to say that he is unjust, inflicting wrath; rather, he is just, carrying out judgments—for punishment is sin’s penalty—so that infants are punished as sinners, not in action but in origin.

“For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother bore me”; and, “A heavy yoke is upon the sons of Adam, from the day they leave their mother’s womb until the day of their burial in the mother of all.” It was not I who invented these words; the Prophets spoke them, moved by the holy Spirit of God’s truth.

## CHAPTER IV

### 7.

Hear also another athlete, exceedingly strong, passing through all the scourges of the devil and overcoming his impatience by his own patience. I mean blessed Job. Consider what he thought about the stain of human nature through the Spirit of God, by whom he was tested and made strong. He declares that even infants cannot be free from the filth of sin and that they must be brought to judgment before God.

“Man,” he says, “born of woman, is short-lived and full of wrath [Col. 1652]; and like a flower, when it has bloomed, he falls; he flees like a shadow and does not remain. Have you not also taken care of this one, and caused him to come before you for judgment? For who will be clean from filth? Not even one, even if his life upon the earth should be only one day” (Job 14, according to the Septuagint).

Is anything doubtful, in the face of such an exceedingly clear authority, about infants being born stained with the defilement of sin? When he says, “Have you not also taken care of this one, and caused him to come before you for judgment?” he immediately indicates, on account of God’s most just judgments, the preceding reason why he comes to judgment: “For who,” he says, “will be clean from filth? Not even one, even if his life upon the earth should be only one day.” That is, he comes to judgment because of the filth of sin, which he draws from the sinful nature through which he is born unclean into the world.

We have stated this according to the edition of the Seventy interpreters, which was translated from Greek into Latin. Hear the same thing more plainly, to your own rebuke, in the manner in which it has been translated from the Hebrew wording:

> “Who can make clean one conceived from unclean seed? Is it not you alone?”

Can there still be an argument? Indeed, should there be any contradiction on your part? You hear it said of an infant: “Who can make clean one conceived from unclean seed? Is it not you alone?” And you still doubt that, through grace, Christ’s Baptism possesses what cleanses an infant?

Unless the infant were unclean, the text would not say, “Who can make clean?” But when it adds, “conceived from unclean seed,” it declares that the parents are stained by sin. Their seed is unclean, not by the condition of nature, but by the vice of the transgressing first parent.

Whether, therefore, the Seventy translated from Hebrew into Greek, or another translator similarly translated from Hebrew into Latin, they have said one and the same thing, though in different words but not with a different truth: infants are guilty of the filth of sin.

### 8.

What injustice is there in God? As I have often asked when setting forth the various issues, tell me: if, according to your error, there is no cause—as we said above Job declared—for an infant to be short-lived and full of wrath, when he has absolutely no knowledge of what wrath is through the use of reason; or why, like a flower, he falls and flees like a shadow and does not remain through a life of many days or years, as we know happens to many infants; or why God causes him to come before him for judgment when he has neither known the commandment of God’s Law that he should obey nor despised his will?

According to you, as I have said, infants suffer these things unjustly from a just judge if they are not held liable through any contagion of sin. But however widely you build walls around your heresy with the words of your lies, truth prevails. Its battering ram, driven by the hands of grace, shatters and destroys everything on which you resist and place your confidence.

For the Lord is just and does nothing unjust, and the truthful one cannot be a liar. Infants, therefore, as the Apostle says, are “by nature children of wrath” (Eph. 2:3), bound, as we have often said, through the offense of their parent Adam. They would not be called children of wrath unless, having been sown, they drew with them wrath—that is, the sin of the first parent, who, by sinning, first provoked God to wrath within our race.

Therefore it is also said: “For who will be clean from filth? Not even one, even if his life upon the earth should be only one day.” Or, as it is expressed in another way, though with the same meaning: “Who can make clean one conceived from unclean seed? Is it not you alone?”

Because of this single filth of sin, which the infant draws not from the good of marriage but from the evil of lust, he is short-lived and full of wrath. He withers like a flower, flees like a shadow, and does not remain; and he will come before the Lord for judgment, to be judged.

Unless the grace of Baptism through Christ comes to his aid, he will perish from the Christian people, just as the Law said that an infant would perish from the Jewish people unless he had been circumcised on the eighth day. For it is written:

> “The infant who has not been circumcised on the eighth day—that soul shall perish from his people” (Gen. 17:14).

Tell me, then: from what crime does circumcision free an infant? Or why did the uncircumcised person perish from the circumcised people of God, if he possessed nothing from which he could be healed or because of which he could perish?

Rather, the loss should have been threatened against his parents, if he had not been circumcised, since they possessed the practice of obedience and free will [Note: [Col. 1653] Several manuscripts omit “and.”], and not against an infant ignorant of the knowledge [Note: [Col. 1653] “Knowledge” is added here from the manuscripts.] of good and evil.

But suppose that, because of this negligence—which is not stated in the text—the parents undergo the punishment of those who are to perish. Can their condemnation, if the infant died uncircumcised, abolish the destruction of the infant’s soul? For God, not man, spoke, saying: “The infant who has not been circumcised on the eighth day—that soul shall perish from his people.”

Tell us, then, if you can, about God’s justice [Note: [Col. 1653] The Colbertinus codex reads, “into which”; other manuscripts, “because.”], in which you boast that you possess great power—or rather, that you possess everything by the powers of nature. Why does he destroy uncircumcised innocence? And why does he command circumcision if circumcision grants no remission of sins?

You answer plainly: “God is just in judging.” This is what you usually say as though you were lovers of God, but with your mouths, while in your hearts you lie to him [Note: [Col. 1653] The manuscripts read: “For this is what you usually say, namely, that you love him with your mouths.”].

If, then, God is just in judging, I ask you: state the cause of the uncircumcised infant who is to perish. Certainly he has no actual sins. What actual sins could there be in eight days? You do not wish to believe that he bears original sin and is condemned on that account. From where, then, do God’s just [Note: [Col. 1653] The printed editions and some manuscripts read, “unjust.”] judgments arise? Speak openly now: “God is unjust and impious, since he condemns an infant whom no condemnable cause preceded.”

For it is recognized that you think nothing else in the darkness of your heart—if indeed you believe that, in accordance with God’s faithful Law, an uncircumcised infant perishes. Or, if some other judgment must be formed about you, let the orthodox decide.

## CHAPTER V

### 9.

But in your accustomed manner, having abandoned and been refuted by the light of truth, you say: “God, foreknowing the evil deeds that he was going to commit when he reached mature age, declared that he would perish from his people.”

Is this how you think, insane Pelagian, that God—who is just in all his ways and holy in all his works (Ps. 144:17)—should be believed to judge an uncircumcised infant, so that he punishes him as though he were responsible for crimes not committed; imputes to him a period in which he did not live his life; and charges him with willing and unwilling, when there was no exercise of will?

Far be this, far be this from the just judge, who gives to each person who obeys or despises through the exercise of free will according to his works. But in the uncircumcised infant God hates and punishes only the offense that is the work of the devil, which the infant, sown from Adam, has drawn with him and from which he was not freed because he was deprived of circumcision.

The same thing now occurs in the Christian people. For that circumcision on the eighth day carried the figure of the Savior’s resurrection day and the grace of Baptism [Note: [Col. 1653] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have, “of the Lord Savior.”].

### 10.

Yet you promise eternal life to infants even if they have not been baptized, because, evidently, you believe that baptism confers nothing upon them and that the grace of Christ takes nothing away from them.

For if you understood why Christ said, “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick” (Matt. 9:12), you would certainly believe that they are brought to the physician and Savior at the station of Baptism, not as healthy people but as wounded ones, so that they may be healed. Nor would they have life unless they ate the flesh and drank the blood of the one who is life itself.

For he said:

> “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves. Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life” (John 6:54–55).

How, then, do you promise infants the life of the kingdom of heaven when they have not been born again of water and the Holy Spirit, when they have not been fed with the flesh or drunk the blood of Christ, which was poured out for the remission of sins?

For his decree is:

> “If anyone has not been born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (John 3:3).

To enter the kingdom of heaven is nothing other than to live the blessed life that endures for ages of ages. Behold: one who has not been baptized and has also been deprived of the life-giving food and drink is excluded from the kingdom of heaven, where Christ, the fountain of the living, remains.

Give me another place besides this where there can be everlasting rest. The Catholic faith, on the authority of God, believes the first place to be the kingdom of heaven, from which, as I have said, the unbaptized person is excluded; the second is Gehenna, where every apostate and everyone alienated from the faith of Christ will experience eternal punishments; the third we entirely do not know, nor will we find—or even discover—such a place in the Holy Scriptures [Note: [Col. 1654] All the manuscripts add, “or discover.”].

Invent, Pelagian, from the workshop of your perverse doctrine a place where infants alienated from the grace of Christ can possess a life of rest and glory.

There is the right hand and the left hand of the just judge seated; there is the kingdom and Gehenna, life and death, the just and the wicked. On the right hand, therefore, are the just; on the left, the workers of iniquity. In the kingdom is the rest of the baptized; in Gehenna, the punishment of unbelievers. Life leads to the joy of glory; death to weeping and the gnashing of teeth. The just are in the kingdom of the Father with Christ; the wicked are in the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.

In saying these things, I have not posited many divisions of places, but only two, because everything mentioned refers to two destinations, namely, the kingdom and Gehenna, even if more terms are used.

The right hand—that is, life, the just, and, if we add what I said, justice, holiness, blessedness, and all other good things—refers to the rest of the kingdom of heaven. The left hand, however—that is, those who will stand on the left—refers to the wicked, death, injustice, deceitfulness, impiety, and every kind of evil, to the torments of Gehenna, where the death called “the second death” will be not an ending but a death enduring in torment.

Therefore, one who has not been baptized cannot be found among the things that belong to the kingdom of heaven. And if he is not there—for truly he is not there—do you think, Pelagian, that you now understand where he is? Or at least say where he is.

## CHAPTER VI

### 11.

Answer in your customary manner: “The Lord says, ‘In my Father’s house there are many dwelling places’” (John 14:2). In these dwelling places, unbaptized infants have their own dwelling places of life and refreshment.

Is this, you think, that third place which a little earlier I demanded should be invented from the workshop of your doctrine? May Christ strike this work with his iron rod, by which he rules the nations—his inheritance—and the ends of the earth—his possession (Ps. 2:8–9); by which he tests the vessels of his mercy and rejects those of dishonor. If it remains unshaken, let him permit your infants whom you have received, to whom you promise life without him, to dwell there.

Come, state your case; support your assertion and refute mine. It is certain, since Truth says so, that these many dwelling places which you have brought forth from the treasures of the Gospels are with God the Father. But I ask you whether they are in the kingdom of heaven or outside it.

For God the Father is in the kingdom of heaven, and these dwelling places are certainly there. But if they are not in the kingdom of heaven, then the Father is alien to the kingdom of heaven, because, as he said, where the Father is, there are also many dwelling places.

What do you say, heretic? Choose one of the two positions whose defender you can be. Is the Father and the dwelling places in the kingdom, or outside it?

If you say, “In the kingdom,” you have lost the place which you had constructed with such elaborate skill for infants. For the unbaptized person does not enter these dwelling places. The one who said, “In my Father’s house there are many dwelling places,” himself also said, “Whoever has not been born again of water and the Spirit will not enter the kingdom of heaven.”

Behold how Christ’s strong rod shatters your work.

But if you say, “Outside,” consider what you are saying to Manichaeus. According to you, the Father, having been defeated in some conflict by someone, is excluded [Note: [Col. 1654] Perhaps, “cast out.”] from the kingdom of heaven. The Baptism of infants does not concern the work of his Son, nor do the Father’s dwelling places belong to Christ. Consequently, their kingdom has been divided: Christ receives the baptized into the kingdom of heaven, while the Father receives the unbaptized into the dwelling places of his own realm.
