Behold what thoughts your heresy, impregnated by the devil, has brought forth; behold what a place that Pelagian—or Coelestian—workshop has fashioned for miserable infants. You have advanced to destruction, excessively clever and sharp-witted as you are, so that the Father appears excluded from the kingdom and Christ from the Father’s dwelling places.

What will the infants deceived by you do thereafter? Catholic reasoning, while you teach them otherwise, does not allow them to enter the Father’s dwelling places without Christ the physician. While you promise them life without Christ, you take life away from them; while you promise them health, you lead them to death; while you guarantee rest, you plunge them into Gehenna.

These dwelling places with the Father, therefore, are not separate chambers allotted for the habitation of the just. Rather, they are the joined rewards of good merits, which are in the kingdom of heaven. That kingdom is undivided in the possession of the united [Note: [Col. 1655] Thus all the manuscripts; the printed editions read, “unique.”] concord of the Godhead—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. It is not like some enormous palace from which one might be shut in or shut out; nor does it have a boundary, as an earthly kingdom does, beyond which it has no power to reign.

For the one who fills and surpasses all things—the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, one God, all in all, one who is powerful and all-powerful—is without end in his kingdom. “Great is the Lord and exceedingly worthy of praise, and there is no end to his greatness” (Ps. 47:2); “his kingdom is a kingdom of all ages, and his dominion is through every generation and lineage” (Ps. 144:13).

The glory of the saints and the blessedness of eternal life may be said to be divided from Gehenna, from which the impious, sinners, and every unbaptized person are separated and assigned to Gehenna’s portion. But God’s power is not partly present and partly absent, because he himself reigns forever and ever both over the rest of the saints and over the condemnation of sinners.

## CHAPTER VII

### 12.

Let the infants come to Christ, so that through his medicine he may restore to them the life they lost through Adam. For he came not in vain to seek and save what was lost.

By his foreknowledge he saw that you would become heretics, and he rebuked you through his Apostles when he said:

> “Let the infants come to me, and do not hinder them; for of such is the kingdom of heaven” (Mark 10:14).

He said “of such” in comparison with those who come to him, not of all infants generally, including those who have not been reborn in him. Therefore he says, “Let the infants come to me”—that is, “Do not suppose that they have no need of me. They cannot come into the kingdom of my Father except through me.”

Finally he says:

> “I am the way, the truth, and the life; no one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14:6).

How, then, do you believe that unbaptized infants will remain in the Father’s house, among the dwelling places, when no one goes to the Father except through Christ, who is the way; and no one has eternal life or remains in the truth except through him, who is life and truth?

“Without me,” he says, “you can do nothing” (John 15:5).

For just as no one comes to the Father except through Christ, so no one who is to be saved comes to Christ unless the Father draws him. For he said:

> “No one comes to me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (John 6:44).

No one can come to the Father and the Son unless the Holy Spirit of the Father and the Son is at work. He breathes where he wills and distributes grace to each as he wills. This grace [Note: [Col. 1655] All the manuscripts have, “salvation.”] is not separated from him, but by an undivided hand and power the one God and Trinity works wholly in the human being [Note: [Col. 1655] The old Remigianus manuscript has, “remaining undivided and one in power.” Other manuscripts have, “with an undivided hand and as one in power.”].

Whoever, therefore, does not have the work of the Trinity in himself—that is, saving Baptism—cannot attain eternal life with the living saints in the kingdom of heaven.

For Baptism is the work of the Trinity, because Christ is, as the Apostle Paul says, “the fullness of divinity” (Col. 2:9). And, as Peter also says in the Acts of the Apostles, salvation is not in anyone else:

> “For there is no other name under heaven given among human beings by which we must be saved” (Acts 4:12).

Behold, Peter, the prince of the Apostles, speaks truth in truth: salvation has been given to human beings under heaven in no other name except Christ’s. You, in your lie, give another name that could save infants who have not been baptized in the name of Christ, who, as I have said, is the fullness of divinity.

For whoever is baptized in Christ is baptized [Col. 1656] in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit—which is the fullness of divinity—with the grace of salvation for the remission of sins.

## CHAPTER VIII

### 13.

“And we,” you will say—as we have heard you say several times—“baptize both adults and infants for the remission of sins.”

And when we have contradicted you in this way—“Then there is sin in infants which is remitted for them in holy Baptism”—you answer:

> “None. They are baptized only for adoption as sons. Grace has in them something it can adopt, but the water has nothing it can wash away. They are immersed for the remission of sins only so that the established custom may be maintained through the formula of the Creed. Adults, however, because through the exercise of free will they could contract sins, are baptized for the remission of sins.”

O blind hearts of your understanding! O teaching that the devil has administered to you, wrapped in mortal darkness! What wise Catholic could endure this? Who would not rather shudder to hear you named than look upon you, when you proclaim that the word of God is true in one part and false in another—that is, true in the case of adults, because they really are baptized for the remission of sins, but false in the case of infants, because they are immersed for the remission of sins in such a way that they are not immersed for the remission of sins?

When, then, will anything you say be true—or ever become true—since, in that very place where Christ, baptizing in the Holy Spirit, the Truth himself, heals all who come to him wounded by sin, you are not afraid to tell God a lie?

For the words of the Creed are God’s words. God did not deceive himself when, through his Apostles, he entrusted to his holy Catholic Church the belief that those who believe are baptized for the remission of sins. Why, then, did he command them to be baptized for the remission of sins if he does not truly effect remission? Rather, he commanded it because he does effect it.

“For God is truthful, and every human being is a liar” (Rom. 3:4).

### 14.

Infants are entirely baptized for the remission of sins; otherwise they will not have life in the kingdom of heaven. Through spiritual regeneration, what they have drawn, as I have often said, from Adam through carnal generation is remitted to them.

Foolish heretic, look to Jesus, who was therefore called Jesus—that is, Savior—because, as the Evangelist says, “He will save his people from their sins” (Matt. 1:21).

Attend to his decree: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick” (Matt. 9:12). And cease speaking falsely against him about infants. He procured Baptism in his own blood as a draught for them, the sick and not the healthy [Note: [Col. 1656] The manuscripts read, “begot” (procreavit).], and for this reason they are catechized, subjected to exsufflation, and baptized: so that the prince of this world, the devil, may be driven out from them.

Or, if the devil is not expelled from them by exsufflation—by whose work, that is, by whose vice of sin through Adam, they are held liable—tell us why an insult is done to the image of God. You, I suppose, do not exorcise those whom you baptize with your baptism, lest you insult not the image of God but the devil.

Or, if you exorcise those who, as you think, have no crime, declare whom you are driving from them. Thus, in the Catholic Church, the work of the devil is expelled by exsufflation and rebuked in them—not because they themselves are the devil, but because the devil’s work is in them.

Insofar as they are human beings, they are God’s work; but insofar as sin is in them, it is the devil’s work. God hates this in them, not them, who are his work.

For this reason, unless they are cleansed by his grace, which is not owed, through Baptism, they will have no part at all in the life of Christians and will not enter the kingdom of heaven. They will be where the uncircumcised infants of the Jews are.

Certainly, although you yourselves, walking in darkness, do not recognize it, no Catholic is unaware that you have two faiths and two baptisms. For, as I showed above, according to what you say, you baptize adults with one faith and infants with another: you baptize them with the words for the remission of sins, but in your hearts you do not believe it [Note: [Col. 1656] The printed editions have: “since, although you baptize them with the word for the remission of sins, you do not believe in your hearts that they receive baptism for the remission of sins.” The manuscript reading has been corrected here.].

But we, anathematizing you, listen to and follow Paul, in [Col. 1657] whom Christ spoke, proclaiming that the Catholic Church in Christ is one body and one Spirit, one faith, [Col. 1658] one Baptism, one God and Father of all, who is above all, through all, and in us all (Eph. 4:4–6).

# BOOK SIX

In which the matter of predestination is argued against the Pelagians.

[Col. 1657]

## CHAPTER I

### 1.

Although the subject of grace and free will has already been discussed at greater length above, it is nevertheless necessary to add something especially important to this work, so that both the slander which you customarily bring against us may be refuted—indeed, utterly disproved—through the illumination of the Savior’s grace, and the integrity of our faith may be demonstrated.

You accuse us of believing or proclaiming [Note: [Col. 1657] The printed editions read *suggillatis*; all our manuscripts have *flagitatis*, meaning “you defame” or “accuse,” as in Tacitus and Cicero.] that, when we speak of predestination together with the Law and the Prophets, the Gospel of Christ and his Apostles, we mean the following:

> “God predestines certain human beings to the life of the kingdom of heaven in such a way that, even if they do not wish to pray, fast, or remain vigilant in every divine work, they cannot perish at all and need not be concerned for themselves in any way, since God, because he willed it, once chose and predestined them to life. But he predestines others to the punishment of Gehenna in such a way that, even if they wish to believe, fast, pray, and subject themselves entirely to the divine will, God is not pleased with them and eternal life cannot be given to them at all: they are predestined by election in such a way that they perish. We say that God, acting in this manner, is one who shows partiality.”

We are not surprised that you, human beings, can fabricate falsehoods about us, human beings, when we see that you have been so bewitched by the devil [Note: [Col. 1657] The Ambrosian manuscript and the other manuscripts have, “so falsified by the devil.”] that you attempt to alter the holy and truthful Scriptures to fit your own understanding, overthrow the faith founded upon the preaching of the Apostles, and place your false doctrine above the truth.

This is why you cannot recognize the truth; indeed, this is why you have become corrupt and abominable in your desires. Incline the ear of your heart with some patience, and hear how we believe and how we proclaim the mystery of predestination. Lay aside also your obstinacy in contradicting the divine utterances.

You can easily discover or recognize the truth by God’s gift [Note: [Col. 1657] The manuscripts omit “or recognize.”], if you cease being contentious and submit to the discipline of silence.

Let us first explain what the name “predestination” signifies. Then, by the authority of the divine Scriptures, we shall prove that predestination exists with God, who shows no partiality.

## CHAPTER II

### 2.

Predestination is so called from foreseeing [Note: [Col. 1657] The manuscripts read, “from sending forth beforehand” (*a praemittendo*).], anticipating, or preordaining something future. Therefore God, for whom foreknowledge is not accidental but has always been and is his essence, predestines whatever he foreknows before it exists [Note: [Col. 1657] Lovaniensis has: “but was always and is essence. Whoever he foreknows before it comes to be, he predestines.” The correction of this passage, corrupted in the other printed editions as well as in Ambrosianus and Erasmianus, is attempted here from the manuscripts.]. And he predestines it because he foreknows what it will be.

Therefore the Apostle also says: “Those whom he foreknew, he also predestined.” But he does not predestine everything he foreknows. For evils he merely foreknows, whereas good things he both foreknows and predestines.

Therefore foreknowledge predestines what is good—that is, it preordains it before it exists in reality. When this begins to exist through its own author, he calls, orders, and arranges it.

Hence what follows: “For those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified” (Rom. 8:29–30).

Let us now explain more openly what we are saying: how God, through his foreknowledge and predestination, makes use of the human race [Col. 1658], in which there is no iniquity [Note: [Col. 1658] The printed editions have, “God generally uses his foreknowledge and predestination toward the human race.” The manuscripts lack both the adverb “generally” and the preposition “toward,” so that God is understood to make use of the human race through his foreknowledge and predestination. The verb is likewise joined with an accusative below, in section 7.].

The mass of the human race, which through the transgression of Adam and Eve was made liable to condemnation and mortal—not by divine creation—owes universally, as a debt, the punishment and torment of Gehenna. Pardon, however, is granted not on the basis of merit but through the abundant mercy of God the just judge [Note: [Col. 1658] The printed editions add, “is bestowed.” This is absent from the manuscripts.].

Because God is just, merciful, and foreknowing of future things [Note: [Col. 1658] The printed editions have, “and foreknowing of future things,” omitting “is,” which is restored here from the manuscripts], from this condemnable mass he foreknows and prepares—that is, predestines—to eternal life certain persons, not through partiality but by the unblameable, indeed incomprehensible, judgment of his equity and by free mercy [Note: [Col. 1658] The printed editions had omitted “indeed incomprehensible” here. All the manuscripts contain it. The Colbertinus manuscript reads “whom mercy carried” in place of “whom mercy freely foreknows and prepares.”].

But the others he punishes with the penalty they deserve, as I said. He punishes them because he foreknew what they would be; yet he himself neither made them punishable nor predestined them to punishment. Rather, as I said, he merely foreknew them within the condemnable mass.

## CHAPTER III
3. But if you ask me to know why God made two persons so different [Note: [Col. 1658] In the manuscripts: “why God made these two differently.”], if he is not a respecter of persons, since justice ought either to punish generally or mercy to liberate: contend with Paul—or, if you dare, argue with Paul, who, with Christ speaking in him, said: “O man, who are you that you answer back to God? Shall the thing formed say to him who formed it, ‘Why did you make me thus?’ Or does the potter not have authority over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?” (Rom. 9:20–21). But I say what I have said: whatever God does, he does mercifully, justly, and holily, because he alone knows by foreknowledge what man, through ignorance, does not know. For “who has known the mind of the Lord, so as to instruct him?” [Note: [Col. 1658] The printed editions read: “Who instructed him?” But the manuscripts have “so as to instruct him,” as above, book 3, no. 9.] Or who has been his counselor? Or who first gave to him, so that recompense might be made to him? (Rom. 11:34–35). Or who says to him, “What have you done?” God cannot be called merely just, or merely merciful, but both just and merciful. Thus we read; thus we believe. Therefore, when [Note: [Col. 1658] The manuscripts omit “when.”] with David we sing “mercy and judgment” to him (Ps. 100:1), we sing in fear; we do not question what his will is concerning judgment and mercy by investigating it.

4. But if these answers are still wholly insufficient for your contentious spirit, by which, carried away on the chariot of argument, you exult vainly across the fields of questions, hear also what else we bring forward, trembling before the incomprehensible judgments and unsearchable ways of God, from “the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God,” with the sole consideration of faith [Col. 1659]. For if we wish to scrutinize God’s secret, which is known only to his justice, we cannot comprehend it, and what is written is fulfilled in us: “They failed who searched out the searchings” [Note: [Col. 1659] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read “in the scrutiny.”]. Why? Because, he says, “man approaches, and the heart is deep,” and God will be exalted (Ps. 64:6–7). If, although you are blameworthy, you boast that the judgments of God are comprehensible to you, you are evidently pleasing God more than the Apostle Paul, who proclaimed through the Holy Spirit that his judgments are incomprehensible.

Declare, then, by what judgment—as Paul and Barnabas preached the word of God at Lystra—God “in generations past allowed all the nations to walk in their own ways” (Acts 14:15), so that they might perish in the idolatry of images [Note: [Col. 1659] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “He proclaimed his judgments through his Spirit. Consider, then, by what judgment Paul said … so that they might perish in idolatry.”]. And why did the Lord choose for himself only one nation, namely Jacob, and Israel as his possession (Ps. 135:4), giving the law to that nation alone for the knowledge of himself, while, as I have said, setting aside the other nations? Or why did the loss of the Jews occur again, so that the reconciliation of the world—that is, of all the nations—might come about, as the Apostle says: “For if their loss is the reconciliation of the world, what will their acceptance be but life from the dead?” (Rom. 11:15)?

Was it impossible for almighty God to give the law to the whole world at one time, to bestow the salvation of Christ’s grace, or, to put it briefly [Note: [Col. 1659] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read “so to speak.” And below, “yields to free choice.”], to accomplish from the beginning of Adam’s fall what his will determined should be accomplished through a diversity of times?

Explain also why, when Paul and Barnabas had been sent by the Holy Spirit to bear the name of the Lord among the nations for the sake of salvation, and were passing through Phrygia and the region of Galatia preaching, they were forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word of God in Asia. And when they had come to Mysia and wished to go into Bithynia, “the Spirit of Jesus,” he says, “did not permit them” (Acts 16:6–7).

# CHAPTER IV

5. “God knew,” you will say, “that they would not believe, and therefore he did not permit them to go there to speak the word [Note: [Col. 1659] The printed editions add “of God.”].” Fool! God is the one who justifies the ungodly, not preceded by human willing, but himself preceding the human will by his mercy. For “my God,” he says, “his mercy will come before me” (Ps. 59:10). Hear also another prophet saying: “Turn me, Lord, and I shall be turned; heal me, Lord, and I shall be healed” (Jer. 17:14; 31:18). Hence the Apostle says: “Being justified freely by his grace, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus” (Rom. 3:24). Hear: freely—and be silent about merits.

Does this prohibition by the Holy Spirit show anything other than the word of the Lord Jesus, who says in the Gospel: “The Spirit blows where it wills” (John 3:8)? From this consider; from this explain why it blows where it wills, and not everywhere.

Say also why, when the aforesaid Paul and Barnabas were preaching salvation at Antioch in Pisidia to Jews and Gentiles, no one believed except those whom the Lord had then ordained to believe. For the sacred page bears witness concerning them: “And they believed, as many as had been ordained to eternal life” (Acts 13:48)—that is, predestined.

Behold: in all that we have brought forward from divine authority, you have both mercy and judgment. And it is certain that God is not a respecter of persons (Rom. 2:11), nor does he show partiality to anyone. Descend, then, if you are able, into the depth of God’s mercy; ascend, if you are capable, into the height of his just judgment; stretch yourself into the length [Note: [Col. 1659] The printed editions read: “Descend into the length.” The manuscript reading has been restored.] and breadth of his unsearchable ways (Rom. 11:33). And if you have penetrated clearly into these secrets—which are so fearful and incomprehensible to us, and before which Paul himself trembled—then, fearless, explain them to us.

6. But if, as I said above, hurled from the chariot of empty questions you fall into the waves of vain contention, and, like a ship abandoned by its helmsman, are rolled along various and unknown shores, unable to sail there safely at all, return and sit in the harbor of the Catholic faith, where no storm of restless [Note: [Col. 1660] The manuscripts have “unfruitful.”] curiosity can disturb or engulf you.

However much you may strive to know, you cannot and will not be able to comprehend the judgments of God. For just as no one knows the things of a human being except the spirit that is in him, so no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God (1 Cor. 2:11). Therefore, if we are able to grasp anything, we must acknowledge that it has been revealed not by our own skill but by the gift of the Holy Spirit.

But if we are not granted knowledge of what is above us, let it not be sought through our smallness [Note: [Col. 1660] The printed editions read “through timidity.” The manuscripts have “through our smallness,” and continue: “let it be sought.” For it is written, etc.]. For Holy Scripture commands: “Do not seek what is too high for you, and do not scrutinize in vanity what is too strong for you” (Sir. 3:22); and, “Do not be high-minded, but fear” (Rom. 11:20).

The depth of God must altogether be feared and revered, and we rightly confess that we cannot investigate it. “You have ordered all things,” it says, “in measure and number and weight, O Lord” (Wis. 11:21). Who, then, is sufficient to comprehend this measure, this number, and this weight of God, so as to be able to recount all his ordinances within these three definitions?

I think that quality is contained in measure, quantity in number, and proportionate reason in weight. But these three—quality, quantity, and proportionate reason—are established in God’s judgment and mercy, because they are enclosed within these two boundaries, through which he established the world, governs it, and will judge it.

Within these things God the just judge cannot be comprehended; he cannot be reproached. Therefore, everything we have said above, or shall say, now lies hidden from us within the enclosure of these three things. They will be unlocked by the sole keys of God’s judgment and mercy and then become known, when, at the Lord’s coming, “the hidden things of darkness will be brought to light, and the counsels of hearts will be revealed,” so that each may receive praise from God (1 Cor. 4:5)—or punishment.

We must therefore return to the matters we began to discuss above.

# CHAPTER V

7. For we said that from the condemnable mass of the human race God foreknew, by mercy and not by merits, those whom he predestined to life by the election of grace; but that the others, who by the judgment of his justice are made strangers to this grace, he merely foreknew as destined to perish through their own fault, not predestining them to perish.

But, as I said, those whom he foreknew in works of ungodliness and death he did not preordain or compel. These, provoking God to anger, either do not wish to receive the faith of salvation preached to them, or, with God as judge, are unable to do so, or misuse what they have received; and for this reason they are handed over to a reprobate mind, to do things that are not fitting [Note: [Col. 1660] The manuscripts read: “so that they may not do the things that are fitting.”]. We rightly confess that punishment was predestined for them.

To prove this, I think the example of Judas alone is sufficient. For God, having foreknown that he would become exceedingly wicked through the vice of his own will—that is, that he would misuse the discipleship graciously bestowed on him by Christ [Note: [Col. 1660] Erasmus, the Lyon edition, the Venetian edition, and the Louvain edition read: “that he would misuse the election of his discipleship, graciously bestowed by Christ.” M.], and, inflamed with greed, would betray the Lord to the Jews for money—predestined punishment for him according to his merit. The Holy Spirit, speaking through David, said: “O God, do not be silent about my praise, because the mouth of the sinner and the deceitful man has been opened against me” (Ps. 109:2)—that is, the mouth of Judas or of the Jews against Christ.

The mouth of Judas, when he said, “What are you willing to give me, and I will hand him over to you?” and, after the promise of money, gave the sign of betrayal: “Whomever I kiss,” he said, “he is the one; seize him” (Matt. 26:15, 48). Therefore he says, “against me, it has been opened.” For when he gave the sign, he opened with his deceitful mouth the one whom they were to seize.

The mouth of the Jews also was opened against him, when, wishing to destroy him by deceit, as the Gospel makes clear, they cried out: “Crucify! Crucify!” (John 19:6). A little later it continues: “Appoint a sinner over him” [Col. 1661]—that is, over Judas—“and let the devil stand at his right hand. When he is judged, let him go out condemned, and let his prayer become sin. Let his days be few, and let another receive his bishopric.”

And after the other things that follow concerning him: “Because,” it says, “he did not remember to show mercy, but persecuted the poor and needy man, and handed over the brokenhearted man to death” [Note: [Col. 1661] The manuscripts read: “to hand over.”] (Ps. 109:6–8, 16–17), together with the remaining passages that were foretold concerning his person [Note: [Col. 1661] The manuscripts read: “his punishment.”].

For, as the Acts of the Apostles relates, the holy Apostle Peter proves that these things had been foretold concerning him and fulfilled in him, when he declares that one of those who had gathered with the Apostles ought to be appointed in his place, because of the testimony of Jesus’ resurrection. He says:

“Men and brothers, this Scripture had to be fulfilled, which the Holy Spirit foretold through the mouth of David concerning Judas, who became the leader of those who seized Jesus. He was numbered among us and obtained a share in this ministry. And he indeed acquired a field from the reward of his iniquity; and, having been hanged, he burst open in the middle, and all his entrails were poured out. This became known to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so that that field was called in their language Acheldemach, that is, Field of Blood. For it is written in the book of Psalms: ‘Let his dwelling become desolate, and let there be no one who inhabits it,’ and, ‘Let another receive his bishopric.’”

And shortly thereafter: “They appointed two: Joseph, who was called Barsabbas and surnamed Justus, and Matthias. And praying, they said: ‘You, Lord, who know the hearts of all, show which one of these two you have chosen to receive the place of this ministry and apostleship, from which Judas transgressed, so that he might go to his own place’” (Acts 1:16–25), and the rest.

Where, then, the memory of his evil works is made by the Holy Spirit in the Psalms, before he existed he was foreknown—not made—to be such a person as he would become against the Son of God. For if he had been made such, he would have been blameless, and it would have been counted as God’s workmanship, not Judas’s. The condemnation pronounced against him would also have been unjust.

But far be this from the supremely good Judge, God, the author of all good things and the condemner of all evil. For, as I said, he foreknew Judas’s evils; he did not make them. Yet, in those things which he foreknew, he handed Judas over by a just judgment to a reprobate mind and permitted him to fulfill them.

And he permitted this because, through the Holy Spirit, he had foretold beforehand that Judas would perish. For just as Christ had to suffer through Judas, as the Holy Spirit had proclaimed beforehand through the prophet, so Judas had to perish, as the same Holy Spirit proclaimed beforehand. For it was said concerning him: “No one has perished except the son of perdition” (John 17:12).

We clearly recognize that punishment was predestined for him because of his evils—in which, as I have often said, he was merely foreknown, not predestined—where the Apostle Peter says concerning him, “that he might go to his own place,” namely, after the honor of his bishopric had been transferred to another. Or certainly we recognize it where it is read that he was condemned before he was born, according to what we stated earlier in our discussion.

Such, then, is the cause of all who perish, although guilt differs from guilt.

# CHAPTER VI

8. Although what we have said has been fully discussed—that punishment was predestined for those who perish—hear the Apostle Peter, when he says that there will be false prophets, lying teachers, and apostates in the Church, as there were among the ancient people: “For them,” he says, “judgment from long ago is not idle, and their destruction does not sleep” (2 Pet. 2:3).

Likewise the Apostle Jude says: “Certain men have slipped in among you, who were long ago designated for this judgment, ungodly men, turning the grace of our God into licentiousness and denying the only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ” (Jude 4).

And in the Gospel the Lord says to sinners: “Go into the eternal fire, which my Father prepared for the devil and his angels.” But to the predestined he says: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25:41, 34)—that is, predestined.

The rule of this discussion must therefore be held firmly and without wavering, a rule made clear by divine testimonies: sinners, in their own evils, were foreknown before they existed in the world, but not predestined; punishment, however, was predestined for them according to the manner in which they were foreknown.

Infants also, who have not been reborn through water and the Holy Spirit, are subject to predestined punishment. They were foreknown not in their own wills—for they have neither good nor evil wills—but only in Adam’s sin, which they drew along with them at birth; remaining in that sin, they completed the time of their present life.

For anyone who believes with a pure faith the Lord’s statement, “Whoever does not eat my flesh and drink my blood will not have life in himself” (John 6:54), understands what judgment justice makes concerning those whom mercy does not assist, and withdraws from contention.

9. Those, however, who live according to God’s purpose must without hesitation be said to have been foreknown and predestined by the election of his gratuitous grace, and to have the kingdom of heaven predestined for them.

The Apostle Paul proves this when, writing to the Ephesians that they had been predestined and elected before the foundation of the world, he says:

“Just as he chose us in him—that is, in Christ—before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless in his sight in love, having predestined us for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ to himself.”

Let the human tongue be silent, and let it not exalt itself at all over predestination. Attend to what was said: “before the foundation of the world.” This gift belongs to the divine will, not to the merit of human weakness.

Finally, attend to what follows: “In whom,” he says, “we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of his grace, which has overflowed toward us in all wisdom and prudence, making known to us the mystery of his will, according to his good pleasure which he purposed in him, for the dispensation of the fullness of times, to restore all things in Christ, things in heaven and things on earth, in him. In him we have also been called by lot [Note: [Col. 1662] The printed editions omit “called by lot.” It is found in the manuscripts; but in them “predestined” is absent.], having been predestined according to the purpose of him who works all things according to the counsel of his will, so that we might be to the praise of his glory, we who first hoped in Christ” (Eph. 1:4–12).

Hear: “according to the riches,” he says, “of his grace which has overflowed toward us”—that is, by which “he went before us,” he says, “to make known to us the mystery of his will.” Hear also: “who works all things according to the counsel of his will.” Is it according to mine, or yours, or someone else’s, so that it might depend on merits? Far from it. It is according to his will, by which he also prepares works of good will for those whom he predestines [Note: [Col. 1662] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “also in those whom he predestined.”], so that they may walk in them, according to what he says in the same Epistle:

“For by grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not from works, so that no one may boast. For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared so that we might walk in them” (Eph. 2:8–10).

Hear: “for good works which God prepared.” And if you see that you are able to do anything good, give thanks to the one who prepared it—that you are able—not to your own will, by which, entirely apart from him, you can do nothing. For he said: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5).

# CHAPTER VII

10. Do not therefore suppose that, when we say these and similar things, we abolish freedom of the will, although it is clear that what we say depends upon divine authority [Note: [Col. 1662] The manuscripts read “to unfold.”]; as though you falsely accuse us of preventing people from doing good [Note: [Col. 1662] The manuscripts omit “that” and read: “you accuse us of preventing the doing of good.”] and from being diligent in God’s purpose.

Rather, we exhort those who perceive that they belong, by the gift of grace, to God’s mercy [Note: [Col. 1662] The printed editions read “to arrive at.” The manuscript reading has been restored.] to devote themselves to prayers, supplications, fasts, vigils, and every work of the divine will.

For the predestined Apostles are told [Note: [Col. 1662] The printed editions read “the Apostle says,” incorrectly and contrary to the manuscripts.], although what is said to them is general and is said by Christ, predestined according to the flesh from the seed of David, but predestinating according to the power of God the Father, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit:

“Watch and pray, so that you do not enter into temptation” (Matt. 26:41).

Likewise: “Watch at all times, praying that you may be considered worthy to escape all these things that are to come, and to stand before the Son of Man” (Luke 21:36).

Likewise: “Strive to enter through the narrow gate” (Luke 13:24).

Likewise: “You are my friends, if you do what I command you” (John 15:14).

And there are many other such passages, which it would take too long to recount.

But, as I recalled above, those to whom he said, “Without me you can do nothing,” can do through him the things that are commanded. The Apostle says that God’s chosen are such in Christ, in whom they were predestined according to the purpose of him who works all things.

Understand the statement: “who works all things”; and believe that the works of those who walk according to God’s purpose are the work of God.

11. But concerning those who are without the grace of predestination—that is, strangers to God’s purpose—and persist in evil works, if they also depart from this life, we do not say, as you suppose:

“Thus they were ordered by God, the maker of all human beings [Note: [Col. 1663] The manuscripts read “of all people.”], to perish, as though he himself had created their evil character and himself compelled them, against their will, to every work of death.”

Far be this from the divine purpose. For “God is not willing iniquity” (Ps. 5:5); nor has he commanded anyone to act wickedly, nor given anyone license to sin (Sir. 15:21). For he made all things to exist, “and the nations of the world are healthful” (Wis. 1:14). But through the devil’s envy death entered the world. Therefore those who belong to his portion imitate him (Wis. 2:24–25).

Nor do we say, as you fabricate:

“Even if they wish to believe or devote themselves to good works for God, God does not wish to grant them this,”

since such willing is itself God’s gift. If, then, what they will is from God, God wills that what he has given be brought to perfection. But if it is not from God, but arises from the boasting of their own will, by which they think they can win God’s favor through merits, they plainly cannot obtain what they desire. For, the Apostle says, “it is not of him who wills or of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Rom. 9:16); and because a human being cannot do anything from himself unless it has been given to him from above (John 3:27).

The supremely good God does not do this through malice, but through justice; nor through respect of persons, but through the discrimination of hidden causes.

We know that sometimes some people wish to receive the faith of eternal life and to attain it, while others do not. We also know that some attain it unwillingly, when divine grace changes their will so that they may will it, while others do not.

We know also that some who were perfected through the labor of many years have fallen at the end of their lives and perished. Others, however, have persisted in every crime and condemnability from their earliest age into extreme old age, and then, suddenly inspired by salvation from heaven, have been snatched away to the rest of the kingdom of heaven.

We know also that infants, who do not possess the use of free choice by which we might judge their merits in good or evil, have been carried by their parents’ hands to the grace of holy Baptism; and while in one of them the mystery of faith was being fulfilled through the hands of the priest, at times another, in the hands of its parents, became lifeless and was deprived of the Savior’s grace.

Who is wise enough to understand these things? Or who will be capable of giving an account of them?

Let us say with David: “The Lord is just in all his ways and holy in all his works” (Ps. 145:13); and, “How great are your works, O Lord! Your thoughts have become exceedingly deep” (Ps. 92:6).

Let us also say with Paul: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments and unsearchable his ways!” (Rom. 11:33).

# CHAPTER VIII

12. But if, even after this explanation has been given, you wish to remain contentious and refuse to submit to the truth [Note: [Col. 1663] The manuscripts read “to the explanation.”], cease slandering us on the ground that we think wrongly about God, who is just and most merciful. Rather, if you dare, accuse the Lord Christ himself, whose Gospel we follow. Quarrel with him; take up your dispute with him.

God forbid that you should slander him for having thought wrongly about God the Father, when he says:

“Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 22:14);

“No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him”;

“No one can come to me unless it has been given to him by my Father” (John 6:44, 66);

and, “Not everyone receives this word [Note: [Col. 1664] The manuscripts omit “this.”], but those to whom it has been given” (Matt. 19:11).

There are also many other passages.

13. “It is false, then,” you will say, “what the Apostle says about God: ‘who wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of his truth’” (1 Tim. 2:4)?

It is certainly not false, because God can do everything he wills, and human will cannot in any way obstruct what he wills.

But I ask you to say why God, who wills all people to be saved, as the prophet Isaiah says, blinds the eyes of some so that they may not see, and hardens the heart so that they may not understand, lest they turn and be healed (Isa. 6:10).

The Evangelist John confirms that this is true when he says concerning the Jews:

“For this reason they could not believe, because Isaiah said: ‘He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, so that they may not see with their eyes, understand with their heart, turn, and I heal them’” (John 12:39–40).

Likewise in the Gospel according to Mark, when the disciples asked Jesus about the parable of the seed, he said:

“To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God; but to those who are outside, everything is presented in parables, so that seeing they may see and not see, and hearing they may hear and not understand, lest at some time they turn and their sins be forgiven them” (Mark 4:11–12).

Say, then, why God, who is not a respecter of persons and wills all people to be saved, opens the hearts of some to believe, illuminates their eyes to see and to know the mystery of the kingdom of heaven, so that they may be saved, while of others—as I said above from the text of the reading [Note: [Col. 1664] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “as the text of the reading has said.”]—he veils the truth in parables, dulls the heart, blinds the eyes, and closes the ears, so that they may not recognize the Gospel of salvation or receive forgiveness of sins?

Tell me, I ask, how do you understand these Gospel passages? Explain what you think here about God, who wills all people to be saved. Behold: all are not generally saved, since one group is given the means to know the way of salvation, while another is not.

When God does these things, therefore, he does them neither through respect of persons nor through injustice, but through ineffable justice and unmerited mercy.

Since, however, neither side of us is able to say anything clearly on this point, let us believe only that one liable to death depends upon the judge’s will.

But lest anyone suppose that not all people are saved through some fault in God [Note: [Col. 1664] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read “through God’s judgment.”], the Apostle said: “who wills all people to be saved.” Therefore all who are saved are saved because God wills it.

“For our God is the God of salvation, and to the Lord belong the issues of death” (Ps. 68:20); and, “For anger is in his fury, but life is in his will” (Ps. 30:5).

Understand, then, justice in his fury and mercy in his will.

14. To deny predestination, which we have briefly proved to exist with God, is a monstrous blasphemy [Note: [Col. 1664] Thus in all the manuscripts. The printed editions read “a monstrous blasphemy.”]. We must not accept it merely, as you usually say, in the case of the Apostles, but also in the case of the Patriarchs and Prophets, the martyrs and confessors, all the saints, and all who serve God worthily.

Let no one boast because of this; let no one despair. For the Lord alone knows who are his (2 Tim. 2:19).

As far as we are able, let us exhort all people to good work; let us give no one cause for despair; let us pray for one another; let us humble ourselves in God’s sight, saying: “Your will be done” (Matt. 6:10).

It will belong to his power to change the judgment of condemnation that is due to us and to bestow the unmerited grace of predestination.

# ON PREDESTINATION AND GRACE

[Col. 1665]

## PREFACE TO THE FOLLOWING BOOK

The little work *On Predestination and Grace*, which begins, “When, in the volumes of the sacred Scriptures,” held a place among Augustine’s works in the ancient editions. But in the edition later prepared by the Louvain theologians, it was rejected into the Appendix, among spurious little works, as a book by a suspect author. Even its manner of expression argues and proves that it is not Augustine’s. We therefore omit other arguments by which learned men can readily establish that it should not be attributed to the holy Doctor.

Nevertheless, it cannot be passed over that Bellarmine, Possevinus, and others considered it worthy of notice that certain doctrines are found in this book contrary to Augustine’s teaching and appear to bear the imprint of Cassian’s views.

For when the author seeks to explain what God’s grace contributes to good works and what free human choice contributes on its own part, in chapter nine he divides everything between God and the human being in such a way that he first attributes to God the act of calling and illuminating, then to the human being and his free choice the choosing of the ways of God’s commandments, and finally to God once more the crowning of obedience.

In chapter eleven he says that we have willing from God because he calls and illuminates us; and that for the same reason we have completion from him, since it belongs to us to strive toward the good works whose willing he has also given.

Likewise, he says that it belongs to God to call or command, but to the human being to open and enlarge the mouth; and finally to God to fill it, or to add the promised fulfillment.

In chapter twelve, when he presents an argument proposed on behalf of the Pelagians, he gives no other response—according to Bellarmine’s judgment—than the one that Cassian himself would have given.

In chapter fifteen, while treating the question of why Pharaoh became harder under God’s scourges, whereas Nebuchadnezzar was led to repentance, he says that Nebuchadnezzar, because he felt God’s hand and groaned in remembrance of his own iniquity, obtained a different end—as though he wished to assign the beginning of good will to the penitent, and only its completion to God.

In chapter sixteen he holds that some people, even if they were not subject to sin, could have been condemned by God. This is contrary to Augustine’s judgment in book three, chapter eighteen, *Against Julian*: “God is good; God is just. He can liberate some without good merits, because he is good; he cannot condemn anyone without evil merits, because he is just.”

And in Letter 186 to Paulinus, no. 20: “If God is believed to condemn someone who is without merit and subject to no sin, he is not believed to be free from iniquity.”

This same little work was also falsely attributed to Bishop Fulgentius of Ruspe, although unjustly, since Fulgentius was always devoted to Augustine and his teachings as a disciple. Moreover, Fulgentius treats this same subject most eloquently and in accordance with Augustine’s mind, both in the first book to Monimus, *On Double Predestination*, and in the three books addressed to John and Venerius, entitled *On the Truth of God’s Predestination and Grace*.

Finally, Fulgentius customarily dedicates his books to someone, following the example and practice of Augustine; but this book is dedicated to no one’s name. It should therefore rightly be judged not merely unassignable to those Catholic Doctors, but attributable to some writer of suspect faith.

[Col. 1665]

# ON PREDESTINATION AND GRACE: A BOOK BY A SUSPECT AUTHOR (C, G, S)

## CHAPTER I

1. When, in the volumes of the sacred Scriptures—whether they foretell future things through the prophetic spirit, narrate past events with historical truth, or transmit instructions for life with apostolic authority—the reader is moved or the hearer troubled by some statement that seems to sound different, he must hold with certain and unshaken faith that the mysteries of one and the same Spirit—apart from whom there is no truth—sound more openly in one place and somewhat more obscurely in another.

Accordingly, if something has been left suspended in hidden meaning, or briefly indicated by the writer, or explained less fully than the dullness of the human heart required, he must recognize that the matter appears more clearly here and lies more deeply hidden there, but that the truth is nowhere absent.

And if, because of the greatness of the matter under inquiry, understanding does not readily present itself to the mind of the questioner—especially if, concerning the unchangeable will of almighty God, the two statements of canonical authority seem to sound differently—everything must be directed according to the rule of piety, so that one may hold with unshaken conviction neither that God is unjust, nor that he assesses the merits of individuals through some confused respect of persons [Note: [Col. 1665] The codices of Victorinus omit “confused.”] [Col. 1666], nor that he is weak because he was unable to bring about what he willed.

## CHAPTER II

2. Under the yoke of this definition, lest necks wrongly made free luxuriate in sacrilegious recklessness, let us recall, as far as we can with God’s gift, the hidden matter of this question. The blessed Apostle Paul proposes it to diligent investigators in various places, and in language differing considerably; and Truth itself speaks to them through him.

Having completed a very broad and forceful discussion of God’s grace, he concludes it in this way: “Therefore he has mercy on whomever he wills, and he hardens whomever he wills” (Rom. 9:18). Yet in another Epistle he himself speaks in this way about divine benevolence: “Who wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (1 Tim. 2:4).

The question arises why some of these people perish, since almighty God wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth; and then why he hardens some while showing mercy to others; or how he can will all people to be saved when he himself hardens certain people so that they may not be saved.

As far as human justice is concerned, this appears unjust. But who would be so foolish—or rather, who would blaspheme so greatly—as to say that God’s justice should be debated according to the law of human justice? If human justice is opposed to God’s justice, it is plainly unjust. For it is evident that from him who is supremely just flows everything that is just in any manner whatsoever.

Who, then, will subject the wisdom of God, which remains unchangeable and creates, governs, and preserves all things, to the judgment of human wisdom? Concerning this wisdom the same Apostle says: “The wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God” (Rom. 8:7); and elsewhere: “The wisdom of this world is foolishness with God” (1 Cor. 3:19).

The majesty of divine wisdom, therefore, must not be disputed according to the judgment of human vanity.

## CHAPTER III
3. But if someone, by nourishing his sins, is deceived by some figure, shadow, or flattering image of pride, so that he says what the blessed Apostle immediately saw that some would say—for he added: “Someone will say: If he has mercy on whom he wills, and hardens whom he wills, why does he still find fault? For who can resist his will?” (Rom. 9:18–19)—let him understand that by this sentence we are compelled and constrained all the more toward humility and devotion. For when the most excellent teacher refers everything to God and denies it to human powers, what else does he urge us to do than to depend upon God with our whole heart and ask from him the help of salvation?

Whoever, then, is troubled by this diversity in the dispensation of divine grace and thinks it unjust that one should be denied what another has received, should understand how the Psalmist spoke divinely: “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. 24:10). Let him acknowledge that God governs human affairs by such a judgment that he either justly returns the penalties that are due or mercifully remits them.

For the stain of the corrupted root has been spread through the branches of descent by the succession of generations in such a way that not even an infant of a single day is free from the guilt of the first transgression (Job 14:4, according to the Septuagint), unless he has been liberated by the undeserved grace of the Savior. And if even this child is not without sin, although he could not yet have a sin of his own, it follows that he has drawn from another the sin of which the Apostle says: “Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death; and so death passed into all, in whom all sinned” (Rom. 5:12).

Whoever denies this certainly denies first of all that we are mortal. For if, as the Apostle says, “through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death,” death could not have entered unless sin entered. And since death is not a condition of nature but the punishment of sin, it necessarily follows that punishment follows sin. But because death passed into all human beings, sin must necessarily have passed into all.

How original sin is born with infants we cannot see with the eyes of the flesh. But because we see that all who are carnally born from Adam—even those who have already also been reborn in Christ—are held under the law of death, through what we see we are compelled to confess what we do not see.

For it would more easily be possible that, although sin had passed on, punishment might not follow, than that one who has no guilt should share in the punishment without any participation in sin.

[Note: [Col. 1667] The manuscripts read *manente* (“remaining”) instead of *transeunte* (“having passed on”).]

[Note: The Fulgentian edition adds here *qui* (“who”). A little later it reads: “Because we see infants always dying, we are compelled to confess that infants are always born with original sin.”]

Therefore, if—as has been shown—we are all born debtors from the seed of the transgressor, since, as the Apostle says, “all sinned in him,” and the very mass from which we descend was already condemned from the beginning, let no one dare complain either of his hardness or of the punishment that is justly owed even in the absence of personal sins, solely by the condition of birth.

But when God bestows undeserved mercy on some who are converted by a gratuitous calling, this must be attributed not to injustice in the steward of his dispensation, but to the most merciful generosity of the giver, in accordance with the truth.

[Note: In the manuscripts, *libertatem* (“freedom”) is found instead of *largitatem* (“generosity”).]

Would a debtor dare accuse a creditor of injustice if, while forgiving another, he demanded from him what was owed? If, then, even in human contracts there is no room for a debtor to claim that what is owed is unjustly demanded from him because he knows that the same creditor has forgiven another debtor what he owed, who could burst forth in such madness of profane speech as to accuse God of injustice if he grants undeserved grace to one and returns due punishment to another?

## CHAPTER IV

4. Accordingly, in the first part of the foregoing sentence, which says, “He has mercy on whom he wills,” I think that no one except one unworthy of mercy would dare dispute. But where it continues, “He hardens whom he wills,” the human mind is somewhat confused by the novelty of the expression.

It must not, however, be understood as though God produced in a person the hardness of heart that had not existed. For what else is hardness than resistance to God’s commands? Hence the blessed Stephen said to the people: “Stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit” (Acts 7:51).

Whoever thinks that this hardness is produced by God because it is said, “He hardens whom he wills,” should consider the very beginning of the transgression and observe who, when God gave the commandment, produced the guilt of transgression in his heart—although even the tempter could not compel him if he refused his consent.

[Note: [Col. 1668] The manuscripts read *in vecorde* (“in a senseless heart”) instead of *in corde* (“in the heart”).]

Therefore, whatever punishment a human being suffers after that transgression, let him acknowledge that it is justly and deservedly imposed. For God is said to harden the one whom he does not wish to soften; likewise, he is said to blind the one whom he does not wish to illuminate; likewise, to repel the one whom he does not wish to call.

“For those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified” (Rom. 8:30). He himself gave us existence; he himself gives us the ability to be good.

## CHAPTER V

5. His divinity foreknew us, his wisdom created us, his justice condemned us, and his grace liberated us.

Although the world began at the time when it was made, it could have no beginning in that light of divine foreknowledge in which it was to be made. And however many human beings have been born from Adam to the present day, or will be born through the succession of generations after our own age, in God they have already been born and have already passed through the entire course of their lives, while nevertheless remaining in that light of the divine gaze.

For God, who is confined neither by place nor anticipated by time, is full both of the memory of all past things and of the knowledge of things that are imminent. He does not, by remembering, turn toward the past, nor, by hoping, extend himself toward the future. Whatever things exist at all, things that are moved by the changes of time, are seen by him from the beginning in which “the Word was, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word” (John 1:1) to the end of all the ages. Concerning this end, when the blessed Moses spoke, he said: “Lord, who reigns for ever and ever, and beyond” (Exod. 15:18).

These things are neither hoped for as future nor have they passed away as past; rather, they are seen in the presence of the Godhead, in its ever-present light.

Since he is eternal and foreknowing, just and gracious, exercising due severity and displaying undeserved mercy, and since he has power over human beings in creating and choosing them, as a potter has power over clay, from him some vessels were made for honor and others for dishonor.

Before he made us, he foreknew us; and in that very foreknowledge he chose us, although he had not yet made us. But by whom could this have been done except by him who “calls those things that are not as though they were” (Rom. 4:17)?

For the Apostle says: “He chose us before the foundation of the world” (Eph. 1:4). We were made within the world, and we were chosen before the world. Thus, in one and the same time—which neither passes away nor is future, but is continuous, or however else it may be expressed, if it can be expressed—in God there are foreknowing, making, and choosing. And while his foreknowledge remains unchangeable, he chooses those whom he was going to make, so that they might be made as those whom he had chosen.

These statements, insofar as they concern the rule of faith, have been spoken beforehand with God’s illumination.

[Note: The Corbie manuscript reads: “have been spoken piously.”]

## CHAPTER VI

6. But now I see what malicious perversity can object even here. It follows that, if those whom he predestined he also called, and those whom he called he also justified, then those who were neither predestined nor called, and consequently were not justified, ought to be innocent of every fault; and on the day of judgment they would unjustly be required to suffer penalties for the evil life they have led.

Let the Apostle Paul say to such people: “Is there injustice with God?” Let him immediately answer himself: “Certainly not.”

Once this has been firmly established in a human mind sound in devotion—that there is no injustice with God—let it understand “He has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills” as though it were said: “He has mercy on whom he wills, and he does not have mercy on whom he does not will.”

Let it likewise understand the same statement again as though it were said: “He gives to whom he wills, and from whom he wills he demands what is owed.”

Whoever persists in calling this unjust should hear from the Apostle: “O man, who are you to answer back to God?” The apostolic authority rightly rebukes this kind of impiety, striking such weight through the contrast of the names when it says: “O man, who are you to answer back to God?” Man to God; clay to the potter.

For the same Apostle added: “Does the thing formed say to the one who formed it, ‘Why did you make me like this?’ Or does the potter not have power over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?”

If, then, the potter has this power—or rather, because the potter has the power to make from the same lump of clay one vessel for honor and another for dishonor—“O man, who are you to answer back to God,” because he has mercy on whom he wills and hardens whom he wills?

7. But before the blessed Apostle reached this kind of conclusion in the orderly course of his argument, he took this especially from the ancient Scriptures as an example by which he might teach the hardening that is said to be done by God.

“Scripture says,” he declares, “to Pharaoh: ‘For this very purpose I raised you up, that I might show my power in you and that my name might be proclaimed throughout all the earth’” (Rom. 9:14–21).

In the same Scripture God is also said most openly to have hardened Pharaoh’s heart when he spoke to Moses about the signs that were to be performed through him against the Egyptians. For he says: “But I will harden Pharaoh’s heart, so that he will not let the people go” (Exod. 4:21).

At this point the clever slanderer, boasting of his apparent case, weighs the justice of God according to his own judgment and responds with as much shouting as he can: “If he has mercy on whom he wills and hardens whom he wills, why does he still find fault? For who can resist his will?” (Rom. 9:19).

To this arrogance the Apostle should say: “O man, who are you to answer back to God?”

But whoever, piously seeking, desires to discover something should read again that passage of the same Scripture where fire first appeared to Moses in the bush and kindled his heart with the heat of divine love, so that he spoke of God’s testimonies without shame in the presence of kings, as David says (Ps. 118:46). There he will find that everything prefaced by the statement that God hardened Pharaoh’s heart refers not to God’s action but to his foreknowledge.

For, speaking from the bush, the Lord says:

“But I know that Pharaoh, king of Egypt, will not let you go except by a mighty hand. But I will stretch out my hand and strike the Egyptians with all the wonders that I shall perform, and afterward he will let you go” (Exod. 3:19–20).

This is the first word of God by which he declared Pharaoh’s future will, just as he had foreseen it. Later, amid the showers of miracles, he is read to have said: “But I will harden Pharaoh’s heart, so that he will not let the people go.”

Here it is already clearly understood that he repeated the first statement. For what does “I will harden” mean except “I will not soften”?

[Note: [Col. 1669] The manuscripts read *manente* (“remaining”) instead of *manante* (“flowing”).]

It is evident that the statement of Scripture was fulfilled: justice flowing upon some and grace pouring upon others, when God said to Pharaoh, “For this very purpose I raised you up, that I might show my power in you and that my name might be proclaimed throughout all the earth.”

For when God used even evil people for good—through Pharaoh’s hardening, the plagues of Egypt, and the many great miracles performed together and in abundance among that people—what else was accomplished than that the power of God, great in itself and complete in itself, might become known to the human race, benefiting not God but those who would later read and believe?

God foreknew in that profound light of his providence that Pharaoh would not change, and that whole nation which, after so many blows, had scarcely seen the people of God escape and nevertheless attempted to pursue them with arms and war.

But he willed the destruction of those who were to perish to serve as an argument for the salvation of the vessels of mercy predestined by him; and he used the perdition of some for the salvation of others, because the potter has power over the clay to make from the same lump one vessel for honor and another for dishonor.

## CHAPTER VII

8. The blessed Apostle had recalled this judgment of divine power in the choice of human beings shortly before, and he demonstrated it by the strongest examples when he spoke of Rebecca’s offspring, still enclosed within the womb, referring everything to God’s grace.

For he says:

“And not only so, but Rebecca also conceived by one act of intercourse with Isaac our father. For before they had been born or had done anything good or bad, so that God’s purpose according to election might remain—not from works but from the one who calls—it was said: ‘The elder shall serve the younger.’ As it is written: ‘Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.’”

And he immediately added: “What shall we say, then? Is there injustice with God?” And he answered by denying it: “Certainly not” (Rom. 9:10–14).

Thus the other things that follow are to be referred to and understood in relation to this statement, by which he denied that there is injustice with God.

Here the purpose of the apostolic argument is sufficiently clear. He compared not merely brothers but twins; not merely twins, but children conceived in one act of intercourse and brought forth into the world at the same moment. Since there could be no weight of merits in those not yet born and not yet having done anything, nothing—even from the merits of their parents, which could have differed at different times—would be left as an obstacle against grace.

Even if we allow that God either turned away or brought near the divine protection toward the children because of their parents’ merits, whether good or bad, those merits ought to have been equal with respect to the twin offspring, who were conceived in the same intercourse and brought to birth at the same moment.

But if it is said that God’s judgment distinguished their future conduct, then what the Apostle had prefaced will surely be nullified: “Not from works but from the one who calls it was said, ‘The elder shall serve the younger.’”

For he did not say, “Not from past works,” but, having said generally, “Not from works,” he wished both past and future works to be understood: past works, namely, which did not exist at all, and future works, which did not yet exist.

Jacob, therefore, was predestined as a vessel for honor, but not from works; for “not from works but from the one who calls” it was said, “The elder shall serve the younger.”

## CHAPTER VIII

9. And lest those vessels predestined for honor should, by attributing something to their own powers, deny glory to the Creator,

[Note: The manuscripts read as above. The printed editions have: “deny the grace of the Creator.”]

the Apostle elsewhere called them “vessels of mercy,” so that they might recognize that everything they were they were according to mercy.

Thus the same Apostle also says elsewhere: “And this is not from you; it is the gift of God” (Eph. 2:8).

The blessed Moses likewise says to the people in Deuteronomy:

“And do not say in your heart, ‘My strength and the power of my hand made this great power for me.’ But you shall remember the Lord your God, because he himself gives you strength to accomplish power, so that he may establish his covenant that he swore to your fathers” (Deut. 8:17–18).

A little later in the same place he says to them:

“Do not say in your heart, when the Lord your God has destroyed these nations before your face, ‘Because of my righteousness the Lord brought me in to possess this good land.’ It is not because of your righteousness, nor because of the holiness of your heart, that you enter to possess their land; but because of the wickedness of these nations the Lord will destroy them from before your face.”

Behold how the impiety of a novel presumption attempts to overturn an ancient doctrine of the Holy Spirit, preached not only in the apostolic writings but also established by the voice of the Holy Spirit in the prophetic writings and at the very beginnings of the Israelite people.

[Note: The Fulgentian edition reads *impetus* (“impetus”) instead of *praesumptionis impietas* (“the impiety of presumption”).]

[Note: The same Fulgentian edition reads *miserantis* (“of one showing mercy”) instead of *miserante* (“showing mercy”).]

For in one and the same passage of Scripture the blessed Prophet clearly displays the goodness and severity of God, saying that the people were not given possession of that land on account of their righteousness, but only granted it by merciful grace, while the others were driven out on account of their unrighteousness.

Here, in the former, iniquity is justly punished; in the latter, no righteousness is rewarded, but a gift is freely bestowed.

Nor was it enough for the blessed Moses to have said that the inheritance of that land had been granted to the Israelite people not on account of their merits, unless he also added what he did add, by which he showed them to be unworthy of every good thing.

For after the passage mentioned above it continues:

“And today you shall know that it is not on account of your righteousness that the Lord your God gives you this good land to possess, for you are a stiff-necked people” (Deut. 9:4–6).

Who here would say that a reward was returned according to the due of preceding merits? Who would not confess that grace was undeserved?

How often does the Prophet say, “They tested him in the wilderness” (Ps. 94:9)? How often did they deserve God’s anger by turning their hearts away, and yet he saved them on account of his mercy, “to make his power known” (Ps. 106:8)?

The Apostle says this again:

“He endured with much patience vessels of wrath prepared for destruction, in order to make known the riches of his glory upon vessels of mercy, which he prepared for glory” (Rom. 9:22–23).

## CHAPTER IX

10. But lest humanity, again dissolving into the dregs of utter laziness, should believe that the arduous path of virtue—which, even with God’s help, can be walked only through labor—could be carried for it by another, and should apply no diligent effort to its own progress, God distributed times and duties between himself and human beings in such a way that we should take the beginnings of good actions from his calling.

Once called and illuminated, we should recognize the ways of his commandments through the understanding of our innate reason,

[Note: The Fulgentian edition reads: “we should recognize the ways of his commandments through the understanding of a good disposition.”]

and should freely choose either to follow them or to abandon them.

Yet if, supported by his help, we followed them with continual devotion, then at the end he would once again crown in us an obedience that did not resist his commandments but was subject to them.

The free will that we have from him, however, flows with an eager slide toward wickedness; and, since it can do nothing toward the disposition of virtue when deprived of God’s help, it remains capable of every kind of sin, supported by its own strength.

For the law of sin, born in our members, drags us along. And when we withdraw from the gentle yoke and light burden of his commandments, flowing by the free choice of our will into the harshest slavery of sin, God abandons us according to his justice.

But those who receive the gift of calling with suitable devotion, who are not subjected to carnal allurements, who have been free from the vice of boastfulness, the fires of avarice, and the wind of pride, and who, insofar as humanly possible, preserve God’s gifts within themselves and devote every effort to spiritual exercises—these he both helps as they struggle in the contest of this life and bestows eternal crowns upon those who conquer.

Again, he abandons those who transgress, hardens those who resist, and condemns those who despise him.

## CHAPTER X

11. Concerning this distribution of stages, by which God either works in us or commands us to work something, let us ask him from whose words the question arose. With the Lord’s help, we shall attempt to unravel it, so that, when his meanings have been arranged throughout different books in varied expression but with one and the same intention, whatever lies hidden in this passage may be disclosed by comparison with another statement.

We read that the Apostle Paul was called by God either in the book where his deeds are narrated with canonical truth, or where he himself confesses it in his Epistle, saying: “Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, called to be an apostle” (Rom. 1:1).

[Note: The manuscripts read: “where his deeds are narrated with canonical truth.” The Fulgentian edition reads: “where his deeds are narrated with complete truth.” The Corbie manuscript reads: “where his deeds are narrated with canonical authority.”]

In the second place, having followed his calling and accomplished everything that had been worked in him as a human being, he himself says: “I labored more than all of them.”

But lest he attribute even this to himself, he added with watchful devotion: “Yet not I, but the grace of God with me” (1 Cor. 15:10).

Once he had been called and had followed his calling through works of righteousness, what else remained except that, liberated from this body of death, he should attain the blessedness of that other life which has been promised to all the saints by the mouth of Truth?

Teaching that this is not repaid by any human merits but bestowed by the grace of God as a gift, he answers himself after the groans in which he had said: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the body of this death?” He says: “The grace of God, through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. 7:24).

Accordingly, this distribution—which we have said consists in human beings being called by God when no merits yet exist, and in those who have been called being helped by God’s assistance so that they may do something good—the Apostle demonstrates by an example taken from the ancient writings.

After he had referred the election of the two twins entirely to God’s grace and judgment, excluding every praise of merits, he saw what impious chatter could blasphemously utter and said: “Is there injustice with God?” And it follows: “Certainly not” (Rom. 9:14).

And as though someone had said to him, “How do you prove this?” he thought the authority of his own teaching insufficient unless he also taught his judgment by an example from the Law.

Thus he wished Moses’ statement to be understood: “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will show compassion to whom I show compassion” (Exod. 33:19), so that we should believe that the first mercy from God is granted to human beings through calling. This mercy alone, however, is not sufficient for right living if the one who called does not continue to assist.

For this reason it was added: “And I will show compassion to whom I show compassion,” so that it might be clear that even the works of mercy are received from God—works by which, when we seem to show mercy, we merit God’s mercy.

Thus he says in the Gospel: “Blessed are the merciful, for God will have mercy on them” (Matt. 5:7).

If the Apostle had not understood it in this way, he would never, for the sake of proof, have taken care to insert this testimony into his argument.

[Note: The Fulgentian edition reads: “he would never, for the sake of grace concerning good works,” instead of “for the sake of proof.”]

## CHAPTER XI

12. But if anyone is troubled by the fact that not all even of those who have already been called are judged worthy to reach the second grace—that is, the gift of living rightly—as the Lord says in the Gospel, “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 20:16), let him understand from this what sort of thing it is that the person who boasts in his free will attempts to defend against God’s grace.

For whoever, abandoning the gift of the divine calling, again slipped into impious unbelief, found his will sufficient to accomplish what he desired, once God’s grace had abandoned him.

[Note: The same edition reads: “with God’s grace abandoning them.”]

See how the Psalmist, interpreting according to the meaning of Moses the order of God’s mercies that the Apostle interpreted, sings it in the truth of the prophetic Spirit.

“Listen,” he says, “O my people, and I will testify to you.”

What did he want them to hear, to whom he spoke with testimony? What indeed but the commandments of life? As another prophet says: “Hear, O Israel, the commandments of life” (Baruch 3:9).

But the Psalmist adds what these commandments of life are, and continues:

“For I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.”

That these are the commandments of life he shows in the prayer by which the Lord commended his disciples to the Father, saying:

“This is eternal life: that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17:3).

After this calling there follows what he also wishes to pertain to human efforts, while showing that it cannot be completed without him. This is what the Apostle says: “For from him we have both the will and the accomplishment, according to his good pleasure” (Phil. 2:13).

We have the will from him because he calls and illuminates; we have accomplishment from him because striving toward the good belongs to us, and he has granted us even the will to do so.

Nor was it without care that the Apostle, after saying, “From him we have both the will and the accomplishment,” added, “according to his good pleasure,” so that they might see again and again where the free will of which they boast has its place in relation to God’s justice.

Let us also observe in the continuous prayer of this Psalm the order by which the Lord distributes his mercies through different dispensations of time, just as the Apostle understood Moses to have said.

For what does the Psalm say after he had taught the called, saying, “I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt”?

“Open your mouth,” he says, “and I will fill it.”
