Here something once again appears to have been reserved for human beings to do through free will. They are commanded to open their mouth, but God promises that he will fill it.

Thus he had also said to his disciples in the Gospel: “Do not consider how or what you are to speak; for it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. 10:19).

He required of them only that they willingly accept every necessity of suffering for the truth; but he promised that the result would belong to him.

[Note: This is the reading of Fulgentius and the manuscripts. In the Lovaniensis edition it reads: “the result of what was promised.” A little later the manuscripts have *ubi sine* (“where without”); the printed editions read *ut sine* (“so that without”).]

What place, then, is reserved for free will where human nature itself, supported by rational dignity, could suffice to accomplish what it willed without God’s help? The Psalm immediately shows it, saying:

“But my people did not hear my voice, and Israel did not attend to me.”

[Note: The Fulgentian edition reads: “so that human nature, if it should be sufficient for itself.”]

What had he said when he called them? “Listen, my people, and I will speak; Israel, and I will testify to you.”

What had he commended to the minds of those listening in his testimony? “I am the Lord your God.”

What had he commanded those whom he had liberated from the land of Egypt and from the darkness of ignorance, leading them into the light of his commandments in the splendor of his calling?

“Open your mouth,” he said.

And immediately, as though he were saying, “But opening it will do you no good if I abandon you,” he added, “and I will fill it.”

What, then, does the one who had called and instructed the called add in a complaining voice concerning those same people?

“My people,” he says, “did not hear my voice, and Israel did not attend to me.”

13. Let the defender of free will now come forth against God’s grace.

[Note: The same edition reads “the defender of free will against God.”] Let him hear the Apostle saying, when he was speaking of his good labors: “Yet not I, but the grace of God with me.”

Let him hear the voice of God in the Psalm, speaking of those whom he had abandoned: “And I let them go according to the desires of their heart; they shall walk in their own inclinations” (Ps. 80:9–13).

Let him hear the one and the same Apostle, who at the different times of his life attributed only his evil to himself, but all his good to grace:

“I was formerly a blasphemer,” he says, “and a persecutor” (1 Tim. 1:13).

And elsewhere: “By the grace of God I am what I am.”

When he said, “I was formerly a blasphemer and a persecutor,” no mention of grace was joined to the evil deed, because human freedom of nature is sufficient for wickedness, as has been said.

But when he spoke of the blessedness of the present life, he said: “By the grace of God I am what I am.”

The blessed Apostle Paul also preserved, in an uninterrupted account, the order by which God has mercy, first by calling and afterward by assisting the efforts that have begun, just as it has been narrated and arranged in the sequence of the Psalm.

For if the testimonies I have mentioned in scattered form are read in their order, they follow in this way:

“By the grace of God,” he says, “I am what I am.”

This is the first mercy, which the works of free will follow.

But so that good works might follow the calling of the Apostle Paul, what does he say?

“And his grace toward me was not empty.”

What did you do?

“I labored,” he says, “more than all of them.”

Do not become too proud, defender of free will, when you hear Paul boasting of his labors. Attend to what follows:

“Yet not I, but the grace of God with me” (1 Cor. 15:10).

I think that none of those who blaspheme against God’s grace with a heart exalted before its fall, as it is written (Prov. 16:18), would assume such shameless arrogance as to consider himself equal or even superior to the merits of the blessed prophet David.

Leaving aside for the moment that first reward—the kingdom bestowed upon him, which everyone must acknowledge was undeserved—let us consider the earnestness and sentiments of his prayers and confessions.

He himself declares in the Psalm: “Blessed is the person whom you discipline, Lord, and whom you teach from your law” (Ps. 93:12).

But let us see whether this alone was sufficient for blessedness even for one who had already been instructed and adequately trained in all knowledge of the Law according to Jewish teaching.

Why, then, does the same man again cry out to the Lord: “Give me understanding, and I will search your law, and I will keep it with my whole heart”?

It was not enough that he had asked for understanding in order to search the Law, unless he also indicated that help was necessary for keeping it when he said: “And I will keep it with my whole heart” (Ps. 118:34)—as though he were saying, “I will keep it with my whole heart if you give me understanding.”

## CHAPTER XII

14. Let that proud defender of his own will respond to these things: the Prophet, he may say, asked for divine help only to understand the divine commandments, which he was nevertheless going to fulfill by his own power.

If this is so, blessed David, I wish to investigate for a little while the hidden places of your thoughts. From where, I ask, do you have the struggle between flesh and spirit? From where the apostolic contest, as you yourself confess?

Though you had already been illuminated and instructed by the gift of understanding that you had asked for from God, you cry out and say: “Turn my eyes away, lest they see vanity” (Ps. 118:37).

For since you had received, as you requested, the understanding by which vanity is distinguished from truth, why do you not turn your eyes away from the vanity that displeases you?

If you condemn avarice, why do you not, separated from it by your own free will, incline your heart toward the commandments of salvation? Why, rather, do you cry out to God as one weak in every respect: “Incline my heart to your testimonies, and not to avarice”?

Unless it is because the law of sin, born in the members, suggests avarice, and the holy man wishes to turn his eyes away from it but cannot do so by himself. Thus “the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. 5:17), and no one delivers us from this conflict except grace, which is bestowed through our Lord Jesus Christ upon the small and the great.

“For to will is present with me, but to accomplish the good is not” (Rom. 7:18). Yet even the will itself is not from us but is the gift of God: “For from him we have both the will and the accomplishment, according to his good pleasure” (Phil. 2:13).

You are therefore blessed, because you agree with Christ’s Apostles in both teaching and struggle: for in your writings we recognize the battles of the Apostles, and in the apostolic writings we find your contests.

## CHAPTER XIII

15. From where does this diversity of things and wills arise in one and the same human being, who consists of soul and body, except that, by the just judgment of the Godhead, a human being who despises God—the creature the Creator, the lowly the Most High—finds within himself, through the obstinacy of the inferior part, the punishments of disobedience?

[Note: The Fulgentian edition reads: “because, despising the just judgments of God, a human being despises God,” and so forth.]

For by what justice would a creature, though inferior to a better creature, serve another creature if that creature itself had refused to serve the Creator, whatever kind of creature it might be?

But even this is not sufficient as punishment: it is not enough that the inferior part should resist the better affections of the heart, unless it also frequently overcomes them, leads them captive, and possesses them.

The law of sin would not only claim those born in Adam as human beings for the service of its movement; it would also assault those reborn in Christ, while its suggestion remains. For through the gift of regeneration guilt has truly been dismissed, but the condition of grace has not been abolished: the ancient documents of debts have been erased, but the human being who still lives in the flesh has not yet been separated from carnal suffering. Thus every human being must continually implore divine help in the time to come.

And because the Law could not so much take away sin as reveal it—sin which everywhere claimed for itself human beings as they were born into it and, having taken possession of them through consent to concupiscence, plunged them into everlasting destruction—our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, the Word of the Father, equal and coeternal with the Father, “emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. 2:6).

Although he himself was not sin, he became sin by assuming flesh, so that, after the human being had been healed from the sin of the flesh, he might condemn sin in the flesh (Rom. 8:3). He came to seek what was lost (Luke 19:10), to heal what was sick, and to raise up what was lying fallen.

[Note: The passage is corrupt; it should certainly read: “to heal those who were sick … to raise those who were lying fallen.”]

He had authority to forgive sins: to grant what he did not owe, to remit what was owed to him; and, having erased all the stains of the ancient guilt, to restore the nature that he had made.

Of those to whom just severity had decreed punishment, according to the ineffable mercy of his hidden arrangement, he chose vessels to make for honor; he absolved some from the coming wrath by the gift of a gratuitous calling; and, abandoning others, reserved them for the judgment of equality.

Yet he took away from no one the capacity to recognize the truth. Thus the fullness of divine foreknowledge was completed, with justice flowing upon some and grace pouring upon others, so that, through those whom God had foreknown to be destined to perish perishing, and those whom in that secret election he had foreknown to be destined for salvation being saved, the Church might be multiplied throughout the whole world.

[Note: The manuscripts read *manente* (“remaining”) instead of *manante* (“flowing”).]

## CHAPTER XIV
16. Rejoice, therefore, whoever you are who have been enlightened, and acknowledge the grace that you did not deserve; groan, whoever you are who have been hardened, and confess the justice. Say, whoever you rejoice that you have been cleansed from original contagion by the washing of grace: “The Lord is merciful and gracious, patient and of great mercy” (Ps. 144:8). “He has not dealt with us according to our sins, nor repaid us according to our iniquities” (Ps. 102:10). Say, whoever you are who are condemned: “You are just, O Lord, in all that you have done to us, and all your judgments are true, because in truth and judgment you have brought all these things upon us, because of our sins” (Dan. 3:27–28); and do not ascribe the blame for your hardening to God’s injustice. For “all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. 24:10), so that those who have obtained mercy from God may not boast in anything concerning their merits before the judgment of truth, nor may those who have been hardened and condemned suppose that they can derive an excuse for their guilt from the fact that they obtained no mercy by which they might be converted.

Pharaoh, therefore, did not receive this mercy, and consequently his free will was sufficient for his destruction. No one so ignorant of the divine Scriptures would dare say that he suffered all those things unjustly. Or perhaps, if we think piously of God as we ought, we shall also find that mercy was given to Pharaoh? For God’s patience ought to have benefited him unto salvation: by delaying the just and deserved punishment, it repeatedly multiplied the blows of the miracles. Could he not, just as he expelled the people when he yielded to the scourges, likewise, believing in the miracles, have recognized God as possessing such great power?

If it is said that Pharaoh could no longer be changed because God had foreseen that he would not be changed, the answer is that God’s foreknowledge does not compel a person to be such as God foreknew him to be; rather, it foreknows that he will be such as he will be, although God does not make him act in that way. If God compelled him to be so, he would of course compel him to be what he is not. But if God had foreseen that what is not would come to be, that would not be foreknowledge. Anyone who soothes himself in his sins with the thought that God foreknew he would become a sinner understands how impiously this is said of God.

## CHAPTER XV

17. Nevertheless, I think that someone may perhaps say that the way to salvation is less adequate if someone is merely scourged, without being inwardly urged by any calling. How, then, did Nebuchadnezzar obtain fruitful repentance (Dan. 4:33–34)? Was he not scourged after countless acts of impiety, repented, and received again the kingdom he had lost? Pharaoh, however, was made harder by those very scourges and perished (Exod. 14:27).

Let the person who judges the divine counsel with a mind overly confident in its wisdom explain to me why the medicine prepared by one physician proved fatal to one person but beneficial to another for salvation—unless it is because “the good odor of Christ” is “to some an odor of life unto life, to others an odor of death unto death” (2 Cor. 2:15–16).

As regards nature, both were human beings; as regards dignity, both were kings; as regards their situation, both possessed the captive people of God; as regards punishment, both were mercifully warned by scourges. What, then, caused their ends to be different, except that one, sensing the hand of God, groaned in remembrance of his own iniquity, while the other, by his free will, fought against God’s supremely merciful truth?

Whoever answers that divine assistance was present to the one so that he might be changed, but absent from the other so that he might be hardened, and contends that this was unjust—because he assigns the ends of these events to God’s will—should understand the Apostle’s words: “He has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens” (Rom. 9:18); and the Lord’s words: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). Let him understand that all these things are accomplished with the Lord’s assistance or permitted when he withdraws, yet let him know that absolutely nothing occurs against the Lord’s will.

## CHAPTER XVI

18. But we return to the little ones; we return to the twins. It is not enough to say what I have said: we return to those not yet born, who had been conceived in the same intercourse and were destined to be brought into the light at the same moment. The magnitude of the question confounds the human mind, which arrogantly argues about God’s will, when the divine will appears to have made a differing and diverse judgment concerning them.

Now raise your voice with all your strength, unjust accuser of the Just One, and tell me: What evil did the one commit, and what good did the other deserve? And the Apostle Paul—not I—answers you: “Neither had both deserved anything; but the potter has power over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor.” You will say, “Why?” What is the reason for this judgment’s such confused diversity? Let him again rebuke this presumption and say: “O man, who are you to answer back to God?” (Rom. 9:20–21).

Especially since, when the argument is once again directed to a comparison of human actions, the response is that a creditor cannot be accused of injustice if, concerning two debtors, he chooses to make such a judgment that he forgives one and demands from the other what is owed by both.

Certainly, in all the acts and transactions of human society, whenever we distinguish and judge anything, it is evident that the justice by which we seem to approve something [Note: The Victorine manuscripts read, “some seem [to perceive] something”; the printed editions, “by which we seem [to perceive] some [thing].” The text is corrected from the manuscripts.] flows into the humble hearts of human beings from the ineffable fullness of divine justice. Blessed John confirms this in his Gospel: “For from his fullness we have all received” (John 1:16).

If this is so, with what shamelessness will a human being judge God, clay the potter—not only saying, “Why have you made me thus?” but also, with blameworthy curiosity, investigating others and saying, “Why have you made one from the same lump in this way, and another in that way?”

If the human race, which plainly was first created from nothing, had not been born with the debt and origin of death and sin, and yet the omnipotent Creator had wished to condemn some of them to eternal destruction, who would say to the omnipotent Creator, “Why have you made it thus?” For he who had given existence to those who did not exist had the power to determine the end for which they would exist. Nor would the others say, “Why did the divine will differ when the merits of all were equal?” because “the potter has power over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor.”

But now, when just punishment is repaid to the condemned while undeserved grace is given to the saved, who could be so forgetful of the human condition as to investigate the secrets of the divine mind—when he himself has deserved punishment—and ask [Note: Fulgentius reads, “ask.”] why another received grace that was not owed to him?

19. Moses demonstrated that this divine election is not repaid according to merits but bestowed upon human beings solely by the generosity of the One who wills, even though at that time he was teaching a carnal people. For he says plainly in Deuteronomy to the people:

“Behold, the heaven is the Lord your God’s, and the heaven of heaven, the earth, and all that is in it; yet the Lord chose your fathers in order to love them, and chose their descendants after them, you above all the nations. Therefore circumcise the hardness of your heart, and do not harden your neck any longer” (Deut. 10:14–16).

But blessed Stephen showed that this hardness of heart remained in them, as we have already said above, when he rebuked the Jews. For in the Acts of the Apostles he says:

“Stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit” (Acts 7:51).

Why, then, was there a stiff neck in that people, chosen from the whole world, who deserved to be freed from slavery through ten miracles, to whom the Law was given, for whose salvation the mouths of all the Prophets strove, from whom Christ was made according to the flesh and to whom he was sent—unless because “a hardening in part has happened to Israel, until the fullness of the nations should enter,” and adopted Israel should enter the kingdom; and the Lord “concluded all in unbelief, that he might have mercy on all”?

Touching upon the mysteries of this divine counsel and the mystery of its majesty—although he knew them through the greatness of his revelations, yet, overcome by human weakness, even the man who had formerly been a persecutor and blasphemer [Note: Fulgentius and the Victorine manuscripts read, “who, because of persecutions and blasphemies.”] and had deserved to be called a vessel of election—he exclaims in wonder:

“O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How inscrutable are his judgments and unsearchable his ways!” (Rom. 11:25, 33–35).

Let us therefore join him, whenever such matters are questioned, in wonder. While the conviction remains that there is no injustice with God, if the matter under inquiry has exceeded the measure of our understanding and does not accommodate itself to the narrowness of our intellect, let us confess that divine justice, mercy, and foreknowledge remain in the fullness of unshaken equity. Otherwise, by arguing about the secrets of the divine will in a manner beyond what the measure of our condition permits, we may abandon God’s justice while wishing to establish our own, and fall into the deepest abyss of obstinacy (Isa. 10:3).

# ON THE PREDESTINATION OF GOD, A BOOKLET BY AN UNKNOWN AUTHOR

## CHAPTER ONE

1. When we are about to speak of God’s predestination, we are entangled in certain anxieties, because when we examine the consciousness of our own foolishness, we are restrained from desiring so lofty a discussion. But when we turn our mind back to the omnipotence of the One who, through the mouth of an irrational ass, showed words of his will to its rational rider (Num. 22:28, 30), we gain strength to venture forth under the hope of heavenly assistance, knowing that whatever good we say or do, we receive not from ourselves but from God.

## CHAPTER TWO

2. First of all, it is impious to say that God predestines anything except what is good. But some predestinations are predestinations of binding, others of condition; the former belong to power, the latter to justice. To make what is being said clearer, let us demonstrate which belong to binding and power, and which to condition and justice.

God created heaven and earth, the sun and moon, day and night. He further predestined that heaven should always revolve; that earth should be held immovable as the center around which the revolving heaven turns; that the sun and moon should preside over day and night; and that day and night should succeed one another in their appointed seasons. These predestinations belong to power and binding. For each of the things we have mentioned is so bound to its operation by God’s predestination that it cannot be moved away from it.

God created the human being and predestined that, if obedient and abstaining from the taste of the forbidden fruit, he should remain in life; but if disobedient, he should undergo the sentence of death. This predestination belongs to condition and justice. For before the human being’s fall, God did not predestine him to die by the power of binding in such a way that he necessarily had to die, but under the condition that he should sin. Since the human being sinned, it was just that he should die; if he had not sinned, he would not have been bound to death by any bond of divine predestination.

## CHAPTER THREE

3. The predestination of death, therefore, was fixed in God under a condition because of his foreknowledge of the human fall; yet it did not exert force upon the human being through power so as to lead him to the sentence of death. Therefore this kind of predestination is not absolutely the cause of death; rather, sin is the cause of predestination and death.

For the death of the human being is not spoken of in the same way as the revolution of heaven. If someone asks why heaven revolves, we answer, “Because God predestined it.” This answer is absolute and requires no further explanation. But if someone asks why the human being dies, we cannot answer absolutely, “Because God predestined it.” For he would not have predestined it unless he had foreknown that the human being would sin.

Sin in the human being arouses in God the zeal of justice; the zeal of justice arouses predestination; and predestination brings about death. The beginning and end of this chain are in the human being. Why does the human being die? Because God predestined it. Why did God predestine it? Because he is just and acts justly. Why does he act justly? Because the human being sinned. Behold: sin comes from the human being, and death occurs in the human being.

4. Someone may say: How can sin be the cause of predestination, when predestination existed before the human being sinned? Let him hear that God treats all things, before they happen, as though they had already happened; and, in his foreknowledge, judges whether they are to be punished or rewarded.

Behold, the wretched human being is bound to death—not by God’s predestination, but by his own offense. Although predestination precedes the offense in time, the offense nevertheless precedes predestination in actual causation. For predestination would not occur unless the offense were going to occur; and the One who foresaw that offense predestined, as a just judge, the punishment of the offense.

From foreknowledge of the offense, therefore, predestination of punishment proceeded, just as from foreknowledge of virtue predestination of reward usually proceeds. Hence the Apostle says to the Romans: “Those whom he foreknew, he also predestined” (Rom. 8:29).

## CHAPTER FOUR

5. Perhaps someone doubts that punishment for an offense comes from God because it is grave and evil, while he openly acknowledges that the reward of virtue comes from God because it is sweet and good, even though God is the author of no evil but of all good.

Such a person must be told that punishment for an offense, although it is evil for the human being when it imposes suffering, is just with God when he punishes sins. What is just is good. The predestination of punishment, therefore, is good because it is just.

Thus the fountain and origin of good speaks through Isaiah:

“I am the Lord, forming light and creating darkness, making peace and creating evil” (Isa. 65:7).

It is as though he said: “I am the Lord, making peace from myself and creating evil from you for you. Because of your sins I give you the war you deserve. Although it is just with me, it becomes evil for you because you sinned not from me but from yourself. For your sin I create punishment for you, which is just with me but evil for you.”

God therefore creates a kind of evil that is just in itself with him but becomes evil for the human being from the human being. One and the same thing, received in different ways among human beings, is both good and evil: for example, the war mentioned above is evil for the defeated and good for the victorious.

Therefore death, which is punishment for transgression, is both just and evil: just because it comes from a just judge, but evil because it comes upon the wretched sinner. This same death is evil for some people and good for others, because it leads some from disgrace to glory, but others from glory to disgrace.

Fire is harmful to wood, straw, and clothing, but useful to copper, silver, and gold, because it smelts these and makes them purer, while it ignites and utterly consumes the others.

Since these things are so, let us not hesitate to say that death was predestined by God. Although it is evil for us, it was nevertheless predestined by God as just because of his foreknowledge of transgression. Hence the Psalmist says: “For you repay each one according to his works” (Ps. 61:13). From whom do the good receive everlasting glory and the wicked wretched death, if not from him who repays each according to his works?

Death does not come purely from God, however; rather, through God’s justice it arises from the human being’s transgression as punishment for the human being. This is said because some people place the devil as the author of death, as though he were its judge of punishment. He is indeed the author of death through the suggestion of sin, but through the power of retribution he is neither author nor creator. He is also the guardian and dispenser of punishments, yet not by his own power, but by divine permission.

## CHAPTER FIVE

6. But some object to what we have set forth by citing what is written: “God never made death” (Wis. 1:13). We must not pass this over with deaf ears, since elsewhere it is written: “Death and life are from God” (Sir. 11:14).

To the person who objects, “God did not make death,” I reply, “Death and life are from God.” In these apparent oppositions there is no reconciliation in the wording, but neither is there contradiction in the meaning.

Death, like life, can be understood not only in two ways but also in three. In the first human being, God created both soul and flesh immortal. Before sin, therefore, the soul lived and the flesh lived—not under the fear of destruction, but under the condition of immortality.

But when the human being sinned, the soul died. This is the death that God did not make. The flesh, however, lived after the death of the soul, but under the expectation of death. The death of the soul is therefore sin; the death of the flesh is the dissolution of the elements; and the death of soul and flesh is infernal punishment.

Life likewise has several forms: the life of flesh and soul before sin; the life of the flesh after sin; and the life of soul and flesh after the dissolution of the elements.

All life is from God, as are the death of the flesh, which is the dissolution of the elements, and the death of soul and flesh, which is punishment for offense. But God never made the death of the soul, which is the beginning and cause of the others, because it is written: “He committed no sin” (1 Pet. 2:22).

Do not understand the death of the soul, however, in the same way as the death of the flesh. The flesh dies by suffering the dissolution of its parts; the soul dies not in this way, but by changing its life.

7. What the predestinations of binding and of condition are has, I think, now been sufficiently explained. Among those that belong to condition, some lead to glory and others to punishment. Those whom God foreknew would become his own through the work of faith, he predestined to glory; those whom he foreknew would serve the devil’s persuasion without correction, he certainly predestined to punishment.

Unless it is guided by the practice of good meditation, the ship of our mind will drift in various directions as the winds of vain thoughts blow upon it, and at last it will be shaken under the danger of sinking.

# FROM THE BOOK WHOSE TITLE WAS *RESPONSES OF SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, TO ARTICLES FALSELY IMPUTED TO HIM*

This book, which begins with the words, “Some people, forgetful of Christian and fraternal charity, strive in every way to damage our reputation, to such an extent that, in their desire to harm us, they do not see that they are overthrowing their own,” bore the name of Augustine in several ancient manuscript codices. From this arose the opportunity for error given to the earliest editors of Augustine’s works, Amerbach and Erasmus, who included this book among Augustine’s polemical works against the Pelagians, having prefixed the name of that holy Doctor to it. It is in fact Prosper’s book refuting the Vincentian objections, which is presented in its proper place in the third part of this Appendix.

# SECOND PART OF THE APPENDIX, CONTAINING VARIOUS WRITINGS AND DOCUMENTS PERTAINING TO THE HISTORY OF THE PELAGIANS

By comparison with these, Augustine’s polemical works against the same heretics are elucidated.

---

## [WRITINGS AND DOCUMENTS PERTAINING TO THE HISTORY OF THE PELAGIANS]

### GENNADIUS, IN HIS *BOOK OF ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS*

Pelagius the Briton [Note: *Brito* was absent from the printed editions of Gennadius. It occurs in the oldest Corbie manuscript, but with the letter *t* doubled: *Britto*.], a heresiarch, before he was exposed as a heretic, wrote works necessary for students: three books on faith in the Trinity, and one book on practical conduct, entitled *Eulogies*, from the divine Scriptures, marked out by an index of chapters in the manner of the martyr Cyprian. But after he had been publicly declared a heretic, he wrote works favoring his heresy.

The same author, in the same place:

Before joining Pelagius—in fact, while still a young man—Coelestius wrote three letters to his parents from the monastery, in the form of booklets, necessary for everyone desiring God. Their language was moral, and at that time there was nothing blameworthy in them; rather, everything was directed toward encouraging virtue.

# HERE BEGINS THE *COMMONITORIUM AGAINST THE HERESY OF PELAGIUS AND COELESTIUS, OR ALSO AGAINST THE WRITINGS OF JULIAN, BY MARIUS MERCATOR, SERVANT OF CHRIST*

(C)

1. A question against the Catholic faith, long ago stirred up among some Syrians, and especially in Cilicia by Theodore, formerly bishop of the city of Mopsuestia—still gnaws away among a very few of them, although it is not openly proclaimed. Instead, it is retained within the churches by those who indulge in it as though they were Catholics [Note: Garnerius conjecturally emends “indulge in it sexually” (*fornicantur*) to “butt horns” (*cornicantur*)]: namely, that Adam and Eve, the progenitors of the human race, were created mortal by God; that they injured none of their descendants through their transgression, but harmed only themselves and made themselves alone guilty before God of the command, and no one else whatsoever.

[Note: It should be read, “Mopsuestia.” Photius, in *Bibliotheca*, cod. 177, mentions five books of Theodore “against those asserting that a human being sins by nature, not by will.” In reality, they were written against the defenders of original sin, Jerome and Augustine and other Catholics. For in his attacks, Theodore censures the following five points as errors:

I. That human beings sin by nature, not by will—by nature, I say, not the nature with which Adam was created, but that which he acquired after sin, when through transgression and sin he changed the good into the evil and the immortal into the mortal.

II. That infants, even though newly born, are not free from sin, since, because of Adam’s transgression, a nature established in sins is propagated to all his descendants as a sinful nature, in their terminology.

III. That holy Baptism and communion in the sacred Body are brought for the remission of sins and provide this even to infants.

IV. That no mortal is just.

V. That marriage and sexual desire, by which the human race is propagated, are works of a perverse nature, into which Adam fell through sin and which, because of the defect of nature, soon received the whole multitude of evils.]

This foolish question, no less hostile to the true faith, was first brought to Rome under Anastasius, of holy memory, supreme Pontiff of the Roman Church, by Rufinus, a Syrian by nationality. [Note: Anastasius, the predecessor of Innocent, was made bishop of the Roman Church in 398 and died in 402.] And, being clever, he protected himself from the odium of the matter and did not dare to advance it himself; instead, he deceived Pelagius, a monk of British descent at that time, and thoroughly instructed and trained him in the impious folly mentioned above.

Pelagius soon dared to compose commentaries on the Apostle Paul. When he reached that very well-known passage in the Epistle to the Romans, which reads, “Therefore, just as through one human being sin entered this world, and through sin death, and so it passed into all human beings” (Rom. 5:12), and so forth, he says there that “only those are held guilty and liable by that transgression who wished to imitate him in transgressing God’s commandments, not all who have been generated from his seed through the succession of generations.”

From this point he argues at greater length concerning the following passages of the Epistle, and declares: “No human being at all has been injured, or is injured, through generation by Adam’s sin or transgression, but by imitation,” he says, “because that first man sinned within the human race; and the person becomes guilty and liable who imitates him by his own will, not by being born but by sinning.”

3. Coelestius joined this Pelagius. He was indeed noble by birth and an auditorial scholar of that period, that is, a forensic scholar, but he had been born a eunuch because of a defect of nature in his mother’s womb. [Note: *Auditorial scholar* means the same as *forensic scholar*, as is understood from Augustine, *Against Julian*, book 2, no. 37, and book 6, p. 34.]

Instructed by the Pelagius mentioned above, he absorbed this most impious doctrine even more thoroughly and, with incredible loquacity, made many people participants and accomplices in his madness. He dared openly and publicly to disseminate its meaning among the peoples everywhere in the following propositions:

Adam was made mortal, and whether he sinned or did not sin, he would have died.

Adam’s sin injured Adam alone and not the human race.

Infants who are born are in the same condition in which Adam was before his transgression.

Nor does the whole human race die through Adam’s death, since neither does the whole human race rise again through Christ’s resurrection.

Infants, even if they are not baptized, possess eternal life.

These five propositions generate one utterly impious and abominable doctrine. He added further:

A human being can exist without sin and can easily keep God’s commandments, because even before Christ’s coming there were human beings without sin; and the Law leads to the kingdom of heaven in the same way as the Gospel.

4. These and similar teachings also pleased Julian and the others of his faction. [Note: The following material will be found below, where Julian is discussed.] And so forth.

# FROM THE BOOK *ON HERESIES*, PUBLISHED BY SIRMOND UNDER THE TITLE *PRAEDESTINATUS*

1. The Apostolic See, under holy Pope Innocent, declared that it had found the eighty-eighth heresy in Pelagius, when Coelestius, a disciple of Pelagius, was teaching at Carthage that human beings could exist without sin by nature, through human nature alone as sufficient for itself.

A certain Paulinus, a deacon and defender and procurator of the Church of Milan, resisted him. In an assembly of priests he brought many propositions against the Catholic faith before him; Coelestius did not deign to condemn them, saying: “It does not concern me to address the matters you allege, where my name is involved but the crime belongs to someone else.”

Then they presented him with his own books, in which he said that human nature itself could suffice for perfection; that is, “A human being can practice such great justice that he can even be without sin if he wishes.”

He also said:

Adam was made mortal, and whether he sinned or did not sin, he would have died.

The Law leads to the kingdom in the same way as the Gospels.

We confess that infants must be baptized for the remission of sins because of the rule of the universal Church.

Adam’s sin did no harm to the human race.

All these sorts of propositions were brought forward against Coelestius for condemnation. But he said that many things among them were held by his faith, and that because of those he could not condemn the rest.

Then, upon the report of nearly all the bishops of Africa, Pope Innocent drafted a condemnation of both Pelagius and Coelestius. Whether before they were condemned by the universal Church or after they had been condemned, however, they did not cease to write that a human being could be without sin; that Adam had done no harm to the human race; that infants were not baptized because they might have original sin; and that nature had been so well made by God that it was sufficient by itself for being without sin.

2. A certain Constantius, a commentator, took up the cause against them without written authority. After him, Augustine, bishop of Hippo, and Jerome, a Bethlehemite presbyter, also wrote against them.

The Pelagians, or Coelestians, nevertheless mingled with the Catholic people, because they have no other church; and therefore, wherever they happen to be, they do not refuse communion. For they say that in this matter they share the same confession in which the Eucharist is celebrated: “We are separated,” they say, “by a question, not by communion.”

Because of this daring, they are exposed to dangers both from our people, if they are discovered, and to execration among their own. For they have their own presbyters and bishops as well.

3. Pelagius himself writes as follows in his Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans, when dealing with the passage where the Apostle says, “Because through one human being sin entered this world, and through sin death, and so passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Rom. 5:12). Referring to Coelestius, who was the first to write against the transmission of sin, he says in these words:

“Those,” he says, “who oppose the transmission of sin endeavor to attack it in this way: ‘If Adam’s sin harmed even those who do not sin, then Christ’s grace also benefits even those who do not believe.’ They also add this: ‘If Baptism removes that original sin, those born from two baptized persons ought to be free from this sin. For how can they transmit to their descendants what they themselves did not possess at all?’”

We have set down these words just as they were written by Pelagius himself.

4. Concerning the statement, “A human being can be without sin,” the following objection was put to them:

“Either he can, and he does not seek assistance; or he cannot, and he seeks assistance. For whoever seeks help admits that he cannot accomplish what he wishes to do; otherwise he asks mockingly for assistance in accomplishing by himself what he is able to do alone.

“For example, if I wanted to lift ten pounds of any substance and sought assistance, I would appear ridiculous in asking for it. But if I wanted to lift two hundred pounds or more, I would ask for help because I could not accomplish it, and I would seek assistance with immense entreaties—especially if the condition of my life seemed to depend upon this burden, so that, unless I lifted the weight I have mentioned, I could not attain life.”

5. As for someone born from two baptized parents possessing nothing from the faith of his parents, reason teaches us this: those who have been baptized have two births—one by which the flesh generated them, and another by which the Holy Spirit generated them. From these two generations they transmit two generations to their descendants: one from the flesh, through the service of marriage; the other from the Spirit, through the consecration of Baptism.

Therefore, concerning someone born from baptized parents, I ask: From what was he born—from the flesh, that is, from the first generation, or from the Spirit, that is, from the second generation?

If he was born from the Spirit, he ought not to be baptized. Why? Because the Holy Spirit caused him to be born, not marital desire.

But if he was born from carnal marriage, that is, from a male and a female, it remains that those who were regenerated from Christ and the Church should regenerate their offspring again.

For we are born from the first Adam, but we are recreated again from the second Adam, as the holy Apostle says:

“The first man Adam was made a living soul; the last Adam, a life-giving spirit. But not first the spiritual, but the natural; afterward the spiritual. The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man from heaven, heavenly. Therefore, just as we have borne the image of the earthly—that is, just as we have created children carnally—let us also bear the image of the heavenly; that is, let us spiritually recreate those whom we created carnally. Or let us ourselves, who were created carnally by the Creator’s will, be recreated spiritually by his grace.”

“This I say,” the Apostle said, “because flesh and blood—that is, human beings born only by the first generation—unless they have deserved to obtain divine grace, cannot possess the kingdom of God, nor will corruption possess incorruption” (1 Cor. 15:45–50).

# TIMOTHY, PRESBYTER OF CONSTANTINOPLE, IN THE BOOKLET *ON THE RECEPTION OF HERETICS*

[Note: From the edition of John Baptist Cotelerius, in volume 3 of *Ecclesiastical Greek Monuments*, who believes that this same Timothy lived before the Monothelite heresy because he passes over it in silence.]

### ON PELAGIUS AND COELESTIUS

These men held the same opinions as Nestorius, a man of empty understanding, since at the Council of Ephesus they also brought forward many unfavorable statements about them, as though the impious Nestorius wanted to renew the doctrine of Pelagius and Coelestius.

It is reported that, in the time of Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, and Innocent of Rome, they rose up against the Church because the aforementioned bishops had undertaken many struggles against them and because they had been condemned in writing.

[Note: More correctly, this should say Theodotus of Antioch. For, according to Mercator in the *Commonitorium* under Coelestius’s name, Theodotus in fact held a synod at Antioch concerning the Pelagian case around the year 420; afterward Pelagius, when his heresy was discovered, was expelled from those regions. In the time of Theophilus of Alexandria, however, the Pelagian heresy was unknown; it began to emerge from hiding at Carthage around the beginning of 412, the year in which Theophilus died. Photius, who follows Timothy’s error below, should also be corrected in *Bibliotheca*, cod. 54.]

Moreover, these two heretics, Pelagius and Coelestius, were, as they say, neither bishops nor clerics nor members of the sacred order at all; rather, they wandered about like monks, conspiring against the truth. They also held the doctrines of the impious Manichaeans.

[Note: See the book *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, no. 62.]

# PHOTIUS, *BIBLIOTHECA*, CODEX 54

1. A book was read against the Pelagian and Coelestian heresy, bearing the following title: “A Copy of the Proceedings of the Bishops of the West against the Nestorian Doctrines.”

It states that the Nestorian and Coelestian heresies are the same, and it praises Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, as a witness, since he wrote to the emperor Theodosius that the Nestorian and Coelestian heresies are identical.

“It is clear,” he says. “For the Coelestians boldly proclaim this concerning Christ’s body or members, that is, the Church:

‘It is not God himself, that is, the Holy Spirit, who privately distributes faith and everything necessary for life, piety, and salvation to each person according to his will; rather, it is the established nature of the human being’—a nature that fell from blessedness through transgression and sin and, separated from God, was handed over to death—‘that, according to each person’s deserving will, both calls upon and repels the Holy Spirit.’

“But the Nestorians dare to think and assert the same things even concerning Christ himself, the head of the body. For they assert that, since Christ became a participant in our nature and God wishes all human beings alike to be saved, each person should also correct his own sin through the freedom of his will and make himself worthy of God.

“Therefore, it is not the Word himself who was born from Mary; rather, the one who was born from her has the Word accompanying him because of the dignity of his natural will, and shares with the Word only the dignity and designation of sonship.”

## 2.

Moreover, this Pelagian or Coelestian heresy flourished in the East, but it also spread in the West, where it was detected and convicted at Carthage in Africa by Aurelius and Augustine, and publicly condemned in various councils. Those who held such opinions were expelled from the Church as heretics in the time of the bishops Theophilus of Alexandria and Innocent of Rome, by the Roman, African, and other bishops of the West.

## 3.

Pelagius himself was acquitted at a synod in Palestine attended by fourteen bishops, after he had entirely rejected and condemned some of the propositions brought against him as foolish, while admitting that he had indeed stated others, though not in the sense in which his accusers interpreted them, but in a manner consistent with the Catholic Church. His accusers were Nepos and Lazarus, Gallic bishops, who, pleading illness on the part of one of them, obtained permission not to appear at the inquiry conducted against him. Augustine makes this known in what he wrote to Aurelius, bishop of Carthage (*On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, no. 2).

## 4.

After the death of Saint Augustine, certain members of the clergy began to assert that impious doctrine, to speak ill of Augustine, and even to attack him with insults, as though he had taught that freedom of choice had been taken away. But Pope Celestine of Rome, writing about the holy man and against those who were reviving this heresy to the bishops of that region, restrained the error that had recently been recalled.

Later, as the people of this sect were restored to the Church through their renunciation of their heresy, the evil was again renewed by them. But Septimus, bishop [Note: [Col. 1684] The Royal Codex has *Seinpeimos*.], checked the course of the pestilence as it arose again, by sending a letter to Leo, who at that time occupied the Apostolic See at Rome. Leo fought against the impious with fervent zeal.

Not long afterward, when the heresy had once more begun shamelessly to appear and arise, as though from an evil root, certain people at Rome also spoke openly in favor of it. Prosper, a truly godlike man, easily scattered them by publishing books against them for general circulation, while Leo, whom we have mentioned, still occupied the Roman See.

## 5.

This same heresy was again condemned by an anathema at the holy synod of Ephesus. John, bishop of Alexandria, also condemned it in his defense addressed to Gelasius, bishop of Rome—condemning not only the Pelagian heresy but Pelagius himself and also Coelestius, together with Julian, who was discovered to be a follower of theirs. [Note: [Col. 1684] Another codex of Photius’ work *Against the Pelagians* is presented below, under the Council of Carthage of the year 418.]

# Prosper, in the Book *Against the Ungrateful*

## I

The doctrine which, saturated with the dragon’s gall,  
the British serpent vomited in pestilential speech—  
by this doctrine he maintained that the first men, once created,  
whether they transgressed the prescribed commandment  
or remained innocent, having kept the law,  
would nevertheless suffer that death  
by which life abandons the flesh:  
a death not brought about by sin,  
but fixed as the companion of created beings  
by God himself as their maker.

Therefore, he said, those born afterward  
had inherited no guilt from their fathers;  
nor are those now born unlike  
the origin of the first men,  
who sinned by misusing their freedom—  
the harmful form, not the seed,  
having injured their descendants.

He held, moreover, that all the innocent  
could live upon the citadel of virtue  
and preserve in the mind its inborn beauty,  
since the natural dignity of one who wills rightly  
depends upon free choice,  
and the law implanted within the heart  
admonishes what is written externally.

To this he added Christ’s grace,  
which, if they wished to be renewed  
in the sacred font, had established in itself  
a universal refuge for those who had fallen:  
so that, once guilt voluntarily incurred  
had been released by pardon,  
nature might of its own accord return  
to its own powers;  
and, purified, might once more preserve  
the strength of which it had been stripped  
through its errors.

So rich, he maintained, is this gift of Baptism,  
and so much is bestowed upon humanity  
by this covenant,  
that it is suitable even for infants  
who are entirely without fault,  
so that those well born may become better  
and nature’s goodness may be illumined  
by honor added to it.

Yet he held that no one among all people  
was born excluded from this gift  
by God’s judgment;  
rather, each person by his own freedom  
deserved to receive the promises  
of the one who calls—  
promises undeserved by those who turn away,  
but owed to the upright.

## II

When this mad error was spreading widely  
and drawing inexperienced ears  
with deadly fictions,  
the pious care of the holy fathers,  
provided throughout the world by God’s prompting,  
came to its aid. With no differing movement,  
they struck down the savage enemies  
with heavenly weapons.

For with the same decrees  
one Spirit thundered.  
The See of Peter at Rome first cut down  
the approaching pestilence.  
Made the head of pastoral authority  
for the world, it holds by religion  
whatever it does not possess by arms.

Nor did the care of the leaders of the East  
shine less brightly.  
They bound the author of the wicked doctrine  
with a merciful injunction:  
he must condemn his own fiction,  
unless he preferred to be cut off  
from the body of Christ  
and separated from the holy flock.

This judgment may appear gentle,  
and even excessively tolerant toward the wicked;  
but in that examination holy faith  
overcame the offspring  
that had arisen from the accursed seed.

For provision was made,  
and divine care took precautions,  
so that although the beast,  
in avoiding the punishment hanging over it,  
retained within itself the same thoughts of treachery,  
it might nevertheless destroy  
its own offspring by condemning it,  
extinguishing with its mouth  
the evil brood that it had brought forth  
with its mouth.

At that time Jerome also—  
the guest of Bethlehem, renowned in name,  
graceful in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin speech,  
an example of character and teacher of the world—  
cut down the enemy in books of great excellence.  
He made known by what storm  
the darknesses that had arisen  
were attempting to obscure the true light.

What should I say of the care  
which the good priest Atticus exercised  
in the great city of Constantinople,  
refuting the envoys of the heretics  
with the ancient faith, in learned speech?  
Although their impious hearts  
had covered themselves with a veil under the appearance of judgment,  
they endured the torments of judgment  
and the silent rejection that followed.

I pass over how great a tumult  
was rightly stirred in illustrious Ephesus,  
which did not permit the vessels of wrath,  
the breath of disease,  
and the seeds of death  
to remain within its walls.

Nor shall I omit with what faith  
burning Sicily drove the viperous host  
from its own shores.

Africa, you pursued the cause  
of our faith with still greater fervor.  
When the throne of apostolic authority  
joined its strength with yours,  
you destroyed the savage entrails of the war  
and cast down the defeated  
across a broad expanse.

Your holy bishops assembled  
from every city,  
and in a most famous twofold assembly  
of elders  
you decreed what Rome approved  
and what the kingdoms were to follow.

Nor was the power of the councils there  
displayed as though our people,  
unable to defeat the heretics by reason,  
had oppressed them by force.  
Their arts were examined  
and the poison of their heretical mind exposed;  
no argument remained  
that learned faith could not dissolve.

The things that flowed forth  
from the cataracts of the eternal fountain  
in an overflowing stream  
were established and remain in writing,  
and were published in the tongues  
of three hundred leaders—  
with severe goodness so governing its law  
that those who wished to return  
from condemned error  
might receive peace,  
while those who persisted in wickedness  
were driven away.

Could a holy council proceed  
to any other end,  
when Aurelius was its leader  
and Augustine its intellect?  
Augustine, whom the grace of Christ,  
watering him with a more abundant horn,  
gave as a light to our age—  
a light kindled from the Light.

For God was his food,  
his life, and his rest;  
his only delight was the love of Christ,  
and Christ’s honor alone was his.  
And while he attributed no good to himself,  
God became everything to him,  
and wisdom reigned in its holy temple.

## III

Among all those, therefore,  
who drove mad beasts from the holy flock,  
his diligence was greater,  
his work greater,  
and his excellence filled the whole world.

For wherever the crafty enemy  
turned his steps,  
and along whatever winding, uncertain path  
he pursued his hidden course,  
he was forestalled by Augustine’s opposition;  
the snares of a thousand roads  
found no access.

And while the rage of the greedy wolves,  
shut out from without,  
gnashed its teeth  
and turned lies into every kind of artifice,  
so that it could not corrupt the minds  
of any sheep  
or disturb uncertain hearts  
with crooked accusations,  
God made him a mouthpiece of truth.

Through his mouth  
streams of books flowed throughout the world,  
which the gentle and humble drink,  
striving to pour the channels  
of life-giving teaching  
into the fields of human hearts.

# From the Same Prosper: Epitaph of the Pelagian and Nestorian Heresies (C)

I, the Nestorian plague, succeeded  
the Pelagian,  
though I had been engendered beforehand  
in her womb.

An unhappy mother and daughter  
of a wretched birth,  
I came forth from the very seed  
that I had borne.

For I had first begun  
to build a citadel upon merits,  
and I wished to carry the work  
from the head down to the body.

But while my offspring  
was armed from the lowest foundations  
to the highest point,  
I did not have a suitable time  
for waging war.

And after the grievous wounds  
of our shared deceit,  
I joined harsh battles  
to an equal end.

Yet one sentence alone  
delivered me over to death,  
while the other, wishing to rise again,  
fell twice.

It rises with me,  
dies with me,  
and with me enters the grave;  
it descends with me  
into the depths of the prison of hell—  
the place where insane pride  
plunged us headlong,  
stripped of gifts  
and swollen with merits.

For by wishing to make Christ God  
through the merit and reward of works,  
we did not remain within  
the covenant of the Head.

Hoping for a crown  
from the freedom of the mind,  
we lost the justice  
which grace gives.

Therefore, you who pity  
the tombs of a twofold ruin,  
take care not to join yourself  
to our destruction.

For if you believe  
that the gifts of the Lord,  
which we acknowledge only too late,  
are owed to humanity,  
you will be one of us.

# Another Commonitorium of Mercator against the Pelagians

An example of the *Commonitorium* which, concerning Coelestius, Mercator issued in Greek, not only to the Church of Constantinople but also to many most religious men, and which was likewise presented to the most pious emperor Theodosius, always Augustus. The same work was translated from Greek into Latin by that same Marius Mercator, servant of Christ, during the consulship of Florentius and Dionysius, most illustrious men.

Through this *Commonitorium*, once the most disastrous error had become known, the imperial command drove Julian, its defender and follower, together with his other associates and accomplices, from the city, and afterward Coelestius as well. At the Council of Ephesus, too, they were subsequently condemned in person by the judgment of 275 bishops.

## 1.

A certain eunuch named Coelestius, born from his mother’s womb, came forth from the city of Rome a little more or less than twenty years ago [Note: [Col. 1686] That is, approximately in the year 410, since the *Commonitorium* is stated to have been issued during the consulship of Florentius and Dionysius, which fell in the year 429]. He had become a disciple and hearer of Pelagius. He came to Carthage, the metropolis of all Africa, and there was accused before Aurelius, bishop of that city, by a written petition from a certain Paulinus, deacon of Saint Ambrose, bishop of Milan, concerning the propositions written below, as appears from the record that was drawn up and into which the petition itself was inserted. We have copies of these proceedings in our hands.

He was accused as teaching these doctrines himself and as having sent through the provinces various people who were in agreement with him, to disseminate them among the peoples. The propositions were these:

“Adam was made mortal, and whether he sinned or did not sin, he would have died.”

“Adam’s sin harmed him alone and not the human race.”

“Infants who are born are in the same condition in which Adam was before his transgression.”

“Neither through Adam’s death or transgression does the whole human race die, nor through Christ’s resurrection does the whole human race rise again.”

“The law sends people to the kingdom of heaven in the same way as the Gospel.”

“Before the coming of the Lord there were people without sin, that is, impeccable.”

The fathers and bishops of that region, in seven pairs of synodal proceedings, resisted Coelestius concerning all the propositions written above. [Note: [Col. 1687] This passage has been thought corrupt and has been edited in various ways by learned men who first published Mercator’s *Commonitorium*. Since the manuscripts agree among themselves here, the reading of the old books, as given by the distinguished Baluzius, has been retained. We think Mercator intended nothing other than that it should be understood that, concerning Coelestius’ seven propositions, other propositions had been composed against him in an equal number, just as you will see was done against Pelagius in the writing that we place below after the Council of Diospolis. Certainly Coelestius’ seven propositions are reported above in another *Commonitorium* of Mercator, at col. 1681, no. 3. One of them is omitted here by the scribes, namely: “Infants, even if they are not baptized, have eternal life.”]

They ordered him to condemn them, because they contained heretical opinions. But Coelestius in no way yielded; indeed, he resisted in the very proceedings in which he was repeatedly heard, and he was deprived of ecclesiastical communion.

## 2.

He believed that an appeal from this sentence should be made to the judgment of the Roman bishop. But, immediately neglecting that appeal, he himself proceeded to Ephesus, a city of Asia, where he dared by underhanded means to seek a place among the presbyters.

Several years later, under Atticus, bishop of holy memory, he went to the city of Constantinople. There, having been detected in similar matters, he was expelled from that noble city through the great diligence of that holy man. Letters were sent concerning him to the bishops of Asia, Thessalonica, and Carthage; we have copies of them and are prepared to produce them.

## 3.

The aforementioned Coelestius, expelled from there as well, hastened with all speed to the city of Rome under Zosimus, bishop of holy memory.

There, in proceedings whose copies we possess, he was examined. When he was somewhat frightened by the investigator, he sowed hope through frequent replies and statements of his own, promising that he would condemn the propositions over which he had been accused at Carthage.

He was urged to do this with increasing insistence, and it was expected of him even more forcefully. For this reason he was considered worthy of a certain leniency from that holy priest, and thus earned a letter full of kindness addressed to the African bishops. He abused that letter, or continues even now to abuse it, in order to deceive many who are ignorant.

## 4.

But when the bishops from Africa sent a reply, setting out the entire case that had been conducted before them, and also sent the proceedings that had then been drawn up with him or concerning him [Note: [Col. 1687] See *Book Two against the Two Letters of the Pelagians*, no. 5], he was summoned to a fuller hearing so that he might hasten to fulfill what he had promised—that is, so that, after condemning the propositions mentioned above, he might be released from the sentence of the African bishops by which he had been deprived of communion.

He not only failed to appear but also fled from the aforesaid city of Rome. For this reason he was thoroughly and at great length condemned in writing by the aforementioned bishop Zosimus of blessed memory. Those writings contain the very propositions over which he had been accused, and the whole case concerning both the Coelestius mentioned above and Pelagius, his still more wicked teacher, appears to be narrated in them.

We also have copies of these writings here, and we report that similar and identical writings were sent to the bishops of the Eastern Churches, to the diocese of Egypt, Constantinople, Thessalonica, and Jerusalem.

## 5.

The reason Pelagius too was condemned along with him is as follows.

Before the devastation of the city of Rome [Note: [Col. 1687] The devastation of the city refers to that which was carried out by Alaric, king of the Goths, in the year 410], the aforementioned man dared to compose commentaries on the Apostle Paul [Note: [Col. 1688] See *Book Three on the Merits of Sins*, no. 1 and following, and *On Original Sin*, no. 34], and to publish them among those whose friendship he relied upon.

He believed that he was explaining each of the Apostle’s words or meanings. In the Letter to the Romans, when he reached the passage where the Chosen Vessel speaks in this way—“Therefore, just as through one man sin entered into this world, and through sin death, and thus death passed into all human beings”—he believed that it should be explained as follows. We have his book and produce it in order to expose its hostile error.

He says:

“Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death.” He says that Paul “used an example or image: for just as, when sin did not exist, it entered secretly through Adam, so also, when righteousness no longer remained in anyone, life was restored through Christ.

“And death passed into all human beings.” He says: “This means that those who sin likewise die. For death did not pass into Abraham, Isaac, or Jacob, concerning whom the Lord says, ‘For all live’” (Luke 20:38).

“But here,” he says, “he says that all are dead because, on account of the multitude of sins, the few righteous are not excepted; just as there also it says, ‘There is none that does good, not even one’” (Psalm 52:2, 4), “and again: ‘Every human being is a liar’” (Psalm 115:11).

“Or certainly,” he says, “it passed into all those who lived according to human custom and not according to heavenly conduct.”

And shortly afterward:

“But death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression.”

He says: “Either, since there was no one to distinguish between the just and the unjust, death thought it ruled over everyone; or it ruled over those who transgressed the commandment as Adam did—that is, over the sons of Noah, who were commanded not to eat the soul in the blood, and over the sons of Abraham, to whom circumcision was commanded. It also ruled over those who, apart from the commandment, had disregarded the natural law.

“‘Who is the form of the one to come.’ For just as Adam,” he says, “was formed by God without sexual intercourse, so Christ proceeded from a virgin through the creative work of the Holy Spirit. Or, as some say, he is a form by contrast—that is, just as the former is the head of sin, so the latter is the head of righteousness.

“‘But the gift is not like the trespass.’” He says: “This is so that equality might not be supposed in the form. For if by the transgression of one many died, much more did the gift and grace of God abound to many through the one man Jesus Christ” (Romans 5:12–15).

“The Apostle means,” he says, “that grace had greater power in giving life than sin had in killing; for Adam killed himself alone and his descendants, whereas Christ delivered both those who were then in the body and those who were afterward to exist.”

## 6.

“Here the careful Catholic reader should note what he says: that Adam harmed not himself alone but also his descendants.”

Hold fast to his earlier definition. For by “descendants” he does not here mean that absolutely all human beings everywhere were harmed by that sin, but only those who, by imitation, likewise became guilty through their own sins and personal transgression, as Adam did. These, without doubt, are found to be his great-grandchildren and descendants.

## 7.

“But those,” he says, “who hold a different opinion concerning the transmission of sin attempt to attack those who defend its transmission in the following manner.” [Note: [Col. 1688] Garnerius reads: “sharply” (*acriter*).]



“‘If Adam’s sin harmed even those who do not sin, then Christ’s righteousness also benefits those who do not believe, since the Apostle similarly—or rather, he says even more—that through one person more are delivered than previously perished through one person.

“‘Next they say: If Baptism cleanses that ancient and long-standing sin, then those born of two baptized parents ought to be free from this sin; for they could not transmit to their descendants what they themselves did not possess.

“‘They add to this: If the soul is not transmitted through generation, as indeed it is not, but only the flesh possesses the transmission of sin, then only the flesh deserves the punishment.’” [Note: [Col. 1688] See Augustine’s Letter 190 to Optatus, no. 22.]

“For it is unjust,” he says, “that a soul born today, not derived from Adam’s mass, should bear so ancient a sin belonging to another; for it is not reasonable that God, who forgives personal sins, should impute one belonging to another.”

## 8.

Again, in another sermon of his, Pelagius says:

“If a sinner,” he says, “has begotten a sinner, so that the original sin of his infant is removed when he receives Baptism, then a righteous person ought to beget a righteous person.

“If parents,” he says, “are not harmed by their own sins after their conversion, much less could they harm their children through those sins.

“If it happened that the first man caused the cause of death, then after Christ’s coming there should no longer have been any need to die.

“If death arose through Adam’s sin, we would never die after the forgiveness of sins that our Deliverer granted us.

“Adam’s sin, therefore, had greater power in killing absolutely all human beings than Christ’s grace had in saving, since grace benefited not everyone but only believers.

“For not all who are born from Adam are also reborn in Christ”—and so forth.

## 9.

All the propositions written above, as has already been said, are contained in that letter of the bishop Zosimus of blessed memory called the *Tractoria*, by which Coelestius and Pelagius were condemned. It was sent to Constantinople and throughout the world and confirmed by the signatures of the holy fathers.

Julian and his remaining accomplices refused to sign it and were unwilling to make themselves of one mind with those fathers. They were deposed and stripped of office not only by imperial laws but also by priestly statutes, and were expelled from all Italy.

Many of them, coming to their senses and corrected from the error mentioned above, returned as suppliants to the Apostolic See and, having been received, recovered their churches.

## 10.

It is clear that the aforementioned Coelestius and Pelagius were not condemned for the first time by Zosimus of holy memory, but by his predecessor, Innocent of holy remembrance, by whom Julian had also been ordained.

Julian remained in communion with Innocent after their condemnation until the death of the aforesaid bishop Innocent, persevering in a sincere judgment and communicating with the one who had condemned them. He therefore undoubtedly condemned Pelagius and Coelestius as well. We do not know what he now wants or about what he complains.

## 11.

The reason they were condemned by Innocent of holy remembrance was as follows.

After the devastation of Rome, Pelagius was living in Palestine. Certain diligent bishops found his books [Note: [Col. 1689] Heros and Lazarus], in which many and various things appeared to have been written against the Catholic faith.

These books were sent with letters to the fathers and bishops in Africa. There, after three councils had assembled, the books mentioned above were read. [Note: [Col. 1689] Three synodal letters were consequently written to Innocent; among Augustine’s letters they are numbered 175, 176, and 177, although the last is not properly a synodal letter but a personal letter.]

Reports were then sent to Rome, together with the books themselves. The apostolic judgment of the one replying to the aforementioned councils was issued, depriving Coelestius and Pelagius of ecclesiastical communion. We have copies of these writings in our hands.

While Pelagius was still in Jerusalem, he was also accused before the synod [Note: [Col. 1689] The Council of Diospolis]. At first, by evasion, concealing himself behind certain ambiguous professions and continuing with doubtful statements or answers, he appears to have deceived that hearing of the bishops.

But afterward, when he was clearly detected, and the accusers persisted before a later synod presided over by Theodotus, bishop of Antioch, of holy memory [Note: [Col. 1689] Theodotus was created bishop of Antioch after Alexander, probably in the year 411, and died in 427], and he was exposed, he was also driven from the holy and venerable places of Jerusalem.

The written communications of that same holy Theodotus to the most reverend bishop of the city of Rome, and of Praylius, bishop of Jerusalem, of sacred memory, bear witness to this. [Note: [Col. 1689] Praylius succeeded John in the see of Jerusalem at the beginning of the year 417.] We have copies of these writings as evidence. [Col. 1690]

## 12.

In the accusation of the propositions that were then brought against Pelagius, this proposition was also included, together with other abominable opinions held by Coelestius as his disciple:

“Infants, even if they are not baptized, have eternal life.”

We also stated above that the proposition attributed to Coelestius—“The law sends people to the kingdom of heaven in the same way as the Gospel”—was consistent with his teacher’s doctrine. Pelagius openly confirms and declares this in certain writings of his.

Finally, we have in our hands a little book of his containing an exhortatory address to a certain widow named Livania [Note: [Col. 1690] Some think that *Juliana* was written instead of *Livania*, either through a scribal error or by a definite intention of the author]. It says:

“It is fitting for Christ’s servant to follow simplicity—not that which is more folly than simplicity, but that of which Scripture says, ‘Blessed is every simple soul’” (Proverbs 11:25, according to the Septuagint).

“Scripture says elsewhere, ‘Cursed is every person who does not remain in all the things written in the book of the law, to do them’” (Deuteronomy 27:26).

“From this,” he says, “it is shown that true simplicity is not that which, with senseless security, disregards God’s commandments, but that which guards the precepts of the law with wise fear.

“For by saying that the person who does not remain in the things written is cursed, he wishes to imply by contrast that the person who has not kept all the commandments is not blessed; and if every simple person is blessed, then the simple person is the one who has fulfilled all the commandments of the law.”

## 13.

No Catholic who has read this proposition doubts that Pelagius asserted what has already been stated so many times: “The books of Moses send people to the kingdom of heaven in the same way as the Gospel.” Nor can anyone who understands it sustain any difficulty.

And because, in that same most impious proposition, he referred indiscriminately to “the law,” if he meant the Mosaic law, whose testimony concerning the curse he quoted, he is plainly attempting to draw us into Judaism.

But if, in order to conceal himself through deceit, he says that by “the law” he meant the Gospel, then he is not wrong in calling the Gospel “the law.” He is impious, however, in that he does not hesitate to place us who are under the Gospel under a similar and equal [Note: [Col. 1690] The distinguished Baluzius, following the old codices, printed: “in which, under what sort of likeness, us,” and so forth.] curse, equating evangelical grace with the law of circumcision and with all Judaism.

Hence his disciple Coelestius also openly dared to declare:

“The law sends people to the kingdoms of heaven in the same way as the Gospel.”

For according to Pelagius it is clear that if we are still under the same or a similar bond, even in the time of the Gospel, then, if we err in any way as human beings or fail to fulfill one of the Gospel’s commandments, we are cursed.

But if this is so—which God forbid—then, as he wishes the statement to be understood, the Gospel has been equated with the old law. Where, then, will be the Apostle Paul’s statement: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13), since it is written: “Cursed is every person who does not remain in all the things written in the book of the law, to do them”?

Moreover, descending into a fuller exposition of this same meaning, he develops and commends it at greater length in the same sermon of this little book. After many other things he says:

“To hate, to curse, and to envy; to lie, to slander, and to believe those who slander is considered a light or nonexistent sin. But those who think this have forgotten that we read that even those guilty of a light commandment are destined to be handed over to Gehenna.

“For it is clear,” he says, “that the Lord said: ‘Whoever says to his brother, “Fool,” or, “Raca,” will be liable to Gehenna’” (Matthew 5:22).

## 14.

Let Julian and his other associates now condemn Pelagius and Coelestius, who have been detected in such impious errors, in order to satisfy the Church. If they are confident that any people hold opinions contrary to the Catholic faith, let them not hesitate to identify them by name, [Col. 1691] and they will receive from us, according to our ability, an ecclesiastical response—or certainly from the person whom they say [Note: [Col. 1691] *Dicent* had been substituted, and the Bellovacensis Codex was cited in support of that reading, but falsely, as Baluzius testifies; he found *dicunt* in that very codex] deviates from Catholic belief.

For, as we stated above, many who had followed Coelestius and Pelagius, and who had also become Julian’s associates and companions, abandoned him and, after Pelagius had been condemned, submitted themselves to the Apostolic See. They professed repentance for the opinions they had wrongly held and were judged worthy by the holy fathers to be received with mercy.

# On the Pelagian Heresy and Its Author and Defenders

Prosper, in his *Chronicle*, under the year of Christ 413.

At this time Pelagius the Briton, with Coelestius and Julian as his helpers, advanced a doctrine bearing his own name against the grace of Christ and drew many into his error. He preached that each person is governed toward righteousness by his own will and receives as much grace as he has deserved, because Adam’s sin harmed Adam alone and did not bind his descendants. Hence it is possible for those who wish to be entirely without sin, and all people are born as innocent as the first man was before his transgression. They are not baptized, therefore, in order to be stripped of sin, but in order to be honored by the sacrament of adoption.

# The Pelagian Heresy Comes to Augustine’s Knowledge

Augustine, in *The Gift of Perseverance*, no. 53.

Although I published these books—the *Confessions*—[Note: [Col. 1691] Approximately in the year of Christ 400] before the Pelagian heresy arose, I certainly said in them to our God, and said it often: “Give what you command, and command what you will.”

When these words of mine were recalled at Rome in the presence of Pelagius by a certain brother and fellow bishop, he could not tolerate them. He objected rather vehemently and almost quarreled with the one who had recalled them.
