The Same, in *The Proceedings of Pelagius*, no. 46.

At first I learned of the name of Pelagius, who was absent and living at Rome, together with much praise of him. Later rumor began to reach us that he was arguing against God’s grace.

Although I was grieved by this, and although it was reported to me by people whom I believed, I nevertheless wished to know something of the kind from Pelagius himself, or from one of his books, so that, if I began to refute him, he could not deny it.

Afterward, when he came to Africa, he was received in my absence on our shore—that is, at Hippo. There, as I learned from our people, nothing of this kind was heard from him at all, because he departed from there sooner than expected.

Later I saw his face once or twice at Carthage, as I recall, when I was fully occupied with the business of the Conference that we were to hold with the heretical Donatists [Note: [Col. 1691] In June of the year 411]. He, however, also hastened overseas.

Meanwhile, these doctrines were growing hot in the mouths of those who were regarded as his disciples, until Coelestius came before an ecclesiastical tribunal and received a sentence worthy of his perversity.

# On the Council of Carthage Held against Coelestius around the Beginning of the Year 412

[Note: [Col. 1691] We learn the date of this first council against the Pelagian heresy from a letter of another Council of Carthage to Innocent, numbered ninety among Augustine’s letters, in these words: “Hence it came about that we asked that what had been discussed here concerning Coelestius’ name nearly five years ago should be reviewed,” and so forth. This synodal letter was written in the year 416. The council against Coelestius, therefore, which preceded it by approximately five years, belongs either to the end of 411 or the beginning of 412.]

Augustine, in *The Proceedings of Pelagius*, no. 62.

When this heresy had deceived many and disturbed the brothers whom it had not deceived, a certain Coelestius, who held such opinions, was brought before the judgment of the Church of Carthage and condemned by the judgment of the bishops.

[Col. 1692]

The Same, in Letter 157 to Hilary, no. 22.

Coelestius had already begun to creep into the honor of the presbyterate in the Church of that same city, Carthage. But because of these very arguments against the grace of Christ, through the exceptionally faithful freedom of the brothers, he was brought before the judgment of the bishops.

Nevertheless, he was compelled to confess, on account of the infants who were to be baptized, that redemption was necessary for them also, and so forth.

But because he departed having been more thoroughly convicted and detested by the Church than corrected and reconciled, and so forth.

The Same, in *On Original Sin*, nos. 2–3.

From the ecclesiastical proceedings at Carthage we have transcribed these words of his:

“Aurelius the bishop said: Let the following be read.”

And it was read:

“That Adam’s sin harmed Adam alone and not the human race.”

When it had been read, Coelestius said:

“I stated that I was uncertain concerning the transmission of sin, but in such a way that I agree with the knowledge of grace which God has granted, since I have heard different opinions from those who are presbyters established in the Catholic Church.”

The deacon Paulinus said: and so forth. [Note: [Col. 1692] See what follows in *On Original Sin*, nos. 3 and 4.]

The Same, in *The Proceedings of Pelagius*, no. 23.

These matters were brought forward in such a way that you and the other bishops with you said that they had been heard and condemned at Carthage in your presence [Note: [Col. 1692] He is addressing Aurelius, bishop of Carthage].

I myself was not present, as you recall; but afterward, when I came to Carthage, I reviewed the same proceedings.

# Pelagian Doctrines with Their Refutation

From Jerome’s Letter to Ctesiphon. [Note: [Col. 1692] In the most ancient Colbertine Codex the heading reads: “To Atesiphon Urbicus.” Orosius, however, says that at the gathering in Jerusalem held in the year 415 it was addressed to Ctesiphon, or Tesisphon, and that it had recently been published by Jerome.]

1. You did not act rashly, as you falsely suppose, but lovingly and earnestly, in sending me a new question drawn from an old one—a question that previously deceived many in the East, so that, under the guise of humility, they might learn pride and say with the devil, “I will ascend into heaven; above the stars of heaven I will set my throne; I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14:13–14). For what greater presumption can there be than to claim for oneself not merely likeness to God, but equality with God, and in a brief statement to embrace all the poisons of the heretics—poisons that flowed from the fountain of the philosophers, especially Pythagoras and Zeno, the leader of the Stoics? They assert that what the Greeks call πάθη (*pathē*), which we may call “disturbances”—namely, grief and joy, hope and fear, two of which concern the present and two the future—can be eradicated from the mind, and that no fiber or root of vice can remain at all in a human being through meditation and the constant practice of virtues, etc.

Well did one of our writers say: “The philosophers, patriarchs of the heretics, have stained the purity of the Church with perverse teaching” (Tertullian, *Against Hermogenes* and *On the Soul*). Thus they do not know the saying concerning human frailty: “Why do you glory, earth and ashes?” (Ecclus. 10:9). This is especially so when the Apostle says: “I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive”; and again: “For I do not do the good that I wish, but the evil that I do not wish, that I practice” (Rom. 7:23, 19). If he does what he does not wish, how can this statement stand: “A human being can be without sin, if he wishes”? How can he do what he wishes, when the Apostle asserts that he cannot accomplish what he desires?

And when we ask them who those people are whom they consider to be without sin, they try to evade the truth by a new device. They say that they are not speaking of those who are or have been without sin, but of those who can be so, etc. David says: “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities” (Ps. 50:7), etc. And in another psalm: “No living person will be justified in your sight” (Ps. 142:2). Under the name of piety they evade this testimony by a new argument, saying that no one is perfect in comparison with God, etc.

**[Col. 1693] 2.** Those who applaud themselves in this kind of perfidy assert nothing new. They deceive the simple and uneducated, but they cannot deceive ecclesiastical men who meditate day and night on the law of God. Let them therefore be ashamed of their leaders and associates, who say that “a human being can be without sin, if he wishes”—what the Greeks call ἀναμάρτητον (*anamártēton*, “sinless” or “without sin”). And because the ears of the Churches throughout the East cannot tolerate this, they pretend that they do say “without sin,” but that they do not dare to say ἀναμάρτητον—as though “without sin” were one thing and ἀναμάρτητον another, and as though the Greek expression they have coined had not been rendered in Latin by two words.

If you say “without sin” and deny that you say ἀναμάρτητον, then condemn those who proclaim ἀναμάρτητον. But you do not. For you know what you teach your disciples inwardly, mentioning one thing with your mouth and concealing another in your conscience; you speak to us, outsiders and the uneducated, in parables, but confess mysteries to your own people. You boast that you do this according to Scripture, because it says: “Jesus spoke to the crowds in parables”; and to the disciples in the house he says: “To you it has been given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, but to them it has not been given” (Matt. 13:10–11).

But, as I began to say, I shall briefly set out the names of your leaders and associates, so that you may observe the kind of company in which you glory. Mani—which is Manichaeus—says that his Elect, whom he places among Plato’s celestial apsides [Note: [Col. 1693] Printed editions read “among the souls.” But several very ancient manuscripts read “among the apsides,” by which name, according to Pliny, *Natural History* 2.15, the Greeks call circles among the stars.] are entirely without sin and cannot sin even if they wish to. For he says that they have surpassed such heights of virtue that they mock the works of the flesh.

Priscillian, a Manichaean party in Spain, whose obscenity your disciples greatly love, rashly claiming for themselves the word of perfection and knowledge, etc. Hence you too assert that those who lack knowledge of the law cannot avoid sins, etc.

Evagrius the Iberian [Note: [Col. 1693] One manuscript has “the Ebionite”; another, “the Iborite.” The Erfurt edition has “the Hyperborean.”], etc., published a book and teachings *περὶ ἀπαθείας* (*peri apatheias*), which we may call “freedom from suffering” or “imperturbability,” etc. His Greek books are read throughout the East, and in the West many read them in Latin through the translation of his disciple Rufinus, etc.

Do you still wish to know another founder of your error? Your teaching is a branch of Origen, etc. Nor should you be ashamed of the company of such men, while rejecting the names of those whose blasphemies you share. The second question of Jovinianus is a discipline suited to your ingenuity. Whatever answer was made to him, consider it an answer to you, etc.

**3.** But the statement that they later fitted to this opinion in order to deceive people—“not without the grace of God”—although it deceives readers at first glance, cannot deceive anyone who examines and scrutinizes it carefully.

They place “the grace of God” in such a way “that we do not rely upon and receive his assistance in each individual work, but refer the matter to free choice and to the commandments of the law,” setting forth the saying of Isaiah: “For God gave them the law as an aid” (Isa. 8:20, according to the Septuagint), so that thanks should be given to God because he created us such that, by our own choice, we can both choose good and avoid evil.

Those who say this do not understand that through their mouths the devil is hissing intolerable blasphemy, etc. One of his disciples—or rather, by now his teacher and leader of the entire army, and, contrary to the Apostle, a vessel of destruction—running through thickets of solecisms, not, as his followers boast, of syllogisms, philosophizes and argues as follows:

“If I do nothing without God’s help, and everything I accomplish is done through his action, then it is not I who labor who will be crowned, but God’s help in me. And he gave me the power of choice in vain, since I cannot fulfill it unless he is always helping me. For the will is destroyed if it needs the aid of another. Yet God gave free choice, which will not otherwise be free unless I do what I wish. Therefore either I use once and for all the power that was given to me, so that free choice may remain free; or, if I need another’s help, the freedom of choice in me will be destroyed.”

What blasphemy does the man who says this not surpass? What poison of the heretics does he not exceed? They assert that through the freedom of choice they have no further need of God beyond what is necessary, etc.

**[Col. 1694] 4.** As for what they constantly proclaim, up and down, namely, that we destroy free choice, let them hear the contrary: those destroy the freedom of choice who misuse it against the beneficence of the giver, etc.

Listen, I beg you—listen to the sacrilegious man. “If,” he says, “I wish to bend a finger, move a hand, sit, stand, walk, run about, spit, flick the dirt from my nostrils with two fingers, relieve my bowels, or pass urine, will God’s help always be necessary for me?” etc.

Do you think that you are being insulted and that the freedom of choice is destroyed if you always have recourse to God as its author, if you depend upon his will, and say: “My eyes are always toward the Lord, for he will draw my feet out of the snare” (Ps. 24:15)? How then do you dare utter with your reckless tongue, “Each person is ruled by his own choice”? If he is ruled by his own choice, where is God’s help? If he does not need Christ as his guide, how does Jeremiah write: “A person’s way is not in himself” (Jer. 10:23); and, “The steps of a person are directed by the Lord” (Ps. 36:23)?

**5.** You say that God’s commandments are easy. Yet you cannot produce anyone who has fulfilled them all, etc. You also commonly say this: either the commandments are possible and were rightly given by God, or they are impossible, in which case the fault does not lie with those who received the commandments but with the one who gave impossible commandments.

Did God command me to be what God is? To have nothing between myself and the Lord the Creator? To be higher than the summit of the angels? To possess what the angels do not possess? Of him it is written as something peculiar to him: “He committed no sin” (1 Pet. 2:22), etc.

Otherwise your own position will destroy itself. You assert that a human being can be without sin, if he wishes; and then, after a most profound sleep, you vainly try to add, for the deception of inexperienced souls, “not without the grace of God.” For if a human being can once and for all be without sin by himself, what need is there for God’s grace? But if he can do nothing without God’s grace, why was it necessary to say that he can do what he cannot?

“He can,” you say, “be without sin; he can be perfect, if he wishes.” What Christian does not wish to be without sin? Or who refuses perfection? etc.

“God gave possible commandments,” he says. And who denies this? But how this statement is to be understood, the Vessel of Election teaches most clearly, etc.

**6.** You will object and say that we follow the doctrine of the Manichaeans and of those who stir up wars in the Church over different natures, asserting that nature is evil if it cannot in any way be changed.

Attribute this not to me, but to the Apostle, who knows that God is one thing and a human being another; that the weakness of the flesh is one thing and the strength of the spirit another. “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh; and these oppose one another, so that you do not do what you wish” (Gal. 5:17).

You will never hear me say that nature is evil. But let us learn from the very author who wrote it how the weakness of the flesh should be explained, etc.

**7.** You blaspheme in vain and thrust into the ears of the ignorant the charge that we condemn free choice. Let the one who condemns be condemned.

For the rest, we differ from brute animals in that we were created with free choice. But free choice itself, as we have said, relies upon God’s help and needs his assistance in every individual act. You do not want this, since, according to you, whoever once possesses free choice has no need of God as helper.

**8.** Who could endure that argument of yours? You speak in these words: “It is one thing to be, and another to be able to be. To be is not placed within our power; but ‘to be able’ may be said generally, because, although another person has not existed, nevertheless there can be one who wishes to exist.”

I ask: what sort of argument is this—that what has never existed can exist? etc.

**9.** Speak what you believe; publicly proclaim what you say privately to your disciples. If you say that you possess freedom of choice, why do you not freely say what you think?

Your private chambers hear one thing; the public platform hears another [Col. 1695]. For the uneducated crowd cannot bear the burden of your secrets or take solid food, being content with the milk of infancy.

I have not yet written, and you threaten me with the thunderbolts of your replies, so that, terrified by this threat, I will not dare to open my mouth. You do not notice that we write for this very reason: so that you may be compelled to reply and at last openly say what, according to the time, the persons, and the places, you either speak or keep silent about.

I do not want it to be free for you to deny what you have once written. The victory belongs to the Church when you openly say what you think. For either you will answer with the same things that we are saying, and then you will not be opponents at all but friends; or, if you say things contrary to our doctrine, we shall win in this respect: everyone will learn what you think, and what the Church thinks. To expose your opinions is to overcome them.

Your blasphemy is evident at first glance. What is blasphemous by its own profession does not need to be convicted, etc.

The Eunomians, Arians, and Macedonians, separate in name but united in impiety, cause us no difficulty, for they speak what they think. This is the only heresy that is publicly ashamed to say what it does not fear to teach privately. The silence of the teachers is exposed by the fury of the disciples: what they heard in private rooms they proclaim from the rooftops. If what they say pleases their hearers, it is reported to the glory of the teachers; if it displeases them, the fault belongs to the disciple, not the teacher, etc.

**10.** No individual’s name is directly mentioned in this little work; we have spoken against the teacher of a perverse doctrine. If he becomes angry and replies, he will reveal himself like a mouse by his own evidence, while receiving still greater wounds in the true contest, etc.

Therefore, distinguished teacher, either defend what you have said and support the sharp points of your opinions with the eloquence that follows, so that, whenever it pleases you, you may not deny what you have said; or, if you have indeed erred as a human being, freely confess it and restore harmony among those who disagree.

Let it come to your mind that the Savior’s tunic was not torn apart even by the soldiers. You see quarrels among brothers, and you laugh and rejoice that some are called by your name and others by Christ’s. Imitate Jonah and say: “If this storm is on account of me, take me up and throw me into the sea” (Jonah 1:12), etc.

**11.** As for the fact that righteous people are called righteous in the Holy Scriptures—such as Zechariah and Elizabeth, Job, Jehoshaphat, and Josiah, and the many whose names form the fabric of Holy Scripture—although in the work I have promised I shall speak more fully, if the Lord grants me grace, for the present it is enough to have touched briefly upon this point: they are called righteous not because they are free from every fault, but because virtues predominate in them, etc.

**12.** Through the council of that holy and illustrious household I beg and admonish you: do not let one man—or, at most, three little men—take upon themselves the refuse of such great heresies, or, to put it more mildly, their disgrace; do not let the shamefulness of diabolical presumption and the foulest association exist where virtue and holiness were first praised.

Let those who supply resources to such men know that they are gathering a multitude of heretics, making enemies of Christ, and nourishing his adversaries. It is useless for them to profess one thing with their tongues when their hands prove that they think another.

## ON PELAGIUS

### Jerome, in the Preface to Book 1 on Jeremiah

Recently an unlearned slanderer came forward, who thinks that my commentaries on Paul’s Epistle to the Ephesians ought to be criticized. In his excessive and senseless stupidity he does not understand the laws governing commentaries, in which many opinions of different people are set forth, with the authors’ names either concealed or stated, so that it is left to the reader’s judgment to decide which he ought chiefly to select.

Although, in the preface to the first book of that same work, I stated that I would speak both my own words and those of others, and that the commentaries belonged as much to ancient writers as to us, his predecessor Grunnius [Note: [Col. 1695] Jerome commonly uses this name for Rufinus of Aquileia, distinguishing him from Rufinus the Syrian, who, according to Mercator in the *Commonitorium*, no. 2 above, col. 1681, was also Pelagius’s predecessor.] once tried to attack me for this, without understanding it.

I answered him in two books, and what this man now presents as his own has already been cleared up by another slanderer. I shall say nothing of the volumes against Jovinianus, in which he complains that virginity is preferred to marriage, marriage to remarriage, and remarriage to polygamy. The most foolish man, weighed down by the porridge of the Scots [Note: [Col. 1696] Pelagius is meant; below Jerome says that he had a Scottish ancestry from the vicinity of Britain. Paul Orosius, in *Apologeticus*, ch. 27, says of him: “Nourished on baths and banquets, you carry broad shoulders and a powerful neck, displaying even on your forehead a certain fatness.”], does not remember that I said in that very work:

“I do not condemn men married twice, nor even three times, or, if it could be, eight times. I will go further: I also admit the repentant fornicator. Whatever is equally permitted should be weighed in an equal balance.”

Let him read the apology in that same work, which Rome gladly undertook many years ago against his teacher; then he will realize that he blasphemes in the words of others, and is so ignorant that he does not even possess curses of his own, but uses against us the fury of enemies long since buried.

### The Same, Preface to Book 2 on Jeremiah

I am dictating the second book on Jeremiah, brother Eusebius, in rapid speech, turning my ears aside for a little so that we may not hear the judgment of blood or mourn the souls of those who have been slain—those who, in the opinion that they possess virtues, fall daily into pride and consider themselves like God, attributing to all human beings the equality that the impious heresy of the Arians denies to the Son; those who set their mouths against heaven and leave nothing further to the future blessedness of the saints.

We have answered their madness as best we could; and, if the Lord grants us life, we shall answer it more fully.

### The Same, Preface to Book 3 on Jeremiah

The devil has not allowed me, content with the rest I desired, to devote myself to explaining the Holy Scriptures and to transmit to people of my language the learning of the Hebrews and Greeks. Rather, day and night, openly and by treachery, he mixes falsehood with truth—or rather, he coats all his lies with deceptive honey—so that the one who hears the sweetness of his words will not fear the poison in his heart.

He promises peace in order to wage more grievous wars; he laughs in order to bite; he offers his hand in order unexpectedly to kill the innocent Abner. Surely this is what the Apostle also meant: “For we are not ignorant of his designs” (2 Cor. 2:11).

Here he is silent; elsewhere he accuses. He sends letters throughout the world—formerly golden, now full of curses—and interprets our patience, which comes from Christ’s humility, as a sign of a bad conscience. He himself remains mute but barks through Albinus the dog [Note: [Col. 1696] Printed editions have “Alpinus.” The old Cigirannian manuscript has “Albinus,” perhaps the same as “Briton,” since the island of Britain was once called Albion from its white cliffs], a large and corpulent man, more capable of raging with his heels than with his teeth. For he has Scottish ancestry, from the vicinity of Britain; and, according to the poets’ fables, he must be struck with a spiritual club like Cerberus, so that, together with his teacher Pluto, he may fall silent in eternal silence.

### The Same, Preface to Book 4 on Jeremiah

The devil always lies in wait for a good work and everywhere sets snares for those who proceed, etc.

Occupied by many crowds flowing here from the whole world and by the concerns of the holy brothers and the monastery, I dictated my commentaries on Jeremiah at intervals, so that what was lacking in leisure might be supplied by diligence. Suddenly the heresy of Pythagoras and Zeno—*ἀπάθεια καὶ ἀναμαρτησία* (*apatheia kai anamartēsia*), that is, “freedom from suffering and impeccancy”—which had once been slain in Origen and, more recently, in his disciples Grunnius, Evagrius of Pontus, and Jovinianus, began to revive. It began to hiss not only in the regions of the West but also in those of the East, and to stain many people in certain islands, especially Sicily and Rhodes, growing from day to day while its adherents teach it privately and deny it publicly.

After remaining silent for a long time and devouring my grief in silence, I was compelled by the repeated complaints of the brothers to answer it. Yet I have not proceeded so far as to give the authors’ names, preferring that they be corrected rather than disgraced.

For I am not an enemy of persons but of error. When they tried to inflict upon me the retaliation of like for like and the natural expression of their own pain, composing the old slanders of their teachers, they showed themselves so speechless and wretched that they could not even curse in their own words. Their lamentations were refuted at that time in books published against them. Whoever wishes to read those books will clearly see that, according to Isaiah, they are mute dogs who cannot bark (Isa. 56:10): they possess the will and the madness to lie, but not the skill to fabricate and bark.

I shall address them briefly:

“Either what you teach is good or it is evil. If it is good, defend it freely; if it is evil, why do you secretly slaughter wretched people through error and, by an exposition of the true faith, nourish them to deceive the simple?” [Note: [Col. 1697] So the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “and by an exposition of the true faith you cast them forth.”]

If it is true, why is it concealed? If it is false, why is it written? I ask: what madness is this? The Apostle commands us to be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks for an account of the hope that is in us (1 Pet. 3:15); and the prophet cries out: “I spoke of your testimonies in the presence of kings, and I was not ashamed” (Ps. 118:46). These people flee the public and whisper in the corners of the lost; they grieve as though for doctrines that are their own, which they fear to confess as their own.

When we speak generally against vices and heretics, they complain that they are being attacked; and, after concealing their indignation for a long time, they proclaim the evil of their conscience. If we must beware of appearing to injure an old relationship, even while cutting down a most arrogant heresy with the spiritual sword, then we shall have to endure crosses for the betrayed faith and say with the prophet: “I was caught in misery while the thorn was being fixed in me” (Ps. 31:4).

Rather, let them hear the apostolic saying: “We must obey God rather than human beings” (Acts 5:29); and again: “If I were pleasing human beings, I would not be Christ’s servant” (Gal. 1:10). But we shall treat these matters more fully in the work itself, unless they keep silent.

## ON THE JERUSALEM COUNCIL HELD IN THE CASE OF PELAGIUS BY BISHOP JOHN AT THE END OF JULY, A.D. 415

[Note: [Col. 1697] Augustine mentions this council, held before John, bishop of Jerusalem, before the Synod of Diospolis, in *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*. It belongs to the year 415, when Paul Orosius, summoned to the council itself, arrived in Palestine during the spring season. Below Orosius specifies the day of the council as the forty-seventh before the first day of the Encaenia; that day of the Encaenia was 14 September, according to Nicephorus, *History*, book 8, ch. 50.]

### From the *Apologeticus* of Paul Orosius, chapters 2–4

**1.** I am obliged to make known the injury that I have suffered, so that what they have done may be manifest to all. For it is both God’s will and his ordering that the evil which had been endured patiently should necessarily be exposed, and that, when by the contention of their fury they receive the fitting recompense their error deserves, there should be made known not only their most wicked doctrines but also the persons who must be reproved.

For the fathers, the martyrs who have now entered into rest, and the concordant [Note: [Col. 1697] Perhaps, “confessors.”] men—Cyprian, Hilary, and Ambrose—and those for whom it is still necessary to remain in the flesh, who are pillars and foundations of the Catholic Church—Aurelius, Augustine, and Jerome—have already published many most authoritative writings against this wicked heresy, without naming the heretics. Yet this abomination of most venomous doctrines has even now living dead and dead living. For Origen, Priscillian, and Jovinian, long dead among their own people, live in these men; and they not only live, but even speak.

But now Pelagius and Celestius, if they persevere in these teachings, are living dead. Behold: against the Church—what is miserable—and, what is far more miserable, openly within the Church, they hiss. The impious serpents, licking their infected mouths with quivering tongues while besieging the holy and most strongly fortified see to which they have subtly crept, terrify all the faithful lest we fly to that once most secure refuge in Zion. For the stench of their mouths spreads poison far and wide, turning into death for all those for whom it had been the fragrance of life unto life.

Against this serpent and its suffocating breath, the most blessed men whom I have mentioned prepare many fragrant ointments from the manifold sweetness of the Scriptures, and, to refresh the hearts of the people who are burning with distress, kindle the most fragrant incense with the offering of prayer. But it is too little to contend against an almost unknown author and to moderate the air infected by its pestilential breath merely by setting contraries against contraries, unless the serpents themselves are dragged into the open and trampled down.

When they expose the rest of their body to mutilation and injury solely to protect the head, they think that they have suffered no loss, provided that only that part of themselves which contains within it many and poisonous tongues is free from danger—even if all their limbs are cut off. It seems enough to us merely to counteract the stench; but we do not remove them from their inner recesses, as though there could be any end to the foul exhalation unless its source were ended. And here Solomon’s testimony comes to mind: “One builds and another destroys: what profit have they except toil?” (Ecclus. 34:28).

The monstrous Goliath of pride also stands there, swollen with fleshly power, confident that he can do everything by himself; armed with much equipment upon head, hands, and indeed his whole body, and having his armor-bearer behind him. Though the latter does not himself fight, he nevertheless furnishes every kind of support of bronze and iron. Nor is it surprising that Scripture, foreseeing this place aptly, declares: “The Philistines stood on the mountain on this side” (1 Sam. 17:3). For the opponent of heresy is expelled from the Church, while a heretic is found being nourished in the bosom of the Church; and therefore the Holy Spirit declares that Israel stands on one side, the enemy on the other. And this happens often. Thus King David, a pious father even toward his impious son, is driven from Jerusalem, having laid aside the royal garb; and immediately afterward the tyrant Absalom enters it.

Therefore Goliath stands, alas, on this side—that is, in the Church—and not only stands, but challenges; and for many days at once reproaches holy Israel for its manifest fear.

**2.** I beg you, most blessed priests, let no one suppose that, under the pretext of Goliath’s appearance, I am glorying in David’s name. You wished me to share in your contest, so that I might come as a helper, not as an author. For I was lying hidden in Bethlehem, unknown, a stranger, and poor. Why does wretched I speak thus—perhaps once more to be charged with boasting? Because David too was such a man and came forth from there.

I was therefore hiding in Bethlehem, entrusted by Father Augustine, that I might learn the fear of the Lord, sitting at Jerome’s feet. From there I came to Jerusalem when summoned by you. Then, at Bishop John’s command, I sat with you in your council. Immediately all of you asked my insignificance to state faithfully and simply whether I knew of anything that had occurred in Africa concerning this heresy which Pelagius and Celestius had sown.

I briefly explained to your assembly, as best I could, that Celestius, already stealthily making his way toward the honor of the presbyterate, had at Carthage been exposed, heard, convicted, made to confess, and condemned by many bishops sitting in judgment, and had fled from Africa after being detested by the Church. I also stated that blessed Augustine had replied most fully against Pelagius’s book, after Pelagius’s own disciples had disclosed it and requested a response [Note: [Col. 1698] Timasius and James.]. I further said that I had in my hands a letter of the aforesaid bishop, recently composed for Sicily, in which he set forth many questions of the heretics [Note: [Col. 1698] Augustine, Epistle 157, to Hilary of Syracuse.]. You also directed me to read it there, and I read it.

After this Bishop John requested that Pelagius be brought in to appear before us. Out of reverence for his episcopal office and for the usefulness of the proceeding, since you thought that he could more properly be refuted by the bishop while present, permission was granted for him to be brought in. Once Pelagius had entered, all of you unanimously asked whether he acknowledged that he had taught the things to which Bishop Augustine had replied. He immediately answered: “And who is Augustine to me?”

When everyone cried out that he was blaspheming a bishop through whose mouth the Lord had granted healing to the unity of all Africa, and that he ought to be expelled not only from that council but from the whole Church, Bishop John immediately ordered the man—a layman sitting among presbyters, accused of manifest heresy—to remain seated in the midst of Catholics; then he said, “I am Augustine.” By assuming, as it were, the person of the bishop who was present, he could more freely grant pardon on the authority of the person who had been injured and calm the agitated minds.

We immediately said to him: “If you assume Augustine’s person, follow Augustine’s judgment.” Then the same bishop said to us all: “Are the things being read said against other persons, or do you think that an accusation ought to be made against Pelagius? State, then, what you have to say against Pelagius himself.” With your approval I said: “Pelagius told me that he teaches: ‘A human being can be without sin and can easily keep God’s commandments, if he wishes.’” Pelagius replied, as you heard: “I cannot deny that I both said this and say it.”

I immediately continued: “This is what the African synod condemned in Celestius; this is what Bishop Augustine rejected in horror in his writings, as you have heard; this is what he condemns in Pelagius’s present writings by his reply to them; and this is what blessed Jerome—whose utterance the whole West awaits as dew upon the fleece, for many heretics and their doctrines have already been overthrown while he attacked them—condemned in the letter which he recently published to Ctesiphon [Note: [Col. 1699] In a German manuscript, ‘Tesiphon.’]. Likewise, he refutes it in the book he is now writing, in the form of a dialogue presenting a controversy. For this is to hold the dragon on a slippery hook, lest it escape” (Job 40:19, according to the Septuagint).

**3.** Bishop John, however, hearing none of this, attempted to require us to acknowledge ourselves as accusers, with him as judge. Everyone repeatedly answered: “We are not this man’s accusers. Rather, we are reporting what your brothers, our fathers, have thought and decreed concerning this heresy which a layman now preaches publicly, lest it disturb your Church without your knowledge—especially the Church to whose bosom we have fled.”

But he repeatedly tried, under the pretense of teaching us, to induce us to make some profession, saying that the Lord had said to Abraham: “Walk before me and be without blemish” (Gen. 17:1); and that Zechariah and Elizabeth had both been declared righteous before the Lord, “walking blamelessly in all the commandments of the Lord” (Luke 1:6). It was known to many of us that this had been said by Origen and was being advanced by John.

I replied: “We are sons of the Catholic Church. Father, do not require us to dare to be teachers above teachers or judges above judges. The fathers whom the Church throughout the world approves, and to whose communion you rejoice to adhere [Note: [Col. 1699] Perhaps, ‘we.’ Or immediately below, ‘we rejoice.’], have decreed that these doctrines are condemnable. Since they approve this judgment, it is fitting for us to obey. Why do you ask the children what they think when you hear what the fathers decide?”

After he had argued for a long time—and because of the incompetence of an interpreter unknown to us, whom the most eminent and devout men, the presbyters Passerius and Avitus and Dominus the former military commander, repeatedly refuted as either mistranslating, suppressing much, or presenting one thing in place of another—our proceedings were, as I have said, very often either altered or left unspoken. Bishop John said: “If Pelagius said that a human being could do this without God’s help, it would be most wicked and condemnable; but now that he adds, ‘A human being can be without sin, not without God’s help,’ what do you say? Do you perhaps deny God’s help?”

I replied: “With you and the above-mentioned men as witnesses, both bearing witness now and previously: anathema to anyone who denies God’s help. I certainly do not deny it, especially since I have refuted the heretics on the opposite side.” Then, when we cried out that the heretic was a Latin-speaker, that we were Latin-speakers, and that a heresy better known in Latin regions should be reserved for Latin judges, and when he almost shamelessly put himself forward to judge, although we were not accusers and only one person was suspect, many had to say: “No one can be at once a heretic, an advocate, and a judge.”

After many other matters had been transacted, Bishop John delivered his final judgment, at last confirming our petition and purpose: brothers and letters were to be sent to blessed Innocent, pope of Rome, and everyone would follow whatever he decided. We all agreed to this decision: that the heretic Pelagius should thereafter fall silent under the silence imposed upon him, and that our party should moderate its attacks upon the convicted and confounded John. After thanksgiving had been celebrated, peace made, and prayer completed as a testimony of peace, we departed.

### 4.

Now, forty-seven days later, when, on the first day of the Encaenia, as was my custom whenever I was present, I had hurried to attend Bishop John, I immediately received from him, instead of a greeting, the mark of a false accusation [Note: [Col. 1700] The German manuscript reads, “of the Savior.”]. For he said to me: “Why do you come to me, you who have blasphemed?” He apparently wished it to be understood: “Do not touch me, because I am clean and without sin” (Isaiah 65:5).

But, conscious of nothing, I asked when, in whose hearing, or in what form I had said anything that could be charged as blasphemy. The bishop replied: “I heard you say that a person cannot be without sin even with God’s help.”

I, most blessed priests—and you yourselves are witnesses, as are the whole brotherhood and, in addition, the holy men who, out of love for truth, support this testimony—immediately testified, saying that such a statement as the bishop now intended to attribute to me had never previously come from my mouth. Yet, by repeatedly rehearsing this incontinent piece of wretched falsehood through frequent explanation, I seem less to have approved it than to have exposed someone else.

For I grant that, whatever the statement may have been, I said it: how, then, did a Greek unfamiliar with Latin hear it, when he did not understand Latin? Or, if he heard a sacrilegious statement, why did he not immediately refute the blasphemer, or, acting more gently, admonish an unwary son, as a devout father would, to restrain the license of dangerous speech? Instead, after an extremely long lapse of memory, he himself brought the accusation, he himself gave the testimony, and he himself pronounced the judgment, taking upon the authority of his own person all the functions of every crime—especially since he had been carefully instructed by the Gospel reading that our Lord Jesus was not condemned without the testimony of a ruler.

On one side my brothers stood beside me, and on the other, false brothers. In the same assembly, the presbyters Avitus and Vitalis were seated on one side with me; on the other was some unknown interpreter, and then the men approved both by the world and by God, the presbyter Passerius and Dominus, formerly a military commander. Both of these had been summoned and brought from your company, at the bishop John’s request, so that, in accordance with their experience and faith, they might serve as interpreters.

You yourself were also present in the middle. In those circumstances it is no less astonishing that you heard than that you saw how a speech, released among so many opponents, colleagues, and hearers, passed them all by and entered the unknowing ears of a knowledgeable listener.

But I am being driven on by the heat of truth [Note: [Col. 1700] The same manuscript omits “of truth.”], and I am exceeding the limits of my formal statement. It is more reasonable to grant that the interpreter erred in speaking than to suppose that the bishop invented the matter in hearing it; and now, in order to demand the reward he deserves for the service he rendered to the heretics [Col. 1701], he is seeking false witnesses to support him.

## The Teachings of Pelagius Are Presented under the Name of Critobolus and Examined by Atticus, Who Is Advocating the Catholic Cause

From Jerome’s first dialogue against the Pelagians [Note: [Col. 1701] Orosius, in the *Apology* above, col. 1699, no. 2, near the end, praises Jerome as occupied at that time with writing this work, that is, in the year of Christ 415.]

**ATTICUS.** Tell me, Critobolus: is it true that I hear you have written, “A person can be without sin if he wishes, and God’s commandments are easy”?

**CRITOBOLUS.** It is true, and so forth. I said that a person can be without sin if he wishes—not, as certain slanderers falsely accuse, without the grace of God, for even to think that would be sacrilegious; but simply that he can, if he wishes, with the implication “with God’s grace,” and so forth. Anyone who removes God’s grace is mistaken; indeed, he should be judged impious, since everything is governed by God’s will, and the fact that we exist, possess free choice, and have the inclination of our own will is a benefit of God the Creator. For it is by the grace of the one who created us in his image and likeness that we possess free choice and, by our own will, incline either toward good or toward evil.

**ATTICUS.** But I ask whether you refer this very thing, which you attribute to God’s grace, to the benefit of our creation, or whether you think that it is present in each individual action we perform, and so forth.

**CRITOBOLUS.** I say both: that it is due to God’s grace that we were created as we are, and that in each individual action we are supported by his assistance.

**ATTICUS.** Then those who remove God’s help from each individual action we perform think wrongly, and so forth.

**CRITOBOLUS.** If God’s help must be used in each individual action we perform, then we shall not be able, unless God helps us, either to sharpen a pen for writing, rub the sharpened pen with pumice, and adapt the hand to letters, or to be silent, speak, sit, stand, walk, run, eat, fast, weep, laugh, and perform other things of this kind, and so forth. In what, then, do we have free choice, and how is God’s grace preserved toward us, if we cannot even do this without God?

**ATTICUS.** Was the grace of free choice given in such a way that God’s assistance is removed from each individual action?

**CRITOBOLUS.** God’s help is not removed when the grace of free choice once given to the creature is preserved [Note: [Col. 1701] Another version reads: “when the creature is preserved by . . . grace.”]. For if, without God, and unless he helps me in every particular, I can do nothing, then he will neither justly crown me for good works nor punish me for evil ones; rather, in both cases he will either accept or condemn his own assistance, and so forth. Just as the order of creation is preserved in the other creatures, so, once the power of free choice has been granted, everything has been left to our will, and so forth.

**ATTICUS.** Tell me, if you please: when you said a little earlier, with God’s help, that a person can avoid sin if he wishes, do you mean that he can avoid sin perpetually or only for a short time?

**CRITOBOLUS.** I maintain that whoever can abstain from sin for one day can do so for another; whoever can do so for two days can do so for three; whoever can do so for three can do so for thirty; and in this way he can do so for three hundred days, for three thousand, and for as long as he wishes to keep watch over himself [Note: [Col. 1701] Another version reads “abstain.”].

**ATTICUS.** How is it that, although I wish and earnestly desire not to sin, I nevertheless fall into sin?

**CRITOBOLUS.** Because your will is imperfect. If you truly wished it, you certainly would not sin.

**ATTICUS.** Then, since you accuse me of not truly desiring it, are you without sin because you truly desire it?

**CRITOBOLUS.** As though I were speaking about myself, whom I confess to be a sinner, rather than about the few and rare persons who may wish not to sin.

**ATTICUS.** How, then, is it that, although both of us wish the same thing, neither of us can achieve it?

**CRITOBOLUS.** Because we do not wish it fully.

[Col. 1702]

**ATTICUS.** Then produce those among our ancestors who wished it fully and were able to achieve it.

**CRITOBOLUS.** That is not easy to demonstrate. For when I say that a person can be without sin if he wishes, I am not asserting that anyone has actually been so; I am simply saying that it is possible if he wishes. For it is one thing to be able to be, which in Greek is called *dynamis* (δύναμις), and another to be in actuality, which they call *energeia* (ἐνέργεια). I may be able to be a physician, but meanwhile I am not one; I may be able to be a craftsman, but I have not yet learned the trade. Whatever, therefore, I can be—even if I am not yet so—I will be if I wish, and so forth.

I ask you to answer this: did God give commandments that are possible or impossible? And so forth. When the Lord says, “If you wish to be perfect, sell everything you have and give to the poor; then come, follow me” (Matthew 19:21), he shows that a person, if he wishes and does what has been commanded, can be perfect, and so forth.

Are you not silenced by these two testimonies in which Job, and Zachariah and Elizabeth, are praised? And so forth. If Job is “a true worshiper of God, blameless and without fault” (Job 1:1), and if Zachariah and Elizabeth, “walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord,” are “righteous in his sight” (Luke 1:6), I think that they are without sin and lack nothing pertaining to righteousness, and so forth.

What will you answer to the example given by the evangelist John? “We know that everyone who is born of God does not sin” (1 John 5:18), and so forth.

Moses says to the people: “Be perfect before the Lord your God” (Deuteronomy 18:13). And the Savior says to the Apostles: “Be perfect, just as your heavenly Father is perfect” (Matthew 5:48). Either it is possible for those who hear to do what Moses and the Lord commanded, or, if it is impossible, those who cannot obey are not at fault, but the one who commanded the impossible is.

Nor am I comparing a human being with God, but with other human beings, in comparison with whom a person who applies himself can be perfect. Accordingly, when it is said, “A person can be without sin if he wishes,” this is said according to the measure of humanity, not according to the majesty of God, in comparison with which no creature can be perfect.

**ATTICUS.** I too hold that no creature can be perfect according to true and complete righteousness. Nevertheless, there is no doubt that one person differs from another [Note: [Col. 1702] Another version reads “from another person.”], and that human beings possess different kinds of righteousness, and so forth.

**CRITOBOLUS.** How, then, Atticus, does the divine word summon us to perfection?

**ATTICUS.** In the manner I explained: so that, according to our strength, each person may extend himself as far as he is able, and, if somehow possible, may reach and grasp the prize of the heavenly calling, and so forth. As long as we possess this treasure in earthen vessels and are surrounded by fragile flesh—indeed, by mortal and corruptible flesh—we consider ourselves blessed if in each virtue and in each part of virtue we are subject to God. But when this mortal nature has put on immortality, and so forth [Note: The printed text has “6,” apparently referring to a continuation or chapter division], then God will be all in all. Wisdom will no longer be found only in Solomon, gentleness of spirit in David, zeal in Elijah and Phinehas, faith in Abraham, perfect love in Peter, to whom it was said, “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” (John 21:15), and zeal for preaching in the Chosen Vessel [Paul], with other virtues distributed two or three at a time. Rather, he will be wholly present in all, the entire number of the saints will rejoice in the whole choir of virtues, and God will be all in all.

**CRITOBOLUS.** Then no saint, as long as he is in this little body, can possess all the virtues? And so forth. How, then, do we read that whoever possesses one virtue possesses all virtues?

**ATTICUS.** By participation, not by possession as one’s own. For it is necessary that individuals excel in particular virtues. Yet I do not know where the statement you say you have read is written.

**CRITOBOLUS.** Do you not know that this is a philosophical doctrine?

[Col. 1703]

**ATTICUS.** But it is not an apostolic doctrine. I am not concerned with what Aristotle teaches, but with what Paul teaches.

**CRITOBOLUS.** I beg you: does not the Apostle James write, “Whoever offends in one point is guilty of all” (James 2:10)? And so forth. Grant that no saint possesses all the virtues; surely you will grant this: in the matter that a person can do, if he does it, he is perfect.

**ATTICUS.** Do you not remember what I said above?

**CRITOBOLUS.** What was that?

**ATTICUS.** A person is perfect in what he has done and imperfect in what he has been unable to do.

**CRITOBOLUS.** But just as he is perfect in what he has done, because he wished to do it, so also, in that by which he is imperfect because he did not do it, he could have been perfect if he had wished to do it, and so forth. You persist excessively in one and the same question, as though trying to persuade us that a person cannot possess everything simultaneously—as if God either begrudged his image and likeness, or were unable to grant that it should correspond in all things to its Creator, and so forth.

**ATTICUS.** If I am not mistaken, the answer concerning possible commandments has been postponed. Set it out, then, as you wish.

**CRITOBOLUS.** Either God gave possible commandments or impossible ones. If they are possible, it lies within our power to do them if we wish; if they are impossible, we are not guilty even if we do not do what we cannot fulfill. Accordingly, whether God gave possible commandments or impossible ones, a person can be without sin if he wishes, and so forth.

If a person cannot be without sin, how does the Apostle Jude write: “To him who is able to preserve you without sin and to set you blameless before the presence of his glory” (Jude 24)? And so forth. I am not saying that a person is without sin, which may perhaps seem impossible to you; I am saying that he can be without sin if he wishes. For it is one thing to be, and another to be able. Being requires an example; ability demonstrates the truth of power, and so forth.

**ATTICUS.** I would like to examine your statements briefly, so that your followers may understand what divine intellect they admire in you. You say, “No one can be without sin except the person who has acquired knowledge of the law.” By this you exclude a large part of Christians from righteousness; and, although you are a preacher of sinlessness, you pronounce almost everyone to be a sinner, and so forth.

Yet you are so generous that you win favor among your Amazons by writing elsewhere, “Women too ought to possess knowledge of the law,” although the Apostle says that women must be silent in the church (1 Timothy 2:12), and so forth.

Nor is it enough for you to have given your troop knowledge of the Scriptures unless you also delight in their voices and songs. For you add and place in the title, “That women too ought to sing psalms to God.” Who does not know that women ought to sing psalms in their own bedrooms, without the presence of men and the gathering of crowds? And so forth.

[Note: [Col. 1703] Here the printed editions add “under the fourteenth title.” They also add elsewhere other title numbers, which we refer to below among the variant readings, because they are absent from the ancient Corbie manuscript.]

You further add, “A servant of God ought to utter nothing bitter from his mouth, but always what is sweet and pleasant.” And, as though the servant of God were one person and the teacher and priest of the Church another, forgetting your earlier statement, you place under another title [Note: [Col. 1703] Here the printed editions add “under the twenty-second title”]: “A priest or teacher ought to observe everyone’s actions and correct sinners confidently, lest he have to give an account for them and their blood be required from his hands.””

Nor are you content to have said this once; you repeat and reinforce the same point [Note: [Col. 1703] Here the printed editions add “under the thirty-first title”]: “A priest or teacher ought to flatter no one, but correct everyone boldly, lest he destroy both himself and those who hear him,” and so forth.

But as for what you set down elsewhere, “Everyone is governed by his own will”—which Christian could hear it? And so forth. By this statement you rashly remove all God’s protection; and from this passage it is clear how you wish the phrase you unsuccessfully try to add elsewhere, “not without God’s grace,” to be understood, since you refer his grace not to each individual action but to the power of creation, the law, and free choice.

[Col. 1704] [Note: [Col. 1704] Here the printed editions add “under the seventy-second title.”]

As for what you put in the following chapter, “On the day of judgment the wicked and sinners must not be spared, but must be consumed by eternal fires”—who could endure this? You prohibit God’s mercy and, before the day of judgment, judge the Judge’s sentence, so that, if he wishes to spare the wicked and sinners, he may not do so because you have issued your prior ruling.

For you say: “It is written in the 103rd Psalm, ‘Let sinners vanish from the earth and the wicked be no more’ (Psalm 103:35). And in Isaiah, ‘The wicked and sinners shall be burned together, and those who have forsaken the Lord shall be consumed’” (Isaiah 1:28).

Do you not understand that God’s threat sometimes conveys mercy? For he does not say that they are to be burned by eternal fires, but that they are to vanish from the earth and cease to be wicked, and so forth.

But if Origen says that all rational creatures are not to be destroyed and attributes repentance even to the devil, what has that to do with us? We say that the devil, all his minions, and all the impious and transgressors perish forever; but that Christians, if overtaken in sin, are to be saved after punishment.

[Note: [Col. 1704] Here the printed editions add “under the twenty-first title.”]

You further join together two chapters that contradict one another. If they are true, you will not be able to open your mouth: “No one can know wisdom and the meaning of the Scriptures unless he has learned them” [Note: [Col. 1704] Here the printed editions add “under the twentieth title”], and again, “An uneducated person ought not to usurp knowledge of the law,” and so forth.

Nor is this enough. Suddenly you become a Stoic, and thunder to us from Zeno’s lofty brow [Note: [Col. 1704] Here the printed editions add “under the seventy-third title”]: “A Christian ought to possess such patience that, if anyone wishes to take away his property, he willingly gives it up,” and so forth.

You add, “The splendor of clothing and ornaments is contrary to God.” What, I ask, is hostile to God if I have a cleaner tunic? What if a bishop, presbyter, deacon, and the rest of the ecclesiastical order proceed to administer the sacrifices in white clothing? And so forth.

[Note: [Col. 1704] Here the printed editions add “under the one-hundred-sixty-fourth title.”]

Let us hear the rest. “Enemies are to be loved as neighbors.” Immediately, as though overcome by a profound lethargy, you set down and say [Note: [Col. 1704] Here the printed editions add “under the one-hundred-sixty-first title”]: “An enemy must never be trusted.” That this contradicts the former statement is obvious even without my saying so, and so forth.

[Note: [Col. 1704] Here the printed editions add “under the one-hundred-twenty-third title.”]

You further add, “The kingdom of heaven was also promised in the Old Testament,” and you produce testimonies from apocryphal writings, although it is clear that the kingdom of heaven was first preached in the Gospel by John the Baptist, the Lord and Savior, and the Apostles, and so forth.

Yet you call us Manichaeans because, preferring the Gospel to the Law, we say that in the latter there is shadow and in the former truth, and so forth.

The hundredth title is: “A person can be without sin and can easily keep God’s commandments if he wishes.” This has been discussed sufficiently. Although he admits that he is an imitator—or rather, a completer—of the work of the blessed martyr Cyprian, who wrote to Quirinus, he does not realize that in that work Cyprian said things contrary to him.

For in the fifty-fourth title of the third book Cyprian writes: “No one is without stain and without sin” [Note: [Col. 1704] The printed editions read “can be without stain and without sin.” The word “can be” is absent from the Corbie manuscript], and so forth. You, by contrast, assert, “A person can be without sin,” and so forth.

And, to enlarge upon this and display the greatness of your virtue—so that you may be thought to pour forth words from the good treasury of your conscience—you place under a title [Note: [Col. 1704] The printed editions add “under the one-hundred-twenty-third title”]: “One must not sin even lightly.”

And what do you mean by “lightly”? Lest anyone think that you said this only in connection with an action, you append [Note: [Col. 1704] Here the printed editions add “under the one-hundred-thirty-first title”]: “Evil must not even be conceived.”

Nor do you remember the statement: “Who understands his offenses? Cleanse me from my hidden faults, Lord, and spare your servant from the sins of others” (Psalm 18:13–14). The Church even acknowledges as offenses those things in which we sin through ignorance and sin merely in thought, to such an extent that it commands sacrifices to be offered for error, and so forth.

**CRITOBOLUS.** I ask you: have you not read, “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matthew 5:28)? Therefore, it is not only the sight and the incentives to vice that are counted as sin, but also the things to which we give our assent. Either we can avoid an evil thought, and consequently we can be free from sin; or, if we cannot avoid it, what cannot be avoided is not counted as sin.

## From Jerome’s Second Dialogue against the Pelagians

**CRITOBOLUS.** You have indeed recalled many passages from the holy Scriptures, abundantly and from memory, and so forth. But what does this have to do with the matter? By all these testimonies you seem to accuse human nature and thereby to direct blame toward God, if he created human beings such that they cannot be free from forgetfulness, ignorance, and sin.

From this it is obvious that a person can refrain from sin if he wishes. For he did what he could not avoid. But when possibility is removed, fault is removed as well. No one is condemned for something he could not do, and so forth.

Give me a testimony from the New Testament in which error, ignorance, and inability to fulfill a command are held to be culpable.

**ATTICUS.** The Chosen Vessel speaks plainly: “I consent to the law of God according to the inner person; but I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin that is in my members. Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God, through Jesus Christ our Lord.”

**CRITOBOLUS.** You have produced testimony that supports my case. Therefore, once we have been freed from this body of death through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, we ought no longer to sin.

**ATTICUS.** We have indeed been freed by the Savior’s Baptism [Note: [Col. 1705] The Corbie manuscript reads “saving Baptism.”]. But explain to me why he said, “I see another law in my members,” and so forth. Hear the same Apostle preaching most clearly: “What I do, I do not understand; for I do not do what I wish, but I do the very thing I hate” (Romans 7:22–25, 15), and so forth.

**CRITOBOLUS.** I am surprised that, being a prudent man, you understand the Apostle in such a way that you think he is speaking in his own person rather than in the person of others, and so forth. Therefore, he is not speaking in his own person, but in the person of the human race, which is subject to vices because of the weakness of the flesh—in the person of the sinner.

**ATTICUS.** And who will grant you that the Apostle speaks in the person of the sinner?

**CRITOBOLUS.** At least you will grant me that many people are called righteous in the Scriptures.

**ATTICUS.** Not merely many, but countless people.

**CRITOBOLUS.** If countless people are righteous—and this cannot be denied—what evil have I said in asserting that a person can be without sin if he wishes?

**ATTICUS.** I grant that they are righteous; but I do not agree that they are completely without every kind of sin. For I say that a person can be without fault, which in Greek is called *kakia* (κακία), but I deny that he can be *anamartētos* (ἀναμάρτητος), that is, without sin. That belongs to God alone [Note: [Col. 1705] The same Corbie manuscript reads: “which in Greek is called *anamartētos*, belongs to God alone,” omitting the intervening words]. Every creature is subject to sin and needs God’s mercy, as Scripture says: “The earth is full of the mercy of the Lord” (Psalm 32:5), and so forth.

I pass over that ridiculous interpretation of your Demosthenes: “Job did not say, ‘Who will be clean from sin?’ but ‘Who is clean from filth?’” (Job 14:4, according to the Septuagint). By this he attempts to prove that “the filth of clothing is signified in infancy, not the vices of sinners.” Or, if he does not understand it in this way, tell us what he does mean.

For he is such an obscure speaker, and so covered with the excessive squalor of his words, that he offers the reader suspicion rather than understanding, and so forth.

Answer me, I ask: where are the easy commandments? “Do not be anxious,” he says, “about tomorrow,” and so forth (Matthew 6:34). Do you not think about tomorrow, and are you content, like birds, with what is present? Your letters, written on papyrus, fly across the rivers of Ethiopia, so that new gifts from Ophir may be sent to Solomon among monkeys and peacocks, and so forth.

Jesus, son of Josedec, whose name is interpreted as “Righteous of the Lord,” the high priest, is described as clothed in filthy garments, and so forth. After the struggle and victory, it is said to him: “Take the filthy garments away from him”; and, “See, I have taken your iniquity away from you” (Zechariah 3:3–4).

And the heir of Jovinian speaks: “I am entirely without every kind of sin; I have no filthy garments; I am governed by my own free choice; I am greater than the Apostle. He does what he does not wish, and does not do what he wishes; I do what I wish, and do not do what I do not wish. The kingdoms of heaven have been prepared for me—or rather, I myself have prepared them for myself by my virtues.

“Adam is held guilty, as are the others who consider themselves guilty in the likeness of Adam’s transgression; but I alone, with my company, am not held guilty. Others, shut up in their cells and not seeing women, are tortured by desires because they are wretched and do not hear my words. But even if I were surrounded by troops of women, I would have no desire. For it has been said of me, ‘Holy stones roll upon the earth’ (Zechariah 9:16, according to the Septuagint). Therefore I feel nothing, because by the power of free choice I carry the trophies of Christ,” and so forth.

As for what Daniel says in his prayer—“We have sinned, we have acted wickedly, we have behaved unjustly, and we have departed from your commandments and ordinances,” and other statements of this kind—you are accustomed to say that Daniel and all the prophets spoke not on their own behalf, since they were holy, but in the person of the people.

Against this opinion he himself will answer and say: “While I was still praying and confessing my sins and the sins of my people Israel” (Daniel 9:5, 20), and so forth.

You ask where Abel, Enoch, Jesus son of Nun, Elisha, and the other saints sinned. There is no need to search for a knot in a reed; if only I could remain silent even about manifest sins, and so forth.

## From the Third Dialogue of the Same Author

**CRITOBOLUS.** Surely you will admit this: those who have received Christ’s Baptism do not have sin; and if they are without sin, they are righteous; and once they have become righteous, if they act carefully, they can preserve righteousness forever and thus avoid every sin.

**ATTICUS.** Are you not ashamed to repeat the rejected and condemned doctrine of Jovinian? For he too relies upon these testimonies and upon your arguments. Indeed, you follow his inventions, wishing to teach in the East what was long ago condemned at Rome and more recently in Africa, and so forth.

**CRITOBOLUS.** Then commandments are given in vain if we cannot fulfill them, and so forth. Argue as you please: you will never wrest from me the free choice that God once granted; nor will you be able to take away the capacity he gave me, if I wish, to do what is commanded, and so forth.

Your entire argument comes down to this: you accuse nature and attribute the blame to God, who created nature in this way, and so forth. I grieve that ecclesiastical men, those who arrogate to themselves the title of teachers, remove free choice; for once it is removed, the sect of the Manichaeans is established, and so forth.

**ATTICUS.** It has been established by a long discussion that the Lord, by his grace—which granted us free choice—helps and sustains us in every individual action, and so forth.

**CRITOBOLUS.** Then, if we did not do what he commanded, either God wished to help us or he did not. If he wished to help us and did help us, and yet we did what we did not wish to do, it was not we but he who was overcome. But if he did not wish to help us, the fault lies not with the one who wished to do what was right, but with the one who could have helped and did not wish to do so.

**ATTICUS.** You do not understand that your dilemma plunges into a great abyss of blasphemy, so that on either side God is either powerless or envious. It would then be no more to his praise that he is the author and helper of good things than to his blame that he did not restrain evil, and so forth.

**CRITOBOLUS.** Your entire argument aims at this: to attribute the word to what the Greeks call *autexousion* (αὐτεξούσιον), which we call free choice, while removing the reality it signifies. For you make God the author of sins when you assert that a human being can do nothing by himself, but only with God’s assistance, so that everything we do is to be attributed to God, and so forth.

[Col. 1707]

**ATTICUS.** In this way, even if he does not help, he will nevertheless, according to your reasoning, be the author of evil, because he was able to prevent it and did not prevent it, and so forth.

**CRITOBOLUS.** It is evident that your argument does not proceed from the sources of truth and Christian simplicity, but from the subtle distinctions and technique of the philosophers.

**ATTICUS.** Do you want me, then, to use the testimonies of Scripture again? And what becomes of the boasts of your disciples that no one can answer your arguments and problems?

**CRITOBOLUS.** Grant that no one could avoid every sin in childhood, adolescence, or youth. Can you deny that many righteous and holy men, after their vices, devoted themselves wholeheartedly to virtues and through these became free from sin? And why are we summoned in the holy Scriptures to perfect righteousness? And so forth.

**ATTICUS.** If the person who is still walking on the road and proceeding according to the law is blameless and perfect, what more will the person possess who has reached the end of the road and of the law? And so forth.

You deserve to hear the words addressed to the Corinthians: “You are already perfect; you have already become rich,” and so forth.

From this swelling of pride there also bursts forth that boldness in prayer with which, when writing to a widow, you declare how the saints ought to pray:

“For he,” you say, “raises his hands to God with good reason and pours forth prayers with a good conscience who can say: ‘You know, Lord, how holy, how innocent, how pure from every deceit, injustice, and robbery are the hands that I extend toward you; how just and immaculate, how free from every lie, are the lips with which I pour forth prayers to you, asking you to have mercy upon me.’”

Is this the prayer of a Christian or of a Pharisee boasting? And so forth.

Flattering the same widow, you are not ashamed to say that piety, nowhere to be found on earth, and truth, everywhere an exile, dwell especially in her, and so forth. You praise her with words attributed to God and say:

“O exceedingly happy woman, O blessed woman, if the righteousness that is now believed to exist only in heaven is found in you alone on earth!”

Is this teaching or killing? And so forth.

You and your disciples habitually swear that these two passages of prayer and praise are not yours. Yet the brilliance of your style clearly shines through them, and such is the beauty of their Ciceronian eloquence that, proceeding at a tortoise’s pace, you do not dare publicly to profess what you teach and circulate privately for sale.

O happy man, whose books no one except your disciples copies, so that whatever you appear to dislike you can claim is not yours but someone else’s! And who could possess such great talent as to imitate the charm of your speech?

**CRITOBOLUS.** I ask you: what have infants sinned? Neither can the consciousness of guilt be imputed to them, nor ignorance, since, according to the prophet Jonah, they do not know their right hand from their left (Jonah 4:11). They cannot sin, yet they can perish? Their knees give way, their cries do not articulate words, their tongue appears to stammer, and eternal torments are prepared for these wretched beings!

**ATTICUS.** You have begun to be excessively articulate—not to say eloquent—now that your disciples have been turned into teachers, and so forth. Do not, then, play with the flowers of orators rather than your own, and so forth.

**CRITOBOLUS.** Grant me at least that those who cannot sin are without sin.

**ATTICUS.** I will grant it if they have been baptized in Christ, and so forth.

**CRITOBOLUS.** You force me to approach that odious question and say to you, “What have they sinned?”—so that you may immediately hurl the stones of the crowds at me and kill by your will the person whom you cannot overcome by force, and so forth. If you know that we are heretics, why do you not accuse us?

**ATTICUS.** Because the Apostle teaches me to avoid a heretic after one and a second admonition (Titus 3:10), not to accuse him, and so forth.

**CRITOBOLUS.** Tell me, please, and free me from every question: why are infants baptized?

**ATTICUS.** So that their sins may be forgiven them in Baptism, and so forth.

The holy and eloquent bishop Augustine recently wrote to Marcellinus—who was later, though innocent, slain by heretics [Note: [Col. 1708] Donatists] under the charge of the tyranny of Heraclianus—two books on the baptism of infants against your heresy. Through that heresy you wish to assert: “Infants are baptized not for the remission of sins, but for the kingdom of heaven,” according to what is written in the Gospel: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of heaven.”

He also wrote a third book to the same Marcellinus against those who say—that is, you say—“A person can be without sin if he wishes, without God’s grace” [Note: [Col. 1708] The passage has been restored according to the Corbie manuscript].

And recently he wrote a fourth to Hilary against your teaching, which fabricates many perverse doctrines. He is also said to be preparing other works specifically under your name, which have not yet come into our hands.

Therefore, I think this labor should be set aside, lest Horace’s words be applied to me: “Do not carry wood into the forest” (*Satires* 1.10.34). For either we would be saying the same things unnecessarily, or, if we wished to say something new, better material has already been taken up by a most distinguished intellect.

## The Palestinian Synod Held at Diospolis in the Case of Pelagius in December of the Year of Christ 415

[Note: [Col. 1708] The place and date of the synod are disclosed by the presbyter Lucian in his letter concerning the revelation and translation of the body of the martyr Stephen, which we published in the Appendix to volume seven. There, no. 2, he says: “On Friday, which is the third day before the Nones of December, in the tenth consulship of Honorius and the sixth of Theodosius, the Augusti, when night had come, as I slept . . . being in a kind of ecstasy and half awake, I saw a man,” and so forth. Later, no. 8: “Therefore I immediately reported it to the bishop,” John of Jerusalem, “while he was at Lydda, which is Diospolis, holding a synod. He took with him two other bishops, Eleutherius—more correctly Eutonius—from Sebaste, and Eleutherius of Jericho, and they came to the place,” and so forth. Finally, no. 9, he writes: “His relics were translated on the seventh day before the Kalends of January.” In other copies of the same letter, no. 8 reads: “For the bishops who were present at that time were John of Jerusalem, and Eustonius, bishop of the city of Sebaste, and Eleutherius of Jericho, with all the clergy.”]

Augustine, in Book 2 of the *Retractions*, chapter 47.

In the East—that is, in Syria-Palestine—Pelagius was brought by certain Catholic brothers before an episcopal tribunal. Those who had submitted a written accusation against him were absent, since they had been unable to arrive on the day of the synod. Pelagius was heard by fourteen bishops, and, because he condemned the very teachings hostile to God’s grace that had been read against him from the written accusation, they pronounced him a Catholic.

The same author, in *The Proceedings of Pelagius*, sections 2 and 5.

Finally, among the matters read out from the memorandum which the holy brothers Heros and Lazarus had submitted—because they were unable to be present on account of the serious illness of one of them, as we later learned with greater probability—the first charge brought against Pelagius was this: in one of his books he writes, “No one can be without sin unless he has knowledge of the Law.” After this had been read, the Synod said: “Did you publish this, Pelagius?” He replied: “I did indeed say it, but not as they understand it. I did not say that one who has knowledge of the Law cannot sin, but that knowledge of the Law helps one not to sin, as it is written, ‘He gave the Law as a help to them’” (Isa. 8:20, according to the Septuagint). On hearing this, the Synod said: “What Pelagius has said is not alien to the Church.” Let another chapter be read. And it was read that in the same book Pelagius had written, “All are governed by their own will” [Note: [Col. 1708] See the remainder above, in the book *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, no. 5], etc.

The same author, in the first book *Against Julian*, no. 19.

We have fourteen other Eastern bishops—Eulogius, John, Ammonianus, Porphyry, Eutonius, Porphyry, Fidus, Zoninus, Zoboennus, Nymphidius, Chromatius, Jovinus, Eleutherius, and Clematius—whom we may introduce into this gathering, all found together in one place: those very men who presided as judges over Pelagius and, thinking him Catholic as men do, since no adversary from the other side was pressing the matter, pronounced him Catholic as though he were Catholic. For if he had not condemned in their presence and hearing those who say “that Adam’s sin harmed Adam alone and not the human race; and that newly born infants are in the condition in which Adam was before sin; and that infants, even if they are not baptized, possess eternal life,” he would by no means have emerged from that hearing except condemned.

# A WRITING AGAINST THE ERRORS OF PELAGIUS, EXCERPTED FROM AUGUSTINE’S LETTER 186, NOS. 31–33, TO PAULINUS

Also published by Nicolaus Carbachius from a Mainz manuscript in 1523, and afterward by Jacobus Sirmond from the Corbie codex, where it appears under the title: “EXCERPTED CHAPTERS FROM THE PROCEEDINGS HELD AGAINST THE HERETIC PELAGIUS,” together with other passages from his memoranda, which he himself was compelled to condemn when they were brought against him in the Palestinian Synod.

What the Lord cried out against Jerusalem, which was unwilling to gather her children, we cry out against those who are unwilling to gather the children of the Church; and they are not even corrected after the judgment that was rendered concerning Pelagius in Palestine. He would have emerged condemned unless he himself had condemned the statements brought against him concerning the grace of God—statements which he could not obscure.
