For, besides those matters which he dared, as far as he could, to defend by some sort of argument, certain charges were brought against him which, unless he had anathematized them without any evasion whatsoever, would themselves have made him accursed. He was charged with saying:

1. That Adam was created mortal and would have died whether he sinned or did not sin.
2. That his sin harmed Adam alone and not the human race.
3. That newly born infants are in the condition in which Adam was before his transgression.
4. That neither through Adam’s death or transgression does the whole human race die, nor through Christ’s resurrection does the whole human race rise again.
5. That infants, even if they are not baptized, possess eternal life.
6. That baptized rich people, unless they renounce everything, are not credited with whatever good they may appear to do and cannot possess the kingdom of God.
7. That God’s grace and help are not given for individual acts, but exist in free choice, or in the Law and teaching.
8. That God’s grace is given according to our merits.
9. That people cannot be called children of God unless they have become entirely without sin.
10. That free choice does not exist if it needs God’s help, since each person has it in his own will to do or not to do something.
11. That our victory comes not from God’s help but from free choice.
12. That forgiveness is not granted to penitents according to God’s grace and mercy, but according to the merit and labor of those who have become worthy of mercy through repentance.

Pelagius anathematized all these propositions in such a way that the Proceedings themselves sufficiently attest that he brought forward no argument whatsoever in any manner to defend them. It follows, therefore, that whoever accepts the authority of that episcopal judgment and Pelagius’s own confession must hold what the Catholic Church has always held:

1. That Adam would not have died if he had not sinned.
2. That his sin harmed not Adam alone but also the human race.
3. That newly born infants are not in the condition in which Adam was before his transgression.
4. That what the blessed Apostle said also applies to them: “Through one man came death, and through one man the resurrection of the dead. For just as all die in Adam, so also all will be made alive in Christ” (1 Cor. 15:21–22).
5. Hence unbaptized infants cannot possess not only the kingdom of heaven but even eternal life.
6. That baptized rich people are not to be deprived of the kingdom of God, even if they do not rid themselves of their wealth and are such as the Apostle describes in his words to Timothy: “Command those who are rich in this world not to be proud, nor to place their hope in the uncertainty of their riches, but in the living God, who richly provides us with everything for enjoyment; let them be rich in good works, generous and sharing, storing up for themselves a good foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of true life” (1 Tim. 6:17–19).
7. That God’s grace and help are also given for individual acts.
8. That grace is not given according to our merits, so that it may truly be grace—that is, freely given—through the mercy of him who said: “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will show compassion to whom I show compassion” (Rom. 9:15).
9. That those who daily say, “Forgive us our debts” (Matt. 6:12), can be called children of God; they would certainly not say this truthfully if they were entirely without sin.
10. That free choice exists even if it needs divine help.
11. That when we fight against temptations and unlawful desires, although our own will is also involved, our victory nevertheless arises not from that will but from God’s help. Otherwise the Apostle’s statement would not be true: “It depends not on the one who wills or the one who runs, but on God who shows mercy” (Rom. 9:16).
12. That forgiveness is granted to penitents according to God’s grace and mercy, not according to their merits, since the Apostle also called repentance itself a gift of God when he said concerning certain people, “Perhaps God may grant them repentance” (2 Tim. 2:25).

Let anyone who agrees with Catholic authority and with Pelagius’s own words explicitly recorded in the ecclesiastical Proceedings confess all these points plainly, without any evasions. For one must not believe that the propositions contrary to these have truly been anathematized unless the truths opposed to them are held in faith and in the heart and proclaimed in open confession. [Note: [Col. 1710] We reproduce this Writing of Augustine, excerpted from his Letter 186 to Paulinus, at this point according to the Benedictine Fathers, who altered the text of this letter in several places when transmitting it. You will find the fragment in vol. 2, cols. 827–829. M.]

# THE EXTRAORDINARY PERSECUTION OF THE CATHOLICS WHO LIVED UNDER JEROME’S CARE, CARRIED OUT BY THE SUPPORTERS OF PELAGIUS AFTER HIS CONDEMNATION IN THE PALESTINIAN TRIAL

Augustine, at the end of the book *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, no. 66.

As for the things said to have been perpetrated after this judgment there by some band of wicked men—who are reported to have strongly supported Pelagius—with incredible audacity, so that God’s male and female servants under the care of the holy presbyter Jerome were subjected to a most criminal massacre, a deacon was killed, the monastery buildings were burned, and scarcely was Jerome himself protected from this attack and assault of the impious by a stronger fortified tower through God’s mercy: I think we should rather remain silent and await what our brother bishops there judge ought to be done concerning such great evils. For who could believe that they are able to disregard them?

The impious doctrines of such people must indeed be refuted by all Catholics, even those who live far away from those regions, so that wherever they may be able to do harm, they may be opposed wherever they can reach. But impious deeds, whose restraint belongs to episcopal discipline, must be punished where they are committed, most especially by those who are present or nearby, with pastoral diligence and pious severity.

# CONCERNING THE SAME, AS IS BELIEVED, PERSECUTION OF THE CATHOLICS BY THE PELAGIANS

Pope Innocent, to John, bishop of Jerusalem.

Eustochium and Paula, those most noble and holy virgins, lamented that the devil had perpetrated in the places belonging to your Church plunderings, killings, fires, and every crime of extreme madness; for they withheld the man’s name and the cause. Although it is not uncertain by whom this was committed, it was nevertheless necessary for Your Brotherhood to exercise vigilance and provide more carefully for that flock, lest something of this kind arise—something which, endangering others, your negligence allows to enter the Lord’s flock, and concerning which we have heard that such lambs, stripped by fire, weapons, and persecutions, weakened after the slaughter and deaths of their own people, scarcely remain alive.

Nothing moves that priestly piety of yours concerning such great power of the devil being admitted against you and yours—against you, I say; for such an outrage having been completed in the Church plainly condemns the gravity of a priest. Where were your preparations? Where, certainly, if these events occurred, were your assistance or consolations? They say that they still fear more than they complain that they have suffered.

I would have judged the matter more seriously if they had spoken with me more openly about it. See, brother, the snares of the ancient enemy, and remain watchful in the spirit of a good ruler, so that these matters, which have been reported to us as manifest more by rumor than by accusation, may either be corrected or checked. Otherwise ecclesiastical law may compel the one who has failed to defend a weakened cause to answer for it.

The same author, to the presbyter Jerome.

The Apostle testifies that contention has never accomplished anything good in the Church; and therefore he commands that the correction of heretics should first take place (Tit. 3:9–10), and that it should be carried on through a more prolonged discussion. When this rule is negligently observed, the evil that ought to be avoided is not avoided but increased.

Nevertheless, because your grief and groaning shake our inward parts so that there is no opportunity for deliberation and counsel, I address first the faith of your steadfastness. You have often said that whoever awaits blessedness is struck by insult or, as you put it, by danger for the sake of truth; and we recall this well through the words of your preaching. Therefore, stirred by so great a spectacle of evils, we hastened to take up the authority of the Apostolic See in order to suppress every outrage. But we have read neither the name of the person against whom we should rise nor any specific charge laid against him.

Thus, as far as we can, we share your grief. If you submit an open and manifest accusation against certain persons, I shall either assign competent judges or, if something more urgent and attentive can be done by us, I shall not delay, dearest son. Nevertheless, I have written to my brother Bishop John that he should act more cautiously, lest anything further of this kind happen around the Church entrusted to him—something which, to foresee and avert lest it occur or recur, becomes most troublesome even for him afterward [reading uncertain].

# LETTER OF THE CARTHAGINIAN SYNOD, HELD AGAINST THE ERRORS OF PELAGIUS AND COELESTIUS BY MORE THAN SIXTY-NINE BISHOPS—AURELIUS, NUMIDIUS, AND OTHERS—TO INNOCENT [Note: [Col. 1711] Letter 175 among Augustine’s letters.] WRITTEN IN THE YEAR 416 [Note: [Col. 1711] This synod is assigned to the year 416 both because the presbyter Orosius, through whom the letters of Heros and Lazarus against Pelagius were brought to the bishops assembled at Carthage, returned from Palestine in that same year, in the spring; and because Innocent’s letter replying to this same Carthaginian synod is dated the sixth day before the Kalends of February, after the seventh consulship of the emperor Theodosius and the consulship of Junius Quartus, a man of illustrious rank—that is, January 27 of the year 417. The subsequent letters of the synod of Milevis and of the five bishops, brought by the same bearer, the Bishop Julius, and delivered to Innocent at the same time, must be assigned to this period as well; Innocent himself replied on January 27 of that year, 417.]

1. When, according to custom, we had solemnly come to the Church of Carthage, and a synod had been convened from among us for various reasons, our fellow presbyter Orosius handed us a letter from the holy brothers and our fellow priests Heros and Lazarus, whose copy we have decided to append here. After these letters had been read, we recognized Pelagius and Coelestius as the authors of an utterly criminal error that must be anathematized by all of us.

For this reason we requested that the matter which had been debated here at Carthage nearly five years earlier concerning Coelestius’s name should be reread. Once it had been read, Your Holiness will be able to observe from what follows that, although the judgment was clear and it appeared that this great wound had at that time been cut away from the Church by episcopal judgment, we nevertheless decided by common deliberation that the authors of such a persuasion—even though Coelestius is said to have afterward attained the presbyterate—ought themselves to be anathematized unless they most openly anathematized these doctrines. In this way, if their own health could not be secured, at least the recovery of those who have been deceived by them or can be deceived might be pursued once the sentence passed against them was known.

2. We therefore thought it necessary, brother lord, to make this action known to Your Holy Charity, so that the authority of the Apostolic See might be added to the decisions of our smallness, for the protection of the salvation of many and for the correction of the perversity of certain people. These men are working through their condemnable arguments to leave no place for the grace of God—not by defending free choice but rather by exalting it in sacrilegious pride. Through grace we are Christians, and through grace the very freedom of our will truly becomes free, when it is liberated from the domination of bodily desires, etc. We suffer them attacking us with increasing frequency and greater boldness.

3. Therefore, if Pelagius should rightly appear to Your Reverence to have been acquitted by the episcopal Proceedings said to have been held in the East, nevertheless the error and impiety itself—which already has many supporters scattered in various places—must also be anathematized by the authority of the Apostolic See, etc.

4. They also deny that infants should be baptized for the salvation given through Christ the Savior, and thus by this deadly doctrine they kill them eternally, etc. Although Coelestius has already confessed in a memorandum in the Church of Carthage that even infants are redeemed through Christ’s Baptism, many who are said to be or to have been their disciples nevertheless do not cease affirming by every means they can these evils by which they attempt to overthrow the foundations of the Christian faith.

5. Therefore, even if Pelagius and Coelestius have been corrected, or say that they have never held these opinions, and deny that any writings brought forward against them belong to them, and there is no way by which they can be convicted of lying, nevertheless let anyone who generally teaches and asserts that human nature is sufficient for avoiding sins and fulfilling God’s commandments, and who thereby proves himself an adversary of God’s grace—which is more clearly demonstrated in the prayers of the saints—be anathema. And let anyone who denies that infants are freed from perdition through Christ’s Baptism and receive everlasting salvation be anathema.

# LETTER OF THE SYNOD OF MILEVIS, HELD AGAINST THE SAME HERESY OF PELAGIUS AND COELESTIUS IN THE SAME YEAR 416, BY SIXTY-ONE BISHOPS—SILVANUS, VALENTINUS, AND OTHERS—TO POPE INNOCENT [Note: [Col. 1712] Letter 176 among Augustine’s letters.]

1. Since the Lord has placed you in the Apostolic See by the special gift of his grace and has given you to our times in such a way that it would count against us as negligence if we were silent before Your Reverence about what ought to be proposed for the Church, rather than that you could receive it either disdainfully or negligently, we ask you to apply pastoral diligence to the great dangers of Christ’s weakened members.

2. For a new and exceedingly dangerous heresy, hostile to the grace of Christ, is attempting to rise up, etc.

3. The authors of this most dangerous error are said to be Pelagius and Coelestius. We would rather see them healed within the Church than cut off from the Church with their salvation abandoned, if no necessity compels otherwise. One of them, Coelestius, is said to have even attained the presbyterate in Asia, etc. But Pelagius, as the letters sent by some of our brothers report, is said to be deceiving certain people while established at Jerusalem. Nevertheless, many more who have been able to investigate his opinions more carefully are struggling against him on behalf of the grace of Christ and the truth of the Catholic faith, but especially your holy son, our brother and fellow presbyter Jerome.

4. We have sent this letter about these matters to Your Holiness from the council of Numidia, following the example of our fellow bishops of the Church and province of Carthage. We have learned that they have written to the Apostolic See, which you honor, concerning this matter, etc.

# LETTER OF THE FIVE BISHOPS AURELIUS, ALYPIUS, AUGUSTINE, EVODIUS, AND POSSIDIUS TO THE SAME INNOCENT [Note: [Col. 1713] Letter 177 among Augustine’s letters.] WRITTEN AT THE SAME TIME

[Col. 1713]

1. From the two councils, of the province of Carthage and of Numidia, we have sent to Your Holiness letters signed by a considerable number of bishops against the enemies of Christ’s grace, who trust in their own strength and in a certain sense say to our Creator, “You made us human beings, but we made ourselves righteous,” etc.

Therefore the household of Christ, which says, “When I am weak, then I am strong” (2 Cor. 12:10), and to which its Lord says, “I am your salvation” (Ps. 34:3), awaits the Lord’s help with a trembling heart, in fear and trembling, also through the charity of Your Reverence.

2. For we have heard that in the city of Rome, where he lived for a long time, there are certain people who favor him for various reasons: some because he is said to have persuaded them of such things, but more because they do not believe that he holds such opinions. This is especially so because it is boasted that ecclesiastical proceedings were held in the East, where he resides, by which he is thought to have been cleared. If the bishops there pronounced him Catholic, this should not be believed to have happened for any other reason than that he said he confessed the grace of God, etc.

3. The issue is not one Pelagius, who perhaps has now been corrected—would that it were so—but the many with whom everything is already filled everywhere: men who argue volubly, dragging weak and uneducated souls along as though bound, while wearing down the strong and steadfast in the faith by the very force of their disputation.

Therefore, he must either be summoned to Rome by Your Reverence and carefully questioned about what grace he means, and whether he now confesses that human beings are helped by it to avoid sin and live justly; or this same matter must be pursued with him by letter. Once he is found to be teaching the grace taught by ecclesiastical and apostolic truth, he must be absolved without any scruple on the part of the Church and without any hiding-place of ambiguity; then there will truly be cause for rejoicing over his purification, etc.

4. We have sent Your Reverence a book that certain religious and honorable young men, servants of God, gave us; we do not conceal their names, for they are called Timasius and James. As we have heard, and as you also know, through Pelagius’s exhortation they abandoned the hope they had placed in the world and now serve God in continence.

When, through whatever work of ours and with the Lord’s inspiration, they had at last been freed from the same error, they produced this book, saying that it belonged to Pelagius, and earnestly asked that a reply be made to it. This was done, and the reply itself was sent back to them. They wrote in response, giving thanks.

We have sent both documents: the one to which the reply was made and the reply itself. And, so that we would not burden you excessively, we have marked the passages where we ask you not to hesitate to examine how he answered the charge that he denied God’s grace—answering in such a way that he would not say grace exists unless it were the nature in which God created us, etc.

5. For this reason, we have thought it better to send Your Beatitude a letter addressed to him by one of us, to whom he transmitted through an Eastern deacon, though a citizen of Hippo, certain writings as a kind of defense of himself. We judge and request that you yourself be willing to send it to him. In this way he will be less likely to disdain reading it, attending more to the one who sent it than to the one who wrote it.

6. As for what they say—that human beings can be without sin and can easily keep God’s commandments if they wish, etc.—whatever the precise state of this question, even if no person in this life is found to be without sin, it is nevertheless said that this can happen through the help of the grace and Spirit of God, and one must strive and pray for it to happen. Anyone who errs tolerably in this matter is not guilty of diabolical impiety but of human error, affirming something that must be pursued and desired even if he cannot demonstrate that what he asserts is possible. For he believes that something can happen which it is certainly praiseworthy to desire, etc.

# LETTER OF INNOCENT [Note: [Col. 1714] Letter 181 among Augustine’s letters.] REPLIED TO AURELIUS AND THE OTHER BISHOPS OF THE CARTHAGINIAN COUNCIL ON JANUARY 27, 417 (C)

[Col. 1714]

1. In investigating these matters—which ought to be treated by priests, and especially by a true, just, and Catholic council, with the utmost care—we have preserved the examples of ancient tradition and remembered ecclesiastical discipline. You have thereby strengthened the vigor of our religion no less now, in seeking advice, than previously, when you pronounced judgment, by approving that the matter should be referred to our judgment. You knew what is owed to the Apostolic See, since all of us placed in this office desire to follow the Apostle, from whom the episcopate itself and the whole authority of this title arose, etc.

2. I therefore rejoice, dearest brothers, that through our brother and fellow bishop Julius you sent letters to us, etc.

3. Whoever, then, appears to agree with the opinion that we have no need of divine help thereby declares himself an enemy of the Catholic faith and ungrateful for God’s benefits. For they are not worthy of our communion, which they have polluted by preaching such things, etc.

They must be removed farther away and kept at a distance from the Church’s inward parts, lest, remaining unpunished for a long time and occupying many, an incurable error grow stronger, etc. Therefore let the incurable wound be separated from the healthy body, etc.

Farewell, brothers.

Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of February [Note: [Col. 1714] In the year of Christ 417], after the seventh consulship of the emperor Theodosius Augustus and the consulship of Junius Quartus, a man of illustrious rank.

# THE SAME AUTHOR’S LETTER REPLIED TO SILVANUS THE ELDER, VALENTINUS, AND THE OTHER BISHOPS OF THE SYNOD OF MILEVIS [Note: [Col. 1714] Letter 182 among Augustine’s letters.]

1. Among the other cares of the Roman Church and the occupations of the Apostolic See, in which we handle the consultations of various people through faithful and healing deliberation, our brother and fellow bishop Julius unexpectedly brought me the letter of Your Belovedness, which you sent from the council of Milevis with especially devoted concern for the faith. He also appended a similar written complaint from the synod of Carthage, etc.

2. The authors of this new heresy must certainly be avoided. For what more bitter thing could they have contrived against God than to nullify divine assistance and remove the reason for daily prayer? This is to say, “What need have I of God?” etc.

3. As for what Your Fraternity asserts they preach—that infants can be granted the rewards of eternal life even without the grace of Baptism—it is utterly foolish. “Unless they eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, they will not have life in themselves” (John 6:54). Those who defend eternal life for them without regeneration seem to me to want to nullify Baptism itself, since they preach that infants possess what is believed to be bestowed upon them only through Baptism, etc.

4. Therefore, by the authority of apostolic vigor, we judge that Pelagius and Coelestius—that is, the inventors of new expressions, which, as the Apostle said, habitually produce nothing that builds up but rather utterly empty questions (2 Tim. 2:23)—are to be deprived of ecclesiastical communion, etc.

At the same time we order that whoever attempts to defend this with similar obstinacy be restrained by an equal punishment, etc. Let this sentence, therefore, remain fixed, dearest brothers, against those mentioned above, etc.

5. Farewell, brothers. Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of February [Note: [Col. 1714] In the year of Christ 417], in the consulship of the illustrious men Honorius and Constantius.

# THE SAME AUTHOR’S LETTER REPLIED TO THE FIVE BISHOPS AURELIUS, ALYPIUS, AUGUSTINE, EVODIUS, AND POSSIDIUS [Note: [Col. 1714] Letter 183 among Augustine’s letters.]

1. We received with great pleasure the letter of Your Fraternity, full of faith and firmly strengthened throughout by the full vigor of the Catholic religion, sent from two councils through our brother and fellow bishop Julius. Its entire substance and structure consist in consideration of God’s daily grace and in the correction of those who think otherwise, so that it might both remove every error from them and, by offering any suitable example from our law, provide a worthy teacher whom they ought to follow, etc.

For if Pelagius, wherever he has taken his stand, has deceived the minds of those who readily or simply believed an argument put forward by him through this assertion—or whether such people are in this city (whom, since we do not know them, we can neither identify nor deny, for even if they exist they remain hidden and never dare either to defend him when he preaches these things or to boast of such opinions in the presence of any of us; nor, amid so great a multitude of people, can anyone easily be detected or recognized anywhere), or whether they live in any region of the earth—we believe, through the mercy and grace of our God, that they will readily be corrected once they hear the condemnation of the person who is found to have stubbornly persisted and resisted as the author of this doctrine, etc.

2. Nevertheless, we cannot be persuaded that he has been cleared, although proceedings have been brought to us by certain unknown laymen in which he was thought to have been both heard and absolved. We doubt whether these are genuine, etc.

Indeed, since the Proceedings themselves contain certain matters which he partly suppressed by avoiding the charges brought against him and partly confused in complete obscurity by turning many words back upon himself; and since he cleared himself of some points, as it could seem for the moment, more by false arguments than by true reasoning, denying some and twisting others through a false interpretation, etc., we can neither blame nor approve their judgment, since we do not know whether the Proceedings are genuine, or, if they are genuine, whether it is clear that he evaded the matter more than he cleared himself with complete truth, etc.

3. We examined the book said to be his, which Your Charity sent us. In it we read that many things had been written against God’s grace, many blasphemous things, nothing pleasing, and scarcely anything that did not deserve utter displeasure, condemnation, and rejection by anyone. No one other than the person who wrote such things would receive and entertain thoughts like them, etc.

Let him therefore anathematize the opinions he held, etc.

4. May God keep you safe and sound, dearest brothers. Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of February [Note: [Col. 1715] In the year of Christ 417], after the seventh consulship of the most glorious emperor Theodosius Augustus and the consulship of Junius Quartus Palladius, a man of illustrious rank.

# ON THE PELAGIANS CONDEMNED BY THE APOSTOLIC SEE

Gennadius, in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*.

Innocent, bishop of the city of Rome, wrote a decree issued against Pelagius to the Western and Eastern Churches. After him, his successor, Pope Zosimus, promulgated it more broadly.

Prosper, in his *Chronicle*, under the year 416 [Note: [Col. 1715] This is a copyist’s error, transferring to the year 416 what plainly belongs to the year 417. Otherwise Zosimus would have governed the Roman Church not for only one year, or nearly two as stated, but for three years.]

Zosimus assumed the episcopate of the Roman Church as its thirty-ninth bishop, for one year, nine months, and nine days. During this period, after the Pelagians had already been condemned in advance by Pope Innocent, they were resisted by the strength of the Africans and especially by the learning of Bishop Augustine [Note: [Col. 1715] Elsewhere, “industry.”].

# ON PELAGIUS’S LETTERS, SENT BY HIMSELF TO POPE INNOCENT WITH A MEMORANDUM OF FAITH BUT DELIVERED TO ZOSIMUS

Augustine, in the book *On the Grace of Christ*, nos. 32, 35, 36.

Pelagius recently sent a letter and a memorandum of his faith to Rome, writing to Pope Innocent of blessed memory, whom he did not know to be dead [Note: [Col. 1715] Innocent died on March 12 in the year of Christ 417]. In this letter he says that there are certain things with which people try to defame him: one, that he denies the sacrament of Baptism to infants and promises certain people the kingdoms of heaven without Christ’s redemption; another, that he says a human being can avoid sin in such a way as to exclude God’s help, and trusts so greatly in free choice that he rejects the help of grace, etc.

But in this letter Pelagius wants the reader to pass over to his book of faith . . . in which he discussed at length many matters about which he had not been questioned . . . . For after he had completed as lengthy a discussion as he wished, from the unity of the Trinity to the resurrection of the flesh—something no one had asked him about—he says: “And we hold one Baptism, which we say must be celebrated in infants with the same words of the sacrament with which we also say it is celebrated in adults,” etc.

But let us consider more carefully what Pelagius thought about the help of grace, even in the memorandum of his faith that he sent to Rome. “We confess free choice,” he says, “in such a way that we say that we always need God’s help.”

The same author, in the book *On Original Sin*, nos. 19, 24.

But observe carefully how Pelagius attempted to insinuate himself in order to deceive even the episcopal judgment of the Apostolic See in this very question concerning the Baptism of infants. In the letter he sent to Pope Innocent of blessed memory—since they did not find him alive and the letter was delivered to the holy Pope Zosimus and sent from there to us—he says that “people defame him because he denies the sacrament of Baptism to infants and promises certain people the kingdoms of heaven without Christ’s redemption,” etc.

But in the book of his faith, which he sent to the same Pope Innocent along with the letter, and to whom he had also written, he exposed himself much more clearly while attempting to conceal himself, saying: “We hold one Baptism, which we say must be celebrated in infants with the same words of the sacrament with which we also say it is celebrated in adults,” etc.—as though the remission of sins were spoken of infants merely through the sound of words and accomplished not in reality.

For a time he seemed to say something compatible with the Catholic faith; but he was unable to deceive that See to the end.

# PELAGIUS’S MEMORANDUM OF FAITH, SENT BY HIMSELF TO INNOCENT AND DELIVERED TO ZOSIMUS [Note: [Col. 1716] It was found in an old Vatican codex together with the following letters of Zosimus and reported by Baronius in the *Annals* under the year 417. It had already existed in a sermon formerly numbered 191 among Augustine’s sermons *On Time*, now number 236 of the Appendix, and also among Jerome’s works under the title “An Explanation of the Creed to Damasus.”] (G)

1. We believe in God the almighty Father, creator of all things visible and invisible.

2. We also believe in our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom all things were created: true God, the only-begotten, and true Son of God, not made, not adopted, but begotten, and of one substance with the Father—which the Greeks call *homoousion* (ὁμοούσιον), “consubstantial”—and in every respect equal to God the Father, so that he cannot be inferior in time, rank, or power. We confess that the one who was begotten is as great as the one who begot him.

When we say that the Son was begotten by the Father through a divine and ineffable generation, we do not thereby assign any time to him; nor do we say that the Father ever began to exist, or the Son either. For we cannot otherwise confess the Father to be eternal unless we also confess the Son to be coeternal. The Father is called Father because of the Son, and the one who was always Father always had a Son.

3. We also believe in the Holy Spirit, true God proceeding from the Father, equal in every respect to the Father and the Son in will, power, eternity, and substance. There is absolutely no rank within the Trinity, nothing that can be called lower or higher; rather, the entire Godhead is equal in its perfection. Thus, except for the terms that indicate the distinct property of the persons, whatever is said of one person may most properly be understood of all three.

And just as, refuting Arius, we say that the Trinity has one and the same substance and confess one God in three persons, so, avoiding the impiety of Sabellius, we distinguish the three persons by the expressed particularity of each. We do not say that the Father is himself the Son, or himself the Holy Spirit, but that the person of the Father is one, that of the Son another, and that of the Holy Spirit another.

For we confess not merely names but also the particular properties of the names—that is, persons—or, as the Greeks express it, *hypostases* (ὑποστάσεις), that is, subsistences. The Father never excludes the person of the Son or of the Holy Spirit; nor, conversely, does the Son or the Holy Spirit assume the name and person of the Father. The Father is always Father, the Son always Son, and the Holy Spirit always Holy Spirit.

Thus they are one in substance and are distinguished by persons and names.

4. We say that the very Son of God, who from eternity without beginning possessed eternity with the Father and the Holy Spirit, at the end of the ages assumed from Mary, ever-virgin, a complete human being of our nature; and that the Word became flesh by assuming humanity, not by changing the Godhead. Nor do we say, as certain men most wickedly suppose, that the Holy Spirit served in place of seed, but that he acted through the power and might of the Creator. Thus we confess one person of the Son in Christ, while saying that there are two perfect and complete substances, namely, of the Godhead and of the humanity, which consists of soul and body.

And just as we condemn Photinus, who confesses in Christ only a human being, a mere man, so we anathematize Apollinaris and those like him, who say that the Son of God assumed something less than the full human nature, and that the human being assumed in flesh, or soul, or consciousness was unlike those for whose sake he was assumed. We confess him to be like us in all things except the stain of sin alone, which is not natural. We likewise execrate the blasphemy of those who attempt, with a novel doctrine, to assert that, from the time when flesh was assumed, everything that belonged to the Godhead migrated into the human being, and, conversely, that everything belonging to humanity was transferred into God. Thus—something that no heresy has ever dared to say—it would appear that by this confusion both substances, namely, the Godhead and the humanity, were emptied of their reality, and changed from their proper state into something else. Such people are understood to confess both an imperfect God in the Son and an imperfect human being, so that they cannot be believed to retain either the true God or the true human being.

5. We say, however, that our passible nature was assumed by God the Son in such a way that the Godhead remained impassible. For the Son of God suffered, not apparently but truly, everything that Scripture testifies to: hunger, thirst, weariness, pain, death, and other things of this kind. He suffered according to that which could suffer—that is, not according to the substance which he assumed, but according to the substance that was assumed. For the Son of God himself, according to his divinity, is impassible like the Father, incomprehensible like the Father, invisible like the Father, and unchangeable like the Father.

And although the Son’s distinct person—that is, the Word of God—assumed a passible human being, nevertheless, by its indwelling, the Godhead of the Word according to its substance suffered nothing, just as the whole Trinity must be confessed to be impassible. Therefore the Son of God died according to the Scriptures, according to that which could die. He rose again on the third day. He ascended into heaven. He sits at the right hand of God the Father, while the same nature of flesh remains—the flesh in which he was born and suffered, and in which he also rose again. For the substance of humanity was not emptied of its reality, but glorified, and will remain eternally with the Godhead. Having therefore received from the Father all authority over the things that are in heaven and on earth, he will come to judge the living and the dead, both to reward the righteous and to punish sinners.

6. We also confess and believe in the resurrection of the flesh, so that we say that we shall be restored in the same bodily reality in which we now exist, and that whatever condition we shall once have after the resurrection will remain forever. There is one life for all the saints, but different rewards according to their labor; conversely, there are punishments for sinners according to the measure of their offenses.

7. We hold one baptism, which we affirm must be administered to infants with the same sacramental words as to adults. If a person falls after baptism, we believe that he can be saved through repentance.

8. We receive the New and Old Testaments in the number of books handed down by the authority of the holy Catholic Church.

9. We believe that souls are given by God, and we say that they were made by him, anathematizing those who say that souls are, as it were, a part of the divine substance. We also condemn the error of those who say that souls sinned previously, or lived in heaven, before they were sent into bodies.

10. We also execrate the blasphemy of those who say that God has commanded something impossible for human beings, and that God’s commandments can be kept not by individuals but collectively by everyone; or of those who condemn first marriages with the Manichaeans, or second marriages with the Cataphrygians.

11. We also anathematize those who say that the Son of God lied because of the necessity of the flesh, and that, because of the human being he assumed, he was unable to do everything he wished.

12. We also condemn the heresy of Jovinian, who says that in the future there will be no distinction of merits, and that we shall possess there the virtues which we neglected to possess here.

13. We confess free choice in such a way that we say that we always need God’s help. We declare equally erroneous those who, with the Manichaeans, say that a human being cannot avoid sin, and those who, with Jovinian, assert that a human being cannot sin; for each group removes freedom of choice. We, however, say that a human being is always able both to sin and not to sin, so that we always confess that we possess freedom of choice.

14. This is the faith, most blessed pope, which we have learned in the Catholic Church, and which we have always held and continue to hold. If something has perhaps been stated in it with insufficient skill or inadequate caution, we wish it to be corrected by you, who hold both the faith and the see of Peter. But if this confession of ours is approved by the judgment of your Apostolate, whoever wishes to stain me will thereby prove himself ignorant, malicious, or even non-Catholic, and will not prove me a heretic.

## Concerning the memorandum of Coelestius, which he gave to Zosimus at Rome

Augustine, in *On Original Sin*, no. 26, and nos. 5, 7.

1. In the memorandum which he gave at Rome, after he had explained, as much as he wished, his faith from the Trinity of one Godhead to the future form of the resurrection of the dead—matters about which no one had questioned him and concerning which no issue had been raised against him—when his speech came to the matter under discussion, he said:

“But if questions have arisen beyond the faith, about which there has been disagreement among many, I have not, as the author of any dogma, established these matters by a definitive authority. Rather, what I have received from the source of the Prophets and Apostles I offer for approval to the judgment of your Apostolate, so that, if perhaps some error of ignorance has crept in—as may happen to human beings—your judgment may correct it.”

Clearly, by this prefatory statement he intended that, if any error appeared in him, it should seem that he had erred not in the faith but in questions lying beyond the faith.

2. In the memorandum which he issued at Rome and which was cited in the ecclesiastical proceedings there, his words are as follows:

“We confess that infants ought to be baptized for the remission of sins, according to the rule of the universal Church and according to the teaching of the Gospel, because the Lord established that the kingdom of heaven can be granted only to the baptized; and since they do not possess this by the powers of nature, it must necessarily be granted through the generosity of grace.”

3. Coelestius adds and says:

“But we did not say that infants are to be baptized for the remission of sins in order to appear to affirm original sin as transmitted by descent; this is far removed from Catholic understanding. For sin is not born with a human being—what is subsequently practiced by the human being—since it is shown to belong not to nature but to the will. It is therefore fitting to confess the former, lest we appear to create different kinds of baptism; and it is necessary to secure the latter in advance, lest, under cover of the mystery, an evil be said to be transmitted by nature to a human being before it is committed by the human being, to the injury of the Creator, and so forth.”

But the very merciful bishop of the aforesaid See [Note: [Col. 1719] Zosimus.]—when he saw him being carried headlong by such presumption, as though in a frenzy, until, if possible, he might come to his senses—preferred gradually to bind him by his own questions and the man’s answers, rather than drive him by a harsh sentence into the precipice toward which he already seemed to be inclining. This is why I did not say plainly, “he had fallen,” but rather, “he seemed to be inclining”; for earlier in the same memorandum, before speaking about such questions, he had said:

“If perhaps some error of ignorance has crept in—as may happen to human beings—your judgment may correct it.”

## Letter of Pope Zosimus to the African Bishops concerning the case of Coelestius

**Zosimus, to Aurelius and all the bishops established throughout Africa, beloved brothers, greeting in the Lord.**

1. Great matters of examination require a great weight, so that the scale of judgment may not be inferior to the matters themselves that are being handled. To this is added the authority of the Apostolic See, to which the decrees of the Fathers, in honor of the most blessed Peter, have established a particular reverence. We must therefore pray—and pray without ceasing—that by God’s continuous grace and everlasting help, peace of faith and of Catholic fellowship may be sent forth from this source into the whole world, unobscured by any clouds. For charity, which, as it is written, is God (1 John 4:8), rejoices in the perfect abundance of fullness when anything involving suspicion is corrected either by the anxious diligence of faith or by a prolonged dispute, or through amendment.

2. The presbyter Coelestius presented himself for our examination, requesting that what had been reported about him to the Apostolic See otherwise than was proper should be cleared. Although many occupations, through the greater obligations of ecclesiastical affairs, were drawing our care and concern in different directions, nevertheless, so that your Fraternity [Note: [Col. 1719] Elsewhere, “Paternity.”.] might not remain any longer in suspense concerning the arrival and examination of the aforesaid man, we set everything else aside and sat in judgment on the appointed day in the basilica of Saint Clement—he who, instructed in the discipline of the blessed Apostle Peter, corrected ancient errors by such teaching and made such progress that he consecrated by martyrdom the faith which he had learned and taught—so that the authority of so great a priest might serve as an example to the salutary correction undertaken in the present examination.

3. We therefore examined everything that had previously been done, as you will learn from the account attached to this letter. After Coelestius had been admitted, we had his memorandum, which he had submitted, read aloud. Not content with this, we repeatedly investigated whether he was speaking from his heart or merely with his lips what he had written. Judgment concerning the hidden things of hearts can belong only to our God, before whom not only what has been thought but also what is about to be thought is already present.

We thought it more concise that Your Holiness should learn by reading what his words contained. One thing certainly troubles us: since you had Coelestius present there, nothing has been clearly decided. As for the letters sent in the earlier report by Heros and Lazarus, it is quite evident that they were hastened by the fervor of faith. But when he was questioned about them, he asserted that he had never had any conversation with the aforesaid men concerning such disputes, and that he had not even known them by sight before they wrote about him. He said that he had met Lazarus only in passing, while Heros, after an apology had been offered for having formed a contrary opinion about an unknown and absent man, had withdrawn with thanks.

Since the accusation was unknown and rested on such a fragile and worthless foundation, it was unquestionably appropriate to inquire into the character of men whose charge had proved so windy and insubstantial—if at least the circumstances of their position and their way of life were known, so that faith might properly be given by the absent to the absent, and their letters might possess enough weight to deserve the authority of testimony.

It became clear that these men, despite irregular ordinations and the opposition of the laity and clergy, had, as strangers and foreigners, claimed priestly offices within Gaul, from which they had themselves resigned by their own decision. Although there were other considerations, we followed their repentance concerning themselves and removed them from priestly rank and from all communion. The case is sufficiently strengthened by the fact that such men proceeded by letter to accuse an absent person who is defending himself in person, setting forth his faith and challenging his accusers.

4. It has never displeased me to turn a judgment toward what is better. As a young man and an executor of the Holy Spirit, Daniel found Susanna innocent, although she had been condemned through the falsehood of the elders; the chaste woman was led back from punishment by a boy, though the old men had represented her as immoral (Dan. 13:46). Therefore, as it has been commanded, we must not believe every spirit (1 John 4:1), but must examine for a long time and with particular care, especially concerning a person’s faith, in which his condition and lifelong conduct are involved.

Nor did Solomon’s investigation fail amid the dispute over the newborn child. He did not bring forward one child belonging to two women who were quarreling with each other; rather, as an arbiter hesitating in his trust, he discovered the truth where he recognized the feeling of genuine devotion (1 Kings 3:16–28). How rare it is for long and disciplined hesitation not to reach the bedchamber of truth. It is a sign of the best judgment to believe wrongdoing with difficulty. For many whose good confession concerning themselves is accepted only reluctantly are driven by necessity into the precipice of that error, and an incurable wound is created when people despair of healing it.

5. Therefore, in the present case, we have judged nothing prematurely or immaturely. We have made known to Your Holiness our examination concerning the unshaken faith of Coelestius. His earlier memorandum ought also to have been a testimony on his behalf among you within Africa, so that people would not believe so readily what had not been investigated and what rumor had broadcast.

Accordingly, either those who would prove that he thinks otherwise than he has woven together in his memoranda and confession should come within two months, or Your Holiness should understand that, after the clear and manifest statements he has produced, we have remained in no doubt.

I warned Coelestius himself, and all the priests who at that time were present from various regions, that these snares of questions and foolish disputes—which do not build up but rather destroy—flow from that contagion of curiosity, while each person abuses his own ingenuity and intemperate eloquence, or Scripture. Even the writings of great men sometimes become endangered, together with their authors, after a very long passage of time, by the interpreter’s discretion. Thus it was divinely foretold: “Sin is not avoided through much speaking” (Prov. 10:19); and holy David asked that a guard be placed around his lips and a watch over his mouth (Ps. 140:3).

6. I admonish your Charity, both by the authority of the Apostolic See and by the mutual affection of love, that now your intellects submit themselves to the precepts and observances of all the holy Scriptures that have been prescribed according to the tradition and ordinances of the Fathers and ancestors. What is not abundant there? What is not full of the Spirit of God and of his words?—unless each person wishes to trust himself more and rely on his own judgment concerning himself.

Issued … [Col. 1721] in the consulship of Honorius Augustus for the eleventh time and Flavius Constantius. [Note: [Col. 1721] In the year of Christ 417.]

## Letter of Pope Zosimus to the African Bishops concerning the case of Pelagius

**Zosimus, bishop, to Aurelius and all the bishops established throughout Africa, beloved brothers, greeting in the Lord.**

1. After the presbyter Coelestius had been heard by us and had clearly expressed what he thought concerning the faith, and had strengthened by repeated professions the same statements that he had presented in his memorandum, we sent Your Affection a fuller written account concerning him.

Behold, we have received the letter of Praylius, bishop of Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 1721] See above, in Mercator’s *Commonitorium*, col. 1689, near the end of no. 11.], who was ordained bishop in place of the former Saint John [Note: [Col. 1721] John died at the beginning of the year 417.] and who intervened as a vigorous supporter of Pelagius’s case. Pelagius himself also sent a very extensive letter containing his defense, in which he fully set out, without any deception, what his profession of faith followed and what it condemned, so that the snares of every interpretation might cease.

This letter was read publicly. It contained everything equivalent to, and formed in the same sense and with the same judgments as, what Coelestius had previously put forward. Would that some one of you, beloved brothers, could have been present at the reading of the letter! What joy there was among the holy men who were present! What astonishment among them all! Some could scarcely restrain themselves from weeping and shedding tears that men of such unshaken faith could have been defamed.

Is there any place in which the grace or help of God has been omitted? Whoever can say or conceive anything beyond this is subject to that heavenly sentence which was pronounced concerning the Holy Spirit: that it will not be forgiven or remitted either in this age or in the age to come (Matt. 12:32).

2. I also see that this Pelagius has been defamed in letters written by Heros and Lazarus. Is it so, dearest brothers, that no report has reached your ears concerning who these storms and tempests of the Church are? Were you unaware of their lives and their condemnation?

But although the special authority of the Apostolic See has removed them from all communion, learn from this letter, even if only briefly, the character of these men. It is an old habit of Lazarus to accuse innocence. In many councils he was found to be a diabolical accuser of our fellow bishop Britius of the city of Tours. At a synod in the town of Taurini, he received the sentence of a slanderer from Proculus of Marseille.

Many years later, through the same Proculus, he became a priest and defender of a tyrannical judgment in the city of Aix. When he opposed the afflicted man, he burst into the very inner sanctuary and priestly throne, which was almost stained with the blood of an innocent person. The shadow of priesthood remained over him there only so long as the image of imperial power stood in the tyrant [Note: [Col. 1721] Constantine, who had usurped power in Gaul.]. After the destruction of his patron, he voluntarily stripped himself of that position and condemned himself by his own resignation.

As for Heros, everything was similar: the same tyrant [Note: [Col. 1721] Constantine.] as patron, the massacre of the crowd, the imprisonment and confinement of the presbyters who opposed him, the affliction of the entire city [Note: [Col. 1721] Elsewhere, “addition.”.], and a similar repentance concerning the resignation of his priesthood.

2. It is astonishing if these men, who contrived so much against brothers and fellow bishops and brought so many storms upon the Church, did not wish to strike a layman striving toward good conduct through a long life of service to God with false letters. It is not fitting for episcopal authority—and especially for your prudence—to depend upon the writings of frivolous whisperers.

Behold, Pelagius and Coelestius are present before the Apostolic See in their letters and confessions. Where is Heros? Where is Lazarus? Their names are made shameful by their deeds and condemnations. [Note: [Col. 1722] Nevertheless, Augustine calls these men “good brothers” in *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, nos. 2, 53.] Where are those young men, Timasius and Jacobus, who, as was alleged, produced certain writings?

You yourselves must judge whether, when such men make confessions at the Apostolic See, the things reported about those same men by corrupt and frivolous authorities, on doubtful rumor, ought to be believed. Love peace, love charity, strive for concord. For it is written: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matt. 19:19). Who are more truly neighbors to one another than all of us who ought to be one in Christ?

Not every wind that enters your ears is a messenger of truth. Therefore a governing mind, always stationed on watch, is needed, lest everything be granted to rumor and everything to witnesses.

Review the sacred Scriptures and the divine archives. False witnesses occupy the greater part of the places where we find the accusation or dangers of the saints. I say the greater part—indeed, the whole—since false witnesses rose up even against our Lord and Savior himself, the sacrificial victim and saving high priest of the whole world, pretending that they had heard him blaspheme.

Consider what deception might still pass unnoticed, when it has attacked the God of faith—or rather, faith itself and the truth—with perjuries.

3. We have written these things so that, in future, if absent and lesser-known persons should, from mere desire, lie about anyone in this way, your feet may stand firm against the ram of deceit. Hence the holy man asks for a lamp for his feet and a light for his paths (Ps. 118:105), namely, so that our footsteps may not be blind and wandering amid deceptive darkness.

And in the Gospel: “Does our law judge a person unless it first hears him from him and considers the matter?” (John 7:51). Likewise in the Old Testament: “You shall not believe a false report, and you shall not join with the wicked as an unjust witness.” And lest perhaps the multitude of accusers should be believed before judgment had been examined, it adds:

“You shall not be with the many in wickedness, and you shall not accept sin through them” (Exod. 23:1–2, according to the Septuagint).

And elsewhere again: “Before you inquire, do not blame anyone; and when you have inquired, rebuke justly” (Ecclus. 11:7). And again: “Speak what your eyes have seen” (Prov. 25:8, according to the Septuagint).

In the Acts of the Apostles, when the chief priests and elders of the Jews were demanding the condemnation of the absent Apostle Paul, the gentile tribune Festus delivered a most just sentence, which we too ought to bring before the faces of believers as a rebuke, saying:

“It is not the custom of the Romans to condemn any person before the accused has his accusers present and receives an opportunity to defend himself in order to clear away the charges” (Acts 25:16).

If, then, a man outside the enclosure of our faith maintained such moderation, it is wholly unworthy of priestly modesty to believe absent persons concerning absent persons. Who will be found free from injury if a credulous breast is opened to every blow struck by an assailant?

Let earthly moderation teach us, since in secular judgments and legal cases there is first such care in choosing and rejecting the judges themselves, and such great hesitation. How many delays have been inserted? How often has an adjournment, even at the very end of the contest, allowed the judgment to be prolonged for an innocent defendant?

People flee to the sea and to documents from beyond the sea, so that the truth—which is often strangled in the tighter constrictions of the present—may at least come from a distance. I would be lying if all these measures had not been discovered for the protection and defense of innocence. It is more tolerable for an innocent person to be found late than for him to be condemned quickly as guilty.

4. It was a serious burden for Lazarus and Heros to be merely the bearers of their own letters. Did they not know that Your Affection would report the matter to the Apostolic See? They would certainly have sailed here by the short route of slander.

When the resignation of a bishopric is at issue, they traverse seas and lands and omit no assistance. But when the reputation of innocent people is attacked, these idle and pampered men—whether accusers or witnesses, for in either case the name of those who deceive is infamous—abuse their letters from their chambers and beds. Two plagues cloud all Africa and the entire calm of Catholic serenity according to their desires.

We shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ. No one will be able to be absent there, nor will anyone be able to evade the judgment of the Lord, whose immensity is present in every place and in all things.

5. If our God was so concerned for the lost sheep that the Word became flesh and, from being Lord, assumed the form of a servant in order to restore the freedom that had long been taken away, then let it be your joy to recognize that those whom false judges accused have never been torn away from our body and from Catholic truth.

Certainly, what our expectation desired has shone forth: they condemn what must be condemned and follow what must be followed. If the head of the household rejoiced at the return of the son who had been dead and came back to life, who had been lost and was found, and ordered a clean robe to be brought for his use—that is, the insignia of a pure mind—and a fattened calf (Luke 15:22–24), how much greater is this rejoicing of faith, that those about whom false reports have been circulated are neither dead nor lost?

We have therefore sent Your Affection copies of the writings that Pelagius sent. We have no doubt that their reading will bring you joy in the Lord concerning the soundness of his faith.

Issued on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October.

## Concerning the error of the Palestinian bishops and of Pope Zosimus himself in the judgment concerning Pelagius or Coelestius

Facundus, bishop of Hermiane, book 7, chapter 3.

They will also find Pelagius, the arch-heretic from whom the Pelagians are named, absolved in the judgment of the Palestinian bishops through the very ignorance that concealed what he thought against the grace of Christ and allowed him to interpret his perverse opinions by cunning.

Finally, they will find even the blessed Zosimus, bishop of the Apostolic See, praising the faith of Pelagius and of his accomplice Coelestius—as though it were true and Catholic—in opposition to the judgment of his predecessor, the holy Innocent, who first condemned the Pelagian heresy. Zosimus himself had examined Coelestius by formal proceedings in the Church of Carthage, after Coelestius had been convicted and appealed to the Apostolic See. He even blamed the African bishops for believing them to be heretics, although, before the African bishops had exposed their deceptions much more clearly, he considered the aforesaid Pelagius and Coelestius orthodox.

And yet … the Church does not consider those Palestinian bishops and Zosimus heretics because they thought well of heretics; rather, according to the merit of their faith, it judges and honors them as Catholics, since the failure of simple people to understand the cunning of the wicked ought not to be counted as a crime.

## Concerning the African Council of 214 bishops against the heresy of Pelagius and Coelestius, held, as is believed, toward the end of autumn in the year 417

Prosper, in *Book of Responses to the Objections of the Gauls*, objection 8.

And together with the 214 priests, whose decree against the enemies of God’s grace the whole world has embraced, let us say, in a truthful profession, as their own statement has it, that the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord assists us in each individual act not only to know righteousness but also to do it, so that without it we are able neither to possess, think, say, nor do anything of true and holy piety.

The same author, in *Against the Collator*, no. 15.

According to you, the 214 priests erred—those who, in the letter which they prefixed to their decrees, addressed the blessed Zosimus, bishop of the Apostolic See, in these words:

“We have determined that the sentence pronounced against Pelagius and Coelestius through the venerable Bishop Innocent from the See of the most blessed Apostle Peter shall remain in force until they openly confess that the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord assists us in each individual act not only to know righteousness but also to do it, so that without it we are able neither to possess, think, say, nor do anything of true and holy piety.”

Prosper, in his *Chronicle*, under the year 418.

At this time Constantius [Note: [Col. 1724] He is praised by Palladius in the *Lausiac History*: “Constantius, assessor of the prefects of Italy.”], a servant of Christ living in Rome as a former deputy governor and resisting the Pelagians most devotedly on behalf of God’s grace, suffered many things through their faction, which joined him to the holy confessors.

The synodal decrees of the council of 214 bishops held at Carthage were brought to Pope Zosimus. After these had been approved [Note: [Col. 1724] The decrees were indeed approved by Zosimus in the year 418; but the council at Carthage in which they were enacted is thought to have been held in the year 419.], the Pelagian heresy was condemned throughout the whole world.

## Memorandum of the deacon Paulinus presented to Pope Zosimus against Coelestius

[Note: [Col. 1724] In the year of Christ 417.]

1. I beseech the justice of your Blessedness, venerable Pope Zosimus. True faith is never disturbed, especially in the Apostolic Church, in which teachers of corrupt faith are easily detected and are punished truthfully, so that, unless they correct themselves, they die in the things they have perpetrated for the worse. In that Church there is the true faith which the Apostles taught and which the Roman Church, together with all teachers of the Catholic faith, holds.

If, like the other authors of heresy, who were judged long ago by the Apostolic See or by the Fathers, expelled from the bosom of the Catholic mother Church, and condemned to perpetual death, these men who have now been detected or will be detected remain in their perfidy, let them be handed over to the spiritual sword by which they may be destroyed—just as Pelagius and Coelestius were condemned by Pope Innocent, the predecessor of your Blessedness of blessed memory, if they reject the right faith and persist in their perverse doctrine.

2. Following that judgment, Your Blessedness, when Coelestius was being heard by the Apostolic See, among other things ordered him in these words:

“Do you therefore condemn everything contained in Paulinus’s memorandum—that is, concerning the questions?”

And elsewhere:

“Have you learned what sort of letter the Apostolic See sent to the brothers and fellow bishops of the African province?”

And it was added:

“Do you condemn everything that we have condemned, and hold what we hold?”

And again:

“Do you condemn everything that has been circulated under your name?”

And again:

“Or the matters which Paulinus set out in his memorandum?”

When he said that he could be proved a heretic from the things brought against him, you, filled with the Holy Spirit, rejected by apostolic authority the words of the madman and slanderer, delivering this sentence, by which you yourself would be proved a Catholic and would undertake to heal him if he wished to be healed:

“I do not want you to lead us around in circles. Do you condemn everything that Paulinus has brought against you, whether charged against you or circulated by rumor?”

What person would not be satisfied with such a sentence? Who other than one who has strayed from the faith would reject something so salutary, so worthy of embrace, and so devout?

The man who had earlier professed that he would condemn whatever had been brought against him if I proved it contrary to the faith hears the command, “Condemn it,” and not only does not condemn it, but persists in such a great insult to the See. Thus the Roman Church now knows him to be guilty, since with such audacious spirit he has dared to resist and not condemn what Your Blessedness decreed should be condemned.

3. Nevertheless, I give thanks to God and Christ the Lord, because he wished the case of his Church to be conducted in such a way that the Apostolic See, from which it was proper that the heresy be condemned by the voice of two pontiffs, ordered those things to be condemned which I had brought against Coelestius. I have always desired, and continue to desire, not his condemnation but his correction.

Now his case is no longer with me but with the whole Church of God, as the writings sent to Your Blessedness testify, since he attempts to oppose the apostolic judgment by denying original sin, which has passed into all human beings and retains, until the end of the world, the inheritance of that Adam who first sinned. Unless this sin is remitted in infants through the sacrament of baptism, they cannot possess eternal life or the kingdom of heaven.

His teacher Pelagius also disputes against these truths. In the judgment of the East, Pelagius condemned the very things that Coelestius is attempting to affirm in the assembly of the Apostolic See.

He also has against him many ancient Catholic teachers of the Churches, Eastern and Western, from the southern and northern regions, who can teach him in their books about original sin—if he desires to be healed. He has the blessed martyr Cyprian, the blessed confessor Ambrose, Gregory of Nazianzus, and the blessed Pope Innocent. He also has, even now, those who may contend with him in the body—if indeed he judges them capable of such a great contest—or certainly those whom he ought to follow, if he wishes rather to learn what is right than to teach what is wrong.

Above all, he has Your Blessedness, whose judgment he ought to have obeyed when he heard the command: “Condemn it.”

Finally, he has the infants themselves, whom he ought to pity if he does not wish to pity himself. To use the words of the martyr, sins not their own but another’s are forgiven them (Cyprian, *Epistle* 64, to Fidus).

4. Therefore I beg your Blessed Apostolate to order that this little book of mine be received, so that I may return thanks to so great a See and to the most just judgments issued in my favor. I sent it for this reason: although Basiliscus the subdeacon, [Note: [Col. 1725] Namely, according to Morel, *Elementa Critica*, p. 231. M.] by order of Your Beatitude and together with the Acts of the Apostolic See, met me at Carthage on the fourth day before the Nones of November, so that I might appear before the Apostolic See and submit to the judgment of Your Holiness, it was reported that I had fled to you, and that I would not be absent if a judgment had been issued against me rather than in my favor.

At that time, however, I could do nothing, because the man who had appealed to the Apostolic See was absent; he ought certainly to have established the merits of his appeal, especially since, when an appellant does nothing, even according to human laws, the one who has prevailed is always in the stronger position. For what interest did I then have in appearing before Your Reverence as an advocate of his perverse teaching? I could have rejoiced if, after those charges which I had brought against him had been condemned, he had deserved to be absolved in such a way that they were confirmed by the judgment of the Apostolic See, and if he had not been permitted to be ordained before being cleared.

But the little fox has always been intent on deceits and does not know how to change his character. He did not believe that he could be caught, since he has always placed his confidence in holes, where he attempts to conceal the buried head of his conscience. This could no longer remain hidden; rather, having been more openly exposed, it is cut away by the spiritual sword of Your Beatitude, lest the Lord’s flock, which you guard with vigilant and watchful care as a good shepherd, should any longer be torn apart by bestial teeth.

I sent this little book to Your Beatitude through Marcellinus, subdeacon of the Church of Carthage. Given on the sixth day before the Ides of November.

# Letter of Pope Zosimus to the African Bishops concerning the Case of Coelestius

**Zosimus**, to Aurelius and the other most beloved brothers who were present at the Council of Carthage, greeting in the Lord.

## 1

Although the tradition of the Fathers has granted such authority to the Apostolic See that no one would dare dispute its judgment, and although it has always preserved this authority through canons and regulations, while ecclesiastical discipline—still proceeding according to its own laws—continues to pay to the name of Peter, from whom it too descends, the reverence that it owes; for canonical antiquity wished such power to belong to this apostle, through the judgments of all, by the very promise of Christ our God, that he might both loose what had been bound and bind what had been loosed; [Col. 1726] and an equal condition of authority was given to those who, with his approval, had deserved to inherit the See.

For he himself has care of all the churches, and especially of this one where he had sat, and he does not permit any privilege or any breath of judgment to waver—he who established the foundations of his own name firm and dulled by no disturbances, and which no one may rashly attack without danger to himself.

Since, then, Peter is the head of so great an authority, and since he strengthened the successive efforts of all our predecessors so that the Roman Church might be upheld by all human and divine laws and disciplines—and you are not unaware, but know well, most beloved brothers, that we govern his place and possess the authority of his name, as you ought to know as priests—nevertheless, although we possess such authority that no one can reopen our judgment, we have done nothing which we would not voluntarily report to your knowledge by our letters.

We give these things to your fraternity so that, consulting together, we may act in common—not because we did not know what ought to be done, or because we would do anything displeasing as contrary to the welfare of the Church, but because we wished to deliberate together with you concerning the man who, as you yourselves state in your letter, had been accused among you and had come to our See, claiming innocence and not refusing judgment by means of his former appeal; he even demanded that his accusers be brought forward and condemned the crimes which, as he said, rumor had falsely charged against him.

We thought, and now know, that his entire petition had been explained in the earlier letter that we sent you, and we believe that sufficient answer was given in the writing that you sent in reply.

## 2

But after the letter sent by your subdeacon Marcellinus, we examined the whole volume. When we had finally read it through, we found that you had understood the entire text of the letter as though we had granted Coelestius credibility in every respect and, without examining his words, had given our assent to every syllable, so to speak.

Matters that require long consideration are never decided rashly, nor should anything be determined without great deliberation when it must be examined by the highest judgment. Therefore let Your Fraternity know that, after the letters mentioned above—or the letters that we have now received from you [Note: [Col. 1726] Some copies read: “the former letters,” others: “the letters now received.”]—we have changed nothing, but have left everything in the same condition in which it had long stood, when we informed Your Holiness of these matters by our letter, so that the appeal which had been sent to us by you might remain in force.

I have subscribed. Farewell. Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, in the twelfth consulship of Augustus Honorius. Received on the third day before the Kalends of May. [Note: [Col. 1726] In the year of Christ 418.]

# Sacred Rescript against Pelagius and Coelestius

[Note: [Col. 1726] In the codex of the canons of the Roman Church it is entitled, “Sacred Rescript issued after receiving the Acts of the aforementioned synod.” That it is properly a rescript, rather than merely an unsolicited constitution, is clear from these words of Augustine, *Against Julian*, book 3, no. 1: “Certainly, as you say, if the emperor’s response was given rather on your behalf.” The Acts which were received and to which the rescript was issued appear to be those of the African synod—not of the synod held on 1 May 418, since the Rescript itself is dated 30 April, but of the earlier synod belonging to the end of autumn in the year 417.]

The emperors **Honorius** and **Theodosius**, Augusti, to **Palladius**, prefect of the praetorium.

## 1

We have learned through widespread report that, for the disturbance of the light of Catholic simplicity, which always shines with pure radiance, a new cunning has suddenly emerged through the ingenuity of deceitful art. Shaded by the lies of false knowledge, it has raged in such a frenzied struggle that it has attempted to touch the settled peace of the heavenly faith, while devising the inventions of a new crime and considering it a notable mark of plebeian lowliness to think along with everyone [Note: [Col. 1726] Another reading: “while, commended by the wind of new cleverness, it considers it a notable mark of plebeian lowliness.”], and believing that it would be the crown of singular wisdom to destroy what is commonly approved.

Pelagius and Coelestius are widely reported to have been the authors of this impious speculation. They assign such savage cruelty to the parent and creator of all things, to the supreme and ever-majestic God, limitless and transcending every beginning, that when he undertook the work of forming the world and weighed, in the profound conception of his spirit, the nature of the human being to be constructed, he placed a foul beginning before the work entrusted to him and promised death to the one who was about to be born. [Note: [Col. 1727] Another reading: “he placed an end before the beginning and sent death beforehand to the one who was about to be born.”]

They say that this did not flow from the ambush of forbidden sin, but that it completely enacted the law of an unchangeable decree; that abstaining from wrongdoing is of no help in avoiding the fatal attack of death, whose force was thought to have been so firmly established that it could not afterward be abolished.

They say that the error of the first human being, into which the helpless blindness of a mind seized by irrationality had rushed, did not descend to later generations; that transgression existed only as a point of distinction in the case of that man whom the unhappy allurements of seductive favor had carried away.

Yet the evident authority of Catholic law, in every respect, bears witness that he was the vestibule of the destruction of all, since it is clear that the diligent observance of the divine command was corrupted by him. There are many other things of this kind, which speech rejects and the law refutes, and which we are weary of recalling, even under the arrangement of punishment.

These things must be cut off by a timely remedy and swift haste, lest, once the practice of wickedness has grown strong, those who are young should scarcely be able to be restrained.

For a recent report has touched the ears of Our Clemency: within our most holy city and in other places, the pestilential poison of certain people has so taken root in their hearts that, with the path of straightforward belief interrupted and their efforts divided into factions, the material for unresting dissension has been introduced. The tranquility of the most blessed Church, which has been assailed, now wavers, as some pursue one interpretation and others another in doubtful fashion. The clarity of the sacred writings, which is complete and explains plainly what all should follow, is thrown into confusion according to the capacity of a deceitful mind, while certain people raise a profane question concerning new authors.

To Palladius, our most beloved and cherished father.

## 2

For this reason, let Your Illustrious Authority know that we have established, by a law destined to endure forever, that Pelagius and Coelestius—the principal heads of this detestable doctrine—shall first be driven from the city and punished by the judgment of good men. If, thereafter, any followers of this sacrilege should be found anywhere, or should utter any discourse concerning the condemned perversity, they are to be seized by anyone and brought before the competent judge.

Whether the person be cleric or layman, anyone shall have the power to report them and to press the charge without any proscription, if he discovers that they have abandoned the light of common knowledge and introduced the darkness of a new disputation against the Apostolic discipline and the clear, error-free judgment of the Gospel, fighting with the crafty cleverness of an ignorant sect and enveloping the shining faith by discussing it through deceptive circumlocutions.
