Therefore, wherever they are found speaking about this most unspeakable crime, we order that they be seized by anyone, brought to a public hearing, and accused indiscriminately by all, so that the public record may pursue the proof of the crime once established, while the guilty themselves are condemned to inexorable exile.

For it is fitting that the source of the evil be separated from public gatherings, and that those who are detestable not only because of their wicked deed but also because of the example of their poisonous spirit should not stand in the midst of the public assembly.

It is useful that this proclamation be disseminated throughout our entire empire, wherever the world extends [Note: [Col. 1727] Another reading: “through almost the whole world, wherever our empire extends.”], lest perhaps the concealment of knowledge provide nourishment for error and anyone suppose that he may act with impunity because he has pretended not to know what has been condemned by public authority.

Given on the day before the Kalends of May at Ravenna, in the twelfth consulship of Our Lords Honorius and the eighth of Theodosius, Augusti. [Note: [Col. 1727] In the year 418, on 30 April.]

# Copy of the Edict of Junius Quartus Palladius

Junius Quartus Palladius, Monaxius, and Agricola, again prefects of the praetorium, issued the following edict. [Note: [Col. 1728] According to the Theodosian Code, book 16, title “On Bishops, Churches, etc.,” Monaxius was prefect of the praetorium of the East. Agricola was prefect of the praetorium of Gaul, as is shown by the letter of Honorius addressed to him on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May concerning the annual assembly of the seven provinces at Arles, as Henry Norisius observes in book 1, chapter 13 of his *History of Pelagianism*.]

Against Pelagius and Coelestius, who were destroying faith in Catholic doctrine by wicked arguments, an imperial judgment was made forceful [Note: [Col. 1728] Another reading: “prevailed”], so that they were removed from the venerable city and punished by the council of good men.

Accordingly, all must be warned by this edict not to lend credulous assent to the errors of a sinister persuasion. If a commoner or a cleric should fall into the obscenities of this darkness, he shall be dragged before the judge by anyone, without distinction concerning the identity of the accuser; stripped of his property by its confiscation, he shall suffer irrevocable exile.

For just as the heavenly majesty gathers reverence from ignorance of its secrets, so it receives insult from the presumption of foolish disputation.

# The Universal Council of Africa Held at Carthage in the Year 418 against the Heresy of Pelagius and Coelestius

In the consulship of the most glorious emperors Honorius for the twelfth time and Theodosius for the eighth time, on the Kalends of May, at Carthage in the secretary of the Basilica of Faustus, when Bishop Aurelius had taken his seat in the universal council [Note: [Col. 1728] The codex of the Church of Saint Bavo at Ghent reads: “At Carthage in the Basilica of Faustus, when Bishop Aurelius, together with Donatianus, bishop of the first see of the province of Byzacena at Telepte, and two hundred and three other fellow bishops from the provinces of Byzacena, Mauretania Sitifensis, Tripolitania, Numidia, Mauretania Caesariensis, and Spain, had taken their seats in council.” The codex of the canons of the Roman Church reads likewise.], with the deacons standing by, all the bishops whose names and subscriptions are recorded, assembled in the holy synod of the Church of Carthage, agreed as follows.

### 1

If anyone says that the first man Adam was created mortal, so that whether he sinned or did not sin he would die bodily—that is, depart from the body—not on account of the merit of sin but by the necessity of nature, let him be anathema.

### 2

It was likewise resolved that if anyone denies that newborn infants should be baptized after emerging from their mothers’ wombs, or says that they are indeed baptized for the remission of sins but derive nothing from Adam of original sin that is cleansed by the bath of regeneration—with the result that the formula of Baptism “for the remission of sins” is understood in them to be not true but false—let him be anathema.

For the Apostle’s words, “Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin, death; and so it passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Romans 5:12), must not be understood in any other way than that in which the Catholic Church, spread throughout the world, has always understood them.

For because of this rule of faith, even infants, who have not yet been able to commit any sins personally, are truly baptized for the remission of sins, so that by regeneration what they have drawn from generation may be cleansed in them.

### 3

[Note: [Col. 1728] Some codices lack this canon; several others contain it, and Photius too recounts it in third place. Augustine also writes in book 2 of *On the Origin of the Soul*, ch. 12: “The authority of the Catholic councils and of the Apostolic See most justly condemned the new Pelagian heretics, because they dared to assign to unbaptized infants a place of rest and salvation even outside the kingdom of heaven.”]

It was likewise resolved that if anyone says that the Lord spoke the words, “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places” (John 14:2), so that it should be understood that there is some intermediate realm in the kingdom of heaven, or any place anywhere, where infants who have departed this life without Baptism live in blessedness—although without Baptism they cannot enter the kingdom of heaven, which is eternal life—let him be anathema.

For when the Lord says, “Unless someone is born of water and the Holy Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (John 3:5), what Catholic would doubt that the one who has not deserved to be a fellow-heir with Christ becomes a participant in the devil? For whoever lacks the right-hand side will undoubtedly incur the left-hand portion. [Col. 1729]

### 4

It was likewise resolved that if anyone says that the grace of God, by which we are justified through Jesus Christ our Lord, is effective only for the remission of sins that have already been committed, and not also as help to prevent them from being committed, let him be anathema.

### 5

Likewise, whoever says that the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord helps us not to sin only because through it the understanding of the commandments is revealed and opened to us, so that we know what we ought to desire and what we ought to avoid, but that through it we are not granted the ability to love and to carry out what we have understood must be done, let him be anathema.

For since the Apostle says, “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up” (1 Corinthians 8:1), it is exceedingly impious to believe that we have Christ’s grace for that which puffs up, but not for that which builds up, since both are gifts of God: both knowing what we ought to do and loving in order to do it, so that, when love builds up, knowledge cannot puff up.

And just as it is written of God, “He teaches human beings knowledge” (Psalm 93:10), so it is also written, “Love is from God” (1 John 4:7).

### 6

It was likewise resolved that if anyone says that the grace of justification is given to us so that what we are commanded to do by free choice we may more easily fulfill through grace—as though, even if grace were not given, we could indeed fulfill the divine commandments, not easily but nevertheless by our own ability—let him be anathema.

For the Lord was speaking of the fruits of the commandments when he did not say, “Without me you can do it with greater difficulty,” but said, “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5).

### 7

It was likewise resolved that, when the holy apostle John says, “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us,” whoever thinks this should be understood as meaning that, out of humility, one ought not to say that one has sin—not because it is truly so—let him be anathema.

The Apostle continues and adds: “But if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:8–9). It is sufficiently clear there that this is to be said not only humbly but also truthfully.

For the Apostle could have said, “If we say that we have no sin, we exalt ourselves, and humility is not in us.” But when he says, “We deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us,” he clearly shows that the person who says he has no sin is not speaking the truth but falsehood.

### 8

It was likewise resolved that if anyone says that the saints say in the Lord’s Prayer, “Forgive us our debts” (Matthew 6:12), not because they say this concerning themselves—for this petition is no longer necessary for them—but on behalf of others who are sinners among their people; and therefore that each of the saints does not say, “Forgive me my debts,” but “Forgive us our debts,” so that the righteous person is understood to ask this rather for others than for himself, let him be anathema.

For the apostle James was holy and righteous when he said, “For we all offend in many things” (James 3:2). Why was “all” added, unless so that this statement would correspond also with the Psalm where it is written, “Do not enter into judgment with your servant, for no living person will be justified in your sight” (Psalm 142:2), and with the prayer of the wisest Solomon, “There is no one who does not sin” (Ecclesiastes 7:21), and with the Book of Job, “He marks the hand of every human being, so that every person may know his own weakness” (Job 37:7)?

For this reason the holy and righteous Daniel also, when he said in the plural in his prayer, “We have sinned; we have acted wickedly,” and the other things which he confesses there truthfully and humbly, lest anyone should think—as certain people hold—that he had said these things not about his own sins but rather about the sins of his people, later said, “When I was praying and confessing my sins and the sins of my people to the Lord my God” (Daniel 9:5, 20). He did not say “our sins,” but spoke of the sins of his people and his own, because, like a prophet, he foresaw those who would understand these things so badly.

### 9

It was likewise resolved that if anyone wishes the very words of the Lord’s Prayer, where we say, “Forgive us our debts,” to be spoken by the saints in such a way that they say this humbly but not truthfully, let him be anathema.

For who could endure someone praying and lying not to human beings but to the Lord himself—saying with his lips that he wishes his debts to be forgiven, while saying in his heart that he has no debts requiring forgiveness?

# Concerning the Same Council of Carthage

Photius, in the *Bibliotheca*, codex 53.

## 1

A book, or synod, against Pelagius and Coelestius, held at Carthage in the great church of Faustus, was read. Honorius was holding the helm of the Western Empire. Bishop Aurelius presided, together with Dotianus of Ptentesii [Note: [Col. 1730] Read: “and Donatianus of Telepte.”], bishop of the first see of the province of Byzacena. Bishops from various provinces attended, numbering two hundred and twenty-four.

This synod condemns with anathema those who asserted that Adam was created mortal and was not condemned to death on account of transgression. Likewise, it condemns those who said that newborn infants did not need Baptism because they did not think them subject to original sin from Adam. It also anathematizes those who affirmed that unbaptized infants live in blessedness in some intermediate place between paradise and hell. It likewise anathematizes six other related propositions favorable to the Pelagians and Coelestians.

## 2

The emperors Theodosius and Honorius also wrote against the same heretics to Bishop Aurelius. After this, Constantius [Note: [Col. 1730] Read: “Constantius.”], the husband of Placidia and father of the younger Valentinian, wrote a decree to Volusianus, prefect of the City, concerning the banishment of the heretic Coelestius.

This Volusianus, the uncle of the holy Melena [Note: [Col. 1730] Read: “Melania.”], at that time shared the beliefs of the pagans; but when death overtook him while he was serving as ambassador at Constantinople, he converted to the orthodox faith and was baptized by the blessed Proclus of Constantinople. At that same time he happened to meet that holy woman, when she herself had come from Jerusalem to the imperial city.

## 3

Pope Leo also wrote concerning converts from Pelagianism, stating that if they wished to be received after returning, they ought to condemn their error in written documents.

In a letter of Pope Celestine of Rome to Nestorius, the same heretics are also rebuked. He likewise wrote to the bishops of Gaul concerning the faith of the blessed Augustine and against those who, excessively emboldened by the license of heresy, grew insolent.

The presbyter Jerome also wrote to Ctesiphon against those asserting ἀπάθεια (*apatheia*, that is, impassibility or freedom from disturbance), or against Pelagius.

This Pelagius was a monk who had taken Coelestius as his disciple.

# Concerning the Judgment and *Tractoria* of Zosimus against Pelagius and Coelestius

[Note: [Col. 1730] See above, the *Commonitorium* of Mercator, nos. 4 and 8.]

Augustine, in Letter 190 to Optatus, no. 23.

For, to use now the words that are found in the letter of the most blessed bishop Zosimus:

> The faithful Lord is faithful in his words, and his Baptism, both in reality and in words—that is, in deed, confession, and the true remission of sins—possesses the same fullness in every sex, age, condition, and class of the human race. No one is made free unless he is a slave of sin, nor can anyone be called redeemed unless he was truly held captive beforehand through sin, as it is written: “If the Son makes you free, you will truly be free” (John 8:36).
>
> Through him we are spiritually reborn; through him we are crucified to the world. By his death, for every soul the bond contracted by propagation—the bond of the death introduced and transmitted to all of us from Adam—is broken; and absolutely no one born is free from liability under it before being freed through Baptism.

In these words of the Apostolic See, the Catholic faith is so ancient, so firmly established, certain, and clear that it is impious for a Christian to doubt it.

Prosper, in his book *Against the Collator*, no. 15.

The most holy See of blessed Peter speaks to the whole world through Pope Zosimus as follows:

> Nevertheless, by the prompting of God—for all good things must be referred to their author, from whom they arise—we reported everything to the awareness of our brothers and fellow bishops.

The African bishops, writing back to the same Pope Zosimus and praising him for the salutary character of this judgment, say:

> But what you placed in your letter, which you ordered to be sent to all, saying, “Nevertheless, by the prompting of God—for all good things must be referred to their author, from whom they arise—we reported everything to the awareness of our brothers and fellow bishops,” we understood in this way: as you passed swiftly by, you cut down with the unsparing sword of truth those who exalt human free choice against God’s help.
>
> For what did you do more freely than to refer everything to the awareness of our humility? And yet you rightly and wisely saw, and truthfully and confidently said, that this was done by the prompting of God.
>
> This is so, certainly, because the will is prepared by the Lord; and, so that they may do something good, he himself touches the hearts of his children with paternal inspirations. For as many as are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God. Thus we do not feel that free choice is absent from us, yet in every good action and in each movement of the human will we do not doubt that his help is more powerful. [Note: [Col. 1731] See below, the letter of Celestine to the bishops of Gaul.]

The same work, no. 57.

Pope Zosimus of blessed memory added the strength of his judgment to the decrees of the African councils and armed the right hands of all bishops with Peter’s sword for the mutilation of the impious.

# Imperial Letter to Aurelius, Bishop of Carthage

[Note: [Col. 1731] This is Letter 201 among Augustine’s letters.]

The emperors **Honorius** and **Theodosius**, to Aurelius the bishop, greeting.

It had previously been decreed that Pelagius and Coelestius, the inventors of an unspeakable doctrine, should be expelled from the city of Rome as certain contagions threatening Catholic truth, lest they corrupt the minds of the ignorant by a wicked persuasion.

In this matter Our Clemency followed the judgment of Your Holiness, by which it is established that they were condemned by all after a just examination of the judgment, and so forth.

Given on the fifth day before the Ides of June at Ravenna, in the consulship of Monaxius and Plinta. [Note: [Col. 1731] In the year of Christ 419.]

A letter was also given to the holy Bishop Augustine in the same terms.

# Letter of Aurelius, Bishop of Carthage, to All Bishops Established throughout the Provinces of Byzacena and Arzugitana concerning the Condemnation of Pelagius and Coelestius

(C)*

To the most beloved and desired brothers and fellow priests Donatianus of the first see, Januarius, Felix, Palatinus, Primianus, Gaianus, another Gaianus, Januarius, Victorinus, and the others established throughout the territory of the provinces of Byzacena and Arzugitana: Aurelius the bishop.

Your Holy Belovedness remembers, most beloved and desired brothers, that it participated in the plenary council concerning the condemnation of Coelestius and Pelagius and their doctrines.

But because, for the honor of God, in whose hand the heart of the king is established, the authority of the most glorious Christian princes, who guard the right and Catholic faith, has been added—and because they wished this authority to be made known to all my fellow bishops through my humility—I therefore hastened to instruct Your Honorable Fraternity by sending copies, lest the serpent-like persuasion of the aforementioned men, excluded from the universal Church of the entire world, should perhaps creep into some part of the province.

Your Belovedness ought not to remain ignorant of this necessary decree of the Christian princes, and the letter they sent to me ought to be forwarded to you. When you have read its copy together with the other copies, Your Belovedness will know how each of you ought to subscribe—whether your subscription is already recorded in the synodal Acts, or whether you were unable to attend that plenary council of all Africa.

When the subscription of all of you concerning the condemnation of the aforementioned heretics has thereby been completed, there will be absolutely no ground from which any suspicion of dissimulation, negligence, or perhaps hidden perversity may rightly appear to have remained.

And in another hand:

I wish you well, brothers; may you live well and remember me. Given on the Kalends of August at Carthage, in the consulship of Monaxius and Plinta. [Note: [Col. 1732] In the year of Christ 419.]

# Booklet of Faith of the Holy Priests of Jesus Christ

[Note: [Col. 1732] In the Veronese codex from which Sirmondus extracted the booklet, nothing remains in place of the title except certain traces of fading letters, which he represented as “IV LI,” perhaps for “Here begins the booklet of faith,” since at the end it read, “Here ends the booklet of faith of S. I. C.” Garnerius interprets these final three characters as “of the Sicilians”; it may perhaps be better to interpret them as “of the priests of Jesus Christ.” For it is hardly credible that the Pelagian bishops, whose leader was Julian—an Italian bishop, certainly—would have called themselves Sicilians.]

Apparently written by Julian and sent to the Apostolic See [Note: [Col. 1732] Perhaps toward the end of the year 418.] in the name of the bishops who, refusing to subscribe to the condemnation of Pelagius and Coelestius, appeal to a plenary synod.

## 1

We believe in God the Father almighty, creator of all things visible and invisible.

## 2

And in our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of the living God, through whom all things were created: not born or made from outside, but begotten from the substance of the Father, true God from true God, so that the one who was begotten is what the one who begot him is.

And because God the Father is without any father of his own, the Son begotten from this Father could not be inferior to the Father. The Son has no beginning, because neither does the Father have an origin.

## 3

We also believe in the Holy Spirit, true God, proceeding from the Father, equal in every respect to the Father and the Son—in will, operation, eternity, and substance.

While distinguishing the persons by the properties of their names, we nevertheless confess the Godhead of the Trinity to be inseparable. We believe that nothing in the Trinity is to be called higher or lower, because the whole Trinity is joined together in the power of the Godhead and the unity of its substance.

## 4

In the fullness of time the Son of God was sent—not by the command of a greater power but by the sharing of will—and the Word became flesh. This did not happen so that God would cease to be God through a transformation, but so that, through the assumption of flesh, he might begin to be human, which he had not been; and so that the human being might ascend to God, God descended to the human being.

He was therefore born for us from the Holy Spirit and Mary, ever-virgin, while according to his divinity he never ceased to be with the Father.

Thus we have received Jesus Christ, the Son of God, from two complete and perfect substances, God and human being. We confess him to have been like the Father according to his divinity and like us according to his humanity, except for the single stain of sin, which is not natural.

He did this so that he might both recall the whole world from sins by his example and redeem it by suffering: as God, removing sin by forgiving it, and as a human being, showing through the likeness of his nature how, thereafter, it could be overcome.

## 5

Beginning with John’s Baptism, by which he was baptized in order to give an example—not, as some wish, because of his own sin, as he himself said to John, “Let it be so for now; for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness” (Matthew 3:15)—he subjected himself to all the sufferings of the flesh, enduring hunger, thirst, weariness, pain, death, and other things of this kind. He became obedient unto death, even death on a cross (Philippians 2:8).

The blessed Peter taught us this when he said:

> Christ suffered for us, leaving us an example so that we might follow his footsteps; he committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth (1 Peter 2:21–22).

## 6

We therefore believe that he suffered and was buried according to the flesh for our salvation, rose on the third day both to destroy death and to open for us the way of resurrection.

Ascending into heaven, he sits at the right hand of the Father, with the substance of his humanity remaining—not emptied but glorified—and remaining forever with the Godhead. We believe that he will come to judge the living and the dead.

By his power and example, we believe that all human flesh will be raised in the same reality of its members in which it was made by God, so that sinners may receive punishments and the righteous glory.

There will be one life for all the saints, but rewards will differ according to labor; and, conversely, punishments will differ for sinners according to the measure of their offenses.

## 7

Following the example of the Church and the command of God, we confess one Baptism, which we truly teach and maintain to be necessary for all alike at every age. We say that no one can obtain forgiveness of sins or the kingdom of heaven unless he has received Baptism.

We believe that someone who has sinned after Baptism can be saved through repentance.

## 8

We accept the New and Old Testament in the number of books handed down by the authority of the Catholic Church.

## 9

We say that the commandments of the divine law are possible to fulfill because of God’s justice. We confess that all of them can be fulfilled through the grace of Christ, which is always the helper and companion of every good act, and through the free choice of the human being, which itself is also a gift of God.

Nevertheless, we understand the grace of God in such a way that it neither follows someone unwilling nor abandons someone obedient.

We judge that one person becomes righteous and another unrighteous not by the will of God but by human fault. For the one who said, “God wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (1 Timothy 2:4), denied that this difference comes from God.

If, then, God wills to save all, and there is no partiality with God (Romans 2:11), sin will most justly be attributed to each person through free choice, according to what is written:

> Before a human being are good and evil, life and death; whatever pleases him will be given to him (Sirach 15:18).

It follows, therefore, that we must confess that we are sinners not because we are unable, but because we neglect to avoid sin.

For this reason the day of judgment has been established, so that the good person may receive a reward for labor, and the wicked person may not escape punishment for contempt.

### 10

We testify that human nature is good and whole, since it was made by the good God. We confess that every human being is made by God, as the patriarch says: “Am I in God’s place, that I should give you children?” (Gen. 30:2); and likewise the prophet declares: “And now, Lord, we do not know Abraham; for you are our father, and we are all the work of your hands” (Isa. 64:8). Hence God also says to Jeremiah: “Before I formed you in your mother’s womb, I knew you” (Jer. 1:5). Likewise, in the Book of Maccabees: “I do not know,” she says, “how you appeared in my womb; for I did not give you spirit, nor did I put together the limbs of each of you” (2 Macc. 7:22). Job, too, refers the very beginning of a conceived human being to God, saying: “Did you not milk me like milk, and coagulate me like cheese, fit me together with bones and sinews, cover me above with skin, and give me life and mercy?” (Job 10:10–12).

All the divine Scriptures are filled with testimonies of this kind, which for the sake of brevity we have omitted here. We also confess that human beings were not only made in the image of God but are made in it, since the Lord says to Noah: “Whoever sheds human blood, his blood shall be shed in return, because God made the human being in his image” (Gen. 9:6). The apostle Paul likewise asserts: “A man ought not to veil his head, since he is the image and glory of God” (1 Cor. 11:7). The apostle James also proclaims: “With it we bless God and Father, and with it we curse human beings, who were made in the image and likeness of God” (James 3:9).

### 11

We say that marriages were instituted and joined together by God as their author, since God said to Noah: “But you, increase and multiply, and fill the earth.” And lest anyone wish to obscure the straightforward history with the mists of allegory, he added: “And multiply upon it” (Gen. 9:7). Hence, when the Jews questioned the Lord in the Gospel about divorce, he replied: “Moses, because of the hardness of your hearts, wrote this commandment for you; but from the beginning it was not so. For he who made them made them male and female” [Col. 1734] “and said: ‘For this reason a man shall leave father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh.’” And lest any misguided person should say that he foretold this as something to be undertaken rather than commanded, he added: “Therefore, what God has joined together, let no human being separate” (Matt. 19:4–8; Mark 10:4–8).

The holy Apostle, too, following Christ’s teaching, says: “Marriage is honorable and the marriage bed undefiled; but the sexually immoral and adulterers God will judge” (Heb. 13:4). And elsewhere: “He who gives his virgin in marriage does well; and he who does not give her in marriage does better” (1 Cor. 7:38). Virginity is therefore to be praised because it is preferred to marriage, which is good: whatever is praised by comparison with evil lacks its proper dignity.

### 12

Since, therefore, we have prefaced our discussion with the goodness of nature, and with the blessing and honor of marriage, we consequently reject natural sin—or whatever other name it may be called—lest we inflict an injury upon God, the creator of all, by maintaining that something could have been made by him together with sin. We would also thereby accuse the testimonies of his Scriptures of falsehood, since they say in the Old Testament: “Fathers shall not die for sons, nor sons die for fathers; each shall die for his own offense” (Jer. 31:30).

Another prophet says: “What is this proverb among you in the land of Israel, saying, ‘The fathers have eaten a sour grape, and the children’s teeth have been set on edge’? As I live, says the Lord, this proverb shall no longer be spoken in Israel. For all souls are mine: as the soul of the father is, so also is the soul of the son; all are mine. The soul that sins shall itself die.” Likewise there: “The son shall not bear the iniquity of his father, nor shall the father bear the iniquity of his son; the justice of the just shall be upon him.” And again there: “I shall judge you, house of Israel, each according to his way, says the Lord” (Ezek. 18:2–4, 20, 30).

And the Apostle says: “We must all be manifested before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive what belongs to the body, according to what he has done, whether good or evil” (2 Cor. 5:10). Likewise the same Apostle: “Each of us shall give an account of himself to God” (Rom. 14:12). And elsewhere: “Each of us shall bear his own burden” (Gal. 6:5).

### 13

We cannot accuse the saints of the Old Testament, who were justified by God and often praised by his judgment, since the Apostle says: “Who shall bring an accusation against God’s elect? It is God who justifies; who is he who condemns?” (Rom. 8:33–34). The Lord likewise testifies in the Gospel: “From you will be required all the righteous blood that has been shed upon the earth, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah” (Matt. 23:35).

Hence, in another passage, the Lord himself, strengthening the Apostles to endure patiently by the example of the Prophets, says: “Rejoice and exult, because your reward is great in heaven; for so they persecuted the Prophets who were before you” (Matt. 5:12). And, which is even greater, he confirmed by his own testimony that those men had been called gods by the prophet David, saying: “If he called those gods to whom the word of God came—and Scripture cannot be annulled—do you say of him whom the Father sanctified and sent into this world, ‘You blaspheme,’ because I said, ‘I am the Son of God’?” (John 10:35–36).

For it is established that they were justified through their own labor and through faith in Christ, since they foresaw that God would come in the flesh, as the Lord himself asserts: “Abraham your father rejoiced that he might see my day; he saw it and rejoiced” (John 8:56). And the Apostle says: “And all these, though commended through faith...” (Heb. 11:39). Again: “By faith Moses, when he had grown up, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter, choosing to be afflicted with the people of God rather than to have the enjoyment of sin for a season, considering the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of Egypt; for he looked toward the recompense” (Heb. 11:24–26).

Hence another Apostle says: “Concerning this salvation those who came before us inquired; the Prophets searched into the time and circumstances to which the Spirit of Christ within them was testifying, when he foretold the sufferings destined for Christ and the glories afterward” (1 Pet. 1:10–11). The Lord himself also proves that they will obtain the kingdom of heaven when he says: “Many will come from east and west and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven; but the children of the kingdom will be cast into the outer darkness” (Matt. 8:11–12).

Therefore we choose to say with the prophet: “But your friends, O God, are exceedingly honored; their dominion is exceedingly strengthened” [Col. 1735] (Ps. 138:17), rather than join those who err and, with reckless speech, disparage both the merits of the saints and the testimony of God’s own mouth.

### 14

Having duly confessed all these things according to the rule of the catholic faith and the authority of the divine Scriptures, we consequently condemn all heretics, especially those who are known among the Latins both by their proper names and by their error, and whose impiety we shudder at: namely, the Arians, who impiously divide the divine substance; the Sabellians, who more wickedly confuse the distinct properties of the persons; the Eunomians, who assert that the Son of God was made from things that did not exist [Note: This is how the Benedictine edition printed at Antwerp in 1703 reads; but Garnerius, in the Augustinian Appendix appended to that edition, restored the passage from the Vernensis manuscript, which Sirmondus had copied in his own hand, as follows: “the Eunomians, who assert that the Son of God was made from things that did not exist.” In B., “the Eunomians, that the Son of God was made, from things that did not exist, assert.” M.]; the Macedonians, who deny divinity to the Holy Spirit; the Apollinarians and their like, who say that the Son of God assumed something less than human nature; the Novatians, who deny repentance to those who have fallen; the Jovinianists, who say that a human being cannot in any way sin after Baptism; and the Manichaeans, who assert two principles, namely, one of good and one of evil, and who say that the soul derives from the good principle but the flesh from the evil, and therefore that there is perpetual conflict between the two natures.

We also condemn those like them who, under the assertion of natural sin, maintain that marriages originated with the devil as their author and that their children are fruits of the devil’s tree. Also those who say that, until the Lord’s Passion, all people were possessed by the devil with the fullest legal right because they had been conceived through the pleasure of marriage. Or those who say that the Son of God only began to benefit the human race from the time of his Passion. Also those who assert that sins are not entirely removed in Baptism. Or those who affirm that the saints of the Old Testament departed from this life with sin. They also say that a human being is driven into sin by necessity.

We likewise abominate the claim that the Savior, because of the necessity of the flesh, lied, and that because of the hindrance of the flesh he was unable to do everything he wished. We condemn those who, with the Manichaeans, condemn first marriages, and, with the Cataphrygians, second marriages. We also condemn those who say that sins cannot be avoided even with the grace of God.

### 15

We also utterly detest anyone who says that human beings can avoid sins without God’s grace or assistance. Likewise anyone who denies that infants need Baptism, or who asserts that Baptism ought to be celebrated for them with words other than those used for adults. If anyone also says that one born of two baptized persons, or born of a baptized woman, does not need the grace of Baptism. Or whoever asserts that neither through Adam does the entire human race die, nor through Christ does the entire human race rise again. Or if there are any other claims that oppose the catholic faith or belong to undisciplined disputes, we condemn them with a similar abhorrence.

All these matters now under discussion—that is, those we have condemned at the end—were themselves also condemned in their own writings by the very persons against whom these charges are made, even though they falsely testify that such things were attributed to them.

### 16

We have written and sent these matters to Your Holiness as they seemed right to us according to the catholic rule. If you think they ought to be held otherwise, write back. But if these things cannot be contradicted, and someone nevertheless wishes to stir up scandal against us, let Your Holiness be certain that we appeal to the hearing of a plenary synod.

### 17

We particularly admonish Your Holiness not to think that we have acted in this way as a reproach to you, because, out of fear of God, we do not dare to subscribe to the condemnation of absent persons. We have been taught by the Scriptures that human will must not be preferred to God’s commands. He says: “You shall not accept a vain report, nor shall you agree with the wicked to become an unjust witness.” And lest anyone think that the multitude should be followed, he added: “You shall not follow the many in evil” (Exod. 23:1–2, according to the Septuagint).

And again: “Before you inquire, do not blame anyone” (Ecclus. 11:7). And again: “Speak what your eyes have seen” (Prov. 25:8, according to the Septuagint). Likewise in the Gospel: “Do not judge, so that you may not be judged; do not condemn, so that you may not be condemned. For with the judgment with which you judge, you will be judged; and with the measure with which you measure, it will be measured back to you” (Matt. 7:1–2).

In another passage, even the Jews, as the Evangelist relates, confess that “our law does not judge a person unless it first hears from him and learns what he is doing” (John 7:51). And in the Acts of the Apostles, a similar judgment was pronounced by Festus among the Gentiles: “It is not the custom of the Romans to condemn anyone before the accused has his accusers present and receives an opportunity to defend himself in order to clear away the charges” (Acts 25:16).

Hence the holy Apostle Paul, establishing a rule for bishops in judging, says: “Do not receive an accusation against a presbyter except on the evidence of two or three witnesses” (1 Tim. 5:19).

Strengthened, therefore, by these and other testimonies, we fear to pronounce judgment against the heads of absent persons whom we have not heard, unless they have been refuted in person. Although it is the duty of priestly office and Christian charity to defend with free authority those who clear themselves in written statements, confess themselves catholic, and condemn the charges brought against them, and to form the better opinion of each person in doubtful matters, nevertheless, preserving the balance of equality promised long ago, midway between the two sides, we neither condemn those whom we have not heard nor defend those who are absent.

Let Your Holiness therefore be certain that, however much this sea may swell when the winds blow and rage against us in bitter waves, it will never be able to shake the house of sound judgment, which is founded upon the justice of Christ.

### 18

We also thought it necessary to repeat this, holy and venerable brother and father Augustine [Note: It appears that this should be corrected to “Zosimus.”]: in your letter you most rightly praised the bishop John, of blessed memory, affirming that he had not destroyed the Churches but had even strengthened them. In a short work addressed to the Neophytes, we have appended, in his own words, what he thought about the Baptism of infants, so that you too, holy brother [Note: Elsewhere: “O holy brothers.”], may know the opinion of the aforementioned man on this matter.

“Blessed be God,” he says; “let us say again, who alone works wonders, who made all things and transformed all things. Behold, those who a little earlier were held captive enjoy the serenity of freedom; those who had been wandering in exile are citizens of the Church; and those who had been in the confusion [Note: Elsewhere, “confession.”] of sin now stand in the lot of righteousness.

“For they are not merely free, but also holy; not merely holy, but also just; not merely just, but also sons; not merely sons, but also heirs; not merely heirs, but also brothers of Christ; not merely brothers of Christ, but also co-heirs; not merely co-heirs, but also members; not merely members, but also a temple; not merely a temple, but also instruments of the Spirit.

“Blessed be God, who alone works wonders. Do you see how many are the gifts of Baptism? Some think that heavenly grace consists only in the forgiveness of sins; but we count ten honors. For this reason we also baptize infants, although they have not been defiled by sins: so that holiness, justice, adoption, inheritance, and brotherhood with Christ may be added to them; so that they may be his members; so that they may become the dwelling-place of the Spirit” (John Chrysostom, *Homily to the Neophytes*).

### 19

Instructed, therefore, by these divine and priestly examples, we have submitted these matters to Your Holiness. It is your responsibility, having considered God’s judgment, to weigh everything with careful examination, so that the peace which we undertook to preserve as commended to us by Christ the Lord may not be dissolved by the intervention of any scandal.

## On Julian, Bishop of Eclanum, Defender of the Pelagian Heresy

Gennadius, in his *Book on Ecclesiastical Writers*, revised against the old Corbie manuscript.

Julian was a man of vigorous intellect, learned in the divine Scriptures, and a scholar in both Greek and Latin. Before he revealed within himself the impiety of Pelagius, he was distinguished among the teachers of the Church. Later, when he defended Pelagius’s heresy, he wrote four books against blessed Augustine, its opponent, and then eight more books. There is also a book presenting a dispute between the two men, each defending his own side [Note: This is Augustine’s *Unfinished Work*, in which he refutes the first six of the eight books of Julian mentioned above.].

This Julian, by distributing alms during a time of famine and scarcity to those in need, drew many people—especially religious persons—into fellowship with his heresy under the appearance of compassion. He died while Valentinian, son of Constantius, was emperor.

## Mercator, in the *Memorandum of Annotations on Julian’s Writings* [Note: See the beginning above, cols. 1680–1682.]

### 1

These and similar [Pelagian] chapters also pleased Julian and his other fellow-members. Once they had been recognized and exposed, and had been condemned by ecclesiastical authority together with the aforementioned persons [Pelagius and Coelestius], Julian defended them also by the sheer number of his books. He therefore chose to be counted third with Pelagius and Coelestius in their condemnation.

### 2

Then, against his childish audacity, the bishop Augustine, of holy memory, composed different books at different times. From among all these, Julian selected one of two books first published to Valerius, so that he might oppose it with four books which he completed for Turbantius [Note: Julian’s first work, consisting of four books written against the first book of *Marriage and Concupiscence*.]. Later he boasts that he responded to one of the last eight volumes sent to Florus [Note: The latter work of the same Julian, consisting of eight books against the second book of *Marriage and Concupiscence*.], pretending that he was completely unaware of many other works which that holy man had composed on the subject.

In those final eight books, wandering through them with dreadful verbosity, and wishing to display himself as more eloquent and learned, after hurling countless insults and abuses against the holy man mentioned above, he shamelessly—or rather, by now impiously—dared to defend the propositions which, as we have stated above, he had learned from Pelagius and Coelestius to his own destruction. Yet, just as in the earlier four books, he continually turns over the same things, always the same things, finding no prudent way out, and filling his parchment or paper more with injuries and insults than with any sound reasoning of the faith.

Although the issue could have been treated with the greatest brevity and by the authority of the holy and divine Scriptures, he composed for himself a vast, distorted, and wholly unnecessary mass of verbosity, from which he forged impieties and accomplished absolutely nothing. For he accomplishes nothing who devotes himself to impiety.

### 3

Nevertheless, the holy bishop Augustine, so often mentioned, overthrew that man’s first four books in six books of his own [Note: Augustine’s first work against Julian.], and also refuted the eight later books, with individual responses attached to each individual chapter [Note: His second work against the same man, which he left unfinished]. Thus, with the hammer of catholic truth, he blunted—or rather shattered—his vain and leaden daggers.

When the work of both men came into our hands, the whole substance of Julian’s foolish and rather impious labor seemed reducible to one perverse proposition, namely: “Adam and Eve’s transgression did not make them mortal, nor did their guilt pass by original succession to their descendants; only the person who, by imitating them, has despised the divine commands becomes guilty.” When, therefore, as I said, I had read through the entire work with particular care, I too responded briefly, as far as the capacity of our strength allowed, adding annotations from his books wherever the opportunity required it. Thus, after the trumpet of so great a Father and teacher, the reader, not disdaining to take up also our little straw pipe, may understand with complete brevity that Julian spent his labor on the composition of his numerous books vainly and with great impiety, in work full of boasting [Col. 1738], and so forth.

### 4

“Are you then the son of Memorius, bishop of holy and blessed memory? Were you born from the womb of Juliana, a woman whom you could find no more honorable among the most reverend matrons? Far be it, far be it from me to dare believe this about you. I would rather believe you the son of their servants, and that you were substituted for them, as is often said to have happened—and this is something you yourself rather approve by the great wantonness and obscenity of your speech. Or, if that is not so, no one who knows the holy character, holy life, and discipline of those people and who has carefully examined your speech in these writings will doubt that they degenerated in you.

“After the death of those holy people, you rightly instructed your two sisters in such lessons through the teaching of your mouth. We know, we know what one of them said or reproached you with when, being excessively severe, you rose up against the ruin of her modesty; and then you immediately fell silent, not daring to inflict any further troubles of your censure upon her grief, and so forth.”

### 5

“Now hear, you yourself and those who have deigned to read both me and you, what you once pronounced against this most impious, most perverse, most shameless, and most wanton opinion of yours—namely, in your letter which you dared at that time to send to the Apostolic See, when you refused to meet with the universal Church in condemning Pelagius and Coelestius throughout the whole world. Before it came into the hands of that holy Roman Church’s bishop, it was circulated through almost all Italy by the efforts of certain people whom you had deceived, and it is known to have been presented to the ears of many as something of great importance.

“For there, among other things, you say as follows: ‘Whoever, therefore, asserts that neither through Adam’s death does the entire human race die, nor through Christ’s resurrection does the entire human race rise again, is opposed to the Apostle, who says: “As all die in Adam, so also shall all be made alive in Christ”’” (1 Cor. 15:22).

“We know and understand by what fraud and deceit you say and mean ‘all’: namely, not absolutely all human beings—that is, the entire human race—but all those who may wish to be imitators of Adam. And when that Apostle said that ‘through Christ’s resurrection all shall rise again,’ you must likewise, without doubt, say that not the entire human race will rise again, but only the righteous and holy, who have imitated Christ’s righteousness and holiness. Yet it is established that absolutely everyone will rise through Christ, although some will rise to the kingdom and others to judgment.”

### 6

“You add: ‘It is therefore rightly rejected when anyone contradicts this statement: “Through one human being came death, and through one human being the resurrection of the dead”’” (ibid. 15:21). “Likewise: ‘Adam’s sin harmed him alone and not the human race.’ And this opinion,” you say, “is rightly refuted by us. For it must be believed that it harmed not him alone but the human race.”

“Here, even though you think you preserve your most perverse and twisted meaning, you could not conceal from us what you are doing. For, as you wish to teach, those people themselves, although few in comparison with the entire race, are the human race.”

### 7

“Likewise,” you say, “the proposition that infants are in the state in which Adam was before his transgression I count among undisciplined questions. Those who are born today are not in every respect in the state in which Adam was before sin, although it cannot be denied that they, like him, are the work of God.”

“We know very well what state you say and mean here, while you imagine that you preserve your own meaning: not, of course, Adam’s state before sin, but the smallness and littleness in which infants are born, and so forth.”

### 8

“Likewise you add that Adam was also made mortal, and that whether he sinned or did not sin, he would have died; and you said that this was not supported by reason. ‘For it must be believed,’ you say, ‘that he was indeed made immortal, but that, if he had not sinned, he could have acquired the power of immortality by tasting the tree of life. It was therefore badly said that, whether he sinned or did not sin, he would have died,’ and so forth.”

[Col. 1739]

### 9

“For we remember how, at the time when you were present in the city of Rome and were troubling the Church among certain simpler people together with the leaders [Note: “Rigberius,” for “participants.”] of this most insane error of yours, you would ask: ‘What is sin?’ you would say. ‘Is it something evil or something good?’ ‘Evil,’ you were answered. To this you would add: ‘Is God the author and maker of this evil?’

“‘Far be it, far be it!’ they cried out to you. ‘How far—how very far—is such madness!’ Not even the most impious Manichaean has dared to profess this. He neither believes nor professes God to be the author of evil, but most wickedly demands that evil has from eternity its own principle, its own essence, and its own nature.

“At that point you would say that it must immediately be asked whether sin was a substance, or a nature, or some accidental thing. When Christian simplicity hesitated for a little, you proceeded in this fashion:

“‘Sin cannot in any way be a substance or a nature. For if it were this,’ you said, ‘it would have God as its maker and author. There is no nature that God did not create. But since it has already been established that God is not the author of evil, sin is therefore neither a substance nor a nature, since it has been made perfectly clear that it is evil. And since it is not a substance,’ you say, ‘it must not be believed by any right or reason that sin could pass into a substance or nature, which is the human being.’

“And you concluded: ‘It is therefore wrongly and foolishly believed that sin is transmitted from Adam,’ and so forth.”

### 10

In your letter, which, as we have mentioned, was sent to Pope Zosimus, of holy memory, you disapprove of and condemn the person who believes “that Adam was made mortal and that, whether he sinned or did not sin, he would have died.” You say: “Nor is this supported by reason. For I believe that he was indeed made immortal, but that, if he had not sinned, he could have acquired the power of immortality by tasting the tree of life.”

You also add: “The person who contradicts the Apostle’s proclamation, ‘As all die in Adam, so all will be made alive in Christ,’ is rightly disapproved.” Then you add this other testimony: “Through one human being came death, and through one human being the resurrection of the dead.”

When a simple Christian hears these words, believing that no deceit or fraud is being introduced, he judges the speaker to be an excellent and reliable teacher, in the manner in which the Church is accustomed to be taught by the Apostles. He decides to listen attentively to the rest of the same Apostle’s words, which you pursue in this case.

But you, having one thing concealed in your heart and another ready upon your tongue, a new and remarkable disputant, now thrust this into your work, composed after so long a time in Cilicia. Since it is necessary to repeat the chapter, let us examine again what new and unheard-of material you brought back after traversing the sea and surveying the East.

“Therefore,” you say, “according to the Apostle, sin entered this world through one human being, and through sin came death, since the world saw him both as guilty and destined for the condemnation of everlasting death,” and so forth.

Let us leave to Christian and prudent readers, after reading you, the judgment of what they ought to think about your vanity. For who could have suspected from your earlier statement that you meant anything other than what all those priests of God meant when, under the presidency of Pope Zosimus, of holy memory, they condemned Pelagius, Coelestius, and you concerning all these chapters about Adam—chapters which you had previously rejected and condemned, but which now, as if gathered together and brought forth from concealment, deserved to be received into your confession? And so forth.

## Preface of the Same Mercator to the Refutation of the Creed Published by Theodore of Mopsuestia

Theodore’s discourse is in Greek. He was once bishop of the town of Mopsuestia in the province of Cilicia. I have therefore attempted, as far as I am able, to transfer it into Latin word for word. I wished to make its perverse meaning concerning the Lord’s dispensation, alien and quite estranged from the catholic faith—by which he wickedly deceived Nestorius, once bishop of Constantinople, together with himself—known to Latin ears as something to be avoided in every way and not followed.

At the same time, I wished to point out that Julian, the former bishop of the town of Eclanum, a Pelagian or Coelestian heretic [Col. 1740], followed this Theodore. After traveling through the lands, traversing the sea, and surveying the East, Julian made his way with his associates, fellow-participants, and συνταλαιπώροις—his fellow sufferers—with great effort to this man, whom he regarded as a celebrated teacher of Christian doctrines, so that Theodore might confirm for him the Pelagian or Coelestian heresy which Julian had undertaken to defend and follow. From there, as though better instructed, he composed those eight volumes which he considers exceedingly wise, directed rather against the catholic faith than against Augustine, of holy memory.

Let the aforesaid Julian therefore recognize from this translation, if he does not disdain to read it, that, while the bad faith by which we said Theodore wickedly deceived Nestorius with himself remains in Theodore, he is nevertheless opposed also to Julian himself and to his own doctrine, about which he composed books in a state of bad swelling and bad health of mind. Let him also recognize that, after his departure from Cilicia, he was condemned by Theodore with an anathema in an assembly of the bishops of that province.

Let him therefore not become angry or resentful against us if we justly expose, convict, and lament that he is alien from the catholic faith and rightly condemned together with Theodore, whose endless praises he expounds in his books and whose authoritative opinion he boasts of relying upon in his error. For Julian is more to be lamented than persecuted with any hatred.

## Julian’s Opinions, Expressed from His Short Works, with Their Refutation

The Venerable Bede the Presbyter, in the preface to his book on the *Song of Songs*.

### Chapter One

#### 1

Since, with the help of heavenly grace, I am about to write on the *Song of Songs*, I first thought the reader should be warned to read with the greatest caution the short works which Julian, bishop of Eclanum in Campania, composed on the same book. Otherwise, through the abundance of his flattering eloquence, the reader may fall into the mire of harmful teaching. Rather, as the saying goes, let him pluck the grape in such a way that he also avoids the thorn—that is, let him search out and choose the sound meanings in Julian’s statements, so that he may no less avoid the unsound ones.

Or better, let him do what Maro says:

> You who gather flowers and strawberries growing upon the ground,  
> Flee from here, O boys: a serpent lies hidden in the grass.  
> (*Eclogue* 3.92–93)

That is, let him restrain himself entirely from reading Julian, since there are writers who have expounded the same book both with sound meanings and in simpler words.

For Julian is, on the one hand, a most accomplished rhetorician and, on the other, after Pelagius, a most fierce opponent of the grace of God, as his writings more clearly demonstrate—those writings in which he raged against Augustine, the most vigorous defender of that same grace.

As the occasion of this quarrel, Julian first composed a short work on Love, under the pretext that he wished to rescue love from the foulest pleasure, but in reality to confirm his own heresy. In brief, though many matters are compressed into it, he teaches: “By the exercise of free choice, we are able to do the good things we wish, although through the help of God’s grace we may accomplish them more easily”—just as we are able to complete a journey on foot, but undoubtedly with less labor when horses are available to carry us.

He forgets the apostolic admonition: “Work out your salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God who works in us both to will and to accomplish” (Phil. 2:12–13). And what is more serious, he opposes the one who did not say, “Apart from me you can do a little,” but: “Apart from me,” he says, “you can do nothing” (John 15:5).

#### 2

He teaches that “only those whom learning and piety have made clear-sighted and learned can contemplate the mysteries concealed in the law.” He has forgotten the grace of God, which revealed the secrets of the Scriptures even to the uneducated and untutored, as the Evangelist says: “Then he opened their minds so that they might understand the Scriptures” (Luke 24:45).

The same evangelist testifies that these people were uneducated when he says: “When they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and realized that they were unlettered and uneducated men, they were astonished” (Acts 4:13).

[Col. 1741]

#### 3

He says: “A holy and noble love, implanted in us from the very beginning of life by nature’s uniting power, and relying upon the soul’s own powers all the way to extreme old age, persists in its vigor without any loss to itself.”

He is plainly incredulous toward the Lord’s statement: “Without me you can do nothing”; and also toward the apostolic saying: “We all stumble in many things” (James 3:2).

It is remarkable where Julian learned that “a holy and noble love, implanted in us from the very beginning of the light, with nature bringing it into harmony,” when the Apostle, himself born from the stock of the Patriarchs, says: “We too were once by nature children of wrath” (Eph. 2:3).

How could it be nature, unless, after the first human being sinned and abandoned holy love, vice grew in place of nature?

It is remarkable where Julian found—or thought he could find—even one human being in whom “holy love, relying solely upon the powers of the soul, persisted in its vigor without loss all the way to old age.” Yet the one who, because of his supreme love, deserved to recline in the bosom of his Creator could find no such person among those who enjoy God’s grace. Rather, he testified by humble confession: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8).

#### 4

He says: “Just as we draw from the body that which is disturbed and rapid, so from the soul we draw that which is elevated and continuous.”

Both parts of this statement are also shown to be contrary to the truth. If “our love drew from the body,” rather than from the soul, “that which is disturbed and rapid,” the Lord would not say:

“For from within, out of the human heart, evil thoughts proceed: adulteries, fornications, murders, thefts, greed, wickedness, deceit, sexual impurity, an evil eye, blasphemy, pride, foolishness. All these evils proceed from within and defile the human being” (Mark 7:21–23).

Again, if our love derived its character as “elevated and continuous” not from God’s daily grace but from “nature” or “the powers of the soul,” the Apostle would not say of his own holy labors, in which he certainly persevered through elevated and continuous love:

“I labored more abundantly than all of them; yet not I, but the grace of God with me” (1 Cor. 15:10).

And again: “Not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think anything as though from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God” (2 Cor. 3:5).

Even if he possessed his good works—which, without any contradiction, are crowned by elevated and continuous love—not from the Lord but from himself, he would have thanked the Lord in vain for things he had not received, saying: “But thanks be to God, who always leads us in triumph in Christ Jesus” (ibid. 2:14).

5. He says, “The same [love], so long as he desires nothing of genital pleasure, is moved, as it were, solely by the mind’s decision, and in its actions possesses delight—free from disturbance and likewise rejoicing in liberty.” This is plainly to say that, apart from what pertains to the stimuli of the flesh, it lies within the decision of our mind to what love it submits itself and to what extent; and that this same love, governed solely by the movement of the mind—that is, without being acted upon by any grace of God—possesses the free perfection of good works, subject to no disturbance. How far this is from the truth, every prudent person readily understands.

For why does so great a multitude of the faithful, seeking to love their Creator “with all their heart, with all their soul, and with all their strength,” and every neighbor “as themselves” (Matt. 22:37, 39), not always obtain what it desires, unless because that love is not moved by the mind’s decision, as Julian supposed, but, as Paul knew, “the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5)? Therefore it is not equal in everyone, because each of us has different gifts of grace that have been given.

Why, moreover, are we so often hindered by adversities arising not only from outside but also from the mind itself, and are unable to accomplish all the good things we desire, unless the one who says, “Our love, solely by the mind’s decision, possesses delight in its actions, free from disturbance and likewise rejoicing in liberty,” is mistaken? The Psalmist truly sings when he says:

> By the Lord a man’s steps are directed,  
> and he greatly desires his way.  
> When the righteous man falls, he will not be shaken,  
> because the Lord strengthens his hand.  
> (Ps. 36:23–24)

Here he plainly indicates that we cannot be free from the disturbance of vices even amid the frequent aids of the Lord’s protection; nor ought we to rejoice in all the steps of our actions because of the freedom of nature, but because of divine direction.

But Julian vainly wishes to exempt “genital pleasure,” “which alone is not moved by the decision of our mind,” as though the rage of anger, pride, love of money, gluttony, vainglory, and the rest of this kind were not overcome with far greater labor than the incitements of lust. These disturbances arrive to trouble our mind even before the age of puberty; and even when lust has often been subdued or has ceased by nature, they nevertheless do not cease to attack us.

## CHAPTER II

6. He says, “The assistance of the Holy Spirit is given to our preceding efforts and merits, and is given for this purpose: that we may love the human race more intensely.” It is useful to set out his words in order:

> “Therefore, when the mind of the wise person, subordinating pleasure to the dignity of love, both stimulates and orders desire, it never crosses the limits of duty, but advances through efforts and merits toward such greatness and beauty that the grace of the Holy Spirit begins to fan its noble fire, then that love comes into being which endeavors to embrace not only relatives or fellow citizens, but the entire human race in its bosom.”

In this one sentence, a Catholic reader readily observes how many and how great the blasphemies are. For it is clear what he attributes to the decision of human freedom and what to spiritual grace: he testifies that the human mind can by itself become wise; can by itself possess the dignity of holy and noble love; can by itself subordinate the pleasure of the flesh to this love; and can by itself both stimulate itself toward virtues and order its desire—so much so that it never crosses the limits of that duty by which the same love must be cultivated.

He says that the mind itself, through its efforts and merits, advances toward such greatness and beauty that it becomes worthy of the assistance of the Holy Spirit. At the arrival of this Spirit, he does not say that the mind is helped as a dark house is helped when a flame or torch is kindled and illuminates it; rather, he says it is helped as wind helps a burning or shining fire, so that it may shine more brightly. The fire, indeed, could be kindled and burn without the wind’s breath and could consume a great forest; yet, driven by the wind, it flames more and more. This is what he means when he says, “so that the grace of the Holy Spirit begins to fan its noble fire.”

He had placed so many goods of the mind beforehand, and after all these he says that the grace of the Holy Spirit begins within it—as though arriving afterward as an assistant, and not preceding it as the inspirer and author of our good efforts and merits. Consider what he believes is accomplished in the noble fire of the wise mind by this fanning:

> “Then that love comes into being,” he says, “which endeavors to embrace not only relatives or fellow citizens, but the entire human race in its bosom.”

You therefore see what he attributes to the spirit of grace, since he grants so much power to our mind. He says that grace comes late to assist the mind and then infuses into it not that love by which God is loved, but only that by which the human race is loved—forgetful, or heedless, of the apostolic faith, which says: “The love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.”

It would be a lengthy task to bring forward and refute with testimonies of the truth all the absurdities that he set forth in this book. Let these few examples suffice, from which it may be inferred how detestable the rest are.

## CHAPTER III

7. After these and countless similar arguments, with which he completed his first book by disputing against the grace of God, he stained the second book with no lesser plague of the same heresy. In explaining the words, “For your breasts are better than wine” (Song 1:1), he first philosophized most foully about the nature of milk; then, much more foully, he attempted to transfer the quality of that nature to confirm his error.

Since setting out the whole passage would be both repellent and excessively long, we have thought it sufficient to quote a part. Assuming, then, the persons of those against whom he was fighting under the name of Manichaeans, he says, among other things:

> “For he maintained that our opinions lead directly to such foaming surges of error that we turned our slander against the author himself; and, in order to lighten the guilt with which the crimes of the will were burning us, we subjected the very nature of the body to infamy, swearing that we came into this light incapable of goodness and full of iniquity; finally, that scarcely anyone could be led to justice—not by reason, I say, but not even by the instruction of the sacred law. This opinion, then, disparaged the nature of flesh and blood. But after the Mediator of God and human beings took up the mystery of salvation, so that, intending to give an example of perfect virtue, he might assume the nature of mortal humanity, he showed that all crimes belonged to conduct, not to seed. Finally, when wills had been turned toward better things, he showed that not only the law’s commands but also those of the Gospel could be fulfilled.”

A brief answer must be given to these words. We do not in any way turn slander against the author of our nature when we say that we were conceived in iniquities and born in transgressions. Rather, we confess that in the first parents of our nature we were made in his likeness, so that, immortal and without sin, we might live in the delights of paradise with the aid of his grace.

If those first parents had taken care to preserve that most blessed purity of primordial life, and had trusted the enemy no more than the Creator, their holy and undefiled offspring would still today inhabit the delights of paradise, knowing neither death nor sin. But when, without any necessity imposed by nature, they consented to sin solely through the carelessness of a wandering mind, and soon, by the just judgment of the Creator, were excluded from the place of paradise’s pleasure and punished with death, they left to their stock and race the contagion of the sin they had rashly contracted. Thus it came about that, although they themselves had committed sin willingly, we too were bound by its guilt unwillingly, so that not even infants—who cannot will anything good or evil—can be free from it unless by the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord.

Thus Julian is proved mistaken when he says, “Guilt was kindled in us solely by the crime of the will,” and, as he later expressed his meaning more openly, when he says, “All crimes belong to conduct, not to generation.” Those things are of seed which we have drawn from Adam as original; those of conduct, or will, or weakness and ignorance, are the crimes that we ourselves add.

He is proved mistaken when he reproves those who subject the nature of our body—not that nature in which the first human being was created holy and immortal, but that which became corrupted after their transgression—to infamy, saying: “I know that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh” (Rom. 7:18); and again, as the same Apostle says: “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh; for these oppose each other, so that you do not do what you wish” (Gal. 5:17).

He is proved mistaken when he censures those who “testify that we come into this light incapable of goodness and full of iniquity.” For we truly confess that all human beings come into this light full of iniquity through the guilt of the first transgression; but far be it from us to swear that we are born incapable of goodness. The heretic, in order to deceive the weak more artfully, joined the truth of Catholic confession to the falsehood of his perfidy.

He is proved mistaken when he says that “we swear that no one can be led to justice, not only by reason, but not even by the instruction of the sacred law.” On the contrary, we confess that, with the Lord’s help, we are led to justice both by reason and by the teaching of the holy law. Without his grace, however, we cannot be justified either by the aids of natural reason or by the precepts of the divine law, as the Apostle testifies: “The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3:6). That is, the letter that commands kills if the Spirit is not present to grant that the commands of the letter be fulfilled; and the Spirit gives life by granting that the letter can be fulfilled.

But when he says of the Lord, “so that, intending to give an example of perfect virtue, he might assume the nature of mortal humanity,” he has more secretly spewed out the poison of his heresy. For he says that the Lord who came in the flesh bestowed upon us not gifts but examples of virtue. Hence, shortly afterward, he says:

> “By his very assumption of flesh,” I say, “he condemned the sins of conduct—not, of course, by changing the nature of the flesh, but its works, so that the justification of the law might be fulfilled in us according to his example.”

## CHAPTER IV

8. Likewise, in explaining the verse, “Your neck is like necklaces” (Song 1:9), he says:

> “When a neck beautiful by nature is adorned with gems, diligence undoubtedly increases its felicity; and things worthy of each other come together, namely, the honor of the necklaces and the loveliness of the neck. So also in you, whose nobility instruction shapes, so that the virtues which nature begins, discipline may complete.”

Instead of saying, “Grace begins, grace completes, grace crowns.”

Likewise, after countless statements of this kind—which a pious reader will very easily detect in his own works—in explaining the verse in which it is said, “I will seize you and bring you into my mother’s house; there you will teach me” (Song 8:2), he revealed more openly the mad opinions he held against the faith, saying of the Lord:

> “Already in infancy he showed many things that we ought to learn. First, that he himself is the maker of all those born from the union of male and female, since he fashioned for himself a body from a virgin without the agency of a man. Next, that no sin is innate in human beings, since he existed both clothed in the reality of flesh and free from stain. Finally, that our origin can be attributed only impiously to the works of the devil, even though it rejoiced in the true God not only as creator but also as indweller.”

In saying these things he not only constructs his error, but also does so by introducing this very example. For Scripture testifies that sin is innate in human beings when it says:

> “A heavy yoke is upon the children of Adam, from the day they come forth from their mother’s womb until the day of burial in the mother of all.”  
> (Ecclus. 40:1)

Indeed, blessed Job testifies that this is coeval with human beings from conception itself when, pleading with the Lord, he says:

> “Who can make the clean thing from unclean seed? Is it not you, who alone are?”  
> (Job 14:4)

And what consistency could there be in saying that no sin is innate in human beings born from the union of male and female because the Son of God, who fashioned for himself a body from a virgin without the agency of a man, existed clothed in the reality of flesh and free from stain?

What logic would follow by which a mere human being could establish the innocence of his birth from the example of the Mediator of God and human beings born in the flesh, when the archangel said of his birth to the virgin mother:

> “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God.”  
> (Luke 1:35)

Yet to our first mother, after the guilt of transgression, the just Judge said:

> “I will multiply your hardships and your conceptions; in pain you will bear children, and you will be under the power of the man.”  
> (Gen. 3:16)

Nor did he deal either Catholicly or consistently with what he says: that our origin can be attributed only impiously to the works of the devil, although it rejoiced in the true God not only as creator but also as indweller. For although the devil introduced sin to the first parents, he did not remove from them the natural course of the blessing, by which they had heard: “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth” (Gen. 1:28).

We are not therefore deceived by the impiety that Julian charges us with, namely, that we attribute our origin to the works of the devil; for we know that our origin was created by God’s primordial work of blessing. But far be it from us to say that, after the evil of transgression and before the remedy of the second regeneration—which occurs through water and the Holy Spirit by the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord—our origin rejoiced in God.

## CHAPTER V

9. We have thought it necessary, for the protection of readers, to note these few passages from the many in Julian’s aforementioned work. Warned by these examples, they should examine his remaining writings more carefully, since he often inserts statements that are no less harmful among salutary words.

For in other short works as well, despite the vigorous opposition of the most holy and learned bishop Augustine, he does not hesitate to affirm the same heresy of his. In the book he wrote *On the Good of Perseverance*, he defends, as he himself claims, the goodness of nature and the freedom of our will with great insistence against the perfidy of Manichaeus; but, as the truth demonstrates, he persists with great obstinacy against the faith of heavenly grace.

“This,” he says, “is perseverance, which above all asserts the power and goodness of free choice, and the freedom of that nature and of the movements of the human mind, since it shows that every good of the mind is voluntary and never subject to any accident.”

But not only the apostolic writings, but my own thoughts as well, teach me that I do not have free movements of the flesh—or even of the mind. They do not permit me, though willing and striving, to devote myself with fixed mind and tireless desire to the practice of prayer, to say nothing of other matters.

If I had free movements of mind, I would wish to keep my mind continuously intent upon prayer during the time of prayer just as I can very easily arrange the members of my body, whenever I wish, in whatever position or place is suitable for prayer.

A little later he says:

> “For it arms and kindles the excellent mind of each person, while it always reminds him of his freedom and drives every fear away from him.”

How much better he would have defeated Manichaeus if he had said:

> “The grace of God has made the mind of each of the elect excellent and has kindled it toward the practice of virtue, while always reminding it of its weakness and that it can do nothing without grace; and while driving away from it all confidence in its own virtue, it urges it to sing to God: ‘I will guard my strength for you’” (Ps. 58:10).

Again, after many statements in which he praises the freedom of our will, he says:

> “For if, as the most learned and orthodox have splendidly argued, no one can ever truly be harmed except by himself, and no one can in any way become miserable against his will, what, then, will virtue fear except its own failure, by which a human being is harmed eternally?”
