This opinion can stand nowhere except among heretics. For it is plainly established that Adam’s sin harms all human beings—not by themselves, certainly, but by him whose guilt from the first crime condemned the whole human race perpetually, except those whom the grace of Christ frees.

The malice of heretics harms those whom it drags unknowingly and unwillingly to destruction, although they desire to know and hold the Catholic faith.

But Julian feared that, if in so large a volume he attributed everything by which we might live rightly to the freedom of our will, he would be detested and anathematized by all as an open enemy of the grace of God. Therefore he mentioned grace here as well, but so covertly that he did not say that it gives all virtues; he said only that it assists and strengthens one virtue in us—perseverance:

> “For it is the work of divine grace to assist and strengthen perseverance, which can preserve the other virtues and defend virtue against everything that resists.”

Here too he used a very cautious word: he did not say that grace gives us perseverance, as though it had not previously been possessed, but rather that it assists and strengthens it, as though it had already arisen from us. Thus wind helps a flame of fire—which it did not itself kindle but which was kindled from elsewhere—to flame more brightly, and, by blowing, strengthens it so that it will not be extinguished. As we have shown, he clarified this meaning more fully in the book *On Love*.

Near the end of this little work, Julian himself openly reveals the purpose for which he labored throughout the various short works he examined:

> “It is a scandal to Manichaeus,” he says, “that we confess his fabrication—that is, that we deny our Lord, who is true—and it offends him because we maintain that nature is good and that human beings have free choice.”

[Note: [Col. 1745] In another version: “we confess that it offends.”]

10. In the book that he wrote to Demetrias, a virgin of Christ, *On the Institution of a Virgin*, he likewise reveals what he thinks about the power of free choice.

Some of our people, reading this book carefully, rashly believe it to be by the holy and Catholic teacher Jerome. They fail to see that both the sweetness of its seductive eloquence and the perversity of its misleading heresy plainly prove that this little work is not his. Indeed, in his dialogue between Atticus and Critobulus, which he published while Pelagius was alive, Jerome himself had already vanquished and crushed Pelagius’s faith—or rather, his perfidy—with divine eloquence. At that time Julian, still a young boy, was being nourished by Pelagius like a little serpent in a serpent’s den.

In this book, then, and in other short works, Julian declares that he has confirmed the same heresy of his, writing as follows:

> “Whenever I have to speak about the formation of morals and the conduct of a holy life, I customarily first display the power and quality of human nature and show what it can accomplish.”

A little later:

> “Since I have followed this order of exhortation in other short works as well, I think it should be observed especially here, where the goodness of nature must be declared more fully, in proportion as the life to be formed is more perfect.”  
> (*Letter to Demetrias*, chap. 2)

Likewise, in the course of the same book:

> “For how many philosophers have we heard of, read about, and ourselves seen who were chaste, patient, modest, generous, abstinent, kind, who rejected alike the honors and pleasures of the world, and were lovers of justice no less than of wisdom? Whence, I ask, did people alienated from God possess these qualities that please God? Whence did they have these good things, unless from the goodness of nature? And since we see that the qualities I have mentioned are possessed either all together by one person, or individually by different persons, and since all share one nature, they show by their example that everything can exist in everyone which is found individually in individuals. But if human beings show, even without God, what they were made by God to be, consider what Christians can do, whose nature has been restored for the better in Christ, and who are helped by the assistance of divine grace.”  
> (Ibid., chap. 3)

And later, speaking of blessed Job:

> “O man evangelical before the Gospels, and a disciple of the Apostles before the apostolic commandments! By opening the hidden riches of nature and bringing them into the open, he showed from himself what all of us could do.”  
> (Ibid., chap. 6)

A little later:

> “Nor do we defend the goodness of nature in such a way as to say that it cannot do evil, since we certainly confess that it is capable of good and evil. We only vindicate it from this accusation: that we should not seem to be driven to evil by its fault, since we do neither good nor evil without the will, and since we are free always to do one, while we can always do both. For why are some to judge and others to be judged, unless it is because in the same nature there are different wills, and because, although we can all do the same things, we do different things?”

A little later, while recalling that Adam was expelled from paradise and Enoch was taken from the world, he added:

> “For neither would the one have deserved punishment nor the other election from a just God, unless each had been capable of both. The same must be understood of the brothers Cain and Abel, and also of the twins Esau and Jacob; and it must be recognized that the sole cause is the will when merits are different in the same nature.”

And again, a little later:

> “Nor does any other cause make it difficult for us to live well than the long habit of vices, which infects us from childhood and gradually corrupts us over many years; then, after binding and enslaving us to itself, it seems to possess a certain force of nature.”  
> (Ibid., chap. 8)

Likewise, after many passages in which he most effectively instructs the virgin dedicated to God (and he would indeed produce a highly useful and salutary work if he taught her to seek in every respect the aid of divine grace rather than trust in the freedom and powers of her own mind; likewise, the book which we have said he wrote *On the Good of Perseverance* would greatly benefit those devoted to virtue if he did not intermingle the poisonous faults of error. But if, as the Apostle testifies, a little leaven corrupts the whole lump, how much more does the greatest poison do so?), he says:

> “We attribute iniquity to the just and cruelty to the pious when we complain that he first commanded something impossible. Therefore we think that, on account of these things, a human being should be condemned by him which he could not avoid.”

And a little later:

> “He who is just could not command anything impossible; nor will he who is pious condemn a human being for those things which he could not avoid.”  
> (Ibid., chap. 16)

11. In each of these statements, which I have excerpted from one of his little books, the magnitude of the errors is readily apparent to every learned person. I have set down so many of them together for this reason: that those who contend that this book was written by the Catholic blessed Jerome’s pen might be convicted by the numerous proofs of its errors [Col. 1747], and that they might become more cautious in reading a work they had learned to be heretical.

I also thought it useful to respond briefly to all these statements together, since, as I have said, their wickedness is clearer than daylight to everyone.

When he says that “many philosophers possess patience, chastity, modesty, and other virtues from the goodness of nature,” it is certain that whatever philosophers did not know Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God, could possess neither true virtue nor true wisdom. To the extent that they possessed any taste of wisdom or an image of virtue, they received the whole of it from above—not only through the gift of the first creation, but also through his daily grace, since he does not abandon his creature, nor does he abandon the creature that has not abandoned him; rather, he distributes his gifts to human beings as he himself has judged, great gifts to the great and small gifts to the small.

When he says that “everything can exist in everyone which is found individually in individuals,” he contradicts Scripture, which says:

> “All the members do not have the same function; and although we are many, we are one body in Christ, and individually members of one another, having gifts that differ according to the grace given to us.”  
> (Rom. 12:4–6)

But when this mortal nature has put on immortality, then at last all the good virtues can exist in everyone; and even then this will not be from the goodness of nature, but through the grace of him of whom it is written: “So that God may be all in all” (1 Cor. 15:54, 28).

The daily evidence of our weakness also proves that everything cannot exist in everyone, since many are found who, striving with the greatest persistence, are nevertheless unable to attain the virtues they see others possessing.

When he says that “human beings, even without God, show what they were made by God to be,” he is so far from the truth that even people close to God cannot show, in this life alone, what they were made by God in the first progenitor to be. [Note: [Col. 1747] According to Morel, *Elem. Critic.*, pp. 259–260, *protoplasti* should be read here. M.]

For who could be greater in wisdom or life than the one who, before paying the debt of the flesh, was caught up into paradise or into the recesses of the third heaven, and contemplated the society of the heavenly citizens and heard their conversations (2 Cor. 12:4)? Yet he says:

> “I delight in the law of God according to the inner person, but I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind.”  
> (Rom. 7:22–23)

The parents of the human race, while they preserved the goodness of nature undefiled, plainly could not have said this.

When he says that “the nature of Christians has been restored for the better through Christ” and that “they are helped by the assistance of divine grace,” if he wishes this to be understood solely of what was granted to us in the remission of sins through Baptism, it is heretical; but if it also concerns his daily grace, by which he does not cease to restore and assist us in mind and body, it is Catholic.

When he says that “blessed Job opened the hidden riches of nature in his outstanding virtues and showed from himself what all of us could do,” how much better would he have said that Job opened the ineffable riches of divine grace and showed in himself that God could give these things to all whom he wished?

When he says that “we are not driven to evil by the fault of nature, since we do neither good nor evil without the will,” he contradicts the Apostle, who says:

> “I know that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh. For to will is present with me, but to accomplish the good I do not find. For I do not do the good that I will, but I do the evil that I do not will.”  
> (Rom. 7:18–19)

When he says that “it is free for us always to do one thing, although we can always do both,” he contradicts the prophet, who addresses God in supplication:

> “I know, Lord, that a person’s way is not his own, nor is it in a man to walk and direct his steps.”  
> (Jer. 10:23)

He also makes himself greater than the Apostle, who said:

> “I myself, with my mind, serve the law of God, but with my flesh the law of sin.”  
> (Rom. 7:25)

When he says that “some are judges and others are judged because in the same nature there is a different will, and because, although all can do the same things, they do different things,” he contradicts the Catholic faith, which also confesses that infants are to be judged—those who, placed in the same nature, were taken away without Baptism before they could do or will, or even know, anything good or evil.

When he says that “Esau and Jacob and others like them were distinguished solely because of the will, so that they had different merits in the same nature,” he contradicts the Apostle, who, speaking of the same persons, says:

> “For when they had not yet been born or had done anything good or evil, so that God’s purpose according to election might remain—not from works, but from him who calls—it was said to her, ‘The elder shall serve the younger.’ As it is written, ‘Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.’”  
> (Rom. 9:11–13)

When he says that “no other cause makes it difficult for us to live well than the long habit of vices,” he contradicts Scripture, which says:

> “A heavy yoke is upon the children of Adam from the day they come forth from their mother’s womb.”  
> (Ecclus. 40:1)

When he says that “the Lord, because he is just, did not command anything impossible,” he speaks truly if he is referring to the help of him to whom the Catholic voice makes supplication:

> “Lead me in the path of your commandments.”  
> (Ps. 118:35)

But if he trusts in the powers of his own mind, he is refuted by the truthful saying of that same just Creator, who says:

> “Without me you can do nothing.”  
> (John 15:5)

When he says that “he who is pious will not condemn a human being for what he could not avoid,” he contradicts the judgment of that same pious Redeemer and just Judge, who says even concerning infants:

> “Unless someone is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot see the kingdom of God.”  
> (John 3:5)

Nevertheless, as Saint Augustine says, the punishment or condemnation of all those who, besides the original sin they have drawn with them, have added no further sin will be exceedingly mild (*Against Julian*, book 5, no. 44). Yet such people cannot be entirely exempt from condemnation, since the Apostle plainly says:

> “Death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who did not sin.”

And as though someone might ask why it reigned over all who had not sinned, he immediately gives the reason, adding:

> “In the likeness of Adam’s transgression.”  
> (Rom. 5:14)

That is, not on account of their own sins, but because Adam, the transgressor, fathered children like himself.

Therefore, in this part of the question, we must say what we have heard the same Apostle Paul say. Discussing the unequal lot of Esau and Jacob, twins born from one intercourse, he says:

> “What then shall we say? Is there injustice with God? Certainly not. For Moses says, ‘I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will show compassion to whom I show compassion.’ Therefore it depends not on the one who wills or the one who runs, but on God who shows mercy.”  
> (Rom. 9:14–16)

And, after being greatly wearied by this question, he concluded:

> “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How inscrutable are his judgments and how unsearchable his ways!”  
> (Rom. 11:33)

We have thought it useful to offer these preliminary observations from Julian’s short works as a warning to readers.

## CONCERNING ANNIANUS, THE FALSE DEACON OF CELEDA

Jerome writing to Augustine and Alypius toward the end of the year 419.

[Note: [Col. 1748] Letter 202 among Augustine’s letters.]

1. Through your cooperation and leadership, the Coelestian heresy has been slain. It infected the hearts of many so thoroughly that, although they realize they have been overcome and condemned, they nevertheless do not abandon the poisons of their minds; and, since they think that through us they have lost the freedom to teach their heresy, they hate us—which is the only thing they can do.

2. As for your question whether I have replied against the books of Annianus, the false deacon of Celeda, who is nourished so abundantly that he supplies frivolous words of blasphemy belonging to another [Col. 1749], you should know that I received the books themselves, sent in loose sheets by the holy brother Eusebius the presbyter, only a short time ago. Since then, either because illnesses overtook me or because of the death of your holy and venerable daughter Eustochium, I have been so grieved that I almost thought the books should be disregarded.

For he remains stuck in the same mud and, apart from tinkling and beggarly words, says nothing else. Nevertheless, we have accomplished much in making him reveal himself more openly while attempting to answer my letter and expose his blasphemies to everyone. Whatever he denies having said in that miserable synod of Diospolis [Note: [Col. 1749] In that synod Pelagius was acquitted in the year of Christ 415, while concealing his errors.], he professes in this work; and it is no great task to answer his most foolish drivel.

If the Lord grants me life, and if we have an adequate supply of copyists, we shall reply in a few brief works—not to refute a dead heresy, but to confute his ignorance and blasphemy by our arguments. Your Holiness could do this better, lest we be compelled to praise our own work against a heretic.

[Note: [Col. 1748–1749] Evidently the heretic Pelagius, whose armor-bearer they therefore believe this Annianus himself to have been called in Orosius’s *Apology*, above, col. 1698. When Orosius was writing the *Apology*, Jerome was writing his *Dialogue against the Pelagians*; at that time, according to Bede, above, col. 1746, no. 10, Julian had already attached himself to Pelagius. Augustine also said of this man in book 2, chapter 51, of his *Unfinished Work against Julian*: “You are idly nourished by deceived wretches”; and he says similar things in book 3, chapters 1 and 44. Moreover, Julian’s manner of speaking clearly agrees with that of the person who wrote the letters presented below to Orontius and Evangelus. And just as Annianus customarily calls Orontius “father” and “most blessed,” so Julian, in the books dedicated to Florus, although Florus was then a bishop, customarily calls him “most blessed father,” not “brother.”]

## SAYINGS OF THE SAME ANNIANUS, FROM HIS LETTER TO ORONTIUS THE BISHOP, WHICH IS PREFACED TO THE HOMILIES OF JOHN CHRYSOSTOM ON MATTHEW
The affection of a most devoted father and the skill of a most learned teacher you exercise equally toward me: amid these storms of temptation that we endure together for love of the faith, you draw me away both from grief and from torpor, and send my spirit, languishing with anxiety, back to the study of the Scriptures. For you command, most blessed sir, that I transfer into the Latin language, in whatever manner I am able, the commentary of Saint John, bishop of Constantinople, which he expounded in ninety-one books on Matthew the Evangelist. Would that this could be done by us as conveniently as it is commanded by you both opportunely and usefully. For what could be offered to our ears more learned for prudence, more ardent for exercise, or purer in doctrine than these splendid monuments of so distinguished a mind and genius?

And this especially at a time when, under the pretext of certain exceedingly difficult questions, the building up of morals and ecclesiastical discipline is being opposed with sufficient insolence. In defense of these, certainly, blessed John rises so greatly and so vigorously everywhere—not only in his other works but also in this one—that, by interpreting the Evangelist’s words, he seems to be fighting alongside us for evangelical perfection. For what does he impress upon human beings more than the nobility of their nature, which, against the madness of Manichaeus, is praised by the unanimous agreement and harmony of all right-minded thinkers? It is praised either for the glory of the admirable Creator, or to arouse zeal for virtue, or to chastise the vices of pleasure.

What, I ask, does he commend more insistently than the dignity of the freedom implanted in us by God? Confession of this is the chief distinction between us and the Gentiles, who believe that a human being, created in the image of God, is so unhappily bound by the violence of fate and the necessity of sinning that he is compelled even to envy the beasts. What does he suggest against those same teachers more effectively than that God’s commandments are possible, and that a human being is capable of every virtue that God either commands or counsels? By this alone, injustice is driven back from the one who commands, and guilt is fastened upon the transgressor.

But when this glory of the learned man discusses the grace of God, with what abundance and also with what caution does he celebrate it! For he is neither careless nor excessive in either respect, but moderate in both. He displays human wills as free, yet everywhere acknowledges that the help of divine grace is necessary for carrying out God’s commandments; he commends the continuous assistance of divine grace in such a way that he does not extinguish the efforts of the will, etc.

## FROM A LETTER OF THE SAME ANNIANUS TO EVANGELUS THE PRESBYTER, PREFIXED TO JOHN CHRYSOSTOM’S HOMILIES ON THE PRAISES OF PAUL

Blessed John, by contemplating Paul more deeply and bringing him clearly into view, seems to me to have examined his very veins and expressed the marrow of his virtues. All of these live so fully in this eulogy, and are so adorned with their own flowers and fruits, that we scarcely admire them less as explained by him so sublimely than we might admire them in the Apostle himself.

This work ought to be all the more beloved and welcome to you because, shining with the light of the Holy Scriptures, it assails the darkness of the Manichaean error like a brilliant star.

[Note: [Col. 1750] He calls the Catholic doctrine concerning grace and original sin the Manichaean error.]

For how great a consolation rises within us when we see so learned and distinguished a teacher of the East asserting the truth that the Traducianist attacks among us?

[Note: [Col. 1750] Augustine is repeatedly called this by Julian. See Book Three of the *Unfinished Work*, no. 93.]

Certainly blessed John, here as in all his books, guards, arms, and kindles this truth, fortified on every side, so that he seems not so much to have instructed his contemporaries as to have prepared aid for us against the assault upon the true faith.

How great is his opposition to necessity! How vigorously he rises in defense of free choice! How, everywhere echoing the books of our teachers, while preserving the right of the will, does he commend the supports of divine grace! How splendidly, against the darkness of all vices and in defense of the mirror of every virtue, does he set forth the chosen vessel!

First, by preferring blessed Paul in his little book to all the saints and comparing him with the angels. Second, by asserting the goodness of nature from his virtues and teachings, etc. Sixth, by resolving all those questions through which the Traducianist, in opposition, stains blessed Paul with the obscurity of vices, so that he might thereby reconcile sins to his faithful by apostolic example. Seventh, by exalting above all others the fire of his zeal for Christ and the fervor of his teaching even before the honor of the apostolate, so that it may be perfectly clear that the necessity of sinning has been extinguished—a necessity against which both the Apostle’s teaching and his life wage war, etc.

## DECREE OF THE EMPEROR CONSTANTIUS, FATHER OF VALENTINIAN THE AUGUSTUS III, ADDRESSED TO VOLUSIANUS, PREFECT OF THE CITY, GIVEN IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 421

[Note: [Col. 1750] We learn from Theophanes that in that same year of Christ 421, on the eighth day of February, Constantius, the father of Valentinian, obtained the imperial power; he held it for no more than six months, for Olympiodorus reports that he died of pleurisy in the seventh month of his reign.]

The Emperor Flavius Constantius, Pious, Fortunate, Augustus, Victor, to Volusianus, Prefect of the City.

[Note: [Col. 1750] Photius mentions him in the *Bibliotheca*, codex 53. See above, cols. 1729–1730.]

We had long ago ordered that the practices full of both ancient superstition and recent vanity be corrected, but we are informed that they are becoming greater through daily insinuations. And since discord stirs the minds of peoples, we order that what we commanded long ago be repeated.

Accordingly, when you have read this, Your Eminence shall diligently investigate all who begrudge the worship of God and shall immediately have them expelled from the walls of the City; yet in such a way that they are not permitted to remain even within the hundredth milestone. We also command that Celestius be driven ever farther from the City. For it is clear that, once these have been removed from our midst, grace and concord retain their former stability.

Indeed, henceforth, if anything of this kind is reported, know that the office of Your Excellency is to be subjected to capital punishment. For we do not permit our commands to be prolonged through negligence in their execution.

Farewell, dearest and most loving father.

And the appended subscription: “Let what we have commanded be carried out, because this is advantageous to your reputation.”

## EDICT POSTED BY VOLUSIANUS, PREFECT OF THE CITY

[Col. 1751]

Volusianus, Prefect of the City, issued this edict:

Until now, judicial proceedings, and secrets favorable to the accused, have withdrawn from judgment Celestius, the disturber of the divine faith and public tranquility. Now the laws and edicts will pursue him even in his absence. First of all, residence in the Eternal City is denied him, so that, even if he stays in the neighboring regions, he will not escape the death he deserves.

In proportion to the recklessness and audacity of his conduct, we warn everyone by the provision of this edict not to regard any hiding place as something that ought to be offered to an evildoer. When such a penalty has been established, whoever thinks that an accused person ought to be concealed from the divine and human laws must necessarily incur both punishment and the stroke of proscription.

## CONSTITUTION OF VALENTINIAN III, ADDRESSED TO AMACIUS, PREFECT OF THE GAULS, CONCERNING CERTAIN PELAGIAN BISHOPS TO BE SUMMONED THROUGH PATROCLUS, BISHOP OF ARLES

The Emperors Theodosius and Valentinian Caesar, to Amacius, Illustrious Prefect of the Gauls.

### 1.

We restore, with ready devotion, all the privileges of the churches and of all the clergy which the tyrant had begrudged in our age, etc.

### 2.

We command that various bishops who follow the wicked error of Pelagian and Coelestian doctrine be summoned through Patroclus, the bishop of the sacred law. Because we trust that they can be corrected, if within twenty days from the time of their summons—the period in which we grant them an opportunity for deliberation—they do not correct their errors and restore themselves to the Catholic faith, they are to be expelled from the regions of Gaul, and a more faithful priesthood is to be substituted in their place. Thus the stain of the present error may be wiped from the minds of the peoples, and the good of a more just future discipline established.

### 3.

Since it is not fitting that religious peoples be corrupted by any superstitions, we command that all Manichaeans and all heretics, schismatics, astrologers, and every sect hostile to Catholics be expelled from the very sight of the various cities, so that they may not be defiled even by the contagion of the criminals’ presence.

We also deny Jews and pagans the license to conduct legal proceedings or to serve in the military. We do not wish persons of the Christian law to serve them, lest, by occasion of dominion, they alter the sect of the venerable religion.

Therefore we order that all persons of this unhappy error be excluded, unless timely correction comes to their aid.

Given at Aquileia on the seventh day before the Ides of July, in the consulship of Theodosius Augustus for the eleventh time and Valentinian Caesar.

[Note: [Col. 1751] In the year of Christ 425, on the ninth day of July.]

## ON THE HERESY DERIVED FROM THE PELAGIAN ERROR AT THE CITY OF BELIGARUM

Cassianus, *On the Incarnation*, Book 1, chapters 2 and 3.

Recently also—that is, in our own days—we have seen a poisonous heresy emerge, and especially at the city of Beligarum.

[Note: [Col. 1751] Elsewhere, “from the great city of Veligarum.”]

Its error was certain, though its name was uncertain, etc.

We do not think that this one distinctive and proper feature of the aforementioned heresy, which had descended from the Pelagian error, should be passed over. Certain people said that the solitary man Jesus Christ had lived without any contact with sin. They proceeded so far as to assert that human beings, if they wished, could be without sin.

For they considered it a necessary consequence that, if the solitary man Jesus Christ had been without sin, all human beings likewise could be without God’s assistance—whatever that solitary man could have done without communion with God. Thus they made no distinction at all between any human being and our Lord Jesus Christ, since the same human being could, by his own effort and industry, merit what Christ had merited by application and labor.

As a result, rushing into still greater and more monstrous madness, they said that our Lord Jesus Christ had come into this world not to provide redemption for the human race but to offer examples of good actions: namely, so that human beings, by following his discipline and walking along the same path of virtue, might arrive at the same rewards of virtue. To the extent of their power, they thereby emptied the whole gift of his sacred coming and the whole grace of divine redemption, since they said that human beings could attain by living what God had accomplished by dying for human salvation.

## ON LEPORIUS

Cassianus, same work, chapter 4.

Leporius, then a monk and now a presbyter, who, as we said above, descended from the instruction—or rather the depravity—of Pelagius, was among the first or greatest defenders of the aforementioned heresy in Gaul. Warned by us and corrected by God, he condemned his wrongly formed persuasion so magnificently that his correction is scarcely less admirable than the unshaken faith of many others. For the first thing is never to fall into error; the second is to reject it rightly.

Thus, coming to his senses, he confessed his error with grief but without shame, not only in Africa, where he then was and where he now is,

[Note: [Col. 1752] Around the year of Christ 425 or 426.]

but also sent letters of mournful confession and lamentation to all the cities of Gaul, so that where his deviation had first become known, his correction might also become known, and those who had previously been witnesses of his error might afterward be witnesses of his correction.

Gennadius, concerning the same man, in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 59.

Leporius, still a monk and afterward a presbyter, had presumed that the purity of life he believed he had obtained solely by his own choice and effort, rather than by God’s assistance. He had begun to follow the Pelagian doctrine. But, warned by teachers in Gaul and corrected by God in Africa through Augustine, he wrote a little book of his correction, in which he both makes satisfaction for his error and gives thanks for his correction.

Leporius himself, in his *Little Book of Correction*.

I also judge that this must by no means be left unmentioned: in the same letter, straying into a similar error, I added that Christ our Lord had fulfilled all that belonged to the sufferings in such a way that, as a perfect human being, he was helped in nothing by the assistance of divinity. I wished, that is, to present the human being in Christ as perfect, so that I might both assert that the Word of the Father was alien to these sufferings and attempt to prove that the human being alone, by himself, had accomplished all these things through the capacity of mortal nature, without any assistance from divinity.

## ON THE PELAGIANS EXPELLED FROM ITALY AND THE BRITONS FREED FROM THEIR ERROR, ETC., THROUGH THE CARE OF POPE CELESTINE

Prosper, *Against the Collator*, chapters 41 and 42.

### 1.

The pontiff Celestine, of venerable memory,

[Note: [Col. 1752] Celestine succeeded Boniface in the year of Christ 423; he was made Roman pontiff on the third day of November and died in the year 432, on the sixth day of April.]

to whom the Lord granted many gifts of his grace for the protection of the Catholic Church, knowing that the condemned ought to be granted not an investigation at trial but only the remedy of repentance, ordered Celestius, who was requesting a hearing without having had his case examined, to be expelled from the whole territory of Italy.

[Note: [Col. 1752] Around the year of Christ 425.]

So inviolably did he consider the statutes of his predecessors and the decrees of synods necessary to be preserved that he would by no means permit the reconsideration of what had once deserved to be cut off.

### 2.

Nor did he free Britain from this same disease with less care, when he excluded certain enemies of grace, who occupied only their native land, even from that remote place beyond the Ocean. By appointing a bishop for the Scots, while striving to preserve the Roman island as Catholic, he also made the barbarian land Christian.

[Col. 1753]

### 3.

Through this man, within Gaul, freedom of malicious speech was taken away from those very people who criticize the writings of Augustine of holy memory. When their consultation had been received and the books displeasing to those in error had been praised for their piety, he made clear, in holy eloquence, what ought to be thought about their authority. He plainly declared how displeasing to him was the novelty of that presumption by which certain people dared insolently to rise up against ancient teachers and, through undisciplined slander, obstruct the preaching of the truth.

Prosper, in the *Chronicle*, under the year of Christ 429.

Agricola the Pelagian, son of the Pelagian Severianus, corrupted the churches of Ireland by insinuating his doctrine. But through the action of the deacon Palladius, Pope Celestine sent Germanus, bishop of Auxerre, in his place, so that, after the heretics had been driven out, he might lead the Britons back to the Catholic faith.

Constantius, *Life of Germanus, Bishop of Auxerre*, Book 1, chapters 19, 23, and 24.

### 1.

At the same time, an embassy sent from Britain announced to the bishops of Gaul that Pelagian perversity had widely seized the peoples in those regions through a few agents, and that aid ought to be brought to the Catholic faith as soon as possible. For this reason a large synod was assembled, and by the judgment of all, two distinguished lights of religion were sought through the prayers of everyone: Germanus and Lupus, apostolic priests who possessed the earth in their bodies and heaven through their merits.

And the more laborious the necessity appeared, the more promptly those most devoted heroes undertook it, hastening the business through the incentives of faith.

### 2.

The authors of the sinister persuasion lay hidden, and like an evil spirit they groaned because the peoples who were escaping were being lost to them. At last, after long deliberation, they presumed to enter the conflict, etc.

The people were present as spectators and future judges. The parties stood before them, unequal and unlike in condition: on one side divine authority, on the other human presumption; on one side faith, on the other perfidy; on one side Christ, on the other Pelagius as author.

At first the most blessed priests gave the adversaries an opportunity to debate. Their crude use of words alone occupied both ears and time for a long while, uselessly. Then the venerable bishops poured forth torrents of their eloquence, together with apostolic and evangelical thunder. Their own speech was mingled with the divine, and testimonies from the Scriptural readings followed their most forceful assertions.

Vanity was convicted and perfidy refuted, so that, unable to respond to each individual objection, they confessed themselves guilty. The people, acting as judge, could scarcely restrain their hands; they expressed their judgment with shouting.

### 3.

Suddenly a man of tribunitian rank came forward into the midst with his wife, carrying in the folds of his garment their ten-year-old blind daughter. The priests ordered her to be presented to the adversaries. But the latter, deterred by the punishment inflicted by conscience, joined their prayers with those of the parents and begged the priests for the child’s healing.

Seeing the expectation of the people and the adversaries inclined toward them, the priests briefly poured forth a prayer. Then Germanus, filled with the Holy Spirit, invoked the Holy Trinity. Immediately he grasped with his hands a small reliquary hanging at his side, which had been torn from his neck with the relics of the saints, and applied it before everyone’s eyes to the girl’s eyes. At once, when the darkness had been driven from them, he filled them with the light of truth.

Author of the *Life of Saint Lupus, Bishop of Troyes*, in Surius, under July 29.

Since he was powerful in intellect, distinguished in eloquence, and outstanding in holiness, he went with Saint Germanus, who was full of every perfection and spiritual grace, to Britain against the Pelagian heresy, which attacked the sound faith. United by one spirit and harmonious in equal purpose, they entrusted themselves to the terrifying waves of the Ocean in the winter season and upon an unexplored sea, calming them by the rudders of their prayers, etc.

Finally, they recalled everyone from error to the confession of the sound faith, when the Pelagian plague had already seized almost the whole of Britain.

[Col. 1754]

Constantius, *Life of Saint Germanus, Bishop of Auxerre*, Book 2, chapters 1–4.

Meanwhile, word was brought from Britain that Pelagian perversity was again being spread by a few agents. Once more the prayers of everyone were brought to the most blessed Germanus, so that he might defend the cause of God, which he had previously won.

He hastened to answer their request, since he delighted in labors and gladly devoted himself to Christ. At last, the envy of the enemy, overcome by his virtues, yielded; he did not dare to attack one whom he had already recognized as a friend of God.

Accordingly, Bishop Severus was added to him, a man of complete holiness who had then been ordained bishop at Trier, etc. The preaching to the people was turned toward the correction of transgression, and by the judgment of all, the authors of the depravity were expelled from the island and brought to the priests to be taken to the interior, so that both the region might enjoy absolution and they might enjoy correction.

## ON THE PELAGIANS’ COMPLAINTS ABOUT THEIR EXPULSION FROM THE WESTERN CHURCH

Nestorius, in a letter to Celestine.

A certain Julianus, and Florus, and Orontius, and Fabius, saying that they were bishops of the western regions, repeatedly approached the most pious and most renowned Emperor

[Note: [Col. 1754] At this very time, namely in the year of Christ 429, Marius Mercator presented to that same emperor Theodosius and to the Church of Constantinople a *Memorial* against Julian and his associates, which is set out above, cols. 1686 ff.]

and lamented their cases, as though they were orthodox men suffering persecution in orthodox times. They repeatedly lamented the same things before us as well, and, often rejected, did not cease doing the same things. Day after day they persist, filling everyone’s ears with tearful cries.

We used the speeches that were appropriate in addressing them, since we did not know the truth about their case. But because we need a clearer knowledge from you concerning their circumstances, lest our most pious and Christian Emperor continue to be troubled by them, and lest we, ignorant of their case, become divided over the resolution of the matter, deign to grant us information about them. Thus, lest, even through ignorance of the justice of truth, they be disturbed by importunate compassion, or regard as something other than this your Beatitude’s canonical indignation against them, perhaps rightly proved on account of their religious sects, etc.

The same man, in another letter to the same person.

I have often written to Your Beatitude concerning Julianus, Orontius, and the others who usurp episcopal dignity and make frequent approaches to the most pious and most renowned Emperor. They cut us down with frequent lamentations, as though they had been expelled from the West in orthodox times.

But up to now we have received no written statement about them from Your Veneration. If I had one, I could answer them and give a concise response to their laments. For now, from their uncertain statements, no one knows what course to take: some call them heretics and say that for this reason they were expelled from the western regions, while they themselves swear that they have suffered slander and endured danger through a subterfuge against the orthodox faith.

We are gravely ignorant as to which of these accounts is certain. For if they are truly heretics, it is a crime to sympathize with them; and again, if they are suffering slander, it is harsh and impious not to sympathize with them.

Therefore may your soul, which loves God most dearly, deign to instruct us, since until now we are divided between both impulses toward them—that is, hatred and compassion. We wish to be taught what judgment we should hold concerning them. For each day we keep these same men waiting, pretending that we are relying upon and awaiting Your Beatitude.

Celestine, in his reply to a letter of Nestorius.

For some days of our life, after the wicked and frequently condemned doctrine of Pelagius and Coelestius, the Catholic faith enjoyed peace, when East and West struck them and the followers of their opinion with the weapons of united judgment.

Finally, Atticus, of holy memory, teacher of the Catholic faith and truly the successor even in these matters of the blessed John, persecuted them for the sake of the common King in such a way that he did not even grant them the opportunity to stand there, etc.

These heretics also, concerning whom you wished to consult us as though unaware of what had occurred, were expelled from their places by a just condemnation because they spoke unjustly. We do not think it surprising that they found rest there. For they found an impious preaching, in comparison with which they might consider themselves innocent.

At this point, since the opportunity for discussion requires it, we cannot remain silent about what astonishes us. We read how well you hold the doctrine of original sin, how you assert that nature itself is indebted, and that the one who descends from a debtor’s lineage rightly pays that debt. What have those who were condemned for denying these things to do with you?

Those who are opposed to one another never come together without suspicion. They would have been expelled, finally, if these matters had similarly displeased you. Yet why are the actions once taken against these men now being questioned, when it is certain that what was done there was transmitted to us by Atticus, who was then the Catholic bishop?

Why did Sisinius, of holy memory, not investigate these matters? Certainly because under his predecessor he had approved that they had been rightly condemned.

Let the wretched men lament that they were deceived by the hope they placed in human beings, when now, because of their communion, only repentance could have come to their aid. Behold, you are beginning to learn about them, if there was anything you did not previously know, etc.

Given on the third day before the Ides of August, in the consulship of Theodosius Augustus for the thirteenth time and Valentinian Augustus for the third time.

[Note: [Col. 1755] In the year of Christ 430, on the eleventh day of August.]

## ON THE DEATH OF AUGUSTINE

Prosper, in the *Chronicle*, under the year of Christ 430.

Augustine, a bishop outstanding in every respect, died on the fifth day before the Kalends of September, answering Julian’s books amid the attacks of the besieging Vandals at the very end of his days,

[Note: [Col. 1755] The response is the second against Julian, commonly called the *Unfinished Work*.]

and gloriously persevering in defense of Christian grace.

## LETTER OF POPE CELESTINE ON BEHALF OF PROSPER AND HILARY, OR ON BEHALF OF AUGUSTINE HIMSELF, CONCERNING THE GRACE OF GOD

[Note: [Col. 1755] Written after Augustine’s death, perhaps in the year of Christ 431. We have checked it against two old Corbie manuscripts of the collection of canons compiled by Dionysius Exiguus. From this letter and the constitutions on grace appended to it, that compiler made the first thirteen “Decrees of Pope Celestine.” He gave the first decree the title, “On Prosper and Hilary, who accuse certain presbyters of Gaul as followers of Pelagius.” The second: “A marvelous assertion of praise concerning Saint Bishop Augustine.” The third: “The authorities of the bishops of the Apostolic See of earlier times concerning the Grace of God.” The fourth: “That Adam injured all human beings, and that no one can be saved except by the grace of Christ,” etc. Quoting the same letter, Peter the deacon, in his *Little Book on the Incarnation and Grace*, no. 7, below, cols. 1775–1776, says that it ends with the words, “which appears to be contrary to the judgments set forth above.”]

TO THE BISHOPS OF GAUL. (G)

To our most beloved brothers Venerius, Marinus,

[Note: [Col. 1755] Some printed editions have Marius. But the manuscripts have Marinus; on their authority, below we restore Filtanius in place of Philtatius.]

Leontius, Auxonius, Arcadius, Filtanius, and the other bishops of Gaul, Celestine.

### 1. PREFACE

The words of the apostolic commandment are that we ought to be without offense among Jews and Gentiles (1 Cor. 10:32). Every Christian preserves this with the whole strength of his soul. Since this is so, a person who refuses even to display this toward the faithful may face no small danger before God.

For the Lord’s saying in the Gospel bears witness to how these things grieve us, who wish that no one should perish—these things which, through Christian authors, strike Christian minds. The Savior himself says that it is better for the one who causes one of the little ones to stumble to be sunk into the depths of the sea (Matt. 18:6). Therefore let us ask what punishment already awaits the one for whom we read that such a penalty is better.

### CHAPTER ONE

### 2.

Our sons Prosper and Hilary, whose concern for our God deserves praise, have laid before us how much license certain presbyters there, of whom I know not, have to pursue the dissension of the Churches: bringing undisciplined questions into the open, they say that these men persistently preach things opposed to the truth.

But we more justly charge this to your affection, since they have the opportunity to dispute over you. We read that the disciple is not above his master (Luke 6:40), that is, no one ought to claim a doctrine for himself to the injury of his teachers.

For we know that these very men were appointed by our Lord to teach, since, as the Apostle says, the third place within the Church has been assigned to them (1 Cor. 12:28). What hope is there in a place where these people speak while their teachers remain silent—people who, if this is so, were not their disciples?

I fear that to connive at this is to remain silent. I fear that those who permit them to speak in this manner are themselves speaking even more. In such cases silence is not free from suspicion, since truth would intervene if falsehood were displeasing. The matter rightly concerns us if we silently favor error.

Therefore let such people be rebuked. Let it not be permitted them to have speech according to their own will. Let novelty cease, if these things are so,

[Note: [Col. 1756] Vincent of Lérins twists this passage, at the end of the *Commonitory*, away from its true meaning against Prosper and Hilary, so that he not unjustly comes under suspicion of Semi-Pelagian error: “For it follows,” he says, “‘Let novelty cease, if the matter is so,’ that is, if it is as certain people accuse your cities and provinces before me.”]

to assail antiquity; let disturbance cease to trouble the peace of the churches. They often try to plunge into shipwreck those whom a secure station makes safe while they stand within the harbor. Secure indeed is the station of all whose footprints are not moved from their perfected steps.

The aforementioned men have appealed to the Apostolic See, complaining to us of this very disturbance that is attempting to cause turmoil. Accept this, dearest brothers, as a measure taken for the peace of the Catholic people.

Let them know—if they are in fact reckoned as presbyters—that in dignity they are subject to you. Let them know that all who teach badly ought to learn more and more rather than teach. For what are you doing in the churches if they possess the chief authority to preach?

Unless perhaps this consideration stands in the way: that it has not yet been gathered, either by authority or by reason, that some among the number of the brothers—perhaps recently admitted from the company of the laity into our college—do not know what they ought to claim for themselves.

Much has already been said about these matters, at the time when we sent a written reply to our brother Tuentius. Even now, however, we repeat our admonition again and again: such people must be avoided, for they labor to sow throughout the land something other than what our farmer commanded.

Nor can we be surprised that these men now dare to attempt such things against the living, since they strive even to disperse the memory of their brothers who have fallen asleep.

### CHAPTER TWO

### 3.

We have always counted Augustine, a man of holy memory, among those in our communion because of his life and merits, and never even a rumor of sinister suspicion touched him. We remember that he was once a man of such great learning that he was always regarded, even by all my predecessors, as one of the best teachers.

All therefore rightly formed a common judgment about him, since everywhere he was loved and honored by everyone. Hence such people must be resisted, for we see them growing in an evil manner.

It is impious to allow religious souls to suffer these things. Since they are our members, their affliction ought also to wear us down, although the promised blessedness awaits all who are proved to suffer persecution for righteousness. What the Lord promises them in the future, the following saying declares (Matt. 5:10).

This is not the cause of those alone who are acting; the universal Church is being struck by this novelty wherever it appears. Let us understand that the very things displeasing to us are displeasing to you.

We will be able to prove this only if, after the wicked have been silenced, complaint about such a matter ceases in the future. May God keep you safe and sound, dearest brothers.

### CHAPTER THREE

### 4.

Because certain people who glory in the Catholic name, lingering either through perversity or ignorance in the condemned opinions of heretics, presume to oppose the most devout disputants, and, although they do not hesitate to anathematize Pelagius and Coelestius, nevertheless speak against our teachers as though they had exceeded the necessary measure, claiming that they follow and approve only what the most sacred See of blessed Peter the Apostle decreed and taught against the enemies of God’s grace through the ministry of its bishops, it was necessary to inquire carefully what the rulers of the Roman Church had judged concerning the heresy that arose in their time, and what they had determined should be thought concerning the grace of God against the most pernicious defenders of free choice.

We therefore also joined certain judgments of the African councils, which the apostolic bishops certainly made their own when they approved them.

Thus, so that those who are uncertain about any point may be instructed more fully, we set forth the constitutions of the holy fathers in a concise list. Anyone who is not excessively contentious may recognize that the connection of all the disputations depends upon this brevity of the authorities set out below, and that no basis for contradiction remains if one believes and speaks with Catholics.

### CHAPTER FOUR

### 5.

Pope Innocent, of blessed memory, declared that in Adam’s transgression all human beings lost their natural capacity and innocence, and that no one can rise from the depth of that ruin through free choice unless the grace of a merciful God raises him. He said this in his letter to the Council of Carthage:

“For that man, experiencing free choice, while using his own goods too carelessly, fell and was submerged in the depths of transgression. He found nothing by which he could rise from there, and, deceived by his own freedom, would have remained concealed beneath the oppression of this ruin,

[Note: [Col. 1757] This is how the manuscripts and the edition of 1524 read. Some other editions have, “he would have lain oppressed in the ruin.”]

unless the coming of Christ, in accordance with his grace, had afterward raised him up. Through the cleansing of a new regeneration, he purified every past fault by the washing of his Baptism.”

[Note: [Col. 1757] In the manuscripts: “the fault of the past.”]

### CHAPTER FIVE

### 6.

No one is good by himself unless the One who alone is good grants him participation in himself. The judgment of the same Pontiff, in the same writings, bears witness to this when he says:

“For what proper judgment shall we henceforth form of the minds of those who think that they owe their goodness to themselves and do not consider the One whose grace they receive daily, although they confidently believe that they can attain so much without him?”

### CHAPTER SIX

### 7.

No one renewed by the grace of Baptism is capable of overcoming the snares of the devil and conquering the desires of the flesh unless, through God’s daily assistance, he receives perseverance in a good way of life. The teaching of the same bishop confirms this in the same pages, saying:

“For although the One who redeemed a human being from past sins knew that he could sin again, he preserved many remedies for his restoration, so that he might also correct him after these things. He provides daily remedies; unless we strive, relying and trusting in them, we shall in no way be able to overcome human errors. For it is necessary that, with the One whose aid enables us to conquer, we should again be conquered when he does not assist us.”

(*Among Augustine’s Letters*, 181.7, 4.)

### CHAPTER SEVEN

### 8.

No one uses free choice well except through Christ. The same teacher proclaims this in a letter given to the Council of Milevis, saying:

“Understand at last, O perverse doctrine of the most depraved minds, that the first human being was so deceived by freedom itself that, while using its reins too indulgently, he fell through presumption into transgression. He could not be rescued from it unless the coming of Christ the Lord, through the providence of regeneration, restored the condition of his original freedom.”

(*Ibid.*, Letter 182.3.)

### CHAPTER EIGHT
### 9. That all the endeavors, works, and merits of the saints must be referred to the glory and praise of God, because no one pleases him for any other reason than what he himself has bestowed

The regular authority of Pope Zosimus, of blessed memory, directs us toward this position. For, writing to the bishops of the whole world, he says:

> “But we, at God’s prompting—for all good things must be referred to their author, from whom they arise—have reported everything to the conscience of our brothers and fellow bishops.”  
> [Note: [Col. 1758] This letter, as well as the following letter of the African bishops, is not extant.]

The African bishops venerated this statement, radiant with the light of the most sincere truth, with such honor that they wrote to the same man as follows:

> “As for what you placed in the letter which you saw to be sent throughout all the provinces, saying, ‘But we, at God’s prompting,’ etc., we have understood it as spoken so that, as you passed swiftly by, you might cut down with the unsheathed sword of truth those who exalt the freedom of the human will against God’s assistance. For what did you do more by free will than refer everything to the conscience of our humility, and yet faithfully and wisely recognized and truthfully and confidently declared that it had been done at God’s prompting? This is so, certainly, because ‘the will is prepared by the Lord’ (Prov. 8, according to the Septuagint), and, so that they may do some good, he himself touches the hearts of his children with paternal inspirations.”  
> [Note: [Col. 1758] Printed editions read *of the faithful* (*fidelium*). The manuscripts more aptly read *of his children* (*filiorum*).]

> “For ‘all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God’ (Rom. 8:14), so that we may neither feel that our will is absent nor doubt that, in each movement of the human will toward good, his assistance is more powerful.”

### CHAPTER IX

### 10. That God works in human hearts and in free will itself in such a way that holy thought, devout counsel, and every movement of a good will are from God, because through him we can do something good, whereas without him we can do nothing

The same teacher instructs us in this confession. Speaking to the bishops of the whole world about the assistance of divine grace, he says:

> “What time, then, passes in which we do not need his assistance? Therefore, in all actions, causes, thoughts, and movements, he must be entreated as helper and protector. For it is presumptuous that human nature should claim anything for itself, while the Apostle cries out: ‘Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the principalities and powers of this air, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places’ (Eph. 6:12). And, as he says again: ‘Wretched man that I am, who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God, through Jesus Christ our Lord’ (Rom. 7:24–25). And again: ‘By the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace toward me has not been empty; rather, I labored more than all of them—not I, however, but the grace of God with me’ (1 Cor. 15:10).”

### CHAPTER X

### 11. That the grace of God by which we are justified through Jesus Christ our Lord is not effective only for the remission of sins already committed, but also for assistance in preventing their commission

We also embrace as something proper to the Apostolic See what was established in the decrees of the Council of Carthage, namely, what was defined in the third chapter:

[Note: [Col. 1758] What is here called the third chapter is the fourth in the universal Council of Africa, above, Col. 1728. Likewise, shortly below the fourth and fifth chapters are cited, whereas in the Council of Africa these are chapters five and six. M.]

> “If anyone says that the grace of God, by which we are justified through Jesus Christ our Lord, is effective only for the remission of sins already committed, and not also for assistance so that they may not be committed, let him be anathema.”

And again, in the fourth chapter:

> “If anyone says that the grace of God through Jesus Christ assists us in not sinning only because through him [Note: [Col. 1758] The Council of Carthage reads *through it* (*ipsam*).] the understanding of God’s commandments is revealed and opened to us, so that we know what we ought to seek and what we ought to avoid, but that through it we are not granted the ability and love to do what we have recognized must be done, let him be anathema.”

For when the Apostle says, “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up” (1 Cor. 8:1), it is utterly impious to believe that we possess the grace of Christ for that which puffs up, but not for that which builds up, since both are gifts of God: both knowing what we ought to do and loving it so that we may do it, so that, when love builds up, knowledge cannot puff up. Just as it is written of God, “He teaches human beings knowledge” (Ps. 93:10), so it is also written, “Love is from God” (1 John 4:7).

Likewise, in the fifth chapter:

> “If anyone says that the grace of justification is given to us for this reason: so that what we are commanded to do by free will we may more easily fulfill through grace—as though, even if grace were not given, we could indeed fulfill the divine commandments without it, though not easily—let him be anathema. For the Lord was speaking of the fruits of the commandments when he did not say, ‘Without me you can do it with greater difficulty,’ but said, ‘Without me you can do nothing’” (John 15:5).  
> [Note: [Col. 1759] See above, Col. 1728.]

### CHAPTER XI

### 12. The testimony of priestly prayers

Beyond the inviolable decrees of the most blessed Apostolic See—which, after casting down the pride of destructive novelty, our most devout fathers taught us to refer to the grace of Christ both the beginnings of good will, the growth of worthy endeavors, and perseverance in them to the end—let us also consider the sacramental character of priestly supplications. These prayers, handed down from the Apostles, are celebrated uniformly throughout the world and in the whole Catholic Church, so that the law of praying establishes the law of believing.

When the bishops of holy congregations, fulfilling a delegated embassy before the divine mercy, plead the cause of the human race, they petition and pray, with the whole Church groaning together with them:

- that faith may be granted to unbelievers;
- that idolaters may be freed from the errors of their impiety;
- that, when the veil of the heart has been removed from the Jews, the light of truth may appear to them;
- that heretics may come to their senses through acceptance of the Catholic faith;  
  [Note: [Col. 1759] The manuscripts read *perfection* rather than *perception*.]
- that schismatics may receive the spirit of renewed charity;
- that remedies of repentance may be granted to those who have fallen;
- and, finally, that when catechumens have been brought to the sacraments of regeneration, the court of heavenly mercy may be opened to them.

That these things are not requested from the Lord superficially or in vain is shown by the outcome itself. For God deigns to draw many from every kind of error, transferring them, rescued from the power of darkness, into the kingdom of the Son of his love (Col. 1:13), and making them, from vessels of wrath, vessels of mercy (Rom. 9:22–23). It is recognized that all this is so entirely the work of God that thanksgiving and the confession of praise are always offered to God, who brings it about, for the illumination or correction of such people.

### CHAPTER XII

### 13. The exorcism of those who are to be baptized

Let us not contemplate casually what the holy Church does uniformly throughout the whole world concerning those who are to be baptized. Whether infants or young adults come to the sacrament of regeneration, they do not first approach the fountain of life until the unclean spirit has been driven from them by the exorcisms and exsufflations of the clergy. Then it truly becomes evident how “the prince of this world is cast out” (John 12:31), and how “the strong man is first bound, and afterward his goods are plundered” (Matt. 12:29), transferred into the possession of the victor, who “leads captivity captive and gives gifts to human beings” (Ps. 67:19; Eph. 4:8).

### 14. The cooperation of free will with grace

Accordingly, shaped by these ecclesiastical rules and by the authoritative testimonies drawn from divine teaching, and with the Lord’s assistance, we confess that God is the author of all good affections, works, and endeavors, and of all the virtues by which one turns toward God from the beginning of faith. We do not doubt that all human merits are preceded by his grace, through whom it comes about that we begin both to will and to do something good.

By this assistance and gift of God free will is not taken away but liberated, so that what was dark becomes luminous, what was crooked becomes straight, what was weak becomes sound, and what was imprudent becomes prudent. For God’s goodness toward all human beings is so great that he wills our merits to be his gifts, and for what he has bestowed he will grant eternal rewards.

Indeed, he works in us so that we both will and do what he wills. He does not permit the gifts he has granted us for exercise to remain idle in us or to be neglected, so that we may be fellow workers with God’s grace. If we see anything in us growing weak through our own negligence, let us hasten anxiously back to him who heals all our illnesses and redeems our life from destruction (Ps. 102:3–4), and to whom we say every day, “Do not lead us into temptation, but deliver us from evil” (Matt. 6:13).

### CHAPTER XIII

### 15. On more profound and difficult questions

As for the deeper and more difficult parts of the questions that have arisen, which those who resisted the heretics treated at greater length, we neither dare to disregard them nor need to establish them here. For confessing the grace of God, from whose work and gracious favor absolutely nothing must be subtracted, we believe that whatever the writings of the Apostolic See have taught us according to the rules set out above is sufficient. Accordingly, we must in no way regard as Catholic anything that appears contrary to the stated judgments.

## THE JUDGMENT OF THE COUNCIL OF EPHESUS AGAINST THE PELAGIANS

From the fifth session, held after the consulship of Theodosius XIII and Valentinian III, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of August.  
[Note: [Col. 1760] In the year of Christ 431, on July 17.]

> “We anathematize Apollinarius and Arius, etc. In addition to these, we anathematize Nestorius, the inventor of new blasphemies, and those who share and agree with him; and those who follow the teachings of Coelestius or Pelagius, whose doctrines we have never accepted.”

### From the synodical letter to Coelestine, in the same session 5

#### 1

John, bishop of Antioch, having assembled certain persons who had withdrawn together with Nestorius, etc., and having gathered, as it were, a council of approximately thirty men who bore the name of bishops—some of whom were exiles, idle, and without churches, while others had been deposed many years earlier by their metropolitans on account of grave offenses—and with them also the Pelagians and Coelestians, as well as some of those who had been expelled from Thessaly, dared to undertake this impious act, etc.

[Note: [Col. 1760] As regards the Pelagians who had been admitted to communion, the bishops adhering to John of Antioch in turn brought the same accusation against Cyril and his associates. They wrote to Rufus of Thessalonica: “For those who had been struck by excommunication from various dioceses and provinces, they immediately received into communion. Moreover, others accused of various heresies, and holding the same opinions as Coelestius and Pelagius . . . and therefore excommunicated by their own diocesan or metropolitan, they restored to communion, disregarding ecclesiastical discipline.” The letter exists among the acts of the Council of Ephesus.]

#### 2

When the records of the proceedings concerning the deposition of the impious Pelagians and Coelestians—Coelestius, Pelagius, Julian, Persidius, Florus, Marcellinus, Orontius, and those who held the same opinions as they—had been read in the holy synod, and when we had considered the decrees and decisions that Your Piety had issued concerning them, we too judged that they must remain solid and firm. Together with you, we all reached the same decision, treating them as deposed.

### From the seventh session

#### Canon 1

If any metropolitan of a province, having abandoned the holy and ecumenical synod, either joined the assembly of those who had seceded or should join it in the future, whether he has agreed or should agree with Coelestius, let him be deprived by the synod of the entire ecclesiastical communion, etc.

#### Canon 4

If any members of the clergy should defect and dare, whether privately or publicly, to hold the opinions of Nestorius or Coelestius, it has been decreed by the holy synod that these too are to be deposed.

## AGAINST THE SAME PELAGIAN HERETICS

Pope Coelestine, in a letter written to the Council of Ephesus after the condemnation of Nestorius, on the Ides of March, during the consulship of Aetius and Valerius.  
[Note: [Col. 1760] March 15, in the year of Christ 432.]

As for those who appear to have shared Nestorius’s impiety and who added themselves as accomplices to his crimes, although your judgment against them is recorded, we too decree what seems appropriate. In such cases many things must be carefully considered. The examples of the Coelestians bear witness to what we say: they have continued up to now to place their hope in the council.

The same pope, in a letter given on the same day, March 15, 432, to Maximian, who had been appointed in Nestorius’s place:

Let no place be given to novel impiety. Let your vigilance resist the Coelestian error, whose condemnation was once known throughout the whole world, so that all who follow this doctrine may be driven from every human association. Let the Holy Spirit oppose them through you in all these matters, wherever they attempt to reach any of these provinces, so that their impious preaching may not revive. Resist them.

For wherever they go, they become known as condemned; and, as though the sentence repeatedly pronounced against them were not sufficient, they disturb distant lands and remote provinces. Yet the one whose faith they tried to persecute by their perversity pursues them, and, by exposing their own impiety, they cannot find where to hide or to what refuge they may flee.

The same pope, in a letter to the people of Constantinople, written on the same day:

We have heard what forms of consolation came to Nestorius as he acted against the law and iniquitously. Among others, the Coelestians, workers of iniquity, were present and did not abandon him. The manifest judgment of our hymn-writer pursues them: “For a long time now the enemies of God have been scattered and have perished, those who work iniquity” (Ps. 91:10); just as the same psalm says, “They devoured the Lord’s people as though they were eating bread” (Ps. 13:4).

Thus he had with him teachers of his exile, and fully trained instructors in this very matter. For it is difficult to separate those whom crimes alone have joined, since the bonds of vices are fastened by a stronger glue.

## JULIAN’S FRAUDULENT ATTEMPT TO ENTER THE COMMUNION OF THE CHURCH

Prosper, in his *Chronicle*, under the year 439.

At this time Julian of Eclanum, a most boastful defender of the Pelagian error, driven by an unrestrained desire for the episcopate he had long ago lost, attempted by many deceptive arts to enter the communion of the Church while presenting the appearance of correction. But Pope Xystus, vigilantly thwarting these ambushes at the urging of the deacon Leo, allowed no opening for his pestilential efforts. Thus he caused all Catholics to rejoice at the rejection of the deceitful beast, as though the apostolic sword had then for the first time decapitated the most arrogant heresy.

## PELAGIANS ARE NOT TO BE RECEIVED INTO COMMUNION UNLESS THEY HAVE RENOUNCED THEIR ERROR

### Letter of Pope Leo to the Bishop of Aquileia  
[Note: [Col. 1761] Formerly numbered 86 among Leo’s letters, now 6. Written around the year of Christ 444.]

### CHAPTER I

#### 1

From the report of our holy brother and fellow bishop Septimius, which is included below, we have learned that certain presbyters, deacons, and clerics of various orders who had been entangled in the Pelagian or Coelestian heresy have entered Catholic communion in your province without any condemnation of their own error being required of them. While pastoral watchmen were sleeping too soundly (Matt. 13:25), wolves clothed in sheep’s skins have entered the Lord’s fold (Matt. 7:15), without laying aside their bestial dispositions. They have even usurped what, by the authority of the canons and our decrees, is not granted to the innocent: namely, that after abandoning the churches in which they had either received or recovered their clerical office, they should be carried about by their instability from place to place, always loving to wander and never remaining on the apostolic foundation.

Those who have not been examined by any investigation and have not been bound by any prior judgment concerning their profession seek this benefit above all: that, under the cover of communion, they may visit many houses and corrupt the hearts of many through knowledge falsely so called. They could not accomplish this if the bishops of the churches had exercised the necessary diligence in receiving such people and had not allowed any of them to wander in different directions.

### CHAPTER II

#### 2

Therefore, so that this may not be dared any longer, and so that the destructive influence introduced through the negligence of some may not proceed to the overthrow of many souls, by the authority of this command we instruct Your Fraternity’s diligence as follows: once a provincial synod of priests has been assembled among you, all—whether presbyters, deacons, or clerics of any order—who have been received into Catholic communion from the company of the Pelagians and Coelestians with such imprudence that they were not first compelled to condemn their error must now, at least after their hypocrisy has been partly exposed, be compelled to true correction, which can benefit them and harm no one.

Let them condemn in explicit professions the authors of their proud error and detest whatever the universal Church has abhorred in their teaching. Let them declare, in full, open statements signed by their own hands, that they embrace and approve in every respect all the synodal decrees that the authority of the Apostolic See has confirmed for the destruction of this heresy. Nothing obscure, nothing ambiguous, must be found in their words. For we know this to be their cunning: if they distinguish themselves from the stupidity of the condemned in some small part of the detestable doctrine, they think that none of their opinions has been forfeited.

### CHAPTER III

#### 3

Although they pretend to reject and renounce all their definitions in order to make it easier to insinuate themselves, they use this entire art of deception: unless their meaning is understood, they qualify their statements so that “the grace of God is given according to the merit of those who receive it.”

But unless grace is given freely, it is not grace, but a wage and repayment of merits. The blessed Apostle says:

> “You have been saved by grace through faith, and this is not from yourselves; for it is the gift of God, not from works, so that no one may boast. For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand so that we might walk in them” (Eph. 2:8, 10).

Therefore every bestowal of good works is a divine preparation. No one is justified by his own power, because grace is the beginning of righteousness for each person and the fountain and source of merits. [Note: [Col. 1762] Alternatively: “For no one is justified by his own power before grace, which is for each person, etc.”]

But these people say that grace is preceded by natural industry for this reason: so that what is already radiant through personal effort before grace may appear not to have been wounded by the injury of original sin. Then the statement of Truth would be false: “The Son of Man came to seek and to save what was lost” (Luke 19:10).

### CHAPTER IV

#### 4

Your Dilection must therefore be on guard and provide with the greatest diligence that, through such people, scandals long ago extinguished may not be revived, and that from the doctrine once cut down some new shoot of the same evil may not arise in your province—one that may not only grow from its roots but also infect the offspring of the holy Church with the poison of its odor.

Those who wish to appear corrected must clear themselves of every suspicion and, by obeying us, prove that they are ours. If any of them should refuse to comply with salutary commands, whether he is a cleric or a layman, let him be expelled from the fellowship of the Church, lest one who destroys his own soul lie in wait for another’s salvation.

### CHAPTER V

#### 5

We also admonish you to restore in full that part of ecclesiastical discipline which was long ago decreed by the holy fathers and often by us: that no one may pass freely from one church to another, whether in the rank of the presbyterate, in the order of the diaconate, or in any subsequent clerical office.

Let each person remain where he was ordained, not enticed by ambition, not led astray by desire, and not corrupted by human persuasion. If anyone, seeking his own interests rather than those of Jesus Christ (Phil. 2:21), neglects to return to his own people and church, let him be regarded as an outsider both to the privilege of honor and to the bond of communion.

Your Dilection should not doubt that, if—which we do not expect—those things we decree for the protection of the canons and the integrity of the faith are neglected, we will be moved with greater severity. For the faults of those in the lower orders must be attributed to no one more than to negligent and careless rulers, who often nourish great pestilence while pretending not to apply the harsher medicine.

## ANOTHER LETTER OF THE SAME POPE TO SEPTIMIUS, BISHOP OF ALTINUM  
[Note: [Col. 1763] Formerly numbered 85, now 7. Written around the year of Christ 444.]

**Leo, bishop, to Septimius, bishop: greetings.**

Having read the letters of Your Fraternity, we recognized the vigor of your faith, which we had known long ago. We congratulate you because you vigilantly carry out pastoral care for the protection of Christ’s flocks, lest the wolves that have entered under the appearance of sheep (Matt. 7:15) tear apart the simple with bestial savagery, and lest they not only make no progress through correction themselves but also corrupt what is sound.

So that the viper’s deceit might not prevail, we sent a letter to the metropolitan bishop of the province of Venetia. Through it he was to understand that his own position would be endangered if anyone coming from the company of the Pelagians and Coelestians were held in Catholic communion without a legitimate profession of satisfaction.

For it is most salutary and wholly filled with the usefulness of spiritual medicine that presbyters, deacons, or clerics of any other order who wish to appear corrected should plainly and unambiguously confess that they condemn both their own error and the authors of that error. Thus no opportunity would remain for the perverse opinions, already put to death, to breathe again. No member of the Church could be violated by association with such people once their own profession had begun to oppose them in every respect.
