Concerning them we also command that the canonical constitution be observed: they must not be permitted to leave the churches to which they properly belong or to move at their own discretion to places not assigned to them. If this is rightly forbidden to those who are free from blame, much less should it be permitted to those who are under suspicion.

Therefore, Your Dilection, whose devotion gives us joy, should join your care to our arrangements and, together with the metropolitan mentioned above, see to it that those measures which have laudably been undertaken [Note: [Col. 1763] Alternatively, *suggested*] and salutarily ordered for the safety of the whole Church are carried out carefully and promptly.

## AGAINST THE PELAGIAN HERESY REVIVING IN DALMATIA

### Letter of Pope Gelasius to Honorius, Bishop of Dalmatia  
[Note: [Col. 1763] Numbered 5 among the letters of Gelasius.]

**Gelasius to his most beloved brother Honorius.**

#### 1

Although, amid the various difficulties of the times and our continual occupations, we can scarcely draw breath, nevertheless, in governing the Apostolic See, we attend without interruption to the care of the entire Lord’s fold, which was entrusted to blessed Peter by the voice of our Savior himself: “And when you have turned back, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22:32); and again: “Peter, do you love me? Feed my sheep” (John 21:17).

We neither can nor ought to disregard anything that affects our concern, sharing the mind of the Apostle Paul and saying: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not on fire?” (2 Cor. 11:29).

A sudden, grievous, and scarcely credible report has therefore overwhelmed us, confusing, wounding, and afflicting our mind. For it has been reported to us that in the regions of Dalmatia certain people have sown the tares of the resurgent Pelagian plague, and that their blasphemy has become so powerful there that they deceive the simple by insinuating a deadly madness.

The error itself is impious, all the more dangerous in its stealth because it is more cunning in deception through the coloring of resemblance to truth. [Note: [Col. 1764] *But* may perhaps need to be supplied.] Yet, by the Lord’s provision, the pure truth of the Catholic faith is present, drawn from the concordant judgment of all the fathers. It exposes the subtle poison of fatal perversity and, from the Scriptures, provides medicine for the salvation of the human race.

Therefore, let hearts not yet strengthened by an abundance of discernment be disturbed in any way until the hidden wound is exposed and the singular remedy shines forth. For no matter how skillfully the spirit of destruction arms itself with deceit, it is both exposed and slain by the holy sword of the principal Spirit.

#### 2

Accordingly, through Your Dilection we fraternally admonish all the priests of the Lord who are there to fight, with the Lord who instructs you, against these novel errors. You must not receive again a perversity condemned long ago throughout the whole world.

Or is it thought that we should rashly undertake something that would allow a heresy properly extinguished by our predecessors to challenge us again and openly engage us after regaining new strength? Is it permissible for us to undo what was condemned by the venerable fathers and to reopen the impious doctrines they cut down?

Why, then, do we take such great precautions to prevent the destruction of any heresy once cast down from coming again under examination, if we strive to restore what our ancestors knew, investigated, and refuted in ancient times? Would we not ourselves—God forbid, and may the Catholic Church never endure it—offer all the adversaries of truth an example by which they might rise against us?

Where is it written, “You shall not move the boundaries of your fathers” (Prov. 22:28), and, “Ask your fathers, and they will tell you; your elders, and they will declare it to you” (Deut. 32:7)?

Why, then, do we reach beyond what our predecessors have defined? Or why is it not enough for us, if we desire to learn what we do not know, to discover how the orthodox fathers and elders instructed us to avoid or adapt each matter to Catholic truth? Why are these things not judged by their decrees? Are we perhaps wiser than they, or could we stand with firm stability if we overturned what they established?

#### 3

Or do you perhaps not know that this heresy of which we speak was long ago struck down by the Apostolic See through the successive and unceasing judgments of Innocent, of blessed memory, and afterward of Zosimus, Boniface, Coelestine, Sixtus, and Leo? It was condemned not only by the laws of the Catholic Church but also by the Roman emperors, to such an extent that its followers were not permitted to have anywhere in the world a place in which to live.  
[Note: [Col. 1764] Alternatively, *at the time*.]

All this is taught both by the records composed in each region of the Church concerning their perversity and by the sanctions of public authority.

Behold how readily some ears, supposedly Catholic, listen to their doctrine, accept their questions, discuss their snares, and patiently admit their blasphemies. If only they would take pains to learn the books and replies of our predecessors against them! There it would be seen in every way that there is absolutely nothing that has not been debated by these men and crushed by those others through magnificent truth.

In this way all the faithful would be instructed to refute all their wickedness, so that nothing further would be sought. But if perhaps certain proposals concerning their opinions have disturbed uneducated minds, the teachings of the venerable fathers both expose all their madness and show by what remedies it is to be cured. Once these things have been foreseen by God’s provision, everything they have woven together in the succession of their teaching will appear both dangerous to those who follow it and foolish to those who recognize it.

Thus, if anyone thinks that they must be opposed, he is an opponent not merely of the judgments of the ancients, but openly and plainly declares himself an enemy of human salvation and Catholic teaching. For this reason the shepherds’ attentive and vigilant care must all the more keep the wolves’ savagery away from the sacred flocks.

For whatever harm happens to the holy sheep will condemn the negligence—God forbid—of their bishops, just as the expulsion of harmful beasts from the regenerated flocks will bring perpetual increase to the rewards of their guardians.

Certainly, if—as we hope more earnestly—these reports have been conveyed falsely, we desire to learn this as soon as possible, so that we who tremble at the affliction of Christ’s members may rejoice all the more in their stability.

Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of August, in the consulship of Albinus Faustus, a man of distinguished rank.  
[Note: [Col. 1765] July 28, in the year of Christ 493.]

## ANOTHER LETTER OF THE SAME POPE TO THE SAME HONORIUS  
[Note: [Col. 1765] Numbered 6 among the letters of Gelasius.]

**Gelasius to his most beloved brother Honorius.**

#### 1

We are astonished that Your Dilection was astonished that the care of the Apostolic See—which, according to the custom of our predecessors, is owed to all the churches throughout the world—should also have been concerned for the faith of your region.

When it was reported to the Apostolic See that certain people throughout Dalmatia were attempting to corrupt Catholic integrity and to reintroduce the poison of the Pelagian plague, already condemned by divine and human laws, we did not think that action should be postponed in any way. We wished either to investigate these matters more carefully and, if they had perhaps crept in, to heal them promptly, or, if they proved to have been falsely reported, to relieve our anxiety. We judged that it was better to appear overly impatient in investigating such matters than, by concealing them, to allow the danger to grow.

For we ought neither to suppress such cases in silence nor to foster them by delay, since, as the Teacher of the Gentiles says, we must be “not sluggish in diligence,” and again, “the one who presides, with diligence” (Rom. 12:11, 8). Unless we immediately investigated—even if the reports had been empty—we would unquestionably be found guilty.

It does not matter through whom these reports reached our ears. Once they had entered our conscience, we could not neglect pastoral watchfulness in investigating them truthfully, so that either the wolves lying in wait might be confronted at the first trace, or, if no wild beasts were present, the sheep might remain secure under protection.

The Apostle testifies that he had learned from those of Chloe about the dissensions among the Corinthians (1 Cor. 1:11), and he did not fail to write immediately, so that either the pious physician might confront the quarrels as they arose or might soon rejoice upon learning of their safety. We too remember that we indicated this in the letter sent concerning the matter: namely, that we might resist encroaching madness, or, if none of these things had occurred at all, rejoice in the integrity of Catholic truth.

Therefore Your Dilection ought not merely to be disturbed by our vigilance. Rather, after receiving the greeting of this present conversation, join your own diligence to ours, so that, if such things have been attempted, they may immediately be corrected, or, if they have not, they may be more carefully prevented from entering by any stealthy intrusion.

#### 2

If those whom Your Charity has sent wish to be more fully instructed concerning these matters, the following headings, together with their replies, will make them known. Since they have already professed that they accept these teachings to the extent of affirming that they held them from the beginning, but wished that what had been brought into question by anyone should first be clarified more explicitly, we have tried, insofar as possible amid the occupations that scarcely permit us to breathe, with the Lord’s favor and following the footsteps of our fathers, not to remain silent about matters that we have received [Note: [Col. 1765] Perhaps: *received* (*accepimus*).]. Whoever follows this rule of sober judgment with a faithful heart ought rightly to be regarded as orthodox. Whoever thinks that these teachings must be rejected should recognize that he has departed from the Apostolic doctrines.

Certainly, if there is anything capable of disturbing the mind, Your Fraternity should not hesitate to consult us confidently [Note: [Col. 1766] *not* may perhaps need to be supplied], so that, with the Lord’s grace supplying assistance, brotherly discussion may dispel every ambiguity of obscurity.

## ON SENE, NAMED SENECA, WHO FELL INTO THE PELAGIAN HERESY, WITH A REFUTATION OF THE THREE ERRORS THAT HE HAD ESPECIALLY ADOPTED FROM THE PELAGIANS

### Letter of the same Gelasius to all the bishops throughout Picenum  
[Note: [Col. 1766] Numbered 7 among his letters.]

**Gelasius, bishop, to all the bishops throughout Picenum: greetings in the Lord.**
1. Until now we had grieved that the provinces neighboring the City were being devastated by barbarian incursions and the savage storms of war; but amid the very perilous heat of these recent calamities we have discovered that the devil has inflicted a more destructive stain upon the minds of Christians than the ferocity of the enemy has inflicted upon their bodies. This evil chiefly concerns the priests of those regions, who, with such sluggishness and such disregard for the ministry they have undertaken, neglect the governance of the souls entrusted to them, so that they even allow those souls to be torn apart with impunity before their own eyes by the smallest beasts. Indeed, by fostering creeping wickedness and yielding to those who corrupt the faithful, they not only fail to restrain them in the least, but themselves provide more readily the nourishment of destruction by their example.

What, moreover, would such bishops do if—God forbid—some new and previously unknown plague should break out, or if men of sharper intellect and more crafty judgment, skilled in some secular learning, should bring forth sacrilegious words of blasphemy, when they neither remember nor refute the worn-out inventions of an error so ancient, an error already convicted both by the greatest teachers of the Churches and in our own age, and when they do not reject what is uttered by the ignorant and foolish? We give thanks to almighty God, because through such persons he tests the hearts of his own people—persons who do not even know what poison they are uttering. For what would the leaders of the peoples do under more cunning enemies, when they willingly submit themselves to the unlearned? Even if there were such complete indolence among the rulers of the Lord’s flock that they could neither understand nor restrain so contemptible and dull-witted a person, they ought nevertheless, rather than rashly surrendering their will to his absurd persuasions, to have sought from us the information that should be known concerning him through pastoral care.

2. For there was brought before us a pitiable old man named Seneca, who is not only alien to all learning but wholly estranged even from ordinary understanding. He has been shamelessly plunged into the filth of the Pelagian abyss, like one of the frogs of which we read in the Apocalypse (Apoc. 16:13), and has been horribly wallowed in that mire, finding no way by which he might emerge from it. For, abandoning the purity of catholic truth, the more he tries to raise himself through the slippery path of falsehood, the more he is overwhelmed, enclosed by its muddy pits. He is one of those of whom the apostle Peter says:

> “But these men, like irrational animals, creatures of instinct, born for capture and destruction, blaspheming in matters they do not understand, will perish in their own corruption, receiving the reward of unrighteousness” (2 Pet. 2:12–13).

Indeed, his mind is so stupid and dull that, concerning the poisons he has wickedly swallowed and vomited forth, he is utterly unable either to understand any account or to give one. Hardened by diabolical blindness and already handed over to himself, he is condemned by the deadly obstinacy of his heart. Nothing remains for him except that our God, who said that things which seem impossible to human beings are possible with him, should pierce such a mind with powerful compunction, so that, according to the blessed apostle Paul, he may recover from the snares of the devil by which he is held captive, in accordance with the sentence of divine judgment.

We disclosed to him many things concerning Pelagian opinions that had never entered his mind, not even in dreams, and demonstrated that they had long ago been refuted. We also showed that the very opinions which he appeared to be putting forward [Col. 1767] had formerly been produced by the Pelagian heretics and suitably shattered by catholic preachers. We proved that Pelagius, Caelestius, Julian, and many other men of rhetorical eloquence had been convicted in this assertion and struck down both by ecclesiastical decrees and by imperial commands. Accordingly, we established that this man cannot withstand positions on which such great men were overthrown—men whose arguments he can neither grasp nor even set forth in comparable language. But, as has been said, a diabolical mind possessed by inspiration, having descended into the depths of evil, consents to no remedies.

3. Therefore, among the countless kinds of blasphemy produced by the authors of the Pelagian heresy, we have judged that three doctrines, which this pitiable old man has especially taken up for himself, should not be left unmentioned, so that once they had been more clearly exposed, their overthrow might more readily be seen, with God destroying them:

> “Infants are created in their mothers’ wombs by the work of God. For that reason they do not think it just that God’s workmanship should be bound by any sin without any action of its own; and they make God unjust if infants are made guilty before they are born.”

They put forward this as the sharpest argument of their doctrine, failing to notice that the first parents of the human race were certainly created from no parents at all, but from harmless material of clay, and were powerfully fashioned purely and sincerely by divine skill [Note: [Col. 1767] Perhaps, “by divine power and skill.”]. Having been made rational, they followed the devil, their seducer, by their own will and were infected with perverse desires through the excess of transgression.

In them, therefore, human nature sinned, and human nature became vicious—a receiver, undoubtedly, of the evil it had previously not known. Having departed from what was good and right [Note: [Col. 1767] “The construction of the words requires that one read here ‘than . . . . . . of those falling away.’” M.], it plainly fell back into an affection for evil and perversity, as the very course of subsequent events makes clear. Thus constituted as the leaders of our nature, they made themselves subject to suffering and corruption, violating the gifts of the divine constitution to such an extent that they were punished by the retribution of death. For there can be no doubt that on the day when they became mortal they became dead.

Whatever, therefore, these parents produced from their own stock is indeed the work of God according to the institution of nature, but not without the contagion of that evil which they drew upon themselves through their transgression. Certainly, this very contagion of evil is not the work of God. Thus the defect is not from God’s creation: it is a fault which nature acquired by a voluntary movement. Yet even from a nature corrupted through itself God carries out the institution of his own creation; the creation produces a defect which it did not receive from the Creator’s institution, but which it assumed through the fall of its transgression.

For if the first human beings themselves, born—as has been said—from no parents and formed without any contagion, could corrupt themselves through an unlawful reach of presumption and attach the work of diabolical fraud to God’s work, what is surprising if those same corrupted people produced corrupted offspring? Did not God, although he created the human substance free in its own creation, nevertheless allow an external slavery, arising under human laws, to make it naturally bound and liable? People are born liable by their origin and are generated subject by a condition of slavery; by being born they become obligated before they have been begotten.

If this occurs with things situated outside nature, how much less surprising is it that it should occur with those in whom human substance itself is known to have been corrupted? Accordingly, just as the human substance itself made itself guilty through the institution of its sincere acts, polluted by its will through evil deeds, so it produced offspring and descendants stained by the guilty will of its own nature, because it generated children of the kind that it had made itself through the excess of its transgression. Therefore it brings forth not only what God instituted well in it, but also what it itself added badly and inconsequently.

Moreover [Col. 1768], just as the quality of an inner desire can alter nature, this is confirmed by the authority of divine Scripture. Thus, when that flock of sheep entrusted to Jacob was drinking while a variety of rods was placed before the channels, it conceived, attracted by the delight of its desire, what it did not possess by nature, and transferred into its offspring, through its senses, what it had not received in creation (Gen. 30:37–39) [Note: [Col. 1768] Perhaps, “what was not implanted.”]. What was then enacted figuratively both signified what would happen among the ecclesiastical flocks, and God, foreseeing the Pelagians’ accusations and the controversies that would be stirred up among his faithful, prepared the understanding of the matter.

4. Divine testimonies, the ecclesiastical sacraments themselves, and the tradition of the catholic teachers handed down by the Lord and Savior himself teach that the beginnings of human generation have been discolored. Hence the prophet cries:

> “Who can boast that he has a pure heart, or that he is clean from sins?” (Prov. 20:9).

Not even an infant whose life upon earth is one day old (Job 14:4, according to the Septuagint). Hence Scripture likewise says:

> “Who can make clean what has been conceived from unclean seed? Is it not you alone?” (ibid., according to the Vulgate).

And elsewhere:

> “For their seed was accursed” (Wis. 12:11).

The prophet David also testifies:

> “Behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother bore me” (Ps. 50:7).

If he says this, who can claim to have been begotten otherwise? The blessed apostle Paul likewise asserts:

> “We too were once by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Eph. 2:3).

Concerning this wrath he says in the Gospel:

> “Whoever believes and is baptized will have eternal life; but whoever does not believe has already been judged, and the wrath of God remains upon him” (John 3:36, 18).

This is the wrath of which it was said:

> “You shall surely die” (Gen. 2:17).

The Lord Jesus Christ himself declares with a heavenly voice:

> “Whoever does not eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood will not have life in himself” (John 6:54).

Here we certainly see that no one is excepted; nor has anyone dared to say that a little child can be brought to eternal life without this saving sacrament. Without that life, it is undoubtedly destined to remain in perpetual death.

Why, then, is an infant enclosed within this condition if it has no sin at all? Indeed, God would appear more unjust—God forbid—if punishment were inflicted where there was no fault. Since the infant is not held bound by any guilt arising from its own actions, nothing remains except that it has been polluted solely by a defective birth; and unless it has been cleansed through participation in the Christian mystery, it cannot attain everlasting life.

Hence infants are exorcised and catechized. Because, in God’s work—which was well instituted in its author—the work of diabolical malignity intervened, they are rescued from the power of darkness and, as the Apostle teaches, transferred to the proper inheritance and purification of the children of God (Col. 1:13, 12) [Note: [Col. 1768] Perhaps, “by which.”].

Unless the first generation, which God instituted as good, had fallen into guilt through transgression and become rejected, a second generation would not have needed to be substituted. Therefore the blessed apostle Paul says:

> “Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin, death; and so death passed to all human beings, in whom all sinned. … Therefore, just as through one offense condemnation came upon all human beings, so through one act of righteousness justification of life came upon all human beings” (Rom. 5:12, 18).

When he says “all” for condemnation, he certainly means those who were begotten from Adam as their parent; but when he says “all” for the justification of life, he refers only to those who have been reborn in the mystery of Christ.

The Pelagian heresy’s deadly doctrine has been convicted by countless such texts, both by our ancestors and now by their abundant teaching. Simple minds should not be disturbed by these matters; for them it is enough to have believed, according to the ecclesiastical rule, what they do not understand. If anyone desires knowledge, it is appropriate to ask.

5. As for the claim concerning infants—that without holy Baptism they cannot be condemned for original sin alone—it is a sufficiently impious and profane proposition [Col. 1769]. Although every Christian knows that infants, newly born from their mothers’ wombs, are baptized for the remission of sins, the catholic Church celebrates this truthfully, not deceptively, lest it appear—God forbid—to be lying in the heavenly sacraments. Since infants have no sins of their own, it is therefore clear that only their original sins are entirely remitted.

Thus, when these alone have also been remitted, they obtain eternal life through Baptism. Consequently, when these alone have not been remitted, they cannot attain eternal life. Hence the Lord also says, as we stated above—and this certainly applies only to the baptized:

> “Whoever does not eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood will not have life in himself.”

What is it to be without perpetual life except to be established in everlasting death? Although the kingdom of heaven and eternal life are the same thing, nevertheless, in order that God’s providence might cut off every Pelagian wickedness, it was said not only:

> “Whoever has not been reborn of water and the Holy Spirit will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (John 3:5),

but equally:

> “Whoever does not eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood will not have life in himself.”

No one doubts that this was said concerning eternal life, since many who do not eat this sacrament appear to possess the present life.

There is therefore no reason to say that unbaptized infants can only be unable to enter the kingdom of heaven, but are not punished by perpetual condemnation, since without Baptism they can neither eat nor drink the body and blood of Christ; without this they cannot have life in themselves; and without life they will necessarily be dead. Let them say, then, if they do not consider those established in perpetual death to be condemned. Let them therefore remove from the midst this alleged third place that they invent for deceiving little children. Since we read only of the right side and the left (Matt. 25:33), let them not make infants remain without Baptism in the left-hand region, but allow the baptized to be transferred by holy regeneration to the saving right hand.

6. In a third chapter they now circulate the delirious teachings of the Pelagians, known and refuted throughout the world [Note: [Col. 1769] Perhaps, “he circulates”]. They say that a human being becomes blessed through free will—which he has corrupted, defiled, and destroyed—with the support of the good of nature. Yet from the blessedness of paradise, where the substance had been constituted good, he could not have been expelled unless he had lost his own good. He became mortal because, through transgression, he had passed from good to evil and had transferred himself from participation in God to diabolical deeds. Therefore he was rightly handed over to his deceiver, to whom he had willingly assented; therefore he was excluded from the love of his happiness and condemned by a heavenly voice to thorns, thistles, and manifold miseries (Gen. 3:18). Such a punishment, imposed by a just judgment, would certainly never have been inflicted so severely and harshly upon one who persevered in the good; nor would it properly have been imposed unless it had been brought about by evil.

Behold: without divine support—which, while placed in that blessedness, he is never read to have sought—not only could the natural good of humanity not help, and not only did it not make him blessed, but when he trusted in this alone and did not return to its giver, he both lost blessedness and took up the beginning of every evil.

As for the claim that he attains blessedness through free will, though he has used it badly and fallen into perpetual slavery, Scripture says:

> “Whoever commits sin is a slave of sin” (John 8:34);
>
> “By whatever anyone is overcome, to that he is enslaved” (2 Pet. 2:19).

Is this not that natural presumption which descended into the rights of detestable captivity, of which holy Scripture says:

> “A heavy yoke lies upon the children of Adam, from the day they come forth from their mother’s womb until the day of burial in the mother of all” (Ecclus. 40:1)?

From this the human race was redeemed by our Lord Jesus Christ alone, through the exchange of his passion, and was rescued through a changed birth. He alone came to seek and save what had perished (Luke 19:10), so that the freedom cast down through reckless [Col. 1770] pride might be restored and renewed through grace. Thus, in reciprocal fashion, just as the free choice of the human will had merited everlasting captivity by following the devil, so, by following the author of restored freedom, it might return to the reward it had lost.

Hence the Lord himself says:

> “When the Son has set you free, then you will truly be free” (John 8:36).

The blessed apostle Paul explains:

> “When you were slaves of sin, you were free from righteousness,” that is, alien from righteousness; “but now, having been freed from sin, you have become slaves of righteousness” (Rom. 6:20, 18).

And again the same apostle says:

> “With the freedom with which Christ has set you free” (Gal. 4:31).

Does not the chosen Vessel himself affirm and say:

> “It is God who works in you both to will and to accomplish, according to his good pleasure” (Phil. 2:13),

lest anyone think that God works both willing and accomplishing in an evil will as well?

7. The Pelagians’ particular and long-worn poison is the opinion by which they think that “the grace of God can be bestowed according to human merits.” May this be far from Christian minds, since the Apostle testifies:

> “It is grace that is given freely; otherwise, if grace is from works, it is no longer grace” (Rom. 11:6).

For a reward is paid, not freely; but grace receives its name because it is bestowed freely.

What Christian would dare to say that anyone possesses anything good without grace, when the Teacher of the Nations cries out, summing up all gifts in himself:

> “By the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace toward me has not been empty” (1 Cor. 15:10)?

He showed that the gift of grace had not been preceded by himself, but that he had followed after it. And to demonstrate that he was grace’s fellow-worker by following it, he says:

> “I labored more than all of them.”

Then, fearing that he might seem to presume upon himself, he added:

> “Not I, but the grace of God with me” (1 Cor. 15:10).

He did not say, “I and the grace of God with me”; rather, he placed the preceding grace before himself and then added his own words.

What, moreover, can be possessed without grace, when faith itself comes through grace? The same apostle teaches us:

> “I received mercy so that I might be faithful” (ibid. 7:25).

Divine mercy is nothing other than grace.

Let us also hear how he instructs the Church:

> “You have been saved by grace through faith” (Eph. 2:8).

He was explaining that the beginning of salvation and faith had begun from grace, as he immediately adds:

> “And this is not from yourselves; it is the gift of God—not from works, so that no one may boast” (Eph. 2:8–9).

Elsewhere he declares the same thing generally and absolutely:

> “What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Cor. 4:7).

Who could be sufficient to enumerate each point? These passages clearly show that free will arising from nature does not merit grace; rather, through grace it receives the ability to be mercifully released from the slavery it had merited by sinning. This redemption was prepared by eternal providence before the foundation of the world. Whether the law had not yet been given, or whether the legal observance was in force, the ancient origin of all holy men and women was cleansed through figurative signs and sacrifices; and through the Spirit of grace, remedies of eternal salvation came to all the righteous who worshiped from afar this mystery, whose fullness, manifested to the nations in Christ, purifies and renews the world and truly makes them participants in perpetual blessedness.

8. Therefore we severely censure our brothers and fellow bishops, especially those governing the Church of the Lord throughout the provinces of Picenum, who not only failed to deter the wicked conversation of a most foolish old man and contemptible person, but even nourished it by their consent. Who could hear of it, who could endure it, that bishops allowed some contemptible corpse of a man to deprive of communion a presbyter who refused to listen to him [Note: [Col. 1770] Perhaps, “dared to deprive him of communion.”]? How was such a man either received by anyone or patiently heard?

He even issued laws, which were willingly accepted, so that servants of God might mix with consecrated young women in a most disgraceful assembly. For when spiritual minds are assailed by imagined enticements even when such associations are absent, [Col. 1771] how much more strongly are they aroused by the sight of the opposite sex, even when they do not wish to be illicitly aroused [Note: [Col. 1771] Thus according to Morel, *Elementa Critica*, pp. 192–193. In B., “who, even when unwilling, are not more intensely incited illicitly.”]?

An even greater crime was added: in the sight and presence of priests, he attempted to tear apart Jerome and Augustine, teachers who were lights of the Church, like a dying fly, as it is written, ruining the oil of sweetness (Eccles. 10:1).

But why should we marvel that the leaders of the Churches neglect these matters, when it is evident—as we have heard from many—that they do everything contrary to the canons and indiscriminately mix everything contrary to apostolic discipline? They ordain without observing the rules; they permit not only monks but also ministers of the Church to migrate abroad with women and return again; and they allow them to be advanced into the clerical service by other bishops.

Although none of these individual practices should be tolerated, who could endure the perpetration of so many and such great crimes, by which they rightly appear to offer a spectacle to Gentiles, Jews, and heretics and, God forbid, to be directing themselves toward the destruction of religion itself? The Apostle’s sentence is rightly applied to those who do such things:

> “For the name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you” (Rom. 2:24).

9. Let it suffice, then, that these offenses have been committed thus far; and, so that God may be appeased concerning human affairs, let divine matters henceforth be cared for more diligently. Let no advocate of the aforesaid plague be found anywhere at all, nor let him find access to the Church or participation in catholic communion anywhere, if he prefers, by his wicked profession, to join the company of heretics.

Those with whom he is shown previously to have mingled in harmful conversation must, unless they repent and withdraw from his association, be removed from ecclesiastical service and punished with a devoted [Note: [Col. 1771] Perhaps, “due”] vengeance, so that an example may be provided for the others to avoid. Let him approach no one, nor let him ever again be permitted to speak the blasphemy long ago condemned.

Men’s and women’s residences are to be kept separate, and vigilant devotion is to be practiced as a holy purpose demands. No one is to be admitted to ecclesiastical office contrary to the established canons. The governors of each province must understand that they will not obtain pardon for past errors if henceforth they neglect to avoid what has been exposed. Nor will any opportunity for excuse remain if, after these present commands—which we have decided to send through the deacon Romulus, whose vigilance and diligence on behalf of the catholic faith and religion we most gratefully recognize—any bishop is found to be either contemptuous or negligent concerning all these matters.

For just as it belongs to the administration of the Apostolic See to provide fittingly for all the Churches with the necessary care, so it must not conceal the power divinely entrusted to it against the contumacious and negligent.

Issued on the Kalends of November, during the consulship of Albinus, a man of illustrious rank [Note: [Col. 1771] On the first day of November, in the year of Christ 493.]

## Profession of the Scythian Monks concerning the Grace of God against the Pelagians (C)

From the booklet given in Constantinople to the legates of Pope Hormisdas in the name of John Maxentius and his companions, in the year of Christ 519.

1. Since these matters stand thus, most blessed fathers, we now think it necessary to make clear to Your Holiness, by a brief exposition, what we believe concerning the grace of God—not the grace by which we are created, but that by which we are recreated and renewed. For even in this respect the enemies of God’s grace—that is, the followers of Pelagius and Caelestius—appear to be exceedingly hostile to us.

2. Accordingly, we confess that Adam was created by God upright in all respects, neither mortal nor immortal, but capable of either condition. He possessed, within the power of his own will, both the willingness and the ability to do everything—that is, both good and evil. Deceived by the cunning of the serpent, he became, by his own choice, a transgressor of the divine command. Therefore, by God’s just judgment, he became subject not only to the death of the body but also to the death of the soul; stripped of his former honor, he was made like the beasts [Col. 1772]—not because he became irrational, but because his rational power was bound by carnal delight.

Immediately, as the deserved consequence of disobedience, he experienced in his own members a contrary law, resisting the law of his mind and taking him captive under the law of sin (Rom. 7:23). We believe that this evil and the punishment of evil passed into the whole human race—not merely the death of the body, which is the punishment of sin, as some wish to say, but also the sting of death, that is, sin, which entered the world.

For we follow the Apostle rather than such men. He testifies that both sin and death passed to all human beings, saying:

> “Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin, death; and so death passed to all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Rom. 5:12).

Therefore we believe that infants, newly born from the womb, are baptized for the remission of sins, so that they may not perish eternally—not merely so that they might merit adoption as children or on account of the kingdom of heaven, as do the disciples of Pelagius, Caelestius, and Theodore of Mopsuestia, who try to assert that natural sin and original sin are one and the same.

3. The strength of nature, therefore, disarmed by the evil of transgression, was entirely unable to rise by itself from the place to which it had fallen by its own will. Consequently, we believe that from Adam until now no one has been saved through the strength of nature, except by the gift of the grace of the Holy Spirit, through faith in the name of Jesus. For:

> “There is no other name given among human beings under heaven by which we must be saved” (Acts 4:12),

except the name of Jesus Christ.

We believe that natural free will is capable of nothing other than discerning and desiring merely carnal or worldly things, which may perhaps appear glorious not before God but before human beings. But concerning those things that pertain to eternal life, it can neither think, will, desire, nor accomplish them except through the infusion and inward operation of the Holy Spirit, who is also the Spirit of Christ:

> “Anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him” (Rom. 8:9).

If anyone believes in Christ, he already belongs to Christ. This is true not through the gift of nature, but through the Holy Spirit, who belongs to Christ. Whoever believes in him who justifies the ungodly (Rom. 4:5) confesses that Jesus is Lord (Rom. 10:9); and:

> “No one can say, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ except in the Holy Spirit” (1 Cor. 12:3).

Therefore we anathematize those who say that sin is something natural or some substance. We also abominate those who dare to say, contrary to the Apostle’s word, “Willing is ours, but accomplishing belongs to God.” The same teacher testifies that both willing and accomplishing are divine gifts, saying:

> “For it is God who works in you both to will and to accomplish, according to his good pleasure” (Phil. 2:13).

We also believe that all who were saved from Abel until Christ were saved by the same grace by which we too are saved, according to the word of the blessed apostle Peter:

> “Why are you testing God by placing upon the necks of the disciples a yoke which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear? But we believe that we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they were” (Acts 15:10–11).

## From the Letter of the Deacon Peter and His Companions, Who Were Sent from the East to Rome on Questions of Faith, Written to the African Bishops in Exile in Sardinia

[Note: [Col. 1772] Approximately the year of Christ 520.]

What the Churches of the entire East believe with them concerning the grace of Christ and defend against the heretics.

To the most holy lords, worthy of being named with all reverence—Datianus, Fortunatus, Albanus, Orontius, Boethus, Fulgentius, Januarius, and the other bishops adorned by confession of Christ—Peter, an unworthy deacon, John, Leontius, another John, and the other brothers sent to Rome on the matter of the faith.

## Chapter One

1. We believe that it will be useful and exceedingly necessary, and especially beneficial to the holy Churches of God, to present to Your Holiness what all the holy Churches of the East defend with us against the heretics concerning the Incarnation and the divine dispensation [Col. 1773]—heretics who do not cease to disturb the ancient faith of the Church with wicked and unjust arguments—and humbly to seek the agreement of Your Blessedness concerning these matters.

For we believe that you differ in nothing from our holy and glorious confession, especially since we have no doubt that the holy Church of God is everywhere animated by one Spirit. The entire East will be filled with no small but rather great joy if they learn that Your Holiness agrees with them—or rather, agrees with the catholic faith—in all doctrines.

Therefore we humbly ask and beseech Your Blessedness to examine carefully what is contained below and, as befits the truest and most fearless preachers of Christ, to command that your judgment be made known to us in writing [Note: [Col. 1773] Fulgentius replied in the name of the fifteen bishops with him in a written book on the Incarnation and Grace, which begins: “Our blessed brother John the deacon, sent by your company, presented to us the letter you sent. After reading it, we joyfully recognized both your faith and your salvation; indeed, through your acknowledgment of the faith, our salvation became known to us.”].

Thus, if, by God’s favor, our exposition is found among you to agree with the catholic faith and the apostolic traditions—as we do not doubt that it will—and if it is approved, we shall be able, strengthened by the authority of so many tested and proven priests, to silence the mouths of those who speak wickedly. Remaining steadfast in the faith of the holy Fathers, we shall give thanks to God, who has glorified you through your confession of holiness, most holy lords and most worthy servants of God.

We now ask you to examine more diligently the matters that follow, etc. [Note: [Col. 1773] Four chapters concerning the Incarnation are omitted.]

## Chapter Six

2. After this it follows that we must also declare to Your Blessedness how we understand the grace of Christ, by which he rescued us from the power of Satan (Col. 1:13), according to what has been handed down to us, since your authority is also greatly necessary to us in this matter.

We therefore believe that Adam was made good by God, the Creator of all things, without any opposition from the flesh, and endowed with great freedom, so that he had the power both to do good by his own ability and, if he wished, to admit evil. Death and immortality were placed, in a certain sense, within the freedom of his will. For he was capable of either condition: if he kept the commandment, he would become immortal without experiencing death; but if he despised it, death would immediately follow.

Thus corrupted by the serpent’s cunning, he voluntarily became a transgressor of the divine law. Therefore, according to what had been foretold to him, he was condemned by God’s just judgment to the punishment of death. Entirely—that is, in body and soul—he was changed for the worse; having lost his own freedom, he was enslaved to the service of sin.

From that time no human being is born who is not bound by the chain of this sin, except the one who was born through a new mode of generation in order to break this bond of sin: the man Christ Jesus, Mediator between God and human beings (1 Tim. 2:5).

For what else could or can be born from a slave except a slave? Adam did not beget children while he was free, but only after he had become a slave of sin. Therefore, just as every human being comes from him, so every human being through him is a slave of sin.

Hence the Apostle says:

> “From one man came condemnation upon all human beings”;

and again:

> “Through one man sin entered this world, and through sin, death; and so death passed to all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Rom. 5:18, 12).

They are therefore completely mistaken who say that only death, and not sin also, passed into the human race, since the Apostle testifies that both sin and death were brought into the world through him.

3. No one at all is freed from this condemnation and death except by the grace of the Redeemer. Although he was Lord, being God, in order to free us from perpetual slavery and from the power of the devil and restore us to true freedom, he became a slave, taking the form of a slave (Phil. 2:7).

Hence he says to the Jews:

> “Then you will truly be free, if the Son sets you free” (John 8:36).

They thought themselves truly free while serving human occupations with utterly vain devotion. Therefore, in order that false freedom might become true freedom—that is, in order that human freedom might become Christian freedom—that same freedom needed a liberator, so that, through his grace, it might turn away from human occupations and be able to think about and desire the things that pertain to eternal life.

Without this grace, therefore, a person can indeed think about and desire human things; but he cannot think about, will, or desire divine things. The first and chief of these, the foundation, as it were, and source of all good, is to believe in the crucified Lord of glory.

This does not arise from the freedom of natural will, because it is not flesh and blood that reveal this, but the heavenly Father, to whomever he wills (Matt. 16:17). He draws that person into true freedom not by violent compulsion, but by infusing sweetness through the Holy Spirit, so that believers immediately say:

> “Jesus is Lord.”

No one can say this through the natural freedom of the will except in the Holy Spirit (1 Cor. 12:3).

They therefore babble in vain who say, “It is mine to will to believe, but it belongs to God’s grace to assist.” For the Apostle testifies that even believing itself—which is giving assent to the truth—is given to us by God, saying:

> “It has been granted to you by Christ not only to believe in him, but also to suffer for him” (Phil. 1:29).

## Chapter Seven
4. But they say: If God makes those who are unwilling want to believe, while no one, as you maintain, can naturally believe or will anything good that pertains to eternal life, why then does he not make everyone willing, since there is no partiality with God (Rom. II, 11), especially since it is written of him, “Who desires all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (I Tim. II, 4)? Either he desires this and is unable to accomplish it, or divine Scripture is lying. But if it is impious to hold either of these positions, it remains that he does not arouse the human will but awaits it from human beings, so that there may be a fair reward for those who are willing, and just condemnation for those who are unwilling.

If matters are as the heretics boast, the inscrutable and incomprehensible judgments of God have been grasped by them. For if, as they wish, he condemns the unwilling but saves the willing, there is absolutely nothing further to investigate. And, as far as they are concerned, divine Scripture is false when it bears witness to the incomprehensible judgments of God (Rom. XI, 33). We, however, believing and demonstrating that the judgments of God are incomprehensible, say that, from one mass of perdition, some are saved by the goodness and grace of God, while others are abandoned by a just and hidden judgment.

Otherwise, let those who judge this contrary to divine justice and goodness say, if they can, why he who desires all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth performed so many mighty works in Chorazim and Bethsaida, yet did not wish to perform any of them in Tyre and Sidon, where, if they had been performed—as he himself testifies—they might perhaps have repented in ashes and sackcloth (Matt. XI, 21). Or why did he forbid the Apostle to announce the word of salvation in Asia and Bithynia (Acts XVI, 6–7)?

And if these things cannot be comprehended, let them return to themselves; and, finding themselves to be human beings, let them cease asking why he saves some by a free gift and abandons others by a just and hidden judgment—he who has authority from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor (Rom. IX, 21). Let them cry out with us, or rather in the words of the Apostle:

“O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How inscrutable are his judgments and unsearchable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor? Or who has first given to him, so that it might be repaid to him? For from him and through him and in him are all things. To him be glory forever and ever. Amen” (Rom. XI, 33–36).

Clearly, therefore, it is not against us but entirely against the Apostle that the person who says, “Unless I first will, grace does not come to me,” resists. For this is nothing other than saying that one must first give something to God in order that God may repay him.

## CHAPTER VIII

5. But, following the same Apostle [Col. 1775], we say that the origin of all good thoughts, their assent, and the will concerning them come from God, through God, and in God. He releases and corrects the perverse wills of human beings, entangled in earthly actions, through the inward infusion and operation of the Holy Spirit, as it is written: “The will is prepared by the Lord” (Prov. VIII, 35, according to the Septuagint).

Hence also blessed Basil, bishop of Caesarea, says in the Prayer of the Sacred Altar, which nearly the whole East frequently uses, among other things:

“Grant, Lord, power and protection; we ask you, make the evil good, preserve the good in goodness. For you can do all things, and no one can resist you; for when you will to save, no one resists your will.”

See how briefly and decisively that eminent teacher once brought this controversy to an end, teaching through this prayer that evil human beings are made good not by themselves but by God, and that they persevere in goodness not by their own power but with the assistance of divine grace.

6. Likewise blessed Innocent, bishop of the Apostolic See, says in his letter to the Council of Milevis:

“All the zeal, all the works, and all the merits of the saints must be referred to the glory and praise of God, because no one pleases him for any other reason than that which he himself has given.”

[Note: [Col. 1775] This sentence is found in chapter eight of Celestine’s letter, above, col. 1757, immediately after Innocent’s words, but it does not in fact belong to him. Again, below, at the end of the present section 6, the beginning of chapter 9 of that same letter of Celestine was taken, through a quite similar error, for the words of the African bishops.]

The African councils, repeating and explaining more carefully and clearly the judgment of Pope Zosimus himself in their letter to him, say:

“But what you placed in the letter which you arranged to have sent to all the provinces, saying, ‘Yet we, at God’s prompting—for all good things must be referred to their author, from whom they arise—have referred everything to the conscience of our brothers and fellow bishops’: we understand this statement to mean that, passing swiftly over those who exalt the freedom of the will against God’s assistance, you cut them down, as it were, with the drawn sword of truth.

“For what did you attribute so freely to free choice as the fact that you referred everything to the conscience of our humility? And yet you correctly and wisely perceived that this had been done at God’s prompting, and you spoke truthfully and confidently. This is so precisely because the will is prepared by the Lord, and because, in order that they may do something good, he himself touches the hearts of his children with paternal inspirations. ‘For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God’ (Rom. VIII, 14).

“Thus we do not fail to recognize the presence of our own will, yet in each movement of the human will toward good we do not hesitate to acknowledge that his grace comes first. God works in human hearts and in free choice itself in such a way that holy thought, pious counsel, and every movement of good will come from God; for through him we are able to do something good, and without him we can do nothing.”

[Note: [Col. 1775] Celestine: “to prevail.”]

7. In harmony with these statements, the most blessed Celestine says in a letter sent to the Gauls:

“For when the bishops of holy peoples, fulfilling the mission entrusted to them, act as advocates for the human race before divine mercy, and, with the whole Church groaning together with them, ask and pray that faith be granted to unbelievers; that idolaters be freed from the errors of their unbelief; that, once the veil of their hearts has been removed, the light of truth appear to the Jews; that heretics come to their senses through acceptance of the Catholic faith; that schismatics receive the spirit of renewed charity; that remedies of repentance be granted to those who have fallen; and, finally, that the court of heavenly mercy be opened to catechumens brought to the sacraments of regeneration.

“That these things are not sought from the Lord superficially or in vain is demonstrated by the outcome of the things themselves: for he deigns to draw many from every kind of error, and, rescuing them from the power of darkness, transfers them into the kingdom of the Son of his love (Col. I, 13); and from vessels of wrath he makes vessels of mercy. This is perceived to be so entirely the work of God that, for the illumination or correction of such people, thanksgiving and an acknowledgment of praise are always offered to God who accomplishes it” (chapter 11).

Again, shortly afterward:

“Therefore, confirmed by these ecclesiastical rules and by documents taken from divine authority [Col. 1776], with the Lord God assisting us, we profess God to be the author both of all good effects and works, and of all zeal and every virtue by which, from the beginning of faith, one strives toward God. We do not doubt that the merits of every human being are preceded by his grace, through whom it comes about that we begin both to will and to do something good.

“By this assistance and gift of God free choice is not taken away but set free: so that what was dark becomes bright, what was crooked straight, what was weak healthy, and what was imprudent prudent.”

The same teacher ends and concludes this very letter by saying:

“Because we believe that, for confessing the grace of God—nothing whatsoever being taken away from its work and gracious favor—it is sufficient to accept whatever the writings of the Apostolic See have taught us according to the rules stated above, we in no way consider Catholic whatever appears contrary to the propositions set forth.”

8. Most holy brothers, we have not considered it necessary to offer these things as reminders to people who were ignorant of them. Rather, to refute the madness of those who reject them as new doctrines, entirely unheard-of in the Churches, we have thought it useful to insert them into this little work of ours.

Instructed by the teachings of all these holy Fathers, we anathematize Pelagius and Coelestius, and likewise Julian of Eclanum [Note: [Col. 1776] Elsewhere, “of Eclana.”], and those who hold similar opinions; especially the books of Faustus, bishop of Gaul, who was promoted from the monastery of Lérins—books which were unquestionably written against the doctrine of predestination. In them he not only contradicts all these holy Fathers but also departs from the tradition of the Apostle himself, making the assistance of grace subordinate to human labor and entirely emptying Christ’s grace of its force. He impiously declares that the ancient saints were saved not by the grace by which we too are saved, according to the teaching of the blessed Apostle Peter, but by the possibility of nature (Acts XV, 11).

Peter, by the mercy of God, deacon, subscribed.

John, by the mercy of God, monk, subscribed.

Leontius, by the mercy of God, monk, subscribed.

John, lector, by the mercy of God, subscribed.

# ANATHEMAS AGAINST THE PELAGIANS, ISSUED AT ROME—AS IS SUPPOSED—in THE YEAR 520 BY THE SCYTHIAN MONKS SENT AS ENVOYS TO POPE HORMISDAS

1. If anyone does not confess that original sin entered the world through Adam’s transgression, according to the Apostle’s statement, “Through one man sin entered into the world” (Rom. V, 12), and so forth, let him be anathema.

2. Likewise, we anathematize every opinion of Pelagius and Coelestius, and of all who hold similar views, accepting everything that was done and written against them by the bishops of the Apostolic See, namely Innocent, Boniface, Zosimus, Celestine, Leo, Atticus of Constantinople also, Augustine, and the bishops of the African province.

# ON THE BOOKS OF FAUSTUS, BISHOP OF RIÉZ IN GAUL

## Letter of Possessor, an African bishop, sent from Constantinople to Pope Hormisdas

To the most blessed lord, Pope Hormisdas, Possessor, bishop: eternal salvation in the Lord.

It is fitting and expedient to return to the remedy of the head whenever the health of the limbs is at issue. For who shows greater concern for those subject to him, or from whom should the stability of wavering faith be more expected, than from the ruler of that See whose first ruler heard from Christ, “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. XVI, 18)?

I suppose that Your Beatitude is not unaware of the many plots by which the Church in Constantinople is troubled, and how, following the pattern of an old disease, a raging wound seeks again to break out—one believed to have been covered by a scar.

Accordingly, when the minds of certain brothers were stirred to scandal by a book [Col. 1777] of a certain Faustus, a Gaul by nationality [Note: [Col. 1777] Possessor is mistaken: Faustus reveals himself in many places to have been British by nationality.], bishop of the royal city, who appears to have written eloquently about various matters, and more frequently about the grace of God, while others, as human intellectual efforts tend to do, resisted in the opposite direction, they thought that I should be consulted about this uncertainty.

I said that the matters debated by interpreters according to the capacity of their own intelligence are not to be received as canonical, nor preserved as law in place of synodal decisions. Rather, we possess certain things—namely, those written in the Old or New Testament and established by the general judgments of the Fathers—as the complete foundation and firmness of faith and religion. The writings composed by various bishops, however, are customarily judged according to their quality, without prejudice to the faith.

But when, as I perceived from their repeated requests, this seemed to them more an excuse than an answer, either to comply with their request or to take the opportunity of rendering service to your apostolate, I presumed to submit, through my deacon Justin, these lines of my insignificance. In them, chiefly asking for the protection of your prayers, I beg that, after consulting what should be thought about the statements of the aforementioned author, they may learn it through the authority of an apostolic response. This is especially so because the sons of the master of soldiers, Vitalian and Justinian, also particularly desire to be instructed on this matter by a rescript of Your Beatitude, and so forth.

Received on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August, in the consulship of Rusticus, a man of the highest distinction.

[Note: [Col. 1777] On July 18, in the year of Christ 520.]

# LETTER OF POPE HORMISDAS TO POSSESSOR

[Note: [Col. 1777] Number 70 among his letters.]

1. Just as it accords with reason that those who are uncertain should consult, so it is proper that those consulted should reply; for the person who does not instruct the ignorant himself drives him into error, and so forth.

2. Where are there not the barbs of varied temptation? What subtle deceits, concealed by cunning, have we endured for almost a whole uninterrupted year from certain Scythians who presented themselves as monks in appearance but not in truth, in profession but not in conduct, and who, under the pretext of religion, carried poisons serving their hatreds? We endeavored to heal them of their inward wound by the moderating treatment of patience, without withholding the admonitions of blessed Paul: “Do not contend in words; for it is useful for nothing except the ruin of those who hear” (II Tim. II, 14), and so forth.

We have thought that these matters should be reported to Your Dilection on this occasion, lest, if they should perhaps be delayed there, they might deceive you by some simulation of words, while you were unaware of how they had conducted themselves in the city of Rome.

3. As for those whom you have indicated in your letter that you consulted concerning the statements of a certain Faustus, a bishop of Gaul, let them have this answer: neither should that man be received [Note: [Col. 1777] This refers to the Decree of Pope Gelasius, composed at the Roman synod in 494, in which the “little works of Faustus of Riéz in Gaul” are judged apocryphal and included under the same heading as the books of heretics: “The other things written or preached by heretics or schismatics the Catholic and Apostolic Roman Church in no way receives, of which a few . . . we believe should be set forth below.” At the end of the Decree it is likewise declared: “Not only rejected, but also . . . condemned forever under the indissoluble bond of anathema.”]; nor can anyone whom the examination of the Catholic faith does not receive among the authority of the Fathers be able to generate ambiguity concerning ecclesiastical discipline or bring prejudice against religious people.

The institutions established by the Fathers, which the faithful ought to follow, are fixed. Whether it is interpretation, preaching, or a word composed for the edification of the people, it is admitted if it agrees with right faith and sound doctrine; if it disagrees, it is abolished.

There is one foundation; whatever structure rises outside it is weak. Whoever builds upon that foundation, whether with cheap or precious materials, should take this into consideration. The person who departs from what the choice of the Fathers has demonstrated strays from the road.

Nor is diligence that examines many things condemned; rather, it is the mind that turns away from the truth. Instruction is often provided concerning matters about which the very opponents are proved to be mistaken. Nor can it be counted a fault to know what one should avoid. For that reason, those who read incongruous things do not incur blame [Col. 1778], but those who follow them do.

If this were not so, that teacher of the nations would never have consented to announce to the faithful, “Test everything; hold fast what is good” (I Thess. V, 21), and so forth.

The venerable wisdom of the Fathers, acting with faithful authority and not without foresight, defined which doctrines were Catholic and, with the Holy Spirit instructing it, established which books of earlier times were to be received as authoritative, lest a reader, indulging his own opinion, assert not what was suitable for the edification of the Church but what his own pleasure had conceived.

What need, then, was there for accusers to extend their questions beyond the established boundaries of the Church and to provoke disputes about statements that are accepted, as though they had not been stated, when the Christian faith is bounded by the canonical Books, synodal precepts, and the regular decrees of the Fathers with a stable and unshaken limit?

As for free choice and the grace of God, what the Roman—that is, Catholic—Church follows and asserts can indeed be learned from the various books of blessed Augustine, especially those addressed to Hilary and Prosper [Note: [Col. 1778] An excellent confirmation of Augustine’s doctrine and an unmistakable condemnation of Faustus himself, who departed from it in his books.]. Nevertheless, the ecclesiastical archives contain explicit chapters which, if you do not have them and consider them necessary, we shall send.

Although anyone who carefully considers the Apostle’s statements clearly understands what he ought to follow.

Given on the Ides of August.

[Note: [Col. 1778] On August 13, in the year 520.]

# FROM THE WRITING OF JOHN MAXENTIUS AGAINST THE FOREGOING LETTER

1. Since a certain letter is said to be circulated everywhere by our enemies, as though sent by the Roman bishop, in which many things are pointlessly set out against the Scythian monks, I considered it necessary to respond to the statements of that letter itself and to show that those same monks are free from every such accusation, and so forth.

It is not easy to believe that this is the letter of the person whose name is attached to it, especially since, as we have said, nothing reasonable or coherent is found in it. Rather, the whole letter appears to be filled with empty accusations and slanders, which usually proceed from the resentment of an opposing mind, and so forth.

2. Or is it perhaps not Catholic to confess that Christ, the Son of the living God, is one of the holy and undivided Trinity? It is precisely for this single proposition that the Scythian monks are known to have gone to the Roman bishop, as is known to nearly all Catholics not only in this royal city [Note: [Col. 1778] Constantinople.] but also throughout Italy.

For, as was said above, the heretics themselves produce this very letter, to which we are responding, everywhere for this purpose: both to stir up hatred against the monks just mentioned and to prohibit everyone, as though on the authority of the same Roman bishop, from confessing that Christ, the Son of God, is one of the Trinity, and so forth.

But far be it from us to suppose that the Roman bishop contradicted Catholic confession in any respect. For he would never have allowed the Scythian monks, whom he knew to confess in speech and in writing that Christ the Son of God is one of the Trinity, to remain in communion with him for nearly fourteen months, as long as he detained them there, if he judged this preaching contrary to the Catholic faith, as the heretics wish, and so forth.

Who, then, would readily dare to believe that this letter was sent by the man mentioned, as we have often said? Unless perhaps—something inappropriate to believe of so great a bishop—we must suppose that, after being corrupted by the aforementioned Dioscorus, he wrote these things against his own judgment, and so forth.

3. In what follows he speaks at length, and unnecessarily, about the books of a certain Faustus, bishop of Gaul, and so forth.

Nevertheless, because at the end of this letter he testifies that the Roman Church receives the books which blessed Bishop Augustine wrote to Hilary and Prosper, and asserts that from those books it can be sufficiently learned what that Church holds and preserves concerning the grace of God and free human choice, I have thought it appropriate—omitting what is shown to have been set out superfluously and at length [Col. 1779] in that letter itself—to extract certain definite chapters both from Faustus and from the aforementioned books of the same holy Augustine and insert them into this little work of ours. Thus, when they are placed side by side briefly and found to contradict one another, it will become plainly evident that Faustus’s books are heretical. In this way all who have hitherto defended them as Catholic will be confounded; their chief leader and author is Possessor, the African bishop, and so forth.

# SYNODAL LETTER OF THE AFRICAN BISHOPS EXILED IN SARDINIA TO JOHN, VENERIUS, AND OTHERS [Note: [Col. 1779] Written in the year of Christ 523.] CONCERNING THE GRACE OF GOD AND HUMAN FREE CHOICE (C)

To the holy brothers greatly worthy of affection by the grace of God, John the presbyter and archimandrite [Note: [Col. 1779] John the archimandrite is, as is thought, the same person as the abbot Maxentius, whose short works are presented above among the Excerpts, col. 1778.], Venerius the deacon, and the faithful men whose subscription is contained in your letter, Datianus, Fortunatus, Boethus, Victor, Scholasticus, Orontius, Vindicianus, Victor, Januarius, Victorianus, Photinus, Quodvultdeus, servants of Christ: greetings in the Lord.

## CHAPTER I

1. Just as the members of the ecclesiastical body are held together in the unity of faith by the bond of charity through Christ’s grace, so it is necessary that the members be concerned for one another, so that, once the disease of any perverse doctrine has been driven away, unceasing and indefatigable attention may be devoted both in speech and in prayer not only to preserving health but also to restoring it.

For in this way it comes about that, while concern for fraternal purity keeps watch, the Holy Spirit himself—through whom the love of God has been poured into our hearts—works all things together for good in those who love God and their neighbor in God.

For just as we receive love itself as a gift of spiritual grace, so, while we are concerned for our brothers, we demonstrate not only that divine grace is present within us [Note: [Col. 1779] In the manuscripts: “that the grace of divine reading is present within us.”], but also that, the more generously the purity of charity is exercised by us, the more abundantly the grace of divine recompense increases for us.

## CHAPTER II

2. We have therefore received the letter of Your Charity, which partly relieved and partly saddened our exile [Note: [Col. 1779] They received the letter of John and Venerius while in exile, but they did not give this response to them until after the exile had ended. For in chapter 18 they praise three books On the Truth of Predestination and Grace, which Fulgentius, as is read in his Life, chapter 29, “composed after he had already returned from exile.” Hilderic, who succeeded King Thrasamund, who died on May 28 in the year of Christ 523, immediately arranged for their recall from exile: “For he,” as Gregory of Tours writes, “bound by an oath imposed by his predecessor Thrasamund not to open churches or restore privileges to Catholics in his kingdom, before he became king, lest he transgress the terms of the oath, ordered both the Catholic priests to return from exile and the churches to be opened.”].

For we rejoice because you hold a correct view of the grace of God, by whose gift free choice of the human mind is enlightened and by whose assistance it is governed. But we are affected by a certain cloud of sorrow because you have indicated that certain brothers, in the question of the grace of God and human free choice, do not follow the straight path of Catholic faith but wish to raise the freedom of human choice against the grace of God.

First of all, dearest brothers, you ought to recognize—and we do not doubt that you have recognized it—that these things have been permitted by divine providence so that through them the power of divine grace may be understood by a clearer demonstration.

For grace itself is in no way recognized unless it is given. As long as it is not in a human being, that person must necessarily oppose it either in speech or in conduct. He opposes the grace of God in speech when he holds a view contrary to Christian faith; he opposes it in conduct when he does not maintain the rule of Christian life in his behavior.

For this is what grace, divinely given, accomplishes in a human being: once the mind has received the gift of faith and charity, it both speaks a good word and devotes itself earnestly to good action.

That these things are divinely given to the faithful the blessed Apostle both demonstrates and requests, saying: “But our Lord Jesus Christ himself, and God our Father, who loved us and gave us eternal consolation and good hope through grace, may encourage your hearts and strengthen you in every good work and word” (II Thess. II, 15–16).

## CHAPTER III

3. All grace for good speech and action therefore comes to us from God; from him it is also clear that sufficient power for good thought itself is granted to us, so that a human being may learn to glory not in himself but in the Lord.

For the blessed Apostle attributed a good thought of a human being to divine grace when he said: “Such confidence we have through Christ toward God—not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think anything as though from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God” (II Cor. III, 4–5).

## CHAPTER IV

4. Therefore, even if some who do not yet possess grace do not understand that they do not possess it, those who have received grace from God ought all the more to be firm in asserting that grace, precisely because they see that it is not bestowed on everyone.

It is necessary that grace be unknown to those to whom it is not given and recognized by those to whom it is granted through divine generosity.

For the Apostle testifies that the gifts of the Holy Spirit are recognized through the reception of the same Holy Spirit. Therefore he says:

“We have not received the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God, so that we may know the things given to us by God. These things we also speak, not in words taught by human wisdom but in the teaching of the Spirit, comparing spiritual things with spiritual things.

“But the natural person does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God; for they are foolishness to him, and he cannot understand them, because they are spiritually discerned. The spiritual person judges all things, but he himself is judged by no one” (I Cor. II, 12–15).

Through the Holy Spirit, therefore, we receive grace; and when that Spirit has been received, it comes about within us that we know what we have received.

## CHAPTER V

5. Therefore, dearest brothers, both the needy poverty of human free choice and the unfailing generosity of divine grace must be known and confessed in the true faith’s proper course.

“For what do you have,” says the Apostle, “that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (I Cor. IV, 7).

Before the generosity of grace, there is indeed free choice in a human being, but it is not good because it has not been enlightened. Therefore, unless grace is given, the good form of free choice is not possessed.

For human free choice without the gift of grace is like an eye without light. The eye was made for seeing, but unless it receives light, it will not see.

That light, however, is the true light that enlightens every human being coming into this world (John I, 9). It enlightens a human being by giving itself through grace.

Therefore, just as the eye of the body always needs to receive light in order to be able to look upon the light itself, so no knowledge can assist the free choice of a human being unless the infusion of spiritual grace itself is given.

Accordingly, so that we may make clear what the truth of Catholic doctrine contains concerning the matters you have included in your letter, we have thought it appropriate to define each point briefly, following the gift of that same grace, which grace itself has deigned to infuse into the hearts and tongues of the holy Fathers so that they might speak of it.

## CHAPTER VI

6. You said that, when you maintain that, although Esau and Jacob had not yet been born, Jacob was chosen by gratuitous mercy, while Esau, held under original sin, was hated by the just judgment of God (Rom. IX, 11–13), they, on the contrary, say that Esau represents the people of the Jews, condemned on account of future evil works, while Jacob represents the people of the Gentiles, saved on account of future good works.

It is good that you join these two propositions, which each side advances, in Catholic agreement. For in this way God’s grace is appropriately recognized by them, while the prophetic mystery is not denied by you.

In those two brothers the representation of two peoples is rightly understood, especially since, when Rebecca herself consulted the Lord, two peoples were foretold who would be separated from her womb (Gen. XXV, 22–23).

Nevertheless, both gratuitous goodness and just severity must be recognized in this distinction. Since every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights (James I, 17), and since all who are saved are distinguished by grace, it is clear that human works were neither chosen nor loved in Jacob, but divine gifts.

Again, since our iniquity commends God’s justice (Rom. III, 5), beyond doubt the wickedness of human iniquity was condemned in Esau.

In Jacob God demonstrated the gratuitous benefit of his mercy, in that grace freely deigned to adopt him. He did not choose him on account of the merits of any future good work, although he foreknew that he would give him himself, faith, and good works.

That is why the blessed Apostle says to the seed of Abraham, whose figure had gone before in Jacob: “You have been saved by grace through faith.” To show that faith is not given on account of some good merits, but that every good merit begins with the gift of faith itself, and that faith itself is the gift of God, he continued: “And this is not from yourselves; it is the gift of God.”

And lest anyone dare claim for himself the merit of any good works, or suppose that he received faith on account of whatever works, he added: “Not from works, so that no one may boast.”

To show, however, that not only faith but also good works are divinely bestowed, he immediately added: “For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works.” He testifies that these works were not only given by God but also prepared by him, saying: “which God prepared beforehand, so that we might walk in them” (Eph. II, 8–10).

Thus Jacob was saved by grace through faith, and by grace he obtained the capacity for good works.

## CHAPTER VII

7.
