Therefore, since it is certain that Esau was a vessel of wrath and Jacob a vessel of mercy, it must be held with absolute certainty that Esau justly deserved wrath in order to be condemned—for God is not unjust when he inflicts wrath—whereas Jacob received, freely, the gift of preceding mercy in order to be saved.

Jacob, therefore, justified freely by the grace of God, became a vessel of mercy through undeserved grace, and by that same grace was mercifully prepared for glory. Esau, however, was justly prepared for punishment through just wrath. “Our iniquity commends God’s justice” (Rom. III, 5).

Thus in Jacob God displays the mercy of gratuitous goodness, while in Esau he displays the judgment of just severity.

Esau, having received the sacrament of circumcision on the eighth day according to the ordinance of the divine constitution (Gen. XVII, 12), was free from the guilt of original sin; yet through the wickedness of his heart he remained in the oldness of the earthly human being, abandoned there by the judgment of him who saves freely and condemns justly.

In his person are signified not only those who deny the faith but also those who, remaining within the Church until the end of their lives, persevere in evil works. Of them the Apostle says: “Those who do such things will not inherit the kingdom of God” (Gal. V, 21).

For just as that circumcised man perished because he loved darkness more than light (John III, 19), so everyone who does not put off the old human being, who is being corrupted according to the desires of error (Eph. IV, 22), will be condemned in the judgment, because he did not use the sacrament of Baptism worthily.

For the old human being includes not only those who are ignorant of God but also those of whom the Apostle says: “They profess to know God, but by their deeds they deny him” (Tit. I, 16).

## CHAPTER VIII

8. Concerning little children, the rule of Catholic truth must be held without hesitation: the little child who is baptized is saved by the gratuitous goodness of God, while the one who dies without Baptism is condemned on account of original sin.

Nor should one say that one who died without the grace of justification and was assigned to the company of the impious was, by some benefit of God, snatched away from future impiety. From that impiety, whether one is a child or of more mature age, each person is rescued by one remedy alone: if he is redeemed by the blood of Christ.

## CHAPTER IX

[Col. 1782]

9. Whoever thinks that grace is given to all human beings does not have a worthy understanding of grace, since not only is faith not possessed by everyone (II Thess. III, 2), but certain nations are still found to which the preaching of faith has not reached.

The blessed Apostle says: “How then will they call upon him in whom they have not believed? Or how will they believe him whom they have not heard? And how will they hear without someone preaching?” (Rom. X, 14).

Grace therefore is not given to everyone, since those who are not believers cannot share in grace itself, nor can those believe to whom the hearing of faith is found not to have reached at all.

The grace itself, however, is not given equally to all to whom it is given, but according to the measure of Christ’s gift (Eph. IV, 7), and to each as God has allotted the measure of faith (Rom. XII, 3). He does not accept the persons of human beings, but one and the same Spirit accomplishes everything, distributing his own gifts to each as he wills (I Cor. XII, 11).

## CHAPTER X

10. As for your statement that a human being is saved by the mercy of God alone, while they say that unless a person cooperates with his own will and labors, he cannot be saved: both positions are rightly maintained if the proper order of divine mercy and human will is preserved—so that the former goes before and the latter follows; so that the mercy of God alone bestows the beginning of salvation, and afterward the human will becomes a co-worker in its own salvation.

Thus God’s preceding mercy directs the course of the human will, while the obedient human will, with the same mercy following after it, runs according to its purpose toward the prize (I Cor. IX, 24).

Accordingly, when the human will runs and labors profitably, it should recognize that the running and labor are a gift from God’s mercy, and it should not be ungrateful for the mercy through which it receives the beginning of salvation, so that through that same mercy it may reach the full outcome of eternal salvation.

For the will is good when it is preceded by God’s gift, and it remains good when it is not deprived of God’s assistance.

Whoever thinks that grace is bestowed by God as though someone, having received suitable security, were giving money, is mistaken. For the Lord himself both grants the pledge of the Holy Spirit (II Cor. V, 5) to whomever he wishes and distributes his money, to be put out by the moneychangers, to the care and service of his servants, as he himself says in the Gospel (Matt. XXV, 27).

## CHAPTER XI
11. That apostolic statement—“Therefore he has mercy on whomever he wills, and he hardens whomever he wills”—is better understood as spoken in the person of one who confirms this; but if anyone does not wish to take it as spoken in the person of one who confirms it, let him attend without controversy to what follows: “Or does the potter not have authority over the clay, to make from the same lump one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?” (Romans 9:18, 21). Since, in making both vessels, the potter’s authority is acknowledged, let him understand in the vessel of honor the undeserved grace of the merciful God, and in the vessel of dishonor let him recognize the deserved judgment of God who hardens—that is, abandons. God is said to harden not because he compels anyone to wickedness, but because he does not rescue someone from wickedness; and, because he is just, he does this justly. Thus, when God shows mercy, a person is saved without his own merits; but when God hardens, he justly receives what he deserves. For God saves by the gift of his goodness and hardens by the judgment of his severity.

## CHAPTER XII

12. You also say, “For it is God who works in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure”; but they say, “If you are willing and listen to me, you shall eat the good things of the land” (Isaiah 1:19). If the mind, tranquil in faith, receives both statements as it ought, no question concerning God’s grace and human free choice will remain. God commands a person to will, but God also works in the person to will; he commands him to act, but he also works in him to act. Therefore blessed Paul joins both together, saying: “Work out your salvation with fear and trembling; for it is God who works in you both to will and to accomplish, for his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:12–13). Thus, for each person to work out his salvation with fear and trembling is the work of a willing human being; but the Lord himself works this in his own people. And so, because a human being possesses free choice, he hears commandments that he is to carry out; yet free choice is in no way made capable of fulfilling the commandments unless it is divinely assisted. In this way a person recognizes, when he receives the commandment, that he ought to act; and he knows that he always owes to God every good thing that he wills and does. For, as the Apostle testifies, he recognizes that God works in a person “both to will and to accomplish, for his good pleasure.” Through the Prophet, God has deigned to promise this grace to his faithful, saying: “I will put my Spirit within you, and I will make you walk in my statutes and observe and carry out my judgments” (Ezekiel 36:27).

When God therefore begins to work in a person the will to act, the person is converted to God; and, with God working in him, he acts in a way pleasing to God. For the Apostle says of God: “May he fit you for every good work [Note: Several manuscripts read, “for every good work,” in accordance with the Greek], so that you may do his will, accomplishing in you what is pleasing in his sight” (Hebrews 13:21). A person can stretch out his hand toward life only to the extent that he has the Lord as his protection over his right hand (Psalm 120:5).

## CHAPTER XIII

13. It is exceedingly absurd to suppose that those who possess either secular or ecclesiastical rank are vessels of mercy, while clerics, monks, and laypeople are vessels of dishonor. The Apostle plainly calls those vessels of mercy “which God prepared for glory” (Romans 9:23)—not, of course, present glory but future glory. To them he says: “When Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory.” Therefore, a little earlier, he says to them: “Set your minds on things above, not on things on earth” (Colossians 3:4, 2). The vessels of mercy are those to whom it is said: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom”; whereas the vessels of dishonor are those to whom it is said: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25:34, 41). Vessels of mercy are therefore made not by ecclesiastical or secular rank, but by spiritual charity in the Church. Accordingly, whatever profession a person may hold, if he possesses the faith that works through charity (Galatians 5:6), he will be a vessel sanctified for honor, useful to the Lord, and prepared for every good work (2 Timothy 2:21).

## CHAPTER XIV

14. To enter into or maintain a dispute against the predestination of the saints is the height of obstinacy, since no one dares oppose apostolic preaching. It says not only of God: “Those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son” (Romans 8:29); and elsewhere: “He predestined us for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ unto himself” (Ephesians 1:5); but blessed Paul also confidently proclaims that our very Head, the firstborn among many brothers (Romans 8:29), was predestined, saying: “He was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh, and predestined to be the Son of God in power, according to the Spirit of sanctification” (Romans 1:3–4). Whoever therefore denies that Christ and his saints were predestined perversely attacks the apostolic faith.

All the predestined are those whom God wills to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Timothy 2:4). They are called “all” because people of every kind, rank, age, and condition, of both sexes, are saved. For the will of almighty God is always fulfilled, since his power is in no way overcome. He is the one who “does whatever he wills in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the depths” (Psalm 135:6), and no one resists his will (Romans 9:19).

It is true what the Son testified about himself: “He gives life to whom he wills” (John 5:21). In giving life, he does not await any beginning from human will; rather, by making the will good, he gives life to the will itself. This applies to adults. But as for little children, in whom a good will cannot yet be formed, he brings about their salvation by the operation of grace alone.

## CHAPTER XV

15. Free choice, which was sound in the first human being before sin, is now indeed shaken in the children of God by its own weakness, but it is raised up by the greater grace of the divine gift.

## CHAPTER XVI

16. We ought either to leave the question of the origin of souls unspoken or to discuss it without controversy. Whether souls come through propagation or are newly created for individual bodies, since the authority of the holy Scriptures does not state the matter plainly, it must be investigated cautiously—especially since the faithful can remain ignorant of it without harm to the faith. This, above all, must be observed and held: the souls of newborn children are bound by the chain of original sin, and the sacrament of holy Baptism is necessary for all. Through it the bond of original sin is broken, and the adoption of sons, lost in the first human being, is received through the second human being.

## CHAPTER XVII

17. Therefore, beloved brothers, stand firm and immovable through the grace of God. Holding the true faith, show charity toward brothers who think otherwise, and despair of no one; for one who today does not acknowledge the truth in some matter may tomorrow come to know it when God reveals it. Power belongs to God to act whenever he wills (Wisdom 12:18). Let us therefore pray for them, that God may work in them. Let us show them good will, for which we may receive a reward, knowing that in God’s sight whoever belongs to the number of the predestined will not perish. The will of the Almighty will be fulfilled in everything, so that they may be saved by grace and, with God enlightening them, receive the knowledge of the truth.

Above all, make every effort to place before the brothers mentioned above for reading the books that Saint Augustine wrote to Prosper and Hilary. The glorious bishop of the apostolic See, Hormisdas, of blessed memory, also inserted mention of these works, with high praise of Catholic teaching, in the letter he sent in reply to our holy brother and fellow priest Possessor, who had consulted him. His words are these:

> “As for free choice and the grace of God, what the Roman—that is, the Catholic—Church follows and preserves can certainly be abundantly recognized in the various books of blessed Augustine, and especially in those addressed to Prosper and Hilary; nevertheless, explicit chapters are also contained in the ecclesiastical archives.”

## CHAPTER XVIII

18. These matters, beloved brothers, we have wished to answer briefly in a common reply to your questions. Moreover, one of us [Note: Namely Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe, who began the work entitled “On the Truth of Predestination and the Grace of God” with these words: “I give thanks to God, holy brothers, the presbyter John and the deacon Venerius, through whose assistance you are such men that you contend with great spirit and fervor for the grace by which we are saved”], insofar as the Lord deigns to grant his servants the grace of sound speech, has answered with sufficient argument, in three books dedicated in your name, everything that you reported those brothers as thinking or saying against grace and predestination. Against the two books of Faustus of Gaul he also published seven books [Note: This work of Fulgentius against Faustus is greatly praised by the author of his Life, chapter 28, who says that he labored more to explain Faustus than to refute him. “For,” he says, “to explain his obscure statements was to refute the arguments of a madman.” He adds immediately: “Clearly, the great labor of this work quickly received its due reward: for as soon as his dictation was completed, the chain of his very long captivity was immediately broken”]. When you have reviewed these works, you will immediately recognize how the discussion exposed Faustus’s notions as contrary to the truth and utterly hostile to the Catholic faith, how clear reasoning convicted them, divine authority suppressed them, and the harmonious testimony of the preceding Fathers completely refuted them.

We hope in the Lord that he will so generously provide the assistance of his grace that he will grant increase to those who think rightly [Note: Some manuscripts read, “grant increase of holy knowledge”] and give those who believe otherwise than they ought the help of recognizing the truth [Note: Another version reads, “the insight”]. For he makes those whom he predestined for life participants in his grace, so that in all their good works they subject the choice of the human will to the grace of God and recognize that every good gift and every perfect gift comes down to them from him (James 1:17). They should also know that help must always be expected from him, since he grants both grace and perseverance to his predestined, so that they may receive the gift of eternal life as grace for grace (John 1:16).

# THE SECOND COUNCIL OF ORANGE: ON GRACE AND FREE CHOICE

[Note: In an old manuscript from Lyon the title is: “Constitution of the Bishops in the City of Orange, on Grace and Free Choice.”]

Held at the dedication of the basilica constructed by the patrician Liberius, on the fifth day before the Nones of July, during the consulship of Decius the Younger, a man of illustrious rank—that is, in the year of Christ 529, in the third year of Pope Felix IV.

## PREFACE

When, with God’s favor and at his invitation, we had gathered for the dedication of the basilica which our son, the most illustrious prefect and patrician Liberius, had constructed in the most faithful city of Orange, and a spiritual discussion had arisen among us concerning matters pertaining to ecclesiastical discipline, it came to our attention that there were some who, through simplicity and insufficient caution, wished to think about grace and free choice otherwise than according to the rule of the Catholic faith.

Therefore, in accordance with the authority and admonition of the apostolic See, it seemed just and reasonable to us that we should present for observance by all, and sign with our own hands, a few chapters transmitted to us by the apostolic See. These chapters had been compiled by the ancient Fathers from the volumes of the holy Scriptures, especially with reference to this matter, in order to instruct those who think otherwise than they ought. When these chapters have been read, anyone who until now has not believed about grace and free choice as he ought should not delay inclining his mind toward what agrees with the Catholic faith.

## That through Adam’s sin not only the body but also the soul was harmed

[Note: See Book 2, *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, chapter 34.]

**I.** If anyone says that through Adam’s transgression the human being was not wholly changed for the worse—that is, in both body and soul—but believes that only the body was made subject to corruption while the soul’s freedom remained unharmed, he is deceived by the error of Pelagius and contradicts Scripture, which says: “The soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezekiel 18:20); and: “Do you not know that to whomever you present yourselves as slaves for obedience, you are slaves of the one whom you obey?” (Romans 6:16); and: “By whatever anyone is overcome, to that he is enslaved” (2 Peter 2:19).

## That Adam’s sin harmed not only him but also passed to his descendants

[Note: From Book 4, *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, chapter 4.]

**II.** If anyone asserts that Adam’s transgression harmed Adam alone and not also his descendants, or testifies that only bodily death—which is the punishment of sin, but not sin itself, which is the death of the soul—passed through one human being to the whole human race, he does an injustice to God and contradicts the Apostle, who says: “Through one human being sin entered the world, and through sin death; and so death passed to all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Romans 5:12).

## That God’s grace is not given in response to invocation, but itself causes invocation

**III.** If anyone says that God’s grace can be conferred in response to human invocation, but does not acknowledge that grace itself causes us to invoke God, he contradicts the prophet Isaiah—or the Apostle, who says the same thing: “I was found by those who were not seeking me; I openly appeared to those who were not asking for me” (Isaiah 65:1; Romans 10:20).

## That God does not wait for our will in order to cleanse us from sin, but prepares it

**IV.** If anyone maintains that, in order for us to be cleansed from sin, God waits for our will, but does not confess that, through the infusion and operation of the Holy Spirit in us, he also brings it about that we wish to be cleansed, he resists the Holy Spirit, who says through Solomon: “The will is prepared by the Lord” (Proverbs 8:35, according to the Septuagint), and against the Apostle’s salutary proclamation: “It is God who works in you both to will and to accomplish, for his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:13).

## That the beginning of faith is not from ourselves but from God’s grace

[Note: See *On the Predestination of the Saints*, from chapter 1 through chapter 9.]

**V.** If anyone says that not only the growth but also the beginning of faith, and the very inclination to believe by which we believe in him who justifies the ungodly and proceed to the regeneration of holy Baptism, is naturally present in us—not through the gift of grace, that is, through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit correcting our will from unbelief to faith and from ungodliness to godliness—he is shown to be an adversary of apostolic teaching. Blessed Paul says: “We are confident that he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion until the day of our Lord Jesus Christ”; and: “To you it has been given for Christ, not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him” (Philippians 1:6, 29); and: “You have been saved by grace through faith, and this is not from yourselves; it is the gift of God” (Ephesians 2:8).

For those who say that the faith by which we believe in God is natural thereby define, in a certain sense, all who are alienated from the Church of Christ as believers.

## That mercy is not conferred on believers and petitioners without God’s grace, since grace itself causes us to believe and petition

[Note: See *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 23, and Prosper, *Against the Collator*, chapter 6.]

**VI.** If anyone says that divine mercy is conferred on us without God’s grace when we believe, will, desire, strive, labor, keep watch, apply ourselves, petition, seek, and knock, but does not confess that through the infusion and inspiration of the Holy Spirit in us we are enabled to believe, will, or perform all these things as we ought; and if he subordinates the assistance of grace to human humility or obedience, refusing to acknowledge that it is the gift of grace itself that makes us obedient and humble, he resists the Apostle, who says: “What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Corinthians 4:7); and: “By the grace of God I am what I am” (1 Corinthians 15:10).

## That by the powers of nature we cannot think or choose any good thing pertaining to salvation without grace

[Note: See *On the Grace of Christ*, chapter 26.]

**VII.** If anyone affirms that by the vigor of nature he can think as he ought of some good thing pertaining to eternal life, or choose it, or consent to salvation—that is, to the preaching of the Gospel—without the illumination and inspiration of the Holy Spirit, who gives everyone sweetness in consenting to and believing the truth, he is deceived by a heretical spirit. He does not understand the voice of God saying in the Gospel: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5); or the Apostle’s statement: “Not that we are capable of thinking anything from ourselves, as though from ourselves; rather, our sufficiency is from God” (2 Corinthians 3:5).

## That no one can attain the grace of Baptism through free choice

[Note: Prosper, *Against the Collator*, chapters 13 and 38, and *Response to Cassian’s Definition 6*.]

**VIII.** If anyone contends that some can come to the grace of Baptism through mercy, but others through free choice—which is plainly corrupted in all who are born from the transgression of the first human being—he is shown to be alien to the true faith. For he either does not assert that everyone’s free choice was weakened by the sin of the first human being, or he thinks it was harmed in such a way that some are nevertheless able, without God’s revelation, to seek out the mystery of eternal salvation by themselves. How contrary this is, the Lord himself proves, for he testifies that no one—not merely some people—can come to him unless the Father draws him (John 6:44). Likewise he says to Peter: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 16:17). And the Apostle says: “No one can say, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ except in the Holy Spirit” (1 Corinthians 12:3).

## On God’s assistance, through which we do good works

[Note: Prosper, *Sentences* 22.]

**IX.** It is a divine gift when we think rightly and restrain our feet from falsehood and injustice. Whenever we do good things, God works in us and with us so that we may act (Philippians 2:13).

## On always imploring God’s assistance

[Note: Prosper, *Against the Collator*, chapter 24.]

**X.** God’s assistance must always be implored even by those who have been reborn and are holy, so that they may reach a good end or persevere in a good work.

## On the obligation of vows

[Note: From Book 17 of *The City of God*, chapter 4, and Prosper’s *Sentences* 54.]

**XI.** No one would rightly make a vow to the Lord unless he received from him what he vowed, as it is written: “What we have received from your hand, we give to you” (1 Chronicles 29:14).

## What kind of people God loves

[Note: Prosper’s *Sentences* 56.]

**XII.** God loves us as we are going to be by his gift, not as we are by our merit.

## On the restoration of free choice

[Note: Book 14 of *The City of God*, chapter 11, and Prosper’s *Sentences* 152.]

**XIII.** The choice of the will [Note: Some manuscripts read, “the choice of freedom”] that was weakened in the first human being cannot be restored except through the grace of Baptism. What was lost cannot be given back except by the one from whom it could have been given. Hence Truth himself says: “If the Son sets you free, then you will truly be free” (John 8:36).

## That, in order to be freed from misery, we must be preceded by God’s mercy

[Note: Prosper’s *Sentences* 211.]

**XIV.** No miserable person is freed from any misery except one whom God’s mercy precedes, as the Psalmist says: “May your mercy, O Lord, quickly come before us” (Psalm 78:8); and: “My God, his mercy will come before me” (Psalm 59:11).

## That through God’s grace the believer is changed for the better

[Note: From the sermon on the title of Psalm 68.]

**XV.** Adam was changed from what God had formed, but for the worse, through his iniquity. The believer is changed from what iniquity had brought about, but for the better, through God’s grace. The former change, therefore, was that of the first transgressor; the latter, according to the Psalmist, is “the change of the right hand of the Most High” (Psalm 77:11).

## That we must not glory in what we possess, since it comes from God

[Note: *On the Spirit and the Letter*, chapter 28, and Prosper’s *Sentences* 259.]

**XVI.** Let no one glory in what he appears to possess, as though he had not received it; nor let him think that he received it because the letter appeared outwardly either to be read or sounded forth to be heard. For, as the Apostle says: “If justification were through the law, then Christ died for nothing” (Galatians 2:21). But if he did not die for nothing, then, ascending on high, “he led captivity captive and gave gifts to human beings” (Ephesians 4:8). From him possesses whatever anyone possesses. But whoever denies that he possesses anything from him either truly does not possess it, or what he possesses will be taken away from him (Matthew 25:29).

## On Christian fortitude

[Note: Book 1 of the *Unfinished Work*, chapter 8, and Prosper’s *Sentences* 295.]

**XVII.** Worldly desire produces the fortitude of the Gentiles, but the fortitude of Christians is produced by the love of God, which has been poured into our hearts—not through the choice of the will that comes from us, but through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (Romans 5:5).

## Grace is preceded by no merits

[Note: Book 1 of the *Unfinished Work*, chapter 133, and Prosper’s *Sentences* 297.]

**XVIII.** A reward is owed to good works if they are performed; but grace, which is not owed, precedes them so that they may be performed.

## No one is saved except through God’s mercy

[Note: Augustine, Letter 186, no. 37, and Prosper’s *Sentences* 308.]

**XIX.** Even if human nature had remained in the integrity in which it was created, it could in no way preserve itself without the help of its Creator. Since, therefore, without God’s grace it cannot preserve the salvation it received, how can it, without God’s grace, restore what it lost?

## A human being can do no good without God

[Note: Book 2 of *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, chapter 8, and Prosper’s *Sentences* 312.]

**XX.** God does many good things in a human being that the human being does not do; but a human being does no good things that God does not grant him to do.

## On nature and grace

[Note: *On Grace and Free Choice*, chapter 13, and Prosper’s *Sentences* 315.]

**XXI.** Just as the Apostle says with complete truth to those who wished to be justified by the law and thereby fell away from grace, “If justification is through the law, then Christ died for nothing,” so it is said with complete truth to those who think that the grace which the faith of Christ commends and receives is nature: “If justification is through nature, then Christ died for nothing.” The law already existed, and it did not justify; nature also already existed, and it did not justify. Therefore Christ did not die for nothing: through him the law was to be fulfilled, for he said, “I have not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it” (Matthew 5:17); and nature, lost through Adam, was to be restored through him, who said that he had come “to seek and save what was lost” (Luke 19:10).

## On those things that belong to human beings

[Note: Treatise 5 on John, and Prosper’s *Sentences* 323.]

**XXII.** No one possesses anything of his own except falsehood and sin. But if a human being possesses any truth or justice, it comes from that fountain for which we ought to thirst in this wilderness, so that, sprinkled by it as though by drops, we may not fail along the way.

## On the will of God and the human will

[Note: Treatise 19 on John, and Prosper’s *Sentences* 336.]

**XXIII.** Human beings do their own will rather than God’s when they do what displeases God. But when they do what they will in such a way that they serve the divine will, although they willingly do what they do, it is nevertheless the will of the one by whom what they will is both prepared and commanded.

## On the branches of the vine

[Note: Treatise 81 on John, and Prosper’s *Sentences* 364.]

**XXIV.** The branches are in the vine in such a way that they contribute nothing to the vine, but receive from it the source of their life. The vine is in the branches in such a way that it supplies them with vital nourishment rather than receiving anything from them. Thus, for the disciples, both to have Christ abiding in them and to abide in Christ benefits the disciples, not Christ. For when a branch is cut off, another can sprout from the living root; but the branch that has been cut off cannot live without the root.

[Column 1789] ## On the love with which we love God

[Note: Treatise 102 on John, and Prosper’s *Sentences* 368.]

**XXV.** It is entirely God’s gift to love God. The one who, though not loved, loved us, gave himself in order to be loved. We were loved when we were displeasing, so that there might come to be in us something by which we could become pleasing. For the Spirit of the Father and the Son pours love into our hearts, and through this Spirit we love the Father and the Son.

Accordingly, in keeping with the statements of the holy Scriptures and the definitions of the ancient Fathers written above, we ought, with God’s favor, both to preach and to believe this: through the sin of the first human being, free choice was so inclined and weakened that afterward no one could love God as he ought, believe in God, or perform for God what is good, unless grace and divine mercy preceded him.

Therefore, we believe that the distinguished faith of righteous Abel, Noah, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and the entire multitude of the ancient saints—faith which the Apostle Paul praises in their honor—was bestowed not through the good of nature previously given in Adam, but through the grace of God. After the Lord’s coming also, we know and believe that this grace is conferred on all who desire to be baptized, not as something possessed through free choice, but as a gift bestowed by Christ’s generosity, in accordance with what has already been said above and what the Apostle Paul proclaims: “To you it has been given for Christ, not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him”; and: “God, who began a good work in you, will bring it to completion until the day of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Philippians 1:29, 6); and: “You have been saved by grace through faith, and this is not from yourselves; it is the gift of God” (Ephesians 2:8); and what the Apostle says about himself: “I received mercy so that I might be faithful” (1 Corinthians 7:25). He did not say, “Because I was faithful,” but “so that I might be faithful.” Also: “What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Corinthians 4:7); and: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (James 1:17); and: “No one possesses any good thing unless it has been given to him from above” (John 3:27).

There are innumerable testimonies of the holy Scriptures that could be offered to prove grace, but they have been omitted for the sake of brevity. For, in truth, whoever is not satisfied by a few things will not be helped by many.

We also believe, in accordance with the Catholic faith, that after receiving the grace of Baptism [Note: The Lyon manuscript reads, “after receiving Baptism’s grace”], all baptized persons, with Christ helping and cooperating, can—and, if they are willing to labor faithfully, ought to—fulfill what pertains to salvation. But we not only do not believe that some have been predestined by divine power for evil; if there are any who wish to believe so great an evil, we pronounce anathema upon them with complete abhorrence.

We also salutarily profess and believe this: in every good work, we do not begin and afterward receive help through God’s mercy; rather, he himself, without any preceding good merits of ours, first inspires in us both faith and love of himself, so that we may faithfully seek the sacraments of Baptism and, after Baptism, with his help, fulfill what pleases him.

Therefore it must be believed most clearly that the remarkable faith of the criminal whom the Lord restored to the homeland of paradise, of the centurion Cornelius to whom the Lord’s angel was sent, and of Zacchaeus, who was deemed worthy to receive the Lord himself, did not come from nature but was a gift of divine generosity [Note: The same manuscript reads, “but was given by the generosity of grace.” The manuscripts of Reims and Beauvais read, “but from the gift of divine generosity”] [Note: Against Cassian. Compare below Prosper’s *Against the Collator*, chapter 7, column 1809].

And because we desire and wish that the definition of the ancient Fathers and our own definition, written above, should be a remedy not only for religious persons but also for laypeople, it pleased us that the illustrious and magnificent men who had gathered with us for the aforementioned festival should also sign it with their own hands.

CAESARIUS, bishop, in the name of Christ: I have reread our constitution and, subscribing below, have signed it, on the fifth day before the Nones of July, during the consulship of Decius the Younger, a man of illustrious rank.

JULIANUS AMARTOLUS, bishop: I have reread it and signed it.

CONSTANTIUS, bishop, in the name of Christ: I have agreed and signed.

CYPRIANUS, [lacuna], bishop, [lacuna], have signed.

EUCHERIUS, [lacuna], bishop, [lacuna], have signed.

EUCHERIUS, likewise, [lacuna], bishop, [lacuna], have signed.

HERACLIUS, [lacuna], bishop, [lacuna], have signed.

PRINCIPIUS, [lacuna], bishop, [lacuna], have signed.

PHILAGRIUS, [lacuna], bishop, [lacuna], have signed.

MAXIMUS, [lacuna], bishop, [lacuna], have signed.

ALETHIUS, [lacuna], bishop, [lacuna], have signed.

VINDEMIALIS, [lacuna], bishop, [lacuna], have signed.

# LETTER OF POPE BONIFACE II TO CAESARIUS OF ARLES, BY WHOSE REQUEST HE CONFIRMS WHAT WAS DEFINED AT THE SECOND SYNOD OF ORANGE

[Note: In the Fossatensis and Laon manuscripts used by Jacobus Sirmondus, this letter was placed before the Council of Orange. The letter was prefaced by the following note: “This manuscript contains the Synod of Orange, which holy Pope Boniface confirmed by his authority. Therefore, whoever believes otherwise about grace and free choice than what either this authority contains or what was established in that synod should recognize that he is opposed to the apostolic See and to the universal Church throughout the whole world.”] (C)

To his most beloved brother CAESARIUS, BONIFACE.

**1.** Through our son Armenius, presbyter and abbot, we received a letter from Your Fraternity, which you had sent to us in the charity by which we are bound in God. In it you believed that you should ask that what you had requested from our predecessor, Pope Felix of blessed memory, for the security of the Catholic faith might be explained through my intervention.

But since divine will ordained that what you had hoped to obtain from him through us should instead be obtained from us by you, we did not delay giving a Catholic response to your petition, which you conceived out of praiseworthy concern for the faith.

You indicate that certain bishops of Gaul, although they have already agreed that all other good things proceed from God’s grace, wish to say that faith alone—the faith by which we believe in Christ—is of nature and not of grace; and that it remained in human beings from Adam by free choice—which it is impious to say—and is not now also conferred on each person through the generosity of divine mercy.

You therefore ask that, to remove ambiguity, we confirm by the authority of the apostolic See your confession, by which you, in opposition to them, define according to Catholic truth that right faith in Christ and the beginning of every good will are inspired in the mind of each person through the prevenient grace of God.

## 2.

And therefore, since many Fathers, and above all Augustine, bishop of blessed memory, as well as our predecessors, the bishops of the Apostolic See, are demonstrably known to have discussed this matter at such length and with such reason that no ambiguity ought any longer to remain for anyone—that faith itself also comes to us from grace—we judged that a lengthy response was unnecessary. Especially since, according to the passages from the Apostle that you sent, in which he says, “I obtained mercy in order that I might be faithful” (1 Cor. 7:25), and elsewhere, “To you it has been granted for Christ’s sake not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him” (Phil. 1:29), it is plainly evident that the faith by which we believe in Christ, just as all good things, comes to each individual from the gift of heavenly grace, not from the power of human nature.

We rejoice that your Fraternity too, after conferring with certain priests of Gaul, has understood this in accordance with the catholic faith—namely, in those matters in which, as you indicated, they unanimously defined that the faith by which we believe in Christ is bestowed through the preceding grace of the Godhead. They also added that there is absolutely no good thing according to God which anyone can either will, begin, or complete without God’s grace, as our Savior himself says: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5).

For it is certain and catholic that, in all good things—of which faith is the chief—divine mercy precedes us even when we do not will it, so that we may persevere in faith, as the prophet David says: “My God, his mercy shall go before me” (Ps. 58:11); and again, “My mercy is with him” (Ps. 88:25); and elsewhere, “His mercy follows me” (Ps. 22:6). Likewise blessed Paul says: “Or who has first given to him, and it shall be repaid to him? For from him, and through him, and in him are all things” (Rom. 11:35–36).

Thus we are exceedingly astonished that those who hold the contrary view are still so weighed down by the remnants of an ancient error that they do not believe one comes to Christ by God’s gift but by nature; and that they say the good of that very nature—which is known to have been corrupted by Adam’s sin—is more the author of our faith than Christ. They do not understand that they are contradicting the Lord’s declaration: “No one comes to me unless it has been given to him by my Father” (John 6:44); and that they are likewise resisting blessed Paul, who cries out to the Hebrews: “Let us run with perseverance the contest set before us, looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith” (Heb. 12:1–2).

Since this is so, we cannot discover what they assign to the human will, without God’s grace, as contributing to belief in Christ, when Christ is the author and perfecter of faith.

## 3.

Therefore, greeting you with fitting affection, we approve the confession written above as agreeing with the catholic rules of the Fathers. But those who, as you indicate, wish to attribute everything else to grace while placing faith first, we constrain by their own profession to ascribe faith even more to the gift of grace, apart from which no one can perform any good thing according to God, as the blessed Apostle says: “Whatever is not from faith is sin” (Rom. 14:23).

Since this is so, either they will attribute no good thing to grace if they attempt to remove faith from it; or, if they say that something is good because it comes from grace, then faith itself must necessarily be attributed to grace. For if there is no good thing without faith, while they deny that faith itself comes from grace, then—God forbid—no good thing will be attributable to grace.

The Apostle James says: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights” (Jas. 1:17). And they themselves admit, as you say, that the other gifts are bestowed through grace; yet they do not hesitate to affirm that those good things subsist through faith itself. Therefore faith as a whole must necessarily be attributed to grace, since they cannot separate from it the good which they attribute to grace.

## 4.

Having briefly established these points, we did not think it necessary to respond to the remaining absurdities of Pelagian error which that letter appears to contain—the letter that you instructed a certain priest to send to you. For we hope in the divine mercy that, through the ministry and teaching of your Fraternity, he will deign to work in the hearts of all those whom you said dissent, so that from this point onward they may believe that every good will proceeds not from themselves but from divine grace, when they find themselves already willing to defend what they had stubbornly attempted to oppose.

For it is written: “The will is prepared by the Lord” (Prov. 8:35, according to the Septuagint); and elsewhere: “I knew that I could not be continent unless God gave it; and this itself was wisdom, to know whose gift it was” (Wis. 8:21).

May God preserve you safe and sound, dearest brother.

Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of February, in the consulship of the most illustrious men Lampadius and Orestes.

[Note: January 25, in the year of Christ 530.]

## Cyprian, *On the Life of Caesarius*, Book 1, no. 35 (C,S)

Many indeed arose as rivals to resist his teaching concerning grace. But what happiness worthy of emulation! For, through the whispers and malicious interpretation of certain people, a groundless sinister suspicion arose in the regions of Gaul against the preaching of the man of God.

For this reason the bishops of Christ residing beyond the Isère, gathered together by the love of charity, assembled in the city of Valence. Blessed Caesarius himself, however, was unable to hasten there as he had arranged, because of his customary illness. Nevertheless, he sent distinguished men from among the bishops, together with priests and deacons.

Among them the holy Cyprian, bishop of Toulon, distinguished and renowned, shone forth. He supported everything he said with the divine Scriptures and demonstrated it from the ancient institutions of the Fathers: no one can seize for himself any advancement in divine matters unless he has first been called by the preceding grace of God.

But while they sought to establish their own righteousness, they were not subject to the righteousness of God, failing to remember that the Lord had said, “Without me you can do nothing,” and, “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John 15:5, 16); and, “No one has anything unless it has been given to him from above” (John 3:27); and the Apostle Paul: “By the grace of God I am what I am” (1 Cor. 15:10); and another passage: “Every excellent gift is from above” (Jas. 1:17); and the prophet: “The Lord will give grace and glory” (Ps. 83:12).

And a person will truly recover free will when he has been redeemed by Christ’s liberation, under which release he can attain the effect of perfection. To their arguments the man of God gave a true and evident explanation derived from apostolic tradition.

For Pope Boniface of the Roman Church, of blessed memory, having learned of the same conflict, trampled down the contention of those who quarreled and confirmed the cause of holy Caesarius by apostolic authority. Thus, with Christ granting it, the bishops of the Churches gradually accepted what the devil had hoped would cease through sudden hostility.

# Third Part of the Appendix

## Prosper of Aquitaine’s Apologetic Works on Behalf of Augustine against the Unjust Reprovers of His Teaching concerning Grace and Predestination; and Also Prosper’s *Book of Sentences* from Augustine

## Letter of Prosper of Aquitaine to Rufinus concerning Grace and Free Will

[Note: Written while Augustine was alive, around the year of Christ 429.]

To my lord, brother most beloved in Christ and deservedly venerable Rufinus,

Prosper sends everlasting greetings.

[Note: We have collated this letter with the most ancient manuscript of the Abbey of Saint Remigius at Reims, which here reads *fratri* (“to my brother”) rather than the printed *Domino fratri* (“to my lord, brother”); at the end, however, it agrees with the printed editions in having *venerantissime mihi frater* (“my most venerable brother”).]

## Prologue

### 1.

Through a mutual friend I received signs of your fraternal concern for me, and I gladly recognized your care of the most sincere charity. And lest malicious rumors, insofar as they cannot keep themselves from your ears, bring you fear or anxiety, I have taken care, as far as the language of a letter permits, to free you from every scruple. I have endeavored to disclose everything to you with the fullest truth, so that, since you have not been able to hear in its entirety what is being spread by our opponents, you may through me learn whatever is said and repeated about us to arouse empty envy.

But first I must explain to Your Holiness the character of the question from which these things arise, so that the falsehood of the slanderers may become clearer to you and you may see what light they are attempting to cover with what darkness.

## Chapter I

### 2.

The Pelagian heresy—what doctrine it adopted in its attempt to destroy the catholic faith, and with what poisons of impiety it wished to occupy the inner parts of the Church and the very vital organs of Christ’s body—is too well known to require a narrative.

Among its teachings, however, there is one blasphemy, the most wicked and subtle offspring of the others: they say that God’s grace is given according to human merits. For when they first wished to assert such great health in human nature that, through free will alone, it could attain the kingdom of God—on the grounds that it was so fully assisted by the support of its own constitution that, naturally possessing rational understanding, it could easily choose the good and avoid the evil—and when, since the works of the will were free in either direction, they held that those who are evil lacked not the ability for good but only the desire for it; when, then, as I have said, they wished the whole of human righteousness to subsist upon natural uprightness and ability, and sound doctrine rejected this definition, they preserved among themselves the condemned position, subsequently disguised in many variations of heretical fraud, by professing that God’s grace was necessary for a human being to begin, advance, and persevere in the good.

## Chapter II

### 3.

But in this profession the grace of God revealed to the vessels of mercy how the vessels of wrath were attempting to insinuate themselves by deceit (Rom. 9:22–23). It was understood, and recognized with the greatest benefit, that they confess grace only in the sense that it is a teacher of free will and, through exhortations, the law, instruction, contemplation of creatures [Note: The printed editions read: “through the creature, through contemplation.”], miracles, and external terrors, displays itself [Note: The printed editions read “may display”; Morel has “may exhibit.” See *Elementa Critica*, p. 102. M.] to its judgment, so that each person, according to the movement of his will, may find if he seeks, receive if he asks, and enter if he knocks.

For, according to them, the calling of grace itself does this first in our regard: it prompts the decision of our own ability. Grace is nothing other than the law, the prophet, or the teacher, whose common and universal concern toward all human beings throughout the world is that those who wish may believe, and that those who believe may receive justification as a reward for faith and good will.

Thus God’s grace is given according to human merit, and in this way grace is no longer grace; for if it is paid in return for merits, and is not itself the creator of good things, it is called grace in vain.

## Chapter III

### 4.

When both the judgments of the Eastern bishops, the authority of the Apostolic See, and the vigilance of the African councils detected these tricks by which the sons of darkness wished to transform themselves into the likeness of the sons of light, blessed Augustine—certainly, in this age, a foremost portion of the Lord’s priests—also destroyed them abundantly and beautifully in many discussions contained in his books.

[Note: The Remigius manuscript reads: “He destroyed it in an abundant and beautiful discussion contained in many books.”]

Among the many gifts of God with which the Spirit of truth filled him in the greatest abundance, he also possessed this power of knowledge and wisdom arising from God’s love: not only to strike down this heresy, still gasping in the mutilated remnants of its own writings, but also to defeat many earlier heresies with the unconquered sword of the word.

Yet, amid so many palms of combat and so many crowns of triumph, while he shines forth for the illumination of the Church and the glory of Christ by whom he himself was enlightened, certain of our own people—something for which we must deeply grieve—slander him in secret but not unknown whispers. Whenever they find ears subject and receptive to them, they defame his writings against Pelagian error, saying that he entirely removes free will and preaches a fatal necessity under the name of grace.

They add that he wishes two masses of the human race, and two natures, to be believed, so that the impiety of pagans and Manichaeans may be attributed to a man of such great piety.

If these things are true, why are they themselves so negligent—or, I should say, so impious—as not to drive such an abrupt ruin from the Church, resist such insane preaching, or at least confront in writing the man from whom such a doctrine proceeds? They would have done a great service to the human race if they had recalled Augustine from error.

Unless perhaps these modest men and novel censors mercifully and respectfully spare an old man of such great prior merits, and, confident that no one anywhere receives his books, remain silent. Or perhaps they have not merely forgiven but have recognized that not only the Roman and African Churches, but also throughout all the regions of the world all the children of the promise agree with this man’s teaching both in the entirety of the faith and in the confession of grace.

Indeed, even in those very places where complaint is stirred up against him, there are, by God’s favor, very many who are instructed in the reception of evangelical and apostolic teaching by his most salutary discussions and who daily expand among the members of Christ’s body, insofar as Christ himself multiplies them.

If we are rightly reproved, why are we not openly accused? If we ought not to be accused, why are we attacked by hidden slander?

## Chapter IV

### 5.

But who does not know why they mutter these things privately in resentment and remain silent publicly out of deliberation? For they wish to glory more in their own righteousness than in God’s grace (Jer. 9:23–24; 2 Cor. 10:17), and they resent the fact that we resist what they asserted against a man of outstanding authority during many conferences.

[Note: He means the *Conferences of the Fathers*, published by the presbyter John Cassian around the year 426. Cassian dedicated the second section of these conferences, beginning with the Eleventh Conference, to Honoratus and Eucherius while they were not yet bishops, since he calls them “brothers” in the preface. Honoratus, however, obtained the episcopate of Arles in the year mentioned, 426. Because the definitions of the Thirteenth Conference were contrary to Augustine, Prosper judged that they should first be resisted orally and verbally, and afterward in writing, through the volume called *Against the Conference*.]

Nor do they doubt that, if they raise any question about this in any gathering of priests or assembly of peoples, hundreds of Augustine’s most blessed volumes will confront them. When these books begin to reveal to the hearts of their hearers the most powerful truth of the Christian faith and to flood their minds with the waters of divine eloquence, what believer, what devout person, having recognized and commended to himself the causes of his salvation, will wish to receive this bitterness of smoky vanity?

For my part, I also hope this from the riches of God’s mercy: that those whom he now permits to be deceived by their free will and to wander from the path of humility, he will not deprive of understanding forever or altogether. Rather, I believe that the very fact that he recalls them more slowly from this further advance is intended to celebrate the work of his grace with greater glory, when he has subjected even the hearts of his opponents—those in whom danger has arisen from zeal for virtue and crisis from moral uprightness.

This is not because anyone ought to lack these qualities, but because their use is most wretched when they are thought to have proceeded from natural ability, or to have come from the abundance of grace only after some merit of a good work or good will had preceded it.

## Chapter V

### 6.

They do indeed assert these things by certain testimonies of the holy Scriptures, but they do not assume them reasonably. For, in defending a particular definition, one must bring forward passages that do not yield to the interpretation by which the definition appears to be contradicted, and that do not abandon the rule to which they have been adapted.

They therefore say that the following was spoken to those using free will:

“Come to me, all who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart; and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy and my burden is light” (Matt. 11:28–30).

They wish this to apply to all human beings who labor in the uncertainty of this life and are burdened by sins, so that those who wish to imitate the gentleness and humility of the Savior and take up the yoke of his commandments may find rest for their souls in the hope of eternal life. But those who do not wish to do these things, they say, lose salvation through their own fault—a salvation which, had they wished it, they could have obtained.

But let them also hear what the Lord said to those using free will: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5); and, “No one comes to me unless the Father who sent me draws him”; and, “No one can come to me unless it has been given to him by my Father” (John 6:44, 66); and, “As the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he wills” (John 5:21); and, “No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son wishes to reveal him” (Luke 10:22).

Since all these statements are unchangeable and cannot by any interpretation be twisted into another meaning, who could doubt that free will obeys the exhortation of the one who calls only when God’s grace has produced in it the disposition to believe and obey?

Otherwise it would be enough merely to admonish a person; there would be no need for a new will to be created within him, as it is written: “The will is prepared by the Lord” (Prov. 8:35, according to the Septuagint); and as the Apostle says: “For God is the one who works in you both to will and to accomplish, for his good pleasure” (Phil. 2:13).

For what good pleasure, unless it is the one God has worked in them, so that he who had granted the will might also grant the ability to act?

## Chapter VI

### 7.

They also say, to demonstrate the capacity of free will, that the centurion Cornelius provides a notable example: before receiving grace, he feared and prayed to God, devoted himself spontaneously to almsgiving, fasting, and prayer, and, having been praised for this by divine testimony, received the gift of regeneration.

They do not understand that all this preparation of Cornelius was bestowed through God’s grace. For when Saint Peter was taught through a vision concerning every kind of animal, with reference to the baptism of Cornelius and, correspondingly, of all the nations, and when he rejected as unclean and common the food forbidden by Jewish observance, a voice came to him three times, saying: “What God has cleansed, you must not call common” (Acts 10:15).

This clearly shows that all the good works which preceded in Cornelius were begun by God’s grace for his cleansing.

[Note: See above, the Council of Orange.]

Thus, because the Lord had already bestowed this gift upon him, the Apostle did not hesitate to confer the sacrament, lest the beginning of a new and previously unrevealed calling waver, if God’s action in receiving him were not established through the very indications of his preceding devotions.

“For not all have faith” (2 Thess. 3:2), nor do all obey the Gospel (Rom. 10:16). But those who believe are led by the Spirit of God; those who do not believe turn away through free will.

Therefore our conversion to God comes not from us but from God, as the Apostle says: “By grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not from works, so that no one may boast” (Eph. 2:8–9).

## Chapter VII

### 8.

Let human weakness acknowledge itself, together with the succession of all generations condemned in the first human being. When the dead are brought to life, the blind are given sight, and the ungodly are justified, let them confess that Jesus Christ is their life, their light, and their righteousness. “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord” (1 Cor. 1:31), not in himself—he who, while ungodly, blind, and dead, freely received righteousness, light, and life from his liberator.

For he was not acting righteously and his righteousness was increased; nor was he walking toward God and his course strengthened; nor did he love God and his love become inflamed. Rather, while he was without faith and therefore ungodly, he received the spirit of faith and became righteous: “The righteous one lives by faith” (Rom. 1:17); and, “Without faith no one can please God” (Heb. 11:6); and, “Whatever is not from faith is sin” (Rom. 14:23).

Thus he should understand that the righteousness of unbelievers is not righteousness, because nature without grace is defiled.

[Note: The manuscript lacks *juste* (“righteously”).]

## Chapter VIII

### 9.

Having lost his natural innocence, the human being, an exile and one who was lost, walking without a path, entered ever deeper errors. But he was sought, found, and brought back, and was introduced into the way that is truth and life. He was set ablaze with love for God, who loved him first when he did not love God.

[Note: The printed editions read: “He was introduced to the love of God.”]

As blessed John the Apostle says: “Not as though we had loved God, but because he himself loved us”; and again: “Let us therefore love God, because God first loved us.” The same Apostle also says: “Beloved, let us love one another, because love is from God; and everyone who loves is born from God and knows God. Whoever does not love does not know God, because God is love” (1 John 4:10, 19, 7–8).

Blessed Paul agrees with him, saying: “In Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision has any value, but faith working through love” (Gal. 5:6).

From where does one possess this faith joined to love, unless from the source where he himself shows that it was received, saying: “To you it has been granted for Christ’s sake not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him” (Phil. 1:29)? This certainly could not happen without great love.

And again: “God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5). Without this love, the Apostle testifies that however great a faith, however great knowledge, whatever virtues, devotions, or labors one may possess, they accomplish nothing (1 Cor. 13:1–3).

For many praiseworthy and wondrous things can indeed be found in a person which, without the marrow of love, have the appearance of piety but do not possess its reality.

## Chapter IX

### 10.

No one, therefore, was found worthy of this great and ineffable good. But whoever has been chosen by God has been made worthy, as the Apostle says: “Giving thanks to the Father, who has made us worthy to share in the inheritance of the saints in light, who has delivered us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love” (Col. 1:12–13).

The same Apostle says to Timothy: “Work with me for the Gospel according to the power of God, who saved us and called us with a holy calling, not according to our works but according to his purpose and grace, which was given to us in Christ Jesus before eternal times” (2 Tim. 1:8–9).

And to Titus: “For we too were once foolish and unbelieving, wandering and serving various desires and pleasures, living in malice and envy, hateful and hating one another. But when the kindness and humanity of our Savior God appeared, he saved us, not because of works of righteousness that we had done, but according to his mercy” (Titus 3:3–5).

Therefore, whatever people God’s grace justifies, it does not make better from good people but makes good from evil people. Afterward, through growth, it will make those who are good better—not by taking away free will but by freeing it.

As long as free will existed alone, without God, it was dead to righteousness and lived for sin. But when Christ’s mercy enlightened it, it was snatched from the kingdom of the devil and made the kingdom of God. Yet, in order that it may be able to remain in that kingdom, it is not sufficient even with that ability by itself unless it receives perseverance from the same source from which it received zeal.

[Note: Perhaps *iustitiam*, “righteousness,” instead of *industriam*, “zeal.”]

## Chapter X

### 11.

For even the most ardent faith of Saint Peter would have failed in temptation unless the Lord had prayed for him, as the Evangelist makes clear:

“Jesus said to Peter: ‘Simon, Simon, behold, Satan has demanded to sift you like wheat; but I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail. And you, when you have turned back, strengthen your brothers; and pray that you may not enter into temptation’” (Luke 22:31–32).

And so that it might be demonstrated even more clearly that free will can do nothing without grace, the one to whom it had been said, “Strengthen your brothers, and pray that you may not enter into temptation,” and who had replied—certainly from free will—“Lord, I am ready to go with you both to prison and to death” (Luke 22:33), is told that before the cock crows he will deny the Lord three times (Luke 22:34; Matt. 26:34; Mark 14:30).

What else does this mean than that he would fail in faith? Certainly the Lord had prayed for him, that his faith might not fail; and he had not prayed in vain, since the one who prayed and the one for whom he prayed were joined in a single operation.

But lest the one who had made great promises about himself appear to stand by free will, he is permitted to be endangered, so that the Lord may look upon and restore him when he is troubled and failing—without whom no one stands firm and no one perseveres.

## Chapter XI

### 12.

Certain people recoil from this confession of God’s grace because, once they confess it to be such as it is proclaimed in divine eloquence and recognized in the operation of God’s power, they would also have to confess that, from the whole number of human beings born throughout the ages, a certain and determinate number of people predestined for eternal life has been fixed with God and chosen according to the purpose of God who calls.

To deny this is no less impious than to oppose grace itself. For it is not hidden from common observation how, over so many ages, innumerable thousands of human beings, abandoned to their errors and impieties, have perished without any knowledge of the true God.

The words of Paul and Barnabas in the Acts of the Apostles likewise make this clear. They said to the Lycaonians:

[Note: The printed editions read “Iconians.”]

“Men, brothers, why are you doing these things? We too are mortal human beings like you, proclaiming to you that you should turn from these vanities to the living God, who made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them; who in past generations allowed all the nations to walk in their own ways. Yet he did not leave himself without testimony, doing good, giving rain from heaven and fruitful seasons, filling your hearts with food and gladness” (Acts 14:14–16).

[Note: The Remigius manuscript reads “and indeed leaving himself with testimony,” omitting *non* (“not”).]

[Note: The printed editions read “their hearts.”]

If either natural understanding or the use of God’s benefits had been sufficient for them to attain eternal life, then even in our own time rational contemplation, the moderation of the air, and the abundance of crops and food would save us, because, using nature better, we would worship our Creator on account of his daily gifts.

## Chapter XII

### 13.

But let the minds of the devout, redeemed by Christ’s blood, be far from this foolish and exceedingly dangerous persuasion. Human nature does not liberate human nature; outside the one mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, there is salvation for no one.

Just as he himself made us, and not we ourselves, so he himself restores us, and not we ourselves. And lest human ability appear able to repay the price of this restoration, either before or after its renewal, through works of righteousness, the riches of God’s goodness were poured forth upon the very beginnings of certain infants, in whom there is neither preceding choice nor subsequent devotion; neither obedience, discernment, nor will.

I speak of those who, as soon as they are born, are born again, and, snatched from this life, are assigned to eternal blessedness. Yet an innumerable multitude of infants of the same nature and condition dies without regeneration; and of them there can be no doubt that they have no share in the city of God.

## Chapter XIII

### 14.

And what of that statement which those who do not understand continually set against us as though it were contrary: that God wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Tim. 2:4)?

Are not those who have perished without knowledge of God from past generations down to the present time included among all human beings? And if, in the case of adults—which is not rightly said—the evil works they committed through free will harmed them, as though the good, rather than the wicked, were liberated by grace, what distinction of merits could there have been between the infants who were saved and those who were not?

What brought these into the kingdom of God? What excluded those from God’s kingdom? Certainly, if you consider merit, neither group deserved to be saved; both deserved to be condemned. For when all had been cast down in Adam’s transgression, unless merciful grace took up some of them, an unimpeachable justice would remain over all.

What the cause or reason of this distinction is within the secret counsel of God is sought beyond the capacity of human understanding and is unknown without any diminution of faith.

Let us only confess that no one is lost undeservedly, no one is liberated through merit, and that the Lord’s omnipotent goodness saves all and instructs all whom he wills to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.

For unless he himself calls, teaches, and saves, no one comes, no one is instructed, and no one is saved. For although teachers are commanded to preach indiscriminately to all human beings and to sow the word everywhere, “neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything, but God who gives the growth” (1 Cor. 3:7).

## Chapter XIV

### 15.

Therefore, when the Apostles began to preach the Gospel to the nations, Scripture records concerning a certain portion of those who heard:

“When the Gentiles heard this, they rejoiced and glorified the word of the Lord, and as many as had been ordained to eternal life believed” (Acts 13:48).

And elsewhere, when many women were listening to Paul’s teaching: “A certain woman named Lydia, a seller of purple from the city of Thyatira, a worshiper of God, was listening; the Lord opened her heart to attend to what was spoken by Paul” (Acts 16:14).

Again, at the very time when the preaching of the Gospel was being sent to all the nations, the Apostles were forbidden by the one who wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth from entering certain regions. Many in those places would consequently be delayed and turned away by the postponement of the Gospel and would die without knowledge of the truth and without the consecration of regeneration.

[Note: Perhaps: *retardati atque aversi Evangelii* (“delayed and turned away from the Gospel”).]

Let Scripture state what happened:

“Passing through the region of Phrygia and Galatia, they were forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia. When they had come to Mysia, they attempted to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus did not permit them” (Acts 16:6–7).

What wonder, then, if at the very beginnings of evangelical preaching the Apostles could not go except where the Spirit of God wished them to go, when we see that even now many nations are only beginning to become participants in Christian grace, while others have not yet touched any fragrance of this good thing?

## Chapter XV

### 16.

Should we say that human wills resist God’s will, and that the character of these people is so savage and intractable that they do not hear the Gospel because their impious hearts are not open to preaching?

And who changed their hearts, except the one who formed each of them individually: “He fashioned their hearts one by one” (Ps. 32:15)? Who softened the hardness of this severity into a disposition to obey, except the one who is able to raise children for Abraham from stones (Matt. 3:9)?

And who will give preachers fearless and unharmed perseverance, except the one who said to Paul:

“Do not be afraid, but speak, and do not be silent; because I am with you, and no one will attack you to harm you, for I have many people in this city” (Acts 18:9–10)?

I think no one would dare say that any nation of the world or any region of the earth should be omitted in which the tabernacles of the Churches are not to be enlarged, since God says to the Son:

“Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Ps. 2:8);

and again:

“All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations shall worship before him” (Ps. 21:28);

and the Lord himself says:

“This Gospel will be preached throughout the whole world as a testimony to all nations, and then the end will come” (Matt. 24:14).

Therefore, whatever nations have not yet heard will hear the Gospel, and as many of them as have been ordained to eternal life will believe. For no others will come into fellowship with Christ’s inheritance except those who were chosen, predestined, and foreknown before the foundation of the world, according to the purpose of the one who accomplishes all things according to the counsel of his will (Eph. 1:14).

## Chapter XVI
### 17

Let us therefore acknowledge the works of the Lord and glorify his mercies; nor let us impatiently bear the fact that we do not know what or how great the vessels of election are. For even in earlier ages, when it was said concerning the people of a single nation, “God is known in Judah; his name is great in Israel” (Ps. 75:2), the future election of the nations was hidden; afterward it became known, though it had not previously been revealed, as the Apostle says: “That which in other generations was not made known to the sons of men, as it has now been revealed to his holy apostles and prophets in the Spirit: that the Gentiles are fellow-heirs, members of the same body, and fellow-partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus” (Eph. 3:5–6). And in the Acts of the Apostles: “The faithful from the circumcision who had come with Peter were astonished, because the grace of the Holy Spirit had also been poured out upon the nations” (Acts 10:45).

If, then, the Lord concealed and postponed this purpose of his calling for as long as he wished, and revealed it when he wished—and this ignorance did not harm his saints—why do we think it harms our hope if it is hidden in what number and among which people the vessels of mercy are prepared for glory? Yet it is certain that all the good will enter the kingdom of heaven, by God’s grace granting this to them; and that no evil people will enter it, their wickedness deserving this outcome.

### 18

It is said with excessive foolishness and thoughtlessness by those who oppose us that, through this grace of God, nothing at all is left to free choice. Although, in infants passing through Baptism, there is manifestly no work or desire of their will, and although liberating regeneration sanctifies many who do indeed exercise free choice but are turned away from the true God and spend their lives in crimes, even at the very moment when they breathe out their spirit: nevertheless, if we piously consider that portion of the children of God which is reserved for works of devotion, shall we not find in them that free choice has not been destroyed but reborn?

When it was alone and left to itself, it moved only toward its own ruin. It had blinded itself, and could not enlighten itself. But now that same choice has been turned, not overthrown; and it has been granted to will otherwise [Note: [Col. 1800] From an old manuscript we have added “to will otherwise.”], to understand otherwise, to act otherwise, and to place its well-being not in itself but in the physician. For it does not yet possess health so perfect that the things which had harmed it can no longer harm it, or that it can now, by its own strength, abstain from what is unhealthy.

Accordingly, the human being who was evil in free choice has, in that same free choice, been made good: evil through himself, good through God. God restored him to that original dignity by another beginning, so that he not only forgave him the guilt of evil willing and acting, but also granted him the ability to will well, act well, and persevere in these things. For the apostle James says: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (Jas. 1:17).

He clearly shows what kind of free choice is moved by the human spirit and what kind is governed by God when he says: “If you have bitter jealousy and contention in your hearts, do not boast and lie against the truth. This is not the wisdom descending from above, but earthly, natural, demonic. For where jealousy and contention are, there are instability and every evil work. But the wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, open to persuasion, full of mercy and good fruits, not judging, without hypocrisy” (Jas. 3:14–17).

Whoever, therefore, strives for and clings to these virtues has been enlightened not by his own wisdom but by wisdom from above: “For the Lord gives wisdom, and from his face come knowledge and understanding” (Prov. 2:6). And this is their truest glory, if they glory not in themselves but in the Lord.

### 19

As for the things which they foolishly and most falsely allege concerning fate, and concerning two masses and two natures, to the injury of so great a man [Note: [Col. 1800] The printed editions read: “they cast about the injury of an intent man.” This is corrected from the old codex, except that it reads *iacitantur* for *iactitantur*.], they do not even burden the man himself, since such errors are thoroughly refuted in his books [Note: [Col. 1800] See Augustine, *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, book 2, chapters 6 and 7; and *Against Julian*, book 4, chapter 8.]; nor do they disturb us, [Col. 1801] since we curse such opinions together with their authors.

But let those who can invent such absurdities see how they may free themselves from the disgrace of this falsehood, if those whose ears they abuse should devote even a little diligence to learning what that most distinguished minister of grace discussed. Indeed, the very men who speak these things ought to have forestalled the entire delay of this investigation by producing and explaining the books, or by pointing out any passage of them which the holy man published and which could even doubtfully be subjected to such an interpretation.

But they have heard nothing of this sort from us, nor have they read anything of the sort. For we know that nothing is carried out by fate, but that everything is ordered by God’s judgment. Nor do we know of two masses or two natures; rather, from one mass—which is the flesh of the first human being—we know that one nature of all human beings was created and is being created, and that this same nature was cast down through the free choice of that first human being, in whom all sinned (Rom. 5:12). It is in no way freed from the debt of eternal death unless the grace of Christ, through the second creation, restores it to the image of God and, by acting, breathing, [Note: [Col. 1801] So the manuscript.
