The printed editions, however, read “hoping.”] assisting, and going before it to the end, preserves its free choice.

## Epilogue

[Col. 1802]

### 20

Since, therefore, Your Holiness perceives—provided that the obscurity of my speech does not stand in the way—that certain people complain about us without cause, and that all those absurd accusations have been woven together to anger and turn away the minds of those whom they wish to persuade of something else, I trust in the power of God’s mercy that this opposition, in these regions as in other parts of the world, will subside, so that the preaching of the eminent man who is at this time in the Church may even be assisted by those by whom it is presently rejected [Note: [Col. 1802] So the manuscript. The printed editions read “is torn away.”].

But you, my dearest and most venerable brother, if you truly desire instruction concerning these questions—as indeed you ought to desire it—devote yourself to learning the disputations of blessed Augustine, so that, in confessing God’s grace, you may attain the purest and most salutary understanding of evangelical and apostolic teaching. May the grace of God and the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ guard you at all times and guide you by the way of truth into eternal life.

[Col. 1801]

# PROSPER OF AQUITAINE, *BOOK AGAINST THE COLLATOR, ON BEHALF OF AUGUSTINE* [Note: [Col. 1801] In the very ancient Corbie codex, written approximately nine hundred years ago, the title of this little work is: “The Book of Saint Prosper on Behalf of the Preachers of the Grace of God against the Book of Cassian the Presbyter, entitled *On the Protection of God*”; that is, against the thirteenth Conference, held with Abbot Chaeremon.] (C)

## [Preface]

He examines the twelve definitions of John Cassian concerning grace and free choice, contained in his thirteenth Conference, and teaches that, with the single exception of the first, they wholly disagree with Catholic truth. He demonstrates that the critics of Augustine both make empty accusations, attack what is right, and defend what is wrong; and that, by turning against the Church an internal war with the weapons of the already defeated Pelagians, they rebel alike against the divine Scriptures and against ecclesiastical and imperial constitutions.

## Chapter One

[Col. 1801]

### 1

Certain people dare to say that the grace of God, through which we are Christians, was not rightly defended by Bishop Augustine, of holy memory; and they do not cease to attack his books, written against the Pelagian error, with immoderate calumnies.

Their domestic malignity, resounding within, would deserve no less contempt than the heretical loquacity barking from without, if, after the wolves had been driven outside the Lord’s sheepfold, those who support them under the name of sheep were not such that neither their standing in the Church nor their abilities seem worthy of contempt. For, while bearing the appearance of piety in their devotion, the power of which they deny in their understanding, they draw many uneducated people to themselves and disturb hearts that do not possess discernment of spirits [Note: [Col. 1801] The Leuven and Antwerp editions read “discernment of the spirit.” The Mainz edition, the earliest of all, which appeared in 1524 from a manuscript exemplar of the Benedictines of Mount Saint James, has “discernment of spirits,” as does the Corbie manuscript. Prosper alludes to 1 Cor. 12:10.]. They endeavor to bring the Church’s cause into such a condition that, while they assert that our people did not speak truthfully on behalf of grace, they persuade others that the enemies of grace were unjustly condemned.

This evil, therefore, must not be neglected. It grows daily from hidden and insignificant seeds and spreads farther and wider from its origin. We must strive, insofar as the Lord assists, to expose the hypocrisy of deceitful accusers, who, because of the very magnitude of the injury they have inflicted upon everyone, and especially upon the pontiffs of the Apostolic See, are judged by the unlearned and unwary to possess superior knowledge; and, through a miserable and perverse success, they easily elicit assent to their falsehood, because they have presumed to claim reverence for themselves.

For, since they are men of good reputation, no one believes that they could possibly have burst into the clamorous expression of a useless complaint through slowness of understanding or rashness of judgment. Rather, people suppose that they labored with great intelligence and intense zeal so that, after comprehending the disputations of a most subtle theologian, a stricter judgment and more discerning examination might now discover what secure approval and careless kindness had not previously seen.

### 2

From where, then, has this diligence of such a severe examination emerged? From where has arrogance armed itself with the grim front of austerity, so that an insidious investigator may weigh the measures of meanings, the values of expressions, and the number of syllables, and presume that he is accomplishing something great if he brands a Catholic preacher with the mark of error? Is some unknown work being attacked, something that has until now remained hidden? Is it not rather that the doctrine which scattered the inventions of the new heretics and shattered the devilish pride of Pelagian arrogance is being torn apart by these attacks?

More than twenty years have passed since the Catholic ranks, under the leadership of this man, have fought and conquered the enemies of God’s grace [Note: [Col. 1802] So the Corbie manuscript and the Mainz edition. Later editions read “more than twenty years,” omitting “have passed since.”]. And I say “conquered,” because he does not allow those whom he conquered to recover their breath, and because, for their destruction, he wrote the judgment of all the priests with one hand. [Note: [Col. 1803] The Mainz edition connects the following sentence with the preceding one as two parts of a single sentence; and, instead of “let them complain,” it has “they complain and arm.”]

Driven out by the pontifical judgment and deprived of communion, let them complain about the happiness of our victory and arm their tongues against us—those who preferred to be exiles from the truth rather than citizens of the Church. But since we are fellow-members and fellow-partakers of the grace of Christ, why do they complain about the weapons by which the common faith was defended? Why do they reopen a war that has been concluded and weaken the fortifications of the peace long since secured?

Do the victors displease them and the defeated please them? Are condemned errors being cherished with such insolence that, through hatred of wickedness, both our authors and our judges are attacked? Or has the standard of the new censors been so precisely adjusted that they affirm none of the things which have been destroyed and reject some of those which have been defended?

Behold: while the Catholic victory remains safe and the authority of the indissoluble decrees remains revered, we are ready to hear the advocates of a more corrected doctrine and to recognize the lines of the most subtle discrimination, cut away from every error. Let what has emerged from new minds be placed before us [Note: [Col. 1803] Perhaps various questions against Augustine had already emerged at that time. But since Prosper had received them only by hearsay, as he seems to indicate below in section 3 and later in section 55, he temporarily sets them aside and undertakes to refute above all Cassian’s definitions, which had been published in writing and circulated among the people.]

## Chapter Two

### 3

And lest we seem to attack, in order to obscure the knowledge of the learned, the things which the ignoble crowd and the brazen loquacity of fools pour out immoderately, we shall report the definitions of one particular man, who unquestionably excels all of them in the study of the holy Scriptures. For the present, these alone ought to be brought into debate for this reason: there can be no doubt whether they are as stated [Note: [Col. 1803] The Mainz edition reads: “Whose decrees for this reason alone ought for the present to be brought forward.” The same wording occurs in the Corbie manuscript, but inserted after “ought to be assumed.” In that codex, before “these alone for this reason,” stands the particle “elsewhere,” indicating that one of the two statements had been taken from another place.].

They have been written down and published in an edition by their author [Note: [Col. 1803] The Corbie manuscript reads “corrected”; the Mainz edition, “corrected,” referring to “decrees.”]. It is no longer necessary to ask whether they exist; rather, it is necessary to demonstrate what they teach.

Therefore, in a book whose title is *On the Protection of God*, a certain priestly man [Note: [Col. 1803] Later editions add “of the clerical order.” This was absent from Corbie and Mainz.], who excels among those with whom he lives in the practice of disputation, introduces a certain abbot discussing the grace of God and free choice. He shows that he approved and embraced the abbot’s opinion in every respect. Thus we are no longer dealing with the abbot, who might perhaps have refuted such opinions of his own by denying them or dissolved them by correcting them, but with the man who chose to bring forward such a doctrine as a weapon for the enemies of God’s grace.

### 4

Nevertheless, at the beginning of the discussion he does not disagree with the piety of truth and would deserve to be honored with a just commendation, had he not deviated from his initial correctness through a headlong and misguided advance. For, after comparing him to a farmer whose model he adapted to one living under grace and faith, and whose labor he declared fruitless unless it were assisted in every respect by God’s help, he introduced a thoroughly Catholic definition, saying (*Conference* 13, chapter 3):

“From this it is plainly gathered that the source not only of good actions but also of good thoughts is God. He both inspires in us the beginnings of holy desire and grants the strength and opportunity to carry out the things which we rightly desire. For every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights (Jas. 1:17), who both begins the good things in us, carries them out, and brings them to completion, as the Apostle says: ‘He who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will also supply and multiply your seed and increase the fruits of your righteousness’ (2 Cor. 9:10).”

Lest anyone think that nothing remained to be accomplished through free choice, he added, not unreasonably, an argument demonstrating that free choice is not removed by these gifts but rather strengthened—unless, turning back toward its own iniquities, it should prefer to withdraw from God’s assistance.

“But it is our responsibility,” he says, “to follow humbly the grace of God, which draws us daily; or else, by resisting it with a stiff neck and uncircumcised ears, as it is written (Acts 7:51), to deserve to hear through Jeremiah: ‘Does he who falls not rise again? Or does he who has turned away not return? Why, then, has this people in Jerusalem turned away with a stubborn turning? They have hardened their necks and have refused to return’ (Jer. 8:4–5).”

Again, below, after teaching that every pursuit of virtue requires God’s grace, he reasonably added:

“All these things, just as they cannot continually be desired by us without divine inspiration, so likewise they cannot in any way be brought to completion without his assistance” (chapter 6).

### 5

But in the seventh chapter [Note: [Col. 1804] It is now chapter eight.]—wishing to show the universal grace of Christ, which leaves no human being entirely untouched and does not abandon even the rebellious and hostile—he says:

“Divine protection is therefore inseparably present with us, and the Creator’s goodness toward his creature is so great that providence not only accompanies it but continually goes before it.”

Here he may have called providence a companion because it often does not abandon even those who abandon it, or because it follows all those whom it precedes.

He continues:

“When it perceives in us a certain beginning of good will, it immediately enlightens, strengthens, and urges it toward salvation, granting increase to that which it has itself planted or which it has seen emerge through our effort” [Note: [Col. 1804] Corbie and Mainz read: “it enlightens it, strengthens it, and directs it toward salvation.”].

Here he may still say that he meant the beginning of good will whose beginnings had been planted or inspired by God. For, from hearts already enlightened, salutary efforts can emerge; and these are therefore said to belong properly to the human being because he has already received the ability to make good efforts, while their seeds are referred back to their author.

### 6

But in chapter nine he adds and says:

“Therefore, human reason does not easily discern how the Lord gives to those who ask, is found by those who seek, and opens to those who knock; and again, how he is found by those who do not seek him, openly appears among those who were not questioning him, stretches out his hands all day to a people that does not believe in him and contradicts him (Isa. 65:1–2), calls those who resist and are far away, draws the unwilling toward salvation, removes from those who desire to sin the opportunity to fulfill their will [Note: [Col. 1804] Corbie and Mainz read “desire” rather than “will.”], and in his kindness obstructs those who hasten toward wickedness.”

Here, as though through an inscrutable diversity, a definition is introduced which teaches that many come to grace without grace, and that some possess the desire to ask, seek, and knock through the vigilance of free choice. Yet this same desire is said to be so blinded in others by great aversion that it cannot be recalled by any exhortations unless it is unwillingly led by the force of the one drawing it.

It is as though the entire manifold work of grace were not carried out in the minds of all so that the unwilling may become willing; or as though anyone among those who already exercise rational judgment could receive faith except by an act of will. It is therefore just as foolish to say that anyone moves toward participation in grace unwillingly as to assert that anyone comes to it without being stirred by the Spirit of God.

### 7

Thus this disputant quickly forgot the definition he had previously stated; quickly, with unstable fickleness, he departed from his own position [Note: [Col. 1804] Later editions read: “he departed through instability and fickleness.”].

For he had stated as a rule: “The source not only of good actions but also of good thoughts is God.” And lest this be understood as a matter of instruction supplied from outside, he had attentively added:

“He inspires in us the beginnings of holy desire and grants the strength and opportunity to carry out the things which we rightly desire. For every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights, who both begins the good things in us, carries them out, and brings them to completion.”

Catholic teacher, why do you abandon your profession? Why, leaving the clearest light of truth, do you roll down into the smoky darkness of falsehood [Note: [Col. 1805] So the Corbie manuscript. The editions read “famous darkness.”]?

When you marvel at what occurs in those who ask, seek, and knock, why do you not attribute it to that same grace which is desired? You see good efforts and devout pursuits, and you hesitate to regard them as gifts of God? The work of grace may have remained hidden while the faith implanted in thought was enclosed in secrecy; but once humble prayer, diligent inquiry, and persistent knocking appear, why do you not understand, from the character of the action, the provision of the one who urges it on?

## Chapter Three

### 8

You think that you have sufficiently armed yourself against the calumnies of the Pelagians [Note: [Col. 1805] So the Corbie manuscript and the Mainz edition. Later editions read: “And you think that you have sufficiently guarded yourself against the calumnies of the Pelagians if you grant us,” etc.] if you grant us, in a limited portion, what ought to be understood concerning all those who are called. But you are in full agreement neither with the heretics nor with the Catholics.

They defend the beginnings of all righteous human works as belonging to free choice. We always believe that the beginnings of good thoughts proceed from God. You have discovered some shapeless third position, unsuited to either side, by which you have gained neither the agreement of the enemies nor a place within the understanding of our own people.

How do you fail to see that you fall into the very condemnation which, whether you wish it or not, you are shown to express—namely, that God’s grace is given according to our merits—when you assert that some good work must precede in human beings, on account of which they obtain grace?

The faith of one who asks, the devotion of one who seeks, and the persistence of one who knocks cannot be regarded as wholly without merit, especially since all such people are said to receive, find, and enter (Matt. 7:7–8). In this it is superfluous, indeed impious, to make room for merits existing before grace in such a way that the Lord’s statement would not be entirely true: “No one comes to me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (John 6:44).

For otherwise one would have to believe that someone’s conversion could occur without God’s illumination, or that the human will could in any way extend itself toward God without God. God draws the one who has been called to the Son; he does not compel one who resists and is unwilling, but makes the unwilling willing. In whatever ways he can, he bends the unbelief of the one who resists, so that the heart of the hearer, once the delight of obedience has been generated within it, may rise where it had been weighed down; learn where it had been ignorant; trust from the place where it had distrusted; and will from the place where it had been unwilling.

“For the Lord will give goodness, and our land will give its fruit” (Ps. 84:13).

### 9

But let us see what follows:

“Who could easily understand how the fullness of salvation is attributed to our free choice? For it is said: ‘If you are willing and hear me, you shall eat the good things of the land’ (Isa. 1:19). And how is it that ‘it depends not on the one who wills or on the one who runs, but on God who has mercy’ (Rom. 9:16)? What also is meant by the statement that God ‘will repay each according to his works’ (Matt. 16:27), and that ‘God is the one who works in you both to will and to accomplish, according to your good will’ [Note: [Col. 1805] Here we have added “your,” on the authority of the Corbie manuscript and the Mainz edition.] (Phil. 2:13), and that ‘this is not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not from works, so that no one may boast’ (Eph. 2:8–9)?”

And he collected other passages gathered from Scripture as though they contradicted one another in alternating senses, so that he might entrust the pursuit of grace’s gifts to human effort; and, having divided all human beings into groups, might make some those whom God’s grace saves and others those whom law and nature justify.

But the law can command that nothing evil be done; it cannot free anyone from evil. It makes the commandment known, but does not supply the desire to obey—unless what kills through the command of the letter is made life-giving through the Spirit of grace.

### 10

After this he concludes:

“Thus, in all these things, both the grace of God and the freedom of our choice are in some manner revealed; for at times a human being can extend himself toward the desire for virtue through his own movements, but he always needs to be assisted by the Lord” [Col. 1806] [Note: [Col. 1806] Later editions read “and because.” The word “and” is absent from the older Mainz edition and from the Corbie manuscript.].

Where, then, is what was stated earlier as a rule: “The source not only of good actions but also of good thoughts is God,” who both begins the good things in us, carries them out, and brings them to completion?

Behold: although here you acknowledge that God’s help is necessary for good beginnings, you nevertheless attribute to bare free choice, apart from God’s grace, the very laudable movements and desires toward virtue. Thus good and salutary efforts cannot indeed advance unless God helps them, but they can nevertheless begin even if they are not inspired by God.

## Chapter Four

### 11

Then, in order to define more clearly what a human being possesses from free choice and what he receives from grace, you add and say:

“For no one enjoys health simply when he wishes, nor is freed from the disease of sickness according to the desire of his free choice.”

You therefore teach that a human being cannot indeed seize health by himself, but that he possesses from himself the desire for health; and that he comes to the physician solely by his own spontaneous will, so that it is not also the physician’s work that he comes.

As though the soul itself were not sick, and, once healthy, could discern a remedy for its body! Yet the whole human being, together with the soul itself, fell into the depth of his misery. There the soul delights in lying until it receives from the physician knowledge of its calamity, always loving its errors and embracing falsehoods in place of truths.

Its first salvation is to begin to be displeasing to itself and to hate the oldness of its weakness. Its next is to desire to be healed and to know by whom it must be healed. These things precede its cure in such a way that they are implanted in it by the one who will heal its sickness. Otherwise, since these things cannot in any way be present in it without purpose [Note: [Col. 1806] So the Corbie manuscript and the Mainz edition. Later editions read: “since these things can be present in it in no way.”], it might rightly appear to have been saved by merit rather than by grace.

### 12

Then you add (*chapter 9*):

“But so that it may become clearer that, through the good of nature—which was bestowed by the Creator’s kindness—the beginnings of good wills sometimes emerge, although they cannot reach the completion of virtues unless they are directed by God, the Apostle is witness when he says: ‘For the willing is present with me, but I do not find the means of accomplishing the good’ (Rom. 7:18).”

According to this definition, then, you previously spoke falsely when you said: “The source not only of good actions but also of good thoughts is from God,” who both begins the good things in us, carries them out, and brings them to completion.

But this cannot in any part be false. No contrary statements should have been brought against it, so that what you rightly professed to begin from grace you would later affirm that we possess through the good of nature and through free choice.

Blessed the Apostle did say: “For the willing is present with me, but I do not find the means of accomplishing the good.” But he also said: “Not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think anything as though from ourselves; our sufficiency is from God” (2 Cor. 3:5). And he likewise said: “For it is God who works in you both to will and to act [Note: [Col. 1806] Later editions read “to accomplish” instead of “to act.”] according to good will” (Phil. 2:13).

The Apostle, therefore, is not contradicting himself. But when the will to do good has been granted to us, we do not immediately find the ability to act, unless the one who gave the desire grants its fulfillment to those who ask, seek, and knock.

The voice of the one who says, “For the willing is present with me, but I do not find the means of accomplishing the good,” belongs to one who has been called and already established under grace. He delights in the law of God according to the inner person, but sees another law in his members, warring against the law of his mind and taking him captive in the law of sin (Rom. 7:18, 22–23). Although he has received knowledge of how to will rightly, he does not find within himself the strength to do what he desires—until, for the good will he has received, he merits finding the power for virtue which he seeks [Note: [Col. 1806] So the Corbie manuscript and the Mainz edition. Later editions, after “which he has received,” add: “he may merit finding one who acts.”].

## Chapter Five

### 13

After this you set forth numerous testimonies [Col. 1807] by which free choice is shown now to be strong and now weak—as though there were some who fulfilled by their own powers what others cannot do without God’s assistance; or as though a command were given to a human being for any reason other than that he should seek divine help.

You conclude and say:

“And thus these things are in some manner mixed and confused indiscriminately, so that among many people the great question is debated as to what depends on what: that is, whether God has mercy on us because we have supplied the beginning of good will from ourselves, or whether, because God has mercy, we obtain the beginning of good will. For many people, believing each of these points and asserting them beyond what is right, have become entangled in various errors that contradict one another” (chapter 11).

Behold: as it seems to you, what was mixed has been separated, and what could not be explained has been resolved. For you define two errors as mutually opposed, errors in which those who do not know what ought to be held concerning free choice and grace are entangled.

In one group you place those who say that God has mercy on us because the beginnings of good will have been supplied from us—plainly indicating the followers of Pelagian doctrine, who say that God’s grace is given according to our merits. In the other group you place those who say that the beginnings of good wills proceed from God’s mercy, intending these to be understood as those who defeated the enemies of grace.

If, then, it is an error to attribute the beginnings of good will to a human being who is not assisted by God, and if it is an error to confess that the will is prepared by the Lord, where are we to be directed so that we may avoid both?

### 14

“If we follow both,” you say, “we submit to neither error.”

You subject us to two errors and, by dividing what you understand as two forms of depravity, condemn them separately but justify them by mixing them together. By this law and rule you could proclaim that those who say that one must always be deceived are as much in error as those who define that one must never be deceived; yet, so that no error is committed in either direction, both positions should be followed, because falsehood is neither always to be avoided nor truth always to be neglected.

Your opinion completely deceives you. Two evils cannot become one good. Two vices do not produce one virtue. Two falsehoods do not make one truth. Things which are rightly equal are not diminished by coming together but increase.

It was therefore not right to criticize those who assert that the beginnings of good wills are generated by God’s inspiration with the same judgment by which those are accused who think that free choice can suffice for these things without the help of grace. One of these definitions has been defeated by the Church; the other has been defended. Nor does the covenant of this new alliance in any way fit them—a covenant by which Catholic doctrine becomes more corrupt than Pelagian doctrine has been corrected.

### 15

“You say that many, believing each of these propositions and asserting them more strongly than is just, have become entangled in various errors contradictory to one another. Is it therefore pleasing to you to condemn Catholics together with heretics, and the victors together with the vanquished; and to brand as erroneous those who drove error from the Church? For according to your judgment—by which you do not wish the beginning of holy and faithful wills in all human beings to be from God (as though you were granting grace a great deal if you allowed that it operates this in the minds of some)—blessed Pope Innocent, most worthy of the See of Peter, erred when, speaking of those who glory in free will, he said:

‘What, then, are we henceforth to judge rightly about the minds of those who think that they owe to themselves the fact that they are good?’

And again, when he was writing about the fall of the first man:

‘For he had formerly experienced free will; but, while using his own goods too rashly, he fell and was plunged into the depths of transgression. He found nothing by which he could rise from there and, deceived forever by his own freedom, would have lain hidden, crushed beneath the weight of this ruin, unless Christ’s coming had afterwards raised him up by his grace.’

[Note: [Col. 1807] Thus in the Corbie manuscript. But in the Mainz edition, *jacuisset oppressu*—‘would have lain oppressed.’ In later editions, *jacuisset oppressus*—‘would have lain oppressed.’]

This is from Letter 181 among Augustine’s letters, section 7.

The Eastern bishops erred, at whose judgment Pelagius was compelled, in order to appear Catholic, to anathematize those who say that God’s grace is given according to our merits.

[Note: [Col. 1808] See the book *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, chapters 11, 33, and 35.]

The African councils of bishops erred, which established in their decrees—at the Council of Carthage, canon 4 or 5—that both are gifts of God: knowing what we ought to do, and loving in order to do it; so that, when love builds up, knowledge cannot puff up. For just as it is written of God, ‘He is the one who teaches human beings knowledge’ (Psalm 93:10), so it is written, ‘Love is from God’ (1 John 4:7).

The two hundred and fourteen priests erred, who, in the letter they placed before their constitutions,

[Note: [Col. 1808] The Corbie manuscript has *protulerunt*—‘brought forth’—instead of *praetulerunt*—‘placed before.’]

spoke as follows to the blessed Zosimus, bishop of the Apostolic See:

‘We establish that the sentence pronounced against Pelagius and Coelestius by the venerable bishop Innocent from the See of the most blessed Apostle Peter shall remain in force, until they openly confess that by the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord we are assisted, through each individual act, not only to know but also to do justice, so that without it we are able to have, think, say, or do nothing belonging to true and holy piety.’

The most holy See of blessed Peter erred, when through the mouth of Pope Zosimus it spoke thus to the whole world:

‘Nevertheless, at God’s prompting—for all good things must be referred to their author, from whom they arise—we have referred everything to the conscience of our brothers and fellow bishops.’

The African bishops erred when they wrote back to the same Pope Zosimus and praised him for the salutary soundness of this judgment, saying:

‘But that statement which you placed in your letter, which you arranged to be sent to all the provinces, saying, “Nevertheless, at God’s prompting—for all good things must be referred to their author, from whom they arise—we have referred everything to the conscience of our brothers and fellow bishops,” we understood in this sense: that, passing swiftly by as it were, you cut down with the drawn sword of truth those who exalt the freedom of human will against God’s help.

‘For what did you do so freely as to refer everything to the conscience of our humility? And yet you rightly and wisely recognized that this was done at God’s prompting, and you truthfully and confidently declared it.

‘For surely this is so because the will is prepared by the Lord, and he himself touches the hearts of his children with paternal inspirations, so that they may do something good. “For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God” (Romans 8:14). Thus we do not feel that our free will is absent, and yet in each individual movement of the human will toward what is good we do not doubt that his help is more powerful.’

Do you see your rules shattered by the solidity of invincible decrees, and the crooked and ruinous joints in the structure of the faith collapsing, like the walls of Jericho, at the sound of the priests’ trumpets (Joshua 6:20)?

## CHAPTER VI

### 16

When, then, a dispute arose among our people and the Pelagians concerning the origin of holy wills and the beginnings of faith and love, the contest was settled by no uncertain victory and no doubtful conclusion, so that we must still discuss the wicked peace of this covenant of yours.

The enemy line has been overthrown; the war is finished. We are victors through him who made power manifest in his arm, who scattered the proud in the thoughts of their hearts, brought down the powerful from their thrones, and exalted the humble; who filled the hungry with good things and sent the rich away empty (Luke 1:51–53); through him who, showing mercy to our fathers, remembered his holy covenant and the oath which he swore to Abraham our father, that he would grant us, delivered from the hand of our enemies without fear, to serve him in holiness and righteousness before him all our days (ibid., 72–75); through him who gave us victory through Jesus Christ our Lord (1 Corinthians 15:57); through him from whom we received not the spirit of this world but the Spirit who is from God, so that we might know the things given to us by God (ibid. 2:12).

Why do you strive to gather up weapons broken by the petty arguments of exhausted disputations? Why, by reviving the ashes of a dead doctrine, do you try to kindle the smell of dying smoke into a renewed flame? There is no danger to free will from the grace of God, nor is the will taken away when the very capacity to will rightly is generated within it.

For if it must not be considered ours because it is formed, governed, directed, and instructed, then the children of God who are led by the Spirit of God are stripped of their freedom. Those to whom the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, counsel and fortitude, knowledge and piety, and the fear of the Lord is given are deprived of the vigor of their rational mind and of every praise belonging to voluntary devotion (Isaiah 11:2–3).

Those who do not think they need these restorations have plainly passed from the habit of an old illness into madness. They reject the remedy, cry out, rave, and resist. But if they are children of the promise, they will become quiet and will be healed.

## CHAPTER VII

### 17

But now let us see what the sobriety of this disputant brings forward. In order to drive out one vice by another and cure one error with another, he confused definitions contradictory to one another by a novel device; and, so that he might offer this mixture as a drink to unsuspecting hearers, he wished to disguise what he had mixed with examples.

For he says:

‘If we say that the beginning of a good will is ours, what was there in the persecutor Paul, or in the tax collector Matthew? One of them was engaged in the bloodshed and punishments of the innocent, the other in public violence and plunder, yet each was drawn to salvation. But if we say that the beginnings of a good will are always inspired by the grace of God, what shall we say about the faith of Zacchaeus, or about the piety of that thief on the cross, who, by forcing his way into the heavenly kingdoms through their desire, as it were, anticipated the particular promptings of a call?’ (Chapter 11.)

### 18

By this difference among the beginnings of good things,

[Note: [Col. 1809] In place of *bonorum*—‘of good things’—later editions have *quorumdam*—‘of certain persons.’]

therefore, he attempts to prove that some people can do without God’s help through free will what others cannot do unless God cooperates; and he wants this to be understood from the slower obedience of some and the more eager assent of others.

As though, where hard unbelief submits to God and suddenly yields to the Gospel which it had long opposed, the right hand of the Most High were at work bringing about the human being’s change (Psalm 76:11); but where a willing hearer embraces a calm exhortation or mere report without hesitation or distrust,

[Note: [Col. 1809] Thus the Corbie manuscript and the Mainz edition. Later editions read: ‘after a calm exhortation, [he embraces] only true morals without any hesitation,’ and so forth.]

the goodness of such conversion were merely a matter of human will.

As though the power of God drew to the Son only those whom he had either rebuked with his voice, crushed with punishment, or made to tremble with fear, while he applied none of his power to the minds of those who ran toward the promises of their Redeemer with joyful hope and eager desire.

But the Truth says: ‘No one comes to me unless the Father who sent me draws him’ (John 6:44). If, therefore, no one comes unless drawn, all who come in whatever manner are drawn.

The contemplation of the elements, then, and the perfectly ordered beauty of all that is in them, draws people to God. ‘For his invisible attributes are understood and perceived from the creation of the world through the things that have been made’ (Romans 1:20).

The narrators of past events draw them; in recounting the praises of the Lord, his powers, and his wonders which he performed, they inflame the mind of the hearer (Psalm 77:4).

Fear draws: ‘For the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom’ (Proverbs 1:7).

Joy draws: ‘I rejoiced in the things that were said to me: We shall go into the house of the Lord’ (Psalm 121:1).

Desire draws: ‘My soul longs and faints for the courts of the Lord’ (Psalm 83:3).

[Col. 1810] Pleasures draw:

[Note: [Col. 1810] Later editions read: ‘The delight of reading draws.’]

‘How sweet are your words to my palate, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth’ (Psalm 118:103).

[Note: [Col. 1809] Thus the old Corbie codex; the Mainz edition does not differ, except that it has *relationes*—‘reports’—rather than *relatores*—‘narrators.’ Later editions read: ‘The knowledge of past events draws, and the reports of divine works inflame the mind of the hearer,’ and so forth.]

And who could perceive or recount through what emotions God’s visitation leads the human mind, so that it follows what it was fleeing, loves what it hated, and hungers for what it found distasteful; so that, by a sudden and marvelous transformation, what had been closed to it becomes open, what was burdensome becomes light, what was bitter becomes sweet, and what was obscure becomes luminous?

Yet all these things are worked by one and the same Spirit, distributing to each as he wills (1 Corinthians 12:11). For God, who said that light should shine out of darkness, has shone in our hearts, for the illumination of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Christ Jesus (2 Corinthians 4:6)—that is, in the manifestation of his Son, who is in the glory of the Father.

[Note: [Col. 1810] The Corbie manuscript and the Mainz edition have *in faciem*—‘in the face’; later editions have *in facie*—‘in the face.’]

[Note: [Col. 1810] Later editions have *in sinu Patris*—‘in the bosom of the Father.’]

### 19

The one, therefore, who illumined the heart of Matthew the tax collector and of Paul, then a persecutor of the Church, also illumined the heart of Zacchaeus and the heart of the thief crucified with the Lord.

Otherwise, was the Lord’s voice idle when he graciously addressed Zacchaeus, who was seeking to see who Jesus was, saying, ‘Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, because today I must stay in your house’? Did he not prepare the mind of the man whose hospitality he had chosen?

Finally, when everyone murmured because he had gone in to lodge with a sinful man, and Zacchaeus, already doing penance, promised to give half of his possessions to the poor and to repay fourfold whatever he had defrauded, the Lord said:

‘Today salvation has come to this house, because he too is a son of Abraham.’

And, so that the cause of this salvation might not remain concealed, he added:

‘For the Son of Man came to save and seek what had perished’ (Luke 19:2–10).

Thus, when we recognized that the man had been saved, we might know that he had been anticipated by the one who sought him.

In the justification of the thief also, even if no indications of grace at work were understood, would we not receive him, together with all believers, as one who had been drawn, since the Lord says:

‘All things have been handed over to me by my Father’ (ibid. 10:22);

and:

‘When I have been lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things to myself’ (John 12:32)?

Among all things, the confession of the thief himself teaches that he too was either handed over or drawn. After he had for some time blasphemed Jesus Christ, he was suddenly changed and said:

‘Lord, remember me when you come into your kingdom’ (Luke 23:42).

But let blessed Paul the Apostle instruct us how such a diversity of contending voices arose in one human being, and let him say:

‘No one speaking in the Spirit of God says, “Anathema to Jesus”; and no one can say, “Lord Jesus,” except in the Holy Spirit’ (1 Corinthians 12:3).

Thus we do not doubt that, in the will of the same person, what he blasphemed came from himself, while what he believed came from the Holy Spirit.

In vain, therefore, did this disputant attempt to fit the argument of his definition to the inscrutable variety of one grace, so that one portion of those justified might be believed to come to Christ solely through the movements of their own will, while another portion, resisting, might be dragged and compelled against its will. For it is God who works all things in all people (ibid., 6), whether he wishes to draw some in one way and others in another; no one comes to him unless he is drawn in some manner.

## CHAPTER VIII

### 20

After this he added testimonies from sacred history, by which he showed that observance of God’s commandments and the completion of the virtues should be attributed to divine grace. This we also most readily confess.

He recalled the examples of Balaam, whom God transformed from wishing to curse Israel into words of blessing (Numbers 23); of Abimelech, who was not permitted to sin against Rebecca

[Note: [Col. 1810] Later editions have ‘Sarah.’]

(Genesis 26); and of Joseph, sold by his brothers, whose evil intention God turned to good (ibid. 37–50).

Then he returns to confirming his definition, so that free will—which he says joins itself to grace—may, as far as it lies in his power, be removed from one part of the human race and established in another, saying:

‘For these two things—that is, grace and free will—seem indeed to be opposed to each other; but both are in harmony. And we understand by the reasoning of piety that we ought to accept both together, lest, by taking one of them away from humanity, we appear to have departed from the rule of ecclesiastical faith’ (Chapter 11).

### 21

The rule of ecclesiastical faith is proclaimed by the Apostle:

[Note: [Col. 1811] Later editions read: ‘The ecclesiastical rule is.’]

‘No one can say, “Lord Jesus Christ,” except in the Holy Spirit’ (1 Corinthians 12:3).

The rule of ecclesiastical faith is:

‘What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?’ (ibid. 4:7).

The rule of ecclesiastical faith is:

‘By the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace toward me was not empty; but I labored more than all of them—not I, however, but the grace of God that is with me’ (ibid. 15:10);

and:

‘I received mercy so that I might be faithful’ (ibid. 7:25).

The rule of ecclesiastical faith is:

‘We have this treasure in earthen vessels, so that the surpassing power may belong to God and not come from us’ (2 Corinthians 4:7).

The rule of ecclesiastical faith is:

‘You have been saved by grace through faith, and this is not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not from works, so that no one may boast’ (Ephesians 2:8–9).

The rule of ecclesiastical faith is:

‘In nothing be terrified by your adversaries; this is for them a sign of destruction, but for you of salvation—and this is from God. For it has been granted to you on behalf of Christ not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him’ (Philippians 1:28).

The rule of ecclesiastical faith is:

‘Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling; for God is the one who works in us both to will and to work, according to his good will’ (ibid. 2:12).

The rule of ecclesiastical faith is:

‘Not that we are competent to think anything from ourselves, as though from ourselves; rather, our sufficiency is from God’ (2 Corinthians 3:5).

The Lord confirms this rule, saying:

‘No one can come to me unless it has been given to him by my Father’; and, ‘Everything that the Father gives me will come to me’ (John 6:66, 37);

and:

‘Without me you can do nothing’; and, ‘You did not choose me, but I chose you’ (ibid. 15:5, 16);

and:

‘No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son wishes to reveal him’ (Matthew 11:27);

and:

‘Just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he wishes’ (John 5:21);

and:

‘Blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah, because flesh and blood did not reveal this to you, but my Father who is in heaven’ (Matthew 16:17).

### 22

By this rule no human will is taken away, because the power of grace does not work in wills so that they cease to exist, but so that from evil they become good, and from unbelieving they become faithful; and so that what in themselves was darkness may become light in the Lord; what was dead may be given life; what lay fallen may be raised; and what had perished may be found.

We believe that the grace of the Savior works this in absolutely all human beings who are rescued from the power of darkness and transferred into the kingdom of the Son of God’s love, without exception of persons.

For, just as this same author defined plausibly, though not firmly, we say and defend that the beginning not only of actions but also of good thoughts is from God. He inspires in us the beginnings of holy will and grants us the strength and opportunity to carry out what we rightly desire.

‘Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights’ (James 1:17), who both begins what is good and carries it out and brings it to completion in us.

If the author had remained in this position, he would not have exceeded the ecclesiastical rule. He would neither have been hostile to free will nor ungrateful toward God’s grace.

[Note: [Col. 1811] The same editions have *offensus*—‘offended’—instead of *infensus*—‘hostile.’ The Corbie and Mainz editions rightly have *infensus*: he appears, that is, to remove free will as far as lies in his power.]

But when he says that one of these two things operated in Paul and Matthew and the other in Zacchaeus and the thief, he does not understand that in the former he has taken away free will, and in the latter grace.

## CHAPTER IX

### 23

Then he added:

‘For when he sees us turning our will toward the good,

[Note: [Col. 1811] Thus the Corbie manuscript and the Mainz edition. Later editions have *deflectere*—‘turning away.’]

he comes to meet us, directs us, and strengthens us. “As soon as he hears the voice of your cry, he will answer you” (Isaiah 30:19); and, “Call upon me,” he says, “in the day of your tribulation, and I will rescue you, and you will glorify me” (Psalm 49:15).’

Who does not see that this doctrine assigns to free will a merit by which grace is anticipated, so that grace serves it by paying what is owed rather than conferring a gift? This definition was condemned at the synod of the bishops of Palestine, even with Pelagius anathematizing it.

In the one who begins to will what is good and desires to depart from iniquity and error, we confess that God’s grace itself is at work. For:

‘The steps of a man are directed by the Lord, and he will take pleasure in his way’ (Psalm 36:23);

and:

‘Every person seems righteous to himself, but the Lord directs the hearts’ (Proverbs 21:2);

and:

‘The steps of a man are directed by the Lord; but how can a mortal understand his ways?’ (ibid. 20:24);

and as the Apostle says:

‘You did not receive the spirit of slavery again into fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, “Abba, Father”’ (Romans 8:15).

[Note: [Col. 1812] The editions have *in timore*—‘in fear.’ The Corbie manuscript has *in timorem*—‘into fear,’ in accordance with the Greek, *eis phobon*.]

### 24

After this he continues and says:

‘For one must not believe that God made a human being of such a kind that he would never will or be able to do good. Otherwise, he did not grant him free will, if he granted him only the ability and desire to will evil, but neither the desire nor the ability to will good. And how will that sentence of the Lord, pronounced after the transgression of the first man, stand: “Behold, Adam has become like one of us, knowing good and evil” (Genesis 3:22)? For one must not think that he had previously been such a person as was wholly ignorant of good. Otherwise, we would have to admit that he was formed as some irrational and senseless animal; and that is altogether absurd and wholly foreign to the Catholic faith.

‘Indeed, according to the judgment of the wisest Solomon, “God made the human being upright” (Ecclesiastes 7:30), that is, so that he might continually enjoy the knowledge of good; but they themselves sought many inventions. For “they became,” as it is said, “knowing good and evil.” Adam therefore acquired after the transgression the knowledge of evil, which he had not possessed; but he did not lose the knowledge of good, which he had received’ (Chapter 12).

### 25

There can be no doubt that the first human being was created upright and free from every vice, and that the nature of all human beings was created together in him. He received free will of such a kind that, if he did not abandon God who was helping him, he could remain, because he wished to, in the good things he had received by nature; and, through the merit of voluntary perseverance, could reach that blessedness in which he would neither wish nor be able to fall into worse things.

But by that same free will, through which he remained good for as long as he wished, he departed from the law appointed for him. He did not fear the punishment of death announced to him, but abandoned God and followed the devil, rebelling against the Lord his Savior and obeying his murderous enemy.

Adam therefore existed, and in him we all existed; Adam perished, and in him we all perished.

[Note: Ambrose, *Commentary on Luke*, book 7, on Luke 15.]

Blessed Ambrose said this no less truly than the Truth itself truly said:

‘The Son of Man came to seek and save what had perished’ (Luke 19:10).

For in the ruin of that universal transgression, neither the substance nor the will of human nature was taken away; rather, the light and beauty of the virtues were stripped from it by the fraud of the envious one.

Once it had lost the things by which it could reach the eternal and imperishable incorruption of body and soul, what remained to it except what belongs to temporal life, which is wholly condemnation and punishment?

Therefore those born in Adam must be reborn in Christ, lest anyone be found in that generation which perished. For if Adam’s descendants naturally acted in those virtues in which Adam existed before sin, they would not be by nature children of wrath (Ephesians 2:3); they would not be darkness (ibid. 5:8), nor under the power of darkness (Colossians 1:13). Finally, they would not need the Savior’s grace, since they would not be good without cause and would not be deprived of the reward of righteousness, possessing those good things whose loss caused our first parents to deserve exile from paradise.

But now, since no one can escape eternal death without the sacrament of rebirth, does it not become perfectly clear from the uniqueness of this remedy into what profound evil the nature of the whole human race has been plunged through the transgression of the one in whom all sinned, and through whom they lost whatever he lost?

He first lost faith; he lost self-restraint; he lost love; he was stripped of wisdom and understanding; he lacked counsel and fortitude; and, impiously pursuing higher things, he was cast down from knowledge of the truth and from the piety of obedience. Nor was even fear itself left to him, by which he might have guarded himself from the forbidden things through fear of punishment, since he did not refrain from them through love of righteousness.

[Note: [Col. 1813] Thus the Corbie manuscript and the Mainz edition. Later editions have *qui abstinebat amore justitiae*—‘who refrained from them through love of righteousness,’ without the negative particle.]

Free will, then—that is, the spontaneous desire for what pleases it—when it grew weary of using the good things it had received and, as the supports of its happiness became worthless to it, directed an insane desire toward the experience of transgression, drank the poison of all vices and saturated the whole nature of the human being with the drunkenness of its intemperance.

From then on, before digesting the deadly crudity by eating the flesh of the Son of Man and drinking his blood, the memory totters, judgment errs, and one’s steps falter.

[Note: [Col. 1813] Elsewhere, *labitur*—‘totters.’] The human being is in no way capable of choosing and desiring that good of which he voluntarily deprived himself, because just as he was able to fall without God’s impelling him, so he cannot rise without God’s raising him.

### 26

It was therefore not rightly said:

‘One must not believe that God made a human being of such a kind that he would never will or be able to do good.’

As though we were saying that this weakness of humanity was created by the Creator, rather than contracted by humanity as the penalty of sin.

Whoever therefore thinks it follows that, if free will is said to have been blinded, the blindness itself must be referred to the author of nature, wishes to persuade us that free will is as sound in Adam’s descendants as it was in Adam before sin. We regard this as wholly foreign to the Catholic faith.

For what has been injured by sin, if that has not been injured from which sin arises?

Unless perhaps it is said that punishment, but not guilt, passed over into Adam’s descendants. That is altogether falsely said—and perhaps for this reason it is not said. For it is exceedingly impious to think this of God’s justice: that he wished those who were free from transgression to be condemned together with the guilty.

Guilt is therefore evident where punishment is not hidden, and participation in sin is proved by sharing in punishment, so that what belongs to human misery derives not from the Creator’s institution but from the Judge’s retribution.

### 27

It was also ineptly stated, and contrary to the sense of all interpreters, when he joined the following to his proof of the soundness of free will:

‘And how will that sentence of the Lord, pronounced after the transgression of the first man, stand: “Behold, Adam has become like one of us, knowing good and evil”?’

As though the devil had made a true promise to Adam, and Adam had advanced by transgressing God’s command into likeness with God, and God had declared that this had been granted to him. In those words, however, what is signified is rather what he failed to attain: having entered upon the path of pride, he lost what he had, while desiring what he had not received.

Nor is the sin any less in the conclusion of this interpretation, where it is said:

‘Adam therefore acquired after the transgression the knowledge of evil, which he had not possessed; but he did not lose the knowledge of good, which he had received.’

Adam possessed the knowledge of good when he faithfully kept God’s good and holy commandment, and was righteous, remaining in the image of his Creator and not forgetting his law.

But after he sold himself—that is, the image and temple of God—to his deceiver,

[Note: [Col. 1813] Later editions have *subdidit*—‘subjected’—instead of *vendidit*—‘sold.’]

he lost the knowledge of good because he lost a good conscience. Iniquity drove out righteousness; pride destroyed humility; desire overthrew self-restraint; unbelief snatched away faith; captivity removed freedom. No portion of the virtues could remain there, where so great a crowd of vices had rushed in.

For:

‘No one can serve two masters’ (Luke 16:13);

and:

‘Whoever commits sin is a slave of sin’ (John 8:34);

and:

‘By whatever anyone is overcome, to that he is enslaved’ (2 Peter 2:19).

No one serves except with some freedom, and no one is free except with some servitude. The Apostle says:

‘For when you were slaves of sin, you were free with respect to righteousness. What fruit did you have then in those things of which you are now ashamed? For the end of those things is death. But now, having been freed from sin and made slaves of God, you have your fruit in sanctification, and the end is eternal life’ (Romans 6:20–22).

Whoever therefore serves the devil is free in relation to God; but whoever, having been freed, serves God is free in relation to the devil.

Thus it becomes clear that an evil freedom could be possessed through the defect of the human will, but that good freedom could not be received without the help of the liberator.

[Note: [Col. 1814] The Corbie manuscript and the Mainz edition read *voluntatem*—‘will’—instead of *libertatem*—‘freedom.’]

## CHAPTER X

### 28

But lest this calamity of the first man appear to have passed into his offspring, this teacher adds that the soundness of the nature of all human beings is proved by the example of the nations, and says:

‘Finally, that the human race did not lose the knowledge of good after Adam’s transgression is most clearly declared even by the Apostle’s judgment, who says:

“When the Gentiles, who do not have the law, naturally do what belongs to the law, these, although they do not have the law, are a law to themselves. They show the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience bearing witness, and their thoughts accusing or even defending them among themselves, on the day when God will judge the hidden things of human beings”’ (Romans 2:14–15).

### 29

If the Apostle is speaking of those who were called from uncircumcision and, although far away, were brought near (Ephesians 2:13), believing in the one who once had not shown them mercy but now shows them mercy (1 Peter 2:10); and if he is speaking of the one who justifies circumcision by faith and uncircumcision through faith (Romans 3:30), who created the two in himself, destroyed the dividing wall of hostility between Jews and Gentiles, and made peace in one new human being (Ephesians 2:14–17), concluding all things under unbelief so that the promise might be given to believers through faith in Jesus Christ (Galatians 3:22)—if, I say, the Apostle is speaking of these people, in whose hearts God writes the New Testament with his finger, that is, with the Holy Spirit, so that they may naturally fulfill the fullness of the law and the works of love, their nature having been restored and renewed, then how does this novelty of an exceedingly proud interpretation receive any support from it, when the reconciliation of enemies can be attributed only to the grace of the Mediator?

‘For all have sinned and lack the glory of God, being justified freely by his grace’ (Romans 3:23–24).

Therefore grace is the glory of God, not the merit of the one who has been freed.

‘For who has given to him first, so that recompense might be made to him?’ (ibid. 11:35).

No good work proceeds from the dead; no righteousness proceeds from the impious. Their entire salvation is gratuitous. Therefore it is the glory of God, so that whoever boasts may boast in the one whose glory he needed.

### 30

But if—and this is what the disputant here more strongly wishes to be understood—these words are spoken about those who were alien to Christian grace and, by their own judgment, established certain practices resembling the commandments of the law, understanding that the customs of cities and the harmony of peoples could not otherwise be maintained unless rewards were assigned to right actions and punishments to sins, just as Wisdom itself is said to have spoken to God:

‘From the mouth of the Most High I came forth, and I held primacy in every nation; I sought rest in Jacob, and found it’ (Ecclesiasticus 24:5–11).

[Note: [Col. 1814] Later editions omit this citation from Ecclesiasticus. It is found in the Corbie manuscript and the Mainz edition.]

then who could doubt that this wisdom survived in the human race for the usefulness of temporal life from the remnants of the nature created by God?

For if the rational mind did not retain enough vigor even to organize earthly affairs, nature would not have been damaged but extinguished.

[Col. 1815]

Yet even if this nature excels in the highest arts and possesses mastery of all the disciplines of mortal learning, it cannot justify itself. For it uses its goods badly; in them it is convicted of impiety and uncleanness because it lacks the worship of the true God, and by the very things through which it thinks to defend itself, it is accused.

Since, therefore, the Apostle declares that ‘no flesh is justified by works of the law’ (Romans 3:20), and that in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision has any power, but only a new creation (Galatians 6:15), why does this man equip the impious freedom of unbelievers with natural goods and wish to justify it by its own principles?

Why does he define the nakedness of transgressive knowledge as fit for the renewal of assailed antiquity?

[Note: [Col. 1815] Later editions have *miserae*—‘wretched’—instead of *lacessitae*—‘assailed’ or ‘provoked.’]

As though this knowledge, whether acquired from the remnants of nature or sought through instruction in the law,

[Note: [Col. 1815] The word *consecuta*—‘acquired’—is added here from the Corbie manuscript and the Mainz edition.]

could, by its own perception, bring it about that what we know ought to be done we would also love to do; or as though there were any movement of good will except one created by the outpouring of love through the Holy Spirit.

‘Without faith it is impossible to please’ (Hebrews 11:6);

[Note: [Col. 1815] Later editions have *placere Deo*—‘to please God.’ *Deo* is absent from the Corbie manuscript and the Mainz edition. Augustine sometimes omits it, and it is also absent from the Apostle’s Greek wording.]

and:

‘Everything that is not from faith is sin’ (Romans 14:23);

and:

‘In Christ Jesus neither circumcision has any power nor uncircumcision, but faith working through love’ (Galatians 5:6).

## CHAPTER XI

### 31

After this, in concluding the testimonies by which he wished to prove that those who are called deaf and blind through prophetic rebuke can, by the capacity of nature, open their ears to hear and their eyes to see—as though the Lord did not speak of these same people when he said, ‘I will give them another heart, and I will give them a new spirit; I will remove the heart of stone from their flesh and give them a heart of flesh, so that they may walk in my commandments, observe my judgments, and perform them’ (Ezekiel 11:19–20; 36:26–27)—he adds and says:

‘Finally, to signify that the possibility of good exists in them, when rebuking the Pharisees he says: “Why do you not even judge for yourselves what is good?”’ (Luke 12:57).

[Note: [Col. 1815] The Corbie manuscript and the Mainz edition have *quod justum est*—‘what is just.’]

‘He certainly would not have said this to them unless he knew that they could discern what is equitable by natural judgment.’

He now attributes not only the will of good but also the possibility of good to free will, as though understanding were demanded of them and justice required of them precisely because they could produce these things from the goods of nature without God’s gifts.

Yet these things are commanded to a human being so that, from the very command by which what he has received is enjoined upon him, he may recognize that he lost it through his own fault; and so that he may not regard the demand as unjust because he is not capable of returning what he owes, but may flee from the letter that kills to the Spirit that gives life, and seek from grace the capacity he does not find in nature.

If he does this, God’s mercy is great; if he does not, the punishment of sin is just.

32. Finally, to complete the foregoing discussion, he pronounces a definitive rule, saying: “We must therefore take care lest, by referring all the merits of the saints to God, we ascribe to human nature nothing except what is evil and perverse” (Chapter 12). What could any disciple of theirs have defined more clearly or explicitly in accordance with the theory of Pelagius and Coelestius? They say, “God’s grace is given according to our merits”; and they likewise say, “God’s grace is not given for each individual act.” Here, within a single sentence, he has combined both blasphemies, saying: “We must take care lest, by referring all the merits of the saints to God, we ascribe to human nature nothing except what is evil and perverse.” He therefore wants there to be many merits belonging properly to human beings, which were not bestowed by the generosity of grace, and for which certain gifts from above are owed in order to increase their natural riches. He wants us to receive God’s grace not for each individual act, and consequently not always to pray for every [Col. 1816] good work. It will therefore follow that we should believe that there is no merit in God’s gifts, since the one whom God always assists in everything is without merit; or, if some merits are also assigned to those things which God bestows, it must likewise be acknowledged that these too could have been acquired by one’s own ability, and therefore that we ought to be assisted in certain matters so that, through grace, what was not impossible by nature may become more possible.

Behold: even in this brief handful of words there is already a numerous chain of not merely two but many impieties. If it is examined with the more scrupulous discrimination of careful inquiry, it will be shown to have been released in no respect from the chain of condemned error.

## CHAPTER XII

33. But lest we seem to proceed by suspicions and to probe the hiding places of his meaning beyond his words, let what follows show what is added to what we already know. At the beginning of his discussion he had said: “Not only the beginning of actions but also of good thoughts is from God: he inspires in us the beginnings of holy willing, and grants the ability and opportunity to carry out the things we rightly desire.” Now, wishing to prove that religious thoughts and holy purposes, conceived without any inspiration from God, can arise from natural wisdom, he introduces Solomon’s words:

“My father David wished to build a house for the name of the Lord, the God of Israel; and the Lord said to my father David, ‘Because you conceived in your heart to build a house for my name, you did well in having this in mind; nevertheless, you shall not build the house for my name’” (1 Kings 8:17–19).

Then, to show how this should be understood, the author himself adds:

“Was this thought and this plan of King David to be judged good and from God, or evil and from man? For if that thought was good and from God, why is its fulfillment denied him by the one by whom it was inspired? But if it was evil and from man, why is it praised by the Lord? It remains, therefore, that it should be believed both good and from man. In the same way we can judge our own thoughts each day: for it was not granted to David alone to think something good from himself, nor are we denied the natural ability ever to understand or think anything good” (Chapter 12).

34. This testimony and argument in no way proves that pious thoughts arise solely from free choice and not from God’s inspiration. David’s will—which was certainly good—is not for that reason to be considered unrelated to God, because the Lord wished the temple to be built not by him but by his son. We must therefore ask from what spirit the impulse of this will proceeded: surely from that Spirit of God in whom he said:

“If I enter the tent of my house, if I climb upon the bed where I lie; if I give sleep to my eyes, or slumber to my eyelids, or rest to my temples, until I find a place for the Lord, a dwelling for the God of Jacob” (Psalm 131:3–5).

When the Prophet longed for this, he did not fail to understand that the true and perfect temple was to be founded by the one who, while being the Son of God, also became the son of David; and who, when he saw the temple built by Solomon, said: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” He was speaking about the temple of his body (John 2:19, 21).

Thus, in order that this temple might be prefigured—the temple that was to be established in Christ and in the Church—it was rightly not David but David’s son who was chosen for its construction [Note: [Col. 1816] Later editions read “for its building.” The Corbie manuscript and the Moguntia edition read “for its construction.”], so that through the Son of Man the Son of God and of man might be signified; and through the destructible temple the incorruptible dwelling might be indicated. To construct the image of this temple, David’s will was approved, but the work was transferred to the one whose person corresponded more suitably to that image. Thus David’s willing was from God, and Solomon’s doing was from God.

35. To make this clearer by examples, let us inquire where God did not wish something to be done that human beings wished to do with God’s approval. The Lord commanded the Apostles, saying: [Col. 1817]

“Go, go forth and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, and teaching them to observe all things that I have commanded you” (Matthew 28:19–20).

When the Apostles heard this, they certainly did not receive mere words through bodily sounds only in their outward ears; rather, through the power of the living Word [Note: [Col. 1817] So Corbie and Moguntia. Later editions read “of the commanding Word.”], an unquenchable flame of charity was kindled in their hearts, by which they most ardently desired to preach the gospel of Christ to all nations. But when they were forbidden to speak the word in Asia, and when they attempted [Note: [Col. 1817] Corbie omits “when they attempted.”] to go into Bithynia, they were prevented by the Spirit of Jesus (Acts 16:6–7). Did they not have this desire from God, since they also wished to convert to the faith the hearts of those whom, by a hidden judgment, God did not then wish to hear the gospel?

Or when the Church prays daily for her enemies—that is, for those who do not yet believe in God—does she not do this from the Spirit of God? Who would say so, except one who does not do this, or who thinks that faith is not God’s gift? And yet what is sought for all is not obtained by all. Nor is there injustice in God, who often does not grant what he has given us to ask.

36. A good will, therefore—namely, the will by which one adheres to God—must not be denied to belong properly to man, but it must be confessed to have been conceived through God’s inspiration. For since no one is good except God alone (Luke 18:19), what kind of good can there be that has no good author?

Human nature, whose creator is God, retains even after transgression its substance, its form, its life, its senses, its reason, and the other goods of body and soul, which are not absent even from the wicked and vicious. But it does not possess in these things the perception of the true good—those goods that can ennoble mortal life but cannot bestow eternal life.

Nor is it unknown how much the Greek schools [Note: [Col. 1817] Moguntia reads “how much of Greek”; Corbie reads “how much Greece.”], Roman eloquence, and the inquiry of the whole world accomplished, through the most intense studies and the most excellent talents, in seeking the highest good: nothing except that they “became futile in their thoughts, and their senseless heart was darkened” (Romans 1:21), because they used themselves as guides in coming to know the truth.

If, then, someone, ashamed of the wretched vanities and deceptive madnesses in which he had taken delight, understands that everything he had embraced as light and life is darkness and death, and tries to withdraw from these things, this conversion is not from him, although it does not occur without him; nor does he strive toward the beginnings of salvation by his own power. Rather, the hidden and powerful grace of God accomplishes this. Removing the ashes of earthly opinions and dead works, it stirs the log buried beneath the heart and sets it aflame with the desire for truth—not in order to subdue a man against his will, but to make him desirous of submission; not to drag one who is ignorant, but to go before one who understands and follows.

Free choice remains—the free choice that God certainly created together with the human being—and it is changed from its vanities and desires, into which it had slipped by neglecting God’s law, not by itself but by the Creator. Thus whatever is restored for the better in it is neither without the one who is healed, nor from anyone other than the one who heals: we are his new creation and new workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, “which God prepared beforehand, that we should walk in them” (Ephesians 2:10).

## CHAPTER XIII

37. Let us now see how far the intention of the disputant proceeds:

“There can be no doubt, therefore, that the seeds of virtues are naturally present in every soul, implanted by the Creator’s gift; but unless these are aroused by God’s assistance, they cannot reach the growth of perfection, because, according to the blessed Apostle, ‘neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth’ (1 Corinthians 3:7). That freedom of choice lies open to man in either direction is also taught most plainly by that book called *The Shepherd*, [Col. 1818] in which two angels are said to adhere to each one of us, namely a good one and an evil one; and the choice rests with man, so that he may choose which one to follow. For this reason free choice always remains in man, so that he may either neglect or love the grace of God” (Chapter 12).

If there can be no doubt that “the seeds of virtues are naturally present in every soul, implanted by the Creator’s gift,” then only Adam transgressed, and no one sinned in his sin (Romans 5:12); we were conceived in no iniquities, and our mothers bore us in no offenses (Psalm 51:5); we were not by nature children of wrath (Ephesians 2:3), nor were we under the power of darkness (Colossians 1:13)—we who, with virtues naturally remaining in us, were born instead as children of peace and light.

Far be it from the minds of the faithful that they should be ensnared by the deceptive fraud of a false doctrine. Virtues cannot dwell together with vices. For what partnership, the Apostle says, is there between righteousness and iniquity? Or what fellowship does light have with darkness? (2 Corinthians 6:14).

Virtue is, in the first place, God himself; for to possess virtue is nothing other than to be virtue. When we partake of him, Christ dwells in us—he who is the virtue of God and the wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24). Faith, hope, charity, self-control, understanding, counsel, fortitude, and the remaining virtues dwell in us as well. But when we depart from this good, everything contrary arises in us from ourselves. When beauty departs, what takes its place except deformity? When wisdom leaves, what remains except folly? When righteousness does not reign, what dominates except iniquity?

38. The seeds of virtues, therefore, which were implanted by the Creator’s gift, were overturned by the transgression of our first parent; nor can they be possessed unless they are restored by the one who gave them. Human nature is capable of being reformed by its maker, and is capable of recovering the goods it possessed, so that through the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, it may recover, in that very part which remains to it, what it lost.

What remains to it is the rational mind, which is not virtue but the dwelling place of virtue. For through participation in wisdom, righteousness, and mercy, we become wise, righteous, and merciful; we do not become wisdom, righteousness, or mercy.

These goods can nevertheless flow back into the rational faculty, even though our rational nature is occupied by vices and, when we transgress, an unclean spirit has invaded God’s temple. They can return through him who casts out the ruler of this world (John 12:31), who binds the strong man and carries off his goods (Mark 3:27), and who, after the spirit of this world has been driven away, gives the Spirit who is from God, so that we may know the things that have been given to us by God (1 Corinthians 2:12). But whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him (Romans 8:9).

39. I think that he is deceived by a likeness to the truth and mistaken in the appearance of false virtues, since he judges that those goods which can be possessed only as God’s gift are also found in the minds of the impious. He does so because many of them pursue justice, temperance, self-control, and benevolence. They do not possess all these things without reason or benefit, and they gain from them much honor and glory in this life; but because in these pursuits they serve not God but the devil, although they receive a temporal reward from empty praise, they nevertheless do not belong to the truth of those blessed virtues.

Thus it is most plainly evident that no virtue dwells in the minds of the impious. All their works are unclean and polluted, since they possess wisdom that is not spiritual but animal, not heavenly but earthly, not Christian but demonic, not from the Father of lights but from the prince of darkness. Even those things which they would possess only if God gave them, they subject to the one who was the first to depart from God [Note: [Col. 1818] So the Corbie manuscript and the Moguntia edition. Later editions read: “while through those very things which they would possess only if God gave them, they are subjected to him,” and so forth.].

40. When he therefore says that “the seeds of virtues are naturally present in every soul without any work of grace,” what is he laboring [Col. 1819] to demonstrate except that, from these seeds, certain sprouts [Note: [Col. 1819] Corbie and Moguntia read “seeds.”] of preceding merits spring forth before God’s grace?
