Finally, to appear to attribute something to grace, he says: “These seeds cannot reach the growth of perfection unless they are aroused by God’s assistance.” Thus God’s assistance is made to consist in exhortation and teaching, while the mind, rich in the seeds of virtues, uses the ability it possesses and needs help only to grasp the heights of those virtues whose beginnings it knows to be present within itself.

According to this man, therefore, the human soul will be built into God’s temple without receiving the foundation “other than which no one can lay,” which is Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 3:11). But when does this foundation begin [Note: [Col. 1819] The Moguntia edition reads “is received.”], unless when faith is generated in the heart of the hearer? If faith was naturally present, then nothing began there; something was merely built upon it. The unbeliever, who had faith before he believed, would therefore be superfluous.

The same can be said of the beginnings of other virtues: grace ought to increase them because they exist, not give them because they are absent. But all the words of the Holy Scriptures teach us something else.

We read that “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Proverbs 1:7), and we read that this virtue is God’s gift: “The fear of God has placed itself above all things; blessed is the man to whom it has been given to possess the fear of God” (Sirach 25:14–15). Since, then, the fear of God is the beginning of wisdom, what virtue can be possessed without wisdom, for which fear is the beginning?

The blessed Apostle Peter says: “Grace and peace be multiplied to you in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has now given us, by his divine power, all things that pertain to life and godliness” (2 Peter 1:2–4). Does he say, “He has aroused within us, by his assistance, the seeds of virtues that we naturally possessed as implanted in us”? No. He says: “He has now given us all things that pertain to life and godliness.”

By saying this, what beginning of virtue did he place in nature that was not bestowed by the one who bestowed everything? For this reason the blessed Paul also says: “What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Corinthians 4:7).

41. We therefore possess all things that pertain to life and godliness not through nature, which has been corrupted, but through grace, by which nature is restored. Nor should we think that the beginnings of virtues exist in natural treasures because many praiseworthy qualities are also found in the abilities of the impious. These qualities certainly arise from nature, but since those who possess them have departed from the one who created nature, they cannot be virtues.

What is truly illuminated by light is light, and what lacks that same light is night. “The wisdom of this world is foolishness with God” (1 Corinthians 3:19). Thus what is thought to be virtue is vice, since what is thought to be wisdom is foolishness.

But how can one who glories in the seeds of natural virtues that he extols [Note: [Col. 1819] The Corbie manuscript and Moguntia edition read: “how can one who thinks himself to abound in the seeds of natural virtues, which he himself boasts are magnificent.”] submit his virtues to the teaching that says, “If anyone among you thinks that he is wise, let him become foolish, so that he may become wise” (ibid., 18), and: “Since the world did not know God through wisdom in the wisdom of God, it pleased God through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe” (ibid., 1:21)?

What could consider that presumption of knowledge and wisdom more inept, or more laughable, unless the Spirit of God has subdued the contempt of the proud and, by the power of his grace, destroyed those arguments that resisted the unknown truth with canine eloquence? Then the soil of the heart, furrowed [Note: [Col. 1819] Corbie and Moguntia read “furrowed” with a masculine plural form, referring to the furrowers rather than the soil.] beforehand, may receive the seed of the word, and the cultivation of God’s field may produce fruits worthy of the eternal storehouses.

42. After that testimony of no authority, which he inserted into his discussion from the little book *The Shepherd*, in order to show that every human being is so entrusted to natural judgment and personal discernment amid the contrary persuasions of the good and evil [Col. 1820] angels [Note: [Col. 1820] We add “angel” from Corbie and Moguntia. See above, §37], that he receives no more protection from God than danger from the devil, he added a rule to his definition, saying:

“For this reason free choice always remains in man, so that he may either neglect or love the grace of God.”

Even in this statement—that “free choice always remains in man”—the matter is not entirely established. Many thousands of infants who are admitted into the kingdom of God, or excluded from the kingdom of God, receive or lose God’s grace without any exercise of their own will; and many who are utterly senseless and foolish in every respect are rescued from the bonds of eternal death through the sacrament of regeneration.

Let us nevertheless accept this statement as applying properly to those who are able to use free will. Is this freedom really so free that it possesses from itself only enough aversion to neglect God’s grace, and enough delight to love it? Did no spirit of noonday heat loosen the icy hardness of that ancient unbelief, and did the torpor of the bound mind grow warm from its own frost? When the Lord says, “I have come to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke 12:49), did no spark reach the cold heart, and did dead ash blaze into the flame of charity from itself?

Nothing of this kind happened in those who love this grace [Note: [Col. 1820] Later editions read “in those condemned by this grace.” Corbie and Moguntia read “in these lovers of grace,” so that this sentence and those immediately following are understood not as simple assertions but figuratively, by way of interrogation.], as happened to those who experienced it and said: “Was not our heart burning within us while we were with him on the road, and while he opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke 24:32).

Nor did that happen in the same way in the case of Lydia, the purple-seller of the city of Thyatira, who alone among the women to whom the Apostle preached there is then shown to have believed: “God opened her heart,” he says, “to attend to the things that were spoken by Paul” (Acts 16:14).

And is the soundness and capacity of free choice, according to this man, so great that people possess charity—the chief of all virtues—not as God’s gift but solely by their own will? What, then, is restored in the soul by its builder, or by what generosity of grace is it made more beautiful, if those things are proper to it without which the things bestowed cannot be beneficial?

But the Apostle, who declares that without charity neither the working of miracles, nor knowledge, nor faith, nor prophecy, nor the distribution of wealth, nor even the endurance of the most savage punishments is of benefit (1 Corinthians 13:2–3), does not remain silent about where charity itself is obtained:

“Because,” he says, “the charity of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Romans 5:5); and again: “Peace to the brothers, with charity and faith, from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ” (Ephesians 6:23).

Let the holy Apostle John also instruct us from where we began to share in this good:

“Beloved, let us love one another, because love is from God.”

And lest we suppose that love is said to be from God because this affection had been sown in human nature, he says a little later:

“Not because we loved God, but because he loved us”; and again: “Let us love God, because he first loved us” (1 John 4:7, and following).

Let human poverty therefore acknowledge that what is rightly said about any good is much more rightly said of the one without whom all goods are of no benefit:

“What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Corinthians 4:7).

## CHAPTER XIV

43. After this, having attributed to man before grace as much as it is most fruitful for him to possess through grace, [Col. 1821] he added certain perplexing and confused statements to demonstrate the strength of free choice; and concerning what he does with the powers already granted to him [Note: [Col. 1821] The Moguntia edition reads “virtues”], he wishes to reinforce what he defines as naturally present in him, so that what he has perfected through God’s assistance should be said to have begun through free choice.

But let us pass over these matters as tolerable, since we too say that free choice, through grace at work, conceives the inclination of a good will and the beginning of faith, so that through these gifts—which were given to it without any preceding merit—it may merit those things promised to the one who will work, always asking the one who said, “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5), for the ability to do something good.

Passing over these matters, then, let us reconsider what he stated concerning the sufferings of holy Job. For he says:

“We read that divine justice also made provision in Job, its most proven athlete, when the devil had demanded him for a single combat. For if he had confronted the enemy not by his own strength but under the protection of God’s grace alone, and if, supported solely by divine assistance and without any strength of patience of his own, he had endured those manifold masses and destructions of temptations, sought with the enemy’s entire cruelty, how could the devil not justly have repeated against him that slanderous cry which he had uttered before:

‘Does Job worship God for nothing? Have you not fenced him around, and his house, and all his possessions on every side? But take away your hand—that is, let him contend with me by his own strength—and see whether he will not bless you to your face’ (Job 1:9–11)?

But since, after the struggle, the slanderous enemy did not dare to repeat any such complaint, he confesses that he was overcome not by God’s strength but by Job’s.

It must nevertheless be believed that God’s grace was not wholly absent from him, since it granted the tempter as much power as it knew Job to have in resistance. Grace did not protect him from the enemy’s attack in such a way as to leave no place for human virtue; it merely ensured that the most violent enemy, by driving his soul into madness and depriving it of understanding, would not weigh him down with an unequal and unjust burden of conflict” (Chapter 14).

44. Who would believe that such things were proclaimed by Catholics among Catholics, unless they also read them written down which had often been defended in private conversations? Has the vision of understanding become so clouded in all human beings, and has the spirit of knowledge and piety departed from all the sons of the Church, that they are not ashamed to thrust such empty tales and such dishonorable lies [Note: [Col. 1821] Later editions omit “such empty tales.” The Moguntia edition rearranges the text: “let a serious man be ashamed to thrust upon the judgment of readers . . . lies,” etc.] upon the judgment of their readers?

Serious man, wise doctor, truthful teacher, give us again the Catholic definition with which, at the beginning of your discussion, you captivated our ears and minds. You had proclaimed in ecclesiastical language the Christian faith [Note: [Col. 1821] So Corbie and Moguntia. Later editions read “the Christian faith in ecclesiastical language.”]:

“Not only the beginning of actions but also of good thoughts is from God: he inspires in us the beginnings of holy willing, and grants the ability and opportunity to carry out the things we rightly desire. For every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights (James 1:17), who both inspires what is good and performs and completes it in us.”

By the solidity of this statement you had shattered all the contrivances of the enemy’s remaining forces. Why, after changing your profession, do you build up what you destroyed and attack what you defended? Why, abandoning the unconquerable fortress of truth, do you gradually rush toward the Pelagian precipices?

You had defined that neither the beginnings of holy thoughts, nor of pious wills, nor of good actions, come from us, but that all good things are generated in us by God’s inspiration and by the help of his grace, and brought to growth and perfection. Shortly afterward, however, you began trying to make the gifts of grace equal to free choice, in order to show that human beings could have from themselves the beginnings that you had assigned to God, saying: [Col. 1822]

“Because sometimes a human being can extend himself toward the desire for virtues by his own impulses, although he always needs to be assisted by the Lord”; and again:

“Even through the good of nature, which was granted by the Creator’s gift, the beginnings of good wills sometimes arise; yet unless they are directed by the Lord, they cannot reach the completion of the virtues.”

After this, in order to show that some are preceded by grace while locating in the prior merits of others the reason for receiving grace, you said:

“What depends on what is uncertain: whether God has mercy on us because we have supplied the beginning of a good will, or whether, because God has mercy, we attain the beginning of a good will.”

To prevent these two rules from remaining ambiguous, you took care to support each with examples that seemed suitable to you: confirming one by the compelled conversion of Paul and Matthew, and strengthening the other by the voluntary faith of Zacchaeus and the thief. You say that their desire was so violent “that they anticipated the special summons of vocation in seizing the kingdom of heaven.”

Then, as the discussion proceeded, in order to reveal the soundness of the inner man, you affirm that “Adam did indeed conceive a knowledge of evil that he did not possess, but did not lose the knowledge of good that he had received.”

And when you wished to prove this also by comparison with the impious, you went so far as to proclaim:

“We must take care lest, by referring all the merits of the saints to the Lord, we ascribe to human nature nothing except what is evil.”

And lest we believe that human nature had lost those virtues in Adam’s transgression, you defined the souls of all human beings as naturally as sound as the first man’s soul had been before sin, saying:

“There can be no doubt, therefore, that the seeds of virtues are naturally present in every soul, implanted by the Creator’s gift.”

When your definitions are considered, it is not hidden how far you have departed from the soundness of that statement in which, by falsely proclaiming what ought to be attributed to grace, you wished to win the judgment of Catholic ears. Once those ears had been made secure by the appearance of your preceding profession [Note: [Col. 1822] Corbie and Moguntia read “promise”], the statements that followed could easily creep in, if the first ones had pleased them.

## CHAPTER XV

45. But thus far, lest you should appear entirely to disagree with the rule you had established, you transferred the beginnings of virtues and merits from free choice to grace [Note: [Col. 1822] Later editions read “from grace to free choice, so that good desires themselves,” etc.] in such a way that you admitted that the voluntary impulses of those good desires could neither advance nor be perfected without God’s help [Note: [Col. 1822] Later editions read “you allowed”]; now, however, having removed God farther away and separated him from the support of man, you attribute such power to free choice that it not only steadfastly and calmly accepts the bitterest loss of manifold possessions and of an entire household, family, and circle of relationships all at once, but also overcomes, by the resolve of bare will, the unspeakable torments of its own body.

And so that there might be no doubt, given your argument, about this point, you set forth the example of holy Job, who contended without God’s protection against that conspicuous cruelty of diabolical savagery. You strive to prove your argument by saying that the most bloodthirsty enemy himself confessed that he had been overcome by Job’s strength, not the Lord’s, because he did not say that God’s grace had opposed him in the more severe conflict. It is as though that man ought to have been surrounded by heavenly protection in his losses and bereavements, but did not need assistance in the torments of his flesh and soul.

If, therefore, nothing more memorable is found among the palms of the saints, nothing more glorious, than this greatness of spirit—which is not overcome by the punishment of so many deaths inflicted upon every limb and upon all the limbs [Note: [Col. 1822] The Corbie manuscript reads “nothing more within the palms of the saints,” etc.]—and if you assert that it subsists solely through human virtue, what praise or merit will remain for free choice to obtain amid the pursuits of quiet and peace, when you have crowned it by its own strength at the end of so great a conflict?

46. I therefore ask you: when that man was being tested by the punishments [Col. 1823] we read about, does it seem to you that he had the Holy Spirit within him? If you say that he did, it is certain that God, whom he had not abandoned, assisted him. But if you say that the Holy Spirit had departed from him, his own prophetic speech refutes you, saying:

“For I know that my Redeemer lives, and on the last day I shall rise from the earth; and again I shall be clothed with my skin, and in my flesh I shall see God, whom I myself shall see, and my eyes shall behold, and not another: this hope of mine is stored in my bosom” (Job 19:25–27).

If this is rightly understood as a prophecy concerning the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, his resurrection as the firstfruits of those who sleep, and the hope of redemption placed in him for all the saints, it plainly appears that God’s grace did not depart from his temple. Even then the Lord was doing in this holy man what he later promised to do in his Apostles and martyrs, saying:

“When they hand you over, do not be anxious about how or what you should speak; for what you are to speak will be given to you in that hour. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matthew 10:19–20).

What of the fact that the same holy man, when replying to his foolish comforters, relied upon God’s help, saying: “The one who is mocked by his friend, as I am, will call upon the Lord, and he will hear him”?

Or did he not know that he had from God what he possessed—the God of whom he says, “With him are wisdom and strength; he possesses counsel and understanding,” and of whom he says, “In whose hand is the soul of every living thing and the spirit of all human flesh” (Job 12:4, 13, 10)?

And again he says:

“I await until my change comes: you will call, and I will answer you; you will extend your right hand to the work of your hands. You have indeed numbered my steps, but you spare [Note: [Col. 1823] Corbie and Moguntia read “sparing.”] my sins; you have sealed up my offenses as though for a certain age, but you have healed my iniquity” (Job 14:14–17).

The Lord, therefore, had not abandoned the one whom he was healing; nor had he withdrawn his assistance from the one to whom he was applying purifying remedies, by which he might shine more brightly.

47. To this endurance of sufferings, in which this holy man excelled, that one too had been prepared by the Lord who said, “Even though I walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me” (Ps. 22:4); and, “The salvation of the righteous is from the Lord, and he is their protector in the time of tribulation” (Ps. 36:39). To this endurance that one too had been prepared by the Lord who referred both believing in Christ and suffering for Christ back to Christ, saying, “Therefore, justified by faith, let us have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ; through whom we also have access [Note: [Col. 1823] Here the Moguntine edition adds, “through faith.”] to this grace in which we stand, and we glory in the hope of the glory of the children of God. And not only this, but we also glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation produces endurance, endurance probation, probation hope, and hope does not disappoint, because the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:1–5); and again, “Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation? Or distress? Or persecution? Or famine? Or nakedness? Or danger? Or the sword? As it is written, ‘For your sake we are put to death all day long; we are regarded as sheep for slaughter’; but in all these things we overcome through him who loved us” (ibid. 8:35–37). From whom the strength of this endurance descended, blessed Peter—and in him the whole Church—was learning from the voice of Truth itself, which said, “Behold, Satan has asked to sift you like wheat; but I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail” (Luke 22:31). Therefore, whoever does not fail in tribulations should not doubt that he is helped by him to whom the hearts of all the faithful cry out daily, “Do not lead us into temptation, but deliver us from evil” (Matt. 6:13). “For the Lord guards the souls of his servants; he will deliver them from the hand of sinners” (Ps. 96:10).

48. But when you say, “The grace of God should be understood not to have wholly departed from Job from the fact [Col. 1824] that God gave his tempter as much power to tempt as he knew Job possessed strength to resist,” would you not speak more rightly and truthfully if, where you said, “as much strength to resist as he knew him to possess,” you said instead, “as much strength to resist as he knew himself to have given him”? The correction of a single word would have moderated with some restraint that entire glory which you wished to assign to human powers, so that the marvelous patience displayed amid such great affliction would be attributed both to God’s help and to the human will’s freedom. [Note: [Col. 1824] Corb. and Mog.: “For in the correction of that word … you would have moderated …”]

But you feared diminishing the praise of human nature if you acknowledged that its strength had been given by God. Therefore, you do not wish God to be believed a collaborator in that struggle and victory, but merely a spectator: so that whoever you have persuaded that so arduous a contest was conquered by the natural capacity of free choice will dare not doubt that, in lesser matters, the effects of good will are much freer. Thus he falls into the pit of that condemned opinion [Note: [Col. 1824] Moguntine: “falls into that condemned opinion.”] which says, “The grace of justification is given to us so that what we are commanded to do through free choice we may more easily fulfill through grace”—as though, even if grace were not given, we could indeed fulfill the divine commands without it, though not easily.

Since Catholic bishops judged this view worthy of anathema, we must use the testimony they used, saying (Council of Carthage, canon 6, above, col. 1729): “For the Lord was speaking of the fruits of the commandments when he did not say, ‘Without me you can do them with greater difficulty,’ but said, ‘Without me you can do nothing’” (John 15:5).

## CHAPTER XVI

49. To these definitions of yours, which you believed fortified by adequate authority, you add, as though secure of the readers’ agreement: “God sometimes customarily offers more than is sufficient for the testing of our faith, so that the firmness [Note: [Col. 1824] Later editions read “weakness”; corrected from Corb. and Mog.] of believers’ faith may be recognized.” You demonstrate this with the example of the Centurion who, when he sought healing for his servant and the Lord promised that he would go to his house, replied, “I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof; but only say the word, and my servant will be healed.” In this the Lord praised him with such admiration that he declared he had not found such great faith in Israel (Matt. 8:5–10). And with a brief conclusion you almost entirely confirm the Pelagian doctrine by saying: “For it would have been no matter of praise or merit if Christ had preferred in him what he himself had bestowed” (ch. 14).

Then it was falsely written, “No one can be continent unless God grants it” (Wis. 8:21); falsely the Apostle proclaimed, when speaking of the same virtue, “I wish that all people were as I myself am; but each has his own gift from God, one in this way and another in that” (1 Cor. 7:7); falsely also taught the one who said, “If anyone lacks wisdom, let him ask God, and it will be given him.” Nor was it said truthfully, “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (James 1:5, 17); and, “No one can receive anything unless it has been given him from heaven” (John 3:27).

Or should we say that all virtues must indeed be counted among God’s gifts, but that in those virtues which a person possesses from himself he is praiseworthy, and that merit exists where God’s gifts have not existed? Therefore, according to your rule, those to whom it was granted not only to believe in Christ but also to suffer for him have lost both praise and merit; nor do those possess true glory who glory not in themselves but in the Lord.

Rather, we rightly hear the prophet saying, “Cursed is the man who places his hope in man, makes flesh his arm, and turns his heart away from the Lord” (Jer. 17:5); and the one who says, “I will love you, O Lord, my strength” (Ps. 17:2); and, “In the Lord my soul shall be praised” (Ps. 33:3); and, “The Lord is my strength and my praise” (Ps. 117:14). Thus we may know most clearly that those in whom the things which they would not possess unless the Lord gave them are not found have neither praise nor merit.

50. You thought that a presumption against the gifts of grace could be generated from the testimony of faith that had been praised, as though faith, when shown to have been praised, were not thereby taught to have been given. The Apostle praises the faith of the Romans and gives thanks to God for this good in them, saying, “First, I give thanks to my God through Jesus Christ for all of you, because your faith is proclaimed throughout the whole world” (Rom. 1:8). To the Corinthians also he writes with similar affection, saying, “I give thanks to my God always for you, for the grace of God that was given to you in Christ Jesus, because in everything you have been enriched in him, in every word and in all knowledge” (1 Cor. 1:4–5).

By giving thanks to God, did he take praise away from believers? Or by praising believers, did he deny God to be the author of their merits? Let us also hear what he thinks of the faith of the Ephesians: “Therefore I too,” he says, “having heard of your faith in the Lord Jesus and your love toward all the saints, do not cease giving thanks for you, remembering you in my prayers, that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give you the Spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him, with the eyes of your heart enlightened” (Eph. 1:15–18).

These people therefore had faith, and they had works of love as well—works that could not lack either praise or merit. Yet for these virtues the Apostle does not cease giving thanks to God, knowing that these gifts had come from the Father of lights. He declares that he also asks him to give the Spirit of wisdom and understanding to those to whom he gave faith working through love. Thus the Ephesians should know that they received from him what they possess, and from him they should learn to hope for what they do not possess.

For the Philippians also he gives similar thanks to God, without suppressing their merit and praise, saying: “I give thanks to my God at every remembrance of you, always in all my prayers making supplication for you all with joy, because of your fellowship in the Gospel from the first day until now, being confident of this very thing: that he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion until the day of Jesus Christ” (Phil. 1:3–6).

Whose cause of human praise and merit is here now dependent upon God? [Note: [Col. 1825] Corb. and the Moguntine edition read: “Whose cause of human praise and merit is not here dependent upon God?”] What virtue or piety has been excepted that did not flow from the fountain of grace, when both the beginning and the perfection of the good work, from beginning to end, are attributed to the Lord? Of the saints he is sung to say: [Col. 1825] “Lord, they shall walk in the light of your countenance, and in your name they shall rejoice all day long [Note: [Col. 1825] Corb. and Mog. omit “all day long.”], and in your righteousness they shall be exalted; for you are the glory of their strength” (Ps. 88:16–18).

## CHAPTER XVII

51. It must certainly be considered how greatly, in this statement of yours, you assist those who say, “The grace of God is given according to our merits.” Yet, in order to defend yourself under the shelter of the Catholic faith, you declare them adherents of a profane opinion, saying: “Let no one suppose that we have said these things in order to attempt to establish that the sum of salvation rests in the power of our faith, according to the profane opinion of certain people who, attributing everything to free choice, define the grace of God as being dispensed according to each person’s merit.”

But I am greatly astonished that you do not see—or think that others do not see—how you condemn yourself with your own mouth. For by saying that “the Centurion, whose faith was praised by the Lord’s voice, would have possessed no praise or merit if God had preferred in him what he himself had bestowed,” you have defined that the Centurion possessed not a faith that had been given, but his own faith, and that consequently nothing had been conferred upon its beginnings by grace. You have also asserted that in that faith lay the cause both of praise and of merit—neither of which it would have possessed if the Lord had conferred what deserves both praise and merit.

Therefore, in vain, to escape the odium of a condemned error, do you deny that the sum of salvation rests in the power of our faith, since salvation cannot in any way exist except through faith. “The righteous person lives by faith” (Rom. 1:17). For Truth says, “Amen, amen, I say to you: whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life and shall not come into judgment, but has passed from death to life” (John 5:24); and again, “This is the will of my Father, that everyone who sees the Son and believes in him should have eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day” (ibid. 6:40); and again, “This is eternal life: that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (ibid. 17:3).

Since eternal and blessed life is clearly prepared for this faith—which you honored with merits and praises because you prefer to number it among the goods of free choice rather than among God’s gifts—how will you avoid the wound with which you stab yourself, by declaring profane those who define grace as being dispensed according to human merits, while asserting that those who are faithful by the gift of grace clearly possess neither praise nor merit? [Col. 1826]

Whichever way you turn, you are both defeated and bound by yourself. For if merits do not precede grace, and faith cannot exist without merits, then faith does not precede grace and is in every respect possessed from grace [Note: [Col. 1826] Corb. and Mog.: “is possessed for the sake of grace”]—whatever it is from which merit arises, which is not possessed before grace.

## CHAPTER XVIII

52. Thus, so that the absurdity of your definitions may not appear self-contradictory, you attempt to mix incompatible things and, with novel presumption, establish the unity of the members of Christ’s body in two classes of believers. One class, namely, to which belongs what you said at the beginning: “The beginning not only of actions but also of good thoughts is from God, who both initiates what is good and carries it out and perfects it in us.” The other class, however, is governed by this rule, in which you say: “The Centurion would have possessed neither praise nor merit if the Lord had preferred in him what he himself had bestowed.”

Although you have brought the entire course of your discussion to these two formulas, which can in no way be made consistent, you now state more distinctly and explicitly what you wish to establish, saying:

“From these examples, therefore, which we have brought forward from the records of the Gospels, we shall be able to observe most clearly that God provides for the salvation of the human race in diverse, innumerable, and inscrutable ways: that he incites the course of some who willingly desire and thirst toward a greater ardor; that he compels others even when unwilling and resisting; that at one time he helps us so that those things may be fulfilled which he has seen us usefully desire; at another time he even inspires the beginnings of holy desire itself, and grants either the beginning of a good work or perseverance. Hence, when we pray, we proclaim the Lord not only our protector and savior, but also our helper and receiver. In that he first calls us and draws us, ignorant and unwilling, toward salvation, he is protector and savior; but in that he customarily helps us when we strive and receives and fortifies us when we flee to him, he is called receiver and refuge.”

53. According to this distinction, then, which you have laid down, there will be in one Church such a diversity that our Lord Jesus Christ—of whom it was said, “You shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins” (Matt. 1:21), and of whom it was said, “There is no other name under heaven given among human beings by which we must be saved” (Acts 4:12)—will be the savior not of all Christians but of some, and the receiver of others.

Thus only those will be saved whom God, when they turned away [Note: [Col. 1826] Corb. and Mog. read “opposed”] and resisted, compelled to receive grace; while those will be received who anticipated the call by the ardor of their spontaneous course. [Col. 1827] To the former a free gift will be conferred; to the latter a due reward will be repaid. The former will have neither praise nor merit, since they possess nothing good except what they have received; the latter will abound in glory and grow rich in recompense, since, devoted by their own ability, they offered what they had not received.

And so Jesus Christ will find some already liberated [Note: [Col. 1827] So Corb. and Mog.; later editions read “free.”] and liberate others; and the statement, “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John 15:16), will not apply to everyone, if there are some by whom he was chosen without having chosen them. Nor will the statement, “No one can come to me unless it has been given him by my Father” (ibid. 6:66), apply to everyone, if there are some who were able to come to the Son without the Father giving it. Nor will the evangelist’s statement, “He was the true light that enlightens every person coming into this world” (ibid. 1:9), apply to everyone, if there are some who came into this world in such a way that they were not darkness, or who began to be light in such a way that they did not need the illumination of the true light.

Nor should the Apostle’s statement concerning all the adopted be understood of everyone: “He rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love” (Col. 1:13), if they themselves break their chains and, shaking off the yoke of their former captivity, run freely from the dominion of the devil into the kingdom of God.

If these things can be preached within one Church, so that neither opinion yields to the other but each is mutually overthrown, then it could happen that we accept what the Pelagians hold and the Pelagians accept what we hold. But in that case they would not so much be Catholics as we would be Pelagians—which God forbid. For the mingling of opposites is the abandonment of what is better, because when virtue admits vice, it is not vice but virtue that is abandoned.

54. Therefore Christian hearts in no way accept what you have tried to persuade us of: that those who are what they are by the grace of God possess neither praise nor merit, and that, while he came to save what had perished, one portion of Christians has been saved by him and another merely received. For the disciples of evangelical and apostolic teaching, not setting their minds on high things but associating with the lowly, shudder at this madness of proud exaltation.

Throughout the whole body of the Church, and in each of its members, what was dead has been made alive; what was captive has been redeemed; what was blind has been enlightened; what had perished has been sought; what was wandering has been found. Nor, according to this new division, is he the savior of some and the receiver of others; rather, Christ is both savior and receiver of all the faithful everywhere.

Those who receive from him the means by which they may merit eternal goods are not deprived of merit and praise. They become happier in proportion as they possess fewer things that are their own and more things that belong to God. The foolish complaint of the proud does not disturb us—the complaint in which they allege that free choice is taken away if the beginnings, progress, and perseverance in good works unto the end are said to be gifts of God—for the aids of divine grace are supports of the human will.

We pray willingly; and yet God sent the Spirit into our hearts, crying, “Abba, Father” (Gal. 4:6). We speak willingly; and yet, if what we speak is pious, it is not we who speak, but the Spirit of our Father who speaks in us (Matt. 10:20). We willingly work out our salvation; and yet it is God who works in us both the willing and the working itself (Phil. 2:13). We willingly love God and our neighbor; and yet love is from God (1 John 4:7), poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (Rom. 5:5).

We confess this concerning faith, concerning endurance of sufferings, concerning marital chastity, concerning virginal continence, and concerning every virtue without exception: unless these things had been given to us, they would not be found in us.

And we confess that free choice, naturally implanted in human beings, remains in nature, but with its quality and condition changed through the Mediator between God and humanity, the human being Jesus Christ. [Col. 1828] He turns the will away from what it perversely desired and converts it toward willing what is good for it, so that, its affection delighted, its faith cleansed, its hope raised up, and its love kindled, it may embrace a free servitude and cast off servile freedom. [Note: [Col. 1828] So Corb. and Mog.; later editions read, “and lose its freedom.”]

## CHAPTER XIX

55. From these definitions, then, which we have examined thus far by passing over certain matters, it is neither obscure nor ambiguous what those who contradict the most sincere defenders of God’s grace think about grace [Note: [Col. 1828] Corb. and Mog.: “how they dissent concerning grace”]; and they disturb the peace of the victorious Church by reviving little questions from the school of the condemned. If, as we have heard, we were to unravel them, the length of our discourse would become excessive. Yet the pious reader can easily understand, from what has become known through their own writings [Note: [Col. 1828] Later editions: “what has become known through their school.” Corb. and Mog.: “what has become known through their own writings.”], to what precipices these paths lead and into what miry bog of muddy streams the moisture of what abyss seeps.

Before bringing the volume to its conclusion, I consider it necessary briefly and jointly to arrange the points we have shown not to agree with Catholic truth, so that those matters which, interposed among our replies, might escape the reader’s memory may be recalled together with greater fidelity.

The first definition therefore said:

“The beginning not only of actions but also of good thoughts is from God; he inspires in us the beginnings of holy desire and grants the strength and opportunity to carry out what we rightly desire. For every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights (James 1:17), who both initiates what is good, carries it out, and perfects it in us.”

This we too embrace wholeheartedly and profess to be Catholic.

The second definition said:

“Therefore divine protection is inseparably present with us; and so great is the Creator’s devotion toward his creature that providence not only accompanies it but continually goes before it. The Prophet, having experienced this, confesses, saying, ‘My God, his mercy will go before me’ (Ps. 58:11). When he has observed in us some beginning of good will, he enlightens it, strengthens it, and urges it toward salvation, granting increase to what either he himself planted or saw emerge through our effort.”

Here there is already a departure from the preceding definition, and what had been wholly attributed to grace is now partly assigned to free choice.

The third definition said:

“Nevertheless, in all these things both the grace of God and the freedom of choice are declared: by the latter a human being can sometimes, through his own movements, extend himself toward the desire for virtues, though he always needs to be helped by the Lord. For when someone wishes, he does not thereby enjoy health, nor is he freed from the disease of sickness according to the desire of his own choice.”

As though our physician did not also grant this to the sick: that they should desire true health.

The fourth definition said:

“But so that it may be more clearly evident that, even through the good of nature granted by the Creator’s kindness, beginnings of good desires sometimes arise—which nevertheless cannot reach the completion of virtue unless they are directed by the Lord—the Apostle is a witness, saying, ‘To will is present with me, but to accomplish the good I do not find’ [Note: [Col. 1828] Corb. and Mog.: “I am not able.”]” (Rom. 7:18).

As though the Apostle possessed good will from a natural inclination, and not from the gift of grace, when he confesses that even the ability to think comes from God (2 Cor. 3:5).

The fifth definition said:

“And so these matters are in some way mixed and confused indiscriminately, so that among many people a major dispute turns on what depends on what: that is, whether God has mercy on us because we have supplied the beginning of good will, or whether, because God has mercy, we obtain the beginning of good will. For many, believing each of these separately and asserting it more than is just, have become entangled in various errors contradictory to one another.

“If we say that the beginning of good will is ours, what was there in the persecutor Paul, what in the tax collector Matthew? One of them was occupied with the blood and punishments of the innocent, the other with public violence and plunder, yet each was drawn to salvation. But if we say that the beginnings of good will are always inspired by God’s grace, what shall we say of Zacchaeus’s faith, or of the piety of that thief on the cross? By their desire they exerted a certain force upon the heavenly kingdom and anticipated the special summons of their calling.”

It is said that both the one who says good will arises from grace and the one who says grace depends on good will are in error; yet it is decided that both opinions must be accepted, while the form of one is set forth in Paul and Matthew, and that of the other in Zacchaeus and the thief.

The sixth definition said:

“These two things, therefore—that is, grace and free choice—seem indeed to be opposed to one another, but both are in harmony, and we conclude, by the rule of piety, that we must accept both equally, lest, by taking one of them away from human beings, we appear to have exceeded the rule of ecclesiastical faith.”

As though both must be accepted in such a way that in some people will precedes grace, while in others grace precedes will, and not in such a way that in everyone will follows grace. For according to them, if free choice is taken away when grace precedes, grace is taken away when free choice precedes.

The seventh definition said:

“After the transgression, Adam acquired knowledge of evil, which he had not possessed; but he did not lose the knowledge of good that he had received.”

Both claims are false. For, when God warned him, Adam had already learned how great an evil he ought to avoid; and, while he believed the devil, he forgot the good condition in which he had been established. Just as the worst knowledge of evil is that evil exists, so the worst ignorance of good is that good does not exist.

The eighth definition said:

“Therefore we must beware lest we refer all the merits of the saints to God in such a way that we attribute nothing except what is evil to human nature.”

As though nature before grace were not under condemnation, were not in blindness, and were not wounded; or as though those whose merits arise from the same source as their righteousness had not been justified freely.

The ninth definition said:

“Therefore it cannot be doubted that the seeds of virtues are naturally present in every soul, implanted by the Creator’s kindness; but unless these have been stirred up by God’s help, they cannot advance toward the increase of perfection.”

As though Adam lost nothing of his spiritual goods through his transgression, and virtue had to be encouraged not so that it might be possessed, but so that it might more easily attain perfection. [Note: [Col. 1829] Here we restore “goods” from Corb. and Mog.]

The tenth definition said:

“This divine justice, we read, was also provided [Col. 1830] in Job, his most approved champion, when the devil demanded him for single combat. For if he had engaged the enemy not through his own strength but protected solely by the grace of God, and if, without any strength of his own patience, he had endured, supported only by divine assistance, the manifold burdens of temptation sought through the enemy’s entire cruelty, together with destruction, how could the devil not more justly have repeated against him that slanderous cry which he had uttered earlier: ‘Does Job worship God for nothing? Have you not enclosed him and all his possessions on every side? But withdraw your hand’; that is, ‘Allow him to contend with me by his own strength; ‘surely he will bless you to your face’” (Job 1:9–11)?

“But since the slanderous enemy dared not repeat any such complaint after the struggle, he confesses that he was conquered not by God’s strength but by Job’s. Nevertheless, it must not be believed that God’s grace was entirely absent from him, since God gave his tempter as much power to tempt as he knew Job possessed strength to resist.

“If God knew only what Job was capable of, and did not also grant him the capacity, then he was a witness of his patience, not his helper. And what need would there be for the help of grace if so great a victory had been won by human strength alone?”

The eleventh definition said concerning the Centurion’s faith:

“The Lord marvels at him and praises him highly, preferring him to all those who had believed from the people of Israel, saying, ‘Amen, I say to you, I have not found such great faith in Israel’” (Matt. 8:10). “For he would have possessed no praise or merit if the Lord had preferred in him what he himself had bestowed.”

An impious notion—one that thinks the person to whom God has given nothing happier than the person to whom he has given everything.

The twelfth definition said:

“Hence, when we pray, we proclaim the Lord not only our protector but also our receiver. In that he first calls us and draws us, ignorant and unwilling, toward salvation, he is protector and savior; but in that he customarily helps us when we strive and receives and fortifies us when we flee to him, he is called receiver and refuge.”

Only someone who does not wish to be saved by Christ can assent to this opinion.

## CHAPTER XX

56. These definitions therefore teach, write, and proclaim in published disputations the following: that when Adam sinned, his soul was not injured and remained sound in the very condition from which he sinned, since he did not lose the knowledge of good that he had received; nor could his descendants lose what he himself had not suffered to lose.

They teach that the seeds of virtues are naturally present in every soul, implanted by the Creator’s kindness, so that whoever wishes may, by natural judgment, anticipate God’s grace and merit his help, by which he may more easily reach perfection—for no one possesses praise or merit if, adorned with gifts that have been given, he is not adorned with things of his own.

They teach that we must beware of referring all the merits of the saints to God as though human nature itself could do nothing good by its own power, since its strength is so intact that it can fight against the devil himself and his savagery, even unto the final punishments, without God’s help.

They teach that this possibility is natural in all human beings, but that not everyone wishes to use the virtues implanted in him. They teach that the Creator is so good toward all human beings that some, because they come willingly, are received by him with praise, while others, because they resist, are drawn against their will; and therefore he is the receiver of those who will and the savior of those who do not will.

And when one portion of the Church is justified by grace and another by free choice, those whom nature has advanced are more glorious than those whom grace has liberated, because among Adam’s descendants the will is as free for every good work as Adam’s will was before sin.

## CHAPTER XXI

57. Behold the teachers of this doctrine. In order to corrupt the purity of Catholic minds by slandering the defenders of grace, they tear apart with savage speech the outstanding man of ecclesiastical teaching in our time [Note: [Col. 1830] Corb. and Mog. read concerpunt (“tear to pieces”)], and believe that they can tear down every defense of authority if they strike this strongest tower of the pastoral watchtower repeatedly with the battering ram of Pelagianism.

“God’s firm foundation stands” (2 Tim. 2:19); but in this respect they fittingly do not fall short of their fathers. It is appropriate that those who follow their opinion should imitate their madness. For they cannot say anything other than what has been made public in the complaints of the condemned and the insults of the most shameless Julian. The shoots of one seed are alike, and what lay hidden in the roots is revealed in the fruits.

We therefore need not fight these people with a new battle line, nor undertake special combats as though against unknown enemies. Their engines were broken, and they fell together with the leaders and companions of their pride, when Innocent of blessed memory struck the heads of their wicked error with the apostolic sword; when the Palestinian bishops’ synod compelled Pelagius to pronounce judgment against himself [Col. 1831] and his followers; when Pope Zosimus of blessed memory added the force of his judgment to the decrees of the African councils and armed the right hands of all the bishops with Peter’s sword for the decapitation of the impious; when Pope Boniface of holy memory rejoiced in the Catholic devotion of the most pious emperors and used not only apostolic but also royal edicts against the enemies of God’s grace; and when that same man, although most learned, nevertheless requested the replies of the blessed bishop Augustine against the books of the Pelagians.

58. Hence also the pontiff Coelestine of venerable memory—upon whom the Lord bestowed many gifts of his grace for the protection of the Catholic Church—knowing that the condemned were to be granted not the scrutiny of judgment but only the remedy of repentance, ordered Coelestius, who was requesting a hearing as though the case had not been examined, to be expelled from the entire territory of Italy. He judged the statutes of his predecessors and the decrees of synods so inviolably binding that he would in no way permit what had once deserved to be cut off to be reconsidered. [Note: [Col. 1831] The same books read “the remedy of the sentence”; and in the following line, “of the case not examined.”]

Nor did he free Britain from this same disease with less care, when he excluded certain enemies of grace, who had occupied only the region of their own origin, even from that hidden place beyond the Ocean. Having appointed a bishop for the Scots [Note: [Col. 1831] Evidently Palladius], while striving to preserve the Roman island as Catholic, he also made the barbarian people Christian.

Through this man the Eastern Churches too were cleansed of a double plague, when he aided Cyril, bishop of Alexandria and a most glorious defender of the Catholic faith, with the apostolic sword to cut out Nestorian impiety; by that same sword the Pelagians were again overthrown when they allied themselves with kindred errors.

Through this man the freedom of malicious speech was taken away within Gaul from those very people who criticize the writings of Augustine of holy memory. When he received the action of those who consulted him and praised with devotion the books displeasing to the erring, he made clear in holy speech what ought to be thought concerning their authority. He plainly declared how displeasing to him was the novelty of this presumption, by which certain people dared insolently to rise up against ancient teachers and, through undisciplined slander, obstruct the preaching of truth:

“Augustine, a man of holy memory, we have always held in our communion on account of his life and merits; nor has even a rumor of sinister suspicion ever touched him, whom we remember to have once possessed such great learning that my predecessors always counted him among the best teachers. Therefore all rightly held the same opinion of him, since everywhere he was both loved and honored by all” (Letter of Pope Coelestine, no. 3, above, col. 1756, ch. 2).

59. Against this trumpet of the most splendid praise, against the dignity of this most sacred testimony, does anyone dare to emit the murmur of a malicious interpretation and cast a cloud of oblique ambiguity over a clear and wholly sincere statement? Namely, because in the pope’s letter the title of the books on whose behalf the action was undertaken was not expressed, should it therefore appear that they were not approved, and that this praise of Saint Augustine was bestowed on account of the merits of his earlier writings? Let this condition stand plainly—let it stand—that the novelty of these books be regarded as rejected if, in the same matter, the antiquity of the same man disagrees; and let anything found discordant with what he wrote against the Pelagians be judged useless or inappropriate.

To pass over, then, those volumes in which, from the beginning of his episcopate—long before the opponents of grace arose—he argued on behalf of grace: let his three books addressed to Marcellinus be read [Note: [Col. 1831] *On the Merits and Remission of Sins*]. Let the letter to Saint Paulinus, bishop of Nola, be reviewed [Note: [Col. 1831] Letter 186]. Let the pages sent to the most blessed Sixtus, then a presbyter of the Apostolic See but now [Col. 1832] its Pontiff, be consulted [Note: [Col. 1832] Letter 194]. Let the separately published volumes addressed to Saint Pinianus [Note: [Col. 1832] *On the Grace of Christ and Original Sin*], to the Count Valerius [Note: [Col. 1832] *On Marriage and Concupiscence*], and to the servants of Christ, Timasius and James [Note: [Col. 1832] *On Nature and Grace*], be examined in turn. Let the first six books against Julian be read; also one addressed to Saint Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, on the proceedings in Palestine [Note: [Col. 1832] *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*]; another to the priests Paul and Eutropius, against the questions of Pelagius and Coelestius [Note: [Col. 1832] *On the Perfection of Human Righteousness*]; and let the four volumes addressed to Pope Boniface of blessed memory be reviewed [Note: [Col. 1832] *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*].

And if in all these works, and in many others whose enumeration would be lengthy, the same spirit of doctrine preceded, and the same form of preaching, let the slanderers recognize that they object pointlessly that no special and separate testimony was borne to these books, whose rule is praised throughout all the volumes. For the Apostolic See approves along with what it had previously recognized whatever does not disagree with it; and what it joins in judgment it does not separate in praise. Therefore, let those who reject these recently published books accept the earlier ones, and agree with what was previously written in defense of Christian grace. But they do not do so: for they know that all those writings are contrary to the Pelagians [Note: [Col. 1832] Later editions: “that Pelagian writings are contrary to themselves.” Corrected from the Corbeiensis and Moguntinus manuscripts], and that they can contribute nothing to resolving what follows if they admit that the truth stands in the earlier works.

60. The perversity of such people must therefore be resisted not so much by the zeal of debate as by the privilege of authoritative testimony, so that no limb of a doctrine long ago overthrown may be allowed to rise again. For it is known that the stratagems of this falsehood are such that, if it is permitted, under the pretext of correction [Note: [Col. 1832] Thus the Corbeiensis and Moguntinus manuscripts. Later editions read: “that the stratagems of this falsehood are such that, if they are permitted to accept some shoot of its root favorable to them under the pretext of correction,” etc.], to preserve for itself some shoot of its root favorable to it, it can restore itself in its entirety from a small part of itself. For where the whole possesses nothing more than a portion, to have given almost everything is not devotion, but to have retained even the smallest part is fraud.

To prevent this from being secured by the snares of hypocrites, we trust that, by the Lord’s protection, what he accomplished through Innocent, Zosimus, Boniface, and Celestine he will also accomplish through Sixtus [Note: [Col. 1832] Sixtus succeeded Celestine in the year of Christ 431, on April 26]; and that in guarding the Lord’s flock this portion of glory may be reserved for this shepherd: just as those former shepherds drove away the manifest wolves, so may he drive away the hidden ones. The most learned old man’s speech rang in the ears of that shepherd as he exhorted his fellow laborer, saying:

“For there are some who think that impieties justly condemned must still be defended more freely; and there are some who enter houses more secretly, and do not cease sowing in private what they are now afraid to proclaim openly. There are also some who have remained completely silent, overcome by great fear, but still retaining in their hearts what they no longer dare to utter with their mouths; nevertheless, they can be recognized by the brethren from their earlier defense of that doctrine itself. Therefore, some must be restrained more severely, others must be investigated more vigilantly; others must indeed be treated more gently, but taught no less diligently, so that, even if they are not feared lest they perish [Note: [Col. 1832] Later editions read: “they do not fear,” or “they may not fear.” Corrected according to the Corbeiensis and Moguntinus manuscripts and Augustine’s Letter 194], they may nevertheless not be neglected lest they perish.””

## CHAPTER XXII

61. It has been sufficiently demonstrated, I think, that the critics of Saint Augustine both make empty objections, attack what is right, and defend what is wrong; and that, waging an internal war with the weapons of those already defeated, they rebel against divine words and human constitutions. Nevertheless, since they have not yet been separated from the fellowship of the brethren, their disposition should be endured rather than their correction despaired of. Until the Lord, through the leaders of the Church and the legitimate ministers of his judgments, sets in order these matters that have been disturbed by the pride of a few and the ignorance of certain others, may it be our concern, with God’s help, calmly and moderately to repay hatred with love, to avoid conflicts with foolish people, not to abandon the truth, and not to fight with falsehood; and may we always ask God that in all our thoughts, in all our wills, in all our words and actions, he himself may hold first place—he who said that he was the beginning.

“For from him, and through him, and in him are all things; to him be glory forever. Amen” [Note: [Col. 1834] In an old Corbeiensis copy the following is appended: “Here ends the book of Saint Prosper against the book of the former abbot Cassian, which is entitled *On the Protection of God*, or *Against the Dogma of Pelagius and Coelestius, Discoverers and Defenders of a Wicked Dogma and Enemies of the Grace of God and of Our Lord Jesus Christ*, and *In Defense of the Holy Roman Bishops and of Saint Bishop Augustine*, asserting the truth of his books against the heretics mentioned above. Thanks be to God.”].

[Col. 1833]

# PROSPER OF AQUITAINE’S RESPONSES ON BEHALF OF AUGUSTINE TO THE CHAPTERS OF THE GALLIC SLANDERERS [Note: [Col. 1833] We add “of the slanderers” from an old manuscript of the Abbey of Saint Remigius at Reims, written nearly nine hundred years ago.]

One book. (C)

[Col. 1833]

## PREFACE

The doctrine that Bishop Augustine of holy memory had defended apostolically for many years against the Pelagians, enemies of Christ’s grace and disparagers [Note: [Col. 1833] The old Remigianus manuscript originally read “deceivers”; a second hand wrote “defenders.”] of free will, and had committed to writing, seemed to certain people worthy of criticism—either because they did not understand it or because they did not wish it to be understood. They offered it, as though it were a summary of knowledge, to those who were guided by their judgment, publishing in brief chapter headings what they boasted they had found condemnable in the books of the aforesaid man. By such a contrivance they both secured hatred for the man whom they attacked and, by frightening the reader, diverted his attention from what they had defamed.

Therefore, lest anyone rashly accept this persuasion and think that the Catholic Teacher’s writings contain the meaning that those who slander him without cause display, I answer each chapter that they have prefaced with the title of condemnation in a brief and definitive statement, departing in no respect from the path of those definitions contained in the holy man’s disputations. Thus even an observer of modest diligence may easily notice with what unjust reproaches the memory of the Catholic Preacher is assailed, and into what sin fall those who, moved by another’s instigation, are readier to condemn a writer of the most celebrated name than to know him.

## FIRST OBJECTION

That, compelled by God’s predestination as though by a fatal necessity, human beings are forced into sins and driven to death.

## RESPONSE

No Catholic denies God’s predestination; but many even of those who are not Christians reject fatal necessity. Sin therefore drags a person to death, but God compels no one to sin. For he commanded no one to act impiously (Sirach 15:21): “You hate, Lord, all who work iniquity; you will destroy those who speak falsehood” (Psalm 5:7). Therefore, whoever proclaims fate under the name of predestination is no more to be approved than one who, under the name of fate, defames the truth of predestination.

The opinion of fate is vain and conceived from falsehood; but faith in predestination is fortified by the authority of many holy Scriptures. In no way may the evil actions of human beings be ascribed to it—those who came into a tendency to fall not from God’s creation, but from the transgression of the first father. No one is freed from the punishment of that transgression except through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, prepared and predestined in God’s eternal plan before the foundation of the world.

## OBJECTION II

That, for those who are not predestined to life, the grace received in Baptism does not remove original sin.

## RESPONSE

Every person who, believing in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, is regenerated in Baptism is absolved both from his own sins, which he contracted through evil will and action, and from original sin, which he inherited from his parents. But whoever denies that one who has fallen back after Baptism into unbelief and impious conduct was cleansed from original sin holds as false an opinion as one who asserts that the same person is not to be condemned to eternal death.

For one who departs from Christ and ends this life estranged [Note: [Col. 1834] In the same Remigianus manuscript, an ancient hand corrected this to “alienated.”] from grace—what does he do except fall into perdition? Yet he does not fall back into what was forgiven, nor will he be condemned for original sin. Nevertheless, because of his final crimes he will suffer the death that was owed to him on account of those things that had been forgiven. Since God’s foreknowledge neither overlooked nor failed to foresee this, he plainly never chose such a person, never predestined him, and never separated him from eternal perdition as one who would perish.

## OBJECTION III

That those who are not predestined to life, even if they have been regenerated in Christ through Baptism and have lived piously and justly, gain nothing from this; rather, they are kept until they fall and perish, and are not taken from this life before that happens to them.

## RESPONSE

There is no doubt that many pass from holiness to uncleanness, from righteousness to iniquity, and from faith to impiety; and it is entirely certain that such people do not belong to the predestination of God’s children, Christ’s co-heirs. Therefore, when such people have fallen into these evils and have died without the correction of repentance, they did not possess a necessity of perishing because they were not predestined; rather, they were not predestined because they were foreknown as going to become such through voluntary transgression.

But the fact that God did not take them from this life at the time when they were in right faith and good conduct must be referred to his hidden judgments, which nevertheless are never unjust. For who does not know that, within the one condition of human mortality, from the infancy of a single hour to the most advanced old age, the deaths of the dying occur at unequal ages, and that no one’s soul departs from the body it vivifies either earlier or later than God wills?

If, therefore, someone deserted God during the length of his life, he made bad use of the good [Col. 1835] that came from God. For longevity comes only from God; and what comes from God is only good; and what is good is not the cause of evil. Thus the person who thinks that the one who prolongs life is the author of sin for those destined to fall does not hold a correct opinion. For living a long time is not sin, but living badly is; and that can happen even within a few years.

Accordingly, just as good works are to be attributed to God, who inspires them, so evil works are to be attributed to those who sin. They were not abandoned by God in order that they might abandon God; rather, they abandoned him, were abandoned, and changed from good to evil by their own will. Although they had been reborn and justified by him, they were nevertheless not predestined by the one who foreknew them as such.

## OBJECTION IV

That not all human beings are called to grace.

## RESPONSE

It is not correctly said that those to whom the Gospel is preached are not all called to grace, even if there are some who do not obey the Gospel—unless we are speaking of those who have not yet learned of the sacrament of Christ’s cross and of his blood-redemption.

For even if it were established that the whole world had already received the Gospel among all nations and to the ends of the earth—which was most truly foretold as something that would happen—it would nevertheless be beyond doubt that from the time of the Lord’s resurrection to the present age there have been people who passed from this life without knowledge of the Gospel. Of them it could be said that they were not called, because they did not even hear the hope of calling.

But if someone always asserts this complete universality of calling in such a way that, from the Lord’s ascension into heaven, not even a single year passed in which preaching did not reach everyone, let him see how he can then prove that the Asians were called, when the Apostles, as it is written, were forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word of God in Asia; or that the Bithynians were called, when the same Apostles attempted to go to them and the Spirit of Jesus did not permit them (Acts 16:6–7).

Let him also see how he can defend the declaration of Truth itself, which says: “This Gospel of the kingdom will be preached throughout the whole world as a testimony to all nations, and then the end will come” (Matthew 24:14). For faith in the word totters—which it is impious to say—if the world was filled with the Gospel four hundred years ago and the Lord’s coming is still being delayed.

Finally, let him also consider among Christian peoples the many thousands of infants who have passed from this life without Baptism, and let him somehow prove that they were called when neither the planter could preach to them nor the one who waters could assist them.

## OBJECTION V

That those who are called are not called equally, but some are called so that they may believe and others so that they may not believe.

## RESPONSE

If calling is understood only as the preaching of the Gospel, it is not truthfully said that the Gospel is preached differently to different people, since there is one God, one faith, one regeneration, and one promise.

But if we look to the effect of planting and watering, something different was done with those whose outer ears were struck by a bodily voice, and something different in those whose inner sense God opened and in whose hearts he laid the foundation of faith and the fervor of love.

To say that some were called so that they would not believe is utterly absurd, as though calling had become the cause of their unbelief and the preaching of faith had made them unbelievers. Although the ministers of God’s word are, to some people, as Scripture says, “the aroma of death leading to death” [Note: [Col. 1835] In the Remigianus manuscript a second hand adds: “but to others, the aroma of life leading to life.”], they are nevertheless “the good aroma of Christ to God” (2 Corinthians 2:16, 15), preaching Christ crucified, “a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles, but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:23–24).

Therefore, the fact that Christ crucified, when preached, was a stumbling block to the Jews and foolishness to the Gentiles was produced by the aversion of the human will; but the fact that Christ was the power of God and the wisdom of God to those called, both Jews and Greeks, was brought about by the operation of divine grace.

[Col. 1836]

## OBJECTION VI

That free will is nothing in human beings, but that God’s predestination operates in them either toward good or toward evil.

## RESPONSE

It is wrongly said that free will is nothing, or does not exist. But it cannot rightly be denied that before the illumination of faith it acts in darkness and in the shadow of death. For before it is freed by God’s grace from the domination of the devil, it lies in that deep place into which it plunged itself by its own freedom.

It therefore loves its illnesses and considers itself healthy because it does not know that it is sick, until this first remedy is applied to the sick person: that he begins to recognize his sickness and is able to desire the physician’s help by which he may rise.

Thus a justified person—that is, one made pious from impiousness—receives, with no preceding good merit, the gift by which he may acquire merit. What has been begun in him through Christ’s grace is then increased through the exercise of free will [Note: [Col. 1836] Thus the Remigianus manuscript. The printed editions read: “by which means.”], yet never without God’s assistance, without which no one can either advance or persevere in the good.

But it is most foolishly said that God’s predestination operates in human beings either toward good or toward evil, as though some necessity compelled them toward both. In good actions, the will must be understood together with grace; in evil actions, the will must be understood without grace.

## OBJECTION VII

That God does not give perseverance to certain of his children whom he regenerated in Christ and to whom he gave faith, hope, and love, because in his foreknowledge and predestination they were not separated from the mass of perdition.

## RESPONSE

Among those regenerated in Christ Jesus, there are some who, abandoning faith and pious conduct, apostatize from God and end their lives in impiety; this is demonstrated by many examples, though it is grievous. But to ascribe their fall to God is extreme perversity, as though he were the instigator and author of their ruin because he foreknew that they would fall by their own will and therefore did not separate them from the children of perdition by any predestination.

For how could a predestined election in Christ have included those whom a just condemnation was going to claim as they departed from Christ? Since it is beyond doubt [Note: [Col. 1836] The printed editions read: “a predestined election in Christ, since it is beyond doubt,” omitting the words “those who depart,” and so on. The passage is restored from the Remigianus manuscript, although that manuscript originally lacked the word “just,” which was later added by an ancient corrector], that perseverance in the good unto the end is God’s gift, and since it is clear that these people did not have it precisely because they did not persevere, God must not be slandered by asking why he did not give them what he gave others. Rather, we must confess both that he mercifully gave what he gave and that he justly did not give what he did not give. Otherwise, just as the cause of falling seems to arise from free will, so the cause of standing might also seem to arise from it, whereas the former is accomplished by human action and the latter is fulfilled by a divine gift.

## OBJECTION VIII

That God does not will all human beings to be saved, but only a definite number of the predestined.

## RESPONSE

If, concerning the salvation of the whole human race and its calling to the knowledge of the truth, God’s will is to be declared indifferent throughout all ages in such a way that he is shown to have passed over no human being anywhere, then the unfathomable depth of God’s judgments is being challenged.

Why, then, in former ages did God allow all nations to walk in their own ways, when “the Lord chose Jacob for himself” (Psalm 134:4), and “he did not deal so with every nation, nor did he reveal his judgments to them” (Psalm 147:20)? Why is one who was once not a people now the people of God, and why are those whom he once did not pity now receiving mercy? Why, where it was said, “You are not my people,” are they called “children of the living God” (Hosea 2:24; Romans 9:26; 1 Peter 2:10)? And why did Israel not obtain what it was seeking, while the elect obtained it and the rest were hardened (Romans 11:7)? It is impossible to comprehend these things, and it is dangerous curiosity to inquire into them.

Nevertheless, no one is permitted to ignore that there is no injustice with God (2 Chronicles 19:7). Nor should anyone believe that any human being, whether before the Law or under the Law, was justified by any other grace or faith than this same grace and faith through which our Lord Jesus Christ, according to the purpose of his will, came at the end of the ages to seek and save what was lost.

But whoever refers the causes of God’s works and judgments entirely to human wills and actions, although he finds them nowhere in the adoption or rejection of infants, and wishes God’s dispensations to vary according to the mutability of free will, is declaring that God’s judgments are searchable and his ways traceable. He thinks he can disclose publicly what Paul, the teacher of the Gentiles, did not dare to approach (Romans 11:33). And—something no less impious—he either teaches that the grace by which we are saved is repaid for good merits or asserts that it is held back because of evil ones.

Let us therefore set aside the whirlwind of obscure questions and turn to the breadth of the grace that has been revealed. Let us say with the Apostle: “God wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (1 Timothy 2:4). And again let us say with the Apostle: “He is the Savior of all, especially of believers” (1 Timothy 4:10).

Let us hear the Lord saying to his Apostles: “Go therefore and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them” [Note: [Col. 1837] In the Remigianus manuscript a second hand adds: “to keep all things”] “everything that I have commanded you” (Matthew 28:19–20).

Let us also hear God’s promise to Abraham: “In your offspring all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed” (Genesis 22:18). And if we are children of the promise, let us not hesitate in distrust, but, with our father Abraham, give glory to God and be fully convinced that what he promised he is able also to accomplish (Romans 4:20–21).

Let us hear David prophesying: “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations shall worship before him” (Psalm 21:28). And elsewhere: “All the tribes of the earth shall be blessed in him; all nations shall magnify him” (Psalm 71:17). And elsewhere: “All the nations that you have made shall come and worship before you, Lord, and shall glorify your name” (Psalm 85:9).

Because these promises are utterly true and cannot waver in any respect, they are fulfilled in those who are saved throughout all the ends of the earth, since he who promised is able also to accomplish it.

This, then, is the taking up of the entire human race; this is the adoption of the children of God; this is the fullness of the nations, foreknown and predestined in Christ before the foundation of the world.
