This is the Jerusalem that from beginning to end is built of living and chosen stones (1 Peter 2:5), as a city founded upon Christ Jesus, the cornerstone, “in whom the whole structure, joined together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord” (Ephesians 2:20–21).

Nothing is cast out from these stones, nothing is diminished, nothing is snatched away. For the Truth says: “Everything that the Father gives me will come to me, and whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37). And again: “You do not believe because you are not among my sheep. My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me; and I give them eternal life, and they will never perish forever, and no one will snatch them from my hand” (John 10:26–28).

God therefore cares for all human beings, and there is no one whom either the preaching of the Gospel, or the testimony of the Law, or even nature itself does not address. But let us ascribe human beings’ unbelief to the human beings themselves; and let us confess that human beings’ faith is God’s gift, without whose grace no one runs toward grace.

And together with the two hundred and fourteen priests whose decree against the enemies of God’s grace the whole world embraced, let us say in a truthful confession, in the words of their own statement:

“By the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord, we are assisted not only in knowing but also in doing righteousness through each individual act, so that without it we are able neither to possess, think, say, nor do anything belonging to true and holy devotion” (See above, *Book Against the Collator*, no. 15).

Nor should we think that these gifts come from God merely because he is the author of our nature, as though he had already bestowed them through the condition of nature. For he did indeed give human beings this capacity at the beginning; but we all lost it in the one in whom we all sinned. Hence we need to be renewed in Christ through another creation and another beginning. In him we are a new creation and a new work; and through him, with no preceding good merits and many preceding evil ones, it is granted to us to become vessels of mercy instead of vessels of wrath.

## OBJECTION IX

That the Savior was not crucified for the redemption of the whole world.

## RESPONSE

There is absolutely no human being whose nature was not assumed by Christ our Lord, although he was born in the likeness of sinful flesh (Romans 8:3), whereas every human being is born in sinful flesh.

Therefore, the Son of God, having become a participant in human mortality without sin, bestowed this upon sinners and mortals: that those who shared in his birth might escape the bond of sin and death.

Just as it is not sufficient for the renewal of human beings that the human being Jesus Christ was born, unless in that same Spirit from which he himself was born they are reborn, so it is not sufficient for the redemption of human beings that the Lord Christ was crucified, unless they die with him and are buried with him in Baptism.

Otherwise, if the Savior was born in the flesh of our substance and crucified for all of us, it would not have been necessary for us to be reborn and planted together in the likeness of his death. But since no human being obtains eternal life without this sacrament, the one who has not been crucified in Christ has not been saved by Christ’s cross.

Now the one who is not a member of Christ’s body has not been crucified in Christ; nor is anyone a member of Christ’s body [Note: [Col. 1838] On the authority of the Remigianus manuscript we add: “nor is anyone a member of Christ’s body.”] who has not put on Christ through water and the Holy Spirit. For this reason he shared in death in our weakness, so that through his power we might share in the resurrection.

Thus, although it is entirely correct to say that the Savior was crucified for the redemption of the whole world, because he truly assumed human nature and because all human beings were jointly lost in the first man, it can nevertheless be said that he was crucified only for those whom his death benefited.

For the Evangelist says: “Jesus was going to die for the nation, and not only for the nation, but also to gather into one the scattered children of God” (John 11:51–52). “He came to his own, and his own did not receive him. But to all who received him he gave power to become children of God, who were born not of bloods, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God.”

Their lot is therefore different from that of those who are counted among the people of whom it is said: “The world did not know him” [Note: [Col. 1838] In the Remigianus manuscript, in place of “The world did not know him,” these words are read: “The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it.”] (John 1:10–13).

Accordingly, in this sense he may be called the Redeemer of the world: he gave his blood for the world, and the world did not wish to be redeemed, because the darkness did not receive the light. Yet the darkness did receive it, for the Apostle says to those who had been darkness: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Ephesians 5:8).

The Lord Jesus himself, who said that he had come to seek and save what was lost (Luke 19:10), said: “I was sent only to the sheep that had been lost from the house of Israel” (Matthew 15:24).

But let the Apostle Paul explain who these sheep of the house of Israel are. He says: “Not all who are from Israel are Israel; nor, because they are Abraham’s offspring, are they all children. Rather, ‘In Isaac shall your offspring be named.’ That is, it is not the children of the flesh who are children of God, but the children of the promise are counted as offspring” (Romans 9:6–8).

Among these, therefore, are those of whom we recalled above that it was said: “Jesus was going to die for the nation, and not only for the nation, but also to gather into one the scattered children of God.”

For not only from the Jews but also from the Gentiles, through him who calls things that are not as though they were, and who gathers the scattered of Israel, the children of God, the children of the promise, are gathered into one Church. Thus is fulfilled what was promised to Abraham, to whom it was said [Col. 1839] that all the tribes of the earth would be blessed in his offspring (Genesis 22:18).

## OBJECTION X

That the Lord withdraws the preaching of the Gospel from certain people so that they may not be saved after receiving the preaching of the Gospel.

## RESPONSE

If it can be proved that, from the time the Gospel began to be preached, absolutely no one existed to whom Christian grace was not announced, then it is not correctly said that what is shown to have been preached was kept silent.

But if people are found in some way [Note: [Col. 1839] The Remigianus manuscript, corrected by an ancient hand, reads “at some time.”] to whom the Gospel was not preached, it cannot be said that this happened without God’s judgment. It is impious to criticize what cannot be comprehended.

## OBJECTION XI

That by his power God compels human beings to sin.

## RESPONSE

No Catholic has said or says that God, by his power, compels people living piously and righteously to sin, or that divine power uses force against human innocence so as to shake it from its purpose of good conduct.

These are not God’s works but the devil’s, whose joy is the ruin of the saints. But the Lord lifts up all who fall and raises all who are bowed down (Psalm 144:14), granting them repentance so that they may recover from the snares of the devil, by whom they were held captive for his will (1 Timothy 2:25–26).

When we read that some were either handed over by God to their desires (Romans 1:24), hardened, or abandoned, we confess that they deserved this through their great sins, because their crimes preceded it in such a way that they themselves owed the punishments [Note: [Col. 1839] The same corrected manuscript reads: “that punishment should befall them.”] which would also turn into guilt for them.

Thus we neither complain about God’s judgment, by which he abandons those who deserve to be abandoned, nor fail to give thanks for his mercy, by which he frees those who do not deserve to be freed.

## OBJECTION XII

That obedience is withdrawn from certain people who are called and who live piously and justly, so that they cease to obey.

## RESPONSE

If God drives a person obedient to him away from piety and makes one who is running well fall, then he repays good with evil and unjustly punishes what he himself compels to occur. What could be said or imagined more perverse, more insane than this?

But people who think that in all things God’s foreknowledge is the same as his will are dragged into such a notion. His will never wills anything except good; but his foreknowledge knows both good and evil. He bestows good things, either by doing them himself or by granting that we do them [Note: [Col. 1839] The printed editions read “commands.” Corrected according to the Remigianus manuscript]; but he did not himself do the evil things at all, nor did he advise or compel them to be done.

Therefore, he did not withdraw the power of obedience from anyone because he did not predestine that person; rather, he did not predestine him because he foresaw that he would withdraw from obedience itself.

## OBJECTION XIII

That certain human beings were not created by God for the purpose of attaining eternal life, but merely to adorn the condition of the present age and to be born for the benefit of others.

## RESPONSE

We know that all human beings are created individually by God, and that from this whole number some will be condemned with the devil while others will reign with Christ. The fact, therefore, that even those who will not share in eternal life are created involves no fault in the Creator, who is the author of nature, not of the defect that nature contracted.

Who could fail to understand that even the condition of such people adorns the variety of this world, when he sees so many advantages of the present life furnished through the studies and works of certain impious people—in the invention of arts, the construction of cities, the establishment of laws, and the confederation of peoples?

If it is asked whether divine providence has brought some benefit from these people—whom impious error has turned away from true religion—to the progress of the saints and the growth of the Church, let us first consider Christ’s own cross. There, through the great crime of the Jews, God’s merciful will was fulfilled: that his only Son should be killed for our redemption.

Let us consider the glorious endurance of the Apostles, who amid the roar of their persecutors cried out to God with one voice: “For truly in this city there gathered together against your holy servant Jesus, whom you anointed, Herod and Pontius Pilate, together with the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel, to do whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place” (Acts 4:27–28).

Finally, let us consider the palms of countless martyrs, to whom a blessed victory was granted over the most savage cruelty of unbelievers.

Let us also hear the Apostle instructing the Church of God in perseverance in piety. “In nothing,” he says, “be frightened by your adversaries. This is for them an indication of destruction, but for you of salvation, and that from God. For it has been granted to you for Christ’s sake not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him” (Philippians 1:28–29).

Let us also perceive God’s goodness in those errors that God permitted to arise in the Church against the Church—not creating or fostering them, certainly, but exercising through them the diligence of his children in seeking and guarding the truth. For the Apostle says: “There must be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest among you” (1 Corinthians 11:19).

And when someone looks toward the darkness of the impious and the illumination of God’s children, who would not become more fervent in giving thanks to God through this very comparison, and learn from the ruin of those who perish into what evils he would plunge by free will unless the grace of God came to his aid through our Lord Jesus Christ?

## OBJECTION XIV

That those who do not believe the evangelical preaching do not believe by God’s predestination; and that God has so determined it that whoever does not believe does not believe by his own ordinance.

### RESPONSE

The unbelief of those who do not believe the Gospel is in no way generated by God’s predestination. For God is the author of good things, not of evil things. God’s predestination, therefore, is always directed toward the good, whether it pertains to the recompense of justice or to the bestowal of grace. For all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth (Ps. 24:10). Accordingly, the unbelief of those who do not believe must be referred not to God’s ordinance but to his foreknowledge. That foreknowledge did not thereby impose the necessity of not believing, merely because it could not be mistaken about the unbelief that was going to occur.

Faith, however, the works of charity, and perseverance in them to the end—since these are bestowed upon human beings through God’s grace—are rightly said themselves, as well as the things to be recompensed for them, to have been predestined. This follows from the authority of the Apostle, who says: “You have been saved by grace through faith; and this is not from yourselves, but is the gift of God—not from works, lest anyone should boast. For we are his workmanship, created in good works, which God prepared so that we might walk in them” (Eph. 2:8–10). He is therefore equally mistaken who refers the unbelief of the impious to God’s ordinance, and he who does not profess God to be the author of the faith and righteousness of the saints. For the one who has lost what he had received does not receive it from the source from which he lost it; rather, he receives from the one from whom he had received what he lost whatever he is to possess.

## OBJECTION XV

That foreknowledge is the same as predestination.

### RESPONSE

Whoever distinguishes God’s foreknowledge in no respect from his predestination attempts to attribute to God, with respect to evil things, what must be attributed to him with respect to good things. But since good things must be referred to God as their giver and co-worker, while evil things must be referred to the voluntary wickedness of rational creatures, there is no doubt that—without any temporal difference—God both foreknew and predestined those things that were to be done with him as their author, or those that were justly to be repaid according to evil merits. But he merely foreknew, and did not also predestine, those things that were not going to have their operative cause from him.

Foreknowledge, then, can exist without predestination; predestination, however, cannot exist without foreknowledge.

[Note: [Col. 1840] To each chapter of the objections he opposes a separate statement.]

Although, therefore, I think that a clear and complete answer has been given, insofar as the Lord has granted it, to all the objections—whether arising from the querulousness of ignorance or from deceitful envy—let us nevertheless compress our profession of our position into a shorter form, so that, under the simplicity of a few words, it may become increasingly clear that we are not concealing what we understand concerning the chapters written above by any art of circumlocution, but are openly and freely rejecting what is erroneous while not refusing assent to what is probable.

### I

Whoever says that, by God’s predestination as though by a fated necessity, human beings are driven and compelled into sins and thereby into death is not a Catholic. For God’s predestination in no way makes anyone wicked, nor is it the cause of anyone’s sin.

### II

Likewise, whoever says that, in those who are not predestined to life, the grace of Baptism they have received does not remove original sin is not a Catholic. For the sacrament of Baptism, by which all sins whatsoever are erased, is genuine even in those who will not remain in the truth and therefore are not predestined to true life.

### III

Likewise, whoever says that those who are not predestined to life—even if they have been regenerated in Christ through Baptism and have lived piously and justly—derive no benefit from this, but are kept until they fall, and are not taken from this life before that happens, as though the fall of such people were to be referred to God’s ordinance, is not a Catholic.

For God did not prolong anyone’s period of life so that the person might collapse through prolonged living and fall away from the right faith in the course of a long life. Indeed, longevity itself must be counted among God’s benefits, by which a person ought to have become better, not worse.

### IV

Likewise, whoever says that not everyone is called to grace cannot be criticized if he is speaking of those to whom Christ has not been proclaimed. For we certainly know that the Gospel has been destined for all the ends of the earth; but we do not think that it has already been preached in every region of the earth. Nor can we say that the call of grace exists where there has not yet been any regeneration through the mother Church.

### V

Likewise, whoever says that those who were called were not called equally, but that some were called so that they might believe and others so that they might not believe—as though the call had been the cause of anyone’s unbelief—does not speak rightly. For although faith is only from God’s gift and the human will, unbelief is nevertheless only from the human will.

### VI

Likewise, whoever says that free choice in a human being is nothing, but that God’s predestination operates in human beings either toward good or toward evil, is not a Catholic. For God’s grace does not abolish human choice but cultivates it; it recalls and restores it from error to the way, so that what was crooked through its own freedom may become straight through the action of God’s Spirit.

God’s predestination, moreover, is always directed toward the good. It knows either to forgive sin, committed solely by the human will, with the praise of mercy, or to punish it with the praise of justice.

### VII

Likewise, whoever says that God did not give perseverance to certain of his sons whom he regenerated in Christ and to whom he gave faith, hope, and love, because by God’s foreknowledge and predestination they had not been distinguished from the mass of perdition—if he means to maintain by this that God did not wish such people to remain in the good things he had given them, and that he himself became the cause of their turning away—holds an opinion contrary to God’s justice.

For although God’s omnipotence could have supplied the strength to stand to those who were going to fall, his grace did not abandon them before they abandoned it. And because he foresaw that they would make this defection voluntarily, he did not include them in the election of predestination.

### VIII

Likewise, whoever says that God does not wish all human beings to be saved, but only a fixed number of the predestined, speaks more harshly than one ought to speak concerning the height of God’s inscrutable grace. For God both wishes all to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Tim. 2:4), and fulfills the purpose of his will in those whom, having foreknown, he predestined; whom he predestined, he called; whom he called, he justified; and whom he justified, he glorified (Rom. 8:29–30). He loses nothing from the fullness of the nations or from the whole seed of Israel, for which an eternal kingdom was prepared in Christ before the foundation of the world (Matt. 25:34).

For the whole world is chosen from the whole world, and all human beings are adopted from all human beings. Nor can God’s promise in any way waver because of the unbelief and disobedience of many, when he said to Abraham, “In your seed all the nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22:18; 26:4). What God promised, he is also able to do (Rom. 4:21): so that those who are saved are saved because God wished them to be saved, while those who perish perish because they deserved to perish.

### IX

Likewise, whoever says that the Savior was not crucified for the redemption of the whole world looks not to the power of the sacrament but to the portion of unbelievers. For the blood of our Lord Jesus Christ is the price of the whole world. Those who are strangers to that price are those who, either delighted with their captivity, refused to be redeemed, or, after redemption, returned to the same servitude.

The word of the Lord has not failed, nor has the redemption of the world been made void. For although the world did not know God in the vessels of wrath, the world nevertheless knew God in the vessels of mercy, which God—without any preceding good merits of theirs—rescued from the power of darkness and transferred into the kingdom of his beloved Son (Col. 1:13).

### X

Likewise, whoever says that the preaching of the Gospel is withheld by the Lord from certain people so that they may not be saved after receiving the preaching of the Gospel can evade the hostility of this objection by appealing to the Savior himself. He did not wish to perform miracles among certain people who, he said, would have believed if they had seen the signs of his miracles (Matt. 11:21; Luke 10:13). He also forbade the Apostles to preach the Gospel to certain peoples (Acts 16:6–7), and even now permits some nations to live outside his grace.

Nevertheless, we hold with the firmest faith that the Church is to be extended into all parts of the world (Ps. 19:4; 22:28; 72:8; Isa. 11:9–10; 27:6, etc.), and that this age is not to end before the Gospel is directed to all the ends of the earth and every tongue confesses that Jesus is in the glory of God the Father (Phil. 2:11).

### XI

Likewise, whoever says that God compels human beings into sins by his power is rightly censured. For God, who is the author of justice and goodness, and whose statutes and commandments are all directed against sin, must not be believed to compel anyone to sin or to hurl anyone from innocence into crimes.

If there are people of such profound impiety that they are regarded as beyond the remedy of correction, they do not receive from God an increase of wickedness; rather, they become worse through themselves. For because of their preceding sins they deserved to be abandoned by God and handed over to themselves and to their deceivers, so that sin itself might become for them the punishment of sin.

### XII

Likewise, whoever says that obedience is withdrawn from certain people who have been called and who live piously and justly, so that they cease to obey, has a bad opinion of God’s goodness and justice. This would make it appear that he compels the pious to impiety and takes innocence away from the good, although he himself is both the giver and guardian of piety and innocence.

Whoever, therefore, adheres to God is moved by the Spirit of God; whoever withdraws from God ceases to obey by his own will.

### XIII

Likewise, whoever says that certain human beings were not created by God for the purpose of attaining eternal life, but merely to adorn the condition of the present age and to be born for the benefit of others, would speak better if he said that God, who is the creator of all things, does not create even those in vain whom he foresaw would not become participants in eternal life.

For even in wicked people, nature itself is God’s good work, and justice is praiseworthy in the condemnation of the impious. Nor can the person who says that the world is adorned even by the condition of such people be rightly censured, or that those who will harm themselves through their own wickedness are born for the benefit of others.

For no multitude, however countless, of impious people is unbecoming to the world or useless to God’s kingdom. Even through their offspring comes the generation that is to be regenerated; and, by enduring and loving them, the people of God becomes more illustrious, learning [Note: [Col. 1843] Thus the Remigianus manuscript. The printed editions have “leading.”] goodness and patience from him who makes his rain fall upon the just and the unjust and makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil (Matt. 5:45).

### XIV

Likewise, whoever says that those who do not believe the evangelical preaching do not believe by God’s predestination, and that God has so determined it that whoever does not believe does not believe by his own ordinance, is not a Catholic.

For just as faith, which works through love, is God’s gift, so unbelief is not God’s ordinance. God knows how to order punishments for crimes, not crimes; it does not follow that, because he has not forgiven something, he himself committed it. The predestined, therefore, lives by the faith given to him; the non-predestined perishes through voluntary, not compelled, unbelief.

### XV

Likewise, whoever says that foreknowledge is the same as predestination undoubtedly confuses these two with regard to our good works. For the things we have from God’s gift, which are called foreknown, cannot fail also to be predestined; and the things called predestined cannot fail also to be foreknown.

But in our evil works only God’s foreknowledge is to be understood. For just as he foreknew and predestined the things that he himself does and gave us to do, so he merely foreknew, and did not also predestine, the things that he neither did himself nor required us to do.

[Col. 1843]

# PROSPER OF AQUITAINE’S RESPONSES TO THE CHAPTERS OF THE VINCENTIAN OBJECTIONS, ON BEHALF OF AUGUSTINE’S TEACHING

[Note: [Col. 1843] The Remigianus manuscript, written approximately eight hundred years ago, had in the first hand “Vincentiarum”; corrected long ago by a second hand, it now presents “Vincentianarum” (as is read without correction at the end of the book). The Louvain scholars observe that some believe the author of the Objections to have been Vincent of Lérins, whose Commonitorium against the profane novelties of heresies survives. It was written around the year 434, or, as the author himself testifies in chapter 42, nearly three years after the Council of Ephesus celebrated against Nestorius.]

One book.

[Col. 1843] **PREFACE**

Certain people, having forgotten Christian and fraternal charity, strive by every means to damage our reputation so greatly that, in their desire to harm us, they do not see that they are overthrowing their own. For they compose and, in whatever statements they can, gather together the monstrous falsehoods of certain utterly foolish blasphemies; and they circulate these publicly and privately, displaying and thrusting them upon many people. They assert that such things are present in our position as are contained in a diabolical little catalogue.

We could easily and sufficiently prove by the subscription of a single anathema that these things are falsely hurled against us to arouse envy, were it not that the malignity of those who think themselves burdened if people think well of us would regard the brevity of our subscription itself with suspicion.

Therefore, lest an occasion for this complaint be found, we have judged it necessary and appropriate—whether to calm the minds of the accusers or to instruct the ears of those who have heard something of this sort—to set forth fully and clearly, insofar as this can be done with the Lord’s help, what judgment we hold concerning these perverse definitions.

Accordingly, after setting out sixteen chapters one by one, we shall place beneath each one the words expressing our position and the faith that, by the authority of the Apostolic See, we defend against the Pelagians. Thus those who deign to devote a little time to reading these words may clearly recognize that no trace of impious and profane opinions has adhered to our hearts, and may judge that the blasphemies they see condemned by our profession ought to be punished in those who produced them.

## FIRST OBJECTION

That our Lord Jesus Christ did not suffer for the salvation and redemption of all human beings.

[Col. 1844] **RESPONSE**

Against the wound of original sin, by which the nature of all human beings was corrupted and put to death in Adam, and from which the disease of all desires took root, the true, powerful, and unique remedy is the death of the Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ. He, free from the debt of death and alone without sin, died for sinners and debtors to death.

Therefore, with respect to the greatness and power of the price, and with respect to the one cause that concerns the human race, Christ’s blood is the redemption of the whole world. But those who pass through this age without faith in Christ and without the sacrament of regeneration are strangers to redemption.

Since, then, because of the one nature of all and the one cause assumed in truth by our Lord, all are rightly said to have been redeemed, while nevertheless not all have been rescued from captivity, the possession of redemption undoubtedly belongs to those from whom the ruler of this world has been cast out, and who are now not vessels of the devil but members of Christ.

His death was not expended upon the human race in such a way that even those who were not going to reign would belong to its redemption; rather, it was expended in such a way that what was accomplished for all through one unique example might be celebrated in individuals through a singular sacrament.

For the cup of immortality, which was prepared from our weakness and divine power, does indeed possess within itself the capacity to benefit everyone; but if it is not drunk, it does not heal.

## OBJECTION II

That God does not wish to save all, even if all wish to be saved.

### RESPONSE

Since the Truth says, “If you, although evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father give good things to those who ask him?” (Matt. 7:11), how could it be that God, who saves even those of whom it cannot be said that they wish to be saved, does not wish to save some even if they wish to be saved—unless there exist certain reasons about which, although they are unknown to us, he nevertheless judges well, and of whom it cannot be said that he ought to have done otherwise than he did?

Setting aside, therefore, this distinction, which divine knowledge holds within the secret of its justice, we must sincerely believe and profess that God wishes all human beings to be saved. For the Apostle, whose statement this is, most earnestly commands what is devoutly observed in all the churches: that supplications be made to God for all human beings (1 Tim. 2:1–4).

Of these, the fact that many perish is the merit of those who perish; the fact that many are saved is the gift of the one who saves. For that the guilty person is condemned is the blameless justice of God; but that the guilty person is justified is the ineffable grace of God.

## OBJECTION III

That God creates the greater part of the human race for the purpose of destroying it eternally.

### RESPONSE

God is indeed the creator of all human beings, but no one was created by him for the purpose of perishing. For the cause of being born is one thing, and the cause of perishing another. That human beings are born is the Creator’s gift; that they perish is the transgressor’s merit.

For in Adam, in whom the nature of all human beings was preformed, all sinned, and they are bound by the same sentence that he incurred. Nor are they released from this bond, even if they are free from personal sins, unless they are reborn through the Holy Spirit in the sacrament of Christ’s death and resurrection.

He is therefore exceedingly impious and ignorant who does not distinguish the defect of nature from the author of nature. Whatever is deserving of condemnation in any person is wholly alien to him. He creates human beings so that they may be human beings, nor does he withhold his workmanship while multiplying the succession of generations; according to the purpose of his good will, he will restore in many what he himself made, and punish in many what he himself did not make.

“For just as through the disobedience of one human being the many were constituted sinners, so through the obedience of one human being the many are constituted righteous” (Rom. 5:12, 19).

## OBJECTION IV

That God creates the greater part of the human race so that they may do not God’s will but the devil’s.

### RESPONSE

It is altogether insane and contrary to reason to say that God’s will is not done by God’s will, and that the one who condemns the devil and his servants wishes the devil to be served.

But the Pelagians consequently suppose that they can raise this objection against Catholics, who deny that Adam’s sin passed into all people. For if original guilt does not bind at the first birth, infants are not liable to the devil, nor do those who have never departed from their creator need to be rescued from the power of darkness.

We, however, who profess that all perished in Adam—for the Son of Man came to seek and save what was lost (Luke 19:10)—do not therefore say that anyone is created so as to do the devil’s will. We acknowledge that every unredeemed person is the devil’s captive.

For the transgression of human beings could not disturb the order of creation established from the ages; and the sinful creature rightly suffers the punitive domination of the one to whom, having abandoned the true Lord, it willingly sold itself.

This servitude is not God’s institution but his judgment: through it, the fraud of the deceiving devil has become punishment for the deceived and wrongly believing human being. No one is rescued from it except through the mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus. His gratuitous grace is not bestowed because of the evil merits of many, nor is it preceded by the good merits of any.

## OBJECTION V

That God is the author of our sins, because, by making the human will evil, he fashions the substance that by natural impulse can do nothing but sin.

### RESPONSE

The vanity of this objection also proceeds from that school in which human nature is defended as free from Adam’s sin and unharmed. Thus, because we assert that all human beings are born guilty of transgression and liable to condemnation, and that they will perish unless they are reborn in Christ, we may appear to say that the one whom we profess to be the creator of nature is also the author of guilt.

We utterly reject this from our position. We know God, just and good, to be the creator of human substance and of its inward and outward senses, so that whatever belongs to nature is wholly from him, while whatever is contrary to nature is wholly not from him.

Sin, however, is contrary to nature, and from it death and all things belonging to death arise. With these evils human beings clothed themselves when the devil, having deprived them of faith and obedience, led them away from God’s law into his own promises, and bound all the offspring of their posterity to himself through the condition of a corrupted stock.

Therefore, if anyone is a new creation in Christ, he is freed from the devil and subjected to God, restored from his deformity to the image of the one who created him. If this does not happen, he remains in the one in whom all die, having no share in the one in whom all will be made alive.

God, therefore, is not the author of anyone’s sin but the creator of nature. Nature, although it possessed the power not to sin, sinned voluntarily and subjected itself to its deceiver by its own will. It is not by a natural but by a captive impulse that it moves in vice, until it dies to sin and lives to God. It cannot do this without God’s grace, because it does not recover the freedom it lost through freedom unless Christ sets it free.

“For there is no other name under heaven given among human beings by which we must be saved” (Acts 4:12).

## OBJECTION VI

That God fashions in human beings a free choice like that of demons, which by its own impulse can wish nothing other than evil.

### RESPONSE

The whole world, as the Apostle John says, lies in the evil one (1 John 5:19), and the wickedness of many human beings is like that of demons. To such people the Lord said, “Brood of vipers, how can you speak good things when you are evil?” (Matt. 12:34), and, “You are born from the devil as your father, and you wish to do your father’s desires” (John 8:44).

But this distinguishes wicked human beings from demons: even very wicked human beings retain the possibility of reconciliation if God has mercy, whereas no conversion has been reserved for demons eternally.

Therefore, just as God did not implant in the transgressing angels the will that did not stand in the truth, so he did not implant in human beings this disposition by which they would imitate the devil. The liar speaks from what is his own, and he will not be free from lying unless the truth sets him free (ibid., 36).

## OBJECTION VII

That it is God’s will that a large part of Christians neither wish nor are able to be saved.

### RESPONSE

If this is said of those who, abandoning the piety of Christian conduct and faith, have irrevocably passed into profane errors or damnable ways of life, there is no doubt that, having such a will, they do not wish to be saved; and as long as they do not wish to be saved, they cannot be saved.

But it must in no way be believed that such people fell into this despair by God’s will, since the Lord rather raises up all who fall and lifts up all who are cast down (Ps. 145:14). No one is raised up except by his grace, and no one is established except by his grace.

God’s will, therefore, is that one remain in a good will. He abandons no one before being abandoned, and he often converts many who have abandoned him.

## OBJECTION VIII

That God does not wish all Catholics to persevere in the Catholic faith, but wishes a large part of them to apostatize from it.

### RESPONSE

The impiety of this blasphemy is no different from the preceding statement. Therefore, what was the answer to that objection should also be the answer to this one, which differs from it in no respect.

## OBJECTION IX

That God wishes a large part of the saints to fall from their purpose of holiness.

### RESPONSE

The madness of this definition says nothing other than what the twofold preceding objection has already stated. It is therefore surprising that the objector repeated for a third time what it would have been sufficient to say once. But, as matters stand, he wished to increase the number of his accusations because he could not vary their meaning.

## OBJECTION X

That adulteries and the seductions of consecrated virgins occur because God predestined them to fall.

### RESPONSE

This is a detestable and abominable opinion, which believes God to be the author of anyone’s evil will or evil action. His predestination is never outside goodness and never outside justice, for all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth (Ps. 24:10).

[Col. 1847] Holy divinity knows not how to institute the adulteries of married women [Note: [Col. 1847] The Remigianus manuscript reads “of husbands.”] or the seductions of virgins, but to condemn them; not to ordain them, but to punish them.

When human beings commit these evils, they serve their own desires and cravings, which they drew from that first stain of voluntary transgression. But when they turn away from evil and do good, the Lord directs a person’s steps and takes delight in his way (Ps. 37:27, 23).

For this reason the Apostle says: “We pray to God that you do no evil—not so that we may appear approved, but so that you may do what is good” (2 Cor. 13:7).

The fall of those who collapse, therefore, the wickedness of the unjust, and the desires of sinners were not aroused, advised, or compelled by God’s predestination. Rather, it plainly predestined his judgment, by which he will repay each person according to what he has done, whether good or evil.

This judgment would certainly not exist if human beings sinned by God’s will. But it will most certainly exist, and every person whom the distinction of divine knowledge places on the left will be condemned, because he carried out not God’s will but his own.

## OBJECTION XI

That when fathers commit incest with daughters, mothers with sons, or servants kill their masters, this happens because God predestined it to happen.

### RESPONSE

If the devil were accused of being himself the author and instigator of such crimes, I think he could in some way free himself from this accusation and prove that the perpetrators of such crimes acted according to their own will. For although he delighted in the fury of sinners, he could nevertheless show that he had not imposed the force of the crimes upon them.

With what folly, then, or madness is it determined that what cannot wholly be attributed even to the devil should be referred to God’s plan? The devil, who assists the allurements of sinners in their crimes, must not be believed to be the creator of their wills.

God therefore predestined none of these acts to occur. Nor did he prepare that soul, which would live wickedly and shamefully, so that it might live in this manner. Rather, he was not ignorant that it would become such, and he foreknew that he would justly judge it as such.

Thus nothing else can be referred to his predestination except what pertains either to the due recompense of justice or to the undeserved generosity of grace.

## OBJECTION XII

That by God’s predestination children of God become children of the devil, temples of demons emerge from temples of the Holy Spirit, and members of a prostitute emerge from members of Christ.

### RESPONSE

God’s predestination, although it is uncertain to us while we move amid the dangers of the present life, remains unchangeable with him who made the things that were to come. He does not blind what he has illuminated, destroy what he has built, or uproot what he has planted.

“For the gifts and calling of God are irrevocable” (Rom. 11:29), and “God’s firm foundation stands, bearing this seal: The Lord knows those who are his” (2 Tim. 2:19).

God’s predestination, therefore, in no way makes some of the children of God children of the devil, or some of the temples of the Holy Spirit temples of demons, or some of the members of Christ members of a prostitute. Rather, predestination makes children of God out of children of the devil, a temple of the Holy Spirit out of temples of demons, and members of Christ out of members of a prostitute.

For he himself binds the strong man and plunders his vessels (Mark 3:27), rescuing them from the power of darkness and transferring them from dishonor into glory (Col. 1:13).

Those of whom it is said, “They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us” (1 John 2:19), went out by their own will and fell by their own will. And because they were foreknown as going to fall, they were not predestined. They would have been predestined, however, if they were going to return and remain in holiness and truth.

Accordingly, God’s predestination is the cause of standing for many; it is the cause of falling for no one.

## OBJECTION XIII

That all those faithful and holy people who have been predestined to eternal death, when they relapse into their own vomit, seem indeed to do this through their own fault; but the cause of that fault is divine predestination, which secretly withdraws good wills from them.

### RESPONSE

The same spirit of blasphemy persists, and the succeeding impiety does not depart from the preceding falsehoods. Sound reason utterly rejects it, and sound teaching unhesitatingly condemns it.

For all who fall back from faith into unbelief and from holiness into shamefulness, and who are not cleansed by any correction before the end of life, deserve nothing other than eternal death. But it is sacrilegious to attribute the causes of such falls to God. Although, from his eternal knowledge, he has foreknown what he will repay to each person according to that person’s merits, he has not thereby—because he cannot be deceived—imposed upon anyone either the necessity or the will to sin.

If, therefore, someone falls away from justice and piety, he is driven headlong by his own choice, drawn by his own desire, and deceived by his own persuasion. The Father does nothing there, nor the Son, nor the Holy Spirit; nothing of the divine will intervenes in such an affair. By God’s work, we know that many are held back so that they do not fall; none, however, are driven so that they may fall.

## OBJECTION XIV

That the large part of Christians—Catholics, faithful, and holy—who have been predestined to ruin and destruction will not obtain perseverance in holiness from God even if they ask for it, because the divine predestination cannot be changed, having preordained, prepared, and fitted them to fall.

### RESPONSE

There is absolutely no predestination of God toward transgression of the law, neglect of religion, corruption of discipline, abandonment of faith, or commission of any kind of sin. Nor can it happen that the one through whom a person rises from such evils should be the one through whom he falls into them.

If, therefore, a person lives in holiness, advances in virtue, and perseveres in good pursuits, this is manifestly a gift of God, without which the fruit of no good work is obtained. But if a person withdraws from these things and passes over to vices and sins, God introduces nothing of the evil temptation. He does not abandon the one who is going to withdraw before that person withdraws; indeed, he often acts so that the person will not withdraw, or even, if he has departed, that he may return.

Why he retains one person and does not retain another is neither possible to comprehend nor lawful to investigate. It is enough to know both that what is stood in comes from him, and that what is fallen into does not come from him.

## OBJECTION XV

That all those faithful and holy people who have been predestined to eternal death, after they have fallen, are so disposed by God that they can neither be freed nor wish to be freed through repentance.

### RESPONSE

This is not said truthfully or wisely. For those who have fallen away from faith and holiness do not rise by their will, just as they fell through their will; they willingly endure the domination of the desires to which they succumbed.

But if some grieve over their captivity and, judging themselves, flee with changed hearts to the mercy of God, they do this not without the spirit of divine visitation. For this is “the change of the right hand of the Most High” (Ps. 77:11), who grants countless fallen people repentance so that they may recover from the snares of the devil, by whom they were held captive for his will (2 Tim. 2:26).

God deprives no one of the path of correction, nor does he strip anyone of the possibility of doing good. For whoever turns himself away from God has himself taken away from himself both the will and the ability to do what is good.

It does not follow, therefore, as those who raise such objections suppose, that God, because he has not given repentance to some, has taken away their recovery, or that, because he has not lifted up some, he has cast them down. For it is one thing to have driven an innocent person into crime, which is alien to God; it is another thing not to have granted forgiveness to a criminal, which proceeds from the sinner’s merit.

## OBJECTION XVI

That when that large part of the faithful and holy who have been predestined to eternal death says to God in the Lord’s Prayer, “Your will be done” (Matt. 6:10), it is asking nothing other than something against itself—that is, that they may fall and collapse—because God’s will is that they perish in eternal death.

## Response

Truth does not say that this is God’s will: that the faithful and the saints should fall away from faith and innocence and perish eternally. Rather, Truth says: “This is the will of him who sent me, the Father: that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me, but should raise it up on the last day” (John 6:39). Whatever, therefore, the Father has given the Son, the Son does not lose at all. For he also says: “Everything that the Father gives me will come to me, and whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (ibid., 37).

If, however, through the universality of the calling and the abundance of God’s goodness, those who will not persevere have been mingled with those who will persevere, then when the former fall away from piety, they fall away not through God’s action but through their own will. They are neither driven to fall nor cast out so that they may depart; yet their future fall and departure are foreknown by him who cannot be deceived.

Therefore, as long as they say in the Lord’s Prayer, “Your will be done” (Matt. 6:10), they are not asking against themselves for something God will in no way or by any means do—that is, that they should fall and collapse. Their own wickedness will bring this about; their own freedom will complete it. But plainly they do ask against themselves for what is unquestionably God’s will: namely, that when the Son of Man comes in his majesty and sits upon the throne of his glory, all the nations should be gathered before him, and he should separate them from one another, setting some at his right hand and others at his left; that the right-hand ones should hear him say, “Come, you blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world”; and that the left-hand ones should hear, “Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire which my Father prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:34, 41).

Thus those who do not intend to do God’s will, yet ask that God’s will be done, are heard in that matter which must be accomplished by God’s will, so that, as imitators of the devil, they may be judged with the devil. For those who rejected God’s will when it invited them will experience God’s will when it exacts punishment.

[Col. 1849]

**RESPONSES OF PROSPER OF AQUITAINE ON BEHALF OF AUGUSTINE TO THE EXCERPTS SENT FROM THE CITY OF GENOA. One book. (C)**

[Col. 1849] To the venerable priests **Camillus and Theodorus** [Note: [Col. 1849] The Remigianus Codex reads *Theudulo*.], Prosper sends greetings.

In the books of Bishop Augustine, of blessed memory, whose title is *On the Predestination of the Saints*, certain passages have disturbed Your Holiness, either because they are unfamiliar or because they are less clear. You sent them to my humility as excerpts from the course of his argument, so that you might learn with what understanding and judgment I received them—as though I possessed greater intellectual ability than you to examine these matters; and as though, rather, you ought not to have exercised the measure of your own capacity in this investigation, and, if some obscurity delayed you, to have hastened to the Father of lights, from whom every good gift and every perfect gift comes down (James 1:17), and from whom the Spirit of wisdom and understanding is given.

Nevertheless, I will not withhold my obedience to your instructions. With the Lord’s assistance—he who grants wisdom to the simple (Ps. 18:8)—I will briefly indicate what I think about these chapters with my holy and learned brothers, asking you not to regard as doctrinal presumption what arises from the simplicity of obedience. Of the excerpts, then, you first set forth the following, in which the words are those of Bishop Augustine.

### FIRST EXCERPT

“Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Rom. 9:13; Mal. 1:3). I carried my reasoning to this point, so that I said: God did not, then, choose anyone’s works—works which he himself would give—but chose faith in his foreknowledge, so that he might choose as his own the one whom he foresaw would believe, and give the Holy Spirit to him; so that, by doing good works, he might also attain eternal life. I had not yet investigated more carefully, nor had I yet discovered what the election of grace was like (*On the Predestination of the Saints*, §7).

### EXCERPT II

And then I added: “What we believe is ours; but what we do well belongs to him who gives the Holy Spirit to those who believe.” I certainly would not have said this if I had already known that faith itself is also found among God’s gifts, which is given in the same Spirit. Both are ours because of the freedom of the will; yet both have been given because of the Spirit of faith and love (ibid.).

### EXCERPT III

Accordingly, what I said later also is entirely true: “For we cannot even will unless we are called; and when, after the calling, we have willed, our will and our progress are not sufficient unless God both supplies strength to believers and leads them where he calls them.” Then I added: “It is therefore manifest that what we do well belongs not to the one who wills or to the one who runs, but to God who shows mercy” (Rom. 9:16). But I discussed too briefly the calling itself, which takes place according to God’s purpose. For the calling of all who are called is not of this kind, but only that of the elect (*On the Predestination of the Saints*, §7).

### RESPONSE

Although these three chapters have been separated from the body of the argument, and have thereby been made more obscure because they are no longer connected with what precedes, what lies between, or what follows, I nevertheless understand that the writer is dealing with one and the same matter. He is speaking about those who said that, at the beginning of his conversion, he had held better views, when he thought that the faith by which we are Christians did not come from grace and was not possessed as God’s gift, but came from the human being himself and from the freedom of the will. Now, they said, he was in error because he asserted that faith itself was also God’s gift, and that the saying “What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Cor. 4:7) applied to it as well.

They also said that he was wrong now to refer Jacob’s election to God’s purpose, since previously he had referred it to foreknowledge. To this objection, therefore, he replies that before he knew the truth of grace, and before he was placed over the governance of the Church, he had ignorantly erred in this opinion. But at the very beginning of his episcopate, after consulting the blessed Simplician, bishop of Milan, about Jacob’s election and Esau’s rejection, he had examined the entire question concerning these two brothers with more penetrating diligence and had recognized beyond doubt, with every power of reasoning, that no human merits precede the election of grace, and that faith—from which all merits begin—is God’s gift. Otherwise grace would not be grace (Rom. 11:6), if something preceded it for which it was bestowed.

Thus, in the statement “Jacob I loved,” what was given to the human being was shown; and in the statement “But Esau I hated” (ibid., 9:13), what was owed to the human being was shown. He carefully recalled this in the second book of his *Retractations* (ch. 1); and when he reviewed all his opinions with censorial rigor, he rejected the one which his detractors choose—the one which he foresaw, before the rise of the Pelagian heresy, as friendly to the error that would later arise, and which he rejected once the truth of grace had been revealed to him.

What reason, then, is there for us not to approve this man’s confession, by which he instructs us, through the example of his own correction, to correct our opinions if we have perhaps fallen into them imprudently, and by which he teaches that we receive from God what we are commanded to ask in order to receive? For if we consider the arguments of Pelagian impiety, what does it strive more earnestly to establish than that God’s grace is given according to our merits? Thus, precisely in the matter in which it confesses the necessity of grace, it weakens grace by attributing it to human will.

Anyone who thinks that faith does not belong among God’s gifts falls altogether into this perversity. Or he boasts that he refers faith to God only because human nature was created by him, and because he implanted in that nature rational freedom, through which each person has it in his own power to believe or not to believe; and that, from this natural good—which he received when he was created without any preceding merits—he merits the other gifts.

But whoever asserts this, I think, acknowledges with us that in the first Adam the nature of all human beings was corrupted; nor does he deny that in that fall it lost the virtues which it cannot possess unless it receives them through grace. What, then, is the meaning of his refusal to admit that faith alone was taken away from that nature, when, had it not first lost faith, it would not have been deprived of all the other goods?

By believing the devil, Adam did not believe God. When his spirit had been intoxicated with pride, his heart departed from the Lord, and he became the slave of the apostate while he wished to be free from righteousness. Since, then, we would not possess continence unless God gave it (Wis. 8:21), nor holy love unless the love of God had been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who was given to us (Rom. 5:5), and since, finally, no one would possess wisdom and understanding, counsel and strength, knowledge and piety, or fear of the Lord unless the Holy Spirit gave these virtues (Isa. 11:2–3), how could faith, lost in Adam, be found in any of his children unless the same Spirit, who works all things in all people (1 Cor. 12:6), infused it?

If Adam’s descendants did not lose what Adam lost, then his sin harmed him alone and not the human race. But “all sinned in one” (Rom. 5:12), and by the guilt of transgression his entire posterity was condemned. Therefore all lost what Adam lost. He lost faith first; and because we were able to lose it first, we need to receive it first.

Let us therefore approve this proclamation of grace, by which faith is defended as God’s gift. The Pelagian error will then be unable to deceive us in anything: for, in order to persuade us that grace is owed, it refuses to acknowledge that faith has been given.

Since, therefore, the persuasion of those who brought this man’s knowledge—built up through so many stages of progress and refined through so many years of study—back to the beginnings of his adolescence was neither just nor reasonable, so that what he had ineptly thought at the beginning of his conversion might support the heretics more than what truth had revealed through his episcopal diligence might benefit Catholics, the gravity of the pious teacher rightly censures those who use this prejudice and linger over what had long ago been renounced. They took care to investigate all his thoughts, but refused to advance with his learning.

Now let us consider what sort of matter it is that you have noted from what follows.

### EXCERPT IV

“Not because believing or not believing is not within the power of the human will, but because in the elect the will is prepared by the Lord” (*On the Predestination of the Saints*, §10).

### RESPONSE

Let us join what follows to this, so that what has been proposed may be clearer from the connected discourse. “Therefore the saying also applies to faith itself, which is in the will: ‘For who makes you differ? What do you have that you did not receive?’” (1 Cor. 4:7), says the Apostle.

Many hear the word of truth, but some believe and others contradict it. These wish to believe, while those do not wish to believe. Who does not know this? Who would deny it? But when the will is prepared for some and not prepared for others by the Lord, we must certainly distinguish what comes from mercy and what comes from judgment.

“What Israel was seeking, it did not obtain; but the election obtained it, while the rest were hardened, as it is written: ‘God gave them a spirit of compunction, eyes that they should not see, and ears that they should not hear, to this very day.’ And David says: ‘Let their table become a snare, and a trap, and a stumbling-block, and a recompense for them; let their eyes be darkened, so that they may not see, and always bend their back’” (Rom. 11:7–10).

Behold mercy and judgment: mercy in the election that obtained the righteousness of God; judgment in the others who were hardened. Yet the former believed because they wished to; the latter did not believe because they did not wish to. Mercy and judgment, therefore, were exercised in the very wills. For this election is an election of grace, not of merits.

Earlier he had said: “In this present time a remnant has been saved according to the election of grace. But if it is by grace, it is no longer from works; otherwise grace is no longer grace” (Rom. 11:5–6). Grace, then, obtained what the election obtained. Nothing preceded them that they might first give and that could then be repaid to them: “He saved them for no reason” (Ps. 55:8). But in the others who were hardened, as the passage does not leave unsaid, it occurred by way of recompense.

“All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. 24:10). Yet “his ways are unsearchable” (Rom. 11:33). Unsearchable, therefore, are both the mercy by which he freely delivers and the truth by which he justly judges (*On the Predestination of the Saints*, §§10–11).

What offense do all these things cause for a devout and Catholic reader? What contradiction do they encounter? Is it false that the will is prepared by the Lord (Prov. 8, according to the Septuagint)? Are not all who are led by the Spirit of God sons of God (Rom. 8:14)? Is it nature that distinguishes one human being from another, rather than grace that distinguishes the believer from the unbeliever? Can anyone say that he has something he did not receive, or boast as though it were his own of something he did not receive—which, had he not received it, he certainly would not possess?

When the word of truth is preached, is it doubtful that some believe by their will while others do not believe by their will? But when God opens the heart of some and does not open the heart of others, we must distinguish what comes from mercy and what from judgment.

After recalling the apostolic statement, which he reinforces with prophetic testimonies—that the election obtained by grace the righteousness of God which Israel did not obtain while seeking it, whereas the others were blinded in recompense—is it not most truly said: “Behold mercy and judgment: mercy in the election that obtained the righteousness of God; judgment in the others who were blinded”? And shortly afterward: “Freely, therefore, the election obtained what it obtained. Nothing preceded them that they might first give and that could be repaid to them: ‘He saved them for no reason.’ But in the others who were blinded, as the passage does not leave unsaid, it occurred by way of recompense.”

What room is there here for complaint, except among the enemies of grace? Unless they refer what is given freely to recompense, they wish what is repaid to belong to injustice.

Further, who has denied what he added from the prophetic words: “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. 24:10)? Or what he attached from the apostolic meaning: “His ways are unsearchable” (Rom. 11:33)—“unsearchable, therefore, both the mercy by which he freely delivers and the truth by which he justly judges”?

It is not characteristic of sound minds to criticize these things, or to count the unsearchable ways of the Lord—that is, the gifts of mercy and the judgments of truth—as penetrable by Pelagian arrogance. For, according to the Pelagians, God’s plan is not hidden, nor is the reasoning of his divine will concealed, if both God’s grace and his anger toward every human being arise from merit.

After this you set down what is said below:

### EXCERPT V

“Faith, therefore, both begun and perfected, is God’s gift. And let no one who does not wish to resist the most manifest sacred Scriptures doubt that this gift is given to some and not given to others” (*On the Predestination of the Saints*, §16).

### RESPONSE

If someone does not accept this, whose view does he appear to hold except that of one who says: “The faith by which I am justified comes from myself; and this good by which the just person lives (Hab. 2:4) I did not receive through grace, but possess by nature”?

If faith is not God’s gift, then the Church prays in vain for unbelievers to believe, and it is enough for the impious merely to be provided with the instruction of the law. Concerning the law it was said: “If righteousness comes from the law, then Christ died for nothing” (Gal. 2:21). The same can likewise be said of nature.

The Apostle also gives thanks to God in vain for those who received the Gospel (2 Thess. 2:12–13), if, according to the Pelagians, this was not bestowed by God’s gift but is possessed solely through the human will. And the same Apostle prays in vain for some that they may have peace and love with faith from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ (Eph. 6:23). Thus the arrogance of the heretics would be convicted of claiming as its own not only faith, but also peace and love.

But if these things come from the human being, what prevents him from possessing by himself the other, lesser goods, when he dares to claim for himself the highest goods, without which the others, however numerous and splendid, are of no benefit?

The statement “Faith, therefore, both begun and perfected, is God’s gift” cannot rightly be refuted. It is also the voice of the Apostle, who says: “By grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not from yourselves; it is God’s gift, not from works, so that no one may boast” (Eph. 2:8–9); and, “To you it has been granted for Christ’s sake not only to believe in him, but also to suffer for him” (Phil. 1:29); and again, “Let us run with endurance the race set before us, looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith” (Heb. 12:1–2).

Through these and very many other testimonies of the divine Scriptures it is recognized beyond doubt that, as this man defined it, faith, both begun and perfected, is God’s gift. And he says that no one who does not wish to resist the most manifest sacred Scriptures doubts that this gift is given to some and not given to others.

Let us not think this was said truthfully if all human beings are believers. But when some believe and others do not, and the Apostle says, “Faith is not possessed by all” (2 Thess. 3:2), who does not see that those who have received faith possess it, while those who do not have it have not received it?

### EXCERPT VI

Then he says:

“Why it is not given to all should not disturb the believer who holds that all proceeded from one person into condemnation—condemnation unquestionably most just—so that there would be no just complaint against God even if no one were delivered from it. Hence it is clear that great is the grace by which many are delivered; and in those who are not delivered they recognize what was owed to them, so that the one who boasts may boast not in his own merits—which he sees to be equal to those of the condemned—but in the Lord.

“Why he delivers this person rather than that person: his judgments are unsearchable and his ways are inscrutable” (Rom. 11:33). For here too it is better that we hear or say, ‘O man, who are you to answer back to God?’ (Rom. 9:20), than that we dare to say, as though we knew it, what he wished to remain hidden, although he could not will anything unjust” (*On the Predestination of the Saints*, §16).

### RESPONSE

If all these things have not been correctly stated, then God’s judgments are searchable and his ways traceable. It is not hidden why this person rather than that person is saved; and the one who is found worthy by election will boast in himself, not in the Lord, while others perish through their own fault.

In that case it will indeed be justice that many are condemned, but it will not be grace that many are delivered. Far be this from Catholic hearts; far be such impiety, that we should think anyone rescued from the power of darkness by his own merits and transferred into the kingdom of God’s Son through a deserved rather than a gratuitous adoption.

Adam perished through a great sin, and all perished in him. Since every human being born under condemnation is owed this in Adam: that he should perish. And just as we cannot complain that in former ages God permitted all the nations to walk in their own ways, so we would have no just cause for complaint if, along with those with whom we shared a common cause, we were to perish while grace still remained absent.

Yet just as grace then rescued a few from the whole world, so now it saves countless people from the entire human race—not according to our works, but according to his purpose and grace, which was given to us in Christ Jesus before eternal times (2 Tim. 1:9).

You also added what he says after discussing many matters:

### EXCERPT VII

“It is therefore within the power of the wicked to sin. But that, by sinning, their wickedness should do this or that is not within their power, but within the power of God, who divides the darkness and orders it, so that even what they do against God’s will does not come to pass except according to God’s will” (*On the Predestination of the Saints*, §33).

### RESPONSE

Although this is a most evident truth, it has been cut out strangely from the midst of obscurity, as though the reader’s every hesitation could not be resolved from the connected context. Consider, therefore, what follows.

“We read,” he says, “in the Acts of the Apostles that, after the Apostles had been released by the Jews, they came to their own people and reported all that the chief priests and elders had done to them. They raised their voices together to the Lord and said:

‘Lord, you are the one who made heaven and earth and everything in them, who through the mouth of our father David, your holy servant, said:

“Why did the nations rage, and the peoples devise empty things? The kings of the earth stood by, and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ.”

“For in truth they gathered together in this city against your holy servant Jesus, whom you anointed, to do whatever your hand and your plan predestined to take place’” (Acts 4:23–28).

If, then, what the Holy Spirit prophesied through the mouth of our father David cannot in any way be understood otherwise than as the Apostles understood it, and Herod, Pilate, and the people of Israel did whatever God’s hand and plan predestined to take place, what inappropriate thing did this remarkable disputant say when he said:

‘It is within the power of the wicked to sin; but that, by sinning, their wickedness should do this or that is not within their power, but within the power of God, who divides the darkness and orders it, so that even what they do against God’s will does not come to pass except according to God’s will’?

For it is very easy for the wicked to will evil; and there is no doubt that their damnable will is confined by God’s power, so that they cannot obtain the result of their desire unless he permits it.

No one who has been even slightly instructed in piety is unaware that God employs his wisdom and justice through the deeds even of the wicked—deeds that proceed from their own desire—to fulfill his plans and judgments. Such a person sees that the supremely good will of God the Father, who did not spare his own Son but handed him over for us all, was fulfilled through the exceedingly evil will of the betrayer Judas and of the Jews.

He also reads in the Gospel pages that Pilate said to Jesus, ‘You do not speak to me? Do you not know that I have authority to crucify you and authority to release you?’ The Lord answered, ‘You would have no authority over me at all unless it had been given to you from above’ (John 19:10–11).

God therefore divides between light and darkness. The darkness is not thereby blameless because God makes good use of it—he who also ordained that, through its work, something should proceed for the good of the children of light. He merely permits the malice of those who desire to do harm to advance as far as he knows it to be useful either for correcting or for testing his saints. Thus even what they do against God’s will does not come to pass except according to God’s will.

The book proceeds next with what is found in its second part.

### EXCERPT VIII

“Would anyone dare to say that God did not foreknow to whom he would give the ability to believe, or whom he would give to his Son so that he would not lose any of them (John 18:9)? If he certainly foreknew these things, then he also foreknew his benefits by which he graciously deigns to deliver us.

“This predestination of the saints is nothing other than the foreknowledge, namely, and preparation of God’s benefits, by which all who are delivered are most certainly delivered. But where are the others left except in the mass of perdition, where the Tyrians and Sidonians were left (Matt. 11:21)? They too could have believed if they had seen those wondrous signs of Christ. But because it was not given to them to believe, even the means by which they might believe was withheld from them” (*On the Gift of Perseverance*, §35).

### RESPONSE

Those who resist these statements are shown most clearly to hold the view that faith is not God’s gift, that grace does not precede free will but follows it, and that God’s grace is given according to our merits.

For if they confess that something is bestowed upon a human being through grace, but that no one receives it except through faith—and faith is not given—then merit lies in the person to whom a gift is not given but a debt is repaid.

Holding this view, they consequently believe that those are predestined to eternal life whom God foreknew would become believers through the exercise of free will. Thus the predestination of the elect is nothing but recompense. In those who are predestined according to the purpose of him who works all things, God does not work faith; and if God works all things, there are no merits belonging to the human being.

Those who think this way truly have not received faith, or have lost the faith they had received by following the utterly empty pride of the Pelagians and boasting in themselves rather than in the Lord, who works all things in all people—good things, certainly, not evil ones. If he works all good things, then he also works faith, without which no one can please God (Heb. 11:6), and which is the foundation of all virtues.

What sort of position is it, then, that although the building belongs to God, and unless the Lord builds the house those who build it labor in vain (Ps. 126:1), these people either refuse to let the foundation belong to the building or wish to begin themselves what the Lord can construct?

The Son of God will not be their beginning. They will not be founded upon Christ Jesus, the cornerstone, nor does the saying “God’s firm foundation stands” (2 Tim. 2:19) apply to them, because they place their entire election upon shifting sand and crumbling ash. [Note: [Col. 1855] The Remigianus manuscript reads *elationem* (“their entire arrogance”) instead of *electionem* (“their entire election”).]

Let us therefore acknowledge wisely and confess piously that God unchangeably foreknew to whom he would give the ability to believe, and whom he would give to his Son so that he would not lose any of them. If he foreknew these things, then he foreknew his benefits by which he deigns to deliver us. This, therefore, is the predestination of the saints: the foreknowledge, namely, and preparation of God’s grace, by which all who are delivered are most certainly delivered [Note: [Col. 1855] Perhaps *all who are delivered* should be added.].

As for all the others who are not delivered—those whom grace did not remove from the general perdition of the human race—let us know that they were not removed by a just judgment. Let us learn from them what has been remitted to us, since we cannot complain about their condemnation. For there is no injustice with God (2 Chron. 19:7), nor does anyone innocent perish under his judgment.

As this distinguished preacher of grace himself says elsewhere: “God certainly repays evil with evil, because he is just; good with evil, because he is good; and good with good, because he is just and good. He does not repay evil with good, because he is not unjust. Thus he repays evil with evil—punishment for injustice; he repays good with evil—grace for injustice; and he repays good with good—grace for grace” (*On Grace and Free Will*, §45).

When some perish, let us not doubt that their perishing is attributed to their own merits; God could indeed mercifully deliver them if he wished. And when some are delivered, let us not dare to define that they were worthy to be delivered; God could indeed justly condemn them if he wished.

Why he does not deliver all, or why he delivers these rather than those, is neither necessary to ask nor possible to discover. For, leaving aside the reasons for this distinction, it is enough to know that with him mercy does not remove justice, nor justice mercy: from him no one is condemned except justly, and no one is delivered except mercifully.

As for the Tyrians and Sidonians, what else can we say than that it was not given to them to believe—although Truth itself says that they would have believed if they had seen such signs of power as had been performed among those who did not believe (Matt. 11:21)?

Let those who make accusations say, if they can, why this was denied to them, and let them show why the Lord performed miracles among those for whom they would not be beneficial, but did not perform them among those for whom they would have been beneficial.

Even if we cannot penetrate the reason for what he did or the depth of his judgment, we nevertheless know with complete clarity that what he said is true and that what he did is just. We know not only that the Tyrians and Sidonians, but also Chorazin and Bethsaida, could have been converted and could have become believers from unbelievers if the Lord had wished to work this in them.

For no one can regard as false what Truth says: “No one can come to me unless it has been given to him by my Father” (John 6:65); and, “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of heaven, but to them it has not been given” (Matt. 13:11); and, “No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son wishes to reveal him” (Matt. 11:27); and, “Just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whomever he wishes” (John 5:21); and, “No one can say ‘Lord Jesus’ except in the Holy Spirit” (1 Cor. 12:3).

Instructed by these authoritative divine utterances, let us give thanks to God, who has given us the spirit of faith and power, of continence and love, of wisdom and understanding, of counsel and strength, of knowledge and piety, and of fear of him.

If he had not given us these goods—he who works all things in all people—we would certainly not possess them in ourselves.
