With those who did not know God, or who, although they knew him, did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but attributed this very knowledge to their own wisdom and thus became fools, with darkened hearts and futile thoughts (Rom. 1:21–22), we would be sitting in darkness and in the shadow of death, having neither complaint concerning punishment, nor defense based on ignorance, nor protection based on nature.

Now let us see what sort of thing follows.

### EXCERPT IX

“But they say, as you write, that no one can be stirred by the goads of correction if it is said in the assembly of the Church, with many people listening:

‘This is how the fixed decree of God’s will concerning predestination stands: some of you will come from unbelief to faith after receiving the will to obey, or, after receiving perseverance, will remain in the faith. But the rest of you, who linger in the pleasure of sins, have not yet risen for this reason: because the assistance of merciful grace has not yet raised you.

‘Nevertheless, if there are some among you who have not yet been called, but whom grace has predestined to be chosen, you will receive that same grace by which you may will and may be chosen. And if there are some who obey but are predestined to be rejected, the strength to obey will be withdrawn from them, so that they will cease to obey’” (*On the Gift of Perseverance*, §38).

**RESPONSE.** I am astonished that Your Holiness could not distinguish the objection of the detractors from the person of the defender of grace, and that you applied the words of the detractors to the very man who responds to his detractors. For certain men were wickedly and foolishly asserting this about the teaching of the Catholic man: that if one preached such a grace of God that faith and obedience and the other virtues, together with perseverance in them to the end, were believed to be obtainable only as a gift of God, it necessarily followed that one would address the people in such words and, by such declarations, remove every exercise of free choice.

Since the most devout teacher had recognized this in the letters of those to whom he was writing, he therefore says, “But they say, as you write”; and afterward, “When they say these things.” From this, then, you could have understood that he himself was not saying these things, but those of whom he said, “But they say, as you write,” and, “When they say these things.” The Apostle similarly says, “As some say that we say, ‘Let us do evil, that good may come’” (Rom. III, 8).

Further below, when he responds to these matters more fully, it is much more clearly evident that such things were never said by him in this manner, and how displeasing to him is this form of preaching. Correcting, purifying, and amending it, he makes it more tolerable to his hearers, moderating what is true and cutting away what is false. After much else he adds:

“Now as for what is connected with those words, I wonder whether any weak person in a Christian congregation can hear it patiently in any way, when it is said to them: ‘And if there are some of you who obey, but if you have been predestined to be rejected, the powers of obedience will be withdrawn, so that you will cease to obey.’ For what else does this seem to mean than cursing, or in some way prophesying evil?” (*On the Gift of Perseverance*, no. 61).

After this, when he explained how these matters ought to be discussed before the people, he connected the words of his own judgment, saying:

“I do not think that the manner which, as I have said, ought to be used in preaching predestination should suffice for one speaking to the people, unless he adds this or something of the kind, saying: ‘Therefore, you too ought to hope for that very perseverance in obedience from the Father of lights, from whom every good gift and every perfect gift comes’ (James I, 17), and to ask for it in your daily prayers; and by doing this to trust that you are not strangers to the predestination of his people, because he himself also grants that you should do this. But far be it from you to despair of yourselves because you are commanded to place your hope in him, not in yourselves. For cursed is everyone who places his hope in man (Jer. XVII, 5); and it is good to trust in the Lord rather than to trust in man (Ps. CXVII, 8), because blessed are all who trust in him. Holding fast to this hope, serve the Lord in fear, and exult before him with trembling (Ps. II, 11).

“For concerning eternal life, which God, who does not lie, promised to the children of promise before eternal times, no one can be secure until this life—which is a time of testing upon the earth (Job VII, 1)—has been brought to completion. Yet he will make us persevere in him until the end of this life, to whom we say daily, ‘Do not lead us into temptation’” (*On the Gift of Perseverance*, no. 62).

Do you see, I ask, how far this discourse differs from the one fabricated by the malice of the detractors, who even strove, by a contrived deception of words, to corrupt the things he says rightly? Concerning this the same teacher most rightly says: “It is the mark of a deceitful or unskilled physician to bind on even a useful medicine in such a way that it either does no good or does harm” (*ibid.*, no. 57). And again, concerning a similar absurdity:

“Indeed,” he says, “this is most true—quite so—but most reprehensible, most inappropriate, and most incongruous; not false in its wording, but not applied beneficially to the health of human weakness” (*On the Gift of Perseverance*, no. 61).

It is therefore not necessary to give an account of matters which, as we have shown, were spoken by others and disapproved by him himself—yet in such a way that he allowed nothing true to be taken from him through its admixture with falsehood. For although he never spoke so foolishly to the Christian people and recoiled from what lying detraction most absurdly invented, he nevertheless proved abundantly, by his devout and steadfast teaching, that the Church must preach predestination, in which grace is prepared; grace, in which the effect of predestination is realized; and the foreknowledge of God, by which he foreknew before the eternal ages to whom he would bestow his gifts. Whoever opposes this preaching is an utterly manifest ally of Pelagian self-exaltation.

Now the point which you placed at the end ought to have been joined to the preceding chapter, where mention was made of the Tyrians and Sidonians, because in the body of the book it too is connected with that same subject, without the insertion of any different discussion. Hence the response which I appended to the preceding matters can also suffice for these, in which there is no obscurity, provided that concerning faith in the predestination and grace of God—from which comes the origin of all good things and the perseverance of merits—one holds what the truth contains.

[Col. 1857]

## EPIGRAM OF PROSPER OF AQUITAINE AGAINST AUGUSTINE’S DETRACTOR. (C)

[Col. 1857]

Against Augustine, it is said, there creeps a certain  
writer whom long ago consuming envy burned:

who, with his head somehow concealed in dark caverns,  
drove the wretched little snake to raise itself from the ground.

Either the Britons of the sea fed this creature on its own grain  
[Note: [Col. 1857] Pelagius the Briton.],  
or its heart swelled with Campanian grass  
[Note: [Col. 1857] Julianus of Campania.].

Let it bring forth what it has conceived and cherished; let it produce what it has labored to bear:  
whether it is armed with an old doctrine or a new one.

However many coils of its spirals it twists into whatever recesses,  
and however deceptively it conceals its head by manifold art,

the viper will not be able to turn the old man aside  
as he advances over worn-down asps and basilisks.

[Col. 1857]

## AGAINST THE SAME, OR SOME OTHER DETRACTOR

[Col. 1857]

A certain learned speaker is said to have attacked  
the books of the aged Augustine and composed a work against them.

Could he display his fine talent and wealth of eloquence  
in no other way than by exhibiting his skill,

unless he aroused new wars against ranks already laid low  
and gave impious weapons to enemies already extinguished?

This battle, instigator, is your death; this stylus  
destroys you, and you perish by your own words.

While you teach how powerful the free mind is,  
you show that your own willing is sufficient for you to perish.

Turn back your steps; flee destruction; and everywhere behold  
the rebels struck down by the thunderbolt of the apostolic mouth.

Nor should you think that, by changing your name, you can be defended:  
if you wish to injure the shepherd of the sheep, you are a wolf.

## [SELECTED SENTENCES FROM AUGUSTINE]

[Col. 1857]

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING BOOK

The printed books contain three hundred and ninety sentences. The first thirty-seven, together with a very few among those that follow, have been excerpted from Prosper’s own *Commentaries on the Psalms*; the remainder are from the works of Augustine. Since we sometimes find that the words of this holy Doctor have been altered, we judge it best, for that reason, to advise readers to consult the passages from which Augustine’s thought has been reproduced more fully than his wording. We indicate this by appending the word “See” to sentences of this kind.

The Colbert manuscript, marked 393—which is the only handwritten exemplar of this book that we have been able to find, and is itself not especially old—represents only seventy-six sentences, no more: namely, the first eighteen, then, with the nineteenth omitted, the twentieth and twenty-first, and others selected from the sequence that follows. It has this preliminary note concerning them:

“This Prosper of Aquitaine was a citizen of Toulouse who, having abandoned secular affairs, devoted himself entirely to divine concerns; and, selecting certain passages from the sentences of blessed Augustine, composed this book,” and so forth.

Several sentences from this book are included among the canons of the Second Council of Orange; and very many are cited under the name of Prosper by Florus, or by the commonly published Bede, in his work on Paul. The author who compiled the decretal letters of Zephyrinus, Callistus I, and other Roman Pontiffs also made use of some of these sentences.

[Col. 1859]

## SENTENCES OF PROSPER OF AQUITAINE SELECTED FROM AUGUSTINE

One book. (C)

### I. What true innocence is

[Col. 1859]

True innocence is that which harms neither oneself nor another. For “whoever loves iniquity hates his own soul.” And no one sins against another before first sinning against himself  
[Note: [Col. 1859] From Prosper’s exposition of Psalm C, 2. See Augustine on the same Psalm, no. 4.].

### II. On those who are to be loved

People are to be loved in such a way that their errors are not loved; for it is one thing to love what they have been made, and another to hate what they do  
[Note: [Col. 1859] Prosper on the same Psalm C, 3. See Augustine on the same Psalm, no. 5.].

### III. On true eternity

True eternity and true immutability exist only in the divinity of the Trinity, for in it being is perpetual. Since its nature is without beginning and requires no increase, it admits no end, and just as no end, so no change. Those creatures, however, to which God has given or will give eternity are not entirely free from every end, because they are not outside change, since for them there is both a temporal establishment, a local movement, and the very change by which they are made to increase  
[Note: [Col. 1859] Prosper on Psalm CII, 28.].

### IV. On the patience of God

The patience of God, by which he spares the despiser and also the one who denies him, and prefers the sinner’s life to his death, is instruction toward repentance and an offer of correction. None of his works is without mercy, since he provides both indulgence and the scourge for human beings  
[Note: [Col. 1859] The same, on Psalm CII, 8. See Augustine on the same Psalm, no. 16.].

### V. On God’s vengeance

Divine goodness is especially angry in this age so that it may not be angry in the age to come; and mercifully applies temporal severity so that it may not justly inflict eternal vengeance  
[Note: [Col. 1859] Prosper on Psalm CII, 9.].

### VI. On the true praise of God

The confession of one who blesses is true when the sound of the mouth and of the heart is the same. To speak well but live badly is nothing other than to condemn oneself with one’s own voice  
[Note: [Col. 1859] The same, 21.].

### VII. On the virtue of charity

Love of God and neighbor is the distinctive and special virtue of the devout and the saints, whereas the other virtues can be shared by both the good and the wicked  
[Note: [Col. 1859] Prosper on Psalm CIII, 3. See Augustine on the same Psalm, sermon 1, no. 9.].

### VIII. On apostolic teaching

Apostolic teaching is so wholesome and life-giving that, according to the capacity of those who use it, it leaves no one excluded from its benefits. For whether they are little or great, weak or strong, it contains for them both what will nourish them and what will satisfy them  
[Note: [Col. 1859] Prosper on Psalm CIII, 11.].

### IX. On seeking God

The one who seeks God seeks joy. Let him therefore seek in such a way that he rejoices not in himself but in the Lord. For as he approaches God, his ignorance is illuminated and his weakness strengthened; he is given both understanding by which he may see and charity by which he may burn  
[Note: [Col. 1859] The same, on Psalm CIV, 4.].

### X. On spiritual disgust

Just as it is harmful to the body not to be able to take bodily food, so it is dangerous to the soul to be disgusted with spiritual delights  
[Note: [Col. 1859] The same, on Psalm CVI, 18.].

### XI. On the ends of the good and the wicked

Those who are heading toward nonbeing are never numerous. For what is as subject to fewness as that which is destined for destruction  
[Note: [Col. 1860] Prosper on Psalm CVI, 39.]?

### XII. On the tranquility of God’s vengeance

God does not desire the punishment of the guilty as though he wished to be satiated with vengeance; rather, he calmly decrees what is just and disposes it by a right will, so that even the wicked may not be without order  
[Note: [Col. 1860] The same, on Psalm CVIII, 5.].

### XIII. On good understanding

The person who does what he rightly understands ought to be done possesses good understanding. Otherwise, understanding without action is like wisdom without fear, since it is written: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. CX, 10)  
[Note: [Col. 1860] The same, on Psalm CX, 10.].

### XIV. On the rest of one who still lives in the flesh

Even in this life the soul that has been rescued from the death of unbelief has its rest. It abstains not from works of righteousness but from the practice of iniquity, so that, alive to God and dead to the world, it may rest in the peaceful tranquility of humility and gentleness  
[Note: [Col. 1860] The same, on Psalm CXIV, 8.].

### XV. On making vows to God

Whoever rightly considers what he should vow to God and what vows he should fulfill should vow and give himself. This is what is required; this is what is owed. Let Caesar’s image be given back to Caesar; let God’s image be given back to God. But just as one must consider what one offers and to whom one offers it, so one must also consider where one offers it, because outside the Catholic Church there is no place for true sacrifice  
[Note: [Col. 1860] The same, on Psalm CXV, 18.].

### XVI. On justice and grace

There are two retributions of justice: when either good things are returned for good things or evil things for evil things. There is a third retribution, that of grace, when through regeneration evils are forgiven and good things are repaid. Thus it is shown that all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth. But God does not know that retribution of the wicked by which evil is repaid for good; for unless he repaid good for evil, there would be no one to whom he could repay good for good  
[Note: [Col. 1860] The same, on Psalm CXVIII, 17; from Augustine, sermon 7 on the same Psalm, no. 1.].

### XVII. On the citizens of the heavenly homeland

Everyone who belongs to the heavenly city is a stranger in the world; and while he makes use of temporal life, he lives in a homeland not his own. There, amid many attractions and many deceptions, to know and love God is the portion of the few, for whom the Lord’s commandment is clear, enlightening the eyes, so that they are not deceived either in love of God or in love of neighbor  
[Note: [Col. 1860] Prosper on Psalm CXVIII, 19.].

### XVIII. On overcoming the desire of the flesh

There is no one whose soul is not weighed down by a corruptible body and an earthly dwelling. But one must strive so that the desires of the flesh are overcome by the vigor of the spirit; and the inner person, who continually feels resistance within, should continually expect to be helped by divine assistance  
[Note: [Col. 1860] The same, 25.].

### XIX. On the narrow way of life

Narrow is the way that leads to life; yet no one runs along it unless the heart has been enlarged. For the path of the virtues on which Christ’s poor walk is broad for the hope of the faithful, even if it is narrow for the vanity of unbelievers  
[Note: [Col. 1860] The same, 35.].

### XX. On the reward of the Christian religion

[Col. 1861]

God must be worshiped with such affection and desire that the worship of him itself is the reward. For whoever worships God in order to merit something else more than God does not worship God, but that which he desires to attain  
[Note: [Col. 1861] Prosper on Psalm CXVIII, 36. See Augustine on the same Psalm, sermon 11, no. 6.].

### XXI. On things hidden, which are not to be judged

It is a sin rashly to judge the hidden things of another’s heart; and it is unjust to condemn on suspicion someone whose works appear to be nothing but good. For God alone is the just judge of what is hidden from human beings, and he is its true observer  
[Note: [Col. 1861] Prosper on Psalm CXVIII, 39; and it is read in the First Letter of Pope Zephyrinus.].

### XXII. On God’s assistance

It is a divine gift when we both think what is right and restrain our feet from falsehood and injustice. Whenever we do good things, God works in us and with us so that we may act  
[Note: [Col. 1861] Prosper on Psalm CXVIII, 59; and this is canon 9 of the Second Council of Orange.].

### XXIII. On the sufferings of the saints

By God’s just judgment, sinners are often given power to persecute his saints, so that those who are helped and led by the Spirit of God may become more renowned through the exercise of hardships  
[Note: [Col. 1861] Prosper on Psalm CXVIII, 62.].

### XXIV. On knowledge of the good

There is no true knowledge of the good unless it is understood for the purpose of being put into practice. For the person who labors to retain God’s law in memory but does not fulfill it in action does not meditate on it profitably  
[Note: [Col. 1861] The same, 71, 77.].

### XXV. On love of the law

The person who loves God’s law shows, in the case of wicked people, that he hates what is contrary to the law, not the people themselves  
[Note: [Col. 1861] The same, 113.].

### XXVI. On examining God’s commandments

No one can examine God’s commandments unless his mind is tranquil. Therefore, so that devout study may be exercised, the quarrels of the malicious must be driven away  
[Note: [Col. 1861] The same, 115.].

### XXVII. On making progress

No one is so educated, no one so learned, that he does not need heavenly illumination. For no increase of divine goods is sufficient in such a way that there does not always remain something for the rational mind both to desire to understand and to carry out  
[Note: [Col. 1861] The same, 125.].

### XXVIII. On the twofold work of God

If we consider all human beings together, some of whom are saved by mercy and others condemned by truth, the ways of the Lord—that is, mercy and truth—are distinguished by their respective ends. But if we look only at the saints, these ways of the Lord are not distinguished: for there mercy is inseparable from truth, and truth from mercy, because the blessedness of the saints comes both from the gift of grace and from the retribution of justice  
[Note: [Col. 1861] The same, 151.].

### XXIX. On the observance of peace

It belongs to Christian perfection to be peaceful even with the enemies of peace, out of hope for their correction, not out of agreement with their wickedness. Thus, if they follow neither the example nor the exhortation of love, at least they may have no grounds on which they ought to hate us  
[Note: [Col. 1861] The same, on Psalm CXIX, 7.].

### XXX. On God’s protection

The Lord protects us from every evil—not so that we suffer nothing adverse, but so that our soul is not harmed by the adversities themselves. For when temptation is present, an entry of a certain kind is made into that which attacks us; and when the temptation is brought to a good end, that is, without a wound to the soul, we emerge from the depth of temporal labor into eternal rest  
[Note: [Col. 1861] The same, on Psalm CXX, 7.].

### XXXI. On God’s assistance

[Col. 1862]

No one ascends to the fellowship of the heavenly Jerusalem except those who confess with their whole heart that their ascent is not the work of their own effort but a divine gift  
[Note: [Col. 1862] Prosper on Psalm CXXI, 4.].

### XXXII. On the world’s hatred of Christians

All who wish to live devoutly in Christ must suffer reproaches from the wicked and those unlike them; and they are despised as foolish and insane because they abandon present goods and promise themselves invisible and future ones. But this contempt and mockery will be turned back upon the wicked when their abundance has passed into poverty and their pride into disgrace  
[Note: [Col. 1862] The same, on Psalm CXXII, 3.].

### XXXIII. On the patience of the faithful

The whole salvation of the faithful and the whole strength of their patience must be referred to him who is wonderful in his saints, because unless the Lord were in them, human weakness would succumb to the fury of the wicked  
[Note: [Col. 1862] The same, on Psalm CXXIII, 3.].

### XXXIV. On due obedience

Subjects must endure rulers, and servants their masters, in such a way that temporal things are borne under the exercise of patience and eternal things are hoped for. For the merit of virtue is increased by the fact that one’s resolve does not violate religious devotion  
[Note: [Col. 1862] The same, on Psalm CXXIV, 3.].

### XXXV. On enduring worldly diversity

Those who are upright in heart do not complain about God’s commandments and ordinances, because it is just to accept with equanimity everything that the one who will judge has willed to be endured  
[Note: [Col. 1862] The same, 4.].

### XXXVI. On the building of God’s house

Every structure of a holy edifice progresses as God works  
[Note: [Col. 1862] The Colbert manuscript reads “as God cooperates.” And below, in place of “there is protection,” it has “there is order.”]  
and stands firm as God protects it. For the protection of those placed in authority is useful when the Spirit of God presides over his people, and deigns to protect not only the flocks but also the shepherds themselves  
[Note: [Col. 1862] The same, on Psalm CXXVI, 1.].

### XXXVII. On eternal joys

The joys of the eternal city are eternal, and the perpetual infinity of its unchanging days will neither vary nor decline, because those who possess it will enjoy unchangeable peace, and the good of all will also belong to each individual  
[Note: [Col. 1862] The same, on Psalm CXXVII, 5.].

### XXXVIII. On the law of charity

The perfection of Christ’s law is charity, by which God and neighbor are loved, and through which one says to the Lawgiver, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. IV, 12). The person who fulfills God’s commandments rightly awaits his promise; nor does the one who forgives others hope in vain that his own sins will be forgiven  
[Note: [Col. 1862] The same, on Psalm CXXIX, 4.].

### XXXIX. On God’s commands

God commands nothing for his own benefit, but for the benefit of the one to whom he gives the command. He is therefore truly Lord: he does not need a servant, while the servant needs him  
[Note: [Col. 1862] Augustine, Letter 138, to Marcellinus, no. 6.].

### XL. On temporal knowledge

What is new in time is not new to God, who created time and possesses all things without time, distributing them to each according to the variety of their respective times  
[Note: [Col. 1862] The same, no. 7.].

### XLI. On God’s providence

The unchangeable reason contains the ordering of mutable things. In it, without time, those things exist together which do not occur together in time, because times do not run together  
[Note: [Col. 1862] The same, no. 8.].

### XLII. On the impunity of sinners

Nothing is more wretched than the prosperity of sinners, by which punitive impunity is nourished and an evil will, like an inner enemy, is strengthened  
[Note: [Col. 1862] The same, no. 14.].

### XLIII. On the letter of the law

The letter of the law, which teaches that one must not sin, kills if the life-giving Spirit is absent. For it makes one know sin rather than avoid it, and therefore causes it to increase rather than diminish, because the transgression of the law is added to evil desire  
[Note: [Col. 1863] Augustine, *On the Spirit and the Letter*, chapters 5, 14.].

### XLIV. On law and grace

The law was given so that grace might be sought; grace was given so that the law might be fulfilled. For it was not fulfilled because of any defect in the law itself, but because of the defect of the wisdom of the flesh. This defect had to be demonstrated through the law and healed through grace  
[Note: [Col. 1863] The same, chapter 19.].

### XLV. On God’s promise

God promises what he himself brings about. For he does not promise while someone else accomplishes it; that would no longer be promising but predicting. Therefore it is not from works but from the one who calls, so that it may belong not to them but to God; and the reward may not be reckoned according to grace but according to debt. Thus grace would no longer be grace  
[Note: [Col. 1863] The same, chapter 24.].

### XLVI. On the faults of the faithful and the good works of unbelievers

Just as certain pardonable sins, without which this life is not lived, do not prevent the righteous from attaining eternal life, so certain good works, without which the life of even the worst person is scarcely found, contribute nothing to the eternal salvation of the wicked  
[Note: [Col. 1863] The same, chapter 27.].

### XLVII. On the effect of an evil will

When an evil will receives the power to accomplish what it desires, this comes from God’s judgment, with whom there is no injustice. For he also punishes in this way, and not unjustly merely because the punishment is hidden. The wicked person, however, does not know that he is being punished until, through manifest punishment, he unwillingly experiences how great an evil was what he willingly perpetrated  
[Note: [Col. 1863] The same, chapter 30.].

### XLVIII. On pride

All vices have force only in evil deeds; pride alone must be guarded against even in good deeds  
[Note: [Col. 1863] The same, *On Nature and Grace*, chapter 21.].

### XLIX. On the unequal use of fortune

It matters greatly what use is made either of those things that are called prosperous or of those that are called adverse. For the good person is neither lifted up by good fortune nor broken by misfortune; but the wicked person is punished by this kind of unhappiness because he is corrupted by prosperity  
[Note: [Col. 1863] The same, from Book 1 of *The City of God*, chapter 8.].

### L. On the death of the saints

A death preceded by a good life should not be considered evil. For nothing makes death evil except what follows death. Therefore those who must die should be little concerned with what happens in order that they may die, but with where they are compelled to go by dying  
[Note: [Col. 1863] The same, chapter 11.].

### LI. On purity, which one does not lose involuntarily

Thus the holiness of the body is not lost while the holiness of the soul remains, even when the body is violated; just as the holiness of the body is lost when the purity of the soul is violated, even when the body remains untouched  
[Note: [Col. 1863] The same, chapter 18.].

### LII. On the strength of endurance

The person who chooses to endure a troubled life rather than escape it, and to despise human judgment—especially popular judgment, which is usually wrapped in the darkness of error—in favor of the light and purity of conscience, must rightly be called the greater in spirit  
[Note: [Col. 1863] The same, chapter 22.].

### LIII. On the humility of the righteous

Whatever evils are inflicted upon the righteous by unjust masters are not punishment for crime but a testing of virtue. For the good person is free even if he serves; the wicked person is a slave even if he rules—not merely the slave of one human being but, what is worse, of as many masters as he has vices  
[Note: [Col. 1863] The same, from Book 4 of *The City of God*, chapter 3.].

### LIV. On the offering of vows

[Col. 1864]

No one could rightly make a vow to the Lord unless he received from him what he was to vow  
[Note: [Col. 1864] From Book 17 of *The City of God*, chapter 4; and this is canon 11 of the Second Council of Orange.].

### LV. On the essence of the Godhead

Every substance that is not God is a creature; and what is not a creature is God. Therefore there is no difference in the divinity of the Trinity, because whatever is less than God is not God  
[Note: [Col. 1864] From Book 14 of *The City of God*, chapter 11; and this is canon 12 of the Second Council of Orange.].

### LVI. How God loves us

God loves us as we are going to be by his gift, not as we are by our merit.

### LVII. On God’s temporal work

The order of times exists without time in God’s eternal wisdom; and nothing is new to him who made the things that are going to be.

### LVIII. On the principal cause of all things

The will of God is the first and highest cause of all bodily and spiritual movements. For nothing takes place visibly and perceptibly that is not either commanded or permitted from the invisible and intelligible court of the supreme ruler, according to the ineffable justice of rewards and punishments, of gifts and retributions, in this vast and immeasurable commonwealth of the whole creation  
[Note: [Col. 1864] From Book 3 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 4.]

[Note: [Col. 1864] At this point the Colbert manuscript adds the following sentence, taken from chapter 59 of Prosper’s *Book of Epigrams*, “On the ends of evils and goods”: 

> Wishing to know in what part of things you are to be placed,  
> Examine what you fear, and what it is that you love.]

### LIX. On the devil’s pride and Christ’s humility

The proud devil led proud humanity to death; humble Christ led obedient humanity back to life. For just as the former fell when exalted and cast down the one who consented, so the latter rose when humbled and raised up the one who believed  
[Note: [Col. 1864] The same, from Book 4, chapter 10.].

### LX. On spiritual increase

In spiritual things, when the lesser adheres to the greater, as a creature to the Creator, the lesser becomes greater than it was, not the greater. And this is what it means to be greater: to be better. For a creature adhering to the Creator becomes greater not in bulk but in virtue  
[Note: [Col. 1864] The same, from Book 6, chapter 8.].

### LXI. On the ineffable excellence of the Godhead

The transcendence of the Godhead surpasses not only the capacity of our customary speech but also the power of our understanding. For God is thought more truly than he is spoken, and he is more truly than he is thought. It is no small part of knowledge if, before we are able to know what God is, we are able to know what he is not  
[Note: [Col. 1864] The same, from Book 8, chapter 2.].

### LXII. On true blessedness

All the blessed have what they want, although not all who have what they want are immediately blessed. Those who either do not have what they want or have what they do not rightly want are immediately miserable. A right will, therefore, even when it has not obtained what it desires, is nearer to blessedness than a perverse will, even if it has obtained what it desires  
[Note: [Col. 1864] The same, from Book 13, chapter 5.].

### LXIII. What it means to be with God

There is great misery for a human being in not being with the one without whom he cannot exist. For since he exists in him, he is undoubtedly not without him; yet if he does not remember him, understand him, or love him, he is not with him  
[Note: [Col. 1864] The same, from Book 14, chapter 12.].

### LXIV. On the incarnation of the Word of God

The divinity of the Word, equal to the Father, became a participant in our mortality—not from what was his own but from what was ours—so that we too might become participants in his divinity, not from what is ours but from what is his  
[Note: [Col. 1865] See Augustine on Psalm CXVIII, sermon 16, no. 6, and sermon 19, no. 6.].

### LXV. With what hatred the wicked are to be hated

Perfect hatred is that which lacks neither justice nor knowledge: namely, that you neither hate people because of their vices nor love vices because of people. Thus in the wicked we rightly hate wickedness and love the creature, so that neither is nature condemned because of vice nor vice loved because of nature  
[Note: [Col. 1865] Prosper on Psalm CXXXVIII, 22. Compare Book 14 of *The City of God*, chapter 6.].

### LXVI. On the labor of fabricating lies

The inventions of falsehood are difficult and laborious. But the person who wishes to speak the truth does not labor; for the good are more at ease than the wicked, and the words of truth-tellers are more straightforward than the fabrications of deceivers  
[Note: [Col. 1865] See Augustine on Psalm CXXXIX, no. 13.].

### LXVII. On the divine Scriptures

The profundities of mysteries in the holy Scriptures are good: they are concealed so that they may not become cheap, sought so that they may exercise us, and opened so that they may nourish us  
[Note: [Col. 1865] The same, on Psalm CXL, no. 1.].

### LXVIII. On the Lord’s prayer

The Lord Jesus Christ, praying with bloody sweat, signified that the sufferings of the martyrs would flow forth from the whole body, which is the Church  
[Note: [Col. 1865] See the same, no. 4, and on Psalm LXXXV, no. 1.].

### LXIX. On receiving the sacraments

The unworthy person takes the sacrament of piety to his own condemnation. For what is good cannot benefit the person who receives it badly  
[Note: [Col. 1865] Augustine on Psalm CXLII, no. 16.].

### LXX. On praising God

The person who praises God for the miracles of his benefits should also praise him for the terrors of his punishments. For he both soothes and threatens. If he did not soothe, there would be no exhortation; if he did not threaten, there would be no correction  
[Note: [Col. 1865] Prosper on Psalm CXLIV, 5; from Augustine on the same Psalm, no. 8.].

### LXXI. On hastening conversion

The remedies of conversion to God must not be delayed by any hesitation, lest the time for correction be lost through tardiness. For the one who promised forgiveness to the repentant did not promise tomorrow to the one who delays  
[Note: [Col. 1865] See Augustine, the same, no. 11.].

### LXXII. On humility in prayer

The person who rightly invokes God is the one who accuses himself, not God, in all the evils he suffers, and who does not praise himself but God for the good things he does. For just as God rejects the person who defends his sins, so he receives the one who confesses them  
[Note: [Col. 1865] See the same, no. 22.].

### LXXIII. On the wonder of creatures

The structure of the world is wondrous, but its Maker is more wondrous. The person who departs from the Creator is wrongly occupied with created things; if he clings to what is above, he will trample what is below, lest what he has loved contrary to nature be turned into punishment  
[Note: [Col. 1865] See Augustine on Psalm CXLV, no. 5.].

### LXXIV. On the disordered soul

A rational soul that prefers lower things to higher cannot govern what it used to govern, because it refused to be governed by the one who governed it  
[Note: [Col. 1865] Augustine, the same.].

### LXXV. On the punishment of sin

The body of our flesh was an adornment for us; we sinned, and from it received fetters, so that the whole course of human action might be impeded by the bonds of mortality  
[Note: [Col. 1865] The same, no. 17.].

### LXXVI. On the proper manner of singing psalms

The person whose works accord with his voice rightly sings praise to God. For when the song has ended, the voice falls silent; but a life that persists in good works never ceases to proclaim the glory of the one whom it rejoices to have working within it  
[Note: [Col. 1866] See Augustine on Psalm CXLVI, no. 2.].

### LXXVII. On fear

Everything that is feared is rationally avoided; God is to be feared in such a way that one flees from him to him  
[Note: [Col. 1866] The Colbert manuscript adds the following, which is the beginning of Prosper’s Epigram 73:

> It is useful for the prudent to beware of worldly adversities.]

[Note: [Col. 1866] See the same, no. 20.].

### LXXVIII. On rightly ordered concern

Just as misplaced security drives one into danger, so rightly ordered concern produces security  
[Note: [Col. 1866] From Augustine on Psalm CXLVII, no. 3.].

### LXXIX. On virginity

Virginity of the flesh is an untouched body; virginity of the soul is incorrupt faith  
[Note: [Col. 1866] The same, no. 10.].

### LXXX. On the proper manner of possessing

We shall be found to possess many superfluous things among our resources if we retain only what is necessary. For nothing is sufficient for those who seek vanities, and the person who uselessly possesses things that would benefit the poor is, in a certain sense, a keeper of what belongs to others  
[Note: [Col. 1866] Prosper on Psalm CXLIV, 5; taken from Augustine’s sermon on Psalm CXLVII, no. 12.].

### LXXXI. On thoughts

Our ears are directed toward our voices just as God’s ears are directed toward our thoughts. It cannot happen that good thoughts result in evil works, because action expresses what is conceived in the heart  
[Note: [Col. 1866] From Augustine on Psalm CXLVIII, no. 2.].

### LXXXII. On the new song

Just as the old song of the old person belongs to temporal things, so the new song of the new person belongs to eternal things; and each person sings as he lives. The new song is the song of faith that works through love  
[Note: [Col. 1866] See Augustine on Psalm CXLIX, no. 1.].

### LXXXIII. On true humility

The true humility of the faithful is to be proud of nothing and to murmur about nothing; to be neither ungrateful nor complaining; but in all God’s judgments to give thanks to God and praise God, whose works are all either just or benevolent.

### LXXXIV. On those who despair
The man is exceedingly wretched who does not hope in God and promises himself favorable outcomes from himself, since, by the very fact that he does not seek God’s help, he has fallen away from all hope of true salvation. [Note: [Col. 1866] See Augustine, on Psalm 33, Exposition 2, no. 13.]

### LXXXV. On riches

Those who are rich in iniquity are in great poverty: they possess neither the wealth of justice nor the treasures of wisdom. But those who serve the Lord acquire goods that cannot perish. [Note: [Col. 1866] See ibid., no. 15.]

### LXXXVI. On true goodness

It is not enough to abstain from evil unless one does what is good; and it is little to harm no one unless one strives to benefit many. [Note: [Col. 1866] See ibid., no. 19.]

### LXXXVII. On the impunity of evil

A sinner who sins is not for that reason unseen by the Lord merely because the punishment of the evildoer is delayed. A more severe sentence, however, is decreed against the one to whom even correction itself is denied. [Note: [Col. 1866] See ibid., no. 21.]

### LXXXVIII. On the goodness of humility

One does not approach the height of God except through humility; and the submissive person draws near to him, while the exalted person withdraws far from him. [Note: [Col. 1866] See ibid., no. 23.]

### LXXXIX. On burial

Just as splendid funerals benefit rich sinners nothing, so the burials of poor saints, whether humble or nonexistent, do them no harm. [Col. 1867] [Note: [Col. 1867] See Augustine, on Psalm 33, Exposition 2, no. 25.]

### XC. On rightly ordered joy

The person for whom Christ is joy can never be deprived of his delights. For the rejoicing that takes delight in the eternal is itself eternal.

### XCI. What unites a person to God

With God, who is everywhere, we are either far from him or near to him not by places but by actions, since, just as dissimilarity separates us, imitation unites us to him. [Note: [Col. 1867] See Augustine, on Psalm 34, Sermon 2, no. 6.]

### XCII. On the good battle

It is a weakness of human mortality to take delight in sinning in mortal flesh. But the disciple and lover of virtues ought not to grant peace to this desire; he ought to declare war against it. [Note: [Col. 1867] See Augustine, on Psalm 35, no. 6.]

### XCIII. On the hope of the faithful

Let it not frighten you, Christian, that what has been promised is delayed. Although the promise is hidden, prayer nevertheless perseveres in hope. Exercise yourself in good works; grow in virtues. While the constancy of faith is being tested, the glory of recompense is increased.

### XCIV. On times

Every time of evils is short. For what is so brief as that which tends toward not existing?

### XCV. On the increase of charity

The capacity for charity always grows: through use it becomes greater, and through generosity richer.

### XCVI. On the end of evils

The wickedness of the evil must perish, either by its own judgment or by God’s sentence. For no iniquity endures when correction or condemnation brings it to an end.

### XCVII. How one clings to God

The person who clings to God and always does his will is never abandoned by the one who dwells within him. Even if he suffers certain hard and adverse things, he is not forsaken but tested.

### XCVIII. On justice

The whole substance of justice is that evils be avoided and good things be done. This pattern of conduct must be maintained amid every kind of adversity, because the only thing never lost is what is devoted to a work of piety.

### XCIX. On endurance

Let present evils be endured until the promised blessedness comes. Let the faithful bear with unbelievers, and let the uprooting of the tares that have arisen among the wheat be postponed. However fiercely the ungodly rage, even in the present time the cause of the just is better: the more fiercely they are attacked, the more gloriously they are crowned. [Note: [Col. 1867] See Augustine, on Psalm 36, Sermon 3, no. 17.]

### C. What a cry to God is

A cry to God is the intentness of the heart and the ardor of love, because what is always desired is always requested. This, however, is not hidden from God, since what proceeds from him returns to him. [Note: [Col. 1867] See Augustine, on Psalm 37, no. 14.]

### CI. On confessing sin

Confession of sin is good if healing follows as well. For what benefit is there in exposing a wound and not applying medicine? [Note: [Col. 1867] See ibid., no. 24.]

### CII. On perfection

In this life, which is wholly a time of testing, even the most exalted saints do not attain that perfection beyond which no further ascent remains.

### CIII. On the labors of the present life

While the course of the present life is being run, even if the person whose outer self is corrupted and inner self renewed makes great progress, it is nevertheless necessary that, while subject to the condition of death, he endure the labors of old age. [Col. 1868] [Note: [Col. 1868] See Augustine, on Psalm 38, nos. 8 and 9.]

### CIV. That the human being, the image of God, is now subject to vanity

The human being is indeed the image of God, and whoever walks in the ways of justice tends toward the likeness of his creator. Yet, while he lives in this life, he encounters the disturbances of vanity. [Note: [Col. 1868] See ibid., no. 11.]

### CV. On divine instruction

The first grace of the divine gift is that it instructs us to confess our humility and makes us recognize that, if we do anything good, we can do it through him without whom we can do nothing. [Note: [Col. 1868] Augustine, ibid., no. 18.]

### CVI. That the whole life of unbelievers is sin

The whole life of unbelievers is sin, and nothing is good without the highest good. For where recognition of the eternal and unchanging truth is absent, virtue is false, even in the best conduct.

### CVII. On the spiritual foundation

Just as the foundation of a bodily structure is at the bottom, so the foundation of a spiritual structure is at the top. An earthly building begins from the earth; a heavenly edifice grows from a beginning above.

### CVIII. That remembrance and forgetfulness do not apply to God

God is said to remember when he acts, and to forget when he does not act. For neither forgetfulness applies to God, since he is in no way changed, nor remembrance, since he forgets nothing. [Note: [Col. 1868] From the Exposition on Psalm 87, no. 5.]

### CIX. Who see God’s miracles

Those see God’s wonders to whom they are beneficial. For what is not understood, or from which no progress is made, is not seen. [Note: [Col. 1868] See ibid., no. 10.]

### CX. On joining mercy and truth

Let truth not take mercy away, nor mercy impede truth. For if you judge against truth in the name of mercy, or, as though rigidly devoted to truth, forget mercy, you will not walk in the way of the Lord, in which mercy and truth have met one another. [Note: [Col. 1868] From Sermon 1 on Psalm 88, no. 25.]

### CXI. On Christ’s temptation and imitation

Christ’s temptation is the Christian’s instruction. For disciples ought to be imitators of their teacher—not in performing miracles, which no one demands, but in preserving humility and patience, to which the Lord invited us by his own example. [Note: [Col. 1868] See Sermon 1 on Psalm 90, no. 1.]

### CXII. On desire and charity

Just as desire is the root of all evils, so charity is the root of all good things. [Note: [Col. 1868] Ibid., no. 8.]

### CXIII. On the Christian’s joy

For a Christian, the proper cause of rejoicing is not the present age but the future one. Temporal things must be used in such a way that they do not hinder eternal things, so that, on the road along which pilgrims walk, what pleases them may be what leads to their homeland.

### CXIV. On the Sabbath

The person who abstains from good works celebrates the Sabbath badly. Idleness from iniquity, however, ought to be perpetual, because a good conscience produces not unrest but tranquility. [Note: [Col. 1868] See the Exposition on Psalm 91, no. 2.]

### CXV. Good must be done with joy

When you do good, do it cheerfully. For if you do something good sadly, it is done more to you than you do it. [Note: [Col. 1868] Augustine, ibid., no. 5.]

### CXVI. That it is not people but the perversity of people that must be avoided

If the good do not adopt the ways of the wicked, there is a great division even among those who live together. It is therefore not people—who can be corrected by the example of better people—but the iniquity of people that must be avoided.

### CXVII. That sins should be avoided not from fear of punishment but from love of justice

God approves that innocence by which a person is innocent not through fear of punishment but through love of justice. For whoever does not sin from fear, although he does not harm the one whom he wishes to harm, nevertheless harms himself greatly; and, while abstaining from an evil deed, is nevertheless guilty in will alone. [Note: [Col. 1869] From the Exposition on Psalm 93, no. 1.]

### CXVIII. On the Pharisee and the Publican

In evil deeds, humble confession is better than proud boasting in good deeds. [Note: [Col. 1869] Ibid., no. 15.]

### CXIX. That the wickedness of the unjust benefits the good

The good person is scourged by the wicked person’s malice, and the son is corrected through the servant. [Note: [Col. 1869] Ibid., no. 25.]

### CXX. On worldly iniquity

Just as night does not extinguish the stars of heaven, so worldly iniquity does not obscure the minds of the faithful who cling to the firmament of holy Scripture. [Note: [Col. 1869] Ibid., no. 29; and it is read in the first letter of Pope Zephyrinus.]

### CXXI. On one’s own ability

A person has sufficient ability of his own for sinning; but for doing good he is not sufficient for himself unless he is justified by the one who alone is just. [Note: [Col. 1869] From the Exposition on Psalm 98, no. 7.]

### CXXII. On contrary dispositions

It is a great labor for the good to endure contrary dispositions; whoever is not troubled by them makes little progress. For another person’s iniquity torments the just person to the extent that he departs from his own. [Note: [Col. 1869] Ibid., no. 12.]

### CXXIII. How one approaches or withdraws from God

One approaches or withdraws from God not through distances between places, but likeness makes one near and dissimilarity makes one far away. And it is the height of misery to be far from that good which is everywhere. [Note: [Col. 1869] From the Exposition on Psalm 99, no. 5.]

### CXXIV. On true freedom

Service to God is always free when it is not necessity but charity that serves. [Note: [Col. 1869] Ibid., no. 7.]

### CXXV. On endurance

The person who refuses to endure anyone because he thinks he makes great progress precisely by not tolerating others shows that he is making little progress instead. [Note: [Col. 1869] Ibid., no. 9.]

### CXXVI. On the supreme craftsman

All the good that we possess we possess from our craftsman. But if what is in us is what we ourselves have made, we will be condemned for it; if it is what God has made, we will be crowned for it. [Note: [Col. 1869] Ibid., no. 15.]

### CXXVII. On the Word of God

The Word of God, through whom all things were made, preordained the time at which he would assume flesh; he did not submit to time in order to be changed into flesh. For humanity approached God; God did not withdraw from himself. [Note: [Col. 1869] From Letter 137, no. 10.]

### CXXVIII. On faith and understanding

Faith opens the way to understanding; unbelief closes it. [Note: [Col. 1869] Ibid., no. 15.]

### CXXIX. On the person who is conquered

The vice by which a person was first conquered is the one he conquers last. For when he has overcome all sins, the danger remains that a mind conscious of doing well may glory in itself rather than in the Lord. [Note: [Col. 1869] From the Exposition on Psalm 7, no. 4.]

### CXXX. On the perfection of desires

The end of anxieties is the perfection of desires, and each person strives and struggles toward what he finds delightful. It is therefore the mark of a wise person to desire what makes one good, not to love what deceives. [Col. 1870] [Note: [Col. 1870] From the Exposition on Psalm 7, no. 9.]

### CXXXI. On the two gifts of grace

Just as there are two functions of medicine—one by which sickness is healed, the other by which health is preserved—so there are two gifts of grace: one that removes the desire of the flesh, and another that enables the virtue of the soul to persevere. [Note: [Col. 1870] Ibid., no. 10.]

### CXXXII. On the end of labor

Human labor cannot come to an end unless one loves what cannot be taken away from him. [Note: [Col. 1870] Ibid., no. 16.]

### CXXXIII. On the wound caused by iniquity

It is impossible for iniquity to wound the just person toward whom it is directed before it wounds the unjust heart from which it proceeds. [Note: [Col. 1870] Ibid., no. 17.]

### CXXXIV. On miracles

The visible miracle calls a person to illumination; the invisible miracle illuminates the one who comes when called. Therefore the person recounts all God’s wonders who, believing in visible things, passes on to understand invisible things. [Note: [Col. 1870] From the Exposition on Psalm 9, no. 2.]

### CXXXV. On those who flee from the devil

The condition of those who flee from the pursuing devil is better than that of those who follow him as he leads, because it is more advantageous to have him as an enemy than as a ruler. [Note: [Col. 1870] Ibid., no. 4.]

### CXXXVI. On depraved desires

All depraved desires are gates of hell, through which one goes to death. Whoever rejoices that he has attained for enjoyment what he desperately desired submits to its dominion. [Note: [Col. 1870] Ibid., no. 14.]

### CXXXVII. On flattery

The tongues of flatterers bind souls in sins. For it is delightful to do things in which one not only does not fear a reprover but even the hearer is praised. [Note: [Col. 1870] Ibid., no. 21.]

### CXXXVIII. On the ill-conscious mind

While a mind conscious of evil seems to itself to suffer no punishment, it thinks that God does not judge. Yet to abuse God’s patience and fail to understand the kindness of the one who spares is already a great condemnation. [Note: [Col. 1870] Ibid., no. 23.]

### CXXXIX. That nature precedes vice

In a creature that sins by its own choice, nature precedes vice. Vice is so contrary to nature that it can do nothing except harm nature. Thus it would not be a vice to depart from God unless it were more proper for the nature whose vice this is to be with God. [Note: [Col. 1870] From Book 11 of *The City of God*, chapter 17.]

### CXL. On angels and human beings

God would not have created any angel or human being whom he foresaw would become evil unless he likewise knew for what useful purposes of the good he would employ them. Thus he adorned the order of the ages, like a most beautiful poem, even from certain antitheses. [Note: [Col. 1870] From the same book, chapter 18.]

### CXLI. On the condition of creation

Three things in particular concerning the condition of creation ought to have been made known to us: who made it, through what he made it, and why he made it. “God said,” it says, “‘Let there be light,’ and there was light; and God saw that the light was good” (Genesis 1:3–4).

If, then, we ask who made it: it is God. If we ask through what he made it: he spoke, and it came to be. If we ask why he made it: because it is good. No author is more excellent than God, no art more effective than God’s word, and no cause better than that the good should be created by the good. [Note: [Col. 1870] From the same book, chapter 21.]

### CXLII. On good and evil love

There is a love by which one loves what ought not to be loved; and the person who loves the love by which what ought to be loved is loved hates that other love in himself. Both can exist in one person. It is good for a person that, as the love by which we live well progresses, the love by which we live badly should decline, until it grows old completely [the printed reading *senetur* is uncertain] and everything by which we live is changed into goodness. [Col. 1871] [Note: [Col. 1871] From Book 11 of *The City of God*, chapter 28.]

### CXLIII. On the good of creation

The good of a rational or intellectual creature, by which it is blessed, is God alone. This good is not from the creature itself, since it was created from nothing, but from the one by whom it was created. When it obtains him, it becomes blessed; when it loses him, it becomes miserable. [Note: [Col. 1871] From Book 12 of *The City of God*, chapter 1.]

### CXLIV. On the vice of nature

Vice can exist neither in the highest good nor except in some good. Therefore only good things can exist somewhere; evil things alone can exist nowhere. For even those natures that have been corrupted from the beginning of an evil will are evil insofar as they are vicious, but good insofar as they are natures. [Note: [Col. 1871] Ibid., chapter 3.]

### CXLV. What ought to be believed

It is not right to believe that God is affected one way when he is at rest and another way when he acts, since he ought not to be said to be affected as though something occurred in his nature that had not existed before. For whatever is affected suffers, and everything that suffers is changeable.

God’s activity, therefore, should not be conceived either as idle rest or as laborious exertion, because he knows how to act while resting and to rest while acting. What in works is earlier or later is to be referred not to the one who makes them but to the things made. For his will is eternal and unchanging, and it is not altered by shifting plans; in that will exists simultaneously whatever in the creation or ordering of things has preceded or will follow. [Note: [Col. 1871] Ibid., chapter 17.]

### CXLVI. That God alone is creator

No one may believe or say that anything other than God is the creator of any nature, however small. For even if angels, commanded or permitted, apply their activity to things that are generated in the world, they are no more creators of living beings than farmers are creators of crops and trees. [Note: [Col. 1871] Ibid., chapter 24.]

### CXLVII. On the first condition of death

It may be said of the first death of the body that it is good for the good and bad for the wicked. The second death, however, is without doubt good for no one, just as it belongs to no good persons. [Note: [Col. 1871] From Book 13 of *The City of God*, chapter 2.]

### CXLVIII. On the death of the godly

The death even of the godly is the punishment of sin. Yet it is called good for them because they make good use of it: for them it is an end to temporal evils and a passage to eternal life. For just as injustice makes bad use not only of evil things but also of good things, so justice makes good use not only of good things but also of evil things. [Note: [Col. 1871] Ibid., chapter 5.]

### CXLIX. On martyrs who have not been baptized

For those who die in confession of Christ before receiving the washing of regeneration, that death avails for the abolition of sins as much as if they had been cleansed in the font of Baptism. [Note: [Col. 1871] Ibid., chapter 7.]

### CL. That every sin is a lie

When a person lives according to himself and not according to God, he is like the devil. For even the angel had to live not according to the angel but according to God, so that he might stand in the truth and speak the truth from his lie, not from his own. Hence it is not said without reason that every sin is a lie, because one sins only by a will that is contrary to the truth—that is, to God. [Note: [Col. 1871] See Book 14 of *The City of God*, chapter 4.]

### CLI. On the different will of the emotions

The diversity of human emotion arises from the diversity of the will. If the will is depraved, it will be restless in perverse conduct; but if it is upright, human emotion will not only be free from blame but also worthy of praise. [Note: [Col. 1871] Ibid., chapter 6.]

### CLII. On true freedom of choice

The choice of the will is truly free when it does not serve vices and sins. Such freedom was given by God; once lost, it cannot be restored except by the one who was able to give it. Hence the Truth says: “If the Son sets you free, then you will be truly free” (John 8:36). [Note: [Col. 1872] From Book 14 of *The City of God*, chapter 11.]

### CLIII. That the heart must be directed toward God

It is good to have one’s heart above—not toward oneself, which is pride, but toward God, which is obedience. The person who desires more is less, when, trusting that he is sufficient for himself, he falls away from the one who truly suffices for him. [Note: [Col. 1872] Ibid., chapter 13.]

### CLIV. On the blessed life

If the blessed life is not loved, it is not possessed. If it is loved and possessed, it must necessarily be loved more excellently than all other things, since everything else that ought to be loved must be loved for its sake. But since no one can be blessed unless he loves it as he ought, it follows that he must wish it to be eternal. It will then truly be blessed when it has no end. [Note: [Col. 1872] Ibid., chapter 25.]

### CLV. God alone is good

Not all the wicked progress so as to become good; nevertheless, no one becomes good except from evil. [Note: [Col. 1872] From Book 15 of *The City of God*, chapter 1.]

### CLVI. On the citizens of the earthly city

The citizens of the earthly city are produced by nature corrupted through sin; they are vessels of wrath. The citizens of the heavenly homeland, however, are produced by grace, which frees nature from sin; they are vessels of mercy. [Note: [Col. 1872] Ibid., chapter 2.]

### CLVII. On the wrath of God

God’s wrath is not a disturbance of him but the judgment by which punishment is inflicted for sin. His thought and reconsideration are the unchanging order of changing things. For God does not repent of any deed of his as a human being does, since his judgment concerning everything is as fixed as his foreknowledge is certain. [Note: [Col. 1872] Ibid., chapter 25.]

### CLVIII. On those who persecute the Church

However the enemies of the Church may be blinded by error or corrupted by malice, if they receive the power to afflict her bodily, they exercise her patience; if they oppose her merely by holding evil opinions, they exercise her wisdom; and, so that even enemies may be loved, they exercise her benevolence. For God works all things together for good for those who love him. [Note: [Col. 1872] From Book 18 of *The City of God*, chapter 51.]

### CLIX. On the end of good and evil

The end of good is not that by which it is consumed so that it no longer exists, but that by which it is perfected so that it is complete. The end of evil is not that by which it ceases to exist, but how far it proceeds in causing harm.

Thus there is one supreme good and another supreme evil. The former is that for whose sake other goods are to be desired, while it is desired for its own sake; the latter is that for whose sake other evils are to be avoided, while it itself is avoided for the sake of the supreme [the supplied text breaks off]. [Note: [Col. 1872] From Book 19 of *The City of God*, chapter 1.]

### CLX. On nature

There is a nature in which no evil exists or can exist. But there cannot be a nature in which no good exists. [Note: [Col. 1872] Ibid., chapter 13.]

### CLXI. On peace of mind

Peace of mind is better than bodily health, and it is more fitting for an unjust person to grieve in punishment than to have rejoiced in wrongdoing. [Note: [Col. 1872] Ibid.]

### CLXII. On the commandment of charity

In the commandment of charity a person finds three things to love: God, oneself, and one’s neighbor. And because the person does not err in loving himself who loves God, it follows that he should counsel his neighbor to love God, whom he is commanded to love as himself. [Note: [Col. 1872] Ibid., chapter 14.]

### CLXIII. On concord and obedience

Domestic peace is the ordered concord of those living together in commanding and obeying. Those who provide care command—for example, a husband his wife, parents their children, and masters their servants. Those for whom care is provided obey—for example, wives their husbands, children their parents, and servants their masters.

But in the household of a just person who lives by faith and is still a pilgrim from that city, even those who command serve those whom they seem to command. They do not command out of a desire to rule but as a duty of providing care; not from the pride of exercising authority but from the benevolence of providing for others. [Note: [Col. 1873] From Book 19 of *The City of God*, chapter 14.]

### CLXIV. On the condition of servitude

Guilt, not nature, produced the name and condition of servitude; and the first cause of this subjection was sin, because, as it is written, “Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin” (John 8:34). Hence the condition of the person who serves a human being is better than that of the person who is enslaved to his own desire. [Note: [Col. 1873] Ibid., chapter 15.]

### CLXV. On those in authority

True heads of households counsel their subjects, as sons, to worship and win the favor of God, desiring to come to the heavenly household where the duty of commanding will not be necessary. Until that is reached, fathers ought to bear more heavily the fact that they rule than servants the fact that they serve. [Note: [Col. 1873] Ibid., chapter 16.]

### CLXVI. On governing the people

A position of superiority, without which a people cannot be governed, ought indeed to be held and administered as is fitting; nevertheless, it is sought improperly. Hence the love of truth seeks holy leisure; the necessity of charity should undertake just business. [Note: [Col. 1873] Ibid., chapter 19.]

### CLXVII. On the life of the soul

Just as what makes the flesh live is not from the flesh but above the flesh, so what makes the soul live a blessed life is not from the soul but above the soul. For just as the soul is the life of the flesh, so God is the blessed life of the human being. [Note: [Col. 1873] Ibid., chapter 25.]

### CLXVIII. On pardon

Although our justice is true because it is directed toward the true end of the good, it is nevertheless so limited in this life that it consists more in the remission of sins than in the perfection of virtues. [Note: [Col. 1873] Ibid., chapter 27.]

### CLXIX. On complete peace

As long as one resists vices, complete peace does not exist. For the things that resist are conquered in a dangerous battle, and the things that have been conquered are not yet celebrated in secure leisure as a triumph, but are still held under anxious rule. [Note: [Col. 1873] Ibid.]

### CLXX. On the first and second death

The first death drives the unwilling soul from the body; the second death holds the unwilling soul in the body. Both deaths have this in common: the soul suffers from its body what it does not wish. [Note: [Col. 1873] From Book 21 of *The City of God*, chapter 3.]

### CLXXI. On unknown causes

Although the causes of divine works are unknown, we know something when we know that the Almighty does not act without reason, even when the weak human mind cannot explain that reason. [Note: [Col. 1873] Ibid., chapter 5.]

### CLXXII. On negligence

A person vainly promises himself after this body what he neglected to acquire in this body. No one does good unwillingly, even when what he does is good, because the spirit of fear is of no benefit where the spirit of charity is absent. [Note: [Col. 1873] See the *Enchiridion*, chapter 110; from Book 1 of the *Confessions*, chapter 12.]

### CLXXIII. On human society

Just as, among the powers of human society, the greater power is placed over the lesser for the purpose of obedience, so God over all. [Note: [Col. 1873] From Book 3 of the *Confessions*, chapter 8.]

### CLXXIV. On loving God

Blessed is the person who loves God, a friend in God, and an enemy for God’s sake. For only the person to whom all are dear in him loses no beloved person, and he never loses the one who does not abandon him. [Col. 1874] [Note: [Col. 1874] From Book 4 of the *Confessions*, chapter 6.]

### CLXXV. On things that are not to be corrupted

It is evident that the things that are corrupted are good. Yet if they were the highest goods, they could not be corrupted, because if they were the highest goods they would be incorruptible; but if they were no goods at all, there would be nothing in them to be corrupted. [Note: [Col. 1874] From Book 7 of the *Confessions*, chapter 12.]

### CLXXVI. On the unchanging God

Since the unchangingly good God made all creatures good, and no nature whatsoever was created except by him, there is no substance of evil. For whatever does not have God as its author does not exist. Thus the vice of corruption is nothing other than either a desire or an act of the will that is disordered. [Note: [Col. 1874] See ibid.]

### CLXXVII. That justice is hateful to the unjust

Just as food that is pleasant to a healthy palate is a punishment to an unhealthy one, and light at which a sound eye rejoices is hateful to diseased eyes, so God’s justice displeases the unjust. If they were subjected to it, they would not be disturbed. [Note: [Col. 1874] Alternatively: “would be diminished.”] [Note: [Col. 1874] Ibid., chapter 16.]

### CLXXVIII. On sickness of soul

The sickness of a rational soul occurs when a person, delighted by inferior goods, desires superior goods in part and does not desire them in part. Therefore the will is divided into two wills; and when one exists, the whole will does not exist. What is present to one is absent from the other. [Note: [Col. 1874] From Book 8 of the *Confessions*, chapter 9.]

### CLXXIX. On the religious person

It ought to be too little for a kindly person merely not to arouse or increase the hostility of others by speaking evil, unless he also strives to extinguish it by speaking well. [Note: [Col. 1874] From Book 9 of the *Confessions*, chapter 9, no. 21; and it is read in the first letter of Pope Callistus I.]

### CLXXX. On truth that is hated

The blessed life is joy in the truth, which is God. Yet truth is hateful to many, and they do not wish to hear it teaching. Though unwilling to be deceived, they want their own lies to appear to be the truth. They are therefore justly repaid by this: they themselves do not escape the truth, while the truth escapes them. [Note: [Col. 1874] From Book 10 of the *Confessions*, chapter 23.]

### CLXXXI. On courageous patience

No one loves what he endures, even if he loves enduring it, because courageous patience is one thing and secure happiness another. The labor of battle and the blessedness of victory do not belong to the same time. [Note: [Col. 1874] Ibid., chapter 28.]

### CLXXXII. On abundant poverty

The poverty of human understanding is often abundant in discourse because inquiry speaks more than discovery, and asking is longer than receiving. [Note: [Col. 1874] From Book 12 of the *Confessions*, chapter 1.]

### CLXXXIII. On eternity

God is true eternity, for he alone possesses immortality, since he is changed by no form or movement and his will is not temporal. For a will that is one thing at one time and another at another is not immortal. [Note: [Col. 1874] Ibid., chapter 11.]

### CLXXXIV. On not despairing of sinners

One must not despair of the wicked; rather, one must pray for them more earnestly, so that they may become good. For the number of the saints has always been increased from the number of the ungodly. [Note: [Col. 1874] From the Exposition on Psalm 39, no. 8.]

### CLXXXV. How peace is to be sought from God

When seeking peace from God, let a person be at peace with himself, so that one thing is not in the profession of his mouth and another in the secret place of his heart. For it is of no benefit for the heart to contain what is true if the voice says what is false, because truth must both be believed and spoken. [Note: [Col. 1874] Ibid., no. 16.]

### CLXXXVI. That a person should not grieve when justly scourged

[Col. 1875]

A person should not complain when he suffers adversities in things that he possesses justly. Through the bitterness of inferior things he is taught to love better things, lest the traveler journeying toward his homeland love the inn as his home. [Note: [Col. 1875] From the Exposition on Psalm 40, no. 5.]

### CLXXXVII. That the sinner should be displeasing to himself

The person who is displeasing to himself runs well toward the remission of sins. For before the just and merciful judge, the person who accuses himself excuses himself. [Note: [Col. 1875] From the Exposition on Psalm 41, no. 12.]

### CLXXXVIII. On seeking aids

The teaching of wisdom must be acquired in the tranquility of peace, for it is difficult to recognize amid the storms of tribulations. Nor are aids in adversity easily found if they were not sought in peace. [Note: [Col. 1875] See ibid., no. 16.]

### CLXXXIX. On the altar of God

The person who approaches the present altar justified reaches the invisible altar of God, to which the unjust does not draw near. For the person who has discerned his own case here will find his life there. [Note: [Col. 1875] From the Exposition on Psalm 42, no. 5.]

### CXC. On the law

Christ is the end of the law; in him the law of justice is not abolished but fulfilled. For all perfection is in him, beyond whom there is no further point to which the hope of faith and charity can extend. [Note: [Col. 1875] See the Exposition on Psalm 45, no. 1.]

### CXCI. On a bad conscience

There are no punishments more severe than a bad conscience. When God is not possessed in it, no consolation is found. Therefore the liberator must be invoked, so that the person whom tribulation has brought to confession may be brought by confession to pardon. [Note: [Col. 1875] See ibid., no. 2.]

### CXCII. On the sick person

What sin is more serious for a sick person than the killing of a physician? But if this is forgiven in Baptism, what is not forgiven? [Note: [Col. 1875] Ibid., no. 4.]

### CXCIII. On ruminating on the word of God

The hearer of the word ought to be like the animals that are called clean because they ruminate. He should not be sluggish about thinking over what he has received in the belly of his heart. When he hears, he should be like one eating; when he recalls what he has heard to memory, he should be like one ruminating. [Note: [Col. 1875] From the Exposition on Psalm 46, no. 1.]

### CXCIV. On the rational soul

The rational soul is mistress of its body; but it will not rule its inferior well unless it has served its superior, God, with complete submission in charity. [Note: [Col. 1875] See ibid., no. 10.]

### CXCV. On the mercy of God

Just as the earth awaits rain and light from heaven, so a human being ought to await mercy and truth from God. [Note: [Col. 1875] Ibid., no. 13.]

### CXCVI. On the good children of the Church

The good children of the Church should rejoice that divine justice does not err in distinguishing them. But they should not rashly divide those who have been gathered, because it is theirs to wish to gather, while it is the Lord’s to separate. [Note: [Col. 1875] From the Exposition on Psalm 47, no. 11.]

### CXCVII. On earthly love

The person who is ensnared by no desire is master of the things he possesses. For whoever is bound by love of earthly things does not possess them but is possessed by them. [Note: [Col. 1875] From the Exposition on Psalm 48, Sermon 1, no. 2.]

### CXCVIII. On Christ’s inheritance

The inheritance in which we are coheirs with Christ is not diminished by the multitude of sons, nor made narrower by the number of coheirs. It is as great for many as for few, as great for each as for all. [Note: [Col. 1875] From the Exposition on Psalm 49, no. 2.]

### CXCIX. On happiness

Happiness should never be secure, because favorable circumstances are more dangerous to the mind than adversities are to the body. Prosperity first corrupts them, so that adversity may find something to break. [Col. 1876] [Note: [Col. 1876] From the Exposition on Psalm 50, no. 4.]

### CC. On the remedies of repentance

The first salvation is to avoid sin; the second is not to despair of pardon. For the person who does not turn to the remedies of repentance before the merciful judge destroys himself forever. [Note: [Col. 1876] See ibid., no. 5.]

### CCI. On the hidden goods of the saints

The good lie hidden because their good is hidden. What they love is neither visible nor bodily, and their merits are established in concealment just as their rewards are. [Note: [Col. 1876] See the Exposition on Psalm 53, no. 7.]

### CCII. On the enemies of the good

No good person has an enemy except an evil person. The latter is permitted to exist either so that he may be corrected or so that the good person may be exercised through him. Therefore one must pray for enemies, so that either their conversion may be obtained or imitation of divine goodness may be found in us. [Note: [Col. 1876] From the Exposition on Psalm 54, no. 4; and it is read in the first letter of Pope Callistus I.]

### CCIII. On the vigor of Christian faith

The vigor of Christian faith begins at three times: evening, morning, and midday. In the evening the Lord was on the cross; in the morning, in the resurrection; at midday, in the ascension. One pertains to patience in being put to death, another to life in being raised, and the third to the glory of the majesty of the one seated at the Father’s right hand. [Note: [Col. 1876] See the Exposition on Psalm 54, no. 18.]

### CCIV. On the purification of the elect
For this reason people are assailed by tribulations, so that the vessels of election may be emptied of wickedness and filled with grace. [Note: [Col. 1876] From the Exposition on Psalm LV, no. 13.]

### CCV. On the good things that no one loses unwillingly

A person can unwillingly lose temporal goods; but no one ever loses eternal goods unless willingly. [Note: [Col. 1876] See the same place, no. 19.]

### CCVI. On the goal of the faithful

The goal of the faithful is Christ. When the intention of the one who runs has reached him, it has nothing further that it can find, but it has in him that in which it ought to remain. [Note: [Col. 1876] See Expositions on the Psalms, Psalm LVI, no. 2.]

### CCVII. On sadness

The sadness of one who suffers injustice is better than the joy of one who commits injustice. [Note: [Col. 1876] From the Exposition of the same psalm, no. 14.]

### CCVIII. On past sins

The mind must be recalled from remembering past things with a certain pleasure, lest desire creep in and we return in heart to Egypt. [Note: [Col. 1876] On Psalm LVII, no. 10.]

### CCIX. On truth

It is good to be overcome by truth. For correction, let truth overcome the willing person; for truth itself will overcome even the unwilling person. [Note: [Col. 1876] In the same place, no. 20.]

### CCX. On the impunity of sins

Sins, whether small or great, cannot go unpunished, because they are punished either when a person repents or when God judges. Divine vengeance ceases if human conversion comes first. For God loves to spare those who confess, and not to judge those who judge themselves. [Note: [Col. 1876] See Expositions on the Psalms, Psalm LVIII, sermon 1, no. 13.]

### CCXI. On the wretched person

No wretched person is freed from however great a misery unless he is preceded by the mercy of God. [Note: [Col. 1876] See sermon 11 on the same psalm, no. 11. It is canon 14 of the Council of Orange.]

### CCXII. On remedies for tribulations

One who faithfully beseeches God concerning the needs of this life is mercifully heard, and is mercifully not heard. For the physician knows better than the sick person what is useful for the sick person. But if he asks for what God both commands and promises, what he requests will certainly come to pass, because love receives what truth prepares. [Note: [Col. 1877] See Expositions on the Psalms, Psalm LIX, no. 7.]
