### CCXIII. On the advancement of the good

The advancement of the faithful does not occur without temptation; nor does anyone become known to himself except through the test of trial. No one will be crowned unless he has conquered, and no one will conquer unless he has struggled. But who struggles unless he has an enemy and resists temptation? [Note: [Col. 1877] From the Exposition of the same psalm, no. 2.]

### CCXIV. On prophecies to be fulfilled

He is foolish who does not believe the Prophets’ announcements concerning the few things that remain, when he sees so many things fulfilled that did not yet exist when they were foretold as destined to be fulfilled. [Note: [Col. 1877] From Expositions on the Psalms, Psalm LXIII, no. 1.]

### CCXV. On idols

Those who worship idols are like people who see empty things in dreams. But if their soul awakens, it understands by whom it was made, and does not worship what it itself made. [Note: [Col. 1877] In the same place, no. 4.]

### CCXVI. On human bodies

All the parts of our body, whether torn apart, rotted, or even burned and dissolved into certain ashes, cannot perish for God. For they pass into those elements of the world from which they were taken by the hand that holds all things. [Note: [Col. 1877] In the same place, no. 6.]

### CCXVII. On good thirst

Those who thirst for God ought to thirst with their whole substance, that is, with soul and flesh alike. For God gives the soul its bread, that is, the word of truth; and God provides what the flesh requires, because he himself made both and makes both. [Note: [Col. 1877] In the same place, no. 7.]

### CCXVIII. On the faithful person’s meditation

If a person who is idle and at rest does not think of God, how will he be able to think of him amid many activities and laborious business? Therefore, when he has leisure, let the faithful person meditate on the things of God and seek the substance of good works, lest he fail in action. [Note: [Col. 1877] See the same place, no. 15.]

### CCXIX. On simulated innocence

Simulated innocence is not innocence; simulated equity is not equity. Rather, the sin is doubled, since it contains both iniquity and pretense. [Note: [Col. 1877] From Expositions on the Psalms, Psalm LXIII, no. 11.]

### CCXX. On light

The soul that withdraws from the light of justice is driven farther from the light of truth the more it seeks what it may find against justice, and is plunged into darkness. [Note: [Col. 1877] In the same place.]

### CCXXI. On the two cities

Two loves make two cities throughout the world: love of God makes Jerusalem, and love of the world makes Babylon. Let each person therefore ask what he loves, and he will discover of which city he is a citizen. [Note: [Col. 1877] From Expositions on the Psalms, Psalm LXIV, no. 2.]

### CCXXII. On God’s commandment

Every commandment of God is light to one who loves. The statement “My burden is light” (Matthew 11:30) is understood in no other way than that he gives the Holy Spirit, through whom love is poured into our hearts, so that by loving we freely do what one who does it through fear does slavishly. Nor is a person a friend of what is right when, if it were possible, he would prefer that what is right not be commanded. [Note: [Col. 1877] From Expositions on the Psalms, Psalm LXVII, no. 18.]

### CCXXIII. On love

Love is the fullness of the law, because the law is fulfilled through love, not through fear. The commandments of righteousness are carried out to the extent that the Spirit of grace gives assistance. [Note: [Col. 1877] In the same place, no. 24.]

### CCXXIV. On good works

[Col. 1878]

Works are not good unless they are performed through faith and love, because either one without the other produces the fruit of no virtue. [Note: [Col. 1878] Expositions on the Psalms, Psalm LXVIII, no. 41, and On the Grace of Christ, chapter 26.]

### CCXXV. On Adam’s fall

Adam was changed from what God had formed him to be, but for the worse, through his own iniquity. The faithful are changed from what iniquity had brought about, but for the better, through the grace of God. The former change, therefore, was that of the first transgressor; the latter is the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High. [Note: [Col. 1878] From Expositions on the Psalms, Psalm LXVIII, sermon 1, no. 2; it is also canon 15 of the Council of Orange.]

### CCXXVI. On temporal pleasures

In the present life, temporal pleasures are sweet and temporal tribulations are bitter. But who would not drink the cup of tribulation, fearing the fire of Gehenna? And who would not despise the sweetness of the world, yearning for the goods of eternal life? [Note: [Col. 1878] Augustine, in the same sermon, no. 3.]

### CCXXVII. On the Trinity

In the divine Trinity the unity of substance is so great that it maintains equality and admits no plurality. [Note: [Col. 1878] In the same place, no. 5.]

### CCXXVIII. That there is no nature belonging to evil

“All things were made through the Word, and without him nothing was made.” Since, therefore, all natures were made through the Word of God, iniquity was not made through him, because iniquity is no substance. Sin is not a nature but a defect of nature, which desires what does not belong to its proper order. [Note: [Col. 1878] In the same place.]

### CCXXIX. On the devil’s iniquity

When the devil was bound by his iniquity, what was taken from him was not what he possessed as his own, but what he had seized as another’s. For in taking away what had been lost from his great household, Christ did not commit theft but recovered a theft. [Note: [Col. 1878] In the same place, no. 9.]

### CCXXX. On the depth of iniquity

The depth of iniquity encloses a person when he not only lies immersed in sins but, wishing to defend them, also loses access to confession. [Note: [Col. 1878] From the Exposition of the same Psalm LXVIII, sermon 2, no. 14.]

### CCXXXI. On God’s help

When God permits or causes us to be afflicted by some tribulation, he is merciful even then. For by stirring up faith and delaying help, he does not deny assistance but awakens desire. [Note: [Col. 1878] In the same place.]

### CCXXXII. On Christians

Christian rich people, if they are truly Christians, are altogether poor; and, in comparison with the heavenly goods they hope for, they count all their gold as sand. For each person has his riches where he has his delight. [Note: [Col. 1878] In the same place, no. 14.]

### CCXXXIII. On Abraham’s faith

Abraham’s faith is Abraham’s offspring. Accordingly, those who belong to the likeness of faith belong also to the promise of the heirs. [Note: [Col. 1878] See the same place, no. 21.]

### CCXXXIV. On perseverance in the good

Let no one among the faithful, however greatly he may have advanced, say, “It is enough for me.” For whoever says this has remained and stuck fast on the road before the end, since he will not persevere to the end. [Note: [Col. 1878] From Expositions on the Psalms, Psalm LXIX, no. 8.]

### CCXXXV. On God

There is no place outside God, nor is there anywhere to flee from him except to him. Whoever wishes to escape the one he has offended should take refuge in the one who has been appeased. [Note: [Col. 1878] From Expositions on the Psalms, Psalm LXX, sermon 1, no. 5.]

### CCXXXVI. On the two lives

There are two lives: one of the body and the other of the soul. As the soul is the life of the body, so God is the life of the soul. And just as the body dies if the soul abandons it, so the soul dies if it abandons God. [Note: [Col. 1879] From Expositions on the Psalms, Psalm LXX, sermon 2, no. 3.]

### CCXXXVII. On the human being

From the one by whom a person has being, from him he has well-being. [Note: [Col. 1879] In the same place, no. 6.]

### CCXXXVIII. On obedience

God clearly and perfectly demonstrated how great a good obedience is when, having placed the human being in paradise, he forbade him something that was not evil. There, obedience alone could hold the palm; disobedience alone incurred punishment. [Note: [Col. 1879] Augustine: “found.”] [Note: [Col. 1879] In the same place, no. 7.]

### CCXXXIX. How the good are instructed

Sometimes God instructs the good through the wicked, and through the temporal power of those destined for condemnation he disciplines those destined for liberation. [Note: [Col. 1879] From Expositions on the Psalms, Psalm LXXIII, no. 8.]

### CCXL. On confession

With God’s mercy, the confession of the penitent has the greatest power. By confessing, the sinner makes God favorable; by denying, he does not make him ignorant. [Note: [Col. 1879] From Expositions on the Psalms, Psalm LXXIV, no. 3.]

### CCXLI. On knowledge

It is the virtue of the humble not to boast of knowledge, because participation in truth is common to all, just as light is. [Note: [Col. 1879] See Expositions on the Psalms, Psalm LXXV, no. 17.]

### CCXLII. How bodies are to be governed

A person does not lack royal power if he knows how to command his body rationally. The true ruler of the earth is the one who governs his flesh by the laws of discipline. [Note: [Col. 1879] See the same place, no. 18.]

### CCXLIII. On punishment and justice

As far as outward actions are concerned, both the one who fears punishment and the one who loves justice do not act against the commandment. Thus they are equal in hand but unequal in heart; alike in action but unlike in intention. [Note: [Col. 1879] From Expositions on the Psalms, Psalm LXXVII, no. 11.]

### CCXLIV. What is to be loved

A person worships what he loves. Since God is found to be greater and better than all things, he must be loved above all things in order that he may be worshiped. [Note: [Col. 1879] In the same place, no. 20.]

### CCXLV. On the heart

The heart is right with God when God is sought for God’s sake. [Note: [Col. 1879] In the same place, no. 21.]

### CCXLVI. On benevolence

It is benevolence, not malice, when a righteous person rejoices that vengeance has overtaken the wicked. For he does not rejoice in the sinner’s destruction, whom he wished to be corrected, but in God’s justice, by which he knows that many can be converted. [Note: [Col. 1879] From Expositions on the Psalms, Psalm LXXVIII, no. 14.]

### CCXLVII. On pretense

One who is good on the surface but evil within, sparing in deed but raging in heart, gentle in hand but cruel in intention, does not overcome evil with good. [Note: [Col. 1879] In the same place.]

### CCXLVIII. On love and fear

Love and fear of God lead to every good work; love and fear of the world lead to every sin. Therefore, in order to grasp the good and avoid evil, one must discern what ought to be loved and what ought to be feared. [Note: [Col. 1879] From Expositions on the Psalms, Psalm LXXIX, no. 13.]

### CCXLIX. On happiness

No unhappiness breaks the one whom no happiness corrupts. [Note: [Col. 1879] From Expositions on the Psalms, Psalm LXXXIII, no. 3.]

### CCL. On the rich person who is poor

The rich person who is such that he despises in himself whatever ordinarily causes pride to swell is poor before God. [Note: [Col. 1879] From Expositions on the Psalms, Psalm LXXXV, no. 3.]

### CCLI. On the steps of piety

The steps of ascent to God are the affections of piety. Your will is your road: by loving you approach; by neglecting you withdraw. Though established on earth, you are joined to God because you love what is dear to God. [Note: [Col. 1880] From Expositions on the Psalms, Psalm LXXXV, no. 6.]

### CCLII. On petitions contrary to God

When something evil is asked of him, God is angered by granting it and shows mercy by not granting it. [Note: [Col. 1880] See the same place, nos. 8 and 9.]

### CCLIII. On lying

It is unbelievable that a person who lies in order to catch someone else does not lie lest he be caught. [Note: [Col. 1880] From the book Against Lying, chapter 4.]

### CCLIV. Also on lying

Although everyone who lies wishes to conceal what is true, not everyone who wishes to conceal the truth lies. Often we hide the truth not by deceiving but by keeping silent. For the Lord did not lie when he said, “I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now” (John 16:12). [Note: [Col. 1880] In the same place, chapter 10.]

### CCLV. On free choice

In the first human being it became clear what human choice could accomplish toward death; in the second, what God’s help could accomplish toward life. For the first human being was human only, whereas the second human being was God and human. Sin, therefore, is committed by abandoning God; righteousness is not achieved without God. [Note: [Col. 1880] From Augustine’s Letter 187, to Dardanus, no. 30.]

### CCLVI. On the law and sin

The letter of the law, which teaches that one must not sin, kills if the life-giving Spirit is absent. For it makes a person know sin rather than avoid it, and therefore causes it to increase rather than diminish, because violation of the law is added to evil desire. [Note: [Col. 1880] From On the Spirit and the Letter, chapter 5.]

### CCLVII. On God’s commandment and fear

If God’s commandment is carried out through fear of punishment and not through love of justice, it is done slavishly and not freely; therefore it is not truly done. For the fruit is not good if it does not proceed from the root of love. [Note: [Col. 1880] In the same place, chapter 14.]

### CCLVIII. On the law

The law of God is according to nature when people do what belongs to the law naturally, having overcome the defect that even the protection of the law had not removed. When, therefore, through grace the law of God is written in hearts, what belongs to the law is done naturally—not because grace was preceded by nature, but because nature was restored through grace. [Note: [Col. 1880] See the same place, chapter 27.]

### CCLIX. On having glory only in God

Let no one boast of what he appears to possess, as though he had not received it, or think that he received it because the letter appeared outwardly either to be read or to sound so that it could be heard. For if righteousness comes through the law, then Christ died for nothing. But if he did not die for nothing, then, ascending on high, he led captivity captive and gave gifts to human beings. From him, therefore, comes whatever anyone possesses. Whoever denies that he possesses it from him either does not possess it or will have what he possesses taken away from him. [Note: [Col. 1880] From the same book, chapter 29; it is also canon 16 of the Second Council of Orange.]

### CCLX. On the human being and pride

The human being had been made immortal. He wished to be God. He did not lose what he was as a human being, but he lost what he was as an immortal; and from the pride of disobedience arose the punishment of nature.

### CCLXI. On the praise of faith

The praise of faith is to believe what has not been seen; its reward will be to rejoice in attaining what has been believed.

### CCLXII. On wisdom

Just as milk passes only through flesh in order to nourish a little child who cannot eat bread, so, unless the wisdom of God—which is the bread of angels—had deigned to come to human beings through flesh, no one could approach the contemplation of the divinity of the Word. Since the light could not be grasped by darkness, the light itself assumed the mortality of darkness and, through the likeness of sinful flesh, gave participation in the true light. [Note: [Col. 1881] See sermon 1 on Psalm XXXIII, no. 6.]

### CCLXIII. On a good reputation

A good fragrance is a good reputation, which each person acquires through the works of a good life. While following Christ’s footsteps, he somehow bathes Christ’s feet with the fragrance of precious ointment. [Note: [Col. 1881] From book 3 of On Christian Doctrine, chapter 12.]

### CCLXIV. On desire

There is no difficulty in going without something except when there is desire to possess it. Therefore only that is rightly loved which can never be rightly lost. [Note: [Col. 1881] In the same place, chapter 37.]

### CCLXV. On the eloquence of a foolish person

One who abounds in foolish eloquence must be guarded against all the more because the listener takes greater pleasure in hearing from him things that are useless to hear, and considers the person whom he hears speaking elegantly to be speaking truthfully as well. [Note: [Col. 1881] From book 4 of On Christian Doctrine, chapter 5.]

### CCLXVI. On talent

The clear mark of good minds is to love the truth in the words of those who discourse, rather than the words themselves. For what use is a golden key if it cannot open what we wish? Or what harm is there in a wooden one if it can? We seek only that what is closed be opened. [Note: [Col. 1881] In the same place, chapter 11.]

### CCLXVII. On the sinful human being

No sinner, insofar as he is a sinner, is to be loved; and every human being, insofar as he is human, is to be loved for God’s sake. God, however, is to be loved for his own sake, since from him all who love him have both what they are and the fact that they love him. [Note: [Col. 1881] From book 1 of On Christian Doctrine, chapter 27.]

### CCLXVIII. On the unchangeable good

The Lord says, “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). This means: through me one comes; to me one arrives; in me one remains. When one arrives at him, one also arrives at the Father, because through the one who is equal, the one to whom he is equal is known. The Holy Spirit conquers and joins us fast together, so that we may remain forever in the highest and unchangeable good. [Note: [Col. 1881] In the same place, chapter 34.]

### CCLXIX. On lying and deception

We find many who wish to deceive, but no one who wishes to be deceived. Since one person knowingly does this while another unknowingly suffers it, it is sufficiently clear that, in one and the same matter, the person who is deceived is better than the person who lies, since it is better to suffer injustice than to commit it. [Note: [Col. 1881] In the same place, chapter 36.]

### CCLXX. On love of eternal goods

The difference between temporal and eternal things is that what is temporal is loved more before it is possessed but becomes worthless when it arrives; for nothing satisfies the soul except the true and certain eternity of incorruptible joy. What is eternal, however, is loved more ardently once attained than when desired. No one thinks more highly of it than he possesses it, so that it becomes less valuable because it was hoped for more greatly. But its excellence is so great that love will receive far more there than either faith believed or hope desired. [Note: [Col. 1881] In the same place, chapter 38.]

### CCLXXI. On spiritual hunger and famine

Those who do not find in the Holy Scriptures the truth they seek suffer hunger. But those who do not seek what they have readily available waste away from the languor of disgust. The danger is equal for both, since blindness takes the nourishment of wisdom from the former and famine takes it from the latter. [Note: [Col. 1881] From book 2 of On Christian Doctrine, chapter 6.]

### CCLXXII. On the sufferings of sinners

“The sufferings of this present time are not worthy of comparison with the glory that is to come and will be revealed in us.” Let the world rage and roar, rebuke with its tongues, and flash with weapons: whatever it does, how little will it be compared with what we are to receive? I weigh what I suffer against what I hope for: I feel the one, I hope for the other; yet what is hoped for is incomparably greater than what is inflicted. Whatever rages against the name of Christ, if it can be overcome, is bearable; if it cannot, it hastens the reward by bringing it sooner, and the end of temporal evil passes into the attainment of eternal good. [Note: [Col. 1882] From Augustine’s sermon 279, On the Apostle Paul, no. 4.]

### CCLXXIII. On love

Since the whole Law and the Prophets depend on the two commandments of love, how much more does the Gospel, by which the law is not abolished but fulfilled, and concerning which the Lord says, “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another” (John 13:34)? Love makes people new; and just as malice makes them old, so love makes them new.

### CCLXXIV. On the scourge

When God chastises the human race and assails it with the scourges of pious correction, he exercises discipline before judgment, and very often loves the one whom he scourges, unwilling to find someone whom he must condemn. [Note: [Col. 1882] Alternatively: “does not choose.”] He scourges the just and the unjust alike, because no one can boast that he has a pure heart or is clean from sin. Thus even the crowns of the righteous come from his merciful grace.

### CCLXXV. On the sufferings of the faithful

The labor of the devout is exercise, not condemnation. We should not be troubled when some holy person suffers grievous and undeserved things, if we have not forgotten what the Just One of the just and the Holy One of the holy suffered. His passion surpasses all passions, because no creature can be compared with the Author of the universe.

### CCLXXVI. On original sin

The misery of the human race, from which we see no human being exempt from birth to death, would not pertain to the just judgment of the Almighty if original sin did not exist. [Note: [Col. 1882] From book 1 of the Unfinished Work, chapter 3.]

### CCLXXVII. On God’s providence, which is always active

The omnipotence of the all-sustaining Creator is the cause of every creature’s continued existence. If this power ever ceased to govern what it had created, the form and nature of all things would collapse simultaneously. Accordingly, when the Lord says, “My Father is working until now” (John 5:17), he indicates a certain continuation of his work, by which he simultaneously contains and governs all things. His wisdom also perseveres in this work, concerning which it is said, “She reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things gently” (Wisdom 8:1). The Apostle likewise expresses this when, preaching to the Athenians, he says, “In him we live and move and have our being” (Acts 17:28). If he withdrew his work from created things, we could neither live, nor move, nor exist. Therefore God is to be understood as having rested from all his works in such a way that he no longer creates any new creature, not in such a way that he ceases to sustain and govern the creatures he has made. [Note: [Col. 1882] From book 4 of On the Literal Meaning of Genesis, chapter 12.]

### CCLXXVIII. On the true Sabbath

Once the observance of the Sabbath, which was signified by a day of rest, has been removed, the person observes a perpetual Sabbath who is devoted to holy works in hope of the future rest. He does not boast of his good acts as though they were his own and as though he had not received them, recognizing that the one who works and rests at the same time is at work within him. [Note: [Col. 1882] In the same place, chapter 13.]

### CCLXXIX. On God’s rest

For those who understand correctly, God’s rest is that which needs the good of no one. Therefore our sure rest is in him, because we are blessed by the good that he is, not because he is blessed by what we are. We too are something good from him, who made all things very good, among which he made us. There is no other good besides him that he did not make; therefore, he who does not need the good he made needs no alien good. [Note: [Col. 1882] In the same place, chapter 16.]

### CCLXXX. On the beginning of time

[Col. 1883]

Time began to run with the movements of created things. Hence time is sought in vain before creation, as though it could be found before time. For if there were no movement of either spiritual or bodily creation, by which future things would succeed past things through the present, there would be no time at all. But creation could not move unless it existed. Time, therefore, began from creation rather than creation from time. Yet both are from God. For from him, through him, and in him are all things. [Note: [Col. 1883] From book 5 of On the Literal Meaning of Genesis, chapter 5.]

### CCLXXXI. That all things are governed by God’s will

When the Savior says that not even one sparrow falls to the ground without God’s will (Matthew 10:29), and that he himself forms and clothes the grass of the field, which shortly afterward is to be thrown into the furnace (ibid. 6:30), does he not confirm that divine providence governs not only this part of the world, assigned to mortal and corruptible things, but also its most worthless and lowliest elements? Thus we should not suppose that those things whose causes we cannot comprehend are thrown into confusion by chance movements. [Note: [Col. 1883] In the same place, chapters 21 and 22.]

### CCLXXXII. On the rational soul

The rational soul ought to raise itself toward those things that are most excellent in the nature of spiritual beings, so that it may set its mind on what is above, not on what is upon the earth. [Note: [Col. 1883] From book 6 of On the Literal Meaning of Genesis, chapter 12.]

### CCLXXXIII. On natural miracles

God, the Creator of natures, does nothing in miracles contrary to nature, nor is what is new by custom opposed to reason. Things unfamiliar to us therefore seem contrary to nature because we have learned the course of nature in another way, but not to God, for whom what he has made is nature. [Note: [Col. 1883] In the same place, chapter 13.]

### CCLXXXIV. On the unchangeable rational order of God’s works

It is credible that every body can be changed into every body; but it is absurd to believe that any body can be converted into a rational soul. For God is omnipotent in such a way that he never overturns the ordinances of his own reason. [Note: [Col. 1883] From books 7 of On the Literal Meaning of Genesis, chapters 12 and 20.]

### CCLXXXV. On the merit of the will

Just as air is not made luminous by the light that is present but becomes luminous—for if it had been made luminous rather than becoming so, it would remain luminous even when the light was absent—so a human being is illumined when God is present and darkened when he is absent. One departs from him not by distances of place but by turning away of the will. [Note: [Col. 1883] In the same place, from book 8, chapter 12.]

### CCLXXXVI. God must be obeyed

It is greatly beneficial for a human being to serve God who commands, even when the reason for the command is unknown. By commanding, God makes useful whatever he chooses to command. There is no fear that he will command what is not beneficial. Nor can it happen that one’s own will does not fall upon a person with the weight of a great ruin if, by elevating it, he places it above the will of his superior. [Note: [Col. 1883] In the same place, chapter 13.]

### CCLXXXVII. On the goodness of human nature

How excellent a good human nature is appears above all from the fact that it was given the capacity to cling to the nature of the highest and unchangeable good. If it does not wish to do so, it deprives itself of the good, and this is evil for it; hence, through God’s justice, torment also follows. For what is as unjust as for the deserter of the good to fare well? Sometimes the evil of having lost the higher good is not felt while the lower good that is loved is possessed. But divine justice requires that the one who willingly lost what he ought to have loved should lose with pain what he did love, and that the Creator of natures should everywhere be praised. For that which grieves for a lost good is still good. If some good had not remained in nature, there would be no pain in punishment over any good lost. [Note: [Col. 1883] In the same place, chapter 14.]

### CCLXXXVIII. On the power to harm

The desire to harm can arise perversely from each person’s own mind. But power is only from God, and these are his hidden and lofty judgments, because there is no iniquity with God. [Note: [Col. 1884] From book 11 of On the Literal Meaning of Genesis, chapter 4.]

### CCLXXXIX. What kind of good God is

How great and what kind of good God is is also clearly shown by this: no one who departs from him fares well. Those who rejoice in deadly pleasures cannot be without fear of pain; and those who, through an even greater stupor of pride, do not at all perceive the evil of their abandonment appear to others who know how to discern these things to be weighed down by how great a misery. Thus, if they refuse to accept the remedy by which such things are avoided, they may serve as an example by which such things can be avoided. [Note: [Col. 1884] In the same place, chapter 5.]

### CCXC. That no creature is evil by nature

Just as sound reason teaches that the creature whom nothing illicit delights is better, so the same reason teaches that the creature who has it in his power to restrain illicit pleasure, and rejoices not only in other lawful and rightly performed acts but also in restraining that very wrongful pleasure, is good. [Note: [Col. 1884] In the same place, chapter 7.]

### CCXCI. On the great works of the Lord

“Great are the works of the Lord, sought out according to all his wills.” He foresees those who will be good and creates them; he foresees those who will be evil and creates them; he offers himself for the enjoyment of the good and bestows many gifts even on the evil; mercifully pardoning and justly punishing, and likewise mercifully punishing and justly pardoning; fearing nothing from anyone’s wickedness and needing nothing from anyone’s righteousness; taking no advantage for himself from the works of the good, yet providing for the good even through the punishments of the wicked. [Note: [Col. 1884] In the same place, chapter 11.]

### CCXCII. On pride

Since pride is love of one’s own excellence, while envy is hatred of another’s happiness, it is readily apparent which gives rise to which. By loving his own excellence, a person either envies his equals because they are made equal to him, his inferiors lest they become equal to him, or his superiors because he is not made equal to them. Thus, by being proud, a person is envious; he is not proud by being envious. [Note: [Col. 1884] In the same place, chapter 14.]

### CCXCIII. On the fullness of divinity in Christ

The fullness of divinity is said to dwell bodily in Christ, not because divinity is a body, but because the sacraments of the Old Testament are called shadows of things to come. By comparison with shadows, the fullness of divinity is said to dwell bodily in Christ because everything prefigured by those shadows is fulfilled in him. Thus, in a certain way, he himself is the body of the preceding shadows—that is, he himself is the reality of those figures and signs. [Note: [Col. 1884] From book 12 of On the Literal Meaning of Genesis, chapter 7.]

### CCXCIV. On conquering vices

The pious activity of this life is to worship God, to fight against inward vices with the help of his grace, and not to yield to them when they incite or compel us even toward what is unlawful. When one does yield, one should ask with religious devotion for pardon; and, so that one may not yield, for God’s help. But in paradise, if no one had sinned, the pious activity of conquering vices would not exist, because it would be the permanence of happiness not to have vices. [Note: [Col. 1884] From book 1 of the Unfinished Work, chapter 70.]

### CCXCV. On Christian and Gentile fortitude

The worldly desire of the Gentiles produces fortitude, whereas the love of God produces the fortitude of Christians. This love has been poured into our hearts not through the choice of the will, which comes from us, but through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us. [Note: [Col. 1884] In the same place, chapter 83; it is also canon 17 of the Council of Orange.]

### CCXCVI. Vice cannot exist except in some good

There can be no evil except in some good, because it can exist only in some nature; but every nature, insofar as it is nature, is good. [Note: [Col. 1885] From book 1 of the Unfinished Work, chapter 114.]

### CCXCVII. Grace is preceded by no merits

A reward is owed to good works if they are performed; but grace, which is not owed, comes first so that they may be performed. [Note: [Col. 1885] In the same place, chapter 133; it is also canon 18 of the Council of Orange.]

### CCXCVIII. On circumcision and Baptism

Circumcision of the flesh was commanded by the law because nothing could better signify through Christ that the author of regeneration removes original sin. Every human being is born with a foreskin, just as every human being is born with original sin. The law commanded the flesh to be circumcised on the eighth day because Christ rose on the Lord’s Day, which is the eighth day after the Sabbath. The circumcised man begets one with a foreskin, passing on to him what he himself has already lost; likewise, one who has been baptized nevertheless passes on to the son whom he begets in the flesh the guilt of his origin, from which he himself has already been freed. [Note: [Col. 1885] From book 2 of the Unfinished Work, chapter 73.]

### CCXCIX. On the first and second Adam

The first human being, Adam, died long ago, yet after him there was to be the second human being, Christ, even though many thousands of human beings arose between the one and the other. It is therefore clear that everyone who is born through that succession belongs to the former, just as everyone who is reborn in him through the gift of grace belongs to the latter. Thus the entire human race is, in a certain sense, two human beings: the first and the second. [Note: [Col. 1885] In the same place, chapter 163.]

### CCC. On the judgments of God

God’s judgments must in no way be compared with human judgments. We must not doubt that he is just even when he does what appears unjust to human beings. [Note: [Col. 1885] From book 3 of the Unfinished Work, chapter 24.]

### CCCI. On the birth of the righteous

The righteous person is born from God, not from human beings, because he becomes righteous by being reborn, not by being born. Hence those who are reborn [Note: [Col. 1885] Alternatively: “regenerated.”] are also called children of God. [Note: [Col. 1885] In the same place, chapter 51.]

### CCCII. On the quality of human nature

Human nature, although evil because it has been corrupted, is not itself evil, because it is nature. No nature, insofar as it is nature, is evil; rather, it is wholly good, and without that good no vice can exist, although nature can exist without vice, either because it was never corrupted or because it was healed. [Note: [Col. 1885] In the same place, chapter 206.]

### CCCIII. On the death of sinners

It is God’s just judgment that each person should perish through his own sin, since God does not create sin. He likewise did not create death, yet he kills the one whom he judges worthy of death. Hence it is written, “Death and life are from God” (Sirach 11:14). Anyone who distinguishes divine judgments from divine works clearly sees that these two things are not contrary to one another, because it is one thing not to have established a mortal being in creation and another to punish a sinner in judgment. [Note: [Col. 1885] From book 4 of the Unfinished Work, chapter 32.]

### CCCIV. On the punishment of sin

God indeed made the world and absolutely all bodies. But that the corruptible body should weigh down the soul and the flesh desire against the spirit is not part of the original nature of the human being as created; it is the subsequent punishment of the condemned. [Note: [Col. 1885] In the same place, chapter 67.]

### CCCV. On the work in every nature
However many vices may disfigure any nature, its constitution is always good. For just as the constitution of the body is good even when someone is born diseased, and the constitution of the soul is good even when someone is born foolish, so the constitution of the human being himself is good when he is born subject to original sin [Note: [Col. 1885] Ibid., chapter 115.].

### CCCVI. On the abolition of sin

Just as certain parents aggravate original sin, so certain others lessen it; but no one removes it except he of whom it was said, “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1:29). For him no human good is impossible, and no evil is incurable [Note: [Col. 1886] From book 4 of *The Unfinished Work*, chapter 132.].

### CCCVII. On the grace of God

It pertains not to human merits but to the mercy of God when someone is delivered from that mass of the first human being, to whom death is deservedly owed. For there is no injustice with God: neither in forgiving nor in exacting what is owed is he unjust; and gratuitous mercy exists where punishment could justly have been exacted [Note: [Col. 1886] From Augustine’s Letter 186 to Paulinus, no. 16.].

### CCCVIII. No one is saved except through God’s mercy

Even if human nature had remained in that integrity in which it was created, it could in no way preserve itself without the help of its Creator. Therefore, since without God’s grace it could not preserve the salvation it had received, how can it recover, without God’s grace, what it lost [Note: [Col. 1886] Ibid., no. 37; and it is canon 19 of the Council of Orange.]?

### CCCIX. No excuse belongs to the sinner

Every sinner is without excuse, whether because of the guilt of origin or because of the addition of his own will, whether he knows or is ignorant, whether he judges or does not judge. For ignorance itself is undoubtedly sin in those who were unwilling to understand; but in those who were unable to understand, it is the punishment of sin. Therefore, in neither case is there an excuse, but only just condemnation [Note: [Col. 1886] From Augustine’s Letter 194 to Sixtus, no. 27.].

### CCCX. On those who are led by the Spirit of God

To be led is unquestionably more than to be governed. For one who is governed does something, and is governed in order to act rightly; but one who is led scarcely seems to do anything himself. Yet the grace of the Savior grants so much to our wills that the Apostle does not hesitate to say, “As many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are sons of God” (Romans 8:14). Nor can free will do anything better in us than commend itself to him who cannot do evil [Note: [Col. 1886] From the book *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, chapter 3.].

### CCCXI. On the resurrection

To be delivered from this body of death, with every sickness of carnal desire healed, is to receive the body not for punishment but for glory [Note: [Col. 1886] From book 1 *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, chapter 11.].

### CCCXII. That human beings can do nothing without God

God does many good things in a human being that the human being does not do; but a human being does nothing that God does not enable the human being to do [Note: [Col. 1886] From book 2 *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, chapter 8; and it is canon 20 of the Council of Orange.].

### CCCXIII. On true righteousness

The righteousness by which the righteous person lives from faith, since it comes to the human being from God through the spirit of grace, is true righteousness. Although it is not undeservedly called perfect in certain righteous people, insofar as this life permits, it is nevertheless small in comparison with that great righteousness which the equality of the angels can receive. The one who did not yet possess that righteousness, because of the righteousness already present, called himself perfect, and because of the righteousness still lacking, imperfect. But plainly, this lesser righteousness produces merit; that greater one produces the reward. Therefore, whoever does not pursue the former will not attain the latter [Note: [Col. 1886] From book 3 *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, chapter 7.].

### CCCXIV. On Christ’s mortality according to the flesh

Concerning the one mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus, the catholic faith knows that he deigned to undergo death for us—that is, the punishment of sin—without sin. For just as he alone became the Son of Man so that through him we might become sons of God, so he alone accepted punishment without evil merits, just as through him we receive grace without merits. For just as no good was owed to us, so no evil was owed to him. Therefore, commending his love to those to whom he was going to give life that was not owed to them, he willed to suffer for them a death that was not owed to him [Col. 1887] [Note: [Col. 1887] From book 4 *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, chapter 4; and it is canon 2 of the Council of Orange.].

### CCCXV. On nature and grace

Just as the Apostle most truly says to those who, wishing to be justified by the law, have fallen away from grace, “If righteousness is through the law, then Christ died for nothing” (Galatians 2:21), so it is most truly said to those who think that the grace which the faith of Christ commends and receives is nature: “If righteousness is through nature, then Christ died for nothing.” For the law already existed here, and did not justify; nature also already existed here, and did not justify. Therefore Christ did not die for nothing: so that the law might be fulfilled through him, who said, “I have not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it” (Matthew 5:17), and so that nature, lost through Adam, might be restored through him, who said that he had come to seek and save what had perished (Luke 19:10) [Note: [Col. 1887] From the book *On Grace and Free Will*, chapter 13; and it is canon 21 of the Council of Orange.].

### CCCXVI. On mercy and judgment

To be able to have faith, just as to be able to have charity, belongs to human nature; but to have faith, just as to have charity, belongs to the grace of the faithful. Yet when the will to believe is prepared by the Lord for some and not prepared for others, one must distinguish what comes from his mercy and what from his judgment. For all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth. His ways, however, are unsearchable. Therefore unsearchable are both the mercy by which he freely delivers and the truth by which he judges justly [Note: [Col. 1887] From book 1 *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapters 5–6.].

### CCCXVII. On helping

No one raises anything to the level at which he himself is unless he descends somewhat to the level at which the other person is [Note: [Col. 1887] From Letter 11, to Nebridius, no. 4.].

### CCCXVIII. On despising worldly glory

The power that love of human glory has to do harm is felt only by one who has declared war upon it. For although it is easy for anyone not to desire praise while it is withheld, it is difficult not to delight in it when it is offered [Note: [Col. 1887] From Letter 22, to Aurelius, no. 8.].

### CCCXIX. On relinquishing temporal goods

The person who despises all the riches of the world is the one who despises having not only as much as he could have but also as much as he wished to have. In this matter one must beware lest elation creep in. For it is more useful to hold earthly wealth humbly than to abandon it proudly [Note: [Col. 1887] From Letter 31, to Paulinus, no. 5.].

### CCCXX. On restraining anger

No angry person thinks that his anger is unjust. Therefore one must quickly return from every indignation to the gentleness of meekness. For persistent agitation easily turns into hatred of the person whom one does not quickly forgive [Note: [Col. 1887] See Letter 38, to Profuturus, no. 2.].

### CCCXXI. On law and grace

The one who gave the law also gave grace; but he sent the law through a servant, whereas with grace he himself descended. Thus, because the law shows sins but does not remove them, those who wish to carry out the law by their own strength, yet are unable to do so, are compelled to turn to grace, which removes both the sickness of inability and the guilt of disobedience [Note: [Col. 1887] From Tractate 3 on the Gospel of John, no. 2.].

### CCCXXII. On the Sabbath

The Christian observes the true Sabbath by abstaining from servile work, that is, from sin, since whoever commits sin is a slave of sin [Note: [Col. 1887] Ibid., no. 19.].

### CCCXXIII. On those things that belong properly to human beings

No one has anything of his own except falsehood and sin. But if a human being possesses anything of truth and righteousness, it comes from that fountain for which we ought to thirst in this wilderness, so that, watered from it as if by certain drops, we may not fail along the way [Note: [Col. 1887] From Tractate 5 on John, no. 1; and it is canon 22 of the Council of Orange.].

### CCCXXIV. On the inseparable work of the Father and the Son

What the Father does with Christ, Christ does; and [Col. 1888] what Christ does with the Father, the Father does. Inseparable love, majesty, and power do nothing separately, just as the Lord himself says, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30) [Note: [Col. 1888] From Tractate 5 on John, no. 1; and it is canon 22 of the Council of Orange.].

### CCCXXV. For whose benefit the sacrament of Baptism is

Those who do not preserve the gifts of the grace of regeneration do not thereby diminish it, just as unclean places do not pollute the brightness of light. Therefore, you who rejoice in receiving Baptism, live in the holiness of the new human being; and, holding the faith that works through love, possess the good that you do not yet have, so that the good you do have may benefit you [Note: [Col. 1888] See the same work, no. 15.].

### CCCXXVI. On truth

Christ is truth in such a way that everything true is understood in Christ: the true Word of God, God equal to the Father; a true soul, true flesh, true human being, true God, a true birth, true suffering, true death, and true resurrection. If you call any one of these false, corruption enters. From the serpent’s poison worms of falsehood are born, and nothing whole will remain; for wherever there is the corruption of any falsehood, there the integrity of truth will not exist [Note: [Col. 1888] From Tractate 8 on John, no. 5.].

### CCCXXVII. On charity

How great is charity: if it is absent, the other things are possessed in vain; if it is present, all things are possessed [Note: [Col. 1888] From Tractate 9 on John, no. 8.]!

### CCCXXVIII. How Christ left his Father and mother

Christ left the Father because, although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant. This is what “he left the Father” means—not that he deserted or departed from the Father, but that he did not appear to human beings in the form in which he is equal to the Father. He left his mother by leaving the synagogue of the Jews, from which he was born according to the flesh, and cleaving to the Church, which he gathered from all nations [Note: [Col. 1888] Ibid., no. 10.].

### CCCXXIX. On the comparison of the first Adam and the second

Adam sleeps so that Eve may be made; Christ dies so that the Church may be made. While Adam sleeps, Eve is made from his side; when Christ dies, his side is pierced by a lance, so that the sacraments may flow forth by which the Church is formed. Therefore the Apostle rightly calls Adam a figure of the one to come. For just as all die in Adam, so also all will be made alive in Christ [Note: [Col. 1888] Ibid.].

### CCCXXX. On the incarnation of the Word

God became human; what, then, will the human being become, for whose sake God became human [Note: [Col. 1888] From Tractate 10 on John, no. 1.]?

### CCCXXXI. On the two births of human beings

One birth is from earth, the other from heaven; one is from flesh, the other from spirit; one is from eternity, the other from mortality; one is from male and female, the other from God and the Church. Yet these two are each singular: for just as the womb cannot be repeated, so Baptism cannot be repeated [Note: [Col. 1888] From Tractate 11 on John, no. 6.].

### CCCXXXII. On the diversity of goods

If you attend to visible things, neither is bread God, nor is water God, nor is this light God, nor is clothing God, nor is this house God. For all these things are visible, and each exists separately. What is bread is not water; what is clothing is not a house; and what these things are is not God, for they are visible things. But God is for you everything that you rightly desire, and the variety of all goods flows forth from one fountain. For when he gives his gifts, he bestows himself under the various names of his gifts [Note: [Col. 1888] From Tractate 13 on John, no. 5.].

### CCCXXXIII. On understanding

[Col. 1889]

The soul desiring carnal things is compared to a woman who does not have a governing husband, namely, the intellect, by whose wisdom it ought to be guided—not as though the intellect were something other than the soul, but because it is a certain hidden sight of the soul. For just as the external eyes are something belonging to the flesh, so the mind is something belonging to the soul, which excels within it through participation in divine reason. And it presides well over all its movements when it is illumined by heavenly light, so that there may be in it the true light that enlightens every human being coming into this world [Note: [Col. 1889] See Tractate 15 on John, no. 19.].

### CCCXXXIV. On the place of prayer

When you seek a suitable and holy place in which to supplicate God, cleanse your inner being and, having driven every evil desire away from it, prepare for yourself a secluded place in the peace of your heart. If you wish to pray in a temple, pray within yourself; and always act so that you may be the temple of God. For God hears there where he dwells [Note: [Col. 1889] Ibid., no. 25.].

### CCCXXXV. On the inner human being

The senses of the body report bodily things to the heart. Nor is the capacity of all of them the same: a thing is not seen from the same place from which it is heard; nor is flavor perceived from the place from which odor is perceived. Nor are these servants sufficient without touch to distinguish smooth and rough, hot and cold, wet and dry. But the mind judges incorporeal things by its own sense alone, and reaches all varieties in a single movement. Whatever distinction it rationally discovers between good and evil, just and unjust, is a single affection of intention, so that the image of God may appear there where the mind is one and the same thing as what it is able to be, to the extent that it is able [Note: [Col. 1889] See Tractate 18 on John, nos. 3, 10.].

### CCCXXXVI. On the life of the Son of God

The Son of God, God, did not obtain life in himself, as the Father has it, by participation, but by being born. For the Father, who is life, begot life; nor does the essence of the begetter and the begotten differ in anything, since the Son is from the Father in such a way that, in coeternal equality, there is not one person but one divinity [Note: [Col. 1889] See Tractate 19 on John, nos. 12–13.].

### CCCXXXVII. On judgment

Although the Father never departs from the Son, it is nevertheless said that, for judging the living and the dead, not the Father himself but the Son will be present. For there neither the divinity of the Father nor that of the Son will be seen, but that form of the Son which he united to himself through the sacrament of the incarnation. Therefore the very one who stood under judgment will be the judge; the very one who was judged will judge, so that the wicked may see the glory of him against whose gentleness they raged [Note: [Col. 1889] Alternatively, “acted violently.”]. Thus the judge will appear in such a form as can be seen both by those whom he will crown and by those whom he will condemn. The Father, however, will not appear, because he did not put on the form of a servant; but he gave the power of judgment to the Son, who also became human [Note: [Col. 1889] Ibid., no. 16.].

### CCCXXXVIII. On the will of God and the human being

Human beings do their own will, not God’s, when they do what displeases God. But when they do what they wish in such a way that they serve the divine will, although they willingly do what they do, it is nevertheless the will of the one by whom what they wish is both prepared and commanded [Note: [Col. 1889] Ibid., no. 19; and it is canon 23 of the Council of Orange.].

### CCCXXXIX. On the Father’s teaching through the Word

If the Father teaches the one who hears his Word, ask what Christ is, and you will find his Word: “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1:1), not “In the beginning God made the Word,” as it says, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” (Genesis 1:1). For the Word of God is God, not a creature; nor was it made among all things, but through it all things were made. Therefore, so that a human being established in the flesh might approach the teaching of such a [Col. 1890] Word, “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:1, 3, 14) [Note: [Col. 1890] From Tractate 26 on John, no. 8.].

### CCCXL. On the body of Christ

The flesh of Christ is the life of the faithful, if they do not neglect to be his body. Therefore, if they wish to live from the Spirit of Christ, let them become the body of Christ; for no one lives from that Spirit who is not the body of Christ [Note: [Col. 1890] Ibid., no. 13.].

### CCCXLI. Who eat the body of Christ

The person who remains in Christ, and in whom Christ dwells, receives the food of life and drinks the cup of eternity. For whoever is at odds with Christ neither eats his flesh nor drinks his blood, even if he daily and heedlessly receives the sacrament of so great a thing, to the judgment of his presumption [Note: [Col. 1890] See the same work, no. 18.].

### CCCXLII. On the happiness of the wicked

Worldly wisdom would have it that God never permitted those who are evil to be happy. He certainly does not permit this; but the wicked are thought happy when they have what they want because they do not know what happiness is [Note: [Col. 1890] Augustine: “happiness is unknown.”] [Note: [Col. 1890] See Tractate 28 on John, no. 7.].

### CCCXLIII. On the change of heart

It is one thing to move from place to place in body, another to move in heart. One moves bodily who changes location by bodily movement; one moves in heart who changes his affection by the movement of his heart. If you love one thing and once loved another, you are no longer where you were [Note: [Col. 1890] From Tractate 32 on John, no. 1.].

### CCCXLIV. On chrism

The name “Christ” comes from *chrism*, that is, from anointing. For every Christian is sanctified in order to understand that he shares not only in priestly and royal dignity but also becomes a fighter against the devil [Note: [Col. 1890] See Tractate 33 on John, no. 3.].

### CCCXLV. On light

Let us follow Christ, the true light, lest we walk in darkness. The darkness to be feared belongs to morals, not to the eyes; and, if to the eyes, then not to the external eyes by which one distinguishes not white from black but the just from the unjust [Note: [Col. 1890] From Tractate 35 on John, no. 4.].

### CCCXLVI. On the incarnation of the Word

The catholic faith believes and proclaims the Lord Jesus Christ to be both true God and true human being. For both are written, and both are true. Whoever asserts that Christ is only God denies the remedy by which he was healed; whoever asserts that Christ is only human denies the power by which he was created. Therefore, faithful and upright soul, receive both: Christ is God, and Christ is human. What kind of God is Christ? Equal to the Father, one with the Father. What kind of human being is Christ? The son of a virgin, deriving mortality from a human being but not deriving iniquity [Note: [Col. 1890] From Tractate 36 on John, no. 2.].

### CCCXLVII. On the sending of the Word

The Lord Christ was sent by the Father; he did not depart from the Father. His mission was the incarnation, and for the invisible divinity to come into this world was the same as for it to appear. If he were quickly grasped, there would be no need for him to be believed. Therefore, what is grasped by believing is never understood unless it is believed [Note: [Col. 1890] Ibid., no. 7.].

### CCCXLVIII. On the Father and the Son

In order that the Father and the Son may rightly be believed, the Son himself must be heard saying, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). In two words, two heresies are cut down at once. By saying “one,” he struck Arius; by saying “are,” he laid Sabellius low, because he would say neither “are” of one person nor “one” of persons who are different [Note: [Col. 1890] Ibid., no. 9.].

### CCCXLIX. On God and the human being Jesus Christ

[Col. 1891]

We must know both realities in Christ: in what respect he is equal to the Father, and in what respect the Father is greater than he. The former is Word, the latter flesh; the former is God, the latter human being. Yet Christ is one, God and human being [Note: [Col. 1891] From Tractate 37 on John, no. 10.].

### CCCL. On the unity of the divine Trinity

There are undoubtedly many souls and many hearts among many human beings; but when they cling to God through love and faith, they all become one soul and one heart. Therefore, if the love of God, poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us, produces such unity among many souls and many hearts, how much more certainly and securely does an eternal and unchangeable unity remain in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, where the undivided Trinity is one God, one light, and one principle [Note: [Col. 1891] From Tractate 39 on John, no. 5.]?

### CCCLI. On the Father’s teaching of the Son

The Father did not teach the Son as though he had begotten an untaught being and conferred knowledge upon one who did not know. Rather, temporal teaching is an atemporal essence; and to be taught by the Father is the same as to be begotten by the Father. For, in the simple nature of truth, being and knowing are not two different things but the same [Note: [Col. 1891] From Tractate 40 on John, no. 5.].

### CCCLII. On faith and truth

Faith always precedes vision. For we believe in order to know; we do not know in order to believe. Faith, therefore, is believing what you do not see; truth is seeing what you have believed [Note: [Col. 1891] Ibid., no. 9.].

### CCCLIII. On the good fragrance of Christ

The good fragrance of Christ is the preaching of truth. Through this fragrance the person who serves and conforms to the Gospel by good works [Note: [Col. 1891] Alternatively, “by good conduct.”] receives life; but the person whose life disagrees with what he speaks well incurs death. This condition also binds the hearers: when sound preaching is heard by some through unbelief unto death, it is received by others through faith unto salvation [Note: [Col. 1891] See Tractate 50 on John, no. 8.].

### CCCLIV. On the capacity to believe

The faith of Christ is to believe in the one who justifies the ungodly; to believe in the Mediator without whom no one is reconciled to God; to believe in the Savior who came to seek and save what had perished; to believe in the one who said, “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). But the person who, ignorant of the righteousness of God by which the ungodly are justified, wishes to establish his own righteousness by which his pride may be convicted, does not grasp this faith. For those who think such things are hardened and blinded by their own elation, because, by denying God’s grace, they are not helped [Note: [Col. 1891] From Tractate 53 on John, no. 10.].

### CCCLV. On true love

The person who possesses charity, which comes from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith, loves God and his neighbor as himself. For the lover of God is a lover of himself; and the person who does not love God does not love his neighbor, because he does not love himself. For the sake of this love, the hatred of the world must also be patiently endured. For it is necessary that the world hate those whom it sees hating what it loves [Note: [Col. 1891] From Tractate 87 on John, nos. 1–2.].

### CCCLVI. On the twofold meaning of “the world”

Two kinds of human beings are designated under the single name “world.” For just as “world” is used of the ungodly, so it is used of the holy. Therefore, since the whole world is divided against itself both in hatred and in love, we are commanded both to hate it and to love it: we are told, “Do not love the world” (1 John 2:15), and, “Love your enemies” (Matthew 5:4), so that, while we detest their iniquity, we may desire their salvation [Note: [Col. 1891] Ibid., no. 4.].

### CCCLVII. On avoiding the glory of learning

To avoid the temptation of empty glory, the condition of the learner is better than that of the teacher. For truth is heard more safely than it is preached. When instruction is received, humility is preserved; but when debate is pleasing, it is scarcely possible for even the slightest boastfulness not to strike the person who is arguing [Col. 1892] [Note: [Col. 1892] From Tractate 57 on John, no. 2.].

### CCCLVIII. On the praise by which God proclaims himself

It is dangerous for a human being to take pleasure in himself, since he must beware of becoming proud. But however much God praises himself, the Most High does not exalt himself, nor does he wish to appear greater in majesty than he is. When he tells human beings of his power, he does this not to make himself more glorious but to make them better and more learned. For it benefits us to acknowledge our author and submit to him who is above all things; nor, concerning one whose nature we cannot comprehend, can we suppose that he is what he is not [Note: [Col. 1892] From Tractate 58 on John, no. 3.].

### CCCLIX. On forgiving sins

Christian observance reaches the advancement of perfect piety chiefly through mutual forgiveness of sins, with the Lord giving us the example of his goodness. For if he in whom there was absolutely no sin intercedes for our sins, how much more ought we to pray for one another concerning our own? A person who cannot be entirely free from sin must embrace this gracious condition: by forgiving the offenses of others, he may wash away his own [Note: [Col. 1892] Ibid., no. 5.].

### CCCLX. On the eternity of the saints

Nothing will then be lacking from the fellowship of righteous desires, when God is everything in everyone. Those reach this blessedness who, before the separation of soul and flesh, die to this age in the flesh and are not found in those desires which only the love of God overcomes, so that iniquity may suffer what it chose and righteousness enjoy the good that it loved [Note: [Col. 1892] See Tractate 65 on John, no. 1.].

### CCCLXI. On confessing Jesus Christ as human

Whoever confesses Christ as God in such a way as to deny that he is truly human—namely, possessing the nature of our flesh and soul united to himself—has no Christ who died for him, because Christ died according to his humanity. Such a person is not reconciled to God through the Mediator, for there is one God and one mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus. He is not justified through Christ, because just as through the disobedience of one human being many were made sinners, so through the obedience of one human being many will be made righteous. He will not rise in the resurrection of life, because through a human being came death and through a human being the resurrection of the dead; for just as all die in Adam, so also all will be made alive in Christ. Nor should anyone defend himself by the example of blessed Peter, who both accused and washed himself with many tears, so that the Church might follow its leader by imitating not denial but repentance [Note: [Col. 1892] From Tractate 66 on John, no. 2.].

### CCCLXII. On eternity

Among certain eternal things there can be some difference; eternity itself, however, is without difference of measure. For the many dwelling places in one life signify various degrees of merit. But so that God may be everything in everyone, even in unequal brightness there will be unity through joy, so that what each individual has may be common to all. For through the bond of love, no part of the body will be alienated from the glory of the head [Note: [Col. 1892] From Tractate 67 on John, no. 2.].

### CCCLXIII. On faith

The faith of those who will see God believes what it does not see; for if it sees, it is not faith. Merit is promised to the believer [Note: [Col. 1892] Alternatively, “is gathered in.”]; the reward is given to the one who sees [Note: [Col. 1892] From Tractate 68 on John, no. 3.].

### CCCLXIV. On a contrary petition

A person who would use badly what he wishes to receive does not receive it, through God’s merciful preference. Therefore, if one asks him for something by which the person whose prayer is heard would be harmed, one should fear all the more that God may give in anger what, in his mercy, he could refuse to give [Note: [Col. 1893] From Tractate 73 on John, no. 1.].

### CCCLXV. On love

“The one who loves me,” says the Lord, “will be loved by my Father; and I will love him, and I will reveal myself to him” (John 14:21). What does “I will love” mean? Does it mean that he will love then and does not love now? Far from it. For how would the Father love us without the Son, or the Son without the Father? Since they work inseparably, how do they love separately? Rather, “I will love him” refers to what follows: “And I will reveal myself to him.” “I will love and I will reveal,” that is, “I will love him in order to reveal myself.” For now he loved us in order that we might believe and hold fast to his commandment [Note: [Col. 1893] Alternatively, “faith.”]; then he will love us in order that we may see and receive that very vision as the reward of faith. For now we also love by believing what we will see; then we will love by seeing what we believed [Note: [Col. 1893] From Tractate 75 on John, no. 5.].

### CCCLXVI. On the branches of the vine

The branches are in the vine in such a way that they contribute nothing to the vine but receive from it the source of their life. The vine is in the branches in such a way that it supplies them with vital nourishment rather than receiving anything from them. Thus, both having Christ remain in oneself and remaining in Christ benefit the disciples, not Christ. For when one branch is cut off, another can sprout from the living root; but the branch that has been cut off cannot live without the root [Note: [Col. 1893] From Tractate 81 on John, no. 1; and it is canon 24 of the Council of Orange.].

### CCCLXVII. On the measure of human righteousness

It was said by divine authority, “Do not be excessively righteous” (Ecclesiastes 7:17). By this, not the righteousness of the wise person but the pride of the presumptuous person is condemned. Therefore, whoever makes himself excessively righteous becomes unjust through that very excess. But who makes himself righteous except the person who says that he has no sin [Note: [Col. 1893] From Tractate 95 on John, no. 2.]?

### CCCLXVIII. On simplicity

No substance, even of an incorporeal creature, is truly simple if its being is not the same as its knowing; for it can exist without knowing. But the divine substance cannot, because it is identical with what it possesses. Thus it does not possess knowledge in such a way that the knowledge by which it knows is one thing and the essence by which it exists another; rather, both are one, although what is supremely simple and one should not be called two things. For the Father has life in himself, and he is not something other than the life that is in him; and he gave the Son to have life in himself—that is, he begot the Son, who himself is also life.

Thus we must understand what was said about the Holy Spirit: “For he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears he will speak” (John 16:13), so that we may understand that he is not from himself. For the Father alone is not from another. The Son was born from the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father. The Father, however, was neither born from another nor proceeds from another. Yet human thought should not on this account imagine any inequality in that supreme Trinity, because the Son is equal to the one from whom he was born, and the Holy Spirit is equal to the one from whom he proceeds [Note: [Col. 1893] From Tractate 99 on John, no. 4.].

### CCCLXIX. On the atemporality of the divinity

Although an unchangeable nature does not admit “was” and “will be” but only “is”—for it truly exists because it cannot exist otherwise than it is—nevertheless, because of the mutability of the times in which our mortality and mutability move, we do not falsely say both “was,” “is,” and “will be”: it was in the past, is in the present, and will be in the future. It was, because it was never absent; it will be, because it will never be absent; it is, because it always is. It does not pass away with past things as though it no longer existed, nor slip away with present things as though it did not remain, nor arise with future things as though it had not existed.

Accordingly, when human speech varies [Col. 1894] according to the sequences of time, the words of whatever time are truly spoken of the one who could not, cannot, and will not be subject to any times. The Holy Spirit therefore always hears, because he always knows; and for him knowing and hearing are the same as always existing. For him always to exist is to proceed from the Father. No one can say that the Holy Spirit is not life, since the Father is life and the Son is life. Therefore, just as the Father, having life in himself, gave the Son to have life in himself, so he gave the Holy Spirit to proceed from him as life, just as he himself proceeds from him [Note: [Col. 1894] From Tractate 99 on John, nos. 5, 9.].

### CCCLXX. On the love with which we love God

It is wholly a gift of God to love God. The one who loved us when he was not loved himself gave us the ability to love him; we who were displeasing were loved so that something might come to exist in us by which we might become pleasing. For the Spirit of the Father and the Son has poured love into our hearts, and through this Spirit we love the Father and the Son [Note: [Col. 1894] From Tractate 102 on John, no. 5; and it is canon 25 of the Council of Orange.].

### CCCLXXI. On the peace of Christ

The peace of Christ has no end in time, and it is the perfection of every godly intention and action. For its sake we are imbued with his sacraments; for its sake we are instructed by his wonderful works and words; for its sake we have received the pledge of the Holy Spirit; for its sake we believe and hope in him, and are kindled with love for him insofar as he grants it. Finally, for its sake we endure every tribulation bravely, so that in it we may reign happily without tribulation. For true peace creates unity, since whoever clings to God is one spirit [Note: [Col. 1894] From Tractate 104 on John, no. 6.].

### CCCLXXII. On times

All time has been ordered by the one who is not subject to time. For the things that were going to occur at the several times have effective [Note: [Col. 1894] Alternatively, “efficient.”] causes in the wisdom of God, in which there are no times. Therefore, one must not believe that the hour of the Lord’s passion came under the pressure of fate, but rather through God’s ordering. For no astral necessity brought the cross upon Christ, nor did the stars compel the creator of the stars to die. He, who is atemporal with the Father, chose the time when he would die in the flesh just as he chose the time when he would be born from his mother [Note: [Col. 1894] Ibid., no. 2.].

### CCCLXXIII. On the unity of the Trinity

In the statement, “This is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17:3), the order of the words is: “that they may know you and Jesus Christ whom you sent as the only true God.” The Holy Spirit is consequently understood as well, because the Spirit is of the Father and the Son, as the substantial and consubstantial love of both. For there are not two gods, the Father and the Son, nor three gods, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; rather, the Trinity itself is the one true God. Yet the Father is not the same as the Son, nor the Son the same as the Father, nor the Holy Spirit the same as the Father or the Son. For the three are the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; but the Trinity itself is one God [Note: [Col. 1894] From Tractate 105 on John, no. 3.].

### CCCLXXIV. What the Father gave the Son

Whatever God the Father gave to God the Son, he gave by begetting him. For the Father gave the Son those things without which the Son could not exist, just as he gave him existence itself. For how could he give words to the Word, in whom he ineffably spoke all things [Note: [Col. 1894] From Tractate 106 on John, no. 7.]?

### CCCLXXV. On God’s protection by which he preserves his own
We must not understand God’s protection of us in a merely carnal way, as though the Father and the Son successively guarded us, each taking turns to preserve us, as if one departed and the other took his place. For the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, who is one true God, guard us together. But Scripture does not lift us up unless it first comes down to us. Thus the Word became flesh and came down [Col. 1895] in order to raise us up; he did not fall in order to lie prostrate. If we have recognized him as the one who came down, let us rise with the one who raises us up; and let us understand that, when he speaks in this way, he distinguishes the persons without separating the natures.

[Note: [Col. 1895] From *Tractate 107 on John*, no. 6.]

## CCCLXXVI. On the grace of God, by which every human merit is preceded

If we consider the nature in which we were created—since the Truth created us all, who is not from the Truth? Yet not all are granted by that very Truth the ability to hear and believe the truth, plainly with no preceding merits, lest grace cease to be grace. For if he had said, “Everyone who hears my voice is from the truth,” such a person would be thought to be from the truth because he obeys the truth. But he does not say this. Rather, he says: “Everyone who is from the truth hears my voice” (John 18:37). Accordingly, he is not from the truth because he hears its voice; rather, he hears because he is from the truth—that is, because this gift has been bestowed on him by the Truth. And what else does this mean than that, Christ granting it, he believes in Christ?

[Note: [Col. 1895] From *Tractate 115 on John*, no. 4.]

## CCCLXXVII. On the love with which we ought to love God

Whoever loves himself, not God, does not love himself; and whoever loves God, not himself, loves himself. For whoever cannot live from himself certainly dies by loving himself. But when the one from whom he lives is loved, he loves himself more by not loving himself, so that he may love the one from whom he lives.

[Note: [Col. 1895] From *Tractate 123 on John*, no. 5.]

## CCCLXXVIII. On the undivided work of the Father and the Son

Whatever it is that the Father ought to do toward the Son is done only through that same Son—toward him, that is, because he is the Son of Man and was made among all things; but through him, because he is the Son of God, and through him all things are made by the Father.

[Note: [Col. 1895] See Book 1 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 7.]

## CCCLXXIX. On the subjection of the Son

There is no difficulty in the Apostle’s saying that, even in the future age, the Son will be subject to the Father, where he says, “Then the Son himself will also be subject to him who subjected all things to him.” For the human form will remain in the Son, and in that form the Father is always greater. Nevertheless, there have been some who thought that the Son’s subjection at that time should be understood as the transformation of his human form into the divine substance, as though each thing were subjected to whatever it is converted and changed into. But the Apostle may rather be understood to have said that the Son would then also be subject to the Father so that no one would suppose that the human spirit and body would be consumed by some transformation. Thus God will be all things, not merely in that human form of his, but in all things (1 Corinthians 15:28), when the glory of the Head fills the whole body.

[Note: [Col. 1895] See the same work, chapter 8.]

## CCCLXXX. That nothing among any creatures is left disordered by the Creator

However many good things there are, whether great or small, they cannot exist except from God. For what is greater among creatures than an intelligent life? Or what can be less than a body? However much these may decline and tend toward nonexistence, some form nevertheless remains in them, so that they exist in some fashion. Whatever form remains in a declining thing derives from that form which does not know decline; and he does not permit the movements of declining or advancing things to exceed the laws of their numbers. Therefore, whatever praiseworthy feature is observed in the nature of things—whether small or great, whatever is judged worthy of praise—must be referred to the most excellent and ineffable praise of the Creator.

[Note: [Col. 1895] From Book 2 of *On Free Choice of the Will*, chapter 17.]

## CCCLXXXI. That God’s foreknowledge does not compel anyone to sin

God compels no one to sin; yet he foresees those who will sin by their own will. Why, then, should the just God not punish what, in his foreknowledge, he does not compel to happen? For just as no one, by his memory, compels past events to have happened, so God, by his foreknowledge, does not compel future events to happen. And just as a person remembers some things he has done, though he did not do everything he remembers, so God foreknows everything of which he himself is the author, though he is not the author of everything he foreknows. Of those things of which he is not the evil author, he is the just avenger.

[Note: [Col. 1896] From Book 3 of *On Free Choice of the Will*, chapter 4.]

## CCCLXXXII. On knowing creatures that are not seen

The human soul is naturally joined to the divine principles on which it depends. When it says, “This would be better made than that,” if it speaks truly and sees what it says, it sees it in those higher principles. Let it therefore believe that God made what it recognizes, through right understanding, ought to have been made by him, even if it does not see this among created things. For even if it could not see the heavens with its eyes, yet by true reasoning concluded that something of this kind ought to have been made, it ought to believe that it was made, although it had not seen it with its eyes. It would not discern by thought that it had been made except through those principles in which all things were made. But no one can truly see in thought what is not there, any more than what does not exist can be seen.

[Note: [Col. 1896] The same work, chapter 5.]

## CCCLXXXIII. By what remedy human wounds are healed

What is so worthy of mercy as the miserable person? And what is so unworthy of mercy as a proud miserable person? Hence it came about that the Word of God, through whom all things were made and whom all angelic blessedness enjoys, extended his clemency even to our misery; the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.
