For in this way a human being, not yet made equal to the angels, could eat the bread of angels, if that very bread of angels deigned to become equal to human beings. He did not therefore descend to us in such a way as to abandon them; rather, he remained whole among them and whole among us: inwardly nourishing them through what he is as God, and outwardly admonishing us through what we are; and by faith makes fit those whom he may nourish equally by sight.

[Note: [Col. 1896] The same work, chapter 10.]

## CCCLXXXIV. That no defect of nature comes from its author

There is no doubt that every defect is contrary to the nature of the thing whose defect it is. Therefore, since nothing is blamed except its defect, and since it is a defect because it is contrary to the nature of the thing whose defect it is, the defect of no thing is rightly blamed unless that thing’s nature is praised. For what displeases in a defect is only that it corrupts what pleases in nature.

[Note: [Col. 1896] The same work, chapter 15.]

## CCCLXXXV. On the punishment of sin

Every sinful soul has two punishments: ignorance and difficulty. From ignorance comes error, which distorts it.

[Note: [Col. 1896] Alternatively, “dishonors it.”]

From difficulty comes the affliction of torment. But to approve false things as true, so that one errs unwillingly, and, because of the resistance of the carnal bond, to be unable to refrain from illicit deeds—this is not the nature in which humanity was established, but the punishment of the condemned.

[Note: [Col. 1896] The same work, chapter 18.]

## CCCLXXXVI. On the variety of remedies

Just as the art of medicine, while remaining the same and in no way changing in itself, nevertheless changes its prescriptions for the sick because our health is changeable, so divine providence, although itself wholly unchangeable, comes to the aid of the changeable creature in various ways. According to the diversity of diseases, it commands or forbids different things to different people, so that it may restore and strengthen what is failing—and tending toward nothingness—from the vice where death begins and from death itself, bringing it back to its own nature and essence.

[Note: [Col. 1896] From *On True Religion*, chapter 17.]

## CCCLXXXVII. On the first transgression of humanity

The first defect of the rational soul is the will to do what the highest and innermost Truth forbids. Thus humanity was driven from paradise into this age—that is, from eternal things to temporal things, from abundance to want, from stability to weakness. It was not therefore driven from a substantial good to a substantial evil, because no substance is evil, but from an eternal good to a temporal good; from a spiritual good to a bodily good; from an intelligible good to a sensible good; from the highest good to the lowest good. There is, then, a certain good which, if the rational soul loves it, it sins, because that good has been ordered below the soul. Accordingly, sin itself is evil, not the substance that is loved in sinning.

[Note: [Col. 1896] The same work, chapter 20.]

## CCCLXXXVIII. On Truth, the teacher of all the arts

Since the law of all the arts is wholly unchangeable, while the human mind, to which it has been granted to see such a law, can suffer the changeability of error, it is sufficiently clear that the law called truth is above our mind. Nor should there now be any doubt that the unchangeable nature which is above the rational soul is God, and that the first life and the first essence are there, where the first wisdom is. For this is that unchangeable Truth which is rightly called the law of all the arts and the art of the omnipotent Craftsman. Therefore, when the soul recognizes that it does not judge the form and movement of bodies according to itself, it must at the same time recognize that its own nature is superior to the nature about which it judges, while that nature according to which it judges, and about which it cannot judge in any way, is superior to it.

[Note: [Col. 1896] The same work, chapters 30–31.]

## CCCLXXXIX. By what the heart is stirred to learn

[Col. 1897]

We are necessarily led to learning in two ways: by authority and by reason. In time, authority comes first; in the nature of the matter, reason comes first. For one thing is what is given precedence in action, and another is what is valued more highly in desire. Since, then, “the beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord,” and humility is the path toward sublime things, let human ignorance proceed through faith, so that faith may deserve to see what it believes.

[Note: [Col. 1897] *On Order*, Book 2, chapter 9.]

## CCCXC. On riches

You flourish in riches and boast of the nobility of your ancestors; you exult in your homeland, the beauty of your body, and the honors that [Col. 1898] people bestow upon you. Look upon yourself, because you are mortal; and because you are earth, you will go into the earth. Look around at those who before you shone with similar splendors. Where are those whom the powers of their fellow citizens courted? Where are the unconquerable emperors? Where are those who arranged assemblies and festivals? Where are the splendid riders of horses?

[Note: [Col. 1898] Alternatively, “trainers.”]

Where are the commanders of armies, the satraps, the tyrants? Is not everything dust? Is not everything ashes? Is the memory of their life not preserved in a few bones? Look at the tombs, and see who is servant, who master, who poor, who rich. Distinguish, if you can, the vanquished from the king, the strong from the weak, the beautiful from the deformed. Remembering nature, therefore, do not at any time exalt yourself. You will remember it if you look upon yourself.

**One Book of St. Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, *On the Spirit and the Letter*, to Marcellinus.** —Marcellinus wrote that he had been disturbed because in the preceding work he had read that it is possible for a person to be without sin in this life, if he wishes and is assisted by God, although no example of such perfect righteousness has ever existed among human beings. Augustine seizes this as an occasion to argue against the Pelagians concerning the assistance of God’s grace, and shows that God does not assist us in performing righteousness merely by giving the law, full of good and holy commandments; rather, he assists and raises up our will itself—without which we cannot do good—by the imparted Spirit of grace. Without this assistance, the teaching of the law is a letter that kills, because it holds people guilty of transgression instead of justifying the ungodly. Returning thereafter to the proposed question, which he begins to resolve at the start of the book and takes up again at its end, he demonstrates that many things are possible with God’s help, as no one denies, although no example of any of them exists anywhere; and thus he concludes that perfect righteousness among human beings exists without an example, yet is not impossible. 199–202

**Notice to the Book *On Nature and Grace*.** 245–246

**One Book of St. Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, *On Nature and Grace*, to Timasius and James, against Pelagius.** —At the beginning it establishes what is certain concerning nature and grace: namely, that nature, propagated from the flesh of Adam the transgressor, since it is no longer as God originally created it—innocent and sound—needs the assistance of grace, by which it may both be redeemed from God’s wrath and directed toward the perfection of righteousness. The punitive defect of nature belongs to a most just retribution; grace itself, however, is not given in return for merits but freely; and those who are not liberated through it are justly condemned. Pelagius’ book, which defends this same nature against grace, is then refuted point by point in replies to each of its arguments. The chief point is that, while attempting to persuade people that it is possible to be without sin, Pelagius maintains that nature has not been weakened and changed by sin; otherwise, he thinks absurdly, the very material for sin would become a punishment, if the sinner had been weakened for the purpose of committing more sins. Further, when he recalls righteous persons of both the Old and New Testaments whom he believes to have been without sin, he says that the possibility of not sinning is inherent in human nature, and that it must therefore be attributed to God’s grace because God is the author of that nature, in which the possibility of not sinning is inseparably implanted. Finally, the opinions of the ancients whom Pelagius adduces on his side—especially Hilary, Ambrose, and Augustine himself—are examined. 247–248

**LXI.** He answers the testimonies of Catholic writers that Pelagius had produced on his side: Lactantius, Hilary, Ambrose, and Jerome. 282  
**LXII.** To do and to perfect righteousness. 283  
**LXIII, LXIV, LXV.** On the same subject. 284–286  
**LXVI.** A certain necessity of sinning. 286  
**LXVII.** Just as illnesses are avoided in two ways, so are sins. Ibid.  
**LXVIII.** How people are to be exhorted to faith, repentance, and progress. 288  
**LXIX.** God commands nothing impossible, because everything is easy for charity. Ibid.  
**LXX.** Degrees of charity produce degrees of righteousness. 290

**Notice to the Book *On the Perfection of Human Righteousness*.** 289–290

**Letter, or Book, of St. Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, to the Bishops Eutropius and Paul, *On the Perfection of Human Righteousness*.** —After Augustine was given a sheet containing definitions said to be those of Coelestius, he first dismantles, in brief replies, each of the arguments by which Coelestius—or anyone else sharing his error—wrongly defined the possibility of a person’s being without sin in this life. He teaches that the perfection and fullness of righteousness by which a person is entirely without sin is impossible by the powers of nature, especially fallen nature, without grace, and that it never exists in the present life. He then proceeds to the authorities gathered from Scripture on the same sheet: some command a person to be blameless and perfect; others state that God’s commandments are not burdensome; and still others appear contrary to those authorities commonly brought forward by Catholics against the Pelagians. 291–292

**Notice to the Book *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*.** 317–318

**One Book of St. Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, to Aurelius the Bishop.** —Each point of error brought against Pelagius at the Palestinian synod, together with his responses to those charges, is examined in detail. Although Pelagius obtained acquittal from the synod, Augustine shows that suspicion of heresy nevertheless remained in him; and finally he demonstrates that the man was acquitted by the synod’s decision in such a way that the heresy itself, on account of which he had been brought to trial, was unequivocally condemned. 319–320

**Two Books of St. Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, *On the Grace of Christ and on Original Sin*, against Pelagius and Coelestius.** 359–360

**Book One: On the Grace of Christ.** —He shows that Pelagius disguises his opposition to grace by professing it; for Pelagius places grace either in nature and free will or in the law and teaching. Moreover, he says that divine grace assists only what he calls the possibility of willing and acting, not willing and acting themselves; and he further thinks that this assisting grace is given by God according to human merits and helps people only so that they may fulfill the commandments more easily. Augustine examines passages from Pelagius’ short works in which Pelagius boasted that he had explicitly commended God’s grace, and demonstrates that these passages can be interpreted as referring to the law and teaching—that is, to divine revelation and Christ’s example, which likewise belong to teaching—or to the forgiveness of sins. He shows that it is entirely unclear whether Pelagius truly acknowledges Christian grace, namely, assistance in doing good added to nature and teaching through the inspiration of the most ardent and radiant charity. Finally, Pelagius is bidden to listen to Ambrose, whom he had praised so highly, speaking outstandingly in commendation of divine grace. Ibid.

**Two Books of St. Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, *On the Grace of Christ and on Original Sin*, against Pelagius and Coelestius.** 385–386

**Book Two: On Original Sin.** —Augustine shows that, in the question of original sin and the baptism of infants, Pelagius in reality dissents in no respect from his disciple Coelestius. Coelestius, unwilling to confess original sin and even daring openly to deny it, was condemned first at Carthage and afterward at Rome by episcopal judgments. Augustine argues that this question is not, as those heretics wished, one in which error may occur without danger to the faith; rather, their error directly attacks the very foundations of the Christian faith. He then refutes those who maintained that the doctrine of original defect detracts from the goodness of marriage and wrongs God himself, the creator of the human being generated through marriage. Ibid.

**Notice to the Books *On Marriage and Concupiscence*.** 409–410

**Letter to Valerius the Count**, to whom Augustine sends the first book of *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, dedicated to him. 411–412

**Two Books of St. Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, to Valerius the Count.** 413–414

**Book One.** —He explains the proper and natural goods of marriage. He proves that carnal concupiscence is not to be counted among those goods: it is wholly an evil that does not arise from the nature of marriage but has befallen marriage from the ancient sin. Nevertheless, marriage makes good use of this evil for the procreation of children. Because of this concupiscence, even from the lawful marriages of children of God are born not children of God but children of the world; they are bound by the chain of sin, although their parents have been freed from it by grace, and are captives under the power of the devil unless they too are freed by the same grace of Christ. He explains how concupiscence remains in the baptized in act but not in guilt. He teaches that through the holiness of baptism not only this original guilt but also all other sins and every evil of human beings must be removed. Finally, he confirms by the authority of Ambrose that the evil of concupiscence must be distinguished from the goodness of marriage. Ibid.

**Chapter One.** The subject of this work. Ibid.  
**II.** Why he wrote the work to Valerius. Ibid.  
**III.** Conjugal chastity is a gift of God. The difficulty of chastity among unbelievers. No one is truly chaste unless he is a believer. 415  
**IV.** The natural goodness of marriage. Every society naturally shuns a deceptive partner. What true conjugal chastity is. Virginity and chastity are not true unless devoted to true faith. 415  
**V.** Condemnation of lust is not condemnation of marriage. The origin of bodily shame in human beings. Adam and Eve were not created blind. What the opening of the eyes in the first parents means. 416  
**VI.** Humanity’s disobedience of its own flesh justly repaid. Shame at the disobedient members. 417  
**VII.** The evil of lust does not remove the goodness of marriage. 418  
**VIII.** The disease of concupiscence in marriage belongs not to the will but to necessity. What the will of the faithful ought to be in the use of marriage. How one is judged to use the evil of concupiscence without being conquered by it. How the holy fathers formerly used marriage. Ibid.  
**IX.** Why a man was sometimes permitted to have several wives, but women were never permitted to have several husbands. 419  
**X.** The sacrament of marriage. Marriage is indissoluble. The law of the world concerning divorce differs from the law of the Gospel. 420  
**XI.** A mutual vow of continence does not dissolve a marriage. The true marriage of Mary and Joseph. How Joseph was the father of Christ. All the goods of marriage existed in the marriage of Mary and Joseph. Ibid.  
**XII.** Every flesh born from intercourse is the flesh of sin. 421  
**XIII.** Before Christ was the time for marrying; after Christ is the time for continence. 422  
**XIV.** A certain excess tolerated among married couples. The use of marriage for the sole pleasure of lust is not free from fault, but because of marriage it is venial. 423  
**XV.** In marital intercourse, what is without fault, what carries venial fault, and what carries mortal fault. Ibid.  
**XVI.** The weakness of incontinence, lest it fall into the ruin of disgraceful acts, should be received within the honor of marriage. 424  
**XVII.** The goods of marriage. Ibid.  
**XVIII.** Why children of wrath are born from a holy marriage. 425  
**XIX.** Thus sinners are born from the righteous, as wild olive trees from cultivated olives. Ibid.  
**XX.** Even unbaptized infants are under the power of the devil. Exorcism over infants and renunciation of the devil. 426  
**XXI.** Sin did not arise from the goods of marriage. The sacrament of marriage is great in Christ and the Church, but small in husband and wife. 427  
**XXII.** Lust and shame arise from sin. The law of sin. The shamelessness of the Cynics. Ibid.  
**XXIII.** In the regenerate, concupiscence without consent is not sin. In what sense concupiscence is called sin. Whatever is born through concupiscence is not unjustly subjected to the devil on account of sin. The devil is to be punished more severely than human beings. 428  
**XXIV.** Original sin is transmitted through lust. Venial sins among married couples. The concupiscence of the flesh, daughter and mother of sin. 429  
**XXV.** Concupiscence remains after baptism like weakness after an illness has been healed. Concupiscence diminishes in those who make progress and increases in the incontinent. Ibid.  
**XXVI.** How concupiscence remains in the baptized in act but passes away in guilt. 430  
**XXVII.** The evil desires of concupiscence. We must will that they not exist. Ibid.  
**XXVIII.** Who could say, “It is no longer I who do it”? 431  
**XXIX.** When the good will be perfected. Ibid.  
**XXX.** How concupiscence held the Apostle captive. What the law of sin means for the Apostle. 432  
**XXXI.** Flesh and the affection of the flesh. Ibid.  
**XXXII.** The law of sin with guilt in unbaptized infants. Through Adam’s sin the human race became a wild olive tree. 431  
**XXXIII.** All forgiveness of sins through baptism, and complete healing in the resurrection, must be acknowledged as gifts received. Daily cleansing. Ibid.  
**XXXIV.** Through the holiness of baptism not only sins but every evil must be removed. The Church is not yet free from every stain. 435  
**XXXV.** The Pelagians, who praise carnal concupiscence as a natural good, are refuted by the authority of Blessed Ambrose. 436

**Book Two.** —In this later book Augustine refutes statements of Julian, excerpted from the first of the four books that Julian had written against the earlier book *On Marriage and Concupiscence*. The excerpts were copied out by an unknown hand and, through the agency of Count Valerius, brought to Augustine. Augustine defends the Catholic doctrine of original evil against the calumnies and sophistries of his opponent and demonstrates above all that it is far removed from the wicked heresy of the Manichaeans. 437–438

**Notice to the Four Books *On the Soul and Its Origin*.** 473–474

**Four Books of St. Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, *On the Soul and Its Origin*.** 475–476

**Book One, to the Monk Renatus.** —After receiving two books by Vincent Victor, who disapproved Augustine’s opinion concerning the nature of the soul and his hesitation concerning its origin, Augustine shows that the young man, thinking arrogantly of himself and passing judgment on so obscure a matter, fell into intolerable errors. He then demonstrates that the testimonies of Scripture by which Victor thought he could prove that souls come from God rather than by propagation, and that new souls are breathed into each person at birth, are ambiguous and wholly unsuitable for confirming Victor’s opinion. Ibid.

**Book Two, to the Presbyter Peter.** —Augustine warns Peter not to give the impression, by praising the books on the origin of the soul that Vincent Victor wrote to him, that he approves them, or to regard as Catholic dogmas the things Victor rashly wrote contrary to the Christian faith. He points out Victor’s various and extremely serious errors and refutes them briefly. Finally, he urges Peter himself to bring Victor to correct them. 495–496

**Book Three, to Vincent Victor.** —Augustine shows Vincent Victor what he must amend in his books on the origin of the soul if he wishes to be Catholic. These matters, already refuted in the preceding books to Renatus and Peter, he briefly touches upon in this third work addressed to Victor himself, reducing them to eleven points of error. 509–510

**Book Four, to the Same.** —First, Augustine demonstrates to Vincent Victor that his hesitation concerning the origin of souls was unjustly criticized, and that Victor wrongfully compared him to animals because he had dared to define nothing on this subject. He then considers Victor’s unhesitating assertion that the soul is spirit and not body. Victor rashly criticized this position as well, attempting to establish that the soul is bodily by nature and that the spirit in human beings is distinct from it. Refuting him, after carefully examining the arguments by which Victor tried to prove that the soul is bodily, Augustine shows that this same entity is also called spirit in Scripture, although in truth that name properly designates the part of the soul by which we reason and understand. 523–524

**Notice to the Work *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*.** 547–548

**Four Books of St. Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, to Boniface, Presbyter of the Roman Church.** 549–550

**Book One.** —Augustine replies to the letter reportedly sent to Rome by Julian. First he defends Catholic doctrine against Julian’s calumnies; then he exposes and refutes the heretical Pelagian meaning concealed in the profession of faith that the author of the letter set against the Catholics. Ibid.

**Chapter One.** He begins with the preeminence of the Roman episcopate. Ibid.  
**II.** He attacks Julian for asserting that free will perished through Adam’s sin. 551  
**III.** Grace is not given according to merits. 552  
**IV.** The Pelagians, destroyers of free will. 554  
**V.** Julian’s second calumny: that marriage is said not to have been instituted by God. His third calumny: that conjugal intercourse is condemned. Ibid.  
**VI.** The Pelagians’ strategy in praising the innocence of conjugal intercourse. 555  
**VII.** His fourth calumny: that the saints of the Old Testament are said not to have been free from sins. Ibid.  
**VIII.** His fifth calumny: that Paul and the other apostles are said to have been polluted by lust. 556  
**IX.** One who does not sin solely from fear sins by the will. 558  
**X–XI.** The discussion continues concerning the Apostle’s words. 559  
**XII.** His sixth calumny: that even Christ was not free from sins. 562  
**XIII.** His seventh calumny: that all sins are not forgiven in baptism. Ibid.  
**XIV.** Serious offenses and venial sins. 563  
**XV.** Julian opposes the faith of his own people to the judgments of Catholics. The first antithesis: concerning free will. The second: concerning marriage. The third: concerning conjugal intercourse. 564  
**XVI.** The coverings that Adam and Eve sewed for themselves. The opening of Adam’s and Eve’s eyes. Shame at nakedness. Ibid.  
**XVII.** Whether lust could have existed in paradise before sin. 565  
**XVIII.** Julian’s fourth antithesis: that the human being is God’s work, and so forth. [Col. 1906] 567  
**XIX.** The beginning of good will is a gift of grace. To come to Christ means to believe. The power of grace. 567  
**XX.** The power of God’s grace is demonstrated. 568  
**XXI.** Julian’s fifth antithesis, concerning the righteous of the Old Testament. 569  
**XXII.** The sixth antithesis, concerning the necessity of grace for all and the baptism of infants. 570  
**XXIII.** The seventh antithesis, concerning the effect of baptism. Ibid.  
**XXIV.** He refutes the conclusion of Julian’s letter. Ibid.

**Book Two.** —He undertakes to examine a second letter of the Pelagians, filled with calumnies against the Catholics like the first, which they had sent to Thessalonica in the name of eighteen bishops. First, he shows that Catholics do not fall into the errors of the Manichaeans when they detest the Pelagian doctrines, by comparing the two heresies with each other. He repels from the Roman clergy the charge of prevarication allegedly committed in the later condemnation of Pelagius and Coelestius under Zosimus, demonstrating that the Pelagian doctrines were never approved at Rome, although Zosimus’ clemency dealt with them more leniently for a time.

Coelestius, so that he might be brought to correct his errors. Under the name of grace, Catholics neither assert fate nor attribute partiality to God; although they do say that God’s grace is in fact not given according to human merits, and that the first desire for what is good is inspired by God, so that a person cannot at all begin to be changed from evil to good unless God’s unmerited and gratuitous mercy is at work in him. 571–572

**CHAPTER ONE.** The Pelagians accuse Catholics under the name of Manichaeans. Ibid.

**II.** The heresies of the Manichaeans and Pelagians are mutually opposed and equally rejected by the Catholic Church. In what respects Manichaeans and Pelagians are united in error, and in what respects they are separate. Ibid.

**III.** The Pelagians’ slander against the clerics of the Roman Church. 573

**IV.** On the same subject. 575

**V.** He replies to the Pelagians’ slanders. What free will is without grace. What Catholics think about fate. 577

**VI.** The charge of fate is turned back against the adversaries. 578

**VII.** He refutes the slander concerning partiality. 580

**VIII.** Even the desire for imperfect goodness is a gift of grace; otherwise grace would be given according to merits. 583

**IX.** He interprets the Scriptures that the Pelagians misuse. 585

**X.** According to whose purpose the elect are called. 586

**BOOK THREE.** He continues to refute the other charges maliciously brought by the Pelagians in the same letter sent to Thessalonica; and against their heresy he explains what Catholics truly say about the usefulness of the Law, what they teach about the effect and power of Baptism, what they teach about the difference between the two Testaments, the Old and the New, what they teach about the righteousness and perfection of the Prophets and Apostles, what they teach about the designation of sin in Christ, when he is said to have condemned sin “in the likeness of sinful flesh,” or to have himself been made sin; and finally what they profess about the fulfillment of the commandments in the future life. 587–588

**CHAPTER ONE.** Introduction. Ibid.

**II.** The Pelagians’ slander concerning the use of the Old Law. Ibid.

**III.** The slander concerning the effect of Baptism. 589

**IV.** The slander concerning the Old Testament and the ancient righteous. The Old Testament is a figure of the New. The saints of the Old Testament belong to the New. 591

**V.** The slander concerning the righteousness of the Prophets and Apostles. 597

**VI.** On sin in Christ. 599

**VII.** On the fulfillment of the commandments in the future life. 600

**VIII.** The three principal doctrines of the Pelagian heresy. The Pelagians’ clouds and the five heads of their slanders. 600

**IX.** He shows that the Catholic position, midway between the Manichaeans and Pelagians, refutes both. 607

**X.** The Pelagians still seek a place of concealment by introducing the unnecessary question of the origin of the soul. 608

**BOOK FOUR.** After dispelling in the preceding books the accusations brought against Catholics, Augustine here exposes the snares hidden in the remaining portion of the Pelagians’ second letter, namely, in the five heads of their teaching: praise of the creature, praise of marriage, praise of the Law, praise of free will, and praise of the saints. With respect to these five heads, the Pelagians maliciously boast that they are no more opposed to the Manichaeans than to Catholics, although they are known to refer all five to this purpose: the first two, to deny original sin; the next two, to establish that grace is given according to merits [Col. 1907]; and the fifth, to say that the saints did not have sin in this life.

Augustine shows that both heresies, those of the Manichaeans and of the Pelagians, are opposed to one another in different ways and are equally hateful to the Catholic faith. That faith professes, first, that nature is good, having been created by the good God; but that it nevertheless needs a Savior because of original sin, which passed to all from the transgression of the first human being. It then professes that marriage is good and truly instituted by God; but that the concupiscence itself which attaches to marriage as a consequence of sin is evil. It likewise professes that God’s Law is good, but in such a way that it merely reveals sin and does not remove it. It certainly professes that free will is implanted in human nature; yet that it is now so enslaved that it cannot perform righteousness unless it has been liberated by grace. Finally, it professes that the saints of either the New or the Old Testament possessed true righteousness, but not perfect righteousness, nor such fullness that they were without every sin.

At the end he produces the testimonies of Cyprian and Ambrose in support of the Catholic faith: some concerning original sin, others concerning the help of grace, and the last concerning the imperfection of present righteousness. 609–610

**CHAPTER ONE.** The Pelagians’ five hiding places. Ibid.

**II.** Praise of the creature; praise of marriage; praise of the Law; praise of free will; praise of the saints. Ibid.

**III.** Catholics praise nature, marriage, the Law, free will, and the saints in such a way as simultaneously to condemn both Pelagians and Manichaeans. 611

**IV.** On praise of the creature. Pelagians and Manichaeans. Ibid.

**V.** On praise of marriage. On praise of the Law. 615

**VI.** On praise of free will. An inscrutable question. 617

**VII.** On praise of the saints. The Church of the present time is not without spot or wrinkle. The Pelagians’ snares. 621

**VIII.** Testimonies of the ancients against the Pelagians. 623

**IX.** Cyprian’s testimonies concerning the grace of God. 626

**X.** Cyprian’s testimonies concerning the imperfection of our righteousness. 629

**XI.** Ambrose’s testimonies against the Pelagians: concerning original sin, the grace of God, and the imperfection of present righteousness. 632

**XII.** The Pelagian heresy arose long after Ambrose. The Catholic faith is always vigilant in repelling error. The convening of a synod is not always necessary for condemning heresies. 636

**NOTICE TO THE BOOKS AGAINST JULIAN.** 637–638

**AUGUSTINE’S LETTER 207.** 639–640

**THE SIX BOOKS OF SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, AGAINST JULIAN, DEFENDER OF THE PELAGIAN HERESY.** 641–642

**BOOK ONE.** He undertakes to defend the Catholic position concerning original sin, which he explained in the first book of *Marriage and Concupiscence*, against Julian, who dared to attack it in four substantial books and did not hesitate to apply the name of Manichaeans to its defenders. Augustine shows that this detestable accusation rebounds upon the most distinguished Fathers, both Greek and Latin, adducing their testimonies on the matter, together with specific replies to those passages of Basil and John Chrysostom that Julian thinks support him. In the final part of the book he shows that the Manichaean heresy is greatly assisted by certain rash opinions of Julian himself. Ibid.

**BOOK TWO.** The author demolishes the Pelagians’ arguments against original sin by the authority and opinions of Catholic teachers who had previously shone in the Church—namely, ten distinguished bishops: Irenaeus, Cyprian, Reticius, Olympius, Hilary, Gregory of Nazianzus, Ambrose, Basil, John of Constantinople, and Innocent; as well as the presbyter Jerome, a holy and exceptionally learned man. 671–672

**BOOK THREE.** Julian must next be refuted with such method and diligence that each of his four books is answered separately in an equal number of books. Accordingly, in this third book Augustine first refutes Julian’s first book, acting so that it may clearly appear that, although God is the true and good creator of human beings, and marriage is good and instituted by him, concupiscence is nevertheless evil, by which the flesh lusts against the spirit. Conjugal chastity makes good use of this evil, while holier continence makes better use by not using it. This evil is not mixed with us from another substance that God did not create, as the Manichaean madness claims; rather, it arose and was transmitted through Adam’s disobedience and must be cleansed and healed through Christ’s obedience. By the obligation of this evil, the one who is born is entangled in a deserved penalty; by undeserved grace, the one who is reborn is released. Julian’s own statements also demonstrate that lust is evil, since he acknowledges remedies against it, wishes it to be restrained by reason, and finally says that those who practice continence wage glorious battles against it. [Col. 1908] 701–702

**BOOK FOUR.** Augustine responds to Julian’s second book, examining each of his statements, as he did in the refutation of the first, while passing over in silence only those that contain no issue relevant to the question. Here he proves especially two things: first, that the virtues of unbelievers are not true virtues; and second, that concupiscence is evil, demonstrating this even from the opinions of the Gentiles, with the adversary providing the opportunity. Around the middle of the book he briefly teaches how grace is not given according to merits and yet is not to be attributed to fate; and how the Apostle’s statement that God wills all human beings to be saved is to be understood. 737–738

**BOOK FIVE.** He takes up Julian’s third book and first explains why the Christian multitude detests the new heresy that rejects original sin: plainly because it sees the image of God suffering such great torments in infants, and knows that if they die without the Sacrament of regeneration, they are excluded from the kingdom of God. He proves that the *perizomata*—the coverings of the loins—were assumed by the first parents because of the shame arising from sin. Sin can be the punishment of a preceding sin, as when God gives the impious over to a reprobate mind so that they do what is improper. From the same mass of condemnation, some sinners are freely elected and predestined, and God brings them to repentance through merciful goodness; others are made vessels of wrath, whom he does not bring to repentance according to his just judgment.

Concupiscence is not worthy of praise because through it human disobedience is punished; rather, it is a vice and remains evil even in those who do not consent to its depraved impulses. He explains how the Apostle’s statement, “Let each one know how to possess his own vessel,” and so forth, is to be understood. Marriage can exist without intercourse, as was the case with Mary and Joseph. Julian argues in vain against sin transmitted from parents by means of Aristotelian categories. He shows how Christ’s flesh differs from the sinful flesh of other human beings. Catholics do not favor the Manichaeans by acknowledging the evil of lust and original sin; rather, the Pelagians favor the Manichaeans when they say that sins are not born from that which is free from sin. Throughout, he shows that the adversary strives in vain to extract something in his own favor from Augustine’s statements as though they contradicted one another. 781–782

**BOOK SIX.** He responds to Julian’s fourth book and to his cavils and slanders concerning the remaining portion of the first book of *Marriage and Concupiscence*. He confirms that human beings are born with sin from the Baptism of infants, from the Apostle’s words to the Romans and Corinthians, and from the rite of exorcism and exsufflation performed when infants are baptized. He shows that the example of the olive tree and the wild olive tree was appropriately given so that it may be understood how sinful children in need of regeneration are born from regenerated and righteous parents. Original sin was voluntary in the first parents and is alien to us in the particularity of the act, but ours through the contagion of descent. By the guilt of this sin it happens that the human race is worn down from infancy by such great miseries, and that infants who die without the grace of regeneration are excluded from the kingdom of God.

He teaches that through Baptism sanctification is now conferred both on the soul and on the body itself, although in this life the corruption of the body—which also burdens the soul—is not removed. He explains how concupiscence remains in act but passes away in guilt. He restores to the Catholic understanding the testimonies of the Apostle Paul perversely interpreted by Julian. Finally, he interprets according to its proper meaning the authority of Ezekiel, which Julian had misused. 821–822

**TWO LETTERS OF AUGUSTINE TO VALENTINUS AND THE MONKS OF ADRUMETUM WITH HIM, SENT TOGETHER WITH THE BOOK ON GRACE AND FREE WILL.** 875–876

**ONE BOOK OF SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, ON GRACE AND FREE WILL, TO VALENTINUS AND THE MONKS OF ADRUMETUM WITH HIM.** He teaches that care must be taken lest free will be defended by denying grace, or grace by denying free will. For that free choice of the will exists in human beings is established by testimonies of Scripture; and the same Scriptures provide divine teachings concerning the grace of God, without which we can do no good thing. He then proves against the Pelagians that grace is not given according to our merits.

He explains how eternal life, which is repaid for good works, is truly grace. He then shows that neither knowledge of the Law, nor nature, nor the forgiveness of sins alone is that grace which is given through Jesus Christ our Lord; rather, grace itself causes the Law to be fulfilled, nature to be liberated, and sin not to rule. He overthrows that vain refuge of the Pelagians in which they say that, although grace is not given according to the merits of good works, it is nevertheless given according to the merits of a good will that precedes the believer’s faith and prayer.

He considers the question why God commands what he himself is going to give, and whether he commands anything that we cannot do. He proves that charity, without which the commandments are not fulfilled, is in us only from God himself. He shows that God works in human hearts to incline their wills wherever he wishes—toward good according to his mercy, or toward evil according to their merits—by a judgment that is sometimes manifest and sometimes hidden, but always just. Finally, a clear example of gratuitous grace, not given in return for merits, is found in those infants who are saved while others, sharing the same condition, perish. 881–882

**LETTER OF VALENTINUS TO AUGUSTINE, REPLYING AFTER THE BOOK ON GRACE AND FREE WILL AND HIS EARLIER LETTERS.** 911–912

**ONE BOOK OF SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, ON CORRECTION AND GRACE, TO THE SAME VALENTINUS AND THE MONKS OF ADRUMETUM WITH HIM.** At the beginning he states what the Catholic faith teaches concerning the Law, free will, and grace. He teaches that the grace of God through Jesus Christ is that by which alone human beings are freed from evil, and without which they do absolutely no good—not merely because grace shows what must be done, but because it also grants that they do it with love, when God bestows on them the inspiration of a good will and a good work.

The correction of evil people who have not received this grace is neither unjust, since they are evil by their own will, nor useless, although it must be admitted that only through God does it become beneficial. Perseverance in the good is truly a great gift of God; nevertheless, the correction of one who has not persevered is not for that reason to be neglected. One who, without receiving this gift, has by his own will fallen back into sin is worthy not only of correction but also—if he remains in evil until death—of eternal condemnation. Why one person receives this gift and another does not is inscrutable.

None of the predestined can perish. Accordingly, perseverance—which not all those who are called children of God here receive—is given to all who are truly children according to God’s foreknowledge and predestination. He responds to the question that arises concerning Adam: how did Adam sin by failing to persevere if he did not receive perseverance? He shows that Adam was given such assistance that, if he wished, he could remain in the good without it being the cause of his willing to do so. Now, through Christ, assistance is given not only without which we cannot remain in the good even if we wish, but also assistance of such a kind and degree that it causes us to will it.

He proves that the number of the predestined, whose distinctive possession is this kind of gift, is fixed and can neither be increased nor diminished. Since it is unknown who belongs to that number and who does not, medicinal correction must be applied to all who sin, lest they themselves perish or destroy others. He concludes that grace does not prohibit correction, nor does correction deny grace. 915–916

**NOTICE TO THE BOOKS ON THE PREDESTINATION OF THE SAINTS AND ON THE GIFT OF PERSEVERANCE.** 945–946

**LETTER OF PROSPER, NUMBERED 225 AMONG AUGUSTINE’S LETTERS.** 947–948

**LETTER OF HILARY, NUMBERED 226 AMONG AUGUSTINE’S LETTERS.** 953–954

**THE FIRST BOOK OF SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, ON THE PREDESTINATION OF THE SAINTS, TO PROSPER AND HILARY.** In this book the truth of predestination and grace is defended against the Semi-Pelagians—people who had by no means withdrawn entirely from the Pelagian heresy, since they wished the beginning of salvation and faith to come from ourselves, so that, as though this were a preceding merit, they might obtain the other good things as gifts from God.

Augustine shows that the gift of God is not only the increase of faith but also its very beginning. He does not deny that he once thought otherwise on this matter and erred in works written before his episcopate, such as the *Exposition of Certain Propositions from the Epistle to the Romans*, which they bring against him. But he indicates that he was later convinced especially by this testimony: “What do you have that you did not receive?” He proves that this testimony must also be understood of faith itself.

Faith must be numbered among the works by which the Apostle denies that God’s grace is preceded, when he says, “Not from works.” By grace the hardness of the heart is removed; and all who are taught by the Father come to Christ so that they may come. Those whom he teaches, he teaches through mercy; those whom he does not teach, he does not teach through judgment.

The passage from his own Letter 102, Question 2, concerning the time of the Christian religion, which the Semi-Pelagians cite, can be correctly explained without compromising the doctrine of grace and predestination. He teaches the difference between grace and predestination. Moreover, by predestination God foreknew those things that he himself was going to do.

He is astonished that the adversaries of predestination, who are said not to wish to be brought to the uncertainty of God’s will, prefer to entrust themselves to their own weakness rather than to the firmness of God’s promise. He shows that they misuse the authority, “If you believe, you will be saved.” The truth of grace and predestination shines forth in infants who are saved, although they are distinguished from the others who perish by no merits of their own. They are not distinguished by a foreknowledge of merits that they would have possessed had they lived longer.

The adversaries unjustly reject as though it were a noncanonical testimony the passage he cited for this purpose: “He was taken away, lest wickedness…,” and so forth. The Savior himself is the most splendid example of predestination and grace: that human being, assumed by the Word coeternal with the Father into the unity of person, should become Savior and the only-begotten Son of God—attained through no preceding merits either of works or of faith.

The predestined are called by a certain distinctive calling proper to the elect. They were chosen before the foundation of the world, not because they were foreknown as those who would believe and become holy, but so that they might become such through that very election of grace, and so forth. [Col. 1910] 959–960

**NOTICE TO THE BOOK ON THE GIFT OF PERSEVERANCE.** 991–992

**THE SECOND BOOK OF SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, ON THE GIFT OF PERSEVERANCE, TO PROSPER AND HILARY.** In the first part of the book he proves that the perseverance by which one perseveres in Christ to the end is a gift of God. For it would be mockingly asked of God if one did not believe that it is given by God. Moreover, according to the exposition of the martyr Cyprian, almost nothing other than perseverance is requested in the Lord’s Prayer; by that exposition the enemies of grace were convicted before they were born.

He teaches that the grace of perseverance is given to some through God’s mercy and denied to others through his just judgment, not according to the merits of those who receive it. Why one adult rather than another is called, and likewise why one of two infants is taken up while the other is left, is inscrutable. More inscrutable still is why, out of two devout people, perseverance is given to one and not to the other. Yet this is absolutely certain: the former is among the predestined, the latter is not.

He observes that the mystery of predestination is shown by the Lord’s words concerning the Tyrians and Sidonians: had the same signs been performed among them as among Chorazin, they would have repented. He shows that the example of infants is useful for confirming the truth of predestination and grace in adults, and he answers the adversaries’ misapplication of a passage from the third book of his work *On Free Will*.

In the second part of the work he refutes their claim that the definition of predestination is contrary to the usefulness of exhortation and correction. He asserts that predestination is beneficially preached so that a person may glory not in himself but in the Lord. Whatever they object against predestination can likewise, in no dissimilar way, be directed against God’s foreknowledge or against that grace which they agree is necessary for all other good things, except the beginning of faith and the perfection of perseverance.

For the predestination of the saints is nothing other than the foreknowledge and preparation of God’s benefits, by which all who are delivered are most certainly delivered. Nevertheless, he commands that predestination be preached in a suitable manner, and not in such a way that among the uninstructed multitude it may seem to be refuted by its own proclamation. Finally, he commends the Lord Jesus to us as the most illustrious example of predestination placed before our eyes. 993–994

**NOTICE TO THE UNFINISHED WORK AGAINST JULIAN’S SECOND REPLY.** 1035–1030

**ON JULIAN AND HIS WRITINGS.** Ibid.

**ON THE SUBSEQUENT WORK.** 1043–1044

**THE UNFINISHED WORK OF SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, AGAINST JULIAN’S SECOND REPLY, COMPRISING SIX BOOKS.** 1049–1050

**PREFACE.** Ibid.

**BOOK ONE.** The first book of Julian’s work addressed to Florus is answered. [Col. 1911] In this first book Julian directs his slanders especially against Augustine and the Catholic faith, in which we confess original sin, on three principal grounds. First, he argues that if God is just, sin belonging to another cannot be imputed by him to infants. Second, since sin is nothing other than an evil will, which is free to abstain from what it wickedly desired, there is therefore no sin in those who are being born, since the exercise of will cannot be found in them. Third, the freedom of choice granted to human beings consists in the possibility of admitting sin and abstaining from sin; therefore free will is denied by those who say that sins are natural.

In some matters between these arguments, he maliciously attacks passages drawn both from the opening sections of the second book of *Marriage and Concupiscence* and from the second chapter of the first book *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*. He also attempts to interpret, according to Pelagian dogma, the authorities cited in defense of God’s grace, by which we are freed from slavery and condemnation—namely, John’s Gospel, chapter 8; the Apostle to the Romans, chapters 6, 7, and 9; and the Second Epistle to Timothy, chapter 2. 1051–1052

**BOOK TWO.** Julian’s second book is refuted. It concerns the Apostle’s words in Romans 5: “Through one man sin entered into this world, and through sin death; and thus into all human beings,” and so forth. Having rejected the Catholic meaning—according to which Augustine explained those words in chapter 27 of the second book of *Marriage and Concupiscence* as referring to Adam’s sin transmitted by generation to all his descendants—Julian labors in vain to have them understood according to the Pelagian heresy as referring to the example of sin, which passes not to all descendants but only by imitation to those who sin. 1141–1142

**BOOK THREE.** Julian’s third book is examined. First, he is shown to misuse the testimonies of Scripture—namely, Deuteronomy, chapter 24; the Fourth Book of Kings, chapter 14; and Ezekiel, chapter 18—in an attempt to persuade people that God imputes the sins of parents to their children in no way. He then labors in vain to extricate himself from the passage in the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 11, by which the response he so emphatically repeated in the preceding book would have to be overturned—namely, that the Apostle said “one” through whom sin passed so that generation would not be understood.

Afterward Julian returns to statements from the second book of *Marriage and Concupiscence* and acts unjustly toward Augustine. He again complains that Augustine denies both free will in human beings and God as the creator of those who are born. Moreover, comparing Augustine’s statements with a certain heretical letter of Manichaeus, Julian slanderously claims that Augustine offers no arguments other than those found in Manichaeus, and that he declares human nature evil just as Manichaeus does. 1247–1248

**BOOK FOUR.** Augustine continues to refute Julian, who in his fourth book argues against the statements in the second book of *Marriage and Concupiscence*, chapters 4 through 11. He defends the teaching that the concupiscence of the flesh is evil and was not implanted in human beings by God the creator. For this purpose he employs the passage from the First Epistle of John, chapter 2, verse 16: “Everything that is in the world is the concupiscence of the flesh … which is not from the Father,” and so forth.

He maintains that this concupiscence belongs to the nature of animals, but nevertheless to the punishment of the human being himself. The shame of the bodily members arose only after sin, because of the rebellious impulses of lust. Further, lest anyone think that there was any concupiscence of the flesh at all in Christ, he vigorously contends against Julian that infants are born liable to original guilt—not through the exercise of their own will, but through the contagion of sin voluntarily committed by the first parent.

He also shows that the passage he brought forward from the Book of Wisdom, chapter 12, verses 10 and 11—“Not ignorant that their race was wicked,” and so forth—serves to demonstrate the defect of our origin. 1337–1338

**BOOK FIVE.** Augustine confirms and vindicates against Julian’s slanders what he wrote in the second book of *Marriage and Concupiscence*, chapter 12 and certain following chapters—especially that a sound nature did not possess that shameful union or agitation of the bodily members which a corrupted nature possesses, and consequently that the one born from it needs to be reborn.

Next, he confirms what he argued there in chapters 14, 20, and 26: that Julian improperly misused two apostolic testimonies, 1 Corinthians 15:36 and 38, and the Gospel saying in Matthew 7:17 or 12:33. He confirms what he asserted in chapter 28: that evil, or an evil will, could arise from God’s good work because that work, although good, was made from nothing and not from God. Finally, he confirms what he taught in chapter 17: that God creates the wicked when he feeds and nourishes the wicked. [Col. 1912] 1431–1432

**BOOK SIX.** Augustine shows that Julian argues in vain in his sixth book against what was asserted in chapter 34 of the second book of *Marriage and Concupiscence*: that through the first human being’s sin human nature was changed for the worse, so that it not only became sinful but thereafter also produced sinners.

He teaches that by sinning human beings lost the powers of free will with which, while they remained intact, a person could act rightly when he wished and not sin if he did not wish to sin. He utterly rejects that definition of freedom which the adversary habitually brings forward: “the possibility of sinning and not sinning,” and so forth.

He proves that the pains of women in childbirth, thorns, labors, sweats, and the other miseries of mortals are punishments for sin; but above all, that death itself is a punitive consequence for the human being, who had been divinely constituted in such a way that, unless he sinned, he would not die.

In the final part of the book he examines and refutes Julian’s exposition of the Apostle’s statement in 1 Corinthians 15:22, “As in Adam all die,” and the subsequent statements of the same chapter. Finally, throughout almost the whole book he demonstrates that the Catholic doctrine of original corruption—which Julian everywhere strives to drag toward the Manichaean heresy—not only lies far from that heresy, but also that the Manichaean heresy can never be overcome by the Pelagians except through the aid and profession of this very Catholic doctrine. 1507–1508
